source: Comprehensive Research Report, Completed Edition (2026-10-22), Tier 2 catalogue master (tier2_upgrades.json)
note: The programme's catalogue: entries collected and field-completed, NOT opened-and-studied — for studied rows see evaluation/source-index.jsonl (the two sets are disjoint by name). good / bad / took / didnt and licence are the catalogue's own recorded fields. Contact emails appearing in listing text are redacted. Data only — no per-project pages.

name: Gemma 4 wiki plugin
good: Obsidian plugin that runs Gemma 4 E4B entirely inside Obsidian's own process via LiteRT-LM and WebGPU — no server, API key or account — and builds a Karpathy-style wiki layer above untouched notes: one summary card per note, an index, concept pages over shared tags, gaps and contradiction sweeps, and chat grounded in one note or the whole wiki with sources listed by the plugin rather than cited by the model. Every page is previewed in full before anything is written, and quizzes/flashcards are built in.
bad: Desktop only and structurally so: it needs WebGPU and about 3 GB for the model, and the README's own 'Not for you if' section says a 4B model is weak at general knowledge and sources are Markdown notes only — PDFs, images and Office files must be clipped or converted first. GPL-3.0 copyleft also bars copying its code into our stack.
didnt: Corroboration — sources listed by the plugin rather than generated by the model, preview-before-write, and a separate wiki layer over immutable notes confirm our citation-locking and approval-gated design; GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only in any case (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: InfraNodus
licence: custom licence (repo shows Other / NOASSERTION; README: 'available under our custom license')
good: Text-to-network visualisation built on Node.js and Neo4j: every word is a node and every co-occurrence a connection, with network-science algorithms surfacing topical clusters, the most influential terms, topic modelling, text statistics and the structural gaps in a discourse where new ideas could connect. It works in several languages, accepts natural-language, hashtag and voice-to-text input, and offers API and JSON export.
bad: The README states this open-source version is the old version last updated in 2020, that the new version with AI capabilities lives only at the paid infranodus.com cloud service, and that no support is provided for the open-source version. Its stack is dated (Neo4j 3.x) and its custom licence is not a standard open licence.
didnt: Rejected — custom licence (ideas-only at best), an unsupported pre-2021 open-source codebase, and a Neo4j database / paid cloud product rather than a local Markdown tool; its cluster-and-gap graph analysis is already covered by our Lens graph analytics (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Nodus Labs

name: AKBP
good: Turns the LLM Wiki pattern into a protocol surface for agent runtimes: a local-first, file-backed knowledge base with typed claims, source hashes, lifecycle relations, review-gated writes (dry_run preview plus approved:true), JSON schemas, a JSONL tool server, SQLite FTS5 retrieval with citations, export manifests with SHA-256 hashes, and conformance tests run in CI across Python 3.9–3.12.
bad: The README itself says it is still alpha, usable for demos and early dogfooding but 'not a 1.0 compatibility promise', and that it still needs larger retrieval-quality benchmarks, broader adapter dogfooding, a clearer migration policy and more long-document ingest proof before it should be treated as mature.
didnt: Corroboration — typed claims, source hashes, lifecycle relations and review-gated writes with conformance tests independently confirm the core design of our wiki; no adoption, as the reference implementation is explicitly alpha (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: secure-llm-wiki
good: A persistent Karpathy-pattern wiki hardened against indirect prompt injection and source poisoning: a fully implemented 7-stage pipeline with input sanitising (zero-width, bidi, HTML, base64, instruction patterns), nonce-delimited claim extraction with provenance, URI-pattern trust tiering, an independent second-model adversarial review (4-eyes principle), a 5-check fail-closed write gate that commits, quarantines or escalates, and read-time hygiene. Its injection corpus maps 8 attack vectors to their stop-gate, OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS, backed by 79 tests.
bad: The README frames it as a portfolio / reference artifact for AI red-teaming consulting, and the repo is small (35 commits, 14 stars, no releases). Supported inputs are limited to plain text, HTML and PDF, and the design requires two different LLM models for extraction and review to preserve independence.
didnt: Corroboration — its quarantine write gates, trust tiering and dual-model adversarial review confirm our Ask-door injection defence and approval-gated write design; a reference artifact, not a stack component for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: knowledge-worker
good: Local-first personal knowledge graph in portable flat JSON-LD with a strict promotion lifecycle — source note to candidates to deterministic validation to human review to merge — where high-confidence claims require a literal source excerpt that matches after whitespace/case normalisation, and unmatched excerpts demote the candidate. It exports a compact LLM-ready context snapshot and audits the graph with PageRank, betweenness, communities and provenance coverage; the core CLI is stdlib-only Python.
bad: Small, young project (39 commits, 14 stars). The README's own persistence principle concedes the store is 'compact JSON-LD until it becomes the limiting factor', so the canonical store is a single graph file rather than human-readable Markdown wiki pages, and durable memory depends on producing a correctly schema'd candidates file.
didnt: Corroboration — excerpt-matched provenance ('provenance-or-bust') and review-before-merge independently confirm our citation-locking and approval-gated write design; its JSON-LD graph store does not fit our Markdown-canonical wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Patina
good: Single-binary Rust CLI that makes the LLM Wiki pattern engineering-grade: Git is the source of truth, the SQLite FTS5 index under .patina/ is disposable and fully rebuildable from the Markdown files, every page declares source_refs whose SHA-256 is recorded at index time, and patina stale warns when a referenced source changed or a review_after date passed. Retrieval is deterministic, with a transparent seven-component scoring formula, plus lint for broken links, frontmatter and duplicate aliases.
bad: The README is explicit about what it is not: no vector database (lexical FTS5 first, semantic retrieval only a planned future layer), no MCP server and no hosted service in the core, and its page-type schemas are described as 'documentation / future enforcement' rather than enforced. It indexes and queries a wiki but does not itself compile one.
didnt: Corroboration — Git-canonical Markdown, a rebuildable local index, source-hash staleness checks and review_after dates confirm mechanisms our wiki already implements; no adoption needed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kenjaku
good: Local-first Karpathy-style second brain in Git-backed, Obsidian-compatible Markdown: it ingests Slack, Gmail, Drive, transcripts and notes, answers in seconds with the source and date for every claim (stale-while-revalidate, with background catch-up and amendment), auto-commits and can auto-push every change, and ships wiki-health skills (/lint, /consolidate, /file-back) plus on-device embedding search. The project is heavily engineered (2,436 commits, 37 releases, mutation testing).
bad: Its own honesty table concedes it is not 100% private end-to-end — search is local but the reasoning LLM is still Claude in the cloud — that it is not yet multi-AI (Claude-only driving layer), and that one-time setup assumes git and Node. Its automated multi-source ingestion runs without a per-item approval gate.
didnt: Rejected — scope and fit: a full second-brain platform duplicating our wiki, whose automated Slack/Gmail/Drive auto-ingest conflicts with our no-auto-discovery, approval-gated capture rules, and whose reasoning layer is Claude-cloud-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Lexicon
good: LLM-compiled personal knowledge base: multi-source ingest (URLs, PDFs, files, tweets, images, audio, video) is chunked, embedded and stored in SQLite, then an LLM groups chunks by topic and writes Markdown articles with citations, backlinks and auto-generated wikilinks, preserving manual edits across recompilation. It adds semantic search and cited Q&A, knowledge linting for contradictions and staleness, a web UI and graph view, and can run on local models via Ollama.
bad: Very small project (1 star, 59 commits, no releases) whose quickstart requires a cloud LLM provider API key by default, with web research tied to a paid Exa key. Its canonical ingest store is SQLite rather than the Markdown files, and its watch mode performs recurring auto-research and recompilation without a human review gate.
didnt: Rejected — fit and maturity: SQLite-canonical storage and un-gated watch-mode auto-research conflict with our Markdown-canonical, approval-gated design, and the project is at single-star maturity (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm_wiki_rag_pipeline
good: Python CLI implementing the Karpathy pattern as route-synthesise-embed-index: init/ingest/query/lint commands scaffold a local wiki, ingest sources into interlinked Markdown pages with YAML frontmatter, build a MiniLM cosine-similarity index over the compiled wiki pages rather than the raw documents, stream cited answers, and lint for orphans, broken cross-references and stale embeddings, with a deep mode that checks page pairs for contradictions.
bad: A demo-scale project: 3 commits and a README that is a worked transcript over three sample sources and five wiki pages, with no releases. It requires an Anthropic API key to run, and the README documents no test suite or evaluation beyond that single demo.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and duplication: a three-commit demo of RAG over a compiled wiki, a capability our Ask door already provides with citation locking and scored abstention (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memwiki
good: Zero-dependency persistent-memory protocol for AI coding agents: one npx memwiki init command scaffolds a .memory/ directory with an immutable .raw/ source folder and a wiki of hot.md (a ~500-word hot context cache read first), index.md, an append-only log.md, stack, patterns, bugs and decisions pages, plus hook files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, Copilot instructions) that make any agent read the memory before working. A protocol update command refreshes the hooks without touching the wiki contents.
bad: Tiny, early project (9 commits, no releases) with no licence stated at the source, so its code is not reusable. Its protocol instructs agents to maintain the wiki proactively and autonomously — editing pages whenever they learn something and updating hot.md before ending a session — with no human review or approval gate, and a freshly initialised wiki starts mostly blank.
didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at the source (ideas-only at best) and its autonomous, un-gated agent updating conflicts with our approval-gated writes; its hot-cache and append-only log patterns already exist in our wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dream-cycle (digital-me)
good: Nightly knowledge-distillation pipeline for the Digital Me Living Knowledge Wiki that turns raw inputs (chat transcripts, scratch notes, brain learnings) into curated, cross-linked wiki entries through a compile, index, citations, crosslink, lint, drift-check and consolidate loop, mixing LLM steps (via an OpenClaw gateway or Gemini/OpenAI/Anthropic directly) with deterministic file operations. It is a small Python >=3.11 package whose only runtime dependency is pyyaml, with a doctor command to verify the install.
bad: The PyPI page states its status as alpha, ported from the maintainer's prior personal setup, and it is built specifically for the Digital Me wiki and its OpenClaw gateway rather than as a general tool. The rendered package page shows no licence, so reuse terms are unstated.
didnt: Rejected — alpha, tied to the Digital Me / OpenClaw stack, no licence stated at the source (ideas-only at best), and its nightly consolidation, lint and drift-check loop duplicates our existing nightly sweep (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: braindb
good: Upgrades the LLM Wiki idea to a real database: typed entities (thought, fact, source, datasource, rule) with explicit supports/contradicts/elaborates/derived_from relations, certainty and importance fields and automatic provenance, served over an HTTP API with hybrid retrieval — pg_trgm fuzzy plus pgvector semantic matching, graph traversal up to 3 hops and temporal decay — plus a built-in natural-language agent, a file-ingestion watcher and a wiki-scheduler sidecar that auto-maintains generated Markdown pages.
bad: Its whole premise is replacing Markdown-canonical memory with a PostgreSQL database, and it runs as a Docker stack (API, watcher, scheduler, frontend, Postgres with pg_trgm and pgvector) whose internal agent needs an external LLM provider key, with DeepInfra recommended by default. The watcher auto-ingests dropped files hands-off — 'you never call the pipeline by hand' — with no approval gate.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a database-canonical store replaces the owner's chosen Git/Markdown-canonical design, and its hands-off auto-ingest watcher conflicts with approval-gated capture (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mindbase
good: Packages the Karpathy LLM-wiki pattern as a local server, web UI, 49-tool MCP server and Claude Code plugin over plain Markdown: sources/ is append-only, the synthesised context.md is human-approved, and ingest is approval-gated by design — the AI shows takeaways plus a checkbox plan and writes only approved items, with per-agent tool allowlists where the builder has no direct file-write tool except an atomic-write MCP call. It runs free and local by default via a hardware-detect wizard that installs a fitting Ollama model, and its lint re-reads the whole wiki and quotes the exact conflicting sentences for contradictions.
bad: The README itself labels it early access / beta through 2026-Q4, with team projects, a browser capture extension, audio input and a desktop app still on the roadmap rather than shipped. The full 8-step approval ingest is Claude Code-only; other MCP clients get a manual prompt-driven version, and synthesis is centred on a single context.md per project.
didnt: Corroboration — its approval-gated ingest (takeaways plus checkbox plan, writes only on approval) and builder-with-no-file-write-tool allowlist confirm our approval-gated write design and per-agent tool boundaries. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Stigmergy
good: A team version of the Karpathy wiki: immutable source material enters one durable Postgres queue, one librarian agent files it into a plain Git-and-Markdown wiki, and every search and answer is scoped to what the caller may see, with hybrid search and citations verified by code. It adds what a shared deployment forces — identity, visibility layers/ACLs, Slack and MCP-bridge capture, explicit dated contradictions, and a full audit trail of one operation, one commit, one change record with the exact patch.
bad: The repo is brand new (a single commit and no stars at source) and AGPL-3.0 licensed. Its write path deliberately removes the approval gate — the README states 'Nobody approves a queue' and the librarian 'creates, rewrites, consolidates, and deletes pages without approval' — and it requires a Postgres/pgvector cloud deployment rather than a local-first file store.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us, its no-approval librarian write/delete path conflicts with our approval-gated writes, and the project is a single-commit new release. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mana
good: An AI-maintained wiki for markdown/Obsidian-style knowledge bases: drop papers, PDFs, transcripts and articles into /raw and the agent reads, cites, cross-references and weaves them into structured wiki pages, turns questions into cited synthesis pages, and surfaces connections, gaps and contradictions. Every agent operation is a git commit and every change returns as a reviewable git diff, with plain markdown files, git history, local review and an offline iOS app for capture and diff review.
bad: It is a hosted assistant service with no licence, pricing or self-hosting terms stated on its homepage, so custody and continuity depend on the vendor despite the portable-files pitch. The site gives no evaluation, scale limits or test evidence for its self-maintaining claims.
didnt: Corroboration — returning every agent change as a reviewable git diff over plain owned markdown confirms our diff-reviewable, no-lock-in wiki design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wikihub.md
good: A publishing platform for markdown knowledge bases where every wiki is a real git repo (push, pull, branch, blame, clone and leave anytime), with first-class rendering (KaTeX, syntax highlighting, wikilinks), Cmd+K full-text search, and fork/star social features. Access is public, private, unlisted or shared per page via one declarative ACL file, and agents get a native MCP server, REST endpoints and a CLI with one-call registration.
bad: Hosting custody sits with a third-party service whose licence and terms are not stated on the homepage. Agent registration grants an agent account 'full read/write access' with an API key shown exactly once — a broad, ungated write surface that does not match approval-gated writes.
didnt: Board — the per-file declarative ACL file (.wikihub/acl, a CODEOWNERS-style pattern) as an idea for per-page visibility control in a published wiki surface. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agent Wikis
good: Hosted, maintained knowledge bases compiled from messy fast-moving sources (repos, changelogs, video transcripts, community Q&A) into structured Markdown wikis that humans browse and agents read natively via llms.txt and MCP, each with sources, freshness metadata and a declared scope. The vendor publishes eval numbers on its own harness (89% vs 48% correct answers and 7% vs 48% hallucination rate against live web search) and public wikis are free for humans and agents.
bad: The catalogue is the vendor's own curated public-topic wikis, not a bring-your-own private knowledge base: the homepage shows no way to host your own corpus, and the deeper XL editions, skills library and specialist agents sit behind the $19.99/mo Pro tier. The headline accuracy figures come from the vendor's own eval harness.
didnt: Corroboration — compiling sources into curated pages with freshness and scope metadata, rather than raw RAG retrieval, confirms our compiled-wiki approach and its accuracy rationale. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graphite Atlas
good: Turns a business into one connected operational map — 'looks like a diagram, thinks like a database' — modelling processes, systems, roles and handoffs so a team and AI can trace dependencies, gaps and key-person risk, then uses that map to design and deploy automation and AI systems. Its directory description adds that AI can generate SOPs, onboarding materials and process guides from the established graph structure.
bad: It is a consultancy-led service (the team embeds with your business through Discover/Design/Deploy) aimed at established 100-to-1,000+ employee firms in process-heavy sectors, with no self-serve product, pricing or licence stated on its site. It is an enterprise operations-mapping engagement, not a personal or local-first knowledge base.
didnt: Rejected — enterprise consultancy scope and fit: built for embedded engagements with large process-heavy firms, with no adoptable local-first software for a personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Northern Logic KB
good: A Business Knowledge Base / 'company second brain' service that organises approved company knowledge — definitions, procedures, policies, decisions and exceptions, with owners, effective dates, access classes and review dates — so people and AI assistants answer from one shared, sourced foundation instead of separate copies. Its operating model is explicitly human-led: temporary working context and model-generated answers do not become durable company guidance without approval.
bad: It is a bespoke consultancy service run by a single founder, with audits and builds 'scoped to the work involved' and no product, licence, self-hosting or published price on the site — there is no software to adopt or run locally. Ongoing value depends on the vendor's managed-operations engagement.
didnt: Rejected — it is a one-person consulting service rather than adoptable software, and its business-KB scope duplicates what our own wiki already does under our custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: second-brain-cloudflare
good: One memory layer for every AI tool, self-hosted in your own Cloudflare account on the free tier: a Worker backed by D1, Vectorize, Workers AI and KV exposes REST and MCP memory tools (remember, append, update, recall by meaning, brief, history, forget/undo, link) with automatic classification, duplicate detection, relationships and time-aware ranking — including as-of recall over facts that keep the dates they were true for. Team Edition adds a private personal layer plus a deliberately shared team layer in the same Worker.
bad: Memory lives in Cloudflare's proprietary stack (Workers, D1, Vectorize) rather than plain markdown files you own and can grep, so custody is platform-bound despite being your account. It is a memory store, not a compiled wiki — no citation-locked pages — and the README notes its shipped embedding models read English best.
didnt: Rejected — duplicates the memory layer we already have, and its Cloudflare D1/Vectorize custody conflicts with our local-first, plain-markdown corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Portable LLM Wiki
good: A hosted personal LLM wiki: sign in with GitHub, paste a bio/resume or profile URL, and a model digests it into a starter wiki you share as a URL or QR code that any LLM (Cursor, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Gemini, local models via URL fetch or MCP) can read for cited answers about you. Ingest digests Slack threads, screenshots, voice memos, PDFs and notes into entities and wikilinks without losing provenance, retrieval is graph-aware, and a four-agent lint swarm (contradictions, stale claims, missing pages, public-tier leaks) surfaces issues for review and never silently rewrites.
bad: It is a hosted multi-tenant service with no licence stated on its homepage, and its scope is a personal profile/bio wiki rather than a general research corpus. Custody of the wiki sits with the service, and sign-in is GitHub-only.
took: Self-describing briefing (Lens llms.txt / llms-full.txt open with a briefing on the wiki's rules and standing questions), leak lint (scans export surfaces for secret-shaped content), and lint in four lanes (contradictions / stale / missing / leaks, filed nightly, surfacing only) — all built 2026-10-19 with Portable LLM Wiki recorded as source/inspiration in lane8-dispositions.md.
didnt: Corroboration — its self-describing briefing URL, graph-aware cited answers and four-lane surfacing-only lint swarm confirm the Lens briefing, leak-lint and nightly lint design we built from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wiki-skills (kfchou)
good: A Claude Code plugin implementing the Karpathy LLM-wiki pattern as seven skills (init, ingest, query, lint, update, audit, merge) over plain markdown with a generated (never hand-maintained) index and a git-derived operation log. Its wiki-audit fact-checks one page at a time — flagging uncited claims, then dispatching one subagent per source in parallel to verify each footnote (quote citations string-matched, synthesis citations judged against the cited range), with a strong mode adding cross-provider adversarial review — and wiki-init installs deterministic pre-commit gates that block commits with unresolved contradiction flags or structural faults.
bad: It is Claude Code-only and small (11 commits, no releases), and strong-mode audit degrades to a same-provider Claude subagent labelled 'the weaker signal' when no codex or gemini CLI is present. Its safety gates depend on the wiki being a git repo; a non-git wiki gets no hooks or scripts.
didnt: Corroboration — its per-source parallel citation audit and deterministic pre-commit gates blocking unresolved contradictions confirm our citation-locking and gated-commit design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Open Knowledge Format (OKF) spec v0.2
good: Defines a minimal, tool-free interchange format: a directory of Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, only 'type' required, that makes provenance (sources with author/usage_count/last_modified signals, not stored scores), trust tiers, freshness/lifecycle (generated, verified, status, stale_after) and Attested Computation first-class. Consumers must preserve unknown keys on round-trip and must not reject documents for unrecognised fields, so bundles stay portable and diffable in git.
bad: Still a v0.2 draft: §12 lists the full runtime protocol, attester ABI/portability/sandboxing and attestation caching as considered and deferred, and §13 records deliberate breaking v0.1-to-v0.2 renames. Conformance (§11) is permissive — only a parseable frontmatter block with a non-empty type is required and consumers must not reject missing optional families or broken cross-links, so the trust/provenance fields are optional in practice.
took: OKF conformance export — built 2026-10-20 (Batch 3.4 in lane8-dispositions.md; source/inspiration not named there).
didnt: Corroboration — first-class provenance, trust, lifecycle and attestation frontmatter, signals-not-scores, and the preserve-unknown-keys round-trip rule confirm our own frontmatter and exporter design; the format itself is already reflected in our conformance export. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: YANP Vault Specification
good: A complete, implementable vault spec on one page: .md/UTF-8 files with optional YAML frontmatter that is written once (temporal evolution goes in appendices, not frontmatter rewrites), wikilink resolution by title then aliases then filename stem with conflict warnings, rename behaviour that rewrites all inbound wikilinks, delete warnings for inbound links, and a publish transform to valid CommonMark that never modifies source files. It ships an implementer's reference with regexes, a resolution algorithm and a minimum viable conforming tool.
bad: The spec page states no licence, so nothing in it can be adopted as code. Its frontmatter is entirely optional and covers only tags/author/hostname/date/status/aliases/priority/due/scheduled/project — there are no provenance, citation, trust or lifecycle-verification fields — and embed transclusion is explicitly not part of the spec; its listed browser editor is Chromium-only.
didnt: Board — the rename/delete safeguards (rewrite every inbound wikilink on rename; warn and list affected notes before deleting a linked note) and frontmatter-written-once as an anti-drift idea for the ideas board; ideas only, as the spec states no licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LLM Wiki v3 belief engine (HousamKak)
good: Formalises the wiki as a rendered view of a state-space system — 'The LLM observes. The state updates. The wiki renders.' — with raw evidence immutable, LLM extractions kept as observations (source ID, evidence span, confidence, extractor model/version, stance, claim key) rather than truth, and a belief updater that decides new/supporting/contradicting/superseding claims. Claim states are typed (active, uncertain, disputed, superseded, stale, archived, rejected), contradictions trigger named outcomes including human review, and every state update is an append-only transition.
bad: Self-labelled a draft architecture specification at version 0.1: the gist is a design document with example JSON schemas, not an implementation, and it presents no evaluation or running code. Its model also demotes Markdown to a rendering of JSONL claim/entity/relationship state, transitions, graph snapshots and BM25/vector/graph indexes — a much heavier stack than a files-first wiki.
didnt: Board — the observation-versus-belief separation (extractions carry evidence spans and extractor identity and are never themselves truth) and the typed claim-state machine as design ideas for our claim lifecycle; ideas only, as the gist states no licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LLM Wiki V3: Segmentation (ahumanft)
good: Names segmentation — narrow, purpose-built components — as the scaling answer instead of one ever-larger schema: separate Ingestor (classify only), Librarian (retrieve and route in its own context, so search drift does not bias the requesting team) and Linter roles, plus two coexisting ingestion modes, a deeply curated 'restricted section' and a shallow-indexed 'open stacks'. It also gives a concrete schema discipline (explicit triggers invoke implicit guidance at a defined step) and cache rewarming for long sessions.
bad: The author states plainly that it is intentionally incomplete — 'This is a concept, not a finished system' — with only early ingestion pipelines and a routing librarian working and the full architecture 'what is being worked toward, not what has shipped'. The gist contains no code, no evaluation and no licence.
didnt: Board — role segmentation (ingestor/librarian/linter with the librarian retrieving in an isolated context) and the restricted-section versus open-stacks dual ingestion modes as ideas for scaling our ingest/query/lint split; ideas only, as the gist states no licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Personal Wiki Skill (Farza)
good: A single Claude Code skill file that compiles personal data into a linked wiki of one person's life and mind: mechanical ingest scripts convert Day One JSON, Apple Notes, Obsidian vaults, Notion exports, plain text, iMessage, CSV, email and Twitter/X archives into one dated Markdown entry per item, then an absorb loop weaves entries into articles with explicit anti-cramming and anti-thinning rules and a quality checkpoint every 15 entries. Query is read-only, index-first and surgical (3-8 articles), and cleanup/breakdown commands audit articles and mine missing pages with parallel subagents.
bad: It is a single gist skill with no licence stated and no tests or evaluation shown. Its absorb discipline is expensive by design — re-read the index before each entry and re-read every article before updating it — and cleanup requires reading every article, so cost grows with the whole wiki rather than with the new material.
didnt: Corroboration — the immutable raw entries, absorb-into-existing-articles compilation, index-first read-only query with an explicit 'don't guess, say so' rule, and periodic quality audits confirm our own ingest/compile/query design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: myKG
good: Builds a confidence-scored knowledge graph from mixed documents (Markdown, text, PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, HTML, images, websites and repos) grounded in an induced, rdflib-validated RDFS/OWL ontology, with every node, edge and attribute carrying a 0.0-1.0 confidence score. It offers a human review gate after schema induction, locked (--base-schema) and frozen (--freeze-schema) ontology modes, SKOS thesaurus support, incremental/resumable sessions, and five output families including an Obsidian vault of wikilinked notes, plus an MCP server with 13 query tools.
bad: The README itself cautions that the locked base-schema mechanism 'is controlled by the LLM, and may not be strictly enforced', and its troubleshooting section documents token-budget failures, HTTP 429 rate limits and non-reproducible extraction (a different graph each run). Running it requires Python 3.11+ and an Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini/OpenRouter API key, a local Ollama model, or the claude CLI.
didnt: Board — the human review gate between schema induction and extraction, and the frozen-schema mode that extracts strictly against an owner-supplied ontology with no invented types, as ingest ideas for our schema-guided extraction. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Commonplace (zby)
licence: MIT (code in src/ and package tooling); CC BY 4.0 (knowledge-base content, documentation, templates and bundled instructional artifacts)
good: A file-backed, agent-operated knowledge system whose doctrine is developed by running one: note titles are assertions rather than topics and links state how claims relate (grounds, extends, contradicts, exemplifies), structure is earned progressively (a frontmatter-free file is valid), and authored knowledge stays in Markdown and Git with derived indexes for scale and review execution state as a scoped SQLite exception. It ships typed contracts, validators, deterministic commonplace-* commands and cp-skill-* procedures including ingest, ground (retain the minimum quotations needed to ground a claim) and validate.
bad: The README states its central theory-builder bet is untested — 'No test of the bet has been run yet' — and that people still perform many of its operations. Full installation is heavy (uv, git, ripgrep, curl, Trafilatura and Poppler all required), and ordinary test runs exclude the expensive 'slow' analysis-workflow tests by default.
didnt: Corroboration — claims-as-titles, typed link semantics (grounds/extends/contradicts), file-backed authored knowledge with derived indexes rather than a database, and exact operations carried by code and validators rather than repeated model interpretation all confirm our own wiki design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: EverOS
good: A local-first, Markdown-native memory runtime for agents: conversations, files and agent trajectories are stored as readable, Git-versioned Markdown (the source of truth, directly editable with a cascade watcher syncing the indexes) over a local SQLite + LanceDB stack needing no managed services. User episodes/profile and agent cases/skills are separate first-class tracks, retrieval is scoped by user/agent/app/project/session, and offline reflection merges episode clusters and refines profiles and skills between sessions.
bad: The one-key setup is only Tier 1 (keyword search): the README's own table makes hybrid/vector search, reflection and skill extraction require an added embedding provider, agentic search and the Knowledge Wiki require a rerank provider too, and the API defaults to hybrid search that fails without embeddings. Office-document ingestion additionally requires LibreOffice installed on the host, and the full system duplicates a memory stack (SQLite + LanceDB indexes, server, API v2) alongside a wiki.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: a full agent-memory runtime with its own server, indexes and self-evolving reflection would sit beside or replace our Markdown wiki and its approval-gated writes, rather than fill a gap in it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OpenKB
good: Compiles raw documents (PDF, Word, Markdown, PowerPoint, HTML, Excel, CSV, text and URLs) once into a persistent, interlinked wiki of summary, concept and entity pages instead of re-deriving answers per query, using PageIndex tree indexing for long documents (PDFs of 20+ pages) with vectorless, reasoning-based retrieval and native handling of figures and tables. It adds cited query/chat with persisted sessions, a lint command, a bundled Knowledge Workbench web UI, a Skill Factory that distils redistributable agent skills from the wiki, and wiki pages that follow Google's OKF specification.
bad: The bundled web UI has auth off by default (a bearer token must be set before exposing the server), and the README's command table states recompile 'Regenerates summaries and rewrites concept pages; manual edits are overwritten'. It also requires an LLM provider key via LiteLLM and depends on PageIndex for its long-document path.
didnt: Corroboration — compile-once-into-a-cited-wiki over per-query RAG, OKF-ready pages, entity pages kept in sync, and a structural/knowledge lint confirm our own compilation design; the system as a whole duplicates our stack rather than filling a gap. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-wiki
good: A multi-agent framework of 39 Markdown skills (any agent — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Gemini CLI and more — reads and runs them; no runtime, API keys or vendor) that compiles what an agent learns into interconnected Obsidian Markdown, with session hooks that inject the vault's memory at start and capture reusable material at end. Ingest is delta-only via a source manifest, every claim is tagged extracted, ^[inferred] or ^[ambiguous] with lint flagging speculation drift, index/log/hot/owner files go through one locked atomic writer so parallel agents cannot drop each other's updates, and queries return [[wikilink]] citations.
bad: Its own evidence is small: the README's comparison study is n=2 per cell on one 38-page vault, says the exact percentages should be treated as indicative, and records one 'with' run failing outright. The README also states what it is not — not a transcript recorder, not a sync service or backup, not a file converter — and audio and video inputs are skipped.
didnt: Corroboration — claim provenance tags (extracted/inferred/ambiguous), manifest-gated delta ingest, a single locked writer for shared memory files, and titles/tags/summaries read before page bodies confirm our own vault hygiene and query-cost design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llmwiki-harness
good: A zero-dependency, agent-agnostic context-memory harness — context window as RAM, local Markdown wiki as disk — exposed over MCP (stdio, streamable HTTP and SSE) to any MCP host, with five memory tools (search, recall, capture, curate, stats) and a host-loadable memory-protocol prompt. Retrieval fuses keyword, wikilink-graph and temporal strategies with RRF, carries explainable via/strength metadata, respects a token budget when assembling context, supports CJK-aware FTS5 search and multiple named vaults served by one server.
bad: Very young and small at source: 5 stars, 1 fork and 55 commits, created 2026-07-30. Its curation falls back through host MCP sampling to a configured endpoint and then to regex when no LLM is available, and the README notes the legacy OpenClaw adapter is kept only for existing users while MCP is the only path under active development.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and maturity: its MCP memory tools, three-layer vault and curate loop duplicate doors and compilation we already have, and the project is too young and small to build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: expo-llm-wiki
good: A cross-platform TypeScript library (Expo, React Native, React web, vanilla JS and Node) giving LLM apps offline-first, SQLite-backed, tiered multi-entity memory: background fact extraction, semantic embedding search with an in-process MiniSearch keyword fallback when offline or when embedding throws, SQL-only GraphRAG traversal with a recursive CTE, and OKF v0.2 import/export. Facts carry source_type (document-derived facts are immutable and preserved from librarian/heal rewriting), a draft review tier that reads can exclude, opt-in evidence grounding that demotes unquoted facts to draft, and a read-only lint reporting dangling edges, untyped facts and unverified inferences.
bad: Its source of truth is SQLite tables, not Markdown files, so knowledge is not directly readable, diffable or git-versioned the way a file wiki is. Grounding and the ontology classifier are opt-in and off by default, ontology inheritance is single-level only (chains and cycles are rejected at validation), and lint is read-only — it never repairs what it reports.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a SQLite-backed app-embedding library replaces Markdown custody with a database and targets Expo/React/Node applications, not a personal file-based knowledge OS; its draft-tier and grounding-to-draft mechanics are already covered in our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-monorepo
good: A single monorepo bundling a Python CLI, an MCP server (15 stdio tools), a graph engine with community detection, a Chrome clipper, a web viewer, an Obsidian plugin and 20 domain templates, all reading and writing the same Markdown wiki with portalocker advisory locks and atomic page writes so concurrent agents and CI jobs cannot corrupt pages. It adds two-step ingest with SHA256 caching, hybrid BM25 + semantic search fused by RRF with a committed search gold set, typed/directed/bitemporal graph edges, reversible entity resolution, and contradiction detection with evidence-grounded confidence written to frontmatter.
bad: Adoption at source is minimal — 3 stars and 0 forks — despite 'production-grade' claims and a dense self-certification release narrative. The surface is very large (six-plus packages to build in dependency order), the base install is lexical/keyword-only, and the semantic, Leiden, entity-resolution and NER extras are explicitly 'outside the supported default story'.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: adopting it means replacing our wiki engine with an entire monorepo (CLI, MCP server, graph engine, clipper, viewer and plugin) whose maturity is unproven at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agentic-stack
good: Keeps one portable .agent/ folder of memory, skills and protocols across 13 coding-agent harnesses (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex and others) so switching tools does not reset the agent. It adds DAG orchestration that judges completion by evidence (exit status, truncation, per-node verify) with exception reports, gated self-evolution (candidates are paired-screened on a fixed task sample with validity and activation gates before install, with backup), Markdown memory tracks (episodes, agent cases, foresight with a validity window, source-backed knowledge pages) served over a stdio MCP server, and a skill forge with quality facets and lineage.
bad: The README states its loop supervisor 'is not an operating-system sandbox', that schedulers should invoke one bounded loop run at a time, and that removing an adapter is a confirm-and-delete with 'no quarantine, no undo'; memory search is labelled BETA. The scope is also very broad — 13 harness adapters, dashboards, a data layer and a flywheel — well beyond a knowledge wiki.
didnt: Board — gated evolution for skills (diagnose failures from episodic memory, scaffold a candidate, paired-screen it on a fixed task sample, install only with backup) and evidence-judged DAG completion as ideas for our own skill and agent governance. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agent-swarm
good: A self-hosted agent operating system in which a lead agent receives work from Slack, repositories, issue trackers, email or API and delegates to workers (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Grok and others) running in isolated Docker containers, with schema-validated task results, deferred tasks that wake on watched outcomes or deadlines, workflows and schedules, and memory and identity that persist across sessions with citation ratings. Extensions are installed as inert drafts and activated only by a trusted lead, operator or dashboard user.
bad: It is a heavy company-scale platform — Docker Compose or Kubernetes/Helm deployment, Bun, an API key and an encryption key to manage, and a very large integration surface (Slack, GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Linear, Jira, WhatsApp, Telegram, Teams, Discord and more) — and its persistent brain is vector-search memory rather than user-owned Markdown. The README warns the repo 'evolves every single day', and its optional public ranking makes token totals public and exact.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a multi-agent company operating system with containerised workers and a Slack lead is far outside a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS, and its vector-search memory does not match our local-first Markdown custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Beever Atlas
good: Pulls Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams and Mattermost conversations through a 6-stage pipeline that extracts atomic facts, deduplicates them and clusters them into auto-maintained per-channel wiki pages with citations, backed by a semantic store plus an entity graph store. Answers are cited back to source messages via a dashboard or an MCP server (28 tools, per-agent auth) into Claude Code and Cursor.
bad: Scope is team chat platforms only, and deployment is heavy: the README ships a Docker Compose stack of backend, bot and web front-end backed by four datastores (Weaviate, Neo4j, MongoDB, Redis), and real use requires GOOGLE_API_KEY and JINA_API_KEY before installation.
didnt: Rejected — team-chat-platform scope and a four-datastore Docker stack duplicate our local-first, directed-ingest wiki while adding heavy operations; its cited-answer design corroborates ours but fills no gap in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Linkly AI / Link
good: Local, source-backed memory for agents shared across Codex, Claude, Cursor and other MCP clients: raw sources become an inspectable Markdown wiki, explicit 'remember this' requests become reviewable memories, and writes are review-gated with no LLM in the memory layer, so ingestion and recall are deterministic. It publishes measured benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval evidence retrieval, a memory-poisoning suite) rather than only asserting quality.
bad: The README's own numbers show the default pip lexical tier is weak (bundled recall benchmark hit@1 0.589, rising only with the provisioned local or optional quality tiers), and its disclosed LongMemEval end-to-end re-judging trails Mem0's answers under the same referee. It is a young, single-author-style project built around coding-agent memory rather than a general research wiki.
didnt: Corroboration — review-gated writes, source-backed plain-Markdown memory and provably local storage mirror our approval-gated, citation-locked, local-first design; it duplicates our stack, so no adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lacuna-wiki
good: Exposes a personal research graph to agents through a single composable MCP tool, `wiki`, over plain-Markdown Obsidian-readable vault files indexed in DuckDB with hybrid BM25 + vector search. It ingests YouTube URLs, arXiv links, PDFs and web pages, and ships structured agent skills — ingest, cited query, an 'adversary' skill that re-verifies old claims against their cited sources, plus sweep and synthesise passes that audit wikilinks and queue synthesis clusters.
bad: The README labels it an early release with Windows support still in progress, and it requires a separate OpenAI-compatible embedding endpoint (e.g. Ollama) plus a running daemon — without the daemon, no MCP client can connect. Changing the embedding model or dimension invalidates existing embeddings, and the planned in-place reindex command does not exist yet: the documented remedy is to delete the vault index and re-run init.
didnt: Board — the 'adversary' skill that re-verifies old claims against their cited sources, and sweep-queued synthesis clusters with coverage scores, as candidate ideas for our lint and truth-checking passes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-memory (ctxr-dev)
good: Local, git-versioned memory for AI coding agents with no RAG stack, Docker or cloud: sessions are captured and compiled into plain-Markdown wiki leaves, recalled through a local MCP server with on-device transformer embeddings. Self-improvement lessons are write-gated — proposed one at a time and saved only on explicit approval — and the README reports a 1,961-test unit + e2e suite.
bad: Hook-driven automatic capture works only in Claude Code; every other MCP client gets the same tools but must follow bundled rule files instead. It requires Node 22.18+ and a ~219 MB embedding-model download on first run, and its scope is coding-agent session memory, not a general personal research wiki.
didnt: Corroboration — a per-lesson approval gate, git-versioned plain-Markdown leaves and fully on-device recall confirm our approval-gated writes and local custody; the capability is already present in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Memora
good: An MCP memory layer giving agents persistent, collective memory in SQLite (with optional S3/R2/Cloudflare D1 sync): its absorb step classifies each incoming fact as duplicate, update, contradiction, related or new, and updates supersede old knowledge through a lineage chain that retrieval can follow in active, latest or full-history modes. It adds semantic and hybrid search, typed memory linking, topic digests bundling memories with source IDs, and an interactive knowledge-graph UI.
bad: Absorb depends on an LLM classifying facts in the write path, so memory writes are model-mediated rather than deterministic. The documented container install path is narrow and fragile — it targets Apple's container CLI on Apple-silicon Macs running macOS 26, the README warns the supervised proxy can come back while its upstream is still stopped, and local embeddings need an optional ~2 GB PyTorch extra.
didnt: Board — supersession lineage with active / latest / full-history follow modes as a retrieval idea for our truth-aware handling of superseded wiki pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-llm-wiki
good: A self-maintaining, Obsidian-compatible Karpathy-pattern wiki with native Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2 support: sources are captured as immutable structured packets, ingested into interlinked canonical pages, and guarded against direct edits to raw sources. A standalone stdio MCP server exposes 15 wiki tools (bootstrap, recall, ingest, lint, reindex and more) usable from Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf and other clients, with deterministic linting and layered personal + project vaults.
bad: It is built primarily for the pi / oh-my-pi agent harness — the company/team vault layer is still marked as future work in its own README, and semantic reindexing may download roughly 2 GB of embedding models. As a complete Karpathy-pattern wiki + MCP server it substantially duplicates our existing stack.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and harness fit: a pi-first Karpathy-pattern wiki with its own MCP server, where our wiki already has its own MCP doors and OKF-style portability is not a missing capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: QMD
good: An on-device search engine for Markdown knowledge bases combining BM25 full-text search, vector semantic search and LLM re-ranking, fused with reciprocal rank fusion and typed query expansion (lex / vec / HyDE), all running locally via node-llama-cpp with GGUF models. It offers a CLI, an SDK and an MCP server whose query tool accepts metadata filters and score thresholds, plus per-collection context descriptions that help an agent choose documents.
bad: Embeddings are a separate step (`qmd embed`) from adding a collection, so newly added pages are invisible to vector search until it runs, and the local GGUF embedding/reranker models stay loaded in VRAM for the HTTP MCP mode. The README also warns that unknown MCP tool parameters are silently ignored rather than rejected, and that the HTTP endpoints are unauthenticated and need the operator's own auth if reachable off-host.
didnt: Corroboration — local BM25 + vector + LLM-rerank hybrid search exposed over MCP is exactly the scale path our wiki's qmd-style design already follows; this pass takes nothing new from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SwarmVault
good: A local-first LLM Wiki implementing Karpathy's three layers (immutable raw/, generated wiki/, schema file) with a typed knowledge graph, hybrid SQLite full-text + embedding search, an MCP server, and a built-in offline heuristic provider that needs no API keys. Every graph edge is tagged extracted, inferred or ambiguous, contradiction detection flags conflicting claims, and compiles can be staged into reviewable approval bundles with new concepts landing in a candidates folder first.
bad: The CLI requires Node >= 24, and the project is a large multi-package surface (CLI, engine, viewer, desktop app, many model providers and agent integrations) to adopt wholesale. Its documentation is English-first and the README itself warns that wording in the translated READMEs may drift from the canonical English source.
didnt: Corroboration — approval bundles, candidate staging and extracted / inferred / ambiguous edge tagging confirm our approval-gated, provenance-tagged design; as a full duplicate wiki stack there is nothing to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: code-review-graph
good: Builds a persistent structural map of a codebase with Tree-sitter — functions, classes, imports, call sites, inheritance and test coverage stored in a local SQLite graph — and serves compact context over MCP and CLI so an assistant reads only the files a change touches. Blast-radius analysis traces callers, dependents and tests for a changed file, incremental updates re-parse only SHA-256-changed files, and the README reports a ~63x median per-question token reduction across six benchmark repositories, plus risk-scored PR reviews as a GitHub Action.
bad: Its scope is code structure only — it indexes no knowledge or wiki content — and the headline benchmarks come from the project's own evaluation runner. Files the parser cannot handle are not silently covered: the README states a build can return a partial status naming the failed files, which keep their previous graph rows.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a code-structure graph for coding agents, not knowledge content; our need is wiki retrieval and citation integrity, which this does not address. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: codebase-memory-mcp
good: A local code-intelligence MCP server shipped as a single static C binary with no runtime dependencies: it indexes a codebase into a persistent knowledge graph using vendored tree-sitter grammars for 158 languages plus Hybrid LSP type resolution, and exposes 17 MCP tools for structural search, call-path tracing, impact analysis, dead-code detection and Cypher-style queries. Indexing and queries run entirely on the user's machine with no hosted service or API key, and it also links documentation and infrastructure (Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform) into the same graph.
bad: Its visual companion, CBM Lens, is explicitly still open beta (v0.0.1) and its Smart CI test selection is labelled experimental in the README, falling back to broader test runs when evidence is insufficient. Its scope is code, docs-as-code and infrastructure — not a personal knowledge wiki — and the README carries a standing note about a known Microsoft Defender false-positive flag on its release binaries.
didnt: Rejected — scope duplication within the code-graph category (alongside code-review-graph and CodeGraph): strong code intelligence, but it serves coding agents, not our knowledge-wiki retrieval or citation needs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CodeGraph
good: A pre-indexed, 100% local code knowledge graph with a Rust kernel: one `codegraph_explore` MCP call returns the relevant symbols' verbatim source, the call paths between them (including dynamic-dispatch hops) and a blast-radius summary, instead of a grep-and-read loop. The index auto-syncs on every file change, the installer auto-configures nine-plus agent clients, and the README's re-measured benchmarks report 88% fewer tool calls and zero file reads across seven real repositories.
bad: The README itself discloses the trade-off: CodeGraph's dense one-call payloads leave about 80% more retrieval context resident in the window at the end of multi-turn sessions than a file-reading agent's results, which matters in small context windows. Installing the CLI also does not index anything or connect an agent by itself — `codegraph install` and a per-project `codegraph init` are separate required steps — and the project ships a telemetry component documented in its own TELEMETRY.md.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a code knowledge graph for coding agents, duplicating the code-graph category; it does not serve our wiki's knowledge retrieval, citation locking or abstention needs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GitNexus
licence: PolyForm Noncommercial (README licence badge; GitHub reports the licence as Other / NOASSERTION)
good: A zero-server code intelligence engine that indexes a codebase into a local knowledge graph — dependencies, call chains, clusters and execution flows — and precomputes that structure at index time so its 19 MCP tools return complete context in one call, including blast-radius impact analysis with confidence scores, change detection against a git diff, and graph-driven renaming. One MCP server serves multiple indexed repos from a global registry, and there is also a browser Web UI for exploring a repo's graph.
bad: The licence is PolyForm Noncommercial — source-available rather than open source, so commercial use falls outside the free terms. Its `analyze` command is also invasive by design: in one step it indexes the repo, installs agent skills, registers Claude Code hooks and writes AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md context files into the project, and the Web UI mode is limited by browser memory to roughly 5,000 files.
didnt: Rejected — licence and scope: PolyForm Noncommercial code is ideas-only under our licence discipline and can never be adopted, and its subject is code intelligence rather than our knowledge wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: quicky-wiki
good: LLM-powered knowledge compiler: ingests files and URLs, extracts atomic claims with confidence scores and provenance, surfaces contradictions automatically, tracks claims temporally (strengthen/weaken/decay via its 'metabolism' commands), and compiles to wiki pages, slides, flashcards, graph and timeline, with a dashboard and a built-in MCP server.
bad: Very small and young: 24 stars, 10 commits and a single release. Extraction requires an LLM API key (local Ollama excepted), and the README documents no evaluation of extraction or confidence-scoring quality.
didnt: Corroboration — confidence-scored claims with provenance, automatic contradiction surfacing and temporal decay confirm our claim-lifecycle design; the tool as a whole duplicates our own compiler, so no code or component was taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PENgram
good: Three-pass pipeline (deterministic tree-sitter code extraction, local faster-whisper transcription, LLM entity/relationship extraction) that turns code, documents, PDFs, audio, images and YouTube channels into a typed knowledge graph: every inferred edge is assigned one of 24 semantic relationship types (including supports / contradicts / supersedes) plus an EXTRACTED / INFERRED / AMBIGUOUS confidence label, with SHA256-cached resumable runs and graph.json / graph.html / Obsidian / Penfield outputs.
bad: Early-stage: v0.1.0, 3 commits and 13 stars. The README itself states the pipeline is idempotent but not byte-reproducible across machines or model versions, because the LLM extraction passes are inherently non-deterministic.
didnt: Board — the 24-type typed-edge vocabulary with EXTRACTED / INFERRED / AMBIGUOUS confidence labels on every edge, for the ideas board as a candidate edge taxonomy. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sage-wiki
good: Single Go binary LLM wiki compiler with an evidenced knowledge graph: typed entities and relations carrying evidence span, confidence and source document, per-fact citations on answers, review-gated entity resolution, bi-temporal edges (contradiction invalidates rather than collides, as_of queries), hybrid BM25 + vector + graph-proximity search, and 19 MCP tools; tiered compilation claims 100K+ documents.
bad: The evidenced-graph features are opt-in passes that cost extra LLM calls per document (the triples pass adds one call per doc), and team/company deployment moves storage to PostgreSQL/pgvector with auth and hub federation — a much larger operational surface than the single-binary pitch suggests.
didnt: Corroboration — evidenced edges with per-fact citations, review-gated entity resolution and bi-temporal invalidation confirm our citation-locking and approval-gated design; the full Go stack duplicates our own system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tesserae
good: Local knowledge compiler that builds a byte-deterministic typed graph (70+ schema-validated node kinds) from markdown, code, PDFs/Office docs and agent sessions; serves cited context documents via Personalized PageRank under a character budget over CLI and MCP, keeps tool outcomes as Event nodes, derives its single causal edge ('recovers') only from observed outcomes, and offers per-agent layered memory with distillation that folds but never deletes.
bad: Its own Status & limitations section: first-run compiles over thousands of files take minutes, incremental compile is experimental, the domain charter is built but not yet produced by compile, RAG-Anything image description is not wired end-to-end, and there is deliberately no live editing UI.
didnt: Board — the derived-never-asserted causal edge discipline and the two composing temporal clocks (as_of vs observed_as_of) in its temporal queries, for the ideas board. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Understand Anything
good: Coding-agent plugin (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI and more) whose tree-sitter + LLM multi-agent pipeline builds an interactive knowledge graph of every file, function, class and dependency, with plain-English node summaries, a business-domain view, guided tours ordered by dependency, fuzzy/semantic search, diff impact analysis, and a /understand-knowledge mode that graphs Karpathy-pattern LLM wikis with community clustering.
bad: The README's own heads-up: the initial /understand run analyzes the whole codebase and can consume a significant number of tokens on large projects; the graph is a snapshot that must be incrementally re-run as code changes, and summary quality rests on the LLM passes.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a codebase-onboarding and code-comprehension graph for development teams, not a personal knowledge system with citation locking and approval-gated writes; nothing in it fills a gap in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WikiMoth
good: Deterministic, token-minimal memory over a plain-markdown [[wikilink]] vault: retrieval is pure-stdlib code with no LLM, GPU or vector DB in the loop, returns the exact auditable note-chain behind an answer in one pass (~99% fewer tokens than dumping the vault in its benchmark), captures Claude Code sessions into notes with code-computed (never model-computed) edges, and ships a no-LLM hygiene suite (conflicts, lint, dedup, decay, bitemporal recall --as-of, supersede-without-delete) also exposed over MCP.
bad: Its own Honest limits section: on a typical real vault retrieval roughly ties BM25 (direct-lookup recall@8 = 1.00 for both), the multi-hop win appears mainly on curated, link-heavy corpora, and the −99% figure is versus dumping the whole vault, not versus a tuned BM25 baseline; young and small at 8 stars.
didnt: Board — deterministic authored-link retrieval with an auditable note-chain, plus the no-LLM hygiene suite (conflicts / dedup / decay / supersede), for the ideas board as candidate retrieval and lint lanes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: EKOS
good: Rust knowledge compiler that observes code, SQL, ETL, Git history and docs without interpreting them, compiles them through deterministic passes into a Canonical Knowledge Model stored in an append-only, replayable semantic ledger where every fact carries its evidence (file and line), serves agents read-only over MCP, redacts secrets/PII at observation time, and keeps human decisions (conflict settlement, promotions, approvals) unreachable from the MCP surface by design; first benchmark: 34s cold ingestion of a 2,022-file repo and 67–93% fewer tokens than grep-based search.
bad: Only Phase 1 of a six-phase roadmap is shipped — the knowledge network, plugin marketplace, enterprise platform and knowledge economy are all 'planned, not shipped' per its own site; the repo is young (created 2026-07-11, 22 stars, small core team) and the project carries a community token and TOKENOMICS.md alongside the code.
didnt: Corroboration — an append-only evidence ledger with provenance on every fact, deterministic compiler passes and human-only decision actions confirm our ledger and approval-gate design; its enterprise data-estate scope is far beyond a personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lat.md
good: Agent Lattice: a codebase knowledge graph written as interconnected markdown files in a lat.md/ directory beside the code, with [[wiki links]] between sections, [[src/file#symbol]] links into code and // @lat: backlink comments in source; `lat check` enforces referential consistency (links, symbols, section structure, test-spec coverage — specs marked require-code-mention must be referenced from test code), semantic search works offline by default via a bundled local embedding model, and the graph is served to agents over MCP.
bad: Scope is codebases only — architecture, product rules and test intent for coding agents, not general personal knowledge; higher-quality semantic search needs a hosted OpenAI or Vercel AI Gateway key, and building from source requires Node.js 22, pnpm and a Rust toolchain.
didnt: Corroboration — a markdown knowledge graph living beside its subject with a check command enforcing referential integrity on every change confirms our schema-and-lint approach; codebase-scoped, so nothing to adopt for the personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CodeAlmanac
good: Self-updating codebase wiki that lives in the repository as plain markdown: compiles decisions, architecture and dead-ends out of agent sessions (Codex / Claude Code) so later sessions can reference them, offers local search / show / serve commands over a local index, a 'garden' pass that reviews the wiki for stale, duplicated or poorly connected knowledge, and a cloud mode where a team shares one wiki delivered back to the repo as commits or pull requests for Git review.
bad: Pre-1.0 and under active development — its own Status section warns breaking changes are possible before 1.0, and its Python rewrite notes describe the local product as an alpha; cloud setup enables session capture per provider (reversible, but a custody-relevant default for a local-first system).
didnt: Rejected — fit and duplication: a team codebase-session wiki with a hosted cloud capture path; it duplicates our own wiki while its custody model runs against our local-first, approval-gated design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graft
good: Builds a codebase understanding graph once — deterministic tree-sitter parsing of every file, function and caller across 23 languages, no model and no network for the structural graph — and writes it as a folder of linked plain-markdown nodes agents open and grep like any repo file; every query first refreshes the graph against the working tree (uncommitted edits included), and the vendor's benchmarks report 46% fewer tool calls and 42% fewer uncached input tokens across 162 runs, with optional plain-English summaries written by the user's own provider key. Now part of Trail-Code, which adds session 'learnings' files.
bad: The graft map is a gitignored local cache (like node_modules) that each teammate must regenerate rather than a committed artifact; the explanatory summaries require your own model provider and key, and Trail-Code's team learnings place is still marked 'soon' in the README.
didnt: Corroboration — a deterministic, model-free code map carried as plain linked markdown files in git confirms our plain-files, local-first approach; it is codebase-scoped tooling, not a personal knowledge system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lorewiki
good: Local-first knowledge base for LLM-assisted coding: indexes a team's markdown wiki into SQLite FTS5 and retrieves with hybrid BM25 + hierarchy-tree navigation fused by Reciprocal Rank Fusion, with CJK-friendly trigram tokenization, per-domain 'topic' vaults shared across projects, a single CLI plus an opencode skill (and optional MCP server) for shell-using agents, zero external services, and optional Ollama / OpenAI-compatible LLM answers that degrade gracefully to top-k chunks when the model is offline.
bad: Tiny project (2 stars, 93 commits). Its headline benchmark is 10 hand-authored queries on a bundled example wiki, and the README itself notes hierarchy-only retrieval regressed to 40% recall@5; the REST API surface was removed in 0.2.0 and Azure OpenAI endpoints are explicitly not supported.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and maturity: FTS5/hierarchy retrieval over markdown duplicates search we already have, at 2-star maturity with a 10-query self-benchmark as its only evaluation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-manager (dotdrelle)
good: Local cockpit for several isolated llm-wiki workspaces: it creates workspace folders, assigns ports, starts Docker services, exposes MCP endpoints, and its donna shell dispatches capability-based agent plans with idempotency, bounded approvals, per-run budgets and recovery after restart. Startup health gates report Ready, Degraded or Setup required across Docker, connectivity, agents, containers and MCP handshakes.
bad: The README states it is a single-user deployment baseline with no true multi-user identity or attributed audit trail, and that it orchestrates rather than implements the wiki engine or agents. It requires Docker, Node 22 and the bundled Bun runtime, has only 3 stars, and its PolyForm Noncommercial licence bars commercial use.
didnt: Board — the deterministic capability dispatcher with bounded approvals, per-run budgets, idempotency and crash recovery, as a design idea for the gateway; its PolyForm Noncommercial code is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LLMWikiNG
good: Local-first OKF v0.2 wiki platform with a wiki.sh CLI (init, ingest, lint, search, watcher, history), a FastAPI web interface with dual-mode editor and interactive canvas knowledge graph, SQLite Matrix FTS5/BM25 search, multi-wiki tenancy, audit logging, and a native MCP server with 47 tools. It compiles sources once into interlinked Markdown instead of re-retrieving on every query.
bad: A very large, fast-moving single-author platform (363 commits, release 3.2.3) whose self-update runs git reset --hard, whose Tailscale Funnel option exposes the wiki publicly, and whose AGPL-3.0 licence makes its code unusable for our stack. Its breadth duplicates a full portal, search and MCP stack we already have.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code and a duplicate full wiki platform; fit and licence both fail for our local-first, git-canonical system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: waikiki
good: A local wiki built for a human and an LLM to edit the same page at the same time: one SQLite file per wiki, fully isolated wikis, live Yjs/pycrdt CRDT co-editing with presence, hybrid FTS5 BM25 plus sqlite-vec search fused with RRF, version history, trash and automatic backups, and an MCP server whose merge-safe edit tools let Claude write into the live document.
bad: The README states its Elastic License 2.0 is source-available, not open source, and bars offering it as a hosted or managed service. Collaborative editing loads Yjs and EasyMDE from esm.sh/unpkg so the editor needs an internet connection, Markdown export loses images, history, comments and templates, and the repo has only 1 star.
didnt: Board — live CRDT human-LLM co-editing of one page and merge-safe, read-before-write MCP edit tools, as ideas; the Elastic-licensed code itself is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WeKnora
good: Tencent's self-hostable knowledge platform with three modes — RAG quick Q&A, a ReAct agent that decomposes complex questions into sub-queries and orchestrates retrieval, MCP tools, sandboxed skills and web search, and Wiki Mode (GA in v0.5.0) where agents auto-generate structured, interlinked Markdown wiki pages with a knowledge graph, editing, revision history and rollback. It adds 4-tier workspace RBAC with per-workspace audit logs, MCP human-in-the-loop tool approval, many document connectors and 20+ LLM providers.
bad: It is an enterprise-scale platform — wiki ingest scaled to 40k-document knowledge bases, multiple vector stores, sandboxes, IM channels and tenant skill catalogues — far heavier than a personal single-user wiki needs. The catalogue's original verdict of not-for-us stands on scale and scope, however capable the platform is.
didnt: Rejected — enterprise multi-tenant RAG/wiki platform at the wrong scale for a personal, local-first LLM wiki, despite its MIT licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Memory OS
good: A 7-layer memory operating system for Hermes Agent: workspace files, FTS5 session search, structured facts with trust scoring and a feedback loop, cross-session Fabric recall, Qdrant hybrid vector search with a 4-level fallback, an auto-curated LLM Wiki layer, and a Ground Truth hierarchy that instructs the agent to treat injected memory as authoritative. It runs locally, is provider-agnostic, and uses relevance-gated, deduplicated surgical context injection.
bad: It is built specifically for Hermes Agent and requires Docker services (Qdrant, Redis, ARQ worker) plus Python 3.11+, so it is not portable to our agent stack. Its bundled Icarus fork is explicitly not upstream-compatible, and the whole design is agent-session memory rather than a citation-locked wiki.
didnt: Corroboration — trust-scored structured facts, decay/dedup scanning and an explicit ground-truth hierarchy confirming our own trust, lifecycle and authority-ranking design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SelfBrain
good: A private personal knowledge system in a GitHub repo you fork and own: 11-plus hubs (calendar, career, documents, finance, health, media, sensors, social, wiki and more) with frontmatter/hub search, Cursor Skills for repeatable routines such as meal logging and Strava CSV to wiki summaries, and Obsidian as the browsing view. There is deliberately no separate cloud service — you run your own copy.
bad: The README calls it an early research project (13 commits, no releases) whose layout will evolve. It depends on a Cursor Cloud Agent linked to GitHub, so the assistant runs in Cursor's cloud rather than locally, and planned plug-and-play extensions and scheduled sync pipelines are still future work.
didnt: Rejected — a promising shape, but its assistant is a Cursor Cloud Agent over a GitHub-hosted vault, which conflicts with our local-first custody and existing agent team. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: whoami.wiki
good: Turns digital archives — photos, chats, documents, location history, transactions and other data dumps — into a living personal encyclopedia written by agents, private by default with the wiki and archive on your own machine and full export to Markdown and original files at any time. It is open source under MIT and is tested with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode harnesses.
bad: The homepage gives no repository, installation or evaluation detail beyond the harness list, and it warns that with online-hosted models your data is sent to those providers — a fully offline experience requires OpenCode with local models. Life-archive auto-ingest of chats and transactions also sits against our no-auto-discovery rule.
didnt: Board — cross-referencing unrelated life-archive metadata timelines into interlinked encyclopedia pages with Wikipedia-style sidebars, event logs and relationship networks, as an idea for personal-history pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: claude-obsidian
good: A local-first Claude Code plugin of 15 skills that turns sources into linked, source-cited Obsidian pages: immutable content-addressed source capture, source and claim ledgers tracking authority, freshness, contradiction, confidence and review state, and grounded refusal over invented citation. Parallel workers return drafts only and one orchestrator applies one recoverable, SHA-checked transaction with a vault lock, journaled backups and approved-plan hashes for mutating setup commands.
bad: Its own capability table limits it: PDF and EPUB get metadata, hash and size only with no built-in semantic extraction, and URL, YouTube and OCR ingestion need a configured external runner. It is an Obsidian/Claude Code substrate, not a standalone wiki, and it states it is not a cloud sync service, transcript recorder or factual oracle.
didnt: Corroboration — claim ledgers with contradiction and confidence state, draft-only parallel workers and single-transaction approval-gated writes confirming our citation-locking and approval-gate design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-llm-wiki (green-dalii)
good: A one-click Obsidian plugin with zero dependencies and no backend that ingests Markdown, PDF, images and Office files into entity and concept wiki pages, with mandatory aliases, tiered duplicate detection and a lint/Smart Fix maintenance flow. Retrieval is zero-embedding Personalized PageRank over the wikilink graph, it supports 16+ providers including local Ollama/LM Studio, and answers carry wikilinks back into the graph.
bad: Its README states answers come from the vault only, bulk external-corpus RAG is out of scope by design, and there is no backend, server or team collaboration — it is a single-user Obsidian plugin. Quality and cost therefore ride entirely on the chosen LLM provider.
didnt: Corroboration — zero-embedding graph retrieval (Personalized PageRank over wikilinks) and alias-first duplicate detection confirming our graph-first, index-first retrieval choices. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-knowledge-bases
good: A Claude Code plugin that compiles raw multi-modal sources (papers, repos, YouTube transcripts, images, datasets) dropped into raw/ into an interlinked Obsidian wiki with summaries, backlinks and auto-generated indexes. Querying runs at three depth levels — Quick from indexes, Standard cross-referencing the full wiki plus web search, and Deep via a multi-agent parallel research pipeline — with outputs as Markdown reports, Marp slides and charts, and automated health checks for broken links, orphans and inconsistencies.
bad: A small, early project: 20 commits, 35 stars and no releases, requiring Claude Code and Obsidian. Its optional X/Twitter integration relies on Smaug using X session cookies, which the README itself notes is not officially supported by X's terms of service.
didnt: Board — the three explicit query depth levels (Quick / Standard / Deep multi-agent research) as a named depth ladder for our own query door. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Matryca Plumber
good: A local-first governed memory plane for Logseq OG graphs: Markdown stays authoritative while a disposable external Shadow DB (FTS5) accelerates reads, writes go through a parser-aware plane with optimistic concurrency control and page locks that reject stale updates, and a Strict Read Only mode blocks graph mutation while keeping the cache useful. It exposes structured CLI and FastMCP access instead of ad hoc file edits, with fail-closed fallbacks to Markdown-backed BM25 reads.
