bad: It requires a Logseq OG graph and Python 3.12+, and its README is dominated by intricate release-qualification history — failed and superseded release candidates, exact parser profiles and gates — signalling high operational complexity. Several headline capabilities (Logseq DB writes, proactive adaptive runtime) are explicitly future work, and evaluators are told to start on a clone of their graph before enabling writes.
didnt: Corroboration — Markdown-as-authority, optimistic concurrency control, strict read-only mode and a disposable rebuildable shadow index confirming our write-safety and read-door design; the Logseq substrate itself does not transfer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SiderMem
good: A Chrome extension and companion CLI that captures web pages, notes, files and chats from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek, automatically extracts entities and topics, and merges them into a connected personal wiki with a graph view and grounded Q&A. Local memories in browser IndexedDB are unlimited and free, Markdown export is offered, and cloud sync is opt-in.
bad: A commercial subscription product: the free tier caps cloud sync at 100 memories and 100 monthly AI summaries and Ask queries, quotas do not roll over, and sync runs through Supabase-hosted cloud storage. No open-source licence is stated at the source, and automatic capture of AI chats runs against our no-auto-discovery, no-session-transcript-ingest rules.
didnt: Rejected — closed commercial cloud-sync product with no licence stated, metered quotas, and automatic chat capture that conflicts with our custody and ingest rules. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki for TiddlyWiki (twillm)
good: TWILLM serves an Obsidian-compatible Markdown vault through TiddlyWiki, with changes from browser, Obsidian or a coding agent picked up live by filesystem watching. Its computed views replace materialised index files — live filter expressions render at view time so indexes cannot go stale — and YAML frontmatter becomes first-class queryable tiddler fields, while the LLM can also author interactive wikitext applets and dashboards. It is agent-agnostic and calls no model itself.
bad: It requires Node.js 22 and bundles a TiddlyWiki build from a non-standard bidirectional-filesystem branch — the README warns the standard tiddlywiki npm release will not work. It is a small project (49 commits, 23 stars, no releases), and the README notes smaller local models produce rougher notes needing more curation.
didnt: Board — computed live-filter views replacing materialised index files, eliminating index staleness, as a design idea for the Lens. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vault-operator
good: An agentic Obsidian plugin that plans, searches, reads, writes and reports back with every action visible, every write approval-gated and every change undoable via checkpoints in a shadow git repository; it is fail-closed by default with per-category auto-approve toggles and a permission centre. It captures sources with block-level provenance, searches by meaning with a local vector index plus full-text, graph expansion and a cross-encoder reranker, maintains three-layer memory, runs vault health checks, and serves the vault as an MCP server to other AI clients.
bad: Desktop-only and requires Obsidian 1.8.7 or newer, plus a configured LLM provider and embedding model for semantic search and ingest. PowerPoint output is beta with no corporate template cloning, and the plugin uses Node.js filesystem capabilities beyond the standard Obsidian API.
didnt: Corroboration — fail-closed, approval-gated writes with checkpoint undo, a revocable permission centre and block-level provenance confirming our approval-gated write design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graph Explorer Base View
good: An Obsidian Bases view that renders only the notes a Base filter returns as an interactive force-directed graph, with a rich visual language: node shape encodes wiki role, and borders and indicators encode explored state, maturity, confidence and graduated children. It adds explored/unexplored and maturity tracking stored in frontmatter, per-view configuration and presets including an LLM Wiki Explorer preset, a side reading panel, batch actions, a minimap and coverage statistics.
bad: It requires Obsidian 1.13.0 or later for the Bases and declarative settings APIs and will not load on older versions, and the README warns BRAT bleeding-edge installs may break. It is purely a visualisation and tracking layer — no ingest, compilation or query of its own — and is a small project (17 stars).
didnt: Board — a filtered graph view colouring nodes by explored status, maturity and confidence with coverage statistics, as a design reference for the Lens. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WikiMind (project 2, distinct)
good: Personal LLM knowledge OS that ingests articles, papers, PDFs, YouTube and RSS, compiles them into wiki articles carrying key claims, confidence scores and source citations, and auto-extracts concepts with bidirectional backlinks. It lints for contradictions, orphans and stale content, offers cross-cutting synthesis, and exposes an MCP server (13 tools) plus exports to Markdown, JSON, PDF and Obsidian.
bad: It is a heavy database-backed stack — PostgreSQL, Redis/ARQ, FastAPI and a React frontend, deployed via Docker or Fly.io — so the knowledge base is not a plain-markdown, git-canonical folder. README documents multi-user OAuth auth and 138 API endpoints, far beyond a personal local wiki, and synthesis depends on a configured cloud LLM provider key.
didnt: Rejected — database-backed (Postgres/Redis) architecture duplicates our markdown-canonical wiki while abandoning plain-file custody, and its claim/confidence compile is already covered in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XTrace MemHub
licence: CC BY 4.0 (documentation in the guide repo only; the MemHub product itself carries no open licence at the source)
good: Turns ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini chat histories, captured via a Chrome extension, into an LLM-Wiki mindmap: MemHub extracts memories, stores them in an encrypted vector database, and exports a Markdown ZIP (beliefs, artifacts and episodes, with wikilink styles for supersession and linked facts) that opens directly as an Obsidian vault, with no local CLI setup.
bad: The GitHub repo is only a five-commit usage guide — the actual product is a hosted, sign-in web service, so the memory extraction happens on the vendor's platform rather than in local files the user controls. The guide documents no self-hosting, no evaluation, and no local-first custody of the extracted memories before export.
didnt: Rejected — hosted chat-history mining into a vendor's encrypted database conflicts with our local-first custody and with the bar on session-transcript ingest; only the guide documentation is openly licensed, not the product. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yopedia
good: Dual-surface wiki: a human surface of Markdown pages with YAML frontmatter, wikilinks, inline citations, and confidence and expiry on every page, plus an agent surface explored by six specialised agents that run ingest, query, lint and graph work on a schedule through GitHub Issues. Its harness enforces quality mechanically — build failures get fix attempts, then automatic revert and re-queue — and pages visibly decay when stale instead of silently persisting.
bad: The README states the agent surface is still 'an open research question' and that the app was grown with zero human code and no human backlog management — agents decide what to build. It is framed as a public, multi-writer commons rather than a private personal wiki, and the repo carries no licence file.
didnt: Rejected — no licence at source, and its autonomous agent-driven writing with no owner approval gate conflicts with our approval-gated writes and private custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Astucia
good: Flat-file, self-hosted wiki with no database: Markdown pages, draw.io diagrams, spreadsheet-style lists and per-file team chat all stored as plain files, with Git auto-commit on save, full-text search (optional SQLite FTS5), a knowledge graph from links, hierarchy and tags, and AI agent jobs plus an MCP server and MCP client so its AI users can call external tools while answering.
bad: Authentication is optional and off by default, in which state, by the README's own wording, every visitor has full admin access. Scope is a multi-user team workspace (chat, mentions, spaces, email digests) in PHP, well beyond a personal wiki, and the GPL-3.0 licence bars code adoption for us.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence (ideas only under our licence discipline) and a team-chat workspace scope that does not fit a private personal knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ambient Context
good: macOS menu-bar app that reads the focused window's text through the accessibility tree and appends it to plain-Markdown daily logs, then has the user's own agent CLI compile each day into six cited knowledge pages (People, Commitments, Threads, Products, Issues, Reading) and a daily summary whose citations are checked against the record before saving. It exposes 20 MCP tools, scrubs credential- and card-shaped strings, skips password fields and private windows, and keeps everything local with no account or telemetry.
bad: macOS 14+ on Apple Silicon only, and built and maintained by one person. Capture is inherently ambient and indiscriminate — the README warns its redaction is heuristics, not a guarantee, and to treat the folder as sensitive — and capture from Chromium/Electron apps and GPU-rendered terminals is thin or missing, per its Known limits section.
didnt: Rejected — continuous ambient screen capture is the auto-discovery / ambient-ingest pattern our system has already refused, and the app is macOS-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ars Umbris
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) — no standard licence name stated in the repo sidebar or README
good: Agent-native IDE for typed knowledge built on a Rust graph engine: it reads composable, interdependent repos of Markdown and YAML as one typed, queryable live graph, checks fields and references, and gives agents diagnostics they can act on, with an Electron host mounting editable typed projections (views) over the graph and an MCP layer providing typed tools and skills.
bad: The README labels it early alpha with breaking changes expected, macOS only for now, and states it runs code on your machine with no sandboxing yet. The entry repo has only 2 commits and no releases, and its licence is not a standard recognised licence at the source.
didnt: Rejected — early-alpha maturity, macOS-only, unsandboxed code execution, and a non-standard licence make it unfit to adopt; the typed-graph diagnostics idea is noted only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BYO-LLM-WIKI
good: Local-first Flask wiki whose deepagents curating agent builds an 8-layer on-disk knowledge graph (source through entity, topic, synthesis, memory and agent skills), with Anthropic-style contextual retrieval over a two-layer HNSW index giving grounded, cited Q&A. Its skill-synthesis loop is gated behind human review — drafts land in pending_review and only a human promotes them — MCP writes are deny-by-default, and it publishes offline evaluation (retrieval hit@k/MRR, RAGAS, a five-family judge panel) on a version-controlled 28-document corpus.
bad: No licence file or licence statement appears at the source, so its code cannot be adopted. RAG requires an OpenAI API key for embeddings regardless of the chat provider, its stores are JSON, HNSW vectors and SQLite checkpoints under data/ rather than a plain-markdown wiki, and its evaluation corpus is only 28 documents.
didnt: Board — the human-gated skill-synthesis loop (draft, deterministic checks plus judge panel, pending_review, human-only promotion) and deny-by-default MCP writes as design ideas for our proposal machinery; no code, as no licence is stated at the source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Curated Thoughts
good: Privacy-first Tauri/Rust desktop second brain with a three-tier memory (working, episodic RAG over SQLite, semantic wiki as real .md files under wiki/) in which an Active Librarian's proposals reach the long-term wiki only through a human-verification gate — approval is stamped with who reviewed it, agents cannot approve, and no MCP approval tool exists. Sources are immutable and read-only to the app's write tools, embeddings default to local Ollama for offline use, and it offers OKF bundle import/export, a headless ct CLI and a unified MCP server.
bad: The knowledge base itself lives in a SQLite brain.db, so the Markdown wiki is a replica of database state rather than the canonical store, and switching vaults discards the knowledge layer built from the current vault. The README also documents an exception to its own gate: MCP wisdom write tools record agent entries straight into the wiki as confirmed facts without the proposal gate, and the build is a complex Rust/Tauri workspace with a required MCP sidecar placeholder step.
didnt: Corroboration — its human-in-the-loop gate, in which librarian proposals wait in a review queue and agents are mechanically unable to approve, confirms our approval-gated write design; its immutable-source separation likewise confirms our raw/wiki split. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nohmitaina
good: Memory editor for people and AI that structures shared memory as Concepts (background and reasons), Procedures (ordered steps with each step's role, required inputs, checks and explicit points where a person decides), Tasks and Episodes (what actually happened), with a Persona as role instructions for reading shared material. It works alongside Claude Code or Codex CLI on macOS and Windows, is free to use, and procedures are drafted by AI then revised by the user from real results.
bad: The site is at version 0.3.0, offers no source repository and no licence, and requires a Claude Code or Codex CLI environment with the user's own subscription and API fees. The site itself states that sharing a process does not guarantee the quality of the result, and it documents no wiki compilation, citation or retrieval machinery — its focus is work procedures, not a knowledge base.
didnt: Board — the Procedure as a first-class memory type, with explicit human-decision steps and per-step checks, as an idea for structuring recurring work in our wiki; the product itself is closed and unlicensed at the source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SecondBrain (PieroSierra)
good: Folder-based personal knowledge base with a one-way flow — append-only raw/ (never modified by AI) is ingested into a cross-linked wiki/, and questions are answered with sources into dated outputs/ — driven by agent skills that run identically on Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode. Capture covers notes, PDFs, Office files, spreadsheets, images, URLs and Craft, with a local web dashboard, a macOS app, a Chrome capture extension, and a lint skill that flags contradictions, unsupported claims and gaps; ingest is explicit, so nothing enters the wiki until the user runs it.
bad: No licence file or licence statement appears at the source, so its code cannot be adopted. The native app and dashboard flow are macOS-centred, the README's own security note says the Codex and OpenCode engines can run shell commands inside the vault (unlike Claude Code's denied shell/network), and the text sent to the agent's model is the one thing that leaves the machine.
didnt: Corroboration — its append-only raw/ to wiki/ to outputs/ flow with explicit, user-run ingest confirms our raw-record plus compiled-wiki design and our bar on automatic ingest. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graph Knowledge Base (gknowledge)
good: Native GNOME (GTK 4 / Libadwaita) LLM-Wiki app, offline by default with a built-in heuristic engine that ingests and answers with no account and no API key, keeping plain Markdown with YAML frontmatter in an Obsidian-compatible vault. Ingest is two-step with per-page source provenance, answers cite pages, a review queue holds uncertain model changes, and it ships an MCP server (gknowledge-mcp) so Claude Code, Codex or Cursor can search, read and grow the same wiki; local Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint can be added.
bad: Linux/GNOME only, with Ubuntu/Debian packaging first-class. The README's own workflow table marks lint (orphans, contradictions, stale pages), the knowledge graph view, web clipper, folder watch and Git diff review as planned rather than done, so several core wiki-maintenance features do not yet exist in the app.
didnt: Corroboration — its offline heuristic engine with per-page provenance and a review queue for uncertain changes confirms our local-first, provenance-carrying, review-gated design, including working with no model at all. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-system
licence: MIT (stated in the README; no separate LICENSE file in the root listing)
good: Web implementation of the Karpathy pattern — FastAPI backend and vanilla-JS frontend that ingests URLs and PDF/DOCX/TXT/Markdown files, synthesises them into source, entity, concept and analysis pages in an Obsidian-compatible vault, and maintains index, log and overview files. Its Graphify knowledge graph labels edges EXTRACTED, INFERRED or AMBIGUOUS by confidence, offers path finding and natural-language graph queries, and rebuilds incrementally (debounced, manual, or nightly cron) using a SHA256 cache, with an async JSON-lines job queue needing no Redis.
bad: Very immature: 8 commits and 6 stars, no releases, and the README states the whole system was built autonomously by AI agents with no manual code editing. By default the server binds to 0.0.0.0 with no built-in authentication (the README recommends bolting on Caddy Basic Auth and a firewall), and synthesis is tied to a single hosted model route (Kimi via OpenRouter).
didnt: Rejected — immature, autonomously built and unauthenticated by default, and it duplicates the web wiki and confidence-labelled graph our stack already has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Row-Bot
good: Local-first desktop AI assistant whose memory layer is a personal knowledge graph with recall, review and Dream Cycle refinement, plus documents and an Obsidian-compatible wiki vault, running on local Ollama models or opt-in cloud/subscription models with data kept on the user's machine. Risky actions wait for Approve or Deny across the conversation, Home and connected channels, and it adds goals with delegated agents, scheduled and webhook workflows, and OS credential-store storage for provider keys.
bad: The wiki is one small feature inside a very large general assistant — shell, browser automation, computer use, messaging channels, health tracking, design and code panels — with installers of about 420 MB (Windows), 930 MB (macOS) and 790 MB (Linux). It is explicitly single-owner and not multi-user hosting, and its breadth is the opposite of a focused, file-canonical knowledge wiki.
didnt: Rejected — scope mismatch: a full personal-AI operating system whose knowledge graph and Dream Cycle are peripheral to our wiki, offered only as part of a near-gigabyte assistant install. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Silica
good: Transactional write path for a Markdown vault: the LLM proposes, a parser and an FSM verify each write against its source, and any edit that fails structural or coherence checks is reverted — a model the README likens to a compiler, test suite, git rollback and formatter combined — claiming 100% write integrity across a real 796-note vault. Retrieval fuses embedding, BM25-weighted co-occurrence and an optional lexical leg by rank, with legs able to abstain; it publishes its abstention rate (87.2% correct refusals on LoCoMo) alongside accuracy, preserves the source's own words instead of summarising (measured worth about 15 points), and works through a web GUI, terminal, Obsidian plugin and MCP server, with a model-free core.
bad: AGPL-3.0 (with a separate commercial licence file), so its code is ideas-only for us. Its own Measured section is candid that the samples are small — LoCoMo here is 2 of its 10 conversations, judged by a local-grade model, and explicitly not comparable to vendor numbers — scanned PDFs yield nothing without the user separately installing MinerU for OCR, and the project is very new (created 2026-10-09, 0 stars at the source).
didnt: Board — the FSM verify-or-revert write gate (propose, parse, structural check, post-write verify, per-file rollback) and publishing correct-refusal rates beside accuracy, as ideas for hardening our write path and Ask door; AGPL-3.0 bars adopting its code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Curator (the-curator)
licence: MIT, except ten Shared Brain backend files that are source-available under the custom Curator Enterprise License
good: Local app that compounds dropped-in documents into an interlinked Markdown wiki readable in Obsidian and synced through the user's own private GitHub repo, distinguishing three kinds of context with different update rules: compounded knowledge that accumulates, volatile working state that supersedes, and canonical foundation documents replaced whole and read verbatim, all delivered to agents in a single MCP call with a per-project reading budget ('the right context, not all of it'). It is vendor-neutral by construction (plain files, no proprietary store), answers cite the pages they came from, and it measures its own handoff effect, reporting that with working state present an agent stopped re-proposing already-failed commands and ruled-out architectures.
bad: Its own honest boundaries state that capture is advisory — nothing forces an agent to save, a missed save returns stale state, and a measured harness saved 0 of 4 times from the skill alone — and that its MCP bridge is a stdio child process, so browser-only assistants cannot reach it. The local server has no per-request authentication, the Mac app is not notarised, ten backend files sit under a custom enterprise licence whose text the README says has not been reviewed by a lawyer, and sync is hard-wired to ordinary github.com with no configurable endpoint.
didnt: Corroboration — its three update rules (knowledge accumulates, state supersedes, canonical documents are replaced whole) and its single-MCP-call bootstrap confirm our supersession and standing-state design; the ten custom-licensed backend files are excluded from any code consideration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graphify
good: Turns a codebase together with its docs, SQL schemas, configs and PDFs into a queryable knowledge graph. Code parsing is local and deterministic (tree-sitter AST, no vector store), every edge is tagged EXTRACTED (explicit in source) or INFERRED, and cross-file calls/imports/inheritance are tracked across roughly 40 languages; outputs graph.html, GRAPH_REPORT.md and graph.json with query/path/explain commands, and the README's benchmarks claim 0.497 recall@10 at zero LLM credits.
bad: Only the code pass is local and deterministic — the semantic pass over docs, PDFs, images and video uses the assistant's model or a configured API key. It requires Python 3.10+ with uv/pipx, and the README pushes a separate paid hosted Graphify Cloud upsell.
took: EXTRACTED-vs-INFERRED edge tags (edge provenance) — built in Round 3, lane TA5 — source/inspiration: Graphify (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — per-edge EXTRACTED vs INFERRED provenance tagging confirms our citation-locking stance that inferred content must never be dressed up as extracted fact; the mechanism was already taken in Round 3, so nothing further is needed from the tool itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OpenKnowledge (inkeep)
good: A true-WYSIWYG markdown editor built for knowledge bases, LLM wikis, specs and notes — private, local and free — with desktop apps (macOS/Windows/Linux) plus a web UI offering a file navigator, search, tabs and a graph wiki-link viewer. It supports side-by-side AI editing with Claude, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and others via MCP/CLI, ships MCP, skills and agentic search out of the box, and offers git/GitHub team sharing with auto-sync and embeddable rich components.
bad: Licensed GPL-3.0, so its code is copyleft and cannot be adopted into our stack. The web app requires Node.js 24+ and git, and the contribution guidance steers contributors to file a detailed issue first, with PRs mainly for small fixes and larger changes only after maintainer acceptance.
didnt: Board — the WYSIWYG-over-plain-markdown editor with MCP side-by-side agent editing is worth boarding as a pattern; GPL-3.0 makes the code itself ideas-only for us. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wikiwise
good: A native Mac app for setting up and managing a local-first markdown wiki with an AI agent: point it at a folder and markdown files become interlinked wiki pages with no database, config or account. Claude Code is built in (custom skills, Readwise-highlight import, article ingest), there is a 3D knowledge-graph view, and the wiki compiles in one click to a clean, fast website; it is explicitly inspired by Karpathy's llm-wiki pattern with no lock-in — just markdown on your Mac.
bad: Readwise labels it experimental, it is macOS-only, and despite the 'open source' claim the product site names no licence, so reuse terms are unstated at source. Its agent story is built specifically around Claude Code.
didnt: Board — folder-pointed, zero-config local-first wiki compilation to a static site is a pattern worth boarding; with no licence stated at source its code is ideas-only, never adopt/build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CartaStudio
good: Captures a practitioner's judgment as a typed, scoped, sourced decision graph stored in portable markdown: every claim is pinned to a source the user chose, unsourced nodes are shown as 'thin', scoped exceptions override general rules with their reasons recorded, and the agent only drafts and proposes — nothing becomes part of a Carta until the user ratifies it. It runs as a local desktop app (macOS & Windows) with data staying on the machine, can check a draft document against the Carta, and explicitly abstains ('no judgment is offered rather than one invented') where the Carta holds nothing.
bad: It is a closed commercial product: the site publishes no repository, licence or technical documentation, publishing is still in beta, and the pricing model charges once other people or their agents start relying on your Carta. Verification of its claims rests entirely on the vendor's own page.
didnt: Corroboration — ratification-gated settling, source-pinned claims with visible thinness, and refusal to judge where nothing is sourced closely mirror our approval-gated writes and scored abstention; as a closed, unlicensed-at-source product it is corroboration only, not a build source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DeepWiki-Open
good: Automatically generates an interactive wiki for any GitHub, GitLab or BitBucket repository — analysing code structure, generating documentation and visual diagrams, organising it into a navigable wiki, and producing a codemap for code-centric guided tours. It supports private repositories via personal access tokens, a RAG 'Ask' feature and a multi-turn DeepResearch process, with provider choice across Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter and local Ollama.
bad: The repository page shows 0 releases and 0 tags despite its popularity, and wiki generation depends on external LLM provider API keys (Google/OpenAI/Azure/OpenRouter) unless the user runs local Ollama.
didnt: Rejected — it is a repository-documentation generator, a different job from a personal LLM-wiki/knowledge OS, and it duplicates repo-reading tooling we already have; its codemap idea does not fill a gap in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cabinet
good: An AI-first knowledge base and startup OS where everything is markdown files on disk — no database, no vendor lock-in, self-hosted — with a WYSIWYG (Tiptap) plus markdown editor. Its AI agents each carry goals, skills and scheduled (cron) jobs; every save auto-commits to git with a diff viewer and page restore; it is BYOAI (Claude, Codex, OpenCode, local models) and ships 20 pre-built agent templates, embedded HTML apps, missions/Kanban, internal chat and full-text Cmd+K search.
bad: It requires Node.js 22+ (the README notes Node 20 triggers an EBADENGINE warning) and at least one supported CLI provider such as the Claude Code or Codex CLI. Its scope is a full startup OS / AI-team product, far broader than a personal wiki, and the optional password protection is a single shared UI gate.
didnt: Board — scheduled cron agents with goals and skills operating over a plain-markdown, git-versioned store is a pattern worth boarding; adopting the product itself would duplicate our existing stack at much larger scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wiki-from-code hook template
good: A drop-in template whose background git post-commit hook diffs each commit, feeds the diff to a chosen AI CLI (Claude Code, Cursor or Codex), and lands a follow-up 'wiki: update' commit, so a codebase wiki stays roughly current with no manual bookkeeping. It ships hard anti-hallucination rules in CLAUDE.md (cite path:line or don't claim), configurable doc categories in .llmwiki/config.yml, and a freshness.sh that compares stored source SHAs against the tree to report stale pages.
bad: A small personal template: 4 commits, no releases, and the README itself says the output is a draft/internal reference, not finished or compliance-grade documentation, and a poor fit for UI-heavy apps. The hook is bash-only — native Windows cmd/PowerShell will not run it and it is untested on native Windows shells.
didnt: Board — the freshness.sh idea (stored source SHAs compared against the tree to list stale wiki pages) as a lint/report, not as the template's unattended auto-writing hook, which conflicts with our approval-gated writes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ByteRover
good: ByteRover CLI (brv) gives coding agents persistent structured memory as a hierarchical Context Tree with an adaptive knowledge lifecycle, git-like version control for the tree, an MCP integration, and a review workflow (brv review approve/reject) for curate operations. It reports strong long-term-memory benchmarks run on the production codebase: 96.1% on LoCoMo and 92.8% on LongMemEval-S.
bad: The GitHub repository is archived, and the code is under the Elastic License 2.0 (a custom/source-available licence, shown as NOASSERTION in the repo sidebar), so the code is not freely reusable. Sync and team sharing push toward the hosted ByteRover Cloud, which sits outside a local-first, self-custodied model.
took: Per-page importance with decay — built in Round 3, lane TB4/TB5 (compound bullet) — source/inspiration: ByteRover
didnt: Corroboration — its FinMem-style importance/recency/maturity scoring and adaptive knowledge lifecycle confirm the per-page importance-with-decay design already built in Round 3 from it; the code itself is not adopted because the Elastic License 2.0 is ideas-only and the repo is archived (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LWC (JanYork)
good: A Rust agent-memory CLI that keeps four traceable layers (immutable raw sources, agent-maintained wiki with citations/links/provenance, temporal memory, schema/purpose), indexes sources and pages at document/passage/sentence level so agents can expand exact spans and detect stale locators, and supports atomic multi-command changesets plus portable archives whose whole-store overwrite requires separate human confirmation. It needs no embeddings or vector database and returns auditable structured JSON from operations.
bad: SQLite is canonical and Markdown is only a rebuildable projection — the inverse of our markdown/git-canonical custody. Its own Limits section states a single-machine, single-user base, lexical search only (no semantic vector retrieval), and a 64 MiB bound per source/page body; the repo is also very young (created 2026-07-29) despite rapid releases.
didnt: Board — the sentence/passage-level bitemporal locators with stale-locator detection after content changes, as a citation-durability idea; the CLI itself is rejected because its database-canonical model inverts our plain-markdown, git-canonical custody (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Trove
good: A local-first macOS app and CLI that aggregates what a user has already saved — X bookmarks/likes, Instagram saves, Substack, GitHub stars, Hacker News favourites, and Claude/ChatGPT exports — into one local workspace with a SQLite FTS5 archive, hydrated markdown content, and agent guide files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/INDEX.md), with no cloud, account, or API keys.
bad: Sync is built on browser cookies and is macOS-only today (cookie sync fails on Linux/Windows by design); the desktop build is unsigned, some sources expose no true saved/liked timestamps so Trove stores approximations, and hydration covers external article links rather than every native page type. It is a small young project (17 stars, 4 releases).
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: it is a social-saves aggregator driven by browser-cookie scraping, not a staged ingest/review pipeline for curated sources, and its cookie-based capture model does not match our deliberate, source-by-source ingest (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: beeweave
good: An agent-native workbench that separates a messy workbench/ staging area (inbox, captures, drafts, with a _staging area in the vault) from a compiled markdown vault/ of concepts, entities, references and synthesis pages with wikilinks, then loops collect → create → distill → reuse so published output becomes the high-signal source for durable knowledge. The same knowledge base is shared across many agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and others) via portable ingest/query/update skills.
bad: Very small and young: 6 stars, 38 commits, created 2026-07-05, with no evaluation or benchmark evidence in the README. Its centre of gravity is a creative-writing flywheel (article/social writers and publishers), not knowledge governance, citation locking or approval-gated maintenance.
didnt: Corroboration — its workbench-staging → compiled-vault split, with durable knowledge distilled from finished pieces rather than every rough note, confirms our updates/raw → compiled wiki staging design; its creation-flywheel scope is not needed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wikidesk
good: A Rust companion server that turns named wiki repos into shared multi-agent knowledge services: agents read local mirrors directly, and an optional research tool (over MCP and REST) queues a question, dispatches a dedicated research agent to update the server wiki, returns the answer with wikilinks resolved to the client's mirror path, and auto-syncs local copies. Read-only versus read+research access is controlled simply through agent rules.
bad: Its own Security section states the research agent runs with full permissions (typically --dangerously-skip-permissions) and is unsandboxed by default — the server must be run inside a container or sandbox, and the author's own sandboxing tool is not yet released. The project is small (51 commits, 17 stars).
didnt: Rejected — its write path delegates to a full-permission, unsandboxed-by-default research agent, which conflicts with our approval-gated writes and safety posture, and it builds the shared/hosted wiki door whose go-ahead remains the owner's undecided decision (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: codeglance
good: A Python CLI that turns a repository into a visual map (interactive glance.html graph), a readable wiki.html, and compact agent context files (llms.txt, agent.md, knowledge-graph.toon), deterministically and offline by default with no Node, hosted service, or API key required. Its ask command answers repo questions with cited graph evidence, and its 'hippocampus' mode budgets context into short-term, working-set, long-term and recycle lanes for long agent sessions.
bad: Very early software: package version 0.0.4 with Development Status 'Beta' on PyPI. The README itself warns large repositories produce large self-contained HTML files, unknown extensions and very large files are skipped by the scanner, and Python is first-class while other languages get only tree-sitter symbol extraction.
didnt: Board — the deterministic, offline codebase-graph → llms.txt/agent.md context-brief pattern (with the hippocampus memory-budget lanes) for documenting code repositories, as a complement to our prose-wiki tooling (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: notionwiki
good: A one-way bridge that polls a Notion workspace, converts changed pages (detected by content_hash over the converted body, gated by last_edited_time) to markdown, and files them into the immutable raw/notion/ layer of an LLM wiki, with overwrite-plus-archive on re-pull, deletions detected by a periodic full reconciliation sweep and archived rather than hard-deleted, and a single-instance lock protecting state. It also generates the wiki index/graph from the agent-built layer independently of Notion.
bad: Intentionally one-directional — there is no write-back, push, or conflict resolution — and the README states raw-layer immutability is convention, not enforcement (agents are merely instructed not to edit raw/). It is tiny and young (4 stars, 30 commits, created 2026-07-08) and depends on a Notion token and the Notion API.
didnt: Board — the one-way feeder pattern (content-hash change detection, overwrite-plus-archive, full-sweep deletion detection) for any future external-source feeder, with the caveat that our raw layer needs enforcement rather than convention-only immutability (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-tools
good: Two strictly local CLIs (wiki-read, wiki-manage) implementing a three-tier updates/ → raw/ → wiki/ flow with no MCP server or remote backend: surgical block-level patching via STDIN (append/prepend/replace/delete), a schema/health lint (broken links, orphans, empty sections), automatic archival of successfully read updates into raw/, [REPLACEMENT] tagging when an update supersedes a raw file, and failed conversions left in updates/ rather than silently dropped. Pages are concept-oriented, aggregating many sources with inline source-slug citation markers.
bad: The README states updates/ → raw/ archival is automatic and irreversible with no backup, the wiki conventions (including provenance) are not enforced by the CLI but by an external agentic system, and provenance is only an inline slug marker — there is deliberately no YAML frontmatter or metadata, which is weaker than citation locking. The package (v0.4.1) is only the execution layer; the analyst/ingest-agent orchestration lives in a separate scaffolding repo built around Claude Code.
didnt: Corroboration — its three-tier staging, surgical patching, replacement tagging and never-silently-drop ingest discipline confirm our own ingest design; nothing is adopted because its slug-only provenance and no-frontmatter stance fall short of our citation locking (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-knowledge
good: A Python toolkit giving Claude Code or Codex persistent memory in an Obsidian vault: keyword search works with no server, semantic ranking is available locally via Ollama (bge-m3), and its hooks provide session recall, selective memory capture, vault protection and secret scanning — direct overwrites, edits and deletions of existing published notes require human approval. Maintenance tooling (garden commands, vault-organizer skill) maintains indexes, filenames and links and reports ambiguous cases.
bad: There is no file watcher, so notes must be reindexed manually or on a schedule to stay searchable, and vault organization requires the Obsidian CLI with specific Obsidian settings enabled. The guard system depends on an external tool (i-insist 0.4.0+), and despite 357 commits the project has 4 stars and no releases.
didnt: Corroboration — its vault-protection hooks, under which overwrites, edits and deletions of published notes require human approval (backed by secret scanning), confirm our approval-gated write design for the wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pieces
good: A desktop long-term-memory product that builds a living, chronological timeline of a user's work across the apps they already use, so they can search, filter and ask questions by time, topic, person or tool, and generate standup updates, morning briefs and meeting prep from that captured context in one click.
bad: Its capture model is continuous and on by default: the homepage states Pieces forms memories every 2 seconds from the currently focused application and from copy-and-paste activity, which is ambient surveillance-style capture rather than deliberate ingest. It is a closed product with no licence stated at the source and no plain-file, git-canonical custody of the memory it captures.
didnt: Rejected — its default continuous capture of everything on screen is the auto-discovery/session-capture model the owner has already rejected, and as a closed, no-licence product it offers no local-first, plain-markdown custody to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wiki (plasma-ai)
good: A Python CLI (plasma-wiki on PyPI) plus Claude Code/Codex plugin that keeps a wiki as plain markdown indexed at every level by _index.md files, where a deterministic CLI — not the agent — generates the indexes and cross-links, and a custom git merge driver auto-resolves merges in the generated region of _index.md. It adds ranked SQLite FTS5/BM25 search weighted toward titles, descriptions, headings and tags, a structured wiki lint (exit-code and --json output), and tool-owned frontmatter timestamps.
bad: Very young: created 2026-07-01, 106 stars and no releases yet. The README documents real fragility around formatters — mdformat/prettier-style hooks can mangle the load-bearing *** delimiter and wikilinks — and authored content below the index delimiter still merges (and can conflict) like any other text; custom .wiki/wiki.py hooks also execute with the user's privileges and need an explicit trust step.
didnt: Board — the deterministic index generation plus the custom git merge driver that auto-resolves the generated region of _index.md, as a candidate fix for index/log merge contention in our own wiki tooling (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: KnowledgeX
good: A personal knowledge library built as local OKF markdown bundles via MCP: the AI offers to save what is worth keeping and saves only what the user approves, answers cite which note was used, whether it was confirmed and whether it may be out of date, changed notes need re-confirming, and changed minds are handled by marking the old note replaced — never by silently editing a past decision. KnowledgeX itself never connects to the internet, and a check-up flow lists notes that are stale, conflicting or unconfirmed.
bad: The README flags it as early (v0.3, 'things may still change') and lists known gaps: evals have only been run against a small local model, search ranks within each notebook rather than across notebooks, and importing existing notes is not yet built. It also acknowledges a trust hole — a symlink inside a notebook can point outside it because the folder check compares paths as text, and anything that can write to the notes folder counts as the user.
didnt: Corroboration — its save-only-what-you-approve flow, confirmed/unconfirmed note status, per-note provenance and expiry, and non-destructive replacement chains confirm our approval-gated writes and claim-lifecycle design; no code adoption while it is at v0.3 with the stated gaps (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-llm-wiki
good: A containerised, git-backed MCP server exposing a Karpathy-style wiki as eight tools, with ETag optimistic concurrency on writes, custom merge-drivers for the two write-contended hotspots (log.md and index.md), a paranoid markdown sanitiser (stripping HTML comments, zero-width and bidi characters, raw HTML and data: images), realpath/symlink path safety, and a read-only lint that grades provenance drift (source_missing/source_drift, stating how many of a page's sources survive). Every write is an atomic commit-and-push, and ingest/query/lint ship as companion agent skills.
bad: Pre-1.0 by its own badge ('interfaces may still shift') and tiny: 13 commits and 3 stars. The server is deliberately schema-blind — it validates nothing about page structure, leaving all conventions to the consuming agent's skills — and its search is fixed-string (ripgrep) only, with no ranked or semantic retrieval.
didnt: Board — its ETag-guarded write path plus merge-drivers for index.md/log.md contention and graded source-drift lint, as design input for our wiki MCP door when the owner rules on that door (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ai-memory
good: A mature, heavily used Rust system (12,154 stars, 133 releases) giving coding agents long-term memory that follows them across 20+ harnesses, projects and machines: the source of truth is a git-backed markdown wiki with a rebuildable derived index, typed claim-once handoffs pass work between agent vendors, and memory ages without an LLM — per-tier decay, access-weighted retention, extractive compaction, dedup and contradiction flagging, all reversible (supersede-not-delete, restore-page) and off by default where they rewrite content. The default capture/search/handoff path uses zero LLM calls and every mutation is audit-logged.
bad: Its capture model is automatic and silent: lifecycle hooks record prompts, tool calls and session boundaries without the user asking it to remember anything, which is session-transcript capture. It is also scoped to coding work — its own comparison table notes it remembers 'this repo', not a general vault — native Windows support is only experimental, and team use means running and trusting a shared server.
didnt: Board — the typed, claim-once handoff protocol between agent vendors (owner plus exactly-once claiming) for our multi-agent team; the product itself is not adopted because its silent lifecycle capture of prompts and sessions is the session-transcript ingest the owner has rejected (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-skills (dexio-wiki)
good: A suite of 12 Agent Skills (setup, orient, capture, record, ingest, query, lint, verify, review, conflicts, refactor, shared) in the open Agent Skills format for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Hermes Agent and OpenClaw. Its wiki-lint skill ships a zero-dependency Python checker (3.8+) that reports broken links, credential-shaped strings (masked in output), orphans, frontmatter gaps, stale and duplicate pages, can rank a --verify-queue of pages most worth fact-checking, and exits 1 on a broken link or possible secret so it can gate a commit or CI job.
bad: Very young and unproven: the repo page shows 7 commits, 1 star and no releases. The skills are maintenance rules only — retrieval, hosting and multi-agent write coordination are delegated to the separate Dexio hosted wiki, and the README presents no evaluation of lint accuracy or skill behaviour.
didnt: Board — the checker's --verify-queue idea: rank wiki pages by how far an error on them would spread and fact-check those first, as a lint-prioritisation addition to our health checks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-manager (sametbrr)
good: Implements Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern as a Claude Code skill with 8 operating modes (bootstrap, ingest, query, update, lint, schema-evolve, multi-wiki routing, teach), 5 idempotent Python-stdlib scripts (init, append_log, update_index, lint, migrate), 8 page templates and 11 reference docs. Its Update mode propagates a superseding claim across paraphrased pages with a semantic sweep and diff-before-write per page under one log entry, and lint writes auto-dated reports (wiki/reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md) that accumulate as a longitudinal health record and exit 1 on block-severity issues for CI.
bad: Requires Claude Code or another agentskills.io-compatible agent plus Python 3.9+, so it is bound to that skill ecosystem. The README documents no scored abstention, citation locking or evaluation results — quality rests on the operating-mode instructions and the structural lint (orphans and index drift) alone.
didnt: Corroboration — idempotent bookkeeping scripts, an append-only greppable log, diff-before-write change propagation and auto-dated lint reports independently confirm our own wiki-manager design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-plugin (praneybehl)
good: Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern as a skill and Claude Code plugin (also installable for Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, OpenClaw, Pi and Hermes) with local-first hybrid retrieval: FastEmbed with the BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 model, sqlite-vec vectors and BM25 lexical fallback fused via RRF, plus a compiled graph layer (graph.sqlite) for relational questions. v3.2.0 adds /wiki:learn and /wiki:evolve — capturing verified experience and proposing whole-skill improvements through training, validation and independent final testing, with explicit apply/rollback and retained rejected attempts.
bad: Setup is heavy: uv plus a pinned runtime (FastEmbed 0.8.0, sqlite-vec 0.1.9, PyYAML) and a downloaded embedding model must install and verify before the wiki reports ready, and the nine slash commands are Claude Code-only (other agents use natural language). The README is candid that its own evolution study rejected both skill proposals — 'no quality improvement was demonstrated' — and claims no measured model gains.
didnt: Corroboration — local RRF hybrid retrieval over compiled Markdown, cited query answers filed back, and a validation-gated learn/evolve loop with rollback confirm our retrieval and maintenance design; its negative evolution result is a useful caution for our own skill-evolution ideas. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hstack
good: A Claude Code skill stack for using LLMs as healthcare advisors: four specialist skills (prepare-for-visit, understand-results, summarize-research, discuss-case) sharing a common preamble with a red/yellow/green escalation framework and safety protocols, dispatching clinical subagents for unbiased assessment before empathetic delivery. Its wiki skills build a personal disease wiki on Karpathy's pattern — wiki-init searches for real sources into raw/, ingest, refresh, lint, and a battle-plan skill that tiers actions from clinically validated to long-tail community wisdom — under source-first compilation and evidence-tier labelling.
bad: Deliberately narrow: it is a healthcare-advisor stack, not a general knowledge tool, and the README stresses it is not a doctor and cannot replace professional care. It is Claude Code-only, development requires bun, and its LLM quality checks need an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and cost roughly $0.10 per run.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a healthcare-domain specialist stack whose wiki skills duplicate our general ingest/lint machinery; its domain (personal disease wikis and clinical advice) is outside our knowledge-OS scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Engram Skill
good: A Claude Code plugin that turns scattered digital touchpoints — X bookmarks, ChatGPT and Claude.ai conversations, Claude Code sessions, browser bookmarks, GitHub stars, Kindle highlights, Notion pages and Granola meetings — into an interlinked Obsidian wiki: per-source sync adapters feed raw/items.jsonl, Claude derives 8–20 topics from the user's own material, and each cluster is synthesized into a page with TLDR, inline author attribution, direct quotes for high-engagement items, required counter-arguments on concept pages and wikilinks. Everything runs locally and incremental sync only regenerates changed batches.
bad: macOS/Linux only in v1 (Windows unsupported because of cookie decryption), and sync depends on extracting browser cookies for x.com, ChatGPT and Claude.ai — the README's troubleshooting documents Cloudflare blocks on ChatGPT sync, 429 rate limits, and breakage when X rotates its pinned GraphQL query ID. Bookmarks and conversations are also sent to Anthropic's API as synthesis context, which the Privacy section flags as a concern for private content.
didnt: Rejected — fit and method: it ingests chat-service session transcripts via browser-cookie scraping of internal APIs, a brittle route our system does not use (session-transcript ingest is unapproved), and its cluster-then-synthesize pipeline duplicates our compiler. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agent Knowledge (stjbrown)
good: A portable Agent Skills family for building project knowledge bundles in plain Markdown conforming to Open Knowledge Format v0.2: a kb hub skill holding the spec, glossary, trust model and templates, model-invoked kb-ingest/kb-document/kb-query skills, and user-invoked kb-init, kb-lint (deterministic OKF conformance checks plus a semantic drift audit for contradictions, stale claims, orphans and coverage gaps) and kb-visualize. OKF v0.2 adds structured provenance, producer identity, lifecycle/freshness signals and Attested Computation contracts; accumulated claims are append-only on meaning, and the repo documents itself as a conformant OKF bundle under knowledge/.
bad: It is bound to the young OKF v0.2 specification (repo created 2026-07-01) and its fallbacks for v0.1 bundles, so format churn is a live risk — the README already records a package split in which the former CLI package was withdrawn and the companion Janet agent moved to a separate install. The vendored OKF spec inside is Apache-2.0 (per NOTICE), separate from the repo's own MIT terms.
didnt: Corroboration — an explicit trust model with append-only claim meaning, structured provenance and lifecycle/freshness signals in an open Markdown format confirms our frontmatter and claim-lifecycle design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-agent (SamurAIGPT)
good: A widely starred (3,645) coding-agent skill that builds a self-maintaining personal wiki from sources dropped into raw/, working with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Gemini CLI with no API key: non-Markdown files (PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, EPUB, audio and more) are auto-converted via markitdown at ingest, entity and concept pages are auto-created and cross-referenced, contradictions are flagged at ingest time, and a living overview is revised on every ingest. Its two-pass graph build parses wikilinks deterministically, adds agent-inferred edges with confidence tags, applies Louvain community detection, and emits a self-contained graph.html with a SHA256 cache so only changed pages are reprocessed.
bad: Despite 115 commits the repo page shows 0 releases and 0 tags, and the root listing has no test suite — correctness rests on the schema files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/GEMINI.md) and agent behaviour. The semantic graph pass relies on agent-inferred relationships labelled only by confidence, with no verification step documented.
didnt: Corroboration — compile-once interlinked pages, ingest-time contradiction flags, a living overview and cached graph rebuilds confirm the core shape of our wiki; its scale of adoption is a useful popularity signal for the pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ThinkWiki
good: An agent-native local knowledge-base skill (Agent Skills format, for Claude Code, OpenClaw, Trae, Hermes and other skills hosts) that turns documents, web pages, notes and conversations into a Markdown workspace through conversation: captures land in an inbox review console grouped ready/review/weak before formal ingest, and it generates browsable HTML outputs — workspace home, local viewer, interactive graph explorer and a graph governance report. Its content knowledge graph goes beyond file links: page-backed nodes (source, topic, concept, decision, synthesis, query, entity) plus claim nodes with typed relations including supports and contradicts, and entity-merge governance surfaces alias collisions with a dry-run merge preview before any structural change.
bad: It requires a local environment with Python 3 and a shell-capable agent — the README states pure cloud chat without local file or shell access cannot run it. Content-generation and entity-embedding features are off unless the user supplies API keys, and the default embedding setup points at an external provider (SiliconFlow BGE-M3); the repo is young (23 commits).
didnt: Board — two interface ideas for our review surface: inbox staging tiers (ready/review/weak) for captured material awaiting ingest, and an entity-merge dry-run preview page before merges are applied. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VitaeContext
good: An agent context layer for career work: a Context Builder skill interviews the user and turns raw career material (CVs, profile sections, portfolio links, project notes) into a private, evidence-bounded Markdown Career Context file holding facts, goals, constraints, proof links and claims to avoid, while the VitaeGraph skill maintains deeper hierarchical records (projects, roles, degrees, certifications, publications) with typed cross-links and rebuildable indexes. A stateless MCP server (protocol 2024-11-05) serves both across agents, bounded summary packets tailor context per destination (e.g. --for cv, --for github), and the repo carries a groundedness evals directory.
bad: Scope is deliberately narrow — career context only, not a general knowledge base — and validation fails until the context file's placeholders are replaced, so the file must be built through its interview workflow before anything works. Downstream drafting/automation is explicitly out of scope: it is only the context layer before those tools.
didnt: Board — the 'claims to avoid' list inside an evidence-bounded context file: an explicit negative-claims section our own person/context pages could carry so agents know what not to assert. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: owledge
good: A Markdown-first persistent-memory and project-planning layer for AI agents and existing knowledge bases: durable local artifacts (plans, tasks, workpackages, evidence, reviews, handoffs, decisions) under .owledge/ with an OWLEDGE.md entrypoint, context packs that give the next agent explicit source files, decisions and next actions, a wikilink audit that checks valid/broken/ambiguous links without rewriting notes, and doctor/test-contracts/release-trust quality gates. Its lifecycle runs intent → project truth → scoped context → agent work → evidence and handoff → reviewed promotion, with a person remaining responsible for decisions and promotion; an optional benchmark kit reports token/context-pollution metrics on synthetic fixtures.
bad: The README's own V1 boundary excludes much infrastructure: no hosted Team Hub, no remote sync, no background scheduler, and its HTTP adapter is local, experimental and loopback-only. Its headline benchmark numbers (88.36% less context pollution, 83.54% fewer tokens per correct answer) come from a synthetic Markdown fixture, and the README cautions real-world savings vary and that the published runs do not use a personal vault.
didnt: Corroboration — evidence-linked handoffs, Markdown as canonical truth with generated views on top, and reviewed promotion with a person responsible confirm our approval-gated write and handover design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: project-wiki (giodra96)
good: An IDE-neutral agent skill giving codebases durable, traceable project memory in a .project-wiki/ directory beside the source: requirements, decisions (ADRs) and change requests carry permanent IDs (REQ-*, ADR-*, CR-*) with explicit bidirectional links to code paths, agents load context progressively from INDEX.md instead of flooding the context window, and deterministic governance runs structural validation and repairs before semantic linting for contradictions, stale meaning and risks. Its Knowledge Provenance Principle treats ingested raw documents as evidence, never canonical truth — information becomes canonical only when classified into official wiki records — and a .wikiignore scopes what a scan may see.
bad: Its scope is software-project memory, not personal knowledge: the wiki lives inside a code repository and its records are requirements/ADRs/technical state. It is very young (19 commits, created 2026-08-19), and its five modes (init, scan, update, sync, maintain) are invocation hints rather than a strict CLI, so behaviour depends on the host agent interpreting the skill.
didnt: Corroboration — permanent record IDs with bidirectional code traceability and the rule that intake is provenance, never unreviewed canonical truth, confirm our citation and compilation discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: okf-knowledge (sniperunder123)
good: A portable Claude Code skill (/okf) to create, read, maintain and visualize Open Knowledge Format bundles — one concept per Markdown file with YAML frontmatter, links as the graph, git as the versioning layer and no SDK, database or lock-in. Commands cover init, update (sync, fix links, append log, validate), index-first query, add, and viz (viz.html + graph.mmd); its validate.py enforces the three hard OKF conformance rules as a CI gate and, with --strict, producer lints, and OKF v0.2 fields add provenance (sources), verified-based trust tiers and stale_after freshness.
bad: The README disclaims itself prominently: 'this is vibe-coded', an unofficial indie project shipped as-is with zero guarantees, and the repo page shows only 2 commits and no releases. It is Claude Code-only, and its headline efficiency claim (a 2,762-line doc becoming 83 concepts, ~1.5k tokens per question) is a single anecdotal migration, not a benchmark.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and maturity: it covers the same OKF ground as stjbrown/agent-knowledge with a far thinner record (2 commits, self-described vibe-coded, zero guarantees), so the other OKF skill is the reference worth keeping. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wiki Builder (Hyperagent)
good: A Hyperagent-platform skill for starting, structuring, growing, querying and maintaining reusable research wikis: each wiki is a standalone folder governed by its own wiki.config.md (purpose, audience, page types, style rules), with seven flavors (research, paper, domain, product, person, organization, project), provenance preserved in sources.md, reusable prompt templates for compiling index/source/concept pages, query-and-file and linting, and a self-contained init_wiki.sh scaffolding script that needs no credentials. The page states it is a port of DAIR.AI's wiki-builder Claude Code plugin (v1.0.0, MIT-licensed) with the templates embedded as heredocs so it runs without an external templates directory.
bad: It is platform-bound: the page's runtime notes say wikis are created on the Hyperagent container filesystem and must live under /agent/workspace/ to remain available across turns in a thread, and delivery to the user means saving or zipping individual Markdown files out of that container. As a port, it adds no capability beyond the open DAIR.AI original it credits.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and platform lock-in: a hosted-platform port of the DAIR.AI wiki-builder plugin, tied to Hyperagent's container filesystem, where the MIT original is directly usable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wiki Builder (DAIR.AI)
good: A Claude Code plugin for starting, structuring, growing, querying and maintaining reusable research wikis, intentionally general rather than hard-coding one layout: it scaffolds a clean structure (wiki.config.md, raw/, wiki/, derived/, prompts/, logs/, sources.md) and defers to each wiki's local wiki.config.md for purpose, audience, page types, style rules and update workflow. Seven flavors ship out of the box (research, paper, domain, product, person, organization, project), provenance is preserved for every claim via sources.md, bundled prompts cover compile-index, compile-source-page, compile-concept-page, query-and-file and lint-wiki, and a manual init_wiki.sh scaffold is provided for use without Claude.
bad: It is a scaffolding-and-prompts plugin for Claude Code only: the page documents no retrieval or search engine, no deterministic linting (lint is a prompt template), and no evaluation — quality depends entirely on the agent following the prompts and the stated quality bar. The parent marketplace repo is small (19 commits, no releases).
didnt: Corroboration — a per-wiki config file governing compilation boundaries, raw/ separated from compiled pages, and provenance recorded in sources.md confirm our schema-file and source discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-skill (lewislulu)
licence: MIT (stated in the README License section; no LICENSE file in the repo root listing)
good: A Karpathy-style LLM knowledge-base Agent Skill for OpenClaw/Codex in which compile, ingest, query, lint and audit passes compound a cross-linked Markdown wiki the human steers through feedback rather than writing. Its distinctive piece is a human-in-the-loop audit loop: an Obsidian plugin and a local Node.js preview server (mermaid, KaTeX, wikilinks) both let the reader select text on a page and file a severity-tagged comment as an anchored Markdown file under audit/, written byte-identically by a shared TypeScript library, and audit_review.py groups open/resolved audits by target for the agent to process; the skill also ships scaffold.py and a 7-pass lint_wiki.py health check.
bad: The README labels it 'Experimental — will iterate over time', and the repo page shows 7 commits and no releases despite 656 stars. Using the audit loop's viewer or Obsidian plugin requires building the shared TypeScript library and the web app (npm install/build steps) rather than a single install, and the licence is asserted only in the README — there is no LICENSE file in the root listing.
didnt: Board — the anchored audit-comment file: reader feedback filed as small severity-tagged Markdown records anchored to page text, processed by the agent as a review queue, as a human-in-the-loop channel for our Lens. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: basemouse-core
good: Remote MCP server for shared, versioned agent memory: context packs (basemouse.context_pack.v1) carry citations, provenance, document versions, checksums, relevance and truncation state; writes are append-only revisions, DELETE is a tombstone, PUT supports expectedVersion/If-Match optimistic locking, and hybrid retrieval annotates each result per-signal.
bad: Very young repo (6 commits, 0 stars, v0.3) and its 'vector' signal is admittedly local hashed-feature token overlap, not a semantic model; durable mode needs a managed Postgres (DATABASE_URL), otherwise it runs an in-memory seed store.
didnt: Corroboration — cited, checksummed, versioned context packs with append-only revisions and tombstone deletes confirm our citation-locking and history-preserving design, without needing this implementation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 0CompactMem
good: Persistent agent memory modelled on OS virtual memory: demand paging, kswapd-style eviction, mlock-style pinning and CRIU-style session snapshots in a single SQLite file, MCP-native and shared across agents, claiming ~0.1 ms hot-path retrieval and 3,500+ tests.
bad: The repo has been renamed to vMem so the catalogue name no longer matches; it requires Python 3.12+ and Claude Code hooks, and its own roadmap still lists distributed vMem, adaptive watermarks and the arXiv evaluation preprint as future work.
didnt: Board — demand-paged working-set memory with pinning for never-evict constraints and capacity-aware eviction, as an idea for context-window management. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: seamless
good: Local-first shared memory and task coordination in one Go binary: durable knowledge is plain markdown files with YAML frontmatter under ~/.seamless (SQLite only indexes them), with supersession preserving provenance, hybrid recall, a dependency-aware task queue with lease-based claiming, and a gardener that only proposes curation while humans dispose.
bad: README states it is early days with frequent releases, and explicitly not a hosted team knowledge base or a RAG framework; scope is one owner's fleet of agents on that owner's machine, localhost only.
didnt: Corroboration — markdown files as source of truth, supersession with provenance, and propose-only curation with explicit human application confirm our local-first, approval-gated design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: robrain
good: Self-hosted decision memory on Postgres with passive capture and a structured rejected[] field on every decision, plus corpus-wide Synthesis passes for drift, contradictions and entity promotion; VetoBench reports 0/50 re-proposals of rejected approaches through its full pipeline versus Mem0 dropping the veto from 38% of retrieved contexts.
bad: Self-hosting needs Postgres plus LLM and embedding API keys (default Anthropic + OpenAI), and its own comparison table reserves calibrated extraction, task-boundary injection, the dashboard and team memory for the paid Rory Plans cloud; the repo has tags but 0 GitHub releases.
didnt: Board — the rejected[] first-class field and VetoBench-style measurement of re-proposed rejections, for our decisions record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agentpack
good: Repo-native task-state ledger in .agentpack/: a Task Passport holds goal, status, constraints, write scope, next actions and verification, with decisions, dead ends, evidence and checkpoints resumable by any MCP client; source conclusions carry file hashes so changed files are flagged, it is local-first with no telemetry or network calls and zero runtime dependencies.
bad: It deliberately covers only task state, not long-lived memory; the optional task gate only warns by default (blocking must be opted into), it requires Node.js >= 20, and the README notes its resumed context still consumes tokens.
didnt: Board — the reviewed Task Passport ledger with hash-bound source conclusions and explicit checkpoints, as a handoff format for multi-session work. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentRecall
good: Correction-first persistent memory (MCP server + SDK + CLI) in local markdown under ~/.agent-recall/: corrections become structured rules with severity, evidence, applies_when and retraction, a check tool can return verdict blocked before risky actions, and heeded-versus-recurred outcomes are measured per correction across five memory layers.
bad: The design is heavy — RRF, Ebbinghaus forgetting, FSRS-lite, salience and calibrated confidence with several constants self-labelled provisional and one open problem in the README — and the README's own Automaticity Law reports pull tools saw zero organic calls across 44 projects, so it depends on wired hooks.
didnt: Corroboration — a correction-first ledger that loads rules before acting and measures whether corrections actually stopped recurring confirms our corrections-as-primary-memory approach. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: facthouse
good: Local memory engine in a single owned SQLite file that consolidates agent activity through Data (session events) to Information (extracted facts) to Knowledge (integrated beliefs on an entity graph), linking entities, dropping duplicates, reconciling conflicts and superseding rather than deleting, with BM25 + graph + optional embedding hybrid search via RRF over MCP.
bad: Extraction is capped at 50 transcript lines per run, semantic search is off by default, and without the Claude Code CLI the fallback heuristic does not extract facts from transcripts at all; copy mode only reads Claude Code, Cursor or Grok Build logs and Cursor cannot load its MCP resources.
didnt: Corroboration — the Data-to-Information-to-Knowledge consolidation pipeline with immutable, superseded-only history confirms our raw-to-compiled ingest layering. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alcove
good: Rust MCP/HTTP server giving coding agents on-demand access to private project docs kept out of public repos: BM25 + vector hybrid search, tree-sitter code indexing across 12 languages, CWD project auto-detection, global cross-project search, and policy enforcement with validate and lint for missing, stale or orphaned docs.
bad: Pre-built Windows binaries are not published (source build only), nothing is searchable until a required alcove setup run, and building from source needs the full-macos/full-cross feature flags for hybrid search — without them only BM25 is available; scope is coding-project docs, not a general knowledge store.
didnt: Rejected — duplication: its on-demand BM25 retrieval over private local documents overlaps retrieval our wiki already has, and its coding-project doc layer does not fit our general knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Myco (Battam1111)
good: Cross-session agent memory substrate that ingests material as immutable history, prunes stale parts with tombstones, carries tamper-evident causal history and a hash-chain-sealed doctrine, and persists across model generations via MCP with TypeScript operator, Rust substrate and Python kernel in one repo.
bad: Self-described v0.9-genesis alpha that 'awaits its first real cultivation'; the README is metaphor-led (living armour, devour/evolve) with no retrieval evaluation or concrete graph-from-AST/markdown detail on the page, and getting started requires Rust 1.80+, Node 22+ and Python 3.13+ together.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and fit: an alpha, three-language self-evolving substrate whose sealed-doctrine scope goes well beyond our citation-locked wiki and is not yet proven in real use. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memory-arbiter-mcp
good: Local SQLite MCP memory layer where every tool reads the same verified facts: full original text is the source of truth with derived indexes, provenance on every write, trust levels that lock user_confirmed memories against silent edits, full version history with supersede chains, one immutable conflict record per event with a judge that proposes no winner, and governance actions requiring per-action user authorization; LoCoMo-Refined reports 61.00% overall with a writer-agent.
bad: Setup is demanding: the server refuses to start without an explicitly configured client/agent identity, setup downloads a ~330 MB embedding GGUF and the mDeBERTa conflict judge is a separate manual install, and in HTTP mode caller headers are stated to be advisory provenance, not authentication or multi-tenant isolation.
didnt: Corroboration — authorized governance, locked user-confirmed facts, conflict records that never auto-pick a winner, and relevance-floor abstention in recall confirm our approval-gated, scored-abstention design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gingugu
good: Local MCP memory server in one SQLite file with typed memories, namespaces, a typed relationship graph (supersedes, contradicts, caused_by), a verified-to-deprecated confidence lifecycle, and hybrid FTS5 BM25 + local embedding retrieval fused with RRF (in-repo bench: MRR 0.828, recall@5 0.983) plus a keychain credential vault and 21 tools.
bad: README states it is still early, an early cognitive-runtime framework rather than a finished product, not yet benchmarked at 100k+ memory scale, and its retrieval numbers come from 30 labelled questions against the author's own ~1,100-memory store, not a public benchmark.
didnt: Corroboration — typed memories with a confidence lifecycle, staleness flags the server never auto-mutates, and hybrid local retrieval confirm patterns already present in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GistPad-MCP
good: Mature MCP server (208 stars) for managing personal knowledge, daily notes and reusable prompts stored as GitHub Gists, with full gist/file/comment CRUD, gist:/// resources with update notifications, and optional daily-notes, starred, archived and prompts tool sets kept off by default.
bad: All notes live in GitHub Gists in the cloud, requiring a GitHub personal access token with gist scope, which breaks local-first custody; the server caches the gist list and only refreshes hourly or on its own writes, so external edits can be stale.
didnt: Rejected — fit: gist-backed cloud custody contradicts our local-first custody of the wiki, however clean the MCP notes surface is. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: contextforge
good: Persistent-memory MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor and Copilot with semantic search, project-based organisation, Git commit/PR sync, task tracking and team collaboration across 69 tools, plus compaction-survival hooks that re-inject the session objective and relevant memories after Claude Code compacts.
bad: Use requires signing up at contextforge.dev and an API key for the hosted service (free tier), so memory is not local-first; the tool surface is large (69 tools, only 11 shown by default) and the repo is small (2 stars, 84 commits).
didnt: Rejected — fit: a hosted, API-key memory service contradicts local-first custody, and its knowledge tools duplicate what our wiki already does. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DecisionNode
good: Local CLI + MCP store recording development decisions as structured JSON (scope, decision, status, rationale, constraints) in ~/.decisionnode/, shared across Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf and other MCP clients, with semantic search, 75%-similarity conflict detection before saving, deprecate/activate soft deletes, global decisions, and a full audit history naming the tool that made each change.
bad: Semantic search depends on a Gemini API key and Gemini embeddings stored in a local vectors.json file, retrieval is explicit-only with nothing pre-injected, and the project is small (42 commits).
didnt: Board — structured decision records with constraints, write-time conflict detection and tool-attributed audit history, for our decision pages, noting the Gemini embedding dependency would need replacing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: doc-manager
good: Zero-knowledge document vault on Azure Blob Storage in one Rust binary with a Streamable-HTTP MCP server: documents are encrypted in the browser with AES-256-GCM (PBKDF2-SHA256, 600k iterations), plaintext docs can be listed, fetched, searched, created and updated from Claude, access is OAuth 2.1 gated by a required GitHub allowlist, and an MCP_READ_ONLY mode hides write tools.
bad: It requires an Azure Storage account and access key, search is only case-insensitive substring over titles and plaintext content, and encrypted documents are deliberately opaque — their contents and writes are refused server-side, so the agent cannot read the private half of the vault; single small project (1 star).
didnt: Rejected — fit: an Azure-hosted cloud vault with substring-only search and agent-opaque encrypted docs does not serve our local-first, citation-searchable wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OKF Harness (pumblus)
good: Byte-level citation verification: okfh evidence checks whether each citation really lands on the bytes of a registered source; bounded evidence briefs and bounded reads by default; the graph report is emitted as a local HTML file; explicitly agent-first, local-first and terminal-native (217 commits, 16 releases, created 2026-06) — the closest external match in this batch to our citation-locking discipline.
