bad: The harness checks citation placement, not claim correctness, and does not require every sentence to be cited, so unsupported prose passes; first use of each pinned runtime is fetched from npm, so it is local-first but not air-gapped; requires Node.js 22+; the README explicitly scopes out GUI, cloud sync, Obsidian helpers, source connectors and vector retrieval (roadmap only), so it is a verification shell, not a full wiki system.
didnt: Board — its byte-landing citation check and bounded-read discipline are the pattern to mirror in our own evidence/lint gates; no code adopted in this pass. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: okf-gem
good: Mature Ruby implementation of the Open Knowledge Format bundle ecosystem (397 commits, 180 stars): okf validate and okf lint return exit codes so format drift fails CI; okf index/search support progressive disclosure; OKF v0.2 frontmatter carries provenance and trust tiers (unverified, machine-confirmed, human-reviewed) via generated/verified/sources/status/stale_after fields; ships four gems, a Docker image and a Claude Code plugin; installs on Ruby 2.4+ with three small dependencies.
bad: Ruby-only in a Python/TypeScript estate; the trust-tier frontmatter is richer than our current page metadata and would need an explicit mapping decision; companion pieces (okf mcp with 14 read tools, okf tui, okf pro) install separately, so the full surface is fragmented across packages.
didnt: Board — the OKF v0.2 trust-tier frontmatter and CI-failing lint are worth mirroring when our own OKF conformance export is next revised; the Ruby runtime keeps the code itself off the adopt path. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: engram CLI
good: Minimal, honest design: the mnemo_wiki CLI (init/validate/lint/status/search/links/BM25) never calls a language model itself — all writing is done by a Claude Code agent following the wiki's CLAUDE.md — over the same three layers we use (immutable sources/, wiki/, schema file), with relative Markdown links only.
bad: Tiny and young (21 stars, 32 commits); without Claude Code only the checking commands work, so the compiler half is not portable to other agents; relative-links-only rules out wikilink-based tooling; no provenance or citation-verification machinery beyond lint; requires Node.js 18+.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent implementation of our exact three-layer, agent-writes/CLI-checks split; nothing in it exceeds what we already run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cartographer
good: The strongest write governance in this batch: a shared git-backed team wiki accessed only through MCP tools, with schema validation, link checks, lint, immutability gates, optimistic concurrency, one commit per write and a signed audit log, in a single Go binary with a read-only Atlas web UI in the same binary; secrets handled via SOPS encryption (547 commits, 43 releases).
bad: Explicitly pre-1.0 — breaking changes bump the minor version — and the README calls it a personal project maintained on a best-effort basis; requires git plus an empty git repository per knowledge base; its multi-user team model is heavier than our single-owner custody model.
didnt: Board — the signed audit log, optimistic-concurrency and one-commit-per-write gates are the reference design if our MCP door ever grows a write path; not adopted while the door stays read-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: quarry-kb
good: Implements exactly our deterministic/generative split: the config-driven harness owns fetch, immutable raw storage and the compile-manifest, then stops — it never calls a model — so it runs and tests with no API keys; the separate finish step verifies provenance, lints, then commits (push only with --push); adapters cover YouTube, web, GitHub, PDF and Instagram; self-described as feature-complete for v1 and fully tested; requires Python 3.11+.
bad: Pre-1.0; the Reddit adapter was removed in 0.4.0 as fragile/blocked, showing adapter maintenance is a live cost; the generative article-writing step between ingest and finish is entirely on the operator or agent, so it is a harness, not a compiler.
didnt: Board — its ingest/finish provenance gate is a clean external statement of our own two-phase ingest rule; worth re-checking at its 1.0, no code taken now. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Oh My Wiki
good: Two-surface design matching our governance split: a deterministic omw CLI (setup, vault create, lint, schema, supersede, review, links, fields, view, doctor — no LLM anywhere) plus an omw skill whose personas (librarian, auditor, curator, fact-checker, consistency-checker, terminology-manager) propose while the human confirms and deterministic ops execute; 13 built-in page schemas, confidence frontmatter, explicit supersede, and a spaced-repetition review queue (omw review due/done) — the closest match in the batch to a Socratic review wizard; FTS5 search with optional local embeddings; public/private visibility with serve exposing only public pages; next-step suggestions never auto-run (809 commits).
bad: Very small audience (8 stars) for its commit count; the review queue assumes the owner will work a spaced-repetition habit, a real ongoing time commitment; dual CLI-plus-skill packaging means two surfaces to keep in sync.
didnt: Board — the propose-confirm-execute persona split and the supersede/review-queue mechanics are the strongest governance patterns in this batch and candidates for our claim-lifecycle work; not adopted in this pass. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Open Knowledge CLI (ok)
good: Full OKF bundle lifecycle in one Go CLI (setup, check, search/view, review, publish/upgrade; 565 commits, 21 releases): check combines validation, link, freshness, retrieval, claims and publication checks over repository Markdown, and publish refuses unmanaged or blocked input, with published Markdown public unless okf_publish is set false.
bad: Anonymous usage and error telemetry is enabled by default (opt-out via --no-telemetry) — the wrong default for a private personal wiki; the publish-to-public orientation fits open OKF bundles, not local-first custody; the Go installers (okn and openknowledge binaries) are another toolchain to carry.
didnt: Board — its combined check (validation plus freshness plus claims plus publication) is a good model for a single health gate, but default-on telemetry and the public-publish orientation keep it off our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Synto
good: Local-first vault compiler (successor to obsidian-llm-wiki-local; 263 stars, 132 commits) with the batch's best hand-edit protection: a SHA-256 content hash per article means manual edits are never overwritten; incremental compiles recompile only articles tied to a changed note; local by default via Ollama with cloud providers optional; confidence scores, a draft to verified to published lifecycle, a rejection-feedback loop (five rejections auto-block a concept), pack export for agents, and an MCP server with 12 tools including verbatim source access.
bad: Documented state hazards: synto concept keep writes the state DB directly, is not auto-committed and cannot be reversed with synto undo, and git revert does not restore .synto/state.db because it is gitignored — state can silently diverge from the git record; article writing expects a 14B+ heavy model, so compile quality is hardware-bound.
didnt: Board — SHA-256 hand-edit protection is the single most adoptable mechanism in this batch for protecting owner-edited pages, with the state-DB divergence hazard as the caution that comes with it; no code taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agent-wiki-cli
good: Builds and maintains an architectural wiki for a codebase — structure extracted from source, prose added by agents — with bounded, searchable context for agents, a read-only MCP server, and per-agent instruction files for Claude, Aider, OpenCode, Copilot, Cursor and generic agents (754 commits); inputs cover Python (stdlib ast), TypeScript/JS, Go, Rust and Haskell.
bad: Very small adoption (2 stars); non-Python inputs need prepared helper binaries and toolchains (Node/npm, Go, Cargo, GHC), so the multi-language surface is setup-heavy; the README's security model treats project plugins as trusted Python code; the project states it does not maintain a formal contribution process; its domain is codebases, not personal knowledge.
didnt: Corroboration — its read-only MCP plus per-agent instruction files mirror our own door design; codebase-wiki scope does not transfer to the personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Quant_LLM_Wiki
good: A domain LLM wiki done end-to-end for quantitative research: a single qlw CLI with nine subcommands (ingest, enrich, embed, sync, ask, brainstorm, agent, lint, compile), a documented pipx install path, and an unusually candid README stating plainly that the tool generates investment strategy ideas, does not produce trade-ready strategies or financial advice, and is used at the reader's own risk.
bad: Single-domain (quant research) with no transfer to a general personal wiki; the pipx flow needs a one-time manual fetch of the schema/ directory into the workspace for full compile/lint quality — an install seam the clone flow hides; evidence in this pass is the search-rendered PyPI page only, the weakest verification level in the batch.
didnt: Corroboration — a worked example of the pattern applied to one research domain, including an honest risk disclaimer worth imitating on generated research pages; nothing to adopt for the general wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki OKF harness (dotdrelle)
licence: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 (custom/noncommercial; GitHub reports Other/NOASSERTION; separate COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md)
good: The deepest provenance machinery in the batch: under the TAXO ingest contract the engine — never the model — anchors each fiche to the exact archived line range with a SHA-256 anchor, with idempotent per-section input/content hashes and stable/verified pages never rewritten; a per-deliverable provenance page reads a build's frozen evidence down to the exact archived passage; agent curation runs on a git branch per objective and nothing reaches the wiki unless a human merges the proposal; wiki doctor migrates older pages to OKF v0.2; local-first with the workspace on disk as source of truth (575 commits).
bad: Licence is PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 with separate commercial terms — source-available, not open source; the README scope note limits it to a single-user deployment baseline and warns against exposing runtime write access as a shared multi-user surface; the generated .wikirc.yaml keeps provider API keys directly in the config file; a heavy system (manager, agents, runtimes) with only 3 stars of external validation; requires Node.js 22+.
didnt: Rejected — the PolyForm Noncommercial licence bars adoption of the code for our purposes; the engine-anchored citation ranges and human-merge proposal queue are noted as ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-claude-skills (vanillaflava)
good: Six agent skills (config, ingest, query, lint, integrate, crystallize) that build and maintain a local markdown wiki following the agentskills.io standard, working across Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and GitHub Copilot. Adds a source-tracing convention the base pattern lacks: a `source:` frontmatter field per page, an agent-assessed `reliability:` rating, and a `## Pending Review` section flagging claims from a single low-confidence source; /crystallize files durable session signal back into the wiki as a first-class operation.
bad: The author states plainly it is a personal implementation, 'not a product', with no backend, API or sync, and that the skills are structured instructions to a language model, 'not code' and 'not infallible' — quality depends entirely on the host agent and the sources fed in. Claude Desktop use needs a separate filesystem MCP, and Claude.ai web/mobile is 'not recommended for primary use'.
didnt: Board — the `## Pending Review` section written onto pages built from a single low-confidence source, paired with a `reliability:` frontmatter field, as a visible per-page review queue (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Research Wiki Skill (NousResearch hermes-agent)
good: Hermes is a self-improving agent whose built-in learning loop creates skills from experience, improves them during use, keeps agent-curated memory with periodic persistence nudges, and offers FTS5 session search with LLM summarisation for cross-session recall; its research-wiki capability ships as one of the bundled skills in the repo's skills system, and the agent runs on seven terminal backends plus Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp/Signal gateways with any model provider.
bad: The research-wiki skill is a minor built-in inside a very large general-purpose agent (57,484 commits, 42 releases at open); the README never documents the wiki skill itself, so taking it means taking the whole agent, its gateway and its autonomous self-modifying skill loop. No approval-gated write model or citation-locking discipline is described at the source.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: a whole self-improving agent platform, not a wiki component; our agent stack already covers its role and its autonomous skill self-modification runs against our approval-gated writes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Nous Research

name: Obsidian Second Brain (eugeniughelbur)
good: A mature, widely used skill (4,844 stars, 596 commits): 48 commands giving Claude Code, Codex and six other CLI agents persistent memory as plain markdown in an Obsidian vault, extending Karpathy's pattern so new sources rewrite existing pages instead of only appending, with four scheduled agents (morning brief, nightly consolidation, weekly review, vault-health), an OKM layer where every fact is timeless, dated or a pointer, and Crew — one shared logbook so several agents see what each other did, where a lesson becomes a rule only when a human runs `keep`.
bad: Its headline mechanism contradicts our governance: /obsidian-reconcile resolves contradictions automatically and pages are AI-first ('for LLM retrieval, not human review'), where our system flags conflicts for the owner and never auto-resolves. Research commands route through external services (Perplexity Sonar Pro, Grok live X access), so vault content leaves the local-first boundary by design.
didnt: Board — Crew's shared multi-agent logbook in a plain folder, with agent lessons becoming rules only on a human `keep`, as a model for cross-agent handoff state (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: second-brain-skill (ChavesLiu)
licence: MIT (stated in the README License section; no LICENSE file appears in the root listing)
good: Packages the Karpathy pattern as a single Claude Code skill with a clean three-layer split (raw/ you write, wiki/ the LLM writes, the Skill as co-evolving spec) and six commands — /wiki init, ingest, query, lint, wipe (with a recoverable trash), test — all also triggerable in natural language; one ingest can create or update 10–15 pages with summaries, entity/concept splits and cross-references maintained automatically.
bad: Very early and thin: 6 commits, no releases, a single skills/wiki directory, and documentation centred on the Chinese README with the English version secondary. It offers no citation locking, abstention scoring or write-approval mechanism beyond the base pattern, so it adds nothing over an existing ingest/query/lint loop.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and maturity: a 6-commit single-skill restatement of the ingest/query/lint loop our wiki already runs, with no mechanism we lack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hippocampus
good: A deliberately lite, zero-dependency OKF-adjacent template: inbox originals preserved untouched in inbox/_done with the archive path recorded on every source page, a deterministic stdlib-Python linter (dead wikilinks, orphans, duplicate names, alias collisions, frontmatter gaps, index drift) that costs no tokens, contradiction callouts placed on both conflicting pages with nothing silently overwritten, and a hot.md ≤500-word session cache auto-injected at session start for cheap 3-step retrieval (hot cache → master index → 3–5 pages).
bad: Deliberately minimal by design: no vector DB, embeddings, BM25 or MCP, batch ingests run strictly one source at a time, and retrieval rests entirely on the index staying current. It is a young, small template (12 commits, 29 stars, single author) with no evaluation or scale evidence at the source.
didnt: Corroboration — independently confirms three of our load-bearing choices: a deterministic non-LLM linter, contradiction flagging on both sides with no silent overwrite, and index-first retrieval backed by a small hot cache (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-context-base
good: A git template implementing the Karpathy pattern with three additions: a human-in-the-loop training period (the system starts chatty for ~30 days, learning the owner's patterns and logging what it learns, and is quiet by day 45, so no taxonomy is designed upfront), a metadata standard on every file (type, summary, tags, status, date) so the agent scans headers instead of loading full files, and a lint system surfacing stale files, missing metadata and orphaned docs — plus inbox-first capture with a 7-day TTL and bootstrap shims for Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and Windsurf.
bad: Scale claims are modest — the metadata approach 'scales cleanly to hundreds of documents' — and the plain template route deliberately disconnects the copy from upstream improvements (a separate Framework Track setup is needed to keep receiving them). The README documents no citation verification, abstention or write-approval gate.
didnt: Board — the 30-day training phase in which the agent starts deliberately chatty, logs the owner's patterns as it learns them, and quiets down by day 45, as an onboarding shape for a new wiki owner (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-knowledge-base
good: Formalises the pattern into a versioned AGENTS.md schema (v1.1.0) and adds a learning layer no other template here has: flashcards auto-generated whenever a concept article changes, a review queue scheduled by a simplified FSRS spaced-repetition algorithm, gap tracking that turns open questions found in linting into a research agenda, and Socratic Q&A graded against the wiki rather than general knowledge. Its contamination model is explicit: the agent writes freely to output/ and learning/, promotion to wiki/ requires explicit instruction or passing the schema's quality rules, a human-only insights/ directory is never touched, and contradictory articles are quarantined by status flag.
bad: Tiny and unproven: 3 commits, no releases, single author, and the FSRS implementation is described as 'simplified' with no evaluation of scheduling quality at the source. Its own comparison table concedes the compiled-wiki sweet spot is 50–2,000 articles and RAG wins at scale.
didnt: Board — the learning layer: an FSRS review queue over wiki concepts plus gap tracking that converts lint-detected open questions into a research agenda, as an owner-facing mastery layer our wiki lacks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cerebro
good: An installable kit (Claude skill or plain templates for Codex/Cursor/Gemini CLI, plus a query-only ChatGPT prompt) that turns books and PDFs into a maintained wiki: a normative BLUEPRINT.md instead of an abstract description, per-page confidence levels distinguishing 'both sources agree' from 'one author's opinion', explicit contradiction handling, anti-hallucination query rules that answer 'no coverage' instead of inventing, an idea-validation output format (Supports / Contradicts / Not covered / Verdict), and a markitdown wrapper that converts sources to markdown once and prints the token saving. Ships a complete worked example brain built from two public-domain books.
bad: Very young and small: 10 commits, 5 stars, single author, created July 2026, with no tests, evaluation or scale evidence at the source; the ChatGPT route is query-only because pages must be uploaded manually. Beyond confidence labels and the validation format it is the standard ingest/query/lint pattern.
didnt: Board — the idea-validation answer format (Supports / Contradicts / Not covered / Verdict) with per-page confidence levels, as a fixed shape for 'validate this idea against the wiki' queries (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: copilot-llm-wiki
good: The most mechanically complete starter in this batch, zero-dependency Python stdlib throughout: a file-based semantic index for sub-cent query routing, a directed property graph (graph.json) with a closed relation taxonomy including `supersedes` and `contradicts`, per-source volatility classes (30/90/365-day) the linter checks against Last Verified timestamps, a 3-way delta reingest engine with reference-counted attribution — an assertion dropped by one source but backed by another stays cited, and an unbacked one moves to a Deprecated / Historical Claims section instead of being silently erased — plus git-tag semantic snapshots with rollback and a strict deterministic linter covering claim-provenance footnotes.
bad: Small and single-author (36 commits, 18 stars, no releases) with large self-descriptions ('production-grade') and no independent evaluation at the source; despite the name it is really a multi-agent template (Copilot, Claude Code, Gemini, Cursor adapters kept in sync by a drift engine), so the Copilot orientation is a packaging choice rather than a distinct capability.
didnt: Board — volatility classes with per-class freshness cycles, and reference-counted delta reingest that retires unbacked claims to a Deprecated section instead of deleting them (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki template (Bashir Aziz)
licence: MIT (stated in the README License section; GitHub's licence detector reports NOASSERTION)
good: A reusable template whose distinctive third layer is sessions/: agent session transcripts auto-exported via Claude Code hooks (PreCompact + SessionEnd + SessionStart), indexed locally in SQLite FTS5 and searchable across every wired project repo, with adapters for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Aider, worked domain examples (research, personal, business, government contracting), and a three-layer confidentiality model — skip-export flag, .exportignore exclusions, and GPG-encrypted confidential session archives.
bad: The README's own tool table shows the full experience exists only on Claude Code: Codex gets a manual export step and Cursor/Aider are manual entirely, and Windows has documented hook failures needing workarounds. At 15 commits with no releases it is a small single-author template, and its transcript layer is exactly the kind of capture that needs an explicit owner decision before use.
didnt: Rejected — its distinguishing layer is automatic session-transcript ingest, which our owner has not approved in any form; the remaining two layers duplicate our existing raw/wiki/schema structure (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-karpathy (balukosuri)
good: A minimal ready-to-clone starter for the Karpathy pattern aimed at technical writers: Karpathy's original llm-wiki.md idea document, a CLAUDE.md schema tailored for technical writing, pre-configured Obsidian vault settings (graph view, hotkeys, sidebar), and a wiki/ folder seeded with index, log, overview and glossary starter pages. The documented ingest flow discusses takeaways with the user, then creates source, feature, product, persona and concept pages (a single source touches 5–15 pages), and lint checks contradictions, stale claims, orphans and terminology.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source — the root listing has no LICENSE file and the README names none — so nothing in it is copyable. It is also a thin scaffold: 4 commits, no releases, no scripts or linter of its own (every operation is a manual prompt to Cursor or another agent), and the schema is pre-tailored to technical-writing page types.
didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at the source makes it ideas-only, and as a bare scaffold it contains nothing our wiki lacks; it duplicates the starter shape we already run (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-nocode
good: A zero-code implementation with dual configuration for Claude Code (.claude/) and GitHub Copilot (.github/) driven by three natural-language commands (ingest, query, lint), built around a human-gated compounding loop: generated answers wait in questions_pending/ and lint reports in lint_pending/, and only what the human moves to the approved folders is integrated into the wiki. Queries are retrieval-only — reads 3–8 pages, cites every claim with wikilinks, never uses external knowledge — and lint runs in two phases, deterministic (broken links, orphans, missing frontmatter) then semantic (contradictions, stale claims).
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source — there is no LICENSE file in the root listing — so nothing in it is copyable. It is also tiny and new (4 commits, 9 stars, no releases), and by its author's own account it has no vector or semantic search, no built-in web ingestion, and multi-user collaboration is deferred in favour of a single human curator.
didnt: Corroboration — its pending → approved folder flow for both answers and lint fixes independently confirms our approval-gated write design; with no licence stated at the source it is ideas-only in any case (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Omnia Vault
licence: MIT (README badge; GitHub's licence detector reports NOASSERTION)
good: An all-in-one clonable project brain: an Obsidian LLM wiki plus Graphify code graphs, 22 vendored skills and 16 slash commands, and a 'war-room' living plan — /intel triages every new video or meeting against the locked roadmap (plan digest loaded before watching a frame), ranking items by phase fit / impact / effort / confidence into ADOPT · TRIAL · WATCH · SKIP with one honest verdict (INCORPORATE, WATCHLIST or PASS) and a logged brief so the same item is never re-litigated; adopted items land in phase files with provenance and phases rebalance only when argued and approved. Answers route through the cheapest layer that can answer (code graph → wiki catalog → one raw file), claims trace to sources, a pre-commit maintenance gate runs doctor → build → lint → source-lint → audit, and a relay baton (_relay/STATE.md) hands work between Claude Code and Codex with a stale-baton detector.
bad: Brand new and unproven (7 commits, created August 2026, no releases) and deliberately maximal — wiki, code graphs, video ingest with Whisper and keyframes, sparring and a five-seat council — so most of the surface is far beyond a personal wiki's needs. The licence is ambiguous at the source: the README badge claims MIT while GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION, so code reuse would need the LICENSE file verified first.
took: Triage verdicts — built in Round 3, lane TB4/TB5 (compound bullet) — source/inspiration: omnia (as recorded)
didnt: Corroboration — its plan-first intel triage with ADOPT · TRIAL · WATCH · SKIP verdicts is the recorded inspiration for our own triage verdicts, and its cheapest-layer-first answer routing confirms our index-first discipline; licence ambiguity at the source keeps it inspiration-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: second-brain-template
good: A self-filing Obsidian vault whose capture layer is a Telegram bot: plain-language messages ('ate paneer bhurji and 2 rotis', 'spent 12.50 on lunch', a photo of a plate or receipt) are parsed by Claude into typed markdown trackers with fixed headers that the bot, Dataview and Claude Code all parse identically, while /ingest, /query and /lint commands compile captures into a cross-linked wiki with [[citations]]. It adds life-tracking the wiki pattern usually lacks — habits, food, money, spaced-repetition vocabulary, reminders, scheduled morning/evening digests — with git committing per capture and everything degrading gracefully without an API key.
bad: Scope is a personal life-tracker, not a knowledge system: Mandarin learning, Oura sleep, Goodreads, chess ratings and bank feeds dominate, and running it means handing a Telegram bot plus Anthropic, Oura, calendar and optional bank tokens continuous access. It is also embryonic — 3 commits, 5 stars, created September 2026, no releases.
didnt: Rejected — scope and maturity: a 3-commit personal life-tracking bot (food, habits, language drills) rather than a knowledge wiki; its capture surface and credential spread do not fit our local-first, approval-gated custody (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PM Wiki
licence: MIT (stated in the README; GitHub's licence detector reports NOASSERTION)
good: The Karpathy pattern specialised for product management with a deliberately minimal four-entity model: problem pages carrying an evidence chain and mention counts with emerging → confirmed → addressed status, decision pages that are never deleted and record options with the evidence for each plus explicit reversal conditions, an assumption register whose status (untested / validated / weakening / invalidated) flips are dated and tied to the source that caused them, and an open-questions queue tagged by resolution path that generates interview scripts. Ingest has a real write gate — the agent proposes assumption or decision changes and the human approves or corrects — and deliverables (PRDs, briefs, 'why did we decide X?') are generated from source-cited evidence, with a complete worked FitLoop pilot included.
bad: A single-commit repository (1 commit, no releases) created July 2026, so the 'battle-tested' schema claim rests on the author's word and one bundled pilot. The entity model is PM-specific by design, and the README itself names the real cost as ~30 minutes a week of human discipline feeding it and running the weekly lint.
didnt: Board — the assumption register with dated, source-attributed status flips, and decision pages carrying explicit reversal conditions that lint checks for triggers (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agentic Memory Index (Verging Labs)
good: Independent benchmark that runs 12 agent-memory systems (Cognee, Karpathy Wiki, Mem0, Mnemosyne, Hindsight, Mitosis Cortex, gbrain, Supermemory, Hyperspell, Membase, Stash, Honcho) through the same simulated-work workload and publishes a single comparable leaderboard of index score, cost per 1,000 questions and lookups per answer, plus failure-attribution categories, long-term retention probed at five checkpoints across 56 working sessions, and onboarding / time-to-ready / time-to-store speed tables. Cognee and a plain Markdown Karpathy Wiki tie for first at 97.1.
bad: The homepage publishes summary scores only: no licence, code or downloadable harness is shown on the page, so the runs cannot be re-derived from the source opened. Coverage is uneven — the Karpathy Wiki row's onboarding, time-to-ready and time-to-store cells are all 'not measured' — and the index is a single v0.2 (Sep 2026) snapshot.
didnt: Corroboration — a plain folder of Markdown notes run as the Karpathy Wiki tying for first place (97.1) against eleven dedicated memory products confirms our compiled-wiki-as-memory design choice over a specialised memory store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: okf-model-bakeoff
licence: Apache-2.0 for the code and for the fixtures written for the benchmark; the corpus is mixed (US Government public-domain works, Wikipedia articles under CC BY-SA 4.0, arXiv papers under other licences)
good: A reproducible model-choice benchmark for OKF / LLM-wiki generation: 14 models run over the same 16 public documents with hand-authored gold ground truth, scored by one cross-vendor judge, with costs taken from a per-call ledger rather than a rate card. Every published number is regenerated from committed scorecards, and a verifier script recomputes all of them — including figures inside sentences — and exits non-zero if any cannot be recomputed. Its headline finding is that six of fourteen arms sit within 0.06 of each other across a 43.9x price range, and it insists on reading the per-document gate column rather than the mean.
bad: The README's own caveats are substantial: the judge has never been calibrated against a human yet carries 50% of the rubric weight and no kappa has been computed, so judged criteria are marked not citable by the project's own gate; the leaderboard is one trial per document; the corpus is only 16 documents / 146,041 source tokens, smaller than the enterprise documents the pattern targets; and one arm (a10-deepseek) has no measurement at all because its route returned HTTP 404 on all 16 documents.
didnt: Board — the bakeoff method itself: a small gold-document set, a doc-gate read over mean scores, and a per-call cost ledger for choosing which model compiles wiki pages, with a verifier that recomputes every published figure before it ships. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TrajWiki
good: Represents each memory as a source-grounded evolution trajectory rather than a static entry: dialogue is stored as immutable episodic snapshots linked by claim-level operations ADD, REVISE and DEPRECATE, so revised or deprecated claims are never deleted and stay linked to their original snapshots and source messages. A persistent Memory Wiki layer compiles the trajectories into structured, interlinked pages (index, entity, topic, inventory) capturing entities, events, quantities, topics and conflicts, and queries route hierarchically from wiki pages to trajectories to snapshots to source messages for evidence-grounded answers. Evaluated on LoCoMo and MedMT, it improves long-horizon dialogue performance across both open-source and closed-source backbones, and wiki routing cut the candidate trajectories considered per query from 130.4 to 55.6 on average.
bad: The paper is explicit that provenance-aware does not mean provenance-perfect: the pipeline depends on structured LLM outputs for extraction, updating, wiki construction and validation, so malformed outputs trigger costly fallback and repair paths, and LLM-generated summaries can shift the salience of specific facts across repeated abstraction. Its diagnostics are offline proxies rather than human-verified audit accuracy, and the cost is concentrated in memory construction — 43.28M deployment tokens for the LoCoMo run with GPT-4o-mini. Evaluation is limited to two dialogue benchmarks, so transfer to document wikis is untested at source.
didnt: Corroboration — typed claim mutations (ADD / REVISE / DEPRECATE) over immutable, source-linked snapshots, with deprecated claims retained rather than deleted, independently confirms the claim-lifecycle and append-only-history design already in our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: The University of Manchester (lead affiliation); also The University of Melbourne, The University of Edinburgh, University of Southern California, The University of Texas at Austin

name: WiCER
good: Formalises the compilation gap in LLM wikis — blind compilation scores 2.14-2.32 against 3.46 for raw full context, with a 53-60% catastrophic failure rate across 17 RepLiQA domains and 6,800 questions — and closes it with a CEGAR-inspired compile-evaluate-refine loop: the compiled wiki is tested against one diagnostic probe per source document, any probe scoring 1/5 triggers a diagnosis that extracts the specific facts the compiler dropped, and those facts are fed back as explicit preservation constraints in the next compilation. One to two iterations recover 80% of the lost quality and reduce catastrophic failures by 55% relative; an ablation across all 17 topics shows targeted diagnosis (+0.95), not generic pinning (+0.16), drives the gains. All code and benchmarks are stated as released for reproducible research.
bad: The paper's own limitations narrow the claim: results are specific to Llama 3.1 8B running on an Apple M4 Pro, the RAG baseline uses fixed-size chunking without reranking, WiCER validation covers eight of the 17 topics and includes one failure case, and scoring rests on an LLM-as-judge. Within-topic runs are deterministic (greedy decoding), so the reported variation is across topics only.
didnt: Board — a probe-driven recompilation pass for our wiki compiler: generate one diagnostic question per source, diagnose the facts a failed probe exposes, and pin those facts as preservation constraints on recompile — as an idea only, since the paper is CC BY-NC-ND. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Zinnia Tech Solutions

name: Obsidian Day Planner
good: An Obsidian community plugin that turns timed tasks written in daily notes into editable calendar and timeline views, with a multi-day planner and a status-bar mini-timeline of the upcoming three hours. It also surfaces tasks from anywhere in the vault via the Tasks plugin's scheduled dates, overlays internet calendars (Google, iCloud, Outlook) from an ICS link, and records time spent on tasks as Dataview clock properties shown as blocks beside the planner.
bad: The README flags its time-tracking feature as experimental and liable to break or change, and clock time blocks cannot yet be edited by dragging. It only sees daily notes if the core Daily Notes plugin or the Periodic Notes community plugin is enabled, so the planner is dependent on other plugins for its primary data source.
didnt: Rejected — a day-planning and time-blocking UI for a note vault is peripheral to a citation-locked knowledge OS; it adds no ingest, provenance or retrieval capability our stack lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Flashcards / Anki sync
good: Lets a user author Anki flashcards directly in ordinary Markdown notes — basic, reversed, cloze, heading and reminder card types, with LaTeX, wikilinks, images and audio in card content — and syncs them to Anki through AnkiConnect, creating or updating the matching Anki notes while Anki keeps review history and scheduling. Obsidian stays the source of truth: each Anki card links back to its exact source location, decks and tags come from frontmatter or folder, re-running an update does not duplicate unchanged cards, and destructive changes ask for confirmation first.
bad: The sync is deliberately one-way authoring, not two-way editing: a linked card edited inside Anki is overwritten from Obsidian on the next update. It requires the desktop version of Anki plus the AnkiConnect add-on running locally, and the small anchors and managed properties the plugin writes into notes to link cards to Anki must not be hand-edited.
didnt: Board — generating retrieval-practice cards from compiled wiki pages (Obsidian as source of truth, Anki owning scheduling) as a study layer for the homeschool work, rather than a feature of the knowledge core. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shell commands
good: An Obsidian plugin for defining shell/terminal commands once in settings and running them from the command palette, hotkeys, URI links or automated events, with built-in variables that inject the current file's title, name, path, parent folder, tags, selected text, clipboard and formatted date/time into the command. Command output can be directed back into the active note, and variable values are escaped per-shell so clipboard or note text containing characters like '>' is not interpreted as redirection.
bad: The README warns the plugin is still in early development, comes with no warranty, and can destroy files if a command is misunderstood; it is desktop-only with no mobile support because it relies on Node's child_process. Listed main issues include corruption of non-English characters in output on Windows/PowerShell and an escaping system the author still describes as experimental, which the README itself notes can be dangerous.
didnt: Rejected — arbitrary shell execution launched from note content runs against approval-gated writes and local-first custody, and GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only in any case; neither the code nor the pattern is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notion-to-Obsidian converter
good: A single Node script that cleans a Notion workspace export for use in Obsidian: it strips the long UUID Notion appends to every directory and file path (which also works around Windows path-length limits), converts Markdown, CSV and notion.so links into Obsidian wikilinks, turns exported CSVs into a companion Markdown table file, rewrites image links, and replaces characters that are illegal in Obsidian filenames.
bad: The README states plainly that the script is not made to be robust and must not be run twice on the same export, as a second run is likely to fail and truncate paths unnecessarily; link conversion is described as imperfect because of name collisions. The maintainer's note at the top says they are tied up with work and will address issues only when life settles, and the repo shows no releases.
didnt: Rejected — a one-shot, admittedly non-robust migration script for a source format our ingest pipeline does not take; no ongoing fit and no capability gap it fills. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yarle
good: Converts Evernote .enex exports — a single notebook or a folder of them — into Markdown, preserving text, code blocks, inline images, attachments and web clips plus all metadata: original creation and modification times, tags, GPS location, notebook name and source URL. Output is template-driven so metadata lands in the Markdown in a user-defined shape, converted files keep the notes' original filesystem timestamps, internal links between Evernote notes are carried over, attachments are organised into a resources subfolder, and dedicated output formats exist for Obsidian, LogSeq, Tana and Heptabase alongside standard Markdown.
bad: It is a one-way Evernote-only converter with no sync or round-trip, and full metadata output depends on hand-writing a config file and template from a large configuration surface. The README carries a dedicated limitations section for the Tana target and per-target format caveats, so fidelity varies by destination rather than being uniform.
didnt: Rejected — Evernote export migration is a niche our programme has no source material for, and its metadata-preserving conversion is already covered by our own ingest path for the formats we actually receive. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: crbro-memory
good: Local MCP memory server storing plain JSON on the user's own disk: fact-level search (Orama) with an optional local semantic layer, corrections that supersede or retract old facts, per-fact shelf life (volatile/normal/durable/permanent) after which claims move to possibly_stale with a source-check warning, explicit evidence records, credentials replaced with a marker before anything touches disk (real values go to the OS keychain), and per-project team sharing through Git of only explicitly shared neurons.
bad: Very small, young project (8 stars, created 2026-05). The README itself notes project scope is organisation, not an access-control boundary, and that relevance/provenance/freshness labels are not a truth guarantee; the semantic layer costs ~500 MB on disk and ~0.5 GB RAM per running server.
didnt: Corroboration — its shelf-life classes with possibly_stale demotion, explicit evidence labels separate from relevance, and refusal to let repetition count as verification confirm our freshness/provenance design for the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rag-kb
good: Local-first, offline-capable agent memory and knowledge service in a single process exposing both REST and MCP: hybrid retrieval (vector + BM25 with normalised weighted fusion, optional reranker and sparse third leg), document and webpage ingestion, per-project sub-stores physically isolated from a global store, full read/write/search audit logs per client and project, and storage/retrieval that works with no LLM configured (optional local Ollama powers RAG answers).
bad: The README states all memories are fully shared with every client, task and AI (client identity is audit metadata only), which is the opposite of scoped custody. Install is heavy (core Python dependencies ~400-600 MB including torch) and the default embedding model is the Chinese-oriented bge-small-zh-v1.5; changing embedding models invalidates existing vector stores.
didnt: Rejected — its hybrid retrieval duplicates what our stack already does, and its all-clients-share-everything memory model contradicts our approval-gated, scoped-custody design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: klypix-mcp
good: Shared project memory for MCP coding tools in a single brain.klypix file committed with the code: decisions and corrections where corrections supersede stale cards, evidence anchors (ev:) that flag code drift, a brain_challenge call that pushes back before a decision by surfacing a previously reversed one, declared-file overlap warnings between concurrent sessions, handoffs, and a conformance command that verifies 15 coordination behaviours against the installed build.
bad: Its own Current limitations section states coordination is machine-local and OS-user-local only (no cross-machine transport ships in the package), overlap warnings are advisory and block nothing, drift detection is single-host, opt-in per card and runs only in the Claude Code hook path, and the eval harness behind its published recall numbers is not in the repo; the companion desktop/web apps are separate proprietary products.
didnt: Board — evidence-anchored memory cards whose freshness is computed from their anchors, plus a pre-decision challenge call that surfaces reversed decisions before an agent acts, for the ideas board. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: coldstart
good: Self-maintaining codebase memory for coding agents with no embeddings, model or service: a deterministic AST index answers which files are relevant to a task with checkable evidence, and an in-repo notebook of agent-written notes (file notes, flow notes, lessons) is anchored to real files and symbols with content hashes stamped at write time, so a note whose evidence drifted is flagged [evidence changed] instead of being served as truth; writes pass a dedup gate and the append-only log makes parallel branches merge as unions.
bad: The README itself says the notebook is young and that its compounding value is a stated bet, not a measured result; symbol-level freshness only exists for languages the navigation index parses, and the tool is scoped to codebases for coding agents, not general knowledge.
didnt: Corroboration — content-hash anchored notes that degrade into labelled hypotheses when their evidence changes confirm our truth-aware freshness direction: stale knowledge must be flagged, never served with fresh confidence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agenthelm
good: Shared, versioned Project Brain for AI coding agents behind an MCP server with git-style history (log/diff/blame via get_history): agents fetch compiled context, propose knowledge, and a Brain Compiler validates evidence and resolves conflicts before a new brain version is released; a human-in-the-loop gate routes @irreversible actions to Telegram approve/reject, with fail-closed safety classification and budget guardrails.
bad: It is a hosted control plane, not local-first: the MCP setup requires a live AGENTHELM_CONNECT_KEY against the agenthelm.online service with a Supabase backend, so memory custody sits in someone else's SaaS; the repo has zero releases and mixes the marketing site, SDKs and server in one tree.
didnt: Rejected — its approval-gate idea duplicates our approval-gated writes, but the hosted, key-gated SaaS custody model contradicts our local-first design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BovedIA
good: Personal memory for Claude Code as an MCP server over plain Markdown notes on the user's own disk (syncable via iCloud/OneDrive/Drive/Dropbox): a router note (Inicio) read at every session start decides what to load and when, branch cover pages load only when a topic enters, and the 38 tools include cheap partial reads (frontmatter, single sections), wikilink/backlink maintenance, orphan and broken-link detection, snapshots with restore, and optional per-author attribution annotations.
bad: The README's own status note (28 Aug 2026) says the public repo is deliberately frozen at v2.8.1 while daily development moved to a private repository, so the open code no longer receives the author's work; documentation is Spanish-only and search is plain-text AND logic — local semantic search is named only as possible future material.
didnt: Corroboration — its router-note pyramid (one always-read note that decides what to load, branch covers loaded on demand, content last) independently confirms our index-first, pull-only-what-the-question-touches query protocol. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shadowgraph
good: Local-first decision memory for AI agents (MCP, CLI, HTTP; zero runtime dependencies): decisions are stored as structured data with the chosen approach, rejected alternatives and their reasons, assumptions, evidence, failed attempts, outcomes and provenance sourceClass (agent_claimed / tool_observed / human_confirmed / production_verified), plus structured reopenWhen rules — a review pass re-evaluates those rules against stored facts after a restart and resurfaces a decision whose rejection reason no longer holds; facts and memories are bi-temporal and reads/writes are strictly project-scoped.
bad: The README labels it Technical Preview / Early Access (0.42.0), states it is not published to npm (install is from GitHub, and the npm name is unreserved), and carries a dedicated Limitations and Technical Preview section; the project is tiny (3 stars) despite its 398 commits.
didnt: Board — machine-checkable reopenWhen conditions on decision records, re-evaluated against stored facts so a settled decision reopens itself when the world changes, for the ideas board. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lockstep
good: Shared decision memory for teams of AI coding agents: a decision ledger plus a usage/dependency graph ranks each decision and change by blast radius (how many services consume the affected surface), routes changes only to the repos that declared a dependency, briefs each agent at session start with what changed and what is binding (highest blast radius first), keeps cross-cutting decisions open until affected teams acknowledge them, and can fail a PR whose contract change has no binding decision.
bad: Pilot-stage software: the README states CLI 0.3.0 is published but hosted rollout and a real authenticated Claude-session verification are still pending, the repo has no releases, onboarding requires GitHub sign-in against a hosted API/dashboard (hosted is the default), and the whole design targets multi-developer teams rather than a personal knowledge base.
didnt: Rejected — team-scale coordination machinery (hosted ledger, GitHub sign-in, blast-radius routing across services) built for engineering orgs; out of scope for a personal LLM-wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memini
good: Local-first project memory as enforced guardrails, not a notebook: memories (failed attempts, fragile files, decisions, deployment rules) live in a .memini/ folder as SQLite plus PR-reviewable Markdown, and hooks intercept an edit to a guardrailed file before it happens — warn once per session or block until a human archives the memory — backed by a git pre-commit gate; memories hash the files they reference so stale ones stop firing until re-verified, secrets are auto-redacted before storage, and wider workspace/user scopes only fire when human-verified so an agent cannot plant rules that spread across repos.
bad: The README's Status section says it is early (v0.1) with team sync only on the roadmap; the repo is minimal (0 stars, 24 commits), and its Security section concedes guardrails intercept edit tools, not arbitrary shell commands, and warn severity is advisory.
didnt: Board — enforced guardrail hooks that inject the recorded lesson at the moment an agent is about to repeat a mistake (warn/block severities, human-verification required before a rule widens in scope), for the ideas board. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memanto
good: A memory agent (Moorcheh) that manages other agents' memory rather than merely storing it: it extracts durable knowledge from interaction streams, consolidates duplicates, reconciles contradictions by superseding while preserving what was believed and when, briefs each agent before it acts, and runs retention as a policy you write — a per-type retention table plus named first-match rules that can pin memories — where expiry is stamped with the date and the rule that retired the item, expired is not deleted (restore is a separate act, hard delete separate again), policy application offers dry-run then confirm, and recall supports point-in-time --as-of queries; the estate exports as portable Markdown (Open Knowledge Format) and runs fully on-prem with Docker + Ollama.
bad: It is a second autonomous agent that curates, merges and expires on its own judgment on a daily scheduled loop, and offers a hosted cloud backend — adopting the whole system would hand governance of the estate to an external agent's judgment, the opposite of our owner-approved write gates.
took: Retention as a git-kept policy file (show-policy → dry-run → confirm; restore and hard-delete kept separate) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 2 — source/inspiration: Memanto mechanics
didnt: Corroboration — its retention mechanics (policy file, dry-run → confirm, expiry stamped with the retiring rule, restore and hard-delete kept separate) are exactly the pattern our programme built in Phase 2; the fleet-agent itself was not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memheaven
good: Self-hosted, remotely accessible shared long-term memory for hosted AI clients: a Cloudflare Worker exposes an OAuth 2.1 + PKCE remote MCP endpoint with tenant-scoped access keys, D1 for metadata/indexes, R2 for verbatim drawer/diary bodies, Vectorize + Workers AI for semantic search, inspectable and deletable records, quota guardrails, redacted audit logging, and synthetic behaviour evals for retrieval and tenant isolation — deployable on a Cloudflare free account with no VM or database administration.
bad: Total Cloudflare platform lock-in (Worker/D1/R2/Vectorize/Workers AI) contradicts local-first custody; the README's client table marks only ChatGPT as Confirmed end-to-end, with Claude.ai, local IDEs and Copilot merely Expected or unknown, and it explicitly does not promise unlimited free usage; the project is small (2 stars, no releases).
didnt: Rejected — a remote memory door is a real need, but binding it to Cloudflare's proprietary stack trades one vendor's custody for another's; our hosted-door question stays open on our own terms. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: people-context
good: Local-first memory about the people in your life for AI agents (MCP server + CLI on one SQLite file, no account, no network calls): explainable identity resolution over names, nicknames, aliases and handles that returns ranked candidates with match reasons and never a silent guess, relationships/roles/time-bounded affiliations, durable facts, interaction summaries, reminders and communication guidance; imports from email, mbox, vCard, calendar, LinkedIn, Outlook and WhatsApp are staged as reviewable candidates that a human approves before anything is recorded, raw source content is never kept, writes are audited, forget is a real hard delete, and sensitive records sit behind an operator-only gate a prompt cannot open.
bad: The README's security model states the database is plaintext SQLite by default — file permissions are a boundary between accounts, not encryption, with SQLCipher only as an opt-in extra — and the optional loopback HTTP server is unauthenticated by design; scope is deliberately narrow (people only, not general knowledge).
didnt: Board — staged import candidates with human review before commit, and identity resolution that surfaces ambiguous candidates with reasons instead of guessing, for our people pages and ingest pipeline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: solucortex
good: Official MCP server for the SoluCortex hosted technical-memory service: solucortex_recall builds task context at the start of work ranked by semantic similarity plus importance over a typed memory vocabulary (architecture, decision, risk, convention, bug_history, tech_debt, sensitive_module, learning), and its governance is explicit — agents propose and humans govern: agent edits return a memory to pending for human re-approval, agents can never change a memory's status or delete it, and deletions happen only from the human panel.
bad: The open-source server is a thin client: it requires a SoluCortex account and a project API key (scx_) and all memory lives in the hosted backend at solucortex.ai, so there is no local-first custody option; the PyPI page also warns never to store real secrets in a memory.
didnt: Corroboration — its 'agents propose, humans govern' rule (edits fall back to pending, status changes and deletions reserved to humans) independently confirms our approval-gated write design, even though its hosted custody is not for us. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agenthold
good: An MCP server giving multiple agents shared, versioned state: optimistic concurrency control rejects a write whose version has moved with a ConflictError carrying the current value, and register/claim/release/status/wait tools add claim/release locks with outcomes preserved for the next claimant. It also works as a plain Python library and connects to any MCP-speaking framework.
bad: Very young and small as shown on the repo page: 2 stars, 48 commits, created 2026-03-14 and no releases. State lives in a single SQLite (WAL) store, and the README documents no multi-host or distributed coordination.
didnt: Corroboration — its version-checked writes and claim/release locks confirm our approval-gated, conflict-denying approach to shared agent state, but our wiki already has its own coordination record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zettelkasten-mcp
good: An MCP server implementing the Zettelkasten method: atomic notes with timestamp IDs, typed bidirectional semantic links (extends, refines, contradicts, supports, questions), tags, and search by content, tags or links via zk_* tools. Markdown files with YAML frontmatter are the source of truth and the SQLite index is a rebuildable layer on top.
bad: The README's own Important Notice calls the software experimental, provided as-is, and warns it may contain bugs that could lead to data loss or corruption. Editing Markdown files outside the system requires a manual zk_rebuild_index run, and the operation model is synchronous.
didnt: Corroboration — Markdown-as-source-of-truth with a disposable, rebuildable SQLite index and typed note links confirms the shape our wiki already uses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: remem
good: Local-first persistent memory for Claude Code and Codex: hooks capture sessions into an append-only ledger, a background process distils them, and recall is project-scoped with source attribution, staleness labels, suppression, review queues and injection audits. Storage is SQLite with SQLCipher encryption by default, exposed through MCP, CLI and an authenticated localhost REST API.
bad: Host support is uneven per the README's own table: Cursor gets MCP only with no SessionStart injection or automatic capture, and compiled command-rule enforcement is Claude Code only. It is scoped to coding-agent session history rather than a general knowledge corpus, and generated memory must pass source-support and lifecycle checks before it is trusted.
didnt: Corroboration — auditable recall with staleness labels, suppression and review queues confirms our citation-locked, governed-memory design; its coding-session scope does not replace the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: flaiwheel
good: A self-hosted memory and governance layer for coding agents: bug fixes, decisions and test cases are stored as structured Markdown in a Git repository and retrieved by hybrid semantic + BM25 search with RRF fusion and optional cross-encoder reranking. Seven category-specific write tools, pre-commit validation and ingest quality gates keep low-quality files out of the index, and a post-commit hook captures fix/feat/refactor commits automatically.
bad: The licence is Business Source License 1.1 — free only for non-commercial use or organisations of up to 10 users, with commercial use beyond that requiring a paid licence (converting to Apache-2.0 in 2030). The README itself says it is not for small hobby projects, plain HTTP remains the default endpoint, and its self-issued TLS requires installing its CA in each client's trust store.
didnt: Board — the git-native structured-relations and timeline idea (replaces/depends_on/fixes frontmatter deriving a knowledge graph from Markdown, with Git history as the validity window) is worth the ideas board; the BUSL licence makes its code ideas-only for us. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NoteDiscovery
good: A lightweight self-hosted knowledge base storing notes as plain Markdown files: full-text search, tags, backlinks, graph view, themes, plugins and HTML export in a responsive web UI. A built-in MCP server lets Claude, Cursor and other clients search, create, edit, organise and append to notes, over stdio or Streamable HTTP.
bad: Authentication is optional and described in the README as simple password protection for self-hosted deployments, so an unconfigured instance is open. The README documents no citation, provenance or abstention machinery — it is a notes app surface, not a governed knowledge layer.
didnt: Rejected — plain-Markdown notes with graph view and MCP is exactly the shape our wiki plus the Lens already provides; it adds no capability our stack lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: smart-tree
good: A Rust directory-visualisation tool claiming 10–24x the speed of tree, with token-efficient AI-oriented output formats (70–90% token reduction claimed), semantic analysis, content search and git status inline. It exposes 30+ MCP tools spanning discovery, search, analysis and AST-aware editing (smart_edit).
bad: The scope is sprawling for a directory tool — the README presents it as a replacement for 20+ tools and bundles a web dashboard, TUI, daemon, hooks and a 'consciousness' memory system (MEM8), much of it unrelated to listing trees. Its headline compression and speedup figures are the project's own claims presented in its README.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: our agents already traverse the wiki tree directly, and its extra subsystems overlap tooling we already have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Chisel
good: Rust file tools for agents built around token economy: patch_apply applies a unified diff atomically so only changed lines cross the wire, and targeted grep/sed reads avoid loading whole files (the README's worked comparison claims roughly 23x fewer tokens over six tasks). Every path is canonicalised and confined to a configured root inside chisel-core — traversal and symlink escapes are rejected — with bearer-token auth, a compile-time shell-command whitelist, atomic writes and a read-only mode; the core is also embeddable via Rust or WASM.
bad: No licence is stated at the source: the repository details show no licence and the root contains no LICENSE file, so the code is not reusable by default. It is also very young — 16 commits and 3 releases as shown on the repo page — and the shell whitelist is fixed at compile time and cannot be extended at runtime.
didnt: Board — unified-diff atomic patch edits plus library-level root confinement is a strong pattern for our agent file doors, worth the ideas board; with no licence stated at source its code itself is not adoptable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agent-coherence
good: A coordination layer that stops one agent silently clobbering another's work on shared files: MESI-style ownership and invalidation plus optimistic commit-CAS turn a stale write into a loud, typed, retryable refusal instead of a lost update, with multi-artifact snapshot sessions and an effect-ordering gate. Its safety invariants are machine-checked in TLA+, it ships an MCP server (stale-write-guard-fs), framework adapters, and ~12-token invalidation signals instead of rebroadcasting artifacts.
bad: The README states it is Alpha — APIs may change before v1.0 — and its guarantees honestly cover only writers going through a single coordinator on a single host, with cross-host fencing still on the roadmap. It also documents one open lost-write gap (issue #248) in a narrow write/write_cas_at interleaving.
didnt: Corroboration — a stale writer being denied fail-closed and forced to reacquire and re-read confirms the stale-write denial at the heart of our shared-file coordination. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hledit-mcp
good: An MCP server exposing hash-anchored file edits to standard MCP clients: read annotates each line with a stable LN#HASH anchor, and edit/batch operations recompute the hash before writing, rejecting a stale anchor with a stale error and a remap hint instead of corrupting the wrong line. A demo transcript in the repo shows the stale-write rejection over the real MCP stdio surface.
bad: Very small and young as shown on the repo page: 1 star, 16 commits and no releases. It is a single tool with three operations, and it depends on a separately installed hledit CLI (Go 1.21+) alongside Node.js 18+.
didnt: Corroboration — recomputing a line hash before a write and rejecting stale anchors confirms our hash-checked, stale-denying edit discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yandex-workspace-mcp
good: An MCP server giving agents governed access to Yandex Disk and Yandex Wiki through 50+ typed tools and one unified search across both. It is read-only by default, with separate read/write/delete permissions, path allowlisting against configured roots, and a structured audit log of write and destructive operations, backed by security and permission regression tests.
bad: It is tied entirely to the Yandex ecosystem and Yandex OAuth, so nothing in it serves our local wiki. It is also brand new and unproven as shown on the repo page (0 stars, 33 commits, no releases), and the README states its offline demo uses a mocked upstream and does not validate live API parity or load capacity.
didnt: Corroboration — read-only by default, granular per-operation permissions, path allowlisting and audit logging of destructive operations confirms the permission posture of our own read-only wiki door, though the Yandex platform itself is out of scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-file-tools
good: An MCP filesystem server for legacy non-UTF-8 text: it detects the encoding from the file's bytes (45 encodings read and write, including CP1251, KOI8, ISO-8859, UTF-16 and GBK/GB18030), hands the model UTF-8, and writes back in the original encoding with BOM and CRLF/LF intact. Encoding awareness extends to edit, grep and search tools, detect_encoding reports charset and confidence, and every path is checked against allowed directories. It ships as a single Go binary.
bad: Licensed GPL-3.0, so its code is copyleft and ideas-only for our stack. Its specialism is narrow — legacy Delphi/Pascal, VB6 and old PHP/HTML codebases — and the recommended Claude Code plugin route additionally requires Node.js 18+ on the PATH or the server shows as not connected.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence plus a legacy-encoding niche our Markdown/UTF-8 wiki does not have; the detect-then-preserve-encoding idea needs no adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DirForge
good: A stateless, read-only directory browsing web app: point it at a mounted path and it serves a clean UI with search, previews and archive inspection, folder-as-ZIP downloads, signed expiring share links and file hashes. The same data is exposed through a REST JSON API, a read-only WebDAV endpoint, a read-only S3-compatible endpoint and an MCP server, all in one container with no database.
bad: The README warns its baseline defaults are homelab-oriented, not internet-hardened, and the default compose file falls back to admin/dirforge credentials if not changed. It is strictly read-only browsing for homelab/NAS use — no knowledge, citation or write-governance features — and small (5 stars, 48 commits on the repo page).
didnt: Rejected — a homelab file browser; our Lens already serves the wiki read-only with far richer structure, and DirForge's read-only-by-construction stance adds nothing beyond that. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fast-filesystem-mcp
good: An MCP filesystem server optimised for large files: chunked and sequential reading with continuation support, streaming writes that avoid memory overflow, directory synchronisation, archive create/extract, and precise line/block editing tools including regex search-and-replace. Large writes verify file integrity afterwards and retry with exponential backoff, with real-time progress tracking.
bad: Backup creation before modifications is off by default (CREATE_BACKUP_FILES=false), so the safety net its editing features advertise must be opted into. The README documents no stale-write, hash-check or version safeguards on its broad write/delete/sync tool set, and its Claude-optimised response shaping ties it to that client ecosystem.
didnt: Rejected — a generic fast filesystem server duplicating file access our agents already have, without the stale-write and citation safeguards our wiki doors require. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: keyhole
good: An MCP server that lets a private ChatGPT app reach only the local folders the user opens, via OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel with no public port and no shell. Folders are read-only by default and become editable only by an explicit local CLI grant (per-folder ro/rw); every write requires the file's current SHA-256 so stale-hash updates are refused, the previous content is recorded locally first, and changes can be restored by change id.
bad: It is locked to ChatGPT and OpenAI's tunnel: setup needs ChatGPT Developer mode, creating your own private ChatGPT app and a restricted runtime key (about 15 minutes), with several platforms and plans untested per its compatibility table. Limits are tight — text files up to 8 MiB, 400 lines or 64 KiB per read, no writing Office documents, PDFs or images — and its document parsers run with the user's OS permissions rather than in a sandbox.
didnt: Board — per-folder ro/rw grants managed only from a local CLI, plus hash-checked recoverable edits through a tunnel with no public port, is a pattern worth boarding for any future hosted door to the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markitdown MCP (Microsoft)
good: Microsoft's lightweight MCP server for MarkItDown, exposing a single convert_to_markdown(uri) tool over STDIO, Streamable HTTP or SSE for http:, https:, file: and data: URIs. The underlying converter turns PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, images, audio, HTML, CSV/JSON/XML, ZIP and EPUB into Markdown that preserves headings, lists, tables and links for LLM consumption.
bad: The MCP server's own README warns it has no authentication, runs with the privileges of the user running it, and its tool can read any file that user can access or any network data — it binds to localhost by default and must not be exposed on other interfaces without understanding that. The parent README also notes the Markdown output is meant for text-analysis pipelines and may not be the best option for high-fidelity conversion for human consumption.
didnt: Board — a single-tool convert_to_markdown MCP front-end is worth boarding as an ingest option for document formats our current converter handles poorly, with its no-auth, runs-as-the-user warning kept attached. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Digimindmap
good: A simple online mind-map creator built on a customised, lightweight version of the My Mind JavaScript library, running on PHP 8+ with SQLite by default or MySQL/MariaDB, with environment-variable controls for authorised domains and rate limits.
bad: Deliberately simple in scope — a basic mind-map widget rather than a knowledge system — and the README is in French; the maintainer states pull requests are not accepted for the moment because reviewing code contributions takes hours they may not have.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL code is ideas-only for our stack and a basic mind-map widget adds nothing to a citation-locked markdown wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LibreKB
good: Self-hosted PHP/MySQL knowledge-base web app that installs in minutes or via Docker, with TinyMCE article editing, categories nested to any depth, file attachments, predefined user groups, custom branding/CSS, and an optional read-only JSON API for articles and categories.
bad: Database-backed by design (PHP 8.4+, MySQL/MariaDB and an .htaccess web server required), so content does not live as plain files; the README's API notes state search matches article titles and content only, and the project is small (62 stars, single maintainer).
didnt: Rejected — GPL code is ideas-only, and a database-backed PHP web KB duplicates none of our local-first, plain-file custody model in a usable way. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Marmot
good: Open-source data catalog shipped as a single binary with an intuitive UI: full-text plus structured/boolean/metadata-filtered search over tables, topics, queues, APIs and dashboards, interactive lineage graphs, ownership and glossary collaboration, and certified context exposed to AI agents via MCP, API and UI.
bad: Scoped to enterprise data assets (databases, warehouses, pipelines), not personal knowledge; it is a young project (repo created 2025-03-12) and the README documents no citation, provenance-locking or abstention mechanism for the metadata it serves to agents.
didnt: Rejected — fit: an organisational data-asset catalog solves a different problem from a personal LLM-wiki; its MCP context-layer idea is already covered by our own MCP doors. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TeamMapper
good: Self-hosted collaborative mind-mapping: shared websocket sessions (successor to the discontinued mindmapp), view-only or modification invites shared by QR code or URL with no registration described as a core idea, node images/colours/fonts/links, undo/redo and shortcuts, and import/export in JSON, Mermaid, SVG, PDF and PNG.
bad: Maps are deleted after 30 days by default (GDPR retention setting), which conflicts with a permanent knowledge record; production deployment requires a Postgres backend, and it is a mind-map session tool only — no wiki pages, search over knowledge, or long-term store.
didnt: Rejected — scope: ephemeral collaborative mind-map sessions, with automatic deletion by default, are the opposite of our permanent, local-first wiki record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Docs (suitenumerique)
good: Open-source collaborative editor (Django + React, BlockNote/Yjs) positioned as a Notion/Google Docs alternative: real-time cursors and presence, comments, granular access control, subpages and searchable hierarchy, offline editing, presentation mode, .docx/.md import and .docx/.odt/.pdf export, and optional model-agnostic AI writing helpers.
bad: A heavy multi-service team platform (Django backend, collaboration server, Postgres, Redis and S3 storage in its install docs) built for organisations, not a single local-first owner; the README warns some advanced features such as PDF export rely on GPL-licensed BlockNote XL packages that are not MIT-compatible and must be excluded with a PUBLISH_AS_MIT build flag.
didnt: Rejected — fit and weight: a scaled, multi-user collaborative docs service with a server stack and a mixed-licence export path, where our system is a local-first personal wiki with owner-only custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Many Notes
good: Markdown note-taking web app built for simplicity: multiple vaults per user whose files are also saved in the filesystem for portability, links/backlinks/tags, templates, fast typo-tolerant file search, tree explorer, vault import/export, PDF export, collaboration invites, OpenID Connect/OAuth login and a PWA.
bad: It uses a database to power its features and runs as a PHP/Laravel web service with a Typesense search component — a server app rather than plain files under the owner's direct control; the README documents no citation, provenance or approval-gating layer.
didnt: Corroboration — keeping the real files in the filesystem underneath a database-powered UI confirms our files-first custody principle; the web vault app itself duplicates editors we already have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Writing
good: Lightweight distraction-free browser text editor with Markdown and LaTeX/MathJax support, fast rendering with no keypress delay or math flicker, no server code at all — just open index.html, works offline — with save-as-.md and print/export-to-PDF shortcuts.
bad: A writing surface only: a single-page editor with no storage model, organisation, search, linking or knowledge features, and a small, old codebase (56 commits, no releases) built on legacy Pagedown libraries.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a minimalist editor page, however elegant, is not a knowledge system and adds nothing to our markdown wiki tooling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DailyTxT
good: Encrypted diary/journal web app (Svelte + Go, Docker): everything written and every uploaded file (up to 500 MB each) is encrypted before storage with ChaCha20-Poly1305, keys derived from the password via Argon2id with one-time backup keys for recovery, plus markdown live preview, tags, full search, templates, maps/GPX, HTML export, multi-user accounts each with its own key — and all data stored in JSON files, no database, expressly for portability and long-term availability.
bad: Diary-scoped only, and the README is explicit that there is no client-side end-to-end encryption (server-side search would not work with it) and the encryption key never leaves the server, so trust rests on the server operator; the author also states no backward-compatibility guarantee in versioning.
didnt: Board — the password-wrapped per-user encryption key with one-time backup keys, over portable JSON files, as a pattern for an encrypted private-journal area of the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Blinko
good: Self-hosted AI card note-taking tool for capturing fleeting thoughts the moment they strike, with AI-powered RAG retrieval by natural-language query, notes stored in the user's own self-hosted environment with full Markdown support, and a lightweight Tauri build for macOS, Windows, Android and Linux.
bad: GPL-3.0 code, so reuse is ideas-only for our stack; it runs on a Postgres/Prisma server stack, and its headline AI retrieval is plain RAG — the README documents no citation locking, abstention or approval gating over what the AI surfaces.
didnt: Board — the flash-thought capture-inbox pattern (instant card capture later organised) for the wiki's intake lane; GPL code itself is ideas-only, never adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TriliumNext
