good: Community-maintained Trilium: cross-platform hierarchical PKM with notes in an arbitrarily deep tree (a note can be cloned into multiple places), rich WYSIWYG and code editors, full-text search and hoisting, seamless versioning, attributes for organisation/querying/scripting, per-note encryption, self-hosted sync, relation/note/geo/mind maps, a REST API, and stated scale beyond 100,000 notes.
bad: AGPL-3.0 code and a database-backed application store rather than plain markdown files the owner can read and move directly; the web interface is supported and tested only on the latest Chrome and Firefox, and later TriliumNext versions increment the sync version so direct migration from original Trilium no longer works.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL code is ideas-only, its database store conflicts with our plain-file custody, and hierarchical PKM is already covered in our programme (wave 1 covered Trilium). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BookStack
good: Simple self-hosted documentation platform (PHP/Laravel) organising content as shelves, books, chapters and pages, with WYSIWYG and Markdown editors, full search across all levels, direct links to any paragraph, page revisions and image management, and a full role-and-permission system.
bad: Content is stored in MySQL rather than plain files, and the hierarchy is fixed at four levels; the README's own project definition calls it opinionated and states it is not designed as an extensible platform for other purposes, and the GitHub repo now only points onward to Codeberg where the project is managed.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a database-backed, fixed book/chapter/page web wiki adds nothing to a folder-tree markdown wiki and would break plain-file custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gitit
good: Wiki written in Haskell (Happstack + pandoc) whose pages and uploads live in a git, darcs or mercurial repository and can be edited either with VCS command-line tools or through the web interface; pandoc's extended markdown by default with reStructuredText, LaTeX, HTML, DocBook and Org-mode also supported, plus TeX math, syntax highlighting, categories, Haskell plugins, caching and Atom feeds.
bad: GPL-2.0 code, and an ageing Haskell-era stack: building requires stack or cabal/Haskell Platform, the repo lists no GitHub releases, and there is no search, graph or AI-access layer of the kind our wiki is built around.
didnt: Corroboration — pages as files in a git repository, editable by VCS or web UI alike, is exactly the custody pattern our wiki already follows; the GPL Haskell implementation itself is not adoptable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Otter Wiki
good: Minimalistic Python/Flask wiki whose markdown content is stored in a git repository that keeps track of all changes, with a minimal interface and dark mode, markdown editor with tables, customisable sidebar/page index, full changelog and page history, user authentication, page attachments, and extended markdown including footnotes, alerts and mermaid diagrams.
bad: Deliberately minimal: its git http server for clone/pull/push of wiki content is flagged experimental in the README, and the README documents no graph view, full-text search depth, or AI/MCP access layer.
didnt: Corroboration — a minimal markdown-plus-git wiki with full page history confirms our core storage design; its feature set is a subset of what our wiki already does. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: keep-it-markdown
good: Converts Google Keep notes to markdown via the unofficial Python Keep API without going through Google Takeout; targets Obsidian, Logseq, Apple Notes, Joplin, Notion and Typora output styles, can also import markdown back into Keep, and offers per-app style switches, label/date filtering and a batch mode.
bad: The README itself warns the API is unofficial — Google could change the API at any time and stop the script from working; it requires Python 3.10+ and a fiddly OAuth-cookie/token retrieval flow to authenticate.
didnt: Rejected — a one-way vendor-export converter for Google Keep, a closed source the wiki does not ingest from; it offers nothing toward citation locking, scored abstention, or approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gooseberry
licence: MIT / Apache-2.0 (LICENSE_MIT and LICENSE_APACHE both in repo root; GitHub sidebar reports Apache License 2.0)
good: Rust CLI for Hypothesis: syncs annotations, supports bulk tagging and interactive search, and generates a plaintext knowledge base in mdBook or Obsidian style using Handlebars templates with a configurable hierarchy and index, keeping links back to each in-context annotation.
bad: The README states it currently doesn't work on Windows; it requires a Hypothesis account with a personal API token and the bat tool; the generated knowledge-base directory is cleared at every sync, so annotations must live in a separate folder; tagging and deletions sync back to Hypothesis.
didnt: Board — the annotation-to-plaintext-knowledge-base pipeline with links back to source context is a genuinely relevant pattern for a citation-locked wiki, but it is bound to the hosted Hypothesis service and a personal API token rather than local-first custody; worth revisiting only if annotation ingest is ever scoped. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BibleGateway to Obsidian
good: Fetches Bible text from BibleGateway and saves each chapter as a separate formatted markdown file, automatically creating navigation between files and a book overview file; supports multiple locales and command-line options for translation version, bolding the words of Jesus, editorial headers, YAML front-matter aliases, and Breadcrumbs-plugin navigation.
bad: The README's own disclaimers warn that using the script with some translations is clearly breaking copyright, that it is not affiliated with or approved by BibleGateway.com, and that use is at the user's own discretion; the script manipulates the clipboard while running, setup requires Ruby and gems, and it has not been tested with all translations.
didnt: Rejected — a single-purpose scripture scraper carrying explicit copyright exposure on many translations; it has no role in a personal LLM-wiki/knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DayOne JSON to MD
good: A single app.py converts Day One JSON exports (zips with media) to markdown for Obsidian, using ![[]] embed linking by default; the author reports testing text, headers, tags, dates, photos and audio.
bad: The repository is archived and its title states the author is not supporting it, pointing users to forks for better versions; the README says content beyond the tested types is unverified.
didnt: Rejected — an archived, unlicensed, single-vendor journal-export converter with no maintenance path; the conversion pattern it embodies is already common and needs no adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A thousand notes
good: The actual scripts the author used to move roughly 29,000 notes from Evernote to markdown in January 2021: cleanup, validation and maintenance scripts fixing duplicate-title asset directories, automation-unfriendly special characters in filenames, and HTML instead of markdown asset links, plus workflow scripts covering dates, tagging and summarisation ideas.
bad: A personal, ad-hoc script collection tied to one migration path (Evernote legacy client via Bear on macOS to markdown); no licence and no packaging.
didnt: Corroboration — independent field evidence that large Evernote-to-markdown migrations hinge on filename and asset hygiene (duplicate titles, special characters, HTML asset links), which corroborates the wiki's own ingest-hygiene rules; the scripts themselves are unlicensed and single-purpose. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Copy Selection as Markdown
good: Firefox add-on that copies a selection, a title plus URL, or links as Markdown via context menu, toolbar button or keyboard shortcut; extensive style settings (heading, bullet, code and link styles, GFM tables and task lists, a MathJax experiment, quote prefix, source link, base64 image embedding); conversion runs fully locally — no data is sent to any server.
bad: Firefox-first: Chrome has no store distribution, so Chrome users must build and install at their own risk; the README says the add-on is in maintenance mode and feature-complete for the author, so non-critical issues may not be resolved; it cannot run on Mozilla restricted domains by default.
didnt: Board — a clean, local-only clip-to-markdown capture surface is exactly the kind of low-risk ingest front-end a local-first wiki wants, and the MIT licence permits adoption; boarded rather than adopted because capture tooling is not on the current build queue. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obsidian Clipper (jplattel)
good: Chrome/Firefox extension that clips a page selection into Obsidian via the obsidian:// scheme, with a configurable vault and note and templates using placeholders such as {clip}, {date}, {zettel} and {og:image}; HTML is converted to Markdown via Turndown.
bad: The repository is archived because the official Obsidian Web Clipper now exists; it was only tested on Chrome/Firefox on OS X; it clips selections only, not whole pages; and it needs a GitHub-Pages bridge page (internet access) because extensions cannot open custom URL schemes directly.
didnt: Rejected — archived, superseded by the official Obsidian Web Clipper, and unlicensed; its template-placeholder pattern is noted but the code has no adoption path. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obsidian Bookmark
good: Chrome extension plus a local Node.js server: copies highlighted areas of a page to markdown and saves them as a note in a chosen vault folder; notes receive a Zettelkasten-identifier prefix plus the page title, and highlighted images are downloaded to a custom attachment folder with links updated.
bad: Requires a manual developer-mode extension install plus a separately run local server (packaged via electron-packager); the README itself calls jplattel's clipper 'a much less janky solution'; roadmap items (in-browser tags, a config page) are unfinished.
didnt: Rejected — an unlicensed, self-described janky two-part clipper superseded by maintained alternatives; nothing in it advances the wiki beyond patterns already covered. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-userland/publish
good: An open-source, free alternative to Obsidian Publish for reading and publishing notes, documented through its linked wiki guide and API reference.
bad: The README states the project is under development with acknowledged [[limitations]]; the repository is sparse (24 commits, 0 releases) and the README is little more than links to its wiki.
didnt: Rejected — an unfinished, unlicensed Publish alternative with no releasable artefact to evaluate; the wiki's publishing lane already has maintained routes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obyde
good: Minimal tool that converts a 'standardly' configured Obsidian vault into a Jekyll or Hugo blog, with config-driven paths and exclusions, a post_link_mode for Jekyll/Hugo, and regex find/replace transformations driven from frontmatter.
bad: The README's own caveat: the tool is opinionated — every post must carry a date in frontmatter and only YYYY-MM-DD dates are supported, mainly to align with Jekyll.
didnt: Rejected — an unlicensed, blog-only vault converter with rigid frontmatter demands; the wiki's publishing needs are broader and already served. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fireproof MCP
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) — a LICENSE.md file is present in the repo but GitHub does not classify it
good: A Model Context Protocol server that plugs a Fireproof database into AI systems such as Claude Desktop, implementing a JSON document store with CRUD operations and the ability to query documents sorted by any field, configured through the standard Claude Desktop MCP config and debuggable with the MCP Inspector.
bad: The README itself calls it a simple example/demo: the repo has only 6 commits and 0 releases, and the documented surface is basic CRUD plus field-sorted query only — no access control, permissions, citation or provenance features are documented.
didnt: Rejected — a demo-grade MCP document store with an unclassified licence; our MCP door is read-only and citation-locked by design, and unclassified-licence code is ideas-only at most. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Betula
good: Single-user self-hosted federated bookmark manager: publish bookmarks with Mycomarkup notes and tags, make archive copies of web pages, store the whole collection as a single SQLite file in one binary, with RSS, a bookmarklet, public/private bookmarks, local and mutuals' search, Miniflux integration, and optional Fediverse following/reposting via Mastodon-compatible software.
bad: It is single-user by design, so there is no multi-user or shared-custody model, and its distinguishing feature — Fediverse federation — is outside a private personal wiki's scope. AGPL-3.0 also makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence and a federation-oriented bookmark store of its own; the single-SQLite-file, one-binary packaging is a pattern we already have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Buku
good: Powerful command-line bookmark manager and 'personal textual mini-web': auto-fetched titles/tags/descriptions, auto-import from Firefox/Chrome/Chromium/Vivaldi/Brave/Edge, regex and deep-scan search, smart tag management, a portable merge-able database, import/export to HTML, XBEL, Markdown, RSS/Atom and Orgfile, manual database encryption, Wayback Machine lookup for broken links, and use as a Python library.
bad: It is CLI-first — the browsable GUI is a separate companion (bukuserver) whose HTTP API is stated to be for personal use only — and bookmarks live in its own database rather than in inspectable wiki files, with no citation, provenance or approval-gating model. GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence and a CLI bookmark database that duplicates capture/organisation patterns our file-based wiki already carries, without citation locking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Digibunch
licence: AGPL-3.0 (GNU AGPLv3, stated in the README)
good: A simple online application for creating 'bouquets' (bunches) of links to share, running on PHP 8+ with SQLite by default or MariaDB/MySQL, with author-access protection, configurable rate limits, an optional Digidrive API integration, and a live demo instance.
bad: The scope is link bundles for sharing, not knowledge capture: the README documents no search, archiving, tagging or import/export of a personal collection, and it states that pull requests are no longer accepted for the moment because the maintainer lacks review time. AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence and a link-bundle sharing tool for learners/colleagues, not a knowledge-capture system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Espial
good: Open-source web-based bookmarking server for self-hosted deployments with multiple user accounts, bookmarks stored in SQLite, a bookmarklet that pre-fills URL/title/selected text, file import (including Pinboard and Firefox formats), an API-key-authenticated /api/add and /api/addBulk JSON API, optional archive backends, and internationalisation across 14 languages.
bad: It is a plain bookmark server — no full-text knowledge retrieval, citation or provenance features are documented — and building from source requires Haskell tooling (Stack/GHCup), with Docker as the recommended route. AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence and a plain multi-user bookmark server; its API-key add-bookmark pattern is already covered by our gated write door. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Faved
good: Private bookmark manager built for large collections: customisable nested tags with colour/description, tag rollup into child tags and pinned tags, automatic fetching of titles/descriptions/preview images, duplicate detection, instant search with bulk actions, a PWA with light/dark mode, a Chrome extension, bookmarklet and Apple Shortcuts integration, and import from Chrome/Safari/Firefox/Edge and Raindrop.io/Pocket preserving folder structure as nested tags; self-hosted with all data stored locally on PHP 8/SQLite.
bad: Features the README itself flags as unfinished: automated tagging is only planned and tag icons are 'coming soon'. It is a young project (repo created 2025-06) and a bookmark manager only — no page-content archiving, citation or knowledge-synthesis features are documented.
didnt: Board — nested tags with rollup (a parent tag automatically including its children's items) as a taxonomy idea for wiki topic pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LinkAce
good: Self-hosted link archive with lists and tags, multi-user support with internal sharing, OAuth/OIDC SSO, automated link monitoring that reports unavailable or moved links, automated archiving of saved sites via the Internet Archive, a full REST API covering all features, Zapier integration, advanced filtered search, a bookmarklet, RSS feeds for private and public lists, HTML import/export, and backups to any S3-compatible storage.
bad: The README states it is not meant to replace browser bookmarks but to be a separate curated database — another database store to maintain alongside the wiki — and the maintainer states he offers no free personal support. GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence and a separate Laravel bookmark database; its link-monitoring plus Internet Archive backup pairing confirms our capture design but adds no missing capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linkding
good: Self-hosted bookmark manager designed to be minimal, fast and easy to set up with Docker: clean readable UI, tags, bulk editing, Markdown notes, read-it-later, sharing with users or guests, automatic titles/descriptions/icons, automatic archiving as a local HTML file or on the Internet Archive, Netscape HTML import/export, a PWA, Firefox/Chrome extensions and a bookmarklet, OIDC/proxy SSO, and a REST API.
bad: Minimalism is the stated design goal, so the feature ceiling is deliberately low — no full-text content search, citation or synthesis features are documented — and bookmarks live in the Django app's database rather than in plain files. The README also notes the maintainer may ignore PRs for features that do not align with the project's goals.
didnt: Corroboration — its automatic archiving of each saved page as a local HTML file alongside the bookmark confirms our capture-and-preserve pattern; the manager itself duplicates what our wiki already does. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NeonLink
good: Simple, lightweight self-hosted bookmark service with minimal dependencies and easy Docker installation (images optimised for Raspberry Pi): tags, search, automatic icon/title/description fetching, a customisable-background dashboard, and private local storage on SQLite via a React/Fastify stack.
bad: The documented feature list is only tags, search, auto metadata and a dashboard — the README documents no import/export, archiving, sharing or API, so it is a start-page/dashboard for links rather than a knowledge tool.
didnt: Rejected — a minimal bookmark start-page service; too little capability to board and it duplicates link storage our wiki already provides. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Servas
good: Self-hosted bookmark management with tags, nestable groups and Smart Groups that group bookmarks by their tags, Firefox and Chrome extensions, multiple user accounts with two-factor authentication, JSON and HTML import/export, responsive design with dark/light themes, and Docker deployment preferring SQLite (MySQL/MariaDB also supported).
bad: Another database-backed bookmark server (Laravel/Inertia/Svelte): manual installation requires PHP 8.4, Composer, Node.js and database migrations, and no content archiving, full-text knowledge search or citation features are documented. GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence and a bookmark server duplicating existing capture; its tag-derived Smart Groups are a familiar pattern already expressible in our tag/index layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shaarli
licence: Zlib (zlib/libpng for Shaarli's own files per COPYING; bundled components carry their own licences, including MIT, BSD, CC-BY and LGPL-3+ pieces)
good: Personal, minimalist, super-fast, database-free bookmarking/link-sharing service you install on your own server, designed to be personal (single-user), fast and handy, with a plugin system, a public demo, and a long maintenance history (repo created 2014, 59 releases).
bad: It is deliberately minimalist and single-user, with per-component licensing that must be untangled from COPYING rather than one clean licence, and its linklog model offers no archiving, citation or knowledge-organisation depth beyond sharing links.
didnt: Rejected — a minimalist single-user linklog in its own format; the database-free instinct matches our file-first design but there is no capability here our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shiori
good: Simple bookmark manager in Go, a Pocket-style clone distributed as a single portable binary usable as CLI or web app: add/edit/delete/search bookmarks, Netscape and Pocket import/export, support for SQLite, PostgreSQL, MariaDB and MySQL, and — where possible — automatic parsing of readable page content to create an offline archive of each saved page.
bad: The feature set is basic bookmark management only, and the Firefox/Chrome web extension is explicitly marked BETA in the README; there is no tagging depth, citation or synthesis layer documented beyond the offline page archive.
didnt: Corroboration — its default behaviour of parsing readable content and keeping an offline archive of every saved page confirms our preserve-the-source capture rule; the manager itself is a duplicate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Slash
good: Self-hosted platform for sharing and managing frequently used links: create customisable, human-readable short links (s/shortcut) for any URL, share them publicly or only with teammates, organise with tags and shareable Collections, view analytics on link traffic and sources, and jump to shortcuts from a Chromium/Firefox browser extension; deployable with a single Docker command.
bad: Its purpose is short-link redirection and sharing, not capturing or preserving content — no archiving, content search or knowledge features are documented — and traffic analytics is the opposite of our private, no-tracking custody stance. AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence and a short-link/bookmark-sharing service; human-readable shortcuts are a naming convenience our Lens routes already provide. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SyncMarks
good: Self-hosted synchronisation of Firefox, Edge and Chromium bookmarks with no cloud service, no account and no tracking: a webapp that acts as the central hub for the SyncMarks browser extensions (published on Mozilla Add-ons and the Edge store), lets you add/edit/delete/move bookmarks in any browser, syncs changes back cross-browser, and can also be used standalone as a website.
bad: It is sync plumbing for browser-native bookmarks only — no content capture, search or knowledge features — and the README states the extension cannot be published in the Chrome Web Store (free publication is not allowed there), so Chromium users must sideload it. AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence and browser-bookmark sync plumbing; our sources live in the wiki itself, not in browser bookmark stores that need synchronising. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Atomic Server
licence: MIT (stated in the README's licence section; the Atomic names and logos are reserved trademarks and not covered by that grant)
good: Local-first linked-data workspace and server in one binary (~70MB, with automatic HTTPS): documents, tables with strict schema, kanban/calendar views, full-text search, real-time collaboration, a virtual drive, files, group chat, custom data models in an Ontology Editor, encrypted-at-rest local databases, full versioning where every write is a signed Atomic Commit, hierarchical read/write authorisation, and a RESTful API serving JSON-AD, RDF, Turtle, N-Triples and JSON-LD, with JS/React/Svelte/Rust/Flutter libraries and MCP support for AI features.
bad: The README states the status is alpha and breaking changes are expected until 1.0, and it is a whole database server and workspace that would replace our plain-markdown file store rather than complement it — a custody and migration commitment far beyond a feature adoption.
didnt: Board — signed Atomic Commits (every write a signed, versioned commit with full history) as a provenance-strengthening idea for our hash-chained write ledger. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: server-filesystem (modelcontextprotocol)
licence: Apache-2.0 for new contributions, existing code under MIT (README licence section; GitHub sidebar shows Other/NOASSERTION)
good: The reference Filesystem server in the MCP steering group's repo provides secure file operations with configurable access controls — the client config passes explicit allowed directories (e.g. @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /path/to/allowed/files), so the agent's file reach is scoped by configuration rather than open-ended.
bad: The repo README explicitly warns that its servers are reference implementations meant as educational examples, not production-ready solutions, and that developers must implement their own safeguards for their threat model.
didnt: Corroboration — the allowed-directory scoping of the reference filesystem server confirms our local-first, explicitly-scoped door design for agent file access. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: filestash
good: Storage-agnostic Dropbox-like file manager speaking SFTP, S3, SMB, WebDAV, IPFS, FTP, NFS, Git and about 20 more protocols, with a plugin-driven architecture, web/native/agent clients, gateways that can expose data over protocols including MCP, a workflow engine, and RBAC-style authorisation plugins.
bad: AGPL-3.0 copyleft licence bars code adoption for us, and the scope is a full multi-protocol file-management platform (transcoding, file apps for dozens of formats, commercial support contracts) — far broader than a personal knowledge wiki needs.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence makes the code ideas-only, and a universal file platform duplicates file access our wiki already has through simpler doors. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nodiom-mcp
good: A shared state board for multiple AI agents built on a Markdown-structure engine: agents read current state, claim a card atomically so no two do the same work, edits land by document structure alongside other agents' writes with nothing overwritten, and finished work waits in a human review column — approve or send back, with the decision written into the board. Every board is a plain Markdown file you can download, diff and commit, and the engine is the MIT-licensed @synexiom-labs/nodiom package.
bad: The board itself is a hosted commercial service (free for agents, Pro in private beta at source), and the site documents the board workflow rather than a self-hostable MCP server's tool surface or data-custody terms in detail.
didnt: Board — structure-based (not regex) Markdown edits, atomic card claiming, and an approval review column are a strong pattern for multi-agent work over plain Markdown files like our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: safe-docx
good: Local MCP server and CLI for reading, searching, editing, comparing and saving DOCX/ODT files with coding agents: it preserves document structure and formatting, edits by paragraph anchor, and can save both clean and native tracked-changes (w:ins/w:del) output, including plan-based batch edits that validate all steps before applying any.
bad: Its own README lists explicit non-goals: it is not a visual editor or layout engine, provides no browser rendering, real-time collaboration or pixel-level pagination guarantees, and .dotx templates must be converted to .docx first; the 30-tool surface is also heavy for a single-format editor.
didnt: Board — clean-plus-redline DOCX editing with formatting preservation is a candidate pattern for any future Word-document workflow in our document pipeline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pdf-card-mcp
good: Local-first MCP server and CLI that turns dense local PDFs into portable, source-linked HTML card readers: it preserves source text, renders source pages for verification, crops tables/figures/formulas as faithful images, emits a manifest with card/page/source anchors, and keeps user notes/highlights separate and exportable as Markdown. Default processing is fully local, and optional LLM sampling is validation-bounded so source text cannot be rewritten.
bad: Self-described as an early implementation: useful for text-layer PDFs now, table detection is best-effort (pdfplumber, optional gmft), scanned PDFs need optional OCR support, and annotation import is not yet exposed in the reader UI.
didnt: Board — source-linked PDF cards with a manifest of source anchors are directly relevant to our citation-locking approach for reading long PDFs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MySQL-AIops / Postgres-AIops / Queue-AIops
good: A family of governed database/queue ops tools (Postgres, MySQL, Redis/RabbitMQ queues) shipped as CLI plus MCP server (35 tools in the Postgres member): every tool passes through a @governed_tool harness that logs every call (params, result, status, duration, risk tier, approver/rationale) to an audit database with no unaudited entry point, writes support dry-run previews, reversible writes record an inverse built from the fetched real before-state for undo, credentials live in an encrypted store, and a runaway guard trips on looped calls.
bad: Coverage is intentionally a curated subset of each system's catalog/maintenance surface; irreversible operations (e.g. kill_session, optimize_table) record prior state for audit but declare no undo, and the risk tier is a descriptive audit label that, by the README's own words, gates nothing.
didnt: Corroboration — the unbypassable audit log, dry-run-everywhere and undo-from-before-state harness confirms our approval-gated, audited write design for agent tools. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mnemiq
good: Governed text-to-SQL that pairs a stochastic proposer (a small open-weights model, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B on a 24 GB card) with a deterministic decider: a ten-check pipeline (shape, per-identity access, denied/masked columns, view and value checks, lineage recording, row-filter/mask injection, proof against the real source) refuses, rewrites or approves every candidate, tables a caller may not see never enter the model's context, and the system declines rather than answers when the data cannot support an answer.
bad: The paper itself reports hard limits: a residual wrong-answer rate of 38–41% survives every calibration method, the baseline 14B configuration defers 73.9% of questions, results do not transfer to Spider 2.0-lite (every local configuration sits in a 2–6% band), and the verification judge is fail-open — an unreachable judge scores the answer as approved.
didnt: Board — the proposer/decider split, decline-rather-than-answer obligation and the measured verification cost ladder are strong evidence for our scored-abstention design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Agentic Fabriq

name: schemabrain
good: Read-only trust and intelligence layer between AI agents and a SQL database: the agent never writes SQL — 12 MCP tools compile strictly parameterized read-only SQL from operator-controlled definitions over a semantic layer (column meanings, mined join paths, a knowledge graph), PII and secret categories are classified per column and refused before the query runs (credentials, government IDs and card data hard-blocked), and every call lands in a SHA-256 hash-chained tamper-evident audit log.
bad: Postgres only at source ('Postgres today' in its directory listing; the site's quickstart points it at a Postgres URL), and it is a young, small project (12 tools, single-digit forks in its listing), so the semantic-layer approach is unproven at scale.
didnt: Board — definition-compiled queries (never agent-written SQL) plus PII refusal and a hash-chained audit row are the pattern to copy if our wiki ever grows a database door. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: schemagate
good: Text-to-SQL access control applied at schema selection, before the model writes anything: it filters the schema by the caller's grants (principal + roles over MCP tools select_schema, list_objects, describe_object), so restricted tables and columns are absent from the prompt rather than ranked low, a restricted object and a missing one return the same error so existence does not leak, and selection cuts prompt size by roughly 65–97% on its test schemas across Postgres, Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and SQLite.
bad: By the author's own account it does not learn — it reflects and ranks the schema, with no question/SQL feedback memory like the archived Vanna it positions against — and live dialect certification is incomplete: PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite are live-tested, while SQL Server and MySQL have only been reflected against, with no live instance run.
didnt: Board — per-principal visibility filtering applied before anything reaches the model's context (absent, not ranked low, with existence non-leakage) is the right shape for any future per-reader retrieval scoping in our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: datacharter
good: Local, contract-governed data plane for AI agents: a charter.yaml data contract grants access per source → table → column over files and databases (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Snowflake, BigQuery, Iceberg, Delta) federated by DuckDB; the engine is read-only by construction (writes/DDL refused at the parser), auto-detected PII defaults to no agent access and is masked unless explicitly granted, policies like aggregates-only and k-anonymity group minimums are enforced by query analysis, and every access is written to a tamper-evident hash-chained flight recorder, with optional canary honeytoken tripwires.
bad: The PyPI page states its status plainly: pre-release, V1 still in development; the desktop app is beta and unsigned on macOS/Windows, so the governance surface is not yet a finished product.
didnt: Board — a declarative contract that grants agents exactly the columns chosen, with PII default-deny and a hash-chained flight recorder, is a clean model for contract-governed retrieval over our own sources. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: coremcp
good: Single-binary Go MCP server exposing SQL databases (MSSQL and PostgreSQL adapters) with read-only mode on by default, automatic schema discovery including column comments, custom parameterized query tools defined in YAML config, a fail-closed T-SQL-aware lexer that strips comments/literals and rejects anything but SELECT/WITH (including multi-statement payloads), a forced row cap, and regex-based PII masking of results (credit cards, emails, SSNs, IBANs and custom patterns).
bad: Unfinished edges are visible in its own README: the Firebird adapter factory returns a placeholder error, MySQL and HTTP transport are roadmap items, and audit logging — a headline need for governed database access — is still on the roadmap rather than built; its PII masking is regex post-processing, which the README frames as one layer, not the only layer.
didnt: Corroboration — fail-closed query validation, read-only-by-default sources and forced row caps confirm the hardening shape we want for any agent data door; its unbuilt audit log shows why audit cannot be an afterthought. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: genai-toolbox (Google)
good: Google's open-source MCP Toolbox for Databases: prebuilt generic tools for instant schema exploration and querying across many databases (Google Cloud's AlloyDB, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Spanner, Firestore, plus PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch and more), and a custom-tools framework where production agents get predefined structured queries, semantic search and NL2SQL defined in tools.yaml, with connection pooling, integrated auth and OpenTelemetry observability handled by the server.
bad: Scope is enterprise database connectivity in general, not knowledge-work: its prebuilt toolsets include a generic execute_sql tool, so the safety of a deployment rests on the operator's own tool definitions and auth configuration, and the README documents no PII masking, citation or abstention behaviour.
didnt: Corroboration — predefined structured tools and toolsets over raw free-form SQL confirm our restricted-tool door design, though the toolbox itself is far outside a personal wiki's scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: chroma-mcp
good: Chroma's own MCP server for self-hosted Chroma access: ephemeral, persistent, HTTP and Chroma Cloud client types, full collection management (create/modify/delete, HNSW configuration, embedding-function selection) and document operations with vector search, full-text search and metadata filtering through twelve chroma_* tools.
bad: It is a thin vendor door onto one vector database: the README notes embedding-function persistence is unsupported for collections created on Chroma ≤0.6.3, and several supported embedding functions (Cohere, OpenAI, Jina, VoyageAI) require external API keys, sending embeddings traffic outside local custody.
didnt: Rejected — a Chroma-specific vector-store server duplicates retrieval our stack already covers and would tie the wiki's door to a database we do not run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ArcadeDB MCP
good: ArcadeDB is a full multi-model DBMS (graph, document, key/value, search, time-series and vector models; SQL, Cypher, Gremlin, GraphQL and MongoDB query languages; 70+ built-in graph algorithms, ACID transactions) with a built-in MCP server, so AI assistants can query it directly — its release notes add vector/hybrid/full-text search tools, GraphRAG prompts and per-principal, per-database tool scoping on that MCP surface.
bad: The MCP server is a feature of adopting the whole database: ArcadeDB requires a JVM (Java 21, with a separate Java 17 branch), and migrating a Markdown wiki into a multi-model DBMS is a platform replacement, not an addition; its own comparison page names the JVM dependency as the one genuine tradeoff.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a JVM multi-model DBMS replacement for a plain-Markdown, local-first wiki, however capable its built-in MCP tools are. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Raneto
good: A free, open, simple Markdown-powered knowledge base for Node.js: all content is file-based, it searches file names and contents, offers a Markdown editor in the browser, and has a login system for edit protection.
bad: The feature set is deliberately minimal — the README's top features stop at file-based content, search, the browser editor and login protection; no version history, comments, or multi-user roles are documented at the source.
didnt: Corroboration — a file-based Markdown knowledge base with search and login-gated editing confirms our local-first flat-file design; it adds nothing our wiki portal lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wiki-Go
good: A modern databaseless flat-file wiki in Go: full Markdown editing with Mermaid and LaTeX, smart full-text search with highlighting, hierarchical pages with version history, user management with access control and private mode, comments, Kanban boards, a REST API, and instant setup via Docker or prebuilt binaries.
bad: A very young project (repository created 2025-04-04) from a single studio, and the README itself warns that non-SSL setups need an insecure-cookies setting that reduces security; the GPL-3.0 copyleft also bars code adoption for us.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and its flat-file serving duplicates what our wiki already does. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: django-wiki
good: A mature wiki system for simple integration into Django projects: a stable model and plugin API, a pluggable lightweight core with an extension API, Markdown stored in a structured way in the database, notifications, and full translation into 13 languages, maintained via PyPI with SemVer releases.
bad: It is database-backed through Django models rather than flat files, customisation requires learning Django (the README warns against hard-copying the repo and describes hard-copying Bootstrap SCSS for theming), and the GPL-3.0 copyleft bars code adoption for us.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence plus a Django/database stack that does not fit our local-first flat-file wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docmost
good: An open-source collaborative wiki and documentation platform positioned as a Confluence/Notion alternative: real-time collaboration, diagrams (Draw.io, Excalidraw, Mermaid), spaces, permissions management, groups, comments, page history, search, file attachments and embeds, with translations in 10+ languages.
bad: The core is AGPL-3.0 while enterprise features sit under a separate Docmost Enterprise licence in dedicated directories, so the open edition is deliberately split from the commercial one; the README documents no flat-file/plain-Markdown storage — content lives inside the application, not as files we could keep custody of.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and its database-backed team-collaboration scope does not fit a personal local-first LLM wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MediaWiki
good: An extremely powerful, scalable, feature-rich wiki implementation designed for a site getting millions of hits per day: PHP processing data stored in a database, easy wikitext editing without HTML/CSS knowledge, every edit kept so vandalism or spam can be reverted, image and multimedia management, caching and proxy support, and structured-data handling via extensions.
bad: The manual itself cautions that MediaWiki is geared towards the needs of the Wikimedia projects and that if your needs are radically different the software might not be appropriate, and that operators must keep up with security upgrades; it is a PHP/database server stack using its own wikitext, not Markdown flat files, and GPL code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Corroboration — its keep-every-revision, easy-revert history model confirms our wiki's history-first, never-lose-a-version design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PmWiki
good: A PHP wiki designed to be easy to install, configure and maintain: it stores all data in flat files so no MySQL or other utilities are needed, upgrades are a simple copy-over that preserves local customisations, pages can be password-protected individually or in sections, and custom markup is easy to add for specialised applications.
bad: The core package is deliberately feature-limited under the PmWiki philosophy, with most capability arriving through add-on 'Recipes' rather than the core; it uses its own wiki markup dialect rather than Markdown, and GPL code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Corroboration — flat-file storage with a minimal core and extension recipes confirms our local-first, files-you-can-copy custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XWiki
good: A generic enterprise wiki platform offering runtime services for applications built on top of it: WYSIWYG and wiki-syntax editing, structured data with custom classes and objects, fine-grained permissions, versioning, multi-language support, a large extension ecosystem, and REST and scripting APIs, with a very long development history (56,545 commits in the platform repo).
bad: It is a heavyweight Java enterprise platform requiring a Java/Tomcat and database deployment — far beyond personal-wiki scale — and the platform repo README is only a stub that points to external documentation, guides and a separate Jira issue tracker for everything substantive.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: an enterprise Java platform with structured-data applications is the opposite direction from our personal local-first flat-file wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zim
good: A graphical desktop wiki editor: pages with links, simple formatting and images stored in a folder structure like an outliner, all data in plain text files with wiki formatting, new pages created by linking to a nonexistent page, and plugins adding a task list manager, equation editor, tray icon and version-control support.
bad: It is a desktop-only GTK application (requiring Gtk+ >= 3.18 and Python 3.10+) with no web server, sharing or collaboration documented in the README, and the GPL-2.0 copyleft bars code adoption for us.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-2.0 licence, and a single-user desktop editor duplicates note-keeping our wiki already covers with a web portal on top. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AmuseWiki
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) on GitHub; project licence text is the Perl 5 terms (GPL or Artistic License)
good: A library-oriented wiki engine and publishing platform using Text::Amuse markup (mostly compatible with Emacs Muse) and a Git backend: it produces high-quality EPUB and LaTeX-quality PDF output, has a bookbuilder for merging and customising texts, an OPDS server for reading apps, flat-file/Git archiving, multisite operation on one instance, and can run as a read-only, moderated, open or private site.
bad: It is a Perl/Catalyst application built around the niche Emacs Muse markup rather than Markdown, installation involves a substantial Perl/TeX toolchain per its install documentation, the README warns its extensive test suite must not be run in a production directory, and GitHub cannot classify its licence (NOASSERTION), so its code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Board — the bookbuilder idea: assembling selected wiki texts into print-quality PDF/EPUB editions, which matches our beautiful-PDF delivery preference. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WackoWiki
good: A light and easy to install multilingual wiki engine: WYTIWYG editing, per-page rights (ACLs), design themes (skins), file upload, email notification and much more, compatible with PHP 8.3–8.5 and MariaDB/MySQL/SQLite, with a long release history (70 releases).
bad: It is database-backed (MariaDB/MySQL/SQLite) rather than flat-file, uses its own wiki markup, and is a very small project by visible community measures (55 stars, 10 forks on GitHub) — a traditional PHP wiki with no capability our stack lacks.
didnt: Rejected — fit and duplication: despite the permissive BSD licence, a database-backed PHP wiki engine offers nothing missing from our flat-file system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wiki.js
good: A widely adopted modern wiki built on Node.js, Git and Markdown (29,063 stars, 145 releases): the project site offers Markdown/WYSIWYG/HTML editors, Git storage synchronisation, multiple search backends and many authentication providers, with path-based page organisation and a GraphQL API.
bad: The default branch opened is a BETA of the upcoming 3.0 release that the README itself flags 'NOT FOR PRODUCTION USE', with the stable 2.x line kept in a separate repository; it is database-backed, and the AGPL-3.0 copyleft bars code adoption for us.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and its database-backed server model duplicates our wiki portal without its citation/abstention layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tiki
good: A full-featured, tightly integrated all-in-one Wiki+CMS+Groupware platform in PHP: a wiki engine plus articles, forums, blogs, file galleries, trackers, polls, calendars, maps, spreadsheets and an advanced permission system for users and groups, all administered through a browser interface and described by its project as the open-source web application with the most built-in features.
bad: Its all-in-one design has the drawback, stated at the source, of an extremely large codebase (more than 1,000,000 lines), and it requires a PHP web server with a MySQL/MariaDB database — a monolithic groupware suite far beyond a personal wiki's needs.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a million-line all-in-one CMS/groupware suite is the opposite of our small, auditable, local-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Documize
good: An open-source, self-hosted, enterprise-grade knowledge management solution built with Go + EmberJS and compiled to a single executable binary for Linux, Windows and Mac: organisation through labels, spaces and categories, unification of internal and customer-facing documentation, LDAP/Active Directory/Keycloak/CAS authentication, and localisation in nine languages.
bad: It requires an external database (PostgreSQL, SQL Server or MySQL variants) with mandatory full-text search support, and the README reserves content approval workflows, version management, lifecycle management, feedback capture, PDF export, analytics and audit logs to the paid Community+ enterprise edition; the AGPL-3.0 copyleft also bars code adoption for us.
didnt: Corroboration — its enterprise tier is built around content approval workflows, version management and audit logs, confirming our approval-gated writes and audit-first design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cortex
good: Cortex's service catalog API Explorer supports both OpenAPI and AsyncAPI specifications and lets a single service carry multiple API specs for different versions, types, or environments. API documentation can live inside the Cortex service descriptor itself (a fully compliant OpenAPI spec) or Cortex can point to documentation hosted elsewhere, so it is agnostic to how specs are generated.
bad: Cortex is a commercial hosted internal developer portal, not a self-hostable documentation generator: API documentation is one catalog feature inside a paid SaaS platform, with no open licence stated on the product page. It offers no local-first, files-on-disk publishing path of its own.
didnt: Rejected — hosted commercial portal with no open licence; scope and custody model conflict with our local-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docmd
good: Zero-config documentation compiler: point it at a Markdown folder and it generates a static site with automatic navigation, an offline full-text search index, sitemap and SEO/Open Graph metadata. The same source also compiles to llms.txt/llms-full.txt, Open Knowledge Format bundles and an MCP interface for coding agents, plus a RAG-powered AI assistant, versioning, i18n and OpenAPI 3.x rendering.
bad: Very young project (repository created 2025-05-08) requiring Node.js 20+, and its AI Assistant on a static site depends on the hosted docmd Cloud Relay or a self-run AI backend. The README documents no citation, provenance or approval-gating features.
didnt: Board — single-source multi-output idea: compile one Markdown tree simultaneously to website, offline search index, llms.txt and a structured knowledge format for agents. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Docnado
good: A rapid documentation tool in Python with Jinja2 templates, described in the listing as 'batteries and style included; you just need to type' — i.e. a styled docs site with minimal setup from the author.
bad: A very small project: the listing entry is a single line with no documented search, versioning, or evaluation features, and no fuller primary-source documentation surfaced. It observably duplicates the much larger MkDocs-class Python generators.
didnt: Rejected — minimal, small-scale Python docs generator duplicating MkDocs/Sphinx-class tooling, with no knowledge-layer features. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DocPad
good: File-based dynamic static site generator: content in any markup, templating engine or pre-processor via a plugin system, with metadata, nested layouts, a query engine for content listings, built-in watch recompilation, a built-in server, and dynamic documents for search pages and forms.
bad: A general website engine rather than a documentation tool — the README lists no built-in docs search or navigation model. The repository shows 0 releases despite 263 tags, its GitHub licence detection reports Other/NOASSERTION even though the README names MIT, and the stack is an ageing CoffeeScript/Node ecosystem dating from 2011.
didnt: Rejected — general-purpose ageing SSG, not a documentation/knowledge system; duplicates the static publishing our stack already has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Docsify
good: Turns one or more Markdown files into a website with no build process required: simple and lightweight, with a smart full-text search plugin, multiple themes, a plugin API and emoji support. Deployable from a single index.html on GitHub Pages or any static host.
bad: By design there are no statically built HTML files — pages render in the browser at runtime, so output depends on JavaScript/CDN delivery rather than a build-time artifact that can be validated or citation-checked. Core search is a plugin, and the README lists no versioning or offline guarantees.
didnt: Rejected — runtime-rendered docs conflict with our build-time validated, static, citation-locked publishing model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Doctave
good: Opinionated, batteries-included documentation generator in Rust, distributed as a single self-contained binary: Mermaid diagrams, offline full-text search, broken-link checking, live-reloading local server, mathematical typesetting, dark mode and responsive design with minimal configuration and fast builds.
bad: Deliberately narrow and opinionated — the README stresses it is not a generic site generator and offers fewer customisation paths. It is not published on crates.io (install is via Homebrew compilation or cargo install from a Git tag), and the project is small (670 stars, 214 commits, 8 releases).
didnt: Board — batteries-included single-binary pattern with built-in broken-link checking and offline search as a build gate for a docs/wiki publisher. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Doctor
good: Doctor converts JavaScript source to documentation using rules that rely on conventions so comment tags are mostly not needed: sources are parsed to an AST, refined with transform rules (including JSDoc-style tags for what cannot be inferred), and emitted as a JSON report renderable to HTML, with mergeable views. Its modular design allows custom grammars and rules, doubling as a general AST analysis tool.
bad: Stale and narrow: the npm package page shows version 0.3.0 published about 12 years ago, Markdown support is described in its own README as initial and rough, and it covers JavaScript source only. No licence is stated on the package or listing pages.
didnt: Rejected — stale, JavaScript-only, and no licence stated at source, so ideas-only at best; no fit for a Markdown knowledge wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Docusaurus
good: Meta-maintained generator for building, deploying and maintaining open source project websites easily, shipping the key pages (home, docs section, blog) out of the box, with localization support via Crowdin and deep customisation. Large, actively maintained ecosystem (66,546 stars, 157 releases).
bad: A heavyweight React/Node.js website stack: getting started is via npm init and a JavaScript toolchain, and the customisation model is React components rather than plain Markdown processing. The README describes a project-website tool, with no knowledge-layer, citation or retrieval features.
didnt: Rejected — capable docs SSG but it duplicates the static publishing layer we already run (Lens on Azure Static Web Apps) and adds a React build chain with no knowledge features. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: eziwiki
good: A combined docs + wiki generator whose own documentation shows reader-facing wiki features: sidebar navigation, search, graph and backlink panels, and a generated sitemap.xml. Pages are controlled from frontmatter or a navigation array, including hidden pages that are built and reachable by URL but excluded from navigation, search results, graph/backlink panels and the sitemap, with a noindex robots tag.
bad: Its own documentation warns that a hidden page is still a public file in the static export — hashed URLs are obscurity, not access control, and sensitive content must simply not be published. No licence is stated on the documentation site pages opened.
didnt: Board — hidden/unlisted page pattern (excluded from nav, search, graph and sitemap, with noindex) for draft or direct-link-only wiki pages, with the explicit warning that hiding is not access control. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GitBook
good: Hosted documentation platform: write in the GitBook editor, publish a docs site with customisations and integrations, and use Git Sync for two-way synchronisation with a GitHub or GitLab repository, including branch-based edits, change notifications, in-editor review and preview, and merge — all available on the free plan. A Sponsored plan makes docs sites free for open source projects.
bad: Hosted and proprietary: there is no self-hosted option on the pages opened, advanced capability is split across paid site plans, and the free Sponsored plan places a small ad in the corner of the project's docs in exchange for revenue. Content custody sits with the hosted platform rather than local files.
didnt: Rejected — hosted proprietary platform; its custody and plan-gating conflict with our local-first, owner-controlled wiki, though its Git Sync review flow is noted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HonKit
good: Maintained fork of GitBook (Legacy) for building beautiful books from GitHub/Git and Markdown or AsciiDoc, outputting a website or an ebook (PDF, ePub, Mobi), with multi-language support, glossary, variables/templating, content references and plugins. It keeps near-full GitBook plugin compatibility while improving build/serve performance (file cache by default; serve 28.2s to 0.9s in its benchmark), is rewritten in TypeScript as a monorepo, and ships Docker support.
bad: It inherits the legacy GitBook book model and plugin ecosystem, so it is a book/docs renderer with no search, graph or knowledge-management features in its README feature list, and ebook output depends on the bundled PDF/ePub toolchain in its Docker image.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms the maintained-fork pattern for keeping a deprecated Markdown book/docs toolchain alive, the same publishing shape as our Markdown-to-static wiki layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mdBook
good: Rust utility to create modern online books from Markdown files — 'like GitBook but implemented in Rust' — maintained by the Rust project, mature and widely used (22,237 stars, 103 releases), with a full User Guide that itself serves as a demonstration book.
bad: The README is deliberately minimal and points to the external User Guide for features; the model is a linear book structure, and the repository page documents no search, graph, citation or knowledge-management layer. Its MPL-2.0 licence is file-level copyleft for any code reuse.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms plain Markdown source compiled by a small native tool into a static book/site as a durable publishing layer, matching our wiki's Markdown-first design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MkDocs
good: Fast, simple static site generator geared to project documentation: Markdown source files configured with a single YAML configuration file, extensible with plugins and Markdown extensions, with built-in, third-party or custom themes, and output publishable anywhere static files can be served.
bad: Core is deliberately thin — the README's feature list is four bullets ending in 'Much more!', with capability such as richer themes and plugins living in third-party projects, and support for third-party features explicitly out of scope for the core team. No versioning, citation or knowledge features are documented in the core README.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms the single-YAML-config, Markdown-to-static publishing pattern our Lens already follows; no new capability to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Slate
good: API documentation generator with a clean, intuitive three-part design — descriptions on the left, code examples on the right — putting the entire documentation on a single linkable page. Authoring is plain Markdown including multi-language code sample tabs, with out-of-the-box syntax highlighting for over 100 languages, an automatic smoothly scrolling table of contents, RTL support, and GitHub Pages hosting by default.
bad: The GitHub repository opened is archived and reduced to a migration notice: the creator removed Slate from GitHub in January 2026, leaving only a read-only archive on his own site. It is also a Ruby/Middleman stack, and its single-page model is aimed at API references rather than multi-page knowledge bases.
didnt: Rejected — upstream archived and removed from GitHub, Ruby/Middleman stack, and single-page API-reference scope does not fit our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: swarmclawai/swarmvault
good: Local-first LLM Wiki on Karpathy's three-layer pattern (immutable raw/, generated wiki/, schema) with a typed knowledge graph, hybrid SQLite FTS + embedding search, contradiction detection, approval bundles (compile --approve, candidates first), MCP server, and an offline heuristic provider requiring no API keys.
bad: Duplicates a pattern our wiki already implements, so it is a parallel implementation rather than a missing capability. Requires Node >=24 and its full feature set (graph viewer, context packs, watch mode, scheduled automation) is a large toolchain to adopt wholesale.
didnt: Corroboration — its three-layer architecture, edge typing (extracted/inferred/ambiguous), contradiction lint and approval-staged compiles confirm our wiki design; no code needed as we already have the pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: swarmclawai/swarmclaw
good: Self-hosted multi-agent runtime with durable agent memory, MCP tools, skills, delegation, schedules/heartbeats and 23+ LLM providers, plus desktop, npm and Docker installs and an org-chart view of agent teams.
bad: Scope is an autonomous agent runtime/swarm framework, not a knowledge wiki; adopting it would replace rather than extend our stack. Its breadth (marketplace, social feed, crypto operations use cases) is far beyond a personal local-first wiki.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a multi-agent runtime, not a missing wiki capability, and duplicative of our existing agent setup. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WujiangXu/A-mem-sys
good: Production-oriented A-MEM implementation: Zettelkasten-style dynamic memory organisation, LLM-generated keywords/context/tags, ChromaDB storage with embeddings over content plus metadata, dynamic linking between memories and continuous memory evolution, with OpenAI/Ollama/SGLang/OpenRouter backends.
bad: Small, research-grade codebase (21 commits, no releases) and the README notes paper results are reproduced in a separate repository. Memory evolution is automatic and LLM-driven, with no approval gate or citation locking, which conflicts with our approval-gated writes.
didnt: Corroboration — Zettelkasten note generation, metadata-enriched embeddings and link-based memory evolution confirm our compiled-wiki linking approach, without its ungated auto-evolution. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DEEP-PolyU/Awesome-GraphMemory
good: Curated survey companion for graph-based agent memory with a clear taxonomy — memory extraction, storage (knowledge-graph, hierarchical, temporal, hypergraph, hybrid), retrieval and evolution — plus related surveys, benchmarks and open-source projects, tied to its arXiv survey paper.
bad: It is a reading list, not a runnable memory system: the repo contains only a README and figures. No licence is stated at source, so its content cannot be reused beyond reading.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and fit: a survey list we have already catalogued, with no licence stated at source and no implementable component for our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU)

name: FareedKhan-dev/optimize-ai-agent-memory
good: Hands-on tutorial coding and comparing 9 agent-memory techniques — sliding window, summarisation, retrieval, memory-augmented transformers, hierarchical, graph-based, compression/consolidation and OS-like management — each with stated advantages and drawbacks, in a single notebook with a cheatsheet.
bad: A blog/tutorial notebook, not a library or production system: only 2 commits, a placeholder API key and a hosted Nebius endpoint in the examples, and no tests or packaging beyond requirements.txt.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and fit: teaching material illustrating techniques we already use, not an adoptable component. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: joshuadavidthomas/opencode-agent-memory
good: Letta-style editable memory blocks for OpenCode as plain markdown files with YAML frontmatter (label, description, soft size limit, read_only), five memory tools, cache-stable per-session snapshots, and an optional append-only journal with local-embedding semantic search where no data leaves the machine.
bad: The README itself labels the plugin experimental, and it is tied to OpenCode v2.0.12+ only. Its self-editing model lets the agent overwrite its own memory blocks, with no approval gate or citation discipline.
didnt: Rejected — fit: an OpenCode-specific plugin whose ungated self-editing conflicts with our approval-gated writes; our block/journal ideas are already implemented differently. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: aayoawoyemi/Ori-Mnemos
good: Local-first persistent agent memory where markdown on disk is the truth and a SQLite index is derived: wiki-links as graph edges, ACT-R activation decay, spreading activation, Q-value reranking and co-occurrence edges, exposed via CLI, MCP server and library, with unusually candid published benchmarks including a dedicated forgetting evaluation (ForgetEval).
bad: Young, fast-moving project (created 2026-02, v0.7.0) whose own README documents weak spots: purge at 64% on discriminating ForgetEval cases, and multi-hop (0.528) and temporal (0.565) recall as its weakest LoCoMo categories, with small single-run HotpotQA comparison (n=50). The learned index state is not derivable from the markdown, so it must be exported before rebuilds.
didnt: Board — the forgetting/supersession benchmark discipline and its retrieval-intelligence layers (Q-value reranking, co-occurrence edges) as ideas to test against our truth-aware retrieval gap; the system itself duplicates our markdown-plus-index stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: redis/agent-memory-server
good: Two-tier agent memory (session memory with configurable TTL, plus long-term memory of extracted facts stored as text and vector embeddings with background promotion) offered via Python/TypeScript SDKs and REST API, with a public LongMemEval benchmark harness auditing the shipping API and other systems.
bad: The supported product is Redis's managed Iris/Redis Cloud service; the README states the in-repo V0 server is the original open-source research foundation, kept as a research artifact and not the supported production distribution. That managed, Redis-backed model conflicts with our local-first, file-custody design.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a managed cloud memory service built on Redis, not a local-first store we can hold custody of. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Prompthon-IO/agent-systems-handbook
licence: no licence name stated at source (GitHub sidebar reports Other/NOASSERTION)
good: Practical handbook covering agent systems end to end — foundations, agentic workflows, LangGraph, MCP/A2A, context engineering, agent memory, evaluation, observability and multi-agent architecture — organised into parallel Explorer, Practitioner, Builder and Contributor learning paths grounded in industry practice.
bad: It is documentation/learning content, not software or a memory system, so there is nothing to integrate. The licence name is not stated in the README and GitHub reports it only as Other/NOASSERTION, so reuse terms are unclear at source.
didnt: Rejected — fit and licence: a handbook for learners, duplicative of material already surveyed, with no licence name stated at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yxf203/Awesome-Efficient-Agents
good: Survey and paper list on efficiency-guided LLM agents organised across memory (latent/parametric, textual, graph-based, hierarchical, multi-agent), tool use (selection, calling, tool-integrated reasoning) and planning, with lightweight notes connecting each topic to efficiency and links to the companion survey and project page.
bad: A curated paper list only — the repo contains just a README and assets, with no code, data or evaluation. No licence is stated at source.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and fit: a bibliography on efficient agents, useful as survey corroboration only, with no implementable component and no licence stated at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Prismer-AI/PrismerCloud
good: Agent harness offering cross-agent learning: an Evolution Engine using Thompson Sampling over recorded error/fix outcomes, 4-type memory with consolidation, context compression, 120+ API endpoints, SDKs in TypeScript/Python/Go/Rust, an MCP server with 47 tools, and a DID/Ed25519 Agent Identity Protocol.
bad: Despite the catalogue's self-hosted framing, the README quick start routes through prismer.cloud sign-in, an API key saved to ~/.prismer/config.toml and free credits, and its learning model depends on sharing outcomes across a hosted network — the opposite of private, local-first custody. Its scope (task marketplace with credit escrow, agent social/community features, messaging) is far beyond a personal wiki.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a hosted, networked agent runtime whose shared-learning and credit model conflicts with our private local-first custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IAAR-Shanghai/Awesome-AI-Memory
good: Centralised, continuously updated knowledge base on AI memory for LLMs and agents, systematically organising frontier research, engineering frameworks, system designs, evaluation benchmarks and real applications across long-term memory, reasoning, retrieval and memory-native system design, in English and Chinese editions.
bad: A curated knowledge base/list, not a runnable memory system — the repository is documentation plus screening/scripts folders, so there is no component to adopt. Its value is bibliographic and overlaps the other awesome-lists already catalogued.
didnt: Rejected — duplication: another curated AI-memory list; survey corroboration only, nothing to build from. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: chunxiaoxx/nautilus-compass
licence: Modified MIT (per README licence badge; GitHub sidebar reports Other/NOASSERTION)
good: Pairs an open memory layer for agents with independent verification: a NACRE judge, the caliber-bench meta-benchmark and preregistered criteria, with local-first and MCP topics, extensive benchmark reproduction documentation and published results — memory treated as a reliability problem, not just retrieval.
bad: Extremely sprawling repository (over 2,000 commits and hundreds of root-level handoff, broadcast and scratch files alongside the code), which makes the supported surface hard to identify. Its licence is a modified MIT variant reported by GitHub as Other/NOASSERTION, so the code is not cleanly reusable.
didnt: Board — independent judging of memory with preregistered criteria and a meta-benchmark for the judges themselves, as a reliability idea for our scored-abstention and verification work; code is ideas-only under its modified licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vshulcz/deja-vu
good: Builds coding-agent memory from session history already on disk across 42 harnesses, as one local Go binary with no LLM and no server: fast indexing, session-start and failure-triggered recall via MCP and hooks, cross-agent handoff, decisions marked accepted/rejected, changed-file warnings, and credentials stripped to redaction markers during indexing; it reports 97.2% R@5 on LongMemEval-S.
bad: Its entire premise is mining agent session transcripts, which is a source class outside our ingest rules. Recall quality rests on raw transcript search rather than a compiled, citation-locked wiki, and semantic recall is optional and sends queries to a configured embedding endpoint.
didnt: Rejected — fit: session-transcript ingest is not an approved source for our wiki, and transcript recall is a weaker custody model than our compiled, citation-locked pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fuyuxiang/echo-agent
good: Open-source, self-hostable agent runtime with layered cognitive memory (current task, session summaries, long-term facts, archive) using hybrid retrieval, time decay for environmental memory and conflict detection, plus skill self-evolution where candidates are validated and benchmarked before promotion (high-risk ones go to human review, promoted skills can be rolled back) and permission policies gating tool calls; runs in terminal, as a Gateway service, or embedded in its desktop app.
bad: A full desktop agent runtime, not a knowledge store — adopting it would replace our stack rather than fill a gap — and it requires Python 3.11+ plus at least one model-service API key. Primary documentation is Chinese-language, and its desktop build chain (Node, pnpm, Rust, protoc) is heavy.
didnt: Corroboration — its gated skill promotion (validate, benchmark, human review for high-risk, rollback after promotion) and permission-checked tool calls confirm our approval-gated write design; the runtime itself is out of scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: brat
good: Web-based tool for structured text annotation: typed text-span annotations, binary relations, n-ary event associations, attributes (e.g. factual vs speculative), and normalization annotations linking mentions to resources such as Wikipedia. Annotation categories, types and constraints are fully configurable, and it adds NLP techniques to support human annotation efforts.
bad: The homepage lists the current version as v1.3 'Crunchy Frog' dated 2012-11-08, a very old release line, and running your own annotation effort means creating and managing a local brat installation yourself.
didnt: Rejected — brat builds labelled NLP corpora through span/relation annotation; our wiki needs citation-locked pages and approval-gated writes, not a corpus-labelling UI, and the release line is from 2012. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rubrix (now Argilla)
good: Collaboration tool for AI engineers and domain experts to build high-quality datasets: collecting human feedback for traditional NLP, LLMs (RAG, preference tuning) and multimodal models, with a programmatic approach for continuous evaluation, plus filters, AI feedback suggestions and semantic search to speed labelling. Deployable on Hugging Face Spaces with a Python SDK (pip install argilla).
bad: The README carries a maintainer notice that the original authors have moved on: the codebase is described as mature and stable but no new features will be added, only bug fixes and patches. Use also requires deploying an Argilla Server and connecting the client with an API URL and API key.
didnt: Board — Argilla-style dataset curation and labelling UI for owner-labelled examples, the exact input our judge-calibration work is blocked on; the project being feature-frozen is acceptable for a bounded labelling tool. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Universal Data Tool
good: Web/desktop app for annotating images, text, audio, documents and video in one interface, using extensible .udt.json and .udt.csv formats: image segmentation and classification, text classification, NER, relations/POS tagging, audio transcription, video segmentation and pose annotation. Features real-time collaboration with no sign-up, CSV/JSON upload/download, Docker and Singularity runs, and React integration.
bad: It is a labelling tool only — the README shows no retrieval, memory, provenance or citation machinery — and the README itself steers readers to the maintainer's new project (tscircuit), signalling where development attention has gone.
didnt: Rejected — a broad multi-format labelling app in the same class as brat/Argilla but with no knowledge-memory or citation capability our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemGPT (now Letta)
good: Platform for stateful agents whose advanced memory lets them learn and self-improve over time: an interactive terminal UI, an App Server for local or self-hosted agents, an Agent SDK for TypeScript applications, channels (Slack, Telegram, Discord) and a cloud option that keeps agent memory, identity and conversations available across computers.
bad: This repository is now largely a pointer: the README states the current source code lives in letta-ai/letta-code, and the retired Letta V1 API server survives only on the archive branch for reproducibility, with active projects directed to the new source.
didnt: Corroboration — Letta's tiered, self-editing memory for stateful agents confirms the layered-memory direction our wiki already implements, with custody kept in our own files rather than an agent runtime. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agents (AIWaves)
good: Framework for data-centric, self-evolving autonomous language agents. Agents 2.0 implements symbolic learning: agent pipelines are treated like neural-net graphs, with language-based loss, back-propagated 'language gradients' and prompt/tool updates per node, trajectory storage, and natural support for optimising multi-agent systems.
bad: The repository shows 0 releases and 0 tags and the README's install route is pip-installing from the git master branch; its news section stops at the 2024-06-25 Agents 2.0 release, and the framework is oriented to research on agent training rather than knowledge custody.
didnt: Board — the symbolic-learning loop (language loss and gradients computed over stored execution trajectories) as a candidate pattern for structured post-failure reflection on ingest and QA runs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentForge
good: Low-code framework for rapid development, testing and iteration of autonomous agents and cognitive architectures: declarative YAML 'Cogs' orchestrate multi-agent workflows, branching logic and memory; agents are defined by YAML prompt templates, with personas, dynamic prompt templates, on-the-fly prompt editing and LLM-agnostic operation across OpenAI, Gemini, Claude and local models via Ollama or LMStudio.
bad: Licensed GPL-3.0, so its code is copyleft. The README routes newcomers through a separate docs hub and beginner/advanced/legacy reference layers, reflecting a broad, sprawling surface for what is an agent-orchestration tool, not a knowledge system.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 bars code adoption under our licence discipline, and its agent-orchestration scope duplicates tooling we already have while offering no missing wiki capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Multiagent Debate
good: Code for the ICML 2024 paper 'Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate': multiple agents generate answers and then respond to and critique each other's responses over debate rounds to improve factuality and reasoning.
