Runnable experiment code with generation and evaluation scripts for arithmetic, GSM, biography and MMLU tasks.
bad: The README calls the code a 'preliminary implementation' with more tasks and settings promised; the repository has only 24 commits, no releases, and no licence file at the source, so the code cannot be adopted.
didnt: Corroboration — agents critiquing each other's answers to raise factuality confirms our adversarial-review pattern for wiki answers; with no licence stated, the code itself is ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: MIT CSAIL

name: Adala
good: Autonomous data-labelling agent framework: agents acquire skills iteratively, learning from a ground-truth dataset environment plus observations and reflections, with per-skill configurable outputs and constraints. Ships skills for classification, summarisation, question answering, translation, text generation and ontology creation, supports student/teacher runtime setups, and works natively in Python notebooks over pandas DataFrames.
bad: The documented prerequisites centre on an OpenAI API key, with other LLMs reached via an OpenRouter workaround, and the README roadmap still lists unfinished items including a REST API, an NER skill and multi-task learning; its scope is data labelling, not knowledge management.
didnt: Board — the ground-truth-anchored learning loop (learn until an accuracy threshold against owner-supplied truth data) as a pattern for auto-labelling golden-set candidates that still land in front of the owner for approval. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NirDiamant/Agent_Memory_Techniques
good: Thirty runnable Jupyter notebooks covering agent memory across six families — short-term, long-term, cognitive architectures, retrieval and multi-agent patterns, frameworks, and evaluation/production — spanning conversation buffers, vector stores, knowledge graphs, episodic and semantic memory, and hands-on MemGPT, Mem0, Letta, Zep and Graphiti notebooks plus LoCoMo benchmarks. Includes a taxonomy, a decision tree, a side-by-side comparison matrix and staged learning paths.
bad: It is a teaching repository rather than a deployable memory layer: the notebooks demo other systems, and the README prominently upsells a paid $199 course and a companion book. The repository is also new (created 2026-05-05) with 37 commits.
didnt: Corroboration — its six-family taxonomy and comparison matrix confirm the breadth of memory techniques our design already draws on; as a course artefact there is no production code here for us to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AML-memory/agent-memory-leaderboard
good: Open, unified, reproducible evaluation for long-term memory systems: the answer and evaluation pipeline is held fixed so score differences attribute to the memory system, and results are reported as capability profiles (explicit fact recall, relational/multi-hop reasoning, temporal and event understanding, memory governance, personalisation, rules execution, epistemic safety and privacy) under versioned evaluation contracts. The textual track covers 10+ benchmark datasets, over 1,500 histories and nearly 5,000 questions, plus a coding-memory track; participants expose only Add and Search operations.
bad: The README states this repository is only the public evaluation release — it is not the production leaderboard service and contains no benchmark data, corpora or gold answers — and the repo has a single commit. Participation requires operating and funding your own memory API, obtaining an AML key, and keeping results private until leaderboard review.
didnt: Board — AML's Add/Search-only controlled protocol and its capability taxonomy (especially temporal/latest-valid-state and epistemic-safety dimensions) as a yardstick design for our own golden-set memory benchmarking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WujiangXu/A-mem
good: Code for the NeurIPS 2025 paper 'A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents': an agentic memory system that dynamically organises memories on Zettelkasten principles — generating comprehensive notes with structured attributes, contextual descriptions and tags, analysing historical memories for connections, establishing links, and continuously evolving memories under agent-driven decisions. Experiments on six foundation models are reported against state-of-the-art baselines on LoCoMo, and the robust evaluation supports OpenAI, vLLM and Ollama backends.
bad: The README states this repository is specifically designed to reproduce the paper's results and directs production use to a separate official implementation (A-mem-sys); results depend on tuning the retrieval parameter k per model, and the shipped evaluation is tied to the LoCoMo dataset.
didnt: Corroboration — Zettelkasten-style atomic notes with intelligent linking and continuous evolution corroborate our wiki's linked-page memory design; nothing here needs adopting over it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VectorSpaceLab/general-agentic-memory
good: GAM, a modular agentic file-system memory framework: LLM-based intelligent chunking, a structured Memory + TLDR summary per chunk, automatic hierarchical taxonomy organisation, incremental addition without rebuilding, and text plus video support across four access levels (Python SDK, CLI, REST API, web platform). Its research directory ships benchmark evaluation on LoCoMo, HotpotQA, RULER and NarrativeQA with a dual-agent Memorizer + Researcher implementation.
bad: The repository shows 0 releases and 0 tags and is young (created 2025-10-08); memory building and question answering are driven by external LLM backends configured through API keys and model environment variables, so memory quality rides on the chosen model.
didnt: Corroboration — GAM's file-system memory with hierarchical taxonomy, per-chunk summaries and a Memorizer/Researcher split confirms our file-first wiki memory architecture rather than offering a missing piece. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AVIDS2/memorix
good: Local-first cross-agent memory layer for coding agents via MCP, compatible with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Gemini CLI and many more: SQLite is the canonical store with an FTS5 candidate index and an optional local LanceDB semantic index, project-scoped observation, Git and reasoning memory, a review-gated knowledge workspace where proposals never overwrite reviewed pages silently, and orchestration with task handoffs, file locks and verification gates.
bad: Its scope is coding-agent memory bound to a Git project, not general personal knowledge, and it is a very young, fast-moving project (created 2026-02-14, already 873 commits) with a huge surface including a bundled terminal agent; it requires Node.js >= 22.18.0.
didnt: Board — Memorix's review-gated knowledge workspace, Git-derived engineering facts and reasoning-memory scoping as comparison points for our gateway's scoping and audit design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentMemoryRepo/agentmemoryrepo
good: A spec for a git-backed agent memory repository: a short MEMORY.md entry point loaded each session with an index of [[cross-links]], one-line entries carrying open metadata such as [source: ...; added: ...], composability of several memory repos with per-repo ownership and history, and a periodic 'Dreaming' agent that adds pattern memories and cleans up duplicates, outdated entries and contradictions. Use cases span personal, team and multi-agent swarm memory, with git surfacing conflicting edits.
bad: The spec is very new and small (created 2026-10-04, 13 commits, no releases). Its memory loop updates entries with no human in the loop and pushes after every edit — the opposite of approval-gated writes — and the README notes automatic startup and scheduled Dreaming are not included and the trial works only on the same machine with local storage.
didnt: Corroboration — its MEMORY.md index, sourced one-line entries and cross-link format corroborate our own memory/wiki conventions; its no-human-in-the-loop write loop is precisely the part our approval gates reject. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Cognition

name: yet-another-free-publish-alternative
good: A Jekyll digital-garden template plus a Python script (pip install YAFPA) that publishes only the notes the user marks share: true in frontmatter, converting wikilinks, transclusions and admonitions, moving images into assets, and then committing and pushing to git. The template is fully Obsidian-compatible markdown (including LaTeX delimiters) with a private-folder collection for unlisted notes.
bad: The README banner states the template and script are no longer maintained and points to a new MkDocs workflow, and the repository is archived. The PyPI docs also note the clipboard feature is untested on macOS, Linux and Android because the author could only test on iOS and Windows.
didnt: Corroboration — publishing only files explicitly marked share: true confirms our selective, approval-gated approach to what leaves the private wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Perlite
good: A web-based markdown viewer optimised for Obsidian: drop a whole vault or markdown folder into the web directory and the page builds itself from the folder structure, with no database and no manual conversion. It offers an interactive graph, search, Obsidian themes, tags/links/images support, LaTeX and Mermaid, and Obsidian Canvas support, as a self-hosted open-source alternative to Obsidian Publish.
bad: It is a viewer only — the README presents no editing capability. Its own security section warns that the generated metadata.json exposes the whole vault structure (including excluded files) and that the raw .md files and metadata.json must be blocked from direct browser access, and it advises against allowing untrusted user input despite Parsedown safemode.
didnt: Corroboration — a database-free, self-hosted read-only web view over a plain markdown vault, with graph and search, confirms the Lens's read-only portal design over the same kind of files. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obsidian For Business
good: A template Obsidian vault combined with Microsoft Outlook VBA macros for a plain-text business workflow: macros extract selected emails and calendar meetings straight into the vault as plain text, and Johnny Decimal macros tag or untag email subjects en masse for searchability.
bad: The repository is archived, so it is no longer maintained. The utilities require Microsoft Windows, Microsoft Office and Outlook with VBA macros and specific legacy VBA libraries enabled, tying the workflow to that desktop stack.
didnt: Rejected — an archived, Windows/Outlook-VBA-bound template collection; our wiki is neither Obsidian- nor Outlook-based, and the email-extraction pattern is already covered by our own connectors. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sourcegraph knowledge bases extension
good: The Sourcegraph browser extension connects Sourcegraph to GitHub inside Chrome: open repos, compare revisions and search code directly from the browser omnibox, working on github.com with no setup. It brings Sourcegraph code navigation into the code host and code-review pages a developer already uses.
bad: Using it with private repositories requires setting up and connecting a private Sourcegraph instance, and GitHub Enterprise requires manually updating the Sourcegraph URL in the extension. The store listing's privacy disclosure states the extension handles user-activity data.
didnt: Rejected — a code-search browser extension for GitHub workflows; it addresses developer code navigation, not a personal markdown knowledge base, and offers nothing our citation-locked wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obweb
good: A self-hosted web interface for an Obsidian vault, designed mobile-first for quick memo capture in the style of Flomo, with plain markdown throughout, Git as the database (posts via the API are pushed to the remote repo), deployment on the user's own server with no third-party data storage, and a simple built-in RSS reader.
bad: The README's own notice states the project is deprecated and the author has moved on to a newer app. The README also concedes hard-coded parts in the code and assumes a specific vault layout (Daily and Unsort directories) plus git pull/push permissions on the server.
didnt: Rejected — deprecated by its own README and superseded by the author's successor app; its unauthenticated-by-default write path also runs against our approval-gated write model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Systemsculpt AI
good: An Obsidian plugin bringing an agent workspace into the vault: chat over notes, documents and images with streamed reasoning, citations, tool activity and approvals; a portable semantic index for finding related notes; audio recording/import transcribed to Markdown or SRT; and Studio visual workflows. Its managed chat offers an Ask Approval mode that pauses before vault files are edited, moved or deleted.
bad: Hosted AI features require a paid SystemSculpt account (monthly or lifetime plan plus credit packs), and the README's privacy section states hosted requests send prompts, selected notes, files and audio server-side, where they may be processed through third parties such as OpenRouter, AssemblyAI and Cloudflare R2. Several Studio node types (local CLI, FFmpeg, dataset adapter) are desktop-only.
didnt: Corroboration — its Ask Approval mode, which pauses for the user before any vault mutation, confirms our approval-gated write design for agent access to the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mesh AI
good: An Obsidian plugin that emulates the Fabric tool inside a vault: reusable text-processing patterns can be run over the active note, clipboard content or Tavily search results, in sequential mode (each pattern's output feeds the next) or stitch mode (all outputs collected). It auto-detects YouTube links and processes their transcripts, downloads patterns from the Fabric repository, supports custom pattern folders and workflows exposed as command-palette items, and integrates multiple AI providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq and Ollama.
bad: The README's compatibility section says only Groq, OpenAI and Ollama are tested and confirmed, with Microsoft Azure, Anthropic and Google still under development. Installation is manual (extract a release into the vault's plugins folder) or via the BRAT beta-plugin installer, rather than the standard community directory route described for finished plugins.
didnt: Rejected — an Obsidian-only pattern runner tied to the Fabric pattern ecosystem; it duplicates agent text-processing we already have and brings no citation, abstention or approval discipline of its own. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Arcana
good: A collection of AI tools for Obsidian, each named for a historical figure: Socrates conversation with user-defined chat agents created from markdown templates, Henry Ford frontmatter-metadata automation applicable to a note or a whole folder, Agatha Christie in-note text generation, Marco Polo file-location suggestions the user can accept or reject, Richard Feynman flashcard generation compatible with the spaced-repetition plugin, Charles Darwin auto-tagging, and Nostradamus note naming. It works with the user's own OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or OpenRouter keys.
bad: Use requires the user's own paid API keys for the cloud providers, and the README leads with an appeal for collaborators, signalling thin maintenance for a 2023-era plugin. The README describes no vault-wide retrieval, citation or verification mechanism — each tool acts on the current note or folder only.
didnt: Board — template-defined conversation agents (a markdown file per agent persona) and accept/reject file-move suggestions, as ideas for agent personas and approval-gated reorganisation in our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Chat CBT Plugin
good: ChatCBT is an AI journaling assistant for Obsidian inspired by cognitive behavioural therapy: the user chats inside a note, and a Summarize command turns the conversation into a table of negative beliefs, emotions, thinking categories and reframed thoughts. Conversations are stored privately in local files, the system prompt is editable, it supports 60+ languages, and the user can choose paid cloud models (OpenAI/Deepseek) or a fully local, free Ollama setup.
bad: The README's disclaimer states it is not a replacement for therapy, has not been reviewed or approved by licensed therapists, was built by someone without psychology expertise, and that AI responses are unpredictable. The cloud options send the user's journal messages to OpenAI or Deepseek, which the README itself flags as a privacy caveat.
didnt: Rejected — wellbeing journaling is outside the scope of our knowledge OS, and an unreviewed therapy-adjacent bot is a risk surface we do not need; only its local-first storage choice aligns with our custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Voicenotes Sync
good: An Obsidian plugin that syncs recordings from the VoiceNotes web and mobile apps into a vault on a configurable schedule and directory, bringing transcripts plus AI-generated summaries and actions as note sections, converting TODOs into markdown todos, optionally downloading the audio file, and shaping notes through Jinja-style note, frontmatter and filename templates with rich variables (transcript, summary, topics, subnotes, attachments).
bad: It is wholly tied to the proprietary VoiceNotes.com service and requires the user's account access token from that service. Its optional mode to delete synced notes from the VoiceNotes server is destructive enough that the README notes it requires double opt-in toggles.
didnt: Board — the voice-capture-to-vault pattern (transcript plus AI summary, actions and todos landed as a structured note via templates) as an ingest idea for our wiki, without the proprietary-service tie. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vox
good: Vox transcribes voice memos inside Obsidian fully self-hosted: a local Docker backend running Whisper means no data leaves the machine and no account is needed. It watches an unprocessed folder, files transcripts with frontmatter and tags, categorises notes by filename tokens (importance R1–R5 plus category codes), includes a built-in audio recorder, and generates local-LLM (Ollama) summaries per note plus weekly, monthly and yearly rollup summaries built hierarchically to respect token limits.
bad: The README states the transcription model is fine-tuned for English and may struggle with other languages. It also requires running and maintaining a separate Docker backend (which downloads a ~470 MB Whisper model on first run) alongside the plugin.
didnt: Board — watch-folder voice-memo transcription with token-aware weekly/monthly/yearly summary rollups, as an ingest and synthesis idea for our wiki's spoken-input path. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ossian-mcp
good: An MCP adapter for the Ossian document server: ask_documents answers from the user's own corpus with the passages the answer came from and returns a refusal when nothing in the corpus supports a response, while recall retrieves durable agent memory ranked by relevance, importance and recency — with memory and corpus deliberately kept as separate stores. It starts read-only (four read tools), gates ingest/remember behind read-write mode and forget behind admin mode plus an explicit flag, supports namespace allowlists and protected namespaces, dry-run writes, and a JSON audit log per guarded operation.
bad: It is only an adapter — it requires a separately running Ossian server and an issued API key before any tool works. The repository is very young and small (created 2026-08-31, 11 commits, 2 stars at opening), so it is unproven in production use.
didnt: Corroboration — read-only-by-default tool gating, cited answers that refuse when the corpus cannot support them, and the strict separation of agent memory from the citable corpus all confirm our citation-locked, scored-abstention, approval-gated design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: UCAN
licence: Community Specification License 1.0 for specification materials, MIT for source code in the spec repo
good: The homepage shows a trustless, local-first authorisation scheme whose tokens are cryptographically signed and verifiable without contacting the issuer, work completely offline, and support fine-grained delegation with custom constraints, time limits, composability/chaining and revocation.
bad: UCAN as presented is a specification plus separate libraries (the homepage lists only JavaScript, Rust and Go), not a finished product an application can simply switch on; the homepage itself documents no conformance testing, evaluation or production deployment evidence.
didnt: Board — capability-style delegated, time-limited, offline-verifiable tokens as a model for approval-gated agent authority, boarded as an idea only because the specification's Community Specification License is a custom licence and its code is therefore ideas-only for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Automerge
good: Its docs show local copies of application state on several devices that can be edited independently and offline, automatically merged cleanly with no changes lost when devices reconnect, with a Git-like history for viewing, branching and merging old versions, and a network-agnostic design (WebSocket, WebRTC, Bluetooth or even files sent by email/USB).
bad: The core is a pure data-structure library: networking, storage and access control live in separate libraries such as automerge-repo, and its docs warn the public sync.automerge.org server is experimental with no reliability or data-safety guarantees, so production use requires running your own sync server.
didnt: Board — Git-like CRDT document history, branching and clean offline merging as a candidate model for collaborative wiki editing, to be weighed against plain Git which our wiki already uses (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yjs
good: The docs show a high-performance CRDT exposing shared Map/Array/text types that can be manipulated concurrently and merge automatically without conflicts, with bindings for ProseMirror, Tiptap, Monaco, Quill, CodeMirror and Remirror, network-agnostic providers, and no need for a central source of truth.
bad: The documentation site itself warns it is a work in progress and that the best information is still the README and demos repo, and it notes scaling shared-editing backends is not trivial; Yjs supplies the data model and providers, not auth, permissions or a finished sync service.
didnt: Board — shared-type CRDT editing with pluggable providers as the leading candidate if multi-editor collaborative wiki editing is ever built, since it duplicates nothing in our current Git-based stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Loro
good: The homepage shows a high-performance CRDT library with rich types — MovableList, LWW Map, MovableTree and rich Text using the Fugue algorithm to minimise interleaving anomalies — that turns JSON-like data collaborative and preserves full version history like Git even during real-time collaboration, including in P2P environments.
bad: The homepage is explicit that Loro only powers the collaborative state layer — 'You bring UI, auth, storage, and transport' — so persistence, permissions and sync infrastructure must all be built or chosen separately.
didnt: Board — Fugue rich-text merging plus Git-like version history over JSON state as an idea for structured wiki pages, behind Yjs/Automerge in maturity for our purposes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: json-joy
licence: Apache-2.0 (per its npm packages; GitHub classifies the repo licence as Other/NOASSERTION, with a LICENSES directory)
good: The README shows a full JSON implementation as a CRDT with seamless merging of JSON data models, claiming the fastest list CRDT and text OT implementations in JavaScript, plus very fast CBOR/MessagePack/JSON codecs, JSON Patch, schema validation and editor integrations for Ace, CodeMirror, Monaco, Slate, ProseMirror and Quill.
bad: The repo's scope is sprawling well beyond CRDTs (router, codecs, binary trees, JSON Expression, reactive RPC), its licence is not presented as one clean repo-level licence (GitHub reports Other/NOASSERTION and a LICENSES directory), and the README's headline claims are self-reported performance assertions.
didnt: Rejected — a capable JSON CRDT, but it duplicates the Yjs/Automerge/Loro options already boarded, its repo-level licence presentation is ambiguous, and its extra subsystems are out of scope for a markdown-first wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Diamond Types
good: The README shows a high-performance Rust CRDT for concurrent editing of text by multiple users in a P2P network without a centralised server, designed for interoperability with positional/operational-transform updates, with Cargo, docs.rs and WASM-based npm packages.
bad: The repo titles itself 'WIP' and the README states this version only supports plain text editing (JSON-style types are on a separate branch), that it began as a performance prototype, and that the package published to Cargo is quite out of date in both API and performance.
didnt: Rejected — plain-text-only and explicitly work-in-progress with a stale published package; interesting as a performance reference, not a fit for a structured knowledge OS (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jazz (CoJSON)
good: The homepage shows a local-first relational database using the same Rust engine in browser, React Native, Node and server, with partial per-query sync, row-level security and per-query authorisation defined in code, blobs/streams/JSON/rich text as ordinary columns, deep edit histories with branch-like views, fluid schema migrations, and a self-hostable open-source server.
bad: The current repo README warns this is the Jazz 2.0 alpha with an entirely new API (classic Jazz is a separate line) and that persistent/device-supported runtimes are not available in the Expo alpha; the managed Jazz Cloud alternative is metered per compute, storage and egress.
didnt: Board — per-query authorisation planned together with the query, partial sync and branch-like row histories as design ideas for a future hosted wiki door, not as a database replacement for the Git-backed wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Earthstar
good: The homepage shows a specification and JavaScript library for private, distributed, offline-first apps that are always self-hosted with servers optional: live and streaming sync, ed25519 verification, multiple identities, temporary documents, real deletion, read-only access grants and document write permissions, working in browser, Deno and Node.
bad: Its docs coverage notes the library does not yet support discovering new peers over the internet and that encryption for invite-only workspaces was marked not implemented yet; it is aimed at small-group apps, and its LGPL-3.0-only licence makes its code ideas-only under our licence discipline.
didnt: Rejected — LGPL-3.0-only code is ideas-only for us, and its small-group sync protocol duplicates the local-first custody our Git/Azure wiki already has without citation or approval-gating features (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Syncthing
good: The homepage shows a continuous file synchronisation program that syncs files between two or more computers in real time, protected from prying eyes, with the user choosing where data is stored, whether it is shared with any third party and how it is transmitted over the internet.
bad: As presented it is file synchronisation only — the homepage offers no content-aware merging, data model, querying or knowledge features, so conflicting edits to wiki files would still be file-level conflicts for us to resolve elsewhere.
didnt: Corroboration — mature, server-free, user-controlled file sync confirms our local-first custody model for the wiki working tree, without adding a new component to the stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LiveStore
good: The site and repo show a client-centric data layer with a reactive embedded SQLite database powered by event-sourcing: events are persisted in an eventlog, applied via materializers, reactively queried with instant results, with a type-safe schema, custom merge conflict resolution, devtools and adapters for web, mobile, server/edge and desktop.
bad: The site itself lists what it does not do: it is not a batteries-included framework (no auth or file upload), provides no hosted service, does not sync with an existing database, does not scale for unbounded amounts of data and does not support peer-to-peer/decentralised syncing.
didnt: Board — event-sourced reactive SQLite with materializers as a design pattern for a local wiki index/query layer, where the append-only event log maps naturally onto our citation-locked change history (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Triplit
good: The README shows a full-stack syncing database running on server and client: real-time sync with incremental updates and property-level conflict resolution, a full client-side database cache, durable server storage with an admin dashboard, pluggable storage (SQLite, IndexedDB, LevelDB, Memory), optimistic updates, relational querying, offline mode with reconnection, schemas and server-enforced authorisation.
bad: It is AGPL-3.0, so its code is ideas-only under our licence discipline, and its model is client-server over WebSockets with a Triplit server URL and token rather than peer-to-peer or file-based custody.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code cannot be adopted under our licence discipline, and a server-centric sync database is the wrong shape for a Git-backed, local-first personal wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ZamSync
good: The README shows a single-binary Rust offline-first sync engine built for intermittent connectivity: an append-only WAL with CRC32 and crash recovery, Hybrid Logical Clock ordering, version-vector deduplication so interrupted syncs retransmit only missing events, mTLS with a hub-signed PKI, ChaCha20-Poly1305 WAL encryption at rest, JSON-schema validation, SQLite projection and a REST API.
bad: It is a very young, small project (repo created in 2026, 67 stars at opening) purpose-built for IoT/rural-health event payloads on low-end hardware (512 MB RAM minimum, Raspberry Pi class), with no document, query or knowledge model beyond raw events.
didnt: Board — WAL replication with HLC ordering and version-vector dedup that survives days offline and mid-transfer cuts, as a resilience pattern for syncing a personal wiki across unreliable connections (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TruLens RAG Triad (TruEra)
good: TruLens provides OpenTelemetry-based tracing of every app step plus reference-free feedback functions, including the RAG Triad — context relevance, groundedness and answer relevance — that can run inline or in batch, with its README reporting its judges graded against human annotations (0.81 groundedness F1 on LLM-AggreFact; 0.93 context-relevance NDCG@5).
bad: The triad scores come from LLM-judge feedback functions that require a chosen LLM provider package (OpenAI, LiteLLM, Bedrock, Cortex, HuggingFace and others are listed), so scores inherit that judge's cost and variance rather than being deterministic checks; TruLens is also a broad agent-evaluation platform well beyond the triad.
didnt: Corroboration — the context-relevance / groundedness / answer-relevance triad independently confirms the three-legged scoring shape of our own retrieval evaluation, while our scored abstention and citation locking go further than LLM-judge scores (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LangChain Benchmarks
good: The README shows an open benchmark package organised by end-to-end use cases that publishes how its datasets are collected, what they contain and how each task is evaluated; its retrieval benchmarks provide document collections with retriever and architecture factories (basic, parent-document, HyDE) and evaluators for answer accuracy and faithfulness to retrieved content.
bad: The README states the benchmarks utilise LangSmith heavily, with datasets stored in LangSmith and an API key expected for the eval/debugging experience, and several benchmark sets are relegated to an 'Archived' section that requires cloning the repo, with other directories described as legacy.
didnt: Board — its semi-structured (text plus tables) retrieval task and table-summarisation trick as candidate additions to our golden-set retrieval evaluation (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ARES
good: The README shows an automated RAG evaluation framework that combines synthetic query generation with fine-tuned classifiers and Prediction-Powered Inference to score context relevance, answer faithfulness and answer relevance with statistical confidence intervals, minimising human annotation, in a model-agnostic package that also supports local vLLM execution.
bad: Its own requirements are heavy: a human preference validation set of at least 50 and ideally several hundred annotated triples, few-shot prompts and a much larger unlabeled set are required, and the appendix calls for over 100 GB of disk and a GPU — an A100 is listed as working while smaller tested Azure GPUs ran out of memory.
didnt: Board — synthetic-data plus Prediction-Powered Inference evaluation with confidence intervals as a method for evaluating truth-aware retrieval on our wiki without hand-labelling thousands of examples (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Stanford University

name: jumbocontext/cli
good: Goal-anchored memory and context orchestration for coding agents: every memory, guideline and constraint attaches to a goal, and Jumbo assembles a current context packet per goal from an append-only JSONL event store with SQLite read projections (CQRS/event sourcing). It is harness- and model-agnostic, runs fully locally with no network calls, and hooks into agent sessions to orient agents at start.
bad: Team sharing is explicitly problematic — the README says the .jumbo/ folder is gitignored by default because the event-sourcing pattern is likely to conflict if shared, with a cloud version only promised as coming soon. Extended context-window support only works for harnesses that support hooks, and several integrations (e.g. Cursor) are listed as to be verified.
didnt: Rejected — goal-anchored context packets duplicate our wiki goal workspaces and Lens retrieval, and AGPL-3.0 bars code adoption in any case; ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: codecoradev/uteke
good: Single-binary Rust local-first memory engine, fully offline with local ONNX embeddings and zero LLM tokens per query, reporting 98.2% recall_any@5 on LongMemEval-S with a reproducible in-repo harness. It fuses vector (HNSW) + FTS5 search via RRF, and adds Rooms for multi-agent shared memory with author attribution, native point-in-time time-travel recall, typed relationship edges (supersedes/contradicts/references), smart decay and an MCP server.
bad: Very young project (created 2026-05-29 per repo details) with a single-vendor roadmap/editions split described in the README, and strict recall_all@5 is 88.0% against a 99.4% ceiling — multi-evidence ordering remains its stated residual gap. First run downloads a ~200MB embedding model.
didnt: Corroboration — its fusion RRF, typed supersedes/contradicts edges, time-travel and decay confirm our retrieval and supersession design; a separate embedding store would duplicate the wiki's citation-locked markdown corpus rather than extend it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sachitrafa/YourMemory
good: Implements an explicit Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: memory strength decays exponentially with per-category half-lives (strategy ~38d, fact ~24d, assumption ~19d, failure ~11d), slowed by importance and recall count, with chain-aware pruning that keeps decayed memories alive if a graph neighbour is strong. It also consolidates clusters of related facts into single summaries (archiving originals), uses vector+BM25+entity-graph hybrid retrieval, and logs reads/writes/deletes in a hash-chained tamper-evident audit trail, reporting 59% Recall@5 on LoCoMo-10.
bad: Licence is CC BY-NC 4.0 in the LICENSE file — a non-commercial Creative Commons licence, not a conventional software licence, so code reuse is barred for commercial use. Setup requires registering for a token by email on the project website before local setup, and the self-contained binary is ~2 GB because it bundles Python, dependencies and both ML models.
didnt: Board — the explicit per-category Ebbinghaus decay formula with chain-aware pruning as a candidate staleness/decay model for wiki pages; CC BY-NC licence means ideas only, never code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: qualixar/superlocalmemory
good: Governed local-first memory control plane whose recall returns three honest tiers — a supported answer, closest memories explicitly labelled as not exact, or 'That isn't in SuperLocalMemory' — directly implementing scored abstention. Every save passes an admission check with a receipt, reads respect roles/workspaces/scopes, erasure reaches all copies with a verifiable receipt, and actions land in a hash-chained audit trail; Mode A makes no model-provider call, and it builds in a Karpathy-style LLM-wiki document index and health check.
bad: AGPL-3.0 with a separate commercial licence file, so code adoption is barred. Optional media (pictures/documents/PDFs) needs about 1.5 GB of downloads and 16 GB of memory, the on-device answer-check model Laya is Apple Silicon only (the cloud alternative Jev needs explicit consent), and the system is very large in scope (3,332 commits, mesh, plugins for many harnesses) for a single-user wiki.
didnt: Corroboration — its three-tier abstaining recall, admission receipts and hash-chained audit confirm our abstention contract, approval-gated writes and gateway design almost point for point; AGPL, so no code taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pqpo/pragma
good: Defines portable agent teams once as versioned YAML DSL (Experts, ExpertTeams, Flows, human checkpoints, per-step model/harness/permissions) and runs the same team via Desktop, CLI or SDK across Codex, Claude Code and other harnesses. Its Host-owned ContextStore turns events from different tasks and harnesses into evidence-backed episodic and semantic memory, with policy-controlled promotion to stable knowledge or Skills that activates only after required review, plus versioned evaluation sets for regression checking.
bad: Explicitly a preview: the README badges it 'preview' and the latest Desktop release provides builds only for macOS Apple Silicon and Intel, so other platforms rely on CLI/SDK paths. AGPL-3.0-only licence bars code adoption, and the full platform (Desktop + interpreter + core + adapters) is a heavy runtime to carry for a personal wiki.
didnt: Rejected — portable multi-harness agent teams are orchestration scope outside our personal LLM-wiki, and its review-gated memory promotion corroborates rather than extends our proposal machinery; AGPL in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HezaoHezao/poirot
good: Deep research agent kernel with a clean layered architecture: a ReAct LeaderAgent with 21 pluggable middleware, token-budget context governance that resolves the active provider's real window for compaction/externalisation, and a five-layer long-term memory (frozen MemoryTrace schema, Ebbinghaus-style lazy decay computed at retrieve time, a single traces.md MarkdownFileStore with pure BM25 HybridRetriever, per-call memory injection that protects prompt caching, and non-blocking auto-consolidation). It adds Docker sandbox path enforcement and a three-layer skill system with gated self-evolution and rollback, with 2400+ tests claimed in the README.
bad: No releases or tags at the source (0 releases) despite its breadth, and advanced memory, skill evolution, multi-agent and sandbox features are all off by default behind many POIROT_* environment flags. Its memory store is a single traces.md file and retrieval is BM25-only by design (no vector/graph dependency), which caps semantic recall for a large wiki corpus.
didnt: Board — lazy Ebbinghaus decay computed at retrieve time and per-call memory injection that protects prompt caching, as retrieval-side ideas for the Ask door; the kernel itself duplicates our gateway/research stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Meterless/Meterless
good: Turns a local Mac/Windows PC/DGX Spark into an OpenAI-compatible AI hotspot by day and an overnight 'Nightshift' attempt-racer: it runs a job hundreds of times across several local models, clusters the distinct approaches (25-37 per race), judges and verifies outputs with validators/browser/media checks, and keeps only what passes with a signed receipt per check. Each night distils its strongest cluster into an insight pack the next night starts from, and it publishes failures alongside benchmarks (e.g. judging initially covered only 8% of shortlisted candidates).
bad: The repo itself is thin — 16 commits and 1 release — because Nightshift is the paid product sold from meterless.ai (Mac M5+ edition is a $199 preorder for Q4 2026), so the open repo is mainly the context engines, examples and docs rather than the full product. Its own published results note verified-but-broken output (12 of 12 generated apps passed 'verified' but only 6 of 12 worked), showing the judging layer is still fallible.
didnt: Board — overnight attempt-racing with cluster distillation into an insight pack and signed per-check receipts, as a pattern for sleep-time compute / anticipatory sweep jobs; the product itself is local-inference scope outside the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: santosomar/AI-agents-for-cybersecurity
good: Hands-on training companion (Pearson/O'Reilly courses and books) in eight parts, from foundations through prompt chaining and RAG to MCP security servers, agentic frameworks for security teams, and a dedicated tokenomics part covering context compounding, prompt caching, model routing, per-task budgets and cost per accepted outcome. Part 8 is a vendor-neutral multi-agent security-assessment harness specification with a scope manifest, human approval gates G0-G3, append-only audit and a kill switch.
bad: It is courseware, not a deployable system: Part 8 is explicitly a design specification with no scanner, payload or service to run, and most scripts need an OpenAI API key. Scope is cybersecurity training, so only the governance/tokenomics fragments transfer to a knowledge wiki.
didnt: Rejected — cybersecurity courseware is out of scope for our LLM-wiki; its human-gated harness spec and cost-per-accepted-outcome metric merely corroborate our approval gates and throughput-budget discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zgcagi/Harness-RSI
good: Bilingual companion site and reading list for a 66-page survey of harness self-evolution under a fixed base model, with a precise definition (H_{k+1}=Update(H_k, trajectories), rejected candidates leave the harness unchanged) and a taxonomy splitting interpreted update targets (prompts, memory/reusable procedures, workflows) from executable ones (tools, code, runtime logic). Its evaluation section is unusually rigorous: claim-specific evidence, selection and oracle integrity, runtime activation, attribution controls, and longitudinal/active-set integrity for lifelong testbeds.
bad: It is a survey/reading list, not an implementation — there is no runnable harness code to adopt, only curated entries and a project website. Several cited 2026 works are preprints, so parts of the evidence base are unrefereed, and the framing is research-oriented rather than a personal knowledge system.
didnt: Corroboration — its insistence that a self-improvement claim needs evaluation with oracle integrity, attribution controls and rejected candidates leaving state unchanged confirms our eval-gated promotion and proposal-only machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Zhongguancun Academy; Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence; University of Science and Technology of China

name: LearnPrompt/cc-harness-skills
good: Six portable, installable SKILL.md bundles distilled from a CC-style coding-agent harness and rewritten host-agnostically for Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw: dream-memory consolidation into a durable index, memory extraction into user/feedback/project/reference types, a read-only verification-gate challenge pass that distinguishes verified from merely claimed done, a bounded swarm coordinator, a nine-part structured context compressor for handoffs, and lightweight proactive jobs with schedule/sleep/expiry limits. Each bundle ships prompt templates, source notes and helper scripts, installable in one npx command.
bad: Very small and young — 10 commits and 2 releases — and its own verification section states the Codex runtime smoke test is still pending local auth, so only Claude Code and OpenClaw loads are verified. The skills are prompt/script patterns for coding agents, with no citation, provenance or abstention machinery for a knowledge corpus.
didnt: Corroboration — its verification-gate (never trust 'done') and dream-memory consolidation confirm our verify-before-completion and observations-pass patterns; our skill system already covers the portable-skill need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jiabaobei/skills-constitution
good: A meta-rule 'constitution' that sits above all skills/tools across agent platforms (Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, Gemini and others) with enforceable articles: classify the task first, pre-check memory and the skill index before acting, mandatory use of a matching skill, search-first when there is no match, and honest capability boundaries before refusing. It makes the rule checkable with hook-based gate scripts (dual-channel classification, hard checks that output must name the actual matched skills, and a three-check evidence chain) plus a skill tree and registry that cut full-catalogue scanning.
bad: Documentation and rule text are primarily Chinese (an English README exists), and enforcement depends on host hooks — on rule-file and prompt-injection platforms (Cursor/Windsurf/ChatGPT) it is advisory only, as its own install table notes. The version churn is high (26 releases in about two months) and the regime is heavyweight for a single-user wiki whose skill routing is already governed.
didnt: Board — the checkable-constitution idea (a meta-rule whose compliance is gate-verified and must cite the actual skills matched) as governance inspiration for our gateway rules; the pack itself duplicates our existing skill discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XortexAI/XMem
good: Multi-modal, multi-agent long-term memory layer that classifies incoming data into domains (profile, temporal, summary, code, snippet, image) routed to specialised stores, with a Judge Agent deciding ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP against existing memory to prevent duplicates and staleness, executed deterministically by a Rust 'Weaver' core across Pinecone/Neo4j/MongoDB. It offers a Chrome extension for ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini, agent plugins, repo scanning into a code knowledge graph, agentic retrieval where the LLM picks search tools, and multi-LLM fallback, reporting 91.5% overall on LoCoMo in its README table.
bad: The repository is archived (GitHub marks it 'Public archive', Archived: Yes), so it is unmaintained. The default architecture depends on cloud stores (Pinecone, Neo4j, MongoDB) and an LLM in both ingestion and retrieval paths, with local mode only as an alternative configuration — the opposite of our local-first, citation-locked markdown custody.
didnt: Rejected — archived and unmaintained, and its cloud vector/graph stack duplicates our wiki corpus; its Judge Agent ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP discipline merely corroborates our ingest adjudication. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NodeDB-Lab/nodedb
good: Multi-model memory and storage engine for AI agents in one process: vector (HNSW), graph, document, columnar, timeseries, spatial, key-value, full-text and array engines share one storage core, identity space and planner, exposed over the PostgreSQL wire protocol plus five other protocols. It embeds at the edge as NodeDB-Lite (including WASM) with CRDT sync to the distributed Origin server, supports bitemporal queries, write-time typeguards, RBAC/row-level security and a hash-chained audit log, and publishes ingest/query benchmarks against TimescaleDB, ClickHouse and InfluxDB.
bad: Still public beta (v0.6.2, 2026-10-16): the README warns the CRDT sync and native protocols still change between minor releases and a 0.5.0 data directory cannot be opened by 0.6, with on-disk and stability guarantees deferred to 1.0. The server is BUSL-1.1 source-available (not open source; converts to Apache-2.0 on 2030-05-01), it requires Linux kernel >= 5.1 for io_uring, and the GUI Studio is still 'coming soon'.
didnt: Rejected — replacing our git-kept markdown corpus with a beta, BUSL-licensed database engine would break citation locking and plain-text custody; its bitemporal and CRDT-sync ideas are noted but the engine is far beyond wiki scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XMUDeepLIT/MemGraphRAG
good: KDD 2026 paper code for a memory-based multi-agent GraphRAG system that organises knowledge into three bidirectionally linked layers — schema (abstract ontology triples), facts (extracted relation triples) and passages (source chunks) — so every fact stays grounded in its supporting passage. Construction is conflict-aware (hard conflicts are detected against passage evidence and resolved in connected groups), ontology induction filters low-frequency schema patterns, and retrieval combines embedding similarity with Personalized PageRank, logging answers, retrieved documents, scores, latency and token usage per question.
bad: Research code with only 15 commits and 1 release; the pipeline requires an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint plus a local Hugging Face embedding model (optionally vLLM/llama-factory and GPU via CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES), and indexing/retrieval must use identical model settings or the saved graph/embedding stores do not match. README documents no packaged install or tests beyond the two CLI scripts.
didnt: Corroboration — its schema/fact/passage three-layer memory with conflict resolution against passage evidence confirms our compiled-layer design and citation grounding; as a research GraphRAG pipeline it duplicates, rather than extends, our retrieval stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Xiamen University (XMU DeepLIT)

name: lobu-ai/lobu
good: Open-source event-sourced context layer and runtime for organisational agents: every tool call, data change and conversation becomes an event in an append-only log, resolved to typed entities and identities with provenance, giving all authorised agents (ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, custom MCP clients) one live, permission-aware model of the world instead of per-session re-fetching. Persistent Lobu specialists with their own identity, tools and access policy can be discovered and delegated to over MCP, while identity, source permissions, approvals, credential brokering and audit stay server-side; it self-hosts with an embedded Postgres by default.
bad: Built for company scale (4,526 commits, 122 releases, Kubernetes charts, Mac app and Chrome extension), so operating it for a personal wiki is heavy. Running specialists locally still pulls runtime components and embedding model weights on first use, setup generates an ENCRYPTION_KEY that must be kept with the database or stored secrets become unreadable, and pre-rename Mac installs need a manual DMG reinstall because the updater cannot cross the bundle-identifier change.
didnt: Rejected — an organisational multi-agent context platform duplicates our wiki-plus-gateway custody model at far greater operational weight; its append-only event graph with provenance corroborates our raw/compiled layering. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: liliang-cn/cortexdb
good: Pure-Go AI memory and knowledge graph in a single SQLite file with no service to run and no embedding model required: HNSW/IVF/flat vectors, FTS5, hybrid and graph retrieval, RDF 1.2 with SPARQL, RDFS/OWL inference and SHACL passing W3C suites, scoped agent memory with sourced context packs, and 80+ tools in-process or over MCP. Captured facts that a newer memory makes untrue are marked superseded — kept, but no longer recalled as current.
bad: Very large surface for a personal wiki: plugins for many harnesses, a shared gRPC brain (with a plaintext remote option), and a Claude Code mod the README calls an early-access feature built against one Claude Code version, whose planned recall and idle capture depend on Haiku running through Claude Code's own model access. Memory lives in an opaque database file rather than readable, citable pages.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: a database-resident memory/graph engine duplicates our compiled markdown wiki while losing page-level readability and citation custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alexisfox7/PRO-LONG
good: Radically minimal programmatic memory: a project-local adapter appends prompts, tool activity, handoffs and session boundaries to one append-only .prolong/log.jsonl, and the agent searches only the history it needs with ordinary tools (rg, jq, Python) — no wrapper, server, database, or transcript dumped into the prompt. Reads of the log are excluded from recording so retrieval cannot recursively copy memory into itself; works with Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and pi.
bad: The README states the headline 97.4% ARC-AGI-3 result motivates the design but is not yet a direct benchmark of the coding-tool MVP, and the whole CLI is only three commands (init/status/uninstall). The log is gitignored, stays uncompiled raw history, and the README warns it can contain prompts, tool results and any secrets that appeared in them; hooks run with the user's own permissions.
didnt: Corroboration — an append-only verbatim log searched on demand, never bulk-injected, confirms our conversation-log plus index-first retrieval design; its lack of compilation and gating is exactly the layer our wiki adds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: EvolvingAgentsLabs/evolving-agents
good: A director agent that compiles CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and memory into small linked When/Do/Because statements, plans by walking them and cites the statement each plan step follows, and delegates to frontier or local lanes. Lessons from corrections are proposed, checked against existing knowledge, and kept only on the user's yes as reversible, versioned patches in plain Markdown files; measured 0.929 vs 0.589 rule-following on 14 real situations with Sonnet.
bad: The README itself reports the advantage disappears with the stronger Opus planner (0.964 for a plain session vs the director on the same check) and that every number should be read as Sonnet's, on a small 14-situation sample. Compiling costs about US$5 for ~60 files, only the Claude Code harness is built (Managed Agents and Antigravity lanes are planned), and it requires Claude Code on PATH.
didnt: Board — lessons as gated, versioned patches that must pass lint, their own probes and a targeted guard before a person's yes, as a candidate acceptance mechanism for wiki lesson/memory updates. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Beever-AI/beever-atlas
good: Turns Slack, Discord, Teams and Mattermost conversations into a self-maintaining wiki: a 6-stage pipeline extracts atomic facts, deduplicates them and clusters them into per-channel topic pages with citations back to source messages, backed by a 3-tier semantic store plus an entity graph store. Questions are answered with cited sources via the dashboard or an MCP server (28 tools, per-agent auth) with a router choosing semantic or graph retrieval per question.
bad: Heavy team-chat infrastructure: three services backed by four datastores (Weaviate, Neo4j, MongoDB, Redis) in a Docker Compose stack, and it requires both a Google/Gemini API key and a Jina embeddings key before a real install. Its source universe is workplace chat platforms, not a personal local-first knowledge base.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a multi-datastore team-chat ingestion platform duplicates our wiki-first distillation idea at far greater operational weight and with cloud-key dependence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CodeSoul-co/Hypha
good: TypeScript framework pairing an Agent Core (ReAct, planning, tool selection, memory access) with a Production Harness providing event-sourced execution, FSM control, policy/approval, checkpoints, recovery, replay and audit; product behaviour is declared as a compilable DomainPack rather than hard-coded. Its cache plane is explicitly reuse-without-authority: a cache hit can never authorise a tool, skip policy/approval, or replace event/artifact evidence.
bad: A very large general agent framework (15 packages) whose bundled server requires MongoDB and Redis plus a configured model provider — far beyond a personal wiki's needs. Its own Tau3 comparison is marginal (0.636 total vs 0.626 for direct model calls over 385 tasks, with banking knowledge at 0.206), and the repo was created in July 2026, so it is young.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: a full production agent harness, not a knowledge system; its event-evidence and approval invariants corroborate ours but there is nothing wiki-specific to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: atomicstrata/atomicmemory
licence: Apache-2.0 (README badge; GitHub sidebar reports Other/NOASSERTION)
good: Portable, inspectable, correction-aware semantic memory: memories can be superseded, clarified, deleted or retained as facts change instead of append-only recall, exposed through one protocol via CLI, MCP server, TypeScript SDK, framework adapters (Vercel AI, LangChain, LangGraph, Mastra, OpenAI Agents) and host plugins. README reports leading performance/cost on BEAM-100K/1M and LoCoMo10 under matched methodology.
bad: Default setup steers to its Hosted Cloud; the local path requires Docker and an OpenAI API key and supports only macOS or glibc Linux, and the README says benchmark reproducibility artifacts will be published later and several packages are 'publish pending' or 'coming soon'. The licence presentation is inconsistent at the source (Apache-2.0 badge vs NOASSERTION sidebar).
didnt: Rejected — duplication and custody: another Postgres/pgvector-backed memory service with a hosted-cloud default duplicates our local wiki memory while weakening plain-file custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sidiora-Labs/hyperfide
good: Agent workflow engine in a single pure-C11 binary with one local SQLite database and no telemetry: it indexes code into a queryable graph, keeps content-addressed snapshots, runs a spec engine whose 'done' is verified against graph and history rather than asserted, and stores agent memory (decisions, constraints, outcomes) in the same database linked to the task it was made under, exposed via a 67-tool MCP server.
bad: The README states plainly that this tree is Hyperfide 2.0 in development and 'nothing in it is a production release', and the scope is enormous (fleet supervisor, distributed control plane, editor/LSP, judgement service). Judgement and recap features need external keys (OpenRouter, Centra), and the whole tool is centred on codebases and spec-driven development, not personal knowledge.
didnt: Rejected — fit and maturity: a pre-release codebase-workflow engine; its verified-done and task-linked memory ideas corroborate our evidence discipline but it is not a personal knowledge system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: grpcer/ownmem
good: Git-native memory for coding agents: readable Markdown lives in the repository's .ownmem/ and travels through clone, review and rollback, with deterministic local recall (exact, BM25F, n-gram, fuzzy and graph lanes fused locally; no model or network call by default). Delivery is graded through four gates into a quoted memory, up to three pointers, or an abstention naming the gate that refused; there are no unattended writes — every memory change is a reviewed commit, under a net-zero entry cap.
bad: Deliberately narrow: the README's own fit table says to choose another system for a cross-repository personal profile or global user memory, automatic capture of every conversation, or large-scale cloud vector search. It is scoped to one coding repository, needs Node.js 20.6+, and some hosts need manual hook-trust or MCP setup steps.
didnt: Corroboration — deterministic non-embedding recall, evidence-before-authority receipts, scored abstention that names the refusing gate, and a ban on unattended writes independently confirm core pillars of our wiki design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Lyellr88/marm-memory
good: Local-first 3-in-1 memory layer and MCP server fusing session history, codebase indexing and concept graphs in SQLite with zero cloud: 16 tools over HTTP and STDIO shared across Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Gemini, VS Code and Cursor, with FTS-plus-semantic re-rank, write-time consolidation/deduplication, published latency and LoCoMo retrieval benchmarks, and a bundled local console control plane.
bad: The README carries an 'IMPORTANT' notice that the maintainer has taken a personal pause from active development, a single-maintainer continuity risk for a system of this size (1,100+ commits, 50 releases). Its centre of gravity is coding-agent context sharing and swarm profiles, not a citable personal knowledge wiki.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and maturity: another local SQLite agent-memory layer overlapping our stack, with an announced development pause. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: databrickslabs/ontobricks
good: Turns Databricks Unity Catalog tables into a knowledge graph in four steps (import metadata, LLM-generate ontology, auto-map, synchronise), with visual or AI ontology design, OWL 2 RL inference, SWRL rules, SHACL validation, R2RML/SPARQL standards under the hood, and a governed DRAFT to IN-REVIEW to PUBLISHED domain lifecycle with append-only review audit. Domains can be published to agents over MCP with per-domain control of exposed tools and data.
bad: Total Databricks platform lock-in: it deploys as a Databricks App and requires a workspace with Apps, SQL Warehouse, Lakebase and Unity Catalog, so it cannot run in our local-first stack. The README also states Databricks Labs projects are provided for exploration only, AS-IS with no formal support or SLAs, and the licence is a custom source-available Databricks License rather than an open-source licence.
didnt: Rejected — platform lock-in and licence: Databricks-only deployment, and custom source-available code is ideas-only for us in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: buildingjoshbetter/TrueMemory
good: Automatic capture and recall that is 100% local in one SQLite file with no API keys on its Edge/Base tiers: an LLM extractor pulls atomic facts, a three-signal encoding gate filters noise before storage, dedup resolves ADD/UPDATE/SKIP and contradictions, and a six-layer retrieval pipeline serves Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Claude Desktop via lifecycle hooks. The PyPI page reports 93.0% LoCoMo and 92.0% LongMemEval for the Pro tier with reproducible benchmark scripts.
bad: Licensed AGPL-3.0. Installation downloads about 1.5GB of models and takes minutes, the strongest (Pro) tier needs an LLM API key for HyDE, and the PyPI page notes anonymous usage telemetry is the one exception to local-only data (opt-out via environment variable). Capture is automatic and unattended, the opposite of approval-gated writes.
didnt: Rejected — licence and fit: AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us, and automatic unattended capture/recall conflicts with our approval-gated, citation-locked writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: beevibe-ai/beevibe
good: Self-hosted, open-source agent workspace for teams: named specialist agents each keep persistent memory bounded to their own domain (facts plus core blocks, no shared pool), work in shared rooms with people, and hand off through an agent-to-agent mesh that supports ask, negotiate (with claims tracked end to end), and escalation to a human who decides between side-by-side positions. Bring-your-own model keys, runs on the team's own infrastructure.
bad: Built for companies/teams, not a personal knowledge base: the stated stack is a Next.js web app, Node/TypeScript API, Postgres plus pgvector and a local daemon, deployed via a Railway template, and it requires the team's own model-provider keys. Memory is per-agent chat-graduated facts, not citable, human-readable wiki pages.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a team agent-orchestration workspace; its human-escalation pattern corroborates our approval gates but the product does not fit a personal LLM-wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: halofyai/halofy
licence: AGPL-3.0-or-later (kernel and console); Apache-2.0 for named client/extension subtrees (driver, MCP, integrations)
good: A governed access layer over MCP and HTTP in which credentials resolve actor, role, namespace and source scope server-side, with provenance, exact and semantic dedupe, supersedence chains, append-only audit and independently verifiable signed erasure; Postgres/pgvector is the authority with embedded PGlite as the zero-setup local default, and the README reports 2,678 tests across 205 files plus 6/6 driver-conformance checks in a hermetic offline test lane.
bad: Very young and unproven as a release: the repo shows only 12 commits and zero releases. The managed/commercial tier deliberately withholds model routing, the managed connector catalogue and the tuned extraction prompt pack, and the organisation-wide multi-tenant scope is far broader than a personal wiki needs.
didnt: Board — signed-erasure certificates and server-owned, credential-resolved identity/scope as governance ideas for our approval-gated doors; AGPL-3.0 kernel code is ideas-only, never adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: varun29ankuS/shodh-memory
good: A single offline Rust binary providing agent memory with zero LLM calls: local MiniLM embeddings and cross-encoder reranking via ONNX, local NER and typed relation extraction building a knowledge graph, and mathematical memory dynamics — Hebbian strengthening, activation decay, spreading activation and long-term potentiation — across working/session/long-term tiers, exposed through 51 MCP tools and a REST API, all deterministic and auditable.
bad: Scope is very broad for a memory binary, also bundling GTD todos, projects, reminders and ROS2/Zenoh robotics support. Its headline benchmark figures are self-reported, and the README itself cautions that reranker latency is an order of magnitude, not a promise, with the LoCoMo gate p50 varying up to 2.3x between runs on identical code.
didnt: Board — the explicit, LLM-free decay/strengthening model (Hebbian strengthening plus power-law decay) as a candidate freshness mechanism for wiki pages, where forgetting is a designed, inspectable rule rather than an LLM judgement. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Signet-AI/signetai
licence: Apache-2.0 (stated in README and licence badge; GitHub sidebar shows NOASSERTION)
good: Syncs memories, shared identity files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md), session transcripts and secrets across many agent harnesses; a background 'dreaming' process builds a structured map of people, projects, facts and relationships with every connection linked back to its source, claim traces show competing claims and exact source passages, secrets are stored encrypted with the master key in the OS keyring, and it reports 97.6% LongMemEval answer accuracy on its tracked MemoryBench runs.
bad: Telemetry is on by default (anonymous usage data, token/cost totals and crash reports; opt-out via config or environment variable). Slack, email, Telegram and WhatsApp sources are still 'coming soon', the nightly channel is explicitly warned as able to break, and release churn is extreme (1,180 releases / 1,255 tags shown).
didnt: Rejected — it duplicates the wiki's own memory, identity-file and cross-agent record, and its default-on telemetry and automatic transcript capture conflict with our local-first, approval-gated custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TIMAN-group/PlugMem
good: Plug-and-play long-term memory (ICML 2026 paper code) that organises experience into compact reusable knowledge units in a hierarchical graph with three memory types — semantic, procedural and episodic — integrable in a few lines of code, with reported state-of-the-art results of 90.2 accuracy on LongMemEval and 79.1 F1 on HotpotQA, released trajectories and memory-graph artefacts, and a Memory Inspector UI for browsing the graph and replaying sessions.
bad: Running it requires external inference infrastructure (OpenAI API key / Azure endpoint plus self-hosted Qwen vLLM and NV-Embed-v2 servers), benchmark setup is heavy (the README notes HotpotQA memory structuring can take several hours), memory compression/evolution is described as only 'naively' supported, and of the coding-agent adapters only Claude Code ships today — OpenCode and OpenClaw are planned.
didnt: Corroboration — its semantic / procedural / episodic split over a hierarchical knowledge graph confirms our own separation of facts, procedures and session records in the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mathomhaus/guild
good: A single compiled Go binary with a first-class MCP server over embedded local SQLite, giving parallel coding agents shared context, memory and task coordination: hybrid BM25 + vector search with rank fusion, atomic task claims so parallel agents do not collide, dependency cascading when a task is completed, and a one-call session start that loads the project oath, the last handoff brief and the highest-priority task.
bad: Platform and install-path degradation is significant: on Windows semantic retrieval is disabled (keyword-only), and the go-install path is also keyword-only. First-class lifecycle-hook support exists only for Claude Code and Codex, and the project is young (70 commits, created 2026-04).
didnt: Corroboration — the session-start brief (oath + last parting brief + top task), search-before-research lore discipline and atomic task claims confirm our multi-agent handoff and coordination design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nowledge-co/nowledge-mem
good: A local-first, graph-augmented personal context manager that persists conversation threads across AI tools and distils them into searchable memories, with MCP integration for many clients, a browser extension importing from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity, automatic entity/relationship extraction into a knowledge graph, topic clustering and a global launcher for pasting memories anywhere.
bad: The repository itself is a showcase, not the product: the root contains only a README and a refs directory across 7 commits, with no licence file, no source code, no tests and no evaluation visible at the source — the actual manager is obtained from the vendor's site.
didnt: Rejected — closed product front-repo with no licence and no inspectable code; nothing here can be adopted or audited for our local-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ChristopherKahler/base
licence: Functional Source License 1.1 (FSL-1.1-ALv2) — custom licence converting to Apache-2.0 in future
good: A single Rust binary ('basemode') that maps a workspace into a knowledge graph — code structure via tree-sitter across 35+ languages queryable by SPARQL, plus projects, decisions with rationale, domain rules and markdown documents as graph nodes stored as plain-text NQuads that diff in git — and injects the relevant slice at four hook moments (session start, prompt, before and after a tool runs), with handoff/fork star commands so sessions survive and resume.
bad: It works with Claude Code only today (Codex and Antigravity are 'coming soon') and is inert if installed before Claude Code exists; it silently self-updates at session start via a detached background process, which is an uncontrolled change channel. The FSL-1.1 licence is a custom, use-restricting licence, so the code is not freely adoptable.
didnt: Board — moment-targeted hook briefing (inject only the rules/decisions bearing on the file or prompt at hand, never a dump) and stale-file signals at session start, as ideas; FSL custom licence means ideas only, never its code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ohad6k/emulo
good: Mines the user's own typed messages in Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, OpenCode and Antigravity logs into a local you.md agent profile in which every rule carries dated verbatim receipts, split into work/design/writing/video layers; a zero-dependency Python tool that stays on the machine, plus a no-model-call usage report that counts repeated asks and correction-style openings with the dated messages behind each finding.
bad: The README is unusually candid that benefit is unproven: whether a loaded profile makes work better 'is not shown', in a pre-registered 60-run study the mined profile did not separate from an invented profile on any of 9 comparisons, and profile loading is unreliable in Claude Code (the skill is not reliably opened on its own) and unverified in several other hosts. Mining pointed at a hosted model sends the selected evidence to that provider.
didnt: Corroboration — a profile derived from the user's own session history with dated receipts for every rule confirms our derived-alignment approach, and its placebo-controlled honesty is a standing caution against claiming such profiles work without a controlled test. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AIOSAI/AIPass
good: A persistent agent workspace in which each agent is a 'citizen' with identity (passport.json), session-surviving memory in plain JSON files rolling over into a local vector store, a mailbox, and a home directory on the shared filesystem; a drone bus reaches any agent, work is carried in written plans, hook gates decide which agent may write what, only a project's manager writes to git, and the fleet is audited in CI against one written standard.
bad: Installation is highly invasive by its own documentation: it rewrites user-level Claude Code settings with deny rules applying to every project on the machine, edits shell rc files, can set global git config, rewrites ~/.codex/config.toml if present, and sets up 18 agents plus a local server. It requires Python 3.10+ and a Claude Code plan, runs on Linux/macOS only (Windows via WSL2), and deliberately has no codebase index.
didnt: Rejected — the installer's machine-wide changes to Claude settings, shell and git configuration conflict with our controlled, owner-ruled setup, and its multi-agent citizen/mailbox model duplicates coordination we already run through the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: smaramwbc/statewave
good: A self-hosted memory runtime on Postgres + pgvector that replaces query-time retrieval with compile-then-use: append-only episodes are compiled once per subject change into typed memories with confidence scores and provenance, then assembled into ranked, token-bounded, deterministic context bundles — the same query at the same point in time returns the same bytes. State-assembly receipts are content-hashed, HMAC-signed and replayable, and a YAML sensitivity policy engine supports deny/redact in log_only and enforce modes.
bad: Its own Current limitations section states: rate limiting is per-IP only (not per-tenant or per-key), multi-tenancy is app-layer with no Postgres row-level security yet, there is no built-in auth provider (it validates keys it does not issue), admin actions carry no identity (promoted_by is null), there is no federated cross-region audit, and receipt replay is 'current code + original policy' rather than byte-for-byte historical reproduction; the FAQ also concedes bundles cost more tokens per answer than a plain fact store.
didnt: Board — signed state-assembly receipts with an embedded policy snapshot and replay ('what would today's code say under the original rules?') as a provenance upgrade idea for our compiled context exports. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pax-beehive/paxm
good: A provider-neutral memory adaptor for Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi and MCP agents: one stable agent-facing contract (CLI, MCP, skills, lifecycle hooks) routed to interchangeable providers — built-in local SQLite (FTS5/BM25, no account, API key, embeddings or memory-layer model calls) or Zep, Mem0, MemOS, OpenViking or a private JSON-RPC provider — with passive prompt-time recall, a durable local write queue so provider failures never block the session, and stored memories that distinguish origin from visibility scope.
bad: Its local-provider evidence is thin by its own account: the SQLite quality preview is an exploratory 30-question LoCoMo run (13/30 successful) explicitly 'not an official LoCoMo score or proof'. Remote providers require user-managed credentials, Team Memory depends on a separate paxl device, and passive recall works to tight default budgets (800ms overall, 250ms per provider) returning partial results on timeout.
didnt: Corroboration — a provider-neutral adaptor with a stable agent-facing contract, local-first default storage and an explicit origin-versus-scope distinction confirms our read-door and provider-swap design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fpytloun/mnemory
licence: Apache-2.0 (stated in README licence section; GitHub sidebar shows NOASSERTION)
good: A self-hosted MCP memory server in which a single LLM call performs fact extraction, metadata classification, deduplication and contradiction resolution; two-tier storage pairs fast searchable summaries in a vector store with a detailed artifact store, memories carry configurable TTL with reinforcement for frequently accessed ones, and a built-in three-phase fsck health checker detects duplicates, contradictions, quality issues and prompt injection with scheduled auto-fix; its README reports 73.2 overall on the LoCoMo benchmark.
bad: It requires an OpenAI-compatible API key for both LLM extraction and embeddings, so it is not offline/local-first by default, and production deployment adds Qdrant plus S3/MinIO. The README explicitly warns deletion is 'best effort, not a verified-erasure or compliance guarantee' — normal deletion retracts and preserves history rather than erasing.
didnt: Board — a scheduled memory fsck (three-phase consistency check for duplicates, contradictions, quality issues and injected content, with a report before any auto-fix) as an audit idea for the wiki corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: letta-ai/trajectory
good: Normalises agent transcripts from 16+ harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Hermes, OpenClaw, OpenHands, Pi, Deep Agents and others, plus ATIF) into one validated, deterministic trajectory record format with a published JSON schema, per-adapter documentation of its exact input contract and what it drops, diagnostics for recoverable cleanup, and matched TypeScript and Python packages kept in parity; a separate conversation API handles multi-party Slack channels.
bad: Coverage is uneven by design: ATIF, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenCode are export-only and return listing_unavailable from local discovery, system messages are omitted by default, Slack is the only conversation adapter with recipients, file contents and other metadata deferred, and development requires Node 20+ plus Bun.
