didnt: Rejected — its input is raw session transcripts, whose ingest into our system is not an approved source, and format conversion alone adds no citation, abstention or custody value to the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 0xNyk/awesome-agent-cortex
good: A curated map that connects layers ordinary framework lists leave apart — agent runtimes, coding tools, MCP, evaluation, memory, knowledge graphs, security and observability — organised into Build / Operate / Remember / Own routes, with deliberate, contribution-reviewed cross-listing and operator guides for the Claude Code, Codex and Hermes stacks.
bad: It is a link list, not a system: no runtime, memory implementation or evaluation of its own, and no releases. Much of its breadth (Solana infrastructure, wallets, payments, DeFi and trading agents) is unrelated to a personal knowledge system, and entry quality depends entirely on contributor curation.
didnt: Rejected — a discovery list, not a component; it duplicates our own landscape research and offers no mechanism our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SodaMem/SodaMem
good: Self-evolving temporal memory in which facts are superseded rather than overwritten (ADD-only plus a SUPERSEDES edge closing valid_until), every memory carries a FactEvent → SourceSpan → RawTurn receipt chain to the exact source turn, and time is modelled on four axes (occurred / valid / said / stored). Recall via build_context makes zero LLM calls, is deterministic, returns citations, and the README reports 92.8% on LongMemEval with all 500 answers and 8,427 evidence rows published for re-grading.
bad: Very new and small (created August 2026, 60 commits). The README itself states no per-question artifacts are published for its 86.88% LoCoMo result, ingest requires an LLM extractor, and the recommended DeepSeek Harness plugin lives in a separate repository tracking a developer-preview host with breaking changes.
didnt: Corroboration — its supersede-don't-overwrite edges, four time axes and per-memory receipt chain confirm our citation-locking, claim-supersession and bi-temporal design choices. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Phant0Meow/dsh-meow-memory
good: Cross-session memory plugin with a seven-layer SQLite store (soul / user / project / fact / lesson / topic / rules, one table per layer), BM25-plus-recency retrieval, first-turn injection of a long-term snapshot without rewriting the user prompt, automatic re-injection after compaction, and per-window dream consolidation with dedup-merge on writes. It has zero runtime dependencies and reports 228 logic tests.
bad: Built specifically for DeepSeek Harness (support stated for dsh 0.1.5), so the store and tooling are host-locked. Per-message recall is keyword-based and capped at top-2 hits from the second message onward, and the README warns a mis-set promptLang value fails silently back to the Chinese pack; documentation is primarily in Chinese.
didnt: Rejected — a DeepSeek Harness-specific plugin duplicating our layered file memory and nightly consolidation, with host lock-in we do not run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: libingzheren/Jev-Mem
good: Separates memory management into a lightweight System-One controller (typing, relation judgments, query routing, budget allocation, candidate scoring, evidence assessment) and a System-Two model that synthesises answers, over shared memory with semantic, temporal, causal and entity graph views while preserving original observations, timestamps and provenance. The paper results reproduced in the README report 0.777 overall on LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini, 6.6× faster memory construction and 36.7% lower query latency than the strongest/fastest baselines, with typed decision traces exposing routing, budgets and stopping reasons.
bad: The README cautions that the supplied commands do not reproduce the full paper evaluation by themselves, that the local Laya backend has not been benchmarked for the paper, and that no LongMemEval result is claimed. Live runs require TypeSafe and OpenAI-compatible API keys and send text to those providers, and the repo is very young (September 2026, 17 commits, no releases).
didnt: Board — the budgeted retrieve-assess-expand controller that stops when evidence is sufficient or further search has little expected value, as a formal pattern for our scored-abstention retrieval. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VAMFI/claude-user-memory
good: A portable agent setup delivered through a single INSTALL.md: the usual result is one short addition (targeting 200 words or fewer) to the tool's native project instructions plus a small CORE.md, an installation receipt with private backups and an undo procedure. It deliberately preserves the user's existing model, provider and native memory setting rather than adding a second memory engine, and requires no GPU, database, Docker or background service.
bad: The README calls it an agent-guided portable beta, explicitly not a deterministic installer or a compatibility guarantee: the Hermes live installation test was blocked by the configured provider's balance, other harnesses and Linux/Windows were not exercised end to end, memory persistence was not tested in the migration, and it concedes prompt guidance is not an enforcement mechanism and claims no performance gain.
didnt: Corroboration — its lean always-loaded addition, selective retention and reversible, receipted installation confirm our lean front-page and verify-before-claiming discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kevin-hs-sohn/hipocampus
good: File-only, zero-infrastructure memory harness whose key device is a ~3K-token ROOT.md topic index compressing all past history into an always-loaded overview, so the agent can notice connections search would miss, backed by a compaction tree (raw → daily → weekly → monthly → root) and BM25/vector hybrid search. Memory types govern preservation (user and feedback entries are never compressed away; stale references get markers), and on its MemAware benchmark of 900 implicit-context questions it reports 21.0% overall versus 0.8% for no memory and 3.4% for BM25+vector search.
bad: Absolute benchmark performance remains low — 21.0% overall and only 8.0% on hard cross-domain questions even at the largest index budget, which the README attributes to the answer model. It supports only Claude Code, OpenCode and OpenClaw platforms, the vector option costs roughly 2GB of disk, and the repo has no releases.
didnt: Corroboration — its always-loaded bounded topic index, compaction tree and never-compress user/feedback rule confirm our index-first, lean-front-page memory design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mage0535/hermes-memory-installer
good: An agent-agnostic memory sidecar (for Hermes, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar agents) that runs beside the agent without patching it: it archives sessions into gbrain and a session search index, layers recall across hot, warm, cold and curated knowledge notes, and lets wiki/knowledge notes participate in retrieval. It ships 28 runtime, support and observability scripts including health and acceptance checks, alert queues and a metrics dashboard, so silent memory failure stays visible.
bad: Heavy operational requirements: Python 3.9+, PostgreSQL 16, plus both Hindsight and gbrain running and reachable, and the README says the repo suits technical users running their own such environment. Some helpers are Hermes-oriented with stronger host assumptions and are excluded from the default install, and the memory-quality cron block is registered in a paused remediation state by default.
didnt: Rejected — its PostgreSQL + gbrain + Hindsight stack duplicates our file-based wiki memory at far higher operational cost and custody complexity. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 1105216375-alt/resimind
good: Neuro-symbolic agent architecture in which models, rules or symbolic tools propose steps but independent domain checks decide what becomes a fact; failed checks return residual feedback for self-correction, and completed derivations can yield candidate rules that are independently verified before admission, frozen in memory, and rechecked on every future application. It provides MCP math tools and an algebra verify-and-repair skill, runs its demos offline with no API key, and supported math routes can run with zero model calls.
bad: The README badges the project experimental and bounds its adaptive algebra and rule learning to rational polynomials; it states MiniF2F and LeanDojo scores are still pending and that its latest same-model planning result and rerun establish no planning success-rate gain. Several headline demos use scripted proposals, with only the verification, admission and reuse executing for real.
didnt: Board — independently verified rule admission (derive once, verify, freeze, recheck on reuse) as a pattern for admitting reusable claims and rules into our claim lifecycle. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rekal-dev/rekal-cli
good: A CLI that captures AI coding sessions at every git commit, stores them raw in a .rekal/ directory in the repo, indexes and embeds them locally in the background, and shares them with teammates through ordinary git push/fetch — no server, account or memory service. Transcripts are scrubbed for secrets and home paths before storage, recall returns the reasoning and rejected alternatives behind a decision, and its output carries INJECT / KNOWLEDGE / SILENCE verdicts with absolute confidence so a silence gate can reject a query that is merely the best of a weak set; a companion arXiv paper and benchmarks are linked.
bad: The single binary is about 170 MB to download and 200 MB on disk, runs only on macOS Apple Silicon and Linux, and building from source requires a CGO build bound to a pinned llama.cpp. Its scope is coding sessions in git repos only, and the README notes ranking and the index database deliberately stay unfrozen under its 1.0 compatibility promise.
didnt: Corroboration — git-native raw session capture that travels with the repo, plus a confidence-gated SILENCE verdict, confirm our verbatim conversation-log-in-git and scored-abstention design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 1173591564/Dynamics-memory
good: Bounded, self-correcting long-term memory that distils continuous, contradictory project interaction logs instead of piling them up: candidates flow through candidate / common / archive pools with hard caps (200 / 8 / 2000) under value-and-confidence dynamics with hysteresis, every memory carries provenance back to an append-only L0 evidence layer, and contradictions are never silently overwritten — unresolved conflicts go to a human_reviews queue for human adjudication and contested items cannot be served confidently. It reports extensive testing (534 pytest passed) and crash-recovery and causal-replay evaluation chains.
bad: No licence is stated at the source — the root listing contains no LICENSE file — so its code cannot be adopted. It is tightly coupled to the OpenCode three-agent protocol and a Zhipu (ZAI) API provider, and its own validation section says independent human L3 acceptance of real sessions has not been done (PENDING-08 still open) and that the health endpoint's validation state is fixed as unverified.
didnt: Board — bounded memory pools with value/confidence separation and a human-review queue where unresolved conflicts stay contested rather than being silently resolved, as an idea for our contradiction handling; no licence at source, so ideas only, no code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alibaizhanov/mengram
good: Human-like agent memory across three types — semantic facts, episodic events and procedural workflows — where procedures evolve from failures with per-step success/fail counts, a policy gate and a regression gate that quarantines a fix that would break another workflow. It offers Python and JS SDKs, an MCP server, LangChain/CrewAI/OpenClaw integrations, multilingual retrieval across 23 languages, cited synthesized answers, and a local folder mode whose memory is a human-readable Markdown tree.
bad: The primary path is a hosted API at mengram.io requiring an account and API key, which conflicts with local-first custody. The README's local mode is more limited than the cloud: its search matches words without embeddings or query translation, the folder is not a single crash-atomic transaction, and external editors do not participate in its write lock.
didnt: Rejected — hosted-API-first custody conflicts with our local-first wiki, and its three-type memory duplicates capabilities our stack already has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mainline-org/mainline
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) — layered licensing: local CLI, skills, hooks and specs intended open under Apache-2.0 / CC-BY-4.0 terms per the README badge and licence section, with hosted service surfaces and brand assets separate
good: Git-native memory for coding agents that stores developer intent — the original goal, reasoning path, key decisions, trade-offs, validation, explicit constraints and abandoned routes — in Git refs and notes alongside the code, so agents read prior judgment before editing (preflight / start / append / seal) and can catch logical conflicts and abandoned paths before they become git conflicts. Intent travels through ordinary fetch, branch and merge flows with no separate memory service, and its controlled eval reports 0 forbidden-list violations intent-first versus 9 code-first across 8 scenarios.
bad: The project is in public alpha with its schema, agent workflow guidance and Hosted Hub still evolving, and the eval is small (8 scenarios, 3 seeds). Its layered licence leaves hosted surfaces and brand under separate/commercial terms rather than one clean open licence, and the README itself advises skipping it for typo fixes, formatting and other tiny edits.
didnt: Board — intent-before-the-diff preflight that surfaces abandoned routes and constraints before an agent edits, as an idea for our repo work; the layered licence makes this ideas-only, no code adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tinqiao-oss/engramory
good: A portable, zero-dependency memory protocol for local file-based agent memory: one small Markdown file per fact plus one always-loaded index, loaded as standing rules in the host's rules file, with a validator (engramory_doctor.py). Its curation contract makes dedup-before-write, update-don't-duplicate and delete-when-wrong the spine, feedback notes carry required Why / How-to-apply lines, and the index is bounded — warnings at 150 lines / 20 KB and a hard PreToolUse hook that blocks growth past 200 lines / 25 KB before the write lands.
bad: The README labels version 0.12.1 experimental: the discipline is model-followed and best-effort rather than guaranteed, the cap hook is bypassed by shell tools, MCP file tools, external editors and sync clients, and it assumes a single writer with serialised writes. By design it ships no database, embeddings or search engine, so it does not scale beyond small personal stores.
didnt: Board — a pre-write hard cap hook that denies index growth past its size cap, instead of after-the-fact compaction alerts, for keeping our always-loaded memory front page lean. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nowledge-co/community
good: Community registry and plugin collection for Nowledge Mem, with integrations.json as the canonical source of truth for capabilities, install commands, transport and tool naming across dozens of hosts (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, Hermes and more). It defines an honest shared autonomy contract — automatic, guided or manual — distinguishing having memory tools from actually getting autonomous memory behaviour, and its integrations provide Context Bundle / Working Memory startup context, routed recall and pre-compaction transcript save.
bad: No licence is stated at the source — the root listing contains no LICENSE file. The repo is only the integration shell: the actual Nowledge Mem product must be running locally and the nmem CLI installed, the core memory system is not in this repository, and capture promises vary widely by integration (several are guided or manual, or explicitly do not promise full-thread capture).
didnt: Rejected — a plugin registry for an external proprietary memory product, with no licence at source; it duplicates the agent-door work our own wiki already does. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: congchuanling-dot/Cohort
good: A local-first, proof-carrying agent runtime: its Time Machine records each run (model requests/responses, tool observations, prompts, schemas, git baseline and workspace snapshot) as a Replay Bundle with SHA-256 proof, supporting fully offline exact replay and fork-from-a-turn counterfactual trials in isolated git worktrees, while a Runtime Governor governs context capacity, cost, cache and tool risk from the same evidence log. Long-term memory is verifiable — entries must cite tool evidence and are read back after writing — and multi-agent delivery merges transactionally only after independent verification and human approval.
bad: Its scope is far broader than a knowledge system — Chrome Bridge browser automation and macOS desktop computer use — and the verified install path is macOS-centric (npm binary for macOS architectures, Accessibility/Screen Recording permissions, manual loading of the unpacked Chrome extension). It requires the user's own provider API keys, and the README carries a preview-stage badge and a dedicated current-boundaries section.
didnt: Board — proof-carrying replay bundles with hash-verified exact replay and fork-from-a-turn trials, as an idea for auditing and comparing our own agent runs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sourcey
good: Turns OpenAPI (2.0/3.0/3.1/3.2), MCP, Doxygen XML, godoc, rustdoc and Markdown into one static HTML site you own, with guides, changelog, roadmap and llms.txt from the same build; everything renders at build time with no dashboard or runtime, plus client-side fuzzy search and agent-readable exports (documents.json, llms-full.txt).
bad: AGPL-3.0 copyleft restricts embedding in our stack; the npm CLI requires Node 22.19+, and Rust documentation needs nightly rustdoc JSON or a committed snapshot built on a stable toolchain.
didnt: Board — agent-readable documentation exports (llms.txt, llms-full.txt, canonical page URLs for citation) as a pattern for the wiki portal; AGPL code itself is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sphinx
good: Mature documentation generator that builds HTML, PDF, plain text, EPUB, TeX and manual pages from reStructuredText, with extensive semantic cross-references, automatic indices, code highlighting, Jinja2 templating and a large extension ecosystem including autodoc for API documentation.
bad: Its native markup is reStructuredText, not Markdown — Markdown sources need an extension such as MyST Parser — and it is centred on the Python/Docutils ecosystem rather than on a linked knowledge base with backlinks or search over notes.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms the static, multi-format publishing model (HTML plus PDF/EPUB from one source tree) that our wiki portal and PDF delivery already follow. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ikiwiki
good: A wiki compiler that converts wiki pages to publishable HTML while storing pages and history in a revision control system such as Git or Subversion; it also supports blogging and podcasting and ships a large array of plugins, acting as a flexible static site generator with some dynamic features.
bad: GPL-licensed and Perl-based, presented by its own homepage as a compiler with only some dynamic features; the homepage documents no built-in search, citation or structured-query layer over the compiled pages.
didnt: Corroboration — a git-backed wiki compiled to static HTML is the same architecture as our LLM Wiki and its Lens portal, validating that design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Orchid Wiki
good: Orchid is a plugin-driven Java/Kotlin static site generator whose wiki feature (the OrchidWiki artifact) offers a GitBook-like wiki alongside blogs and Javadoc integration, with multi-theme support, an admin interface, powerful indexing and full-text static search.
bad: The GitHub repository is archived (public archive), its 0.x artefacts were published to the deprecated JCenter repository, and it is GPL-3.0 copyleft on a JVM/Gradle stack.
didnt: Rejected — archived and unmaintained, GPL-3.0, and tied to the JVM ecosystem; no fit for our Markdown/git wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Xlog
good: A fast, git-native Go framework for knowledge bases: it works in any Markdown directory, automatically converts page mentions into links (surfacing implicit links), adds bidirectional backlinks, hashtags and full-text search, serves a live-preview server and builds static sites, with 37 built-in extensions.
bad: The README documents no sync, access control, citation-locking or approval machinery, and editing is deliberately delegated to an external desktop editor rather than done in the browser; it is a small project (233 stars) centred on a single binary server.
didnt: Board — automatic implicit-link surfacing (mention-to-link conversion plus automatic backlinks) as a feature idea for the wiki traverse/Lens layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LightCMS
good: A self-hosted Go CMS that works human or headless: full admin UI plus REST and MCP APIs (130 MCP tools in the current README, grown from the catalogued 41), built-in semantic search and site chat, and content forking, versioning, diff/merge review, templates and approval workflows with static page generation.
bad: Very new and small (repository created 2026-01-23, 32 stars) and scoped to website content management on MongoDB (its quick start walks through MongoDB Atlas setup), not to a file-based personal knowledge wiki.
didnt: Board — the agent sandbox pattern (agents work in an isolated content fork with copy-on-write, humans review a per-field diff and merge, with scoped sandbox-only API keys and a per-session change ledger) as a model for approval-gated agent writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Electric SQL
good: Provides sync primitives for local-first apps: Postgres Sync is a read-path sync engine handling partial replication (Shapes), data delivery and fan-out over an HTTP API, with TypeScript and Elixir clients, alongside TanStack DB and PGlite for reactive local data.
bad: Sync is read-path only in the current architecture — writes must go through the application's own APIs rather than through Electric — and it requires running the Electric sync service against a Postgres database configured with the necessary replication permissions.
didnt: Rejected — our wiki is Markdown files under git, with no Postgres-backed application for Electric to sync; scope mismatch. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OrbitDB
good: A serverless, distributed peer-to-peer database using IPFS for storage and libp2p pubsub for peer sync; its Merkle-CRDT OpLog gives conflict-free, cryptographically verifiable writes and merges, with events, documents, keyvalue and keyvalue-indexed database types running in browsers and Node.js.
bad: It is eventually consistent by design and requires standing up the Helia/IPFS and libp2p stack, including configuring the IPFS instance for persistence and peers for connectivity; there is no central authority or single source of truth to lock citations against.
didnt: Rejected — P2P/IPFS replication conflicts with our single-owner, local-first custody and citation-locking model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PouchDB
good: An open-source JavaScript database inspired by Apache CouchDB that runs in the browser (46KB gzipped) and Node.js, storing data locally while offline and synchronising it with CouchDB and compatible servers when back online, across Firefox, Chrome, Opera, Safari and IE.
bad: Synchronisation is defined by the CouchDB replication protocol, so adopting it means adopting a CouchDB-compatible server ecosystem; the homepage also notes the project is currently undergoing incubation at the Apache Software Foundation.
didnt: Rejected — duplicates storage/sync needs already met by git-tracked files, and would pull in a CouchDB document model foreign to the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Y-Sweet
good: An open-source realtime CRDT document store and sync backend built on Yjs, written in Rust: it persists document data to S3-compatible storage, scales horizontally with a session-backend model, deploys as a native Linux process and provides document-level access control via client tokens, with TypeScript/React client libraries.
bad: It stores Yjs documents only — it is a sync/persistence backend for collaborative editors, not a general database or search layer — and by default `y-sweet serve` does not write data to disk unless a data directory or S3 path is specified.
didnt: Rejected — realtime multiplayer document sync is outside our single-owner wiki's needs; no collaborative editing requirement exists to serve. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GUN.js
good: A decentralised P2P graph database and sync protocol: multiplayer by default with realtime peer-to-peer state synchronisation, local-first and offline with end-to-end encryption, a graph model that can hold key/value, tables and documents, in a roughly 9KB gzipped embedded engine.
bad: By design there is no master, no server and no single source of truth, which conflicts with citation locking; the README's own testing notes warn that tests trigger persistent writes and the database must be cleared before re-running, reflecting a loose operational model.
didnt: Rejected — a no-single-source-of-truth P2P graph is the opposite of our citation-locked, owner-controlled wiki custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: libSQL
good: An open-source, open-contribution fork of SQLite with embedded replicas inside the app, a libSQL server for remote SQLite access, WebAssembly user-defined functions and core extensions (ALTER TABLE type changes, randomized ROWID), with official Rust, TypeScript/JS and Go drivers and full SQLite file-format and API compatibility.
bad: The README states libSQL inherits SQLite's fundamental limitations such as the single-writer model, and that while it is actively maintained, new features are being developed in the separate Turso database rewrite (currently in beta), so the project's centre of gravity is shifting.
didnt: Rejected — the wiki's storage is Markdown files under git, not an embedded SQL database; adopting libSQL would duplicate, not serve, that layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PGlite
good: A WASM build of real Postgres packaged as a TypeScript client library (about 3MB gzipped) that runs in the browser, Node.js, Bun and Deno with no other dependencies, supports many Postgres extensions including pgvector and PostGIS, and can persist to IndexedDB or the filesystem or run as an ephemeral in-memory database, with reactive, realtime bindings.
bad: The README's Limitations section states a single limit plainly: PGlite is single user/connection (it builds on Postgres's single-user mode because WASM cannot fork processes), and its status badge marks it Alpha.
didnt: Board — an embeddable in-browser Postgres with pgvector as a candidate engine for local semantic search/QA experiments over the wiki, related to the undecided instant-answer lane. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Turbolite
good: A SQLite VFS in Rust that serves point lookups and JOINs directly from S3-compatible storage with sub-250ms cold latency (86ms for a point lookup plus join in its published benchmark), with page-level zstd compression and AES-256 encryption usable separately from S3, a local no-S3 mode, and bindings for Python, Node.js, Go and Rust.
bad: The README flags it prominently as experimental — under active development and containing bugs — with one safe writer per database (a single write source), an experimental WAL-shipping path, and no formal releases on the repository (0 releases).
didnt: Board — page-level compressed, encrypted SQLite databases served from object storage as a pattern for hosting many small per-topic databases cheaply, once the project matures past its experimental stage. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VelesDB
good: A local-first memory engine for AI agents in a single small Rust binary that fuses vector (HNSW/SIMD), graph and columnar engines under one query language (VelesQL); its why() returns the evidence path behind every recall by walking typed links, and a deterministic context compiler shrinks agent context with an auditable, reversible decision per fragment — with no cloud, LLM or API key in the memory path, plus an MCP memory server.
bad: Its own Known limitations list single writer per collection, no distributed replication, no advanced RBAC or multi-tenant isolation in Core (those are Premium, commercial-license features), and WASM MATCH queries limited to 2 hops; the core is source-available under a custom licence, not an OSI open-source licence.
didnt: Board — why() evidence-path recall and the deterministic, auditable context compiler as ideas for truth-aware retrieval and context assembly; the custom source-available licence makes the code itself ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wuisabel-gif/MemWhale
good: Records commands, output, failures and the fixes that worked into local SQLite and serves them over MCP to 19 coding agents, with no account and nothing uploaded. It keeps provenance explicit (agent identity separate from source type), groups linked worktrees under canonical repository IDs, reports 97% top-5 retrieval on LongMemEval (470 questions, retrieval only), and leaves MCP-authored lessons pending review by default.
bad: The README itself scopes it narrowly: a debugging memory layer, not a general-purpose personal memory system or a replacement for project documentation. Capture is separate from retrieval — MCP alone does not record terminal activity and automatic capture needs a client-specific hook (Rho's hook payload lacks command text and stdout); its 25%-to-96% bug evaluation is stated to be synthetic tasks, not a field study, and Windows is supported only inside WSL.
didnt: Rejected — debugging-session capture for coding agents, not a citation-locked personal knowledge OS; its local SQLite/MCP shape duplicates parts of our stack without the wiki's compiled, human-readable layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wuxuyun0606-collab/lmc-5
good: Five-axis XYZEM model (timeline, relations, fact evolution, experience signals, metabolism) split into a raw event journal and curated memories, with fact-key supersession, a Z-axis conflict audit that queues contradiction candidates for pending review instead of auto-superseding, a gated night hippocampus pass, and both a zero-dependency SQLite minimal implementation and a PostgreSQL/pgvector production implementation with a three-tier recall cascade.
bad: AGPL-3.0 with a separate commercial licence file. The production implementation needs PostgreSQL plus at least one embedder API key, and the README warns the Y relation graph is not built at write time — unless night_dream is scheduled in cron, two-hop expansion, contradiction and derivation chains silently go silent; several axes still require primary-agent review for splits, supersession and archive/delete decisions.
didnt: Board — the Z-axis conflict-audit queue and the raw-events vs curated-memory split, as ideas only; AGPL-3.0 code is never adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: roandejager/Hillock
good: Local, gradient-free neuro-symbolic engine combining a relational SQLite knowledge graph, Hebbian synaptic memory and hyperdimensional computing: it extracts facts without an LLM pass, applies a hard mathematical gate that blocks unanswerable questions before they reach the LLM, ingests a 30-sentence document in about 5 seconds, runs in under 1.2 GB VRAM (CPU-only possible), and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API server plus a GPU-free verification suite.
bad: Dual-licensed AGPL-3.0 / paid commercial licence (startup $49/mo, enterprise $2,500+/yr) with a CLA for contributors. It is pre-1.0 (v0.8.0 status, roadmap tracked in a single issue), an independent single-maintainer research project, and requires Python 3.10+, a running local Ollama and a downloaded spaCy English model.
didnt: Board — the mathematical abstention gate that blocks unanswerable questions before the LLM, as an idea for scored abstention only; AGPL-3.0 code is never adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: iamtouchskyer/memex
good: Zettelkasten persistent memory on exactly a markdown-plus-git substrate: atomic cards in the agent's own words, links written in context ('this relates to [[X]] because...') rather than bare tags, a curated keyword index, 12 MCP tools shared across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf, VS Code/Copilot and any MCP client from one ~/.memex/cards/ directory, plus privacy guardrails that reject high-confidence raw secrets and redact credentials in URLs.
bad: The higher-quality agentic-memory workflow is experimental and default-off. Cross-device sync auto-creation requires the GitHub CLI (or a self-supplied remote), and memex serve opens a third-party web UI (memra.vercel.app) when sync is set up unless --local is passed; with no embeddings or vector store, recall depends on its ranked keyword card search.
didnt: Board — its link-in-context Zettelkasten discipline and keyword-index entry points, for comparison against our wiki's note-linking rules. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NickCirv/engram
good: A local structural code graph and context spine: source miners extract entities, references and Git co-change into a project-local SQLite graph, queries traverse it and render bounded context through CLI, hooks, MCP and an authenticated local dashboard across 8 IDEs, and recorded mistakes are carried into later sessions.
bad: The README itself qualifies its headline claims: the documentation review was source-inspected, not executed, benchmarks at this revision are unverified, a smaller context packet does not by itself demonstrate equal answer quality or a lower bill, and the whole system is not guaranteed network-free (npm update checks, Context7 and configured MCP/plugin providers can make external calls). Default init also installs a Sentinel hook unless --no-hook is passed.
didnt: Rejected — a code-structure context tool for coding sessions, not a personal knowledge OS; its graph retrieval duplicates investigation aids we already have and its token-reduction claim is unverified at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Uranid/mnem
good: 'Git for AI agent knowledge': a persistent, versioned knowledge graph in a project .mnem/ directory with branch, diff, merge and rollback of any write, deterministic no-LLM ingest (re-ingesting an unchanged file is a no-op), hybrid retrieval fusing vector, keyword and graph traversal in one pass with explicit token-budget reporting, first-class forgetting where revoking a fact filters every retrieval path while preserving the audit trail, all offline in a single binary usable as CLI, HTTP server, MCP server, Python library or WASM.
bad: Install is rough at source: macOS pip and npm binaries are stated not yet published (the v0.1.7 runtime downloader fails on macOS), Cargo install compiles 5-15 minutes and the MSRV is Rust 1.95. Its benchmark lead carries disclosed methodology caveats, including lenient MAX-over-turn-hits scoring on LoCoMo and differing pipelines on FinanceBench.
didnt: Corroboration — versioned, branchable, revocable knowledge with token-budget transparency confirms our git-backed wiki design; the Rust binary itself duplicates our substrate rather than filling a gap. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alex09x/kyb
good: Git-backed shared memory for agent fleets with no database: one markdown file per entry, one commit per change so a commit SHA is a version ID, every write versioned and attributed, writes rejected when the body looks like a secret, hybrid BM25 (Tantivy) plus local vector search over current and historical versions including as-of queries where a superseded version never answers, and incident/task kinds whose closing requires a resolution and archives rather than deletes.
bad: A young project (created 2026-08) with a deliberately flat key space — no projects or namespaces. It requires running a Rust server, and its default KYB_AUTH=off trusts the network (anyone who can reach a non-loopback bind can write); hybrid search degrades to lexical-only when no ONNX model is on disk.
didnt: Board — per-write attribution plus close-with-a-mandatory-resolution and as-of historical search, for comparison against our filings/ledger discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PerryLink/dsh-memento
good: Bounded, layered, approval-gated, auditable cross-session memory: every write path (add/replace/remove/seed) is forced through an approval waterfall inside the service that no model path can bypass, denied writes still land an audit row, replace/remove approvals carry the full text being changed, hard per-track/per-layer character budgets fail with a structured error rather than truncating or auto-compacting, and a frozen snapshot is injected once per session over a zero-dependency SQLite provider.
bad: Maintenance status is stated as FROZEN since 2026-10-05 in the repo description. It is bound to DeepSeek Harness alpha lines (verified against dsh-v0.2.1-alpha.2, Node ^22.19.0), and the README names an audit gap out loud: the harness does not know memory/* session event types, so the session-log side of the audit trail is not written and the gate stays adaptive.
didnt: Corroboration — a non-bypassable approval gate, denied-write audit rows and hard budgets confirm our approval-gated write design; frozen and DeepSeek-Harness-specific, so not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lsaint/aikito
good: One personal Git workspace governing the context coding agents share — instructions, skills, MCPs, subagents and durable memory — across 8 agent consumers, projects and machines, stdlib-only Python with no daemon, vector store, database or hosted service required. Adopt and sync preflight their complete plans before writing, locally edited copies block sync until reviewed, and durable memory is plain Markdown versioned by Git in global and project scopes.
bad: Memory is a skill that guides agents to retrieve and update Markdown notes rather than a retrieval or citation engine, so quality depends on agent compliance with the skill. The README documents no evaluation, search ranking or abstention mechanism, Windows setup needs Developer Mode, and secret governance is manual — the user must review secrets before pushing the workspace repo.
didnt: Rejected — its workspace-governance and Markdown-plus-Git memory duplicate our wiki's substrate, and it offers no citation locking or scored abstention our system lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docmancer/docmancer
good: Indexes the memory, rules and instructions Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini already wrote on the machine and carries the durable parts to every agent as canonical local Markdown, with recall returning cited answers that keep the contributing source attached to every claim. Consolidation proposals link to exact transcript evidence and wait for review, writes go through an approval proposal whose default answer is no, edits are guarded by the content hash last read, and the default profile runs offline on SQLite FTS5 plus sqlite-vec with a vendored embedding model.
bad: Agent backup and restore are stated to be development-preview commands and managed cloud snapshots remain gated on migration and recovery acceptance. Automatic recall and session capture exist only for Claude Code and Codex (other agents recall on demand via skill files), and multi-machine Personal Sync is a paid subscription with trial, grace and hosted-ciphertext deletion windows.
didnt: Board — evidence-linked consolidation proposals that wait for review before becoming shared memory, as a pattern for our ingest review flow. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ali-hey-0/ai-runtime-lab
good: Fourteen self-contained, runnable proof-of-concept phases (30-100 lines per concept) covering FSM state guards, durable execution with memoised replay, retry/idempotency, DAGs, model routing, RAG, memory systems, multi-agent orchestration, security sandboxing and observability. Its core pattern is a deterministic runtime sandwich: FSM guard, validated structured intent, durable idempotent execution, checkpoint, observe — the LLM only proposes and never touches the outside world directly.
bad: It states plainly that it is not a framework and not a product: a personal engineering-education project with intentionally minimal code, only 4 commits and 0 releases, and phases 15-17 (generative UX, distributed systems, final integration) are still roadmap items with no implementation folders.
didnt: Rejected — a teaching lab of minimal proof-of-concepts, not a memory or knowledge system to integrate; its value is mental models we already apply. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Coding-Dev-Tools/engraphis
good: Local-first SQLite memory that works offline, organises memories by workspace/repo/session, and combines vector, lexical, graph and code-aware retrieval packed to a hard context budget. Grounded recall preserves provenance and temporal history: it cites retrieved memories or abstains when evidence is weak, and its timeline can surface superseded (closed) versions instead of silently replacing facts.
bad: Its own benchmark section concedes the registered results are three small deterministic offline fixtures (18-26 samples) that do not establish general task performance. The optional Jev remote-assistance lane is experimental, BYOK, showed no retrieval-quality improvement in its 40-task synthetic comparison, and managed Jev is stated as not yet available; the hosted control plane and managed services are private.
didnt: Corroboration — cite-or-abstain grounded recall over bi-temporal history, keeping superseded versions visible, confirms our citation-locking and truth-aware retrieval design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yantrikos/yantrikdb-server
good: A Rust cognitive memory engine shipped as embedded library, MCP server (15 tools) and HTTP cluster that does three things plain vector stores do not: temporal decay with configurable half-life so stale memories fade, a think() pass that consolidates duplicate fragments into canonical memories, and contradiction detection with a conflicts API. Multi-signal scoring combines recency, importance, similarity and graph proximity, with CRDT multi-device sync and proactive triggers for pending conflicts and approaching deadlines.
bad: The README itself limits contradiction detection to relations its extractor recognises: claims are keyed by subject so inverse-functional conflicts (two different CEOs of one company) are not modelled, and copular attribute claims are off by default. It also carries a correction notice that earlier Phase 3 benchmark writeups used a Python simulator rather than the real engine, and its newest throughput bench has not been re-run in over 20 releases after an earlier fresh-install wedge at 256 writes.
didnt: Board — the temporal-decay fading model (importance plus configurable half-life) and the think() consolidation/conflict pass as one scheduled engine operation, for the ideas board. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sibyl-Labs/Sibyl-Memory
good: Durable file-based long-term memory with no vector database and no embeddings: a SQLite + FTS5 engine with a five-tier hierarchical schema (hot state, warm entities, cold journal, reference, archive) and single-source-of-truth per entity enforced by a UNIQUE constraint. Ships as a five-package family (SDK, CLI, MCP server, Hermes adapter, LangGraph BaseStore) and reports #2 overall at 95.6% on LongMemEval Oracle.
bad: Despite the local-first framing, an activated hosted account is required since client 0.9.0: every memory tool needs a server-signed entitlement renewed by daily check-ins to api.sibyllabs.org, free accounts have a local cap enforced server-side, and paid tiers gate the self-learning and linter features. Native Windows is not supported (WSL2 only).
didnt: Rejected — the mandatory hosted account, entitlement check-ins and server-enforced caps conflict with our local-first custody model, and its file/SQLite memory duplicates what our wiki already does. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BotHarness/DeepSeekBot
good: A personal bot-team platform: multiple bots each with their own identity, persona and pixel avatar that can be chatted with, grouped and delegated tasks, with scheduled jobs and a bot marketplace for sharing bots. Each bot's memory is a plain Git repository the user can browse, diff, correct directly and push to GitHub to share one bot across machines, and bots reply under their own identities inside Slack, Discord, Feishu/Lark, QQ and WeChat.
bad: It is a plugin that only runs inside the DeepSeek Harness desktop host, and the README notes the computer running DSH must stay online for bots to do background work — total platform lock-in rather than a standalone memory engine. Its scope is a multi-bot chat product surface (themes, wallpapers, avatar workshops), not knowledge management.
didnt: Rejected — DeepSeek Harness lock-in and a bot-team chat product scope; our multi-agent coordination already runs through the wiki, not a host-bound bot platform. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: slow-stack/mneme
good: Cross-session memory on local SQLite with editable Markdown mirrors: autoDream background consolidation dedupes and merges, contradictions are frozen for human adjudication rather than silently resolved, and every automatic reorganisation leaves a replayable decision receipt (input snapshot, decision detail, result hash). Recall is 4-way (keyword/vector/BM25/entity) with an offline local-embedding option, plus a standalone daemon and a zero-dependency stdio MCP server usable outside its host.
bad: It is built as a plugin for DeepSeek Harness, with awkward install mechanics the README warns about at length (the installable package is a subdirectory; installing the repo root yields an uninstallable shell). Several headline capabilities are off by default or beta: scope isolation and entity extraction default off, and the M.O. workflow-pipeline feature is v0.9 beta with no run records yet, so every workflow node stays in candidate state.
didnt: Corroboration — contradictions frozen pending a human ruling and replayable, auditable consolidation receipts confirm our approval-gated write design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Patdolitse/piia-engram
good: A local-first, user-owned AI work-identity layer stored as JSON/Markdown under ~/.engram/ and portable across MCP coding tools, holding preferences, lessons, decisions and playbooks rather than task history. High-risk writes (credentials, shell commands, MCP config, permission rules) wait for user review, and its Memory Lens preview shows exactly what an AI caller would receive versus what governance withheld, with secrets redacted.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us. The README's own evidence table shows verification is uneven: only Claude Code and Codex have partial (L4) continuity proof, several listed tools are merely 'expected to work', and by default low/medium-risk writes are auto-absorbed; local files are plaintext by default with encryption only optional and field-level.
didnt: Board — the Memory Lens idea: a read-only preview of exactly what a caller will receive versus what was withheld, before anything is sent; AGPL-3.0 code itself is not adoptable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memoket/memoket-kite
good: A vector-free memory engine: conversations crystallise into typed, dated, topic-indexed facts that keep the original message as evidence, and each question compiles into a readable, validatable symbolic plan executed deterministically over the topic index. Time-aware sorting makes 'now' resolve to the latest fact, answers arrive with source receipts, and an unanswerable question returns genuinely empty; it reports 93.51% on LoCoMo and 85.60% on LongMemEval-S at roughly 1.6K reader tokens per question.
bad: It is very young (13 commits, 1 release) and is a plain Python library only — the README says agent-ecosystem integrations are 'next on the roadmap'. Fact extraction and question planning require an OpenAI API key or OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint, and its technical report is still in preparation with no arXiv paper yet, so the benchmark claims rest on the repo's own reproduction contract.
didnt: Board — the question-to-inspectable-symbolic-plan mechanism over dated, source-linked, topic-filed facts, directly relevant to our truth-aware retrieval gap. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JasonDocton/lucid-memory
good: Local, zero-cloud-cost memory with a Rust core modelled on human cognition: gist compression, MINERVA-style cubing to suppress weak matches, multiplicative recency (relevance times recency), 3-hop spreading activation so related memories surface together, plus episodic, visual and procedural memory types and background consolidation that strengthens recent memories, decays stale ones and prunes weak associations. It reports 2.7ms retrieval and 82.5% recall at fixed token budgets against Pinecone and claude-mem baselines.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us. Its headline numbers come from its own benchmarks on small realistic developer workflows of 50-200 memories, framed as marketing comparisons against Pinecone; installation needs 5GB free disk and an embedding-model download, and supported clients are limited to Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence bars code adoption and its scope is coding-session recall, not a cited knowledge corpus; the spreading-activation ranking idea is noted but the system is not a fit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: eiondb/eion
good: Shared memory storage for multi-agent systems combining PostgreSQL with pgvector for conversation memory and semantic search with a Neo4j knowledge graph fed by an in-house entity/relationship extraction service. It exposes memory and knowledge tools over a built-in MCP server, supports sequential agency hand-offs and controlled external guest-agent access, and provides a register console with agent registration at read, read-write or full CRUD permission levels.
bad: Very early and thin: 10 commits, no releases, and its concurrent live-agency mode is explicitly marked WIP with console monitoring features 'coming soon'. The stack is heavy for what it delivers — Dockerised PostgreSQL plus Neo4j, a Go 1.21+ server and Python 3.13+ extraction services — and AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence, an immature 10-commit codebase, and a heavy Postgres-plus-Neo4j server stack disproportionate to a personal local-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dcostenco/prism-coder
good: Persistent session memory for coding agents as an MCP server: sessions resume with handoff notes, open TODOs and configurable context depth, backed by a knowledge graph with semantic, keyword and graph search, an immutable session audit trail, session drift detection and time-travel history. It routes bounded work to on-device Ollama models (2B-27B fleet) first and meters exactly which token volume local serving kept off the cloud model, reporting tokens rather than invented dollar figures.
bad: The scope is enormous and churning — the README is a long chain of v20.x feature releases mixing memory, inference routing, a browser, a code reviewer and a security scanner — and higher tiers sit behind the Synalux subscription portal (Pro $15/mo, Team $20/seat/mo) with cloud sync and skills entitlement; even in local modes the README notes per-call entitlement checks and telemetry still contact the portal.
didnt: Rejected — a sprawling coding-agent product entangled with a paid subscription portal, duplicating coding-session memory rather than serving a cited personal knowledge corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GuyMannDude/mnemo-cortex
good: A local-first cognitive coprocessor over MCP: active memory that classifies on ingest, consolidates overnight with cross-agent dreaming, and keeps roughly 7,000 verified facts with confidence laddering and full audit history alongside a tamper-evident memory ledger that seals every save. It adds structured-fact exact lookup, a workspace-wide document librarian (SQLite FTS5), encrypted USB sneakernet sync between machines, and agent-to-agent messaging — all with no telemetry and no cloud dependency.
bad: It is built and maintained by one maker (self-described, donation-funded) running his own five-agent fleet, so its production claims (~10,000 memories, 84 versions) are single-operator evidence with no independent benchmark in the README. The feature surface is very sprawling — passports, disco-bus messaging, plan pads, USB couriers — and ChatGPT access needs a bespoke hardened gate because ChatGPT has no local MCP.
didnt: Board — the tamper-evident memory ledger idea: seal each save so a later verify names any record that changed, went missing or arrived unsealed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zilliztech/mfs
good: A context harness that mounts scattered sources — code repos, memory and skill files, docs and PDFs, cloud drives, chat, tickets, databases and SaaS — as one file-like tree under stable URIs, driven by ingest and find skills. Agents get both fast semantic search/grep across the whole namespace and progressive browsing (ls, cat, tree, head, tail) down to exact lines; after a one-time setup the stack runs locally and offline with a local embedding model and no API key.
bad: Setup is a real deployment: a separate server plus a Rust CLI, a first Docker build of minutes and a ~600MB embedding model download, on a Milvus-lineage vector stack that is heavy for a personal wiki. Retrieval is similarity-score based with no citation locking or abstention gate shown in the README, and its breadth across mail, CRM and production databases widens the ingestion surface considerably.
didnt: Board — the file-like unified namespace with browse-then-read progressive disclosure (ls/cat over every source) as an interface idea for our corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Frappucc1no/recall-loom
good: A file-based project-memory layer needing no database, RAG or background service: context brief, rolling summary, daily logs and next steps live in readable Markdown/JSON files beside the project, so a new session, model or tool resumes from current facts first and only digs into history when needed. Continuity files are validated for missing, stale or conflicting state, and long-term-fact updates pass revision, freshness and structure checks with preview-style repair instead of silent writes.
bad: Deliberately narrow by its own account: it is not a knowledge base, task orchestrator or execution framework, offers no semantic retrieval over a large corpus, and refuses unconfirmed automatic extraction or merging of long-term facts. It depends on skills-capable AI coding tools (or bridge files) to be invoked, and the project is small (50 commits).
didnt: Corroboration — current-before-history file memory (brief, rolling summary, daily logs) with validated, non-silent writes mirrors our wiki continuity model almost exactly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zqiren/Orbital
good: A project agent that owns project context so agents are replaceable: it maintains plain local Markdown files (PROJECT_STATE.md, DECISIONS.md, LESSONS.md, CONTEXT.md, SESSION_LOG.md) that every agent reads before starting, hands work to Claude Code, Codex and Kimi Code (and can do work itself), and lets a different agent pick up mid-conversation when one hits its usage limit.
bad: Downloads are offered only for macOS (Apple Silicon, macOS 13+) and Windows 10/11, the Windows installer is not code-signed (SmartScreen 'Unknown publisher'), Hermes and OpenClaw support are listed as 'coming soon', and model calls require the user's own API key. The licence is copyleft GPL-3.0.
didnt: Corroboration — its local, plain-Markdown project files (state, decisions, lessons) read by every agent before work confirm our wiki's local-first, file-based context design; GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only and the agent-manager scope duplicates our stack, so no code adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shy2593666979/AgentChat
good: A full agent application platform (FastAPI + Vue) integrating LangChain, Function Call, MCP, RAG, Memory, HITL and Skills: agents can be bound to tools, MCP servers, skills and knowledge bases with retrieval and reranking, per-user resource isolation is built in, token usage and request tracing are logged, and a first run works on lightweight SQLite, in-memory cache, local files and Chroma.
bad: Scaling means operating MySQL, Redis, MinIO and Milvus/Elasticsearch, knowledge bases need separately configured embedding and rerank models (the chat model's key cannot be reused), the README states its Docker deployment combination was not run-verified in the latest documentation update, and the repo shows 0 releases despite 555 commits.
didnt: Rejected — a general multi-user agent chat platform duplicates platform layers we already have and is not a personal knowledge/wiki memory system; scope and operational weight do not fit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mindscale-noah/MindMemOS
good: A portable, self-evolving memory operating layer: user profiles, preferences, project facts and tool experience persist as reusable assets shared across OpenClaw, Hermes, Claude Code and OpenHands; memory improves through schema learning, offline 'dreaming' consolidation and feedback, experience memories are distilled into skill candidates, and it reports benchmarks (LoCoMo, PersonaMem, MemoryAgentBench, SpreadsheetBench) with HTTP API, Python SDK/CLI and agent plugins.
bad: Very young (repo created 2026-06-23, first released 2026-06-30) and heavy to self-host: local deployment starts a Docker stack of Qdrant, Neo4j and Kafka (plus optional ClickHouse, OTel and Grafana) and requires three separately configured model routers (chat, embedding, rerank); the hosted cloud path is a commercial quota service (starring the repo 'upgrades to a Pro quota membership').
didnt: Rejected — maturity (weeks old) and a heavy Qdrant/Neo4j/Kafka service stack conflict with our local-first, file-custody wiki; its self-evolving auto-write model also conflicts with approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: omdsh-dev/dsh-mnemon
good: Composable, view-based memory for DeepSeek Harness with three memory kinds (runtime memory injected as compact USER.md/MEMORY.md, project documents searched on demand, and durable Memory Spaces recalled from pluggable providers): each turn shows a memory bar listing exactly what it read and wrote, one-click save distils a fact into the right space with a receipt, and self-evolving skills are backtested and change nothing without the user's Adopt click.
bad: It is built specifically for DeepSeek Harness and pins release-candidate host versions (DSH 0.2.1-rc.2 / 0.2.0-rc.2); the repo was created 2026-08-10, the Skills component is labelled experimental, and third-party Memory Spaces providers differ in graph, deletion and enumeration capabilities, with turning a component off not erasing its stored memory.
didnt: Board — the per-turn memory bar (what a turn read/wrote, with receipts) and backtest-before-Adopt skill evolution are ideas for the ideas board; the implementation is DeepSeek-Harness-specific, so no adoption for our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neo4j-labs/agent-memory
good: Graph-native agent memory backed by Neo4j with three memory types (short-term conversations, long-term entities/preferences/facts as a knowledge graph, and reasoning traces/tool usage), multi-stage entity extraction with typed relations, entity resolution and deduplication, an MCP server, Python and TypeScript SDKs, explicit :TOUCHED audit edges from reasoning steps to entities, consolidation primitives and an eval harness.
bad: The README badges it Beta and states it is a Neo4j Labs project that is 'not officially supported. There are no SLAs or guarantees around backwards compatibility'; it requires running Neo4j/Aura or the hosted NAMS service, the SDK is async-only with no synchronous wrapper, and available methods and retrieval scopes differ between the Bolt and NAMS backends.
didnt: Rejected — fit: our wiki is Markdown-file-first with citation locking, and a Neo4j graph database backend (or hosted NAMS) would replace, not extend, that custody model; Beta/Labs support posture adds maturity risk. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Neo4j Labs

name: MaxFreedomPollard/Compartment
good: Encrypted, fully offline agentic memory with a GUI memory map: one claim per memory (enforced, 200-character cap with atomisation of longer notes), every memory records its required source and learned date, superseded records stay readable by id in an audit chain, memories can expire, untrusted content can be marked quarantined, recall is hybrid vector+keyword with a relative cut so an unknown question returns nothing, and there is no LLM, API key, account or telemetry inside.
bad: A single-author project created 2026-07-20; the 200-character claim cap forces splitting of normal notes, the README itself warns a wrong expiry deletes a memory the user wanted, and each vault is locked to one embedding model (changing it requires a re-embed reindex).
didnt: Corroboration — one-claim-per-memory with mandatory source and date, superseded-but-readable audit chains, quarantined untrusted content and returning nothing for unknown questions confirm our claim-lifecycle, citation-locking and scored-abstention design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: huggingface/funes
good: Durable, searchable memory of past agent sessions: it indexes Claude Code, Codex, pi and Hermes sessions into a single local Lance dataset, recall fuses vector and BM25 search with reranking and shows which agent each hit came from, grounded answers name the sessions they drew from, credentials are redacted at index time with an always-on gate refusing to push any chunk still containing a secret, and memory can be published as a private-by-default Hugging Face dataset.
bad: Memory is raw session transcripts rather than curated claims; the README notes the release checksum 'does not authenticate the bucket itself', requests to the Hub carry an anonymous install id unless telemetry is opted out of, each memory holds one embedding model's vectors (changing model means rebuilding from transcripts), prebuilt binaries are listed only for Linux and macOS, and the repo was created 2026-06-18.
didnt: Rejected — scope: raw session-transcript ingest is not our curated ingest model (our conversation log is kept verbatim and compiled into wiki pages, not vector-indexed as memory), and Hub publication of session memory conflicts with local-first custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nossa-y/activity-frames
good: Compiles a locally recorded workday into structured activity frames and agent-ready context blocks deterministically (a real day compiles to 1,371 tokens from 247,563 raw snapshot rows, in under a second, with no LLM in the loop): every frame carries evidence pointers back to raw capture rows, a two-tier contract separates measured facts from inferred interpretation (which must be namespaced, confidence-tagged and evidence-linked), every document declares its blind spots, recurring activities become executable workflows that halt and ask on anything unexpected, and it is served over six MCP tools, 100% local.
bad: Status is v0.2, developed and tested only on macOS (Apple Silicon; the Intel build is 'less exercised') with no prebuilt Linux capture engine, and the README warns the local capture database itself stores what the recorder sees (screen content and OCR), so it must be protected like any sensitive file; entity parsers cover a fixed list of sites with a generic fallback elsewhere.
didnt: Board — the two-tier measured-vs-inferred contract with evidence pointers and declared blind spots is an idea for the ideas board for our wiki's claim handling; continuous screen capture itself is out of scope and a privacy step we do not take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: syncable-dev/memtrace-public
licence: Proprietary EULA (indexer and MemDB closed-source; benchmark suite MIT)
good: Structural memory for coding agents: a bi-temporal episodic knowledge graph built by Rust + Tree-sitter parsing with zero LLM calls, indexing 1,500 files in about 1.5 seconds at $0 API cost, with 25+ MCP tools (impact/blast-radius, evolution, dead code, API topology), six temporal scoring modes for time-travel questions, hybrid BM25 + vector + rerank retrieval, and a reproducible benchmark suite whose ground truth comes from Python ast/pyright rather than its own index.
bad: It is in private beta behind a waitlist, the licence is a proprietary EULA with the indexer and database closed-source, telemetry is opt-out, network traffic includes licence validation, and the README itself states the tradeoff: it is purpose-built for code and 'doesn't handle conversational entity memory' the way general memory systems do.
didnt: Board — bi-temporal memory (valid-time vs record-time, with time-travel queries and temporal scoring) is the idea our claim lifecycle could adopt, boarded as an idea only; the code is proprietary/closed-source, so nothing is adopted or built from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tudoumashu/ai-memory-skillpack
good: Bounded, fail-closed project memory for Codex CLI (optional Claude Code support): a SYSTEM.md constitution sets tiers, byte budgets, attribution and replace-guards, memory is read HOT (whole-file each session) / WARM (rg to a section) / COLD (only on explicit history traces), handoff is a one-page snapshot replaced in place rather than an append-only log, writers are forbidden to store secret values with sanitizers as backstop, and acceptance is an executable VERIFY.md with SHA256-pinned pack bytes and receipt-hash upgrade protection.
bad: Scoped to per-repo coding-project memory, not a personal knowledge wiki; it requires Linux or WSL (macOS needs GNU sha256sum/flock/readlink and newer bash or the installer stops), ships no GUI, and is a very young single-author pack (created 2026-09-08, 0 forks).
didnt: Corroboration — bounded HOT/WARM/COLD tiers with byte budgets, replace-in-place handoffs, mandatory write attribution and a fail-closed verifier confirm our lean front-page memory, index-first reading and verification standards. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TeleAI-UAGI/telemem
good: A Mem0-compatible drop-in memory layer (same add()/search() shapes) with character-aware summarisation, LLM-based semantic clustering deduplication, isolated per-character memory profiles, FAISS + JSON dual storage for fast retrieval plus human-readable auditability, fully local running (Qwen + FAISS), a video-to-frames-to-captions multimodal pipeline with ReAct-style video QA, and a reported 86.33% QA accuracy on the ZH-4O long-dialogue benchmark against Mem0's 70.20%.
bad: Its evidence base is its own run on a Chinese multi-character role-play dialogue benchmark — its stated niche is character/companion and multi-persona dialogue, not knowledge management; deduplication depends on LLM clustering (cost and non-determinism), and the evaluation configuration uses 8B-class LLM and embedding models.
didnt: Rejected — fit: per-character dialogue memory for role-play/companion agents duplicates the Mem0-style layer and does not serve a citation-locked personal wiki; benchmark evidence does not transfer to our workload. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: angelnicolasc/graymatter
good: Persistent agent memory as a single ~10 MB Go binary (no Docker, database, config files or cloud account), working as an MCP server or Go library, offline: recall returns receipts (per-signal ranks, fused score and provenance via recall --explain), knowledge-graph edges carry the fact IDs that produced them, facts decay on a deterministic 30-day half-life with tombstones instead of deletes, a context block projects top facts into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md within a token budget, and a doctor --audit mode measures duplicates, staleness and marker conflicts in instruction files.
bad: The README states plainly what it is not — 'Not a knowledge-base UI. Not a hosted service. Not a framework' — its headline 90% token saving is measured against full-history injection and its own test recalls facts planted 96 sessions back only 83% of the time, the 30-day half-life decay is wrong for a permanent knowledge record, cross-project federation is deferred on the roadmap, and it is a single-author project created 2026-04-08.
didnt: Corroboration — recall receipts explaining why each fact ranked, graph edges carrying their source fact IDs, and tombstone-instead-of-delete retention confirm our citation and provenance design; its 30-day decay is explicitly not adopted for a permanent wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: text2future/flowix
good: A local Markdown notes app whose notes double as agent memory: agents work inside a note and write results back into the same note for checking and continuation, and Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Hermes and other MCP/CLI tools can all work from the same set of notes, while notes stay as plain local Markdown files the user can open in other apps, expose to agents only by choice, and sync or back up with their own tools.
bad: The README's development section states the desktop build connects to its cloud service (cloud.flowix.cc) — the production build always connects for cloud sync — which sits uneasily beside the local-control pitch; the DeepSeek Harness plugin is not yet published to npm and must be installed from a checkout, Windows PowerShell 5.1 stdin encoding can corrupt Chinese Markdown unless files are passed explicitly, the desktop app supports only macOS 14+ and Windows 10+, and the repo was created 2026-05-25.
didnt: Rejected — a notes app with its own cloud sync duplicates our wiki + Lens and would move custody of the user's notes into a second, young product; the shared-Markdown-notes idea is already our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: aerovato/operator-memory
good: A self-improving context engine that gives coding agents a Markdown 'brain' for documenting their work — specs, decisions, standards, research and lessons — kept in three partitions (.operator/ private project knowledge, .operator-shared/ published with the repo, ~/.operator/user/ personal knowledge across projects), run as a consult-build-update loop each session, with zero infrastructure: no background agents, no embeddings, no vector database, no model configuration, and knowledge that is transparent, Git-tracked and shareable.
bad: The README admits a cold start is a sparse brain until the agent is asked to write the first specifications, that agents sometimes hesitate to create, consolidate or split documents and must be steered, and that reliable brain updates during long conversations are still roadmap items — so updates depend on the agent remembering; the repo was created 2026-08-16 and is under active development.
didnt: Corroboration — a curated, human-readable Markdown workspace with private/shared/personal partitions and a consult-build-update loop, explicitly rejecting transcript-RAG, is the same architecture as our LLM Wiki; nothing to adopt that we do not already run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NevaMind-AI/memUBot
good: An 'enterprise-ready OpenClaw' proactive assistant built on the memU memory framework: structured, auto-organised persistent memory with semantic indexing, continuous context capture with auto-flush before context compaction so critical information is not lost, shared memory pools with access control for team deployments, a full memory audit trail with export, local-first operation with no cloud dependencies, and adapters for Telegram, Discord, Slack and Feishu.
bad: The repo has 0 releases and only 63 commits since its 2026-01-27 creation, the installer is obtained by entering an email on its website rather than from the repo, and much of the enterprise pitch is roadmap rather than shipped — Linux support, end-to-end encryption, RBAC and SSO all appear under the roadmap headings; the AGPL-3.0 licence is copyleft.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under our licence discipline, and the product is an immature, team/enterprise assistant platform that duplicates our own agent-plus-wiki stack; its auto-flush-before-compaction idea is noted but nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mmethodz/dreamgraph
licence: DreamGraph Source-Available Community License v2.0 (custom, source-available; GitHub reports Other/NOASSERTION)
good: A graph-governed conceptual development environment: an instance-scoped daemon, CLI, VS Code extension and browser Architect over a persistent knowledge graph grounded in source, ADRs, workflows, tests and runtime observations, so plans and architecture decisions become auditable execution. Cognitive outputs stay advisory until backed by governed evidence or explicit review, and expired, rejected, retired or superseded ideas remain inspectable as project history; the README cites a sealed gate of 2,040 passing root tests and successful upgrades on seven tested instances.
bad: Scope and complexity are far beyond a personal knowledge wiki — multi-repo architecture cognition, Computer Use and spend ledgers — and the README itself cautions that its public GPT-4.1 pilot 'records quality failures and does not establish improved understanding or cost savings' and that the new cost observation is 'a single maintainer run, not a general benchmark'. Native Windows dialogs are supported but Linux/macOS dialogs require operator action.
didnt: Board — the typed plan-authority and lifecycle ideas (superseded/rejected ideas remain inspectable, cognitive output advisory until governed evidence or review) for the ideas board; ideas only, as the custom source-available licence bars adopting its code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemTensor/MemPrivacy
licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (per README badge; no LICENSE file in repo root)
good: A privacy-preserving memory layer for edge-cloud agents: on-device detection classifies sensitive spans by type and a PL1-PL4 privacy level, replaces them with semantically typed placeholders (e.g. a blood-pressure reading becomes <Health_Info_1>), keeps the placeholder-to-value mapping in a local SQLite store, and restores values locally on the way back, so cloud memory never holds raw values. Its MemPrivacy-Bench (200 synthetic bilingual users) reports only 0.71%-1.60% downstream accuracy loss under PL2-PL4 protection.
bad: Very early code: 16 commits and no releases at the source. The README states the framework's effectiveness 'heavily depends on accurate privacy extraction' and degrades substantially with general LLMs in place of its fine-tuned models, and its benchmark users are synthetic rather than real-world.
didnt: Board — the PL1-PL4 privacy taxonomy and local reversible typed-placeholder pseudonymisation as a pattern for any future cloud call from our local-first wiki; ideas only under the CC BY-NC-ND licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentToolkit/altk-evolve
good: Gives coding agents on-the-job learning: it saves trajectories via an MCP server, distils them into reusable guidelines stored in vector or filesystem backends, resolves conflicts with an LLM, and retrieves task-relevant guidelines with provenance/attribution tools plus retention-policy and compliance tooling. The README reports +8.9 points overall on AppWorld, with a 74% relative increase on hard multi-step tasks.
bad: The README warns its Web UI/REST API 'has no authentication, so any local process can read and change memories through it' — the opposite of approval-gated writes. It is also a heavy stack (Python 3.12, embedding providers, optional pgvector/Milvus backends) aimed at coding-agent self-improvement rather than a cited personal knowledge base.
didnt: Rejected — trajectory-to-guideline self-improvement duplicates our own lessons/claims machinery, and its unauthenticated memory API conflicts with our approval-gated, citation-locked writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Thinklanceai/agentkeeper
good: Cognitive-continuity infrastructure in local SQLite with zero required dependencies: identity principles are protected from every compression pass, the same memory renders per-model (XML for Claude, sections for GPT, prose for Gemini), facts and graph triples carry GDPR TTLs, and content-hashed checkpoints snapshot and restore full state deterministically. It also imports ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini exports into scoped namespaces and deterministically compares what each platform knows, with PII excluded unless explicitly included.
bad: Young and partly unfinished: 52 commits, and the README's own architecture diagram marks Postgres as a 'stub available; full implementation in v1.2'. It also states plainly that reconstruction restores state but 'Behaviour is not guaranteed: AgentKeeper restores the agent's state, not the model's next decision.'
didnt: Corroboration — protected identity exempt from compression, content-hashed checkpoints, TTL expiry and scoped, PII-excluding export imports confirm our own continuity, retention and ingest design; no separate SQLite memory store is needed alongside the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: surrealdb/docs.surrealdb.com
good: A well-maintained documentation site for SurrealDB (1,939 commits) built with Vike, React and Mantine, with structured content collections in src/content, reusable railroad-diagram components for the query language, and a Labs programme with tooling (bun run make:lab) for community learning content.
bad: It is a documentation website, not a memory system or database: it only carries the agent-memory topic tag, and adopting it would mean adopting the Bun/Node 20 + Vercel docs stack for content about a database we do not use. The repo root contains no LICENSE file and states no licence.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a vendor documentation site, not a memory project, and with no licence stated its code is ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: namidb/namidb
licence: Business Source License 1.1 (BSL 1.1; converts to Apache-2.0 on the change date in its LICENSE, commercial licence offered separately)
good: A Rust graph engine where the object-storage bucket is the database: Cypher/GQL property graphs with optional declared constraints and indexes, vector and BM25-plus-vector hybrid search fused by reciprocal rank fusion, built-in graph algorithms (PageRank, Louvain, shortest paths, FastRP), and an MCP server. It ingests an Obsidian/Markdown vault in one command, turning wikilinks into LINKS_TO edges, embeds into EMBEDS edges, tags into a tag tree and frontmatter into node properties.
bad: Licence is the blocker: BSL 1.1 is not open source for production embedding/hosting, and the README says a separate commercial licence is needed to embed, redistribute or run it as a hosted service outside what BSL allows.
