It also hard-depends on the bucket supporting PUT-if-absent conditional writes — an S3-compatible store that ignores If-None-Match 'cannot host NamiDB safely'.
didnt: Board — the vault-as-graph ingestion mapping (wikilinks, embeds, tag tree, frontmatter as properties) and bucket-as-database durability idea for the ideas board; ideas only, as BSL code is never adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SpillwaveSolutions/agent-brain
good: Local-first RAG memory packaged as a Claude Code plugin (30 slash commands, 3 agents, 2 skills) plus FastAPI server, CLI and MCP server with OAuth 2.1: hybrid, vector, BM25, GraphRAG and RRF-combined multi search modes, tree-sitter AST-aware code chunking across 11 languages, pluggable embedding/summarisation providers including a fully local Ollama mode, and per-project isolated servers with automatic port allocation.
bad: The README header's own last_validated stamp is 2026-03-16, and its auth note shows security is in transition: data endpoints require an API key only 'as of the next release', with a --no-api-key flag preserving 'the legacy no-auth experience on 127.0.0.1'. The system is also centred on code/document search for coding hosts rather than a personal knowledge wiki with citations and abstention.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and fit: its hybrid + GraphRAG retrieval duplicates retrieval our wiki stack already has, and its coding-plugin scope does not add citation locking or scored abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RapierCraftStudios/ForgeDock
licence: AGPL-3.0 (with a separate commercial licence file)
good: An autonomous dev pipeline that uses GitHub itself as agent memory: issues are the queue, PRs the ledger, and each stage (investigate, context, architect, build, quality gate, review, merge) writes machine-readable FORGE annotations into HTML comments that later agents read back via the gh CLI, backed by an event-sourced, crash-safe run log with leases. Milestone orchestration is conflict-aware across five detection layers including historical co-change coupling mined from git log, with cycle-checked topological waves.
bad: AGPL-3.0 bars adopting its code into our stack. Its headline numbers are self-reported point-in-time figures from its own first 30 days of dogfooding, and the README concedes a reproducible cost-per-issue benchmark is still a future gate — 'no estimated efficiency claims'; it also requires a Claude Code subscription or API key, the GitHub CLI and Node.js 18+.
didnt: Board — the FORGE annotation idea (structured stage findings written into the durable record every later agent reads) and conflict-aware parallel scheduling for the ideas board; ideas only under AGPL-3.0. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nambok/mentedb
good: A ground-up Rust database engine for agent memory rather than a wrapper: WAL storage, HNSW vectors, knowledge graphs and bi-temporal memory nodes, with write-time intelligence — LLM extraction, quality filtering, deduplication, contradiction detection and belief propagation that lowers confidence in memories depending on a superseded fact. Retrieval fuses vector, BM25 and graph traversal, returns token-budget-optimised context, and it ships Python/TypeScript SDKs, MCP, REST and gRPC plus LongMemEval and scale benchmarks.
bad: The README banners it 'Beta — MenteDB is under active development. APIs may change between minor versions', so it is a moving foundation. Richer extraction needs an external LLM provider and key, and adopting it would replace our plain-Markdown, human-readable wiki custody with an opaque engine store.
didnt: Rejected — fit and maturity: a beta, API-unstable storage engine would displace local-first Markdown custody, which is a core design commitment of our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Necmttn/ax
good: A local-first agent-experience layer: it ingests sessions from six harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Omp, OpenCode, Cursor) plus git history and GitHub PRs into one typed local DuckDB graph with no server or account and no outbound call at ingest. Its /retro workflow records structured tried/worked/failed/next retros, turns repeated friction into proposals the user reviews one at a time, and tracks accepted proposals as experiments with verdicts after 3, 10 and 30 sessions, alongside per-branch token cost accounting.
bad: AGPL-3.0 bars adopting its code. The founder's own note in the README calls ax 'early', it is macOS-first (Linux works for ingest and CLI, with the one optional launchd telemetry agent macOS-only), and it requires Bun 1.3+; its subject is coding-agent observability, not a cited personal knowledge base.
didnt: Board — the retro-loop pattern (structured tried/worked/failed/next records, reviewed proposals, experiment verdicts after 3/10/30 sessions) for the ideas board; ideas only under AGPL-3.0. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: moeru-ai/auv
good: A unified orchestration layer for OS automation ('Application Use'): repeated screenshot-click-type-verify tool-call loops are squashed into reusable, scriptable Rust GUI operations at zero token cost, across macOS, Linux and Windows, with a JS SDK, per-app drivers (e.g. Apple Music, macOS media control, even games) and a doctor/probe flow for the platform permissions it needs (Accessibility, Screen Recording, Automation).
bad: It is not a memory or knowledge project at all — it only carries the agent-memory topic tag — so it offers nothing to a wiki. Platform support is uneven in its own README: Linux musl is unsupported, the Nix package does not support Windows or embed the signed macOS helper, and Windows lock/unlock support rests on 'one installed lock and unlock gate on one Windows 11 host', explicitly 'not a general support claim'.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an OS/GUI automation layer with no memory, retrieval or knowledge function relevant to our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ogham-mcp/ogham-mcp
good: A shared-memory MCP server giving multiple clients (Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode and others) one persistent memory: hybrid pgvector + full-text search fused with reciprocal rank fusion in a single Postgres query, a typed-edge graph for two-fact join queries stored in a relationships table, and stdio or streamable-HTTP transport for multi-agent sharing. It reports 97.2% R@10 on LongMemEval for retrieval and 85.8% end-to-end QA on the AMB harness.
bad: Custody is the mismatch: the quick start states 'You need a database first' — a Supabase or Neon cloud Postgres, or self-hosted Postgres — plus an external embedding-provider API key, so memory lives in a database service rather than local files we own. Its own QA table also places it well below extraction-pipeline systems (85.8% vs 95.4% for the top entry).
didnt: Rejected — duplication and custody: another Postgres-backed MCP memory duplicates our existing wiki MCP door and moves memory out of local-first file custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: YuanchenBei/Mem-Gallery
good: Source code for the ACL 2026 Main paper 'Mem-Gallery: Benchmarking Multimodal Long-Term Conversational Memory for MLLM Agents' (arXiv:2601.03515): a multimodal conversational dataset with evaluation QAs (hosted on Hugging Face) and a unified evaluation framework whose run_bench.py currently supports 10+ memory models, with adaptable official-example integrations for A-Mem and MemoryOS.
bad: It is a benchmark harness, not a memory system, and a heavy one: experiments are conducted on CUDA 12.2 with vLLM, torch and transformers, the dataset must be downloaded separately, and several config files ship with empty model paths and API keys the user must fill in. It evaluates multimodal (image-bearing) conversation, which our text-first wiki does not hold.
didnt: Board — a multimodal long-term conversational-memory benchmark as a candidate future evaluation set if the wiki ever gains image-bearing memory; nothing to adopt for the current text corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sherlockwz/AMA
good: Official code and reusable skills for the Findings of ACL 2026 paper 'AMA: Adaptive Memory via Multi-Agent Collaboration': four collaborating agents — Constructor, Retriever, Judge and Refresher — over three memory granularities (raw text, atomic fact knowledge, episode memory), where the Judge checks relevance and consistency and can request another bounded retrieval round, and the Refresher updates or removes conflicting memories. It reports the highest LoCoMo overall LLM score among tested backbones (0.774) and a large knowledge-update gain on LongMemEval_s (0.897 vs 0.568 without the Refresher).
bad: Brand-new research code: 4 commits at the source, and benchmark datasets are not redistributed, so reproduction requires obtaining and placing them yourself plus an OpenAI-compatible chat and embedding endpoint. The README itself names a limitation — on temporal reasoning Nemori outperforms AMA.
didnt: Board — the bounded Judge retrieval loop (verify evidence sufficiency, retry retrieval, refresh contradictions) as a design pattern for truth-aware retrieval, for the ideas board. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: deepmemteam/deepmem
good: A self-hostable, Mem0-API-compatible memory layer — changing one import line migrates Mem0 client code — built as a FastAPI service over Qdrant with LLM fact extraction, hybrid retrieval (vector + BM25 + entity boost + time-decay), semantic caching, async batched distillation that cuts LLM calls by about 80%, GDPR soft/hard delete and export/import, and a built-in MCP server. It runs in open mode with no API key or registration, and benchmark scripts ship in the repo for reproduction.
bad: Immature: 5 commits and no releases at the source. Its own README is explicit that there are no graph relations ('relations is always []'), no temporal graph layer, and that its cloud benchmark column is RTT-dominated with about ±10% jitter and an add-latency row that 'isn't apples-to-apples' against Mem0.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and duplication: a five-commit Mem0 clone with no graph or temporal layer adds nothing over memory systems already studied, and lacks citation locking and abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 23blocks-OS/ai-maestro
good: One dashboard orchestrates Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build and other terminal agents across machines via a peer mesh with no central server, with persistent per-agent memory (nightly conversation-to-memory with entity graph and source passages), code-graph queries, and signed agent-to-agent messaging via AMP. Secrets are used by name from a local vault without the model seeing the value, and approvals/questions surface as clickable cards.
bad: Scope is a full multi-agent operating system, far beyond a personal wiki memory layer, requiring Node 18+, tmux and per-agent installs; the README itself notes true lip-sync needs OpenAI/ElevenLabs keys and that secret scrubbing stops accidents, not a determined agent. Screens in the README are from a demo company with scripted agents.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: an agent-orchestration OS duplicating our existing multi-agent coordination and memory, not a missing wiki capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: verygoodplugins/automem
good: Graph + vector long-term memory: FalkorDB stores memories as nodes with 11 typed relationships and Qdrant stores embeddings, with hybrid recall (semantic, graph traversal, temporal, tags, importance) and multi-hop bridge discovery that surfaces the reasoning connecting facts, with no LLM call in recall. It exposes MCP (local and remote) and REST, runs via Docker or Railway, and reports BEAM 10M and LongMemEval benchmark results with reproduction material in the repo.
bad: Pre-1.0 by its own README: tags are a hard gate before scoring so a missing tag hides a perfect semantic match, recall does not yet reliably prefer the newest version of a conflicting fact or resolve multi-session preference updates, the MCP SSE bridge does not forward state_mode, and entity-node synthesis is experimental and off by default. Requires FalkorDB + Qdrant services and an embedding provider.
didnt: Corroboration — its typed-relationship graph, INVALIDATED_BY/EVOLVED_INTO edges and consolidation cycles confirm our claim-lifecycle and supersession design, but its service stack duplicates our markdown wiki store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rahilp/second-brain-cloudflare
good: A single Cloudflare Worker (D1, Vectorize, Workers AI, KV) gives every MCP client the same memory: remember/append/update/recall with validity dates and as_of recall, history with before-text, canonical/draft/deprecated status, explicit linking, and deterministic Prompt Capsules for gateway prompt prefixes. Capture comes from MCP, CLI, browser, Obsidian, Notion, calendar/email and iOS Shortcuts, with a Personal/Shared team layer where sharing moves one canonical memory.
bad: Tied entirely to Cloudflare Workers/D1/Vectorize, contrary to local-first custody; v3.0.0 supports only one shared team despite multi-team parameters being wired for later, the shipped embedding models read English best, and Windsurf/OpenCode capture is explicitly not yet supported. Contradiction handling demotes protected-memory conflicts to draft rather than resolving truth.
didnt: Corroboration — validity-dated memories, as_of recall and canonical/draft/deprecated status confirm our bi-temporal and lifecycle design; the Cloudflare-hosted store itself is rejected on custody grounds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: supermemoryai/openclaw-supermemory
good: OpenClaw plugin that auto-recalls relevant memories and a persistent user profile before every turn and auto-captures conversations after every turn for extraction, deduplication and profile building in Supermemory cloud, with /remember, /recall and /supermemory-index commands and save/search/forget/profile tools plus custom container tags for routing memories.
bad: Everything runs in the Supermemory cloud with no local infrastructure and requires Supermemory Pro or above and an API key, so custody is external; the repo root lists no LICENSE file and no releases, and capture defaults to sending every conversation turn to the cloud service.
didnt: Rejected — licence and custody: no licence stated at source and a paid cloud-only memory backend contradicts local-first custody; auto-recall/auto-capture pattern already present in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kitfunso/hippo-memory
good: Local SQLite long-term memory for coding agents shared across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw and any MCP client, with markdown mirrors, BM25 search with no model or network call by default and zero runtime dependencies. Memories strengthen on recall, decay by default, error memories get longer half-life, and hippo supersede removes a replaced fact from recall while keeping provenance (kind, scope, owner, artifact_ref) on every row.
bad: The README is unusually candid that measured effects are mixed: decay tied with decay switched off and sleep consolidation lowered recall in its own tests, a sequential-learning magnitude claim was retracted, and supersession benefit is unmeasured. The optional sleep step sends memory text to Anthropic when ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, and capture/compaction coverage depends on per-host hook trust and integration completeness.
didnt: Corroboration — outcome-weighted strengthening, supersede-leaves-recall and provenance-per-row confirm our scored, supersession-aware memory design; the coding-agent store duplicates our wiki memory. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alash3al/stash
good: Self-hosted single-binary persistent memory in Postgres + pgvector with an MCP server over SSE for any MCP client, started with one docker compose up. A 9-stage consolidation pipeline turns episodes into facts, relationships, causal links, patterns, contradictions, goal tracking, failure patterns and hypothesis verification, processing only new data per run, with a fully local Ollama option.
bad: The README documents the pipeline only at headline level — no evaluation, benchmarks or recall-quality evidence are shown on the page — and it requires an embeddings model and a chat reasoning model via an OpenAI-compatible API key unless the Ollama route is used. The hosted Stash Cloud is a separate from-scratch codebase with a differing feature set, so the open repo is not the cloud product.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and evidence: a Postgres episode/fact store duplicating our wiki memory, with no benchmark evidence at source to justify a second store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Playa-Cyrene/Cyrene-Agent
good: Windows Electron + TypeScript desktop Live2D companion agent with four modes (Chat, Work, Code, Learn), L0/L1/L2 layered personalised memory with evidence chains and conflict detection/resolution via its DMAE Worldbook, hybrid RAG (vector + BM25 + reranker) with source retention, voice interaction, and permission-gated code tools confined to a user-bound trusted directory with symlink-escape rejection.
bad: Windows 10/11 64-bit only, with Feishu, WeChat iLink, key/mouse automation and native screenshot features dependent on the Windows environment, and source builds requiring Node 24, pnpm, Rust and Visual Studio Build Tools. It is a character companion product centred on one game character, and embedding-enhanced features degrade or switch off without the separate BGE-M3 download.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a Windows-only character desktop companion, not a knowledge-OS component; its memory evidence-chain and conflict ideas are already covered by our citation and lifecycle design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jaredrhod/ai-memory-vault
good: A build script plus templates that turn an Obsidian vault into an AI's working memory with no vector database, just markdown: a CLAUDE.md boot config, a VAULT-INDEX operating manual inside the vault, daily-note and MEMORY.md pointer templates, and an AI Priming pattern where each recurring job reads a defined set of notes before producing output. Memory lives outside the model with no size ceiling and the AI holds only what the current task needs.
bad: Built and tested on Claude Code, with other terminal AIs described as working with rough edges; the repo is essentially one build file and four templates with 57 commits and a single release, no tests, retrieval mechanism or evaluation documented. The boot config ships with the author's own agent persona filled in, and the CC-BY-SA-4.0 share-alike terms apply to adaptations.
didnt: Corroboration — a markdown vault as working memory, index-first priming and a pointer MEMORY.md confirm our own wiki architecture almost exactly; nothing new to take, and share-alike terms bar code adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zosmaai/pi-llm-wiki
good: Self-maintaining, Obsidian-compatible Karpathy-pattern wiki for the pi harness with native Open Knowledge Format v0.2: immutable source packets, source pages, canonical wiki pages and generated metadata, with ingest, full-text search, mechanical linting (orphans, broken links, duplicate aliases, coverage gaps, stale captures), stable source-ID citations, guardrails blocking direct edits to raw sources, and the same wiki exposed over a stdio MCP server to Claude Code, Cursor and other clients. Personal and project vaults are layered so knowledge compounds across projects.
bad: Built primarily for the pi / oh-my-pi harnesses, with other clients only via its MCP packaging; the company/team layer is listed as future, trajectory-based agent working-memory is opt-in and off by default, and semantic reindexing may download around 2 GB of vector models. It duplicates, rather than extends, a full LLM-wiki stack.
didnt: Corroboration — source packets, canonical pages, deterministic indexes/logs, lint and citation style independently confirm our wiki design; a direct duplicate of our system, so no adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Lumen-Labs/brainapi2
good: Turns raw text into an event-centric knowledge graph automatically: a Scout/Observer/Architect/Janitor agent swarm extracts entities, builds actor-target-context event hubs and validates/deduplicates relationships in a loop, in an append-only graph that preserves provenance and lets answers show the walkable graph path used. It offers REST retrieval endpoints, an MCP server, a web console, accurate and lightweight pipeline modes, and Python/TypeScript SDKs.
bad: Licensed under BUSL-1.1 with Additional Use Grant: None — production use requires a commercial licence until the 2030 change date — and running it is heavy: backing services differ by profile up to Postgres/Neo4j/Milvus/Mongo plus LLM providers, search is off by default, and the console screenshot is still marked coming soon in the README.
didnt: Board — the event-hub Triangle of Attribution and Janitor validation loop as ideas only; BUSL-1.1 bars adopting its code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: supermemoryai/smfs
good: Exposes a Supermemory container as a real mountable filesystem (FUSE on Linux, NFS on macOS) so editors, scripts and agents can read, write and grep memory like a local directory, with background push, 30-second pull sync, scoped memory-generation paths, and a grep wrapper that routes flagless grep inside a mount to semantic search while flagged grep stays literal. A TypeScript virtual bash package covers runtimes with no local filesystem.
bad: Requires a Supermemory API key and the Supermemory cloud service — the filesystem is a view onto a hosted container, not local custody — and FUSE use in Docker needs /dev/fuse and SYS_ADMIN capability. Only files under configured memory paths enter the memory pipeline; everything else is plain durable storage in that cloud.
didnt: Rejected — custody and duplication: a filesystem front-end to a hosted memory service contradicts local-first custody, and our wiki already is a plain-file store agents can grep directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: taylorsatula/mira
good: A single-continuous-thread synthetic entity with first-person memory: conversation segments collapse into first-person summaries with absolute timestamps and chaining over the previous five summaries, memories decay on use-days unless they earn their keep through access, references and links, and a subcortical pre-response retrieval pass plus a Peanut Gallery metacognitive observer prepare and check context. Its Text-Based LoRA loop folds per-segment alignment assessments into an evolving, critic-checked user model in Postgres.
bad: AGPL-3.0 copyleft, a single-author project the author calls his TempleOS, with no new-chat functionality by design and a hosted version whose managed experience sits outside the open repo. The README documents no evaluation or benchmarks for the persistence claims, and the architecture is a whole agent entity, not a separable memory component.
didnt: Board — first-person segment-collapse summaries and use-day decay as ideas only; AGPL-3.0 bars adopting its code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AmeNetwork/aser
good: Lightweight, modular Python agent framework installable from PyPI where an agent is assembled in a few lines with pluggable model, tools, knowledge (RAG), memory, MCP servers, tracing and chat-to-web3 connectors, with worked examples from beginner agents through router/sequential/parallel/hierarchical multi-agent patterns, Text2SQL, workflows and evaluation. It also integrates Google's A2A protocol and a self-coding tool experiment.
bad: The README is a catalogue of example links with no documented evaluation, limitations or production evidence on the page, there are no releases, and much of the advanced surface is Web3/onchain oriented (ERC8004, MSCP, Farcaster) which is outside a personal knowledge OS. Memory is one pluggable example among many, not a studied memory system.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a general Web3-leaning agent framework duplicating our agent stack, with no wiki or memory capability we lack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ADW-19/build_a_product_agent
good: A pure-documentation, production-oriented handbook in Chinese covering agent technology selection, module development (conversation, memory with Milvus + Redis, tools, LangGraph workflow, RAG with Recall@k/nDCG/MRR), single- and multi-agent paths (MCP + A2A, HITL, Plan-and-Execute), and five-dimension system testing. Examples follow a unified Python 3.13+ async skeleton rather than isolated toy demos.
bad: The README states it is a pure documentation project with no runnable framework, no releases, and only 20 commits since 2026-05. It is primarily Chinese-language, warns its tech-stack baseline and model IDs/prices go stale quickly, and its memory coverage is one chapter in a general agent guide, not a memory system.
didnt: Rejected — documentation-only general agent handbook, duplicative of guidance already in our stack and not a memory or knowledge component to build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zjunlp/LightMem-Ego
good: Self-hostable multimodal memory for smart glasses and phones: always-on egocentric camera/audio capture on one aligned timeline, three-tier memory (current, short-term micro-events, long-term episodes/routines/preferences via the EM2Mem event-centric engine), and answers shipped with timestamped visual and transcript evidence. Docker quick start brings up the web UI and backend pipeline.
bad: Evaluation in the README is a small prototype set — 27 queries over five videos (~45.7 minutes) with overall answer accuracy 51.9% (LLM-judge) / 55.6% (human). Every self-host path needs an external OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint plus Xfyun ASR credentials, visual retrieval needs a GPU, the phone client is only a mobile-browser frontend, and the privacy section says a production deployment still needs HTTPS, access control, encryption at rest, retention/deletion policy and explicit consent.
didnt: Rejected — egocentric lifelogging/wearable scope with continuous camera and microphone capture is outside a text-first personal LLM-wiki, and its privacy burden conflicts with local-first custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: ZJUNLP

name: DrDroidLab/open-index
good: Builds a domain 'brain' from typed doc_types with YAML schemas, entities with related_to edges, and connectors, stored in SQLite + FTS5 by default (OpenSearch optional). Writes are validated (add-entity, import with dry-run, validate for CI), file-backed entities stay git-tracked and PR-reviewable while index-backed entities stay in the DB, and the MCP layer offers read plus put_entity/create_doc_type with a --read-only opt-out.
bad: Very young: created 2026-08, 52 commits, no releases shown in repo metadata. The MCP server is read+write by default so an agent can mutate the brain unless --read-only is set, index-backed state lives in a gitignored brain.db that must be backed up or re-ingested, and relationship validation is described as only light (right target type) with undeclared edge meanings still allowed.
didnt: Corroboration — schema-typed entities, a file-vs-index source-of-truth split, validated writes and a read-only MCP mode confirm our wiki's typed, citation-locked, approval-gated design; no separate adoption needed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linggen/linggen-memory
good: One local daemon and store (Rust ling-mem, LanceDB + Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, no model inside the daemon) shared across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Zed and OpenClaw, with per-turn cited recall, directory-scoped filing, and a nightly dream/forget/audit pass that promotes durable rows, fades staging rows after about a week, collapses proven chains by archiving rather than deleting, and queues unsettled contradictions for review with the user. Three tiers (core, long-term, short-term) and a frozen schema/CLI/MCP contract at release 1.8.2.
bad: The full loop is split: the nightly memory agent and dream mission live in the separate Linggen engine repo, so the standalone store does not close the loop alone. ling-mem sends anonymous install/command telemetry to linggen.dev by default (opt-out via env var, file or no-default-features build), and prebuilt binaries are only for macOS Apple Silicon and Linux x86_64.
didnt: Corroboration — three durability tiers, nightly consolidation with archive-not-delete merges, and a human review queue for unsettled contradictions confirm our lean-memory and claim-lifecycle design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dat999zx/knowl
good: Persistent agent memory over MCP/CLI on local SQLite with no API keys, whose central mechanism is supersession: a same-subject write retires the predecessor from normal retrieval while keeping it queryable via timeline. Its own-harness ablation shows supersession raising conflict-resolution top-1 from 47% to 98%, and in MemoryAgentBench's own harness it scores 90 on FactConsolidation single-hop at 262K versus 73 with supersession off; ambiguous replacements are left active with a manual knowl supersede command.
bad: The README itself cautions that benchmark figures are single runs at temperature 0.7, the ablation gap moved 4 points between runs of the same cell, and multi-hop is weak — Knowl scores 7 against a 14-point retrieval ceiling there. It requires Node.js 22+, does not run the CLI under Bun or Deno runtimes directly, and team sharing is pushed to the separate hosted knowl.cloud layer.
didnt: Corroboration — typed, sourced facts retired on change, with a measured retrieval collapse when supersession is off, strongly confirms our truth-aware retrieval and claim-supersession priority. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: proteus-evolve/Proteus
good: Harness-agnostic self-evolution framework: plug in any agent harness via a small HarnessAdapter (bundled minimal, LLM, DeepSeek Harness, Pi, Codex adapters), run context-fresh observe-propose-act-reflect episodes in a Docker or local sandbox, and measure the harness itself with structural distance, a crystallisation/swap test for removable dispositions, and a behavioural-distance permutation test. Supports goal, multi-goal and no-goal regimes with hidden or visible evaluators, and only activates candidates that pass rebuild/validation.
bad: Badged as a research preview at v0.4.0 and created 2026-08, so it is early research apparatus rather than a settled product. Real harnesses need Docker plus provider API keys/auth, and by design it lets an agent rewrite its own prompts, memory, skills, tools and source — the README notes an application-level file sandbox cannot contain a self-editing agent.
didnt: Rejected — autonomous harness self-rewriting conflicts with our approval-gated writes and owner-decision rules, and its research-preview maturity fits a measurement lab, not a personal knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AskTheWay/dsh-auto-memory
good: Claude Code-style auto-memory for the DeepSeek Harness with no servers, embeddings or setup: typed memories (user/feedback/project/reference) as plain Markdown files under $DSH_HOME/memory, workspace plus user scoping, a MEMORY.md index auto-injected into every system prompt within a hard 4 KB byte budget (0 bytes when empty), update-replace consolidation instead of near-duplicate pile-up, and cross-process locking with orphan recovery. Ships 150 tests plus a deterministic no-LLM evaluation layer run in CI.
bad: Scoped entirely to the DeepSeek Harness (requires @deepseek-ai/dsh >= 0.1.5-rc.2, Node ^22.19 || >=24) and very new (created 2026-09). The README pins a known limitation: index truncation under budget pressure is positional, not relevance-ranked, with probe retention dropping to ~38% to 10% as memory count grows unless entries are pinned; full relevance ranking is still on the roadmap.
didnt: Corroboration — a typed-file store with a byte-budgeted MEMORY.md index injected per request and dedupe-and-update discipline mirrors and confirms our own MEMORY.md model; the DeepSeek-only scope makes adoption duplicative. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: donkruger/Kanban
licence: Proprietary — README states 'Kanban Pro is proprietary software. All rights reserved.' (GitHub: Other / NOASSERTION)
good: Kanban Pro is a local-first, filesystem-backed Kanban board whose boards live as Markdown files on disk — portable and AI-agent readable with no vendor lock-in — distributed as signed/notarised macOS DMGs plus Windows and Linux builds, with an embedded CLI per the repo description.
bad: The repo is a download shell: only README, LICENSE, SECURITY and assets, 16 commits, no source code to inspect or reuse, and the product is early access. The Windows installer is unsigned (SmartScreen warning on first launch), and the licence is proprietary, so nothing in it can be built on.
didnt: Rejected — proprietary, closed-source task-board product with no inspectable code and no memory-system substance for our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mtrnix/metronix-memory
good: Self-hosted MCP memory server with durable per-agent facts and preferences scoped by workspace and agent, hybrid retrieval (dense + SPLADE sparse + Neo4j graph context) with source citations, ingestion of files and SaaS knowledge, and REST/OpenAI-compatible APIs alongside MCP. Reports LongMemEval-S Recall@10 95.4% and commits reproducible MuSiQue/2Wiki passage-recall results recomputed from files in the repo.
bad: Heavy stack: Docker with at least 6 GB RAM (8 GB recommended), ~15 GB disk and a 10-15 minute first build. The headline benchmarks are self-labelled directional (single N=1 runs whose run files, manifests and protocol text are absent from the repo) or external and unreproduced, LoCoMo answer accuracy is 52.8% and BEAM 100K 32.1%, and the README documents quick-start inconsistencies in its own API docs (scope casing returns HTTP 422; a documented default workspace lands records in a separate unlisted workspace).
didnt: Rejected — a heavy Neo4j/Qdrant/Docker memory service duplicating our local-first wiki retrieval, with headline benchmark claims that cannot be checked from the repo itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: libenxier-beep/codex-memories
good: Local-first Codex memory with governed recall and no hosted vector DB: Git-backed memory authority plus a disposable SQLite sidecar, capture through Codex lifecycle hooks into candidate quarantine, and a bounded three-round progressive-disclosure retrieval loop where indexes only propose candidates and content is reopened from exact Git authority before entering context. Fail-closed checks cover scope, privacy, deletion tombstones, provenance, revision and content hashes, the installer writes a review-only hook merge plan instead of editing hooks.json, and the public suite reports 289/289 tests passing.
bad: Self-described as an advanced preview / real-world dogfood with only 10 commits since 2026-08. Its own validation snapshot is mixed: the compact hidden seal scored Recall@5 3/6 and was rejected, the independent N=180 Large-B3 evaluation was not executed, Windows is not yet validated in CI, and automatic capture/recall stays inactive until the owner manually reviews and merges the hook plan.
didnt: Corroboration — authority-before-similarity, quarantined candidates, provenance/tombstone checks and reopening exact source before injection confirm our citation-locking and scored-abstention design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yu-Xiao-Sheng/codex-memory-trim
good: A Codex skill that periodically trims global memory: a read-only audit (collect.py) reports file sizes, cross-layer consistency and orphan summaries with usage counts marking KEEP versus delete candidates, then trim/compress/add-global sub-skills dedupe, prune stale threads, compress verbose entries and add global rules. Reported real-world results over three rounds cut MEMORY.md from 162 KB/1482 lines to 46 KB/474 lines and the total memory dir by 46%, with backup-first tarballs, git rollback and a three-layer (files, raw, state DB) consistent removal procedure.
bad: Narrowly bound to Codex's own ~/.codex/memories layout and consolidation pipeline, with unattended scheduling requiring danger-full-access sandboxing on Linux/macOS only. Results are one user's self-reported production directory, deletions are destructive by design (mitigated by backups and git), and trimmed changes only reach new sessions because the memory snapshot is injected once at session start.
didnt: Board — the usage-count audit that flags zero-retrieval memories as delete candidates while explicitly keeping high-usage ones, run backup-first across all memory layers, is a clean periodic-diet idea for our lean-MEMORY.md discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kronic90/Mimir
licence: PolyForm Noncommercial (README badge; GitHub: Other / NOASSERTION)
good: Modular Python library giving agents episodic, procedural, social, temporal and visual memory, orchestrating VividnessMem (neurochemistry) and VividEmbed (semantic retrieval) under 21 neuroscience-inspired mechanisms including reconsolidation, spreading activation, retrieval-induced forgetting and temporal gist extraction. Retrieval is a hybrid BM25 + semantic bridge with 5-signal re-ranking, memories decay organically and compress to gist, and it offers encryption at rest and context-block generation for prompt injection, degrading gracefully when optional engines are absent.
bad: Early and thinly evidenced: 17 commits, no releases, and an expansive feature matrix asserted as tested with no evaluation results visible in the README to support accuracy claims. Core capabilities depend on two separate sibling packages, without which neurochemistry defaults off and recall falls back to BM25 only (and to plaintext JSON without the cryptography package); the PolyForm Noncommercial licence bars commercial use.
didnt: Rejected — noncommercial licence makes its code ideas-only, and its emotion/neurochemistry character-memory scope does not fit a citation-locked personal knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wrste/pheromone-network
good: Zero-dependency TypeScript memory kernel (Node >=18, offline, no GPU or vector DB) that learns local associations with a manual Hebbian rule: each output reads a few tag-compatible neighbours, links used often are reinforced through short- and long-term pheromone trails, and idle links evaporate by half-life via explicit evaporate/decayByFactor calls. The RecallKernel API (observe/score/encode) is small and inspectable with explicit weights and cosine scores, works with any supplied embeddings or the built-in ngramEmbed, and ships a browser demo.
bad: The README itself bounds it: it is an association/recall component, not a text search engine, relational or vector database, or general classifier, and time-based decay does not run automatically. Its scenario tests are small deterministic near-text cases (three candidates per query, 12/12 tests) that the README says are not a benchmark or a measured recall rate on real data, the n-gram encoder does not establish semantic equivalence between different phrasings, and the package is at version 0.1.0 with 16 commits and no forks.
didnt: Board — link reinforcement plus half-life evaporation is a clean, implementable weighting model for the Lens graph, where edges that are never traversed fade. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Facets-cloud/flow
good: A Go task manager and working-memory layer for Claude Code and Codex: interview-driven task capture writes structured briefs, each task gets a dedicated resumable session, a live 'scoop' appends durable facts to a five-bucket Markdown knowledge base during sessions and a 'sweep' on flow done re-reads the transcript for anything missed, and playbooks snapshot recurring work into reproducible runs. All data is local under ~/.flow as plain Markdown beside a rebuildable SQLite index, with no server, cloud or telemetry.
bad: Badged alpha and built around macOS terminal automation (iTerm2/Warp/Terminal.app/kitty/zellij, Accessibility permission needed for stock Terminal), with other harnesses and terminals (Cursor, Linux tmux/wezterm, Windows) explicitly needing contributors. Background-agent mode is Claude-only, sync via a shared folder risks SQLite corruption if run on two machines at once, and the knowledge base is append-only Markdown buckets with no citation, supersession or approval-gating machinery.
didnt: Rejected — a macOS-centric Claude/Codex session and task manager duplicating our wiki-plus-task system, without the citation locking or approval gates our design requires. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: oneal2000/SR-Agents
good: Releases SRA-Bench, the first benchmark for decomposed evaluation of Skill Retrieval Augmentation: 5,400 capability-intensive test instances, 636 manually constructed gold skills mixed with 25,626 web-collected distractor skills (26,262-skill retrieval corpus), and six task families (TheoremQA, LogicBench, ToolQA, MedCalc-Bench, CHAMP, BigCodeBench) scored across the full pipeline of skill retrieval, skill incorporation and end-task execution. The SR-Agents toolkit ships BM25, TF-IDF, BGE, Contriever, hybrid and BM25 + LLM-rerank retrievers plus five skill-use methods (LLM Direct, Oracle Skill, Full-Skill Injection, LLM Selection, Progressive Disclosure) behind a single resumable retrieve → infer → evaluate CLI that works against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (hosted APIs, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama).
bad: A young research artefact tied to a 2026 arXiv preprint: created 2026-04-16 with 25 commits and a single release, Python 3.10–3.12 only. Inference requires an external OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint (no model is bundled), and ToolQA additionally needs an external corpus downloaded from Google Drive. It is an evaluation harness for six fixed academic datasets with rule-based/execution scoring — the README documents no production agent runtime, no citation or provenance machinery, and no approval gating for the skills it retrieves and injects.
didnt: Board — SRA-Bench's decomposed evaluation design (score skill retrieval, skill incorporation and end-task execution as separate stages, plus a distractor-robustness test that mixes the gold skill with hard negatives) is a clean evaluation pattern for our own large skill catalogue, where end-task success alone hides whether the right skill was ever found. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 410979729/scope-recall-hermes
good: One shared SQLite store for Hermes, Codex, Claude Code, WorkBuddy and dsh with source-backed recall: facts are drawn from accumulated evidence, only the owner's explicit correction or confirmation changes a captured fact, and owner tools can browse, inspect history, correct, mute or delete memories (deletion shows dependent sources and facts first) and export a portable package with original sources, facts, history and hashes.
bad: Its own README states the synthetic recall benchmark 'does not establish consolidation quality, semantic embedding quality or performance on private conversations'. Setup is intricate (host-specific install plans, optional extras, a vector threshold to tune by hand), recall is lexical only without the LanceDB extra, upgraded stores cannot be opened by earlier releases, and PostgreSQL/pgvector is explicitly outside this v3 distribution.
didnt: Corroboration — SQLite-as-sole-fact-authority, scope isolation, and facts changeable only by explicit owner correction or confirmation confirm our custody and claim-correction design; the multi-host plugin itself is not needed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Meridiona/meridian
good: Automatic work journal: it reconstructs the day from screen activity into a scrubbable timeline, produces an end-of-day summary and a ready-to-paste standup, and drafts Jira worklog updates that wait for the user to review and send. Activity stays in one encrypted database on the user's machine.
bad: Platform-limited to macOS (Apple Silicon only; Intel unsupported) and Windows 10/11, with no Linux support, and capture is pruned automatically after 30 days at about 20 GB a month. Analysis sends summary material to whichever AI provider the user connects, and the current licence is source-available PolyForm Strict: no modification, no redistribution, and no commercial use without a separate licence (pre-change releases were MIT).
didnt: Rejected — screen-capture work journalling for Jira is a different scope from our knowledge OS, and the PolyForm Strict licence bars modification and commercial use, so its code is ideas-only at best. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemTensor/MemOS-Cloud-OpenClaw-Plugin
good: Official OpenClaw lifecycle plugin: it recalls memories from MemOS Cloud before each run (before_prompt_build hook calling /search/memory) and saves the conversation after each run (agent_end calling /add/message), with a local config UI, per-agent memory toggles and overrides, and multi-agent data isolation via agent_id injected into both calls.
bad: Memory lives in the vendor's cloud (default base URL memos.memtensor.cn) behind a required MEMOS_API_KEY, so custody is not local-first. The README documents a known Windows installer failure (spawn EINVAL) needing a manual-install workaround, and the optional model-based recall filter defaults to fail-open, injecting unfiltered recall when filtering fails.
didnt: Rejected — it sends every conversation to a third-party cloud memory service, which conflicts with our local-first custody; the lifecycle recall-then-save hook pattern is already our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lovstudio/Ataru
good: High-performance local retrieval over past agent history: a Rust Tantivy + Jieba keyword search core with optional semantic/hybrid recall, incremental indexing that never rewrites the original transcripts, and stable Turn/Run/Session/Project IDs that take any hit back to the original session, message and line number. It runs offline by default, degrades to keyword search with explicit fallback warnings, and its search skill refuses to run when the index is not ready rather than disguising a missing index as zero hits.
bad: Retrieval only — it indexes and searches past transcripts but writes, corrects or consolidates no memory — and its source adapters cover only Claude and Codex local session files. The CLI is keyword-only (semantic and hybrid modes exist only in the desktop app), and the README's own measurement shows a turn-level query taking about 48 seconds on a 2,705-session / 847,526-message corpus with a 6.6 GB index.
didnt: Corroboration — stable-ID return to the original session, message and line confirms our citation-locking design, and its refusal to present a missing index as zero hits confirms our honest-abstention posture. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: abraxas914/VESTI
licence: MIT (stated in README licence section; no LICENSE file in repo root)
good: Local-first AI conversation memory hub: a Chrome extension auto-captures chats from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen and Doubao into local IndexedDB, with full-mirror, smart-filter and manual-archive capture modes, and a web dashboard adds a Gardener agent whose classification steps are observable, Library topic organisation, Explore RAG answers with source cards that jump back to the original conversation (with the source type explicitly labelled when local relevance is too low and it falls back to model world knowledge), a similarity Network graph, and curated Notes weighted higher in retrieval.
bad: The README's own known-boundaries section states browser-side vector computation becomes a bottleneck as conversations reach the thousands, there is no cross-device sync, the full Weekly Digest is frozen in a 'Soon' state, Gardener classification confidence drops on fuzzy or personal topics, and platform DOM changes can break its capture parsers. Storage is capped (soft warning at 900 MB, hard stop pausing writes at 1 GB) and summaries and embeddings depend on the external ModelScope API.
didnt: Board — explicitly labelling an answer's source type when local recall falls below threshold and the system falls back to model world knowledge, as an addition to our abstention signalling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LucieEveille/kiwi-mem
good: Self-hosted memory gateway (Python/FastAPI, PostgreSQL + pgvector, Docker) sitting between chat clients and OpenAI- or Anthropic-format providers, with brain-like mechanisms: per-memory heat that decays over time and re-warms when recalled, tiered injection (hot memories in full, warm as summaries, cold withheld), Dream consolidation that cleans fragments and merges them into vector-indexed memory scenes, hierarchical calendar summaries (day to week to month to quarter to year), contradictions retiring superseded memories while user-locked memories never decay, prompt-cache-friendly injection ordering, and automatic project isolation.
bad: Security posture is weak by its own admission: the README warns the gateway and admin panel have no built-in authentication, so anyone who knows the gateway address can reach every API, including a /sync/export endpoint that can export the full configuration (potentially including API keys) and a backup-import endpoint. Scope is AI companions — the README states it is not an enterprise knowledge base and does no document retrieval or knowledge graph — and practical deployment needs a 24/7 server plus a domain and HTTPS for mobile clients.
didnt: Board — memory heat (decay/reinforcement with tiered full/summary/withheld injection) and hierarchical calendar summaries as candidate mechanisms for our retrieval ranking; AGPL-3.0-or-later code itself is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ScottRBK/forgetful
good: MCP memory server (FastMCP) enforcing atomic Zettelkasten memories — one concept per note, with context, keywords and tags supplied at write time — embedded and automatically linked to similar memories to grow a knowledge graph. It also models entities, projects, documents, code artifacts, Agent-Skills-format procedural memory and plans/tasks with acceptance criteria and dependency tracking for multi-agent coordination, exposes only three meta-tools to protect the client context window, and runs fully locally with FastEmbed embeddings plus cross-encoder reranking on SQLite or PostgreSQL.
bad: Memory is only what an agent explicitly chooses to record in the imposed atomic format — there is no automatic capture — and the atomic/context/keyword burden falls on the client agent for every note. The README documents no evaluation or benchmark results for retrieval quality.
didnt: Corroboration — atomic one-concept memories with automatic linking and context recorded at write time confirm our atomic-claim and provenance-at-capture design; the server itself duplicates our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jayminwest/mulch
good: Structured expertise for coding agents stored as typed JSONL records in a .mulch/ directory inside the git repo: agents record conventions, failures and other types with file anchors, evidence links, supersedes and confirmations, and 'ml prime' injects a token-budgeted one-line-per-record index (failures first; superseded records hidden, stale records demoted and marked) into new sessions. It ships stale detection, a corpus health audit, schema validation, a write-time quality gate and lifecycle hooks such as secret scanning at record time, and contains no LLM of its own.
bad: Scope is project-bound coding expertise inside a git repository, not general or personal memory, and search is BM25 text ranking with no semantic/vector recall. Priming is lossy by design: over-budget records are dropped lowest-ranked first, and prime's default auto-context-scoping emits only a subset of the corpus unless --all is passed.
didnt: Corroboration — git-lived typed records with supersedes links, staleness checks and a corpus audit confirm our wiki-in-git conventions and lifecycle discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: supermemoryai/memorybench
good: Pluggable benchmarking framework for conversational memory and RAG: any wired provider (Supermemory, Mem0, Zep) can be run against any included benchmark (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, ConvoMem) through a checkpointed ingest, index, search, answer, evaluate, report pipeline that resumes from the last successful stage, with judge-agnostic scoring, structured failure inspection, a real-time web UI, and MemScore reported as an accuracy / latency / context-tokens triple rather than one collapsed number.
bad: Coverage is narrow as shipped — three providers and three benchmarks are wired into the CLI options — and every run requires paid cloud API keys for both the memory provider and the judge/answering models, sending benchmark data to those external services. Accuracy rests entirely on LLM-judge scoring against ground truth.
didnt: Board — MemScore's discipline of reporting accuracy, latency and context tokens as a separate triple, never collapsed into one number, for our own evaluation reporting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rush-db/rushdb
good: Graph + vector database and memory layer built on Neo4j: push any JSON and it infers types, labels and relationships on write with no schema or migrations, auto-embeds designated properties server-side, and answers graph-filtered semantic search, arbitrarily deep relationship traversal and aggregations through one unified query API, with an MCP server, JavaScript and Python SDKs, ACID transactions, and self-host (Docker) or managed cloud deployment.
bad: Self-hosting is heavyweight — it requires Neo4j 2026.01.4+ with the APOC plugin — and the zero-schema, infer-everything model is the opposite of a curated, schema-governed knowledge base: there is no citation, provenance or approval layer in what the README presents. It is a general database product, not a knowledge OS.
didnt: Rejected — a Neo4j-backed schema-free database conflicts with our schema discipline, citation locking and local-first file custody, and adds a heavy service dependency for no missing capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: typegoose/mongodb-memory-server
good: Mature test tooling (created 2017, about 2.9k stars, hundreds of releases): it spins up a real mongod binary programmatically from Node.js — about 7 MB per fresh instance — so integration tests run against an actual MongoDB isolated from each other, with replica-set support, configurable binary version and platform, mongoose/Jest examples, and compatibility with any CI runner that can run Node.
bad: It is not agent or long-term memory at all: the data is ephemeral test state shut down with the process. Binaries are downloaded on install or first run, so the first run can be slow and depends on network/proxy configuration, slim Linux images need libcurl4 installed, and the README notes there is no official MongoDB release for Alpine Linux so Alpine binaries cannot be pulled.
didnt: Rejected — a MongoDB test fixture misfiled under memory; it has no agent-memory, retrieval or knowledge capability relevant to our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dataojitori/nocturne_memory
good: MCP long-term memory server (SQLite/PostgreSQL) that rejects vector RAG in favour of URI-addressed, graph-like structured memory (core:// and project:// paths) with human-readable disclosure triggers for conditional recall, glossary auto-hyperlinking between memories, and namespace isolation per AI persona. Its visual dashboard gives the owner a memory explorer plus Review & Audit: every AI write auto-snapshots, changes are shown as visual diffs the owner can integrate or roll back, and cleanup of old versions requires human confirmation; only designated core memories load at boot (7.2K characters loaded from a 969K-character store in its worked example), the rest is read on demand.
bad: Framing and scope are companion-persona-centric ('memories are for sovereign AI'), with memory authored autonomously by the AI itself rather than captured and cited from sources, and the README presents no retrieval evaluation or benchmarks. The public demo server is read-only, and proactive use depends on the client AI being given a recommended system prompt telling it to read and write memory.
didnt: Board — rollbackable, snapshot-versioned memory where every AI write is diff-reviewed and cleanup requires human confirmation, to check against our gateway's approval-gated write path. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemTensor/MemRL
good: Official code for the MemRL paper: a non-parametric method that evolves at runtime via reinforcement learning on episodic memory, decoupling stable reasoning from plastic memory and using a two-phase retrieval mechanism to filter noise and surface high-utility strategies from environmental feedback. Ships runnable entrypoints and configs for four benchmarks (HLE, BigCodeBench, ALFWorld, Lifelong Agent Bench) where it reports outperforming state-of-the-art baselines without weight updates.
bad: It is a benchmark research release, not a reusable memory service: runs require external LLM and embedding API keys set in YAML configs, LLB tasks need Docker environments, and the README notes this release supports only the LLB db and os tasks (no kg). It has 0 releases and documents host-specific fragility (a CXXABI_1.3.15 / libstdc++ preload workaround for sqlite3/MemOS initialisation).
didnt: Board — utility-scored episodic retrieval: two-phase retrieval that filters passive semantic matches by feedback-derived utility is a candidate scoring idea for our retrieval/eval work, but runtime self-evolution without weight updates does not fit approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: swapnildahiphale/OpenSRE
good: Self-hosted AI SRE agent that investigates production incidents and learns from each one, combining Neo4j episodic memory (past incidents and what fixed them, surfaced mid-investigation via memory-search) with a Neo4j knowledge graph of service dependencies and blast radius. Ships 51 production skills (Datadog, Grafana, PagerDuty, Elasticsearch, Kubernetes, AWS and more), a web console, Slack and Teams bots, and Entra SSO, with direct Anthropic by default and optional LiteLLM for other providers.
bad: Scope is incident response, not knowledge work, and the stack is heavy: Docker with Postgres, config-service, Neo4j, agent and web console. The README itself warns local-dev simple-mode is cleartext HTTP with no rate limiting and no sandbox isolation, designed for localhost only and not for production exposure without its hardening checklist.
didnt: Rejected — domain and stack mismatch: an SRE incident investigator on Neo4j/Postgres duplicates none of our citation-locked wiki needs and its episodic-memory idea is already covered by closer memory projects. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vasilyevdm/ai-agent-handbook
good: A source-code-derived engineering guide across 30+ agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Claude Code, LangGraph, CrewAI, Hermes and others) covering agent loops, system-prompt assembly, six compaction strategies, context rot (degradation from ~25% window fill, 12 defences), a 5-tier memory hierarchy, tool sprawl / progressive disclosure, multi-agent orchestration, and human-in-the-loop, state and security, with code examples and a quick decision guide.
bad: Documentation only — the repo is a single ~5,000-line guide plus its PDF, with 1 commit, no releases and a single named author, so there is nothing runnable, tested or maintained as software. Its framework star counts are explicitly dated March 2026 and will stale quickly.
didnt: Corroboration — its independently derived findings (context rot starting well below full windows, personality and operational instructions in separate files, sub-agents used primarily for context isolation, skills-as-Markdown with progressive loading) confirm patterns already present in our agent/wiki design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: EGO4D/episodic-memory
good: Code to reproduce the Ego4D episodic-memory benchmark over the large egocentric-video dataset, making past video queryable across four tasks: VQ2D (last-seen object, 2D + temporal localisation), VQ3D (3D displacement to the last-seen object), NLQ (temporal localisation for natural-language questions) and MQ (localising all instances of a named activity).
bad: Vision/video domain only — it needs the external Ego4D dataset download and per-task sub-benchmark setups, and the README flags a known data defect: ~14% of NLQ annotations have a near-0 query window and under-report challenge performance pending a dataset update. No releases are published.
didnt: Rejected — fit: an egocentric-video localisation benchmark has no bearing on a text-first personal LLM-wiki with citation locking and scored abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mem0ai/mem0
good: Production-oriented memory layer offered as a Python/TypeScript library, self-hosted server and cloud platform, retaining user, session and agent state. Its current algorithm uses single-pass ADD-only extraction (memories accumulate, nothing overwritten), entity linking across memories, multi-signal retrieval fusing semantic, BM25 and entity matching in parallel, and temporal reasoning, reporting 92.5 on LoCoMo and 94.4 on LongMemEval.
bad: The README itself cautions that its headline benchmark scores reflect the managed platform, which includes proprietary optimisations not available in the open-source SDK, so open-source users should not expect identical numbers. It also requires an external LLM (gpt-5-mini by default) and an embedding model to function, and its strongest features sit in the hosted tiers.
took: Claim-level append-only index with temporal multi-signal fusion — built in Round 3, lane TB2 — source/inspiration: Mem0
didnt: Corroboration — single-pass ADD-only accumulation, entity linking and parallel semantic/BM25/entity fusion with temporal ranking confirm the direction of our claim-level append-only index; the hosted platform itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memvid/memvid
good: Portable, serverless memory that packages data, embeddings, search structure and metadata into a single .mv2 file instead of a RAG pipeline or vector database. Memory is organised as append-only, immutable Smart Frames with timestamps and checksums, giving crash safety, queries over past memory states, timeline inspection and time-travel branching, with Rust, Python, Node and CLI SDKs and optional PDF, CLIP and Whisper features.
bad: The core is Rust (Rust 1.85.0+ required) and local vector search needs embedding models downloaded manually (about 120 MB to 1.3 GB depending on model), so integration and operational cost are non-trivial for a Markdown-first stack. Its single opaque capsule file also trades away the per-file human readability and git diffability our wiki is built on.
didnt: Board — the self-contained, versioned .mv2 capsule (append-only frames with checksums, rules and expiry) as a portable export/snapshot format idea, not as a replacement for files as the source of truth. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: campfirein/byterover-cli
good: CLI (brv) giving coding agents persistent structured memory as a curated context tree, with an interactive REPL/TUI and web dashboard, git-like version control for the tree (branch, commit, merge, push/pull), 20 LLM providers, 24 built-in agent tools, MCP integration, work with 22+ coding agents, and a review workflow to approve or reject pending curate operations. Reports 96.1% on LoCoMo and 92.8% on LongMemEval-S from the production codebase.
bad: The repository is archived (public archive), its spaces and legacy sync commands are deprecated, and team features push toward the hosted ByteRover Cloud. Its licence is the Elastic License 2.0 (shown as Other/NOASSERTION in the repo sidebar), so the code is not available on open-source terms for adoption.
took: Per-page importance with decay — built in Round 3, lane TB4/TB5 (compound bullet) — source/inspiration: ByteRover
didnt: Corroboration — a context tree with an approve/reject review workflow for curate operations confirms our approval-gated write design; the Elastic License 2.0 terms and archived status bar any code adoption, so only the idea was taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memodb-io/Acontext
good: Skill memory layer that automatically distils completed or failed agent tasks from session messages into agent skill files — readable, editable Markdown you can share across agents, LLMs and frameworks, export as ZIP, and git/grep like plain files. Recall is by progressive disclosure (the agent fetches skills with get_skill / get_skill_file tools) rather than semantic top-k search, and users define the memory structure through SKILL.md schemas.
bad: Running it means operating a backend: the architecture diagram shows PostgreSQL, S3, Redis and RabbitMQ behind a FastAPI core, the self-host path needs Docker and an OpenAI API key, distillation defaults to gpt-4.1, and the cloud path starts from claimed credits and an API key. Automatic LLM distillation of every finished task also writes memory without a human approval step.
didnt: Board — skills-as-memory: procedures distilled from finished tasks into retrievable Markdown skill files, recalled by progressive disclosure rather than top-k search, is a distinct framing worth boarding for our procedural-memory layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemMachine/MemMachine
good: Universal memory layer combining working memory, graph-based episodic memory (Neo4j) for conversational context and SQL profile memory for long-term user facts, persisting across sessions and model changes. Offers Python and TypeScript SDKs, a REST API and native MCP servers (stdio and HTTP), is LLM-agnostic (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Ollama), runs self-hosted via Docker or as a managed service, and integrates with LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Strands, n8n, Dify and FastGPT.
bad: It is a server system, not a library drop-in: the quick start requires a running MemMachine server before any client code works, backed by both a graph database and SQL storage. It provides generic personalisation memory with no citation locking, scored abstention or approval-gated writes, so it duplicates the commodity memory-layer pattern rather than our wiki's guarantees.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and fit: another Neo4j-plus-SQL agent memory server in the same space as Mem0, with none of the citation, abstention or approval machinery our knowledge OS is built around. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zilliztech/memsearch
good: Unified persistent memory shared across Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness, OpenClaw and OpenCode, with Markdown as the source of truth — memories are human-readable, editable, version-controllable .md files and Milvus is explicitly a derived, rebuildable shadow index. Retrieval is progressive and hybrid (3-layer search/expand/transcript recall, dense vector plus BM25 sparse fused with RRF, SHA-256 dedup, live file-watcher indexing), plugins capture conversations automatically, and repeated workflows are distilled into reusable skills.
bad: Truth may live in the files, but operation depends on a Milvus backend (Lite locally, or Zilliz Cloud / a self-hosted server) and the default local ONNX bge-m3 embedding model is a ~558 MB first-launch download. The Codex install path even requires running with --yolo for ONNX model network access, and per-platform capture/summarisation routing adds considerable configuration surface.
didnt: Corroboration — Markdown as the source of truth with the vector store demoted to a rebuildable shadow index, plus hybrid dense/BM25 fusion and content-hash dedup, confirms our files-first, index-second architecture; the Milvus dependency is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kingjulio8238/Memary
good: Knowledge-graph memory layer for autonomous agents (FalkorDB or Neo4j, with multi-graph support for multiple agents) combining a Memory Stream of timestamped entities with an Entity Knowledge Store tracking frequency and recency, inspired by Microsoft Research's K-LaMP. Retrieval builds bounded subgraphs around key entities (max depth 2, multi-hop joins across entities) instead of searching the whole graph, memory updates automatically as the agent interacts, and it runs local models via Ollama.
bad: The implementation is dated and brittle: it requires Python <= 3.11.9, its named model defaults are gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4-vision-preview and LLaVA, setup demands a long list of third-party API keys, and the README says the bundled ReAct demo agent will be removed in a future version. The catalogue record also notes it was last updated in Oct 2024.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and duplication: a 2024-era graph-memory demo with pinned old models and a to-be-removed agent core, whose bounded-subgraph retrieval idea is already covered by our graph and ranking work. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Asymptote-Labs/agent-beacon
good: Cross-harness memory that captures full session history from Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Cline and 20+ other harnesses into one OpenTelemetry-based trace format (prompts, responses, tool calls, commands, edits, approvals, MCP activity, tokens) stored as durable local JSONL. It evaluates what worked, extracts workflows, corrections and debugging patterns, and — after review and approval — makes that knowledge reusable by future agents via MCP or Agent Skills, with a local read-only dashboard and trace lenses.
bad: The orientation is capture-and-telemetry at machine scale (topics include cloud, MDM, SIEM and observability): interactive setup preselects Beacon Cloud and confirming it starts forwarding session history to the hosted service, and the README warns its sandboxed dashboard lenses cannot block every way a browser can send data out. Wholesale session-history capture is also a much broader custody surface than a curated wiki.
didnt: Rejected — custody and scope: continuous cross-harness session capture with a cloud-forwarding default conflicts with our local-first, curated, approval-gated ingest; only harness-normalised trace discipline is of passing interest. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mudler/LocalRecall
good: 100% local memory layer and knowledge base for agents with a WebUI: a lightweight REST API (plus MCP integration) over collections in a file-based Chromem vector store by default, or PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB, pgvector and pgvectorscale for hybrid BM25-plus-vector search in production. Runs with no GPU, internet or cloud services, integrates with LocalAI/LocalAGI, and accepts external sources such as web pages, git repositories and sitemaps on a refresh interval.
bad: Self-described as lightweight and no-frills: file support is only Markdown, plain text and PDF with more formats listed as coming soon, and retrieval is plain chunk-and-vector RAG with no citation locking, abstention scoring or write approval. An embedding endpoint (LocalAI or an OpenAI-compatible API) is still required to vectorise content.
didnt: Rejected — duplication: competent local-first RAG collections, but our wiki already provides Markdown-first storage with stronger provenance, citation and governance machinery on top. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: inikep/lzbench
licence: GPL-2.0 or GPL-3.0 (bench and doc directories only; bundled compressors under their respective licences)
good: In-memory benchmark that compiles dozens of open-source compressors (zstd, brotli, lz4, zlib, xz and many more) into a single executable built with the same compiler and optimisations, loads the input once, and verifies decompressed output matches the original — giving comparable ratio/speed results, including published Silesia-corpus tables with an interactive Pareto-frontier view.
bad: Its method requires access to each compressor's source code, so closed compressors are excluded by design, and its own table flags a set of bundled compressors as having security issues or being unmaintained, with decompression mismatches and segfaults under modern compilers. The GPL terms apply only to the bench and doc directories, with every bundled codec under its own licence.
didnt: Rejected — fit: this is 'memory' only in the hardware/in-RAM sense, a compression benchmark with no bearing on agent memory or the knowledge OS; its GPL terms would in any case make the code ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fengzdadi/memory-bench-registry
good: Structured registry of 207 agent-memory benchmarks, one YAML file per benchmark, browsable online and filterable by memory type, reproducibility level and year across 11 types (conversational long-term, personalisation, episodic, semantic knowledge update, procedural workflow, coding cross-session, parametric, multi-agent, multimodal, embodied, memory security). Every field must be traceable to the paper or official repository, recorded in the entry's sources, with unfound values left null, plus documented coverage gaps and excluded candidates with reasons.
bad: Verification stops at documentation: of its 207 entries, 0 are smoke_tested and 0 are full_run, 37 are paper_only, so nothing in the registry has actually been executed by its maintainers. It is also very new and small-scale (created 2026-10-11, 25 commits, no releases), and its field/reproducibility definitions and gap docs are in Chinese only.
didnt: Board — use its provenance-traced 207-entry map and reproducibility levels as the starting shortlist for expanding our golden set, verifying any chosen benchmark firsthand before adoption since none are run-verified. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kargarisaac/lerim
licence: Apache-2.0 (core, per README License section; hosted/commercial offering sits outside the open-source core)
good: Compiles completed agent traces into cited, reusable context: it filters noisy runs for decisions, constraints, facts, preferences, corrections and handoffs, links each record back to its source session, consolidates overlap, and serves answers and startup context briefs via CLI and MCP tools. It also proposes evidence-backed edits to skill/instruction files, shown as diffs for review before applying.
bad: Node.js 20+ is a hard runtime requirement with no fallback trace parser, and native ingestion is uneven: the README lists Cursor and OpenCode as not supported in 0.4.0 and several agents as MCP-only or experimental. Extraction-quality evidence is aggregate-only (a 47-case diagnostic), and custom-trace users must do their own export, cleaning and redaction before import.
didnt: Rejected — trace-to-context compilation duplicates our wiki ingest/compile layer and citation practice, and the remaining value is a separate runtime we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: talirezun/the-curator
licence: MIT, except ten Shared Brain backend files that are source-available under the Curator Enterprise License (per README Licensing section)
good: Turns dropped-in PDFs, markdown and text into a compounding, interlinked markdown wiki stored locally and synced through the user's own private GitHub repo, readable in Obsidian, with cited answers. It cleanly separates accumulating knowledge, superseding working state/handoffs, and verbatim canonical documents, and delivers agent bootstrap context over MCP with a token-budgeted reading model.
bad: The README states two honest boundaries: the MCP bridge is a stdio child process so browser-only assistants cannot reach it, and state capture is advisory — a missed save returns stale previous state. The Mac app is not notarised, and the mixed licence (MIT plus a custom enterprise carve-out) complicates reuse.
didnt: Rejected — this is a direct duplicate of our own LLM-wiki system (compounding markdown wiki, handoffs, MCP door), and the custom enterprise licence carve-out bars adopting its Shared Brain code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Inspired-by-Atmosphere/pulse-path
good: States pointer hygiene as five explicit laws — delete means relink, modify means check both link directions, add means declare an outbound link, always verify after reorganising, and treat all stores uniformly — and ships portable, dependency-free Python engines for it: a declarative rule table, a dry-run memory health check (mem_guard) and a link-integrity scan (scan_links.py). The three skills are drop-in and independently usable.
bad: Very young and small: 6 commits and a single release at source. The README itself says it is not a database (the pointer dictionary is a plain markdown file and concurrency control is left to the host agent), semantic-store integration assumes an optional OpenViking-like store, and detection scripts always exit 0, reporting only through stdout.
didnt: Board — the five pointer-hygiene laws plus a dry-run link-integrity scan as an explicit lint lane for wiki reorganisations. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pouyahasanamreji/continuum
good: One local MCP server giving coding agents shared persistent memory and orchestration: lessons become 768-dim embeddings in sqlite-vec inside a single SQLite file, recall returns ranked metadata before bodies to keep context cheap, fundamental versus situational knowledge are separated, and a PLOT.md protocol plus an agent registry with reserved-path tracking coordinates parallel agents in isolated worktrees.
bad: No licence file appears in the repository root and there are no releases, so reuse rights are unclear. It is scoped to coding-agent orchestration, requires Node >=22.12 and pnpm 10.33+ on bare metal (or Docker), and its memory is embedding-based with no citation locking or approval-gated writes described.
didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at source (ideas-only at most), and its shared vector memory/orchestration duplicates our wiki plus agent coordination while lacking citation locking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: major7apps/pensyve
good: A persistent agent-memory runtime with a Rust engine and local SQLite storage: it stores facts, conversation episodes, observations and action outcomes, searches by text, embeddings and entity relationships, and offers consolidation that promotes repeated facts and updates retention. Access is broad — Python SDK, MCP server, CLI, REST gateway, and TypeScript/Go clients — with no account or API key needed for local use.
bad: The README states Pensyve is in maintenance mode with no new features planned (security and dependency fixes only), and Pensyve Cloud closed on 1 October 2026. Embedding models may download on first load, so offline use requires preparing model files in advance.
didnt: Rejected — a general memory runtime duplicating our wiki memory layer, now in maintenance mode with its hosted service closed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kunwar-shah/claudex
good: Indexes Claude Code conversation history under ~/.claude/projects with SQLite FTS5 full-text search (filtering by project, session, role and date, with highlighting), auto-detects V1/V2/V3 Claude Code formats, and adds an MCP server with 10 tools plus structured memory (priority, confidence, TTL) and token-budgeted recall prompts. A React web UI provides browsing, analytics and JSON/HTML/TXT export.
bad: Scope is a single vendor's history format: it only works where Claude Code has written local project files, and requires Node.js 18+. The README's troubleshooting section documents recurring failure modes — empty results despite existing messages, missing projects, broken search and port conflicts — around its index rebuild.
didnt: Rejected — a Claude-Code-history viewer/search tool; its scope is transcript indexing, which our wiki deliberately does not adopt as its memory model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yantrikos/yantrikdb-hermes-plugin
