good: A YantrikDB memory provider plugin for the Hermes agent with self-maintaining memory: duplicate canonicalisation, first-class contradiction tracking (conflicts()/resolve_conflict()), explainable recall (why_retrieved per result), recency-aware ranking, proactive hygiene, knowledge-gap detection and a reproducible recall benchmark. Embedded in-process by default — no server, token or GPU — with idempotent writes and owner-scoping for shared agents.
bad: It is built specifically as a Hermes memory provider (other agents need the separate MCP/Python distributions), knowledge packs are embedded-mode only and unavailable over the HTTP backend, and owner scoping is off by default because it changes where new memories are written.
didnt: Corroboration — contradiction tracking, explainable recall and supersession-aware ranking confirm our claim-lifecycle and citation design; the plugin itself is Hermes-specific. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: THUIR/MemoryBench
good: A standardised, extensible benchmark for memory and continual learning in LLM systems (ICML 2026 Spotlight per the README): 28 datasets across academic, legal and open domains, 8 memory-system baselines behind one registry, and four regimes — off-policy, stepwise off-policy, on-policy and training-set performance — with a simulated user-feedback loop, testing whether systems learn from accumulated feedback rather than merely doing long-context reading comprehension.
bad: This repo is the lightweight benchmark interface; the README says the full paper reproduction code lives in a separate repository. Reproducing paper results needs a heavy vLLM deployment (Qwen3-32B main model plus separate 8B, embedding and critic models), and results depend on a simulated feedback model rather than real users.
didnt: Board — the feedback-driven on-policy/stepwise evaluation regime as a model for testing whether our wiki memory actually improves answers over time, rather than only retrieval accuracy. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: THUIR

name: AIPMAndy/dna-memory
licence: Apache-2.0 (per repo LICENSE detection; the README licence footer links it under an MIT label, inconsistent at source)
good: A local-first unified memory layer that processes before it stores: bounded source pointers instead of transcripts, signal filtering, importance/confidence weighting, eight cognitive types, and only verified, traceable conclusions crystallised into a Markdown source of truth (SQLite is a rebuildable index). Superseded conclusions are kept and marked, recall is fed back as useful/misleading, credentials and sensitive content are rejected, and one MCP service serves Codex, Claude Code, Hermes and Obsidian.
bad: Very early: 9 commits at source. Recall is keyword-based (1–4 keywords per call), automatic extraction is capped at 3 candidates of at most 800 characters per session, deduplication is exact-text only with no fuzzy merging, and the primary README is in Chinese with a separate English version.
didnt: Corroboration — process-before-store gating, bounded pointers, verified-only crystallisation and explicit supersedes confirm our ingest and claim-lifecycle discipline almost point for point. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kennethlaw325/awesome-llm-knowledge-systems
good: A unified guide that connects topics usually treated separately — RAG, context engineering, harness engineering, skill systems, agent memory, MCP and progressive disclosure — into one lifecycle/ecosystem map with chapters, a glossary and translations. Its dated entries habitually flag the provenance and limits of the claims they record (vendor figures labelled as such, unreplicated results noted).
bad: It is a curated guide, not software: there is no implementation, test suite or release to adopt, and much of its content is fast-moving 2026 vendor and paper claims that age quickly and, by its own annotations, often rest on a single source's own numbers.
didnt: Rejected — a reference map, not a system; useful reading for landscape surveys but nothing to build from or adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Nimrobo/superdense
good: A local outcome loop and reward layer for coding agents: each goal gets goal.md (protected), run.md (playbook) and gate.md (completion contract); every run first recalls what shipped and how it landed, records a hypothesis/experiment before acting, and writes the measured result back, with gate failures blocking completion claims. It also indexes past sessions into local SQLite with cost, error and tool signals, compaction views, and cohort comparisons — no cloud.
bad: Session adapters cover only Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode, and measuring real-world outcomes depends on wiring external connectors (GitHub, X, npm, analytics) with their own access. It requires Node 20+ and centres on measurable marketing/performance-style goals, a narrower frame than general knowledge work.
didnt: Board — the preregistered hypothesis/experiment/reward record and the gate contract that stops a run being called complete on a failed check, as patterns for goal tracking and completion verification. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vaan21th/daemonkey-agent
good: A local-first companion daemon whose memory is split into two separately governed tracks — a soul layer (identity, user profile, growth journal) and a playbook layer (work distilled into reusable manuals that are auto-loaded for similar tasks) — all stored as readable files on the user's disk, surviving model and machine changes. It adds a workbench for editing documents in place, scheduled jobs, self-repair with rollback to a working core, and a token-frugal prompt-prefix assembly design.
bad: AGPL-3.0 copyleft covers the whole agent, including network-service use. It requires the user to supply an OpenAI-compatible API key and Python 3.10+, its scope is a broad self-extending/self-repairing companion (desktop pet, chat bridges, document engines), and its headline memory benchmark result is its own run on a 31-item benchmark.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under our licence discipline, and a self-modifying companion daemon conflicts with our approval-gated write model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: syiibfs-hash/cc-agent-brain
good: A local-first memory engine for coding agents with zero third-party dependencies (Python stdlib SQLite + FTS5, including CJK bigram tokenisation): hooks capture prompts, replies and tool actions into an append-only event stream, distil them into four-layer versioned, bi-temporal memory where facts are superseded or expired rather than overwritten, and recall via BM25 + RRF through an MCP server, with a human-readable Markdown wiki projection and secret redaction at capture time.
bad: Very early: 5 commits, no releases, and the current version is v0.2 — embeddings and a built-in recall evaluation set are still roadmap items (v0.3), so retrieval is lexical only today. Capture depends on Claude-style lifecycle hooks, tying the loop to harnesses that expose them.
didnt: Corroboration — bi-temporal supersede-never-overwrite versioning, an append-only event stream under a readable markdown projection, and capture-time secret redaction confirm our wiki's memory model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ruvnet/agentdb
good: A self-learning vector memory in a single .rvf file: HNSW search over the RuVector Rust engine, hybrid BM25 + dense retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion, and a feedback loop where recordFeedback drives a Thompson Sampling bandit that re-tunes ranking, RL algorithm choice and compression tier. It ships as an npm library, a CLI and an MCP server with 41 tools covering pattern storage, causal/hierarchical memory, reflexion episodes and a skill library, running in Node, browser and edge runtimes, offline.
bad: The headline performance and quality figures (+36% search quality from feedback, 150x faster than SQLite, sub-millisecond search) are the project's own benchmark claims. Scope is very broad for 20 commits and no releases — 9 RL algorithms, GNN attention, graph queries and enterprise security in one package — and its learning loop optimises ranking opaquely rather than preserving citable sources.
didnt: Rejected — a self-tuning vector database duplicates our retrieval stack while replacing citable, inspectable memory with bandit-optimised ranking; maturity (no releases) does not support adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shamspias/reins
good: A lightweight agent harness you bolt onto an existing app so an LLM can operate it through intent-named functions ('your verbs, not your tables'): decorate existing functions with @capability or auto-expose SQLAlchemy/Django ORM models with Agent.from_orm, and the agent plans and calls those operations through your own code rather than raw SQL. Safety is enforced in code — ask() is strictly read-only, run() writes are opt-in and pass policy, a fail-closed human approval gate, row-level scoping by principal, and a structured PII-redacted audit trail — with sandboxed code-mode execution, budgets, and seven model providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Groq, Z.ai/GLM, Ollama, vLLM) behind one interface across Python, Go and TypeScript packages passing a shared conformance suite.
bad: The README badges it alpha and its Status section says it is at its first Python alpha (0.1.0a1) with APIs that may change before 1.0, and installation notes say the first PyPI release is still coming so users install from source for now. The default sandbox is a whitelisted-import subprocess the README honestly labels 'not a hard security boundary', and the roadmap lists remaining gaps: a native Go code-mode sandbox and the TypeScript <reins-chat> widget are not yet done.
didnt: Corroboration — its code-enforced read-only ask()/write split, fail-closed approval gate, and structured audit trail confirm our approval-gated write design, but it is an app-operation harness for operating external apps via ORM/functions, not a memory or knowledge component for a personal LLM-wiki, so nothing is adopted from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CMU-SAFARI/prim-benchmarks
good: PrIM is presented as the first benchmark suite for a real-world processing-in-memory architecture (UPMEM), with 16 heterogeneous workloads plus CPU and GPU baselines for comparison. It also ships microbenchmarks for compute throughput and memory bandwidth and scripts for weak and strong scaling experiments.
bad: Running it requires the UPMEM SDK — the README notes the official SDK website is deprecated and points to a mirror — and it is designed for a server with real UPMEM modules or the SDK's functional simulator. It benchmarks PIM hardware only and has no LLM or agent-memory content.
didnt: Rejected — hardware processing-in-memory benchmark with no fit for a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: SAFARI Research Group (CMU-SAFARI)

name: OpenHelix-Team/RoboMemArena
good: A robotic memory benchmark with 26 manipulation tasks, demonstration data, evaluation BDDL definitions, a leaderboard, and CSR/TSR metrics. The dataset is organised as full long-horizon HDF5 trajectories plus keyframe-annotated subtask episodes with agent-view and wrist-camera observations, robot state, and an RLDS conversion path.
bad: Evaluation requires a LIBERO-compatible environment and an OpenPI runtime, and the dataset itself is hosted externally on Hugging Face / ModelScope. The README warns the June 2026 dataset update changed data and evaluation logic enough that earlier downloads must be overwritten, and no licence file is present in the repository.
didnt: Rejected — robotic manipulation memory, outside the scope of a text LLM-wiki, and no licence stated at source so its code is ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vectorize-io/agent-memory-benchmark
good: AMB is fully open about its method: datasets, prompts, scoring logic and results are published, with a live leaderboard. Its ingest-retrieve-generate-judge harness tracks accuracy alongside speed and token cost, adds agentic-task datasets beyond chatbot LoCoMo/LongMemEval, and includes PrecisionMemBench, a retrieval-only mode that asserts exactly which memories must and must not be returned.
bad: Answer generation and judging both require a Gemini API key, so scores are tied to that provider's models, and no licence file is present in the repository. It is authored by the Hindsight team to evaluate its own system, as the README itself states.
didnt: Board — the PrecisionMemBench idea of hard per-case must-return / must-not-return retrieval assertions, and publishing judge prompts with results, for our own eval reporting; no licence is stated, so no code is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OpenDataBox/MemoryData
good: A unified benchmark suite that runs four benchmark families (MemoryAgentBench, LoCoMo, LongBench, MemBench) and 22 method presets — spanning baselines, sequential, structural-topological and hybrid memory architectures — through a single main.py launcher selected by two YAML files. Every run emits a result JSON and persisted agent state under a stable results layout, with separate Linux/macOS and Windows dependency manifests.
bad: Datasets are not bundled and must be placed under datasets/ in loader-specific layouts, and most presets assume OpenAI-compatible endpoints and API keys. The repository is very new and small (4 commits at the source) and no licence file is present.
didnt: Board — the one-launcher, two-YAML-config pattern for running many memory methods across several benchmark families as a candidate shape for expanding our eval set; no licence is stated, so no code is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: microsoft/X-Mem
good: A cross-platform, extensible tool for characterising memory-hierarchy throughput, latency and power, with NUMA, multi-threading and large-page support and modular C++11 design for adding new benchmark kernels. It covers sequential, strided and random access patterns across cache and main memory on Linux and Windows, x86 and ARM.
bad: The repository is archived, and the README is dated 2016 (project revision April 2016) with period prerequisites such as Ubuntu 12.04/14.04, Visual Studio 2013/2015, Python 2.7 and SCons. It is a hardware memory-characterisation tool with no LLM or agent-memory relevance.
didnt: Rejected — archived 2016 hardware memory tool, out of scope for a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Microsoft and UCLA NanoCAD Lab

name: ahstat/episodic-memory-benchmark
good: The Tulving benchmark generates synthetic book-like narratives whose events carry date, location, entity and content, with recurring entities tracked across chapters, and releases 11 datasets from 10K to 1M tokens. Its Q&A suite (36 templates in the paper) scores Simple Recall and Chronological Awareness, including a zero-matching-events group that checks hallucination, and reproducibility notebooks are provided.
bad: The narratives are LLM-generated (Claude 3.5 Sonnet / GPT-4o), so the benchmark tests memory over synthetic fiction rather than real personal records, and running new experiments requires OpenAI, Anthropic or OpenRouter API keys. Evaluation is centred on in-context reading of a single narrative.
didnt: Board — synthetic episodic dataset generation with chronological-awareness and zero-match hallucination questions as a gap-filler idea for our golden set, which lacks synthetic episodic data. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: maleadt/pChase
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) — a LICENSE file is present but GitHub does not identify it as a standard licence
good: pChase measures both latency and bandwidth of constant-stride and random access patterns across cache levels and main memory by actually chasing pointers, so the next address depends on retrieved data — unlike arithmetic-address benchmarks such as STREAM. Experiments can vary chain sizes, thread counts and concurrent references per thread to expose NUMA and SMP contention.
bad: The code originates from 2007-2008 with 2011 graduate-project additions (an x86 JIT for the hot path), so it is dated, low-level hardware tooling. Its licence is not identified as a standard licence at the source, and it has no LLM or software-memory relevance.
didnt: Rejected — hardware pointer-chasing benchmark, out of scope, and its unidentified licence makes its code ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cruvolo/ramspeed-smp
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) — a LICENCE file is present but GitHub does not identify it as a standard licence
good: RAMspeed/SMP measures effective cache and memory bandwidth on multiprocessor UNIX-like machines, written in C for portability with assembly routines where available. Its INTmark/FLOATmark and INTmem/FLOATmem suites (plus MMX/SSE variants) cover Copy, Scale, Add and Triad subtests, with a BatchRun mode that averages repeated runs.
bad: The shipped version is v3.5.0 from August 2009, the mirror holds only 6 commits, and supported platforms are legacy i386/amd64/alpha UNIX-like systems. Its licence is not identified as a standard licence at the source, and it is purely a hardware bandwidth tool.
didnt: Rejected — legacy hardware cache/RAM bandwidth tool, out of scope, and its unidentified licence makes its code ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Emmimal/context-graph-benchmark
good: A pure-Python, deterministic benchmark with zero API calls that compares raw history dump, TF-IDF vector RAG and a NetworkX context graph of (subject, predicate, object) triples across five scripted multi-agent scenarios and 18 graded queries; the graph scored 88.9% at 26.9 tokens/query against 50.0% for vector RAG, with the largest gap on join queries needing two separately-stated facts. Fact supersession is built in — a restated (subject, predicate) pair removes the old edge — and regression tests lock the headline numbers.
bad: The scale is tiny and hand-authored: five scenarios and 18 queries, with distractors scripted rather than real. The README itself discloses that TF-IDF stands in for neural embeddings, token counts are a ~4 chars/token estimate, entity linking is a hardcoded alias table covering only anticipated phrasing, and two queries are left intentionally broken.
didnt: Corroboration — its join-query and fact-supersession results confirm our graph/files-over-flat-RAG design choice and our rule that a superseded fact must not be returned with full confidence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: timoheimonen/macOS-memory-benchmark
good: A low-level CLI for Apple Silicon that measures CPU and Metal GPU memory bandwidth, cache and main-memory latency, access patterns, TLB behaviour and two-thread cache-line handoff latency, using native ARM64 kernels and runtime-compiled Metal kernels. It adds a synthetic LLM decode/prefill memory-traffic profile and emphasises reproducibility with explicit seeds, parameter sweeps, JSON checkpoints and machine-readable output.
bad: It requires macOS 26 or later on Apple Silicon (ARM64) only, so it runs nowhere else. The README states the LLM profile is synthetic — query heads do not add executed attention maths and the prefill tile is not a real inference kernel's tiling — and the code is GPL-3.0.
didnt: Rejected — Apple-Silicon-only hardware microbenchmark, out of scope for our wiki, and GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under our licence discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: python/memory.python.org
good: The CPython Memory Tracker benchmarks and analyses CPython memory use across commits and build configurations, with a FastAPI/SQLite backend, a Next.js frontend for trends and commit diffs, and a worker CLI that can benchmark commit ranges in parallel. Docker Compose is the supported setup, and backend tests exercise the full request cycle in CI.
bad: Its scope is solely CPython development: it needs Docker, a CPython source checkout and an authentication token for the worker, and the README says local (non-Docker) development is not recommended. It tracks interpreter memory, not agent or LLM memory.
didnt: Rejected — a CPython-interpreter memory tracker, a different meaning of memory from our agent/wiki memory system and out of scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Backboard-io/Backboard-Locomo-Benchmark
licence: No standalone licence stated at source — the README says the implementation follows the LoCoMo dataset license and terms of use
good: An end-to-end LoCoMo evaluation framework: it ingests conversations turn-by-turn into an isolated assistant per conversation, asks test questions in a separate thread, and scores answers with a GPT-4.1 LLM judge that returns reasoning, producing per-conversation and per-category (single-hop, multi-hop, open-domain, temporal) accuracy plus response times. A comparison table against Mem0, Zep, LangMem and others is published in the README.
bad: It is a vendor framework built to demonstrate Backboard's own system (2 commits at the source) and requires both a Backboard API key and an OpenAI API key, so it cannot run against a local-first system. It filters out LoCoMo category 5 (adversarial) questions, the README notes 2-3% judge variance across runs, and no standalone licence is granted for the code.
didnt: Rejected — a single-vendor, API-key-bound LoCoMo harness for Backboard's hosted system, incompatible with local-first custody, with no standalone licence stated. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: geniesinc/Memora
good: Memora benchmarks long-term memory for personalised agents with explicit credit for both remembering and forgetting: its FAMA score combines memory_presence sub-questions (what should be recalled) with forgetting_absence sub-questions (deleted or updated information that should not surface). It releases data for 10 personas at weekly, monthly and quarterly horizons (up to about 2,000 sessions per persona) across Remembering, Reasoning and Recommending tasks, plus evaluation code for both plain LLMs and six memory agents.
bad: Breadth is limited to 10 personas with 15 evaluation questions per weekly/monthly persona-period (30 for quarterly), and evaluation depends on an LLM judge over yes/no sub-questions plus OpenRouter, OpenAI and per-agent API keys. The repository is small (6 commits at the source) and its published reasoning-task FAMA scores are very low across all systems shown.
didnt: Board — the FAMA idea of scoring forgetting (deleted/updated facts must not surface) alongside recall, as a metric our own supersession and abstention evals could adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Arizona State University (ASU) and Genies

name: wontopos/glasshouse
good: Glasshouse sets auditable rules for publishing memory benchmark results: the per-question record must be published so anyone can recompute the number, each benchmark version fixes the reader, judge and prompts (submitters do not choose them), the harness must be one a customer could use, and three runs count as a result while five are certified. A claims register records vendors' public numbers alongside whether their reader and judge are published.
bad: By its own README, glasshouse-v0.1 is a draft that is not released yet, the submissions directory is empty, and the repository has released no benchmark of its own and verified nothing in its claims register. Governance rests on company/individual voting proposals, run by a host that also competes in the market it administers.
didnt: Board — the publication standard of shipping the per-question record, judge and prompts with any benchmark number we report, so our eval claims stay recomputable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nerdralph/cl-mem
good: A small OpenCL memory benchmark utility that reports sequential write, read and (since v0.3) copy speeds, with a worked example in the README (128 GB written at 111.3 GB/s, read at 164.2 GB/s on an R9 380). Its entire implementation is a handful of files (main.c, input.cl, Makefile).
bad: Scope is narrow and unfinished by its own README: only sequential tests exist and random read/write tests are merely planned for a later version. The code dates from 2016 with 10 commits, and it benchmarks GPU device memory, not LLM or agent memory.
didnt: Rejected — a minimal 2016 OpenCL hardware bandwidth utility, out of scope for a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lsds/sgx-membench
good: A minimal, focused memory benchmark for Intel SGX, split into an enclave component (sgx-membench-enclave) and a host component (sgx-membench), under a permissive Apache-2.0 licence.
bad: The README is a single line ('Simple memory benchmarking of Intel SGX') with no build, run, or results documentation at the source. The repo is tiny and old: 4 commits, created 2016, no releases, and it is specific to Intel SGX hardware, so it offers nothing transferable as a knowledge system.
didnt: Rejected — hardware SGX memory benchmarking is unrelated in scope to a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS with citation locking and approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: techtheist/knowledgedrift
good: An offline, judge-free benchmark for AI memory: one seeded invented world is poured through a twelve-operation protocol (inscribe, link, supersede, release, purge, endorse, settle, recall, suspects, lineage) and probed with tasks whose pass/fail rules are fixed in advance. Its eight families — retrieval, abstention, currency, contradiction, drift, deletion, rationale, temporal (plus an opt-in authority family) — directly test superseded notes, planted contradictions, forgotten items and token/signal efficiency, with a published ladder over 1,500 tested facts and 9,008 tasks comparing systems including Mem0, LangMem, cognee and Supermemory.
bad: It is very early and small: 12 stars, 20 commits, and the shipped worlds are a single invented software-development project, so results do not establish performance on a personal knowledge corpus. The headline ladder also shows most real systems scoring far below the author's own reference system (800 vs 263–580), so independent adoption/replication is not yet shown at the source.
didnt: Board — its judge-free families (currency, drift, deletion, abstention, authority-rung ranking) and the rule that a system that cannot do something declares it N/A rather than scoring a mysterious zero, as an evaluation design for our truth-aware retrieval / scored-abstention testing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sanonone/kektordb
good: Combines HNSW vector search with a temporal knowledge graph and a cognitive engine: a Gardener process consolidates duplicates and detects contradictions, an epistemic engine scores confidence (Consensus/Stability/Friction), 'Semantic Git' versioning preserves superseded memories via superseded_by/evolves_from edges, and decay is configurable per memory layer. It ships as REST server, embedded Go library, MCP server (49 agent tools) and AI gateway, with hybrid AOF+snapshot persistence, CRC32 checks, JWT/RBAC auth, and published benchmarks (Recall@10 0.97) against Qdrant and ChromaDB.
bad: The README's own Current Limitations section states it is single-node only — no clustering, scaling vertically within one machine — and the benchmarks note it is optimised for embedded single-node scenarios, not billion-scale distributed deployments. Adopting it would also mean replacing our file-based wiki store with a separate Go database engine and its LLM-based contradiction analysis.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and scope: a full standalone memory database engine duplicates our local-first wiki store rather than filling a missing capability, despite its permissive licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yantrikos/yantrikdb
good: An embeddable Rust cognitive memory engine with Python bindings providing temporal decay, autonomous consolidation, contradiction detection and a knowledge graph with HNSW recall. It publishes reproducible, CI-gated evidence (recall/latency benchmark, graph-lift test, competitor comparison, LongMemEval-S retrieval scored mechanically) and reports large token savings from selective recall versus file-based memory (about 70 tokens per query at 5,000 memories in its benchmark).
bad: The README itself warns that opening the store with a second SQLite library in the same process corrupts the store silently, with integrity checks refusing writes until cleared — a sharp custody hazard for a file-based workflow. A store's embedding dimension is fixed at creation (switching models requires re-embedding), and its embedder-superiority evidence rests on a self-described small set of 12 probes whose gain it says is corpus-specific and may not transfer.
didnt: Corroboration — its decay, consolidation and contradiction-detection design, and its reproducible CI-gated recall evidence, confirm mechanisms our stack already has; no separate engine adoption is needed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yantrikos/yantrikdb-mcp
good: A drop-in MCP server (21 tools: remember, recall, forget, correct, think, graph, conflict, temporal, procedure, skill and others) giving any MCP client persistent cognitive memory backed by the YantrikDB Rust engine, with temporal decay, contradiction detection and autonomous consolidation. It runs locally on SQLite with no telemetry, and also offers an HTTP cluster mode and an SSE mode, with a digest-first session briefing as its recommended golden path.
bad: The README labels SSE mode legacy and warns SSE connections can drop on idle, recommending cluster mode instead for shared setups. Embedder choice is fragile across versions: bundled (64-dim), ONNX (384-dim) and multilingual (256-dim) databases are mutually incompatible, auto-detection is heuristic, and a missing-extra mismatch fails fast rather than migrating.
didnt: Corroboration — a thin MIT-licensed MCP wrapper over a local memory engine, with local/SQLite/multi-mode deployment, confirms the MCP-door pattern our wiki already uses; the underlying engine duplicates our store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: STiFLeR7/memex
good: Builds a bitemporal knowledge graph of a codebase (modules, symbols, decisions, problems, evidence) in Neo4j via Graphiti, using tree-sitter extraction and Gemini synthesis, and serves bounded, provenance-aware ContextPackets through 14 MCP tools. Its v1 live-context hooks deliver a session-start working set, check edits against current code before they land, and name files to re-read on resume; confidence is computed at query time from base confidence, validation status, reinforcement and access, with hierarchical Leiden clusters scaling from 50 to 5,000+ modules.
bad: It is explicitly codebase-only — the README states memex is not a source of personal memory or raw session state — so it does not address a personal knowledge wiki. It requires a self-run Neo4j 5 server and a Gemini API key for synthesis, and the README notes the first start downloads Python dependencies for about 40 seconds, which can exceed Claude Code's MCP connect timeout.
didnt: Rejected — scope and dependencies: an engineering-context graph for codebases requiring Neo4j and Gemini, not a fit for our local-first personal wiki custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: liza-studio/skillmem
good: A local, self-improving skill memory for coding agents on plain SQLite with no API key or cloud: skills are learned, recalled, reinforced and decayed on an Ebbinghaus schedule, with strength rising only on evidence outside the agent's own judgement (a passing test, an accepted diff, owner confirmation). Every memory carries provenance (owner/agent/imported/derived), only the owner can approve a memory as a rule, unapproved memory is injected framed as data not instructions, edits are appended to a SHA256 hash-chain verifiable with skillmem verify, and it reports hit@5 0.871 / MRR 0.622 on the LongMemEval oracle set with local hybrid FTS5 + ONNX retrieval.
bad: The README is candid that its protections are not a wall: the plugin path has no deny rules for owner-only commands, the deny rules are substring matches an agent with a shell can evade, and reinforce is not idempotent (evidence ids are deferred to a later release). It is also narrow — procedures for coding agents, not general knowledge — and very new (created 2026-08-30, 9 stars).
didnt: Board — provenance on every memory with owner-only trust approval, strength earned only from external evidence, and unapproved memory framed as data rather than instructions, as a hardening idea for our approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alphaparkinc/genpark-hierarchical-memory-consolidation-compressor-skill
good: Distils multi-turn dialogue into dense semantic long-term memory blocks: an ephemeral-chatter sieve drops greetings and small talk, a salience pattern classifier extracts preferences, constraints and facts, and only items at or above a salience threshold are promoted to the permanent tier, pruning token bloat. It is pure Python 3.9+ standard library with zero external dependencies, packaged as an MCP skill (client.py, mcp_server.py, skill.json).
bad: Documentation at the source is minimal — the entire README is an architecture diagram plus two feature bullets, with no evaluation, tests, decay parameters or usage detail beyond example_usage.py. The repo is slight (7 commits, 0 releases, 8 stars) and carries no licence file or licence statement, so its code cannot be reused.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and licence: a thinly documented, unlicensed skill sketch; the salience-gated consolidation idea is already covered by our consolidation design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: withkynam/vibecode-pro-max-kit
good: A spec-driven coding harness (15 agents, 33 skills, 10 hooks) built around a gated 7-phase RIPER-5 workflow, plan-validate-fix and execute-validate-fix self-healing loops, feasibility probes and 36 mechanical validators. Its self-improving project memory keeps shared process/context notes on disk, written every phase so a run survives a memory reset, and its one-command installer is explicitly non-destructive, backing up existing config and never overwriting a user's process folder.
bad: Its pitch is autopilot operation 'with 0 need for human gate', which directly conflicts with an approval-gated write model, and its scope is coding-project delivery, not knowledge custody. The harness is heavy ceremony for small work (mitigated only by its own quick/fast lanes) and installation is a curl-pipe-to-bash script requiring Node.js 22+, git and bash (Git Bash/WSL on Windows).
didnt: Rejected — fit: a vibe-coding delivery harness whose no-human-gate autopilot contradicts our approval-gated writes, and whose memory is a by-product of a much larger coding workflow we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: thClaws/thClaws
good: A native-Rust AI agent harness shipped as one binary across desktop GUI, CLI, headless and webapp surfaces, with multi-provider support (1,100+ models across 27 providers), MCP, skills, plugins and agent teams. Relevant here, its Knowledge Bases (KMS) feature keeps per-project and per-user wikis under .thclaws/state/kms/ following Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern — grep + read with a one-line index.md and no embeddings — and its /dream command mines recent sessions into a dated audit-trail page reviewable with git diff; it also ships OS-level bash confinement by default.
bad: The LLM-wiki element is only one small feature (and a topic tag) inside a very large general agent harness, so adopting it means adopting the whole platform. It is pre-1.0 with rapid churn (638 commits, 194 releases), and the README warns v0.126.0 migrates existing workspaces into .thclaws/bots/main/, breaking anything holding the old absolute path until updated.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: a full agent platform whose embedded KMS wiki corroborates the Karpathy pattern we already implement, but whose harness we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MarceloCaporale/codex-agent-mem
good: Local-first MCP memory layer for Codex CLI/Desktop, Claude Code, Gemini CLI and other runtimes: SQLite + FTS5 storage, compact context packs, session-aware retrieval, an explicit read-only audit mode and governance/audit tooling, with no external memory server. Its reproducible synthetic fixtures report repeated context cut from about 22,950 to about 1,068 tokens.
bad: The README itself cautions that local SQLite memory is plaintext by default and must not be treated as a secrets vault, that its generated-context guardrail is not prompt-injection proof, and that the token savings are fixture results, not a universal guarantee. Validation is uneven across runtimes — Grok/xAI is only a protocol-level note and some model validations are explicitly not claimed.
didnt: Board — the known_pack_hash / not_modified unchanged-pack avoidance and the visible scope warning when a pack spans multiple sessions, as retrieval-efficiency ideas for our MCP door; the SQLite store itself duplicates our wiki memory. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: langchain-ai/langgraphjs-api
good: Provided the LangGraph.js CLI and an in-memory server implementation for LangGraph.js agents, in a 439-commit TypeScript monorepo from LangChain.
bad: The repository is archived and its README says only that it has moved to langchain-ai/langgraphjs, so this repo is superseded and unmaintained; it has no releases, and its server is in-memory rather than a persistent knowledge store.
didnt: Rejected — archived and superseded by the langgraphjs monorepo, and an in-memory agent server is not a durable memory layer for our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: enochchau/vitest-mongodb
good: Small test helper that runs Vitest against MongoDB Memory Server: setup/teardown functions wired through a Vitest setup file, a global __MONGO_URI__ for connecting in tests, and an option to run a replica set instead of a single server.
bad: The repository is archived with no releases, and the README states the jest-mongodb mongoURLEnvName option has 'No plans to implement'. It is a MongoDB test fixture, unrelated to a markdown knowledge store.
didnt: Rejected — an archived MongoDB test helper; no fit for a local-first markdown knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: danielmarbach/mnemonic
good: Local MCP memory server whose memories are plain markdown with YAML frontmatter — readable, diffable and git-synced with no database — offering project-scoped hybrid semantic, exact-match and relationship-aware recall, local gitignored embeddings, and a semantic git commit for every remember/update/consolidate.
bad: The README states it favours simplicity and portability over large-scale knowledge bases: hundreds to low thousands of notes are a good fit, very large collections bring longer reindexing, higher recall latency and more git churn, and many concurrent writers should use a dedicated database and indexing layer instead. Default recall also requires a locally running Ollama embedding model.
didnt: Corroboration — its plain-markdown-plus-git, no-database design, with generated embeddings kept out of git, confirms our exact storage shape and local-first custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sylweriusz/mcp-neo4j-memory-server
good: MCP memory on Neo4j: memories as graph nodes with observations, unified semantic-vector, exact-match and graph-traversal search in four tools, typed relations with strength, source tracking and temporal metadata, batch creation, and per-project databases.
bad: It requires a Neo4j setup where the Graph Data Science plugin is 'not only recommended but necessary' (the README's worked setup is DozerDB), plus sentence-transformer embeddings — heavy external database infrastructure for a personal file-based wiki. It has no releases.
didnt: Rejected — the Neo4j/GDS database dependency contradicts local-first plain-file custody and duplicates graph features we build over markdown. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: akshayaggarwal99/amp
good: MCP-native memory server with a two-layer short-term/long-term design, semantic query showing relevance scores, and a local Galaxy/Force dashboard. Its LoCoMo write-up is unusually honest, publishing method, raw per-question verdicts and bootstrap intervals: AMP-Padded2 scored 72.0% while sending roughly 9–16x fewer input tokens than full context.
bad: Very early: 8 commits and no releases, and the README admits the entity table stores names as nodes only — no edges, no relations, off by default and unused by retrieval — with the graph layer, cloud sync and multi-agent sharing still on the roadmap. On its own N=150 test it is statistically tied with naive RAG and 10 points behind full context.
didnt: Board — neighbour padding around retrieved anchors (w=2, +11.3 points over anchor-only in its own test) as a retrieval experiment for our search; the server itself is too immature to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MyrikLD/memlord
good: Self-hosted MCP memory server with hybrid BM25 + pgvector search fused by Reciprocal Rank Fusion, local ONNX embeddings, 11 MCP tools, multi-user workspaces with an in-process OAuth 2.1 server, a Web UI, and a non-destructive 'dreaming' consolidation pass that surfaces near-duplicate and conflicting memories.
bad: Dual-licensed AGPL-3.0/commercial, and it requires PostgreSQL 15+ with pgvector and Python 3.12 — a multi-user server stack far heavier than a personal file wiki. Its own comparison table notes memory input is manual (explicit store) while competitors offer auto-extraction and richer UIs.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0/commercial licensing makes its code ideas-only for us, and its PostgreSQL multi-user server scope does not fit a single-owner local-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mnemoverse/mcp-memory-server
good: Hosted persistent memory over MCP with a simple memory_write/memory_read pair, shared rooms for multi-agent work, one API key or OAuth login across Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and ChatGPT, and a distinctive memory_feedback call: rating a recalled memory as helpful or misleading re-ranks what comes back next.
bad: The README is explicit that only the MCP server and Python SDK are open source — the memory engine is a hosted service, self-hosting is Enterprise-only by agreement, and the free plan caps use at 1,000 queries a day, 10,000 atoms of storage and 60 requests a minute. That puts memory custody outside our local perimeter.
didnt: Board — the helped/misled feedback re-ranking signal as a recall-quality idea for our retrieval; the hosted closed engine itself is rejected on custody grounds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jexp/neo4j-in-memory-server
good: Runs Neo4j's ImpermanentGraphDatabase as an in-memory test server for Neo4j 3.1.x: it should not access disk, starts and restarts faster with less transactional overhead, and exposes a REST endpoint to delete the database content while the server is running.
bad: The README heads it 'Only for Testing' and warns content is not kept across restarts and RAM use is higher; the repo dates from 2014 with 5 commits, targets Neo4j 3.1.1, distributes a zip via Dropbox, and no LICENSE file appears in its repository root listing.
didnt: Rejected — a 2014 test-only, deliberately ephemeral Neo4j tool with no licence stated at source; no fit for durable wiki memory. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obra/episodic-memory
good: Semantic search over Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode and Oh My Pi conversation transcripts, auto-indexing at session end and exposing MCP search/read tools plus sync/stats/doctor/show CLI commands, so past decisions and the reasons behind them can be recalled in natural language.
bad: Summarisation depends on Claude/Codex authentication with a long list of environment overrides and a metered-API cost warning in the README, and indexing is tied to each harness's transcript locations and hook-trust flow. It indexes raw transcripts rather than compiling cited, curated pages.
didnt: Rejected — raw-transcript episodic indexing duplicates our conversation log without our compile-and-cite step, and adds a metered summarisation dependency. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: daveshap/REMO_Framework
good: FastAPI microservice that organises chat logs into a hierarchical taxonomy — raw logs, message pairs, then clustered summaries stored as human-readable YAML files — using Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings and cosine-similarity clustering, searchable via add/search/rebuild/maintain REST endpoints.
bad: The README warns 'this code is still in early alpha. Testing and bugs should be expected!', the repo is archived with no releases and essentially two Python files, and it requires TensorFlow, TensorFlow Hub and an OpenAI API key file. Its returned-taxonomy example is explicitly imaginary.
didnt: Corroboration — its L1 raw logs rising to higher-rank summary layers corroborates our raw-source/compiled-page layering, though the archived alpha code itself is not usable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: facebookresearch/GradientEpisodicMemory
good: Official source code for the NeurIPS 2017 Gradient Episodic Memory paper (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato): GEM uses episodic-memory samples to constrain new-task gradients so learning a new task does not increase loss on earlier tasks, alleviating catastrophic forgetting while allowing transfer, with a run_experiments.sh replication path and results/metrics code.
bad: Archived research code from 2017 with 11 commits and no releases, demonstrated on MNIST and CIFAR-100 variants — model-training continual learning, not agent or document memory. Its licence is non-commercial, so the code is ideas-only in any case.
didnt: Rejected — a continual-learning training method for neural networks rather than a knowledge-store design, and its non-commercial licence bars code adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: facebookresearch

name: timgordontg/engrim
good: Local-first, project-scoped SQLite episodic memory shared across Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Copilot CLI and OpenCode via hooks and a hardened MCP server: a roughly 4,000-character curated boot pack replaces transcript replay, with hybrid BM25 + model2vec recall, origin_agent provenance, supersede/retire without erasing history, and a self-healing 'engrim doctor'.
bad: Created in June 2026 and single-author, so its 'Universal Cross-Model Episodic Memory Standard' is a self-declared standard with no external governance shown at the source. The open-source tier is single-developer only — team federation, secret/PII scrubbing and a Merkle compliance ledger are commercial Enterprise features — and it is engineered for software-engineering projects, not a general knowledge wiki.
didnt: Board — the budget-capped '[RESUME HERE]' boot pack and the engrim_review 'safe to clear' check for uncaptured decisions as session-handoff ideas; the SQLite coding-agent store itself duplicates our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nemori-ai/nemori
good: Self-organising long-term memory that segments multi-turn conversations into topic-consistent episodes (LLM boundary alignment informed by Event Segmentation Theory), distils durable semantic knowledge via a predict-calibrate loop with temporal anchors and provenance, and serves unified vector + text + hybrid search, with published LoCoMo scores (overall LLM alignment 0.8305) and LongMemEval evaluation code.
bad: The current release is a complete rewrite the README says is not compatible with the previous MVP, and running it requires PostgreSQL 16 plus Qdrant via Docker and external LLM/embedding API keys (OpenRouter or OpenAI). It is research-grade conversational-memory infrastructure, not a file-based personal wiki.
didnt: Board — episode-granularity segmentation with LLM boundary detection and temporal/provenance anchors as a memory-unit design to test against our page granularity; its PostgreSQL + Qdrant stack is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: facebookresearch/agem
good: Official TensorFlow implementation of Averaged Gradient Episodic Memory (A-GEM, ICLR 2019) plus Experience Replay with reservoir sampling, with replicate-results scripts for MNIST, CIFAR, CUB and AWA — an efficient lifelong-learning method that constrains updates against an episodic memory of past tasks.
bad: Archived with no releases and built for TensorFlow >= v1.9-era code; it is neural-network training research on image datasets, with separate dataset downloads required for CUB and AWA — no bearing on document or agent memory storage.
didnt: Rejected — archived TF1-era continual-learning research code; its scope is model training, not our knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: facebookresearch

name: MariPS/learn-build-apply-wiki
good: An Agent Skill maintaining three linked Open Knowledge Format markdown wikis — study, project and job — with agent operations for ingest job/source, tracking applications, query with citations, recap, interview prep, lint and project documentation. Study pages use per-claim OKF footnotes, keep conflicting versions with their footnotes, and a coverage ladder (empty to solid) anchored to the theory section, and it needs only Python 3.8+, markdown and git with no database or dependencies.
bad: Very early and narrow: 0 stars, 12 commits, created 2026-09-27, and scoped specifically to studying to get hired. The study wiki skeleton is deliberately not shipped — the user must supply their own curriculum — and the job wiki holds sensitive personal data (CVs and cover letters) that the README warns must be kept out of any public push.
didnt: Rejected — career/job-application scope duplicates the compiled-wiki, ingest, query and lint machinery already in our stack, with no citation-locking, scored abstention or approval-gated write mechanism beyond our own. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kkonstvol-lab/obsidian-memory
good: Turns an Obsidian vault into a Markdown/Git memory system separating a source-backed LLM wiki from per-agent operational memory, with Codex lifecycle hooks, derived graph and bridge-health tools, and an operator control tower. Its safety model keeps markdown and Git as source of truth, promotion as an immutable proposal requiring explicit approval, and new retrieval patterns behind golden-set/baseline qualification gates.
bad: The README states no DB, vector store, MCP runtime, background job system, dynamic context engine or automatic repair loop is shipped — it is a portable skill source, not the private runtime engine it was derived from. It is small (3 stars, 27 commits, no releases) and requires Obsidian, an agent-skills environment, and recommended Dataview/Templater/Obsidian Git plugins.
didnt: Corroboration — its approval-gated promotion, markdown/Git custody, separation of durable wiki from agent memory, and qualification-before-adoption for retrieval confirm design choices already built in our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rudrathegreat/pulsar-wiki
good: A local-only browser interface for source-backed research workspaces where each folder holds its own wiki, immutable raw sources, saved chats and reading annotations, plus integrated JupyterLab research notebooks with revision history and reproducibility records. Agent writes are tightly bounded: only Markdown under wiki/ may change, raw/ is immutable, index updates are required and failed operations roll back, and NASA ADS literature search is built in.
bad: Licensed GPL-3.0 and tied to a single provider path: it requires an eligible ChatGPT subscription, states there is no API-key or alternate-provider fallback, and is intentionally local-only and not to be exposed via proxy or LAN. Notebooks additionally need a local JupyterLab 4 Python environment, and the included workspace and literature tooling are astronomy-specific.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under our licence discipline, and its ChatGPT-subscription lock-in and astronomy/NASA ADS scope do not fit our local-first, multi-provider wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GD4AI/obsidian-llm-wiki
good: A mature one-click Obsidian plugin (1,254 commits, 85 releases) that ingests Markdown, PDF, images and Office files into typed entity and concept pages, with zero-embedding graph retrieval using Personalized PageRank over wikilinks, graph-powered Q&A with wiki-link citations, lint and smart-fix, a headless CLI, 11 languages and 16+ LLM providers including local Ollama/LM Studio.
bad: Obsidian is the runtime — there is no backend, server or team collaboration, by design. The README itself states answers come from the vault only and bulk external-corpus RAG over sources such as Confluence, Notion or arXiv is out of scope, so it does not provide our citation-locking, abstention or approval-gated gateway machinery.
didnt: Corroboration — the reference implementation family the owner chose; its graph-powered Q&A over typed entity/concept pages and local-first, zero-embedding retrieval confirm the mechanism already known and used in our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mduongvandinh/llm-wiki
good: A fully automatic personal knowledge base on Karpathy's pattern that compiles dropped articles, notes, PDFs and Reddit threads into a cross-referenced wiki, flags contradictions on ingest, and offers ready-made variants for book companion, competitive intelligence and job search. It works across many AI tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, Gemini CLI, Codex, Aider, Continue) via per-tool schema files, with discover, ingest, query, lint, status and digest commands.
bad: Very thin implementation history for its claims: only 9 commits and no releases despite 214 stars and 93 forks. Its headline extension is auto-discovery — web, Reddit, GitHub and RSS scanning driven from config — and several tools in its own comparison lack auto-loop/background support, so operation depends heavily on the host agent.
didnt: Rejected — duplicates our compiled-wiki core, and its auto-discovery-led, fully automatic operation conflicts with our approval-gated, no-auto-discovery stance; maturity is also low at 9 commits. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jackwener/llm-wiki
good: An agent-native CLI plus skill system that compiles knowledge once into interconnected Markdown pages: the tool itself calls no LLMs, instead installing four focused operation skills (ingest, query, lint, research) for Claude Code, Codex and other spec-compliant agents. It provides BM25 search with CJK bigram tokenization, wikilink graph analysis (communities, hubs, orphans, wanted pages), and optional hybrid BM25 plus vector search via DB9.
bad: Small and unreleased: 30 commits, no releases and a single tag. There is no self-built GUI — Obsidian is the human interface — and the vector/cloud path depends on the external DB9 service rather than a local store.
didnt: Corroboration — compile-once/query-forever pages, agent operation skills, BM25 search and graph health analysis confirm mechanisms already present in our stack; nothing missing is offered. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: georgesung/LLM-WikipediaQA
good: Runs document Q&A over Wikipedia articles using Wikipedia-API to search and retrieve articles, LangChain for the Q&A framework, and OpenAI and HuggingFace models for embeddings and LLMs. It provides both a batch notebook for comparing different LLM/embedding combinations and an interactive Gradio app.
bad: A small 2023 demo, not a persistent wiki: 14 commits, no releases, created 2023-05-06, scoped only to Wikipedia articles retrieved at query time. Detailed results live in an external blog post rather than in the repo, and the OpenAI path requires the user's own OpenAI API key for ada embeddings and GPT-3.5.
didnt: Rejected — a dated, single-source Wikipedia Q&A experiment with no compiled, maintained knowledge base, citation locking or abstention; it does not fit a personal LLM-wiki/knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LeoBR84p/wiki_llm
good: Turns mixed document collections (docx, pdf, md, txt, xlsx, pptx) into a generated wiki through a Writer-Evaluator-Editor pipeline, with deterministic content-hash UUIDs so IDs survive renames, automatic term collection and taxonomy normalisation, a LangGraph repair agent for broken links and orphans after every run, and built-in BM25 plus LLM RAG chat with no vector store. Its markdown-hero layer provides semantic chunking, lint, merge and Word export.
bad: Only 2 commits in the repo despite the elaborate README, and its pip-from-repo install example still points at a placeholder your-org/wiki-llm URL. It depends on an external LLM backend (OpenRouter, OpenAI, Bedrock or Ollama) with API keys, and on the separate markdown-hero library for its core Markdown semantics.
didnt: Corroboration — deterministic content-addressed page identity, self-reviewing generation and post-run lint/repair confirm hashing and repair mechanisms already in our citation-lockfile and lint design; the implementation itself is too immature to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hellohejinyu/llm-wiki
good: An LLM-powered personal wiki CLI in pure Markdown with smart ingestion that integrates sources into structured pages with citations, automatic cross-linking, a multi-step ReAct query agent that dives into cited source files and answers with source citations, and two-phase lint (static plus LLM semantic, with auto-fix). Ingest operations require user confirmation before being applied unless explicitly skipped.
bad: Early-stage: 18 commits and 1 release, with roadmap items still unchecked including a wiki log command, Obsidian plugin integration and embeddings/vector search for large indexes. Query retrieval is capped at a 4-iteration agent loop and keyword matching, and it requires an OpenAI-compatible API key stored in .wikirc.yaml.
didnt: Corroboration — confirmation-gated ingest, cited synthesised answers and static-plus-semantic lint confirm patterns already built in our system; it offers nothing missing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NiharShrotri/llm-wiki
good: A fully local LLM-maintained wiki running on Ollama plus Qwen3 plus QMD, with a three-pass ingest (extraction, page drafting/merging, source summary) producing cross-linked source, entity and concept pages, hybrid BM25 plus vector plus LLM-rerank search, cited synthesis with optional write-back as synthesis pages, lint with auto-fix, and a full local web UI. No API keys or cloud services are used and no data leaves the machine.
bad: Heavy local requirements: about 15GB free disk, 12GB RAM recommended (16GB+ for comfort), a roughly 9.3GB Qwen3-14B model plus QMD/Node and Homebrew SQLite on macOS. The README states it was tested on macOS Apple Silicon, should work on Linux, and Windows is untested; the repo has only 8 commits and no releases.
didnt: Corroboration — local-first hybrid search, smart merging preserving provenance, and cited synthesis with write-back confirm our local-custody design; its single-model heavyweight stack is a duplicate, not an addition. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: julianoczkowski/karpathy-llm-wiki
good: A step-by-step guide to building a local Karpathy LLM wiki with Claude Code and Obsidian and no vector database or complex infrastructure: clip sources into a raw folder with Obsidian Web Clipper, paste Karpathy's gist plus a prompt so Claude Code creates CLAUDE.md, index and log, then ingest, with health checks, lint, a hot cache for recent context, and automatic cross-source linking.
bad: Guide only: the repository's root contains only README.md — no code, schema, templates or tests are shipped — across 3 commits with no releases. The README itself limits scale, stating it works well up to a few hundred documents and that millions of documents need a proper RAG pipeline with embeddings and a vector database, and ingest takes 5 to 15 minutes per source.
didnt: Rejected — a tutorial with no reusable code and no licence stated at source, so ideas-only at most; its stated few-hundred-document scale is below our corpus needs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Eamonnn101/Chinese-LLM-Wiki
good: A Chinese-first Markdown wiki scaffold for LLM agents with a four-layer architecture — immutable raw/ in its original language, wiki/ as the sole canonical compiled layer, output/ for non-canonical query and delivery products until promoted, and AGENTS.md as the agent's rule file. It provides page templates, ingest/query/lint workflows, ASCII slugs with Chinese titles and aliases, and an evidence convention of Chinese synthesis plus a short original excerpt plus the raw/ path for key claims.
bad: Scaffold only: 3 commits, no releases, and no code or tooling beyond templates and conventions. By default the public version does not track raw sources or the wiki source/topic/entity/synthesis content in Git, so the published repo is an empty framework, and its conventions are specifically Chinese-first.
didnt: Corroboration — its raw-immutable, output-non-canonical-until-promoted layering and excerpt-plus-raw-path evidence convention confirm our raw/compiled/output separation and citation practice; no licence is stated, so nothing is adopted from its text. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agents-flex/agents-flex
good: A mature lightweight Java AI agent framework (1,817 commits, 35 releases, version 2.3.1) with modular abstractions for chat, embedding, rerank, vector stores, document extraction, a durable agent runtime with snapshot recovery, tool approval and middleware, plus RAG, MCP, Skills, Text2SQL with read-only SQL checks, web search, TTS/STT and an LLM Wiki module that organises knowledge as a navigable hierarchical tree with path-based recursive reading and progressive disclosure.
bad: It is a broad JVM framework, not a wiki product: most modules require JDK 8+ and its MCP module JDK 17+, built with Maven, and the LLM Wiki is one small module among dozens spanning video, image, OCR and many commercial provider integrations. Adopting it would mean adopting a Java application stack wholly unlike our Markdown/Python wiki.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a general Java agent framework whose wiki module is hierarchical tree reading, not a compiled, citation-locked personal wiki; it duplicates no missing capability in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vlasenkoalexey/tpu_performance_autoresearch_wiki
good: A Karpathy-method wiki of TPU performance knowledge hooked to an autoresearch optimisation engine: agents run a disciplined loop of ranked falsifiable hypotheses, minimal code diffs, benchmarks on real hardware, XProf profiling and HLO analysis, and profile-grounded verdicts recorded in a ledger. Its case studies report autonomous agents beating hand-optimised MaxText baselines for Qwen3-8B on TPU v6e-8 and MaxKernel results in a Pallas kernel lane.
bad: Entirely domain- and hardware-specific: it requires TPU hardware (CloudTPU VM or GKE), JAX/PyTorch-XLA and XLA profiling, and its key profiling bridge xprof-cli is a private repository available only by asking the author. The wiki content is TPU optimisation knowledge, not a reusable wiki engine.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a TPU performance experiment whose value depends on private tooling and specialist hardware; its hypothesis-ledger discipline is already reflected in our eval and premortem machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: stevesolun/ctx
good: CTX Fit finds the cheapest AI coding setup that reliably works on a repository: it profiles the repo free, locally and read-only, tests candidate configurations against real repo tasks, and chooses a winner by a fixed rule — discard anything below the reliability floor, then minimise attributable cost, then prefer the simpler configuration — applying it only as a reviewable working-tree change or pull request. It is actively maintained (1,599 commits, 38 releases) with extensive refusal gates that leave the tree untouched on failure.
bad: Not a knowledge wiki despite its wiki/knowledge-graph topics: release 1.0.21 compares capability configurations within one coding-agent harness, not harnesses against each other, and release qualification did not include a paid live-provider trial. Real evaluations need extra harness installs, Node/npx, provider credentials and Bubblewrap on Linux, and native Windows/PowerShell is not supported (WSL2 only).
didnt: Rejected — fit: an AI coding-configuration evaluator for repositories, not a personal knowledge wiki or retrieval system; its reliability-floor-then-cost rule does not fill a gap in our wiki stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ttpears/bookstack-mcp
good: MCP server giving AI assistants full BookStack access: 21 read-only tools plus 22 write tools covering books, chapters, pages, shelves, attachments and comments with full CRUD and recycle-bin support. Write operations are disabled by default, responses are token-efficient compact JSON, and it supports stdio and Streamable HTTP transports for Claude Desktop, Claude Code, LibreChat and other MCP clients.
bad: It is entirely bound to a running BookStack instance and its API token credentials, so it provides no knowledge system of its own. Some features are version-gated (e.g. changelog messages need BookStack v26.09 or newer) and the legacy HTTP+SSE transport was removed in 3.0.0, breaking older clients unless pinned to 2.x.
didnt: Rejected — BookStack-specific MCP bridge; our wiki is file/Git-based with its own MCP doors, so this adds a dependency on a platform we do not use. Its read-only-by-default write gating corroborates our approval-gated write design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alizdavoodi/MCPDocSearch
good: Crawls websites and documentation with crawl4ai (configurable depth, include/exclude patterns, HTML cleaning) into a single consolidated Markdown file, then chunks it by headings, embeds chunks locally with sentence-transformers, caches embeddings, and serves semantic search via fastmcp tools (list_documents, get_document_headings, search_documentation) for Cursor and Claude Desktop.
bad: Small, early project (13 commits) with a README warning that first-run local embedding can take several minutes on large sets, and a security note that its pickle cache is unsafe if the storage directory is writable by untrusted users. Search is vector-similarity only, with no citation locking, abstention scoring, or write path.
didnt: Rejected — crawl-to-Markdown plus embedding search duplicates ingest/retrieval our wiki already does with citation discipline this lacks; its heading-chunking and cache-invalidation approach is corroboration only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fantasticmao/pokemon-wiki
good: Scrapes the 52poke Pokemon encyclopedia with jsoup into a versioned SQLite database shipped in the repo, then serves read-only combined queries over Pokemon, abilities, moves and items via both an HTTP API and a Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint, with a Docker Hub image for quick deployment.
bad: Data is a static snapshot: the query service never contacts the source wiki at runtime, so updates require re-running the spider and replacing the database file. Content and images remain owned by the source encyclopedia under its own copyright statement, and the service is read-only with no editing or mirroring.
didnt: Rejected — a single-fandom Pokemon dataset with no relevance to a personal LLM-wiki; the offline SQLite-plus-MCP read pattern is noted as corroboration only, and CC-BY-SA content terms do not fit our corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Systaro/DocuVault
good: Self-hosted team documentation where documents live as Markdown in a Git repository and every save is a commit, with a TipTap WYSIWYG editor, role-based and team permissions, public share links, and a built-in Streamable HTTP MCP server (19 tools) with OAuth so AI agents get CRUD access under the signed-in user's permissions. Optional AI features include cited Q&A, semantic search (pgvector + OpenAI embeddings) and proposed edits the user applies.
bad: README states it is in early access with occasional breaking changes expected until 1.0, and Tasks and the meeting bot are alpha; GitHub sync is only planned (GitLab or local repo today). It is source-available under BSL 1.1, not OSI open source — offering it as a competing hosted service requires a separate agreement — and public share links deliberately render embedded HTML and JavaScript.
didnt: Rejected — BSL 1.1 licence bars adopt/build of its code, and its heavy Spring Boot/Angular/PostgreSQL/Redis/MinIO stack duplicates our Git-backed wiki; its every-save-a-commit and per-user-permission MCP ideas are corroboration for our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TheWinci/mimirs
good: Local MCP server giving coding agents persistent, searchable codebase memory with no API keys, cloud or Docker — just Bun and SQLite. It provides semantic search, an auto-generated wiki, cross-session memory, dependency graphs and annotations, works with Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, JetBrains and Copilot, and publishes benchmarks (89-97% Recall@10 across four codebases, top file and line coverage on ContextBench).
bad: Scope is codebases, not general knowledge: it indexes project files for coding agents and requires Bun plus, on macOS, a non-Apple SQLite with extension support. README notes recall-first design deliberately yields low file precision, and numbers vary by repo size, query and model; it has no releases listed despite 18 tags.
didnt: Board — its published recall-benchmark methodology and lazy-indexing/cross-session memory pattern are worth borrowing as evaluation ideas for our retrieval, but the tool itself is code-focused and duplicates our wiki MCP doors. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shiquda/mediawiki-mcp-server
good: MCP server that searches and retrieves pages from any MediaWiki site (Wikipedia, fandom.com, wiki.gg and others) via a configurable --base-url, exposing just search (query, limit) and get-page (title) tools over stdio, streamable-http and SSE transports, installable via uvx or Docker.
bad: README opens by declaring itself outdated and directing users to ProfessionalWiki/MediaWiki-MCP-Server instead. It is read-only and minimal (only two tools, 18 commits), and the repo root shows no LICENSE file, so reuse rights are unclear.
didnt: Rejected — superseded by its own README, read-only external-wiki lookup only, and no licence stated at source, so its code is ideas-only and offers nothing our system lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: L3-N0X/Minecraft-Wiki-MCP
good: MCP server for browsing the official Minecraft Wiki with search, page summaries with section lists, per-section raw wikitext access, full-page retrieval, category browsing/membership and redirect resolution, plus multi-language support via a configurable MediaWiki API URL and an optional public hosted Streamable HTTP instance.
bad: Single-game scope with no relevance beyond Minecraft, read-only, and v2 is a complete Python rewrite with breaking tool renames and changed content format (raw wikitext instead of stripped HTML). The repo root shows no LICENSE file and there are no releases.
didnt: Rejected — a single-fandom, read-only lookup server; no licence stated at source makes its code ideas-only, and its search-then-summarize-then-section workflow merely corroborates progressive-disclosure reading we already use. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alirezarezvani/gaios
good: Forkable template AI operating system for Claude Code and Codex: a guided /setup interview fills CLAUDE.md and context files, and bundled skills provide triage/daily/weekly cadence, a raw/-to-wiki/ second brain with a leakage-scanning lint gate, a graphify knowledge graph over code plus wiki, decision logging, self-verifying dynamic workflows and an autoresearch loop, with deterministic Python tools in a Workflows-Agents-Tools layering.
bad: Very young template project (29 commits, created 2026-06) meant to be forked and heavily customized per role, with guardrails that the README warns must not be run unchanged for regulated businesses. It is an opinionated starter blueprint rather than a maintained product, and its frameworks are credited to / trademarked by a third party (Nate Herk) in NOTICE.
didnt: Corroboration — its raw/wiki split with a lint gate, append-only decision log, and deterministic-tools-under-probabilistic-agents layering confirm patterns our wiki already implements more deeply; as a template it would be duplication, not an addition. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: decodingai-magazine/llm-wiki-workshop
good: Self-paced workshop teaching LLM-wiki design from first principles in three exercises (vanilla mechanic, ingest at scale with subagent fan-out and URI adapters, interactive learning from queries), with slides, video and committed reference runs. Its core rules are explicit: immutable raw/ versus LLM-written wiki/, every claim carrying a wikilink citation, a >=2-source threshold before a concept gets a page, and navigation by progressive disclosure through hierarchical indexes.
bad: It is teaching material, not a production system: exercise 01 caps runs at 10 notes, inputs are small curated example sets (5/10/50 notes), and it depends on an external agent harness and the user's own LLM usage. README documents no evaluation, approval gating, or custody model beyond the workshop scope.
didnt: Corroboration — its raw/wiki separation, per-claim citations, >=2-source page threshold and index-first progressive disclosure independently confirm central design choices of our LLM Wiki; as a workshop it is not a component to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alchaincyf/obsidian-ai-orange-book
good: Free book (Chinese PDF, older English PDF) on rebuilding a second brain with Obsidian plus Claude Code: vault architecture, Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern (LLM as compiler/maintainer rather than RAG retriever), seven copyable workflows, a shortlist of 4 plugins from 1000+, and advanced chapters on Git versioning, custom Skills and local AI, updated with tested screenshots against Obsidian 1.14.4 / Claude Code 2.1.287.
bad: It is a book, not software: the repo contains only PDFs, assets and screenshots, with 9 commits and no code or licence file; the English edition lags at v1.0.0 (April) behind the October Chinese revision. Its claims (e.g. CLAUDE.md + index.md doing 80% of the work) are author guidance, not evaluated results.
didnt: Rejected — a how-to book with no licence stated at source and no reusable component; its Markdown-as-agent-interface and LLM-as-compiler arguments corroborate our existing wiki design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: oldwinter/knowledge-garden
good: A real, long-running personal Obsidian vault published as a template and digital garden: complete snapshot of the author's daily notes, plugins and workflows with bidirectional links, evergreen notes, an ACCESS organisation method, a published website with backlink panels, and v2.0 additions covering ChatGPT/Gemini/DeepSeek usage notes.
bad: It is one person's content vault, not a tool: README states contributions of others' notes cannot be accepted, about 90% of notes are written for the author himself, and content is deliberately unpolished for publication. There is no agent, retrieval, citation or write-gating machinery to reuse.
didnt: Rejected — a personal content garden offered as a vault template; useful only as corroboration that plain Markdown plus backlinks sustains a long-lived second brain, which our wiki already builds on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HugoBlox/theme-second-brain
good: Hugo starter template for publishing a Zettelkasten-style second brain from future-proof Markdown: supports audio, video, images, math, code and Mermaid diagrams, editing via GitHub or Git-connected apps such as Obsidian/VS Code, the Wowchemy/HugoBlox site builder and CMS, BibTeX citation import via Hugo Academic CLI, and deployment to GitHub or Netlify.
bad: It is only a static-site publishing theme (20 commits, template from 2022) — no knowledge capture, linking intelligence, search, or agent access of its own — and the repo root shows no LICENSE file. The README is largely a sponsorship appeal and points to external documentation for actual use.
didnt: Rejected — a presentation layer for Markdown notes; our Lens portal already serves that role, and with no licence stated at source its code is ideas-only regardless. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: revezone/revezone
good: Lightweight local-first, graphics-centric second-brain app combining Excalidraw and tldraw whiteboards (with custom fonts and double-linking to notes), a Notion-like WYSIWYG note editor with slash commands and Markdown, folder-based file management and a drag-and-drop flex layout, available as an online version (browser storage) and a desktop app (local storage).
bad: README states it is still in public beta, and that the repository contains only the basic-functionality code which does not fully correspond to the capabilities of revezone.com or the desktop app. It has no agent/MCP, citation or knowledge-compilation features, and its AGPL-3.0 licence is copyleft.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under our licence discipline, and a whiteboard-centric notes app is outside our text-first, citation-locked wiki scope; its local-first custody stance is corroboration only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PandoraReads/apex-dashboard
good: A one-page Obsidian workspace plugin bundling memos, todos, projects, notes, a native calendar, a built-in DQL query engine, RSS reader, web embeds, and sidebar widgets (weather, pomodoro, reading tracker, bookkeeping, habits, music); 15 composable section types and 13 themes, all saved as plain-text markdown.
bad: Locked to Obsidian desktop; no evaluation, tests, or correctness claims documented on the page; README is primarily Chinese; single author; offers no citation locking, abstention, or versioned-knowledge mechanisms — a pretty UI layer, not a memory design.
didnt: Rejected — Obsidian-desktop UI plugin; its dashboard-widget ideas are already covered by our Lens; nothing missing from our stack here (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MimicHunterZ/PocketMind
good: Flutter mobile + Spring backend second-brain app: one-tap link capture via the OS share sheet, four-tier degrading content extraction, local-first storage with incremental multi-device sync, AI summarisation/Q&A/auto-tagging, and reminder-based memory reactivation.
bad: Licence is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — non-commercial, so the code is ideas-only; early stage (v0.3, most of the roadmap still planned); binaries only for Android/Windows; relies on scraping third-party sites; single author.
didnt: Rejected — non-commercial licence, narrow bookmark-collector scope, and early-stage maturity; no fit for our wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nageoffer/ragent
good: A production-grade Java Agentic RAG platform covering the full pipeline: document parsing, hybrid retrieval (vector, keyword, knowledge graph, web search) with RRF fusion and rerank, query rewriting/splitting, tree intent recognition, session memory with persisted summaries, MCP tool calling, model failover, and a React admin console with traces.
bad: Java/Spring AI stack with heavy infra (MySQL, Redis, Elasticsearch, Neo4j); docs are primarily Chinese; README stresses enterprise-level complexity, which is steep for a personal system; our retrieval needs are simpler.
didnt: Rejected — full-stack enterprise agent platform with a stack mismatch for our personal local-first wiki; its hybrid-retrieval and evidence-tracing techniques corroborate our retrieval design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
