name: java-up-up/nexus-agent
good: An enterprise agent platform with a three-layer executor (disambiguation, RAG, ReAct agent), pre-orchestration (routing, rewriting, sub-question splitting, disambiguation), dual-channel hybrid retrieval with RRF fusion, parent-child chunking, evidence budgets with a no-evidence short-circuit, a Neo4j document graph, Skills/MCP support, and three session-memory strategies.
bad: Heavy infra footprint (MySQL, PGVector, Elasticsearch, Neo4j, Redis, Kafka, MinIO); Chinese-first docs; young (141 commits, 667 stars); enterprise multi-tenant SaaS orientation — far from a personal wiki.
didnt: Rejected — enterprise multi-tenant agent stack far from our personal wiki scope; its no-evidence short-circuit idea corroborates our scored-abstention design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: unitedrhino/things
good: A mature Go/go-zero AIoT platform and SaaS base: device/product management, thing models, MQTT/CoAP/HTTP/TCP ingestion, multi-tenancy, digital twins, fused AI agents with RAG knowledge bases and memory, spanning smart energy, buildings, parking, and agriculture.
bad: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft — ideas only, never adopted; README notes the AI capabilities live in separate modules beyond this repo; pure IoT scope mismatch with a knowledge wiki.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL licence plus IoT-platform scope; no fit for our personal LLM wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: junkai-li/NetCoreKevin
licence: MulanPSL-2.0 (repo sidebar; README badge claims MIT — ambiguous)
good: A .NET 9 enterprise AI-agent middle-platform: Qdrant RAG with qwen3-rerank, agent memory isolated by tenant/agent/user, dynamic SKILL.md skill loading, multi-agent collaboration, context compression, MCP server, RBAC, per-user token quotas, and an OpenAI-compatible API for third-party clients.
bad: Enterprise mid-platform heaviness (MySQL, Redis, Qdrant, Hangfire, 25 modules); licence ambiguity at the source — sidebar shows MulanPSL-2.0 while the README badge claims MIT; vendor-heavy (Alibaba/Tencent services); .NET stack mismatch.
didnt: Rejected — enterprise .NET middle-platform scope with licence ambiguity at the source; tenant-isolated agent memory is a boardable idea only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: raia-live/amfs

name: samfoy/pi-memory

name: sverklo/sverklo

didnt: Board — bi-temporal memory with superseded_by lineage (a fact stays queryable with the validity window in which it was true) as a pattern for truth-aware retrieval and supersession in the wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agentscreator/engram-memory

didnt: Rejected — scope mismatch: an appliance OS for autonomous agents, not a personal knowledge/wiki system, and far beyond what our stack needs (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ldclabs/anda-brain
good: A self-hosted graph memory service built on KIP 2.0, which separates Concept, Proposition, Assertion (who said it, how confidently, from when, citing what) and Evidence — 'a statement existing is not the statement being true' — so disagreement coexists, current belief is projected from assertions at read time, and the three kinds of change (world changed, claim was wrong, misrecording) each keep their own history. Recall answers with citations and can return 'contested' or 'insufficient'; background sleep cycles consolidate, flag claims that depended on revised premises, and never purge memory — forgetting decays accessibility, never truth or confidence.
bad: The model rides on a bespoke protocol (KIP 2.0) and the project's own AndaDB graph store, a non-standard stack to adopt wholesale. Formation, Recall and Maintenance all depend on LLM calls (per-Space BYOK model configuration), and the system is young (created 2026-03, v0.13.x) with multi-agent service machinery well beyond a single-user wiki.
didnt: Board — the Proposition/Assertion/Evidence separation with belief projected at read time, plus 'insufficient' as a first-class recall answer, as design input for our claim lifecycle and scored abstention (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cognicore-dev/cognicore-env
good: Zero-mandatory-dependency Python memory/reflection layer that runs in-process: BM25 plus a multi-hop graph adapter that selects chunk sets covering the query's entities jointly (LongMemEval STRICT R@5 85.2% at 5 chunks vs 78.8% zero-shot baseline), reflection that surfaces lessons from repeated failures before the next attempt, replay/branching of recorded runs, and Ed25519-signed portable memory bundles whose import is fail-closed — unverified records land in a quarantine partition invisible to search until fresh verification evidence promotes them.
bad: The README itself states the known limitation: lexical TF-IDF/BM25 retrieval misses when session vocabulary differs from the query's, and semantic search needs the optional sentence-transformers extra; at 20 chunks the multi-hop advantage over brute force disappears. Scope also sprawls into RL environments, an arena and an autonomous coding agent (NEXUS).
didnt: Board — signed, fail-closed memory bundles with a quarantine partition for unverified records as a pattern for transferring memory between agents without trusting it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AQ-MedAI/MedMemoryBench
good: A NeurIPS 2026 benchmark for agent memory in personalised healthcare: 20 longitudinal patient personas with background, life events and trap events across ~2,020 multi-session doctor–patient dialogues and ~1,986 evaluation queries in six clinically motivated types — including state_update (tracking how a patient's state evolves) and multi-hop clinical deduction — with a unified framework running 14 baselines (Long Context, Embedding/BM25 RAG, Mem0, Letta, MemOS, A-MEM, MIRIX, MemRL, LightMem, GraphRAG, HippoRAG-v2, ReMem, Zep) in Chinese and English.
bad: It is an evaluation harness for one domain, not a memory system: the personas and dialogues are synthetic, datasets total ~1 GB of downloads, and running baselines requires paid LLM API keys (OpenAI/Azure/BigModel) plus per-method vendored dependencies. Nothing in it transfers directly to a general personal wiki beyond evaluation design.
didnt: Board — the state_update and trap-event query types as evaluation ideas for testing whether our wiki's retrieval respects superseded facts in our golden set (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: screenpipe/screenpipe
good: Mature (22k stars, 14k commits) local-first 'computer history': event-driven capture pairs screenshots with the OS accessibility tree (OCR as fallback), audio is transcribed locally with Whisper with speaker diarisation, and everything is searchable by natural language over SQLite FTS5 with app/window/date filters and exposed to agents through an MCP server and plugin ('pipes') system — capture stays on-device by default with filters for passwords and excluded apps.
bad: It is source-available under a custom commercial licence — personal non-commercial use only, commercial use requires a licence — and features are gated by paid plans. Continuous screen and audio recording is heavy (README specs: ~5–20% CPU, 0.5–3 GB RAM) and privacy-invasive by design, and what it stores is raw capture, not curated, citation-locked knowledge.
didnt: Rejected — custom commercial licence bars adoption, and indiscriminate screen/audio capture is the opposite of our curated, consent-scoped wiki ingest (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HurricaHjz/SecondSelf
good: A multi-agent harness (Claude Code coordinating, Codex helpers) where each helper may write only the files it is given under a written contract, with independent critic and verifier agents that must first catch a planted case before a silent check counts as clean. Its self-maintaining local Markdown wiki gives every knowledge page a graded trust level and cites the pages behind every answer, with ingest, query, lint and deep-lint skills.
bad: Explicitly pre-1.0 and pre-release — the README warns the design changes often until v1.0. It only runs inside Claude Code or the Claudian Obsidian plugin with an authenticated Codex CLI for helpers, and the real running cost is frontier-model API credits; the repo is young (created June 2026, 52 commits).
didnt: Corroboration — its contract-scoped helper agents, planted-case verifier checks, graded-trust wiki pages and cited answers independently confirm our harness and citation-locking design; the framework itself duplicates our own wiki stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NimaChu/my-wiki
good: Local-first knowledge app where sources are kept as a Reference evidence layer (originals, snapshots, images) and distilled into atomic Concept pages with bidirectional evidence links, so conclusions can be traced back to the source. Document extraction runs through its own per-page quality gates — garbled, sparse or low-confidence pages are locked as needs-followup rather than silently accepted — and knowledge exports in Google Open Knowledge Format v0.2, with a Viki Q&A interface and an interactive knowledge-graph front end.
bad: A very young, fast-moving project (created July 2026, 112 commits) with a large, complex feature surface spanning CLI, dashboard, remote mode and galaxy packaging. The main README is in Chinese (an English version exists), and full document fidelity depends on external parsers (MinerU, Docling) that must be installed separately.
didnt: Corroboration — its evidence-layer-to-concept compilation, extraction quality gates that refuse to fake success, and OKF export confirm our raw-source plus compiled-wiki design; the app itself duplicates a stack we already have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zereight/gitlab-mcp
good: A mature MCP server for GitLab with 276 tools across projects, merge requests, issues, pipelines, wikis and releases, over stdio, SSE and Streamable HTTP. name: nduckmink/arkon
good: Self-hosted enterprise knowledge hub whose MRP pipeline (Map, Reduce, Plan-review, Refine, Verify, Commit) compiles documents into an interlinked wiki: every ingest first produces a human-reviewable plan of pages to create or update, new content is LLM-merged into existing pages rather than overwriting, and every page records its source documents. name: anyproto/anytype-mcp

The README states real limits: filter-schema support is missing (flattened filters fields are omitted), event-stream tools and pairing/API-key management are excluded, and the OpenAPI spec is discovered once at startup so the server must be restarted after an Anytype update.
didnt: Rejected — fit: it fronts the Anytype app, which is not our stack; our wiki has its own MCP doors. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rudra-ravi/wikipedia-mcp

didnt: Rejected — scope: a single-source public-encyclopaedia lookup; our research flow already searches the web and the wiki directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ProfessionalWiki/MediaWiki-MCP-Server

name: aashari/mcp-server-atlassian-confluence

didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at source (ideas only under our licence discipline) and fit: a Confluence connector for a platform outside our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: talosdeus/wiki-js-mcp

name: zzaebok/mcp-wikidata

bad: It is a personal vault snapshot (2 commits, zero stars): the README itself warns that notes contain personal business information and asks others not to reuse them, there is no licence, and the automation depends on the author's own .claude configuration and Feishu/social-platform workflows.
didnt: Board — the dedup-gateway intake that sorts every capture into a typed, ID-prefixed card (insight vs full knowledge card) as an ingest-triage idea for our wiki; the vault itself is a personal instance with no licence, so ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: quanttide/quanttide
licence: Apache-2.0 per the repo LICENSE file / GitHub metadata, but the README licence section states CC BY 4.0 — conflicting licence statements at source
good: The root repository of the QuantTide knowledge system organises 46 domain second brains on four orthogonal axes — categories (how it runs), domains (what it knows), subjects (legal-entity records) and adapters (Feishu/GitHub/agent bridges) — under a unified spec: every domain brain shares one information architecture (data/ declarative + docs/ procedural + apps/ + packages/ + examples/), is the single concentration point for its domain, and is versioned with a CHANGELOG like code.
bad: Almost all substance lives in dozens of submodule repositories, so the root repo is an architecture manifesto and directory map rather than a working system; it has 1 star, and its own licence statements conflict (LICENSE/GitHub say Apache-2.0, the README licence section says CC BY 4.0).
didnt: Board — the four orthogonal axes plus one mandated information architecture per domain brain as an idea for structuring multi-domain wiki growth; the conflicting licence statements bar adopting its code or content as-is. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mo9652962-ai/mo9652962-ai
good: An indie developer's profile/portfolio repo presenting a local-first project matrix; its Second Brain flagship is described as a self-evolving Chinese Obsidian knowledge base of 760+ public notes across 18 domains, with self-healing tooling, a four-level context-memory system, output-style alignment and a 3D WebGL knowledge-topology site plus llms.txt access.
bad: This repository contains only the profile README, LICENSE, PRIVACY.md and SECURITY.md — the second brain and all other projects live in other repositories, so nothing here can be run or inspected. It is 8 commits with 1 star, and the flagship claims are self-reported marketing copy with no in-repo evidence.
didnt: Rejected — a portfolio/profile repo whose second-brain claims point elsewhere; there is no artefact here to adopt or corroborate against. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 1522267053/langgraph-agent
good: A lightweight LangGraph agent platform for non-programmers: visual drag-drop flow canvas with condition branches, three loop modes and nested reusable 'capability cards', a three-tier hot/warm/cold memory with automatic promotion, access-decay demotion (hot 25 days, warm 35 days) and AI self-consolidation on overflow, a three-level knowledge base (document → heading tree → paragraph) with vector/LIKE fallback retrieval, MCP integration with self-healing sessions, LangGraph interrupt() human-in-the-loop, and zero-config SQLite startup or EXE packaging.
bad: Single-author project with 1 star despite 815 commits; its README comparison table is self-authored marketing (e.g. claiming to be the 'only' open platform with visual loops), and there are no releases. Scope is a general desktop agent/flow product, not a knowledge-custody system, and its memory consolidation is AI-autonomous rather than approval-gated.
didnt: Board — the three-tier memory with automatic promotion/decay thresholds and the document→heading→paragraph progressive knowledge navigation as ideas for our retrieval layer; the platform as a whole duplicates our stack and its autonomous memory consolidation conflicts with approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DrTonks/career-agent-lab
good: A TypeScript + LangGraph multi-agent career-planning core for university students (national second prize, China University Service Outsourcing Innovation & Entrepreneurship Competition, per README): an orchestrator dispatches profile/match/path/report experts over 10,000 job records, with structured handoffs carrying evidence citations, hybrid BM25 + local BGE vector retrieval merged by RRF over chunks that keep source, version and offsets, and versioned long-term memory that is written only after user approval and supports correction, withdrawal, expiry and full forgetting.
bad: Narrow and early: only the agent core is included (no front end or other back-end code), it offers a local CLI only with HTTP/SSE adaptation left as separate work, and it has 6 commits and zero stars. It is bound to its competition dataset of synthetic/public sample jobs and a single DeepSeek-style provider configuration, and carries no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — model-proposed memory changes committed only after user approval, with correction/withdrawal/expiry and invalidation of downstream artefacts when facts change, confirms our approval-gated writes and citation discipline; domain-bound and unlicensed, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mark-cell-520/human-future-skill
good: A conversational 'skill' package for civilisation forecasting that bundles six modules — real-time signal monitoring across six dimensions, six-perspective multi-agent debate with cross-examination, interactive scenario projection with Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, cross-domain fusion detection, prediction calibration using Brier scores with bias correction, and personalised roadmaps — over a claimed 250+ source list and 12 technology storylines.
bad: The README is a self-declared build-completion report: headline features such as live APIs, prediction-market integration and causal-inference models are listed as planned for v2.1–v3.0, the stated forecast confidences (e.g. 85% for 2026–27) rest on a flat '28 items of evidence' with no shown evaluation, and the repo has 2 stars and no licence.
didnt: Board — the Brier-scored prediction-calibration log with bias correction as an idea for scoring our own forecasts and abstention thresholds; the speculative simulation scope and unverified claims bar adoption, and the code is unlicensed so ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: endtree-FDE/feishu-group-agent
good: A Feishu (Lark) group-bot template that runs on the owner's own machine via lark-cli long connection + Cursor CLI or any OpenAI-compatible model: it answers @-mentions and approved DMs, reads group history, files, docs, calendars and bitables, keeps per-group long-term memory, and redacts customer names, phone numbers, IDs, emails, secrets and local paths before replying. Writes are triple-locked (user allow-list, resource allow-list, allowed action types) and always require the initiator's confirmation — by card button or 6-digit code — which cannot be switched off; knowledge-base imports land in a review area and only replace the live index after confirmation, and per-group retrieval cites source title and section/page.
bad: It is hard-bound to the Feishu/Lark platform and Windows-first setup (PowerShell installer, lark-cli, Feishu app registration), and per-group knowledge search and most memory/skill features are off by default. Brand-new project (created 2026-10-17, 0 stars, 48 commits), so its security claims are untested by any user base.
didnt: Corroboration — non-disableable initiator confirmation for every write, staged knowledge imports that go live only after review, and per-group memory isolation confirm our approval-gated writes and local-first custody; the Feishu-specific bot itself is out of scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rick2857/sumuwei
good: A Chinese persistent-character agent built on TypeScript, Node.js, ElizaOS, Drizzle and PostgreSQL/PGlite, with persistent memory, source attribution, replayable projections, relationships, emotion, beliefs and goals/commitments. Optional integrations include CLI, QQ, native voice, 3D VRM and Live2D, plus material-driven reminders and controlled web verification.
bad: The README itself marks many capabilities as not verified in the public copy: real-model, QQ, voice and desktop chains are not run in credential-free CI, full database regression is NOT RUN, and there is no automatic periodic backup or PITR. It is a very recent, single-character experiment (12 commits, 2 stars) requiring the operator's own PostgreSQL, model, accounts and resources.
didnt: Rejected — a persistent fictional-character agent with role-play, voice and avatar scope does not fit a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS centred on citation locking and approval-gated writes, despite its permissive licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ytsuchiya-work/agent_memory
good: A minimal demo for verifying the effect of agent memory, provided as two notebooks covering short-term and long-term memory agents on Lakebase. Its small scope makes the comparison easy to inspect.
bad: The README is a single line with no explanation, evaluation results, or usage instructions visible on the repo page. The repo has only 2 commits and 1 star, and is tied to Lakebase notebooks rather than a reusable library.
didnt: Rejected — a two-notebook demo with no documented findings duplicates the memory-effect premise our wiki already implements, and offers no transferable mechanism for citation locking or scored abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: miwaihnt/advanced-data-and-ai-engineering
good: A Japanese production-pattern lab covering memory-efficient data engineering (heapq K-way merge, asyncio merge, O(1) LRU cache, sliding-window aggregation) and AI engineering patterns including a self-correcting ReAct agent, resumable stateful agents, multi-agent consensus debate, and robust structured output with Pydantic. It runs locally on Python 3.11+ with Ollama qwen2.5:3b.
bad: The repo has 0 stars, 12 commits and no LICENSE file, so reuse rights are unclear. It is a collection of pattern exercises rather than a packaged library, and its 'memory' content is mostly RAM/complexity optimisation, not knowledge memory.
didnt: Rejected — generic data/AI engineering exercises matched on RAM 'memory', with no licence stated at source, so its code is ideas-only and none of its patterns address citation locking, abstention or local-first wiki custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ratorin/claude-session-manager
good: A VS Code extension for managing Claude Code sessions and agents: rename, favourites, tags and per-agent memos, a fast viewer for large JSONL sessions, memory-file browsing, multi-agent organisation charts, live status and usage-limit monitoring. The README documents extensive tracking of Claude Code version changes and preserves unknown frontmatter keys when editing.
bad: It is tightly coupled to Claude Code and VS Code (requires VS Code 1.85+ and Claude Code 2.1.113+) and, by its own README, can only see local sessions — cloud, Remote Control and teammate sessions are not visible to the extension. It has 0 stars and no releases despite 234 commits.
didnt: Rejected — a Claude Code session-management UI for VS Code does not serve a wiki/knowledge OS with its own portal and agent doors, and its scope is editor tooling rather than knowledge custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: garyohosu/mind-virus-lab
good: A small, sandboxed, offline-capable Python harness testing whether a benign fictional goal propagates between three agents via messages and persistent memory files, and whether a system-prompt defence warning stops it. It enforces strong safety boundaries: carried memory is delivered as an ordinary user turn never promoted to a system prompt, agents have no shell or filesystem access, and all writes go through a path-traversal-rejecting sandbox.
bad: The README stresses that results from the default deterministic fake provider validate the harness, not real AI behaviour, and real Anthropic runs so far are too few to draw conclusions from. Its evaluator is simple English regex that will miss paraphrases, only one real provider is implemented, and the repo has 6 commits and 0 stars with no licence stated.
didnt: Board — the rule that carried memory must never be promoted to a system-level instruction, and the defence-warning comparison, are directly relevant safety ideas for approval-gated writes and cross-agent filings; code is ideas-only because no licence is stated at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: takehisa-nanba/AI-Health-Guardian
good: A VS Code extension and MCP server that lets AI agents monitor and protect host resources: real-time RAM status, autonomous shutdown of memory-heavy WSL2/background processes below a threshold, an emergency reset for hanging sub-processes, and a get_resource_status tool so an agent can check its own health before heavy tasks. It also ships WSL2 vmmem management and cleanup scripts aimed at low-RAM (8GB/16GB) machines.
bad: The README states the tool is optimised specifically for Windows environments focusing on WSL2 and Windows process management, so it does not fit a Linux-hosted wiki. It has 0 stars, 10 commits and no releases, and installation is via a manually installed VSIX.
didnt: Rejected — system RAM/WSL resource guarding matched on system 'memory', not knowledge memory, and its Windows-only platform scope is outside a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: xugaoyi/vuepress-theme-vdoing
good: A mature VuePress theme for knowledge management and blogging: a Markdown-centred project structure that builds a structured knowledge base readable like books, combined with fragmented blog posting, built-in automation tools and multi-dimensional indexing to locate knowledge points quickly. It is well adopted, with about 4.9k stars, 1,195 forks and 55 releases.
bad: It is a presentation theme only — it provides no ingest, citation, retrieval or write-governance layer, so knowledge correctness and provenance remain entirely the author's problem. It is tied to the VuePress/Vue ecosystem, which our wiki portal does not use.
didnt: Corroboration — its structured, book-like organisation of a Markdown knowledge base with multi-dimensional indexing confirms the value of structured navigation over a flat file pile, a principle our Lens portal already follows; the theme itself is not needed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AlexAnys/awesome-openclaw-usecases-zh
good: A Chinese OpenClaw use-case collection of 50 verified real scenarios across office automation, content creation, DevOps, AI assistance and knowledge management, each in a uniform format (pain point, capabilities, required skills, setup, tips) with copyable prompts and difficulty ratings. It adds an agent-facing layer — AGENTS.md execution/human-division protocol, INDEX.md with risk tags, and a cross-agent concept mapping — so any agent can reproduce a case.
bad: It is a content catalogue, not software: there is nothing to run, and the README itself warns that referenced skills and third-party dependencies are not reviewed by the maintainers and must be source- and permission-checked before use. Cases are centred on the Chinese platform ecosystem (Feishu, DingTalk, WeCom, Xiaohongshu) and on OpenClaw specifically.
didnt: Rejected — a use-case anthology for a different agent platform and ecosystem; its knowledge-management cases duplicate patterns our own agent setup already covers, and there is no code or mechanism to adopt for citation locking or abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: phachon/mm-wiki
good: A lightweight enterprise wiki and team knowledge-sharing system written in Go, deployable as a single binary with a guided installer or Docker: independent document spaces with access levels, Markdown writing with attachments, full-text search, custom roles and permissions, LDAP/external login integration, email notifications on document changes, and sharing/download. It has about 3.8k stars and 12 releases.
bad: The maintainer's note at the top of the README says there has been little energy to maintain it in recent years, the UI and tech stack need a complete refactor, and it has been held at the current version pending a planned rewrite. It is a team/enterprise MySQL-backed wiki with no LLM, citation or provenance features.
didnt: Rejected — an unmaintained enterprise team wiki duplicates the storage/presentation layer our LLM-wiki already has, while offering nothing for citation locking, scored abstention or approval-gated AI writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wx-chevalier/Developer-Zero-To-Mastery
good: A large personal developer knowledge collection — interactive mind maps, roadmaps/learning paths, interview preparation and a weekly — organised as a navigable 'knowledge fence' spanning programming languages, software engineering, web, distributed systems, data science and AI, with links out to companion Awesome Lists, books and mind-map repos. It has about 3.2k stars and 1,594 commits of accumulated content.
bad: It is one author's curated content with no software, search system or retrieval mechanism of its own, relying on external GitBook/website hosting for reading. Its content licence is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (non-commercial, no derivatives), which forbids adapting its material, and it is a public learning corpus rather than a private personal knowledge system.
didnt: Rejected — a public, single-author learning-content corpus under a no-derivatives licence; it confirms the value of navigable knowledge maps but provides nothing adoptable for a private, citation-locked personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kkkirito-123/ZLAgent
good: An IM-first personal AI assistant harness for WeChat / WeCom / Webhook with a substantial implemented core: permission policies, read-before-write policy, approval service, checkpointed long tasks with recovery, persisted plans and DAG execution, a memory store (in-memory/SQLite), a guarded skill system, local stdio MCP tools, and eval/benchmark runners with release gates. Its GeneralAgent facade separates chat (always verified=False) from task execution, and routed task execution stays disabled by default without explicit host opt-in.
bad: The README's own delivery status marks several stages only LOCAL or DEFERRED, states product-specific integrations remain roadmap slices, and explicitly puts model-inferred silent memory, embeddings, RAG and multi-agent delegation out of scope — so the headline GraphRAG/pgvector/Neo4j stack in the repo description is not the implemented core. It is a young rebuild (20 commits, 32 stars) with a heavy intended stack (FastAPI, PostgreSQL/pgvector, Neo4j, Redis).
didnt: Corroboration — its approval service, read-before-write policy, checkpointed recovery and default-off routed execution confirm our approval-gated-write design; adopting its harness would duplicate our existing gateway and wiki stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gentlekk/personal-memory-archivist
good: A personal-memory life archivist web app (Vue 3 + Vite frontend, FastAPI + Pydantic backend, SQLite, REST) for recording thoughts, emotions, decisions, relationships and projects, with LLM-generated summaries, tags and themes for later review. LLM support is pluggable across OpenAI, DeepSeek and Qwen via configuration.
bad: The README documents only the tech stack, how to run it and the directory layout — the headline auto-summary/tag/theme features are not described in any detail, and there are no tests, releases or screenshots visible. The repo has 7 commits, no LICENSE file, and run instructions are Windows-oriented (.venv\Scripts, copy commands).
didnt: Board — automatically deriving summaries, tags and recurring themes across a person's decisions, relationships and projects for periodic review is a useful review-layer idea for our wiki; its code is ideas-only because no licence is stated at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: slicenferqin/universal-memory-mcp
good: A universal, cross-project MCP memory server for any AI CLI (Claude Code, OpenCode, Copilot, Gemini CLI) that is 100% local with no telemetry or cloud: a three-layer memory architecture (Level 0 daily raw logs, Level 1 extracted facts/decisions/preferences, Level 2 consolidated summaries) with daily extraction, weekly consolidation and monthly archiving, plus hybrid semantic (vector) + FTS5 keyword search with time decay and project relevance, stored as Markdown under ~/.universal-memory with a SQLite vector index.
bad: The README announces the main line has migrated to a new runtime-first repo (project-memory-runtime), leaving this repo as a compatibility/maintenance line, and its current version is v0.6.0-beta.0 with recall stated at 60% and v1.0 production readiness still planned. Unit-test coverage above 80% is listed as a high-priority contribution need, indicating thin current coverage.
didnt: Corroboration — its local-first custody, Markdown memory files and daily-to-consolidated layered consolidation strongly confirm our wiki's raw-to-compiled design; it is a CLI conversation-memory layer, not a citation-locked knowledge base, so there is nothing to adopt over our existing stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XCNXNXNX/lingxi-flow-agent
good: A HarmonyOS NEXT personal-assistant agent written in pure ArkTS: one-sentence requests are planned and executed across 25+ system tools (files, reminders, calendar, weather, search, memory), with multiple LLM providers, importable JSON skill packs, RAG knowledge-base Q&A (BGE-M3 vectors with keyword fallback), voice interaction and multi-device sync. Notable engineering includes eager parallel tool calling during streaming and on-demand skill-pack injection by trigger word.
bad: It is a student competition entry (3 stars, 41 commits) locked to HarmonyOS NEXT, requiring DevEco Studio 5.0+, HarmonyOS 5.0+ hardware/emulator and Huawei signing certificates to build and install. Its platform, language (ArkTS) and device scope have no overlap with a Linux-hosted personal wiki.

name: LZZZQ-Lab/smart-assistant-agent
good: A ReAct-pattern smart customer-service / personal assistant with CLI and Streamlit web modes: short-term memory as a 5-turn sliding window, long-term memory via Chroma vector semantic retrieval that auto-captures facts triggered by phrases like 'I am' / 'remember', and tools for company-policy lookup, weather and arithmetic. It offers both an OpenAI/LangChain mode and a no-API-key mock mode, with automatic fallback to a JSON file if the vector store fails to initialise.
bad: The repo is a single commit with 2 stars, its built-in tools are narrow demos (policy lookup by keyword, simulated weather for a few cities, four-function arithmetic), and its README licence section states only that the project is for learning and research use, with no licence file. Long-term memory capture is keyword-triggered rather than governed or citation-backed.
didnt: Rejected — a single-commit teaching demo whose keyword-triggered memory and toy tools are far below the governance bar of citation locking, scored abstention and approval-gated writes, and no licence is stated at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IssacW228/student-llm-wiki

Browsed via Obsidian with a Dataview Home dashboard, cross-course connections and contradictions logs.
bad: Scoped to university course slides and exam preparation, and dependent on Obsidian plus the Dataview plugin and an external AI tool for all ingest/review work. README documents no evaluation, citation-locking or approval-gated write mechanism.
didnt: Corroboration — confirms our existing Karpathy-pattern raw/wiki structure, hash dedup, lint, connections and contradictions tracking; the student/exam layer duplicates what our wiki already has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Drchronx/ai-agent-research-starter-kit
good: A teaching and deployment kit for the full AI-agent research workflow: deploying Codex, Claude Code, OpenClaw and Hermes, reusable Skills organised by function, literature search with BibTeX and citation checking via AMiner/AI4Scholar/Zotero/Obsidian, plus topic generation, experimental design, statistics, EEG/ERP and BCI, writing, review self-check and journal formatting. Its PolyForm Noncommercial licence bars commercial use and covers the teaching materials, prompts and Skills as well as code.
didnt: Rejected — teaching-kit scope aimed at academic research training, not a personal wiki/knowledge OS, and its noncommercial custom licence makes its code and materials ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: patrick-andstar/kaoyan-math-ai

name: zzybrim/douyin-obsidian

didnt: Board — the tiered light/standard/deep structured archiving of extracted social video/image-text content for the ideas board; the Douyin-specific extractor itself is out of scope for our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wwaa321/kiko-ai-assistant

name: CK-bantang/Obsidian-Template
good: A student Obsidian vault template preconfigured with curated community plugins (including Obsidian Git, Excalidraw, Tasks, Linter, Easy Typing, Clear Unused Images), 9 themes, bidirectional links, graph/canvas visualisation and Git multi-device sync. name: Yasikap/Bangumi-Bridge-Obsidian
good: Obsidian automation via QuickAdd/Dataview/Templater scripts that import Bangumi anime data — single-title search in Chinese/Japanese with full metadata, ratings and auto-classification, and batch import of watched/wishlist/watching collections filed by year/season. name: zzyong24/thirdspace-dashboard
good: An Obsidian plugin providing a visual console for the ThirdSpace vault system: file statistics from frontmatter dates, a past-year activity heatmap, 8-workspace counts with hot/cold activity colouring, today's work-log summary and timeline, double-click-toggle todos stored in the daily log, product status and recent files. bad: The README states the plugin is forcibly bound to the thirdspace-vault-template: fixed Chinese directory names, workspace-index.yaml and product-status.md formats, and panels go blank or degrade if those conventions are absent. Only 6 commits, no releases, and install via a release download is described despite no releases being listed.

name: voocel/openclaw-mini
good: A minimal, heavily commented reproduction of OpenClaw's core architecture for learning: dual-loop Agent Loop with typed EventStream, JSONL session persistence, three-stage context pruning and compaction, on-demand bootstrap loading, tool-based keyword memory retrieval with a pre-compaction memory flush, extensible SKILL.md skills, heartbeat proactive wakeups with request merging, and a WebSocket RPC gateway with challenge-response auth. name: yaojit/oh-my-kb
good: A Claude Code personal knowledge base plus assistant framework implementing ingest (tweets, public accounts, web, GitHub, Feishu) → incremental LLM compile with concept extraction → indexing → health inspection → cross-source Q&A, with 27 skills, 3 sub-agents and a pure-Markdown, git-diff-auditable four-layer memory; every knowledge entry is traceable to its raw source and the raw/wiki/outputs layers are strictly separated.
bad: Very new and tiny — 2 commits, 2 stars, created 2026-07-24 — and shipped as a skeleton stripped of all the author's data and credentials. Many skills are strongly bound to external accounts (Longbridge, Xueqiu, Feishu/Lark, Gaode, Cloudflare) and are reference implementations only until the user supplies keys, and the messaging/cron layer depends on the external cc-connect connector.
didnt: Corroboration — its Karpathy-derived raw → LLM-compiled wiki → outputs layering, incremental compile, traceability to source and index-instead-of-RAG at ~100 notes confirms our existing LLM-wiki design, which already covers this stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wangyijin1560/wang-agent
good: A minimal local terminal agent with a tool registry (AST-safe calculator, mock search, real DuckDuckGo web search, todo create/list/complete/delete), per user+session isolation, a strict JSON decision protocol, summary compression of old messages, a FakeLLM test client and end-to-end tests.
bad: A demo-scale build — 5 commits, 2 stars — whose todos and memory live only inside SessionState, whose real model path is a single Aliyun Bailian qwen model (falling back to a rule-based demo mode without config), and which has no persistent knowledge base, citations or licence.
didnt: Rejected — maturity, scope and no licence: a minimal teaching demo that duplicates the agent runtime we already have and offers no citation locking, scored abstention or knowledge compilation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mengtian999/bitjarvis
good: A local-first desktop personal agent with a self-developed memory system, per-agent personality folders, multi-agent collaboration and delegation, file/command/browser tools, a community Skills ecosystem with strict review, cron/heartbeat scheduling, and a two-layer sandbox (PathGuard access levels plus OS sandboxing) with user confirmation for writes, command execution and network requests.
bad: Very young — created 2026-09-17, 19 commits, 1 star — with Windows still Beta and its installer unsigned (SmartScreen warnings), the mobile client in a separate repo, and cross-device IM relayed through the project's own self-built bitjarvis.chat homeserver rather than purely local transport.
didnt: Board — the exportable agent packaging idea: an agent as one folder exportable as a local-first role-card / skill-bundle zip carrying personality, optional memory and Skills under a whitelist. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SpadeFater/Copy_Myself
good: A LangGraph personal assistant where CLI, FastAPI and a PyQt desktop workbench share one execution chain, memory and tool-confirmation policy; approvals are bound to session, normalised tool name, parameter SHA-256 and expiry, the filesystem tool refuses paths outside allowed roots and sensitive .git/.env/key paths, and model-generated MCP tools run in Docker with a read-only root, non-root user, resource limits and no network by default, over SQLite graph memory.
bad: The README itself says the project is still at the basic-capability stage with complex personal-assistant workflows unfinished; no licence is stated at source, the Windows build needs three executables kept together, and it warns the free PyQt6-Fluent-Widgets it uses is GPLv3, constraining closed distribution.
didnt: Corroboration — approvals bound to a specific session and specific parameters rather than a permanent tool pass, plus sensitive-path filesystem guardrails, confirm our approval-gated writes design; no code taken, and no licence is stated for its own code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fantasticit/think
good: An open-source knowledge-management tool that organises online collaborative documents into independent knowledge-base spaces for accumulation and reuse, with multi-user collaborative editing on MySQL, Next.js, NestJS and Tiptap, Docker deployment, 1,117 commits and 2,143 stars.
bad: The README documents features only briefly and points to an external help centre for real documentation; the author notes the deployed site goes down intermittently because of server cost and an expired free SSL certificate. The page shows no AI, LLM compilation, citation or retrieval-evaluation capability, and the repo has 0 releases and 0 tags.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a collaborative document platform duplicates conventional doc tooling and offers no citation locking, scored abstention or LLM knowledge compilation for a personal local-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: xaoxuu/hexo-theme-stellar
good: A mature Hexo theme (1,314 commits, 94 releases, 2,063 stars) that turns a static site into an all-in-one personal knowledge base: articles, a Wiki system for stable project docs, columns for series and notebooks for scattered notes share one navigation, search and reading experience, with rich tag/data components, section-level local search and remotely loaded dynamic data decoupled from static content.
bad: It is a presentation layer only — it requires Hexo 8 and Node.js 22 and provides no ingest, LLM compilation, abstention or private knowledge custody; as a static-site theme its model is publishing content, not keeping a local-first private wiki.
didnt: Board — the content-organisation pattern of Wiki, columns and notebooks sharing a single navigation, search and reading experience, as a presentation idea for a wiki portal. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: riba2534/feishu-cli
good: A complete Feishu open-platform CLI (503 commands across 20+ modules — docs, knowledge base, sheets, bitable, messages, mail, calendar, tasks, approvals and more) whose core is lossless bidirectional Markdown ↔ Feishu document conversion over 40+ block types, with Mermaid/PlantUML rendered as editable boards, a three-stage concurrent pipeline tested on 10,000+ line documents, dry-run writes, idempotency keys, structured --jq output and 9 ready-made agent Skills.
bad: Entirely locked to the Feishu platform: it requires creating a Feishu app, granting an extensive permission-scope list and OAuth user authorisation, and even its conversion has documented approximations (highlight rendered as underline; unreadable cross-document sync blocks exported as warning placeholders).
didnt: Rejected — platform lock-in and scope: Feishu is not part of our stack, and a platform CLI contributes nothing to citation locking, abstention or local-first wiki custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: getrebuild/rebuild
good: A highly configurable, zero/low-code enterprise management platform (4,002 commits, 174 releases) with a graphical entity designer, approval workflows, fine-grained team/role/department permissions and Docker deployment, whose current version adds an AI assistant that operates business data in natural language with 30+ tools, custom Skills, knowledge-base Q&A and MCP server support for building WMS/MES/CRM/HRM/ERP systems.
bad: GPL-3.0 with a parallel commercial licence, an enterprise Java/MySQL scope far beyond a personal wiki, and higher-tier features reserved to the paid commercial edition per its README's commercial-authorisation section.
didnt: Rejected — licence and scope: GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us, and an enterprise ERP/CRM platform does not fit a personal LLM-wiki / knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PenglongHuang/ChatGPT-Java-FunAi
good: A Spring Boot ChatGPT learning project offering unlimited-turn contextual chat with streaming, plus PDF reading built on parsing, recursive text chunking, OpenAI embeddings and vector semantic matching against Pinecone or Milvus to recall similar knowledge-base passages, with multi-source file comparison, an API-key pool with rotation scheduling, quota queries and key-failure detection.
bad: The repository is archived and its own changelog stops in 2023; the front-end repo is stated as not yet open, and the README's disclaimer says the code is for demo and testing only and must not be used commercially — contradicting the plain Apache-2.0 grant — while setup requires MySQL, Redis and an overseas server or global proxy.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and duplication: an archived 2023 embedding-RAG demo, superseded by our markdown compilation approach, with a licence disclaimer that conflicts with its stated licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: luolin-ai/Dify-Enterprise-WeChat-bot
good: A Dify-based Enterprise WeChat knowledge-base bot that auto-replies in private and group chats, keeps a separate session per user inside group chats, maintains conversation context via the Dify API, supports whitelist control of which users/groups it interacts with, and saves daily conversation logs as CSV files; it can point at a locally deployed Dify instance.
bad: Windows-only and pinned to one fixed Enterprise WeChat version (4.1.13.6009 in the introduction) because client API changes break session recognition; the README's known-issues section says republishing a changed Dify agent never propagates — the workaround is creating a new agent and swapping the API key — and its Dify Workflow tutorial is stated as not yet developed. Its licence is a custom, non-standard licence.
didnt: Rejected — platform lock-in, maturity and licence: a Windows/Enterprise-WeChat bot under a custom licence (ideas-only) with no fit for a local-first personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: skrstop/MCPHub-Desktop
good: A Tauri 2 local-first desktop client for managing MCP servers, Skills and RAG knowledge bases on the user's own PC — all processes, config, keys and vector data stay local — with bundled Node/UV/Bun runtimes, semantic chunking (Unicode, Markdown and tree-sitter AST strategies), local GGUF embedding models, one-click Skills install/export to dozens of agents by symlink or copy, keys stored in the OS keyring, and the RAG base exposed to agents as MCP tools (rag_search, rag_get, rag_file_create/update).
bad: The README's troubleshooting documents real rough edges: macOS installs are unsigned so users must clear the 'damaged app' warning with xattr, and Windows can crash on first launch from the installer; the repo also embeds a full read-only snapshot of the upstream mcphub project that is explicitly not this project's code, complicating provenance.
didnt: Board — the idea of exposing a local knowledge base to agents as callable MCP memory tools (rag_search / rag_get / create / update) with strategy-based semantic chunking, as a possible door pattern for our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Samge0/ragflow-upload
good: A focused batch tool that recursively traverses a document directory and uploads and parses files into a RAGFlow knowledge base via the pure API/SDK (no database dependency), with parse-progress monitoring, per-document custom metadata via .meta.json sidecar files, a choice of RAGFlow chunk methods, and resumable progress records that skip already-completed files on re-run.
bad: Tightly coupled to one upstream: it requires RAGFlow v0.26.2+ and Python 3.13+, the README warns the current client is incompatible with older (~v0.19) RAGFlow because of API changes, supported suffixes are only md/txt/pdf/docx, and the knowledge base must be created manually in RAGFlow first.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and dependency: a single-purpose uploader for RAGFlow, which our stack does not use; our ingest compiles Markdown directly rather than feeding a vector RAG service. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Awesome-AI-Pedia/Awesome-AI-Pedia
good: A broad, continuously updated AI resources encyclopaedia organised as real repository directories covering AI coding assistants, MCP, agents, Skills, prompt/rules collections, RAG, MLOps, interview material and learning paths, published as a VitePress site with local full-text search, a dark theme, automatic sidebar generation by scanning the repo, and auto-deployment to GitHub Pages.
bad: It is a curated content collection, not a capability: the README shows no evaluation, citation, verification or curation-quality machinery behind the listings, and the repository sprawls across dozens of top-level topic folders in mixed languages, created 2026-08-03 with 0 releases.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: an awesome-list duplicates our own research catalogue and provides no mechanism relevant to citation locking, scored abstention or approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: weaiw/trove-ai
good: A self-hostable personal read-later plus knowledge base built first-class for Chinese-internet platforms (WeChat public accounts/Channels, Toutiao, Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Bilibili, Zhihu and more) with a trafilatura → headless-Chromium → BeautifulSoup extraction cascade, RAG Q&A that cites the user's own library, an auto-grown knowledge graph linking each article to its 3 closest siblings, AI learning paths, agent knowledge organisation only after explicit confirmation, one-way Obsidian sync that never overwrites local edits, and multi-tenant JWT isolation.
bad: AGPL-3.0 copyleft — the FAQ says closed-source SaaS needs a separate commercial licence — on a heavy self-host stack (PostgreSQL+pgvector, Redis, Playwright; ~4 GB RAM, ~5 GB disk); README screenshots are still placeholders, Pocket/Omnivore migration has no direct importer (workarounds only, direct importer promised for v1.1), and its acknowledgements state it was vibe-coded with 0 lines of human-written code.
didnt: Board — its confirmed-agent-writes plus auto-linking each new item to its nearest neighbours in a knowledge graph, as ideas for our wiki's ingest; AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only, never adopt/build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wzdavid/ThinkRAG
good: A RAG system that runs entirely on a laptop: LlamaIndex + Streamlit, hybrid retrieval with BGE reranking, local models via Ollama with no GPU required, a development mode that needs no database, and Chinese-optimised splitting, title enhancement and prompt templates, with hosted APIs (DeepSeek, Moonshot, ZhiPu, OpenAI-compatible) also supported.
bad: The README's own Known Issues section reports unresolved problems for Windows users and pins Ollama to 0.3.3 because llama_index is incompatible with Ollama 0.4. It is a small single-author project (62 commits, no releases).
didnt: Rejected — plain local RAG Q&A with no citation locking, scored abstention or approval-gated writes; it duplicates retrieval our stack already has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tianclll/Ace-Translate
good: Fully offline, format-preserving translation of PDF/Word/Excel/PPT/Markdown/TXT and images using local llama.cpp models, with a proprietary-term glossary injected for consistent terminology, a built-in document knowledge base with full-text search and tagging, screenshot/selection translation, OCR, ASR/TTS, and an embedded REST API with 16 endpoints.
bad: Windows 10/11 only per its own system requirements, and building from source needs a heavy native chain (Visual Studio 2022, Qt 6.5.2, OpenCV, CUDA/ONNXRuntime). It recommends 16 GB RAM and takes about 5 GB with models, and is a single-author project.
didnt: Rejected — a Windows desktop translation product; translation is peripheral to our wiki and its knowledge base is a translation archive, not a citation-locked knowledge store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gelusus/wxvl
licence: MIT (badge in README; no LICENSE file in repo root)
good: Automatically scrapes WeChat official-account security articles, converts them to Markdown with wechatmp2markdown, filters them by vulnerability keyword patterns (CVE/CNVD/CNNVD/POC/RCE and similar), dedupes processed links via data.json, archives by year-month, and keeps itself updated through GitHub Actions runs every four hours.
bad: Extremely narrow: one content type (WeChat security posts) drawn from two upstream feeds (a picker archive and the Doonsec RSS). It is an extension of another author's original wxvl, and the README describes an article archive with no search or Q&A layer.
didnt: Rejected — a single-domain scraper/archive; its scheduled scrape-to-Markdown ingest resembles our pipeline, but there is nothing here a personal wiki needs to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lhh737/KnowledgeBase-RAG-LLM-System
good: Lightweight local RAG Q&A system (Streamlit + LangChain + Chroma): upload a .txt file and it is chunked and written to a persistent Chroma store with MD5 dedup, then answered over with streaming chat that keeps conversation history for follow-up questions. No GPU is needed.
bad: The README presents it as a RAG learning/intro project. Ingest accepts .txt only (PDF/Markdown/Word support is listed as a future extension), and both the chat model and embeddings are Alibaba DashScope cloud APIs, so it is not an offline system; the bundled sample corpus is an e-commerce customer-service demo.
didnt: Rejected — tutorial-grade, txt-only and cloud-API dependent; far below the standard of our existing wiki stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mingchen666/Reviva
licence: AGPL-3.0 + commercial dual licence (per README badge and licence section; no LICENSE file in repo root)
good: Local-first Electron learning workspace that combines a Wiki knowledge base with source traceability and lint/semantic audit, agents that work under a permission sandbox, 13 creation tools (quizzes, flashcards, mind maps, knowledge graphs, PPT, podcasts, deep-research reports), audio/video transcription with keyframe extraction, and a KBP protocol for plugging in external knowledge bases (Dify, FastGPT, MCP or custom HTTP).
bad: The AGPL-3.0 + commercial dual licence restricts reuse, and multi-user or commercial use requires the author's licence. It is a very young project (created June 2026, at v1.4.x) with headline features still marked Beta (KBP external knowledge bases, growth profile), ships for Windows and macOS only, and some creation tools depend on cloud services.
didnt: Board — the wiki lint/semantic audit with source traceability and the KBP external-knowledge-base protocol are ideas for the ideas board; the code itself is AGPL/commercial dual-licensed, so ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: creditease-sec/insight
good: Three-in-one enterprise security platform: application-system asset management, full vulnerability lifecycle management (submission, notification, acknowledgement, retest, classification, risk and fix-deadline calculation, mail reminders, statistics) and a security knowledge base for cases, policies and training material, with a five-role permission model and a Docker deployment guide.
bad: The repository is archived and the README states this v1 is no longer maintained, pointing users to its successor. The documented stack is dated (Python 2.7, Flask 0.11, MySQL 5.7), and the licence is GPL-3.0.
didnt: Rejected — an archived, GPL-licensed enterprise vulnerability-management platform; its knowledge base is a security-case library, not a personal knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mahonelau/-kykms
good: Elasticsearch-based document knowledge-management system with full-text search inside attachment contents, document classification, fine-grained permission and secrecy-level controls, Flowable workflow review, OCR of scanned attachments into searchable text, and RAG Q&A that supports locally deployed (Ollama/vLLM) or cloud LLMs; it deploys fully offline and runs on as little as 2 cores / 4 GB.
bad: The open-source edition is the basic tier: the README reserves the knowledge graph and other advanced capabilities to paid higher editions or customisation. The stack is legacy (Java 8, Spring Boot 2.3.5, Elasticsearch 7.6.1, Vue 2), and the vendor's README promotes its successor KMatrix while noting the old system has no smooth migration path to it.
didnt: Rejected — an enterprise, sales-tiered KMS on a heavy legacy Java stack, far beyond personal-wiki scale; our stack already covers the underlying need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ischenliang/quickly-picture-bed
good: Web image-hosting system (NestJS + Vue 3) with a plugin market (upload, theme and toolbox plugins covering dozens of object stores), multi-bucket management with migration, albums with tags, operation logs, RBAC, and a built-in knowledge-base module for creating, organising and exporting documents alongside images.
bad: The knowledge base is a minor side module of an image bed: basic document CRUD and export with no retrieval or RAG capability described. Deployment requires MySQL and Node 18, and the README documents a seeded default administrator account, which is a security footgun if left unchanged.
didnt: Rejected — an image-hosting product whose knowledge-base module is peripheral and well below our wiki's standard. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fufankeji/fufan-chat-api
good: Private knowledge-base Q&A system covering five scenarios — general LLM Q&A, local knowledge-base Q&A over Faiss, live web-search Q&A (Serper retrieval indexed into Milvus), agent Q&A and an LLM recommendation system — with fine-grained user permission management, a stated complete RAG evaluation pipeline, and Docker deployment.
bad: It is a secondary development of LangChain-Chatchat v0.2. The README's Fixes section documents fragile workarounds (a forced langchain-core==0.2.5 pin that ignores dependency conflicts, and a Milvus indexing bug), and admits the agent Q&A initially did not meet expectations. No licence is stated anywhere at the source.
didnt: Rejected — no licence at source, derivative of an older Chatchat release, and courseware-grade engineering. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: didilili/shopkeeper-agent
good: Complete NL2SQL agent for e-commerce data warehouses: a metadata knowledge base split across MySQL (authoritative structured metadata), Qdrant (semantic recall of fields and metrics) and Elasticsearch (full-text over field values), with a LangGraph pipeline that recalls context, generates, validates, corrects and executes SQL, streaming the process over SSE; ships as a runnable full-stack project with chapter-by-chapter tutorial branches.
bad: The README's own capability-boundaries section says it deliberately does not cover production governance — no login or data permissions, no multi-tenancy, no SQL security audit or whitelist, no systematic evaluation set, and limited multi-turn memory — because it is a teaching project over a teaching data warehouse. It is young (created April 2026, 36 commits).
didnt: Rejected — data-warehouse question-answering, not knowledge-wiki scope; its metadata-KB hybrid retrieval corroborates hybrid design, but the domain does not transfer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: phpk/godoos
good: Intranet office operating system with a Windows-style web desktop in a roughly 70 MB Go package: office editors, native file storage, LAN chat with automatic peer discovery, per-file encryption and a password vault, an app store, and — since v1.0.5 — a knowledge base generated from folders with one-click indexing and search; it runs fully offline with no registration.
bad: The knowledge base is one small feature inside an office suite, and the README's long changelogs are dominated by bug fixes. The stronger permission, workflow and encryption features are reserved to the enterprise edition; the licence is AGPL-3.0 and the README additionally asks commercial users to purchase a licence.
didnt: Rejected — office-OS scope with a peripheral knowledge base, and AGPL-licensed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zhikunqingtao/zhikuncode
good: Self-hosted coding agent whose unified Tool Gateway runs every tool call through input freezing, risk/resource analysis, system-invariant checks, scoped grant matching (RUN/SESSION/WORKSPACE) or a persistent permission prompt, and a pre-execution recheck, returning structured audit results; it adds an 8-layer bash sandbox, a three-layer memory system, skills and plugins, and reports a SWE-bench Lite resolve rate of 56.0% (168/300) on the official harness.
bad: It is a coding assistant, not a knowledge system. The README is heavily self-promotional and its comparison cases and benchmark are vendor-published single-run records, and the project is young (created April 2026).
didnt: Board — the unified authorisation flow (risk analysis, scoped grant matching, pre-execution recheck and structured audit, with single-use approval for high-risk operations) is a board-worthy pattern for our approval-gated writes; the product itself is out of scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NanGePlus/LangGraphChatBot
good: Worked tutorial series building a LangGraph customer-service bot with short- and long-term memory, PostgreSQL persistence (PostgresSaver checkpoints and PostgresStore cross-thread memory), parallel tool execution, and a RAG triage workflow that grades retrieved documents for relevance and rewrites the query (up to three times) before generating an answer.
bad: A video-course demo repository: numbered case folders that the README instructs readers to copy into their own projects, built around a single telecom data-plan recommendation scenario, with no releases. Dependencies are pinned to early-2025 versions and the README documents patching langchain_openai source to work around an embedding bug. No licence is stated at the source.
didnt: Rejected — a tutorial demo with no licence; its grade-then-rewrite loop parallels our abstention design, but there is nothing here to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: luoguoxiong/aipack
licence: MIT (per README License section; no LICENSE file in repo root)
good: TypeScript agent framework with a self-built runtime: framework-level permission approval (a PermissionPolicy with allow/deny/confirm/pending verdicts, an ApprovalManager issuing persistent approval tickets via FileApprovalStore, verdicts rendered before tool execution so tools cannot bypass them), cross-session long-term memory using BM25 + vector hybrid retrieval, five-level context compression, bidirectional MCP bridging, a built-in eval system with baseline regression gates, and 13+ model providers.
bad: It is an agent framework, not a knowledge system — its only knowledge-adjacent component is the memory plugin. The surface is very broad (ten packages) for a single-author project, and there is no LICENSE file in the repo root despite the MIT statement in the README.
didnt: Board — framework-level permission approval (verdict precedes execution, tools cannot bypass it, persistent approval tickets) is a board-worthy pattern for our approval-gated writes; the framework itself is not needed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cunninger/my-ai-agent
licence: Apache-2.0 (per README licence section; no LICENSE file in repo root)
good: Spring Boot + Spring AI agent service with Kryo file-persisted chat memory, a RAG knowledge base over PGVector (Markdown upload, document CRUD APIs, query rewriting), a ReAct agent with a flexible tool registry, and a separate MCP image-search server module.
bad: A very small, early project: 12 commits, no releases, built on milestone pre-release Spring AI (1.0.0-M6). Its main model path requires an Alibaba DashScope API key, and the README's clone URL is still a placeholder (your-username).
didnt: Rejected — demo-scale agent service; its knowledge base is one small module and the pre-release stack is not a fit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MultiHop-RAG
good: A QA benchmark of 2,556 queries whose evidence is distributed across 2 to 4 documents, with queries that also involve document metadata, reflecting real-world RAG scenarios (COLM 2024). The repo ships retrieval and QA evaluation scripts plus simple, BM25, hybrid and reranking sample pipelines, so a system can be scored on both retrieval and end answers.
bad: The README itself admits the dataset-construction pipeline code is 'not very tidy' and only partly open-sourced. The corpus is drawn from news articles, a single genre, and the repo has no releases; the sample code pins an old llama-index version (0.9.40).
didnt: Board — multi-hop questions with evidence spread across 2–4 documents and metadata-aware queries, as a template for a cross-page retrieval test inside our own golden set; the news-domain dataset itself does not fit a personal wiki's claims. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RAGBench
good: A large-scale RAG benchmark of 100k examples across five industry domains, assembled from 12 sub-datasets (including CUAD, EManual, ExpertQA, FinQA, HotpotQA, PubMedQA, TechQA) with train/validation/test splits. Each example carries sentence-level support annotations — relevant and utilised sentence keys, adherence, and relevance/utilisation/completeness scores alongside TruLens groundedness and RAGAS faithfulness columns — allowing explainable, per-sentence evaluation rather than a single score.
bad: The annotations are model-made, not human: the viewer shows responses generated by gpt-3.5-turbo and annotated by gpt-4o, so its ground truth inherits those models' judgements. The dataset card as opened states no licence, and as a composite of 12 third-party datasets the component terms are not addressed on the card.
didnt: Board — sentence-level support labelling (all-relevant vs utilised sentence keys with adherence and completeness scores) as a model for per-sentence citation-support scoring in our evals; the composite dataset itself is unusable as evidence because no licence is stated at source, so ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CRAG
good: A factual-QA RAG benchmark spanning five domains and eight question categories, varying entity popularity from popular to long-tail and temporal dynamism from years to seconds, with mock APIs that simulate web and knowledge-graph search. Its scoring rates answers perfect/acceptable/missing/incorrect and auto-evaluation awards +1 for correct, 0 for missing and −1 for incorrect, explicitly penalising hallucination over abstention; baselines and a local evaluation script are included.
bad: Licensed CC BY-NC 4.0, so the dataset and code cannot be used commercially. The repo is small (12 commits, no releases) and was migrated from the KDD Cup 2024 GitLab, and its auto-evaluation leans on a mix of rule-based matching and LLM assessment rather than human labels.
took: CRAG confidence gating (gate) — built in Round 3, lane TB6 — source/inspiration: CRAG
didnt: Corroboration — its +1/0/−1 correct/missing/incorrect scoring, which punishes a wrong answer more than an abstention, confirms our scored-abstention design, and its confidence gating is the recorded inspiration for the gate built in Round 3 (lane TB6); the benchmark's own code and data were not adopted, and CC BY-NC 4.0 bars commercial code use in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LegalBench-RAG
good: An IR benchmark for complex legal-contract questions whose ground truth is stored as exact snippets — a corpus file path plus a character index range — so an evaluator can deterministically compute precision and recall even at the exact character level. The full generation code is included, rebuilding the benchmark from ContractNLI, CUAD, MAUD and PrivacyQA, and a benchmark script runs any retrieval system against it.
bad: The README warns that because LLMs are used to create the benchmark, re-running the generation script will not reproduce the distributed benchmark exactly. The data itself is not in the repo — it is distributed through a Dropbox download link — and running the pipeline requires setting up API credentials.
didnt: Board — character-exact ground-truth spans enabling deterministic precision/recall, as a model for exact-span citation checking against wiki pages; the legal-contract dataset itself is outside our scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MTRAG
good: The first end-to-end human-generated multi-turn RAG benchmark: 110 multi-turn conversations converted to 842 evaluation tasks over four document corpora (ClapNQ, Cloud, FiQA, Govt), published in TACL 2025, plus 200 synthetic conversations. Its companion MTRAG-UN adds 666 tasks targeting unanswerable, underspecified, non-standalone questions and unclear responses, and scripts cover retrieval, generation and evaluation, with results viewable in InspectorRAGet format.
bad: The human core is small — 110 conversations — with the larger volume coming from synthetic data. Corpora must be downloaded and uncompressed separately, two of the four are reused existing corpora, and running experiments depends on the external BEIR codebase and on models the user supplies.
didnt: Board — MTRAG-UN's taxonomy of unanswerable, underspecified and non-standalone questions as test categories for conversational retrieval and abstention over the wiki; the benchmark corpora themselves are external domains we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: IBM

name: U-NIAH
good: A unified needle-in-a-haystack framework that tests both raw LLM long-context understanding and RAG systems with multi-needle cases defined in a simple YAML format, sweeping context lengths (defaults run from 1K toward 999K) and needle depth percentages. RAG testing supports topk, half and full context modes with configurable chunking, and batch visualisation scripts turn results into depth-by-length heat maps.
bad: No licence is stated at source: the repo root has no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no licence, so the code is ideas-only. It is a very young, small project (created February 2025, 11 commits, 8 stars), its SDK support is limited to OpenAI/Anthropic-style APIs requiring API keys, and the default haystack is Paul Graham essays, so needle realism is synthetic.
didnt: Board — multi-needle depth × context-length heat-map probing, including the topk/half/full context modes, as a cheap regression probe for retrieval from long wiki pages; no licence is stated at source, so the idea may be boarded but its code may not be adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Tongji University (Tongji-KGLLM)

name: RAGEval
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) at source — no standard licence identified
good: A framework that automatically generates scenario-specific RAG evaluation datasets: it summarises a schema from seed documents, generates diverse documents and question-reference-answer triples, and ships the DragonBall dataset covering finance, legal and medical domains in Chinese and English. It introduces Completeness, Hallucination and Irrelevance metrics and reports experiments across nine generation models and several retrievers, including TopK and chunk-size trade-offs.
bad: GitHub classifies its LICENSE file as Other (NOASSERTION), so no standard licence could be identified at source and the code must be treated as unlicensed. Its documents and QA pairs are LLM-generated, so ground-truth quality depends on the generator, and repo news stops in September 2024 with only 25 commits.
didnt: Board — schema-first synthetic scenario generation (schema → documents → question-reference-answer triples) with Completeness/Hallucination/Irrelevance metrics, as a way to generate domain-specific evals from our own pages; no standard licence is identified at source, so ideas only, never its code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FeB4RAG
good: The repository for the FeB4RAG federated RAG benchmark collection ships three usable pieces: the produced dataset, the code to create, reproduce or expand it, and response-evaluation code that includes a web interface for pairwise judging of generated responses. It is Apache-2.0 licensed, so the collection machinery is freely reusable.
bad: The repo is prototype-scale and thinly documented: only 4 commits, 17 stars and no releases, a minimal top-level README that delegates all detail to sub-folder READMEs, and even a committed .DS_Store file. Nothing on the page evidences ongoing maintenance or adoption beyond the original resource release.
didnt: Rejected — a thin, small collection repo whose dataset-reproduction and pairwise-judging pieces duplicate evaluation tooling already covered by stronger entries in this cluster (RAGBench, CRAG), and it offers no mechanism our eval stack lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: ielab

name: OmniEval
good: An omnidirectional, automatic RAG evaluation benchmark for the financial domain with an end-to-end pipeline: build a retrieval corpus, auto-generate evaluation samples with a quality-filtering pass, run inference, then evaluate with either rules or five model-based metrics — accuracy, completeness, utilisation, numerical accuracy and hallucination — implemented by LoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-7B evaluator models. Code is MIT licensed.
bad: It is finance-only and the repo is minimal (7 commits). The pipeline is heavy to operate: data generation needs an API key, and model-based evaluation requires self-hosting two separate vLLM evaluator servers; the evaluation data itself is model-generated, filtered rather than human-verified.
didnt: Board — automatic matrix-style benchmark generation with trained evaluator models for completeness, utilisation and numerical accuracy, as a pattern for testing numeric and multi-part claims in our pages; the financial-domain benchmark itself does not transfer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Renmin University of China (RUC-NLPIR)

name: Annotorious
good: A mature JavaScript image-annotation library (1,785 commits, 81 releases) that adds annotation to any web page with a few lines of code, distributed as an npm monorepo spanning core, standard-image, OpenSeadragon, React and Svelte packages, with IIIF support. Annotations persist in the W3C Web Annotation format via format adapters (FragmentSelector and SvgSelector), making them interoperable outside the library.
bad: Scope is images only — text annotation lives in a separate project, not this repo — and the library provides no storage or backend: host applications must persist and serve annotations themselves. The project site URL carried in the catalogue (recogito.github.io/annotorious) now returns 404, with documentation moved to annotorious.dev.
didnt: Board — the W3C Web Annotation model with fragment/SVG selectors and OpenSeadragon/IIIF handling, as the interchange shape if the Lens ever annotates scanned pages or images; the library is image-only and brings no annotation store of its own. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Recogito
good: A semantic annotation platform for texts and images, built by the Pelagios Network, that links place, person and event references to URI-based gazetteers and vocabularies (such as Pleiades), supports collaborative accounts and groups with private and shared workspaces, and exports the resulting linked data. It is Apache-2.0 open source for self-hosting, with a free hosted instance offered by Pelagios Commons.
bad: It is built for historical and geospatial humanities work — its tagging vocabularies are gazetteers of the ancient world — not general knowledge management. The hosted service's own terms release users' annotations publicly under CC0 and make no guarantees about access or loss of data, and the platform originated in 2013–2018 research projects rather than a maintained product roadmap.
didnt: Corroboration — annotation grounded by linking mentions to external authority URIs (gazetteers/vocabularies) confirms our entity-linking approach for people and places in the wiki; the platform itself is humanities/geospatial-scoped and its hosted terms publish annotations under CC0, so it is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Austrian Institute of Technology; University of Exeter; The Open University (Pelagios Network)

name: doccano
good: A deliberately simple open-source text annotation tool covering text classification, sequence labelling and sequence-to-sequence tasks (sentiment, NER, summarisation and similar), with collaborative annotation, multi-language and mobile support and a RESTful API. It installs in minutes via pip or Docker with SQLite by default, and is widely adopted (10,802 stars) under MIT.
bad: Its feature list is basic by design — collaboration, language support, themes and an API, with no machine-assisted suggestions, no knowledge-base or entity linking and no inter-annotator agreement or curation tooling visible in the README. It exists to build ML training datasets, not to maintain citation-bearing knowledge.
didnt: Rejected — a solid lightweight labeller, but its three task types target ML training data rather than citation-bearing knowledge annotation, and the richer annotation need in this cluster is already covered by INCEpTION and WebAnno. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Label Studio
good: A multi-type data-labelling platform for text, images, audio, video, HTML and time series with configurable label formats and a large template library, multi-user projects, import from files or S3/GCS cloud storage, and a REST API. Its ML-backend integration supports pre-labelling, online learning and active learning, and the open-source edition is Apache-2.0 with a very large community (28,515 stars, 88 releases).
bad: It is a heavyweight stack to run — Django with PostgreSQL and Nginx in the production compose setup, MinIO for S3 — for what would be a side tool in our system. The vendor splits capability across editions: the README promotes a Starter Cloud trial and an edition comparison, so part of the platform is commercial, and its centre of gravity is ML training pipelines, not knowledge curation.
