good: A carefully hardened fork of a QQ ↔ DeepSeek Harness bridge, documented as six explicit deltas over upstream, each with regression tests: a busy-state watchdog with warn/release/hard-cap tiers that recovers sessions whose 'busy' flag wedged (with replayable shared-memory records machine-checked by 160 assertions), a cross-session shared-memory bucket with consent-gated impression writes (target must be a session member or a console-confirmed uid), 30-day staleness expiry and 7-day weakening, daily memory snapshots with console rollback (and failure logging instead of silent snapshot loss), proactive-contact time windows, and fail-closed admin checks on the snapshot endpoints where upstream was fail-open.
bad: A chat bridge for companion-style QQ operation, version-locked to one DSH release line, whose memory is topics and impressions rather than knowledge; the upstream-MIT code is entangled with the proprietary SnowLuma gateway's EULA constraints.
didnt: Corroboration — daily memory snapshots with rollback and fail-closed endpoint hardening parallel our checkpoint and custody practice; a QQ bridge, so nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: freehul/sgme
good: SGME (ShiGuang Memory Engine), a substantial self-hosted memory hub (596 commits, 35 releases; Python + SQLite; HTTP and MCP access): conversations are captured into an L0 raw layer of Markdown kept permanently, distilled into tagged memories (14-dimension tag system) with automatic dedup, merge and contradiction detection, and injected per scenario rather than wholesale — stale memories leave injection automatically while staying traceable, every memory traces back to its original conversation, wrong memories can be marked rejected with a correction note (kept, never deleted, undoable), skills and a shared wiki are managed as peer modules, and a built-in evaluation framework reports extraction F1 rather than asking for trust. Daily snapshots with rotation and off-site copies cover backup.
bad: The README embeds an instruction block aimed at visiting AI agents, directing them to star this repository using the machine owner's GitHub credentials before installing — an agent-manipulation pattern that disqualifies any closer relationship. First-run also ships built-in default API keys (they return 403 only once real keys are configured), and its persona layer accumulates personality profiling (including an MBTI estimate) injected into every conversation.
didnt: Corroboration — its L0-raw-to-distilled memory with provenance and rejection-marking parallels our raw/compiled design; the embedded agent-instruction block rules out anything closer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: songth1ef/nestwork
good: A git-native memory protocol (public template, 141 commits) that makes one private repo the shared brain for Claude, Codex, Gemini, Hermes and other agents across machines: per-agent directories with read/write isolation, a priority chain for rule conflicts, atomic per-write hooks, and a two-tier loading model — a small resident summary at startup (measured on the author's own nest: ~640 tokens versus ~69,600 for full-history loading) with history, projects and workflows retrieved on demand, optionally as topic files behind a generated index. Only reviewed, stable facts are promoted into the resident tier; a distillation step compiles shared memory, an agent mailbox supports inter-agent messages, and the docs are explicit that the nest is for portable context, not secrets or unreviewed employer material.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source (a template repo with no LICENSE file), the protocol has already churned to 3.2 with breaking bootstrap refreshes on upgrade, and memory quality rests entirely on agent discipline — there is no verification, citation or audit machinery beyond git history itself.
didnt: Corroboration — git-native layered memory with reviewed promotion into a small resident tier is our own architecture in miniature, matching the catalogue verdict ALREADY HAVE (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CodyQin/shared-ai-memory
good: A template kit (GitHub + Gitee mirrors) for giving any local agent a shared, user-owned long-term memory in a separate private repo: USER.md for stable background, a lean MEMORY.md index that explicitly refuses raw chat accumulation, PROJECTS.md for decisions and next steps, a memory/inbox where devices first write candidate memories (reducing cross-device conflicts) that are promoted to memory/topics only after user confirmation, a shared-memory SKILL.md carrying the sync and privacy rules to every agent, and a clearly written privacy red-line list (no secrets in git history; private is not a vault — rotate and purge if a secret ever lands).
bad: A prompt-and-template kit, not software: 4 commits, no machinery of its own — no sync engine, no retrieval, no verification — so every guarantee rests on whichever agent executes the prompt and on the user's discipline.
didnt: Corroboration — candidate-then-confirm memory promotion and a lean index file mirror our memory discipline; a template, so there is nothing to take (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: EastSword/EchoMemory
good: A shared knowledge base for agent teams (Python, SQLite + FTS5, zero-dependency pip install) with three access paths (REST, MCP, CLI) and unusually serious identity machinery for its size: per-agent accounts with PBKDF2 password hashing, HMAC JWTs and Ed25519 keys, per-entry authorship tracking and revocable access. Its seven knowledge types (decision, lesson, process, insight, rule, reference, contact) make one field first-class that most memory systems omit: decisions must record a rejected field — what was turned down and why — so agents stop re-proposing rejected options.
bad: Twelve commits and a tiny footprint: knowledge entries are agent-asserted free text with no source provenance or verification, and the roadmap admits semantic search, automatic extraction and contradiction detection are not yet built.
didnt: Corroboration — decisions carrying their rejected alternatives as first-class data mirrors our own decision records (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: leepandar/RingStory
good: A private family photo-sharing application built on the WeChat ecosystem (Spring Cloud Alibaba microservices, uni-app mini-program): photos are organised on a timeline and into a 'ring tree' atlas clustering year → season → month → day, with a review service generating monthly/seasonal/yearly retrospectives and a Rust + ONNX face-recognition plugin.
bad: A heavyweight microservice stack (gateway, Nacos, RocketMQ, Elasticsearch, sharding) for a family photo album; nothing in it concerns agent memory, knowledge compilation or retrieval for reasoning — the catalogue match was on the word 'memory' in its tagline.
didnt: Rejected — a family photo product, not agent memory or a knowledge system (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RewFa-CEO/AMP
good: A cross-agent memory engine with twin TypeScript and Python cores sharing one storage layer, exposed over MCP and REST: three memory tiers (working, long-term, graph), per-memory importance scores with Ebbinghaus-style decay (half-life plus access gain), scope isolation enforced at retrieval (user/session/agent), an append-only JSON audit log of every store/retrieve/update/delete, optional AES-256-GCM at-rest encryption, and production mode that refuses to start without an API token compared in constant time.
bad: Its headline capture mechanism is a Chrome extension that 'implicitly captures' the user's highlights, reading preferences and frequent searches in the background — surveillance-shaped ingest by design, the opposite of consent-first capture. The marketing ('the HTTP of the AI era') also runs far ahead of the implementation, which the README's own roadmap admits: retrieval is substring + token matching with no embeddings, and the graph tier is an enum placeholder sharing long-term storage.
didnt: Rejected — the catalogue verdict NOT FOR US stands; its decay weighting is one more forgetting-curve data point, and its background-capture extension contradicts our consent-first ingest (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yht20927/my-claude-memory
licence: MIT (per the README licence section; no LICENSE file)
good: mcMemory: a layered memory system for coding agents implemented in pure Bash (312 test assertions) with a four-layer model — L1 project summary, L2 outline index with line ranges, L3 AI-condensed chunks carrying YAML frontmatter (source file, SHA-256, sync time) with large files split by heading, L4 device-keyed links back to raw sources. Sync is hash-driven and incremental; retrieval is BM25 weighted by source and evidence class (agent-asserted content is discounted by default, best evidence wins); a session ledger is append-only with event-sourced resolution; deletions go to a trash folder; mcmStatus scores drift (broken links, orphans, staleness); and git sharing uses union-merge for append-only logs with conflicts surfaced, never silently resolved.
bad: Single-author Bash of considerable intricacy (30 commits); L3 chunks are AI condensations at 10–30% of source length, so fidelity rests on the condensing model with no verification pass, and there is no answer-side abstention or citation enforcement.
didnt: Corroboration — layered memory with evidence-weighted retrieval and an append-only, event-sourced ledger parallels our own design; the catalogue verdict ALREADY HAVE stands (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zzOwOzzZoww/MemWeave
good: A local memory-governance layer for coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, WorkBuddy) built around a closed loop: agents distil candidate knowledge, which becomes active only after human confirmation or objective evidence (explicit stable preferences/decisions may auto-promote on verbatim evidence; model confidence never counts as verification); retrieval arbitrates four paths (direct, term-bridge, sibling, anchor) under project scope, lifecycle state, version and evidence gates and prefers returning nothing over injecting noise; superseded versions stay traceable; and LFHV (Lost Future Hit Value) counterfactually re-checks archived knowledge — an archived item returns to active only if it is actually selected into a live context. The published LoCoMo and anti-noise evaluations are reported with unusually honest caveats about what the numbers do not show, and the regression suite runs 1,260 tests.
bad: Alpha software (0.5.0a2, 18 commits); retrieval is FTS5/BM25 plus a small hand-maintained term bridge — deliberately no semantic search — and background extraction ships redacted session summaries to a configured model provider, with the README conceding redaction cannot cover custom credential formats.
didnt: Corroboration — candidate-to-evidence-to-active promotion and falsifiable forgetting (LFHV) are the strongest memory-governance parallels in this wave; alpha maturity keeps it reference-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: iushiyou/workbuddy-sync
good: A two-way sync tool for Tencent WorkBuddy's personal assets (conversations, tasks, spaces, skills, memory files) across machines via any shared folder, engineered with rare care for a 15-commit project: each machine writes only its own zip package so cloud-drive conflict copies cannot occur; append-only logs merge by line-level union; the SQLite database is snapshotted through the backup API (the README documents a measured case where a naive copy would have lost records still in the WAL); merges are idempotent (INSERT OR IGNORE over column intersections); overwritten files always leave timestamped backups; sync scope is a JSON manifest treated as data, with built-in exclusion of secret-like paths and an unknown-asset detector that flags new client directories the manifest does not cover.
bad: A file-sync transport for one vendor's desktop app, Windows-only: it moves WorkBuddy's data files faithfully but knows nothing about the knowledge inside them, non-append files merge newest-wins with a conflict copy rather than content merging, and correctness depends on users honouring its quit-before-pull rule.
didnt: Rejected — a single-vendor sync utility, not a memory or knowledge system; its merge care is noted but there is nothing here for our stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: archlizheng/AIPM-Wiki
licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (per the README copyright section and badge)
good: A Chinese-language knowledge base for aspiring AI product managers, organised as an Obsidian vault with bidirectional links and a graph view: a numbered learning path (roadmap, AI fundamentals, core PM skills, case teardowns of products like ChatGPT and Perplexity, a large interview question bank with a uniform question → examination points → reference answer → follow-ups format, and a resource index), with a read-only Feishu mirror generated by one-way sync. Technical and market claims are stated to be verified against official vendor documentation with access dates noted.
bad: A content curriculum, not a system: no software, no ingest or retrieval machinery, and its most perishable content (model line-ups, pricing, policy) is exactly what ages fastest — the README dates its verification to 2026-07. The CC BY-NC-SA licence also bars commercial reuse.
didnt: Rejected — a career-content curriculum, not a knowledge system (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linyuxuanlin/Wiki_MkDocs

name: gulagala001/oh-my-dsh

name: asdfaj23/shoppilot
good: ShopPilot: a small e-commerce guide agent with an unusually disciplined design for a practice project — the LLM understands and expresses while deterministic code computes and verifies: a Planner extracts structured constraints (Pydantic-validated) into a sub-task DAG; bounded ReAct execution runs under triple budget guards (steps / tokens / cost) with graceful degradation; recommendation ranking is a seven-dimension weighted score computed inside the tool, never by the LLM, so it is regression-testable; the Composer must attach citation numbers to real tool data and pass five deterministic self-checks (citation bounds, budget, product traceability, false refusal, goal coverage); an out-of-pool entity gate refuses questions about products not in the pool instead of inventing prices; after-sales answers use TF-IDF + BM25 fused by RRF over structure-aware chunks and refuse honestly when material is insufficient; long-term memory is an append-only Markdown file the user can read and delete. Its benchmark reports 96.3% vs 40.7% task completion against direct API calls on its 27-question set, with a McNemar significance test.
bad: A personal learning project by its own declaration: all data is LLM-synthesised (40 SKUs, 138 reviews, a 27-question test set), three days old at study time, unlicensed, and scoped to one narrow shopping domain.
didnt: Rejected as a system — a learning project on synthetic data — though its deterministic-guardrail design (checks as pure functions, refusal gates, forced traceable citations) corroborates our own guardrail philosophy (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zhonglijing-star/research-digest
good: A small personal research-tracking digest （知研） that follows topics including agent long-term memory, memory governance, user modelling and automated research agents: it queries OpenAlex, Crossref and arXiv (plus Semantic Scholar with an optional key) daily via a local server or a GitHub Actions → Netlify pipeline, caches responses in SQLite with backoff on 429/5xx and polite request spacing, and presents each paper with title, authors, abstract, source, date, DOI, type and peer-review status clues. Its honesty details stand out: coverage is explicitly not promised ('does not claim to contain every paper in the world'), unverifiable review status is displayed as unknown/unverified, preprints are labelled separately from published records, and full-text links are shown directly only when the metadata records a Creative Commons licence.
bad: A literature-alert tool, not a memory or knowledge system: it stores metadata and relevance feedback, compiles nothing, and its ranking adjusts to the user's clicks rather than to evidence about the papers. Eighteen commits, no licence stated.
didnt: Rejected — a paper-tracking digest; its metadata honesty is noted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: szc01/smart-medical-assistant
good: A LangGraph medical-triage assistant with unusually careful memory engineering for its size: four role agents (supervisor, examiner, attending doctor, pharmacist) routed by conditional graph edges; short-term memory (per-thread checkpoints) and long-term memory (per-user profile, medical history, allergies) in physically separate Postgres stores; uploaded PDF records extracted into Pydantic-validated structured fields before entering long memory; answers cite the source document and page. Its self-built 25-case evaluation (routing, page-cited retrieval, refusal to drag records into unrelated questions, no-data fallback honesty, cross-user access denial) is published with its caveats, and one eval finding drove a real design fix: examination values were removed from long-term memory into retrieval-only after the system was caught citing blood-sugar values in weather answers.
bad: A two-day-old, zero-star domain demo bound to one model provider, with admitted gaps: memory read/write, routing and PDF extraction are untested, scanned PDFs need external OCR, text is capped at 8,000 characters, and old long-memory records are not backfilled when the memory rules change.

name: PandoraReads/pandora-skills
good: Eleven agent skills whose second-brain set explicitly wires two layers together: PARA as the human-facing layer of original notes and actions, and an LLM-Wiki as the AI-facing, traceable knowledge layer compiled from it. The skill set covers the full loop — onboard (bind and check the vault), triage (route inbox originals by actual use), plan, ingest (build traceable wiki pages from inbox/resources), query (search across PARA and wiki, then return to the original text to verify), lint (check properties, directories, backlinks and the wiki's source chains), review (weekly/annual) and archive/restore — plus three learning skills (pre-reading analysis with active recall, highlight extraction, Socratic language practice).

name: Detachment5879/second-brain

name: zjncs/Uniq-Cluster_Memory
good: Uniq-Cluster Memory (China Mobile): a conflict-aware temporal memory system for medical agents that treats contradiction as first-class data. A five-stage pipeline extracts structured facts from long multi-turn dialogues, clusters them into causal information bundles (with causal deconfounding via backdoor adjustment against lexical-overlap, temporal-proximity and speaker confounders), grounds relative time expressions, and manages uniqueness through a bi-temporal conflict graph — every memory carries t_event, t_ingest, t_valid_start and t_valid_end — resolving value conflicts by confidence-weighted multi-candidate comparison that preserves the full conflict history and provenance rather than overwriting, with deterministic rule-based temporal-logic constraints (medication start/stop ordering, diagnosis-before-test, dose monotonicity) adjusting confidence at no extra LLM cost. On its Med-LongMem benchmark it reports Unique-F1 (strict) 0.8508 and Conflict-F1 0.9762 against 0.3848 / 0.8867 for a long-context LLM, with a full published ablation (removing time grounding collapses Unique-F1 by 85.5%) and an 88-test suite.
bad: Research code with honest limits: the headline benchmark is a synthetic suite at n=20 on the hard split (the generator targets 200 samples for v1.0), the Graphiti comparison is a simulated baseline, the domain is medical dialogue only, and no licence is stated — ideas only for us in any case.
didnt: Corroboration — the strongest external design evidence in this wave for our sharpest open gap (truth-aware retrieval over superseded facts): bi-temporal validity windows, preserved conflict histories instead of winner-takes-all overwrites, and deterministic formal constraints are the same machinery our supersession work needs; nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cabbage2000-lab/paper-tutor-skills
licence: PolyForm Noncommercial (per the README licence badge; GitHub licence detection reports Other / NOASSERTION)
good: An academic-tutoring skill suite (25 commands across the research lifecycle, for Claude Code / Codex / WorkBuddy) engineered around a non-negotiable bottom line: never fabricate — citation verification is decided by real API responses, never model memory, returning one of six honest states (verified / metadata mismatch / retracted / not found / unverifiable / pending human check), with Chinese-language literature always routed to human checking rather than ever being labelled suspect. Other verification machinery: claim-overstatement checks that lay conclusion and results side by side without issuing a verdict, PRISMA screening ledgers with count-conservation checks, and an AI-use disclosure generated only from the project's real trace directory (.paper/), with missing levels marked as placeholders. Process discipline is equally explicit: every command stops at checkpoints for the user's decision with zero writes before confirmation, long work resumes across sessions from the trace directory, the suite publishes a boundary list including four automation mechanisms it evaluated and rejected (a full-chain orchestrator, score-based ranking, silent degradation, auto-rewriting existing files), and it refuses whole request classes — ghost-writing, AI-detection evasion, reviewing other people's under-review manuscripts — each with a legitimate alternative exit.
bad: A tutoring workflow, not a knowledge system: it manages one researcher's project, not a maintained corpus, and its licence (PolyForm Noncommercial) forbids commercial use in any case. Its strictness is also deliberately conservative — Chinese-language citations can never be machine-verified inside it, by design.
didnt: Corroboration — the best-governed skill suite in this wave: API-grounded citation verification with an honest six-state outcome set, a published list of automation mechanisms it evaluated and refused, and checkpoint-gated writes independently match our own honesty and gating rules; nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CalamityXeroc/GIS-agent
good: GIS-agent: an ArcGIS Pro / arcpy agent framework (self-declared early stage) with unusually strong verification engineering. Requirements are first extracted from the task brief into an acceptance checklist; a bounded observe-decide-execute loop (caps on turns, diagnoses, repairs and total runtime) runs tools with automatic code self-repair (traceback + data catalogue + recipe hints fed back); and completion requires passing mandatory acceptance — structural assertions (existence, coordinate-system WKID, fields, feature counts, non-blank rasters/images), semantic checking of every checklist item with evidence (PARTIAL allowed), visual inspection of the rendered map, and delivery-hygiene checks (no process files or redo leftovers) — failing acceptance returns the gaps for bounded repair rather than declaring success. Supporting machinery: 48 methodology recipes each carrying its own validation assertions, automatic backup before any overwrite, a persistent Jupyter kernel for cross-step state, per-run JSONL traces plus Markdown reports, a project log whose relevance+recency retrieval injects pitfalls from similar past tasks into new runs, and ~460 tests under an explicit dependency boundary (the engine must not depend on LangChain/LiteLLM/ChromaDB/Pydantic).
bad: A domain execution tool, not a knowledge system: its 'memory' is an error-fix table and a pitfalls log for GIS tasks; it depends on a licensed ArcGIS Pro environment for real output; and the author states plainly that it is early-stage with many problems. No licence is stated.
didnt: Corroboration — its mandatory acceptance gate (completed is not the same as verified) and backup-before-overwrite rule are the same discipline as ours; it is a GIS tool, nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Leoxia55/agent-from-scratch
good: ScratchAgent: a teaching project that hand-writes an agent in ~3,700 readable Python lines with no agent framework in the core loop, decomposed from first principles (what the model sees, what it can do, how actions execute, where state lives, when to stop, how to observe and recover). Its state discipline is explicit: an ExecutionContext holds an event log that serves simultaneously as model history, debugging record, session-recovery substrate and the raw material for long-term-memory extraction, and state values the program must read reliably are never left only in natural-language prompts. Safety is taught as architecture: tools declare confirmation policies, a side-effecting call returns a pending result instead of executing, approval/rejection/parameter-modification are recorded at the application layer, max_steps is a mandatory fuse, and the docs state plainly that confirmation is an authorisation boundary, not a prompt.
bad: A teaching codebase (thirteen commits, no CLI or server): its memory and RAG are instructional implementations, and it warns itself that default-exported file tools do not automatically acquire approval policies — the safety pattern must be wired deliberately.
didnt: Corroboration — a teaching codebase whose confirmation-as-authorisation-boundary and event-log-as-record principles match our own; nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agent-memory-leaderboard/leaderboard
good: Agent Memory Leaderboard (AML): an open, reproducible evaluation platform for long-term agent memory, launched 2026-07-29 by researchers from more than twenty universities and research organisations (co-organisers listed include Tianjin University, Tsinghua University, Peking University, Oxford, UNSW Sydney and Shanghai AI Laboratory). Cycle 1 drew 100+ teams and 67 representative memory frameworks completed the official evaluation on text memory; the first public leaderboard was released 2026-08-12, and Cycle 2 (opened 2026-09-20) extends to textual, coding and multimodal memory tracks with a RMB 150,000 prize pool for open-source teams.

bad: A teaching demo over a fixed snapshot of first paragraphs: the corpus is only article openings (not full articles), loading takes minutes of model and embedding downloads, results carry no answer synthesis, and no licence is stated in the Space's frontmatter.

bad: A training-systems paper demo: 'memory' is GPU activation memory in distributed training — a catalogue keyword collision, nothing to do with knowledge memory.
didnt: Rejected — a training-systems demo; hardware-memory keyword collision (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SandhyaMadhunagula/GNN-Knowledge-Graph
good: A Flask web app for building a knowledge graph from documents: upload a PDF/DOCX/TXT (or paste text) and it sentence-splits the text, extracts triples with REBEL-large, accumulates them into a NetworkX graph persisted across sessions (pickle file), renders it with PyVis, answers keyword searches with the matching nodes' neighbour triples, and exports the graph as a Subject-Relationship-Object CSV.
bad: The name promises a GNN and the code contains none — extraction is REBEL, the graph is NetworkX, search is substring matching on node names; the graph is persisted as a Python pickle (unsafe to load from untrusted sources), the Flask session secret is hardcoded in the source, and extracted entities are title-cased blindly, mangling acronyms and case-sensitive names.
didnt: Rejected — a REBEL extraction web app with no GNN in it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: schultzhenry/gesda_knowledge_graph_demo
good: An explorer for the GESDA (Geneva Science and Diplomacy Anticipator) knowledge graph — UNESCO concepts, SDG targets, scientific breakthroughs, platforms and their relationships, held in Neo4j with a vector index: a Streamlit app with a connection-status sidebar (live node/relationship counts by type), and three tabs — curated hardcoded queries, vector search ('find nodes using non-jargon language'), and an interactive Cypher query builder.
bad: A front-end only: the graph and vector index live in external services the Space connects to (credentials via .env), so the demo carries no data or method of its own, and no licence is stated.
didnt: Rejected — an explorer UI over an external graph (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sebaaas/create-a-note-taking-app-that-uses-ai-to
good: 'Smart Notes AI — Intelligent Note Taking': a static note-taking web app generated with DeepSite (the Space's name is the truncated generation prompt, 'create a note taking app that uses ai to…'), rendering a notes UI whose initial state reads 'No notes yet — Create your first note to get started'.
bad: An AI-website-builder artefact: a generated front-end shell whose name is the truncated prompt that generated it; whatever AI features it advertises live in generated page code with no backend or knowledge model at the source. No licence is stated.
didnt: Rejected — an AI-website-builder generated page (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Severian/Mycomind-Daemon-Ollama-Mixture-of-Memory-RAG-Agents
good: 'Mycomind Daemon' — a Mixture-of-Memory-RAG-Agents assistant on local Ollama models: three reference agents (Analytical, Historical Context, 'ScienceTruth') answer in parallel and a Synthesis agent aggregates, while memory is split three ways in the Letta style — a core memory of persona/user/scratchpad blocks persisted to a JSON file and editable from the UI, an event memory logging each exchange, and an archival memory (RAG store) the user can add to, search, edit and clear — plus an optional web-search toggle.
bad: A personal assembly of borrowed frameworks (omoa mixture-of-agents, llama-cpp-agent, a local MemoryAssistant package) with parts wired loosely — a stray update_memory method references self inside a module function, memory files are the operator's own, everything depends on a local Ollama serving four models, and there is no verification of what agents write into memory. No licence is stated.
didnt: Rejected as a system — a personal framework assembly; Corroboration for the three-part agent-memory taxonomy (a small editable core-memory file of persona/user/scratchpad blocks, an event log, and a searchable archival store) — the Letta/MemGPT pattern independently re-implemented, with memory editing exposed in the UI rather than hidden (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: siddhartharya/My_NotebookLM_Podcast_Generator
good: A NotebookLM Podcast Generator replication: give it a PDF or a URL (not both), pick a tone (humorous/casual/formal) and length, and Llama 3.1 70B writes a two-host dialogue script from the extracted text, spoken line-by-line with gTTS in two voices (Sarah, American; Maria, British) and stitched into one MP3 with its transcript.
bad: A NotebookLM-audio clone with a hard 2,048-token ceiling on its source (long documents are silently truncated past the warning print), single-vendor TTS voices, and no grounding check between source and script. A media generator, not a knowledge system.
didnt: Rejected — a NotebookLM-style podcast generator clone (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Spyhack225/second-brain
good: Despite its name, a 52-line Streamlit page titled 'Audio Transcript with Whisper': upload an mp3/wav/m4a, it saves the file, loads Whisper-large, and displays the transcript.
bad: A name collision: despite the Space name there is no second-brain functionality — no notes, storage or retrieval; it is a single-purpose transcription page that reloads a large model per upload.
didnt: Rejected — a Whisper transcription page under a second-brain name (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Suchinthana/Sinhala-Wikigen-mT5
good: A low-resource-language generation demo with a clean minimal recipe: google/mt5-base with the author's fine-tuned Suchinthana/MT-5-Sinhala-Wikigen checkpoint, driven by a task prefix ('writeWiki:'+topic) with sampling at max_length 75 - a compact example of steering a multilingual seq2seq model into producing Wikipedia-style Sinhala text from a bare topic.
bad: It GENERATES wiki-style text rather than retrieving or citing anything - synthetic encyclopaedia content with no source, no grounding and no quality check; single hardcoded checkpoint, 75-token ceiling, no evaluation of the Sinhala output's factuality, and a vestigial 'live=loading' hook in the Interface call.
didnt: Rejected - a fine-tuned generation demo whose output is unverifiable synthetic wiki text; a knowledge system built on cited sources has no use for a generator of plausible articles, and its recipe adds nothing beyond the standard prefix-conditioned pipeline pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tipbs/wikipedia_summary
licence: No licence stated in the Space card frontmatter or README.
good: The page-inspector function from the bootcamp family as a standalone: wikipediaapi fetches a page by exact title and returns exists flag, full URL, title, summary and full text in one call, with an explicit not-found branch returning 'Not found' fields instead of raising.
bad: The 'summary' output is page.summary[0:60] - sixty CHARACTERS, a stub fragment mislabelled as a summary; exact-title lookup only (no search or disambiguation), English Wikipedia hardcoded, no error handling beyond the exists check.
didnt: Rejected - a snippet-grade demo with a mislabelled 60-character summary field; nothing here exceeds the wikipediaapi library's own examples. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tyang/electra_wikipedia_qa
licence: No licence stated in the Space card or README.
good: The cleanest standalone of the ELECTRA-over-Wikipedia pattern: deepset/electra-base-squad2 answers from the FULL article content and returns the answer together with the source article URL and the model score - and its confidence output is honestly labelled 'Confidence in answer (assuming the correct wikipedia article)', naming the retrieval assumption inside the UI; a flagging control lets users rate answer relatedness.
bad: Topic resolution is still wikipedia.search top-1 with disambiguation resolved by random.choice among options; the shipped examples include opinion questions ('why did it collapse?', 'Why do his supporters like him?') that extractive QA cannot answer from an article span, inviting confident nonsense; no abstention when the span score is low.
didnt: Rejected - a single-model extractive QA demo; its one transferable virtue, labelling confidence with its retrieval assumption, is a phrasing our own answer surfaces already need and get from the abstention gate rather than from this demo. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: utensil/model-memory-usage
good: A faithful duplicate of the HF Accelerate Model Memory Calculator (the original studied at B076): dtype-and-quantisation-aware estimates of model, gradient and optimiser memory with per-stage Adam training breakdowns, kept available under another account.
bad: A copy, not a project: no code or documentation of its own beyond the duplicated_from pointer, and its estimates age with the upstream original; the catalogue name collides with 'memory' while concerning GPU RAM only.
didnt: Rejected - a verbatim duplicate of hf-accelerate/model-memory-usage already studied at B076; nothing new to learn or take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vaughn/open-notebooklm
good: A deployment of Gabriel Chua's open-notebooklm (the PDF-to-podcast generator studied at B071): PDF in, a Llama 3.1 405B call in JSON mode with a pydantic object produces the two-host dialogue script, TTS renders an MP3 - the README documents the full self-host route including the FIREWORKS_API_KEY setup.
bad: A deployment, not a new system: no code of its own at the Space, wholly dependent on a paid hosted 405B endpoint, and the generated dialogue carries no citations back to the PDF - entertainment-grade transformation with no verification path.
didnt: Rejected - a hosted copy of the open-notebooklm generator already studied at B071; nothing additional to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: virennsinggh/viren-rag-backend
licence: No licence stated in the Space card frontmatter or README.
good: A complete small RAG backend ('FirstRAG') rather than a demo: named collections own a PDF directory, a metadata.json and a Qdrant collection; chat sessions persist full history in SQLite; retrieval knobs (dense_k, bm25_k, rerank_candidates, final_k) are per-request parameters; and each assistant message is STORED TOGETHER WITH ITS SOURCES JSON, while chat responses carry the route taken plus retrieval_metrics and routing_metrics - observability and answer provenance built into the data model, and collection deletion sweeps vectors, files and rows in dependency order.
bad: Single-tenant personal backend with no authentication on any endpoint, CORS pinned to a localhost frontend, collection names sanitised but uploads and storage unmanaged beyond a directory per collection; hybrid weights and reranker live in modules outside the opened file, and there is no evaluation of answer quality.
didnt: Rejected as a system - a personal RAG backend on standard parts - with corroboration for two data-model choices our surfaces share: persisting each answer alongside the exact sources it used, and returning retrieval/routing metrics with the response instead of hiding the pipeline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vishnun/KnowledgeGraphNLP
good: A minimal shell over the author's own nligraphspacy library: one call runs RelationEntityExtract over pasted text and returns the separated entities/relations as JSON - the library-first packaging (pip-installable core, 20-line demo) is the right shape for an NLP utility.
bad: The Space itself contains no extraction logic to study - everything evaluable lives in the external library; the demo returns raw separated components with no graph rendering, no confidence and no handling of multi-sentence text described at the source.
didnt: Rejected - a 20-line wrapper whose substance is an external spaCy utility; nothing to take beyond the packaging pattern, which our own tools already follow. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vssksn/sre-memory-agent
licence: No licence stated in the Space card frontmatter.
good: The strongest memory discipline in this batch, from an autonomous SRE agent built on Hindsight memory: a ten-stage loop (Detect, Classify, Remember, Investigate, Repair, Review, Verify, Regress, Recover/Roll back/Escalate, Learn) under the stated rule 'Memory is treated as evidence, not truth' - a recalled repair matching on error class is still judged for comparability against the current failure before reuse, the demo's second scenario is designed so the agent must REJECT the first incident's fix despite the identical error class, full trajectories including failures are retained for the next incident, and honesty is engineered in: recorded-trajectory runs are labelled 'simulated', a missing LLM key makes the agent report memory as unavailable 'rather than pretending', and a missing Docker daemon is reported as a degradation rather than called isolation.
bad: An SRE-domain system, not a knowledge system: the memory layer is a third-party service (Hindsight, embedded PostgreSQL or its cloud) whose extraction quality bounds everything, live mode burns a shared free-tier token budget between reasoning and memory extraction (the card notes 'reflect' does not fit that budget at all), and verification happens in a sandbox the Space itself cannot provide without an external Docker host.
didnt: Rejected for adoption - a domain agent on someone else's memory cloud - with strong corroboration for our own doctrine: memory recalled is evidence to be re-judged against the present case (never truth by matching), failed trajectories are kept as first-class memory, and simulated or degraded modes must be labelled as what they are instead of presented as live. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vwxyzjn/pyserini-wikipedia-kilt-doc
good: A seven-line window onto a serious retrieval corpus: the bundled pyserini_wikipedia_kilt_doc package's search function exposed directly, giving document lookup over the KILT Wikipedia snapshot - the provenance-fixed corpus the KILT benchmark standardised on - through Pyserini's index.
bad: The Space is only an import shim: no index details, fields or ranking behaviour are visible in the app file, the corpus is a frozen benchmark snapshot rather than living Wikipedia, and there is no query UI beyond a single text box.
didnt: Rejected - a lookup shim over a benchmark corpus; the KILT snapshot's value is as evaluation data, already known to the programme through the benchmark literature. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yadayana/Knowledge-Graph-Visualization
licence: No licence stated in the Space card frontmatter or README.
good: A fuller personal GraphRAG build than its title suggests: uploads (extension-allowlisted, 5 MB total cap) feed a Pinecone index; for each question an LLM first DECIDES whether graph reasoning is warranted ('False only if the prompt is focused on retrieving a single fact'), builds a knowledge graph from the documents when it is, retrieves with query reformulation, and streams the answer with staged progress states; the visualisation half renders the graph (stored as {source: [[relation, target]]} JSON) in 3D with greedy-modularity communities and small communities bucketed into an 'other' class instead of dropped.
bad: A single-user personal app whose routing decision is one uncalibrated LLM yes/no per question - the expensive path (graph construction over the whole corpus) can trigger on a phrasing judgement; state lives in module globals, keys come from a sibling folder's .env, and there is no evaluation of whether Graph RAG answers beat plain retrieval on its own corpus.
didnt: Rejected - a personal GraphRAG demo; its per-question LLM routing echoes the routed-retrieval pattern seen in FirstRAG this batch, and its community-bucketing visualisation choice is a presentation detail, not a capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yasserrmd/NotebookLlama
licence: No licence stated in the Space card frontmatter or README.
good: An implementation of the NotebookLlama recipe with one genuinely good interaction design: the pipeline runs PDF extraction, transcript generation (Llama 3 70B via Groq) and a TTS-rewrite pass, then STOPS and presents the rewritten transcript in an editable box - the human can fix the script before EdgeTTS renders the audio, instead of the audio being generated blind; each run is isolated in its own temp session directory.
bad: Intermediate artefacts are exchanged as pickle files, the pipeline modules sit outside the opened file, there is no citation of the PDF in the generated dialogue, and per-run temp state vanishes with the session - a converter, not a knowledge tool.
didnt: Rejected - a podcast converter; its human-edit-before-render step is a sound pattern our own audio work already follows through script approval, and nothing else transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yogesh18018/knowledge-graph-engine
licence: MIT (per the licence line in the application's own footer; the Space card frontmatter carries no licence field).
good: 'GraphMind' is a tidy rule-based KG workbench: paste or pick a demo text, extract entities across five types (PERSON, ORG, LOCATION, DATE, TECHNOLOGY) with a minimum-mentions filter, infer relationships, and inspect the result across four tabs - PyVis interactive graph, entities table with character offsets, relationships table, and statistics including community and centrality charts - all without an LLM in the loop, so behaviour is deterministic and inspectable.
bad: Rule-based extraction quality is bounded by its patterns (the 'reasoning' in the title is graph analytics - centrality and communities - not inference over facts); no persistence, no source documents beyond pasted text, no evaluation of extraction precision/recall, and the app is a portfolio-grade demo rather than a maintained tool.
didnt: Rejected - a well-finished demo workbench; deterministic no-LLM extraction is a known trade-off, and our extraction needs are claim-level with citations, which this does not attempt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ZENLLC/legalkit-knowledge-graph
good: The LegalKit knowledge-graph viewer under an organisation account: the same minimalist D3 v7 force-layout page over a bundled knowledge_graph.json (orange nodes, hover tooltips showing node text, zoom and drag) - making the demo reachable from the project's org presence as well as the author's personal one.
bad: A second copy of the viewer already studied at B077 (louisbrulenaudet/legalkit-knowledge-graph): identical code, a static snapshot that cannot show how the legal graph was extracted, no search or filtering, and no statement at the Space of how this copy relates to the original.
didnt: Rejected - a duplicate of the LegalKit static viewer studied at B077; nothing new to learn or take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rl-llm-wiki/knowledge-base
licence: CC-BY-4.0 (content, per the dataset card; linked code and data artefacts carry their own licences, recorded per source).
good: The dataset artefact of the agent collaboration whose dashboard, reader and town were studied at B071/B079 - and its card documents a genuinely disciplined knowledge-base design: two layers (topics/ expert articles written to be learned from directly; sources/ one faithful summary per processed source), every non-obvious claim cited inline as [source:<id>] resolving to the source summary and onward to the captured material, every change landing through a REVIEWED pull request ('curated knowledge, not an accumulation'), a non-binding taxonomy.yaml as guidance rather than fixed structure, an article index auto-generated on each merge and marked do-not-edit-by-hand, and per-source licences recorded individually instead of one blanket claim.
bad: The card itself warns 'Early days. This wiki starts empty and grows' - coverage is whatever the agents have processed so far, the richer corpus (raw PDFs, figures, code) lives in an external bucket rather than in the dataset, and the review bar's actual strictness is not observable from the artefact; it is one young domain KB, not infrastructure others can adopt.
didnt: Rejected for adoption - another project's living knowledge base, not a tool - with corroboration for the architecture our own wiki already runs on: compiled layer over faithful source records, inline citation ids that resolve to the source record, writes gated by review rather than accumulation, and a machine-generated index nobody edits by hand. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: THUIR/MemoryBench-Full
good: The extended release of MemoryBench (the balanced version studied at B080 is a subset of this one, train and test alike, in the same proportions): the full-size corpus behind the paper's benchmark, with the card honestly warning that component dataset sizes 'vary significantly', so naive averaging lets one dataset dominate the results - an aggregation caveat most benchmark cards omit; the citation block names all six authors (Ai, Tang, Wang, Long, Su, Liu).
bad: As a separate catalogue entry it duplicates the B080 benchmark: same configurations, same simulated-feedback design, same paper - the delta is size, not method, and usage guidance is deferred wholesale to the balanced version's card.
didnt: Rejected - the full-size variant of the MemoryBench benchmark already studied at B080; recorded separately because the catalogue lists it separately, with the subset relationship and the averaging caveat as its own facts. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Tsinghua University (THUIR - the Tsinghua University Information Retrieval group)

name: Aditya210/knowledge-graph
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter; the card body contradicts nothing but fills in nothing either - its own License field still reads '[More Information Needed]').
good: The single concrete fact the source offers: the dataset is intended for training SVO (subject-verb-object) extraction - the triple shape at the heart of knowledge-graph construction - and it carries an Apache-2.0 frontmatter declaration.
bad: The card is the raw template with every section unfilled: no provenance, no size, no schema, no splits, no source description - nothing about the data itself can be verified from the source, so the dataset is unusable for any serious purpose regardless of its contents.
didnt: Rejected - an undocumented dataset whose own card records nothing about it; an SVO training set of unknown origin and shape cannot be evaluated, trusted or reused. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AGBonnet/augmented-clinical-notes
good: A carefully documented augmentation dataset: 30,000 triplets aligning a clinical note (PMC-Patients), a synthetic patient-doctor dialogue (NoteChat) and a GPT-4 structured patient summary produced against an explicit medical information template (published in the card, JSON included) - the training data for the MediNote-7B/13B note generators; the card is unusually candid about its own synthetic-data problems: ChatGPT dialogues' unrealistic yes-answer pattern, notes truncated before dialogue generation, the deliberate choice to fine-tune on truncated notes so models would not learn to hallucinate note endings, and prompt leaks found inside some generated dialogues.
bad: Two of the three fields in every triplet are model-generated (GPT-3.5 dialogues, GPT-4 summaries), so errors compound invisibly; the source notes over-represent English-speaking clinical settings, and real dialogue data remains legally undistributable (HIPAA), which is the dataset's reason to exist and its ceiling at once.
didnt: Rejected - a medical-domain training dataset - with corroboration for its documentation practice: publishing the synthetic pipeline's known failure modes (prompt leaks, truncation trade-offs, realism limits) inside the dataset card itself, where a user cannot miss them. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: EPFL (repository: EPFL-IC-Make-Team/ClinicalNotes; curators Antoine Bonnet and Paul Boulenger)

name: AI-BRIDGES/wikidata-search-traces
licence: CC-BY-4.0 (per the dataset card; underlying Wikidata facts CC0 1.0, persona source CC BY 4.0).
good: A model of certified question construction: 10,235 reasoning trajectories in which an agent answers questions by writing Python in a REPL over 13 graph functions against a frozen Wikidata dump - and the questions are BUILT from the graph (seed entity, expand a fact tree that identifies it without naming it, render as a natural question), so every question provably has exactly one answer and every clue is necessary; only traces reaching the expected answer are kept for training, while the released corpus also preserves dead ends for failure study; scoring is exact match after canonicalisation with NO judge, and the card publishes a five-system comparison with accuracy, cost, tokens and seconds per question (best: an open-weight Qwen3.8-27B in the RLM harness, 74/100 at about $0.04 per question).
bad: The corpus teaches one harness's search style over one frozen dump - traces date as Wikidata moves, multi-hop questions are only 672 of 10,235, and the published evaluation is 100 questions; question naturalness depends on a persona dataset's style transfer, which no persona text survives into the questions (by design), leaving tone variety claimed rather than shown.
didnt: Rejected for adoption - a training/benchmark corpus for graph-search agents, not a system - with corroboration for our golden-set discipline: questions generated FROM the source graph so answerability and clue-necessity are provable before use, scored by exact match with no judge, and failure traces kept as data rather than discarded. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: AI-BRIDGES project, Digital Humanities Research Hub, School of Advanced Study, University of London (built by Pleias; funded by Wikimedia Switzerland with Wikimedia Deutschland; MSCA fellowship grant 101203096)

name: AI-Ethics/Consciousness_Knowledge_Graph_Exploration
good: As an artefact it demonstrates one thing clearly: how quickly a 'knowledge graph' can be produced by having an LLM expand a concept tree - hundreds of nodes spanning consciousness research, particle physics, sustainability and AI architectures, hierarchically arranged, at zero marginal cost.
bad: The card is an unedited chat transcript pasted as documentation: no schema, no edge semantics, no sources, no curation, and no dataset structure described - the graph asserts connections (consciousness to collider design to circular economy) with nothing behind any of them; it is the accumulation-without-verification anti-pattern in pure form.
didnt: Rejected - an LLM conversation dump presented as a knowledge graph; recorded because the catalogue lists it, and because it marks the exact failure mode (generated structure with no provenance) that a citation-first system exists to avoid. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ai-forever/school_notebooks_RU
good: A properly specified handwriting corpus: photographs of Russian school notebooks with end-to-end COCO-format markup - polygon segmentations per text line with category and a translation field - suitable for training text detection and OCR models, with the annotation schema documented field by field in the card.
bad: A computer-vision training set with no relation to knowledge systems (the catalogue match is the word 'notebooks'); the card gives no dataset size, split or baseline results, and handwritten-schoolchild data carries its own consent/provenance questions the card does not discuss.
didnt: Rejected - an OCR training corpus; nothing in it bears on knowledge organisation beyond the shared word 'notebooks'. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ai-hyz/MemoryAgentBench
good: The sharpest memory evaluation in this section: MemoryAgentBench (arXiv 2507.05257) grades memory agents on FOUR competencies - Accurate Retrieval, Test-Time Learning, Long-Range Understanding and Conflict Resolution - fed incrementally in multi-turn chunks ('inject once, query multiple times'), with two purpose-built datasets (EventQA over novel event chains; FactConsolidation for single- and multi-hop fact conflicts); its published findings are directly decision-relevant: multi-hop conflict resolution is the field's bottleneck (every method at or below 7%; single-hop only 60% even with GPT-4o agents), fact-extracting memory (Mem0) loses decisive context, MemGPT lacks temporal/structural metadata, and construction cost varies by orders of magnitude (Mem0 at 20,000x BM25; Cognee 3.3 hours on one long sample).
bad: Several splits are tiny (Test-Time Learning 6 examples, Conflict Resolution 8), so headline percentages rest on small samples; much content is adapted from existing datasets with the usual inheritance of their biases, and the benchmark measures agents through its own chunking protocol, which favours systems designed for incremental feeding.
didnt: Rejected for adoption - a benchmark, not a system - with strong corroboration for our centrepiece gap: independent measurement says conflict resolution over accumulated memory is where every current approach fails (multi-hop at most 7%), and a four-competency split is a more honest evaluation frame than recall alone - the same reason our truth-aware retrieval gap is stated in supersession terms. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology (HUST-AI-HYZ)

name: ariG23498/quick-notebooks
good: A small, honest collection of four runnable inference notebooks - QwQ and Llama 3.3 70B through hosted API inference, NVIDIA's LogitsProcessorZoo with transformers, and Qwen 2.5 VL 7B on a free Colab tier - useful as copy-and-run starting points.
bad: Four demo notebooks with no unifying framework, no maintenance signals and nothing about knowledge or memory; the catalogue match is the word 'notebooks' in the Jupyter sense.
didnt: Rejected - inference demo notebooks; a name collision, recorded for completeness. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: asi/wikitext_fr
licence: CC-BY-SA-4.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section).
good: WikiText-fr mirrors the classic English WikiText language-modelling benchmark for French: over 70 million tokens drawn only from French Wikipedia articles rated 'quality' or 'good', with train/validation/test splits - a quality-gated corpus design (featured-article status as the filter) that gives French LM evaluation the same footing as the English original (companion paper: Simoulin & Crabbe, TALN 2021).
bad: A static language-modelling corpus - perplexity fodder, not knowledge infrastructure; its splits table is internally garbled (token counts truncated across versions), and a 2021 Wikipedia snapshot ages quickly as a benchmark of current French.
didnt: Rejected - an LM evaluation corpus; the quality-gated extraction idea is standard practice in corpus building and adds nothing to a citation-first knowledge system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Babelscape/wikineural
licence: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section - non-commercial research only).
good: WikiNEuRal (Tedeschi et al., Findings of EMNLP 2021) attacks NER data scarcity with a combined method: knowledge-based annotation from the BabelNet multilingual lexical knowledge base, corrected and extended by transformer models, plus a novel domain-adaptation step - producing silver training data in 9 languages (about 1.05M sentences in total) that improves downstream NER by up to 6 span-F1 points over previous data-creation methods; per-language, per-class counts are published in full.
bad: Silver data is still machine-made: KB coverage and neural errors are baked into every language's corpus, the tagset is the coarse 4-class CoNLL scheme, and the NC-SA licence bars commercial use - a research artefact, not a building block.
didnt: Rejected - NER training data under a non-commercial licence; the knowledge-base-plus-neural silver-data recipe is a known technique, and our extraction is claim-level with citations rather than span-level NER. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Babelscape (point of contact: [email redacted])

name: bharat-raghunathan/indian-foods-dataset
licence: CC0-1.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section).
good: A tidy image-classification set: 4,770 photographs across 15 Indian dish classes (biryani, dosa, dhokla, panipuri and others), uniformly resized to 300x300 with a clean train/test split and a one-line class-label schema - a reasonable starter corpus for food-recognition experiments, public-domain licensed.
bad: Scraped from Google Images with the provenance and label-noise problems that implies (the card's own structure section even names the label field inconsistently); it has no relation to knowledge graphs or knowledge systems at all - the catalogue adjacency is spurious.
didnt: Rejected - a food-photo classification dataset; nothing in it bears on this programme. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: blo05/cleaned_wiki_en
licence: No licence stated - the dataset card consists of a single line of text ('Cleaned wikipedia dataset') with no frontmatter or licensing information.
good: The one thing the source establishes: someone published an English Wikipedia dataset they describe as cleaned - the intent (a pre-cleaned wiki corpus) is a genuinely useful artefact category for retrieval experiments.
bad: Nothing else is verifiable from the source: no cleaning method, no dump date, no schema, no size, no splits and no licence - an unlabelled redistribution of Wikipedia text that no careful project could adopt or even describe beyond its title.
didnt: Rejected - an undocumented dataset; where the source itself contains almost nothing, the honest record is this row stating exactly that, rather than a guess at its contents. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: chaojiang06/wiki_auto
good: WikiAuto is the standard corpus for text simplification, built with a sound bootstrap: crowdworkers manually aligned English-to-Simple-English Wikipedia sentence pairs (the manual config: 565K candidate pairs with aligned / partial / not-aligned labels and GLEU scores), a neural CRF aligner was trained on that seed (paper: Jiang et al., ACL 2020, arXiv 2005.02324), and the aligner then produced the large auto-aligned configs (up to ~592K pairs) with paragraph- and sentence-level alignment maps preserved - human judgement first, machine scale second, provenance of each pair's origin kept in the config structure.
bad: Simplification pairs inherit Simple Wikipedia's coverage and style; truly aligned pairs are a small minority of the manual candidates (about 2.9K of 565K), so most training signal is machine-labelled; the resource serves one NLP task and ages with both Wikipedias.
didnt: Rejected - a text-simplification corpus - while noting its construction pattern (small human-verified seed, model extension, origin preserved per record) is the same shape as our human-ruled, machine-scaled wiki workflows; nothing here needs importing for that. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Ohio State University (point of contact: Chao Jiang, [email redacted])

name: community-datasets/wiki_snippets
licence: Listed as 'unknown' in the card frontmatter; the card body defers to the source datasets' licences (Wiki-40B / Wikipedia dumps).
good: Wikipedia pre-chunked for dense retrieval at serious scale - 17.5M passages from Wiki-40B and 33.8M from the Wikipedia dump at 100-word windows - and, crucially, every snippet carries its exact provenance: wiki_id plus start/end paragraph AND character offsets, article title and section title, so any retrieved passage can be traced back to its precise location in the source article; this is the passage store the DPR-era ecosystem standardised on.
bad: Fixed 100-word windows cut across sentence and argument boundaries; the dump vintage is old, most card sections are unfilled template, and the licence is recorded as unknown at the dataset level - provenance of location is excellent while provenance of rights is not.
didnt: Rejected as a dataset - a frozen passage dump - with light corroboration for its chunk record design: a retrieved passage that knows its article, section and character offsets is citable in a way a bare text chunk never is, the same principle as our page-and-line citations. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: epri/EPRI-Public-Reports-RAG-Database
good: An institution publishing its knowledge the right way for the RAG era: EPRI ships its public reports as a downloadable SQLite database (openrag.db) of chunks with BGE-M3 embeddings and citation-grade metadata on every chunk - product id, content type, the full heading path (h1-h3 plus depth), page start/end, title, publication date, canonical URL, programme, abstract and keywords - together with loader scripts for Qdrant (cloud) and Zvec (local), and a documented path to regenerate the whole database with a different embedding model under the same schema; the corpus is a product an external organisation can ingest without scraping anything.
bad: Non-commercial licence; the corpus is one institution's energy-sector reports, embeddings are single-model by default (re-embedding is a paid API exercise), and the destructive collection-recreate behaviour of the loaders is a footgun the card does at least flag.
didnt: Rejected - an energy-domain corpus under an NC licence - with corroboration for the artefact pattern: a knowledge holder distributing chunks + embeddings + per-chunk provenance (page span, heading path, canonical URL) as one portable database is exactly how a wiki's contents should be exportable, and our exports should carry the same per-chunk citation fields. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: EPRI (Electric Power Research Institute)

name: esdurmus/wiki_lingua
good: WikiLingua is the reference cross-lingual summarisation corpus: article-summary pairs in 18 languages drawn from WikiHow how-to guides (despite the name, the source is WikiHow, not Wikipedia), about 273K pairs across the language configs, each non-English record carrying its English counterpart's URL and section name so the same guide aligns across languages - enabling summarise-in-another-language evaluation without parallel corpora.
bad: How-to guides are a narrow, formulaic domain; summaries are the guides' own step text, so 'abstractive' targets are semi-extractive by construction; per-language sizes vary 40-fold (English 57,945 vs Turkish 1,512), and the corpus is a 2020 snapshot of a commercial how-to site.
didnt: Rejected - a cross-lingual summarisation benchmark; its alignment bookkeeping (each record naming its cross-language counterpart) is good dataset hygiene, not a capability our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Exr0n/wiki-entity-similarity
good: Alias supervision mined from Wikipedia's own link graph: whenever article A links to article B with anchor text C, (B, C) becomes an alias pair - 4.79M pairs at the strictest tier - with three quality levels set by an explicit heuristic ('better articles have more citations', thresholds of 5/10/20 inbound links) and classifier training pairs that are balanced and article-disjoint across splits, so a model cannot memorise entities between train and test; exactly the kind of free, structure-derived ground truth entity resolution needs.
bad: Anchor text is noisy supervision (generic anchors like 'here' or partial names pollute the corpus, mitigated only by the inbound-link threshold); the dump is December 2018, and random negatives make the classification task far easier than real disambiguation, where confusables share context.
didnt: Rejected - an alias-training dataset - with light corroboration for a principle our entity handling already follows: a corpus's own link structure is ground truth about what its names mean, and quality tiers should be set by an explicit, stated heuristic rather than silent filtering. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: facebook/kilt_wikipedia
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card - its Licensing Information section is unfilled (the underlying text is a Wikipedia snapshot).
good: The frozen knowledge source of the KILT benchmark (Petroni et al., 2020): the 2019-08-01 Wikipedia snapshot processed into 5.9M article records that keep everything a provenance-minded system wants - paragraph structure, anchors with paragraph ids and character offsets plus link targets, categories, Wikidata id/label/description/aliases, and the revision identity (pageid, parentid, revid, timestamp) of the exact text; every KILT task (QA, fact checking, entity linking, slot filling, dialogue) is grounded against this one snapshot so results are comparable.
bad: Frozen in August 2019 by design - comparability bought with staleness; 37 GB of downloads for the snapshot; and the card itself is mostly template, its licensing section unfilled, which is careless for a canonical benchmark artefact.
didnt: Rejected - a benchmark substrate, not a system - while noting its record design (anchors with offsets, revision identity, Wikidata aliases on every article) is the provenance standard a frozen corpus should meet, and the contrast with B082's wiki_dpr, whose passages carry no offsets at all. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: facebook/wiki_dpr
good: The DPR passage corpus that defined dense retrieval evaluation: all of English Wikipedia (Dec 2018) split into 21M disjoint 100-word passages, shipped WITH precomputed 768-dimensional embeddings from two training regimes (Natural-Questions-only and multiset) and FAISS index options (exact / compressed / none), so a retrieval experiment could start from download rather than from a week of encoding; the id/text/title discipline made passage-level citation the field's default unit.
bad: An 85 GB, 2018-frozen artefact whose passages carry only an id and a title - no section, no offsets, no revision - so a retrieved passage cannot be traced more precisely than its article; embeddings are inseparable from their two 2020-era encoders, and the NC licence bars commercial reuse.
didnt: Rejected - a frozen retrieval corpus; historically important, and its missing per-passage provenance (contrasted with wiki_snippets at B081 and kilt_wikipedia in this batch, both of which keep offsets) is itself the lesson. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: facebook/wiki_movies
good: WikiMovies is the classic knowledge-base QA benchmark of the memory-network era (Miller et al., 2016): roughly 100K templated questions over 75K movie entities with answers drawn from OMDb, designed so results can be broken down by question type and knowledge representation (KB triples vs raw text) - one of the first datasets built expressly to test whether a system reads structured knowledge or documents better.
bad: Templated questions over a single entertainment domain, generated from the same KB they query - leakage between question generation and answer source makes scores optimistic; the movie KB is a 2016 snapshot, and the task (single-fact lookup) is far below what retrieval systems are now asked to do.
didnt: Rejected - a 2016 templated QA benchmark; of historical interest for memory-network research, with nothing transferable to a citation-first wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fn-aka-mur/llm-japanese-dataset_wikinews
good: A clean, single-purpose slice of the Izumi-lab Japanese instruction dataset: 4,265 instruction/input/output examples for one task - generating a news headline from a Wikinews article - in the standard Alpaca-style schema, small enough to fine-tune or evaluate against in minutes.
bad: A subset of someone else's dataset with no additions of its own; headline generation from the article it titles is a near-extractive task, and 4K examples of one narrow task carry little signal beyond that task.
didnt: Rejected - a small single-task instruction subset; nothing here bears on knowledge systems. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FreedomIntelligence/huatuo_knowledge_graph_qa
good: Scale through structure: 798,444 Chinese medical QA pairs generated by templating questions over a medical knowledge graph, with answers copied from the graph's own entries - so every answer is traceable to a graph fact by construction; part of the HuatuoGPT/Huatuo-26M effort (arXiv 2305.01526) to give Chinese medical LLMs domain grounding, with its graph sources openly credited.
bad: Template questions teach template answers: linguistic diversity is low, the graph's own errors become ground truth at scale, and a model can learn the template distribution instead of medicine; a training corpus for one language and domain, with no evaluation split described in the card.
didnt: Rejected - templated medical QA training data; its answers-are-graph-entries construction is the same traceability trick as B081's graph-built questions, applied to SFT rather than benchmarking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FreedomIntelligence/RAG-Instruct
good: RAG-Instruct targets a real gap - models are rarely taught HOW to use retrieved context: GPT-4o synthesised instruction data over Wikipedia spanning diverse query-document scenarios and RAG task types, and fine-tuning on it lifts Llama-3 models across eleven RAG benchmarks on the card's own table (2WikiMultihopQA +17 points for the 3B model, PopQA +20 for the 8B); the dataset and paper (arXiv 2501.00353) are openly released.
bad: Synthetic supervision from one teacher model: whatever GPT-4o's retrieval habits are - including its failure modes - become the student's ceiling; the card's table also shows how far there is to go (MS MARCO accuracy only 25.0 even after tuning), and instruction tuning for RAG behaviour is a model-layer intervention, not knowledge infrastructure.
didnt: Rejected - synthetic SFT data for retriever-reader behaviour; our answer-quality lever is source discipline and abstention, not fine-tuned context use. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gboleda/wikicorpus
licence: GFDL - GNU Free Documentation License (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section: 'the same license as Wikipedia').
good: The Wikicorpus (Reese, Boleda et al., LREC 2010) was the largest freely available sense-tagged corpus of its era: Catalan, Spanish and English Wikipedia (2006 dump, 750M+ words) annotated with FreeLing lemmas and part-of-speech, and - its distinctive layer - WordNet senses assigned by the UKB disambiguation algorithm, aligned across the three languages through WordNet's InterLingual Index, so lexical-semantic questions could be asked over running text at corpus scale; raw and tagged versions are both published (tagged English alone: 26.35M sentences).
bad: A 2006 Wikipedia snapshot with 2010-era automatic annotation - UKB/FreeLing errors are frozen into every tag; GFDL licensing is awkward for reuse; and sense-tagged text serves lexical semantics research, not knowledge retrieval.
didnt: Rejected - a lexical-semantics corpus; its cross-lingual sense alignment is a WordNet-era technique our claim-level citation model does not use. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Universitat Politecnica de Catalunya (UPC), Barcelona (project homepage: cs.upc.edu/~nlp/wikicorpus)

name: GEM/wiki_auto_asset_turk
licence: Mixed, per component as stated in the card: WikiAuto CC BY-NC 3.0; ASSET CC BY-NC 4.0; TURK GPL v3.0 (frontmatter license: 'other').
good: The GEM benchmark's simplification suite pairs WikiAuto's 483,801 training pairs (the corpus studied above) with the two high-quality human evaluation sets as its tests - ASSET (the same 359 sentences simplified with diverse rewriting transformations, 10 references each lineage) and TURK (lexical-paraphrase-focused references) - and adds challenge sets that perturb the tests (backtranslation, punctuation removal, frequency filtering), so a simplification model is scored on human references and on robustness, not on one automatic split.
bad: A repackaging: the training data is WikiAuto unchanged, the test sets are small by design (359 sentences), and the triple licence mix (two NC licences plus GPL for TURK) makes the bundle awkward to reuse as a whole.
didnt: Rejected - the GEM repackaging of the WikiAuto corpus studied in this batch; its multi-reference + perturbation-challenge test design is good benchmark practice already reflected in our golden-set thinking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GEM/wiki_cat_sum
licence: CC-BY-SA-3.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section).
good: WikiCatSum (Perez-Beltrachini, Liu & Lapata, ACL 2019) is a multi-document summarisation corpus with a twist that matters: for each entity in three domains (animals, companies, film; 56,624 examples) the input is a RANKED cluster of paragraphs from related crawled texts and the target is the entity's Wikipedia summary, with every summary sentence labelled by TOPIC - so a system can be scored not only on text overlap but on whether it covered the right aspects; the GEM edition adds the topic annotations and frames the task as evaluation over noisy, long inputs with factual-correctness metrics alongside ROUGE.
bad: Inputs are deliberately noisy web crawls (the worked example's paragraphs include citation-list fragments), three domains only, and summaries-as-targets inherit Wikipedia's lead-section style; a summarisation benchmark, not knowledge infrastructure.
didnt: Rejected - a summarisation benchmark; its per-sentence topic labels are a nice evaluation refinement (coverage by aspect, not just overlap) that our own answer checks approximate through claim-level citation review. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: University of Edinburgh (with Google Brain co-authors)

name: GEM/wiki_lingua
licence: CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0 (per the GEM data card frontmatter and licensing section; the original esdurmus release in this batch declares CC-BY-3.0).
good: The GEM edition of WikiLingua (Ladhak, Durmus, Cardie & McKeown, Findings of EMNLP 2020): the cross-lingual summarisation benchmark whose gold cross-language alignments were created by aligning the IMAGES illustrating each WikiHow step - a clever grounding signal that avoids machine translation entirely - packaged with unified monolingual and cross-lingual loaders and splits made document-consistent across languages specifically so no document leaks into a test set through another language.
bad: A repackaging of the esdurmus/wiki_lingua corpus studied in this batch under a more restrictive licence line (NC-SA here vs CC-BY-3.0 on the original card - a discrepancy a reuser would have to resolve); the underlying domain remains WikiHow how-to guides.
didnt: Rejected - the GEM repackaging of WikiLingua; recorded for its loader unification, its leakage-proof splitting, and the licence discrepancy between the two cards, which is itself a provenance lesson. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Columbia University (with Stanford University and Cornell University co-authors)

name: glaiveai/RAG-v1
good: A synthetic RAG fine-tuning set (~50K samples) with two design choices worth naming: an explicit ANSWER MODE on every example - the model is trained to either answer only from the provided documents or to combine them with its internal knowledge, making groundedness a declared behaviour rather than a hope - and answers that carry their citations structurally, the cited documents listed first and inline <co: n> tags marking each claim's source.
bad: Fully synthetic (generated on the Glaive platform) with no published quality audit, sampling method or deduplication in the card; 46 lines of documentation for 50K training rows, and citation tags in synthetic answers can teach the FORM of citing without the discipline of citing truly.
didnt: Rejected - synthetic SFT data - with light corroboration for its answer-mode idea: declaring per-answer whether the response is grounded-only or may mix in model knowledge is the same honesty our answer surfaces owe their reader, achieved there by training and here by the abstention/citation gates. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: google-research-datasets/wiki_atomic_edits
good: WikiAtomicEdits decomposes real Wikipedia revision history into atomic operations: each record is a (base sentence, inserted-or-deleted phrase, edited sentence) triple, across eight languages at serious scale (English alone: 13.7M insertions and 9.35M deletions; roughly 43M edits in total) - the corpus behind Faruqui et al.'s EMNLP 2018 work on modelling language and discourse from edits, and still the cleanest large-scale record of WHAT editors actually change when they revise a sentence, one phrase at a time.
bad: Atomic decomposition flattens edits that were really restructurings; insertion/deletion pairs extracted automatically include vandalism-and-revert noise from the raw history; and the card body is largely unfilled template - the schema and counts in the frontmatter carry the whole record.
didnt: Rejected - an edit-modelling corpus - while noting the kinship: our supersession records likewise treat a page's change as a set of claim-level operations with the prior text preserved, rather than an overwrite; nothing here needs importing for that. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Google Research (google-research-datasets)

name: google-research-datasets/wiki_split
