licence: CC-BY-4.0 per the card frontmatter; the card's licensing section states the content is verbatim Wikipedia revision history under CC BY-SA 4.0 - both statements recorded as they appear.
good: WikiSplit (Botha et al., EMNLP 2018) mines supervision from editing behaviour: when a Wikipedia editor split one complex sentence into two, the revision pair becomes a training example - 989,944 of them - for split-and-rephrase models; the supervision is real human editorial judgement harvested at scale from the revision history, with no annotation budget, and the method generalises to any editing operation a community performs repeatedly.
bad: The card concedes 'some inherent noise': the worked example's own split inserts a connective ('Ergo,') that changes the rhetoric, some splits are really deletions or rewrites, and the licence is stated inconsistently between the card's frontmatter (CC-BY-4.0) and its licensing section (CC BY-SA 4.0).
didnt: Rejected - a sentence-rewriting corpus; its construction principle (revision history as free supervision) is already how our wiki treats its own history - as data with provenance, not as noise to discard. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Google Research (google-research-datasets)

name: google/wiki40b
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card frontmatter as opened (the corpus is cleaned Wikipedia text in 40 languages).
good: Wiki-40B is Google's cleaned multilingual Wikipedia corpus for language modelling: forty languages with train/validation/test splits, aggressive cleaning of markup and boilerplate, and - unusually for a pretraining corpus - provenance retained per article (wikidata_id and version_id alongside the text), so any example can be traced to the exact Wikipedia revision it came from; English alone contributes 2.93M articles.
bad: A pretraining corpus, not knowledge infrastructure: text-only, frozen at its 2019 snapshot, and its cleaning choices (which sections survive) are baked in invisibly for most users; the card's frontmatter carries no licence line.
didnt: Rejected - an LM corpus; its wikidata_id + version_id per article is the provenance habit our raw layer already keeps. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Google (dataset paper: Guo et al., 'Wiki-40B: Multilingual Language Model Dataset', LREC 2020)

name: google/WikiProfile
licence: CC-BY-SA-4.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section).
good: WikiProfile profiles parametric factuality at the level of the individual fact: 2,150 subject-object propositions extracted from Wikipedia lead paragraphs (2,125 pages, 9 categories, 19 entity types), each probed by ten questions engineered to separate ENCODING from RECALL - text completion (is it in the weights), direct and naturally-phrased closed-book questions (can it be retrieved verbatim vs conversationally), REVERSE questions with subject and object swapped, multiple choice, and contextual variants - with each fact carrying its page's popularity (2023-2025 page views) and creation date, so recall can be analysed against exposure; the paper's thesis (arXiv 2602.14080) is that recall, not storage, is the bottleneck.
bad: A probe of model weights, not of retrievable knowledge: questions and distractors were Gemini-generated (with search-grounded filtering and manual validation removing under 2%), facts come only from lead paragraphs, and the benchmark measures what a model memorised - the opposite direction from a cited-source system.
didnt: Rejected for adoption - a parametric-knowledge probe - with corroboration for its central distinction: having a fact stored and being able to retrieve it under rephrasing and direction reversal are different properties, and both must be tested - the same asymmetry our supersession coverage measures directionally. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Google (authors: Nitay Calderon, Eyal Ben-David, Zorik Gekhman, Eran Ofek, Gal Yona)

name: Helsinki-NLP/opus_wikipedia
licence: Listed as 'unknown' in the dataset card frontmatter; the licensing section is unfilled.
good: The OPUS collection's Wikipedia bitexts: parallel sentences mined from comparable Wikipedia articles in 20 languages (36 language pairs; the largest detailed configs run to 800K+ pairs), a workhorse corpus for machine-translation training from the OPUS project (Tiedemann, LREC 2012), built by subject-aligned comparable-corpus mining (Wolk & Marasek).
bad: Mined alignments between independently written articles are noisy by nature - comparable is not parallel - and the card leaves licence and curation sections unfilled; a translation-training artefact with no knowledge-system relevance.
didnt: Rejected - an MT bitext corpus; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hqfang/memorybench
good: A name collision worth recording precisely: THIS MemoryBench is a robotics benchmark - scripted demonstrations for three memory-dependent manipulation tasks in RLBench (reopening the drawer you closed, testing 3D spatial memory on the z-axis; putting a block back, 2D x-y memory; rearranging a block, requiring backward reasoning over your own prior actions), 100 training and 25 held-out episodes per task, accompanying SAM2Act+ (Fang et al., arXiv 2501.18564), whose policy adds a memory bank, memory encoder and memory attention so actions condition on prior observations and actions.
bad: Nothing to do with language-model memory: three scripted simulation tasks measure a robot policy's spatial recall, the dataset is small and simulator-bound, and the shared name with THUIR's MemoryBench (B080) guarantees confusion in any catalogue that does not open the source - as this one nearly did.
didnt: Rejected - a robotics dataset; recorded in full because disambiguating it from THUIR/MemoryBench is exactly the kind of collision the completion pass exists to resolve. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: huggan/wikiart
licence: Listed as 'unknown' in the card frontmatter (data files (c) original authors; the card states the dataset may be used only for non-commercial research purposes).
good: The standard WikiArt corpus for computational art history: 81,444 artworks from WikiArt.org, every image labelled on three axes - artist (129 classes, with an explicit Unknown Artist class), genre (11) and style (27) - the training ground for the genre classifiers and art-diffusion models seen elsewhere in this catalogue (the B076 latent-diffusion Space and the B074 WikiArt genre app both descend from it).
bad: Scraped exhibition images under unclear rights (licence 'unknown', research-only note), labels inherited from WikiArt's own crowd taxonomy with its historical biases, and no relation to knowledge systems beyond sharing the 'wiki' prefix.
didnt: Rejected - an art-image classification corpus; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HuggingFaceTB/issues-kaggle-notebooks
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card frontmatter (a reformatted slice of bigcode/StarCoder2-Extras; the Kaggle notebooks component is described in the card as sourced from Meta Kaggle Code, Apache 2.0 upstream).
good: Two large, carefully cleaned code-adjacent corpora from the StarCoder2 effort, reformatted from special-token form into natural text: 15.5M GitHub issue discussions (about 11B tokens, from GH Archive) structured as title/question/answers/status threads, and 580K Kaggle notebooks (about 1.7B tokens) rendered as Markdown with their referenced datasets' descriptions prepended - with documented curation: bot and short-content filtering, multi-party discussion requirements, StarPII anonymisation, and deduplication that cut notebook volume by 78%.
bad: Training data for code models, with the residual PII and licence heterogeneity of any web-scale scrape (the card's anonymisation sentence even garbles what was removed versus preserved); issue threads are other projects' working records, not knowledge curated for reuse.
didnt: Rejected - code-LM training corpora; the notebook-to-Markdown normalisation is competent data engineering, not a knowledge capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: iapp/iapp_wiki_qa_squad
licence: MIT for the dataset as published (iApp's questions, answer spans and assembly, per the card's licence table); the context column is Thai Wikipedia text under CC BY-SA and stays under CC BY-SA in any redistribution - the layering is stated explicitly in the card and its LICENSE.
good: A small dataset with exemplary verification discipline: 7,242 Thai extractive-QA questions over 1,912 Thai Wikipedia articles, human-annotated in 2019 (iApp Technology), in SQuAD format where every answer span is EXACT - the card states context[answer_start:answer_end] == text holds for every row with no exceptions, and ships validate.py to prove it (23 checks, run live against the canonical source, including row-by-row equality with the original release after a packaging migration); splits are article-level so no article leaks across train/test; and the card discloses, in plain language, that the canonical source carries annotator account identifiers and payment fields which the published projection strips - with validate.py FAILING if they ever appear - and that an earlier revision of the card itself once printed a real identifier and payment record, now removed.
bad: Extractive QA over one language's Wikipedia is a narrow task; answers are capped at 100 characters by the SQuAD conversion, biasing toward factoid spans; and the dataset needed a 2026 rescue at all because its original loading-script packaging silently broke when the datasets library dropped script support - a reminder that packaging is part of a dataset's durability.
didnt: Rejected as a dataset - with corroboration for three of its practices, each of which our wiki machinery already honours in its own terms: machine-checked span-to-source exactness (our citation checks), licence layering stated per column rather than per dataset, and errors in one's own documentation admitted in the document itself (our corrections ledger). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ikawrakow/imatrix-from-wiki-train
good: Calibration artefacts for better LLM quantisation: importance matrices (imatrix) for llama.cpp's improved quantisation schemes, computed over the WikiText training text (wiki.train.raw), so models can be quantised (the card's example: Mixtral-8x7B to Q4_K_M) with less quality loss than naive rounding - a small, genuinely useful community service for local inference.
bad: A pure keyword collision: 'wiki' here is WikiText calibration text, the artefacts are opaque numeric matrices per model, and nothing in the repo concerns knowledge, retrieval or memory in the information sense.
didnt: Rejected - quantisation calibration files; recorded to close the collision honestly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jean-Baptiste/wikiner_fr
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card.
good: The French slice of WikiNER (Nothman et al., Artificial Intelligence 2013): 120,682 training sentences of French Wikipedia text with silver-standard named-entity tags (LOC, PER, ORG, MISC) derived automatically from Wikipedia's internal links and category structure - one of the earliest demonstrations that an encyclopaedia's own markup is free annotation, and for years the standard French NER training resource.
bad: Silver labels inherit Wikipedia link conventions (first-mention linking, inconsistent MISC), the tagset is the coarse 4-class scheme, and the data is a 2012-era snapshot; superseded in method by WikiNEuRal (B081), which exists precisely to improve on this generation of silver data.
didnt: Rejected - silver NER training data; its link-derived annotation principle is the same one B082's wiki-entity-similarity exploits, recorded there. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: John6666/knowledge_base_md_for_rag_1
licence: MIT (per the dataset card frontmatter and License section).
good: A hobbyist knowledge base in exactly our genre: a collection of self-contained Markdown 'knowledge packs' about Hugging Face itself - one topic per file, YAML front matter (topic, source, timestamp), and a fixed section discipline (background, official docs/blog/papers, model/dataset/Space cards, community and GitHub Q&A, implementation tips, and a Limitations and open questions section in every pack) - designed to be attached directly as LLM context or chunked and embedded for RAG, with sources separated by authority (official vs community) inside each file.
bad: A personal curation with undefined vetting ('vetted community sources' is asserted, not specified), unstandardised filenames, no per-claim citation to the underlying documents, and coverage bounded by one maintainer's HF interests - the form is right and the verification layer is absent.
didnt: Rejected - a personal notes collection - while recording that its per-pack structure (front matter, authority-separated sections, a mandatory limitations section) independently converges on the shape our own compiled wiki pages take, minus the citation machinery that makes ours trustworthy. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: KlingTeam/Context-as-Memory-Dataset
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card as opened (the card consists of the paper title, venue and links only).
good: The dataset behind a SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 paper from the Kling team on long interactive video generation: 'context as memory' - retrieving relevant prior frames/context so a generated video stays scene-consistent over long horizons, the video analogue of retrieval-augmented memory; its release as a public dataset lets other video models be tested on the same long-horizon consistency problem.
bad: A video-generation artefact: nothing in the card (four lines: title, venue, two links) documents size, format or licence, and the 'memory' here is frame retrieval for visual consistency - a different problem from knowledge memory, sharing only the retrieval pattern and the name.
didnt: Rejected - a video-generation dataset from an unrelated field; recorded because its title pattern (X-as-Memory) is what brought it into a knowledge-memory catalogue. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: legacy-datasets/wikipedia
licence: CC-BY-SA-3.0 and GFDL (per the dataset card frontmatter - Wikipedia's own dual licensing).
good: The canonical Hugging Face Wikipedia dataset in its legacy form: the 2022-03-01 dump processed into clean id/url/title/text records for 300+ language editions (English 6.46M articles) - for years the default text substrate for language-model training and the reference point every other corpus in this section (Wiki-40B, wiki_snippets, wiki_dpr) defines itself against.
bad: Raw article text only: no structure, no links, no revision metadata beyond the dump date in the config name; superseded packaging (hence 'legacy'), and a dump is a starting material, not a knowledge system.
didnt: Rejected - a dump redistribution; recorded as the substrate artefact of this whole dataset run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-jp/extraction-wiki-ja
good: A national-lab instruction dataset for a specific skill: information extraction and structuring from Japanese Wikipedia text, built by LLM-jp (Japan's national LLM project) at growing scale (v0.3: 89,663 four-turn dialogues), with its construction stated transparently in the card - instructions generated by prompting Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct with Wikipedia passages, responses generated by the same model, both filtered by that model.
bad: A fully self-referential pipeline: one model writes the questions, writes the answers and grades both, so its extraction habits and errors are laundered into 'ground truth' with no human or source-side verification pass described; extraction targets are whatever the generator found salient in each passage.
didnt: Rejected - synthetic extraction SFT data; its card is a clean example of why our ingest insists on sources opened and checked independently of the model that summarised them. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: LLM-jp (National Institute of Informatics, Japan - contact [email redacted])

name: llmware/rag_instruct_test_dataset2_financial_0.1
good: A hand-written, closed-context RAG test set from llmware: 100 samples whose short contexts (earnings releases, financial tables, market news; 100-500 tokens) support questions requiring fact extraction, key-value pull, small arithmetic and ordering - and, notably, questions whose correct behaviour is recognising that the information is NOT in the passage; samples were written bespoke for the test (names masked or invented), making it a clean, contamination-free probe of basic RAG competence for any model, designed alongside llmware's BLING instruct models.
bad: One hundred samples is a smoke test, not a benchmark - no statistical resolution, one domain, contexts far shorter than real retrieval output; a series fragment (test dataset 2, version 0.1) rather than a maintained evaluation suite.
didnt: Rejected as an artefact - a 100-sample probe - with light corroboration for its design: a RAG test set that scores not-in-source recognition alongside extraction is testing abstention, the behaviour our Ask door is built around. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llmware/rag_instruct_test_dataset_0.1
good: The general sibling of B083's financial test set: llmware's basic enterprise RAG test - 100 hand-written samples over short contexts (financial news, earnings releases, contracts, invoices, technical articles) for closed-context QA, key-value extraction and bullet summarisation - shipped WITH its own published scoreboard, which is the honest part: GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct and Claude Instant all score a flat 100 while llmware's own 1B-class BLING models score 30-77 (on CPU, with timings), so the card documents both the test and its ceiling.
bad: At 100 samples with frontier models saturating it, the set can only smoke-test small models; no abstention or adversarial cases are described in this basic version, and scores are the vendor's own runs on the vendor's own test.
didnt: Rejected - a vendor smoke test; its published saturation table is the useful artefact, corroborating that tiny fixed test sets measure the test, not the system, once models pass them. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: m3hrdadfi/wiki_summary
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section).
good: WikiSummary: 56,366 Persian Wikipedia articles paired with their lead-section 'highlights' as reference summaries, prepared for Persian summarisation research (the companion work fine-tunes a BERT2BERT model, ParsBERT-based, on it) - one of the early resources that gave a lower-resource language a real summarisation benchmark, with source links retained per article.
bad: Lengths were cut hard to fit the model (articles to 512 tokens, highlights to 128), so the 'summary' task is really lead-paragraph prediction on truncated text; the card body is largely the unfilled template (its Languages line reads 'The text in this dataset is in Percy'), and lead-as-summary inherits Wikipedia's lead-section conventions.
didnt: Rejected - a single-language summarisation corpus; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: macpaw-research/mac-app-store-apps-release-notes
licence: MIT (per the dataset card frontmatter and card body).
good: A tidy software-analytics corpus from MacPaw's research arm: the release-notes text of 24,000+ Mac App Store apps, extracted from store metadata collected via the iTunes Search API (Dec 2023 - Jan 2024), cleaned from 87,000+ raw samples and deduplicated on the notes text itself, with language classification (75% English, 13% German) and app identity fields (name, bundle ID, version dates) - and a card that declares its own status in the first line: a static snapshot, not refreshed on a schedule.
bad: A 'notes' keyword collision - these are app changelogs, not knowledge; the snapshot is frozen at early 2024, collection was shaped by API workarounds (search-term engineering to dodge limits and exclude games), and most of the card's later sections remain commented-out template.
didnt: Rejected - an app-store text corpus; its snapshot-status banner is good card hygiene, nothing more for us. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: MacPaw (curated by MacPaw Way Ltd.; contact [email redacted])

name: MaziyarPanahi/Jev-RAG-Claim-Verification-130K
licence: Listed as 'other' in the card frontmatter: rows record 'mit-with-upstream-review-required' for the seed data (the original RAGTruth project is MIT, Particle Media 2023); the card states it grants no additional redistribution or training rights and that third-party text/model outputs and provider terms need separate consideration.
good: A claim-verification corpus built with unusual evidentiary discipline: 130,000 typed decisions derived from RAGTruth's human hallucination-span annotations (source pinned to an exact revision), organised into four task families - sentence-level claim-span grounding (81,528), hallucination-type presence (24,236), whole-response grounding (12,118) and response quality incl. incorrect refusals (12,118) - where every row keeps the source-derived reference labels and the verifier's (jev-1.13.0) predictions in SEPARATE columns, neither silently substituted for the other, and preserves all 21,181 disagreements (1,265 of them at provider confidence >=0.90) for inspection; the semantics are stated with care (no_annotated_hallucination means no marked span overlaps, not proven truth), the audit reports agreement (83.71%) next to majority-label baselines so the number cannot flatter itself, and the card publishes its own split-leakage audit - 349 shared query/context pairs and 67 identical requests cross splits - with instructions to rebuild splits by connected components, explicitly forbidding the description 'leakage-free'.
bad: Derived decisions, not new annotation: 130,000 rows unfold from only 12,118 upstream responses over 2,019 contexts, classes are heavily imbalanced (response quality is 99.56% majority-label), the verifier's scores are uncalibrated provider outputs, and response-quality 'good' certifies only the absence of marked defects - all of which the card itself states, which is the point, but it bounds what the corpus can evidence.
didnt: Rejected for adoption - a derived evaluation corpus, not a capability - with strong corroboration for four practices our verification machinery shares: reference and prediction never merged into one column, disagreements preserved rather than resolved silently, agreement reported against the majority baseline, and a published leakage audit with the honest label withheld until earned. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: merve/my_notes
good: A student's graduate-school lecture notes published as a dataset: cheatsheets and notes across data science, machine learning (following Mitchell's textbook), statistics, deep learning, image processing and data structures & algorithms - compiled per-lecture and into single PDFs, shared for exam and interview revision with an open invitation to improve the handwritten scans by pull request; a likeable piece of open study culture with real download traction (4,149 per the catalogue).
bad: A 'notes' keyword collision: personal revision material ('not intended to teach a topic from scratch', per the card), partly handwritten scans of varying legibility, no structure a knowledge system could build on.
didnt: Rejected - a personal study-notes upload; recorded to close the collision. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: michaelauli/wiki_bio
licence: CC-BY-SA-3.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section).
good: WikiBio (Lebret, Grangier & Auli 2016): 728,321 Wikipedia biographies aligned as table-to-text pairs - the article's infobox, kept as a structured table (column headers, row numbers, cell contents), against its first paragraph - the dataset that launched neural data-to-text generation as a research area, and still a clean example of exploiting an encyclopaedia's own parallel structure (structured infobox / prose lead) as supervision with no manual annotation.
bad: The alignment is noisy by construction: lead paragraphs routinely say things the infobox does not (and vice versa), teaching models to hallucinate plausible details - the exact failure this dataset family became famous for; text is tokenised 2016-style (-lrb-/-rrb- artefacts throughout).
didnt: Rejected - a generation-training corpus; its infobox-to-lead hallucination lesson is already part of the field's record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: microsoft/wiki_qa
licence: Microsoft Research Data License Agreement for the WikiQA Corpus (full text reproduced in the dataset card): use, copy, modify and distribute for research and technology development purposes only; no use directly in a commercial product without Microsoft's permission; derivatives must carry the same terms and change notices.
good: WikiQA (Yang, Yih & Meek, EMNLP 2015): Microsoft Research's challenge set for open-domain QA as answer-sentence selection - 29,258 question/sentence pairs where the questions are real user queries (from Bing logs), the candidate sentences come from the summary paragraphs of the Wikipedia pages those queries led to, and crowdsourced labels mark which sentences actually answer the question; a foundational benchmark whose realism (real questions, naturally occurring candidate sentences, many questions with NO correct candidate) shaped a decade of QA evaluation.
bad: Sentence selection is a 2015 framing of QA - no generation, no multi-hop, no citations; labels are binary and noisy at the margins, the corpus is small by current standards, and the research-only licence (no commercial product use) bounds reuse.
didnt: Rejected - a historical QA benchmark under a research-only licence; its no-correct-candidate realism anticipates abstention evaluation, noted at B080/B083 in stronger modern forms. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Microsoft Research

name: musabg/wikipedia-tr-summarization
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card (the underlying text is Turkish Wikipedia).
good: A large Turkish summarisation corpus: 119,110 article/summary pairs built from the 2023 Turkish Wikipedia dump with a documented pipeline (standard cleaner plus custom stripping of references sections, mT5-tokenised length filtering to 300-900 tokens) - useful scale for a mid-resource language, with the full method repeated in Turkish in the same card.
bad: The reference summaries are GPT-3.5-Turbo generations, not human text or article leads: the dataset teaches and measures imitation of one model's summarisation habits, errors included, with no quality audit reported; articles over 900 tokens are truncated at a paragraph boundary, so some 'summaries' describe partial articles.
didnt: Rejected - synthetic-reference summarisation data; the same generator-as-reference pattern recorded at B082 (RAG-Instruct) and B083 (llm-jp). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nasa-gesdisc/nasa-eo-knowledge-graph
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter; the v2 authorship layer is sourced from OpenAlex, CC0, noted in the card).
good: A production agency knowledge graph at real scale: NASA's Earth-observation graph links 8,058 datasets (mostly DAAC-archived) to the instruments, platforms, projects, data centers and science keywords around them and - its stated purpose - to the scientific publications that USE them (55,313 USES_DATASET edges inside 982,434 citations), so dataset influence, research trends and collaboration structure become queryable; v2.0.0 (June 2026) grew it to 1,409,253 nodes and 5.84M relationships by adding the OpenAlex authorship layer (905,086 authors, 35,435 institutions with ORCID/ROR identifiers) - and it keeps its epistemics clean: edges computed from the graph's own structure (dataset co-usage, author/institution works-with) are flagged derived:true with weights, kept separable from sourced facts, exports ship in JSON/GraphML/Cypher with published SHA-256 checksums, and the card states OpenAlex's author-disambiguation failure mode plainly.
bad: A domain artefact for Earth science, string-typed properties throughout (chosen for cross-database compatibility), and the citation-expansion layer trades completeness for depth (expansion publications may lack abstracts/authors present in the core set); the graph answers who-used-what, not what is true.
didnt: Rejected as an artefact for adoption - a domain dataset - with corroboration for two of its disciplines that our graph machinery shares: derived edges labelled as derived (never mingled with sourced assertions) with their evidence weight attached, and checksummed exports so a consumer can verify the artefact is the artefact. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: NASA GES DISC (Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center)

name: neulab/wiki_asp
good: WikiAsp (Hayashi et al., from CMU's NeuLab): aspect-based summarisation over Wikipedia - for each article in 20 domains (film, company, town, animal, software, ...), the source text is the article's referenced sentences and the target is a SET of summaries, one per aspect (a film's plot, cast, reception; a town's geography, history, demographics), where the aspects are the article's own section structure; roughly 320K examples in total. It formalises a genuinely useful idea: a good summary of a structured document is not one paragraph but a bundle of facet summaries, and Wikipedia's headings provide the facet supervision for free.
bad: Aspects inherited from section headings are uneven (idiosyncratic headings, missing facets, plot-heavy films), targets are the section texts themselves (long, not abstractive summaries), and the per-domain dumps run to gigabytes of near-duplicate boilerplate phrasing; a summarisation benchmark, not knowledge infrastructure.
didnt: Rejected - a summarisation dataset; the facet-summary framing converges with per-section reading of structured pages and needs nothing from us. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Carnegie Mellon University (NeuLab)

name: neural-bridge/rag-dataset-1200
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the dataset card; users must also abide by the Falcon RefinedWeb terms of use).
good: A small, simple RAG fine-tuning set from Neural Bridge AI: 1,200 context/question/answer triples whose contexts are Falcon RefinedWeb passages and whose questions and answers were generated by GPT-4 - the starter size of a four-dataset family, harmless and clearly licensed for teaching a model the shape of grounded answering.
bad: The card is mostly a generic marketing essay about RAG rather than documentation of this data (no sampling, filtering or quality process is described); GPT-4-generated QA over web passages inherits both web noise and generator error, and 1,200 examples is a demo quantity.
didnt: Rejected - synthetic RAG SFT data with boilerplate documentation; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neural-bridge/rag-dataset-12000
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the dataset card; users must also abide by the Falcon RefinedWeb terms of use).
good: The 10x sibling of rag-dataset-1200: 12,000 context/question/answer triples (RefinedWeb contexts, GPT-4-generated questions and answers) for fine-tuning RAG-shaped answering, Apache-2.0, with clean splits - a usable commodity dataset of its kind.
bad: The documentation is the family's shared boilerplate with the numbers swapped - the same generic RAG essay, nothing about how the larger set was sampled or checked relative to the smaller - so the card evidences packaging, not curation; synthetic QA quality is bounded by its generator and unaudited here.
didnt: Rejected - the same synthetic SFT commodity at a larger size; recorded separately because the catalogue lists it separately, not because it differs materially. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neural-bridge/rag-full-20000
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the dataset card; users must also abide by the Falcon RefinedWeb, GSM8K and RAG Hallucination Dataset terms of use).
good: The family's combined training file: the sibling datasets merged into a single-feature format - one clear_prompt string per example with ##CONTEXT## / ##QUESTION## / ##ANSWER## delimiters, folding in GSM8K problems and the hallucination-refusal examples alongside the RefinedWeb QA - a pragmatic 'everything in one file' SFT pack for RAG behaviour including refusal.
bad: The merge discards the structure it merges (one opaque string; which source an example came from is no longer a field), the name says 20000 while the splits total 21,792, and the card's provenance sentence for its QA content is garbled into self-contradiction - the packaging actively degrades the (already thin) documentation of its parts.
didnt: Rejected - a lossy repackaging of the three sibling sets; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neural-bridge/rag-hallucination-dataset-1000
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the dataset card; users must also abide by the Falcon RefinedWeb terms of use).
good: A thousand abstention lessons: context/question/answer triples where the question was deliberately generated (by GPT-4, over RefinedWeb contexts) to be UNANSWERABLE from the context, and the target answer is uniformly 'This question cannot be answered.' - a crude but real training signal that refusing is a behaviour a RAG model can be taught, distributed as a standalone set and folded into the family's combined pack.
bad: One fixed refusal string for every case teaches the form of abstention without its judgement (no reasons, no partial answers, no 'the context covers X but not Y'), the unanswerability is generator-asserted rather than verified, and 1,000 examples of a single sentence is a narrow signal that can as easily teach over-refusal.
didnt: Rejected as data - with light corroboration for its premise: abstention is trainable behaviour, which the field's better instruments (B083's llmware not-in-source cases, graded by evidence) implement with the reasoning left in. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: omarkamali/wikipedia-monthly
licence: No licence field appears in the dataset card frontmatter as opened (the content is Wikipedia text).
good: Wikipedia as a living dataset rather than a frozen dump: a monthly-refreshed, multilingual mirror of Wikipedia in Hugging Face-native form - a 'latest' config per language edition (300+), each carrying the full article set (English 7.25M articles) plus fixed 1k/5k/10k sample splits for quick experiments. The operational idea is the valuable part: downstream users pin a monthly snapshot instead of everyone re-processing raw dumps on their own schedules.
bad: A mirror, not a curation: whatever Wikipedia's current state is flows in monthly (vandalism windows, mid-edit articles), the card is 76K lines of generated config with no editorial documentation of cleaning choices, and consumers inherit dump-scale storage for marginal freshness gains unless they truly need monthly cadence.
didnt: Rejected - a redistribution with a refresh cadence; the cadence idea is noted against B083's frozen legacy dump, and our own corpus is deliberately source-pinned rather than rolling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: open-phi/rag-textbook-instruct-full
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card.
good: An instruction-tuning set in the Open-Phi 'textbook' style: 8,340 formatted prompt/completion pairs (117 MB) whose name ties them to a retrieval-augmented-generation textbook - the phi-family idea that textbook-quality synthetic instruction data beats raw web text for teaching a small model, applied to RAG subject matter.
bad: The dataset documents nothing about itself: the card body is literally '[More Information needed]', no source textbook is identified, no generation or filtering process is described, and there is no licence - a consumer can verify nothing except the schema and the row count.
didnt: Rejected - an undocumented SFT file; recorded exactly as thinly as its own card allows, which is the honest completion. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OxAISH-AL-LLM/wiki_toxic
good: The Jigsaw Toxic Comment corpus in its simplest usable form: 223,549 Wikipedia talk-page comments from the 2017/18 Kaggle Toxic Comment Classification Challenge, cleaned and collapsed from the original six overlapping labels to a single binary toxic/non-toxic label with ready train/validation/test splits - a durable baseline dataset for content-moderation research, where 'wiki' means Wikipedia's own discussion pages and their moderation problem.
bad: Binarising six graded labels (toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity_hate) into one bit destroys the distinctions moderation actually needs; the underlying crowdsourced labels carry the well-documented identity-term biases of the original challenge, and most of the card's consideration sections are unfilled template.
didnt: Rejected - a moderation classification corpus; nothing transfers to a knowledge system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rag-datasets/rag-mini-bioasq
good: A pocket RAG evaluation kit for the biomedical domain: a passage corpus plus a question-answer test set derived from BioASQ (the biomedical QA challenge), packaged in the standard two-config shape (text-corpus for indexing, question-answer-passages for testing) so a retrieval pipeline can be smoke-tested end-to-end in minutes; the card honestly points to a successor version that fixes NaNs in its corpus.
bad: 'Mini' means toy-scale and self-generated subsets of a challenge training set (with known NaN defects in this version); scores on it evidence plumbing, not biomedical retrieval quality.
didnt: Rejected - a teaching-scale eval kit; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rag-datasets/rag-mini-wikipedia
good: The general-domain sibling of rag-mini-bioasq: a mini Wikipedia passage corpus plus a QA test set (derived from the Kaggle question-answer dataset) in the same two-config shape - index the passages, run the questions, check the plumbing of a DPR-style pipeline on a laptop-scale artefact.
bad: A four-line card and a toy corpus: the subset generation is a script's output with no sampling documentation, and nothing measured on it generalises beyond 'the pipeline runs'.
didnt: Rejected - a teaching-scale eval kit; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ragavsachdeva/popmanga_test
licence: No licence stated in any source opened (the Hugging Face repository is gated; the papers do not state a dataset licence in the material reviewed).
good: PopManga is the evaluation dataset behind the Manga Whisperer line of work (Oxford VGG): manga pages annotated for automatic transcription - speech-bubble detection and text, text-to-tail association (which bubble belongs to which speaker) and character identity - built to make comics accessible to visually impaired readers by generating faithful textual transcriptions; the follow-up (Magiv2, arXiv 2408.00298) extends it chapter-wide as PopManga-X with a character bank (PopCharacters, 11K+ characters) so naming consistency can be evaluated across a whole chapter, not per page.
bad: An accessibility-vision benchmark from an unrelated field; the dataset's HF distribution is gated, annotations centre on a specific commercial-manga sample, and nothing in it touches text knowledge systems - it entered this catalogue on the 'rag' in its author's name (ragavsachdeva), the purest name collision of the run.
didnt: Rejected - a manga-transcription benchmark; recorded with its verification level stated plainly (papers opened, repository gated) rather than dressed up as a full opening. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: raghavprabhakar/commonsense-embodied-ai
good: A commonsense-reasoning QA dataset aimed at embodied agents: questions about the physical affordances of objects (what can be grasped, opened, sat on, poured from) - the kind of tacit physical knowledge a household robot needs and text corpora rarely state; published at 100K-1M scale under MIT with its project code (COAT) linked.
bad: The card documents almost nothing (no construction method, no example, no splits table), so the dataset's quality is unverifiable from its own record; affordance QA for robots is adjacent to, not part of, knowledge-memory infrastructure.
didnt: Rejected - an embodied-AI dataset with a two-line card; recorded as found. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Salesforce/wikisql
licence: Listed as 'unknown' in the dataset card frontmatter; the card's licensing section is unfilled.
good: WikiSQL (Zhong, Xiong & Socher 2017, the Seq2SQL paper): 80,654 crowd-annotated natural-language questions paired with SQL queries over 24,241 real Wikipedia tables, with the query stored structurally (select column, aggregation, conditions) as well as in human-readable form, and tables split disjointly across train/test so systems must generalise to unseen schemas - the dataset that made text-to-SQL a mainstream task; B078's nomic-ai Atlas 'wikisql' map was a visualisation of queries drawn from this corpus.
bad: The SQL dialect is deliberately minimal (single table, no joins, no nesting, a handful of aggregations), so success on WikiSQL long ago stopped evidencing real database competence; questions were crowd-written to fit the constrained grammar, and the licence was never cleanly stated on the card.
didnt: Rejected - a text-to-SQL benchmark; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Salesforce Research (authors: Victor Zhong, Caiming Xiong, Richard Socher)

name: Salesforce/wikitext
licence: Stated inconsistently in the card: the frontmatter lists CC-BY-SA-3.0 and GFDL; the licensing section states CC BY-SA 4.0. Both are recorded as found.
good: WikiText (Merity et al. 2016): the language-modelling benchmark built from Wikipedia's verified Good and Featured articles - over 100 million tokens in WikiText-103 - designed against the Penn Treebank's distortions: full articles (so long-range dependencies exist), original case, punctuation and numbers retained, a realistic vocabulary, in raw and tokenised variants; for years the standard yardstick for LM perplexity, and the source of the wiki.train.raw file that B083's imatrix artefacts were calibrated on.
bad: A 2016 perplexity benchmark: the field long ago saturated and moved past it, its 'verified articles' are a quality-skewed slice of Wikipedia, and a token stream is pretraining fodder, not knowledge infrastructure.
didnt: Rejected - an LM benchmark corpus; recorded as the ancestor artefact several other rows in this run depend on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Salesforce Research (authors: Stephen Merity, Caiming Xiong, James Bradbury, Richard Socher)

name: seungheondoh/music-wiki
licence: MIT (per the dataset card frontmatter; the page texts are Wikipedia's, the entity data MusicBrainz's).
good: A music-domain text corpus built by graph traversal: starting from a Wikipedia music seed page, recursively following referenced pages to depth 20 (167,890 pages), then inverting the direction - taking MusicBrainz's 11M music entities as the index and crawling the corresponding Wikipedia pages (193K) - for 361K pages aligned loosely to a structured music KB (releases, artists, labels, works, genres, instruments as separate splits), groundwork for a music text database / music-language modelling.
bad: Crawl-depth-20 from a seed drifts far off-topic, the two halves overlap without a stated dedup, alignment to MusicBrainz entities is by construction loose (a page per entity attempt, not a verified join), and the card gives no quality or coverage audit - a researcher's working corpus, not a maintained resource.
didnt: Rejected - a domain crawl corpus; the entity-first inversion (start from the KB, fetch the text) is a neat construction trick, noted and not needed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: stanfordnlp/wikitablequestions
licence: Stated inconsistently in the card: the frontmatter lists CC-BY-4.0; the licensing section states Creative Commons Attribution Share Alike 4.0 International. Both are recorded as found.
good: WikiTableQuestions (Pasupat & Liang, ACL 2015): 22,033 crowdsourced questions over 2,108 Wikipedia tables whose answers require compositional operations over the table - filtering, superlatives, aggregation, arithmetic, row joins - rather than cell lookup, with answers as denotations (the value, not a program), which made it the founding benchmark for semantic parsing on semi-structured data and still a clean test of table reasoning; five fixed random splits are shipped for variance reporting.
bad: Tables are small and clean by construction, questions were elicited to be compositional (a biased sample of what people ask tables), and denotation accuracy credits lucky guesses equally with correct reasoning - limits the authors' own research programme spent years addressing.
didnt: Rejected - a table-QA benchmark; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Stanford University (authors: Panupong Pasupat, Percy Liang)

name: starmpcc/Asclepius-Synthetic-Clinical-Notes
licence: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter and licensing section).
good: Asclepius (Kweon et al. 2023) attacks a real constraint head-on: clinical LLMs need discharge summaries, and real ones cannot be shared - so the notes are SYNTHESIsed by GPT-3.5 from published case reports (PMC-Patients), then turned into 157K instruction pairs across eight clinical NLP tasks (entity recognition, abbreviation expansion, temporal extraction, coreference, relation extraction, paraphrase, summary, QA), yielding a publicly shareable clinical training corpus and a model family trained on it; the MIMIC-III-based variant is distributed through PhysioNet's credentialled route instead - the privacy boundary is handled by construction, not by policy.
bad: Synthetic notes inherit GPT-3.5's clinical habits and simplifications (real discharge summaries are messier, more abbreviated, more contradictory), the questions and answers are also model-generated and unverified against the notes at scale, and NC-SA licensing bounds reuse; a model can learn the genre without learning the medicine.
didnt: Rejected - a clinical SFT corpus under a non-commercial licence; its synthesis-for-shareability pattern is the clinical echo of our fictional public demo corpus, noted without need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Technoculture/synthetic-clinical-notes-embedded
licence: MIT per the derivative's own frontmatter - recorded with the conflict stated: the upstream dataset it post-processes (starmpcc/Asclepius-Synthetic-Clinical-Notes) is CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, whose non-commercial ShareAlike terms an MIT re-release does not satisfy; the card does not address this.
good: A convenience derivative of Asclepius: the same 158K clinical instruction pairs converted to Alpaca format with precomputed BGE-small embeddings for both input and output columns (saving every consumer the embedding pass), a clean published lineage diagram back to PubMed Central, and even a GPT-4 'diversity rating' annotation pass with its prompt reproduced in the card.
bad: Two substantive faults: the diversity table shows a uniform rating of 5 on every sampled row, which evidences a rating pass that did not discriminate; and the licence is wrong on its face - an MIT claim over a CC-BY-NC-SA upstream is exactly the kind of silent relicensing that poisons downstream use, whatever the packager intended.
didnt: Rejected - a derivative with a licence conflict and a non-discriminating quality pass; its lineage diagram is good practice wrapped around both. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: unimelb-nlp/wikiann
licence: Listed as 'unknown' in the dataset card frontmatter.
good: WikiANN (also known as PAN-X): named-entity recognition data for 176+ languages built from Wikipedia by transferring annotations through cross-lingual links and knowledge-base properties - PER/ORG/LOC tags in BIO form with a 'spans' field preserving the source annotation - tiered by Wikipedia size (100-sentence sets for the smallest languages up to 20K/10K/10K for the largest) into the balanced benchmark that made massively multilingual NER evaluation possible; B078's nomic-ai 'wikiann' Atlas map was an embedding visualisation of this dataset's sentences.
bad: Silver-standard throughout: labels are only as good as Wikipedia's link graph and KB coverage in each language (heavily skewed to famous entities), the three-class scheme is coarse, and small-language tiers of 100 sentences are smoke tests rather than training data.
didnt: Rejected - multilingual NER silver data; the family record is completed by B081's WikiNEuRal and B083's WikiNER rows. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: University of Melbourne (unimelb-nlp; Pan et al. 2017, with the balanced version by Rahimi, Li & Tiedemann 2019)

name: usc-isi/WikiConvert
licence: MIT (per the dataset card frontmatter and License section).
good: Wiki-Convert (Thawani et al., EMNLP 2021) mines a free annotation layer hiding in Wikipedia's markup: the {{Convert}} template, which editors use to render a quantity in two units, marks numbers that are genuine cardinal quantities - so 900,000+ English Wikipedia sentences arrive with precise number spans (offset, length, magnitude) distinguishing real quantities from nominal/ordinal numbers; the paper uses it to show that better number encodings (exponent embeddings best) improve masked-word prediction by over 2 points on number-bearing sentences, generalising beyond them - numeracy measurably enhancing literacy.
bad: One narrow signal (numbers in sentences) from one template's usage conventions; coverage is wherever editors bothered with {{Convert}}, and the literacy gains, while real, belong to the encoder comparison, not the dataset alone.
didnt: Rejected - a numeracy research dataset; its template-as-annotation trick is the same Wikipedia-markup exploitation as WikiNER/WikiANN, recorded across those rows. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: USC Information Sciences Institute (authors: Avijit Thawani, Jay Pujara, Filip Ilievski)

name: vibrantlabsai/ragas-wikiqa
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card.
good: A small RAG-evaluation artefact in the Ragas style: 232 WikiQA-derived items, each carrying the question, a correct and an incorrect answer, the retrieved context, and two model generations side by side - generated_with_rag and generated_without_rag - so the marginal value of retrieval can be inspected and scored per question rather than asserted in aggregate.
bad: Two hundred and thirty-two rows with an empty card ('[More Information needed]'), no stated generation models, prompts, or scoring, and no licence - an experiment's residue, useful as a schema sketch and nothing more.
didnt: Rejected - an undocumented eval residue; the with/without-RAG paired-generation schema is the one idea, already standard practice. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vishnun/NLP-KnowledgeGraph
licence: CC0-1.0 (per the dataset card frontmatter; the card's licensing section is unfilled).
good: Training data for knowledge-graph extraction in token-classification form: about 15K records where each token is tagged as source entity (SRC), relation (REL), target entity (TGT) or other - the labels produced automatically with spaCy's POS and dependency parsing, companion to the same author's 20-line KG demo Space (B080) - a minimal, CC0 recipe for bootstrapping triple extraction.
bad: Parser-derived labels inherit parser errors with no gold correction described; the SRC/REL/TGT scheme flattens n-ary and nested relations, and the card documents neither the source texts nor any accuracy check.
didnt: Rejected - a small auto-labelled training file; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wikidepia/IndoParaCrawl
licence: No licence stated in the dataset card.
good: A pragmatic low-resource move, documented in one sentence: ParaCrawl v7.1 (a large web-mined English-centric parallel corpus) bulk-translated into Indonesian with Google Translate, manufacturing an Indonesian parallel corpus where natural ones are scarce - synthetic data as a bridge for a language the crawl under-serves.
bad: Translation of a translation corpus: ParaCrawl's noisy web pairs, passed through machine translation, compound both error sources; no filtering, sampling or quality figure is reported, and the card is three lines long.
didnt: Rejected - a synthetic MT corpus; recorded as found. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wikimedia/structured-wikipedia
good: Wikipedia pre-parsed by its owner: Wikimedia Enterprise's Structured Contents release turns English (7.60M articles) and French (2.87M) Wikipedia into Parquet with a pinned, unified schema - abstract, short description, main entity (Wikidata QID), parsed infoboxes, sections, parsed tables as first-class objects referenced by ID, and, most significantly, PARSED REFERENCES: citations extracted as structured objects linked to the in-text citation points, carrying credibility signals (referenceneed, referencerisk) that flag where a claim's sourcing is thin or risky; revision metadata (editor, ML revert-likelihood scores) rides along. It is the difference between scraping an encyclopaedia and receiving its citation graph as data.
bad: Beta scope (two language editions; more by request), 44 GiB of Parquet whose recursive fields still arrive as JSON strings to decode, credibility signals are model scores rather than verdicts, and the snapshot cadence serves the Enterprise product line - the free release trails the paid API.
didnt: Rejected as an artefact for adoption - a data product, not a system - with corroboration for its central design: references parsed into addressable objects with per-reference risk signals is citation infrastructure at exactly the granularity our claim layer works at, arriving here from the source owner itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Wikimedia Enterprise (Wikimedia Foundation)

name: wikimedia/wikipedia
licence: CC-BY-SA-3.0 and GFDL (per the dataset card frontmatter - Wikipedia's own dual licensing).
good: The official current edition of the canonical dataset: Wikimedia's own organisation now publishes the cleaned Wikipedia dataset (2023-11-01 dump generation) for all 300+ language editions in the same id/url/title/text form the legacy copy (B083) pioneered - provenance consolidated under the source owner, which is where a substrate artefact belongs.
bad: Same limits as its predecessor: cleaned article text only, no structure, links or citations - the structured sibling (above) exists precisely because this form is not enough for knowledge work.
didnt: Rejected - a dump redistribution, now from the authoritative source; nothing further transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Wikimedia Foundation

name: wikimedia/wikisource
licence: CC-BY-SA-3.0 and GFDL (per the dataset card frontmatter).
good: Wikisource in dataset form: the Wikimedia library of free source texts - transcribed books, documents, speeches and historical works, proofread by volunteers against page scans - across about 80 languages (English 208,279 texts), in the same clean id/url/title/text shape as the Wikipedia dataset; a pretraining and study corpus of primary sources rather than encyclopaedia prose.
bad: Transcription fidelity varies by edition and era (OCR residue in older proofreading), texts are public-domain-heavy (a strength for rights, a skew for content), and as with its sibling it is raw text without structure or provenance beyond the page URL.
didnt: Rejected - a text corpus; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Wikimedia Foundation

name: BytedTsinghua-SIA/RL-MemoryAgent-14B
good: MemAgent's 14B release: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning to BE a memory agent - the model reads a long document in chunks and, after each chunk, rewrites a fixed-size textual memory, so arbitrarily long input is processed in bounded context; the memory policy itself (what to keep, what to drop, how to phrase it) is learned from reward on downstream questions (multi-conversation RL, arXiv 2507.02259) rather than hand-prompted - memory management as a trained skill instead of a scaffolding heuristic, with framework code public.
bad: The memory is a single overwritten text block: lossy by design, with no provenance (which chunk a kept fact came from is gone), no contradiction handling (newer text simply replaces), and quality bounded by the RL reward tasks; a model release, not a memory system with guarantees - the card itself is minimal and defers everything to the repo/paper.
didnt: Rejected for adoption - a trained model, not infrastructure - with corroboration for its premise from the opposite direction: the field is now spending RL to learn what our wiki does by explicit, inspectable process (write, cite, supersede, keep history); learned overwrite memory and auditable file memory are the two poles of the design space, and this is the clearest artefact of the learned pole. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: ByteDance and Tsinghua University (SIA Lab) - the BytedTsinghua-SIA collaboration

name: BytedTsinghua-SIA/RL-MemoryAgent-7B
good: The 7B MemAgent: the same RL-trained chunk-and-rewrite-memory framework (arXiv 2507.02259) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct - the accessible size for studying whether learned memory policies survive scale-down, and the practical entry point for reproducing the paper's long-document QA results.
bad: Everything the 14B row records applies with a smaller capacity budget: a single overwritten memory block, no provenance or contradiction handling, and a minimal card that defers to the repo; at 7B the compression losses of the fixed-size memory bite harder.
didnt: Rejected - the smaller sibling of the row above; recorded separately because the catalogue lists it separately. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: ByteDance and Tsinghua University (SIA Lab)

name: 0x795E2795/Obsidian-Alpha-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0
licence: Stated inconsistently in the card: the frontmatter lists Apache-2.0; the License section states the model follows the Gemma 4 license and usage terms, with users responsible for complying with them. Both are recorded as found.
good: Despite the name, nothing to do with the Obsidian note app: an experimental sparse-MoE language model (Gemma-4-26B-A4B fine-tune; 128 experts, top-8 routing, ~3.8B active parameters, 262K context) released as a GGUF Q4_0 checkpoint for local-inference and quantisation research - with a card that is more honest than most: alpha status up front, a benchmarks section that publishes NO numbers because the evaluation is unfinished ('preliminary or incomplete benchmark numbers are intentionally not included'), and a thoughtful quantised-release comparison protocol (answer flips and token-level agreement, not just accuracy).
bad: An alpha checkpoint with known backend-compatibility and long-context inconsistencies, a licence conflict between its own frontmatter and its License section, and no verified capability evidence yet - a testing artefact, in this catalogue purely on a name collision with the note-taking app.
didnt: Rejected - an experimental model checkpoint; recorded to close the Obsidian collision honestly, with a nod to its withheld-benchmarks honesty. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: abenzerps/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-Quantized
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the model card frontmatter and Source and Build section).
good: Community quantisations of Tencent's Hy-Memory-30B-A3B - notable in itself: a model trained SPECIFICALLY as a memory operator (a 'memory writer' that does session summarisation, context compaction and entity-memory extraction for agent systems), packaged here in ten formats (GGUF Q4_0-Q8_0, FP8, NVFP4, MLX 4/6/8-bit) with sizes, recommended picks per runtime, and a SHA256SUMS file - the distribution layer that makes a specialist memory model actually runnable on local hardware from llama.cpp to Apple Silicon.
bad: A quantisation is a distribution artefact: quality deltas per format are the packager's unmeasured claim beyond the vendor's benchmark image, the underlying model's memory-writing is a black-box transformation (summaries and extractions with no citation back to source text), and a memory OPERATOR model answers none of the verification questions our system is built on.
didnt: Rejected - a quantised model package; recorded because a major lab now ships a dedicated memory-writer model, which is market evidence for the memory layer's importance - and for the provenance gap (writes without citations) that our design refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AdapterHub/bert-base-uncased-pf-wikihop
licence: No licence stated in the model card.
good: A Pfeiffer adapter (a small trainable module, a fraction of the base model's size) that turns bert-base-uncased into a WikiHop multi-hop QA system - the AdapterHub pattern: freeze the base model, share tiny task modules instead of full fine-tunes; this one comes from a systematic study of intermediate-task transfer (Poth et al., EMNLP 2021), where WikiHop served as a target task for measuring what pre-training transfers.
bad: An artefact of the BERT era: encoder-only extractive QA over a 2018 benchmark, distributed for a forked library (adapter-transformers), with no licence stated and evaluation deferred to the paper; nothing here survives contact with modern LLM practice except the modularity idea.
didnt: Rejected - a legacy adapter module; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AdapterHub/roberta-base-pf-wikihop
licence: No licence stated in the model card.
good: The RoBERTa twin of the adapter above: a Pfeiffer adapter + QA head for roberta-base on WikiHop multi-hop QA, from the same intermediate-task-selection study - the pair together let the paper (and users) compare transfer into the same task across two base encoders while holding the task module format constant.
bad: Same limits as its sibling: BERT-era extractive QA, a forked-library distribution, no licence stated, no local evaluation; a research artefact of adapter science, not a capability to adopt.
didnt: Rejected - the second half of a legacy adapter pair; recorded for completeness. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agents-course/notebooks
good: The hands-on half of Hugging Face's Agents Course: sixteen notebooks walking from a dummy agent library through smolagents code/multi-agent/retrieval/tool-calling agents, LlamaIndex components and workflows, a LangGraph mail-sorting agent, and bonus units on monitoring and evaluating agents - the onboarding ramp a large share of practising agent builders have actually run; catalogued as a model repo, it is really a course artefact (another 'notebooks' filing, cf. B071-B079).
bad: Teaching material, by design shallow per topic and framework-version-sensitive; nothing in it is a system to adopt, and its presence in a models catalogue is a filing quirk.
didnt: Rejected - course notebooks; nothing transfers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ahmed792002/alzheimers_memory_support_ai
good: Almost nothing can be said for the artefact itself; what the card does preserve - accidentally, by being an untouched auto-generated Trainer template - is a complete, honest training log: a GPT-2 fine-tune 'for Alzheimer's memory support' whose validation loss bottoms at epoch 5 and then climbs for 45 straight epochs while training loss collapses to 0.046, a textbook overfitting curve published in full.
bad: A health-adjacent model with every substantive section reading 'More information needed': the training dataset is literally 'unknown', there is no description of what the model does, for whom, with what safeguards, or any evaluation beyond a loss number on an unnamed set - and it was trained 45 epochs past its own best point. As a 'memory support' tool for a vulnerable population it evidences nothing except its training log.
didnt: Rejected - an undocumented fine-tune; recorded as the run's clearest cautionary artefact: a model card can carry a licence, a loss table and a kind intention and still evidence nothing about the thing that matters. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ahmedehabb/Memory-R2-answer-agent
good: The answer half of Memory-R2 (arXiv:2605.21768): a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model given an SFT warm-start then an RL continuation with an answer-F1 reward, trained against the memory manager's rollouts so the two halves of a long-horizon memory system are credited fairly. The card is unusually honest about the architecture's division of labour - this model only answers from the store the separate manager maintains, it is explicitly swappable, and the published table shows an untrained GPT-OSS-120B answers better by the LLM judge (86.08 vs 69.03) while the trained agent wins on F1/BLEU.
bad: Useless alone: it manages no memory and depends entirely on the paired Memory-R2 manager and its store protocol. The judge-score inversion in its own headline table undercuts the case for the specialised training, and the artefact is one checkpoint (sft_cont_step55) from one paper's pipeline.
didnt: Rejected - a trained answer checkpoint for someone else's memory framework; the corroborating point (a general model out-judging the specialist on answer quality) is recorded in this row, and our answering runs over cited files, not a learned store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ai-forever/ReadingPipeline-notebooks
good: A bare weights store for the ReadingPipeline project's OCR, segmentation and handwriting-recognition models trained on the Sberbank school-notebooks datasets (Russian and English handwritten school notebooks) - a genuinely scarce resource: annotated children's handwriting, the input side of any handwriting-to-text pipeline for schoolwork.
bad: Weights only: no model card content beyond two sentences, no architecture, training or evaluation detail at this source - everything of substance lives in the separate GitHub project. Zero downloads at catalogue time; a storage bucket, not a usable artefact in itself.
didnt: Rejected - a weights bucket for a handwriting-OCR pipeline; the underlying problem (children's handwriting recognition for homeschool work) is real but nothing here is adoptable as-is, and our OCR queue works from scanned pages, not notebook-photo models. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ai-forever/scrabblegan-notebooks
good: Weights storage for ScrabbleGAN models trained on the Sberbank school-notebooks datasets - ScrabbleGAN generates handwritten word images, so these weights support synthetic handwriting data generation, the standard trick for augmenting scarce handwriting-recognition training sets.
bad: A one-sentence card: no architecture, sample, or evaluation detail at this source, and zero downloads at catalogue time. The artefact is inert without the separate GitHub codebase, and synthetic-handwriting generation is several steps removed from any need of ours.
didnt: Rejected - generative handwriting weights storage; of archival interest only as a companion to the ReadingPipeline row above. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Akash7897/bert-base-cased-wikitext2
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the auto-generated model card frontmatter).
good: A bert-base-cased fine-tune whose card at least publishes its full training table (loss 7.09 -> 6.86 over 3 epochs, eval loss 6.8544) and exact hyperparameters and framework versions - the complete, if minimal, Trainer-generated provenance record.
bad: The card itself confesses the problem: the training dataset is literally 'None', and the description, intended-uses and data sections all say 'More information needed'. An eval loss of 6.85 for masked-LM is poor, and nothing states what the model is for - an unreproducible checkpoint from a 2022-era training run.
didnt: Rejected - an undocumented personal fine-tune with an unnamed dataset; recorded as part of the long tail of auto-generated HF checkpoints that carry a licence and metrics but no usable knowledge. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Akash7897/gpt2-wikitext2
licence: MIT (per the auto-generated model card frontmatter).
good: A GPT-2 fine-tune with a complete auto-generated provenance record: training loss falling 6.56 -> 6.00 across 3 epochs, eval loss 6.1079, full hyperparameters and pinned framework versions - reproducible in form even though the data is unnamed.
bad: Same failure as its sibling BERT checkpoint: trained 'on the None dataset', every descriptive section 'More information needed', and an eval loss above 6 marks a weak language model by any era's standard. Nothing distinguishes it from thousands of identical tutorial fine-tunes.
didnt: Rejected - undocumented tutorial-grade GPT-2 checkpoint; no capability, data, or method our system lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AliceGomes/notes-knowledge-distillation
licence: MIT (per the card frontmatter and License section).
good: A model of honest research hygiene published in the open: a working note on knowledge distillation that organises motivation, related work, a falsifiable hypothesis, matched-baseline comparison plan, reproducibility checks and failure modes - and states plainly, twice, that plans and hypotheses are not results and that no benchmark claim, code, or checkpoint exists yet.
bad: By its own declaration there is nothing to use: no experiment has been run, no artefact released beyond the note itself (reading.md). Its value is entirely in the discipline of its framing, not in any distillation finding.
didnt: Board - the note's explicit 'hypotheses are not results' labelling and its scope-and-limitations section are a clean template for how research-in-progress should be marked in a knowledge base; the stance matches our own never-invent rule and is worth the ideas board as a documentation pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ANGExllL/obsidian
good: Not a notes artefact at all despite the name: an adversarially fine-tuned EfficientNetV2-L image classifier submitted to the Perturb subnet (netuid 26) on Bittensor, with a neat provenance device - the on-chain hash commits sha256(weights || miner hotkey), binding the exact weights to the miner identity - and exact preprocessing parameters for reproduction.
bad: A single-purpose competition submission: no accuracy or robustness numbers on the card, value only inside the Perturb subnet's incentive game, and the name 'obsidian' is pure collision with the notes app - a catalogue false friend. Nothing transferable except the hash-commitment trick, which our citation lockfile already covers differently.
didnt: Rejected - a Bittensor subnet classifier checkpoint whose only lesson (hash-commit your artefact to an identity) duplicates what our citation lockfile does for pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AT/distilroberta-base-finetuned-wikitext2
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the auto-generated model card frontmatter).
good: A DistilRoBERTa fine-tune nominally aimed at WikiText-2, with hyperparameters and framework versions on the card - the bare minimum of a Trainer provenance record.
bad: The emptiest card in this batch: trained 'on the None dataset', the Training results table is blank, no loss is reported anywhere, and the run was configured for 80 epochs - the card documents a training job, not a model anyone evaluated. Every descriptive section reads 'More information needed'.
didnt: Rejected - an unevaluated checkpoint with an unnamed dataset and an empty results table; there is nothing at the source to learn from beyond the cautionary pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Babelscape/wikineural-multilingual-ner
licence: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (per the card frontmatter and Licensing Information section; restricted to non-commercial research purposes).
good: The trained model from WikiNEuRal (Tedeschi et al., EMNLP 2021 Findings): an mBERT NER tagger covering 9 languages, trained on silver data created by combining knowledge-based Wikipedia linking with neural models plus a domain-adaptation step - up to 6 span-F1 points better than previous data-creation methods, usable in one pipeline call, and with an honest limitations section (Wikipedia-trained, may not generalise to news; combine with CoNLL for robustness).
bad: Silver-standard training data means the ceiling is the automatic annotation's quality, and the licence is CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 - non-commercial research only, share-alike - which bars product use outright. The model is from 2021, pre-dating LLM-based extraction entirely.
didnt: Rejected - licence (CC-BY-NC-SA is ideas-only for us) and scope: our entity handling works over cited prose, not token classification; the Wikipedia-as-annotation-source method is the same pattern recorded across the WikiANN/WikiNER rows. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bdanko/umsb-mpnet-episodic-memory
licence: no licence stated at source (the card frontmatter carries tags, base model and training metadata but no license field).
good: An all-mpnet-base-v2 embedding model fine-tuned with MultipleNegativesRankingLoss on 3,067 episodic-memory examples - the widget shows what 'episodic' means here: whole clinical-agent trajectories (FHIR tool calls, dosing decisions, judge feedback) embedded so a memory system can retrieve a past episode by similarity to the current situation, rather than retrieving isolated facts.
bad: The card is a raw generated_from_trainer dump - over a thousand lines of widget payloads with no written description, no evaluation, and no licence stated anywhere, so the weights are legally unusable by default. The training episodes are one person's clinical-agent experiments; nothing shows the embeddings beat the base model at episode retrieval.
didnt: Rejected - no licence at source (ideas-only at best) and no evaluation; the episode-level retrieval idea is noted here, but our retrieval works over cited pages with provenance an embedding of a whole trajectory cannot give. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: boxwrench/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B-q4nx-wrench
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the card frontmatter and Credits and license section; the base model's licence is included as LICENSE-Hy-Memory).
good: A serious piece of hardware engineering: Tencent's Hy-Memory-30B-A3B memory-writer MoE repacked into q4nx, a 4-bit format for AMD's XDNA2 NPU, so every linear layer runs on a Ryzen AI NPU (12.6 tok/s decode on one Strix Halo), with unusually rigorous reporting - per-layer expert-output error vs the BF16 reference (8.8%, honestly compared with llama.cpp Q4_K_M's 6.7%), exact file layout, and a dated early-release status note.
bad: The weights load only in the author's own npu-wrench runtime - explicitly not GGUF, not llama.cpp/vLLM/transformers - and need exotic consumer NPU hardware; a task-level evaluation of the memory-writing itself has not been run, so the one number that matters for a memory model is missing. It is also a quantisation of a model already studied in this programme (B086's Hy-Memory rows).
didnt: Rejected - a hardware-specific repack of Tencent's memory-writer (already covered at B086); the local-inference direction is interesting but an NPU-only format with no task-level eval is not a route for our file-based stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bryanmildort/gpt-clinical-notes-summarizer
licence: no licence stated at source (the 14-line card carries no licence field or statement).
good: A GPT-J-6B fine-tune for a concrete, well-scoped clinical task - discharge-summary in, summary with pertinent information out - in an era when a 6B open model doing usable clinical summarisation was a meaningful demonstration.
bad: The entire documentation is two sentences: no dataset named, no training detail, no evaluation, no usage example, and no licence stated anywhere - so the weights are both unusable legally and unverifiable technically. Six likes and 16 downloads at catalogue time mark an abandoned personal upload.
didnt: Rejected - no licence at source and no evidence at source; there is nothing here a completion pass can honestly say beyond the task framing, which is recorded. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: burtenshaw/Kimi-K2-notebooks
good: Two runnable Colab notebooks demonstrating Kimi-K2-Instruct's two most API-relevant behaviours - function calling and structured outputs - with one-click badges, so a developer can test the model's tool-use contract in minutes without any local setup.
bad: Two notebooks is the whole artefact: no prose explanation, no results, no failure cases, and everything depends on the hosted Kimi-K2 endpoint staying as it was. It is a pointer to someone else's model, catalogued here only because 'notebooks' matched the wave's note/knowledge sweep.
didnt: Rejected - demo notebooks for a hosted model; our function-calling needs are served by our own gateway tools, and there is no knowledge artefact here to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Capx/Llama-3-Obsidian
licence: Meta Llama 3 Community License (card frontmatter 'llama3'; the License section states the model is governed by the META LLAMA 3 COMMUNITY LICENSE AGREEMENT).
good: A Llama-3 SFT fine-tune series ('Obsidian', Capx AI) aimed at general-purpose instruction following, released in Alpaca format with a standard transformers loading snippet - an ordinary but complete community fine-tune release of its moment.
bad: The card undermines itself: the usage code loads meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct rather than this repository, the 'custom dataset' is never described, no evaluation is offered for the 'state of the art finetune' claim, and the sample system prompt instructs the model to present itself as a 'conscious sentient superintelligent artificial intelligence'. Another catalogue false friend - 'Obsidian' is a model name, not the notes app.
didnt: Rejected - an undocumented Llama-3 fine-tune under Meta's community licence (custom terms, ideas-only for code purposes); nothing in the release is verifiable or needed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cja5553/BJH-perioperative-notes-bioClinicalBERT
good: A clinically serious artefact with a paper behind it (Alba et al., npj Digital Medicine 2025): Bio_ClinicalBERT fine-tuned multi-task over 84,875 real perioperative notes from Barnes Jewish Hospital to predict six postoperative outcomes (30-day death, DVT, PE, pneumonia, acute knee injury, delirium) from the short single-sentence notes clinicians actually write (8.9 words average). The card is commendably explicit about data scale, vocabulary, and the need to train your own predictor head on the hidden states.
bad: The weights are effectively closed: the card states the model 'remains private' because it was trained on patient notes - non-institutional access requests are rejected and institutional ones need approvals - so the MIT tag on the card describes an artefact the public cannot download. Single-centre, single-sentence notes also bound generalisation hard.
didnt: Rejected - a clinical risk model whose weights are access-gated by design and whose domain (perioperative outcomes) is outside our system; recorded for its honest privacy posture: licence stated, access refused, reasons given. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Barnes Jewish Healthcare (BJH), St Louis, MO; corresponding author Charles Alba, Washington University in St. Louis (contact shown on the card)

name: ClaudioItaly/Memory-9
licence: no licence stated at source (the card frontmatter carries base models and tags but no license field).
