bad: Same structural ceiling as every template in this cluster — organisation without ingest, citation or retrieval machinery — sold into the same Notion custody; the 5.0 rating is two ratings, and the name collides with at least two other 'Notion Second Brain' products, which even the catalogue must keep carefully apart.
didnt: Corroboration — a second, independent maker's second-brain template corroborating the category demand; the naming collision with the other second-brain templates in this very batch is itself recorded as a catalogue-disambiguation hazard our register discipline exists to handle. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NotionFlashcard
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial add-on; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Attacks the real failure of note-taking — notes written and never reviewed — by generating flashcards, memory games and exercises from the notes themselves, inside Notion, with a weak-point algorithm and progress tracking to aim the review.
bad: A study add-on for students inside one vendor's notes app; the retention statistics in its pitch are marketing garnish without sources on the page, and everything depends on the notes living in Notion in the first place.
didnt: Rejected — a student exam-prep add-on for Notion, out of scope for a knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Open Paper
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A literature-review workbench with the right core promise: read, annotate and question papers in one place, with every AI response grounded in a citation to the paper — trust treated as a feature, aimed at researchers drowning in PDFs.
bad: The grounding claim is asserted in one sentence, with nothing on the page about how citations are verified, what happens when a paper doesn't support an answer, or where the library lives; its 5.0 rating is a single review — a young product with a trust claim it has not yet evidenced.
didnt: Corroboration — citation-grounded AI answers over a paper library corroborate our citation-first Ask design; the difference is that our lockfile pins each claim to raw source lines and can prove the pin, rather than asking the user to trust the grounding claim. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Orchestra
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A sensible answer to fragmented team work: task-focused communication (one dedicated chat per piece of work, only the relevant people in it) with tasks, docs and calls in the same place instead of scattered across tools.
bad: Team-communication SaaS: the work record it creates is a company's chat history on the vendor's platform, and nothing in its design addresses personal knowledge, provenance, or retrieval over time.
didnt: Rejected — a team messaging/workspace tool, out of scope for a personal knowledge system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PaperGen
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: It automates the genuinely tedious mechanics of long-form writing — structure, formatting in styles like APA/MLA, reference lists, and supporting charts — which is why products like it find buyers among students and professionals facing 8–40 hours of paper assembly.
bad: The product is citation theatre: references are auto-attached to text the user did not research, and evading AI detection is sold as a feature — the precise inversion of a citation discipline; the market's verdict on its page is a single 1.0/5 rating.
didnt: Rejected — generated papers with generated citations are the antithesis of our citation-truth standard; recorded as a cautionary artefact of what citation machinery must never become. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Paperguide
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A research platform aimed at the rigorous end of the literature workflow: evidence synthesis, literature and systematic reviews, and reference management in one place, grown steadily from a chat-with-PDF tool into a full research workspace over five launches.
bad: The research corpus and its synthesis live on Paperguide's platform; the page describes workflow breadth (synthesis, reviews, reference management) without any account of citation verification or of what its AI does when the literature doesn't answer — and its 5.0 rests on three reviews.
didnt: Corroboration — its systematic-review and evidence-synthesis workflow corroborates the deep-study discipline our register enforces (items counted only when opened at source and judged); our corpus stays in owner files rather than a research SaaS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Passionfruit Labs
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A sharp read of a real shift: as AI answers replace search results, it tracks which pages each major AI engine actually cites, benchmarks competitors' cited pages, and ties AI visibility to attributed revenue instead of vanity metrics — citation share treated as a measurable market.
bad: Marketing analytics end to end; here 'citation' means a brand mention in an AI answer to be optimised for revenue — a meaning orthogonal to whether any claim is true — and its attribution claims (the team's '$375M+ attributable revenue') are unaudited marketing numbers.
didnt: Rejected — AI-search marketing tooling, out of scope; recorded because its existence evidences a commercial market pricing 'who gets cited by AI' — the economy our citation discipline answers to for truth rather than for traffic. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Perplexity
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: The product that made cited answers the consumer default: ask a question, get a synthesised answer with its sources attached, on every platform — 'Where Knowledge Begins' — and rated 4.87/5 over 97 ratings while expanding into health, legal and personal-computer lines.
bad: It answers from the live web, not from your corpus: nothing is kept, compiled, or held under your custody, and a citation's presence is not its verification — a linked page can fail to support the sentence it decorates, which is precisely the failure our citation lockfile exists to catch.
didnt: Corroboration — mainstream proof that users now expect sourced answers; our Ask door answers the same expectation from the owner's own corpus, with citations pinned to raw lines and scored abstention when the corpus doesn't know. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pink Piko - AI Emotion Journal
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Goes beyond mood tracking: AI tagging surfaces the specific feelings and events behind each entry, trend charts connect activities to mood, sentiment analysis reads the entries' tone, and recurring-word bubbles show themes — a journal that analyses itself, wrapped in a friendly companion to keep the daily habit alive.
bad: Intimate affect data accumulates on a vendor's service under unstated terms; the analysis features (trend charts, sentiment) are described in marketing language with no evidence of their accuracy, and the 5.0 rating is five ratings deep.
didnt: Corroboration — structured emotional self-logging with automatic pattern extraction corroborates the log-as-data pattern (a daily record becomes more valuable as structure accrues — cf. Journal BuddyAI in B097); its custody of sensitive personal data is the consumer default our local-first design refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Plurai
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A real research idea aimed at a real weakness: LLM-as-judge evaluation is slow, costly, and unstable, so Plurai 'vibe-trains' a small dedicated eval/guardrail model from a task description alone — synthetic data, multi-agent-debate validation, deployment in minutes — making always-on evaluation economically possible.
bad: The headline numbers (43% fewer failures, 8x cheaper) are the vendor's own comparisons on its own page, and its 5.0 rating is a single rating; a trained judge is only as good as the synthetic data and debate process that produced it, which the page summarises rather than evidences.
didnt: Board — task-specific evaluators trained from a plain description of desired behaviour, cheap enough to run on every interaction: a candidate technique for our evaluation machinery, which currently leans on frozen thresholds and fixed batteries. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Powabase
licence: No licence stated at source for the platform (commercial backend-as-a-service; its Product Hunt page names no licence for the product, while noting its cookbook and example apps are open-sourced on GitHub).
good: A coherent unification of the AI-app stack — Postgres with pgvector, file storage, auth, several RAG algorithms, multimodal embeddings, rerankers, OCR, agent orchestration and observability — provisioned as one platform, designed to be token-efficient for coding agents to build on.
bad: A hosted backend: your app's data, memory and RAG context live on Powabase's platform, the 98.7% FinanceBench figure is a vendor claim from its launch post, and the self-hosted open-source version that would answer the custody question is a promise dated after early access, not a present fact.
didnt: Rejected — developer infrastructure for shipping AI apps, out of scope for the wiki itself; its existence corroborates that 'memory + retrieval + agents' has become a standard stack, which is context, not a component we lack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Quivr - Your Second Brain
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: An early, genuinely aimed second brain: connect your files and documents and interrogate them conversationally — reviewers confirm it handles varied files and answers questions over uploaded documentation (e.g. a code framework's docs) better than a general chatbot.
bad: Its own reviewers make the case against it: a web app felt slow and inaccessible next to local clients, and the lack of encryption for an uploaded personal corpus is named as a concern on the page itself — the custody and locality costs of the hosted second-brain model, in users' words.
didnt: Corroboration — Quivr's reception corroborates our founding choice from the market side: people want a second brain that is local and fast, and they notice when it is neither; our wiki is files on the owner's machine for exactly the reasons its reviewers state. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Readever
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Aims at the right moment in reading — getting stuck mid-text rather than summarising afterwards: highlight a sentence and ask in place, receive proactive guidance cards matched to your goals, translate without leaving the flow, and get book recommendations from a natural-language description.
bad: The persona mentors are the tell: answers voiced as Elon Musk or Steve Jobs are theatre laid over the text, not evidence from it, and the advertised 'memory system' is never explained on the page — engagement features dressed as comprehension features.
didnt: Rejected — a consumer reading-entertainment app, out of scope; reading inside the text with help at the point of confusion is a commodity pattern, and persona answers are the opposite of source-grounded reading. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: remio - Your Personal ChatGPT
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A well-aimed personal knowledge hub: it captures your work across channels — notes, files, meetings, recordings — and builds a searchable knowledge base your assistant answers from, combining your personal context with world knowledge; local-first by its own launch billing, and rated 5.0/5 by its early users.
bad: The claims outrun the evidence on the page: 'uniquely accurate insights' is asserted without any account of citation or of what happens when your material doesn't answer, and how local-first the custody truly is — what still transits the vendor's AI — is not specified.
didnt: Corroboration — a local-first, capture-everything personal knowledge hub corroborates our architecture's direction (ingest all channels, compile into one searchable memory); the unexamined gap is the one our register patrols: answers asserted accurate without pinned citations or abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Repeet: Learn Languages with Flashcards
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A thoughtful stance in a crowded category: instead of an algorithm's schedule, the learner chooses what to practise and when, and the creation flow is the product — capture a phrase while browsing via the extension and it becomes a card, on the maker's correct observation that making your own cards is itself learning.
bad: Its honesty exposes the limits: offline practice works but offline editing doesn't, the app covers three interface languages, and its 5.0 rating is one rating; it is a small, single-maker consumer app.
didnt: Rejected — a language-learning flashcard app, out of scope for a knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ReSO AI
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: More serious than a visibility dashboard: it closes the loop from measurement to action — find the questions, measure citation and recommendation share against competitors, diagnose the specific gaps behind losses, issue a weekly prioritised plan, then re-verify that fixes actually moved the visibility.
bad: Marketing instrumentation: its 'trust gap' audit measures a brand's eligibility to be cited, not the truth of anything, and the agentic-employee framing promises outcomes (recommendations by third-party models) that no tool can guarantee.
didnt: Rejected — AI-visibility marketing tooling, out of scope; the second GEO platform in two batches (cf. Passionfruit Labs, B098), confirming a whole industry now prices AI citation share — the traffic side of the citation economy our lockfile serves from the truth side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sagekit
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Whichever of its two presentations is current, the underlying ideas are sound: an AI workspace where research becomes lasting documents, and (per the maker's post) automation built by chatting in natural language while the complexity — integrations, loops, error handling — is handled underneath and shown on a visual canvas.
bad: The source cannot settle what the product is: research-and-writing workspace in the title, Zapier-class automation builder in the maker's text — a rename or repivot visible in the record itself, which makes any stronger claim about the product ungroundable from this page.
didnt: Rejected — under either identity it is a hosted SaaS (research workspace or automation builder), out of scope; recorded with its identity discrepancy stated, as the register requires when a source disagrees with itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Scispace
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: One of the most substantial research tools in this catalogue: highlight any confusing passage, equation or table in a paper and get a plain-language explanation, ask follow-ups, and discover papers by meaning rather than keywords — sustained since 2022 and extended into deep review and an academic agent.
bad: Generated explanations are simplifications with no citation-truth mechanism behind them — nothing on the page describes checking an explanation against the paper's own evidence — and the reading corpus accumulates on SciSpace's platform across its expanding agent tooling.
didnt: Corroboration — paper comprehension at real scale corroborates the research-reading workflow our deep-study programme performs by hand; our register's insistence on judging from the source itself, not from a generated simplification, is the deliberate difference. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Scribble Network
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: The most rigorous thinking in the GEO cluster: instead of counting one-off mentions, it pays only when content holds as a source across repeated AI answers over a week, attributes mentions to specific posts section-by-section, and plans timestamped, publicly verifiable citation proofs — an incentive design that at least points at durability rather than luck.
bad: It is a machine for manufacturing citations: paying for content designed to be picked up by AI answers optimises the appearance of authority, and its own thread concedes the measurement substrate is unstable — one call per prompt per day, citations shifting between identical asks.
didnt: Rejected — a citation-buying marketing platform, out of scope and antithetical to citation-as-evidence; noted that its makers independently document citation churn across re-asks and treat only a source that holds across refreshes as signal — the same instability our reverify queue and lockfile track from the truth side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Second
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A well-shaped agent workflow for a painful job: legacy migrations and upgrades decomposed into selectable modules, with the agent's plan presented for human review before anything executes — automation with a checkpoint, aimed at work teams otherwise postpone for years.
bad: A hosted service that must be given write access to a codebase to do its work, in a domain (framework migrations) where a bad automated change is expensive; its 5.0 rests on four ratings, and the page gives no account of verification or rollback.
didnt: Rejected — code-migration SaaS, out of scope for the wiki; its review-the-plan-before-it-runs step is the approval-gate pattern appearing in dev tooling, noted and left there. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Second Brain Labs
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: As marketing automation it is coherently designed: survey every prospect before the pitch so the pitch answers their actual pain points, then follow up individually after purchase to cut refunds — personalised outreach at a scale a solo seller could not otherwise run.
bad: The name promises a knowledge product and delivers marketing automation; every number on the page is the maker's own unaudited case study, and 'automate your sales using AGI' is the page's own framing — persuasion infrastructure wearing a memory product's name.
didnt: Rejected — sales/support automation, out of scope; recorded as a name-collision caution (it has nothing to do with second-brain knowledge systems) of the same kind the register flags for the Notion template cluster. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SEORCE
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A genuinely unified discovery stack: traditional SEO (crawls, rankings, analytics) and AI visibility (who the engines cite and recommend) in one system, with guided fixes and even a WhatsApp interface for querying your own visibility data.
bad: Another dashboard in the most crowded marketing niche of this catalogue stretch, with no reviews on its page to weigh it by; 'AutoFix' applied to search visibility is optimisation of appearances, and nothing here touches the truth of any content.
didnt: Rejected — SEO/GEO marketing platform, out of scope; the third such platform in two batches, further evidencing the citation-visibility industry noted at Passionfruit Labs (B098) and ReSO AI (this batch). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sider: AI Research Agent & Extension
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A complete research loop in the browser: an agent that scans 100+ sources, reflects, and writes visualised reports, while everything it gathers accumulates into Wisebase — a personal knowledge base that grows with your research instead of evaporating after each answer.
bad: Breadth is the design: 100+ sources scanned per question produces a report, not a studied corpus, and the accumulated Wisebase lives in Sider's custody; nothing on the page describes per-claim citation pinning or abstention when sources conflict.
didnt: Corroboration — a research agent that deposits its materials into a growing personal knowledge base corroborates our research-into-corpus pattern; our programme's difference is the depth standard (each item opened and judged, claims pinned to raw lines) against its scan-and-summarise breadth. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Solid Diary - AI Journal
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A thoughtfully made journal: clean design, multiple themes, no limits on images or voice notes, and privacy as its stated design intent — a personal diary for iOS and Mac by a solo maker who plainly cares about the craft.
bad: Its headline claim is contradicted on its own page: a journal marketed as '100% private' whose AI runs on OpenAI's API, with the maker's silence on the obvious question left standing in the thread — privacy as a slogan, not an architecture.
didnt: Rejected — a journal app, out of scope; kept as a cautionary record that custody claims must be checked against the actual data flow, which is precisely the check our register applies to every 'private' or 'local' claim in this survey. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Spellar AI
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Bot-free meeting capture done thoroughly: it records on-device across Mac, iPhone, iPad, web and Chrome with no bot joining the call, produces summaries and action items, lets the user choose the model (Claude, GPT or Gemini), and in Spellar 3.0 chats across all past meetings, so the meeting archive becomes a queryable memory rather than a pile of transcripts.
bad: The headline word is 'Private', but the page never says where recordings or transcripts are processed or stored, and the model choice it advertises is among three cloud providers — the custody behind the privacy claim is simply not addressed on the page. Everything runs through Spellar's own service and its integrations.
didnt: Corroboration — bot-free capture plus chat-across-all-meetings confirms the consumer shape of meeting memory: record without a bot, then interrogate the archive. Our difference is custody: the archive it chats over lives in the vendor's cloud under an unexamined 'private' headline, where ours is owner-visible files with cited answers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Studyy - Instant Flashcards
licence: No licence stated at source (free app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A tight capture loop for students: photograph a textbook page and get flashcards, summaries and extracted key points without manual note-taking, with the deck positioned for repeated revision.
bad: The page is a single maker's feature list with no reviews or rating to test it against, no statement of extraction accuracy, and no word on what happens to scanned pages; the 'personal tutor' and memory-retention claims are asserted, not evidenced.
didnt: Rejected — scan-to-flashcard drilling is a study aid outside our knowledge-OS scope, and the page evidences no citation, verification or custody machinery to learn from; its extraction quality is exactly the kind of claim our system would have to pin to a source before repeating. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tana Outliner
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: The batch's most architecturally serious notes product: a structured outliner (typed nodes and relationships rather than flat pages) with voice capture, full offline support, a multi-model AI layer — and a local API plus MCP server, so agents like Claude Code can read and write the user's actual structured workspace instead of pasted excerpts.
bad: The workspace lives in Tana's proprietary cloud format; offline support mitigates access, not custody or lock-in, and the page offers no export or self-host story. The AI features ride on third-party models, so the graph's intelligence is rented even where its structure is the user's.
didnt: Corroboration — a flagship notes product shipping a local API and an MCP door so agents can work inside the user's structured notes confirms our read-door design from the market side; its proprietary cloud custody is the contrast our plain-files wiki is defined against. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Trupeer
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: One rough screen recording yields two documentation forms at once — a polished product video and a step-by-step written guide — which is a real answer to the cost of producing tutorials and product docs from demonstrations.
bad: The pitch leans on marketing arithmetic ('100x the power of Loom'), its 4.36/5 is the weakest rating in this batch, and the page shows nothing about the accuracy of the generated steps — a guide that misstates a step is worse than none, and nothing here would catch it.
didnt: Rejected — it generates marketing and tutorial documentation from screen recordings; our documentation is compiled from cited sources, and the page shows no verification machinery standing between a recording and a published guide. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TwinMind
licence: No licence stated at source (free app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Ambient capture engineered seriously: a quiet native app that records calls and conversations in the background, turns them into structured notes, proactively surfaces suggestions and tasks, and doubles as system-wide voice typing — with explicit engineering attention to recording stability across sleep and device changes.
bad: 'Captures everything you say and hear' is the maximal-custody model, and the page says nothing about where that audio and the accumulated life-context are stored or processed, nor about the consent of the other people being recorded; the 'AI Second Brain' it builds lives wherever TwinMind keeps it, not with the user.
didnt: Corroboration — continuous capture flowing into structured notes and proactively extracted tasks is the consumer form of our capture-to-action pipeline; the contrast is that its memory accumulates inside the vendor's system under no stated custody, where ours is written to owner-visible files the user can audit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Twos
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Radical capture minimalism that users reward: a single 'thing' type for notes, tasks, reminders, events and lists removes every categorisation decision at the moment of capture, and 117 ratings at 4.93/5 say the minimalism holds up in daily use; PALs adds AI-generated lists on top without complicating the primitive.
bad: The same flatness is the ceiling: the page shows no retrieval depth, no linking or structure beyond lists, and nothing about export or custody — a system designed to hold everything you write in one undifferentiated stream, which is a capture layer, not a knowledge system.
didnt: Corroboration — Twos is consumer proof of the capture-first premise behind our ingest discipline: write the thing down immediately, in one place, with zero filing decisions. Our system is what happens after that moment — structure, citation and retrieval that Twos deliberately never builds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Typeless
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Dictation that aims past transcription: it rewrites rambling speech into polished, style-matched prose at the point of input, shipping as a system voice keyboard on desktop, iOS and Android — the friction it removes (typing cost on mobile) is real, per its own launch framing.
bad: The polishing is silent rewriting: what you said and what it wrote can diverge, with no original kept — the page presents adaptation purely as a benefit and never mentions a verbatim record; 11 ratings is a thin base, and where the voice is processed is not stated.
didnt: Rejected — for a system whose foundation is a verbatim record of what was actually said, a dictation layer that silently rewrites speech into smoother prose is the failure mode, not a feature: voice capture matters to us, unrecorded transformation of the record does not. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TypingMind - Chat UI for LLMs
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial web app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Custody-conscious by design: your own API keys, chats running locally in your browser, 18 providers behind one interface, and pay-per-use instead of a subscription — it treats model choice and data custody as the user's, and has sustained a perfect rating across two launches three years apart.
bad: It is a front end only: no memory, no knowledge base, no persistence or retrieval model of its own beyond the browser it runs in — everything it knows evaporates with the chat, which is precisely the loss our wiki exists to prevent.
didnt: Corroboration — BYOK, browser-local, provider-agnostic design is market proof that users value custody of keys and conversations plus freedom of model choice, the same posture as our local doors; its total absence of a memory layer marks the exact gap our system fills. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ultimate Second Brain
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial Notion template; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Four years of launches for one idea — a capture-and-organise dashboard inside Notion — shows durable demand for second-brain organisation, delivered as a template: zero code, installed inside a tool the buyer already uses.
bad: It is a template inside someone else's platform: total dependence on Notion's cloud and pricing, no AI, no verification, no custody outside Notion; and its perfect 5.0 rests on exactly 2 ratings, the thinnest evidence in this batch.
didnt: Corroboration — the second-brain template trade corroborates lasting demand for capture-and-organise systems; the template form itself (static, platform-locked, unable to answer questions) is the floor our cited, queryable system is built above. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Voicenotes
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Voice-first capture with the crucial second half built in: you can interrogate your own spoken archive ('ask about every word you spoke'), and a Pages feature turns talking into publishing; a bootstrapped small team has sustained it since 2024 to a Product of the Year award.
bad: The page says nothing about export, custody, or what grounds the answers it gives over your notes — no citation or source-pinning is visible, so 'ask about every word' is a promise the user cannot check from anything shown here.
didnt: Corroboration — interrogable voice notes are the consumer form of our conversation-log plus Ask-door pairing: speak everything, then ask the record. The piece its page never shows — answers tied to a checkable, pinned source — is the piece we built first. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Voz AI Voice Note Taker
licence: No licence stated at source (free app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Impressive breadth for one maker: capture from lectures, calls and even YouTube videos, structured notes generated automatically, Q&A over transcripts, translation into 100+ languages, and an Apple Watch recorder for capture on the go.
bad: A single-maker app with no rating or reviews visible on its page; 'automagically' stands in for any accuracy account, and the translate-and-rewrite features multiply transformations of the original record with no way to check any of them against it; custody of recordings is not mentioned.
didnt: Rejected — a capable solo voice-note app, but it transforms (transcribes, translates, rewrites) rather than preserves, and neither its page nor its evidence base gives our programme anything checkable to take; lecture capture is covered in this batch by entries with visible review records. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Web & Youtube Highlighter + AI Summary
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial browser extension; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Annotation that stays anchored to its source across the three places reading actually happens — web pages, PDFs, and YouTube videos — with highlights, notes and bookmarks organised in one place and AI summaries of the annotated material; maintained since 2022.
bad: The page is thin and the base small (7 ratings): it says nothing about where highlights are stored, whether they export, or how the AI summaries are grounded — the annotations' long-term custody is left entirely implicit.
didnt: Corroboration — a highlight is only worth keeping while it stays pinned to the passage it marks; Web Highlights builds its whole product on that anchoring across web, PDF and video, the reading-side twin of our claim-citation practice. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WordSnap - AI Flashcards Maker
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial iOS app; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: A neat capture loop for language learners — photograph the world, tap the words that interest you, get translations with definitions and context — and a maker unusually transparent in the thread about his stack, timeline and platform limits.
bad: Its 5.0 is a single rating; the app is iOS-only by the maker's own admission; and translation accuracy rests on the maker's 'I think it's pretty accurate' — the page contains no evaluation, and the translations themselves come from a general API with no checking step.
didnt: Rejected — an honestly built vocabulary app, but photo-to-translation drilling sits outside our scope, and its unverified machine translations are an example of the genre our citation discipline exists to refuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Writesonic
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Its pivot is itself a finding: a substantial business (9.3K followers, enterprise and agency customers) now exists to measure what AI systems say about a brand and to act on it — treating AI answers as a monitorable, influenceable surface, with analytics for AI-agent traffic to boot.
bad: 4.42/5 across 53 ratings is mediocre at this scale; the superlatives ('best', 'the only AEO platform') are unverifiable; and the product's purpose is to optimise representation inside AI answers — placement engineering aimed at the answer layer, indifferent to whether the answer is grounded.
didnt: Corroboration — Writesonic's GEO trade exists because AI answers can be gamed into existence; that adversarial reality is the context our citation lockfile, source-pinning and scored abstention are built for: when answers can be optimised, only a pinned source distinguishes knowledge from placement. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Writingmate.ai
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: Aggregation with a clear consumer benefit: every flagship model behind one subscription, meeting users inside Google Docs, Slides and Sheets rather than another destination app, sparing them juggling seats, credits and APIs.
bad: It is a reseller layer: continuity and custody depend on the middleman's survival and upstream providers' terms, the pitch is price arbitrage ('save hundreds of dollars a year') rather than capability, and the page shows no memory or knowledge layer of its own.
didnt: Rejected — a subscription-bundling front end; read against TypingMind in this same batch (same aggregation, opposite custody: your own keys, locally run), it marks the model we refuse — our system holds its own records and calls models directly rather than renting access through an intermediary. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: YouMind
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its Product Hunt page names no licence).
good: The learn-to-create loop in one studio: capture inspiration, explore source materials, draft and polish into finished articles, podcasts and videos without switching tools — aimed squarely at the gap between collecting material and shipping work.
bad: The page is a launch letter: no mechanics are shown for how materials are stored, cited or checked, and 'learning meets writing' is asserted rather than demonstrated; with 9 ratings, the evidence base is the founder's own enthusiasm.
didnt: Rejected — an output-polishing creation studio; its direction (turn material into publishable content) is the reverse of ours (turn content into a checkable record), and its page shows no source or citation discipline to borrow. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Anytype
licence: Any Source Available License 1.0 (source-available, not open source; README of the official client repo).
good: The most complete consumer realisation of the custody posture: offline-first local storage, zero-knowledge encryption with user-held keys, peer-to-peer sync with no server or gatekeeper, self-hosted backups, and a user-defined data model (your own Types) across blocks, databases and graph views — actively developed at scale (302 releases).
bad: The code is source-available, not open source (the Any Source Available License 1.0 restricts use), and the system is a heavyweight app stack (Electron client, Go middleware, sync protocol) whose encrypted vault is opaque to outside tooling — your data is yours, but only Anytype reads it fluently.
took: Local-first P2P zero-knowledge sync posture — Tier C; boarded, Waiting (owner decision) — source/inspiration: Anytype (global harvest), as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md.
didnt: Corroboration — Anytype corroborates the destination (local-first, encrypted, owner-keyed personal knowledge) while marking our fork in the road: its vault is an encrypted app database, ours is plain owner-readable files under git custody; its sync posture is the one our programme boarded as a Tier C owner decision rather than adopting silently. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bear
licence: Proprietary freemium (Bear Pro subscription; no open licence at source).
good: A decade-refined writing surface: seamless live Markdown, flexible nested tags, backlinks, OCR over photos and PDFs, and export to PDF, HTML, DOCX and JPG — plus a credible privacy story (notes stay in your iCloud, optional per-note encryption, Advanced Data Protection supported).
bad: Apple-only — no Windows, Android or web — and sync custody is iCloud under a Pro subscription; it is a writing app, not a knowledge system: no AI layer, no citation or verification machinery, and organisation tops out at tags.
didnt: Corroboration — Bear's long success with plain Markdown notes, flexible tags and export-to-everything corroborates the plain-text, export-always foundation our wiki is built on; its Apple-walled, iCloud-bound custody is where a system meant to outlive platforms must differ. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Capacities
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; freemium, hosted in the EU).
good: The object model done accessibly: notes as typed, property-bearing objects linked into a living network, with the system itself surfacing connections you made but never linked — plus an explicit no-lock-in export promise and an independent, user-funded business model.
bad: Custody is Capacities' EU cloud: export is the exit route, not local possession, and the page's AI features are asserted without mechanics; there is no citation or verification layer — connections are surfaced, never vouched for.
didnt: Corroboration — typed objects with automatically surfaced unlinked mentions corroborate our typed-page and neighbour machinery; the difference is that its network lives in the vendor's cloud while ours is computed over files the owner holds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Capture - Quick Notes
licence: Proprietary freemium (App Store listing: free with in-app purchases; no licence stated at source).
good: Capture as a pure front door: instant notes from widgets, the share sheet or Siri, automatic date and URL recognition — and then it leaves, exporting to 20+ destination apps or to any Siri Shortcut, so the capture layer never tries to become the archive.
bad: It is deliberately only a front door: no storage model, search depth or knowledge structure of its own; Apple-platform only (iOS 18+, macOS 15+); sync is iCloud; and at 205.7 MB it is a large app for a capture box.
didnt: Corroboration — Capture is the capture-triage pattern as a product: seize the thought in seconds, recognise its dates and links, route it onward to the system of record — the same shape as our gateway capture pipeline, with the phone as the door instead of the inbox. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Craft
licence: Proprietary freemium (no licence stated at source; Free and Plus plans).
good: Design-led unification done well: documents, tasks, calendar and daily notes in one polished surface with adaptable structure (folders or collections) and publishing straight from where you write — validated by 25,000 ratings at 4.8 as shown on its own page.
bad: The page is awards and testimonials: nothing on export formats, offline behaviour or data custody, and the structure tops out at collections — a beautiful workspace whose knowledge model is shallower than its surface; proprietary cloud throughout.
didnt: Corroboration — publishing directly from the writing surface is the consumer form of our Lens pattern (the wiki you write in is the wiki that publishes), and Craft's docs+tasks+daily-notes convergence mirrors our own page types; the rest is polish an owner-only system does not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Docmost
licence: AGPL-3.0 (core; enterprise features under the Docmost Enterprise licence) — repo README licence section.
good: The full team-wiki feature set, self-hostable: real-time collaboration, spaces, granular permissions and groups, page history, comments and embeds — a credible open Confluence replacement with 22k stars of momentum.
bad: AGPL-3.0 core with a commercially licensed enterprise tier is a dual-licence gravity well, and its centre of gravity is real-time multi-writer editing — the collaboration model our single-writer, approval-gated design rejected by design; it is a team platform, not a personal record.
didnt: Rejected — licence discipline makes AGPL code ideas-only for us, and its real-time multi-writer model is the one our approval-gated single-writer design deliberately refuses; page history is the one comfort our git history already provides. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: EndNote
licence: Proprietary (paid; Clarivate — no licence stated at source beyond commercial sale).
good: Reference management at institutional depth: one-click capture, 7,000+ formatting styles applied as you write, shared libraries with permissions and activity logs — and retraction alerts, which flag a cited source's changed status at the moment of writing: a real source-status signal rather than a static bibliography.
bad: Proprietary and institution-priced, with the library held in Clarivate's ecosystem and cloud sync; and it manages references — the containers of claims — not claims or knowledge: nothing in it can say whether what you cited is true, only, via the retraction feed, that its status changed.
didnt: Board — retraction and status alerts on cited sources: when a source a page relies on is retracted or superseded, flag it at the point of use. Our citation lockfile pins what a claim rests on; a status watch over those pinned sources is the missing other half, adjacent to the truth-aware retrieval gap. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Evernote
licence: Proprietary freemium (no licence stated at source).
good: The original capture-everything notes service, still defining the category's baseline promise: notes, tasks and schedule unified, capture from anywhere, and a version-11 AI layer added on top of two decades of accumulated user archives.
bad: The homepage sells capture and AI but shows nothing about export, custody or verification: the second brain is rented cloud behind a freemium gate, and its AI features are offered as standalone trials rather than described as working over your archive with any grounding.
took: Email-in capture at the gateway inbox (subject-line grammar; per-purpose revocable drop addresses) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 7 — source/inspiration: Evernote / OmniFocus pattern (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — Evernote's email-in capture pattern is literally built into our gateway (see took); the product itself remains the cautionary baseline: the category's pioneer holds its users' archives in its own cloud, the custody model our files-first design exists to avoid. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Google Docs
licence: Proprietary (free with a Google Account; Workspace plans paid — no licence stated at source).
good: The default document surface of the world: real-time co-editing with sharing controls and a revision history you can revert through, Word conversion both ways, and free with any Google account — its version history is the one genuine record-keeping feature in the consumer office class.
bad: Total platform custody: documents live in Google's cloud and formats, the revision history is Google's to keep, and real-time multi-writer editing — its core virtue — is the collaboration model our single-writer design rejects; there is no claim, citation or knowledge layer at all.
didnt: Rejected — the canonical cloud co-editing word processor; our documents are owner-held files, and its one record-keeping virtue (revertible revision history) is one our git history already embodies with stronger guarantees. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Google Keep
licence: Proprietary (free — no licence stated at source).
good: Capture with zero ceremony, embedded everywhere: notes, lists, photos, drawings and voice memos one tap away inside every other Google app, with family sharing built in — the lowest-friction capture layer in this batch.
bad: Deliberately shallow: cards with no structure, linking or knowledge model, held in Google's cloud; and its sharing is coarse — the FAQ notes anyone in a family group can delete a shared note, so custody and control are traded away for convenience.
didnt: Corroboration — Keep corroborates capture-first at platform scale (a note surface inside every app you already use) while displaying its natural limit: capture without structure, citation or custody is a pile of cards, which is why our capture feeds a compiled wiki instead. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HelixNotes
licence: AGPL-3.0 (maker's posts and project listings; the project site itself says 'free, open source').
good: The local-first Markdown pattern executed with unusual completeness by a solo maker: ordinary .md files, a wiki-link graph, a cross-note Tasks view, per-note version history, automatic backups, sync deliberately left to the user's own tools, and AI that is optional and bring-your-own-key or fully local.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack; it is a young single-maker project (v1.3.6) whose polish is still catching up with its philosophy; and as an editor it has no citation, claim or abstention machinery — it keeps notes faithfully and vouches for nothing.
didnt: Corroboration — HelixNotes is independent proof of the foundation: plain Markdown files, wiki links, local custody, sync-by-files — built by a maker who rejected cloud notes for the same reasons. Our layers above that foundation (citation locking, scored abstention, approval gates) are exactly what it does not attempt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mendeley
licence: Proprietary freemium (Elsevier; 2GB free tier — no licence stated at source).
good: A real researcher's library workflow for free: PDF-first reference management with in-place reading, highlighting and annotation, collections and tags — and an AI layer that works across the whole library rather than one document at a time.
bad: The library lives in Elsevier's cloud under a 2GB free ceiling: custody of a researcher's corpus sits with a publisher whose interests are not the researcher's, and the AI's cross-reference connections are generated inside that closed system with no exportable, checkable record.
didnt: Rejected — a reference manager inside a publisher's cloud; our programme holds its sources as raw files it custodies itself, and Mendeley's AI-over-the-library pattern, like EndNote's, manages containers of claims rather than claims. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Microsoft OneNote
licence: Freemium proprietary (Microsoft — no licence stated at source).
good: The free-form notebook at platform scale: a canvas mixing typing, ink, audio and files, voice transcription built in, and now Copilot Notebooks that reason over the notebook's contents plus your files and email — with Sticky Notes that resurface when you return to a source.
bad: Custody is Microsoft 365: notebooks live in OneDrive in a proprietary package format, the free-form canvas that makes capture easy makes structure and export ragged, and Copilot's work over the notebook is a cloud service, not a checkable record.
didnt: Rejected — a superb capture canvas inside Microsoft's cloud and formats; our capture feeds plain files, and its source-recall Sticky Notes are the consumer shadow of the citation machinery we build properly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notes
licence: Proprietary (free; bundled with Apple's operating systems — no licence stated at source).
good: The default capture surface for a billion devices: quick notes, checklists, sketches, scanned documents with searchable text, smart folders and note links — zero setup, zero cost, always in sync, and lockable per note.
bad: Apple-walled and iCloud-held: no real presence off Apple's platforms beyond a web shell, organisation tops out at folders and tags, and there is no export-respecting knowledge model — notes are easy to make and hard to take anywhere else in structured form.
didnt: Corroboration — Notes is the baseline proof that capture must be instant and everywhere (Quick Note from any screen) before it is anything else; our pipeline starts from the same premise and adds the structure, citation and custody a platform default never will. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Paperpile
licence: Paid proprietary (no licence stated at source).
good: The reference manager that respects where your files already live: PDFs sit in your own Google Drive, capture is one click from anywhere, annotation and citation happen in one Gmail-simple surface, and it is explicit that it never touches your password or unrelated Drive files.
bad: The trade is total Google dependence: sign-in, storage and the writing surface (Google Docs) are all Google's, the library's organisation layer is Paperpile's proprietary service, and citation here means formatting — nothing checks that a cited paper still stands.
didnt: Rejected — an elegant reference manager whose custody answer (your Drive, their organiser, Google's docs) is the inverse of ours (our files, our organiser, our pages); its one-click capture is the only move, and our ingest already has it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Qiqqa
good: A once-commercial research manager (PDF library, OCR, annotation, reference tools) given entirely to its community — every premium feature included — and kept alive by volunteers years after the company wound down.
bad: Its own history is the cautionary tale: when the commercial cloud closed, users' Web Libraries were unrecoverable without local backups; and the codebase is a Windows-only legacy desktop application with sparse releases — a preserved artefact, not a living platform.
didnt: Rejected — Windows-only legacy software whose development has wound down; its enduring value to this survey is documentary: a reference manager's cloud died and took its libraries with it, which is the failure mode our local raw custody exists to prevent. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: QOwnNotes
good: A decade-deep plain-files notes system with the full modern checklist: your Markdown files stay yours, sync is your Nextcloud (or Dropbox, or Syncthing), versioning and trash come from the server app, notes can be AES-256 encrypted — and it ships an MCP server so AI agents can search and fetch your notes, the same door pattern our wiki exposes read-only.
bad: GPL-2.0 makes the code ideas-only for us; the experience is a power user's Qt desktop app (60+ languages, dockable everything) rather than a system with a knowledge model — no citations, claims or verification, and its AI features are provider plug-ins, not a grounded answer layer.
didnt: Corroboration — independent, decade-long proof of our substrate choices (plain Markdown files, sync-by-files, wiki links with backlinks) plus convergent evolution on the agent door: it grew a built-in MCP server for notes just as our wiki exposes a read-only MCP door. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ReadCube Papers
licence: Paid proprietary (subscription tiers — no licence stated at source).
good: Literature management at enterprise scale with verifiability as the headline promise: answers linked to their sources across a 165M-publication corpus, shared libraries, and structured review workflows (PRISMA, dual review) that treat evidence handling as a process, not a chat.
bad: It is an enterprise cloud sold to companies: your library, annotations and questions live on ReadCube's platform, the 'verifiable' claim is a headline whose mechanics the page does not show, and nothing here is a personal, owner-held record.
didnt: Corroboration — a mainstream vendor now sells 'every citation sourced, linked, verifiable' as the headline of a literature platform: the market has arrived at the premise our citation lockfile implements with pinned, checkable evidence rather than a slogan. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RemNote
licence: Proprietary freemium (no licence stated at source).
good: The notes-to-memory pipeline done in one app: write notes, turn them into flashcards without leaving the flow, and let spaced repetition plus an exam-date scheduler decide what to review each day — with AI generation from PDFs and transcripts feeding the deck.
bad: It optimises for passing exams, not for holding truth: AI-generated cards and explanations are unverified by design, the knowledge base lives in RemNote's cloud, and its model of knowledge is what one student can recall — not what a record can prove.
didnt: Rejected — a learning-retention tool for students; our memory problem is the fidelity of the written record, not the owner's recall, and drilling generated cards is the opposite direction from a citation-locked wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SciSpace
licence: Proprietary freemium (no licence stated at source).
good: A broad, popular front end for paper work: chat with a PDF, assisted literature review, citation generation and topic finding in one place, with adoption at a scale (9.6M researchers claimed) that proves the demand for AI over scholarly text.
bad: The gallery includes an 'AI Humanizer' — a tool whose purpose is to disguise machine text as human — which is provenance laundering sold as a feature; the scholarly tools are generation-first (write, paraphrase, summarise) with citation as formatting, the exact inverse of verification.
didnt: Rejected — a generation suite for papers, including a humanizer that exists to obscure where text came from; our system's open gap is scholarly citation truth-checking, and SciSpace is evidence of the flood that makes it necessary, not a source for it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Simplenote
licence: GPL-2.0 for the client apps (catalogue record); the sync service is Automattic's proprietary cloud.
good: Radical simplicity that has outlived fancier rivals: type, tag, search, share — with every change backed up so any note can be revisited as it was, Markdown when you want it, on every platform, free.
bad: The sync and history live in Automattic's cloud and the model stops at tags: no links, no structure, no knowledge layer — a notebook, deliberately; and its version history is a convenience feature, not an auditable record.
didnt: Corroboration — per-change versioned capture ('go back in time') in the simplest notes app on the market corroborates our version-everything instinct; our git history is the same promise kept with proofs instead of a slider. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Standard Notes
licence: AGPL-3.0 (catalogue record; the site states the code is completely open and independently audited).
good: The custody posture as a consumer product, sustained for a decade without venture capital: audited zero-knowledge end-to-end encryption, offline copies, open and audited code, and a business model (users pay, nobody else) aligned with keeping promises — holding everything from journals to health and family records on that basis.
bad: Encryption is also its ceiling: content sealed against the provider is equally opaque to search, AI and tooling beyond the app itself, so the vault can keep knowledge but cannot compute over it; and AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Corroboration — a second independent witness (with Anytype) that users will pay for zero-knowledge, owner-keyed custody of their most sensitive notes; our difference is the same fork: sealed vaults protect the record, plain owner-held files let a system work on it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Super Productivity
good: A full work-management system with a privacy posture most commercial tools will not match: local-first, no account, no telemetry, end-to-end-encrypted self-hostable sync, deep tracker integrations, and MIT licensing — sustained at 23k stars.
bad: It is a task and time manager: notes exist as attachments to tasks, not as knowledge; there is no document, citation or memory model — the unit of thought is the ticket, and when the ticket closes, its context goes with it.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an excellent local-first task system, but our programme's task layer already lives in its own goal and tracking machinery; nothing in Super Productivity answers a knowledge question our wiki poses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Trilium Notes
good: The deepest open personal-knowledge-base feature set in this wave: a tree with cloning instead of single-parent filing, note hoisting for focus, attributes that double as a query and scripting layer, relation maps, per-note encryption and self-hosted sync — proven at 100,000-note scale.
bad: AGPL-3.0 throughout; a single application database rather than owner-readable files; and an Electron app whose richness (scripting, widgets, maps) is a platform to maintain — its record is the database's word, with versioning internal rather than independently checkable.
took: Relation maps + note hoisting — built in Round 3, lanes TB4/TB5 — source/inspiration: Trilium (idea only, as recorded); Trilium is also among the 21 named forms behind the Graph, portal and capture forms built in Round 3 (lane8-dispositions.md).
didnt: Corroboration — Trilium's relation maps and note hoisting were taken as ideas into our Round 3 build (see took); the rest corroborates the large-personal-knowledge-base ambition while its database custody and AGPL licence mark where our files-first stack diverges. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WizNote
licence: Paid proprietary (no licence stated at source).
good: A complete Evernote-class feature set from the Chinese ecosystem: web clipping, Markdown, two-way linking, team wikis with real-time collaboration, and sync across every device class including WeChat — a reminder the category is global, not a Silicon Valley monopoly.
bad: Vendor-cloud custody throughout, with collaboration and WeChat sync as the gravity, positioned for the Chinese market and its platform rules; 'citations' here means two-way links between your own notes, not sources — nothing in it verifies anything.
didnt: Rejected — a cloud collaboration notebook in the Evernote lineage; its two-way links and clipping are table stakes our ingest already covers, and its custody model is the one this programme exists to refuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zettlr
licence: GPL-3.0 (catalogue record; the site confirms free and open source software with files staying on your computer).
good: The scholarly writing desk built on the right custody: your Markdown files on your computer, a real reference manager wired in for citations, and one-click typeset export through Pandoc profiles — the full idea-to-publication path without a platform taking custody at any step.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us; and it is a writing workbench, not a record system — citations are formatted from the reference manager at export time, with no pinning of what a claim rested on when it was written, and no answer or abstention layer.
didnt: Corroboration — Zettlr corroborates the scholarly corner of our design (local files, citation-manager integration, Zettelkasten IDs and links) from the writing side; our citation lockfile exists because formatting a citation at export is weaker than pinning the evidence when the claim is made. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zotero
licence: Open source (AGPL-3.0 — the project's licence; zotero.org states Zotero is open source and nonprofit-developed); freemium — paid tiers sell sync storage.
good: The reference manager as public infrastructure: one-click capture with full metadata from across the scholarly web, a local library you control, 9,000+ citation styles inside every writing tool, and group libraries free — run by a nonprofit whose stated interest is that you keep control of your own data.
bad: It manages references, not knowledge: the library is metadata and PDFs, annotation stays shallow, and citation still means formatting at write time — nothing pins what a claim rested on, or notices when a source is later retracted; sync beyond the free storage tier is a paid subscription.
didnt: Corroboration — Zotero is the scholarly commons our citation machinery presupposes: the capture-and-organise layer run as nonprofit open infrastructure with user control of data as its founding claim; our lockfile starts where Zotero stops, at the claim rather than the reference. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Athena
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS, free while small; its listing names no licence).
good: Consumer software built on our two rarest premises: nothing enters the record without your approval of each piece, and the system's daily job is one honest briefing about what matters — commitments and people tracked from what you actually said, in your words.
bad: The record is life-admin in a startup's cloud: commitments and worries, not sources or claims; approval gates the input, but nothing verifies or cites anything, and 'free while it's small' is the whole business model stated aloud.
didnt: Corroboration — Athena independently arrived at approval-gated capture plus a daily what-matters briefing, the consumer shape of our gateway gates and morning report; it corroborates the interaction design while its cloud custody and uncited memory show the distance to a record system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BookRecall
licence: No licence stated at source (freemium app; its listing names no licence).
good: A tight loop for readers: photograph a passage, keep the highlight, and receive daily recall prompts with questions — capture and spaced recall aimed at exactly the point where reading evaporates.
bad: Highlights without a home: the listing itself concedes no idea detection, no API and no collaboration, and a highlight severed from its page, edition and context is a quotation, not knowledge; three reviews are the whole public evidence base.
didnt: Rejected — a reading-recall gadget; our ingest keeps the whole source precisely so a passage never has to survive as an orphaned highlight. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Brain.fm
licence: No licence stated at source (subscription service, from $14.99/month; its listing names no licence).
good: Functional audio taken seriously as engineering: long, lyrics-free tracks modulated for the target brain state, research backing claimed, and modes for work, rest and sleep — designing explicitly for the attention its users actually have.
bad: A subscription stream with no offline mode: stop paying, or lose signal, and the focus aid vanishes; and whatever its merits as audio, it holds no knowledge and keeps no record.
didnt: Rejected — focus audio, not a knowledge system; noted with respect for its ADHD-aware design, and nothing in it touches the record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Brainbase
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its listing names no licence and publishes no pricing).
good: Website AI as an afternoon's embedding rather than a quarter's project: a co-pilot that answers and guides visitors, aimed at owners with no engineering staff.
bad: The listing itself flags the costs: no explicit user data protection and an opaque algorithm, with a capability ceiling at simple tasks — a widget that speaks for your site without a record of what it said or why.
didnt: Rejected — a website chat widget; it puts generated answers in front of the public with no grounding discipline, the deployment pattern our abstention rules exist to prevent. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Brainfish
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its listing names no licence).
good: It treats a help centre as a living corpus: find the gaps from real customer questions, draft the missing articles, and keep the existing ones proofread and translated — knowledge maintenance as a continuous process rather than a documentation project.
bad: The maintenance is unreviewed generation at the public boundary: AI writes the articles customers will trust, from 'trends', inside the vendor's platform — a knowledge base that updates itself is one whose errors update themselves too.
didnt: Rejected — a support-deflection layer over someone else's help centre; its gap-filling drafts are exactly the write path our approval gates exist to slow down. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BrainSoup
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial desktop software; its listing names no licence).
good: A multi-agent team as a desktop product with the privacy posture stated up front: agents with defined roles and user-set knowledge boundaries, working from your documents, your data held in a local database, and third-party calls anonymised — collaboration without handing the corpus to the platform.
bad: Windows-only and chat-room-shaped: the agents' work product is conversation, with no compiled record, citation or verification layer; and with hosted models only, the local database still phones the cloud for every thought.
didnt: Corroboration — BrainSoup corroborates the multi-agent-over-your-documents shape (role agents, bounded knowledge, local data) that our own agent team works in; the difference is that our agents write to a checked, permanent record rather than a chat room. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Clear Cortex
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; its listing names no licence).
good: Whichever identity is current, the Q&A's workspace design is the right instinct: answers drawn only from explicitly connected sources, each answer citing what it drew from, and shared workspaces so a team gets the same context and the same answers; the studio side likewise keeps one library and one login across every major media model.
bad: A listing that cannot present one product cannot ground trust in either: the sourced-answering workspace is described only in Q&A text with no mechanics, pricing or custody terms, and the studio side is a credit-burning generation aggregator whose discarded renders are a listed cost.
didnt: Rejected — as catalogued, a marketing media studio, which is out of scope; and the grounded-workspace product its own Q&A describes is asserted without evidence, under a page that disagrees with itself about what the product is (discrepancy recorded here, as with Sagekit in B099). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ClickUp Brain
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; freemium, paid from $10/month — its listing names no licence).
good: AI embedded where the work already is rather than in a separate chatbot: search that sees the whole workspace, agents built without code, and meeting-to-follow-up automation — with a stated no-training, no-retention data posture and real compliance badges.
bad: The workspace is ClickUp's cloud and ClickUp's model of work (tasks, docs, stand-ups); the AI's context is everything the company put into ClickUp and nothing it didn't, and its answers carry no citation or abstention discipline — fluency across the corpus, vouched for by nobody.
didnt: Rejected — an AI skin over a team project platform; workspace-wide context search is the commodity form of grounded answering, and our record cannot live inside a task manager's cloud. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

bad: Everything captured lands in Cluing's hosted environment, its agents are hosted-only with no offline use, and the listing itself warns that sharing sensitive data through it raises security concerns; one review is the entire public evidence base.
didnt: Corroboration — Cluing's source-attached insight capture corroborates our raw-source ingest discipline from the browsing side; its hosted-agent, team-cloud custody is the fork where our owner-held raw files diverge. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Constella

didnt: Corroboration — Constella corroborates resurfacing-while-you-write, our neighbour machinery in consumer form; its unresolved custody claims (recorded in-row) are why our version is computed over files whose location is never in doubt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fabric
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial SaaS; paid from $10/month after trial — its listing names no licence).

didnt: Rejected — the anti-pattern to a compiled wiki: an ever-shifting, history-free organisation layer over a vendor-held pile; our wiki's organisation is written down, diffed and kept. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HeyBrain

name: Macaron
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial personal-agent app; its listing names no licence).

name: Mantle
licence: No licence stated at source (MantleOS's own site and its listing both describe it as open source, self-hosted and free with no per-seat fees, but neither names a licence).

didnt: Corroboration — Mantle independently assembles our whole premise in one product: owned custody, total ingest, sourced page-and-line answers, permissioned reading and running, an MCP door and a morning briefing; it corroborates the design end-to-end while its unnamed licence and gate-free autonomy mark exactly where our discipline is stricter. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Medical Brain

name: Mnemosphere

name: mymind

name: Omi AI

name: Orchid

name: OsirisBrain

name: 0spoon/seamless

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 20alexl/claude-engram
licence: No licence found at the repo (the README's contents list no licence section, the LICENSE path returns 404, and a targeted web search surfaced none) — treated as all-rights-reserved, ideas only.
good: The session itself becomes the record: hooks capture every decision, mistake, edit and test result without being asked; a checkpoint is banked before every compaction and the rules, past mistakes and checkpoint are re-injected on the far side; and a completion claim is verified against evidence before it is believed — with run reports the README insists are hook-captured, never self-reported by the model.

didnt: Corroboration — engram independently builds our own survival kit: capture everything automatically, checkpoint before compaction, re-inject the rules and the mistakes, and never let a completion claim stand without evidence; it corroborates the discipline from inside a single tool, and its missing licence keeps the corroboration at the level of ideas. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: a2cr/a2cr
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata shows 'Apache License 2.0'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: The handoff treated as a first-class object: a compact checkpoint carrying goal, state, decisions, blockers, validation and next action — deliberately not the transcript — stored locally, resumable by any MCP client, with the boundary stated in writing that loaded context is work state, not an authority.
