(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Abhigyan-Shekhar/Waggle-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata shows 'Apache License 2.0'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Approval-gated memory correction, fully mechanised: an agent proposes a replacement, a human reviews and approves the exact value, the system checks the target has not moved since the proposal, and the old memory stays in history joined to its replacement — with recall returning supersession provenance, a local SQLite default and a portable graph file for moving memory between clients.
bad: The gate has a stated perimeter: by the README's own admission, direct graph editing and local MCP writes bypass the approval flow, so the discipline holds only on the browser-correction path; the hosted workspace is a disposable preview on free hosting (temporary /tmp state), and the project is young (created 2026-04-12).
didnt: Corroboration — Waggle's propose → human approves the exact value → apply-with-freshness-check → predecessor preserved in history is approval-gated writing and supersession, independently built and honestly scoped; it corroborates the gate design, including the candour about where the gate does not reach. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: adelinamart/robrain
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata shows 'Apache License 2.0'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Memory with judgment about what was refused: every decision is stored with the alternatives that were rejected as a structured field, decisions carry a lifecycle (active / superseded / invalidated) and a conflict graph, a corpus-wide synthesis pass hunts drift and contradiction no single session could see, and the benefit is benchmarked — veto memory measurably stops agents re-proposing what the team already ruled out.
bad: The self-hosted open version is the lesser half: the comparison table reserves write-time supersession detection, conflict auto-resolution and the calibrated taxonomy for the paid cloud, it demands Postgres plus Anthropic/OpenAI keys to run at all, and it is young and unreleased (created 2026-05-04, 0 releases).
didnt: Corroboration — RoBrain corroborates the corrections-ledger principle with the sharpest formulation in this wave: a rejection is structured data with a lifecycle, contradictions are found by scanning the whole corpus, and the cost of forgetting a 'no' is measured, not asserted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: afairai/afair
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo metadata shows 'GNU Affero General Public License v3.0'; the README's License section confirms it).
good: A two-storey memory with the right load-bearing wall: an append-only, content-addressed event substrate that is never rewritten, with every interpretation a versioned view that can be regenerated without touching a stored event; a deliberately frozen three-verb surface, visible beliefs the owner can trace to source and correct, and corrections preserved as history.
bad: AGPL-3.0 puts its code off-limits for adaptation under our licence discipline, ideas only; its organising principle is emergence — 'the user never defines a category' — which surrenders the deliberate schema and owner-set structure our record depends on; and it is young (created 2026-05-25, 6 stars) with the hosted offering not yet live.
didnt: Corroboration — afair is the closest architectural cousin in this wave: preserve everything append-only, derive every view, let corrections accrete as history rather than overwrite — our raw/compiled split arrived at independently; the AGPL licence and its anti-schema stance keep it corroboration, never a source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentBase1/mcp-server
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository; the registry content it serves is stated in the README to be CC0).
good: A tidy, honest piece of plumbing: four well-scoped MCP tools giving any agent searchable access to a shared registry of instruction files, with the registry's contents under CC0 so what an agent retrieves is free to use without restriction.
bad: The mechanism is the hazard: an agent pulling third-party instruction files into its context at runtime, from a hosted registry of unknown curation, is a standing injection door; the implementation is also minimal (15 commits, one file, no releases) and wholly dependent on the vendor's hosted registry staying up.
didnt: Rejected — fit and trust model: our skills are few, local, read before use and changed only by the owner; a runtime marketplace of strangers' instructions is the arrangement that discipline exists to refuse, however open its licences are. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agentcivics/agentcivics
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: A complete, internally consistent on-chain civics for agents: identity as a soulbound object with lineage and death as real events, reputation earned from measured activity rather than self-declared, refusal recorded as first-class negative space, and moderation that no single actor can capture (stake, quorum auto-flag, council, DAO) — all transparent and auditable on-chain.
bad: It answers a public-world problem with public-world costs: identity and memory live permanently on a public chain, memory literally costs money and decays unpaid, the deployed reality is four testnet agents — and a private, single-owner record needs none of the consensus, staking or token economics, while on-chain permanence is the opposite of private custody.
didnt: Rejected — a decentralised registry solves trust between strangers; our record's authority is one owner's, held privately and correctable by him alone, and pay-to-remember with decay is a custody model we would never accept for it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agentic-mcp-tools/memora
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: The most battle-tested memory server in this wave (744 stars, 539 commits, 35 releases): absorb with classification and preview before anything is written, supersession lineage that retrieval follows to the current version by default while keeping the full history one mode away, topic digests that return sources alongside memories, and document fragments guarded against accidental merge or deletion.
bad: Its intelligence is also its risk: an LLM decides whether a new fact duplicates, updates or contradicts the record, so merges happen on model judgment — and by its own documentation the system can degrade silently (a healthy-looking TF-IDF fallback) while the container path demands macOS 26 and hand-built proxy plumbing; cloud sync moves custody outward by design.
didnt: Corroboration — Memora corroborates our ingest shape at the largest scale in this wave: classify-on-arrival with a dry-run before committing, supersede-never-delete with lineage you can walk, and retrieval that returns source IDs with the answer; its documented silent-degradation mode is the caution our verify-the-thing-itself standard answers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentModule/mcp
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository; the knowledge service it fronts is commercial).
good: Compliance as retrievable infrastructure: EU AI Act obligations decomposed into modules whose logic gates are deterministic JSON — pass or fail, traced to the article they implement, with human-in-the-loop escalation points in the directive layer and a provenance chain kept for audit; an agent can check itself against the statute at runtime instead of improvising.
bad: The repo holds no knowledge: it is a thin proxy to a paid hosted API, the content layers sit behind trial keys and membership, several tools exist to run the sales funnel (waitlist, referrals, proof-of-value submission), and the whole thing is 26 commits and 2 stars — compliance certainty rented by the call.
didnt: Corroboration — its one real idea corroborates ours: rules worth executing are deterministic, binary and pinned to a cited source, never a model's impression; everything else about it (hosted, metered, funnel-shaped) is the commercial wrapper that idea does not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ahmetakyurt/zipmem-mcp
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Memory as coordinates, not copies: what survives a session is a blueprint kept verbatim, a set of anchors pointing at exact file lines, and lessons distilled to one line each — the window stays small, the detail is re-read from the file itself when needed, and the staged-checkpoint/authoritative-save split means a crash loses at most the work since the last checkpoint.
bad: The compacting is done by the agent under a prompt directive, so nothing verifies that an anchor or a distilled lesson is faithful — the lossy step is exactly the unverified one; and the project is brand new (created 2026-06-20, 0 stars, no releases) with a single JSON file as the whole store.
didnt: Corroboration — zipmem corroborates two of our mechanisms in miniature: keep the coordinate and re-read the source on demand rather than trusting a stored copy (our citation pointers), and separate the staged checkpoint from the authoritative save (our checkpoint discipline); its candour about the directive being unenforceable is the same honesty. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: aidesignblueprint/integrations
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Doctrine distributed the careful way: one body of design principles served identically as IDE rules, prompt files and a read-only MCP surface, so every agent works from the same text; and its feedback tools carry the strictest consent wording in this wave — a value signal may be recorded only after the user has clearly said something was useful, at most once per session, never silently.
bad: The repo is a mirror of a hosted contract, not the substance: the validators that do the real work are paywalled, authenticated and store your runs server-side, there is no public API schema or CLI by its own 'intentionally not here yet' list, and the audience is 3 stars.
didnt: Corroboration — the corroboration is in its manners: a public read-only doctrine door, and write tools that may fire only on the user's explicit expression, never silently or automatically — our ask-first rule written into someone else's tool contract; the design-UX doctrine itself sits outside a personal record's scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ailenshen/apple-notes-mcp
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; the README's License section confirms MIT).
good: The most careful consumer-notes bridge in the wave: minimal-diff edits that leave the rest of the note — including formatting Markdown cannot express — untouched, optimistic-concurrency refusal when the note changed underneath, a backup before every change, and honest two-way Markdown conversion for the styles Notes actually has.
bad: The price of admission is steep and narrow: macOS 26 only for the current version, a Full Disk Access grant, and Apple's walled store underneath — attachments are read-only, locked notes are invisible, and the record's real custody stays inside Apple's proprietary database whatever the server does.
didnt: Corroboration — its write discipline corroborates ours exactly: refuse the write when the target moved since the read, back up before changing, touch only the difference; careful writing into a store you do not own is the consumer-scale version of our approval-gated, freshness-checked writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AIStorageDepot/aistoragedepot-mcp
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: One library, every client: prompts, rules and skills maintained in a single place and projected into whichever agent tool is open — as MCP prompts, as addressable resources, or as native slash-command files per client, with namespacing that keeps the sync from ever touching the user's own commands.
bad: The library's home is the vendor's cloud: the server is a 14-commit thin client (created 2026-07-23, 0 stars), the account token is all-powerful, and the pull feature's whole job is writing service-held content into the instruction folders of every agent client on the machine.
didnt: Rejected — custody and duplication: our prompts, rules and skills already live as local files under the owner's version control and are read before use; a hosted library that syncs content into agent instruction surfaces adds a vendor, a token and a supply path to gain nothing we lack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AkashGoenka/coldstart
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Notes that know when they have gone stale: every claim in the notebook is anchored to files and symbols with a content hash, the index re-checks the stamps as code changes, and drifted knowledge degrades into a labelled hypothesis with re-verification guidance instead of a confident lie; around it, a deterministic index (no embeddings to drift) and a write gate that kills duplicates at write time rather than cleaning them up later.
bad: Its world is the codebase: navigation parses TypeScript-family languages (the notebook's hash machinery is language-agnostic, the index is not), the notebook's payoff is admittedly unproven over a repo's lifetime, and the audience is still 11 stars.
didnt: Corroboration — the strongest corroboration in this batch: freshness as a mechanical property rather than a hope — hash-stamped evidence, stale knowledge visibly demoted instead of confidently served, the append-only log as truth with pages derived from it — is our change-detection and raw/compiled discipline, built for code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AlekseiMarchenko/central-intelligence
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata shows 'Apache License 2.0'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Verbatim custody as the headline contract: the service decomposes memories into facts for search but returns the user's own content unrewritten, scopes sharing explicitly (agent, user, org), reads the memory files of rival tools so context follows the user across clients, and shows its benchmark numbers — including a mediocre 52.2% on the hardest one — instead of cherry-picking.
bad: The substance lives in their cloud: the local package is a thin client to a hosted API, memories flow to the vendor's Postgres for decomposition, 'forget' is a hard delete endpoint with no history, and the benchmark suite carries a disclosed self-interest (one harness is the author's own).
didnt: Corroboration — CI corroborates the two habits that matter here: return the owner's words verbatim, never a model's rewrite of them, and publish your memory's measured scores with the conflicts of interest stated; its hosted custody is where the agreement ends — corroboration of principle, not a candidate store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alfredoizdev/contextforge-mcp
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Compaction survival treated as an engineering problem with receipts: the session's objective is captured prompt by prompt before any summary can eat it, the post-compaction recall is relevance-ranked, size-capped and deadline-bound so a slow search can never drop the rest, and the privacy note itemises what is local, what is sent and what is never uploaded.
bad: The memory's home is the vendor's cloud behind an account key, the 69-tool surface is sprawl the project itself has to hide behind a lean mode and a gateway tool, and it is young (created 2026-05-16, 2 stars) — the hooks are careful, the custody is rented.
didnt: Corroboration — ContextForge corroborates our compaction discipline from the product side: log the objective before the cut, re-inject it after, keep the injected block small and bounded, disclose precisely what leaves the machine; its freshness/confirm/correct verbs are our reverify habit as tooling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: aliasunder/vault-cortex
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: A serious, heavily-shipped door over files the owner keeps: 1,156 commits and 245 releases behind hybrid search, tasks, link-graph health and append-only memory that shows how a view evolved, reachable from a phone under OAuth while the vault itself never stops being a folder of Markdown the user can walk away with.

didnt: Corroboration — Vault Cortex corroborates the files-first architecture commercially: a disposable server over owner-held plain Markdown, append-only dated memory whose history stays visible, shipped and stress-tested in the field; it is our substrate bet, productised for Obsidian users. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AliceLJY/recallnest
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE file ships in the repository).
good: Evidence and memory kept in separate storeys: transcript fragments live on an evidence layer that can be searched but never mistaken for a decision, promotion to durable memory is a gated step with conflict guards and an audit trail, every recall states its provenance and age, and the store lints itself for contradictions, duplicates and orphans.
bad: The machinery is heavy and speculative in places: 44 tools, a Bun/LanceDB stack with external embeddings, Weibull decay curves, emotion modulation and predictive reminders far beyond what a personal record can verify; one author, 15 stars, and a feature surface that outruns its own evaluation.
didnt: Corroboration — RecallNest corroborates our layer discipline precisely: raw evidence and durable memory are different layers, promotion between them is gated and evidence-bearing, and every retrieved row must declare which layer it came from; its published FAILURES.md and its default-off reversal are the record-keeping honesty itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ambermem/amber
licence: MIT (repo metadata shows 'MIT License'; a LICENSE.md file ships in the repository; the service it runs is commercial and hosted-only).
good: Retrieval engineered around how people actually ask: every fact is embedded under five or more phrasings of itself, so a question phrased unlike the original conversation still finds it; facts are atomic and individually searchable with subjects, topics and dates, time expressions resolve to real ranges, and the whole store exports as JSON on demand.
bad: Custody is the disqualifier: the service cannot be self-hosted at all, the record of a life sits on a newborn vendor's edge infrastructure (created 2026-05-17, 1 star), and the 'no model reads your memories' promise survives only by defining the OpenAI embedding endpoint out of 'reading' — the text leaves the user's control either way.
didnt: Rejected — a personal record that cannot come home fails our custody rule no matter how good the retrieval is; export-as-JSON is an exit door, not custody. The paraphrase-variant mechanism is recorded in this row as the one idea worth remembering. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: andreas-roennestad/openhive-mcp
licence: MIT (stated in the README's License section; no LICENSE file appears in the repository root listing).
good: The pair is the unit: a problem stored together with the approaches that were tried and failed before the one that worked, searchable by the next agent who hits the same wall — collective debugging memory across agents and organisations, with solutions ranked by how often they get used.
bad: Provenance-free by design: anyone's agent can post, the only quality signal is a use counter that increments on retrieval, and nothing vets a 'solution' before the next agent reads it as knowledge — a popularity-ranked pool of untrusted third-party content is an injection surface wearing a knowledge base's clothes.
didnt: Rejected — our record admits material through sourced ingest with the source named, and a score earned by being fetched is not verification; OpenHive's shape (failed approaches recorded beside the fix) is the one sound idea, and it is already how our corrections ledger works. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: atakanelik34/Bilinc

name: bluzername/lennys-quotes
licence: MIT for the code (per the README's License section; no LICENSE file in the root listing). Transcript content remains Lenny Rachitsky's.
good: Citation to the moment: every answer points at the exact second of the source recording, and the corpus itself is kept as committed, diffable transcript files, so the evidence base is inspectable and versioned rather than a black-box index; an offline mode keeps it usable without the network.
bad: A single third-party corpus whose content rights stay with the podcaster; no evaluation of answer quality; thirteen stars - a personal tool, not infrastructure.
didnt: Corroboration - answers that cite the source segment precisely (speaker, episode, second) are this system's citation discipline in miniature, over someone else's corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cachly-dev/cachly-mcp
good: The lesson mechanics are genuinely well thought: typed lessons with symptom and outcome, a token-budgeted tool surface (27 of 124 listed, the rest behind one dispatcher), reviewer confirmation raising a lesson's rank, a governance audit trail, contradiction detection in consolidation, and export as a first-class verb - 'you can leave and take your data'.
bad: The Brain - the memory itself - lives on their EU servers behind an account and an API key, and a test Brain is auto-created before any account exists; the local repo is the client and documentation, not the store; two stars of adoption.
didnt: Rejected - hosted custody of the memory store is disqualifying for this system's local-first design, however good the lesson mechanics built on top of it are. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: caix84476-netizen/personal-understanding
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata; the catalogue's 'MIT (verified)' note agrees).
good: The closest design relative in this sweep: the verbatim record is the ground truth and everything derived is regenerable and labelled by layer, with promotion rules enforced rather than hoped for; its semantic audit names this programme's exact failure modes (a summary impersonating the verbatim record; a hypothesis quietly promoted to fact; attribution swapped); retrieval is staged survey, probe, then deep, with an associative channel beside it; and the discipline is to say 'not yet found', never 'not found' - unconfirmed items decay in weight but are never deleted.
bad: Three stars and one maintainer; the README is a design document as much as a report - the 180+ regression tests are its own, and the associative-retrieval claims rest on the cited papers rather than its own published evaluation.
didnt: Board - its named semantic-audit checks (summary impersonating the verbatim record; hypothesis quietly promoted; attribution swapped) and the five-layer fact stratification are concrete candidates for this system's claim machinery, MIT-licensed and small enough to re-implement faithfully. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cameronrye/openzim-mcp
good: Tool-surface discipline, measured: the author counted the schema cost of every tool, cut 22 tools to 8, and offers a single-tool mode for small models - the same budget thinking as this system's eight read verbs; and the store itself is integrity-checked (libzim archive validation plus checksums) rather than trusted, with per-entry resources and change notifications over static archives.
bad: A read-only window onto other people's static archives: nothing about capturing, governing or correcting a personal record, and its value ends where the ZIM corpus ends.
didnt: Corroboration - a small fixed verb surface sized to a schema budget, and checksum validation of the store itself, match this system's read-door design and verification posture. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: carrasquelalex1/hipocampo
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata and the README).
good: Real retrieval engineering for its size: a named hybrid pipeline with dynamic fusion, a source layer recording authorship and reading fingerprints, and an installer that stands up the whole stack with no manual steps; the README is candid that the hosted demo loses its data on restart.
bad: The substrate is a database server to operate, and its signature compression is lossy: granular history is summarised into 90-day checkpoints, so the record itself thins over time - the opposite of this system's verbatim-first custody; thirty-six commits and five stars.
didnt: Rejected - server-database custody plus lossy time-decay compression of the record run against this system's plain-file, keep-the-original design; its bilingual documentation is its most portable virtue. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: catfish-1234/sessionmem
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata and the README's badge).
good: Capture hygiene done right: secret redaction happens before storage and is on by default, the store is one inspectable SQLite file needing no account, retrieval is offline BM25 with an optional local embedding model, and the benchmark is committed with its methodology and its misses - rare honesty at this size.
bad: A 90-day retention policy prunes old memories automatically by default, and what is stored is the session-end summary, not the session - the record is deliberately thinned twice over, where this system's record is kept whole.
didnt: Corroboration - default-on secret scrubbing at capture and a published benchmark with its misses match this system's leak discipline and evaluation honesty; we part on retention, which prunes where ours preserves. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cavinooo/claude-find
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata and the README's License section).
good: It searches the record itself: raw transcripts, not compressed summaries - 'nothing lost through compression' is its stated design; it is retroactive over existing sessions with no hooks, permanent retention is treated as a feature worth changing a host setting for, and tool-call metadata (files touched, errors encountered) is indexed as a retrieval signal.
bad: One host only (Claude Code); no write, governance or provenance layer - recall with no curation; and it leans on Bun, Ollama and a GPU to be fast; 55 commits.
didnt: Corroboration - searching the raw transcript and refusing summary-loss is this wiki's conversation-log principle built as a tool by someone else. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ccf/agentcairn
good: This system's architecture, independently arrived at and shipped: files are the truth, the index is replaceable, hand edits are honoured on the next reconciled read, every result carries project, validity status and a permalink, and a failed index rebuild preserves the last good cache while the durable files stay untouched; the installer previews before it writes.
bad: Capture distils transcripts into notes before writing - the vault holds the distillation, not the raw record; the multi-host plugin sprawl (eight hosts, marketplace installs) is a maintenance surface this system does not carry; and its validity-window fields are a design commitment, not a free feature.
didnt: Corroboration - canonical Markdown, a disposable index and non-lossy supersession match this system point for point, and its published recall numbers give an external yardstick; its valid_from/valid_until fields are the bi-temporal design already parked as an owner decision in this programme, not adopted here. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cdeust/Cortex
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata and the README's badge).
good: Write-time verifiability grading is the standout: provenance is graded by whether the memory's references actually resolve, dead references are labelled rather than silently trusted, and the README practises what it grades - shipped is separated from planned, limits are listed beside the install instructions, and unmeasured claims are refused outright.
bad: Fifty-seven tools is a very large surface to govern; the 36-neuroscience-mechanisms framing is heavy ornamentation over the engineering; and the managed-PostgreSQL provisioning machinery (pinned binaries, per-version dependency sets, a setup hook that exits 0 even when installation fails, which the README itself warns about) is a lot of apparatus for a local store.
didnt: Corroboration - grading a memory at write time by whether its references resolve, and labelling the unverifiable instead of hiding it, is this system's citation-lock and abstention posture from the memory side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: celiums/celiums-memory
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the repo metadata; 'in full: no open-core split', per the README).
good: Evidence-preserving by stated design: raw events, claims, graph edges, summaries, policy traces, journal chains and audit records are kept as separate kinds rather than collapsed into opaque vectors; retrieval does not silently mutate memory; mutating requests carry operation IDs with receipts and a recovery story; and the not-production-ready status is declared at the top of the README, not buried.
bad: Fifty-two commits and explicitly not ready for production; the target architecture hands custody to Cloudflare Durable Objects and R2 - hosted, tenant-based infrastructure; and the ethics-engine and circadian layers are a product thesis far beyond a personal record's needs.
didnt: Corroboration - a hash-chained append-only journal, typed abstentions, and provenance kept separate from summaries match this system's ledger and abstention design; the hosted target architecture and pre-production state bar adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cg3-llc/prior_mcp
licence: Functional Source License 1.1 (FSL-1.1-ALv2) per the README's License section (repo metadata: Other/NOASSERTION); source-available, ideas only under this programme's licence discipline.
good: Dead ends are first-class: every solution is stored with what was tried and failed, so the next agent skips known failures instead of rediscovering them; the feedback-refund loop ties search cost to usefulness signals; and retraction is a soft-delete, keeping the exchange honest about removals.
bad: The knowledge base is hosted on their service behind accounts and a credit economy: what your agents solved leaves the machine into a shared commercial pool, quality rests on community feedback rather than verified sources, and the licence is source-available FSL, not open source.
didnt: Rejected - a hosted, credit-metered exchange for agent knowledge is the opposite custody direction from this system's private, owner-held record; recording failed approaches beside solutions is the one idea in it, and this programme already practises that. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: chatmcp/mcp-server-chatsum
licence: No licence found at source (three routes checked: no licence in the repo root listing, metadata or README; the LICENSE blob path returns HTTP 404; directory listings for this repo report no licence; all rights reserved by default).
good: An early proof, from the first month of MCP, that a person's own chat history belongs behind a query tool on their own machine: the store is a local SQLite file, and the one tool both retrieves messages and summarises them against a prompt.
bad: Three commits in total - a December 2024 demo that stopped where it started; summarisation is the only verb, so the answer is a model's compression with no verbatim recall path back to the messages; and with no licence the code is all-rights-reserved.
didnt: Rejected - an abandoned single-tool demo; the pattern it pioneered (query your own chat store through a tool) is one this system already runs properly, with the record itself kept. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CheMiguel23/MemoryMesh
good: Schema-driven tool generation is elegant: declare an entity type once and the server builds its tools, complete with relationship edges created alongside required properties; the memory is one inspectable JSON file with a viewer that shows the raw data, not just a rendering of it.
bad: Built for fiction consistency, not evidence: no provenance, no citations, no verification of anything the model asserts; the schema machinery generates delete tools by default, so the connected model can erase the graph ungated; and a single JSON file of free-text metadata cannot carry a sourced record.
didnt: Rejected - a story-consistency graph whose write model (model-generated add/update/delete, ungated) is the inverse of this system's approval discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: chenxiachan/thoughtdag
good: Context you can inspect and edit before it is used: the panel shows exactly which dossiers and excerpts will enter the next request, with sources one click away and exclusion per item; condensing never destroys the path it shortens; and its benchmark reports its own scope limits (selection timing is not end-to-end speed) instead of inflating them.
bad: A canvas application to live inside, centred on the DeepSeek Harness; editable context makes the human the retrieval layer, which does not scale to a whole-life record; and remote model calls send the selected content to configured providers, as the README states plainly.
didnt: Corroboration - a request preview that shows the assembled context and lets the owner exclude items before anything is sent, plus condensing that preserves the original, are this system's approval and verbatim disciplines from the interaction side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ChevalGrand520/local-gpu-imagegen
good: The governance is the product: authority, reproducibility, review and recovery are wrapped around generation rather than left to the operator - identity is cryptographic, downloads are never silent, acceptance stays with the user at original resolution, and the final artifact is byte-identical to the reviewed one or it is not final.
bad: A narrow golden path (Windows 10/11 with NVIDIA plus an already-running ComfyUI), two stars, and not a knowledge or memory system at all - it sits in this catalogue as an MCP control-plane exemplar, and its apparatus serves image runs, not records.
didnt: Corroboration - confirmation-gated execution, byte-bound finalization, and negative evidence published beside the positive are this system's approval and verification discipline operating in another domain. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ChrisGVE/workspace-qdrant-mcp
good: Serious engineering depth with one governance rule worth underlining: persistent behavioural rules are loaded at session start but may only be created on the user's explicit instruction, never autonomously - the store distinguishes what the owner ruled from what the agent inferred, and the scratchpad is explicitly for the reasoning behind decisions.
bad: Heavy apparatus for a personal record - a Qdrant server, a background daemon, and a C toolchain for grammar compilation; four stars against 5,274 commits; the current line is explicitly transitional while v0.2.0 is rebuilt; and its scope is code projects only, with memory living in vector collections rather than readable files.
didnt: Rejected - a code-indexing platform whose weight, mid-rebuild state and database custody do not fit this system; the discipline inside it (rules only on explicit instruction) is noted, not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cipherfoxie/sovereign-mcp
licence: MIT for the server code; the blog content it serves is CC BY-SA 4.0 (both per the README's License section).
good: Exemplary small-door hygiene: every tool is read-only and idempotent and says so in its annotations, schemas are real typed models rather than dictionaries, the knowledge base is Markdown plus a generated JSON index (a pattern the author documents in a linked write-up), and the diagnose tool answers an error with the curated fix and a link to the source article.
bad: A single blog's content and TF-IDF retrieval only; nothing here addresses a personal record - it is a publishing door, not a memory system.
didnt: Corroboration - a public read-only door over a plain-text knowledge base, with its read-only idempotent nature declared in the protocol annotations so clients can calibrate trust, is this system's door pattern in public form. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CodeAbra/iai-personal-memory-engine
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata and the README).
good: Verbatim-first with contradiction as a first-class operation: the original words are the episodic layer, a contradiction does not overwrite but closes a validity interval and links its successor, and retrieval can return the records that argue against an answer as well as those for it; its published numbers include the comparison it did not win.
bad: Idle-time processing still reshapes the store unattended - weak unreviewed edges decay and summaries are induced without a gate; the encrypted store is not plain-readable files, so the record's inspectability depends on the tool; solo-maintained; English-first by default.
didnt: Corroboration - verbatim capture, contradiction handled as a closed validity interval with old and new records linked, recall returning anti-hits alongside hits, and benchmark ties reported as ties corroborate this system's supersession and evaluation machinery from a popular independent build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: contextium-io/contextium-mcp-server
good: Workflow loading in one call is the right shape for shared team context - a workflow bundles its agents, skills and libraries so a session starts with the whole working set, and restorable-trash deletes plus versioned files are sane defaults for team knowledge.
bad: The repo holds no store to inspect: custody, versioning and search all live on the vendor's servers behind an account, in team-cloud scope; eight commits and zero stars - a wrapper around a service, at the opposite pole from a self-hosted record.
didnt: Rejected - a hosted team platform whose local artifact is only a client; there is nothing here a self-hosted, owner-held record can take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: contextstream/mcp-server
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata; the README scopes it to the server, client and release tooling - the hosted backend is not included).
good: Consent discipline unusually well stated for a hosted product: learning is off by default, consent and withdrawal are explicit and human-only, data handling is documented with its controls before signup, and the performance claim is published with its configuration, methodology and limitations rather than as a bare number.
bad: The memory lives on their hosted backend, which the open repo deliberately excludes - the store doing the remembering cannot be inspected; transcript capture defaults to on; and use is metered in monthly credits against an account.
didnt: Rejected - hosted custody with default-on transcript capture is disqualifying; its consent line ('agents cannot consent for you') is worth quoting in our own docs, but the system is not adoptable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: contradictory-body/cc-sensei
good: The two-layer pattern done cleanly: distilled module notes for orientation, the primary source itself for proof, output budgets that keep answers inside a context window, build-time indexing so runtime is a lookup, and path safety treated as a gate rather than a hope.
bad: One corpus (another product's codebase) and five commits; the analyses are one team's distillation, so trust rests on the notes until the reader drops to source - which the tool at least makes one call away; nothing about personal records or their governance.
didnt: Corroboration - a compiled layer over a primary source, with the source itself still readable by line range behind the same small door, is this wiki's raw/compiled two-layer design applied to a codebase. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: conversation-handoff-mcp
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata and the README's badge).
good: The injection defence is genuinely well designed: retrieved conversation is fenced as untrusted with a boundary the content cannot forge, fences are widened past the body's own backticks, and merges refuse to fabricate provenance - ambiguous sender fields are dropped, not merged into a plausible string; saving is verbatim, with summarisation explicitly instructed against.
bad: A clipboard, not a record: in-memory storage with automatic FIFO deletion of the oldest handoffs is anti-custody by design, and a handoff_clear with no argument wipes everything; nothing persists to files at all.
didnt: Corroboration - its load-time treatment of stored conversation as untrusted content, fenced behind an unforgeable boundary token, corroborates this programme's external-content discipline from inside a memory tool; the storage model itself is the counterexample. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cryptosquanch/legends-mcp
licence: MIT (per the repo metadata and the README's License section, 'but include the disclaimers').
good: The engineering hygiene is fine and the honesty apparatus is present: fully local data with no network calls, structured persona files with explicit guardrails ('things they'd never say'), injection hardening, and disclaimers that name the personas as generated interpretations rather than the people.
bad: It manufactures authoritative-sounding first-person speech in real people's voices from public material: an interpretation delivered as the person is the fabrication pattern itself, and a disclaimer does not convert a simulated Buffett answer into evidence about anything except the persona file.
didnt: Rejected - simulated testimony is the inverse of a sourced record; plausibility in a famous voice is precisely what this system's citation discipline exists to refuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ctxfile/ctxfile
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the repo metadata and the README's package table; the paid Pro add-on is a separate closed package).
good: Approval-aware ingest: imported instructions and identity do not take effect until the user approves them, and a rejection is remembered rather than re-asked; capture hygiene matches it - redaction happens before the snapshot, credential files are never opened, the core never writes to the project, and every save is announced, never silent.
bad: Sessions persist as agent-written summaries rather than the conversation itself; the open core excludes the parts that touch real session history (those are the paid Pro connectors); and the project is weeks old with five stars.
didnt: Corroboration - ingest that waits for approval, rejections that stick, and redaction before capture are this system's gate discipline stated as product features by an independent team. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dahshanlabs/klypix-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the repo metadata and the README).
good: A correction culture in machinery form: corrections are cards that supersede, challenges quote the reversing correction before the stale decision is re-taken, completion requires evidence rather than assertion, and the tooling verifies itself - install exits only after a live handshake, and conformance runs against the exact build installed; even its demo is CI-rendered and labelled as scripted.
bad: Project scope only - one brain per repository; 26-plus verbs is a wide surface to govern; and the brain file is a JSON-canvas format tied to the vendor's wider app ecosystem, whose cloud sharing path sits beside the local server.
didnt: Board - the challenge-before-decision pattern (a claim is checked against recorded corrections and answered with the correction card before work proceeds) and evidence anchors that flag drift in what a decision cites are concrete candidates for this system's correction and citation machinery, Apache-2.0 and plainly specified. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: darktw/usecortex-mcp
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page of the resolved usecortex-official/usecortex-mcp repository.
good: Topic-organised project context behind a two-way door is the shape agents want, encryption at rest with per-user keys is at least claimed, and a free tier lowers the cost of trying it.
bad: The memory itself is hosted and auto-extracted: facts are organised by the service with no human gate, custody sits with a paid third party, session history expires on the paid plan, and the repo is a client stub — the actual memory machinery is closed.
didnt: Rejected - a hosted, auto-extracting memory service behind paid tiers with expiring history is the opposite custody direction from this system's owner-held, human-gated record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: davidgut1982/lore-mcp

name: dbwls99706/deadends.dev

name: dcostenco/prism-mcp

name: DollhouseMCP/mcp-server

name: DomDemetz/claude-soul

name: doobidoo/MCP-Context-Provider

name: doobidoo/mcp-memory-service
licence: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0) per the repo page and the README's badge.

name: dot-RealityTest/obsidian-codex-mcp

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: drexthealpha/Knos
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page.
good: Payment gated on verified proof rather than on a worker's say-so, and a disclosure table that counts what is merely written or merely locally tested, are the same honesty discipline this programme runs on; the backtest number — agent pull requests claiming green checks that were not green in roughly 4-8% of cases — is real evidence for evidence-gated completion.

name: dshakes/distil
licence: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0) per the README's License section and the LICENSE file in the root (repo metadata: Other/NOASSERTION).
good: Lossless-by-default with byte-exact recovery is the only compression posture compatible with a verbatim-first record; the measurement practice — publishing parity, inconclusive pilots, a rival's corrected number and its own externally-caught defect — is evaluation honesty of the first order.

didnt: Board - reversible compression with recoverable handles, hash-chained receipts and published parity/inconclusive results are a concrete Apache-2.0 reference for this system's compaction and handoff handling, where the summary must never become the only surviving record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DuhoKim/NebulaMind
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page.
good: Evidence starts provisional and only becomes active on promotion, with claim trust recalculated at that moment; challenges must arrive carrying a contradicting paper; the full version history is kept.

didnt: Rejected - governance by agent vote, with reputation paid for agreeing with the crowd, is the inverse of an owner-ruled, source-checked record; provisional-until-promoted evidence is the one sound mechanism, recorded in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: edobusy/agenthold
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page and the README's License section.
good: Silent overwrite is treated as the defect it is, and the fix is the database world's proven one; releases that declare what the holder did — including where a file moved to — hand the next worker the truth instead of a surprise.
bad: Coordination only: the store holds working state, not a sourced record — no provenance, citation or retention design; tiny and young (48 commits, 0 releases); correctness rests on agents honouring the claim protocol.
didnt: Corroboration - version-checked writes and outcome-carrying handoffs corroborate the coordination half of this system's single-writer discipline, proven from the multi-agent side; nothing needs adopting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: entanglr/zettelkasten-mcp
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page and the README's License section.
good: The storage doctrine is exactly right — files are truth, the database is a cache that can be thrown away; typed links with named inverses, including a first-class contradicts relation, give the graph semantics most note tools skip.
bad: A note tool, not a knowledge system: no provenance or source citation on notes, no gates, no retrieval evaluation; the author's own notice warns of possible data loss; edits made outside the system need a manual index rebuild.

name: epicsagas/alcove
licence: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0) per the repo page.
good: Keeping private docs out of public repos while making them searchable by every agent from one setup is the right custody shape; validate and lint treat the doc corpus as something whose completeness and freshness can be checked mechanically.
bad: The corpus is project documentation only — architecture, decisions, debt notes — with no record-keeping, provenance or answer evaluation behind the search; retrieval quality is asserted through scores in examples rather than a published benchmark.
didnt: Corroboration - private docs served on demand instead of stuffed into agent config, with policy validation and lint over the corpus, is the retrieval-side shape of this system's doors; nothing needs adopting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ErebusEnigma/context-memory
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page and the README's License section.
good: The pre-compact checkpoint is the standout: the full conversation is saved before the context window eats it, and a tool exists to load it back; outcome classification makes past sessions searchable by how they ended; dry-run pruning and data-preserving migrations show care.

didnt: Corroboration - a full-conversation checkpoint taken before compaction and kept recoverable is this system's conversation-log premise in small; we part on the everyday record being summaries rather than the verbatim session. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: evc-team-relay-mcp
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page and the README's License section.
good: The write policy is enforced by credential class rather than by documentation, errors name the remedy instead of failing obscurely, and the availability matrix distinguishes 'forbidden for you' from 'does not exist yet' — a distinction most READMEs blur.

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fabio-rovai/open-ontologies
licence: MIT License (MIT) per the repo page.
good: Consequences are computed before a change lands, proofs are checkable by someone who trusts neither the author nor the engine, forged results are refused by name, and the language of every claim is calibrated to what actually backs it — verification culture of the highest order in this wave.
bad: A specialist tool for formal ontologies (OWL/RDFS/SHACL) — its machinery does not transfer directly to a Markdown wiki; the hosted platform is the commercial gravity around an MIT core; 1,198 stars in seven months suggests momentum that a small team must sustain.
didnt: Board - plan-before-apply with a semantic blast radius and an independently checkable proof certificate is the strongest external form of this system's propose-verify-apply gateway discipline, and its verdict vocabulary (proved vs measured vs opinion) is a standard our own reporting can be held to; MIT-licensed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fenghaochang/LoreRoom
good: Capture happens at the only point where nothing can be silently lost: the plugin source itself, both sides of the conversation verbatim with time and sender, in an encrypted owner-held store. The security boundary is stated with unusual care: it never handles the bot token; the only secret is a 32-byte key in config.json (git-ignored, chmod 600, never logged, never given to Claude, never crossing a network); the README says plainly this is at-rest encryption of the local database, NOT Telegram end-to-end encryption, that it protects against the database file being copied off the machine, and that it does NOT protect against someone who can already read the account's files, because the key sits next to the database by design. Limitations are admitted in the same document: the spool is briefly plaintext (mode 0700 directory, drained continuously and deleted), plugin patching is required, recall is keyword-plus-time only with no semantic search yet, and messages sent by a separate script outside the plugin's reply path are not captured.
bad: Scope is a single channel: Telegram bots driven through one specific plugin, with a patch that must be re-applied after plugin updates. Recall is keyword and time only. The plaintext spool window, though brief and permissioned, is a real exposure the design accepts rather than eliminates.
didnt: Corroboration — capturing the conversation itself, both sides, at the one point where nothing can slip past, into an encrypted local store with the encryption boundary stated as precisely as our own custody rules would require, is our conversation-log premise engineered for a channel that gives the user no record of their own. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FilippoPilo/cortex-connector
licence: MIT (this connector repository only; the memory engine is closed and unpublished)
good: The claimed differentiators are the right ideas: a quality gate on write (a novelty/redundancy check before storing), typed claims whose contradictions are detected and tracked rather than silently overwritten, an entity knowledge graph, a per-memory coherence metric, and answers that can cite the memories and sources behind them. Deletion of a memory always requires explicit confirmation, and the README is candid that the engine is not open source and that disconnecting leaves the memories in the Cortex account until deletion is requested.
bad: The memory itself lives in a closed, patent-pending hosted service the reader cannot inspect; the MIT licence covers only the bridge, not the engine. A continuous background consolidation cycle ('REM') turns episodic memories into long-term knowledge autonomously, and export and deletion are by request to the vendor rather than operations the owner performs on their own files.
didnt: Rejected — the quality gate, typed claims and conflict tracking are asserted for an engine that cannot be opened, audited or self-hosted, and the owner's record would sit on a vendor's infrastructure under a patent application; our memory has to be files the owner holds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fish827-08/rag-kb
good: An offline-first store whose storage and retrieval never require a model at all. Full audit logging: every write, read, update, delete, search and ask is recorded as JSON per client and project under logs/agent-audit/, queryable via REST and CLI. Per-project sub-stores are physically isolated (kb_data/projects/<project>/ — delete the directory to delete the project's memory) and merged with the global store under a project boost. Memory governance (semantic dedup returning HTTP 409 with the duplicate's id and similarity, decay, freshness) all defaults OFF with zero behaviour change. A privacy guardrail forces sensitive namespaces to local answering, never sent out; /ask routes local-first with cloud fallback only for hard questions in auto mode; embedder failure returns 503 EMBED_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE with the model name and a fix suggestion instead of a bare 500; switching embedding models is guarded — the store keeps using the model it was created with (recorded in runtime.json) and warns on mismatch. The published eval reports the light model matching the heavy one on its own set rather than inflating the upgrade.
bad: A service-shaped store (its own database and runtime state) rather than plain files a person can read directly; the eval set is 50 questions, small enough that its own caveat does the honest work; the richest documentation is in Chinese, which raises the reading cost for an English-first team.
didnt: Corroboration — an offline-first store with a complete per-client audit log, governance features that ship disabled, honest small-sample evaluation numbers with the stronger-model caveat printed, and a guardrail that keeps sensitive namespaces off the network matches our posture closely; nothing needs adopting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fisher521/burn-mcp-server
good: The limitations section is candid and specific, and the exact read-only walkthrough — prompt, tool calls, sources and limits — is published for reproduction. The promotion ladder (Flame to Spark to Vault) is a real triage idea: most captures are disposable, a few earn permanence, and the states make that judgement explicit instead of pretending everything saved is equally valuable. The agent-facing surface is deliberately constrained: no delete through MCP at all, state moves only.
bad: The founding gesture is expiry: an unread save is destroyed on a 24-hour timer by default, which is a retention policy pointed the wrong way for a record-keeping system. The vault lives in a hosted app behind an account and a paid tier, and the server is a front end to that account, not a store the owner holds.
didnt: Rejected — auto-deleting unread captures on a deadline is the opposite of a durable record, and the collection lives in a hosted read-later account; the honest limitations section and the published reproducible walkthrough are the parts worth remembering. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: forgemeshlabs/library-mcp
good: Retrieval-only answers that are real cited passages, with the method declared in every response, is exactly the citation posture our lockfile enforces, here sold as a service: a hallucinated quote is treated as worse than no quote. The payment guard is a genuine mechanism rather than a promise — payee, network and asset pinned, per-call and per-session caps that configuration can only lower, a dedicated low-balance wallet required, no redirect-following.
bad: A hosted corpus behind per-call cryptocurrency payment: every lookup spends real USDC, the corpus and index live on the vendor's service, and the book counts are the vendor's own growth claims. Nothing here is a store or a record the owner holds.
didnt: Corroboration — answers restricted to real, cited passages with the method stated in the response itself corroborate our citation discipline from an unrelated direction; the pay-per-call wallet model, even well-guarded, and a hosted corpus are not ours to adopt. Nothing was connected or paid in this study. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: g1itchbot8888-del/agent-memory
good: The diagnosis is ours, stated by an agent that lives it: context truncation eats decisions and the thread. The layering carries a stated token budget — identity plus active context give continuity in roughly 700 always-loaded tokens while the archive is pulled by meaning only on demand. The LearningMachine is the right instinct: corrections, errors and their fixes are stored as first-class memories and surfaced with search results, so a past mistake informs the next decision. The README is honest about who it is not for (no polished install story, no multi-agent shared memory).
bad: The cure is automatic rewriting: auto-capture extracts facts in place of the conversation, consolidation merges similar memories into new text and prunes low-scoring ones, and contradiction resolution silently favours the latest at search time. The original wording — the thing a correction or a decision actually said — does not survive as the record.
didnt: Rejected — the layering and the corrections tracking match our diagnosis, but a memory that merges, prunes and silently supersedes its own contents is a summary engine, not a record; our archive keeps what was said, verbatim, and marks supersession instead of performing it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gamosoft/NoteDiscovery
good: The most-starred self-hosted Markdown knowledge base in this wave stores notes as plain files in folders — no proprietary format, no lock-in — serves its own libraries so it works air-gapped, and exposes both a REST API and an MCP server over the same store. The human surface is complete (editor, graph, search, themes, export) without the files ever stopping being files.
bad: Its MCP surface is broad write access (create, edit, move, organise) with only optional password authentication in front of the app; there is no approval gate, audit ledger or citation discipline — it is a notes application with an agent door, not a governed record. Nothing in its model addresses supersession, provenance or abstention.
didnt: Corroboration — file-first storage, self-hosting, air-gapped operation and a door over the same files corroborate the shape we already run; its agent door is wider than our gated one, and nothing in it needs adopting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: geml-spec/geml
good: Block-addressed editing with re-validated writes is a write discipline with teeth: an agent changes one named block, the document is re-parsed whole, an invalid result is refused with a precise error location, untouched bytes are guaranteed unchanged, and a sidecar history makes any save revertible at block grain. Applied to plain Markdown it needs no conversion and no new files — the address layer sits over the files a person already has. The dual licence is stated cleanly (code MIT, spec CC BY 4.0) with governance documented in the repository.
bad: A young format (created June 2026) asking the world to meet it halfway: the finest grain requires .geml files, profiles are a vocabulary ecosystem that does not exist yet, and adopting a new document format wholesale would be a migration decision, not a tool swap. Its validation guarantees structural integrity, not truth — a well-formed block can still be wrong.
didnt: Board — board the mechanism for evaluation on the Tier A queue: block-addressed, re-validated, revertible edits over existing Markdown are the write safety our editor lacks at block grain, assessable without adopting the .geml format itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: geondongkim/geond-agent-protocol
good: Reservations with an audit trail, handoff packets that carry evidence refs and tested commands, importers that redact secrets before anything is persisted, and a strictly read-only dashboard over shared multi-agent memory: the coordination is structured and inspectable rather than conversational. The payload discipline — evidence refs and snippets by default, raw transcripts only by follow-up — is the same instinct as our citation requirement, and the alpha status and unbuilt areas are declared up front.
bad: The shared store is a PostgreSQL database, not files a person can read or diff; coordination state (reservations, handoffs) lives only inside it. Alpha software with its own audit streams admittedly unbuilt, and the multi-writer shared-database model is the direction our gap map records as deliberately not taken for the wiki itself.
didnt: Corroboration — reservations, evidence-carrying handoffs and a read-only reviewer surface over multi-agent work corroborate the coordination shape our team runs on files and filings; the database custody and multi-writer model are theirs, not ours. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GetCacheOverflow/CacheOverflow
good: The human-verification gate is the honourable part: no agent-published solution becomes available until a person has explicitly marked it safe, and the privacy boundary is stated precisely — the tool sees only the snippet it is handed, never the codebase. Reputation with stricter review for unknown authors is a reasonable trust gradient for a public pool.
bad: A public pool of agent-published fixes is a supply chain our record cannot vouch for: the provenance of a pooled solution is a reputation score and a safety mark, not a primary source we can open, read and cite. Solutions are generic patterns divorced from the codebase and evidence that produced them, and a purged-after-harm model means bad fixes are discovered by being applied.
didnt: Rejected — our ingest rule requires primary sources we can open and cite; a reputation-ranked pool of decontextualised fixes, however well gated, is the opposite direction. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gingugu/gingugu
good: Three mechanisms stand out. Review hints flag staleness on read while the server refuses to mutate — the human reconciles, which is our corrections posture in miniature. The self-generating golden set (a phrase occurring in exactly one memory has exactly one provably correct answer) builds labelled evaluation questions from the store itself, sized to your own data, staying local. And the protocol ships with the store: session-start injection, a stop hook that verifies the session wrote something down, and tripwires that block a forbidden tool call before it runs — designed from the observation that the failure mode is not retrieval but discipline. Migration backups before any upgrade, a keychain-backed credential vault, and honestly framed benchmark numbers complete a careful package.
bad: Memories are extracted statements in a SQLite database, not verbatim source files with citations; consolidation tools merge and summarise clusters on demand, and the confidence lifecycle grades memories without an evidence chain back to a quotable source. Its centre of gravity is a single coding assistant's working memory, not a multi-agent governed record.
didnt: Board — board three named mechanisms for the Tier A queue: review hints (staleness flagged on read, never auto-mutated), the self-generating provable-answer golden set built from the store itself, and the shipped discipline hooks (session-start protocol load, stop-hook write check, tripwires). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: giskard09/giskard-oasis
good: The diagnosis is real — an agent buried in accumulated context and failed attempts does lose the thread — and the response shape (restated purpose, one next step) is the shape of a good handoff. The trails log is privacy-careful: signed, opt-in, metadata only, no content, and unsigned agents are not tracked.
bad: The distillation is an unverifiable model reflection bought with cryptocurrency micropayments inside a reputation economy; there is no record, no citation, no mechanism an owner can audit — the clarity is asserted, and the purpose it returns is generated in the moment rather than recovered from anything the agent actually wrote down. It is also easily confused with the unrelated Giskard-AI evaluation framework of the same name.
didnt: Rejected — a paid contemplative nudge whose answer is generated rather than sourced cannot serve a record-keeping system; when our agent loses the thread it re-reads the log and the state file, which exist precisely so the purpose never has to be re-invented. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: giuliohome-org/doc-manager
good: The encrypted/plaintext split is enforced at the door, server-side: encrypted items are discoverable by title while their contents are refused to the model entirely, so the zero-knowledge guarantee survives giving an agent a door at all. The fail-closed details are right — a required non-empty allowlist that refuses startup, a read-only mode that hides write tools rather than merely discouraging them, and an MCP surface that returns 503 when unconfigured instead of running open.
bad: A single-user vault application, not a knowledge system: search is case-insensitive substring over titles and plaintext, there is no citation, provenance or retrieval model, and custody of the blobs sits in one Azure storage account under one access key. Plaintext documents are fully writable and deletable through the same door that reads them once OAuth is configured.
didnt: Corroboration — encrypted items staying opaque to the agent door while remaining discoverable, plus a fail-closed allowlist and an opt-in MCP surface, corroborate the door discipline our gateway aims at; the vault itself is not a knowledge system and nothing needs adopting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Goldentrii/AgentRecall
good: The corrections ledger measures the thing that matters: not whether a correction was saved, but whether the mistake recurred — heeded versus recurred outcomes with proof counts, published with confidence intervals and the unflattering numbers included. The check-before-action verdict ('blocked') puts the ledger in the path of irreversible operations instead of in a file nobody reads, and the Automaticity Law is a rare measured admission that pull tools go unused while push hooks change behaviour. Constants are labelled by epistemic status throughout (measured, form-only, open problem), corrections never expire by time, and rule rewrites stay owner-gated.
bad: Memory beyond the corrections layer still decays by formula (Ebbinghaus curves, spaced reinforcement), and the five-layer palace is a derived store whose entries are agent-written summaries rather than verbatim sources with citations. The agent-addressed install block in the README is an onboarding device aimed at visiting agents; it is recorded here as evidence of the project's distribution method, not followed.
didnt: Board — board two mechanisms for the Tier A queue: outcome tracking on our own corrections ledger (heeded versus recurred, so a correction's effectiveness is measured rather than assumed) and the check-before-risky-action verdict pattern; the Automaticity Law finding (push channels change behaviour, pull tools go unused) is design evidence for our doors. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gordonkjlee/facthouse
good: Immutability is stated as the law of the store: facts are never deleted, only superseded. The three-layer separation (Data/Information/Knowledge) keeps the raw session lines distinct from the extracted facts and the integrated beliefs instead of collapsing them into one rewritten record. Semantic search is off by default with a reasoned justification, inference is gated behind an explicit opt-in with pending-until-confirmed hypotheses, and the no-model fallback is honest about what it cannot do rather than degrading silently.
bad: The value proposition is automatic: transcripts are copied from client logs, facts extracted, knowledge integrated by a pipeline the owner configures once — the record is a derived store (session_facts, facts) rather than the conversation itself as the primary readable artefact. Extraction defaults to a model pass the owner already pays for, and the pipeline's honesty depends on configuration discipline the README walks through but cannot enforce.
didnt: Corroboration — facthouse independently assembles our stack: raw events kept, extraction as a separate layer over them, facts never deleted but superseded, hypotheses gated behind confirmation with fact-id citations, and semantic search off until the owner chooses it. The bitemporal support is noted as the parked design our own Phase-2 gates hold. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gpitrella/memxus-remote-mcp
good: The trust policy is the creditable part: memory is stated as advisory context, not instruction authority, with an explicit catalogue of what the memory layer never does — a governance document most memory products never write. The GitHub/Notion sync into per-project collections keeps synced content tagged and separable from manually saved memories rather than one undifferentiated pool.
bad: The production record lives on the vendor's infrastructure: a hosted MCP endpoint in front of a managed Postgres, with the owner connecting by OAuth and holding no files. AGPL-3.0 on the server code means any adaptation is ideas-only. The forget tool deletes permanently with no record kept, and the architecture diagram's 'no local files to manage' is the custody stance stated as a feature.
didnt: Rejected — our memory has to be files the owner holds; a hosted context layer whose store is the vendor's Supabase is the wrong custody shape regardless of the governance documents around it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: graphlit-mcp-server
good: The connector breadth shows what a mature ingest layer looks like (document extraction to Markdown, transcription of media, connector enumeration tools for channels, folders and calendars), and the README is upfront that every one of these paths requires the platform account — no local-first claim is made.
bad: The knowledge lives on the vendor's platform: the MIT server is a client of a hosted RAG service where ingestion, extraction and retrieval all run behind an account and a JWT secret. The ingest-everything posture (mail, chat, drives, issues) into one vendor project is the opposite custody direction from ours, and destructive tools (delete collections, delete content) sit in the default tool surface.
didnt: Rejected — a connector surface for a hosted platform is not a record the owner holds; ingest-everything into a vendor's RAG project trades custody for convenience. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gregario/3dprint-oracle
good: Domain knowledge served as shipped data rather than generation: the corpus is embedded, the tools are read-only, there are no keys and no network calls at runtime, and the source of the filament data is named with its licence. The README's headline promise is explicitly that answers are 'backed by real brewing data, not hallucinations' in its sibling project — the same anti-hallucination instinct in the family.
bad: A fixed domain oracle, not a memory or knowledge system: the corpus is a snapshot of someone else's database, the recommendations are generated rather than sourced, and nothing in it records, versions or cites the user's own work. Its value dies with the freshness of the embedded snapshot.
didnt: Corroboration — the embedded-data oracle pattern (a bounded corpus from a named authoritative source, shipped inside the server, read-only tools, zero runtime network) corroborates serving knowledge as data rather than generation; the domain is not ours and nothing needs adopting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gregario/brewers-almanack
good: The provenance table is the standout: every dataset names its record count, its source and its licence or factual basis, down to the attribution owed to the BJCP. Data is embedded (no keys, no runtime network), the tool surface is read-only, and the README's headline promise is answers backed by real data, not hallucinations.
bad: Same structural limits as its sibling oracle: a snapshot of compiled domain data with no recording, versioning or citation of the user's own work; generated recipe suggestions sit beside sourced facts in the same tool surface, and the 'factual data' compilation is the maker's own hand, not a verifiable chain.
didnt: Corroboration — the per-dataset provenance table (record counts, source, licence or factual basis for each of eight datasets) is source discipline most knowledge servers never show; the embedded-oracle pattern again, corroborating the shape, not something to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gregario/lego-oracle
good: Change detection done right for a public dataset: the data is refreshed daily from Rebrickable and new package versions publish automatically when the upstream changes, so the version history of the package IS the freshness record. The data section prints exact counts per category, and the attribution names the source with the trademark disclaimer.
bad: Third instance of the fixed-oracle pattern: no user record, no versioning of the user's own work, nothing citable beyond the dataset itself. Freshness depends on the maker's pipeline staying alive; if the daily refresh stops, the oracle silently ages.
didnt: Corroboration — the automatic republish-on-upstream-change pipeline with an explicit attribution section is change detection applied to a public dataset; third corroboration of the oracle shape in one batch, nothing to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: grooverLab/fable
good: Our conversation-log premise aimed at exactly the failure Usman named: the platform's own compaction takes the record away, so the tool seals the transcripts before that happens and treats the vault as immutable. The verbatim-first discipline is total: recall quotes the actual transcript, surgery and pruning are reversible by construction with the cost shown byte by byte before anything changes, and the mute mode keeps capture running while recall is silenced — an audit that cannot be anchored to yesterday's conclusion. Retrieval numbers are published from a real archive with a reproduction script.
bad: The vault is Claude Code transcripts only: a single platform's session logs, indexed by a tool the user must install and keep running; composition and time-travel are derived artefacts built from those logs, and the surgery operations (removing conversations, pruning) rewrite the working copy even though the vault keeps the bytes. Its 30-day-deletion claim about Claude Code's behaviour is the project's own account of another product's policy.
didnt: Board — board the pattern for the Tier A queue: pre-compaction capture hooks plus a sealed verbatim vault plus reversible pruning/surgery, applied to our own transcript custody where the platform gives us no record at all. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hannesrudolph/mcp-ragdocs
good: The fork provenance is acknowledged rather than laundered, the queue-based ingest with sequential processing and error handling is a sensible intake shape, and the README warns plainly that adding extracted URLs to the queue on large sites risks excessive queuing. The star count shows how early the MCP documentation-search niche arrived.
bad: A first-generation docs-RAG pipe: retrieval depends on a hosted embedding model and a vector database instance the owner must supply keys for; search returns chunk excerpts with no source anchoring, version tracking or provenance; removal is permanent with no record of what was there. There is no citation discipline, no governance, and nothing the intervening waves of memory systems have not superseded.
didnt: Rejected — historically interesting as one of the earliest MCP servers, but its chunk-excerpt retrieval and permanent-destruction tooling have nothing to teach our custody stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HatmanStack/ragstack-mcp
good: Two creditable details: the configuration surface is deliberately read-only through the MCP door (changes require the dashboard's Cognito auth), and the key-similarity check nudges the caller to avoid duplicate metadata keys before adding documents — schema hygiene as a tool. The scrape controls (scope, depth, glob patterns) are precise.
bad: The knowledge base is the vendor-shaped AWS stack: the record lives behind an AppSync endpoint and API key in Lambda/S3, the chat answers are generated with citations asserted by the same system that generates them, and the configuration is read-only through the MCP door — the owner audits the stack but governs it only through the dashboard. Nothing in the record is a file the owner can open.
didnt: Rejected — a client for a serverless knowledge-base product keeps the record in the product's stack, not in the owner's hands; AI-generated answers with self-asserted citations are not a citation discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HBarefoot/engram
good: Write-time secret detection is a genuine guardrail: secrets are blocked before they reach the database, on every write, not flagged after. Conflicts are surfaced side-by-side with keep-both as an explicit option instead of being auto-resolved. The honesty discipline is the batch's best: numbers labelled as footprint not accuracy, the rule-based baseline published next to the improvement, rivals' strengths conceded in the comparison table.
