bad: Memories are extracted statements in the store, not verbatim sources; dedup absorbs near-duplicates into the existing record and decay quietly removes the unrecalled, so the record rewrites and fades itself by policy. The conflict workflow resolves by human button-click rather than by recorded evidence, and the comparison table is marketing despite its fairness.
didnt: Corroboration — write-time secret blocking, conflicts surfaced side-by-side for a human choice rather than auto-resolved, and published numbers labelled as footprint rather than accuracy corroborate our guardrails and our honesty discipline at once. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hermes-labs-ai/fidelis
good: The verbatim-first argument is made with a concrete example of a sentence a summary would drop — the missing sentence matters. The supersession model (correction marks the old record superseded, kept, shown with validity) matches our own. The honest scope section and the printed provider-sees-data caution are exactly the kind of boundary statement our rules require.
bad: A retrieval service over saved notes, not a record-keeping system: notes are what the user puts in, retrieval returns passages, and there is no provenance, citation chain or governance around what those notes assert. Embeddings still require a local Ollama instance, and the pre-release scope means the team and multi-machine story is unbuilt.
didnt: Corroboration — verbatim-by-default retrieval, corrections that supersede without erasing, validity shown rather than silent replacement, and the model-provider data-flow caution are our custody stack independently assembled; nothing needs adopting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HiAi-gg/docsmint
good: The scoped-access design is careful: per-category read/edit/write grants, a global key only for trusted automation, short-lived tokens bound to workspace and scope, and credentials that cannot create or elevate other credentials. The README states plainly that Cloud is a separate hosted listing and that the npm package is only a bridge to the owner's own deployment.
bad: A database application, not a record system: Postgres/Redis/SeaweedFS under Docker, rich-text documents, generated answers from the graph — the knowledge is derived and chunked rather than kept as citable files. The recommended path is the hosted Cloud endpoint, and the search sophistication (typo tolerance, cross-language graph) is retrieval machinery without a citation chain.
didnt: Corroboration — category-scoped keys with explicit per-part read/edit/write grants, one-hour tokens, and credentials that cannot elevate themselves corroborate the scoped-access shape our gateway already enforces; the application itself is not ours to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hifriendbot/cogmemai-mcp
good: Two design ideas are worth recording: the intent document with NEVER/MUST invariants compiled into enforceable patterns (a plain-English spec that acts before an action, not a review after), and the character-budget recall where truncated results keep their identity and real length with nothing hidden — degradation declared rather than silent.
bad: The recommended mode is the vendor's cloud: memory across devices, users and teams lives on their service, with the paid tiers gating the judged guard checks. The benchmark numbers are self-reported superlatives ('top published score', 'above human performance') with no reproducible runner shown at source, and the guard's judged check fails open while the enforceable part is literal pattern matching. The quantum-safe encryption claim is a badge, not a mechanism described at source.
didnt: Rejected — a cloud-first guard product with self-reported superlative benchmarks is not evidence-grade; our guard gates run on our own machines against records we hold, and our numbers are measured or they are not published. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hjqcan/GoodMemory
good: The honesty discipline is the batch's sharpest: a claim gate that currently publishes nothing rather than publish something unvalidated, withdrawn benchmark numbers kept visible but explicitly barred from quotation, internal diagnostics labelled as not claims, and a strict track defined as 'a hard lower bound no LLM judge can inflate'. The read-only MCP with opt-in writeback, installed pre-actions, hosted-host canaries and leakage audits are the door-and-watch machinery our gateway mirrors.
bad: The auditable surface is a database-backed memory layer (SQLite/Postgres) with hooks and canaries, not files a person can read: memory entries are API objects, and the evidence machinery governs benchmark claims about the product rather than the truth of the memories themselves. The read-only MCP plus opt-in writeback is the right door shape, but the store behind it is still a service's tables.
didnt: Board — board the fail-closed benchmark-claim gate for the Tier A queue: no number enters our claims without a validated declaration (no-memory baseline, independent judge, zero execution failures, verified dataset, reproducible run), and withdrawn numbers stay visible as audit-trail artifacts explicitly barred from quotation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hoornet/agentdocs-mcp
good: Two careful details: space-scoped tokens that sandbox an agent to one space are named as the recommended way to run an agent, and the hosted endpoint refuses caller-supplied file paths for uploads because that would be arbitrary file read — a boundary drawn where it is cheapest to attack. import_markdown is idempotent by source path, so re-imports cannot silently duplicate the library.
bad: The documents live on the vendor's platform: AgentDocs is a hosted collaborative product, and the MCP server is its client whether run over stdio or through the hosted endpoint. Write tools (create, update, delete, bulk create) are broad and unprompted once a token is installed; the version history lives on their server, not in a repo the owner controls.
didnt: Corroboration — space-scoped tokens confining an agent to exactly one space corroborate the scoped-access shape, and server-side versioned pages with restorable old versions corroborate our version-keeping instinct; the platform is hosted and nothing is ours to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hubinoretros/deep-thinker
good: The DAG shape itself is honest about reasoning: branches and merges are kept as graph structure rather than flattened into a single chain, node aliases (last/best/root) make the graph addressable, and the metacognitive stuck-detection names a real failure mode of long reasoning sessions. Sessions persist to local files and resume.
bad: The record is a reasoning trace, not knowledge: thoughts are generated in-session, scored by the server's own heuristics, and pruned by design — dead ends and 'redundant' branches are deleted as a feature. Confidence is a multi-factor heuristic presented as a number, strategy auto-selection is keyword matching, and the eight 'high-IQ' enhancement tools (emotional intelligence analysis, social impact modelling) are prompt theatre around the same graph. Nothing is sourced, cited or kept.
didnt: Rejected — a thinking scaffold whose core operations include deleting the branches it judges unproductive is the opposite of a record; our reasoning belongs in the conversation log, kept whole, not in a pruned graph. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hyunjae-labs/lore
good: The right custody relationship to transcripts: they stay where the platform wrote them, unmodified, and the database is explicitly disposable — delete it and re-index. Turn-aware chunking respects the conversation's own structure instead of slicing tokens, both agents' logs are indexed into one searchable store with per-agent filtering, and the whole thing runs locally with no keys.
bad: The index is over two platforms' session logs only, and the opt-out-by-default posture indexes every project on the machine until the owner excludes it — capture first, consent later. Search returns conversation chunks ranked by fused scores with no citation chain back to a compiled record, and there is no curation layer: everything said is equally searchable, nothing is distilled, corrected or superseded.
didnt: Corroboration — transcript search over the platforms' own session logs, fully local with the sources untouched and the index disposable, corroborates the retrieval half of our conversation-log design; the curation layer above the transcripts is what a wiki adds and lore deliberately does not attempt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: idapixl/algora-mcp-server
good: The tool design is tidy: bounded result sets with cursor pagination, explicit filter parameters rather than free-text guessing, aggregate statistics as a first-class tool, and an honest architecture note about which filtering happens locally because the upstream API lacks it.
bad: A one-commit wrapper over a third-party platform's live API: it keeps no record, versions nothing, and its answers are whatever the platform returns at call time. Bounty discovery is a marketplace convenience, not knowledge custody, and the server adds filtering cosmetics over an API the agent could call directly.
didnt: Rejected — a read-only client of someone else's bounty platform has no record to keep and nothing to teach our custody stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IgorGanapolsky/mcp-memory-gateway
good: Pre-action enforcement with the verdicts graded honestly: hard-block for secret leaks and self-disable attempts, warn-and-log for the destructive-but-sometimes-legitimate classes, strict mode as an explicit owner switch. Lessons are local files with provenance (the check names the feedback that created it), the no-weight-update disclaimer is printed rather than implied, and progressive wiring ('prove the pipe before you turn matching on; empty dashboard is success') is installation discipline most guard tools skip.
bad: The gate is only as strong as the hook surface: on advisory clients it is a tool the agent may call, not an interception, and the lesson store lives inside each client's own memory directories, so the record fragments across tools unless the machine-wide scope is shared deliberately. Pattern promotion from repeated failures is a heuristic ladder — a rule can harden into a block from frequency rather than from a reviewed decision.
didnt: Board — board the promotion ladder for the Tier A queue: a recorded failure starts as a warning and hardens into a blocking gate only after it recurs, with the originating feedback cited when the check fires — the enforcement half of our corrections ledger, to be evaluated against the callimachus and AgentRecall guard patterns already boarded. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ihorponom/agentpack
good: The distinction it draws is the right one: memory remembers how you work, the ledger remembers where the task stands — and dead ends are recorded as first-class state, not just successes. Conclusions carry file hashes with the limit stated in one sentence (unchanged is not correct), checkpoints bind verification to a commit, and the security posture (zero runtime dependencies, no network, provenance-signed releases) is engineered rather than asserted.
bad: Task state only, by design: the ledger records where a task stands, not what is known — the durable knowledge still needs a home elsewhere, and the passport's compact resume budget means the ledger summarises rather than preserves. The gate is warn-first and hook-dependent, and the redaction of stored context is best-effort by its own wording.
didnt: Corroboration — a repo-local task ledger with decisions, dead ends and verification evidence as first-class entries, hash-flagged source conclusions and a warn-first scope gate is our own STATE-and-checkpoint practice built independently; our handoff files already do this work. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ikalus1988/MisakaNet
good: The evidence discipline is the strongest in this batch: a five-grade ladder where the top grade cannot be written or voted into existence, an empty top stated on the front page, a benchmark whose own section explains why it does not measure what it might appear to measure, counts generated by CI rather than typed, and abstention built into retrieval — a miss is a named answer (no_match) that opens an intake instead of returning a least-bad lesson.
bad: A public, shared corpus is a different custody shape from a private record: lessons are contributed across strangers' machines and retrieved anonymously from a hosted endpoint, so a fix's applicability to your stack is judged by its evidence grade alone. Intake arrives faster than triage (the README names the queue as the honest bottleneck), and BM25 matches words, not meaning — a failure described in new vocabulary is a miss by construction.
didnt: Board — board the evidence ladder for the Tier A queue: grades that rise only on reproduction, CI verification and observed reuse by distinct clients, with the top grade unearnable by writing or voting, applied to our own corrections and failure records; the miss-that-returns-an-intake pattern belongs with it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: irisxc4/memoryguard
good: The governance framing is exact: persistent memory solves storage, not governance, and this layer governs — writes classified or surfaced as conflicts, corrections preserving their predecessors with reasons, secrets quarantined rather than stored active, and history separated from rules so raw chat cannot leak into future context unexamined. The fail-closed migration (no silent fallback, rollback evidence kept) and the measured/estimated honesty labels match our verification discipline.
bad: The governed store is a set of SQLite domain databases behind a large surface (the cutover closed 233 routes): the record is application state, not files a person can open, diff and cite, and the governance machinery's complexity is itself the risk — mandatory-rule replacement, audience matching and conflict merging are a lot of semantics between the agent and its notes. Classification and dedup still happen automatically on write; the human reviews exceptions after the fact.
didnt: Corroboration — supersede chains that preserve what changed and why, quarantine of sensitive-looking content, conversation history kept as a separate evidence archive, and measured-versus-estimated labelling are our governance instincts independently assembled; the SQLite domain store is where we part. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IvenKooLab/loci
good: Citations are structural: every answer points at file and section, and a claim-by-claim verification pass exists for when the stakes justify it. The custody split is right — files are the record, the index is per-machine and rebuildable — and the demo-data captions and the loopback-admin warning are stated where a user will see them rather than buried.
bad: Answers are generated over the index (with citations attached), and the citation is a file-and-section pointer rather than a checked claim — verification is an optional flag, not the default path. The loopback-admin default is a real exposure if the console is ever tunnelled carelessly, and harness discovery reads other tools' memory stores, which is only as safe as those stores are.
didnt: Corroboration — Markdown memories with a disposable local index, file-and-section citations on answers and a console that shows what each agent remembers corroborate our files-first shape; nothing needs adopting beyond the corroboration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JAAvila-Of/vivac
good: Provenance as the primitive rather than a link somebody remembers to add: the edge is the data model, so 'why are we here' is always answerable by walking it. Closure discipline is enforced by the tool, not by habit (a run marked DONE with findings open is the defect the whole design answers), refuted premises cascade honestly while rescued work keeps its birthplace, and the README's limits section plus its README-commands-tested-by-CI practice are verification culture of the first order.
bad: A single-author instrument: pull requests are not open yet, the tree's value depends entirely on the discipline of recording edges as work happens, and the model is tasks and decisions — the knowledge itself (documents, sources, evidence) lives elsewhere. The token comparisons are the author's own measurements on his own projects, reproducible in spirit rather than independently verified.
didnt: Board — board the provenance edge for the Tier A queue: every work node carrying its parent, decisions keeping their rejected alternatives and the rule they were judged against, and closure refused over open findings — the shape our decision records and run records should take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jagoff/memo
good: Files-first custody done completely: Markdown is the truth, the database is derived and rebuildable, hand edits win. The time-machine answers the question a flat memory cannot (what did we believe on that date, and what changed since), the contradiction radar surfaces changed minds instead of letting stale versions ride, and removing an unsupportable savings claim from the product — with the reason printed — is the honesty standard this whole wave should be judged by.
bad: The Dream pipeline is autonomous maintenance: conflicts resolved, stale memories pruned and cross-cluster insights synthesized overnight with zero intervention — a receipt makes it auditable, but the record is still rewritten by a process nobody approved item by item, and 'newer-wins' is one of the triage resolutions. Ambient injection puts a memory in front of the model before it answers whether or not the memory is right, and the full surface (165 tools, 145 CLI commands) is a very large machine for a notes store.
didnt: Corroboration — Markdown as the source of truth with a rebuildable derived index, as-of reconstruction of what was believed when, contradiction triage, and an unsupportable savings figure deleted rather than defended corroborate our stack and our honesty discipline; the autonomous nightly rewriting is where we part. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jaimenbell/rag-mcp
good: Fail-closed engineering throughout: degradation always goes toward the expensive-but-correct option (full rebuild), never toward a wrong skip; the corpus root is enforced as an authorisation scope, not a convention; errors are structured so the calling agent can react; and the README's own numbers (test count, ingest costs) are either measured on a named live corpus or enforced by CI against the code — claims and code held in lockstep.
bad: Retrieval only: one search tool over an embedding index, with citations at chunk granularity and no answer layer, no abstention scoring and no provenance beyond the chunk pointer. The corpus root is the only access boundary (no per-document scoping), and the doc_class heuristics (filename tokens for handoffs) are necessarily approximate.
didnt: Board — board the change-detection machinery for the Tier A queue: a content-hash manifest gated on run identity so a configuration change can never half-apply, and dated-series chunk de-duplication that keeps repeat dates as metadata instead of dropping the snapshots — plus the handoff/knowledge class separation our own STATE files already observe informally. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JamesANZ/cross-llm-mcp
good: The fan-out comparison use is real (the same prompt to several providers for cross-checking), preferences are stored locally in a plain JSON file the owner can read, and the README is candid that the Hugging Face route is the hosted Inference Router, pointing elsewhere for genuinely local inference.
bad: A provider shim, not a knowledge system: every call sends the prompt to a hosted third-party API under the user's keys, the 'memory' is a prompt log with delete and clear tools, and nothing is sourced, cited, versioned or kept as a record. Tag-based 'best model' tables are hard-coded 2025-era model names presented as intelligent selection.
didnt: Rejected — model routing across hosted APIs is a different layer from record custody; there is nothing here for the wiki's stack, and its prompt log is a convenience cache, not a record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JamesANZ/memory-mcp
licence: ISC per the README License section (repository metadata says MIT — discrepancy recorded)
good: The context-window caching idea is coherent on its own terms: archive proactively at a high-water mark rather than at the moment of overflow, and restore when there is room again. Tag-based organisation and per-provider memory separation are simple and predictable.
bad: Every default points the wrong way for a record: the plain save overwrites, a clear-all tool sits in the basic set, relevance is keyword overlap, and long conversations are condensed into generated summaries that stand in for the original. The store is MongoDB documents — a database nobody opens and reads — with per-LLM silos keyed by caller-supplied user ids.
didnt: Rejected — overwrite-by-default storage with summary condensation is precisely the record loss our verbatim-first custody exists to prevent; the 80%/30% context-window caching thresholds are the only mechanic worth noting, and they belong to session management, not memory. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: japlete/md-vision-mcp
good: Default-deny as a startup condition rather than a setting: no allowlist, no server. The index-first workflow (discover headings and sizes, then read exactly the section needed, images inlined in order) is context discipline — the agent spends tokens on the passage it chose, with its position in the document known. AST-based heading parsing avoids the classic regex failure on code blocks.
bad: A reading aid, not a memory system: it indexes and fetches documentation but keeps nothing, cites nothing beyond the section it returns, and its retrieval quality rests on the calling agent choosing the right sections. The benchmark is explicitly work-in-progress, so the benefit over plain filesystem reading is asserted by design rather than measured.
didnt: Corroboration — a read-only door that refuses to start without an explicit allowlist, and a heading index with line starts for targeted reads, corroborate our default-deny door discipline and index-first reading shape at miniature scale. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jayasukuv11-beep/agenthelm
good: The governance instincts are right: knowledge enters by proposal rather than by direct write, history is kept in git-style log/diff/blame form, action classes are declared by decorator with a fail-closed default, and irreversible actions stop for a human decision with the payload shown. Budget guardrails treat runaway spend as a safety event, which it is.
bad: The brain lives on the vendor's control plane: a live connect key, a hosted dashboard, a Supabase backend — the project's knowledge is in their service, versioned by their compiler, which also resolves conflicts automatically before releasing. The repository root carries the product's marketing and planning artefacts (carousel strategy, video files, audit documents) alongside the code, and human approval runs through Telegram buttons on the vendor's channel.
didnt: Rejected — propose-then-compile with versioned history and irreversible-action approval are the right shapes in the wrong custody: a fleet control plane holding the record on its own service is not a record the owner holds. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jaydubya818/Agentic-KB
good: The pipeline shape and the principles are the strongest independent match in this programme: raw held untrusted, compilation as a named state transition, citations carried through synthesis, contradictions surfaced rather than smoothed, private scopes pinned so they cannot leak through generated surfaces, and promotion of compiled knowledge behind an approver with a hash-chained audit trail behind it.
bad: Compilation depends on a hosted model key — the compile step that turns raw into knowledge runs on a vendor's API, so the pipeline stops where the key does. The scope is a single author's entire operating system (2,262 commits, no releases, 2 stars): the knowledge base cannot be lifted out of the OS around it, and nothing is versioned for anyone else to adopt.
didnt: Corroboration — the raw-to-ingest-to-compile pipeline with citations surviving synthesis, contradictions kept visible, gated promotion and a hash-chained audit is our architecture arrived at independently, down to the principle wording; our compile is the agent's work under the owner's gates rather than a pipeline stage keyed to a vendor. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jcdickinson/simplemem
good: The files stay human-readable (Markdown plus YAML) with DuckDB as a derived index rather than the record, and the candour is genuine: the project calls itself vibe-coded and prints its known issues where a user will read them before adopting, which is more honesty than polished projects manage.
bad: LGPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only for us before anything else is weighed. Retrieval depends on a hosted embeddings API key, delete is destructive across all related data, migrations are admittedly absent, and the whole thing is 25 commits and one star behind a self-applied vibe-coded warning.
didnt: Rejected — licence, hosted-embedding dependency and destructive delete each disqualify on their own; the honest warning label is the most valuable part of the project and is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jessedu29260-netizen/booboo
good: Authority as a file: the org chart is versioned in git, cycle-validated, and is what agents actually boot from — identity, authority, rules and buckets arrive as one slice from a source a human can diff. The nightly Markdown vault export named as an insurance copy, the per-build ingestion-quality line separating authored links from orphans and dump-suspects, and an append journal beside the snapshot are custody instincts we share.
bad: The graph is a model of the system rather than the system's own documents: the record is a JSON spec maintained through adapters, one indirection away from the files it describes. One star and a July 2026 creation date make it very young, the catalogue's 3D framing undersells that the substance is the spec, and a scaffold that ships its own AGENTS.md constitution means adopting projects inherit the author's governance text wholesale.
didnt: Corroboration — an org chart kept as versioned, git-tracked authority that agents boot from, an append journal beside the snapshot, authored links outranking harvested ones and a nightly plain-Markdown insurance export corroborate our files-as-authority design; the graph-spec layer is a model we do not need over the wiki itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jidoseal/jidoseal-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (MCP server wrapper); the scan engine is proprietary (pinned 0.1.4, sha256 published, SBOM shipped)
good: A deterministic corpus validator with no model calls: frontmatter tiers mapped to named clauses of real standards, the corpus graded by its weakest file rather than its average, gaps split by who can fix them, and a Merkle root over the whole corpus. Its self-disclosure sets the wave's standard — its own no-egress claim is labelled unaudited in its own description, and tier is explicitly not certification.
bad: The checker itself is proprietary: the wrapper is Apache-2.0, but the scan engine is a pinned binary the user must trust — the published sha256 and SBOM mitigate rather than remove that. Thirteen commits, one star, created 2026-09; and frontmatter completeness is a proxy for documentation quality, not the quality itself — a Gold file can still be wrong.
didnt: Board — board the weakest-file corpus tier and the AUTO versus NEEDS-CLIENT gap split for the Tier A queue: a corpus graded by its least-complete page, with machine-fixable gaps separated from owner-decision gaps, is the shape our wiki validator should report in. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JinNing6/Noosphere
good: The evidence machinery around shared skills is careful: SHA-256 verification before apply, applicability checked rather than assumed, outcomes counted only when approved (an auditable lower bound, in its own words), digests stated to prove identity rather than correctness, and experience records kept descriptive rather than executable.
bad: The core proposition is a pooled registry of executable skills contributed by strangers: review-gating, digests and applicability checks reduce the supply-chain surface but cannot close it, because applying a skill means running its instructions. A social/consciousness layer rides in the same repository, and the root's hygiene noise sits oddly against the verification story.
didnt: Rejected — a shared executable-skill commons is exactly the supply-chain risk our owner-gated, filings-only agent collaboration is designed to avoid; the verification and outcome-counting discipline around it is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JinyangWang27/people-context
good: The judgement calls are right: ambiguity answered with candidates and reasons, imports held as candidates until the owner approves them, sensitive records behind an environment-flag gate no prompt can open, writes audited, forget implemented as genuine deletion with the audit trail redacted, and the plaintext-database fact printed plainly with its permissions and its encrypted option.
bad: The record is one SQLite file — application state, not pages a person can open, read and cite — and it concentrates exactly the data whose disclosure must be bounded. Raw import sources are never kept, so a fact's provenance ends at the candidate the owner approved; the staged-import discipline is sound, but the discarded source is a provenance cost our ingest rule refuses.
didnt: Corroboration — staged-candidate imports with owner approval, identity resolution that returns its ambiguity instead of guessing, a prompt-proof operator gate on sensitive records, and a forget that really deletes corroborate our people-pages practice and its gates; our record stays readable pages rather than a database. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jinzcdev/markmap-mcp-server
good: A tidy single-purpose tool: server-side rendering gives the client real image and SVG exports, preferences live in startup configuration instead of per-call arguments, retrieval is path-contained, and cleanup can be dry-run before it deletes.
bad: Rendering only: it transforms Markdown for display and keeps no record, checks nothing and cites nothing beyond the diagram it returns. The Playwright/Chromium dependency is heavy machinery for a diagram export, and its 289 stars measure convenience, not knowledge value.
didnt: Rejected — a mind-map renderer is presentation tooling; it touches neither custody, citation nor verification, and our reading surfaces are a separate concern from the record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jmpdsevilla/BovedIA
good: The pyramid is our index-first protocol as a vault design: the router note carries criteria, not work, and is read before anything else; covers route, notes hold substance, and a separate layer keeps the reasons. Cheap partial reads, vault-health maintenance over orphans and broken links, snapshots that simulate before restoring, and human authorship ranges preserved by the annotation spec are all the right instincts.
bad: The public artefact is a frozen snapshot: development moved to a private repository and the README says so, so what is open is what was left behind. Sync is delegated to consumer cloud drives with their own conflict behaviour, and at 34 commits and one star the project is a personal instrument rather than a maintained tool.
didnt: Corroboration — a router note read first, holding criteria rather than content, over plain Markdown kept as files, with simulate-by-default restore and preserved human authorship ranges, corroborates our index-first reading discipline and our caution with restores; the frozen public snapshot is recorded as its maintenance state. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: junnnnnw00/obsidian-everywhere
good: The narrowest Git boundary in the wave: git capability is opt-in, commit requires an explicit file list with preview and confirmation, and push is a separate, stricter capability restricted to the current HEAD, an operator-pinned HTTPS destination and a five-minute one-use approval ID — it never pulls. Writes fail closed when the vault's mount disappears, and semantic search is local and off by default.
bad: The remote bridge exposes a broad write surface (41+ tools) over a tunnel — the guards are strong, but the surface they guard is wide, and ngrok puts a third party in the path of an authenticated bridge. The graph ranking (PageRank, context bundles) is retrieval machinery, not verification: it decides what is central, not what is true.
didnt: Corroboration — push treated as a separate capability with a pinned destination and a one-use approval, writes blocked outright when the vault's storage disappears, and dry-run-first bulk edits with rollback corroborate our gateway scoping and fail-closed posture at vault scale; the bridge's breadth is what our read-only door refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: juyterman1000/entroly
good: Every reduction reversible with a receipt: what was kept, what omitted, why, and the handle that recovers the exact original bytes. Claims are labelled unearned when the engine that would earn them is absent, verification tooling is stated not to prove answer quality, and cross-agent resume reconstructs state from repository evidence while requiring the receiver to acknowledge it before claiming the work.
bad: This is prompt-context selection, not corpus custody: the store exists to serve compression, recovery depends on that store surviving, and the fidelity figures are the project's own measurements on its own harness. At 478 stars it is the wave's most-adopted context tool, but what is adopted is the compression, not a record.
didnt: Corroboration — byte-exact recovery with receipts, claims labelled unearned until verified, and a resume the receiving agent must review and acknowledge extend the lossless-first corroboration distil established in B111; nothing new to board beyond it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kaaustubh/project-memory-mcp
good: The two-layer split is a stated design rule, not an accident: the auto-loaded file stays lean because the high-volume history lives in an append-only JSONL read on demand. Capture is proactive but confirming (notice given, uncertainty asked, secrets skipped), the opt-in Stop hook fires only on the two failures that matter — work done, nothing logged; correction given, no preference saved — and standups are composed from disk evidence rather than the agent's impression.
bad: Project-scoped by design: one repository's issues and decisions, with no cross-project record, no citation layer and no verification of what is recalled. The recall hook injects silently, and a store whose day one is empty is worth exactly the capture discipline its users sustain — the mechanism cannot supply the habit.
didnt: Corroboration — a lean always-loaded file over an on-demand append-only history is our MEMORY.md and wiki discipline in miniature, and a stop hook that fires only when work happened but nothing was recorded mechanises our conversation-log rule; the discipline-hook pattern itself was already boarded with gingugu in B112. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kael-bit/engram-rs
good: Engineering completeness: one Rust binary, one SQLite file, a rule-based fallback when no LLM is configured, CJK tokenization, and session reconstruction that assembles core memory, recent items, the topic index and triggers. The trigger: tag mechanism — lessons recalled before risky operations — is pre-action recall, the recall-side cousin of the guard patterns boarded earlier in this programme.
bad: The lifecycle rewrites the record by design: an LLM gate decides what deserves promotion, decay demotes whatever is not recalled, dedup merges records into new text at a similarity threshold, distillation condenses topics, and a background process runs all of it every 30 minutes. What the agent remembers is continuously re-authored by the engine's judgement — the opposite of a record that stays what was written.
didnt: Rejected — automatic decay, merge and condensation behind an LLM promotion gate is the anti-pattern in polished form: supersession in our record is explicit and human-arbitrated, never a half-life. The trigger-tag pre-action recall is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kage-core/Kage
good: Verification is the product: citations checked at write, recall and diff time, hallucinated citations rejected before they enter storage, stale memory withheld rather than served, and delegated work judged by checks the orchestrator runs itself, itemised on a receipt — never by the agent's report of itself. Memory stays OKF Markdown in the owner's repository, and private spans are never stored.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only for us regardless of merit. The headline metrics are the project's own claims carried as badges, the scope has swollen from memory to orchestrator, desktop app and LAN phone access gated by a pairing secret, and installation rewrites the agent policy files in the user's repository — the memory layer arrives with its own governance text attached.
didnt: Corroboration — checks re-run by the harness rather than trusted from the agent's self-report, citations refused when their target does not exist, and stale memory withheld pending re-verification corroborate our verification standard and the truth-aware retrieval direction; GPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kaliaboi/mcp-zotero
good: A small, honest bridge: five read-only tools over the Zotero Web API, credentials held in environment variables rather than configuration files, and a setup flow that verifies the credentials with a direct API call before the server is ever run.
bad: A pass-through, not a record: the library lives on Zotero's cloud, nothing is stored locally, nothing retrieved is cited or kept, and the documented credential carries write access the server never uses and nothing narrows. Twenty-two commits and no releases since December 2024 mark its maintenance state.
didnt: Rejected — a thin API bridge to a hosted citation library; our sources are ingested as files into the wiki with citations locked at ingest, not queried live through a five-tool shim. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: khwanlabs/khwan-mcp
licence: MIT (this MCP server; the Khwan memory service it connects to is hosted and proprietary)
good: Unusual honesty about mechanism: the README states plainly that memory cannot save tokens inside a caching session and says where the savings actually live; recall is capped and floored so an empty result means 'not known here' rather than a gap to fill with the nearest fact; lessons lead the seed text because a rule earned over months outranks a nearby turn; and the key-out-of-the-repo launcher pattern is documented as carefully as the product itself.
bad: The memory itself lives on the vendor's service: stored turns sit server-side, a nightly pass on Khwan's own model rewrites them into lessons, and what the owner holds is an API key and whatever recall returns — at most three facts at a time. Cores and caps are plan-gated, and continuity depends entirely on the service existing.
didnt: Rejected — hosted, account-bound memory distilled nightly by the vendor's model into standing lessons is custody inverted: our record is files the owner holds, distilled by our own process under his gates. The honest token accounting and the empty-recall-is-an-answer floor are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: knaisoma/data-olympus
good: Governance as data, not habit: proposed versus accepted is a field on every document, retrieval respects it, supersession is a chain in the format rather than an edit, and concurrent agent writes are serialised through a pending queue by a single writer with per-session worktrees. The interoperability evidence is pinned, bidirectional and scoped by its own authors as fixture-level — claims discipline of the first order.
bad: Pre-1.0 beta with 59 releases of churn behind it, and the governance is format-level: status fields and a pending queue govern the store, but nothing here checks a document's claims against the world — a wrong decision, once accepted, is retrieved with the same authority as a right one. The single-writer serialisation that prevents write races is also a throughput ceiling, accepted as the price of the model.
didnt: Board — board status-aware retrieval for the Tier A queue: governance state as a format field (proposed versus accepted) that retrieval filters on by default, with supersedes chains tracing decision history, plus the single-writer pending queue as the serialisation pattern for concurrent agent writes to the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: krimto-labs/krimto
good: The custody split is right — Markdown files in the owner's git are the truth, the SQLite/vector index is derived, and the audit trail is git log rather than an application table. Scope as a server-enforced primitive with most-specific-wins precedence at recall is a clean answer to the personal-versus-shared memory collision, and team disbanding preserves the notes.
bad: Write governance is thinner than read governance: scope is enforced at recall and by the access server, but approval of what enters team or org memory is a roadmap item (the PR approval flow is v0.3), while automatic memory is switched on by the setup wizard's standing rule. Zero releases and seven stars mark its adoption; the hierarchy's value only appears with a team, which is also where its unshipped approval flow matters most.
didnt: Corroboration — facts as Markdown in the owner's git with the index derived and disposable, git history as the audit trail, and scope precedence resolved at recall corroborate our custody shape and our filings model; the org hierarchy is a team shape our single-owner wiki does not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Krzysztof318/MailFathom
good: The write discipline is the best in this wave for a live-communication surface: read, mark, draft and send are separate grants, none implies another, sending is off by default everywhere and impossible in a read-only deployment, and a queued send carries an identity and can be withdrawn before delivery. Reading never mutates the mailbox, answers cite the messages they drew on, and freshness of the local copy is stated with every result.
bad: AGPL-3.0-only makes it ideas-only for us. It is pre-1.0 with admitted breaking upgrades — the stored archive is discarded and re-synced across the 0.8 boundary — and its own screenshot caption warns that until the SensitiveContent option is turned on, the service redacts nothing on its way to a client. The mail copy is a PostgreSQL database: the archive is application state under a heavy .NET deployment, not files the owner reads.
didnt: Corroboration — per-credential grants checked at listing and at call, sends queued with a record identity and withdrawable before they leave, credentials held by reference so configuration is safe to show, and cited answers from a local copy corroborate our email gates and custody rules almost point for point; AGPL keeps it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kskurtveit/echocache
good: The most honest README in the batch: the design rule is argued from token arithmetic, the cases where the cache loses are measured and printed (27 percent worse than the grep slices it tried to replace), the free built-in alternative is recommended over the tool for the common case, and the absence of reuse evidence is admitted on the front page rather than discovered by a reviewer. Freshness semantics and hash-based derived-from invalidation are the right mechanics for what it does cache.
bad: By its own evidence the value case is unproven: zero recorded instances of cross-session reuse in the project's own history, a narrower surviving case (sharing derivations across projects or hosts) that its author calls unproven rather than merely untested, and a host-native free alternative that captures most of the value for its main host. A similarity graph over cached conclusions, with a 0.25 default linking threshold, will also link things that merely sound alike.
didnt: Corroboration — the rule 'cache conclusions, never what was read; a hit must stand in for regenerating, not re-reading' is our derived-view discipline stated with measurements, and the derived-from invalidation cascade is our index-rebuild logic in cache form; its refusal to claim unmeasured reuse corroborates our claims discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kunickiaj/codemem
good: Engineering scale and candour: 133 releases across four hosts sharing one project-scoped store, hybrid retrieval with a keyword-only fallback that keeps working when the semantic runtime fails, a local viewer for inspecting what was captured, and the observer's cost and data-flow disclosed in the quick start rather than the fine print.
bad: The record is manufactured, not kept: an observer model summarises captured activity into memories, those summaries are what get stored in SQLite, and they are injected into later prompts automatically — capture, distillation and injection all happen without a human reading any of it. Sync, team sharing, a coordinator and account linking widen the custody surface well beyond the machine the sessions happened on.
didnt: Rejected — ambient capture distilled by an observer model and auto-injected into future prompts is the custody pole our verbatim-first, owner-gated record exists against; the README's plain statement that local storage is not local-only processing is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: KVANTRA-dev/NOUZ-MCP
good: Two design decisions carry it: the artifact layer and the domain layer are never merged, so a log cannot quietly become knowledge by accumulation; and drift is a first-class report — when what a note says it is and what its content measures as diverge, the server shows the divergence instead of silently reclassifying. Domains are owner-authored prose rather than a vendor taxonomy, everything runs locally, and the privacy table names the one thing that leaves the machine.
bad: Classification by vector projection onto prose reference descriptions is a heuristic wearing a schema's clothes: the thresholds (0.55 for bridges and parent links, spread cut-offs in the config) are judgement calls, and a note's sign is whichever axis its embedding lands nearest. process_orphans auto-fills metadata for unmarked files, the configuration surface is large, and it is a single-author project whose primary documentation is in Russian (an English version is linked).
didnt: Corroboration — the hard separation of artifact form from domain classification ('a log stays a log') and drift reported between a page's declared sign and its measured content profile corroborate our schema discipline and our lint direction; the classification itself we keep human and explicit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kyle-visner/stellarjay
good: Safe write access, engineered rather than promised: append-only history, per-agent attribution tokens, idempotent retries, tamper-evident history, undo scoped by agent and time window with a preview — and expected_root optimistic concurrency, so an agent writing from a stale read is refused instead of silently overwriting a fresher state.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only for us. The domain is business records (CRM, bookkeeping) rather than knowledge, the store is a server with its own data directory and encryption key rather than files the owner reads, and at 83 commits and nine stars the model is young — the hosted platform it powers is the author's business, so the open core's centre of gravity sits elsewhere.
didnt: Corroboration — an append-only store where corrections are new entries, every write carries its agent's name, stale writes are refused by expected-root, and rollback is previewed before it runs corroborates our write discipline in a business-data mirror; AGPL keeps it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kyrzin/kybase
good: Section-level operation is the right granularity for agent memory: search names the section that matched, reads and appends touch only that section, and the human edits the same notes in the same app the agents write to. Per-client OAuth tokens are individually revocable, the embedding providers' data flow is stated where the choice is made, and export to plain Markdown is a first-class feature rather than an afterthought.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only for us. The 'Markdown for humans' headline sits over a Postgres volume in the full app — the Markdown is the interface and the export, the database is the store — and the repository shows 3 commits against 8 releases. The master secret grants full access to the whole instance for non-OAuth clients, and public share links make possession of a URL equivalent to access by design.
didnt: Corroboration — one Markdown base read and edited by both the owner and every agent, section-level reads and writes, per-client revocable tokens and a plain-Markdown export as the exit corroborate our shape; the database-as-store custody in the full app is where we part. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: l33tdawg/sage
good: The instincts underneath the machinery are sound: writes are signed and attributable, admission is a reviewable lifecycle rather than a direct write, access is scoped by enrollment, domain and classification, deprecation retains the audit history, and the README states in its own words that consensus does not prove a remembered claim is true — a limit most governance products leave unsaid.
bad: The governance is disproportionate to its guarantee: on a personal install the single validator votes on its own admissions, so the chain, keys, quorum machinery and fork-ladder upgrades add operational weight without adding a second judge — and by the project's own statement, consensus governs what is committed, not whether it is true. Decay is part of the lifecycle, and 325 releases in under eight months is a churn rate no owner can audit.
didnt: Rejected — Byzantine consensus over memory admission is governance machinery in search of a second party: our gate is the owner himself, a stronger and simpler check than a quorum of one. Signed admission, permission scoping and deprecate-with-audit-history are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LamantinAI/kaeru
licence: BSL 1.1 (source-available per LICENSING.md; converts to Apache-2.0 on the Change Date or four years after a version's first distribution; versions up to v0.7.0 were MIT)
good: The history model is the most careful in the wave: assertions and retractions are the substrate, not a log beside it; supersession distinguishes replacing a record from revising it; and audit events commit in the same transaction as the changes they explain. Re-entry restoring obligations (open tasks, claims, reminders, slot pointers) alongside touched context is our STATE-file discipline recognised as an API, and self-maintenance that proposes findings for the agent to accept or refuse respects the gate.
bad: BSL 1.1 makes it ideas-only for us until each version's conversion date. The store is a CozoDB/RocksDB graph database — the record is application state inside a single binary's vault, with Markdown as an export rather than the substance — automatic hygiene re-layers memory by default (only recall layers, and previewable, but unsupervised), the daemon phones home version telemetry unless disabled, and it is pre-1.0 alpha whose own install section demands a backup before upgrading.
didnt: Corroboration — assertion/retraction history with as-at reads, replace-versus-revise kept distinct, audit committed atomically with the mutations it explains, and re-entry that surfaces what is still owed corroborate our record design in a graph-engine mirror; BSL keeps it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: laradji/deadzone
good: Supply-chain discipline as the design: the index is pinned to the binary version, fetched once, verified against a pinned SHA256, and never trusted unverified — a drifted download aborts rather than degrades. Fail-loud semantics (offline mode refuses to guess), verification failures that drop a document instead of poisoning a run, and stated platform limits make it a small tool with an adult posture.
bad: A reference-lookup utility, not a memory: the corpus is other people's library documentation, fixed at whatever the shipped index contains, and currency is a manual act (upgrade the binary or keep serving the cache forever). Two tools and four stars mark the scale, and the documentation pipeline behind the index is admitted to be the messy half.
didnt: Corroboration — a version-pinned, hash-verified, offline corpus whose failures are loud and whose unverified states are refused outright corroborates our lockfile and verification posture for reference material; it is a lookup tool beside the wiki, not a part of it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: leesgit/passbaton
good: The compaction handover is the sharp piece: instead of letting the host's compaction summarise blindly, a hook re-injects a structured handover at the moment of compaction, and session exit mines the transcript for the artefacts worth keeping (decisions, error-fix pairs) rather than the whole stream. One store shared across three vendors' CLIs, fully local, with upstream limitations documented against their issue numbers.
bad: Continuity by automation: context is injected whether or not it is the right context, and what survives a session is a hook's extraction of the transcript (commits, decisions, error-fix pairs), not the transcript itself — the verbatim record is upstream in the platform's files, and this store is its summarised shadow in one SQLite database. Twenty-five tools and five hooks across three hosts is a wide surface to keep correct.
didnt: Corroboration — a PreCompact handover re-injected at compaction, decisions and error-fix pairs harvested from transcripts into a shared local store, and continuity across three agent hosts corroborate our checkpoint-and-handoff practice; the pre-compaction capture pattern itself was boarded with fable in B113. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: leonardsellem/hypermnesic
good: The strongest files-are-truth statement in the wave, held as an engineering invariant rather than a slogan: the index is disposable by construction, recall returns the repo-relative source path, and a first-run proof demonstrates recall plus a dry-run write diff before anything is installed. Consent-scoped write access, revocable grants, and a doctor that diagnoses without mutating complete a custody posture we recognise.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only for us. v0.1.0 with nine stars is a young instrument, the shared endpoint leans on Tailscale Funnel for its public HTTPS (a third party in the serving path), and the compounding pitch — every connected AI continuously curating the same notes — trusts each client's curation equally, gated by a consent scope rather than by review of each write; the commits are reviewable after the fact, which is not the same as approved before it.
didnt: Corroboration — files as truth with a disposable index, writes as reviewable commits previewed as diffs before they land, read-by-default client scopes with write granted on a consent page, and a setup that verifies the live chain before claiming success corroborate our architecture and our verification standard almost exactly; AGPL keeps it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lfrmonteiro99/memento-mcp
good: Several disciplines are right: typed memories with distinct retrieval behaviour per type, a policy file that lives in the repo where the team can review it, private regions excluded from indexes, injection, embeddings, LLM calls and sync alike (not just from display), secret scrubbing at write time, and team memory serialised as files in git rather than held in the server.
bad: Decay scoring is in the core model: memories lose standing by formula over time, write-time dedup merges near-duplicates when embeddings are on, and capture plus injection are automatic — the record's contents and prominence are continuously adjusted by the server's scoring rather than held as written. The savings figures, however labelled, are modelled estimates, and the store's substance is SQLite rows behind a web inspector, not files.
didnt: Rejected — decay scoring, write-time dedup and automatic injection are the managed-memory profile our verbatim-first record refuses; the repo-resident policy file and the private-region exclusion from every downstream path are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Lians-ai/Lians
good: The typed evidence classes are the sharpest completion-gate design in this batch: which kinds of evidence may open a gate is a property of the evidence, not of the claimant, and an agent's own attestation is structurally incapable of satisfying a criterion.
bad: Young project (created June 2026) whose trusted classes lean on GitHub-specific attestation plumbing; the memory product underneath the guard is comparatively ordinary, and the fixture numbers are self-run on a bounded beta.
didnt: Board — typed evidence classes for completion gates: completion criteria name the evidence classes that can satisfy them, agent-attested and inferred-activity evidence can never open the gate, and checkpoints are bound to current git/task state so stale evidence is refused. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: liftkkkk/owl-mcp
good: A competent, honest bridge between MCP and the semantic-web stack: reasoning is delegated to real reasoners, mutation is explicitly two-phase (change in memory, persist on save), and scale limits are stated rather than discovered.
bad: Twelve commits and no releases; formal ontology files are a specialist substrate the wiki deliberately does not use, and nothing here governs records, provenance or retrieval over Markdown.
didnt: Rejected — a sound semantic-web utility bridge, but OWL reasoning over ontology files is a different substrate from the wiki's Markdown record, and the two-phase save is the only transferable mechanic. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LiLara-AI/shadowgraph
good: reopenWhen is the standout: a decision carries the conditions under which it should be reconsidered as data, evaluated against stored facts, so the rejected alternative resurfaces exactly when its rejection reason stops holding. The completeness blocks and fail-closed scope answers are equally disciplined — absence and incompleteness are reported, never smoothed over.
bad: Technical Preview with three stars and a single release; bi-temporal storage plus four-signal fusion is a heavy apparatus for a store whose differentiation is the decision layer, and the Ed25519 verification path is optional and separately configured.
didnt: Board — decisions that carry their own reconsideration conditions: chosen and rejected alternatives stored with reasons plus structured reopenWhen rules evaluated against stored facts at review time, so a decision reopens itself when the fact that justified rejecting the alternative changes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lildaddyo/braintube-mcp
licence: Elastic License 2.0 (per the LICENSE file at the repo root; repo metadata reports Other/NOASSERTION and the README names no licence; source-available, ideas only under this programme's licence discipline).
good: The shape is sensible — one compiled, citable corpus over everything a user saves, with per-user isolation — and the repo is candid that it is a front end: the deployment machinery is in the tree rather than hidden.
bad: The corpus lives on the vendor's backend under an account, so the record's custody is the service's, not the user's; Elastic License 2.0 makes the code source-available only, and zero stars with no releases gives no adoption signal.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted, account-bound custody model for the compiled corpus, and Elastic License 2.0 keeps it ideas-only under this programme's licence discipline in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linklore/linklore-mcp
licence: Elastic License 2.0 (per the README's licence badge and License section; repo metadata reports Other/NOASSERTION; source-available, ideas only under this programme's licence discipline).
good: The git-diff stale detection between code and its linked docs is a genuinely useful mechanic, and the Source Model disclosure is more honest than most open-core projects manage.
bad: Seven commits; the differentiating core is compiled and closed, sharing depends on a backend outside the repo, and Elastic License 2.0 is source-available only.
didnt: Rejected — Elastic License 2.0 plus a compiled, non-buildable core and backend-dependent sharing; the git-diff code-to-doc stale check is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linxule/lotus-wisdom-mcp
good: As a prompting ritual it is coherent and self-aware about being one, and the analytics note on the hosted worker is candid.
bad: Nothing is recorded, retrieved or governed: the output is a styled reasoning trace, and the wisdom framing does the work that evidence would have to do in a memory system.
didnt: Rejected — prompt theatre of the same family as deep-thinker (B114): a contemplative scaffold over reasoning steps with no record, no retrieval and no governance to study. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lithtrix/lithtrix-mcp
licence: No licence found at source (three routes checked: no License line in the repo details and no LICENSE file in the root listing; the blob/main/LICENSE path returns HTTP 404; no licence named in the README; all rights reserved by default, ideas only).
good: The delegation-signing and passport mechanics show real cryptographic care about agent identity, and the credit metering is at least explicit.
bad: The shape is the inverse of governed memory: an agent enrols itself, agrees to terms on the user's behalf, and stores the record on a metered vendor platform; eight commits, no licence, and the local repo holds none of the memory.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted, credit-metered platform in which the agent self-registers and self-agrees to terms, with memory held server-side and no licence at source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lockstep-team-agent/lockstep
good: Draft-versus-accepted as a hard state boundary, acknowledgement binding for cross-cutting decisions, and the configured-versus-activated distinction are all stated as rules, not vibes — and the consent granularity (setup approval is not upload approval) is exactly right.
bad: Pilot-stage and team-shaped: multi-repo routing, surface IDs and acknowledgement quorums solve coordination problems a single-owner wiki does not have, and the hosted default puts the ledger on Railway unless self-hosted.
didnt: Corroboration — draft-vs-accepted decision states, acknowledgement-bound briefings and activation-is-not-configuration corroborate the wiki's own governance from the team-tooling side; the multi-team machinery itself is a shape our single-owner wiki does not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: louis030195/easy-obsidian-mcp
licence: No licence found at source (no License line in the repo metadata, no LICENSE file in the root listing, and no License section in the README; all rights reserved by default, ideas only).
good: Dataview access and typo-tolerant search over a live vault are convenient, and reusing the vault app's own API keeps one writer of record.
bad: No licence, a hard dependency on weakening Obsidian's Restricted mode and keeping the app running, and no record governance of its own — it is a window into a vault, not a memory system.
didnt: Rejected — a thin, unlicensed bridge whose documented operations are read-side despite the catalogue's CRUD description, and which requires disabling Obsidian's Restricted mode. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LuizEduPP/rememb
good: Non-destructive versioning with restore, a portable folder store, and a read-only supervision UI over an MCP-only write path are a clean small-scale discipline; refusing embeddings and judging relevance agent-side is a stated, defensible trade.
bad: Keyword-only retrieval will miss paraphrase at any real corpus size, sectioned free-text entries carry no provenance or status model, and five stars with a bundled-skills marketing layer gives little adoption evidence.
didnt: Corroboration — non-destructive versioning with diff/restore, soft delete, an audit trail and a supervision-only UI corroborate the wiki's write discipline at personal scale; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict stands. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lumayapartners/memini
good: Two mechanics stand out: a guardrail is bound to the hash of the evidence it cites and goes quiet when that evidence changes, and agent-proposed rules are confined to the narrowest scope until a human verifies them for wider reach — containment designed against a prompt-injected writer.
bad: v0.1 with no releases and no stars; the pre-commit gate fails open by design, warn-mode is advisory only, and the interception covers edit tools rather than the shell, all of which the project itself concedes.
didnt: Board — evidence-bound guardrails with scope containment: a recorded warning stops firing when the file it cites changes hash until a human re-verifies it, and agent-proposed rules live at the narrowest scope, firing wider only once human-verified. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lyonzin/knowledge-rag
good: The most carefully hedged claims apparatus in this batch — every performance statement carries its methodology boundary — and the check-first/cite-sources skills encode retrieval-before-assertion as a habit.
bad: Retrieval only: nothing here keeps, versions, governs or supersedes a record, and 35-format ingestion breadth trades against depth on any one format.
didnt: Corroboration — a well-run local retrieval layer whose methodology-hedged audit claims and path:line citation discipline corroborate the wiki's retrieval standards; it keeps no record and governs nothing, so there is nothing further to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: M-T-D-N/agentmemory-codex-windows
good: Exemplary engineering honesty for a downstream: preview status, AI authorship, unknown root causes and qualification limits are all stated where a user will meet them, and the audit mechanics (trackAccess off-switch, capture exclusions, qualified adoption without silent downgrade) are genuinely careful.
bad: A packaging downstream of an already-studied upstream line rather than a new design; Windows-only, unsigned, two stars, and its 58-tool inherited surface is far broader than the four-hook profile it actually qualifies.
didnt: Corroboration — the AgentMemory line's Windows distribution corroborates through its audit and capture discipline (provenance-scoped writes, bounded federated recall, derived indexes labelled derived); as a downstream of a studied project it adds packaging, not a new pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Magnemo-AI/magnemo
good: The closest match in the catalogue to the owner's own rule that decisions are always his: promotion is a human-only act whose answer never transits the agent, the ledger makes trust a computed property of recorded acts, and retrieval serves canon only — staged material exists but is never silently searchable.
bad: Seventeen commits and three stars, Phase 1 guarantees only, the hosted door still roadmap (0.7.0), and the in-chat approval depends on client behaviour the project can test on only one client so far.
didnt: Board — the trust ledger pattern: promotion as a human-only act whose answer never passes through the agent, every promote/reject recorded append-only with actor and mandatory reason, rejections kept as teaching material, and retrieval that serves promoted canon only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: majiayu000/remem
good: The most thorough treatment in this batch of the problem the wiki's own compile step faces: a distilled claim is a claim about a source, and remem refuses to let it circulate as current truth until the source support, the gate and the receipt all still check out — with drop reasons diagnosable rather than silent.
bad: Mature but heavy: 1,828 commits of machinery (workers, rollups, recovery ranges, claim ordering) around a distillation pipeline whose quality still rests on the background model, and the SQLCipher default and multi-surface eligibility policies make the system hard to reason about from outside.
didnt: Board — distillate governance: auto-captured memory is untrusted until it passes source-support checks against the raw capture, auto-promoted items re-validate an exact activation receipt at injection time, and rows that cannot be verified are labelled legacy_unverified and excluded from default context while remaining visible to explicit search. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MakeaMouse/fish-bridge-mcp
good: The delivery trick is elegant — the summary rides in the instruction file every client already reads, so no injection machinery is needed — and the merge sources (test output, IaC, specs as graph inputs) are broader than most session tools.
bad: The compressed graph overwrites the agent's instruction file on the strength of an LLM extraction whose quality percentages are asserted without a method; session-scoped, with no provenance from graph node back to the turn that produced it and no governance over what the compile keeps or drops.
didnt: Rejected — a token-economy session compressor, not a record: its output is an unprovenanced LLM extract written over the instruction file, and its quality figures are self-rated without methodology. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markmhendrickson/neotoma
good: The closest architectural relative of the wiki's raw-to-compiled pipeline in this batch, with the provenance pushed one level deeper than per-note: per field. The limitation disclosures (including a named idempotency defect in the current release) are a model of how to scope a system's own claims.
bad: Immutability is a write-path convention the database does not enforce, attribution is uneven across its four interfaces (the CLI records no writer at all), and IDs are instance-relative in ways the README has to warn about at length; the full apparatus (federation, peer sync, guest intake) far exceeds a personal record's needs.
didnt: Board — field-level provenance by deterministic reduction: current state is computed from immutable observations by a stable-order reducer under per-field merge policies, and every field in the snapshot names the observation that set it, so 'current' is always explainable and reproducible. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mattjoyce/mcp-persona-sessions
good: The persona-as-Markdown-file convention is tidy, and session frameworks as data (YAML types with goals, topics and durations) are a reasonable way to make guided conversations repeatable.
bad: Not a memory or record system in any sense the catalogue is studying: no store, no provenance, no retrieval — and GPL-3.0 would keep it ideas-only regardless.
didnt: Rejected — persona role-play session scaffolding that happens to sit in the MCP registries; off-domain for a record study, and GPL-3.0 in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: max-ramas/rms-memory-mcp
good: Recall that can refuse is the pattern: instead of always filling the prompt with the least-bad matches, the envelope makes abstention a first-class answer, and the write-path credential refusal (kind and line named, value never echoed) is the right shape for a guard.
bad: Feature breadth is enormous for 150 commits (graph, code memory, HTTP transport, GUI companion, federation), the paid GUI sits on top of the free server, and the auto-stamped confidence field has no stated derivation — a number whose basis is the one thing left unexplained.
didnt: Board — bounded recall as an inject/abstain envelope: retrieval returns either a bounded, score-gated injection or an explicit abstention, fails closed on error, and lets lifecycle frontmatter (status, supersedes, validity windows) decide what may be served at all. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: maxkuminov/obsidian-mcp
good: The self-describing vault is the right answer to per-session briefing, and the no-hidden-pipeline statement is a scope honesty most memory products avoid: what you see in the folder is exactly what the system knows.
bad: Deliberately a storage-and-search layer: curation, lifecycle and truth-maintenance are all left to the agents and the human, and the PostgreSQL/pgvector stack is a heavier operational commitment than the vault it indexes.
didnt: Corroboration — the self-describing vault (conventions carried in the vault and learned on first call) and the explicit refusal to run a hidden extraction or decay pipeline corroborate the wiki's own door design; it is a well-built access layer over ground we already cover. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcasdfgf/mcp-roo-memory
good: The mutation taxonomy (a typo fix, an approach change and a stale-cascade are different operations) is a thoughtful distinction, and the viewport tiers are a sensible answer to context overflow.
bad: Nine commits and a PoC disclaimer; the reference config trains the worst habit — blanket pre-approval of delete and store tools — and the fractal taxonomy is asserted in CONCEPT.md rather than evidenced by use.
didnt: Rejected — an explicitly experimental proof of concept at nine commits, whose shipped configuration pre-approves destructive tools. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memokar/brainy
licence: AGPL-3.0 (dual-licensed with a commercial option and a contributor licence agreement, per the README's License section); ideas only under this programme's licence discipline.
good: The coordination mechanics are exactly the ones a multi-agent wiki needs and are stated as guarantees with a race test behind them; propose-then-approve for knowledge writes matches the owner's decision rule, and the honest comparison table is a small model of evidence discipline.
bad: Eleven commits and zero stars — the design is well-evidenced by its own tests but unproven by adoption; single-node SQLite by the author's own statement, and AGPL plus a CLA keeps the code itself out of reach for this programme.
didnt: Corroboration — atomic task/resource claims with leases, expected-commit optimistic concurrency over a Git-backed Markdown store, and a trigger-enforced append-only audit corroborate the wiki's multi-agent coordination design almost point for point; AGPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memstate-ai/memstate-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the repo metadata and the LICENSE file; the README's badge names MIT — a metadata-versus-badge discrepancy recorded here, not resolved).
good: Keypaths with preserved version chains and built-in conflict detection are a genuinely better shape for facts that change than embedding-only recall, and the fairness notes are more candid than most vendor benchmarks.
bad: The store itself is the vendor's hosted service — the repo holds no memory — so custody, availability and pricing are the SaaS's; the benchmark, however fairly noted, is the maker's suite, weights and win; and the licence badge disagrees with the repo's own metadata and LICENSE file.
didnt: Rejected — a client for a hosted, account-bound memory service; the keypath versioning is credited in good, but the record's custody is the vendor's and the headline numbers are self-benchmarked. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mercurialsolo/counsel-mcp
good: The wrapper itself is competently done — dual transport, standards-based OAuth endpoints, clear tool contracts — and question-sharpening as a pre-step before analysis is a sound interaction pattern.
bad: A thin client over a proprietary hosted reasoning service: nothing is stored, versioned or governed locally, and the analysis itself is a black box behind an account.
didnt: Rejected — an API wrapper for a hosted strategic-reasoning service, in the registries' memory neighbourhood by association only; it keeps no record to study. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: michael-denyer/memory-mcp
good: The delivery mechanism is clever — riding hook stdout to place the hot set in context at zero tool-call cost, and printing only on change — and per-repo isolation is automatic.
bad: Frequency is doing the work evidence should do: use promotes a memory, promotion guarantees more use, and nothing in the loop checks whether the memory was right — the trust score that supposedly demotes the outdated has no stated derivation, and 'predicted next memories' injects speculation into every prompt.
didnt: Rejected — self-reinforcing promotion: recall frequency promotes, promotion drives recall, and no source-support or review gate interrupts the loop, which is the inverse of the evidence-gated promotion boarded from skillmem (B117) and remem (B118). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: michielinksee/linksee-memory
good: The accounting rule is the contribution: most memory tools can say what was decided and some can say what happened, but linksee reconciles the two and only raises the divergences nobody has explained, with held items carrying their own review dates.
bad: The drift engine leans on declared violation signals — string-level tripwires that a paraphrased divergence can walk past — and the comparative claims rest on a single self-run scenario; the six-layer model and anchor taxonomy add ceremony a small store must keep up with.
didnt: Board — drift accounting: declared decisions carry violation signals, observed divergence between the record and reality is flagged only when no recorded resolution accounts for it, and accounted evolution stays quiet — so the ledger distinguishes silent abandonment from deliberate change. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mlorentedev/hive
good: Operational honesty of a rare order: measurements labelled as measurements, deferred-commit risk stated as a contract, partial-failure semantics (a cancel is not a rollback) made visible in the health output, and a security hold published against the author's own feature.
bad: Lesson confidence grows by being read, which is the same self-reinforcement loop rejected elsewhere in this batch — here it only ranks lessons rather than promoting them into canon, but the signal still rewards the already-surfaced; 110 releases in seven months is a fast-moving target for a context layer.
didnt: Corroboration — on-demand vault access with deferred-commit writes and a health surface that reports drift and ghost responses corroborates the wiki's access pattern; its measurement-versus-description footnote and published security hold are candour worth matching. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mnemosyne-OS/Mnemosyne-Neural-OS
licence: Custom 'Engramm License' (open-core; repo metadata reports Other/NOASSERTION, a LICENSE file ships in the root, and the README's licensing sections describe an open core with wallet-verified licensing); ideas only under this programme's licence discipline.
