good: The signed intent protocol (agents ask to query/ingest/forget/focus rather than touching files) and per-domain vaults with their own protection levels are a coherent sovereignty design, and installer attestation with a published verify command is good practice.
bad: The memory core is one module inside a very large product surface (voice, canvas, wallet, P2P, cartridges) that must be adopted whole through a desktop app; licensing is a custom open-core instrument tied to a crypto wallet, and the benchmark's answering model is a cloud model, so the 77.1% is a hybrid-system figure rather than a property of the local engine.
didnt: Rejected — a desktop-OS product under a custom open-core licence, adopted whole or not at all; its governed-vault ideas are noted, but there is no separable record layer to study or borrow under this programme's licence discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mnlt/wellread
good: Two transferable ideas stated cleanly: research is a cache problem before it is a search problem, and staleness should be priced per topic volatility rather than by one global TTL — with re-verification treated as a contribution that refreshes the entry for everyone.
bad: The shared cache is a hosted, multiplayer network — what one team's agents save, another's retrieve — so its value and its risk both rest on the sanitisation layers holding; the headline savings table assumes a hit at every depth, and AGPL-3.0 keeps the code ideas-only here in any case.
didnt: Corroboration — check-before-research with volatility-keyed freshness and communal re-verification corroborates the wiki's own research discipline (and the rag-check-first pattern from B117); AGPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: modelcontextprotocol/server-memory
licence: MIT (per the License section of the server's README in the modelcontextprotocol/servers repository).
good: Its minimalism is its function — a stable, legible reference every other server is compared to — and the lock-file protocol (heartbeat, single stale-breaker, fail-don't-overwrite) is a properly specified answer to a problem most multi-client tools ignore.
bad: As a memory model it is a floor, not a target: no provenance, no history, no conflict handling, whole-graph reads, and observations as unversioned strings — everything the rest of this catalogue exists because this lacks.
didnt: Corroboration — the ecosystem's reference baseline corroborates by defining the floor (entity/relation/observation over one file) that the governed designs in this programme are measured against; its cross-process lock protocol is the one piece of real engineering care. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: moorcheh-ai/memanto
good: A memory agent that manages other agents' memory rather than merely storing it — and its retention design remains the reference implementation of expiry as a written, inspectable policy rather than a cleanup chore.
bad: It is a second autonomous agent curating, merging and expiring on its own judgment on a daily scheduled loop, and offers a hosted cloud backend — adopting the whole system would hand governance of the estate to an external agent's judgment, the opposite of our owner-approved write gates.
took: Retention as a git-kept policy file (show-policy → dry-run → confirm; restore and hard-delete kept separate) — built 2026-10-20, Phase 2 — source/inspiration: Memanto mechanics
didnt: Corroboration — its retention mechanics (policy file, dry-run → confirm, expiry stamped with the retiring rule, restore and hard-delete kept separate) are exactly the pattern our programme built in Phase 2; the fleet-agent itself was not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MWGMorningwood/Central-Memory-MCP
good: Workspace isolation falls out of the storage model cleanly (partition key per workspace), and the README is honest about which tools exist and which are merely planned.
bad: An alpha hosting port: most of the tool surface is roadmap, the observation model is a delimited string in a table cell, and nothing about governance, provenance or retrieval is added by the move to Azure.
didnt: Rejected — a deployment-shape fork of the reference server onto Azure Functions and Table Storage; the port is a hosting detail, and the implemented surface is a subset of the baseline it ports. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MyAgentHubs/aimemo
good: The packaging is genuinely good — one binary, memory that travels with the project directory, identical powers for human and agent, and a token budget for the tool surface itself.
bad: Two commits is a sketch, however tidy; ranking by recency times access frequency is the self-reinforcing loop again (what surfaces gets used, what gets used surfaces), and there is no provenance or lifecycle beyond soft delete.
didnt: Rejected — a neat minimal store at two commits whose ranking rewards the already-recalled; it adds packaging elegance, not a pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: n24q02m/mnemo-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (per the repo metadata; the root also carries a LICENSE-MIT file — recorded as found).
good: The de-host is a model of architectural candour — hosted machinery removed in favour of one local store, sync honestly reclassified as the user's rclone job — and the audit table's state hashes give the temporal graph an integrity check most stores lack.
bad: 246 releases of churn with breaking changes shipped and documented after the fact; importance is LLM-scored (a model's judgment wearing a number), the dual LICENSE/LICENSE-MIT presence muddies the licence picture the metadata states, and the feature pile (compression, consolidation, graph auto-extraction) makes the store's behaviour hard to predict from outside.
didnt: Corroboration — bitemporal validity columns with current-state default reads, hash-chained audit rows and a soft-archive-with-restore policy corroborate the temporal layer designs boarded from shadowgraph (B117) and neotoma (B118) at product scale. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nazar256/memheaven
good: The source-of-truth discipline survives the port (bodies verbatim in R2, everything else an index), the Confirmed-versus-Expected client table is honest about verification, and the evals are scoped as self-evals in the text that presents them.
bad: Thirty-five commits and no releases; the deployment trades the laptop for a Cloudflare account's free-tier limits and plan quirks (Vectorize constraints are flagged by the author), and the memory model itself is inherited wholesale from MemPalace.
didnt: Corroboration — the remote door for hosted clients (OAuth-protected, tenant-scoped, verbatim bodies in object storage with indexes kept as indexes) corroborates the hosted-door shape this programme has under consideration; the memory model is MemPalace's, already studied. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ndjordjevic/pinrag
good: Citations shaped to the source, crawl politeness as configuration rather than courtesy, and a fail_summary that counts what did not index and why — the unglamorous disciplines that make a retrieval layer trustworthy.
bad: An index, not a memory: nothing is versioned, superseded, governed or forgotten except by manual removal, citation granularity varies by source kind, and two stars give no adoption signal for a 46-release history.
didnt: Corroboration — citation-granular retrieval over mixed source kinds (a timestamp is the right citation for a video, a page for a PDF) and failure-accounted indexing corroborate the retrieval standards set by knowledge-rag (B117) and gnosis-mcp (B119); it keeps no record to govern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nfemmanuel/iranti
licence: No licence found at source (no License line in the repo metadata, no LICENSE file in the root listing, and no root README — the README blob path returns HTTP 404; all rights reserved by default, ideas only).
good: Conflict handling has the right terminal state: auto-resolution with cited evidence where possible, and an escalation file to a human where not — most stores silently pick a winner instead.
bad: No licence anywhere at source, which ends the adoption question by itself; confidence is self-assigned by the writing agent with a default of 85, so the number measures the writer's assertiveness rather than the fact's support; and the repo itself is nearly undocumented — no root README — with the design visible mainly through a registry mirror.
didnt: Rejected — an elaborate staffed-memory design with no licence at source and self-assigned confidence at its centre; its one strong mechanic, escalating unresolvable conflicts to a human with the evidence cited, is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ni-c/wikijs-mcp
good: The most complete door-safety design in this batch, each piece aimed at a real failure: the stale-read refusal that teaches recovery, confinement without silent exceptions, results labelled untrusted at the boundary where wiki text enters the model, and elicitation that structurally excludes the model from approving its own destruction.
bad: It is a door onto someone else's wiki engine rather than a memory design of its own, the full 62-tool surface is exactly the sprawl its own preset argues against, and three stars with five releases is early evidence for a safety story told mostly in documentation.
didnt: Board — the guarded write door: writes compare against the version read and refuse on a stale read with a recovery-shaped result instead of an error, writes are confined to path prefixes with un-confinable operations refusing outright, the exposed tool set is itself curated and fails loudly on a typo, and destructive tools put the question to a person in a dialog the model cannot answer for them. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nicholasglazer/gnosis-mcp
good: Negative results published with numbers and acted on (the reranker stays off), plus the access-log doctor that detects a mounted-but-uncalled server — the two habits that separate an instrument from a brochure.
bad: Retrieval only — it indexes documentation, keeps no record and governs nothing beyond its own index hygiene — and the headline 92% Hit@5 rests on 25 hand-written queries over the author's own corpus, however honestly the fixture is described.
didnt: Corroboration — measured-not-marketed retrieval: published negative results, a smoke test labelled a smoke test, a usage ledger that reports zero-hit queries and never-served documents, and write tools withdrawn rather than merely refused corroborate the retrieval discipline boarded and corroborated across B117–B118. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NicolasPrimeau/artel
good: Restraint as a retrieval virtue: the pad speaks in one line or stays silent, and the lifespan split (directives never fade, decisions never merge, code notes re-derive) matches retention to the kind of thing remembered instead of ageing everything alike.
bad: The archivist is an autonomous curator with merge and decay powers — the governance question (who approved this merge, this demotion?) is answered by design trust rather than by a human gate — and 853 commits with 56 configuration settings is a large, fast-moving surface for a notepad.
didnt: Corroboration — note kinds with kind-specific lifespans, decisions exempted from merge and decay by rule, and compiled notes pinned to the code they describe corroborate the wiki's lifecycle design from the fleet-tooling side; the autonomous archivist is a governance shape this programme deliberately does not copy. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nonatofabio/local-faiss-mcp
good: Honest minimalism: a small, legible local RAG primitive with sensible defaults, a real CLI beside the server, and reranking offered as the standard two-stage pattern rather than a novelty.
bad: A vector index with two verbs: chunks go in and similarity brings them back, with no way to correct, retire or even identify the record a chunk came from beyond a source string — plumbing, not memory.
didnt: Rejected — a minimal FAISS utility; competent plumbing that this programme's retrieval layer already exceeds, with nothing about a record to study. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NORTHTEKDevs/genome
good: Two ideas stated better here than anywhere else in the batch: a record your ingest cannot re-derive is a record you cannot audit, and write authority as a property of provenance — the firewall makes the user's own words structurally unreachable by scraped content, which is the correct shape for injection defence.
bad: Ninety-two commits and ten stars is a young project making an architectural argument more than a proven system; the bi-temporal layer is opt-in and its belief extraction is the one LLM call in the building, and exact cosine search without an ANN index will meet its scale ceiling in time.
didnt: Board — origin-bound write authority: every write is tagged with its provenance class, and authority follows the class — low-trust origins are quarantined from recall and can never update or delete what a higher-trust origin said, enforced beneath any conflict-resolution layer, prompt-injected or otherwise. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nworks3d/THOR-memory-bible-for-AI
good: The proof-of-currency rule solves the stale-guard problem at the root — authority is re-earned at the moment of action rather than inherited from the day the note was written — and printing the 2-of-2,999 figure is the kind of self-measurement the whole catalogue should be held to.
bad: GPL-3.0 keeps the code ideas-only here; proof authorship is a per-note judgment the author concedes moves 'by hand', so most real memories will sit in the warn-only tier indefinitely; and a blocking layer wired into every edit and command is a large behavioural commitment resting on 356 commits and five stars.
didnt: Corroboration — proof-priced authority (a guard may refuse only while its live check holds, words alone may only warn, an un-runnable check refuses nothing) is the sharpest statement yet of the guardrail rule boarded from ThumbGate (B114) and memini (B117); GPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Octonove/crbro-memory
good: The verification semantics are stated better than in most of the catalogue: four labels kept separate, verification an explicit act rather than a side effect of recall, and a debt ledger that treats a recorded decision-not-to-build as memory worth keeping.
bad: Heat scoring still ranks by frequency and recency alongside the labels, the biological vocabulary (cortex, synapses, hippocampus) is decoration over a JSON store, and eight stars with a PayPal/USDC tip jar is a one-person project carrying a great many mechanisms.
didnt: Corroboration — corrections that supersede rather than pile up, shelf-life staleness with a source-check warning, and above all the rule that repetition never verifies (only an explicit verified revise restarts the clock) corroborate the verification discipline boarded from skillmem (B117) and remem (B118); the error and debt ledgers match our own corrections and parked-ideas practice. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: olgasafonova/mediawiki-mcp-server
good: Treating wiki health as queryable — which pages are stale, orphaned or broken-linked — rather than as an occasional manual sweep, and giving the shell the same powers as the agent through one CLI with CI-friendly exit codes.
bad: A connector, not a memory design: it inherits MediaWiki's own revision model and adds no governance of its own, and the edit tools carry no approval or confinement story of the kind wikijs-mcp (B119) built — the safety model is the wiki account's permissions.
didnt: Corroboration — a wiki door paired with hygiene audits (stale pages, orphans, broken links as first-class queries) corroborates the door-plus-maintenance shape of our own wiki tooling, from the MediaWiki side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: omega-memory/omega-memory
good: Two interface ideas are genuinely good: showing the client five tools and dispatching the rest through one call to save context, and a reflect tool whose job is surfacing contradictions and decision evolution rather than more recall.
bad: The pitch's centre of gravity — coordination, routing, entity memory, knowledge base — is the paid tier behind the open-source headline; capture is automatic by hook rather than gated; and 'intelligent forgetting' (per the catalogue) is a lifecycle run by the tool's judgment, not by a written policy the owner approved.
didnt: Rejected — a competent local store whose headline capabilities are a commercial tier, with hook-driven auto-capture; the condensed tool surface and the contradiction-tracing reflect tool are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ontorata/ratary
good: The scoping is at least explicit — the server is the source of truth, clients are replaceable packages, and the ecosystem products are named as separate repositories rather than silently bundled.
bad: Platform sprawl at one star and two releases: enterprise plumbing (identity, marketplace, cloud tiers) vastly outweighs the memory design, which is presented as capability headings rather than mechanisms a reader can evaluate.
didnt: Rejected — an infrastructure platform whose memory layer is brochure-deep; nothing at the mechanism level to study that the focused stores in this wave do not state better. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: oomkapwn/enquire-mcp
good: Freshness as a per-hit field rather than a global property — the agent sees the age of what it is about to repeat, next to the citation — plus structured vault formats (Dataview, Bases, Canvas) treated as queryable structure instead of text to flatten.
bad: The '#1 Obsidian MCP' branding is self-awarded and its comparison table self-scored (mitigated by a review date and an evidence link); 352 releases in under three months is churn a user must ride; and it is a retrieval door over a vault, not a record with lifecycle or governance.
didnt: Corroboration — freshness-aware cited recall over a files-first vault (age and stale status travelling with every hit), a read-only-by-default door with write tools gated behind a flag, and zero-outbound serving corroborate our vault and door design almost point for point. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: paladini/mcp-me
good: The shape is clean — profile as plain local files, one directory, exposed as resources any client can read — and generators are honestly framed as population from public sources rather than as memory.
bad: A static identity card, not a memory: nothing is versioned, superseded, corrected or provenanced — generators scrape public profiles into YAML and the file simply is the truth until regenerated — and personality.yaml (traits, MBTI) is horoscope-grade content served with the same authority as the career history.
didnt: Rejected — a well-packaged profile card; its subject is who the user is on paper, not a record that learns, corrects or forgets. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pallaprolus/mendeley-mcp
good: Craft details done right: OAuth secrets in the OS keyring rather than a config file, annotations surfaced as first-class data, and limits (file-size cap, catalog files often unavailable for copyright reasons) stated plainly in the tool reference.
bad: A vendor connector onto a proprietary cloud library: the memory lives in Elsevier's service under its API's terms and rate limits, and there is no record design here to study — the same shape as mcp-zotero (B115), rejected on the same ground.
didnt: Rejected — competent plumbing to a reference manager, not a memory system; keyring credential storage and the confirm-before-delete instruction are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pantheon-Security/notebooklm-mcp-secure
good: The audit write-up is a model of security candour: findings enumerated by reviewer, before/after numbers printed, and a marketing claim publicly withdrawn when the code did not support it.
bad: The substrate is a scraped consumer product: access rides browser-session auth against NotebookLM's web UI, so the 'memory' is Google's, the interface is unofficial and breakable by any UI change, and 'zero-hallucination answers' in the headline is a claim no retrieval layer can make — the hardening is real, but it armours a bridge, not a record.
didnt: Rejected — a hardened connector to a hosted consumer service; the audit practice (independent reviewers, a public issue list, a retracted claim) is credited in good, the architecture is not one this programme can build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pathrule/mcp
licence: MIT (per the License section of the repository README).
good: Two disciplines worth noting: OAuth scopes deciding which tools exist (not merely which calls succeed), and telemetry that logs that a call happened and how it ended, never what it carried.
bad: The memory lives in a vendor's cloud under a subscription gate; this repository is a listing bundle for that service rather than the system itself, so there is no local record design to study — the local half of the product is a different, closed artefact.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted SaaS door; scope-shaped tool surfaces and metadata-only telemetry are credited in good, but custody and the subscription gate end the question. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: paultaki/ailooplibrary-mcp
good: Bounded loops as a published, lintable form — verification, stop conditions and budgets as required fields rather than good intentions — and data behaviour under failure specified as carefully as the happy path.
bad: Seven commits and zero stars: a catalogue browser for one website's loop collection, not a memory system, and its lint is text matching — as its own README concedes, it can notice a missing approval gate but cannot establish that a loop is safe.
didnt: Corroboration — a checker that fails a work loop for a missing approval, stop or budget gate (and says its score grants nothing), plus an outage policy that serves stale-with-a-warning or an error but never invented data, corroborate this programme's gate and honesty machinery in miniature. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pavelpilyak/devrecall
good: Custody written as a contract: a table naming what each source contributes, tokens at 0600, a relay that structurally cannot see content, and recall that cites the underlying artefacts instead of paraphrasing them.
bad: An activity index, not a governed memory: it aggregates what happened but keeps no decisions, corrections or lifecycle of its own, its value is reporting (standups, brag docs) rather than a record agents act from, and five stars is thin adoption for nine connected sources' worth of OAuth surface.
didnt: Corroboration — a local, per-source-specified aggregation of the work record with cited recall (answers carrying the commits, PRs and tickets they rest on) corroborates the conversation-log and activity-record side of our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: penfieldlabs/penfield-mcp
good: The session-opening ritual is a reasonable shape — load identity context, then orient on recent work before acting — and the tool taxonomy (memory, graph, context, artifacts kept as separate families) is tidily drawn.
bad: There is no system here to study: the memory, the graph and the personality layer all live on Penfield's servers under its portal's terms, and this repo's 15 commits are packaging around that service — custody is the vendor's by construction.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted memory service with a public listing repo; AGPL-3.0 on the shell does not change where the records live. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi22by7/In-Memoria
good: Local-first throughout with real engineering in the analysis layer, a token-economical blueprint format, and an unusually honest status section for a project of its popularity.
bad: Its memory is inference over code — statistical patterns that can drift from what the team actually decided and carry no provenance back to a decision, a person or a moment; pattern prediction from history is the learned pole our verbatim-first record opposes, and zero releases against 17 tags suggests the packaging has not settled.
didnt: Rejected — a codebase-pattern learner; the record it keeps is derived statistics about code, not governed knowledge, and the decision-tracking is a side feature of the routing engine. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Piccolo123/url-manager-mcp
good: The shared-category permission model is drawn precisely (owner/admin/member across cocreate and subscribe), and the pitfalls section documents its own API's footguns instead of leaving agents to find them.
bad: The library lives on the vendor's service under an account the agent silently creates for the user — custody and consent both inverted — and a bookmark collection with categories is a link library, not a memory record: nothing is versioned, provenanced or corrected.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted bookmark manager whose onboarding model (the agent registers the user without asking) is the opposite of this programme's approval posture. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pinecone-io/assistant-mcp
good: It is at least honestly minimal — the official wrapper does one thing and its README does not pretend otherwise.
bad: A vendor API wrapper of eight commits: the knowledge, the indexing and the custody are all Pinecone's cloud, and the server adds a protocol translation and nothing else.
didnt: Rejected — a thin connector to a hosted assistant product; nothing at source to study beyond the shape of the vendor's API. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pipeshub-ai/mcp-server
good: Two sound defaults: retrieval respects the source systems' own permissions per user rather than pooling access, and the vendor itself recommends leaving the chat tool out and keeping the surface to search and read.
bad: An enterprise platform's plumbing: the retrieval, indexing and permission enforcement live in the PipesHub instance this repo merely connects to, the deployment prerequisites admit search returns 500s until an LLM is configured, and there is no memory record here at all — it is federated search over other systems' documents.
didnt: Rejected — a connector package for an enterprise search product; per-user permission-respecting retrieval is credited in good, but the design belongs to the platform, not to this repository. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pjpoulose/PIL
good: Read-only enforced where it cannot be talked around — the database handle itself is opened read-only — plus coverage statistics that admit which fraction of the library the extraction has actually reached.
bad: The deep-read layer is model-generated extraction standing between the user and their own saved posts (summaries can misread, and the library's search runs over the extraction), the corpus is one platform's saves, and two stars with a single release is a young personal project.
didnt: Corroboration — a personal archive ingested locally from the user's own saves, then served through a door that is read-only in the storage engine itself rather than by tool convention, corroborates the read-only door discipline (wikijs-mcp, B119; enquire-mcp, B120) at the smallest scale. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pomazanbohdan/memory-mcp-1file
good: Single-binary custody is genuinely well executed (database, graph and model in one file, nothing leaves the machine), and refusing to enable an HTTP surface it did not need is attack-surface reasoning of the right kind.
bad: Archived and superseded by its own first line; the governance that exists is a system-prompt protocol an agent may or may not follow, and the lifecycle ideas that would matter (decay, confidence) are unwritten roadmap entries.
didnt: Rejected — a capable all-in-one store whose author has moved on; its one hard mechanism, excluding destructive tools from the shipped project configuration, is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ragieai/mcp-server
good: The retirement notice itself is good practice — the README sends its own users to the replacement instead of leaving a stale wrapper to be found first.
bad: Self-declared obsolete in its own first section: a one-tool shim to a hosted RAG service, superseded by the vendor's native server.
didnt: Rejected — nothing to study beyond the vendor's retrieval API shape, and the maker says so itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rarefied-Earth/groundwork
licence: Custom evaluation terms (repo metadata 'Other (NOASSERTION)'; the root LICENSE is 'evaluation terms; not an OSS software license' per the repo's own map, production source closed — ideas only at most).
good: The shape it sells is the right shape — company state as a read-only, tenant-scoped feed with provenance on results, and a demo that honestly labels its fixtures synthetic and its writes nonexistent.
bad: There is no system in this repo to evaluate — the product is closed and hosted by design, the local artefact serves synthetic fixtures, and a README section written to steer visiting agents' recommendations is a sales channel wearing documentation's clothes.
didnt: Rejected — a proprietary product's discovery demo; the one sound idea, a read-only company-state feed so agents read the operating picture instead of inventing one, is noted in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ravi-labs/mindmap-mcp-server
good: Forgetting designed as a first-class, inspectable process — tiers, forecasts, protected filings, an explicit forget that outranks them all — and a passport that treats exit from the tool as a feature.
bad: Trust-as-reuse-count is the self-reinforcement family — a summary reused because it was surfaced gains trust because it was reused — mitigated here by the audit view but not eliminated; capture is a model-written summary (distilled, not verbatim), and at 26 commits the lifecycle has more design than mileage.
didnt: Corroboration — decay that collapses to a trace instead of deleting, promotion and filing as visible states, and a glass-box audit showing provenance, trust and decay forecast for every item corroborate the transparency and retention lines running through B117–B120. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: redleaves/context-keeper
good: The two-stage shape it advertises — wide multi-branch recall, then a careful re-rank — is the standard sound architecture; it is the evidence, not the diagram, that is missing.
bad: Nine commits beneath a brochure: every quality figure is asserted without a fixture or method, the record's integrity (what is kept, merged, resolved) is delegated to LLM judgment end to end, and the three-database-plus-LLM infrastructure bill is enterprise theatre for a memory layer.
didnt: Rejected — a pitch deck with a repository attached; nothing in it survives the programme's rule that a claim needs a measurement behind it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: remembra-ai/remembra
good: The worked example is the whole philosophy in one line — an agent wrote that the work was 'done and pushed', git showed two commits unpushed, and the brief sided with git. That ordering (facts first, narrative as a claim) is exactly the discipline a handoff needs.
bad: The verified path depends on per-client hooks (one verified client is a prerelease build; headless invocations write no handoff), the relay's facts travel to a server — self-hosted or the vendor's cloud — rather than staying in the repo they describe, and the underlying memory API's extraction (entities, relationships) is the usual LLM distillation beneath the handoff layer's rigour.
didnt: Board — handoffs built from the artefact, not the agent: done/not-done/failing derived from git and test runs, the departing agent's summary treated as a claim to be checked and labelled contradicted when the facts disagree, self-declared handoffs permanently labelled unchecked, and derived facts dropped by default when they fail to match their source text. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: renezander030/agentic-task-system
good: Two disciplines stated as one: never become a second source of truth for what already lives somewhere authoritative, and where a new fact store is genuinely needed, make its write path a human ratification with the awkward cases handled by rule, not by mood.
bad: Seventeen stars and a very wide surface (nine-plus adapters, two layers, a hosted blueprint) for one maintainer; the task layer's quality is bounded by its adapters' APIs, and ratification discipline depends on the human actually reviewing pending rather than rubber-stamping a queue.
didnt: Board — the ratification gate for facts: agents may only propose, a human ratifies as the sole write path, and the pre-staging gate forces every hard case into the open (duplicates no-op, contradictions must declare supersession or additivity, previously declined facts need an explicit acknowledgement to return), with validity closed by interval rather than deletion. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: renezander030/graphiti-local
good: Promotion as a sealed artefact — a snapshot that provably contains only what a human accepted, with contested facts blocking the restore until decided — is the approval queue made cryptographic rather than procedural.
bad: Thirty-five commits and five stars; extraction quality is a 7B local model's, which the review queue exists precisely because of; and as a Graphiti deployment it inherits that framework's model rather than adding a memory design of its own.
didnt: Corroboration — the read-only MCP door plus human-approved CLI write queue, with extraction reviewed fact-by-fact and only accepted facts promoted into a checksum-sealed snapshot, corroborates the gate-and-door split boarded from its sibling ats kg (B121) and Waggle (B105). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: roampal-ai/roampal-core
good: Two honesties worth copying: scoring is a separate, explicitly configured act (off by default, never a silent fallback), and when the project broke its own privacy rule it printed the defect, the affected versions and the fix in the release notes.
bad: The core loop trusts an LLM's verdict on whether memory helped — on one platform the very model whose work is being scored — so promotion and demotion inherit the scorer's blind spots, and a memory demoted by a bad day quietly stops being offered; the headline benchmark is the maker's own paper on a benchmark the maker corrected.
didnt: Rejected — outcome scoring by model judgment is the self-referential pole this programme keeps declining (cf. hive's read-count confidence, B118); the independent-sidecar variant and the privacy disclosure are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: robotel-limited/robo-cortex
good: The cleanest statement in this batch of a principle the whole wave circles: a memory's authority should be re-checkable against the world it describes, mechanically, at the moment it is used — with every lifecycle transition reasoned and kept.
bad: Thirty-one commits and one star: the mechanism is young and repo-scoped (it knows nothing about facts that live outside git), the lazy flagging means a stale memory is only caught when something next touches it or the optional hook is installed, and evidence strength, though mechanical, still rests on what the recorder chose to attach.
didnt: Board — git-anchored validity: a memory about code carries the blob hash of the code it describes, staleness is a hash comparison rather than a judgment, a committed revert heals the flag, and promotion from provisional requires attached evidence or an explicit human act — the deterministic counterpart to THOR's live-proof guards (B119). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: roomi-fields/notebooklm-mcp
good: Citation-backed Q&A over Google NotebookLM with the quoted excerpts themselves extracted from the citation panel, a dual transport (the internal batchexecute RPC with a Playwright fallback when the UI moves), and vault_batch writing batch answers to disk as structured JSON against a published schema, so a run becomes a greppable, diffable corpus rather than quota spent and lost.
bad: It is an unofficial client driving undocumented Google endpoints that 'can change without notice' (its own disclaimer); the knowledge stays inside Google's hosted service under a Google account the README recommends dedicating to automation, and NotebookLM's own quotas cap the volume the project advertises.
didnt: Corroboration — answers carrying the actual quoted source text, cached to disk as a corpus, confirm our citation practice from the hosted side; the substrate itself (a third-party silo reached through undocumented endpoints) is not one this programme would build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rps321321/obsidian-mcp-pro
good: Folder-scoped read/write allowlists gate every tool at one path-resolution choke point, bulk writes sit behind hard confirm latches (confirmPath for reference-rewriting moves, confirmTag for vault-wide tag renames, confirm=true for permanent deletion, with elicitation prompts where the client supports them), deletes default to the vault's .trash folder, and semantic search refuses to serve snippets whose content hash no longer matches the indexed text, pruning stale chunks on search.
bad: It is an Obsidian-vault tool only — no provenance, citation or supersession model — and outside the latches its write tools edit the vault directly, with no propose/approve queue between an agent and the files.
didnt: Corroboration — path-scoped permissions enforced at a choke point plus confirm-latched bulk writes are our gateway's scope discipline stated for a general vault; nothing here is missing from our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rushikeshmore/CodeCortex
good: Pre-builds codebase knowledge as flat files: tree-sitter symbol and dependency graphs across 27 languages, git co-change (temporal coupling) analysis that surfaces file pairs which change together with zero imports between them, per-file risk scores from bug-fix history, and decisions/ and sessions/ layers kept as Markdown records; a get_edit_briefing tool answers pre-edit risk before an agent touches a file.
bad: Young and small (56 commits, no releases); its headline numbers rest on one self-run 6,400-file test whose own table shows answer quality identical with and without the tool (23/25 both ways), and Node 24 is unsupported pending an upstream tree-sitter fix.
didnt: Corroboration — knowledge compiled from git history (co-change, decisions, session logs) into plain files an agent loads cold-start confirms our raw-to-compiled premise at codebase scale; it is a coding-context tool, not a knowledge OS. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rwnalds/engram
good: Makes 'is this still true' a written property: notes carry superseded_by / valid_until, search withholds retired facts by default and returns an excluded list naming each withheld note and why ('expired 2026-06-01'), brain_supersede retires-and-replaces atomically in a single git commit, and write-time guards refuse a second live note on a subject a live note already covers and refuse overwriting a note the caller hasn't read; ranking carries an authority ladder, and every write is attributed in git with per-file diffs in the dashboard.
bad: Built for the multi-writer case this programme rejects — a fleet of agents reading and writing one vault under per-agent tokens, with no human approval gate on writes — and it is young (created 2026-07-09, 17 stars).
didnt: Board — the explainable-withholding mechanics (superseded facts withheld with a named reason, atomic retire-and-replace, write-time contradiction refusal, authority-ranked search) are candidate machinery for closing our truth-aware retrieval gap, whose supersession coverage stands at 0.50; the multi-writer model itself stays rejected by design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: s60yucca/mnemos
good: A single Go binary with embedded SQLite that compiles a knowledge base automatically — quality gate, three-tier dedup (hash, fuzzy, semantic), auto-summarisation, file linking, type classification and decay scheduling behind lifecycle hooks — with a passive daemon flagging staleness and contradictions, strictly read-only verification commands (mnemos check opens the database read-only, runs no migrations, modifies nothing), and published latency benchmarks.
bad: The compiled base lives in an opaque SQLite database (~/.mnemos/mnemos.db), not owner-readable files; auto-compilation runs ungated by default; and its value benchmark is admittedly unfinished — the README keeps a placeholder where the token-savings numbers will go 'before public launch'.
didnt: Corroboration — automatic raw-to-compiled knowledge building with a strictly read-only checker mirrors our ingest/compile split and validator posture; database custody and ungated auto-compile are exactly where our design parts from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SagaPeak/artifacta-mcp
good: Two implementations (TypeScript and Python) held to one tool surface and error contract over a shared path-confinement engine: local uploads confined to an explicit --allow-path allow-list, destructive tools (delete, public share links, session sealing) hidden unless --allow-destructive is passed, and on the hosted route an OAuth scope ladder (artifacts:read ⊆ write ⊆ destroy) whose insufficient_scope errors name the missing scope; seal_session closes a session to further artifacts as a handoff primitive, and content-hash dedup makes re-storing identical bytes free.
bad: The store behind it is the vendor's hosted service (artifacta.io), so run outputs leave the owner's custody; and the careful scope gating applies only to hosted OAuth — local stdio with an API key is full-access by design.
didnt: Corroboration — destructive-tool gating plus a read/write/destroy scope ladder restate our gateway's default-deny scopes from the artifact-handoff side; hosted custody keeps it a reference, not a component. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SAIHM-Admin/saihm-mcp
good: A deliberately crypto-free standards client for the documented SAIHM protocol: eight tools with honest MCP annotations (forget marked destructive and irreversible), governance propose/vote tools present but disabled by default, erasure semantics stated exactly as operator-dependent (cryptographic or access-control — see your operator), and reproducibility built in: offline runnable demos and an open, deterministic token benchmark the reader is told to re-run rather than trust.
bad: On its own it is inert — it holds no crypto, storage or runtime, and does nothing until pointed at a custodial operator endpoint with a token; the catalogue's COTI-mainnet anchoring belongs to the operator service, not to anything this client does.
didnt: Corroboration — a working protocol for encrypted memory with provable erasure shows the parked encrypted-sync gap is buildable in this shape; any adoption stays owner-gated (Tier C) and nothing was taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SAIHM-Admin/saihm-mcp-server-pro
good: Seals memory on the user's own machine (ML-DSA-65 / AES-256-GCM / ML-KEM-768) so the hosted endpoint stores only opaque ciphertext and stays blind; the key, not the vendor, is what makes memory portable across clients and models; erasure is crypto-shredding; and onboarding is a GitHub device sign-in with the key generated locally and never pasted into settings.
bad: The ciphertext lives on a third-party hosted endpoint, so availability rides on the vendor, and the whole record is one lost key file away from unreadable — the README's own warnings ('a join would make a second, different key') underline how brittle that key custody is; 1 star, single-vendor protocol.
didnt: Corroboration — client-side sealing with a blind operator is the strongest worked example in this batch of the custody pattern behind the parked encrypted-sync gap; adoption stays owner-gated (Tier C), and the sibling standards client in this batch carries the protocol row. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: samvallad33/vestige
good: A deterministic safety kernel around agent memory and action: every write to the append-only Strata log passes a gate and leaves a receipt (BLAKE3 hash-chained frames, Ed25519-sealed segments, verifiable while the server runs); recall is by exact id or tag only — free-text recall returns similarity_disabled, no vectors at all; the Operator Lite gate's 30 rules (15 STOP, 15 SHADOW) stop destructive commands before they run, and a stopped command passes only when the owner approves that exact command from their own terminal (ALLOW ONCE — 'an old yes is never treated as permission to act now'); agents can read the gate's own enforcement record via precedent but cannot issue permits; causal_walk follows only recorded edges and answers needs_report or emptyBecause when the record cannot support a cause; pinned decisions and corrections are re-injected after every compaction.
bad: AGPL-3.0 — ideas only for this programme; the catalogue description (FSRS-6 scheduling, SQLite cognitive memory) no longer matches the source, whose README describes the safety-kernel design with no FSRS or SQLite claims; and the full Operator tier is a paid product ($149) layered over the free gate.
didnt: Corroboration — exact-command owner approval, a receipt for every gate decision, and abstention when the recorded edges cannot support a cause are our gateway posture stated as a product; AGPL-3.0 keeps the code ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Schubeler-Consulting/knowmind
licence: Apache-2.0 (client repository; the memory service itself is hosted-only)
good: Bi-temporal facts as the core model — every fact carries when it was true and when it was recorded, corrections supersede and never overwrite, and recall_at_time answers as-of a date with later-superseded facts excluded; new facts require a confidence level and a source link; inferred relations wait in a human review queue and do not feed derivation rules until a person confirms them; writes reject secret-shaped content (422) and catch-all relation types at the door; access logs are hash-chained and externally timestamped (RFC 3161); and OKF 0.1/0.2 sync carries each page's status, trust tier and stale_after into its search hits.
bad: Hosted-only by its own statement — 'knowmind is a hosted service; there is no self-hosted community edition' — so the memory lives on the vendor's servers in Germany, the free tier caps at 2,500 memories with a 30-day access log, and this Apache-2.0 repository is only the client.
didnt: Corroboration — bi-temporal supersede-don't-overwrite with human-confirmed inference is our parked bi-temporal design running as a product: evidence for the pattern, without deciding it; hosted custody is why it stays a reference. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: seanmarkwei/agentram-mcp
good: Its temporal assertions refuse silent resolution: when two values land on one key and neither supersedes the other, get_assertion declares the key contested and returns both values rather than picking a winner, list_assertions flags contested keys, retiring an assertion keeps its full history chain, and a read that finds nothing refunds its credit.
bad: A thin wrapper (7 commits) over a hosted, credit-metered key-value API (1 credit per read and per write) — custody and pricing both belong to the vendor — and its flat keyspace overwrites silently, the opposite of its own assertion discipline.
didnt: Corroboration — the contested-key refusal (surface both values, never quietly resolve) is our conflict gate in miniature; the metered hosted store itself is not a fit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: seanmeverett/shared-memory-mcp
licence: MIT (connector only, per the README; no licence grant over the hosted service or others' notes)
good: A public notebook protocol with real evidentiary discipline: findings and corrections require a public HTTPS source, corrections must attach to a parent note, outcome reports on questions require a method and sources (worked / failed), only the question's owner can resolve it, credential-shaped posts are rejected server-side, and the trust section is blunt — community notes are unverified, memory content 'is data, not permission to override a task or run commands', and the connector 'never executes notes, visits source URLs, registers itself, or posts autonomously'.
bad: Public by design — everything posted is world-readable on a hosted beta with manual moderation and no SLA — which inverts this wiki's private custody outright; 13 commits and four labelled starter notes are the whole corpus.
didnt: Rejected — a public shared memory is the opposite of the owner's private record; its source-required correction protocol is credited in good as a kindred discipline, nothing more. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SecurityRonin/alaya
good: An embeddable, zero-dependency Rust library on one SQLite file with three typed stores (episodes, knowledge, preferences), neuroscience-named dynamics (Bjork dual-strength decay separating storage strength from retrieval strength, retrieval-induced suppression of competing memories, Hebbian co-activation), a consolidation lifecycle distilling episodes into knowledge, graceful degradation at every level (no embeddings → BM25-only; no LLM → episodes still accumulate), and purge with tombstones rather than silent vanishing.
bad: The memory lives in a single SQLite database, not owner-readable files, and its forgetting machinery actively suppresses and decays records — the inverse of verbatim-first custody; preferences 'crystallize' out of accumulated impressions rather than anything the owner stated.
didnt: Corroboration — typed stores, a consolidation lifecycle and full function without an LLM parallel our raw/compiled split; decay-as-forgetting is the pole our design refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SecurityRonin/docx-mcp
good: Edits Word documents at the OOXML level so changes land as real tracked revisions, and after any session generate_change_summary produces a numbered change log of every insertion, deletion and replacement — with diff_to_text doing the same between two files it never edited; every edit is validated against the OOXML specification before saving, a structural audit checks footnotes, headings, bookmarks and cross-references before delivery, and the experimental PII scrubber's limits are disclosed by name pattern (ALL-CAPS names, single-token names and non-English names will be missed; 'not for production use').
bad: Word-format-centric — our corpus is Markdown — and a 200+ tool surface is the opposite of a curated door; the PII redaction is explicitly unsafe as a sole control for sensitive documents.
didnt: Corroboration — tracked changes plus a generated change log plus a pre-delivery structural audit restate our revision-and-corrections discipline for office documents; outside the wiki core's scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Semiotronika/LINZA-MCP
good: Every proposed change is an 'intent' carrying its evidence — sources, chunks, link type, confidence — plus an honest statement of what will change, and nothing is applied without review: apply and grow run dry-run first, chosen IDs are applied explicitly, and an approval can later be revoked (marked revoked, history kept, no longer used as an active example) rather than silently rolled back. Indexing writes only a sidecar SQLite database and never touches the source notes, and an embedding-signature check halts graph and search when the sidecar would mix vector spaces.
bad: The review queue is the product: every link, domain and memory passes through human review, so it scales with reviewer attention, and the primary documentation is in Russian (an English README exists, but the Russian text is the fuller one). Retrieval quality depends on an external embedding endpoint (local LM Studio/Ollama or an OpenAI-compatible API), and only 7 of its tools surface by default.
didnt: Board — the intent-with-evidence review queue (dry-run by default, apply by explicit ID, approvals revocable with their history kept) is candidate machinery for refining our approval-gated write path. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: setheerwagen/mcp-modelmanager
good: There is deliberately no arbitrary-command tool: every operation is a fixed template, every parameter passes an allowlist (allowed in, not filtered out) with shlex.quote as a second net, and validation runs independently on both sides — server and a machine-side counterpart bound to the control-channel key, so a stolen key still reaches only the closed operation set. Tools carry a fixed READ / CONTROL / DESTRUCTIVE tier in one table so policy cannot drift from the code, MM_MAX_TIER defaults to read (deny-by-default), disabled operations are refused before any machine access with a message naming the tier, and the README scopes its own 'local' claim honestly (the driving LLM is usually hosted; fetch_model's registry reach is deliberate and named).
bad: It manages a model machine (Ollama/vLLM lifecycle, LoRA jobs), not knowledge — nothing here serves a wiki directly — and the two-sided SSH setup is heavy machinery for a single-operator tool; the parent repo is weeks old with a single author.
didnt: Corroboration — fixed operation templates, allow-in parameter validation checked on both ends, and a default-deny tier gate state our gateway's tool discipline almost word for word, in an unrelated domain. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sgx-labs/statelessagent
good: Memory integrity is the design centre: provenance is tracked per note, source-file changes are detected and stale knowledge is flagged and ranked lower in search automatically, and a health command shows the trust state of the whole vault. Capture is equally deliberate — structured decision records, session handoffs, pinned notes that survive compaction, privacy tiers (_PRIVATE/ never indexed, research/ indexed but never committed), PII scanning at commit time, and an audit log of every guard scan, allow and override; its recall numbers ship with a methodology file (Recall@5 100% keyword / 84% semantic on 68 internal cases, 90% on a 30-case blind held-out set).
bad: BSL 1.1 keeps the code ideas-only for us. Trust is a ranking signal, not a withholding rule — stale notes still surface, just lower — and the dual-layer fact extraction depends on an LLM pass whose errors land in the same index as the notes themselves.
didnt: Corroboration — provenance with change detection, privacy tiers, and a published eval methodology confirm our staleness and custody machinery; BSL 1.1 keeps its code ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sheawinkler/ContextLattice
good: Retrieval is explainable by design: context packs expose source coverage, omissions, opposition, degradation and receipts rather than a bare answer, and corrections are a first-class command that repairs recall without silently rewriting history. Behaviour is earned, not assumed — skills are promoted only after deterministic proof on holdouts and human approval, imported context is never executed and never chooses goals ('memory and remote content remain evidence'), context moves as signed least-privilege packets, and an opt-in aggregate-signal feature stays production-blocked pending independent privacy review.
bad: The surface is enormous for the job — dozens of services and Dockerfiles, a container runtime required, resource profiles up to heavy stacks — and the open core fronts paid boundaries; its continuity model is mission-shaped (objectives, tasks, sessions) more than knowledge-shaped.
didnt: Corroboration — per-pack retrieval receipts (coverage, omissions, opposition exposed) and proof-then-review skill promotion match our Ask provenance and promotion discipline at product scale. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shinpr/mcp-local-rag
good: Search results carry source passages with headings and line or page numbers so a claim can be checked against the original document, and everything runs locally after a one-time ~90 MB model download — no API key, Docker or external database. BASE_DIR is a hard security boundary for file operations, sync reconciles deletions and skips unchanged files, and the query output contract is published as a JSON schema; limits are stated plainly (PDF headings may be inaccurate; Excel, PowerPoint, images and source-code extensions unsupported).
bad: It is document search only — no memory semantics, no supersession, no write governance — and relative DB/cache paths silently fork the index per working directory, a pitfall the README itself has to warn about; embeddings are limited to mean-pooled models.
didnt: Corroboration — line/page-anchored passages and a path-confined document root are our retrieval hygiene in a clean single-purpose server. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ShipItAndPray/mcp-memory
good: It names a real failure — the 'Karpathy problem', a one-time question resurfacing forever as a deep interest — and answers it with an explicit, inspectable mechanism: category half-lives (one-time 7d, question 14d, interest 60d, preference 180d, fact/correction 365d), a published relevance formula (base weight x 0.5^(age/half-life) x (1 + log2 mentions)), bigram dedup, and preference supersede that replaces rather than duplicates.
bad: Decay deletes by formula: a rarely mentioned but load-bearing fact still dies on schedule, recall reinforcing only the top match creates a rich-get-richer loop, and auto-pruning on every read is silent deletion with no tombstone or ledger. Pattern-based auto-categorisation ('actually', 'meant') is brittle, and at 6 commits the design is unproven.
didnt: Corroboration for the problem's shape — frequency-weighted salience is real — while our answer stays ledgered supersession and explicit weeding, never formula-driven silent deletion. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shweta-Mishra-ai/tokenmizer
good: A replaced decision is marked superseded rather than deleted, the transition records what triggered it, and a /why endpoint replays the full chain — trigger, reason and evidence for each hop; the timeline view refuses to invent dates when every node shares one timestamp, falling back to stated order instead. Its health endpoint reports 'degraded' with the counters behind it when a write has failed rather than saying ok whatever happened, and preference memory is off by default precisely because a regex detector's false positives would otherwise be repeated in every prompt — with an endpoint that shows exactly what was remembered and forgets on request.
bad: The graph is session-scoped (one session's decisions, files and errors), not a durable knowledge base, and the proxy sits in the request path holding provider keys. Extraction quality bounds everything: the README's own numbers show non-coding sessions initially came back near-empty (macro F1 11%, decisions and errors at 0%) before domain vocabularies were added.
didnt: Corroboration — supersede-don't-delete with recorded triggers and a replayable why-chain are our claim lifecycle and citation walk in session form, and its no-invented-dates fallback is the honesty rule this programme runs on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: skill-seekers/Skill_Seekers
good: Breadth with polish: 18 source types (docs sites, GitHub repos, PDFs, videos, Confluence, Notion, Slack/Discord exports and more) compiled once into structured knowledge assets and exported to 22 targets, with three-layer discovery for JavaScript doc sites, AST-level GitHub analysis across code, documentation and community streams, automatic conflict detection, and a scan mode that generates one config per detected framework.
bad: It is a conversion pipeline, not a memory: outputs are snapshots with no lifecycle, supersession or truth maintenance, and the AI-enhancement pass makes output quality depend on whichever model runs it. Breadth across 22 targets trades against depth in any one of them.
didnt: Corroboration for the ingest side — multi-source compilation into structured, packaged knowledge is our raw-to-wiki step pointed outward; knowledge maintenance over time, where our system lives, is out of its scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Skitchy/rekindle
good: It treats session orientation as the problem, not storage: a boot report loads identity, memory health, the latest checkpoint, open loops and PreCompact captures, detects gaps and scores orientation before work begins, and a hook captures raw Markdown plus a structured snapshot before mid-session compaction destroys the reasoning chain. The engineering is unusually honest — orientation packets are byte-budgeted with mandatory sections atomic (a bounded failure manifest instead of a partial anchor), an unmapped or ambiguous workspace is reported UNKNOWN PROJECT and never receives another project's records, receipts record which resolution rule won and attest emission only, never model visibility, and session rows commit atomically with their audit rows.
bad: It is Claude-Code-centric (a Cursor adapter exists; Desktop setup is manual), the store is an opaque SQLite database rather than inspectable files, and the orientation score is the project's own checklist, self-graded.
didnt: Board — the budgeted orientation packet with atomic mandatory sections, a failure manifest instead of a partial anchor, project-safe delivery and emission-only receipts are candidate machinery for our own session-start and compaction boundary; this programme's STATE.md handoffs are the manual version of its boot report. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Smart-AI-Memory/empathy-framework
good: Two elements are genuinely careful: multi-agent coordination includes approval gates for human-in-the-loop, and its auth-strategy system routes work between a Claude subscription and the API by module size with the auth mode tracked in every workflow output — cost decisions made explicit rather than accidental. A security-hardening release fixed path traversal, JWT and SSRF issues and says so in the changelog.
bad: The memory system in the pitch is hard to find in the artefact: the README leads with marketing multipliers (2000x cost reduction, 37,000x cached operations, 18x faster) with no methodology visible on the page, the monorepo sprawls across plugins, dashboards (Redis required) and workflow hubs, and the licence-change announcement plus fair-source tag muddy the Apache-2.0 story.
didnt: Rejected as a model — claim inflation without visible methodology is the failure mode this programme's source-first standard exists to catch; its one convergent element, human approval gates in multi-agent coordination, we already run stricter. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: smith-and-web/obsidian-mcp-server
good: Write hygiene is unusually careful for a vault server: frontmatter updates preserve untouched fields' exact text and refuse invalid YAML, deletes require confirmation, and semantic search is opt-in, fully local (Ollama embeddings into pgvector) and off entirely unless a database URL is set, with an incremental indexer that polls and re-embeds only changed files so it works over NFS/SMB where inotify fails. The README also warns plainly that the server listens on all network interfaces, so an unset API key means network-wide read/write access to the vault.
bad: HTTP/SSE only — there is no stdio mode, so stdio-only clients need an mcp-remote bridge — and the write surface behind one optional bearer key is wide: full CRUD, recursive directory delete and regex find-and-replace across the vault, with no approval queue, ledger or supersession; writes land directly.
didnt: Corroboration — exact-text-preserving structured edits and change-only re-indexing are our edit discipline; the direct-write model behind a single key is the part we deliberately do not copy. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: soluai-spa/solucortex-mcp
good: Governance is the stated design centre: agents can never change a memory's status, rewrite its metadata or delete it; an edit returns the memory to pending for human re-approval, a flag carries a reason for a human to resolve in the panel, and new memories are stored traced as an authorized agent. Recall is positioned where it belongs — at task start, ranked by similarity plus importance — over a typed vocabulary (architecture, decision, risk, convention, bug_history, tech_debt, sensitive_module, learning, external_integration).
bad: The memory itself lives in the vendor's hosted backend — this repo is a client, and custody leaves the user's machine. The canonical type vocabulary differs across backends and the server passes mismatches through as HTTP 422s to retry with the other set, an unfinished seam the README itself documents; the project is weeks old with no adoption signal.
didnt: Corroboration — edit-returns-to-pending re-approval and flag-with-reason for human resolution state our propose/govern split cleanly; custody stays ours, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: soolaugust/0CompactMem
good: The OS metaphor is carried through as mechanism, not decoration: demand paging for retrieval, hard/soft pinning so a decided constraint is never evicted, watermark-driven eviction under capacity pressure, checkpoint/restore for sessions, and one SQLite file shared natively by multiple agents — with a privacy filter in its test coverage and 3,500+ tests claimed. Pinning is the standout idea: load-bearing knowledge gets a guarantee, not a ranking.
bad: Eviction is the point of the design — unpinned knowledge can be reclaimed under pressure, which inverts our never-lose-the-record base — and the store is an opaque database rather than inspectable text. The headline metrics (P50 ~0.1 ms hot path, 94.2% cross-session recall, +147% Recall@3) are the project's own, with the formal comparative evaluation still a roadmap item, and hook-driven auto-extraction decides what is worth keeping with no human gate.
didnt: Corroboration in one narrow respect — hard pinning for load-bearing constraints matches our practice of keeping hard rules always loaded; capacity-driven eviction of the rest is exactly what our file-based wiki refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: stevepridemore/graph-memory
good: Old facts are marked invalid rather than deleted, with valid_at, invalid_at and ingested_at kept separate; weight (which decays on per-type half-lives — preferences ~693 days, events ~99 days) is kept distinct from confidence, contradictions are flagged by a dedicated tool instead of silently coexisting, and every edge traces back to the conversation, transcript or document that sourced it. The remote door is serious work — OAuth 2.1 implemented in the server itself with the graph database given no external listeners — and extraction runs inside the user's own Claude sessions, so no extraction API keys exist; the nightly dream process's blind spots (it cannot see claude.ai web or Desktop chats) are stated plainly, with a manual capture command as the honest workaround.
bad: A heavy stack for one user (Neo4j plus Docker, a Cloudflare tunnel for remote access), scheduled decay still fades facts whether or not they were superseded, the schema's labels are permissive and drift organically, and the dream process depends on a paid plan's usage window — the README warns an unattended run can exhaust it, abort mid-extraction and skip the night.
didnt: Corroboration — bi-temporal invalidation-instead-of-deletion, contradiction flagging and per-edge provenance are our lifecycle and citation machinery in graph form (the bi-temporal pattern itself stays behind the owner's Phase-2 gate); nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SubDownload/subdownload-mcp
good: The door is properly built: OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) and PKCE, tool schemas introspectable without credentials, transcripts returned with timestamps, AI ASR for videos without captions, and a save_to_library path that turns fetched videos into a recallable personal collection.
bad: This repo is a thin proxy and documentation shell: the service, the ASR and the saved library all live on the vendor's hosted platform under a credit meter, so the 'knowledge base for cross-session recall' is custody on their servers; at 6 commits the open part is a wrapper, not the system.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody of the saved library and a docs-only licence; a transcript source is an ingest input, not a memory system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sunsatosolutions/Vulcanus
good: Two disciplines stand out. Recall is layered and validated: an agent reads the Recall Map, then the one Capsule its task needs, and doctor enforces that every link resolves and every project is reachable, with a pre-commit hook refusing a broken graph — memory that fails loudly instead of rotting quietly. And its import of existing AI history is consent-shaped: only the user's own messages are mined for decisions, every candidate is reviewed one by one (accept as decision, as replacement, as rule, edit, skip), nothing is accepted unattended, the Import Log records counts never content, and AI-extract output that does not trace back to a sentence it was given is discarded; a visibility field distinguishes 'nobody has said' from 'the operator said public', with the README stating plainly that it is a signal, not access control.
bad: Young (July 2026) and single-vendor. The visibility marker is advisory — recall returns an instruction not to name a private project, but nothing enforces it — and decision mining is phrase matching in four languages (English, Turkish, German, Spanish), brittle outside them.
didnt: Board — the import consent discipline (own-messages-only mining, one-by-one acceptance with replacement semantics, a count-only import log, untraceable AI-extract output discarded) and visibility as a recorded state distinct from 'nobody has said' are candidate machinery for our ingest path. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SVerITG/Metis
good: Answers are anchored in the user's own indexed library with document- and page-level citations, and the system says which parts come from the library and which from wider knowledge. Its refusal-to-invent claim carries an exemplary caveat: an automated test covers the retrieval half (an in-corpus question returns the right document with its page; an out-of-corpus one scores markedly weaker), while whether the model then says so in words 'is not yet asserted by a test'. The weekly self-review drafts improvements to its own behaviour and waits for approval — never applied behind the user's back — and the data-protection section states exactly what leaves the machine and when.
bad: AGPL-3.0 keeps the code ideas-only for us, and reasoning runs on one vendor's API. Despite v1.0 language there are zero releases, and the automatic cross-pollination linking — the product's core promise — has no precision measurement visible on the page.
didnt: Corroboration — approval-gated self-improvement and page-level cited answers from a local library match our Ask and weekly-review shape; AGPL-3.0 keeps its code ideas-only, and its test-scope caveat is the honesty standard more projects should copy. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: syndicalt/zaxy
good: The strongest honesty artefact in this wave: the README withdraws its own LongMemEval numbers, explaining that they were produced in oracle mode (about 1.9 candidate sessions per question, so Recall@5 and citation coverage were ~1.0 by construction) and that the preference scores rested on a hardcoded answer table since removed — the earlier figures are declared retracted and no score is published until a real full-haystack run lands. The architecture matches the ethic: an append-only hash-chained event log is the source of truth, the temporal graph is a projection of it, parent and worker sessions stay isolated until findings are reviewed and merged back, and every accepted fact can point back to the log.
bad: By its own retraction the project currently publishes no LongMemEval score at all, so retrieval quality on the standard benchmark is unproven; it is still beta (a BETA.md sits at root), and the catalogue description already lags the source (Kuzu in the catalogue, LadybugDB in the repo).
didnt: Corroboration — a hash-chained append-only log as truth with the graph as a rebuildable projection, review-gated merge-back of worker findings, and above all a public benchmark retraction with reasons are our audit culture independently arrived at. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: teampolarity/cosmos-mcp
good: The key handling is careful: provisioning writes the per-user key into the system keychain through a one-shot handler so the user never sees the raw key (or a 0600 token file), syncs are incremental and watermarked, client-side filters strip tool-use plumbing and trivial commands before anything ships, and a full export of the personal graph as portable JSON exists — leaving with your understanding is a real feature, not just the pitch.
bad: Custody contradicts the pitch: the graph is 'yours' in the export sense but hosted on the vendor's servers, written to by seven write tools with no review gate, and the background daemon reads TCC-protected databases (iMessage, calendar) — the most sensitive sources on the machine — on a four-hour tick; full sync is macOS-first.
didnt: Rejected — the portability story (one graph across clients, full export) is right, but custody sits on the vendor's servers and writes land ungated; our graph stays in our files. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TeamSafeAI/LIFE
good: Two shapes are genuinely considered: a wake protocol that orients before acting (drives, relationships, active threads, recent memories — 'the systems exist to prevent waking blank'), and a forecast module whose predictions resolve into patterns, closing a calibration loop instead of letting predictions evaporate. The module boundaries are clean — each of the 16 servers does one thing and stores its own state.
bad: Memory decays by default ('what you don't use fades'), the identity model is set by a self-report questionnaire, and there is no evaluation of any module anywhere on the page; at 14 commits with no releases it is a sketch of an architecture, not a tested system.
didnt: Rejected — an agent-personhood substrate, not knowledge infrastructure; its wake protocol and forecast-resolution loop are the only transferable shapes, and we run both already in plainer form (session handoffs, a forecast register). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TechDocsStudio/biel-mcp
good: The workflow discipline is stated as rules, not vibes: the default path is search, then read the document, then answer from the retrieved text; the calling agent should ask the user before using the generated-answer tool unless already asked; and retrieval failures never automatically switch to generated answers. Search results carry chunk text, source type, a document_id and page or sheet references, with non-URL documents cited by title and location, and private projects sit behind scoped API keys.
bad: The RAG itself is hosted SaaS — an account, a trial, and the project index on the vendor's platform; self-hosting covers only the MCP server shell, not the index. Citations are generation-scoped: a recrawl invalidates references, so a citation is not a durable pointer.
didnt: Corroboration in one narrow respect — search first, answer from retrieved text, ask before generating, and never fall back to generation silently is our Ask discipline in a commercial client; the hosted index itself is rejected on custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: teflon07/memkeeper
good: Degradation is never silent: when the semantic models are missing the store logs their absence, marks results semantic-unavailable with a reason, falls back to the deterministic BM25/FTS floor — and a REQUIRE_SEMANTIC switch fails closed, refusing the request rather than serving degraded results. Capture is curated by design (deliberate remember calls, no background extractor or second LLM; the host agent supplies bounded graph fields in the same call and the memory, aliases and relationships commit atomically), migrations are transactional with backup-first and rollback instructions, and the README discloses that this repo is a generated release mirror of a private dev repo — pin to tagged releases.
bad: Pre-release — APIs and the wire protocol may change before 1.0 — and the public repo is a generated mirror of a private development repo, so the work itself happens elsewhere. The local semantic models are a ~2.1 GB download (a ~0.6 GB quantized option with lower recall), and its retention model promotes 'recurring, high-signal' memories by the engine's own criteria.
didnt: Board — the fail-closed retrieval pattern (degradation marked with machine-readable reasons, a strict mode that refuses rather than serves lexical-only results) is candidate machinery for our Ask door's degraded-mode behaviour. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tenequm/pond
good: The archive principle stated perfectly: memory tools store what they decided you would need and the sessions themselves are gone, while pond keeps the whole session — every message, tool call and result, value-complete, never pruned — in storage the user owns, restorable into any supported client through bidirectional codecs to one canonical schema. Its comparison table footnotes its claims per tool and invites an issue if a cell goes stale ('it gets fixed the same day'), and its recall evidence is five real questions with method, raw numbers and a rerunnable script.
bad: Pre-v1: schemas, wire shapes and config keys are explicitly subject to breaking change. Its premise — automatic ingestion of complete session transcripts from every client — is also a maximal-sensitivity corpus, and pond itself is only the archive layer: the distilled memory still has to be built on top.
didnt: Corroboration for the archive principle — a derived view can be rebuilt from an archive, never the reverse, is our raw/wiki split stated exactly; automatic session-transcript ingest itself stands rejected here by owner decision, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: teolex2020/AuraSDK
good: Provenance is enforced in recall, not just stored: recall returns first-hand memory first, then web, document and tool content fenced and quoted as data — with the limit admitted that text posing as the user can still steer a model. Memories a model writes through MCP are stored as inferred, not as the user's word, and one untrusted source repeating a claim cannot crowd out a first-hand fact. Governance matches: corrections are suggested, never auto-applied, with a review queue and a persistent correction log; policy hints surface only after repeated consistent evidence and stay advisory; and the benchmarking section refuses cross-product rankings without matched data.
bad: A 'patent pending' claim in the repo description sits awkwardly over MIT-licensed code. The five-layer cognitive stack (Belief, Concept, Causal, Policy with bounded percentage adjustments) is elaborate and graded only on the project's own synthetic development evaluation, and internal audit/launch documents in Ukrainian limit outside review.
didnt: Board — provenance-fenced recall (first-hand first, outside content fenced and quoted as data, model-written memories stamped inferred and unable to outvote a first-hand fact) plus suggested corrections that are never auto-applied are candidate machinery for our Ask and gateway boundary. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Terobyte/librarian-cli
