good: A small tool built around one honest job: ebooks become clean, token-counted Markdown chapters deterministically (byte-identical output, no embeddings, no network, no API keys), and a verify command checks whether a quote actually appears — verbatim verdicts graded exact, close (with a word-diff shown), distorted, or not found, with the edge cases stated (a replaced word in a three-word quote 'really is a distortion'). Every ingested book passes a five-metric quality gate (ok / review / failed), scans and DRM files fail honestly rather than pretending, and all six MCP tools are read-only.
bad: Narrow by design — books only — and young (July 2026, 2 stars). Book-mode verification scans whole chapter text in pure Python (seconds of CPU on long books), shelf mode needs the FTS5 index, and quotes spanning a chapter boundary cannot verify better than distorted in v1.
didnt: Board — graded quote verification (exact / close with the differences shown / distorted / not_found) against a local corpus is candidate machinery for our scholarly citation truth-checking gap. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc
good: Governance is the architecture: every tool call runs through one pipeline — auth, folder ACLs, a read-only kill switch, human-in-the-loop confirmation on destructive operations, and an audit log — with declared scope classes separating read, write, delete, bulk, execute and admin across 164 capabilities, fronted by a five-tool facade that bypasses no gate. The honesty matches: a 'When NOT to use' section names its own weight, its single maintainer and its licence's network copyleft, and headline retrieval figures once on the README were withdrawn as unreproducible, replaced by a statistical ship rule gating every ranking change against a golden set.
bad: AGPL-3.0 keeps the code ideas-only for us. It is heavy — a polyglot TypeScript/Rust monorepo wanting Node 24 or Bun — governance is opt-in (the zero-config start boots with auth off and no folder ACL, fine only because it is local-only), and it is a single-maintainer project, as its own README lists.
didnt: Corroboration — the one-pipeline governance (ACLs, kill switch, human confirmation on destructive operations, audit log) and the withdrawn-figures honesty match our gateway and audit culture; AGPL-3.0 keeps its code ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TheGoatPsy/mneme
good: Its two headline properties are enforced, not promised: 'no LLM call on the critical path' is checked in CI by parsing the hook modules for network-capable imports and re-checking the transitive import closure at runtime, and search quality 'cannot silently degrade' because a regression guard fails the build if nDCG@5 drops more than 0.02 below the locked baseline or the out-of-vocabulary negative probe fails. Markdown is ground truth and the index is derived state you can delete and rebuild; memory-edit proposals queue for a policy drain the server never applies directly; and every figure carries the note that it is a deterministic regression anchor on a seeded synthetic corpus, not a real-world quality measurement.
bad: The production search path is FTS5 BM25 only — the semantic backend is roadmap, stated plainly — and automatic capture is transcript-derived session records, a route that needs its own consent decision. The project is small (3 stars) and its benchmark corpus is synthetic by design.
didnt: Board — a CI-enforced no-network/no-LLM capture path and a locked-baseline retrieval regression guard are candidate machinery for our validator and reverify stack; Markdown as ground truth with a deletable derived index is our substrate, independently built. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TheStack-ai/waypath
good: The split is the design: a Truth Kernel holds canonical decisions, entities and preferences with temporal validity, supersede and history, while a separate Archive Kernel holds raw evidence with content-hash dedup — and knowledge moves between them only through an explicit page, promote, review flow with a review queue and a resolve-contradiction command. Session context packs surface truth highlights including an explicit contradictions array rather than hiding conflicts.
bad: v0.1.0 — a first public release with deferred basics (no hosted or multi-user story, no adaptive ranking yet) — and the truth lives in a single SQLite file: owned and local, but opaque to inspection compared with plain files.
didnt: Corroboration — a canonical truth store kept separate from a raw evidence archive, with promotion through a review queue, is our wiki/raw split in miniature. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Thezenmonster/agentmem
good: Governed memory aimed squarely at truth maintenance: a five-state trust lifecycle (hypothesis -> active -> validated -> deprecated -> superseded) where deprecated and superseded memories are excluded from recall automatically; conflict detection combining topic overlap with sentence-level negation matching and severity grading (critical when both sides are active); staleness detection by age, missing source file, and source-hash drift; a 0-100 health score over conflicts, stale share, orphaned references and deprecated weight; provenance on every memory (source_path, source_section, source_hash); trust-ranked recall with published weights (relevance 25%, trust 20%, provenance 20%, recency 15%, frequency 10%, confidence 10%) packed into a token budget; canonical human-readable markdown as the source of truth, synced into SQLite idempotently (same hash skips, a removed section deprecates with a reason, a restored section resurrects); 13 MCP tools across Python API, CLI and server from one core.
bad: Tiny and young: 20 commits, 6 stars, no releases, one author; the production evidence is the author's own (330+ memories over one video-production workflow, conflicts tuned from 1,848 false positives to 11 findings) with no independent evaluation; conflict detection rests on Jaccard topic overlap plus negation patterns, which will miss paraphrase-level contradictions; FTS5-only retrieval (porter stemming) with no semantic component; the package/repo name split (install quilmem, run agentmem) is a discovery hazard; per-project SQLite stores mean the governance is only as global as the file you point at.
didnt: Board: the trust lifecycle plus hash-drift staleness and trust-ranked recall are candidate machinery for our claim lifecycle and the truth-aware retrieval gap; boarded for the build queue rather than adopted, since the code is 20 commits old and our lifecycle states already exist in schema form (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: thomasjumper/agentbay
good: The remembered layer is scoped sensibly (decisions, setup gotchas, pitfalls, handoffs, project facts) and kept distinct from instruction files the user writes; entries are human-readable, attributed to the agent that stored them, carry provenance and verification status, and can be exported, archived or erased; connection is one command over hosted MCP with OAuth, API keys as a documented fallback for CI; legacy package names are kept working so existing installs do not break.
bad: Hosted-first by design: the memory itself lives on the vendor's service (stremai.com), and this repository is explicitly only the install docs, comparison pages and recipes — the hosted application and parts of the SDK are developed elsewhere, so the MIT licence covers the surface, not the system holding the data; 11 commits and 2 stars; no local store, no lifecycle or truth machinery described, and verification status is asserted rather than specified; erase/export are dashboard acts on someone else's custody.
didnt: Rejected: a shared-memory layer whose store is the vendor's hosted service, with the open repo as a docs surface, fails our custody rule regardless of the attribution and export features (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: threadctx-dev/threadctx-mcp
good: Honest about the pull-based limit of MCP tools and attacks it three ways at once: marker-fenced instruction blocks spliced into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/Cursor rules on first start (preserving surrounding content, idempotent, with a documented opt-out), the same instruction carried in the MCP initialize handshake for clients that never read rule files, and tool descriptions written to bias proactive querying — with the README admitting no mechanism can force a call; git-history capture is off by default precisely because it spends the user's LLM tokens, calls the user's own provider directly with nothing routed through vendor servers, and ships a dry-run; the API key is read from the environment only and never lands in committed files by construction; query results carry a consistent attribution footer; local mode is a plain JSON file you can inspect with a list command.
bad: A third-party server writing instruction blocks into a project's AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md on first start is exactly the kind of ambient write our approval posture exists to prevent, however well fenced; local mode is keyword matching over one JSON file scoped by git remote — no lifecycle, provenance beyond authorship, or conflict handling; team sharing and semantic search are the paid cloud tier, moving custody to threadctx.dev; 16 commits, 1 star, pre-1.0.
didnt: Corroboration: the capture discipline (off by default, own key, dry-run, nothing routed through the vendor) and the candour about pull-based limits match our standards, but a server that auto-edits project rule files is not a pattern we take, and the store itself has no truth machinery to borrow (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: thyn-ai/telys-sdk
good: Exemplary MCP surface hygiene: all 19 tools ship rich descriptions with failure modes and static annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint false throughout — the server makes no network calls); introspection answers initialize and tools/list from a static registry with no credentials and no runtime loaded, so a client can inspect the surface before trusting it; write semantics are precise (upsert as the idempotent write, update strict about existing ids, delete as tombstone with a separate compaction step, collection partitions fixed up front); embedding-agnostic by design (bring your own vectors at any dimension, or the built-in on-device bigram embedder); fully offline after a one-time free device login.
bad: The engine the tools drive is closed: a signed proprietary runtime obtained through the vendor's login, so the Apache-2.0 licence covers the facade, not the memory engine — behaviour inside the kernel is unverifiable from source; created 2026-09-23 with 25 commits and 0 stars, the youngest and least-proven entry in this batch; a vector/lexical store at heart — no lifecycle, supersession, contradiction or provenance machinery; the free community licence for the runtime is a vendor grant that can change.
didnt: Corroboration in one narrow respect: the annotation discipline and credential-free introspection are the standard our own MCP doors should be judged against; the memory engine itself is a closed runtime and unusable as a base under our licence and audit rules (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: timmx7/acheron-mcp-server
good: Solves one real problem cleanly: the same local memory reachable from Claude Chat, Code and Cowork, which normally cannot see each other; fully local SQLite with full-text search, no cloud, no network calls, no telemetry, zero configuration; six small tools with natural-language-shaped descriptions (save, get, search, list with project/surface/type/tag filters, delete, status); install is a single config block.
bad: Two commits total — a sketch, not a maintained project; the recovery story for database trouble is to delete bridge.db and start over (no migration, repair or export discipline stated); no provenance, lifecycle, contradiction or staleness handling — a saved claim is indistinguishable from a superseded one; delete is a plain forget with no history; nothing distinguishes surfaces' trust or scopes writes per project beyond a filter field.
didnt: Corroboration: cross-surface local bridging is a shape we reach through our own read door and gateway rather than a shared writable store, and at 2 commits with no truth machinery there is nothing here to take (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: timowhite88/farnsworth-syntek
licence: Proprietary (README licence section: 'Proprietary — Farnsworth Labs. All rights reserved'; no LICENSE file; GitHub metadata names no licence)
good: Client-side encryption before anything leaves the machine (AES-256-GCM, keys stay with the user, credentials in a local encrypted vault with a revoke command); the seven-layer memory taxonomy (identity, active context, episodic, semantic, procedural, graph with temporal decay, synthesis) is a recognisable cognitive split; session-end consolidation is an explicit act rather than a silent background rewrite.
bad: Proprietary and paid: $100 per 90 days by crypto payment (SOL, MON, USDC), plus per-session gas; the persistence layer is a public blockchain — consolidated memory, even encrypted, is written as Monad calldata through a third-party gateway (ai.farnsworth.cloud) and a second paid service (DropClaw), which is the opposite of our custody model and makes deletion effectively impossible; vocabulary like 'holographic recall' and a token-extraction expansion of the SYNTEK name substitute branding for specification; 10 commits, 2 stars, README-only evidence for every architectural claim.
didnt: Rejected: proprietary licence, subscription paywall, and memory custody on a public chain via a vendor gateway — three independent disqualifiers under our rules (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: tomohiro-owada/devrag
licence: MIT (README licence section, stated in both the English and Japanese halves; no LICENSE file at root)
good: A tight, honest developer RAG: single Go binary, local ONNX embeddings (multilingual-e5-small, 100+ languages) in sqlite-vec, incremental sync, and search filterable by directory and filename glob so retrieval can be scoped the way our index-first protocol scopes reads; the performance claim is published as a table with the environment and corpus stated (M2, 100 files, ~1 MB: 95 ms search at ~300 tokens versus 25 s and ~12,000 tokens for full reads), so the 40x token saving is checkable rather than a slogan; CLI and MCP expose the same operations including dry-run delete; full bilingual documentation.
bad: Document search only: no lifecycle, supersession, contradiction or provenance layer — a stale document retrieves as confidently as a current one; the model auto-downloads on first run from Hugging Face, a supply-chain step the README treats casually; index freshness depends on the server having indexed the file, and the troubleshooting answer to wrong results is to delete vectors.db and rebuild; no licence file at root (the MIT statement lives only in the README), which weakens the grant's discoverability.
didnt: Corroboration: a clean example of the local semantic-search component our own stack reaches with different tooling; nothing taken because it has no truth or lifecycle machinery, which is where our gaps are (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: topoteretes/cognee
good: The heavyweight reference platform of this space at real scale (32,633 stars, 11,602 commits, 156 releases): graph plus vector memory built from documents, code and conversations, runnable with no LLM key via local GLiNER extraction and local embeddings; the MCP server offers three transports (stdio, SSE, streamable HTTP) plus cloud and API modes, a deliberately minimal remember/recall/forget memory API alongside deterministic code_search operations (query_facts, traverse, impact_analysis, delta over an indexed code graph), and session cache versus permanent graph memory through one tool; its documentation of the DNS-rebinding guard is exemplary — 421 for an unrecognised Host, 403 for an unrecognised Origin, loopback explicitly not treated as safe, and a disclosed FastMCP gap (the guard was silently dropped for SSE) that they patched and explained; session distillation curates accepted lessons into permanent memory; a linked research paper (Markovic et al., 2025) backs the graph/LLM interface work.
bad: A platform, not a component: adopting it means adopting its pipeline, stores and improvement stages wholesale, several of which are LLM-dependent and rewrite memory in ways our approval-gated, file-first design refuses; graph construction quality rests on extraction models whose errors become structure; the surface is enormous (dozens of optional dependency groups — Neo4j, Neptune, Turso, scraping, tracing) with the operational weight that implies; nothing in the MCP layer offers per-write approval, a trust ledger, or scored abstention of the kind our doors are built around.
didnt: Corroboration: cognee is already studied as a platform elsewhere in this survey (the catalogue itself marked it ALREADY HAVE); this pass adds the MCP subtree's transport and code-search detail and its first-rate rebinding-guard documentation, but no new disposition — our architecture stays file-first and approval-gated (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: topskychen/tilde
licence: MIT (README licence section; no LICENSE file at root)
good: A genuine human-in-the-loop profile store: agents may only propose updates, which queue until the user approves or rejects them via CLI, with an update history log — the same propose-then-approve shape as our gateway, in miniature; the profile is one structured local YAML file (identity, tech stack, knowledge sources, team context) served over MCP resources with per-skill visibility (public/private/team), so agents see only what they are cleared for; storage backends are pluggable (YAML, SQLite, Mem0); resume and document ingestion bootstrap the profile with a dry-run preview; API keys are kept out of the synced config by design.
bad: Profile and preferences only — no knowledge lifecycle, contradiction or provenance machinery beyond the update log; ingestion depends on a Google (Gemini) API key, so the extraction path is a hosted LLM; the ingest command offers --auto-approve with a confidence threshold, a dial that quietly dissolves the approval guarantee the rest of the design builds; 12 commits and 4 stars; MIT is stated only in the README with no licence file at root.
didnt: Corroboration: the propose/approve/log loop for agent-written profile data matches our own gateway discipline and validates it from an independent design; nothing taken because the domain is identity profiles, not knowledge, and our propose flow already exists (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: tribal-memory/tribal
licence: MIT (README licence section; no LICENSE file at root)
good: Aimed at the right target: an engineering team's tacit knowledge — learnings, debugging insights, heuristics, decision rationale — captured from development work and made retrievable to coding agents over MCP, self-hosted on the team's own Postgres with pgvector; Rust implementation with a serious developer toolchain around it (sqlx offline query metadata, cargo-deny licence/advisory checks, unit tests runnable without a database, a full pre-push gate).
bad: The README is the whole public specification and it specifies almost nothing: prerequisites, setup and run commands, but no tool list, no capture mechanism, no lifecycle, provenance or evaluation claims to judge — the knowledge-engine behaviour is unevaluable from source documentation; the setup burden is heavy (Rust stable plus nightly, Docker, just, sqlx-cli, cargo-deny); the default branch sitting on a chore branch suggests a one-developer project mid-errand (the setup instructions even clone a differently-named personal fork path, samfolo/tribal); MIT appears only in the README with no licence file at root.
didnt: Corroboration: the tacit-knowledge framing matches what our wiki does for a team of agents, but with the public evidence this thin there is no mechanism to evaluate or borrow (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: tstockham96/engram
good: The feature shapes are the right ones: bi-temporal versioning, an audit tool that cross-references external files like CLAUDE.md against the vault and flags outdated claims, an alerts tool surfacing pending commitments, stale follow-ups and contradictions, structured session briefings, and spreading-activation recall over a typed knowledge graph; storage is local SQLite with network calls confined to the user's own LLM provider, and the README discloses the once-per-4-hours npm version check with its opt-out.
bad: Three commits total stand behind a 17-tool surface, a REST API, an SDK and benchmark claims — the maturity gap is the story; the headline LOCOMO figure (80.0% versus Mem0's 66.9% and 28.8% for file memory) is self-run with no harness, corpus or judge published in the README to check it against; operation requires a Gemini API key, so extraction and consolidation costs and behaviour ride on a hosted model; the README contains an agent-addressed install section instructing agents to pitch the tool to their user, and its init performs MCP registration, instruction-file edits and tool auto-approval in one step — auto-approval being precisely what our write posture forbids (the section is characterised here as evidence, not followed).
didnt: Corroboration for the audit/briefing/alert shapes only: at 3 commits, with self-reported benchmarks and an auto-approving installer, this namesake stays a watch item rather than a board candidate — distinct from rwnalds/engram, which was boarded in batch B122 on stronger source evidence (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: TT-Wang/cortex-plugin
good: The most candid engineering record in this wave: a Stop-hook miner writes lessons as markdown in an Obsidian vault, and the write path compares each candidate against its nearest neighbours in one batched call and chooses ADD, UPDATE, SUPERSEDE or NOOP behind safety rails — a protected-target guard, a truncation guard, at most 5 destructive operations per delta, and a global fallback to ADD-all on any exception; SUPERSEDE exercises a real bi-temporal invalidation path (invalid_at / replaced_by); retrieval citations are logged per session (.recall_log.jsonl) so citation rate per tool is measurable and feeds a demotion guard; the project publishes its own failures — 462 memories auto-classified as always-relevant was 'not a layer, it was a full briefing', a recency-decay ranker was prototyped and reverted for a measured regression, a 15% feedback weight reading a file nothing wrote was deleted, deprecated memories leaking through the hook path were fixed; a named 18-query benchmark is re-measured per release (74.7% to 80.0%) with per-release deltas explained, and a v2.9 tool diet cut the MCP surface from 14 tools to 6 with schema size reported (12,827 to 5,474 chars).
bad: The memory source is automatic transcript mining — a Stop-hook miner over conversation turns — which is session-transcript ingest, a route the owner has rejected for our wiki, so the core capture mechanism cannot be taken even where its rails impress; the write-path judge is a small hosted model call (Haiku) whose ADD/UPDATE/SUPERSEDE decisions are only as good as that call, with the rails bounding damage rather than guaranteeing correctness; benchmark is 18 queries over the author's own vault — honest, but small and self-administered; Claude Code plugin only, single maintainer, fast-moving with breaking restructures between minor versions (the L0-L3 layer system was retired wholesale in v2.8).
didnt: Board: the write-path safety rails (bounded destructive ops, protected targets, exception fallback to additive-only) and the citation-log feedback loop are candidate machinery for our gateway write path and claim lifecycle; the board explicitly excludes its transcript-mining capture, which stands rejected by owner decision (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: tverney/mcp-agent-memory
good: A clean separation we recognise: a thin MCP bridge (read the index, append a session summary, substring search) over plain files, with a separate daemon doing consolidation and extraction — the filesystem itself is the contract between them, so either side can be replaced; the read tool is index-first by design (load the lightweight MEMORY.md index cheaply, pull topic files only when needed), which is our own index-first protocol arrived at independently; token discipline is measured, not asserted (a lean consolidation agent cuts per-call cost about 7x, with the credit figures shown); session summaries are specified tightly (300-800 tokens of durable findings, not play-by-play) because consolidation cost is understood; uninstall backs up the memory directory and removes only its own client-config entries.
bad: Consolidation and extraction are an unattended LLM daemon (Bedrock, OpenAI or Kiro credits) rewriting durable memory from session summaries with no approval step, review queue or per-write provenance described — the exact unattended-rewrite shape our gateway forbids; search is plain substring, with no ranking, lifecycle or contradiction handling in the bridge; the system's behaviour splits across two packages, so the guarantees depend on the daemon repo, not this one; small adoption (6 stars).
didnt: Corroboration: the filesystem-as-contract split and index-first reads validate our architecture from an independent implementation; nothing taken because its consolidation is unattended LLM rewriting, which our approval gates exist to prevent (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: TyKolt/kremis
good: A deterministic graph engine built for grounded answers: pure Rust core with no LLM, no embeddings and no floating-point arithmetic, so the same input always produces the same output; every result traces to an ingested signal and missing data returns an explicit not-found rather than a fabrication; BLAKE3 hashing of the full graph state plus a canonical binary export (KREX) make integrity checkable at any point; the standout is proof-carrying knowledge — a /certify endpoint issuing a Verifiable Query Certificate that proves a fact, or proves its absence, bound to the state hash, so an abstention can be checked by someone who does not trust the system; the fabrication benchmark is written with rare honesty: the README itself argues the comparison is not like-for-like, reports that a current frontier model now matches the substrate on its own benchmark, and narrows the claim to the one thing that survives — a certifiable absence; ACID persistence on redb, CLI/HTTP/MCP interfaces to one engine, CI-published operation benchmarks.
bad: Alpha, pre-1.0, with breaking changes expected, 15 stars and one visible author; the graph must be fed structured signals — there is no document ingestion, extraction or prose memory here, so it complements rather than replaces a wiki; determinism is bought by excluding everything probabilistic, including semantic recall, so natural-language questions need resolved entity ids before the engine can help (the README concedes the benchmark hands Kremis pre-resolved ids); redb's exclusive lock means CLI and server cannot run simultaneously; certificates prove facts about the graph state, not about the world — garbage signals certify just as cleanly.
didnt: Board: absence certificates bound to a state hash are candidate machinery for our abstention and citation story — a way to make 'we do not know' a checkable artefact rather than a sentence; boarded as machinery to study, not a store to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: udjin-labs/mnemostack
good: Serious hybrid recall engineering: vector, BM25, temporal and graph retrievers fused by Reciprocal Rank Fusion and refined by an 8-stage pipeline (query classification, exact-token rescue, hub dampening, freshness, inhibition-of-return, graph resurrection), exposed identically over MCP, HTTP and a Python API; the documentation is unusually honest about its own numbers — it states plainly that the returned score 'has no single scale, is not a similarity, not a confidence, and not comparable across queries', and that list order is authoritative; LoCoMo results are reported under two different judges with a fresh-clone reproduction path; the feedback loop is explicit (recalls can apply state, but usefulness updates happen through a feedback call rather than silently training on every response); a graceful-degradation design keeps retrieval working when the LLM is unavailable; multi-tenant isolation via payload filters, with an optional service-key hard boundary and per-tenant quotas.
bad: A heavy stack to stand behind a recall call: Qdrant, a Gemini (or other hosted) embedding key, and optionally Memgraph, before the first memory is stored; several pipeline stages are speculative machinery (Q-learning weights, curiosity boosts) whose contribution is not isolated in the published benchmarks; 9 stars against 412 commits — deep but little independently exercised; the corpus is an embedding store, not human-readable files, so memory cannot be audited by reading it the way a wiki can; no approval, lifecycle-governance or provenance discipline at the write path comparable to our gateway.
didnt: Corroboration: its fusion architecture and its candour about score semantics are a reference point for our retrieval work, but the store is an opaque embedding service on a heavy stack — the opposite of our readable-file custody — so nothing is taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: unibaseio/membase-mcp
licence: Proprietary (the repo's License section: 'Copyright © 2026 Unibase. All rights reserved. Proprietary'; the local engine is a compiled binary under its own Unibase licence)
good: A single memory shared across every AI the user runs: facts, documents, web pages and Claude/ChatGPT chat exports go into one store, partitioned into containers per project, and are read back through Python/TypeScript SDKs, a CLI and an MCP server by Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and ChatGPT alike. It publishes its accuracy method and results (93.1% LoCoMo, 92.6% LongMemEval_S, 92.2% DMR, at roughly 3x and 11x fewer tokens than full history), and offers a local mode (data in ~/.membase) beside the hosted account.
bad: The memory lives in a Membase account by design — the hosted API is the default, and the local mode still needs an OpenAI API key and runs a compiled, closed engine, so neither mode is owner-held plain files. The licence is proprietary (all rights reserved), so nothing here is available to build on; the benchmark figures are the vendor's own, and the README itself notes the answer shown in its demo is illustrative.
didnt: Rejected — proprietary licence and hosted custody: the store is an account at membase.com (or a closed local engine keyed to OpenAI), the opposite custody direction from our owner-held files; the container-as-project-partition pattern is the ideas-only residue (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: uniskela/adhd-hub
good: A self-hosted source of truth for half-finished work across coding agents: threads carry open/blocked/done/dismissed states with a per-project PROGRESS.md wiki; a check_overlap tool ranks open threads against what you are about to start ('am I about to redo something half-done?'); destructive or merging actions are gated — duplicate merges are queued for explicit human confirmation and rename/delete wait for UI confirmation rather than applying immediately; reminders (once/session/daily/random) plus a session_digest give a calm 'where you left off' resume surface; a local stdio MCP mode sits beside the HTTP server, and bearer secrets are never returned to the browser.
bad: Young and small (5 stars, pre-1.0 versioning, a single maintainer who manually merges every release PR); it tracks project work state, not cited knowledge — no provenance, citation or verification machinery; the optional transcript indexer stores heuristic summaries of local transcripts; the HTTP mode's security rests on one bearer token.
didnt: Board — the overlap check plus human-confirmed duplicate-merge queue as candidate machinery for our work-continuity surface: before new work starts, rank it against open threads, and never let a merge of two threads apply without a human's explicit confirmation (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: upstash/context7
licence: MIT (this repository only — the MCP server source; the API backend, parsing engine and crawling engine are private, per the README's own disclaimer)
good: Version-specific, up-to-date library documentation pulled from source into a coding agent's context at query time — the direct antidote to stale training-data APIs: a resolve-library-id step maps a name to a canonical library ID, query-docs returns docs and code examples for an exact version, and it ships as both an MCP server and a CLI+Skills mode across 30+ clients at very large adoption (63k stars).
bad: Scope, not memory: it retrieves public library documentation, nothing of the user's own knowledge; the machinery that does the work (crawling, parsing, the API backend) is a private hosted service — the open repo is the client shell, with an API key 'recommended' for higher rate limits; its own disclaimer declines to guarantee the accuracy, completeness or security of the community-contributed documentation it serves.
didnt: Rejected — scope and split custody: a documentation-retrieval service for public libraries, not a memory or knowledge substrate, and the parts that do the work are closed and hosted (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Vasilispapg/claude-handoff
good: Turns any Claude Code session — even a crashed one — into a clean handoff.md another AI can continue from, post-hoc, with zero dependencies (stdlib only, also shipped as one auditable single file): deterministic by default with no API call; secret-looking strings are redacted from every output because 'the handoff you paste into a web chat is egress too'; SessionEnd and PreCompact hooks snapshot state before compaction squeezes it away; and `chf --brief` distills a project's entire session history into one living memory brief — done / in flight / not started, decisions with their why, an ordered resume plan — where every bullet cites the session id it came from, under a freshness stamp that lists the newer sessions and commits rather than merely warning.
bad: Very young and tiny (1 star, one author, created 2026-08); its input is Claude Code's local JSONL transcripts (plus claude.ai/ChatGPT exports), i.e. the transcript-ingest substrate; the distilled brief is only as truthful as the sessions it mines — citation is to a session id, not to a verified source — and the real-summary mode depends on an LLM call through your own key or CLI plan.
didnt: Corroboration — its PreCompact/SessionEnd snapshotting, egress redaction, and freshness stamp that names what changed confirm our checkpoint-before-compaction, gateway PII-scan and staleness-surfacing design from the consumer side; the transcript substrate it mines is not a route we take (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: vbcherepanov/total-agent-memory
good: Local memory whose recall is built to be measured: BM25, locally computed dense embeddings, fuzzy matching and a knowledge graph fused by reciprocal rank fusion, with an optional cross-encoder rerank — and the default profile makes no LLM call on write or search, so a rerun gives the same result and the published benchmarks (LongMemEval R@5 95.1%, LoCoMo R@5 0.607, BEAM 1M R@5 0.448) reproduce offline from scripts in the repo. Facts carry validity intervals (kg_add_fact / kg_at), and a newer value of a single-valued fact retires the older one; a team mode separates personal/department/company stores behind one gateway with roles, authorship and an audit trail.
bad: The benchmarks are the author's own runs (a JOSS paper is still under review), and the LoCoMo/BEAM figures are middling next to the LongMemEval headline; the surface is sprawling (74-79 tools, 9+ IDE integrations, three Docker team topologies) for a 136-commit project; validity intervals exist but there is no citation or human-arbitration layer — retirement of a fact is automatic on a newer write, not ruled.
didnt: Corroboration — validity intervals with single-valued-fact retirement are the parked bi-temporal pattern working in the wild, and its offline-reproducible, no-LLM-default benchmark discipline matches our own eval rules; automatic retirement without a human ruling is where our designs part (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: vectorize-io/hindsight
good: The most substantial learning-memory system in the wave: retain/recall/reflect over memory banks, where reflect consolidates raw memories into observations and mental models (knowledge pages) rather than only replaying conversation; its LongMemEval results are published live with per-model accuracy, latency and cost, and the README states its benchmark performance was independently reproduced by research collaborators at Virginia Tech's Sanghani Center for Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics and The Washington Post, while other vendors' scores are self-reported.
bad: An LLM is required at the centre — retain and reflect run through one of 25+ providers (hosted or local), so there is no deterministic, no-LLM path and memory content is model-distilled rather than verbatim; the headline 'most accurate agent memory system ever tested' is a superlative its own page qualifies (other scores self-reported); the managed cloud is the path of least resistance, with self-hosting a Postgres-backed server deployment.
took: Four builds recorded in lane 8 as sourced from Hindsight, all built 2026-10-19: wiki search upgrade (temporal stage + coverage rerank in wiki search and the Lens); observations pass (consolidates repeated cited claims into proposed beliefs, filed for a ruling, never auto-applied); standing-question page ([[current-state]], six standing questions answered fresh on every ingest day); gateway secrets/PII scan (blocks secret-shaped content at the gateway door, values never echoed).
didnt: Corroboration — already in the stack by design: the four builds above are our Hindsight adaptations, each hardened past the original (the observations pass files beliefs for a ruling and never auto-applies them, where Hindsight's reflect writes its own conclusions) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: vishalbanwari26/mnemos
good: Forgetting with an audit trail: facts carry status (active / merged / forgotten), confidence and last_reinforced_at; reflection merges near-duplicates and decays stale facts, a fact crossing the forget threshold is archived rather than silently deleted, and every merge/decay/forget action lands in a reflection_log. Storage is genuinely swappable — Postgres+pgvector, embedded Qdrant and Neo4j behind one interface, with the same behavioral test suite run against all three to prove parity — and episodes separate occurred_at (logical event time) from created_at, which is what lets its benchmark honestly simulate 30 days passing; retrieval exposes its real similarity/recency/score per item, a transparency its author spun out as a standalone tracing library (memlens).
bad: Embryonic: 9 commits, 0 stars, one author, not on PyPI; the demo and benchmark are the author's own fictional-user data (seven conversations, six questions); fact extraction and merging run through hosted LLM calls (Anthropic/Groq), so the memory content is model-distilled; its scope honesty is a stated intention, not evidence of use.
didnt: Corroboration — archive-never-delete forgetting with a per-action audit log, backend-parity contract tests and the occurred_at/created_at split confirm our custody, verification and bi-temporal instincts in miniature; too young to build on (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: vishnu-77/openreflex
good: Ambient execution memory that governs itself: lifecycle hooks record how work actually goes into an Experience Graph, compile successful work into project-scoped Reflexes, and — during a task — detect failure loops (repeated failing commands, identical retries, stalled progress, runaway context growth) and raise one alert, with cooldown, advising continue, pivot or stop from a marginal-value estimate. Its Reflex Score (0-100, how strong the recommendation is) is explicitly kept separate from the estimated chance that the task succeeds, and its Path check answers 'better option: none proven' when comparable past tasks don't support one; capture stores only coarse project-relative metadata (never file contents, commands, tool output or transcripts) and is off until the user approves the project (/openreflex approve, revocable).
bad: Tiny adoption (3 stars) and a single author; the loop detection and marginal-value machinery are heuristic and its benchmark is a self-described simulated one; it governs coding-task behaviour only — no citation, provenance or knowledge layer; ambient hooks watching every lifecycle event are a broad capture posture, mitigated by coarse metadata and opt-in approval rather than by a line-by-line audit the user can inspect.
didnt: Board — the live failure-loop verdict (continue / pivot / stop from a marginal-value estimate, raised once with cooldown, its strength score kept separate from success probability) as candidate machinery for our agent-run monitoring, where a looping lane currently surfaces only as activity (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: VonderVuflya/Yggdrasil
good: Local-first memory with governance: session start auto-injects identity, project status and open follow-ups (~300 tokens); duplicates and conflicts are queued for review rather than merged silently, and governance changes are non-destructive (archive, never delete); every memory doubles as a plain-Markdown note the owner can read, edit and grep; seeding from existing transcripts and vaults runs with a --dry-run first; credential hygiene is engineered (the engine token lives in a 0600 file and reaches the daemon as a file path, masked in config listings); the optional self-maintaining model's dedupe/merge is propose-only.
bad: AGPL-3.0 — ideas only for us. Alpha status by its own badge, 22 stars; the zero-config default tier is keyword-only FTS5, so the strong recall figures belong to the optional local-model tiers; an always-on daemon plus per-prompt auto-recall hooks is a broad ambient surface; background consolidation, even propose-only, is a local LLM deciding what looks duplicate.
didnt: Corroboration — the session-start orientation packet (identity + project status + open follow-ups), the review queue for duplicates/conflicts and archive-never-delete governance are our orientation and approval design stated independently; AGPL-3.0 keeps the code ideas-only regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: vornicx/Midas
good: Eval-first memory built around a provenance guard: no LLM at ingest or query, recall returns the verbatim source turn, typed belief revision supersedes old values — and before any memory-justified external or destructive action the agent must call check_memory_use, which blocks unless the user explicitly confirmed that action and the confirmation is still current; a superseded memory cannot authorize an action at all. Its adversarial memory-safety bench blocks 10/10 attacks (a planted confirmation beside a prohibition, a confirmation for a different action, a provenance-laundering supersession, a cross-namespace approval) with no over-blocking (benign-pass 1.00); memory_state returns the live non-superseded decisions and memory_diff the beliefs added and revised (old -> new); and it publishes its failed experiments (hybrid retrieval, reranking, naive distillation measured not to help) alongside the wins.
bad: Young and small (15 stars, 137 commits, one author; the TypeScript port is labelled experimental); the guard is advisory at the client layer — a client that never calls check_memory_use is ungated; its judged-answer figures rest on a gpt-4o judge; and it states its own structural limit plainly: top-k retrieval cannot do whole-conversation aggregation or summarization (marked by design in its own comparison table).
didnt: Board — the provenance guard as candidate machinery for our gateway's write gates: memory may inform planning, but a memory-justified external or destructive action requires a user confirmation that is still current, and superseded memory authorizes nothing; its adversarial bench (including provenance-laundering and cross-namespace approval attacks, with benign-pass measured too) is the test shape to copy (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: whynowlab/jarvis-orb
good: A persistent memory ('Brain Lite') with a live face: four memory tiers (episodic, semantic, project, procedural) auto-classified and ranked by recency, temporal scoring with a 30-day half-life, contradiction detection that flags conflicts and marks superseded decisions stale, entities (projects, PRs, decisions) tracked as objects with full state-transition history, and a memory_verify tool that marks memories verified, superseded or contradicted — all local (SQLite + FTS5, zero cloud dependencies) — while a 3MB Tauri/Three.js orb renders brain events in real time (a contradiction pulses red; an entity change flashes cyan).
bad: Presentation leads ('Not a tool. A presence.'); the brain is thin — 7 MCP tools, 55 commits, auto-classification doing the tiering — and the 30-day half-life decay is recency bias by formula: a true old decision fades exactly because it is old; the orb is macOS/Windows only (Linux 'Not yet'); it is the lightweight extraction of a private 'Jarvis' control plane whose full form is not the open repo.
didnt: Corroboration — entities with full state-transition history and explicit verified/superseded/contradicted states are our claim-lifecycle design in miniature, and the orb shows memory events are worth surfacing live; the half-life decay scoring is the part we don't take (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: wnbhr/being
licence: Apache-2.0 (stated only in the README's License section; no LICENSE file at root)
good: A personality runtime with one genuinely distinctive mechanism: identity as an Ed25519 key pair with a tamper-evident signature chain — cryptographic proof of a Being's ownership and history — wrapped around a SOUL persona definition, episodic memory stored as structured scenes (who, what, when, where, emotion) that decay, merge and consolidate, and a Patrol background cycle that processes conversations into memory between sessions; BYOK throughout, so the platform never spends the user's quota without consent.
bad: Custody points the wrong way: the documented path is Ruddia's hosted worker (being.ruddia.com) over Supabase, and even self-hosting requires a Supabase project plus a provider key — the memory is rows in a vendor-shaped Postgres, not owner-held files; embryonic (53 commits, 1 star, no releases) with much of the surface (extensions, Sense/Act bridge, tool loop, sandbox) marked planned; memory exists to serve persona continuity, with no citation, provenance-checking or user-ruling layer.
didnt: Rejected — scope and custody: a hosted-first personality runtime whose memory serves persona continuity in someone else's database, not a cited knowledge substrate; our Black Box ledger already carries the tamper-evident-chain idea in hash form (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: writerslogic/scrivener-mcp
licence: AGPL-3.0 (with a COMMERCIAL_LICENSE.md at root offering dual licensing)
good: An MCP door over a real file format, engineered the way a write door should be: writes are atomic with a pre-write backup, deletion is a reversible move to trash, create_snapshot takes a Scrivener-native snapshot before editing and compare_snapshot diffs it against the current document (paragraphs added/removed, net word change), and verify_project_integrity is a read-only scan for structural problems (missing/duplicate UUIDs, unreadable content). Project memory persists with the manuscript — character profiles, plot threads, style guides — so a consistency check months later catches contradictions (dialogue out of character, a limp that disappears for a chapter); document management, deterministic analysis and keyword search need no API key at all, and semantic indexing runs locally.
bad: AGPL-3.0 — ideas only for us, with a commercial dual licence beside it. The domain is fiction manuscripts in one proprietary app's format, and if the project is also open unsaved in Scrivener the two can write over each other (its own warning); semantic_search still needs a provider to interpret the query despite the local index; the tool count is stated two ways at source (53 in the header, 67 in the tools section).
didnt: Corroboration — snapshot-before-edit with a diffable compare, atomic writes with pre-write backup, reversible deletion and a read-only integrity scan are our checkpoint-and-verify discipline applied to someone else's files; AGPL-3.0 and the fiction-manuscript domain keep it ideas-only regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Wuesteon/lean-memory
good: Embedded local-first memory (one SQLite file per namespace, no server or mandatory cloud key) whose sleep-time maintenance job is dry-run by default and stages every judgement call — near-duplicate merges, summaries, evictions — as a proposal a human approves, edits, or rejects, in a web console or conversationally; unreviewed proposals expire after 30 days rather than auto-applying ('silence is never consent'). Facts are superseded, never deleted, and stay queryable as-of any past point in time. The README is candid: public LongMemEval/LoCoMo runs are deliberately deferred until after launch, and the default offline backends are named 'semantically meaningless' stubs.
bad: Very young (created 2026-06-21) and small (43 stars); the headline benchmark numbers are still deferred, so retrieval quality rests on an internal 1/5-to-4/5 figure. On the default install roughly 15% of extracted candidates — almost all inferential 'derives' facts — are typed by a deterministic stub rather than a model, making inference-type facts second-class unless the optional Ollama extra is added; its own README buries that in a Known Limitations pointer.
took: The staged-maintenance pattern as corroboration: dry-run-by-default hygiene, only provably-safe transforms auto-applied, judgement calls staged as expiring proposals — silence is never consent — matches and sharpens our own review-queue discipline.
didnt: Not adopted as a component: our store is owner-held Markdown under git, not a per-namespace SQLite fact engine, and its extraction pipeline solves a problem our ingest does not have. Studied as design corroboration only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wynelson94/longhand
good: Genuinely well-engineered verbatim session memory: sources are captured before Claude Code rotates its session files away, search and recall are token-capped by design, results carry explicit stale:true banners with reasons instead of clean-looking empty answers, a reconciler MCP tool lets the agent self-heal index drift, and retired tool names keep answering forever with migration notes rather than hard-failing. Backed by a canary regression corpus anchored to real shipped bugs and 617 unit tests over 792 real sessions.
bad: The whole substrate is bulk session-transcript capture and indexing — including thinking blocks — which is precisely the ingest our system has not approved: our record is a deliberately compiled wiki, not a verbatim transcript store. It is also Claude-Code/Codex-shaped, so its corpus model does not transfer to a multi-source personal wiki.
took: One portable idea noted: staleness signalling — when the underlying record has moved, say so in the result with the reason, never return a clean-looking empty answer. The capture substrate itself was not taken.
didnt: Not for us — verbatim session-transcript ingest is unapproved in our system (the same bar applied to B124's transcript pond and B126's deja-vu), and no part of the tool was adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: xChuCx/agent-memory
good: The closest design cousin in this batch: memory is plain Markdown committed to the repo (readable, git-diffable), durable changes stage for human review as an exact diff before applying, secrets/PII are scanned out before anything is written, a section merge driver handles concurrent edits, and whole-file pre-hash compare-and-set detects drift during rebase so adjacent concurrent edits cannot silently clobber each other. Its VTP-1 protocol adds cryptographic receipts for verifiable task completion, with RFC 8785 canonicalisation verified against the official test vectors.
bad: Scope is per-repository coding-agent memory, not a personal knowledge system; the swarm-consensus/VTP layer is heavy machinery for a single-owner wiki, and the project is young (created 2026-05-26, 15 stars) with a fast-moving 0.x release line whose hardening release notes describe serious attack classes (symlink bypass, manifest tampering) only recently closed.
took: Corroboration for our approval-gated writes, plus one concrete mechanism worth remembering: pre-hash compare-and-set on staged edits, so a staged change whose base has moved fails loudly instead of landing on moved ground.
didnt: Not adopted: our gateway already implements approval-gated writes over the wiki with its own trust ledger, and swapping stores mid-programme would cost more than the CAS mechanism is worth as a transplant (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XJTLUmedia/Context-First-MCP
good: Bundles the four failure modes of long conversations — drift, silent contradiction, vague execution, hallucinated success — into one per-turn orchestrator that returns a single directive with a context-health score: conflicts are checked against locked ground-truth state, an abstention check asks clarifying questions instead of guessing when confidence is low, and verify_execution rechecks whether a tool output actually achieved the stated intent. The abstention and conflict layers are framed on named published methods (RLAAR, ERGO) with arXiv references.
bad: Embryonic (20 commits, 2 stars) with marketing-grade claims: several 'advanced reasoning' layers carry paper names (Coconut, InftyThink, KAG) but are necessarily lightweight TypeScript heuristics, not the papers' methods, and no evaluation of the 37 tools is shown. Its research_pipeline writes files autonomously to disk with 'no LLM cooperation needed' — unreviewed autonomous writes are the opposite of our approval gate.
took: Corroboration only: a single per-turn directive combining conflict-vs-locked-truth, abstention, and execution verification parallels our Ask door's abstention and conflict gates; nothing was built from it.
didnt: Not adopted — embryonic, unevaluated, and its autonomous file-writing pipeline conflicts with our approval-gated write model (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XuebinMa/AIWiki
good: A content wiki with unusually honest apparatus: every pitfall entry follows one structure (what I see you doing → why it happens → consequences → best practice → example → version notes → sources), tags its evidence (official docs / arXiv / CVE & security advisories — three case studies carry CVE numbers), is version-stamped, and labels each tool's coverage depth honestly rather than padding thin coverage. Entries are written from the model's first-person perspective, tracing each pitfall to the mechanism that causes it.
bad: It is a book of advice about coding agents, not a memory or knowledge system we can build on, and its content licence is CC-BY-SA-4.0 (share-alike), so its text is ideas-only for us in any case. Coverage of the four non-Claude tools is admittedly thinner, leaning on security disclosures and official docs.
took: One habit worth keeping: per-entry evidence tags plus a version stamp, and coverage depth labelled rather than padded — the same honesty discipline our claim lifecycle applies to wiki pages.
didnt: Not adopted — a documentation content project under a share-alike content licence; read for its evidence-tagging practice only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yamantaka520/Agent-Memory-OS
good: The strongest multi-agent memory design in this batch: private/agent/team/project/global scopes sit behind a hard ACL enforced before ranking (candidate indexes return IDs only; content is re-read through the gate), federation policy lets a peer only shrink a memory's visibility, never widen it, and revocation actually retracts already-synced copies on peers via an independent ACL clock. Context packs are token-budgeted and auditable — context_pack_report() explains every include and exclude — and associative recall traversal is ACL-safe, so an invisible memory can never bridge two visible ones.
bad: Very young (created 2026-07-10, 7 stars) with a wide, fast-moving feature surface (federation, Hebbian reinforcement, per-agent recall profiles, consolidation) whose claims rest on its own docs; federation convergence is last-writer-wins with tombstones, weaker than a git history. Its store is a SQLite database, not owner-readable files.
took: Three federation rules recorded as design corroboration for our own multi-agent filings mesh: peers may only shrink visibility, revocation must propagate to already-synced copies, and every context selection should be able to explain its includes and excludes.
didnt: Not adopted as a component — our agent mesh shares a git wiki under owner rulings, not a federated SQLite fabric; the rules were noted, the engine was not taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yaminbkk/NexusMem
good: Indexes the one record git cannot give an agent — shell commands with their real exit codes — and links failures to their fixes (same-command retry, or a conversation bridge required to match every significant word). Provenance is explicit: commits are [observed] events, doc sections are [authored] claims that can go stale, and the two compete on equal terms in one ranker. Hygiene is serious: assistant transcripts are off by default precisely because they are 'the likeliest place for a pasted credential', commands are redacted before being written, and the README publishes where its own linking heuristic failed (roughly half its links on the first dogfood pass) and how the fix was verified against the full set.
bad: The capture substrate is the problem for us: shell-history scraping plus optional agent-command hooks is activity surveillance by another name, and our work record is a deliberately kept wiki log, not a harvested shell history. Ranking leans on tuned priors (signal and recency exponents) whose derivation is candid but corpus-specific.
took: Two portable ideas noted: failure → fix chaining (when a past failure surfaces, its recorded fix rides with it) and the observed-vs-authored provenance split for ranking unlike evidence. The capture substrate was not taken.
didnt: Not adopted — shell-history and agent-command capture is not a substrate our system takes; studied for its provenance and failure-chain ideas only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yonro/memory-os-cli
licence: MIT (client repository only; the hosted memory service implementation is private)
good: The client is well-built: a PlanRunner pattern for every mutating command (build the plan, preview it with paths and diffs, confirm once, apply sequentially, stop on first failure), generated project configuration that references a credential without ever embedding its value, dry-run modes throughout, and a deterministic target resolver that never silently writes configuration to unverified paths. Session-continuity snapshots and per-record agent identity/provenance are sensible service features.
bad: The product is the hosted service, and that implementation is private: the actual memory store sits at xmemo.dev under the vendor's custody, so 'user-owned' describes the marketing, not the architecture. The MIT licence covers only this client/distribution repo — the open part does not launder the closed service behind it.
took: Nothing taken beyond corroboration: PlanRunner's preview-then-confirm-once shape matches our staged-apply gates. The catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict could not be verified against any build record and is not repeated here.
didnt: Not adopted — a client for a private hosted memory service; owner-held local files are our custody model, and no XMemo component exists in our system to 'already have' (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yubinkim444/repo-memory
good: Minimal in the right way: shared agent memory as plain files in the repo — an append-only facts.jsonl where every fact carries the evidence needed to re-verify it cheaply (file, line range, the tool and command that verified it, verified_at) and the identity of the agent that added it; stale entries stay and readers consult verified_at. Quality control is deliberately social: facts flow through normal git PR review, and git blame attributes every fact.
bad: Embryonic (11 commits, 1 star, no releases) and deliberately thin: no review gate inside the tool itself, no staleness machinery beyond the timestamp, no search beyond listing/filtering. Its README contains a specification block addressed to discovering agents — evidence of its intended workflow, treated here as data, not instruction.
took: Corroboration for our citation discipline: a fact that carries its own re-verification evidence (source location plus how and when it was checked) is exactly the shape our citation lockfile enforces at wiki scale.
didnt: Not adopted — a per-repo scratch memory, far below the wiki's needs; studied as a miniature of the evidence-carrying fact pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yuelinghuashu/story-cli
good: A directory-convention content store with the two habits our wiki also runs on: indexes and per-entry READMEs are generated from the convention rather than hand-maintained, and a validate command checks the corpus against its own specification (directory naming, UTF-8 encoding, duplicate sequence numbers, config schema) before any build. Its MCP server is designed for token economy — directory scans return slim output by default and chapter reads truncate on demand — and it claims 550+ passing tests across scanner, validator, exporters and the MCP protocol.
bad: Fiction-first and tiny (37 commits, 0 stars, single author): the knowledge-base and tech-doc templates are secondary modes of a story manager. Its own docs warn the MCP server 'reads and writes all files in the working directory' and should only run in trusted repositories — a broad write surface with no approval gate.
took: Corroboration only: validate-before-build as a corpus compliance gate and generated indexes from a directory convention both parallel our lint and index machinery; the token-economical MCP read shapes were noted.
didnt: Not adopted — a single-author fiction CMS whose knowledge mode is a side template; nothing in it displaces our own generator and validator (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ZengLiangYi/ChatCrystal
good: A mature local-first distillation pipeline (485 commits, 38 releases): conversations from five coding tools are parsed locally and distilled into structured notes — titles, summaries, conclusions, snippets, tags — with semantic search, relation-aware expansion, a tag knowledge graph, and an explicit experience quality gate governing what becomes reusable knowledge. Its privacy boundary is drawn carefully: parsing happens on the user's device, and even its optional cloud mode uploads only normalised conversations, never filesystem access.
bad: Its substrate is bulk import of coding-agent conversation transcripts — the ingest our system has not approved; our wiki compiles directed sources, not harvested chat histories. The distillation quality also depends entirely on an external LLM and embedding provider the user must supply, so the gate's judgements are only as good as that model.
took: Corroboration for two standing choices: local parsing before anything leaves the machine, and an explicit quality gate between raw material and reusable knowledge — the shape of our raw → compiled wiki ingest. The transcript-import substrate was not taken.
didnt: Not adopted — conversation-transcript import is unapproved in our system, and its note store does not displace the wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zensation-ai/zenbrain
licence: Apache-2.0 (code); the six Predictive Memory Architecture components of the full architecture are proprietary and not in the open packages
good: The best honesty apparatus in this batch: Zenodo reproduction packages whose scripts re-derive every published value and exit non-zero on mismatch, a mechanism comparison against Mem0/Letta/Zep run at pinned versions with positive and negative controls printed before the result, and a correction notice stating plainly that the measured LongMemEval arm was a Python port of a test-harness class rather than the shipped system — plus 'the paper prints where ZenBrain loses'. The library itself is zero-dependency TypeScript with 945 tests, FSRS retention, Hebbian strengthening and sleep consolidation as tested functions.
bad: By its own correction, the headline benchmark figures do not measure the package being sold here, and the full 15-mechanism architecture is not the open artefact — six PMA components are proprietary, so the open library ships 9 of the 15 mechanisms. Pre-1.0 with an API that can still change, and the neuroscience framing runs well ahead of what the corrected evidence shows.
took: The verification pattern, not the memory engine: publish reproduction packages that fail loudly on drift, print the controls before the result, and correct the record in the README when the measured thing was not the shipped thing — the standard our own evaluation reporting aims at.
didnt: Not adopted as a memory layer — decay-by-spaced-repetition is a retention policy our archive-never-delete wiki deliberately does not run, and the benchmark evidence does not cover the shipped package (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zsxh1990/pr-genius
good: Institutional memory for outbound contributions, built with rare epistemic care: rejected PRs are harvested into an anti-pattern corpus that actually moves the risk tier, while the success-pattern corpus is deliberately kept out of scoring and the README says so; every corpus count it prints is re-verified against the live tree on each release by a verify_claims script; a doctor command 'never lies about what is missing'; and every mutating command is dry-run by default behind an explicit --confirm. Its nine PR states are framed as decisions ('what do I touch today'), including CLEAN — being told what not to spend today on.
bad: Niche and small (3 stars) despite 544 commits; its knowledge is GitHub-PR-shaped and does not transfer to a personal wiki, and its value compounds only for a heavy outbound-contribution practice we do not run — our repos are read-only by owner rule, so there is no outbound PR portfolio to board.
took: Two habits recorded as corroboration: verify printed claims against the live tree at release time (our live-verification standard, independently arrived at), and harvest failures into an anti-pattern corpus that is actually wired into decisions while keeping the success corpus reference-only.
didnt: Not adopted — no outbound PR practice exists here for it to serve under the owner's read-only GitHub rule (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zuneracodes/localkeep
good: The curation-first stance, stated as a principle: the user writes the entries, anchors the dates, and keeps them locally — the model is only a lookup engine over the user's own words, and nothing is silently scraped from conversations. Its privacy section is honest about the boundary that matters (storage is local, but retrieved fragments do enter the model's session), and tests start from an empty database and create memories through the same Hub forms a new user would use.
bad: Embryonic — 3 commits, 1 star, a single small codebase — and activation is fragile: Claude will not reliably call the tools unless the user pastes vendor instructions into personal preferences and clicks 'Always approve', which is a standing-permission pattern our own gates avoid. Chronological banks with lookup only; no search quality, lifecycle, or contradiction machinery is shown.
took: Nothing taken beyond corroboration: user-authored-only memory with an honestly stated egress boundary is the owner's own sovereignty model, independently arrived at.
didnt: Not adopted — embryonic, and our wiki already is the curated, owner-held record this tool prototypes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zzallirog/weighted-compact
good: The most disciplined claims presentation in this batch: the recap's faithfulness is provable (four invariants — coverage, conservation, provenance, determinism — re-checked on 1007/1007 sessions, stdlib-only, no model, no judge), the six-signal importance mixture is published as a null result with numbers ('no measured edge over recency or bm25 at current N'), and the one real win is a control guarantee, not a quality claim — user keep/skip labels are hard constraints in compaction (100% keep-label survival vs the recency baseline's 62%). Zero outbound network is enforced by a CI workflow, and for lossless archival the README points users to zstd rather than shipping a weaker fold of its own.
bad: Its input is the session-transcript corpus: it processes transcripts rather than archiving them, but a transcript-derived substrate is still the ingest family our system has not approved — our answer to compaction loss is the compiled wiki record and conversation log, not transcript mining. Alpha status, 5 stars, and the compaction layer's measured result is a tie with cheap baselines by its own account.
took: The claims discipline as corroboration: separate each claim so none borrows another's credibility, publish the null result with its numbers, and sell the control guarantee you can prove — the standard our own evaluation reporting is held to.
didnt: Not adopted — transcript-substrate tooling stays outside our approved ingest, and our compaction answer is the compiled record (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zzhang82/Agent-Memory-Bridge
good: Governance stated as boundaries, not features: derived repository facts (WHAT, rebuilt from a clean git state) are kept separate from durable human decisions (WHY) so one cannot silently become the other; if HEAD moves or the worktree is dirty the derived snapshot is not presented as current truth, and refresh is an explicit act, never automatic. There is no automatic learning and no transcript archive — 'It is not a system that silently converts every conversation into durable truth' — and changed knowledge is revised or superseded instead of overwritten, with an Inspect view answering why a given memory surfaced.
bad: Per-project coding memory only — no personal-knowledge scope — and its onboarding leans on agent-addressed prompt/skill material pasted into the client, which puts setup trust in copied instructions. Young (7 stars) with a fast 0.x cadence (57 releases since April), so its governance vocabulary is still moving.
took: Corroboration for two of our own rules: derived views must refuse to present themselves as current when their source has moved, and durable knowledge is stored explicitly or not at all.
didnt: Not adopted — our gateway and wiki already implement governed memory with an owner-facing trust ledger; a second per-project store would fragment the record (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: andyliszewski/grounding-ai
good: Citation-grade habits in a small package: the pipeline is deterministic (same inputs, byte-identical chunks), every document and chunk carries triple-hash provenance plus page ranges and section headings, and corpus partitioning is the core data model — each agent's YAML filter gives it its own FAISS index over only its collections, rather than one monolithic index with a query-time filter. Its evaluation was written down before the run, graded by hand blind to condition, and reports its own failed citation-validation gate alongside the headline accuracy gain.
bad: Embryonic (16 commits, 1 star) and its one evaluation is small — 25 documents, 26 questions — so the +50-point figure is a promising pilot, not an established result; the citation check that failed its gate is the very feature a citation-grade pipeline most needs working. Per-agent index rebuilds also multiply storage and maintenance as collections grow.
took: Corroboration for our citation machinery: hash every chunk at ingest, partition retrieval by audience as a data-model decision, and report the gate your own citation check failed — directly relevant to the scholarly citation truth-checking gap.
didnt: Not adopted — a 16-commit pilot cannot displace our ingest pipeline; studied for its provenance and partitioning design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gogabrielordonez/mcp-ragchat
licence: MIT (stated only at the foot of the README; no LICENSE file at root)
good: A complete, small RAG-chat loop in one package: Markdown sections become documents, a ragchat_test tool verifies retrieval quality before going live, and the generated widget is a single self-contained script tag with no framework dependencies. Per-domain stores are plain local JSON files a owner can inspect.
bad: 'Zero cloud dependency' describes only the vector store: every chat and embedding call needs a commercial API key, so the dependency moved rather than vanished. Four commits, no tests visible, a JSON-file vector store with top-3 cosine retrieval, and a README demo presented as a transcript of an interaction that is a script, not a measurement.
didnt: Not adopted — a website chat widget is not a wiki component, and its licence rests on a README footer alone (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: notwhiteblank/scholar-rag-mcp
good: Serious scholarly-ingest engineering: papers are parsed by a real pipeline (MinerU, with metadata normalised via local heuristics, CrossRef and optional GROBID), chunked deterministically, and read back the way a researcher works — outline first, paginated full text with hard size caps. Deletion of a knowledge base is two-phase, ingestion runs as background jobs that survive restart (interrupted jobs are recovered and skipped on re-run), and both parse and annotation caches are keyed by content hash so unchanged papers are never reprocessed.
bad: Preview software (v0.4.0, interfaces and storage layout 'may change') with a heavy runtime: three separately served local models (chat, embed, rerank) via vLLM, a downloaded Qdrant binary, and MinerU's model stack — a GPU-shaped install for what is, at bottom, a paper index. Retrieval quality is asserted by a latency figure (100k-chunk p95 < 1s), not an accuracy evaluation.
took: Three mechanisms noted for our scholarly work: two-phase deletion for corpora, content-hash parse caching, and outline-first paginated reading as the context-safe way to serve full texts.
didnt: Not adopted — preview-stage and operationally heavy; noted as candidate-shaped machinery for the paper corpus, nothing built (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: poll-the-people/customgpt-mcp
good: A complete, honest thin client: the full vendor API surface (agents, conversations, pages, stats, settings) is exposed with pagination, API keys are masked in logs and never stored by the server, and a validate_api_key tool lets a client check credentials before doing work.
bad: The wrapper is open but the thing wrapped is a closed SaaS: your corpus and conversations sit in CustomGPT.ai's custody under its terms, and the server's own statelessness means nothing about the knowledge is owner-held. Two commits total, and the README cannot keep its own provenance straight (install instructions pointing at another organisation's repo).
didnt: Rejected — an open client over a closed hosted knowledge platform; custody is the disqualifier (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vectara/vectara-mcp
good: Two of its tools treat factual consistency as a first-class, callable check: one identifies and corrects hallucinations in generated text against supplied documents, the other returns a factual-consistency evaluation with scoring — the check is a separate step from generation, run against the sources. The server itself is security-conscious: authenticated HTTP by default, rate limiting, CORS origin validation, and explicit warnings that stdio and --no-auth are development-only.
bad: Every tool is a call to Vectara's hosted platform: corpus, index, generation and the consistency checking itself all live vendor-side under an API key, so adopting it means moving the knowledge and its verification out of owner custody. The MCP layer adds nothing testable locally — no evaluation of the checking tools ships in the repo.
took: The shape, not the service: factual-consistency evaluation as a standalone callable step, separate from the generator and run against the sources — the pattern our scholarly citation truth-checking gap calls for, to be built over our own corpus.
didnt: Rejected as a component — hosted-platform custody for both the corpus and its checker (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zaharajabeen13-create/ai-rete-rag-mcp
good: A principled split of labour: the verdict always comes from a deterministic rule engine (auditable, reproducible) and the LLM's only job is explaining it, grounded in the ingested policy documents. Policy handling is bi-temporal in practice — documents are dated (effective_from/effective_until), new versions declare what they supersede, and decide can read the policy in force on an earlier day (as_of). Turning prose policy into rules is itself gated: the importer drafts each rule citing the exact sentence it encodes, saves nothing, and a human reviews before put_rules commits the set; every fact in a decision records its source file in the audit trail.
bad: The engine is hosted and metered: rules, documents and decisions live in a vendor account under a plan quota, and this repository is only the client shim, so none of the auditable-engine benefit is owner-held or inspectable at source. Zero stars and a single month of history give the design no track record yet.
took: Two ideas recorded: keep the verdict deterministic and let the model only explain it; and compile prose into draft rules that cite their source sentence and wait for human review before they take effect — the draft-then-review shape our own proposal pipeline uses.
didnt: Not adopted — a client for a hosted, metered decision service; the two design separations were noted, the service was not taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 8b-is/smart-tree
good: One genuinely valuable component: a security scanner aimed at the MCP supply chain — it detects MCP servers that phone home or fetch mutable content (IPFS/IPNS injection, fake cryptographic verification, auto-execution hooks, hidden directories) and can clean malicious integrations out of a client's configuration, with certificate scanning that reports metadata honestly ('they inspect metadata without verifying signatures, chain trust, or revocation'). The core tree tool is fast Rust with token-conscious output formats, and activity logging is a stated feature.
bad: Claims discipline is poor: 'quantum' compression branding, consciousness language ('Aye Consciousness', save_consciousness.sh), and speed multipliers headline a README that also tries to recruit the reading agent itself with a superpower pitch and a prescribed first move — the agent-addressed marketing pattern at its most explicit.
