Underneath, it is a directory-listing/context utility, not a knowledge system, and its breadth (TUI, web dashboard, daemon, hooks, hub) makes its real maintenance surface hard to judge.
took: One idea noted: audit the installed MCP surface itself — which servers and hooks are configured, and whether any fetch mutable remote content — as a standing security check for an agent-heavy setup.
didnt: Not adopted — a context utility with inflated claims and an agent-recruiting README; only the scanner idea was noted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A1-x-Tech/mcp-google-drive
good: Safety design well beyond its size: 'delete' means the reversible trash, permanent deletion is a separate tool that 'cannot be picked by accident', a write is never replayed after an uncertain failure (retries apply to reads only, so a copy or upload cannot duplicate behind your back), every operation class is published in a confirmation-boundary table, and tools are marked read/write/destructive so the client can distinguish inspection from live change. The OAuth flow is equally careful — the client JSON is handed over by file path, the consent code returns to a one-shot loopback listener, tokens are stored mode 0600 and verified with a real API call at connect time.
bad: Embryonic — 9 commits, 0 stars, created days ago — and it asks for broad Drive scopes for its full surface (the complete `drive` scope covers sharing, trash and deletion on arbitrary files), so its careful tool design sits behind a wide credential. Nothing in the repo yet evidences testing at any scale.
took: Corroboration for our Drive boundary: reversible-trash-by-default with permanent deletion as a separate, unmistakable tool, and reads-only retries so a failed write is never silently duplicated.
didnt: Not adopted — we already work through a connected Drive route under the owner's organise-only boundary; studied as a safety-design peer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: aadilr/changethisfile-mcp
good: The commercial terms are disclosed in the README rather than discovered later: server-side processing, 24-hour auto-deletion, 1-hour download expiry, input caps, and exactly which tools are free, metered or preview-only are all stated up front, and the API key 'is never logged'.
bad: The work happens on the vendor's servers: documents leave the machine for a metered third-party service whose full outputs sit behind checkout links — a pay-per-document egress for operations (format conversion, table extraction) that local tools already do. The open MIT package is only the bridge; the conversion engine is closed and hosted.
didnt: Rejected — hosted, metered document processing is an egress our local toolchain makes unnecessary (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agaveis/hiberden-mcp
licence: MIT (this connector; the hiberden-core archive engine it fronts is a commercial product)
good: Verification done the way our own standard demands: verify_copy is 'proof from the actual medium, not a stored flag' — it re-reads the copy and re-hashes it before stamping Verified, a fast BLAKE3 pass can sustain an already-Verified copy but never promote one, a not-attempted result (cloud copies, checked in the desktop app) is reported distinctly from a failure, and every verify writes an audit-log row naming the algorithm that ran. The permission model is equally strict: the default tier is read+verify, write/delete tools above the tier are neither advertised nor accepted, the tier itself can only be changed in the desktop app, and the process holds no model and no API key and performs zero network I/O.
bad: The connector is a window onto a commercial engine whose own terms gate archive-writing, and the platform is young (22 commits, GA August 2026) with tape support admittedly never run against a physical drive. Its domain is media archives, not knowledge, so only the verification design transfers.
took: Strong corroboration for our preservation work: a backup counts as verified only when the medium is re-read and re-hashed, a lighter check may sustain but never promote a verified state, and 'not attempted' must never be reported as either pass or fail.
didnt: Not adopted — a connector for a commercial media-archiving product we do not run (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: alebgl77/ftp-deploy-mcp
good: Deployment treated as a gated workflow rather than a file copy: transfers are staged and verified before promotion with a rollback path, plans are required by default (legacy direct mutators are blocked except dry runs), every server can be pinned read-only, dry runs are first-class, and local file access is confined to a declared localRoot that refuses symlink escapes. Its protocol matrix is candid about what each transport can and cannot guarantee, and refuses unsafe configurations (unknown SFTP host keys, plaintext FTP, insecure TLS) unless the operator explicitly acknowledges the specific risk being accepted.
bad: Zero stars and two months old, with an elaborate durable-workflow apparatus (state quotas, plan journals, alias locks) whose complexity is itself a risk at this maturity; and its protocol honesty cuts both ways — for FTP/FTPS it concedes the client-side root is not a reliable jail, so the security story depends on server-side chroot discipline outside the tool's control.
took: Corroboration for staged promotion everywhere: scan → plan → approve → transfer → verify → promote with a rollback path, and unsafe modes that must be explicitly acknowledged rather than silently available.
didnt: Not adopted — our deploys do not run over FTP/SFTP; studied as a deployment-gates peer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: arjunprabhulal/superpdf
good: Deterministic local parsing with the right instincts: because the reader works by rules rather than a model, output is reproducible and nothing is uploaded; charts are converted back into the numbers they were drawn from, with values measured from the drawing (rather than printed on it) explicitly marked approximate; SSRF discipline is built in (links to localhost/private addresses refused at every redirect, non-PDFs refused, downloads deleted after reading); and its benchmark presentation is honest — its own run, labelled as such, with stronger competitors listed above it.
bad: A week old at study time (created 2026-10-14, 28 commits, 0 stars): the benchmark is a single self-run, chart values are 52.2 on its own table, and rule-based parsing will lose on irregular layouts where learned parsers win — the honest table shows it mid-pack, well behind the paid leader. Nothing yet proves durability of the project itself.
took: Noted as candidate-shaped corroboration for the wiki's OCR/document queue: local rule-based parsing, approximate-value marking on recovered chart data, and allow-list folder confinement for any MCP file tool.
didnt: Not adopted yet — a one-week-old project cannot carry our document pipeline, but it is the shape of what our OCR/parse queue wants (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: box/mcp-server-box-remote
good: The connection model is clean as far as it goes: OAuth-protected resource metadata and authorization-server discovery are published at standard endpoints, and access is granted per-user from inside the client rather than by shared service keys.
bad: There is no software here to study or reuse — four commits carrying documentation for a proprietary hosted endpoint; content stays in Box under Box's terms, and the tool surface itself is defined elsewhere ('see the remote Box MCP server documentation'), so even the capability list is not in the repo.
didnt: Rejected — a signpost to a hosted enterprise service, not a component (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bzsanti/oxidize-python
good: A local document door with the bounds stated up front: every path must resolve inside the configured workspace root (OXIDIZE_WORKSPACE), inputs are capped (100 MB maximum file, 10,000 maximum pages, bounded output bytes and sessions), and the toolset covers generation, parsing, split/merge, PDF/A compliance checking and signature verification with no C dependencies, no Java and no subprocesses — and explicitly no hosted endpoint, local stdio only.
bad: Young and small (created 2026-03-09, 6 stars) and wholly bound to one upstream Rust library, so its format coverage and correctness rise and fall with oxidize-pdf; the sandbox is a path-resolution discipline inside one process, not an approval gate — nothing in the README describes a human confirmation step before a write.
took: Corroboration for our door design: a document MCP that confines every path to a workspace root and publishes its resource caps is the shape our own read doors take.
didnt: Not adopted — our ingest pipeline already parses PDFs and a second parser stack would duplicate it; studied for its sandbox-and-caps discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ckanthony/Chisel
licence: No licence found at source (metadata silent, no LICENSE file at root, LICENSE path 404, no licence section in the README, and no licence field in the workspace or member-crate Cargo.toml files) — all rights reserved, ideas only
good: Precision with the failure modes engineered out: patch_apply sends only a unified diff and a hunk mismatch returns PatchFailed with the file untouched (atomic writes); shell access is a compile-time fixed whitelist (grep/sed/awk/find/cat and kin — rm, bash, curl and sudo are not in it and cannot be added at runtime); every path is canonicalised and confined to the configured root before any I/O, enforced inside the embeddable chisel-core library including embedded use; bearer-token auth, 127.0.0.1-only binding, read-only mode, rate limiting and audit logging round out a security model the README documents attack by attack.
bad: No licence anywhere at source after four routes, so the code is all-rights-reserved and ideas-only regardless of merit. It is also young (16 commits), and its standalone server is an HTTP transport guarded by a bearer secret — a wider exposure than a stdio door, mitigated but not removed by the localhost binding.
took: Two ideas boarded from the design only: a compile-time-fixed command whitelist that the model cannot extend at runtime, and confinement enforced in the embeddable core so every host inherits it.
didnt: Board — the fixed-whitelist plus core-enforced confinement pattern is worth carrying into our gateway's tool design; the code itself is no-licence and stays untouched (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: colapsis/transfa
good: Transfer hygiene done properly: uploads carry a SHA-256, a TTL, optional password protection and download limits, exposed uniformly through a CLI, an API and an MCP server, and the same code can be self-hosted by anyone who wants the custody back.
bad: The default path is the vendor's custody: no-account guest uploads go to transfa.sh's servers, so a file leaves the machine before the link exists, and the useful tiers are paid (Pro $12/mo, Team $48/mo per the README). Self-hosting exists but is not the product being sold.
didnt: Rejected — ephemeral agent file transfer through a hosted third party contradicts our local-first custody; our sharing runs through storage we control (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: convertica-net/convertica-mcp
licence: MIT (covers the wrapper only; the conversion service is a closed subscription API)
good: An honest thin wrapper: two tools, 35+ converters behind them, and the README states plainly that files are deleted from Convertica's servers right after the response — the egress is at least disclosed rather than hidden.
bad: Every conversion happens over HTTPS on Convertica's servers, so documents leave the machine by design; the server is useless without a paid subscription key, usage is metered against plan quota, and the wrapper itself is embryonic (12 commits, 0 stars). The MIT licence covers the two-tool shell, not the service doing the work.
didnt: Rejected — hosted metered document conversion is document egress as a business model; our conversions run locally (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cyberchitta/llm-context.py
good: Context curation that shows its work before anything is sent: the agent authors composable rules (prm-/flt-/ins-/sty-/exc-), lc-preview reports the exact file list and size, and the code graph flags files that define symbols the selection uses but does not include; packs carry a timestamp that lc-missing and lc-changed resolve against, so drift is checkable. The README states plainly 'A pack is always partial', and the pack header reports full/outlined/excerpted counts so a consumer can verify what it actually received.
bad: It is a code-context packer, not a knowledge store — nothing here governs custody, citation or approval — and its real documentation lives in the installed agent skill rather than the README, so the artefact a human can audit at the repo is thinner than the tool itself. Partiality is honest but structural: every consumer works from an excerpt whether it checks the header counts or not.
took: Corroboration for two of our habits: preview the exact set before it is used, and label partiality in the artefact itself (counts of full vs outlined vs excerpted) instead of letting a partial pack pass as the whole.
didnt: Not adopted — our index-first retrieval already selects context from the wiki; studied for its preview-and-partiality labelling (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dabito/hledit-mcp
good: The stale-write problem solved at the anchor: reads annotate each line LN#HASH, and before any write the hash at the anchor is recomputed — if the file changed underneath, the write is rejected with a stale error and a remap hint, and no write happens. The demo is a deterministic transcript produced by a script driving the real MCP surface, so the evidence offered is the tool's actual behaviour, not a mock-up.
bad: Embryonic (16 commits, 1 star) and deliberately narrow — one tool, no wider file management — so the anchor discipline is proven on a small surface only; a hash check also cannot judge whether the intervening change matters, only that it happened.
took: One mechanism noted: reject the write and return a remap hint when the anchor's hash has moved — the compare-at-write refusal our guarded write doors already practice, in its smallest form.
didnt: Corroboration — hash-anchored stale-write refusal is our own write discipline stated minimally; nothing to adopt from a 16-commit single-tool server (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: denis-samatov/yandex-workspace-mcp
good: The most carefully gated connector in this batch: read-only by default with separate read/write/delete permission flags per service; ALLOWED_ROOTS checked before any call and post-filtered on results; a structured audit log of write and destructive operations; the global destructive operation absent unless root '/', an explicit flag and a literal confirm=true coincide; page deletion returns a random, expiring (15-minute), principal-bound, single-use recovery handle with the upstream token encrypted at rest; search fallback results are explicitly marked degraded=true; invalid or stale cursors fail closed; and an enabled service with no allowed roots fails startup rather than running wide open. Its tool-exposure policy is tested, including a negative control.
bad: It serves the Yandex ecosystem (Disk and Wiki), which is not our stack, and it is brand new (33 commits, 0 stars), so the elaborate gate design has almost no field history behind it yet.
took: Three mechanisms recorded as corroboration for our gateway: degradation marked in the result rather than hidden, destructive recovery as a random expiring single-use handle bound to the principal, and fail-closed startup when a service is enabled without roots.
didnt: Corroboration — its permission-flag, allowlist and audit design independently matches our gateway's default-deny posture; the connector itself targets a platform we do not use (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dimitar-grigorov/mcp-file-tools
good: It solves the silent-corruption problem of legacy text properly: encoding is detected from the bytes rather than the extension, the model is handed UTF-8, and writes go back in the original encoding with BOM and CRLF/LF line endings intact — every tool is encoding-aware, and the sandbox resolves symlink and junction targets before the allowed-directory check. Mature by this wave's standards (398 commits, 41 releases).
bad: GPL-3.0, so the code is ideas-only for us. The source also disagrees with itself on a headline number — the repo description claims 24 encodings while the README body claims 45 — recorded here rather than resolved, and a warning against quoting either figure without checking the code.
took: One idea noted: detect a file's encoding from its bytes, never its extension, and round-trip writes in the original encoding with BOM and line endings preserved.
didnt: Corroboration — byte-first encoding detection with faithful round-trip writes confirms how legacy corpora should be handled; GPL-3.0 keeps the code itself ideas-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dissimilis/DirForge
good: Read-only as an architecture, not a setting: no database, no background workers, no disk writes, and the same tree served through a web UI, a REST API, a read-only S3-compatible endpoint, a read-only WebDAV endpoint (write methods return 405) and an MCP endpoint; signed and one-time share links, sidecar checksum verification (.md5/.sha1/.sha256/.sha512/.sfv), and downloads denied by extension with env/key/pem defaults.
bad: The README warns against its own defaults: the compose file falls back to admin/dirforge credentials if unset, and the baseline configuration is described by its own author as 'homelab-oriented, not internet-hardened' — safe on a LAN, unsafe to expose as shipped.
took: Corroboration for our read door: one tree, several read-only surfaces, write methods refused at the protocol level rather than merely unadvertised.
didnt: Not adopted — our MCP read door and Lens already serve the wiki read-only; studied for its one-tree-many-surfaces shape (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: drolosoft/go-docs-mcp
good: A read-only document door in a single Go binary: 13 tools over PDF/TXT/MD/DOCX/CSV/images, directory-locked with path-traversal prevention, OCR fallback via tesseract, table and image extraction, and an mtime-based cache so unchanged documents are not reparsed; even its read_url tool is capped at 50 MB.
bad: Young (28 commits, 11 stars), and read_url is the one crack in the read-only posture — a tool that fetches remote content into the corpus needs the SSRF and provenance care the README does not dwell on; the mtime cache can also serve a stale parse when a file's content changes without its timestamp moving.
took: Corroboration for our document door: directory-locked, read-only, with extraction and OCR behind the same confined surface.
didnt: Not adopted — our ingest pipeline covers these formats; studied as a clean small example of a confined reader (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: efforthye/fast-filesystem-mcp
good: Large-file handling taken seriously: stream-based writes for files of any size, chunked and sequential reads with continuation tokens, pagination for big directories, precise block-level editing tools, and a large-write path with integrity verification and retry with exponential backoff — all confined to allowed directories, which the server can list on request.
bad: The safety story is weaker than the feature story: the surface includes delete, move, batch operations and directory sync, yet backup creation — advertised under 'Backup & Recovery' — is off by default (CREATE_BACKUP_FILES=false) and otherwise per-call, and the README describes no approval or confirmation gate before destructive operations. Speed is the design centre; restraint is opt-in.
didnt: Not adopted — our file access runs through narrower doors with approval gates; a broad fast write surface with backups off by default runs against that posture (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ellmos-ai/ellmos-filecommander-mcp
good: Fifty tools with the invariants written down as a contract: local stdio with zero telemetry and egress only through an explicit caller-invoked web fetch; content search bounded (max 50 explicit files, 10 MB per file, match and character caps) with API keys and tokens automatically masked in excerpts; metadata-first preview with a 1 MiB inline ceiling; safe delete routed to the Recycle Bin/Trash; and a cloud-lock fallback that copies, SHA-256-verifies, then unlinks when sync filters block a rename. It ships 306 tests and a Level 1 SBOM, and publishes a 48-hour security-response SLA.
bad: Its own Security section states the cost plainly: the server has full filesystem access with the running user's permissions, includes an arbitrary shell-command tool and interactive sessions, performs permanent deletion by default (safe mode is opt-in and does not cover commands or sessions), and has 'no built-in sandboxing — security is delegated to the MCP client layer'. The invariants bound the file tools; the shell tools sit outside them.
took: Two invariants recorded: mask secrets in search excerpts before they can reach context, and make cloud-locked moves copy + hash-verify + unlink rather than fail or force.
didnt: Rejected as a door for our system — a 50-tool surface with an unsandboxed shell is the opposite of our narrow, scope-checked gateway, however well its file invariants are documented (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: exoticknight/mcp-file-merger
good: Deliberately minimal: one tool that merges any number of files into one output, access confined to directories the user allows (with a tool to list them), and a merge summary reporting file sizes — nothing else is claimed and nothing else is exposed.
bad: Minimal to the point of fragility as a dependency: 10 commits, no releases, and a single-purpose function (concatenation to fit chat length limits) that a shell one-liner replaces; merged output also strips the per-file provenance a citation-grade pipeline needs unless the caller rebuilds it.
didnt: Rejected — merging files to fit a chat window is a workaround our index-first retrieval does not need, and the merged artefact would lose the per-source boundaries our citations depend on (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ezpzfile/ezpzfile-mcp
good: Local-first document tooling with rare-format reach: everything runs on the user's machine and 'no file is ever uploaded'; six consolidated tools (related jobs share one tool, an argument picks between them — a deliberate defence against tool definitions eating context) cover reading and converting DOCX, PDF, HWP, HWPX, EML and the Japanese JTD and XDW formats most toolkits ignore, plus PDF editing, image cleanup with EXIF/GPS stripping, background removal and QR codes. Its benchmark is a measured same-task comparison with per-message figures, dated and presented as a floor rather than a ceiling.
bad: Weeks old (created 2026-09-12, 9 commits) and not really an open development repo: it is a read-only export regenerated from a private monorepo (issues, not pull requests), and the HWP/JTD/XDW engines and fonts are kept out of git and ship inside the npm package, so the code you can audit is not the whole artefact you run; background removal also downloads a model and runtime on first use — disclosed, and uploads nothing, but a network touch in an otherwise offline tool.
took: Noted as candidate-shaped corroboration for the wiki's document queue: fully local rare-format reading (HWP/JTD/XDW) exists as an MCP surface, with its export-only provenance recorded alongside.
didnt: Board — local rare-format document conversion is a candidate for our document/OCR queue; adoption would need the npm-package-only engines weighed first, since the auditable repo is an export (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FacundoLucci/plsreadme
licence: MIT (the sharing service itself is the author's hosted deployment on Cloudflare)
good: Sharing with a revision conscience: paste markdown, get a rendered plsrd.me link with inline paragraph comments, a version timeline whose restore is archive-first and non-destructive, and a review mode that defaults to the current draft with history on demand; anonymous docs are owned through an admin_token, signed-in users can claim legacy links by proving that token, and the limits are published in the README (200 KB maximum document, 30 uploads/hour, permanent link lifetime).
bad: The custody is the vendor's: shared documents live in the author's Cloudflare R2/D1 deployment under their domain, so a 'permanent' link lasts exactly as long as that service does; and the local .plsreadme record file stores the admin tokens for everything you have shared in your project root — the README itself has to warn users to gitignore it, since a committed copy hands out edit/delete rights to every shared doc.
took: Corroboration for our sharing design: archive-first restore and a current-vs-timeline review split are how shared documents should behave; the token-in-project-root pattern is recorded as the counter-example.
didnt: Not adopted — our documents are shared through the owner-only Lens, not a third-party link service; studied for its versioning and restore discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FI-Mihej/text_file_read_and_refactor_mcp
good: Token-efficient editing with the addressing done properly: reads and searches work on character slices and on spans defined by boundaries (text, word, dev-word or regex), so an agent can ask for 'the text between this marker and that one' or replace exactly that span instead of shipping whole files; every file's BOM and codepage is resolved automatically and edit tools save with the original encoding and BOM preserved. Read-only and edit tools are kept as separate named sets.
bad: The public repo is a curated mirror: the README states active development (including experimental code and private research notes) happens in a private repository and selected snapshots are published periodically, so the auditable artefact lags the real one. It is also tiny (8 commits, 1 star) and built on the author's own Cengal framework, an extra dependency of trust.
took: Corroboration for our editing discipline: address content by boundaries and slices rather than whole-file rewrites, and never let a save silently change a file's encoding or BOM.
didnt: Not adopted — our editors already do boundary-anchored edits; studied for the span-addressing and encoding-preservation design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: filesystem@quarkiverse/quarkus-mcp-servers
licence: Apache-2.0 (parent repo root LICENSE; the item is a directory inside quarkiverse/quarkus-mcp-servers)
good: A community filesystem MCP server from the Quarkus ecosystem (parent project: 197 stars, nine sibling servers): access is scoped by the paths passed at launch, jbang runs it with no manual Java install, and a native-image build makes startup near-instant; the server lists, reads and modifies files inside the granted paths only.
bad: The directory README is thin — it never enumerates the tools or states any read-only mode, confirmation behaviour or symlink handling, so the safety surface cannot be judged from its own page beyond path scoping; and it grants modify access, not just reads, within those paths.
didnt: Not adopted — a Java-stack general filesystem server adds nothing over our existing doors; recorded as the Quarkus ecosystem's reference implementation (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GuruPDF/gurupdf-mcp
licence: MIT (covers the wrapper only; the conversion service is a closed credit-metered API)
good: Breadth behind a small surface: 126 conversion/OCR/edit operations (PDF ⇄ Office, images, ebooks, compress, merge, split, protect, watermark) exposed through just four MCP tools including job status and a credit check, reading and writing local paths so the agent never handles manual upload/download.
bad: The headline sells local conversion ('right on your own machine', 'works on your local files'), but its own Free tier section states 'Conversions run on GuruPDF's servers; files are deleted automatically within an hour' — the local framing and the server reality sit on the same page, discrepancy recorded rather than resolved. Usage is credit-metered (free accounts: 2 conversions/minute, 10/day), and the MIT licence covers the wrapper, not the service.
didnt: Rejected — hosted credit-metered conversion behind a local-sounding headline is exactly the custody ambiguity our document pipeline refuses (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hmk/box-mcp-server
good: A straightforward community Box connector: search files and read them (PDF, Word and others) over MCP, with two documented auth routes — JWT app auth for a persistent connection, or a short-lived developer token for a quick start — and the credential carried as a base64 env value rather than a file path.
bad: The auth burden is enterprise-grade: the recommended JWT route needs a paid Box enterprise or developer account, an admin-authorised application with App + Enterprise Access and the as-user header enabled, while the easy route is a developer token that lasts 60 minutes. The capability itself is narrow — search and read only, per the README's own list.
didnt: Not adopted — Box is not our storage platform and our Drive custody runs through our own connector; recorded as the community Box reader (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: isaacphi/mcp-gdrive
good: One of the original MCP samples (it credits code originally developed by Anthropic) and still the common ancestor of many Drive servers: search, read files as resources with Workspace files auto-exported (Docs → Markdown, Sheets → CSV, Presentations → text, Drawings → PNG), read Sheets ranges, and update a single cell.
bad: An early sample that stayed one: 11 commits since December 2024, no releases, build artefacts and node_modules committed to the repo, and setup requires creating your own Google Cloud project and OAuth client. The permission shape is also lopsided — Drive is read-only-scoped while Sheets gets the full spreadsheets scope so a single-cell update tool can write anywhere in any sheet the account can reach.
didnt: Not adopted — our Drive work runs through our own connector under the organise-only boundary; recorded as a widely-forked early reference (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: j0hanz/filesystem-context-mcp-server
good: Safety defaults that outrun the reference server, in a heavily-maintained package (2,327 commits, 88 releases): access confined to chosen folders with symlinks resolved before the check; .env files, private keys and cloud credentials blocked by default; the server asks before deleting a non-empty folder, opening an unallowed folder, or overwriting via create/move; --read-only removes every write tool outright; edits are exact-match and all-or-nothing with dryRun diff previews; search uses RE2 (a regex engine that cannot hang), respects .gitignore, and stat returns a token estimate before a read. No telemetry, no network calls.
bad: The catalogue description is stale: this is no longer a read-only exploration server but a full read/search/edit server — judged here on what the source shows. Within that design, content edits (edit, patch, replace_text) apply without asking — dryRun diffs are available but optional — and create/move's confirmation can be bypassed per-call with overwrite: true, so the human gate covers deletion and overwrite but not ordinary edits.
took: Corroboration for our door defaults: block secret-shaped files by default, make read-only a mode that removes write tools rather than a promise, and let a caller price a read (size/token estimate) before paying for it.
didnt: Not adopted — our own MCP read door is deliberately read-only and our writes go through the gateway's approval flow; studied as the strongest safety-defaults example in this wave (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jamalofski/conv2pdf-mcp
licence: MIT (covers the server only; the conversion API is a closed metered service)
good: The most honestly documented hosted converter in this wave: files are processed on OVHcloud servers in France with 'no transfer outside the EU, no US service in the chain'; nothing is ever overwritten (results land beside the input with a suffix, a taken name becomes 'report (2).pdf', and an existing output_path is refused before anything converts); jobs are deleted from the server once the result lands, with a one-hour fallback; and the quota rules are stated in the open, including the ungenerous parts — a conversion conv2pdf refuses after reading the file still counts, one refused on arrival does not. The server itself is dependency-free and tests run against a fake API with no key and no network.
bad: The conversion itself is still hosted egress — files go to a third party's servers, EU-only or not — and it is metered (the Dev plan's 300 free conversions last 12 months; files capped at 10 MB on Dev) with a brand-new codebase (11 commits, created 2026-10-04, 0 stars) between the user and that service.
took: One standard recorded: a hosted tool earns consideration only when it publishes its overwrite, deletion, quota and retry behaviour the way this README does — behaviour stated in advance, not discovered in use.
didnt: Rejected for adoption — hosted conversion remains document egress; its behaviour documentation is boarded as the standard a hosted tool would have to meet to be considered at all (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jeannier/homebrew-mcp
good: Complete brew coverage in one small Python file: install/uninstall/upgrade/cleanup, list/search/info/outdated/deps, doctor/update, tap management, pin/unpin and services, run as real brew commands via subprocess over stdio, with every request and result logged to homebrew_mcp.log.
bad: It hands the model system mutation with no gate described anywhere in the README: no confirmation step, no allowlist of packages, no read-only mode — the same channel that runs brew doctor runs brew uninstall. macOS-only, and a 3-commit single file, so the convenience is exactly as durable as its one script.
didnt: Rejected — an agent channel that can install and uninstall system packages without an approval gate is the anti-pattern our gateway exists to prevent (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: juergenkoller-software/distill-mcp
licence: MIT (covers the bridge only; the Distill app it drives is commercial, credit-metered)
good: Renaming with the safety pieces present: suggest_names previews without renaming, revert_rename undoes, and get_rename_history records timestamps, before/after and which AI provider named each file; the bridge is open source expressly so the wire format can be audited while the app stays closed, and one refusal is correctly agent-proof — the app's legal texts must be accepted by the user in the app window (HTTP 403 legal_not_accepted), a step the README states an agent cannot perform.
bad: The bridge is a shell around a commercial dependency: it needs the Distill app (macOS 15+, direct-download version only — the Mac App Store build has neither API nor MCP) installed and running, the default provider is the vendor's credit-metered Distill Cloud (content leaves the machine unless the user switches to BYO keys or local Ollama), and folder monitoring renames new files in the background once enabled. The MIT licence covers the bridge; everything that does the work is closed.
took: One pattern credited: a consent step the agent structurally cannot perform on the user's behalf, returning a refusal that names the human action required — the shape our own owner-only steps take.
didnt: Not adopted — macOS-app-bound and credit-metered, and automatic background renaming runs against our organise-only, approval-first file boundaries (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kookerella-Ltd/Kookerella.FsOpenXmlDsl
licence: MIT (parent repo root LICENSE; the item is the Mcp directory inside Kookerella-Ltd/Kookerella.FsOpenXmlDsl)
good: A spreadsheet decompiler, not just a writer: any existing .xlsx/.xlsm can be read back and handed over as runnable F# or C# source that rebuilds an equivalent file, or as XML/JSON against real schemas (Xml.xsd / Json.schema.json) whose deterministic ordering makes a workbook git-diffable. Round-trip fidelity is a tested guarantee — build, save, read back, identical structure, validated against the OOXML schema in the library's own test suite — and it runs purely locally over stdio with no Excel install and no hosted service.
bad: The simple tools are deliberately narrow — create_workbook/read_workbook handle plain cell values and formulas only — and there is no formula evaluation engine anywhere in the stack, so generated formula cells carry no cached value until real Excel opens the file; the JSON direction also ships without runtime schema validation, a gap the README explains (it would force a JsonSchema.Net dependency on every consumer) rather than hides. The project is young (parent repo created 2026-08-23).
took: Corroboration for our verification standard: round-trip fidelity claimed only where a test rebuilds the artefact and compares — the same shape as our verify-against-source rule for delivered files.
didnt: Not adopted — a .NET/F# dependency for spreadsheet work our pipeline does not need; studied for its round-trip-as-tested-guarantee standard (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: koraynar/doc-extract-mcp
good: Deterministic tooling around the model, with the failure modes named and engineered against: all file access confined to one allowed root (DOC_EXTRACT_ROOT) with traversal refused and symlink-escaping glob matches dropped; PDF text arrives with explicit '--- page N ---' markers 'so citations of page 3 mean page 3'; chunking is deterministic with overlap and page hints; validate_json returns every schema error with its JSON Pointer path, not just the first, so the model can fix all mistakes in one pass; and output is written by the server, inside the root, with a verifiable row/byte count. Guard failures surface the actual reason to the model instead of a masked generic error.
bad: By its own honest accounting: text-based PDFs only (no OCR, so scanned PDFs yield empty text), no .docx/.xlsx, extraction quality hostage to pypdf's reading order, and 'new and has no production mileage yet… not been hardened beyond that — review before pointing it at sensitive directories'. Two commits and 0 stars; a well-built portfolio piece, not a proven tool.
took: Two habits recorded as corroboration: page markers that make a page citation mean the page, and validators that return every error with its path in one pass rather than failing one mistake at a time.
didnt: Not adopted — our ingest pipeline already extracts with OCR in scope; recorded as an exemplar of deterministic tooling around a model (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: L-Jovi/keyhole
good: The careful way to let a hosted model touch local files: folders are opened by the local CLI only and 'nothing ChatGPT does can widen its own access'; read-only is the default and rw is an explicit local command; every edit requires the file's current SHA-256 (stale-hash updates are refused), the previous content is recorded in an owner-only local history before the file is touched, individual replacements are atomic, and restore_change rolls a change back without overwriting later edits. Secret-shaped names (.ssh, .env*, *.key, credentials.json) are hidden at any depth, symlinks and hard links are refused with paths opened component-by-component under O_NOFOLLOW, every response states when it was truncated, nothing is shared after a reboot until the owner resumes it — and the README is candid about the residue: 'hiding by file name is not secret detection… anything already sent to ChatGPT cannot be recalled by closing the folder'. It reaches the local machine through OpenAI's official Secure MCP Tunnel: outbound long-poll only, no public port, no shell.
bad: Bound to one vendor's surface: it exists to serve ChatGPT (Pro with Developer mode), requires the user to create their own OpenAI tunnel and private app (~15 minutes of setup after account access), and its document parsers 'run with your OS permissions; they are not an OS sandbox' by its own statement. The recovery history is bounded (1,000 records / 450 MiB) and eviction or purge removes replay protection with it — 'history is not a permanent audit log'.
took: Boarded as design evidence for the hosted door: owner-held grants the model cannot widen, hash-checked recoverable edits, and an honest statement of what cannot be recalled once sent.
didnt: Board — its grant and recovery model is direct evidence for the hosted-door decision, which remains the owner's Tier C call; nothing built or decided here (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LincolnBurrows2017/filesystem-mcp
good: A compact Python filesystem server with the basics in place: read/write/list/search/copy/move over nine tools, all operations restricted to one specified root directory, a 1 MB cap on file reads, and an optional --readonly mode that disables writes.
bad: Minimal and unproven: 2 commits, no releases, and the security model is three bullets — no symlink handling, no secret-file blocking, no confirmation before delete_file removes a file or directory; the default mode is read-write, with restraint available only as an opt-in flag.
didnt: Rejected — a 2-commit generic filesystem server adds nothing over the stronger doors already studied in this wave (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ltspace/dowse
licence: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual, at the user's option)
good: Local search with the index treated as the asset: file names, document contents (PDF/Office/code) and OCR'd screenshot text in one persistent tantivy index, fully local with no network and no telemetry, incremental updates via file-watch plus startup mtime/size reconciliation. Its MCP server is read-only by construction — four tools (search, preview, read_file_chunk, index_status) that 'never touch the index writer or open arbitrary paths', reloading the reader before each call so it can run beside the live app. The benchmark table is a model of the genre: design targets printed beside measured values, rows that were not measured say 'not measured', and too-fast repeat OCR readings are named as OS caching artefacts and excluded.
bad: Windows-only, and a full-disk content index is a sensitive corpus by design — the privacy answer is that it never leaves the machine, which the user must trust or verify via the suggested firewall check. The installer is unsigned (SmartScreen flags it; the author explains the certificate cost rather than hiding it), and the roadmap admits the NTFS admin fast path is 'not yet verified on real hardware'.
took: Corroboration for our evaluation reporting: publish the target beside the measurement, mark the unmeasured as unmeasured, and exclude flattering artefacts by name — plus a read-only MCP face over a live index as the safe way to expose local search.
didnt: Not adopted — Windows-only desktop search is outside our stack; studied for its read-only MCP posture and its benchmark reporting (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mamertofabian/mcp-everything-search
good: One search tool over the fastest native index on each platform — Everything's SDK on Windows, Spotlight's mdfind on macOS, locate/plocate on Linux — with the platform asymmetry handled honestly: the tool advertises only the current platform's parameter object in its schema, unreadable matches on Windows are omitted with a warning that counts them ('N matching result(s) could not be read and were omitted'), and failures return an error result whose text starts 'Search failed:' rather than an empty list. The most-adopted item in this batch (367 stars).
bad: It is a filename index, not a content index — content search exists only on macOS via Spotlight, and Linux depends on the locate database's freshness. There is also no allowed-directory scoping on Windows or Linux (only macOS gets a search_directory limit), so the tool discloses paths across the whole disk to the model by design.
took: One habit recorded: when some matches cannot be read, return the readable ones plus a counted warning — partial results labelled as partial, never silently trimmed.
didnt: Not adopted — our wiki search is content- and citation-aware over a known corpus; a whole-disk filename index answers a different question (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MarceauSolutions/md-to-pdf-mcp
licence: MIT (stated in the README's License section only; no LICENSE file at root and the repo metadata is silent)
good: Markdown to PDF on weasyprint + markdown2 + pygments — the same engine family as our own report pipeline — behind three MCP tools (convert_markdown_to_pdf, extract_toc, get_default_styles): automatic table of contents with clickable links, batch conversion of multiple files, and custom CSS styling.
bad: One commit and 8 stars — a wrapper, not a maintained project. Its README's Project Structure section describes a src/ layout and files (VERSION, CHANGELOG.md, SKILL.md, a testing/ directory) that do not exist in the actual root listing (a md_to_pdf_mcp package directory, README.md, pyproject.toml, server.json) — the documentation describes a tree the repo does not contain, discrepancy recorded rather than resolved.
didnt: Not adopted — our report pipeline already drives weasyprint directly; a 1-commit wrapper adds a dependency and no capability (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mark3labs/mcp-filesystem-server
good: The reference filesystem server's semantics reimplemented in Go (692 stars, 14 releases): access confined to allowed directories with path validation and symlink resolution checked for security, inline size limits on responses, and the server also usable as an embeddable Go library.
bad: The full reference surface includes write and delete tools, and the README describes no confirmation behaviour — confinement is the only gate. A general filesystem door is in any case broader than our wiki-scoped, read-only MCP door.
didnt: Not adopted — our MCP read door is deliberately read-only and wiki-scoped; recorded as the Go port of the reference server (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mickaelkerjean/filestash
licence: AGPL-3.0 (parent repo root LICENSE; the item is a plugin directory inside mickaelkerjean/filestash) — ideas only
good: A mature file manager (parent repo: 2,547 commits, 14,816 stars) whose plugin model is the interesting part: runtime wasm plugins run under declared permissions ('no declared network host, no way to phone home'), authorisation plugins return a per-operation Allow/Deny decision, and one interface fronts many backends (FTP/SFTP/S3/WebDAV/SMB/Git/NFS and more) — the MCP plugin exposes that configured storage to agents through the same plugin seam.
bad: AGPL-3.0 puts the code itself in ideas-only territory for us. On the merits, the storage backend interface the plugin fronts includes Rm/Mv/Save, so agent access inherits write and delete operations against whatever remote storage and credentials the operator configured in Filestash — breadth set by configuration, not by the tool.
didnt: Not adopted — AGPL-3.0 (ideas only), and a general remote-storage agent door is far broader than our wiki-scoped doors; the declared-permission plugin model is noted in the row (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: microsoft/markitdown
good: One tool, convert_to_markdown(uri), over STDIO, Streamable HTTP or SSE on top of Microsoft's MarkItDown converter; binds localhost by default. The README's Security Considerations section is candid: the server has no authentication, runs with the privileges of the user running it, and can read any file that user can access or any network data it can reach.
bad: That candour is also the warning: no authentication at all, so on any non-localhost bind the door is as wide as the running user's own access — the README itself says 'DO NOT bind the server to other interfaces… unless you understand the security implications'.
didnt: Board — aligned with the earlier study of this same project: the single-tool convert_to_markdown front-end stands as an ingest option, with its no-auth warning kept attached (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem
licence: Apache-2.0 for new contributions, existing code under MIT (README licence section; GitHub sidebar shows Other/NOASSERTION)
good: The reference filesystem server, tightened since the earlier study: allowed directories come from command-line arguments (the Roots mechanism is deprecated, kept for 2025-era clients), at least one allowed directory is required and the server refuses to serve without one; every tool carries a published annotation row (readOnlyHint / idempotentHint / destructiveHint, openWorldHint false throughout); read-only files are refused rather than replaced, and edit_file offers dryRun diffs while preserving line endings and indentation.
bad: Still a full read/write/delete surface whose safety rests on the operator's allowed-directory arguments; and write_file overwrites in place — the README itself discloses that the overwrite 'is not crash-atomic'.
didnt: Corroboration — aligned with the earlier study: allowed-directory scoping with at least one directory required is the baseline door shape; this pass adds the per-tool annotation table as the labelling standard a door should publish (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Regan-Milne/obsideo-mcp
licence: PolyForm Shield 1.0.0 from v0.6.2 (LICENSE file at root; repo metadata shows Other/NOASSERTION) — a custom non-compete licence, ideas only; versions up to 0.6.1 were MIT, and the storage provider node remains MIT
good: Encrypted object storage with the verification done properly: client-side AES-256-GCM encryption by default before upload, objects replicated to three providers, and chunk-level merkle possession proofs run on a continuous cycle with providers paid only for proofs they pass; the verify tool challenges providers against the merkle root recorded locally at upload time (roots.json), states which trust inputs it relied on, and reports failures first. Keys live only in ~/.obsideo and backup_keys refuses without an explicit destination. Agent payment discipline is structural: upgrade only returns a Stripe checkout link for the human to pay — 'an existing plan is never resized from this server'. A first put auto-creates a free no-email trial account (100 MB, proof-of-work instead of identity); 12 GB free with email signup.
bad: Custody is third-party even though content is encrypted: objects sit with three storage providers and a coordinator chooses the providers and keys, and the README is blunt that a lost encryption key makes every object permanently unreadable. PolyForm Shield is a custom non-compete licence (ideas only), and the project is brand new (0 stars, created 2026-07-19). Its README also carries an agent-addressed setup runbook (the Hermes section, pointing the agent at a hosted page to fetch and execute) — recorded as a pattern to recognise, not a route to take.
took: Corroboration for two owner-boundary shapes: a payment step the agent structurally cannot complete (it can only hand the human a checkout link), and a verification result that states the trust inputs it relied on instead of claiming trustlessness.
didnt: Not adopted — the custom PolyForm Shield licence makes it ideas-only, and third-party custody of our backups is not our model; studied for its proof-of-possession verification and its payment boundary (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Synexiom-Labs/nodiom-mcp
good: Structural Markdown editing for agents: seven tools (tree, read, read_list, write, append, delete, query) addressed by structural selectors — heading paths such as '# Project > ## Tasks', list items by index or by content match — instead of regex or line numbers. A content selector must match exactly one item and keeps pointing at the same item when others are added or removed; YAML/TOML frontmatter is preserved and never treated as a heading; unmatched selectors return fuzzy 'Did you mean' suggestions instead of silence.
bad: Embryonic (7 commits, no releases) and the confinement story is absent: tools take absolute file paths with no allowed-root restriction described, and the delete tool has no confirmation behaviour described. The README also upsells the hosted Nodiom Cloud sibling.
took: One addressing property recorded: a content-matched selector keeps pointing at the same item when neighbours are added or removed — structural identity over positional identity, the same direction as our boundary-anchored edits.
didnt: Not adopted — 7 commits and no described path confinement; studied alongside B112's geml and B123's frontmatter editing as the structural-addressing line (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TrendTweekers/mintpdf
good: HTML/Markdown to PDF via Chromium, as a REST API and an MCP server (generate_pdf, pdf_from_url), and fully self-hostable under MIT with a published image whose CI smoke-tests the image by rendering a real PDF. Its Security section is exemplary: SSRF is blocked at two independent layers (the submitted URL is resolved pre-flight, and every Chromium request is re-resolved at request time), the guard 'caches only refusals, never approvals', unresolvable names fail closed, and addresses are judged from bytes, not text spellings, with IPv4-mapped forms handled. Rendered files are deleted after an hour and contents are never logged; admission control is measured and published (RENDER_CONCURRENCY/QUEUE, 503 with Retry-After, a burst table), as are the limits (anonymous 3 renders/day, free key 100/month, paid tiers $19/$49/$129).
bad: The author states the residue himself: DNS rebinding is 'a narrowed race rather than a closed door', and download links are unauthenticated by design — 'the link is the secret'. The hosted default sends documents to mintpdf.dev, and the Limitations section admits the service was 'two days old at the time of writing, with no paying users yet', is single-instance (SQLite keys/quotas), and has no Office formats or merge/split (it points to Gotenberg).
took: One standard recorded: an SSRF guard that caches only refusals, never approvals — a refusal is stable, while an approval expires with the DNS answer it rested on.
didnt: Not adopted — our report pipeline renders locally with weasyprint and needs no hosted renderer; studied as the SSRF and admission-control standard for any URL-fetching tool (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: UseJunior/safe-docx
good: The batch's mature outlier (772 commits, 37 releases): a local MCP server and CLI for reading, searching, editing, comparing and converting DOCX/ODT files with document structure preserved. A targeted edit produces both a clean copy and a tracked-changes copy for review, and 'the rest of the document stays outside the requested edit'. Conformance is treated as a published artefact: a Conformance Explorer navigates ECMA-376 sections, capability claims, explicit non-goals and measured cross-implementation outcomes, with the generated conformance report kept source-controlled in the repo.
bad: By its own statement it is not a visual editor or layout engine: no browser rendering, no real-time collaboration, no pixel-level pagination guarantees, and .dotx templates must be converted to .docx before use. Our own deliverables are generated PDFs, so the editing gap it fills is narrow for us despite its quality.
took: Boarded as design evidence for the document-editing queue: every edit ships a clean copy and a tracked-changes copy side by side, and conformance is published as claims beside explicit non-goals and measured outcomes.
didnt: Not adopted — our document pipeline is PDF-first and our reports are generated rather than edited in place; boarded for its dual-output edit pattern and its conformance standard (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: velyan/pdf-card-mcp
good: Local-first conversion of a PDF into a portable, source-linked card-based HTML reader: source text preserved, source pages rendered for verification, tables, figures and display formulas kept as faithful image crops, and a manifest.json carrying cards, pages, warnings and source anchors. Notes and highlights are user-authored data kept separate from the source manifest and exportable as Markdown; publishing includes only public annotations by default, redacts the local source path by default, renders read-only, and fails if an included annotation cannot be anchored. MCP sampling is deliberately bounded: the host model may choose validated style tokens or suggest card-boundary polish, but raw CSS and source-text rewrites are rejected, and the sampling postprocess validates exact source-text preservation.
bad: Early and self-described as such ('an early open-source implementation', 32 commits, 2 stars): best on text-layer PDFs, table detection is best-effort (pdfplumber, or gmft as an optional extra), and scanned PDFs need optional OCR support bolted on.
took: Corroboration for bounded model discretion: let the host model choose from validated tokens and reject raw styling or any source-text rewrite outright — discretion inside a validated envelope, with the source text untouchable.
didnt: Not adopted — our reading surfaces are the wiki and its Lens; recorded as a reader-design study (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: willianpinho/large-file-mcp
good: Read-only large-file handling done cleanly: six tools (chunk read, regex search with context lines, file structure, line navigation, summary, streaming) that stream files of any size line-by-line without loading them into memory, with per-file-type chunk sizes and an LRU cache. Performance is reported honestly: a measured latency table from a published benchmark script on named hardware (Apple M1 Pro), the larger tiers explicitly not benchmarked with the reason stated, and the cache caveat printed beside the flattering number — hit-rate 'depends entirely on your access pattern', 95% only on the documented hot-chunk workload.
bad: Tools take absolute file paths with no allowed-directory confinement described — read-only by tool set, but the whole filesystem is in reading scope. It is also line-oriented text only: no document or binary structure awareness.
took: Corroboration for our evaluation reporting: publish the measured tiers, name the unmeasured ones, and print the caveat beside the flattering number.
didnt: Not adopted — our corpus reads are wiki-scoped through our own doors; recorded as a clean read-only large-file design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Xuanwo/mcp-server-opendal
good: One list/read surface over many storage backends through Apache OpenDAL (S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage and more), with automatic text/binary detection on reads; services are configured by OPENDAL_<ALIAS>_ environment variables and addressed as alias://path, so the same two tools reach every configured backend.
bad: A thin wrapper (9 commits): the breadth is OpenDAL's, not this server's. Credentials are carried in environment variables (with .env loading supported), so secret custody is entirely the operator's arrangement, and only list/read operations are documented.
didnt: Not adopted — a general storage-backend door is broader than our wiki-scoped doors, and our Drive custody runs through our own connector; recorded as the OpenDAL front-end (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: adhikasp/mcp-git-ingest
good: A minimal repo-reading server inspired by gitingest: github_directory_structure returns a Unicode tree of a repository and github_read_important_files returns named files' contents; clones land in a deterministic temp directory named from the repo URL's hash, an existing clone is reused, and cleanup runs in finally blocks so temp repos do not accumulate.
bad: The README's Usage section is a pasted model session transcript rather than tested documentation — its closing claims ('robust, flexible') are a model's narration of itself, recorded as such. Cloning arbitrary repositories on request is a network pull surface with no allowlist described, and the project is an early sample (13 commits, no releases).
didnt: Not adopted — our GitHub reading runs through the read-only connector and local mirrors under the owner's read-only rule; recorded as an early ingest sample (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: costajohnt/oss-autopilot
good: A contribution autopilot with the approval shape right: the daily check fetches your open PRs and classifies each (failing CI, changes requested, unanswered maintainer comment, conflict, or waiting on the maintainer), an agent drafts the reply or fix, and 'nothing is pushed or posted until you approve that specific action' — backed by a 'What it will and will not do on its own' section. Overnight mode prepares fix branches in local worktrees and writes a morning report; the unattended run starts with a tool allowlist plus a deny list blocking git push, gh pr comment, gh api and npm publish, and the README states the residue plainly: 'It is not a sandbox: the run executes each project's test suite with your credentials available.' The scheduler installer prints the launchctl command rather than loading it. Issue search vets candidates (already claimed? linked PR? does the repo merge outside contributions? maintainer response speed) and skips repos whose documents say they do not accept AI-assisted contributions; the scoring is explained in linked docs. Heavily shipped: 1,071 commits, 242 releases; also an MCP server (30 tools) and a standalone CLI.
bad: Claude Code-centric: the eight specialised agents exist only in the plugin (MCP and CLI users get the underlying data, not the agents), the default install posture is @latest auto-updating, and Windows is untested. Overnight mode executes each project's test suite with the user's credentials available — disclosed plainly, but a real trust grant.
took: Corroboration for our autonomy shape: per-action approval before anything is pushed or posted, a deny list and not just an allowlist for unattended runs, and the residual trust stated in the README instead of smoothed over.
didnt: Not adopted — it manages a personal open-source contribution workflow we do not run; studied for its approval flow and unattended-run discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: daniloneto/bitbucket-mcp
good: A Bitbucket Cloud PR-review server over stdio with the read/write split made explicit: read tools (repositories, PRs, diff, comments, commits, directory, file) and write tools (comment, approve, request changes) sit in separate README tables with the minimum token scopes named for each. Least privilege is enforced by the credential rather than by instruction: the Security note recommends a read-only scoped token for a first-pass subagent 'so approve/comment fail on permission rather than relying on prompt discipline'. It also documents the platform gotchas an implementer needs — app passwords in brownout since 2026-06-09 and removed 2026-07-28, and the HTTP Basic pair being email:token, since using the username fails with a silent 401.
bad: Brand new and unproven (2 commits, 0 stars), and the write tools (comment, approve, request changes) carry no confirmation step of their own — the token's scope is the only gate, which is the author's own point but leaves nothing behind it.
took: Corroboration for our door discipline: enforce a subagent's read-only posture in the credential's scope, so a forbidden action fails on permission instead of relying on the agent's discipline.
didnt: Not adopted — Bitbucket is not in our stack (GitHub and Azure DevOps are); recorded for its scope-as-enforcement note (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ddukbg/github-enterprise-mcp
licence: ISC (named only in the README's closing License section; no LICENSE file at root and the repo metadata is silent)
good: The GitHub Enterprise Server variant of the GitHub door: repositories, branches, contents, issues and PRs (including create and merge), Actions workflows, enterprise statistics, and enterprise-only user management, with the enterprise-only features flagged as such; the tools table names the PAT permission each tool needs. Runs over HTTP/SSE or stdio, with a Docker image defaulting to HTTP transport, and also works against github.com and Enterprise Cloud with the enterprise features degrading out.
bad: The management surface is as wide as it gets — repository create/update/delete, PR merge, Actions management, and enterprise user create/update/suspend — with no read-only mode, allowlist or confirmation behaviour described anywhere in the README; the token rides in environment variables and CLI arguments (--token). node_modules is committed to the repo.
didnt: Rejected — an ungated enterprise-admin channel is the opposite of our read-only GitHub posture; recorded as the Enterprise variant (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dockndevai/mcp-azure-devops
good: An Azure DevOps server (boards/work items, repos/PRs, pipelines, projects) whose governance model is the design: AZDO_MODE defaults to read-only and tools above the mode are never registered, not merely refused; a project allowlist refuses operations outside it; protected projects stay readable but never mutable; delete_project needs AZDO_ALLOW_DELETE and admin mode; typed confirmation requires confirm to equal the target's name, not a boolean; dry-run validates and logs intent; a JSON audit line is written per guarded operation; and destructive actions prompt the human via MCP elicitation, falling back to the flag gates when the client cannot elicit. Published on npm with SECURITY.md and governance tests in the repo.
bad: Brand new and unproven (23 commits, 1 star, created 2026-08-23), and an admin mode exists (create/delete project) even if it is triple-gated; the PAT rides in environment variables. The governance is config, so a careless config reopens everything the defaults close.
took: Boarded as design evidence for any Azure DevOps door: mode-gated tool registration (tools above the mode are never registered), protected projects that stay readable-but-never-mutable, and typed confirmation — the confirm value must equal the target's name, not a boolean.
didnt: Board — its governance model is direct evidence for how an agent should be let near our Azure DevOps org; nothing connected or configured here, and any adoption stays the owner's call (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Doucs91/hivelore
good: A deterministic policy gate for agent-written code: a .ai/ layer in the repo holds decisions, gotchas and failed attempts as Markdown files anchored to the code paths they describe (stale anchors are detected when code moves); agents start with a get_briefing call; and enforce checks in MCP, Git hooks and CI block the commit that repeats a documented mistake — same diff, same verdict, on every machine. Lessons can carry a command sensor (the team's own test as oracle), and since v0.43.0 prove-RED is mandatory for a blocking sensor: the incident is replayed at the pre-fix commit and the oracle must fail there; a crash before the assertion is red-unrunnable and refuses to claim proof. A sensor-weakening gate stops protection being silently demoted, sensor commands run with a scrubbed environment (no cloud credentials or tokens), and an unrunnable command warns but never blocks — 'a broken harness must not masquerade as a failing test'.
bad: Scoped to code repositories: its own harness table marks architecture fitness only partly covered and behaviour merely bridged, and it says plainly that the oracle problem is unsolved — it routes the team's own tests rather than verifying correctness. Enforcement executes repo-authored commands (opt-in per repo, scrubbed environment — stated, but a trust decision), and adoption is tiny (4 stars).
took: Boarded as design evidence for our corrections ledger: a captured lesson becomes a deterministic gate only after its oracle is proven RED on the pre-fix state — a lesson that cannot reproduce the incident stays a warning, never a block.
didnt: Board — the lesson-to-gate discipline (briefing before work, prove-RED before blocking, a gate against silently weakening the sensors) is boarded for our own corrections/gate machinery; nothing installed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: firelock-ai/kin
licence: Apache-2.0 (covers Kin and its local stack including kin-db; the KinLab hosted product is separate and proprietary — the split is stated in the README)
good: A graph-native code repository: functions, types and their recorded relationships are repository state you commit, branch and merge — the graph is the model, not a search index beside another repository — with exact source preserved byte-for-byte. kin impact answers 'what else should I inspect before changing this?' from recorded callers; kin review shadow returns PASS / NEEDS ATTENTION / WOULD BLOCK with graph-derived evidence and is stated to be advisory ('it does not block a merge… Authorship is declared, not independently verified'). The honesty is specific: a screenshot caption warns 'This illustrates a workflow, not a performance benchmark', and the Beta limits section says coverage is incomplete and 'an empty result does not prove there are no callers or dependencies'.
bad: The repository is archived at source, so the project's own state is frozen and its future uncertain; it is a public beta whose history import costs grow with history rather than checkout size, and Kin-only state (commits, branches, reviews, specs) is not recoverable from Git — deleting the store loses it, a backup burden the README states but cannot remove.
didnt: Not adopted — the repo is archived at source and a replacement code repository is not our stack; the graph-as-model and advisory-review designs are recorded (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: github/github-mcp-server
good: GitHub's official MCP server and the ecosystem's reference door (33,828 stars): repository/issue/PR/Actions/security coverage as selectable toolsets (or individual tools), offered as a GitHub-hosted remote server or a local binary/Docker image. Its gating vocabulary is first-class — toolsets, a dedicated Read-Only Mode and a Lockdown Mode — and its token guidance is concrete: OAuth login keeps the token in memory only, and a Token Security Best Practices section prescribes minimum scopes, separate tokens per environment, rotation and 600-permission config files. Enterprise Server is supported via --gh-host with HTTPS enforced: non-HTTPS hosts are refused so credentials are never sent over cleartext, loopback excepted.
bad: The default surface is full platform management — repositories, issues, PRs, Actions, security findings — so breadth is both the product and the risk, and the classic PAT scopes it asks for are coarse (repo). The remote route also makes GitHub the host of the door: convenient, and a custody choice.
took: Corroboration for our connector posture: the vendor's own vocabulary for a safe door is toolsets, a read-only mode and a lockdown mode — our GitHub work stays on the connected connector under the owner's read-only rule.
didnt: Not adopted as a separate install — our GitHub access already runs through the connected GitHub connector, read-only under the owner's standing rule; recorded as the official reference server (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gitopia/gitopia-mcp-server
good: A 57-tool server for Gitopia, a decentralised Git platform with on-chain governance, DAO management and crypto bounties. The safety machinery exists in named form: trust tiers (readonly < localwrite < chainwrite) gate tool access, chain writes are rate-limited (10/min, 100/hr), a message allowlist restricts signing to Gitopia and Cosmos group message types, DRY_RUN previews transactions, and a Batch & Approval group can hold transactions as pending for confirm_transaction / reject_transaction before broadcast.
bad: The defaults invert the safety story: TRUST_LEVEL defaults to chainwrite — the widest tier — and APPROVAL_MODE defaults to false, so the approval machinery protects only operators who switch it on. A wallet is auto-generated on first use ('zero-config'), making BIP-39 mnemonic custody the user's problem from the first run; the prompts include an autonomous hunt-bounty workflow. Five commits.
didnt: Rejected — a decentralised on-chain forge is not our stack, and a door whose defaults are the widest trust tier with approval off teaches the opposite of our defaults (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HasanJahidul/git-insight-mcp
good: Read-only semantic git queries — the who/what/when/why that raw git log answers poorly: who_touched groups blame by author with lines, commits, last-touched and a primary owner; introducing_pr finds the PR that introduced a line, parsing merge messages first and falling back to the GitHub API; co_change lists files most often changed together; branch_hygiene reports ahead/behind, merged status and a stale flag; recent_work builds a standup from an author's window; commit_context assembles subject, body, files, PR and related issues. The local-git tools work with no token at all — PR linkage is skipped, not failed — and a Limits (v0.1) section states the caps in the open.
bad: v0.1 scale and stated limits: GitHub only for PR linkage, co_change capped at 1,000 commits, blame by line range rather than AST, renames not yet tracked, PR results uncached (rate limits apply). Fourteen commits, 2 stars.
didnt: Not adopted — our provenance questions are answered by git and the wiki record directly; recorded as a clean read-only git-semantics design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jaimenbell/github-mcp
good: A small read+write GitHub server built as a worked example of the hardened pattern: the write group (issue/PR mutations) is env-gated and OFF by default; a disabled write returns a structured policy_refusal error naming the required env var — 'never a silent no-op, never a crash' — and a write with the group enabled but no token returns a distinct auth_required; the group gate and the token precondition are checked independently, both before any network call. Both GitHub rate-limit shapes surface as typed errors with reset/retry times. Its honest-capabilities table maps every claim to the implementing file and the tests that verify it, and CI fails the build if the README's test-count badge drifts from what the suite actually reports; reads degrade gracefully to GitHub's unauthenticated 60 req/hr tier.
bad: A portfolio reference implementation (20 commits, 0 stars) beside the official server in this same batch: REST v1 only, no GraphQL, webhooks, GitHub Apps or Actions tools, single-page list results, and file reads truncating past 100 KB. It demonstrates a pattern; it is not a door to adopt.
took: Corroboration for our refusal design: a gated call returns a structured refusal naming what would enable it — never a silent no-op, never a crash — and the gate and the credential precondition are checked independently, before any network call.
didnt: Not adopted — a 0-star portfolio reference beside the official server we already connect through; studied for its refusal shape and its claims table (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JaviMaligno/mcp-server-bitbucket
good: Full Bitbucket Cloud management in twin TypeScript and Python implementations claimed identical in function: 58 tools across repositories (including create/delete), PRs (merge/approve/decline/request-changes), pipelines (trigger/stop, variables), webhooks, branch restrictions, deployments and permission management, plus MCP prompts and resources. The remote-deployment story is done properly: /mcp can be gated on a bearer JWT from an external authorization server (Entra ID, Okta, Auth0) with an RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata document, JWKS signature verification, iss/aud/expiry checks and a 403 insufficient_scope for under-scoped tokens, while /health stays open. The two Bitbucket credential families (personal API token as Basic email:token, workspace access token as Bearer) are auto-detected, with the 401 trap explained.
bad: Full management behind one workspace credential — delete_repository, permission management, pipeline-variable writes — with no read-only mode described for the stdio server; and the README's own caveat stands: the OAuth gate 'controls who may use the server… it does not attribute actions to individual users'. A hosted third-party deployment (Fronteir AI) is also offered for those who would rather not run it.
took: One limit recorded for the hosted-door file: gating who may use a shared door does not attribute what the door's own credential then does — caller authentication and action attribution are separate problems.
didnt: Not adopted — Bitbucket is not our stack (contrast B131's daniloneto/bitbucket-mcp, the review-scoped pole); recorded for its remote-door OAuth treatment and its stated attribution limit (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jmrplens/gitlab-mcp-server
good: All of GitLab — up to 1,103 actions over the REST and GraphQL APIs, tier-detected from Free to Ultimate — behind two discovery meta-tools (find/execute) by default: 11,343 tokens of startup context (1,941 in minimal surface mode) against a measured 576,788 to 734,051 tokens for listing every action as its own tool, the figures measured with the cl100k_base tokenizer and checked in CI. Guard rails are named: read-only mode, safe mode (a preview of each write instead of the write), tools excluded by name, and a confirmation before anything destructive; each action's reference entry states the token scope and fine-grained permissions it needs. Releases carry signed checksums, an SBOM and build provenance, and the public demo instance carries its warning in the open: 'Your token and every request pass through that machine, so run it yourself.'
bad: The find/execute shape concentrates risk: one execute meta-tool reaching up to 1,103 actions makes the guard rails the entire safety story — a mis-set mode or exclusion list exposes everything at once, where per-action servers fail narrower. GitLab is also not our forge.
took: Corroboration for door economics: publish the tool surface's context cost — tokens of tool definitions, measured and checked in CI — and make safe mode a preview of the write instead of the write.
didnt: Not adopted — GitLab is not our forge; studied for the meta-tool surface economics and its guard rails (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JoeGlenn1213/lgh
good: LocalGitHub: a single Go binary wrapping git http-backend so any directory becomes an HTTP Git remote on 127.0.0.1:9418, with Basic Auth (salted password hashing), an optional read-only serve mode, mDNS LAN discovery, and the same binary doubling as the MCP server. Smart Ignore generates a project-appropriate .gitignore and blocks large files (>50 MB) and sensitive files (.env, *.key) before they enter a repo. Agents get a real-time event stream over a Unix socket (read-only, local user only) and event replay for testing — replayed events carry a '_replayed': true marker in the payload — and MCP calls return exact triggered_job_ids so an agent can track pipeline status 'with zero blind spots'.
bad: The convenience flows run against approval-first habits: lgh add --push and lgh up auto-commit and auto-push, and a one-click tunnel (ngrok/cloudflared) exposes the local server to the internet by design — authentication exists, but the posture is the opposite of localhost-only. One star; a young single-author project.
