took: One habit recorded: replayed events carry a '_replayed': true marker in the payload — synthetic history is labelled as synthetic where it is consumed, never passed off as live.
didnt: Not adopted — our repos live on GitHub and Azure under the read-only rule, and the tunnel posture is the opposite of our localhost-only gateway; recorded as the local-first git-hosting design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kaiyuanxiaobing/atomgit-mcp-server
licence: MulanPSL-2.0 (Mulan Permissive Software License, Version 2 — repo metadata and the root license file)
good: The MCP server for AtomGit, the Chinese open-source collaboration platform: about 25 tools over repositories, issues (including comments, assignees and assignability checks), pull requests, branches and labels, authenticated by a personal access token, with Chinese and English READMEs.
bad: The write tools (create issues and PRs, delete issue comments, set assignees, manage labels) carry no read-only mode or gating described; AtomGit is not our forge; and this repo is a mirror with no releases — the primary home is atomgit.com.
didnt: Not adopted — AtomGit is not our forge; recorded as that platform's MCP server, with its MulanPSL-2.0 licence noted at source (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: klarluft/gitwarren-app
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later (LICENSE at root; copyright held by Klarluft B.V. under a CLA that keeps a commercial licence possible — the dual-licensing posture is stated in the README) — ideas only
good: Local code review built for the agent moment: a review compares two refs PR-style (conversation, commits, files changed, browse files), and if the reviewed branch is checked out in a worktree — wherever it is — its staged, unstaged and untracked changes are folded into the diff, so work is reviewed before it becomes a commit. Markdown diffs render with edits marked like tracked changes and can be commented paragraph by paragraph. Nothing is cached (every diff is read from git at the moment it is shown) and nothing leaves the machine: reviews live in one SQLite file, no account, no telemetry, the desktop app's one outbound request is the update check. Agents are first-class through an MCP server over stdio — they open reviews, read the human's comments, reply in-thread and resolve what they fixed — and headless machines are reached over SSH, wsl.exe or the user's own tailnet, with reviews staying on the machine the code is on.
bad: GPL-3.0-or-later puts the code in ideas-only territory for us, and the CLA copyright consolidation (one holder, commercial licence grantable on request) is a deliberate centralisation — stated openly, but a posture to note. Brand new (created 2026-09-02), and review state lives in one local SQLite file with the app rather than with the repository.
took: One workflow pattern recorded: review the agent's uncommitted worktree — staged, unstaged and untracked folded into a single diff — before it becomes a commit; that is exactly when review is cheapest, and it is the shape of our audit-before-report rule.
didnt: Not adopted — GPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only, and our agent review runs inside the workflow rather than in a desktop app; the pre-commit worktree-review pattern is recorded (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kopfrechner/gitlab-mr-mcp
good: A deliberately narrow GitLab door: ten tools for merge-request and issue review — list projects, list open MRs, MR details/comments/diff, general and line-specific diff comments, issue details, and MR title/description setters. There is no merge tool at all: the surface is review-shaped by construction. The visible project set can be filtered by minimum access level and a search term (MR_MCP_MIN_ACCESS_LEVEL, MR_MCP_PROJECT_SEARCH_TERM), and the troubleshooting section names the token scopes (api, read_api).
bad: No releases cut despite 154 commits, and the write tools (comments, title and description edits) have no confirmation behaviour described; GitLab is not our forge in any case.
didnt: Not adopted — GitLab is not our forge; recorded as the narrow review-scoped GitLab door, the opposite pole from jmrplens' 1,103 actions in this same batch (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linnea-bakshi/gha-doctor
good: A read-only GitHub Actions doctor covering the third leg beside actionlint (correctness) and zizmor (security): speed, cost and reliability. Flake detection comes with receipts — a job that failed and passed on the same commit is flaky by construction — and cost rules map to billable minutes (missing concurrency cancellation, uncached installs, 10x macOS runners, 6-hour default timeouts, full-history checkouts), rolled into a 0–100 health score with a committable badge. --diff previews what --fix would change as a unified diff and writes nothing; the published JSON Schemas are generated from the same Go types that produce the output, with CI failing if they drift; the README displays the tool's own verdict on its own repo. The project discloses its maintainer plainly at the top of the README: 'This project is built and maintained by Linnea Bakshi, an AI agent… a human is not pretending to be behind this account.' Its sampled research is published the same way (the CI waste ledger: 10% of sampled compute spent inside failed runs; one scheduled workflow failing unattended for 396 days).
bad: Young (created 2026-07-24, 3 stars) and single-maintainer — where the maintainer is an AI agent by the project's own disclosure, continuity is an open question a user should weigh. The log-based features need a token with Actions read access on private repos, and the diagnosis is GitHub-Actions-only.
took: Corroboration for diagnosis-before-optimisation: name the flaky job from run history with receipts (failed and passed on the same commit) and price each finding in billable minutes before recommending any fix.
didnt: Not adopted — our Actions footprint is small and WikiCitadel's CI is blocked on a workflow-permissions gap, not on workflow waste; recorded as the read-only CI-cost diagnostic (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: madeinplutofabio/vibe-revert
good: A local safety layer for coding agents that records the project's real working state before a session — staged, unstaged and pre-existing untracked files are part of the checkpoint and are preserved through recovery, so the human's own uncommitted work is never the agent's collateral. Risk findings are deterministic rules, not a model judging a model ('No AI judges the AI'): reproducible, explainable and inspectable, flagging edits that touch auth, payments, databases, secrets, dependencies and infrastructure. Rollback previews by default and only --apply writes; every apply first saves an emergency checkpoint; selective rollback (--only / --except / --risk / --finding, path selectors following renames) is all-or-nothing — drift on any selected path refuses the whole operation and --force does not override; an interrupted apply fails closed and points at the emergency checkpoint. It warns rather than blocks (an opt-in pre-commit hook can reject above a risk threshold), and findings can be emitted as an agent-ready fix prompt: 'Rules decide. Agents fix.' Records stay on the machine; no account, no hosted service.
bad: Beta and unadopted (0 stars, npm @beta, Node 22+), and its own limits are real: it does not reverse effects outside project files — deployments, database writes, API calls, payments and sent emails are gone once done; rollback is state-based, not atomic; sessions ended before 0.8.0 cannot be selectively rolled back (MIGRATIONS.md). Its proof is the author's own beta report: '3 real AI coding sessions. 3 exact project-file restorations' — promising, and self-reported.
took: Boarded as design evidence for agent-session safety: checkpoint the real working state (including pre-existing uncommitted work) before an agent runs, preview restores by default, make partial restores fail closed rather than half-apply, and keep risk findings as deterministic rules an agent can be handed as a fix prompt.
didnt: Board — the checkpoint / preview-first / fail-closed restore discipline is boarded for our agent work; nothing installed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: modelcontextprotocol/server-git
licence: MIT (the directory README's License section: 'This MCP server is licensed under the MIT License'; the item is src/git inside modelcontextprotocol/servers)
good: The reference git server from the MCP project itself: twelve tools over stdio (status, unstaged/staged/between diffs, commit, add, reset, log, create_branch, checkout, show, branch). Its error contract is the teaching point: tool failures return isError: true with 'Error executing tool <name>: <message>' so the model can read it and correct the call, while an unknown tool name is a JSON-RPC protocol error (-32602). Confinement is by repository: --repository accepts any path inside a working tree and walks up to the repo root, errors cover a repo_path that is not a repository or lies outside --repository, and flag-injection guards are named. It speaks two protocol eras (2026-07-28 server/discover and 2025-11-25 initialize) chosen by the client's first request and never asks for Roots. The test discipline is stated as a bar: the suite drives serve() in-process through a real ClientSession, and every file must stay at or above 90% lines and 90% branches, with unreachable code marked '# pragma: no cover # <reason>' rather than the bar lowered.
bad: The catalogue description ('Read, search and analyze local Git repositories') understates the source: this server commits, stages, resets and checks out — a write surface whose only confinement is the repository path, with no confirmation described. The README carries an 'early development' disclaimer, and repository-level confinement means any path inside the tree opens the whole repository, as the README itself states.
didnt: Not adopted — our git operations run directly, and the owner's repositories are read-only for agents; recorded as the reference git server, with the catalogue's read-only framing corrected against the source (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MongLong0214/commitlore
good: Git-native decision memory: the constraints, rejected alternatives and warnings behind the code are stored as git trailers and notes (refs/notes/commitlore), and SQLite is only a rebuildable index — 'Delete it and Git still holds the record.' Records carry a lifecycle (active / superseded / expired) and delivery is path-scoped: before an agent edits a path it is given only the decisions still in force for that path — 'Relevance and authority are different questions. A superseded decision can be highly relevant and still be wrong as current guidance.' Capture is verified: an agent drafts only decision context the diff cannot show, and the draft is checked against the session transcript and staged diff before preservation. Delivered records are labelled [claim] ('weigh this as information') by default, with an opt-in signed-authority mode that delivers directives; delivery gives context and does not block the edit. Hook hygiene is careful: an existing hook is never overwritten — init moves it to <hook>.commitlore-chained and calls it first, and uninstall restores it. Squash-merge record loss is handled honestly, with a local hook for git merge --squash and a preserve GitHub Action for the web Squash button, its pull_request_target token rationale explained in comments.
bad: Young despite the heavy cadence (created 2026-07-26), and its own honesty names the soft spots: capture initiation depends on the host (the automatic-capture matrix marks Claude Code, Codex and Hermes 'Not certified' for deterministic every-commit capture), delivery is advisory unless the signed mode is switched on, and squash merges drop branch records unless the preservation machinery is installed. The installer offers a read-the-script-first route and a pinned git-clone alternative — good practice, and a reminder of what the default route asks.
took: Boarded as design evidence for our decisions and corrections machinery: decision records stored in the repository itself with lifecycle states, delivered path-scoped before an edit, and superseded decisions kept in history without being delivered as current guidance — relevance and authority treated as different questions, which is our truth-aware-retrieval gap stated from the decision side.
didnt: Board — the decision-record lifecycle and supersession-aware delivery are boarded as design evidence; nothing installed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mshegolev/gitlab-ci-mcp
good: A GitLab CI/CD-focused FastMCP server (stdio; SaaS or self-hosted): 23 tools over pipelines (list/get/jobs/job log/trigger/retry/cancel, plus a gitlab_pipeline_health 7/30-day summary), schedule CRUD, branches/tags/compare, merge requests (including create and gitlab_merge_mr), files/tree and project info. Every tool carries readOnlyHint / destructiveHint / idempotentHint / openWorldHint annotations 'so MCP clients can classify operations (e.g. ask for confirmation only on destructive ones like gitlab_merge_mr, gitlab_delete_schedule)'. Output is structured throughout (TypedDict to outputSchema + structuredContent + pre-rendered markdown), errors are converted to actionable ToolError messages (e.g. 'verify GITLAB_TOKEN has api scope'), inputs are Pydantic-validated, and gitlab_get_job_log accepts a grep_pattern with context so megabyte-scale CI logs can be filtered server-side instead of pulled whole into agent context. One cached HTTP session per project_path, per-call project override, and corporate-proxy handling (GITLAB_NO_PROXY_DOMAINS; the server clears HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY in its own process).
bad: Merge and delete tools are present, and the annotation labels are the only stated gate — whether a destructive call is actually confirmed is the client's behaviour, not something this server enforces. Seventeen commits and 2 stars: a small, young project.
took: Corroboration for the per-tool annotation standard: every tool labelled read-only / destructive / idempotent / open-world so the client can gate only the destructive ones — the same labelling B131's server-filesystem published as a table, here carried by a CI server.
didnt: Not adopted — GitLab is not our forge; recorded as the CI-scoped GitLab door with full per-tool annotations (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nikolay-e/diffctx
good: Diff-seeded context for reviewers and agents: instead of packing the whole repo or querying a maintained index, diffctx starts from a change and reports what it reaches outside its diff — the callers, the tests that reach them, the contracts it crosses — then selects the code needed to understand it under a token budget (--budget, counted in o200k tokens by default). Local, deterministic, no index, no model calls. Caller resolution is static and per-language, and 'where it cannot resolve, the answer says so instead of printing a zero'. The same engine runs as CLI, MCP server, Claude Code plugin and GitHub Action; BENCHMARKS.md and COMPARISON.md are published, and .gitleaks.toml plus a secrets baseline sit in the tree.
bad: Small adoption (6 stars), and the native binary answers only --diff and --symbol — whole-tree export, Markdown packs, the graph command and the MCP server need the Python package. Static caller resolution is per-language heuristic work; the says-so behaviour bounds the damage but the coverage limits are real.
took: Corroboration for diff-seeded context: what a change reaches outside its diff, selected under a stated token budget, with unresolvable cases answered as unknown rather than printed as zero — the same honesty as our abstention standard.
didnt: Not adopted — our diffs are reviewed in-tree under the audit rule; recorded as the diff-seeded context selector (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: noordeen123/culprit
good: Offline, read-only root-cause analysis for coding agents: find_suspects ranks the commits that introduced a regression by blaming the fix's removed lines plus git log -L; verify_fix is a pre-commit gate returning complete / partial / risky with the untouched call sites listed as the patch list, skipped symbols named, and whether a test shipped — completeness kept as one axis and confidence (risk_level) as a separate one; blast radius and test impact round out 11 MCP tools. Deterministic, no network, no API key, no test runs. The benchmarking is the honesty exemplar: against 50 real regressions with author-verified Fixes: ground truth it reports top-1 50% and top-5 66%, and its three-arm comparison states plainly that the agent alone beats culprit on accuracy (90% vs 80% top-1) — culprit's value is efficiency, 41% fewer tool calls and 14% fewer tokens, with the caveats printed (n=10, an easier slice). An optional real bisect runs in a throwaway git worktree, and a match stamps the report 'confirmed by git bisect'. CI gating is by exit code only — no PR comments, no writes.
bad: A heuristic, not a proof — the README's own bisect comparison says so (proof belongs to bisect; culprit is a 'strong heuristic'), and its headline accuracy (50% top-1 on the full 50) is modest. Young and small (103 commits, 6 stars, created 2026-06-20).
took: Corroboration for honest evaluation: publish the arm where the tool loses, price its value in tool calls and tokens rather than accuracy, and keep the completeness verdict separate from the confidence score — the standard our own evaluation reporting is held to.
didnt: Not adopted — our root-cause work runs directly through git; recorded as the offline regression-RCA server (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: QuentinCody/github-graphql-mcp-server
licence: MIT (LICENSE.md at root and the README's License section; repo metadata shows Other/NOASSERTION)
good: A minimal bridge to GitHub's GraphQL API: one tool that executes any GraphQL operation with variables against the GitHub API using the caller's PAT, with example queries (repository info, search, user info), error handling, and the authenticated and unauthenticated rate limits stated. For flexible read queries without a curated toolset, the shape is honest about what it is.
bad: The single tool executes mutations as readily as queries, with whatever scope the PAT carries — no read-only mode, query allowlist or confirmation described. That hands the model the token's full authority in one call: the opposite pole from curated toolsets with per-tool scopes.
didnt: Rejected — one arbitrary query-and-mutation tool is the opposite of our door discipline; our GitHub access runs through the curated connector under the owner's read-only rule (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rafim-dev/mcp-smart-git
good: A small smart-git helper (MCP server plus standalone CLI): git_smart_commit generates structured Conventional Commits from diffs with breaking-change detection; git_review_diff statically scans diff lines for secret leaks (AWS keys, OpenAI tokens, private keys), eval() hazards and forgotten debug logs, returning a 0–100 security score; git_resolve_conflicts scans for conflict markers and synthesises merge recommendations; plus changelog generation from history and a token-efficient status. The pre-PR secret audit runs on the diff, before the commit exists.
bad: Brand new and unproven (6 commits, 0 stars, created 2026-09-07); the test claim is '100% passing' with no counts published; the secret scan is pattern-class and its coverage is characterised only by the README's list; distribution leans on a $5+ pay-what-you-want Gumroad/itch.io bundle (the GitHub repo itself is MIT).
took: Corroboration for scanning the diff itself before a commit or PR exists — secrets, eval hazards and debug leftovers caught at the cheapest moment, the same point our pack scan makes at pack time.
didnt: Not adopted — six commits and no track record; recorded as a small smart-git helper (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: raohwork/forgejo-mcp
licence: MPL-2.0 (Mozilla Public License 2.0 — weak copyleft, treated as ideas-only under the licence discipline)
good: The established Gitea/Forgejo door (70 stars): issue management (create/edit, labels, comments, attachments, dependencies), labels and milestones, releases and attachments, PR viewing, Forgejo/Gitea Actions viewing and wiki page management, over stdio or HTTP — HTTP mode is single-user (one token at startup) or multi-user (per-request Bearer). A Security Recommendations section prescribes environment variables over config files, least-necessary scopes and regular rotation.
bad: A management surface whose setup recommends write scopes from the start, with no read-only mode described; and MPL-2.0 is weak copyleft — outside the MIT/Apache class our licence discipline adapts from. Env files (.env, .env.local) are committed in the repo root listing.
didnt: Not adopted — Forgejo/Gitea is not our forge, and the Forgejo/ForgeFed platform question already stands boarded from lane 8 on the owner's hosted-door ground; this server adds nothing to that question (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ReviewGate/reviewgate
licence: Custom proprietary EULA (ReviewGate End-User License Agreement v1.0: free for use including commercial, no fee redistribution, no hosted-service offering, no modification or reverse engineering; source not published) — ideas only
good: Review against the team's own written rules: ReviewGate reads the agreements the team actually wrote — ADRs, conventions, the rules in .reviewgate/config.yml — and reports where a change breaks them: a finding quoting your own rule rather than a textbook. Two passes under the hood: a cheap generator looks for problems and a stronger independent judge refutes them against the code; only what survives is published. It runs in three places on the same rules and judge — a CLI over staged, uncommitted or committed changes, a pre-push hook that refuses a push carrying blocking findings, an MCP server the coding agent calls itself before the request exists, and a PR bot for GitHub/GitLab. Self-hosted with your own model key: code goes only to the provider you configured, no telemetry, no vendor account, source never written to logs or disk; live reviews on 13 real pull requests are published as a demo.
bad: The source is not published — this repo distributes binaries, so the engine cannot be audited at source and its judge-refutation numbers live on the vendor's site. The licence is a custom EULA: free for any purpose including commercial use inside your organisation, but no redistribution for a fee, no hosted or managed-service offering, no modification or reverse engineering, and 'nothing in these terms grants you any right to the source code'.
took: Corroboration for two-pass review: findings generated cheaply, then refuted by an independent judge before anything reaches a human, and a finding that quotes the team's own written rule — the shape of our audit-before-report rule and of the corrections ledger it enforces.
didnt: Not adopted — the engine ships as binaries under a custom EULA with source unpublished, so it can be neither audited nor adapted; recorded for its two-pass pattern only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sadayamuthu/mergelock
good: A git-native merge gate for parallel agent branches: mergelock check compares two branches before they meet and reports the conflicts git cannot see — signature_caller (a signature changed on one branch while the other adds calls that no longer fit), modify_delete (including calls to a deleted symbol), add_add, textual, and duplicate_definition as a warning — computed from commits with git merge-tree and tree-sitter parsers, never touching the working tree, so it is safe in a pre-push hook, CI, or over MCP. Semantic rules cover TypeScript/JavaScript and Python; other languages still get the textual checks. The exit-code contract is scriptable (0 clean, 1 warnings, 2 conflict, 3 operational error), and rule behaviour is pinned by branch-pair fixtures — tiny repos with a base, two branches and the expected findings — inside a suite that includes a 5,000-file performance test. The unsigned-macOS-binary Gatekeeper note is stated in the install section.
bad: One week old at source (created 2026-10-14, 1 star) and semantic coverage stops at TypeScript/JavaScript/Python; it needs git 2.38+ for merge-tree --write-tree, and the Go build uses cgo for tree-sitter. It reports conflicts; reconciling them is still the agents' work.
took: Corroboration for pre-merge semantic checks between parallel agent branches: the conflicts git can't see — a changed signature against new call sites — are exactly what multi-agent branch work risks, and the rule behaviour is pinned by fixtures rather than asserted.
didnt: Not adopted — our branch merges are coordinator-run and small; recorded as the semantic merge gate for parallel agent branches (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TamiShaks-2/git-context-mcp
licence: MIT (stated in the README's closing License section; no LICENSE file at root and the repo metadata is silent)
good: A small local orientation server: five read-only tools over stdio — project_status (branch, cleanliness, sync), code_map (structure and entry points), recent_activity (churn), work_summary (recent work plus TODO/FIXME debt), risk_scan (large, complex or high-churn files) — giving an agent situational awareness before it edits. It reads only git metadata and repository files, executes no project code, uploads nothing and depends on no external service; the README carries an explicit 'What this MCP does not do' section, and discloses that the README itself was generated through the server's own tools.
bad: Eight commits and no releases: a sketch, not a maintained tool. The risk signal is size/churn heuristics, and there is no confinement question to answer only because the surface is read-only summaries.
didnt: Not adopted — orientation context we already produce from the tree directly; recorded as a clean read-only orientation design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tiberriver256/mcp-server-azure-devops
good: The established community Azure DevOps server (396 stars, 49 releases): some forty tools across user/organization, projects, repositories (including create_branch and create_commit from unified diffs or search/replace instructions), work items (create/update/links/attachments), code/wiki/work-item search, pipelines (including trigger and artifact download) and pull requests (including create and comment). Three authentication methods — PAT, Azure Identity (the default) and Azure CLI — and Azure DevOps Server (on-premises) support is its stated niche. Its README leads with an honest signpost: 'Looking for the official server? Microsoft maintains a product-supported Azure DevOps MCP… If you use Azure DevOps Services (cloud), start there.'
bad: A full write surface with no read-only mode, project allowlist or confirmation described — the governance is the PAT's scopes alone. Set beside B132's dockndevai (mode-gated registration, protected projects, typed confirmation), this is the ungated pole of the same platform.
didnt: Not adopted — the owner's Codex ↔ Azure DevOps setup is his own work and unconfirmed, and any Azure DevOps door we build takes its governance from B132's boarded model rather than this one's token-scope-only posture; recorded as the established community server and the contrast case (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wkoverfield/quilt
good: Line-level authorship for several coding agents sharing one Git checkout: capture hooks attribute every edit to its session, and quilt commit --mine commits only your lines, even inside a hunk another actor also touched — so the first git commit -am no longer sweeps everyone else's work into one blob. Symbol-level claims (tree-sitter, ten languages; whole-file claims otherwise) reserve utils.js#formatPrice rather than the file: a write into claimed code is denied before any bytes change, and the denial carries the holder's stated intent and when their lease lapses, so the blocked agent can build elsewhere and re-claim after the holder's commit auto-releases. If one actor overwrites another's uncommitted lines, the victim's version is snapshotted — nothing is silently lost. Quilt writes provenance (actor, session, files, hunks, tree) into the Git commit itself, so it survives pushes and fresh clones, while prompt correlation stays local; all state lives in a deletable .quilt/ sidecar, Git stays the source of truth and is never rewritten. The fleet example runs seven agents with and without Quilt on the same checkout (without: one commit and a silent overwrite; with: six clean commits and one denied write), and bench/ holds the scenario ladder run both ways on the same metrics.
bad: Capture depends on hooks being wired per runtime (Claude Code hooks, or the MCP tools for other runtimes), so an unwired editor bypasses attribution; there is a daily anonymous telemetry heartbeat (its contents and off switches — QUILT_TELEMETRY=0, DO_NOT_TRACK=1 — are documented in the README). Young (created 2026-06-28, 7 stars).
took: Corroboration for attribution discipline: provenance recorded in the commit itself rather than in a side log, and a denied claim that carries the holder's intent and expiry instead of a bare refusal — the shape our own multi-agent coordination uses at branch granularity.
didnt: Not adopted — our agents work in separate branches merged by the coordinator, not in one shared checkout; recorded as the line-level authorship layer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zach-snell/bbkt
good: A Bitbucket CLI and MCP server in Go whose tool surface is shaped by the credential: at startup the server introspects the token's granted scopes via the /user endpoint and silently drops any tool whose required scope is missing — 'preventing the AI from hallucinating successful writes it doesn't have permission for'. BITBUCKET_DISABLED_TOOLS denies tools even when scopes allow them, and a --no-auth mode supports transport testing with tools returning auth-required errors. Nine manage_* tools (workspaces, repositories, refs, commits, source, pull requests, PR comments, pipelines, issues) with required scopes tabulated; the scoped-API-token requirement is documented with the unscoped-token failure detected and explained (Bitbucket has required scoped tokens since the September 2025 app-password phase-out). Multi-profile auth (API token or OAuth 2.0 with refresh) with profile auto-selection from the git config email, and most commands infer workspace/repo from .git/config.
bad: The write surface behind the scopes is full management (repository create/delete, PR merge, source write/delete, pipeline trigger/stop) — the gating shapes what the model can see, but a fully-scoped token still yields the full surface. Four stars; Bitbucket is not our forge in any case.
took: Corroboration for capability-shaped tool surfaces: introspect the credential at startup and drop the tools it cannot use before the model ever sees them, so a read-only token yields a read-only server by construction — the same registration-gating idea as B132's mode gating, derived from the credential rather than a mode flag.
didnt: Not adopted — Bitbucket is not our forge; recorded as the third Bitbucket door in three batches, and the one whose surface is shaped by the credential (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zarcherlot/code-relay
good: Cross-machine verification for coding agents: the Dev Host implements, the Target Host runs the real validation — the exact source commit checked in an isolated worktree, in the environment that actually matters (another OS, special hardware, a private network, real integrations) — and a structured receipt comes back: receipt.json plus a human-readable receipt recording passed, failed or blocked, with expected/actual results to guide the next repair iteration. Runbooks are bound to a repository, branch and source commit; validation commands are allowlisted with bounded output and timeouts; checkpoint execution runs through a code-relay-checkpoint self-hosted GitHub Actions runner. Ten MCP tools over stdio (bind_project, short-lived checkpoint invites, join_checkpoint, watcher status/stop, a non-mutating doctor, publish_runbook which validates before publishing, status, fetch_receipt which loads and validates, analyze), with the MCP JSON-RPC surface implemented directly in Go rather than via an SDK.
bad: Brand new and unadopted (0 stars, created 2026-08-30), and its trust story is the target machine: the checkpoint runs on a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on the Target Host, joined via short-lived links, so whoever controls that host controls the verdict's ground. The primary installation route is an agent-addressed runbook at a raw URL — an onboarding device to treat as evidence, not instructions.
took: Corroboration for verification receipts: a completion claim is backed by a structured receipt from a real run at the exact commit — passed, failed or blocked, with expected against actual returned for repair — and the validating commands are allowlisted with bounded output and timeouts. That is our verify-the-thing-itself standard, split across two machines.
didnt: Not adopted — we have no second verification machine in the loop; recorded as the cross-machine verification design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AIops-tools/MySQL-AIops
good: Governed DBA operations for MySQL 8.x and MariaDB 10.6+: 35 MCP tools (26 read, 9 write) plus a CLI, every call wrapped in a @governed_tool harness. Four flagship root-cause analyses — slow-query (digest numbers mapped to a cited cause and action), InnoDB lock-wait/deadlock (wait-for tree naming the root blocker), replication lag, table fragmentation — each finding carrying its measured number rather than a black-box verdict. The harness guarantees: a unified audit log (every call over MCP and CLI alike lands a row in audit.db — 'there is no unaudited entry point'), a runaway/budget guard, risk-tier labels on the audit row, and undo recording built from the real before-state (drop_index captures the index definition from SHOW CREATE TABLE so undo recreates it exactly; irreversible ops like kill_session declare no undo). Writes support dry-run previews and double confirmation on the CLI; identifiers that cannot be parameterised are charset-validated and backtick-quoted; credentials live in an encrypted store (Fernet + scrypt). Live-verified against MySQL 8.4.10 and MariaDB 11.8.8 including the full create_index → audit → undo loop, the run surfacing a real Decimal/JSON bug the mocks could not see. Its philosophy is stated head-on in 'What this tool does, and does not, decide': the tool does not decide whether a write is allowed — point it at an account with only SELECT/PROCESS/REPLICATION CLIENT and writes fail at the server, 'the place that actually owns the permission'; each tool's risk_level 'is a label, not a gate'.
bad: The governance deliberately contains no gate: there is no read-only switch, policy file or approval step inside the tool, so a write-privileged account plus a confident agent is the whole risk surface — the audit row records the damage faithfully after it happens. The family is brand new (created 2026-07-17, 0 stars), and replication RCA against a real replica remains unverified by its own account.
took: One design position recorded: enforcement can live in the connected account's privileges — 'the place that actually owns the permission' — with the tool guaranteeing instead that nothing is silent (an audit row for every call, no unaudited entry point) and that reversible writes carry an undo built from the fetched before-state. Our doors gate in the tool as well; the audit completeness and before-state undo are the shared standard.
didnt: Not adopted — we run no MySQL/MariaDB operations; recorded as the governed-DBA design whose enforcement lives in the account's privileges (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AIops-tools/Queue-AIops
good: The AIops-tools harness applied to Redis and RabbitMQ: 28 MCP tools (20 reads including four flagship RCAs — memory pressure, latency, queue backlog, connection churn — plus 8 governed writes) and a CLI routing through the same governed functions. The RCAs are transparent heuristics: thresholds are named constants, every finding carries its evidence, 'never a black-box verdict'. Big-key sampling is SCAN-budgeted (at most 10,000 keys walked, at most 200 sized with MEMORY USAGE, never KEYS *) and reports its coverage. Undo is honest about its limits: delete_queue's undo re-declares the queue from its recorded definition and the descriptor says plainly 'the messages are not restored'; irreversible writes (purge_queue, redis_kill_client) record prior state only. Every call lands a secret-redacted audit row, writes take dry_run previews with CLI double-confirmation, credentials sit in the same encrypted store as the family's, and each tool's risk_level is kept in agreement with its [READ]/[WRITE] documentation tag by a test. Live-verified against Redis 7.4.9 and RabbitMQ 3.13.7 including a set_policy → undo_apply loop on the live broker; the run found and fixed a real defect (integer quantities rendered as floats) that equality assertions could not catch.
bad: Same deliberate absence of an in-tool gate as its sibling — purge_queue and delete_queue are governed by dry-run, double confirmation and the broker account's permissions, nothing else. Brand new (created 2026-07-17, 0 stars); Redis cluster/sentinel topologies and AUTH/TLS connections remain unverified by its own account, and the stale top banner (above) shows the verification story being maintained in two places at once.
took: Corroboration for undo honesty: the undo descriptor states what the undo does not restore (a re-declared queue's messages are gone), so a recovery claim never silently covers more than it returns — the sibling of B133 vibe-revert's stated non-goals, at the level of a single operation.
didnt: Not adopted — we run no Redis/RabbitMQ operations; recorded as the queue member of the governed-AIops family (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: aliyun/alibabacloud-tablestore-mcp-server
good: Alibaba Cloud's official MCP collection for Tablestore, its serverless wide-column store: four implementations in Java and Python — a Java starter server, a Java RAG knowledge-base Q&A system built on the MCP architecture (with knowledge-base construction and RAG optimisations), a Python starter server, and a Python Mem0/OpenMemory variant. Documents are added to Tablestore and searched semantically by vector and scalar indexes, the serverless-RAG shape the catalogue describes.
bad: Everything here fronts Alibaba Cloud Tablestore, a hosted cloud database — the data lives in the vendor's cloud under the vendor's account model, which is a custody choice before it is a tool choice. The root README is an index only, so per-server tool detail sits one level down in each subproject.
didnt: Not adopted — Alibaba Cloud Tablestore is not our stack; recorded as the vendor's MCP collection for it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: appwrite/mcp
good: Appwrite's official MCP server (130 releases): the Appwrite API — databases, auth/users, functions, teams, storage, messaging — exposed as tools. Its primary form is a hosted remote server (mcp.appwrite.io) authenticated by OAuth 2.1 through a browser consent screen — 'there are no keys to copy', scopes are approved by the user at connect time — with a self-hosted stdio variant authenticated by a project API key. The README is a thorough per-client connection matrix (Claude Code/Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, OpenCode, Windsurf, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Copilot CLI, Zed, Warp, JetBrains, Cline), including the sharp edges: Antigravity strictly requires the serverUrl key and the wrong key 'will cause tool registration to fail silently', and clients without remote-OAuth support (JetBrains, Cline) bridge through mcp-remote over stdio. An in-process appwrite_search_docs tool searches the product documentation.
bad: Hosted-first: the default route puts the vendor's cloud server in the path, with the project's full backend API behind the OAuth scopes the user approves on a consent screen — convenient, and a custody and blast-radius choice. The self-hosted route falls back to a project API key. The README is almost entirely connection instructions; the tool surface itself is documented off-repo.
didnt: Not adopted — Appwrite is not our backend; recorded as the vendor's hosted-first MCP door with a proper OAuth consent flow (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ArcadeData/arcadedb
good: A mature multi-model DBMS (14,238 commits, created 2021, by OrientDB's founder): graph, document, key/value, time-series, vector and search models in one engine, spoken to in SQL, Cypher, Gremlin, GraphQL and MongoDB Query Language, and reachable over the Postgres, Redis and MongoDB wire protocols as well as HTTP/JSON and Bolt. Fully transactional (ACID), Raft-based HA, 70+ built-in graph algorithms, materialized views, parallel query execution — and a built-in MCP server (an mcp/ module in the tree) so AI assistants can work with it directly, plus an AI assistant in its Studio. The engineering discipline is visible from the repo page: daily HA integration, resilience and load suites, a weekly 60-minute chaos run and weekly benchmarks, REUSE licence compliance, a GOVERNANCE.md and four release variants (full/minimal/headless/base) so an operator ships only the modules they run.
bad: Adopting it means replacing files-as-truth with a JVM database platform — a different architecture, not a tool we lack — and its breadth (six wire protocols, an AI assistant in Studio, a module matrix with four release variants) is the opposite of our plain-files custody. None of that is a defect in the project; it is the fit judgement the earlier row already made.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a JVM multi-model DBMS replacement for a plain-Markdown, local-first wiki, however capable its built-in MCP tools are. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: astandrik/local-ydb-toolkit
good: A Codex skill plus a 39-tool local stdio MCP server (with Claude Code and Gemini/Antigravity plugin forms and a GitHub Action that boots disposable YDB tenants in CI) for operating Docker-based local-ydb deployments, locally or over SSH: prerequisite checks, tenant bootstrap, dynamic-node lifecycle, schema DDL generation/validation/application, auth hardening, storage workflows, dump/restore and upgrades. The discipline is the content: mutating tools are plan-first and require confirm: true; the SQL tool is deliberately narrower than the official ydb-platform/ydb-mcp's (managed YQL only, against the selected configured profile), and the README positions the two servers as complementary rather than competing. Configuration fails closed — an explicit config path must name a readable regular JSON file of at most 1 MiB, and 'missing or invalid explicit files fail closed instead of selecting the default profile'. Failure shapes are designed: a failed Docker inventory returns ok=false with a reason and omits the inventory arrays 'so failure cannot be mistaken for an empty host'. Third-party trust signals are disclaimed in a Discovery and trust section ('External scores, tool counts, and install metrics are directory snapshots, not security attestations'; the VerifyMCP score 'is not a security certification'), and the repo's own CI runs the real stdio server against a live tenant, covering the managed-SQL safety matrix, plan-only behaviour and a confirmed dynamic-node add/remove.
bad: Scoped entirely to Docker-based local YDB deployments — a database we do not run — and the operating surface is powerful by design (host operations over SSH to named profiles, node lifecycle, auth changes), so the confirm:true discipline carries the whole safety story. Four stars; the Claude Code plugin route is still pending community review by its own account.
took: Corroboration for fail-closed configuration: an explicit config path that is missing or invalid fails closed rather than silently selecting a default profile, and a failed inventory omits its arrays so failure cannot be mistaken for an empty result — absence and failure never share a shape.
didnt: Not adopted — YDB is not our database; recorded for its fail-closed configuration and plan-first mutation discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Couchbase-Ecosystem/mcp-server-couchbase
good: The Couchbase ecosystem's MCP server for Capella and self-managed clusters: cluster health, schema discovery, document KV operations, SQL++ query and indexing, full-text and vector search, query-performance analysis and operational insights, over stdio or Streamable HTTP (an Operational Insights server ships alongside). Safety posture is explicit: read-only mode is ON by default — document upserts/inserts/deletes and data-modifying SQL++ are blocked unless CB_MCP_READ_ONLY_MODE=false — individual tools can be disabled, and tools can be gated behind user confirmation via elicitation. The doctrine is stated plainly: 'tool disabling is a convenience layer for guiding LLM behavior; the underlying Couchbase user's role-based access control remains the authoritative security boundary' — the same enforcement-in-the-account position as the AIops family in this batch. Remote deployments authenticate with OAuth 2.1 (JWT/JWKS, provider-agnostic), and the README carries Logging, Auditing, 'Risks Associated with LLMs' and Usage Data Collection sections in the open.
bad: The write surface is full once read-only mode is switched off (document writes, data-modifying SQL++, scope/collection create and permanent delete), several administrative reads require ro_admin or Full/Cluster Admin roles, and enterprise support sits behind the paid Couchbase AI Data Plane. Usage data collection exists and must be read in its own section before deployment.
took: Corroboration, from a second vendor in the same batch, for the doctrine that tool-layer gating guides the model while the connected account's RBAC is the authoritative boundary — paired here with read-only-by-default so the convenience layer and the boundary start out agreeing.
didnt: Not adopted — Couchbase is not our stack; recorded as the vendor-ecosystem server with a read-only-by-default posture (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: devopam/MCPg
good: A broad PostgreSQL MCP server (279 tools: catalog introspection, query intelligence, NL→SQL, structural diffs, hybrid search, graph queries via Apache AGE, pgvector/TimescaleDB/PostGIS integrations, live ops) with production-shaped hardening. Read-only is the default access mode (restricted and unrestricted are opt-ins); every user-supplied SQL statement parses through a validated AST allowlist before execution; capability gates keep higher-blast-radius tools off until enabled (DDL, shell subprocesses via MCPG_ALLOW_SHELL, LISTEN/NOTIFY); and — the step beyond hand-written labels — 'Every tool publishes MCP ToolAnnotations (readOnlyHint, openWorldHint) derived from those same gates, so clients can auto-approve reads and gate writes without guessing.' Every call records a structured audit event with credential-redacted arguments; the HTTP transport refuses to start unless authenticated (bearer token or OIDC JWT), with an explicit allow-unauthenticated escape hatch; multi-tenancy runs per-request SET ROLE against an allowed-roles list; TLS is enforced on startup; the Docker runtime drops its toolchain and runs as a non-login uid. Testing is stated in numbers: 2,500+ unit tests plus an integration suite against a real PostgreSQL container across PG 14–18 in CI (19 beta tracked as non-blocking).
bad: The ceiling is high: unrestricted mode plus the gate variables unlocks DBA operations (DDL, dumps, migrations) and even subprocess tools — all env-config, so the posture is one careless variable away from the widest surface; NL→SQL across 22 model providers adds a model-egress path for schema and data context. Fourteen stars sit oddly against the 'production-grade' framing.
took: Corroboration, one step past B133's annotation standard: the tool annotations are derived from the same capability gates that enforce them, so the label a client auto-approves by cannot drift away from the enforcement underneath it.
didnt: Not adopted — our Postgres needs are served directly and our MCP door is the wiki's own read door; recorded as the broad Postgres server whose annotations are derived from its gates (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: elekto-com-br/elekto-mcp-sql
good: A read-only SQL Server introspection server (.NET, stdio): 21 tools over schema metadata, DDL definitions, dependency graphs, index health and data profiling, plus a guarded query_table (filtering, secure aggregates, sampling, pagination), reading connection strings from the project's own appsettings.json / web.config so no credential is stored in the repo. Its engineering is an honesty discipline: results the login could only partly see carry a visibility block that says so; values that cannot be known are returned as null/'unknown' instead of passing a guess for a fact (a hidden procedure definition used to read as a body of 0 lines; an empty array used to mean both 'does not exist' and 'hidden from you' — now ok: false distinguishes them); check_permissions reports what the connected login can and cannot see, per tool, with the GRANT that completes it; failures come back as content (ok: false) rather than tool errors; a server started with no configuration answers every tool with the file to create, where it looked and an example, instead of exiting; every tool declares readOnlyHint / idempotentHint with destructiveHint: false and openWorldHint: false. A Privacy and Data Security Warning sits at the top of the README spelling out that tool results are transmitted to the LLM provider, and the no-configuration guidance tells the agent to agree with the user before writing anything and never to write a password into the connections file.
bad: GPL-3.0 puts the code in ideas-only territory for us, and SQL Server / .NET is not our stack; 0 stars. The read-only claim rests on the server's own validation, which its warning section is careful not to absolutise ('there is always a risk of unintended consequences').
took: Corroboration for visibility honesty: a result the credential could only partly see says so in a visibility block, and 'hidden from you' is never rendered as 'does not exist' or as an empty body — absence, invisibility and failure each keep their own shape.
didnt: Not adopted — GPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only and SQL Server is not our stack; recorded for its visibility-honesty standard (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ferrants/memvid-mcp-server
licence: No licence in force at source — the root LICENSE file is empty (0 bytes) and the repo metadata shows Other (NOASSERTION); treated as all-rights-reserved, ideas only
good: A small Streamable HTTP MCP wrapper over memvid (text encoded into video, retrieved by semantic search): two actions, add_chunks and search (top_k, 5 by default), run locally against a memory.mp4 file. As a demonstration that the memvid store can sit behind MCP at all, it is complete and honest about its limits.
bad: Four commits and no releases; the server's own README concedes add_chunks resets the memory video on every add ('Unsure if there is a way to incrementally add'), so the store cannot accumulate; the HTTP endpoint documents no authentication; and the empty LICENSE file leaves reuse rights unstated — all-rights-reserved by default.
didnt: Not adopted — a 4-commit demo wrapper; the memvid core already stands in the masters (memvid/memvid) with the .mv2 capsule boarded as an export-format idea, and this wrapper adds nothing to it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fireproof-storage/mcp-database-server
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) — a LICENSE.md file is present in the repo but GitHub does not classify it
good: A minimal Fireproof-backed JSON document store for MCP, by the Fireproof project itself: CRUD operations plus queries sorted by any field, over stdio for Claude Desktop, with MCP Inspector debugging wired as an npm script. As the vendor's own reference example of plugging a ledger database into tool use, it is small and readable. (The catalogue description — 'Fireproof ledger database with multi-user sync' — describes the Fireproof platform; this repo is its demo server, and the row is judged on the repo.)
bad: Self-declared demo grade: 6 commits, no releases, a README that teaches installation and Inspector debugging and nothing about the sync or ledger behaviour the catalogue line advertises; the licence file GitHub cannot classify leaves the reuse terms to be read in LICENSE.md itself before any use.
didnt: Rejected — a demo-grade MCP document store with an unclassified licence; our MCP door is read-only and citation-locked by design, and unclassified-licence code is ideas-only at most. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FROWNINGdev/django-orm-lens
good: Static analysis of a Django project's ORM layer with no database and no django.setup(): one parser core behind three surfaces — a VS Code extension, a CLI (17 subcommands, SARIF + PR annotations, pre-commit hooks, a GitHub Action) and 13 read-only MCP tools 'answering schema questions from ground truth'. It builds the model graph (apps → models → fields → Meta) and live ER diagrams from source alone, detects N+1 loops by following querysets across functions with the select_related to add, and checks schema drift by replaying each app's migrations in order into the field set they imply and comparing against models.py — 'Only the dangerous direction fails the build: a field declared but never migrated means the column will not exist.' Migration risk is weighed against real table sizes: blast-radius --stats turns 'probably populated' into '~41 000 000 rows, 12.0 GB' from a read-only query the operator runs themself, 'with no database credential anywhere near CI'; impact findings carry Certain / Likely / Possibly confidence tags, and time-travel schema diffs treat renames as first-class events with confidence-scored detection, never Add + Drop. Zero runtime dependencies for the CLI, no account, no telemetry, and 'There is no Pro tier, and none is planned.'
bad: Django-only by construction, and young despite the cadence (created 2026-07-12) with heavy traction marketing around the engineering. The --stats mode needs the operator to run a read-only query themselves and feed the result in — a deliberate credential boundary, and a manual step.
took: Corroboration for ground-truth schema answers: derive the schema by static parsing and migration replay instead of asking a running system, tag impact findings Certain / Likely / Possibly rather than flat, and fail the build only in the dangerous direction.
didnt: Not adopted — we build no Django; recorded as the static schema-analysis design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gannonh/firebase-mcp
good: The established community Firebase MCP server (247 stars): Firestore tools (add/list/get/update/delete documents, list collections, collection-group queries), Storage tools (list, file info, upload from content or from URL) and an Auth user lookup, over stdio or an HTTP transport with session management, installed via npx (@gannonh/firebase-mcp) and authenticated with a Firebase service-account key. Its README documents a known issue in the open — the firestore_list_collections Zod validation error is investigated, attributed to the MCP SDK, and stated not to affect functionality — and its tests run against the Firebase emulators.
bad: The credential is the whole security story: a service-account key carries Admin SDK authority over the project (Firestore, Storage, Auth user lookup) and typically bypasses Firestore security rules, yet no read-only mode, tool gating or confirmation is described anywhere; the HTTP transport adds session management with no authentication described for it. For our own Firebase project that is precisely the door shape we do not open.
didnt: Not adopted — Firebase is our platform, but this door hands an agent a service-account key with no read-only mode or gating described; our Firebase work stays inside the owner's cricsfc Google scope and the existing tooling (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: infino-ai/infino-mcp
good: Retrieval over your own data where it already lives: an MCP server for Infino running keyword (BM25), semantic, hybrid and SQL retrieval over Apache Parquet on object storage — a local path, your own S3/Azure/S3-compatible bucket, or a hosted Infino Cloud endpoint. The index discipline is the point: 'The index is a valid Parquet file' — data and search indexes in plain Parquet, openable with DuckDB or pyarrow, 'No export, no lock-in.' Semantic search embeds queries with a local model by default (transformers.js MiniLM; a one-time ~90 MB download, then offline), so nothing leaves the machine for embedding. Its posture is stated in the same doctrine two other servers in this batch use: 'The agent owns the data. Every tool, writes included, is always available. On Infino Cloud the API key's capabilities decide what a connection may do; every tool carries MCP annotations so your client can ask before a destructive call.' INFINO_MCP_VALIDATE probes the store at startup so bad credentials or an unreachable bucket fail then instead of on the first search, and logs go to stderr so they never corrupt the JSON-RPC stream.
bad: Zero stars and young (created 2026-06-16); the 'agent owns the data' posture means local connections get no read-only mode at all — every write tool is always available — and the hosted Cloud endpoint reintroduces vendor custody for those who choose it. The embedding model must match the one that produced the stored vectors or similarity is meaningless, a coupling the README states but cannot remove.
took: Corroboration for portable index formats: the search index itself is a valid Parquet file readable by DuckDB or pyarrow, so the retrieval layer never becomes lock-in — the files-as-truth instinct applied one layer down, to the index.
didnt: Not adopted — our retrieval runs over the wiki's own files and indexes; recorded as the Parquet-native retrieval design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Janadasroor/pg-mnemosyne-mcp
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: A Postgres-backed MCP memory with a deliberately professional shape: asyncpg connection pooling; a tasks schema with status transitions (backlog/todo/in_progress/blocked/done), priorities and deadlines; and an agent_sessions coordination hub where agents register their current file and subtask as a real-time bulletin board against double-coding and merge conflicts. Ships on PyPI with a CLI that can add, list and initialise records and auto-configure nine named MCP clients.
bad: run_sql executes arbitrary SQL including DDL, and sibling tools create databases and add columns dynamically: through one DSN the agent holds full DBA authority, with no read-only mode, allowlist, confirmation or audit described anywhere. Memory in a Postgres database is the opposite custody shape from our files-as-truth wiki, and 11 commits/4 stars is a young base for a coordination-critical role.
took: Corroboration for mutual-visibility coordination: agents publishing their active file and subtask to a shared board so conflicts surface before the merge, not at it — the bulletin-board member of the coordination family B133's quilt works at line level.
didnt: Not adopted: our agents coordinate through the wiki, filings and separate branches, and our memory is the wiki's files — a Postgres-backed memory and task store would replace both with a database we would have to trust and back up. The coordination-hub idea is noted against B133's quilt, which solves the same conflict problem at line level inside git itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: KashiwaByte/vikingdb-mcp-server
licence: No licence found at source (repository page read in full: no licence in the repository details, no LICENSE file in the root listing, and the README names none) — all rights reserved by default; ideas only.
good: A small, early (December 2024) community MCP server over ByteDance's VikingDB vector database: collection and index introspection, upsert and search in four tools, packaged for uv/Smithery with a Dockerfile — a representative of the first wave of vendor-vector-database MCP wrappers.
bad: It fronts ByteDance's hosted Volcengine cloud: collection data lives in VikingDB, access is by access-key/secret-key pairs pasted into client configuration arguments, and one of the four tools is an upsert — a write surface into a third-party cloud store. The README is sparse, with no read-only mode, scoping or data-handling discussion.
didnt: Not adopted: no licence in force at source (ideas only in any case), and a hosted ByteDance vector database is not a store we place the owner's material in; our retrieval runs over the wiki's own files. Recorded as distinct from the Tier 1 OpenViking rows, which are a separate ByteDance project. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kosminus/querywise-mcp
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: Natural-language database querying with the safety story in the execution path, not the prompt: all execution is read-only, enforced twice — a static SQL blocklist (DDL/DML/admin/injection) plus connector-level enforcement (SQLite opened mode=ro, Postgres in a read-only transaction). The tool design separates generation from execution: generate_sql writes SQL but does not run it, so a human or client reviews before run_sql; the recommended MCP loop keeps reasoning in the client's model while the server grounds the question in a business semantic layer (glossary, metrics, data dictionary, example queries) stored in an embedded SQLite + sqlite-vec file — zero external infrastructure, degrading gracefully to keyword-only matching with no embedding provider.
bad: Young and small (13 commits, 3 stars). The semantic layer that grounds every answer is itself writable through the MCP management tools, so a bad or malicious glossary entry steers future queries — a poisoning surface the README does not discuss; authentication for the Streamable HTTP mode is not described in what was read.
took: Corroboration for two of our door standards: generation and execution as separate tools with a review point between them, and read-only enforced at two independent layers (statement blocklist and the connector's own read-only mode) rather than one.
didnt: Not adopted: we query our own files and SQLite stores directly and have no business databases needing a natural-language layer; the catalogue's FOR US verdict is answered by the read-only and generation/execution-split standards it corroborates rather than by adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memgraph/mcp-memgraph
licence: MIT (parent repository root: LICENSE file and GitHub repository details for memgraph/ai-toolkit; the batch item is a directory inside that repository).
good: Memgraph's own MCP server with read-only as the default posture: write Cypher verbs (CREATE, MERGE, DELETE, SET, DROP, REMOVE) are blocked unless MCP_READ_ONLY=false. Results are type-preserving (nodes, relationships and paths return as tagged objects). The optional multi-tenant authentication is carefully bounded: OIDC/JWT validated against issuer, audience, expiry and a required scope; the session's database set is the intersection of the token's tenants claim with the server's tenant catalog, and use_database states it 'cannot expand authorization beyond what the JWT grants'; enabling auth with a required variable missing fails fast at startup. The DCR-intercept workaround is described with unusual candour ('makes the MCP server lie to those clients').
bad: Memgraph is not our stack — our graph needs are served by the wiki's own link structure, and adopting this means adopting the database. run_cypher_query is arbitrary Cypher once read-only is switched off, and the experimental server variant ignores read-only mode entirely (stated, but the escape exists). The parent toolkit also ships a Context Graph that captures coding-agent sessions into the graph — a session-transcript substrate our owner has not approved; noted as adjacent, not part of this server.
took: Corroboration for token-bounded scope: a session may switch context only inside the set its credential already grants — the same registration-gating family as B132's dockndevai and B133's bbkt, derived here from the caller's JWT claims.
didnt: Not adopted: no Memgraph in our systems, and nothing here displaces the wiki's files-and-links graph. The token-bounded tenant switching is filed as design corroboration for the hosted-door question. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neo4j-contrib/mcp-neo4j
licence: MIT (LICENSE.txt at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README License section).
good: Neo4j Labs' MCP collection (maintained by the Neo4j Field GenAI team): four servers — Cypher (schema inspection plus natural-language-to-Cypher execution), memory (entities and relationships as cross-session knowledge-graph memory), cloud-aura-api (create, scale, find and destroy Aura instances) and data-modeling (create, validate and visualise graph models, Arrows.app import/export). The README is candid about status — Labs software, frequently updated, 'not supported by the Neo4j product team', no SLAs or backwards-compatibility guarantees — and signposts the official product server for those who need it. All servers run over stdio, SSE or Streamable HTTP and ship containerised deployment guides.
bad: The cypher server executes generated read and write Cypher with no read-only mode described at this level, and the Aura server can create and destroy cloud database instances from a chat — capability as risk, gated by the account's credentials alone. Labs status means breaking changes arrive without the guarantees a production door wants.
didnt: Not adopted: Neo4j is not in our stack — the wiki's graph is its own files and links — and the Labs no-SLA posture is wrong for anything load-bearing. Recorded as the vendor-adjacent collection it is, distinct from the community Neo4j memory servers already in the masters. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nlqueries/nlqueries
licence: Business Source License 1.1 (README badge and License section; LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub shows Other/NOASSERTION) — converts to Apache-2.0 no later than 2030-06-04, each version also converting on the fourth anniversary of its first publication; until conversion it grants production use except offering the product as a hosted or managed service. Ideas only under our licence discipline.
good: A self-hosted NL2SQL engine with an MCP server, built around validation: generated SQL is checked against the schema before execution across PostgreSQL, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, SQL Server, DuckDB and SQLite. A YAML knowledge base is auto-built from schema and query history; a feedback loop re-validates thumbs-up answers' SQL against the current schema before blending them into later prompts as verified examples; an eval command regression-checks generated SQL against the agent's own mined capsules and a golden set. Its documentation index includes a database-hardening page stating 'the read-only role to grant per engine, and exactly what each connector does and does not enforce' — the enforcement-in-the-account doctrine of B134 stated as a documentation standard. The semantic cache replays the stored SQL so a cached answer's rows are current rather than stale. Document Q&A answers with citations.
bad: BUSL-1.1 until its conversion dates — ideas only under our licence discipline, whatever the production-use grant says. The network-served MCP token 'has full access' (the README's own words), so the read-only posture depends on the operator following the hardening doc's role grants. Needs Qdrant for embeddings, semantic cache and document search; 4 stars against a broad feature surface.
took: Corroboration for two standards: a hardening document that states what each connector does NOT enforce, beside the read-only role to grant; and user-approved example SQL re-validated against the current schema before it is trusted as a prompt example.
didnt: Not adopted: BUSL is outside the adaptation class, and our querying runs over our own files and stores, not a fleet of business databases. Its hardening-doc candour and feedback re-validation are filed as standards corroboration. The catalogue's FOR US verdict is answered at the level of those standards. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: questdb/mcp-server-questdb
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README License section).
good: A different door architecture: instead of holding database credentials, this bridge connects the agent to the user's already-open QuestDB Web Console — every notebook, query and chart action executes in the browser against the user's established session. Pairing is ephemeral and consent-based: each bridge run generates a fresh port and token held only in memory, the user accepts a consent prompt in the console tab, and on restart the old credentials stop working. Distribution is careful: a setup wizard pins the bridge version into each detected agent's config (a version mismatch tells the agent which version to switch to), and an offline route offers a single self-contained .mjs release bundle that makes no network connections except the local WebSocket.
bad: The flip side of session-borrowing: the agent inherits the full power of the user's console session — whatever that session may run, the agent may run, with no narrower scoping described. QuestDB is not in our stack. DEBUG logging records full tool payloads, so the log files become a sensitive artefact of their own.
took: Corroboration for ephemeral pairing: per-run credentials held only in memory, consent taken in the user's own already-authenticated session, and nothing long-lived stored for the agent to hold — acting through the user's session rather than through a stored credential.
didnt: Not adopted: we run no QuestDB, and our doors are the wiki's own. The ephemeral-pairing and session-borrowing pattern is filed as corroboration for door design generally. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SidneyBissoli/ibge-br-mcp
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details). The IBGE data itself is served under Brazil's open-data framework (Lei 12.527/2011 and Decreto 8.777/2016 — unrestricted reuse with source credit), as the README's provenance section states.
good: A read-only MCP server over Brazil's official IBGE APIs (localities, SIDRA tables, census 1970–2022, indicators, municipal panels, geographic meshes, health, news) whose centrepiece is a provenance block on every response since v3.3.0: source, the canonical URL that reproduces the query, data_vintage (the reference period, or null when the source exposes none), retrieved_at (the real upstream extraction instant, preserved across cache hits), a ready-to-use citation and the licence — mirrored in structuredContent, an out-of-band _meta channel and a text footer. Aggregates computed server-side are marked derived. The README is honest about versions: IBGE revises published figures and keeps no earlier version, so every value is the version published at retrieved_at; and it records a fixed defect — indicator tools once mixed every variable of a table, now each is pinned to the one variable its name promises.
bad: Domain fit only: Brazilian official statistics serve none of the owner's work. The claims of 565 tests and 88% coverage are the project's own reporting, not independently verified here. A remote hosted endpoint is offered alongside local install, which would put queries through the author's infrastructure — the local route exists and is the one the provenance design deserves.
took: Corroboration for per-response provenance: source, reproducing URL, data vintage, retrieval instant and citation attached to every answer, with derived values marked as derived — the citation standard our own Ask door is judged against, implemented by a data server.
didnt: Not adopted: no use for Brazilian public data in the owner's systems. The per-response provenance block is filed as corroboration for our citation standard — it is the strongest implementation of it in this wave. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: slotix/dbconvert-streams-public
licence: Split, stated openly in the README: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details) covers this repository's examples, documentation and assets only; the DBConvert Streams product and its bundled MCP server binary are proprietary under the DBConvert Streams licence. The open part does not launder the closed part.
good: The public home of DBConvert Streams (database IDE + migration + real-time CDC) whose MCP surface is read-only by design: 27 tools for connections, schemas, table/view inspection, SELECT-only SQL and federated queries (DuckDB joining PostgreSQL, MySQL, files and S3 in one statement), schema/data comparison and stream diagnostics — 'only SELECT passes the server-side filter — the AI can look and advise, never write'. The desktop app's built-in AI Chat likewise receives a scoped read-only subset and 'cannot change connections, configuration, streams, or data'. A 'When this is probably not for you' section names its own limits.
bad: The software you would actually run — the IDE, the CDC engine and the bundled MCP server binary — is proprietary and distributed under the vendor's own licence; the MIT in this repository covers only the examples, docs and assets around it. The IDE itself edits data directly (outside the read-only MCP surface), and migration/CDC sit behind pricing. Nothing here can be audited at source because the source is not published.
didnt: Not adopted: a proprietary binary is not a door we open, and we have no database migration or CDC workload for it to do. The read-only MCP surface design is noted; the licence split is recorded in the licence line where it belongs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Snowflake-Labs/mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: Snowflake Labs' community MCP server for Cortex AI — and a model of honest deprecation: the README's first line marks it [DEPRECATED], states it is no longer maintained and directs every user to the official Snowflake MCP Server. The legacy design had real governance vocabulary: a configuration file drives the whole tool surface (only explicitly listed Cortex Agent/Search/Analyst services become tools), tool groups are enabled individually, and a sql_statement_permissions section allows or denies execution per statement type (Select, Insert, Create, Drop, Unknown…) across any tool that can change objects — with enforcement ultimately resting on the connected role's RBAC, as the README states.
bad: Deprecated and unmaintained by its own banner. The legacy surface includes object management (create, drop, update) and LLM-generated SQL; the shipped example configuration enables nearly every statement type including Drop, Delete and TruncateTable, so the permissions file is a loaded default an operator must actively narrow. Snowflake is not in our stack in any case.
didnt: Not adopted: deprecated, and Snowflake is not our platform. Recorded with its deprecation and successor pointer intact — a catalogue entry whose source now answers 'use the other one'. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SurajKGoyal/amnesic
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: Persistent semantic memory for SQL databases (Postgres, MySQL, MSSQL, SQLite): a per-database local SQLite store holding what the schema means — table and column annotations (what status = 3 is), a foreign-key graph including hand-annotated relationships for legacy schemas with no FK constraints, and searchable notes — handed to every future session automatically. Read-only enforcement is two-layered: static SQL analysis refuses write statements including writes smuggled inside a WITH CTE, and every query runs inside a transaction that is immediately rolled back, so a parser miss still cannot persist. The knowledge is portable: export hands the next developer everything taught as JSON, outliving access to the database itself. Its 'Honest comparison' table marks its own gaps (no execution plans, no lineage/governance, cached schema) and advises using a query executor instead where those matter.
bad: Small and young (4 stars). The knowledge layer is only as good as what sessions teach it: schema freshness is cached with manual refresh (its own comparison table concedes this), so stale meaning can be served confidently; knowledge import is an unconditional upsert, stated but sharp. It solves a problem — forgotten schema meaning — that our wiki pages already solve in prose.
took: Corroboration for defence in depth on reads: a rollback-wrapped transaction as a second enforcement layer that does not trust the statement parser — if classification fails, the transaction boundary still makes the read harmless.
didnt: Not adopted: our schema and systems knowledge lives in the wiki's compiled pages, not a per-database SQLite store, and we run no fleet of legacy SQL databases for agents to forget. The rollback-wrapped read is filed as corroboration. Cross-reference B135's querywise and dati: three shapes of the semantic-layer idea in one batch — stored meaning, grounded generation, and a publishing gateway. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VictoriaMetrics-Community/mcp-victorialogs
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: The VictoriaMetrics community's MCP server for VictoriaLogs, read-only by API selection: it exposes almost all of VictoriaLogs' read-only APIs (log queries, streams, fields and field values, query statistics) plus something rarer — the product's up-to-date documentation embedded in the server and searchable without online access, so the agent can read the manual offline. Operationally complete: per-tool disabling via MCP_DISABLED_TOOLS, bearer-token and custom-header configuration, a public playground instance to try without installing, Helm chart, Prometheus /metrics and health endpoints, and binaries, Docker and go install routes.
bad: VictoriaLogs is not in our stack. The header-passthrough option forwards named incoming MCP request headers to the VictoriaLogs instance — flexible behind a reverse proxy, but a deployment care point: a caller-supplied header reaches the data store, and the configuration example shows it beside the bearer token without a warning. The README itself notes response quality depends heavily on the client model.
didnt: Not adopted: no VictoriaLogs instances to inspect. Recorded as a competent vendor-community read-only server; the org move from the catalogue's VictoriaMetrics-Community path to VictoriaMetrics is noted in the evidence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: weaviate/mcp-server-weaviate
licence: No licence found at source (the repository as it stands contains only README.md: no licence in the repository details and no LICENSE file; the README names none) — nothing in this repository is licensed for reuse; the built-in server it points to lives in the weaviate/weaviate repository under that project's own terms, not examined here.
