good: The repository now documents a genuine platform evolution: Weaviate absorbed its MCP server into the database itself — from v1.37.1 (preview) the main binary serves MCP at /v1/mcp on the REST port, enabled by one environment variable, authenticating through the existing API-key flow and respecting RBAC, with four tools (collection config inspection, tenant listing, hybrid search, object upsert). The deprecation is handled cleanly: the notice is the README's first line, the successor is named with its documentation, and the old standalone Go implementation is declared unmaintained with its history preserved rather than deleted.
bad: As a repository there is almost nothing left to adopt or audit: the standalone implementation is unmaintained and its source survives only in git history before the notice. The built-in server it points to includes an objects-upsert write tool; its safety rests on Weaviate's own RBAC configuration, which this page does not examine. The catalogue description ('Use Weaviate collections as a knowledge base and as a chat memory store') describes the retired standalone server, not what the repository now documents.
didnt: Not adopted: the standalone server is retired, and Weaviate itself is already recorded as a Tier 1 platform; no MCP door to Weaviate is needed. The row records the signpost state of the repository as found. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yimindev/dati
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: A database semantic gateway (Spring Boot/Java 21 + Vue) that publishes databases as MCP services: connect MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse or Doris, enrich the metadata (business terms, column aliases, automatically extracted enum dictionaries), then compose the published service from built-in tools plus parameterized SQL tools — owner-authored SQL with named parameters, the safe middle ground between no agent access and arbitrary agent-written SQL. Credentials are centrally managed with user-level permissions and data-scope isolation, and services are published over Streamable HTTP from a configuration UI rather than code. Bilingual documentation, an online demo and worked examples (star-schema BI, a family-finance assistant) are included.
bad: A whole platform to operate — Spring Boot service, web frontend, its own database and Elasticsearch for semantic retrieval — to front databases we do not run. The quick start makes the first registered user ('admin') the super admin, a default to handle with care on any network-reachable deployment. Created 2026-08-23: two months old at study time, with its governance claims resting on its own documentation.
took: Corroboration for parameterized SQL tools as a door shape: the owner authors the query once, the agent supplies only parameter values — capability without free-form query text, the database analogue of our fixed-verb read door.
didnt: Not adopted: we have no enterprise databases to gateway and no NL2SQL workload. The parameterized-tool publishing model is filed as corroboration for door design. Cross-reference B135's querywise and amnesic — the batch's three semantic-layer shapes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AceDataCloud/MCPSerp
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details) — the licence covers this wrapper; the AceDataCloud SERP API it calls is a commercial metered service under the vendor's own terms.
good: An MIT MCP wrapper over AceDataCloud's Google SERP API (web, images, news, videos, places, maps and knowledge-graph search in 11 tools, with localisation and time filters) whose README is unusually careful about credentials and metering: it explains that Dynamic Client Registration 'is not an API key', warns against configuring both OAuth and a fixed Authorization header, walks through per-key restrictions, expiry and usage limits, and states plainly that 'Search tools are read-only but consume Credits, and repeating a search can incur another charge' and that the health endpoint 'checks endpoint reachability only'.
bad: Every route — hosted or local stdio — ends at AceDataCloud's metered commercial API: searches consume credits, repeats charge again, and the account balance is part of the tool's behaviour. That is a paid egress dependency for search capability we already have through our own routes, from a 1-star repository.
didnt: Rejected: a metered hosted wrapper around a commercial SERP API, where the open code is the thin part and the service is the product. The credential candour is credited in the good field; nothing else is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AIMLPM/markcrawl
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: A local Python crawler that turns sites into clean Markdown plus a structured JSONL index in which every page carries its URL, fetch timestamp and a pre-formatted citation with access date — provenance built into crawl output rather than reconstructed later. The default embedder is local (no API key); HTTP retries honour the server's Retry-After header. Its benchmark posture is exemplary: the README quotes the independent crawler benchmark that ranks it 1st on cost and 7th of 7 on answer quality and retrieval accuracy, prints the numbers, explains the cause (aggregator print pages stealing 39–49% of top-5 slots, since fixed by a default filter), adds a methodology caveat about the benchmark itself, and includes both a decision matrix steering users to Firecrawl, Crawl4AI or Scrapy where those fit better and a 'When NOT to use MarkCrawl' section. The MCP server is an optional add-on, not the core.
bad: Its own published numbers put answer quality (3.77/5) and retrieval MRR (0.341 against leaders at 0.76) last of seven crawlers — the gap is attributed to its deliberately narrower crawl strategy, with recovery projected, not yet measured. The default install bundles the full ML stack (torch, transformers), a heavy dependency for a crawler; 5 stars.
took: Corroboration for two standards: a citation with access date emitted per fetched page at crawl time, and publishing the benchmark you lose (rank, numbers and cause in the README) beside the one you win.
didnt: Not adopted: our ingest is owner-directed per source and filed into the wiki by hand with provenance recorded; a bulk crawler feeding a vector store is a different pipeline from ours. The catalogue's FOR US verdict is answered by the citation and benchmark-honesty standards it corroborates. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AIweather-Anurag/ottasia-mcp-server
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README License section).
good: A small, honest thin client: three read-only tools (where_to_watch, whats_new_on, search_titles) over the author's own ottasia.com public JSON endpoints for 30 Asian and Middle Eastern streaming markets, with no API key and no configuration — the npm package never holds a credential because all TMDB data, caching and per-country provider logic stay on the backend. It carries an explicit privacy policy: the server sends only the query terms (a title, a provider, a country code) and collects, stores and transmits no personal data, credentials, files or conversation content. A hosted HTTP/SSE endpoint is offered beside the local install.
bad: A thin client whose data lives entirely on the author's backend: if ottasia.com changes or closes, the installed package is dead. Six commits and one star; coverage and freshness of the underlying availability data are the vendor's, unverifiable from the repository.
didnt: Not adopted: streaming-availability lookup for Asian and Middle Eastern markets serves none of the owner's work. Recorded as a clean small example of the keyless thin-client shape. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: andybrandt/mcp-simple-arxiv
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README License section).
good: One of the earliest arXiv MCP servers (December 2024) and a model of API citizenship: it follows arXiv's published API guidelines — rate limited to a maximum of one request per three seconds, a single connection at a time, with error handling and retry logic — and says so in the README. Search covers title and abstract with submission-date filtering and sorting by submission date, update date or relevance, and results report the total matching count so the model can gauge a query's specificity. It returns metadata, abstracts, links to PDF/HTML formats and full text converted to Markdown, runs locally over stdio or as the author's hosted web connector, and needs no API key.
bad: A search-and-metadata wrapper: no local paper store, no section-level reading, no citation export — the literature loop stops at the abstract and a whole-paper Markdown conversion. Capability has been surpassed by richer arXiv servers (B136's blazickjp/arxiv-mcp-server in this same batch is the fuller pole).
didnt: Not adopted: our paper work opens sources through our own fetch and ingest routes. Recorded as the simple, well-mannered pole of the arXiv door pair in this batch. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bartonguestier1725-collab/scout-mcp
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README License section).
good: Parallel fan-out search across 21 sources in one server — code registries (GitHub, npm, PyPI, GitLab), papers (arXiv, Semantic Scholar), community and blogs (Hacker News, Reddit, Lobsters, StackExchange, dev.to, Hashnode, Qiita, Zenn, Lemmy, YouTube, Product Hunt, X) — each tool a direct API call returning normalized JSON with consistent fields (title, url, source, created_at). The multi-source scout_report runs searches with Promise.allSettled, so one failing source does not block the others. Most tools work with no keys at all; optional keys only unlock sources or raise rate limits, tabulated honestly as required/recommended/optional.
bad: Breadth over depth: it returns search results, not readings, and several sources are mediated (X search runs through xAI's Grok with the user's key). The same code also runs as the author's paid x402 HTTP API — the free stdio mode is unaffected, but the business model is part of the artefact. One star; the catalogue understates it as 12 platforms against the README's 21 tools — recorded here.
took: Corroboration for partial-failure fan-out: parallel source searches settled independently so a single source's failure degrades the report instead of voiding it — the shape our own multi-lane research needs when one route dies.
didnt: Not adopted: our research routes already search these source families and then read the sources themselves, which is the step this server stops before. The partial-failure fan-out is filed as corroboration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BenyD/haypile
licence: AGPL-3.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details) — copyleft; ideas only under our licence discipline.
good: Local-first document search with its privacy made measurable: one Go binary (~56 MB, embedding model inside) watches folders and indexes PDF, DOCX, PPTX, Markdown, HTML and mbox into a single SQLite file (FTS5 + vector merged by RRF), serving MCP and REST on localhost only, every result carrying a file and page citation. Its Trust commitments are versioned with the code: the open/paid boundary is declared upfront (the full single-user product is open under AGPL forever; paid team features come later, named in advance), and 'zero external connections' is a verifiable feature — hay status reports outbound connections with a target of 0 and no telemetry. The cloud-LLM boundary is sharp: documents are always indexed locally, opting in sends only the retrieved passages for that one question to an endpoint the user chose, and API keys are refused over plain HTTP to anything but localhost. Retrieval quality is measured by an eval/ query set with expected results, run on every retrieval-affecting change.
bad: AGPL-3.0 — ideas only under our licence discipline. Two stars and three months old. Scanned-PDF OCR currently needs a local vision model rather than a bundled engine (roadmap), and answer generation depends on an external local LLM server the user must run; without one, ask degrades to showing passages.
took: Corroboration for verifiable privacy: a status command that counts outbound connections turns 'we never phone home' from a claim into a measurement the user can check — the standard our own tools' privacy statements should meet.
didnt: Not adopted: AGPL places it outside the adaptation class, and our document search runs over the wiki itself. The catalogue's FOR US verdict is answered by the verifiable-privacy standard it sets, which is the part worth keeping. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: blazickjp/arxiv-mcp-server
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: The established arXiv MCP server (3,228 stars) built as a literature-work loop rather than a search wrapper: paper ID → outline → one section → citations. Nineteen tools include bounded full-text reads (12,000 characters by default, with start/max_chars controls), paginated outlines with stable section IDs, passage search returning source offsets, reads of the original author-submitted LaTeX by section (the source, not a PDF scrape), a citation graph via Semantic Scholar cached on disk, BibTeX exported from authoritative arXiv metadata, and topic watches stored locally with carefully specified update semantics (omit categories to preserve, pass [] to clear). Papers stay on disk under the user's own storage path. The README warns that an unrelated npm package shares the name and must not be installed — namesake hygiene stated where installers will see it.
bad: Semantic search over the local store sits behind a [pro] extra, so the free server's local loop is lexical. Downloads convert HTML-first with a PDF fallback, so fidelity varies by paper. The plugin/skill packaging steers client behaviour — convenient, and one more surface to audit before trusting.
took: Corroboration for bounded section-level reading: outline first, then one bounded section at a time with stable identifiers — the mechanised form of our deep-study counting standard (open the source, read enough to judge, never skim the whole into context).
didnt: Not adopted as an install: our paper programme opens sources through its own routes and files them into the wiki. Recorded as the reference implementation of the arXiv door — the fuller pole against this batch's mcp-simple-arxiv — and as corroboration for the bounded-reading discipline our deep-study standard already practises by hand. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: deficlow/HyperStore-MCP
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README License section, © HyperGPT) — the licence covers this wrapper; the HyperStore catalogue data is the vendor's.
good: A clean thin wrapper over HyperGPT's HyperStore directory (6,500+ listed AI applications): 13 read-only tools (keyword and embedding search, full app details with pricing and screenshots, categories, audiences, use cases, curated alternatives), three resources and three guided prompts, installable by uvx/pipx/Docker or via the vendor's hosted endpoint with no credentials. The How it works section states the shape plainly: a thin async wrapper around the public REST API, 'read-only — no credentials, no writes, no PII', with the website and the MCP server serving the same data.
bad: The catalogue is a vendor's marketing directory: listings, pricing and 'curated alternatives' are HyperGPT's commercial curation, so answers inherit a sales surface's incentives. The wrapper is 12 commits and 1 star, and the hosted-endpoint route makes the vendor's server the data path. Nothing here is a primary source for anything.
didnt: Not adopted: AI-app directory discovery is not a research need of ours — the landscape programme reads projects at their own sources, which is precisely what a directory front-end abstracts away. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: divyanshu-iitian/SearchForge
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: A capability-routed search gateway with honest failure semantics: queries route by intent (code to GitHub, academic to Crossref, community to Hacker News, web to a private self-hosted SearXNG with Wikipedia fallback), providers are isolated so 'one outage cannot erase healthy results', tracking parameters are stripped before deduplication, every contributing provider stays in the result's sources, and rankings fuse by reciprocal rank. Its read_url accepts public HTTP(S) URLs only — credentials, localhost, private IP literals and non-web protocols are rejected, responses size-bounded, timed out and cached. A doctor command performs real bounded probes and reports each provider's access tier, capability, latency and error as degraded rather than all-or-nothing. The Production boundary section states the rule our own house runs on: 'Search results and page content are untrusted input; delimit them and apply prompt-injection defenses.' It generates no answers, hides no citations and sends no telemetry.
bad: Fifteen commits and two stars, created weeks before this study — the design standards are ahead of the track record. The read path depends on Jina Reader's no-key quota (documented at 20 requests/minute), an external dependency inside the 'free' story, and broad web metasearch needs the operator to self-host SearXNG.
took: Corroboration for two reporting standards: provider health reported as degraded with the failing part named, never as a binary up/down; and the untrusted-input boundary for fetched content stated in the tool's own production documentation.
didnt: Not adopted: our search routes are established and read sources directly. The catalogue's FOR US verdict is answered by the degraded-health and untrusted-input standards it corroborates. Recorded as distinct from the masters' searchforge-seo-geo namesake. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dumpling-AI/mcp-server-dumplingai
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details) — the licence covers this wrapper; the Dumpling AI API it calls is a commercial hosted service under the vendor's own terms.
good: A broad MIT wrapper over the Dumpling AI API: 28 tools spanning data APIs (YouTube transcripts, web/maps/places/news search, Google reviews), scraping (scrape, crawl, screenshot, AI extraction against a schema), document conversion (doc-to-text with OCR, PDF conversion and merging, PDF metadata read/write, document/image/audio/video extraction) and AI features, each documented with a full example request. One key unlocks the whole surface, which is the convenience the product sells.
bad: Every call executes on the vendor's hosted API behind a required API key: documents to convert, pages to scrape, images, audio and video all leave the machine, and two tools run arbitrary JavaScript and Python in the vendor's cloud by design. The local MIT code is the thin part; custody, metering and retention are the service's. A knowledge-base add tool writes into the vendor's store as well.
didnt: Rejected: a hosted-API wrapper of the B129 convertica / B130 conv2pdf family — our documents and media are processed locally or not at all. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: echology-io/decompose
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README closing licence line, © Echology, Inc.).
good: Deterministic, no-LLM text decomposition: pure regex and heuristics split any text into semantic units, each classified by authority (mandatory, prohibitive, directive, permissive, conditional, informational), risk (safety_critical, security, compliance, financial, contractual, advisory), type, an irreducible flag (must this be preserved verbatim), an attention score from 0 to 10, and extracted entities (standards, codes, regulations). A filter_for_llm keeps the high-value units under a token budget and reports the reduction percentage (typically 60–80%); routing examples send safety-critical units to full analysis with human review and skip boilerplate. It runs offline in under 500 ms for a 50-page spec, same input always producing the same output, and ships as library, CLI and a two-tool MCP server. The patterns were extracted from a production AEC document-intelligence platform and tested against thousands of real specs and contracts.
bad: The classifiers are regex and heuristics tuned on AEC documents (specs, contracts, RFIs); how authority and attention scores transfer to general prose is unproven, and an attention score from pattern matching is a heuristic ranking, not a calibrated judgement — treated as ground truth it would mislead. Ten stars; the marketing register ('The missing cognitive primitive') runs ahead of the evidence.
took: Corroboration for deterministic pre-classification: authority class and a verbatim-irreducibility flag assigned by rule before any model reasoning begins — classification as a cheap, auditable first pass, with the model reserved for judgement.
didnt: Not adopted as a component: our ingest classifies by reading, and a regex authority layer over the owner's material would need validation we have not done. Recorded as design corroboration — the deterministic end of the claim-labelling family that B133's commitlore works from the git side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gaoshan0971/digeguigui
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: A complete vertical knowledge product for reptile and exotic-pet collectors (the name is 滴个龟龟）: a 633-species knowledge base with per-species gene trees drawn like GitHub commit graphs (breeding routes as branches, merges and key nodes), AI species identification from photos returning a genotype guess with confidence, a genetics calculator computing offspring genotype distributions from the parents, a collection showcase wall, a price-reference 'weather station' (explicitly reference only — no transaction matching, no funds handled), and blockchain provenance certificates, exposed to agents through an MCP server with 9 free tools. The plan is candid about what it is not: not a live-animal trading platform, not a shop, not a medical-help forum.
bad: Entirely outside the owner's domains. The identification and health-diagnosis claims are the product's own marketing, unverified from the repository; the price data is partly user-reported and partly scraped from public sources by the plan's own account, so its authority is soft. The main README is a business plan rather than technical documentation, and the MCP surface is documented in a separate file not opened here.
didnt: Not adopted: a reptile-collector community product has no bearing on the owner's systems. Recorded completely as catalogued — a full study row for an out-of-domain item, per the completion standard. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: giskard09/giskard-search
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: An experiment in agent commerce: pay-per-search with no accounts or subscriptions — get_invoice issues a 10-sat Lightning invoice through a self-hosted phoenixd node (or payment details for USDC/ETH on Arbitrum via the x402 protocol), the agent pays, then search_web/search_news run against DuckDuckGo with the payment hash as the credential. A report tool lets the agent feed back whether a result was useful. The payment contract addresses are published in the README, and the server is one of a small ecosystem of agent services by the same author (memory, identity, marketplace).
bad: The design puts spending authority inside the agent's loop: the agent holds or triggers wallet payments per query, with an owner private key in the server's environment for the Arbitrum route. That is precisely the boundary our house keeps — money moves only on the owner's decision (B131's obsideo standard: the server returns a checkout link and the human pays). The search underneath is DuckDuckGo, a commodity; 29 commits, 1 star; the README's clone instructions point at a differently named repository (giskard09/mcp-server).
didnt: Rejected: agent-held payment authority contradicts the owner's money rules, whatever the catalogue's FOR US verdict says. The micropayment experiment is recorded; the boundary it crosses is the finding. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: goesByhc/cn-scraper-mcp
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README licence section).
good: Search and extraction across eleven Chinese platforms (Taobao, JD, Pinduoduo, Xiaohongshu, Zhihu, ZSXQ, Weibo, Douyin, Bilibili, Douban, Dianping) built on careful credential hygiene: guided_login opens the platform's own login page and the user authenticates there themselves — the tool never sees a password — then harvests the resulting cookies (including HttpOnly, via CDP) into a local store. Cookie values are never written to logs and never returned through MCP tool results; tools report status, field names and local paths only, and credentials are sent solely to the owning platform's domain. Per-platform honesty is tabulated with footnotes (Pinduoduo marked not recommended — its session permits one search only; Douyin experimental), and when a platform demands a human step the tool returns a structured ACTION_REQUIRED naming the platform, reason, action, link and the tool to retry.
bad: The design maintains logged-in scraping against platforms' anti-bot defences — TLS-fingerprint spoofing (curl_cffi, credited in its thanks), residential-IP requirements, captcha polling — and its own FAQ concedes bulk scraping may violate platform terms, for learning and research only, at the user's risk. Harvested cookie stores and persistent Chrome profiles on disk are high-value credential artefacts, and the remote HTTP deployment would put them one misconfiguration from the network — the README warns against bare public exposure itself.
took: Corroboration for the structured hand-back: when a step is genuinely the human's (a login, a captcha), return a named ACTION_REQUIRED — platform, reason, action, link, retry path — instead of failing silently or improvising around the gate.
didnt: Not adopted: we have no Chinese-platform research need, and terms-risk scraping of logged-in platforms is not a route we take. The credential-hygiene and ACTION_REQUIRED patterns are filed as corroboration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kimdonghwi94/Web-Analyzer-MCP
licence: MIT (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details; README License section).
good: A compact two-tool web reader: url_to_markdown fetches a page (Selenium for dynamic content, BeautifulSoup for parsing), scores elements with a custom importance algorithm, strips ads, navigation and duplicates, and emits structured Markdown; web_content_qna chunks the extracted content, matches chunks to the question by relevance and answers with an OpenAI model of the user's choice. A Limitations section is included in the README (Chrome required for JavaScript-heavy sites, an OpenAI key required for Q&A, some sites block automated access).
bad: Small and early (24 commits, 4 stars). The Q&A tool ships page content to OpenAI's API, so 'local server' does not mean local processing; the importance scoring is an unvalidated custom heuristic with no evaluation published; JS-heavy sites need a local Chrome for the Selenium path.
didnt: Not adopted: our own reading route fetches and reads pages directly, without a summarising intermediary whose scoring we cannot inspect. Recorded as a representative small two-tool reader. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lennney/agent-search-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file at the repository root; GitHub repository details).
good: Free-first metasearch engineered around evidence honesty. Sixteen adapters (nine zero-key — DuckDuckGo, Sogou, Bing, Baidu, Wikipedia, Startpage, Yandex, Mojeek, Wiby — and seven optional keyed providers) sit behind routing policies in which the default free_first never spends a configured credential and free_only blocks paid providers outright. Every response carries a Search Evidence Packet: which engines ran, the stop_reason and quality_gate that ended the search, the request and evidence budgets, whether evidence was truncated — and partialFailures kept as a first-class field, because 'an empty result cannot hide an upstream error'. Source independence is counted correctly: source_count counts provider families, not adapter names, so the same upstream reached through several adapters never inflates corroboration. Token savings are measured on a checked-in bilingual fixture with a locked tokenizer (31.1% for compact mode) with the caveat printed beside the table — the fixture verifies formatting and packet behaviour, not live availability or search quality — and an offline demo replays the scorer on synthetic scenarios while making no live claim.
bad: Three months old at study time; the zero-key engines are scraped web endpoints whose availability shifts under it (the design surfaces those failures rather than preventing them), and its quality gate's thresholds are the author's calibration, not independently validated. The measured savings are formatting measurements on a fixture, as the README itself is careful to say.
took: Corroboration for evidence accounting in search: count independent provider families rather than adapters, keep partial failures visible in the result rather than converting them into an unexplained empty set, and expose the stop reason and quality gate that ended the search.
didnt: Not adopted as a component: our search routes are established. Recorded as the search wave's strongest design corroboration — its evidence packet states, in a tool's own contract, the independence and failure-visibility rules our research reporting runs on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lfnovo/content-core
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: One unified async Python API/CLI/MCP front-end over pluggable extraction engines: URLs and HTML, YouTube transcripts, Reddit, the Office/EPUB document family, and audio/video transcription, with the engine selectable per content type (firecrawl/jina/crawl4ai for URLs, docling for documents) and configuration resolved in a stated priority (flags > env > config file > defaults). Engine failure modes are honest: the docling engine raises a ConfigurationError when its optional extra is not installed rather than silently degrading, and auto falls back explicitly. Ships an agent skill and plugin manifests for two harnesses beside the library.
bad: Summarization and transcription route through external LLM/STT providers (keys required), so extraction is local but summarization is not. The YouTube-on-blocked-networks guidance (a logged-in browser's cookies file, a residential proxy) is anti-block circumvention advice — recorded as characterised, not a route we take. The MCP surface is only two tools; the value is the library/CLI, not the door.
took: Corroboration for pluggable extraction engines behind one interface, with a missing optional engine failing loudly by name rather than silently degrading — the error posture our own ingest tooling should keep.
didnt: Not adopted — our ingest extracts through established per-source routes and files into the wiki by hand; a general extraction library adds an engine layer we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linxule/mineru-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A client wrapper that treats a hosted parsing API with unusual custody discipline: submissions carry a durable local journal with duplicate-request protection and resumable checkpoints; downloads retain the complete provider archives byte-identical under SHA-256 names with an inventory covering every member, so nothing the provider returned is silently dropped; partial and unknown states stay explicit (exit 2 for partial or unknown, unknown provider states never flattened); and the offline bundle format records its own provenance limit in plain words — a caller-asserted binding does not prove the provider parsed those exact PDF bytes. CLI and MCP run the same implementation in-process so the two surfaces cannot drift.
bad: The parsing itself happens on mineru.net's hosted API under a MinerU API key — documents leave the machine; the local code is the client. The most distinctive features (durable operations, bundles) are unreleased in the checkout, so the published package is thinner than the README's front half suggests. Local retention paths fail closed on Windows, stated but a real platform limit.
took: Corroboration for retained-artifact discipline around a hosted parser: keep the provider's complete archive under a content hash, inventory every member, keep unknown states explicit, and print what the provenance binding does not prove.
didnt: Not adopted — document parsing for the paper programme runs through our own routes, and hosted-API parsing custody is not accepted for owner documents. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Marvy101/pod-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: The concept is the valuable part: a searchable corpus of firsthand observations agents recorded while doing real work — what actually happened with a product, API, service or place, as opposed to what its documentation promises — searchable before an agent commits to a decision, with a feedback tool to write back what was observed afterwards. The proxy design is honest about itself ('This package is a proxy, not a reimplementation'), the default endpoint is read-only and keyless, and read vs write surfaces are separated by endpoint and token.
bad: One commit: the repository is a release mirror, so the code here is not where the work happens and cannot be audited as the system's source of truth. The corpus, its moderation and its survival all belong to the hosted Pod service; the default endpoint is anonymous and rate-limited per IP, and one listed tool is pending an upstream deployment that does not exist yet.
took: Corroboration for the firsthand-observation corpus as a knowledge type — field reports of what happened in use, kept apart from documentation claims — which is the shape of our own field-report and corrections practice in the wiki.
didnt: Not adopted — the observation corpus is a third party's hosted service, and our own firsthand record lives in the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: n24q02m/wet-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A genuinely self-contained research server: embedded SearXNG metasearch with no API keys, academic search (Scholar, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, PubMed, CrossRef), a library-docs indexer with FTS5 hybrid search and version-aware queries, local file conversion, and local embedding/reranking so the zero-config path phones nothing home. Its deployment discipline is sound: no-auth mode refuses non-loopback binds, the HTTP surface is OAuth-gated, and the token-hashing command never echoes the token. Renames and breaking removals (media analyze removed in v2.0.0) are announced at the top of the README with a migration pointer.
bad: The extraction chain's escalation includes TLS spoofing and stealth bypass of named sites' bot defences — anti-bot evasion as a feature, characterised here as evidence; not a route this programme takes. The project has renamed itself around a CLI with MCP demoted to a secondary surface, and the sister-project sprawl (a dozen sibling servers from the same author) makes the maintenance centre unclear. 1,452 commits and 284 releases in eight months is churn as much as maturity.
took: Corroboration for the zero-key local default (embedded metasearch + local embeddings) with hosted backends as an explicit fallback chain, and for refusing non-loopback binds in no-auth mode.
didnt: Not adopted — our search and reading routes are established, and the evasion-oriented extraction chain is not one we would run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nkapila6/mcp-local-rag
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: Honest minimalism: a local web-search server that calls itself 'primitive' in its own description, needs no API keys, fetches results, ranks them locally with Google's MediaPipe text embedder, and returns extracted Markdown context — no account, no hosted component. It has grown a multi-engine deep-research mode (9+ backends with privacy-focused choices called out) while keeping the local-ranking core, and ships an agent skill teaching tool selection and privacy-aware defaults.
bad: The keyless engines are scraped search endpoints whose availability and terms are the engines' to change; ranking quality rests on a small on-device embedder with no published evaluation; the recommended uvx install pulls unpinned from the git repository. 'Deep research' here means multi-engine result fusion, not source reading.
didnt: Not adopted — our research routes search and then read sources directly; a snippet-ranking layer adds nothing to that discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nyxn-ai/NyxDocs
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: A Context7-shaped idea applied to one vertical: cryptocurrency project documentation across Ethereum, BSC, Polygon and Solana, collected from CoinGecko, GitHub, GitBook, Notion and official sites into a local SQLite/PostgreSQL store, with search by name/category/blockchain, documentation retrieval and an update-monitoring tool. The multi-source collection into one queryable store is a reasonable shape for a fast-moving documentation domain.
bad: Two commits: a scaffold, not a track record — the README describes a fuller system (collectors, scrapers, update monitors, a documentation folder) than the root listing shows. Documentation freshness for fast-moving crypto projects depends on scrapers against GitBook/Notion/websites that change shape often, and nothing at source evidences the monitoring working.
didnt: Not adopted — cryptocurrency documentation is outside the owner's domains, and the repo is a two-commit scaffold. Recorded completely as catalogued, per the completion standard. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: opendatalab/MinerU-Ecosystem
licence: Apache-2.0 — via the parent repository root (LICENSE file at the MinerU-Ecosystem root and its Repository-details block); the mcp/ directory page names no separate licence.
good: The official MCP server for the MinerU Open API: parse_documents converts local files and remote URLs (PDF, images, DOCX, PPTX, spreadsheets) to Markdown with tables as HTML and formulas as LaTeX, page ranges selectable, model and OCR language choosable, over stdio or streamable HTTP. Its tiering is unusually transparent: Flash mode works with no key and no sign-up (free, Markdown only, published limits of 20 pages / 10 MB per file), a token unlocks the precision API (≤200 MB / ≤200 pages, more formats), and a Privacy Policy section in the MCP README states exactly what is sent (the document content), that results are temporarily cached server-side, and that they are not used for training.
bad: Parsing is a hosted service: document content is uploaded to mineru.net in both modes, so the free Flash mode trades custody for convenience — the privacy section says so, but the trade is the product. Full capability needs the vendor's token; the ecosystem repo's centre of gravity is the cloud API, not the self-hostable open-source engine.
didnt: Not adopted — the MinerU engine was already studied at Tier 1 and our parsing routes are our own; the official cloud front-end adds hosted custody we do not take on for owner documents. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: peter-j-thompson/semanticapi-mcp
licence: MIT — stated only in the README's License section; no LICENSE file at root and the repository metadata is silent (recorded as found). The related engine repo is separately AGPL-3.0 per this README's Related section — a licence split: the MIT covers this client only.
good: A small, legible idea: natural-language API discovery as three tools — ask for a capability ('send an email with Gmail', 'convert currencies in real-time') and get back endpoint details, parameters, auth setup and code snippets; deep-discover a named provider against an intent; or analyse an API from its documentation URL into a provider config. Returning auth setup and snippets alongside endpoints is the right answer shape for an agent that must then configure a call.
bad: Six commits and one star — a thin client whose substance is the hosted service, whose catalogue quality and call behaviour cannot be audited from this repo. 'Discover and call any API' through a hosted intermediary puts a third party between the agent and every credential it would use; auto-discover defaults on. The licence split (MIT client, AGPL engine, hosted service) means the open parts are the smallest parts.
didnt: Not adopted — API discovery for our work is done by reading the provider's own documentation at source, and arbitrary API invocation through a hosted intermediary is not a door we open. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pexafy/pexafy-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: Stock-photo search shaped for conversation: describe a scene in a sentence in any language and get real free-to-use photographs back (from an index over Unsplash, Pexels, Pixabay and more), each result carrying its source, its licence and the credit line to display; search-by-image with a natural-language twist ('like this, but at night'); a grid flow in which the human's picks return to the assistant in the order chosen. All five tools are read-only, no API key is needed to search, and account linking is OAuth rather than a pasted key.
bad: The search runs on the vendor's hosted index at pexafy.com — the repo is the server, but the index and its ranking are the service's, and the project is two months old with no independent uptake (0 stars). Visual-similarity search quality is asserted, not measured anywhere at source.
took: Corroboration for attribution travelling with the asset: every returned photograph names its source and licence and carries its credit line — the same discipline as our citation-with-access-date standard, applied to images.
didnt: Not adopted — image search for our work runs through existing routes, and a hosted stock-photo service is peripheral to the programme. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: phpcip/opensolr-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A full-featured front-end to managed Apache Solr: hybrid BM25+kNN search with server-side embeddings (no local model to run), search-by-image (labels/OCR/barcodes turned into query terms, no image vector stored), PDFs indexed one document per page so a hit lands on the answering page with a #page= link, grounded RAG answers, and a check_schema tool that reports whether an index can do what each tool needs and exactly why not. Its README's demo-account section is a candour exemplar: the shared public key's account is shared with every reader, anything created is auto-deleted after 3 days without warning or export, and 'never put anything real, private or client-owned in it' is printed in the setup path itself.
bad: Managed-service custody: local files and folders indexed through this server are read on Opensolr's servers — their text, OCR and picture descriptions are computed there — so 'index your contracts folder' means uploading the contracts. The write surface is wide (add/delete documents, create indexes, apply-schema replacing an index's configuration, force when it holds documents) behind one API key, with no confirmation described. Two months old, 0 stars.
took: Corroboration for printing the custody warning inside the setup path — the demo section states the shared visibility and the 3-day deletion where a user will actually read them, not in a separate policy page.
didnt: Not adopted — hosted search custody over local files is not accepted, and our retrieval runs over our own files and indexes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pragmar/mcp-server-webcrawl
licence: MPL-2.0 — resolved by opening the LICENSE file at root (Mozilla Public License 2.0, © 2025 Ben Caulfield, 'Incompatible With Secondary Licenses'); repo metadata shows Other (NOASSERTION) and the README names no licence. Weak copyleft: ideas only under this programme's licence discipline.
good: Search over crawl archives you already own: one local server reads the outputs of seven crawlers/formats (WARC, wget, HTTrack, Katana, SiteOne, ArchiveBox, InterroBot) and offers fulltext search with a real boolean and fielded syntax (url/type/status/headers/content fields, status ranges, wildcards), plus token-conscious extras — Markdown at roughly a third of the HTML bytes, ~500-byte snippets for refinement before pulling content, XPath and regex extraction — with the README explicitly coaching the trade-off ('Use judiciously'). It doubles as a no-AI interactive terminal search over the same archives, including over SSH against archives sitting on a remote host.
bad: The licence is discoverable only by opening the LICENSE file — the README never names it and repo metadata shows NOASSERTION, so a catalogue reader cannot tell this is MPL-2.0 without the extra step. The shipped prompt routines are copy-paste Markdown procedures a user pastes into their assistant — a distribution shape that blurs documentation and instruction, characterised here as evidence. Search quality over heterogeneous crawl data depends entirely on the operator's own crawl discipline.
took: Corroboration for snippet-first refinement: cheap ~500-byte contextual snippets to narrow a search before any full content is pulled — token budgeting as a search interface feature, not an afterthought.
didnt: Not adopted — MPL-2.0 is outside the MIT/Apache adaptation class in any case, and we hold no crawl-archive corpus to search. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: qune-tech/ocds-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: A privacy-engineered client for German public procurement (OCDS) data: semantic tender search, tender matching against company profiles, notice lineage (PIN→CN→CAN) and raw eForms XML — with the privacy design as the headline: company profiles live in a local SQLite database and queries and profiles are embedded locally with a multilingual ONNX model (multilingual-e5-small), so only embedding vectors, OCIDs and filter values leave the machine. The README's Privacy & data flow section enumerates what stays, what the API sees, and what that still reveals, and names the first-run model download's source and size — data minimisation documented as a data-flow list, not a slogan.
bad: The data and the matching live behind the vendor's API, and the key requires a €99/month Pro plan — the free local server fronts a paid hosted dataset. Embedding vectors still reveal commercial interest (sectors, buyers, value bands), as the README itself concedes. German public procurement serves none of the owner's work.
took: Corroboration for the data-flow list as the privacy document: what stays, what leaves, and what the leaving parts still reveal — including the sentence that minimisation is not elimination.
didnt: Not adopted — domain (German public procurement) and a paid hosted dataset behind the key. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: r-huijts/opentk-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A read-only civic-data door done well: 17 tools over Dutch Tweede Kamer documents, debates, MPs, committees, votes and activities, with an advanced search syntax (phrases, NOT, OR, NEAR), full document reading in targeted/sequential/full modes with character offsets, and a smart-analysis layer that triages before reading — TF-IDF keywords, Dutch-optimised entity recognition and a 0–100 relevance score so an agent can pick the 3 relevant documents out of 15 without loading all of them. Upstream attribution is prominent and specific (the OpenTK project and its creator are credited at the top, with the wrapper's own role stated plainly).
bad: Wholly dependent on one person's upstream service (Bert Hubert's tkconv) for the data — a generous public good, but a single point of failure the wrapper cannot outlive. Dutch parliamentary data serves none of the owner's work, and the 80–90% context-saving figure is the project's own claim, unmeasured at source.
took: Corroboration for analyse-before-loading: cheap deterministic triage (keywords, entities, relevance score) ahead of full-document reads — the same economy as our outline-first, bounded-section reading standard.
didnt: Not adopted — domain: Dutch parliamentary data is outside the owner's work. Recorded completely as catalogued, per the completion standard. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rejifald/StitchAPI
licence: Apache-2.0 — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: An agent-native API runtime with a sharp primitive: a 'stitch' declares one endpoint's contract once (input/output schema, auth, resilience) and becomes a callable whose every live response is validated — hard drift (a required field missing or incompatible) throws, soft drift (coercion, undeclared or defaulted fields) surfaces as a leveled warn/info finding instead of a silent undefined downstream. Resilience (retry with backoff honouring Retry-After, proactive throttling, layered timeouts, circuit breaker, idempotency keys) is declared, not hand-rolled per call site; auth is a boundary — the stitch owns its credential and callers, agents included, get a capability, not the credential; and one definition serves four front doors — in-process function, CLI, HTTP endpoint and MCP tool. Zero runtime dependencies, with the bundle budget enforced in CI and signed provenance plus SBOMs per release.
bad: Still a release candidate (1.0.0-rc.8) after two years — the README's own advice is to pin an exact version. It is a TypeScript library for application code, not a server we would run; adopting it means adopting its runtime model across our API call sites. The catalogue description pointed at a docs-search tool, so the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict was formed against a different surface than this repo presents.
took: Corroboration for three door-design standards in one project: callers receive a capability, never the credential; contract drift is leveled (hard drift fails, soft drift warns) rather than silent; and one definition can serve function, CLI, HTTP and MCP surfaces without forking the contract.
didnt: Not adopted as a component — our connectors are hand-built per provider under the connector docs, and a TypeScript runtime library does not drop into that. Its design vocabulary is taken as corroboration only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ricocf/mcp-wolframalpha
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A small, early (April 2025) Python MCP server putting Wolfram Alpha's computational knowledge behind chat: math, science and data queries with structured results, multi-client handling, and a worked example client (Gemini via LangChain, with a Gradio UI and a CLI) showing the full loop from question to computed answer. Docker routes are provided for both server-side and client use.
bad: A thin wrapper over a metered commercial API — the value and the limits are Wolfram's, and the key is the user's metered appid. Most of the repository and README is the demo client (Gradio UI, Docker files) rather than the server; no releases; the repo's move to a new owner path leaves its own clone instructions pointing at the old one.
didnt: Not adopted — no computational-knowledge need beyond existing routes, and a metered third-party API key is not taken on for it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Savirinc/unfragile-mcp-server
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: Capability discovery as a typed problem: an agent states an intent and gets back ranked artifacts, an invocation-ready resolution for capability URIs (capability://database.postgres.query.readonly), side-by-side comparisons and stack assembly — and, the distinctive part, a trust_passport tool returning machine-readable trust evidence for an artifact: its capability URIs, permissions, data-access risk, failure modes and observed outcomes, so a discovery result carries its risk sheet with it instead of a star count. A feedback tool closes the loop by reporting success/failure back into future routing.
bad: Two commits: this repo is a thin client; the graph, the rankings (UnfragileRank) and the passport evidence are produced by the vendor's hosted API and cannot be audited from here. 'Every query feeds the graph' cuts both ways — your searches and stack queries become the vendor's match records, a data flow a user should notice before adopting it as their discovery layer.
took: Corroboration for the trust passport as a discovery artifact: permissions, data-access risk, failure modes and observed outcomes in machine-readable form beside the capability — the evidence sheet a door should be able to show for anything it recommends.
didnt: Not adopted — capability discovery for this programme is done by opening the candidate projects at their own sources, which is precisely the step a match graph abstracts away; its trust-passport shape is taken as corroboration only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: serkan-ozal/driflyte-mcp-server
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A narrow, well-specified hosted retrieval service: Driflyte recursively crawls and indexes web pages and GitHub content, tags every document with topics, and this server exposes exactly two tools — list-topics so an agent can discover what the corpus actually covers before querying, and search constrained to chosen topics with a bounded topK and a 0–1 relevance score on every returned document. Limits are published in the README (free, no signup, 100 requests per 5 minutes per IP), and both tools' schemas are documented completely, including which fields are optional.
bad: The corpus is the vendor's: which topics exist, what was crawled and how fresh it is are all decided server-side ('Future changes to usage policies and limits may be introduced'), and the local package is a front-end whose two tools cannot be pointed at any other index. Topic tagging quality is asserted, not evidenced.
took: Corroboration for a coverage-discovery tool beside the search tool: list what the corpus holds before asking questions of it, so absence of a topic reads as a corpus limit rather than a negative finding.
didnt: Not adopted — a hosted, vendor-scoped corpus cannot serve as a research source for this programme; our research reads the original sources. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shariqriazz/google-ai-search-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: Google-grounded retrieval on the user's own credentials: seven tools over Vertex AI or the Gemini API — web-grounded answers, documentation-synthesised explanations, doc snippets with version targeting, project guidelines, and code analysis against official documentation with citations and severity categories. The README opens with an implementation-notes box that deserves quoting in any catalogue: a listed tool does not prove its upstream provider is configured or reachable, and model-produced comparisons and analysis are material to verify against the cited primary sources, not deterministic findings. Configuration (model, temperature, streaming, retries) is explicit, and the Docker guidance warns against baking keys into the image.
bad: The analysis tools (code analysis, technical comparison, architecture recommendation) are model synthesis wearing tool names — the README's own notes say to verify them, which is honest, but a caller that skips the notes gets confident prose. Safety filters are set to BLOCK_NONE by design. Ten commits; everything rides on the user's Google billing.
took: Corroboration for the listed-is-not-configured note: a door's tool list is a claim about shape, not about a working upstream — say so where the tools are listed, and frame model-produced analysis as material to verify against primary sources.
didnt: Not adopted — our search and documentation routes are established, and Google Cloud work stays inside the owner's cricsfc scope through existing tooling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sifter-ai/sifter
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: A clear-eyed alternative to chunk retrieval for homogeneous document collections: describe the fields once (in natural language; the schema is inferred and exported as Pydantic/TypeScript types), extract every invoice/contract/receipt into typed records in MongoDB, then answer questions with real filters and aggregations — exact, reproducible database answers ('total unpaid across all invoices last quarter') instead of similar chunks. Its 'Why not RAG?' section makes the argument precisely: RAG breaks where every document looks alike and the question is an aggregation. Natural-language queries compile to MongoDB aggregation pipelines that are inspectable, so the generated query can be read before its answer is trusted. Fully self-hostable (Docker Compose, your MongoDB, your LLM key) with SDKs, a CLI, spec-driven dashboards and HMAC-signed webhooks.
bad: Extraction quality rides on the operator's own LLM key and model choice — the engine is only as accurate as the model you bring, and no accuracy evaluation is published at source. The MCP server includes write tools, and the commercial gravity is the hosted Cloud (Drive and email ingress), where documents would leave the operator's infrastructure.
took: Corroboration for inspectable generated queries — the NL-to-pipeline translation is shown, not hidden — and for the extract-once discipline on homogeneous collections: structured records first, aggregations answered exactly.
didnt: Not adopted — our document work is reading and filing into the wiki, not bulk field extraction over homogeneous collections; the inspectable-pipeline pattern is the take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: smeet666/mcp-recipes
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: Federated recipe search with the most disciplined answer accounting in this wave: six sources in three languages searched with one question, every recipe normalised into one shape, versions of a dish compared side by side rescaled to the same servings, and any ingredient list rescaled offline. The accounting is the design: counts are never added across sources; a failed source is reported as failed, never as having found nothing; each source's reported_total travels with reported_total_means saying what that number counts on that site; names_the_dish states how many of a site's rows actually carry the dish in their title, because 'a search index answers the words it is handed'; a field a source has no notion of comes back absent rather than invented; a part a source withholds for subscribers is named withheld; rescaled quantities carry a rounded flag and the instruction to say they were recomputed when shown. Per-site pacing is honoured as a floor — a global setting can only make the server more patient than the slowest site asks.
bad: Zero stars and two months old; coverage is six scraped sites whose layouts can change under it, and the rescaling arithmetic, however carefully flagged, is heuristic around units, divisibility and language-specific quantity phrasing. The domain is recipes — nothing here serves the owner's work directly.
took: Corroboration, in its strongest form yet, for per-source answer accounting: never sum counts across sources, failed is not empty, every total is labelled with what it counts, and recomputed figures are flagged as recomputed where they are shown.
didnt: Not adopted — recipe search is outside the programme's needs; the row is recorded for its answer-accounting design, which is the transferable part. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: smeet666/mcp-wikibooks-cookbook
licence: MIT for the server code — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block. The content it serves is separately licensed: Wikibooks Cookbook pages are Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0, stated in the README's Licence and attribution section and returned with each recipe.
good: A single-source recipe server over the Wikibooks Cookbook (via the Wikimedia API, no key, no account) whose honesty conventions are meticulous: total_available is always null because the search route publishes no total, and result_count is defined as the rows this call returned; a figure the page states nothing for is null rather than filled; after a redirect, id names the page actually read and redirected_from names the key that was asked for; every ingredient line carries its scaling state (scaled/rounded/unscaled) and rescaled figures are labelled this server's arithmetic; failures come back as one of six typed error codes with a hint naming the next move, including rate_limited with the wait spelled out. Content attribution travels with the answer: get_recipe returns the CC BY-SA licence and the page URL so a repeated recipe carries its credit.
bad: Zero stars, two months old, one upstream (the Wikimedia API) whose search publishes no totals — the server is honest about that, but result completeness is unknowable by construction. Recipe content quality is whatever the wiki's volunteer pages hold, and rescaling inherits the same unit/divisibility heuristics as its sibling.
took: Corroboration for the unknown-total shape: when the upstream publishes no total, the field is null and the returned count is defined as what this call returned — never an implied completeness.
didnt: Not adopted — recipe lookup is outside the programme's needs; recorded for its null-honesty and attribution discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: srezai-team/srezai-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees. (The MIT covers this bridge package; the hosted API it calls is a commercial service.)
good: A candid thin bridge to a hosted search API (SrezAI, strong Russian-web coverage): web and image search, page reading into clean Markdown with offset windows, schema-based extraction, site maps and crawls, YouTube transcripts, ready answers with semantic reranking, an asynchronous deep-research tool that returns a ticket to collect later — and a verify_claim tool returning supported/refuted/mixed/unverified with verbatim quotes from 2–5 independent domains. The README's first section tells most readers not to install the package at all (connect to the hosted server directly if your client speaks Streamable HTTP), the bridge holds zero tool logic so it cannot drift from the API, failed or empty calls are not charged, and a get_usage tool reports balance, quota and the price list for free.
bad: Everything executes on the vendor's hosted API under a metered key — searches, page reads and claim checks all leave for srezai.ru, with a strong Russian-web focus. Nine commits and zero stars; the claim-verification quality rests entirely on the vendor's unseen pipeline.
took: Corroboration for outcome-based metering as the fair shape: errors and empty calls are not charged, and the usage/price tool itself is free — an agent can always afford to check what it is spending.
didnt: Not adopted — a hosted, metered search API is not a route this programme adds; recorded for its metering fairness and its bridge honesty. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sriram-PR/doc-scraper
licence: Apache-2.0 — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees.
good: A complete docs-corpus pipeline in one Go binary: point it at a documentation site and it detects the framework (30+ generators — Docusaurus, Starlight, Sphinx, VitePress, MkDocs Material, mdBook…), validates the content selector on the page, and crawls politely (robots.txt, sitemaps, per-host rate limits, retries with backoff, resumable crawls) into clean GitHub-flavoured Markdown with frontmatter, pages.jsonl, llms.txt and llms-full.txt. The corpus is then served to agents offline over MCP (BM25 search and page reads with no network access). Freshness is a first-class surface — incremental re-crawls, watch mode, crawl history, get_freshness and diff_crawl — and two failure disciplines stand out: JavaScript-only shells are reported instead of being crawled empty, and staged output never clobbers the last good copy.
bad: A crawler is only as polite as its configuration in a given run — the tooling supports robots.txt and rate limits, but the operator chooses the targets and pace. Detection covers 30+ generators; long-tail documentation platforms fall back to Readability extraction with the fidelity that implies. Keeping corpora fresh is a standing re-crawl chore the tooling schedules but the operator owns.
took: Corroboration for three ingest disciplines in one tool: a JS-only shell is reported, not crawled empty; staged output never overwrites the last good copy; and freshness is queryable (get_freshness, diff_crawl) rather than assumed.
didnt: Not adopted as an install — our ingest is owner-directed per source rather than standing documentation crawls; the freshness and staging patterns are the take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: takashiishida/arxiv-latex-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: The focused case for reading papers at their true source: instead of extracting text from a PDF (where equations and notation degrade), this small server fetches the paper's original LaTeX source via arxiv-to-prompt and serves it in four tools — the full flattened LaTeX, just the abstract, the section list, and one section by path — so mathematical content reaches the model exactly as the author wrote it. Section-level access keeps reads bounded instead of forcing whole-paper dumps.
bad: LaTeX-only by design: papers without an arXiv source submission (or outside arXiv) are out of reach, flattened source can be very long for a whole paper, and there is no search, citation graph or alerting — the discovery half of the literature loop lives elsewhere. Fidelity of the flattening is arxiv-to-prompt's, not verifiable from this repo.
took: Corroboration for source-over-rendering in paper reading: where an author-submitted source exists, read the source — the same standard this programme applies when it opens a repository rather than trusting its catalogue line.
didnt: Not adopted as an install — our paper programme opens sources through its own routes; recorded as the narrow pole of the arXiv pair beside B136's blazickjp reference implementation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: talonicdev/talonic-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block. (The MIT covers this client; the Talonic platform it calls is a hosted, credit-metered service.)
good: The official client for a hosted document-extraction platform, with three design surfaces worth recording. First, extraction proper: schema-validated JSON with per-field confidence scores and stable IDs, over a Field Registry whose concepts carry maturity levels (core/proven/candidate), synonyms and occurrence counts. Second, budget as a tool surface: get_balance reports balance, EUR value, burn rate and runway; get_pricing lets an agent predict spend before running a job; get_usage breaks consumption down per function. Third, a decision-task protocol for external agents: work parked at a decision stage is claimed under a lease with an execution epoch; the claim returns a frozen input package with provenance locators, precedents and an output contract; submission is outcome + verbatim evidence locators + a short rationale; and declaring a task undecidable is a first-class act that raises a human review and applies a fallback policy. Its status block separates the seven not-yet-production-verified tools from the verified rest, in the open.
bad: The platform is hosted and credit-metered: documents are uploaded into Talonic workspaces and every extraction burns credits, so the client being MIT does not make the processing local or free beyond a 50/day trial tier. Thirty-six tools is a wide surface whose centre is the vendor's workspace model; the decision-task tier is admittedly not yet production-verified. The default install line is @latest (the pinning advice is present, but the default is the risk).
took: Corroboration for budget-aware tooling (an agent should be able to read its balance, burn rate and the price of a job before running it) and for the decision-task contract: frozen inputs with provenance locators, verbatim evidence locators in the submission, and undecidable as a designed outcome rather than a failure.
didnt: Not adopted — document extraction for the owner's files does not move to a hosted credit-metered workspace; the budget-tooling and decision-contract patterns are the take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vectorize-io/vectorize-mcp-server
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block. (The MIT covers this client; the Vectorize platform it calls is a hosted service.)
good: Vectorize's official server for its hosted RAG platform: retrieve documents from a configured pipeline by question, extract any file to chunked Markdown, and generate a 'private deep research' report from the pipeline's corpus with optional web search. Setup is a single org/token/pipeline triple, with VS Code prompt-string inputs (the token field masked) as a thoughtful install touch.
bad: Everything of substance is server-side on Vectorize's platform: the corpus, the embeddings, the retrieval and the deep-research generation all live behind the token, and the documents for extraction are sent as base64 to their API. The repo is a configuration shell — 28 commits around three API calls — so nothing about retrieval quality can be judged from the source.
didnt: Not adopted — hosted RAG custody; our retrieval runs over our own files and indexes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VoxellInc/forge-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; README License section agrees. (The MIT covers this client; the Forge embedding API it calls is a hosted service.)
good: A deliberately minimal hosted-embedding door: two tools (embed, list_models), stateless, three quality tiers (turbo 1024-d free forever with no card, pro 2560-d, ultra 4096-d) with Matryoshka truncation, and an OpenAI-compatible API that maps existing model names to matching-dimension tiers so a vector store can change engines without re-dimensioning. Its measured-retrieval section is a benchmark-honesty exemplar: the pipeline's numbers on four public corpora are printed with the method, and immediately limited in the vendor's own words — the questions were model-written and therefore easier than a human-written test set, the figures are not a vendor comparison and not what the embed tool alone does — with receipts published including the misses.
bad: Embeddings are computed on Voxell's hosted API, so document text leaves the machine on every call — the no-storage claim is the vendor's word, unverifiable from this client repo. The surrounding marketing register ('It's an upgrade on every path', 'a different league') runs well ahead of the measured section's own caution, and the project is five months old with one star.
took: Corroboration for benchmark self-limitation printed beside the numbers: who wrote the test questions, why that makes them easier, what the figures are not, and the misses published with the receipts.
didnt: Not adopted — our embedding needs are served inside existing tooling, and a hosted embedding API is not added for them. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wd041216-bit/free-web-search-ultimate
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; the README's Attribution section records that the integrated Laya model is separately Apache-2.0 (open weights, Convai Innovations) while the search providers, verification pipeline, MCP server and CLI are the project's own MIT code.
good: Zero-key web search with a local evidence sieve: DuckDuckGo by default (self-hosted SearXNG for cross-validation), then an open-weight, non-autoregressive decision model (Laya, Apache-2.0) scores every result for relevance in a single forward pass before it can burn context tokens, and verifies claims by probabilistic stance (support/conflict/neutral per source) with claim decomposition and citation-ready evidence reports. The engineering is published, not gestured at: the verification blend weights are printed (0.55 neural stance + 0.35 source quality + 0.10 freshness), the payload keeps the full lexical sidecar so both classifiers can be compared on your own data, and every stage degrades gracefully (no sieve → lexical verifier; provider down → next provider; no web footprint → insufficient_evidence, by design). Its Honest Limits section is exemplary: the lexical verifier is pattern-matching, not entailment; 'Laya ships over-confident' (mean ECE 0.466 → 0.081 only after per-domain temperature refitting; 'Our defaults are reasonable, not calibrated'); the base checkpoint's zero-shot score (0.362 vs 0.766 fine-tuned) is printed against its own product.
bad: The production paths lean on a commercial unlocker that auto-retries CAPTCHA- and geo-blocked pages — anti-bot evasion as a feature, characterised as evidence; not a route this programme takes. A 'Jev-class' sieve is only as trustworthy as its calibration, and by the README's own account the shipped defaults are uncalibrated for any given domain; the 111-test claim is the project's own.
took: Corroboration for calibration honesty as a published section: shipped-overconfident stated with the ECE numbers, defaults labelled 'reasonable, not calibrated', both classifiers' outputs kept for comparison, and insufficient_evidence as a designed verdict when there is no web footprint.
didnt: Not adopted — our search routes are established and the unlocker path is not one we would run; the calibration honesty is the take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: XZXZZX-Ai/bilibili-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block; the README's closing section agrees.
good: A local-first Bilibili reader with provenance discipline rare in this wave: video metadata, chapters, comments, creator profiles, favorites traversal, and transcripts in which every text carries its data_source — human subtitle, ai_subtitle (Bilibili's AI recognition, explicitly 'not a human-verified quotation'), or local ASR (faster-whisper, an explicit opt-in fallback that runs once, on one part, within stated bounds) — with AI subtitles double-read and integrity-checked before use, keyword hits returned with context, timestamps and jump-to-moment links, and degradation explicit (no subtitle → SUBTITLE_UNAVAILABLE, never a silent substitution). Credential handling is equally careful: QR login on the user's phone or a hidden local terminal prompt; the agent is never to touch cookie values; diagnostics report configuration state without secrets; temporary audio is cleaned on every path.
bad: Search, favorites and creator content require the user's own Bilibili login — there is no anonymous degradation, stated plainly — and the credential file (~/.bilibili-mcp/config.json) is, by the README's own note, not guaranteed OS-level encryption. High-frequency use can trip Bilibili's rate limits and risk controls, with the risk expressly the user's. Bilibili content serves none of the owner's current work.
took: Corroboration for transcript provenance labelling (human / AI-recognised / locally transcribed as distinct data_source values with different trust) and for the credentials-never-through-the-agent install pattern — the human enters secrets in a local terminal while the agent pauses.
didnt: Not adopted — no Bilibili research need; recorded for its provenance labelling and credential-handling discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: A1-x-Tech/mcp-google-docs
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A Google Docs door designed around the API's real failure modes: 27 tools to read a document as text, structure or Markdown, edit by exact UTF-16 index ranges, style, manage lists/tables/images, work comment threads and export — with the index-shift problem handled as protocol (re-read fresh indexes before every edit; edit from the end backwards) and whole-document Markdown replacement made a separate, explicitly destructive step whose losses are enumerated (comment anchors, positioned objects, headers/footers and extra tabs do not survive). A 'What can change' table gives every operation class a confirmation boundary (No change / Changes local files only / Changes a document / Destructive / Potentially destructive) and tools are annotated so the client can distinguish inspection from live change; the API's own limits are stated as limits rather than smoothed over. OAuth is done carefully — PKCE with a one-shot loopback listener, the client secret never passing through the conversation, tokens in a 0600 file — and no general-purpose Drive tool is exposed beyond what Docs operations need.
bad: Nine commits and zero stars — the careful documentation is ahead of any track record. The default scope request is broad (documents plus full drive), the narrower options exist but must be chosen deliberately, and a raw-API-request tool can call methods without a dedicated tool, which widens the surface past the annotated 27. Our Google Docs access already runs through the connected connector, so this would be a second door to the same account.
took: Corroboration for the confirmation-boundary table as a door document — every operation class labelled by what it can change before it is run — and for making whole-document replacement a separate destructive step with its losses enumerated.

name: amos689/paper-preflight
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: The per-source answer accounting doctrine (B136–B138) in its purest form yet, applied to citation truth: a negative verdict is only issued when every source that could know the work has answered; silence from a source is recorded as 'cannot determine' with the reason, never rounded into 'not found'; no LLM touches a verdict; every finding is backed by a record or by the full set of answering sources; and the accuracy claims are made the hard way — held-out sets committed before the code they measure, flags hand-reviewed, false-alarm rate published beside the catch rate, the misses (9 cannot-determines) left in the table. Rule pages that include 'when it can be wrong' complete the shape.
