It checks citation RECORDS, not whether the cited work supports the sentence citing it (an experimental evidence finder exists but is explicitly experimental).
took: Boarded as design evidence for the scholarly-citation-truth-checking gap (one of the centrepiece's three honestly-open gaps): the verdict taxonomy with cannot-determine as a first-class outcome, not-found gated on every source answering, retraction/withdrawal checks, rule pages stating when each check can be wrong, and held-out evaluation committed before the changes it measures.

name: dvdsosa/zotero-native-mcp

name: Embassy-of-the-Free-Mind/sourcelibrary-v2
licence: MIT — per the mcp-server README's License section (the subtree the batch URL serves).
good: Quoting discipline built into the tool shape: a dedicated get_quote that returns the page's exact text with its citation and a stable shortlink, locators that keep printed page and scan page distinct, and a stated rule against paraphrasing from memory — our verbatim standard, implemented by a library. Pagination honesty matches it: truncation is a flagged field with the continuation values supplied, never something to infer from a short page. The duplicate check before import and findings shared as references rather than copied text complete a careful curation posture.
bad: The corpus and its translations live on one institution's hosted service, and the translations are AI-generated — get_quote's verbatim text is verbatim of a machine translation, a distinction a citer must keep (the tool returns the original OCR alongside, which is the mitigation, but the headline artefact is the translation). The collection is a specialist one; nothing here generalises to our own shelves.
took: Corroboration for quote-from-the-page tooling (verbatim text + stable citation link + printed-vs-scan locators) and for truncation made an explicit flagged field with continuation values — beside B138's total_available honesty, the same rule for pages.
didnt: Not adopted — a specialist hosted corpus outside our current work; the quoting and truncation disciplines are the take, recorded as corroboration. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HasData/google-scholar-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block (the repo/launchers; the MCP service itself is hosted and credit-metered).
good: Commercial honesty of the fair shape: the price is in the tool table itself (10 credits per call), the free tier's real capacity is spelled out (≈100 calls, no card), charges attach to successful calls only — the no-charge-for-errors metering credited at B136/B138 — and the FAQ does not dress the scraping up as an official API or an affiliation.
bad: A scraping intermediary is the whole product: availability rides on Google's tolerance for automated reading of Scholar and on the vendor's infrastructure, and the records returned are whatever Scholar's index holds — search results, not verified records (contrast this batch's paper-preflight, which checks records against registries). Queries transit and are metered by a third party; 17 commits of launcher around a closed service.
took: Corroboration for per-successful-call metering with the price stated in the tool table — predict-the-spend honesty — from a hosted scraping door we do not use.
didnt: Not adopted — scholarly search here runs through open registries and first-party sources, not a metered scraping intermediary; the metering honesty is credited in the took line. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: herbertkokholm/cite-caddy
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: Two disciplines of the first order. Idempotency keys on destructive operations solve the ambiguous-write problem at the protocol level — the retry replays the original outcome rather than re-executing, which is the exact complement to B139 google-tasks' read-back rule (where the platform offers no keys, read back; where you build the door, key the writes). And the key-safety analysis names a silent-breakage mode most Zotero tooling never mentions: a delete does not error anywhere, it just orphans the citations in every Word document that used the item. Aggregate-only status metrics and a registry-generated server card round out a documentation set that treats drift and leakage as design problems.
bad: Full CRUD including permanent delete and library moves, offered remotely and multi-tenant: a hosted deployment holds many users' Zotero API keys (encrypted at rest, but concentrated), and onboarding is self-service with no admin approval — anyone with a key becomes a tenant of the deployment. The key-safety section is candid that the dangerous operations break citations silently, yet the tools still ship without the dry-run/confirmation step the README itself floats as 'worth considering'. 0 stars.
took: Corroboration for idempotency-key replay of the original outcome on destructive writes (the protocol-level answer to the ambiguous-write problem, beside B139's read-back rule) and for key-safety candour — a delete that silently breaks downstream citations must be documented at the tool, not discovered later.
didnt: Not adopted — Zotero is not in our stack and a remote multi-tenant write door to a reference library is the opposite of our door posture; the idempotency and key-safety documentation is the take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Liyux3/scholar-mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: Federation done with the accounting switched on: sources grouped by evidentiary role rather than dumped into one list, identities canonicalised so the same paper reached five ways counts once with five sources' evidence (provider-family independence, the B136 doctrine), a status resource that reports which reranker actually ran, debug provenance per source, partial coverage reported as partial — and a benchmark whose protocol, frozen data and hash manifest are published with the misses counted in both directions. This is what a search tool's evidence sheet should look like.
bad: The Google Scholar channel's automatic session recovery is a bot-check workaround: a fresh browser profile is used precisely to get past a verification challenge the source put in the way — characterised here as evidence; it is a posture we do not take toward sources' defences, however carefully it avoids the user's own profile. The ranking stack is also heavy with external dependencies (a cloud reranker by default, Alibaba-region key subtleties documented at length), so what produced a given ranking takes the debug surface to reconstruct.
took: Corroboration for canonical-evidence pooling across a federation (one record, many sources' evidence), a status surface that names the reranker actually used, and a frozen protocol-published benchmark — beside B136–B138's per-source accounting family.
didnt: Not adopted — our research retrieval runs through first-party and registry sources under our own accounting; the federation's canonicalisation and status honesty are credited, the Scholar recovery channel is a boundary we do not cross. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: michaelellis003/paperboy
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block.
good: A stateless server over an owner-held source of truth is the custody-correct shape, and the separations are drawn where they belong: delivering is not cataloguing, a missing PDF is a record state rather than an error, an unresolvable reference earns a receipt with a reason and a pointer to the right tool. Ambiguity is handled by offering the closest candidate for confirmation — never guessing, never silently failing (the B139 apple-notes candidates pattern in a delivery tool) — and the full-power-token warning is stated in the setup docs instead of discovered later.
bad: The remote mode's single bearer token is all-or-nothing by design — the README's candour about it does not reduce the blast radius if it leaks (send email as the owner, edit the library). Delivery depends on SMTP app passwords and Amazon's approved-sender machinery, both brittle; and the queue's memory living in Zotero tags means the dedup guarantee is only as strong as the user's Zotero hygiene.
took: Corroboration for the stateless-server-over-owner-held-truth shape, delivery/cataloguing separation, confirm-the-candidate ambiguity handling, and full-power-token candour in setup documentation.
didnt: Not adopted — no e-reader delivery need in our stack; the stateless-over-owner-truth shape and the ambiguity handling are the take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mlava/scholar-sidekick-mcp
licence: MIT — LICENSE file at root and the Repository-details block (the repo/client; the API it fronts is a hosted service with free and paid tiers).
good: The fabrication pattern is correctly identified and met head-on: resolution alone cannot catch a real DOI wearing an invented title, so the tool compares the claim against the record field by field and SHOWS the divergence (similarity scores + the resolved record beside the claim) instead of issuing a bare verdict — evidence presented, not asserted. The committed tools.json makes the whole surface inspectable before anything runs, provenance metadata rides every response, and the tools are read-only by annotation and in fact.
bad: The verdicts are computed on the vendor's hosted API — the repo lets you inspect the tool surface exactly, but not the matching engine, its thresholds, or its registry coverage, so a 'matched' verdict cannot be re-derived from here the way paper-preflight's can. The LLM screen, however bounded and disclosed, puts a model inside a verification path on the paid tiers. Bibliography audits cap at 25 entries per call.
took: Corroboration for claim-vs-record citation verification with the divergence shown (per-field scores + the resolved record), and for a committed tools.json making a door's surface inspectable without running it — beside paper-preflight's boarded registry-accounting shape for the same gap.
didnt: Not adopted as a service — verification we rely on must be re-derivable from inspectable machinery (the paper-preflight shape); the claim-vs-record pattern is credited in the took line. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Circleback
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: The read surface is genuinely useful in shape: full-text search across meeting transcripts returning matches with timestamps and speaker labels, action-item search by status and assignee, and people/company lookups across interaction history — meeting records made queryable where the conversation already happens; the server follows the authenticated remote MCP spec and is centrally hosted and managed by the vendor.
bad: Meeting notes, transcripts and connected email live in the vendor's cloud — custody of some of the most sensitive records a team produces; the write surface includes deleting action items and sharing meetings, gated by a connect-time write grant with per-change confirmation delegated to whichever client app is used; no self-host or export route described in the documentation studied.
didnt: Rejected — vendor custody of meeting records; the timestamped transcript search shape was noted: our own meeting material stays in our files, read through our own doors (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Cleve
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial product).
good: A coherent lightweight offer: one workspace holding notes, research and drafts, an assistant that drafts from documents the user selects or it finds, voice notes turned to text, and the same workspace reachable from external AI tools; privacy posture is stated plainly (private by default, no sale of data, no training use, encryption in transit and at rest).
bad: Another hosted notes silo: the working memory lives in the vendor's cloud in their structures, export and exit are not described on the page studied, and nothing in the model — no provenance, no audit trail, no governance of agent writes — reaches what our plain-file wiki already guarantees; no licence.
didnt: Rejected — a generic hosted notes workspace with vendor custody and no governance model beyond sharing settings (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: ColdState — Deterministic Knowledge Infrastructure
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial API service).
good: The retrieval philosophy is ours, argued commercially: deterministic whole-word scoring instead of embeddings, so the same query returns byte-identical rankings every time, evals are stable, failures replay exactly and every ranking can be audited token-by-token through an explain endpoint; the MCP surface is read-only by design — search, fetch an entry verbatim, cite it, verify it later; and the exit is real: IaaS mode builds your index server-side and delivers it as a portable SQLite file you query offline, ending the hosting relationship.
bad: The global knowledge base and the hosted mode keep indexes on ColdState's infrastructure (encrypted at rest) — custody again; the 48.4M-entry corpus is a vendor-curated black box whose provenance is not inspectable from the page studied; commercial API terms, no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — deterministic lexical retrieval with per-term explanation and verify-later citation is the retrieval discipline this system already runs (and the second source in this batch, after Brain Memory, reporting lexical retrieval beating embeddings for this job); the hosted vendor corpus is not for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Contexel
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: The portability and attribution story is better than most of its class: memories are saved in the user's own words, every memory shows who saved it and when, the record of who changed what cannot be quietly edited, a wrong memory can be fixed once and every connected AI uses the new version, and the whole memory downloads as plain text at any time; the manager-access exception is disclosed on the page rather than buried.
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud — the shared memory of a person, family or team sits on Contexel's infrastructure, and the disclosed exception (an account manager can open a private workspace, with notification) shows the encryption claim stops at the service boundary; memory content is free-floating facts with no source-document layer beneath them; subscription pricing; no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — per-memory attribution (who saved it, when), a change record that cannot be quietly edited, and plain-text export are our provenance and no-lock-in rules in consumer form; hosted custody of the memory itself is the rejection ground for adoption (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Context Link
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: The federation shape is right: instead of copying content into yet another store, it indexes where work already lives and searches everything in one pass, returning answers with exact citations, past lookups reviewable and exclusions one click; the Memories feature — save a settled decision once and every AI reads the latest version — is the decisions-as-first-class-records pattern; Modes (weighting the same sources differently per task) is a thoughtful retrieval touch.
bad: The unified index of a business's Drive, email, Notion and files sits in the vendor's cloud, resynced daily — the most sensitive aggregate a business owns, held by a third party; semantic search is a black box with no deterministic or inspectable ranking; per-seat subscription; no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — federated single search over where work already lives, citations on every answer, and settled decisions saved as shared Memories corroborate our index-first federation and decision-record design; the hosted index custody is not for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Corvio
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial hosted service; the help page references a public GitHub repository for the client source but states no licence).
good: The Work Model idea is genuinely close to our synthesis layer: approved fragmented sources are reconciled into a governed knowledge tree with stable owners, preferences kept in the right Memory, and only evidence-backed reusable methods admitted as Skills or Patterns — later agents retrieve the owners instead of rebuilding context; the operating doctrine in its own guide is unusually strict — preserve originals before transforming, a terminal result counts only after the canonical readback is consumed, resume a partially-completed operation once from its receipt rather than duplicating the work.
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud workspace — the Work Model, its tree and its receipts live on Corvio's infrastructure; reconciliation decisions are the service's, taken inside its own model rather than in inspectable files; no licence stated; the guide's agent-facing instruction style (long prescriptive doctrine addressed to installing agents) is exactly the surface our evidence-not-instructions rule exists for — it is characterised here, not followed.
didnt: Corroboration — evidence-gated admission of reusable methods as Skills, originals preserved before reconciliation, and completion counted only on canonical readback match our synthesis and verification discipline; the hosted Work Model itself is not for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: NeoFlux AI Pte. Ltd. (Singapore UEN 202556091C), operator named on the vendor's own help page

name: Darwin
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial platform).
good: The access model is stated plainly and chosen by the user up front: read-only to look, full access to change knowledge, agent wording and opening tests, disconnect at any time; the answers come from the workspace's real numbers — results, leads, meetings, conversations — and the gap-finding loop (ask what visitors wanted that the agent could not answer, then add the missing knowledge in the same chat) is a genuinely useful knowledge-maintenance pattern.
bad: Customer conversations, leads and meetings live in the vendor's hosted workspace; full access lets an assistant change the agent's wording, knowledge and opening tests on a public website; even the read-only mode exposes lead names and emails by default — the privacy-safe path requires knowing to use a scope-limited API key instead; no licence.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a hosted website-chat agent platform) and vendor custody of customer conversation data; its read-only/full-access choice at connect time was noted as the right shape for a door grant (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: DeepDNA
licence: No licence stated at source (free knowledge API; terms referenced for the future beta but no licence named in the documentation studied).
good: The epistemic discipline is exemplary: every drug–gene pair names its guideline (CPIC/DPWG) and carries a cited summary, every variant returns its sources and a reading block (assembly, strand, countability, strand ambiguity), and the disclaimer travels inside every payload so an agent forwarding the answer forwards the caveat; the tools accept only gene symbols, rsIDs and drug names — a genotype argument is refused and not used, stored or counted; knowledge endpoints receive and store nothing personal; endpoints that are specified but not deployed are labelled private beta in plain words rather than mocked.
bad: Scope is pharmacogenomics — a vertical knowledge API, not a component for this system; coverage starts with the pharmacogenes and most-searched genes and grows from there; the personal-data endpoints (DNA/bloodwork parsing) are not deployed at all, so half the documented surface is contract only; the knowledge base is vendor-curated and hosted; no licence stated for the API or data.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a pharmacogenomics knowledge API with no place in this system; its refusal to guess (the evidence-grade field left null until the CPIC dataset fills it, a cited source on every claim, undeployed endpoints labelled undeployed) corroborates our never-invent and citation rules and was recorded as that corroboration (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: DispatchMind
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial SaaS).
good: Within its scope the operating discipline is strong: one record per job from first call to last dollar, technicians see only their own jobs, nothing a tech closes is final until the owner approves it, open balances chase themselves with scheduled reminders, and the owner wakes to a plain-language morning report of money in, jobs booked and what is still owed; data export is self-serve at any time and the account can be deleted by the owner from the account menu.
bad: Scope is field-service business operations (HVAC, plumbing, locksmith and similar trades) — a whole business system of record on the vendor's hosted platform, on Cloudflare's network per the page; a business's jobs, customers and balances sit in that custody; the MCP surface the catalogue lists is an access door into that system, not a knowledge component; no licence.
didnt: Rejected — scope and hosted custody of a business's operational records; the AI dispatcher's check-with-the-owner-first rule for money, cancellations and big changes was noted as corroboration of our approval gates (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: DoneThat
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial product).
good: The privacy posture is the product's centre and is concrete: capture is automatic but publication is not — every day is reviewed by the person before anything is shared, any task can be hidden, screenshots are deleted after processing, shared views omit when work happened, and a bring-your-own-AI option keeps raw data from ever reaching the vendor; it positions itself explicitly against monitoring spyware while still giving managers visibility.
bad: Scope is employee work-tracking — a hosted service whose raw material is a person's working day, which is surveillance-adjacent however gently framed; the catalogue's 'AI-ready long-term memory' claim rests on the vendor's cloud holding that history; not a knowledge component for this system; no licence.
didnt: Rejected — scope (work-tracking SaaS) and third-party custody of a person's workday record; its private-until-reviewed, share-only-what-you-approve posture corroborates our review-before-anything-leaves rule and was recorded as that corroboration (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: ENYAL by Greenland AI
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial platform; SDKs offered without licence terms on the page studied).
good: The proof model is the strongest in this batch: agent decisions and actions are encrypted before they reach the service, anchored on a ledger with timestamps, and provable at three tiers up to quantum-resistant STARKs, with a small client-side verifier anyone can run without an account; selective disclosure lets a holder prove compliance from records re-encrypted for one recipient without exposing the knowledge base; the graph layer detects contradictions across archived material rather than merely storing it; local memory is free and only permanence is sold.
bad: The permanent record lives on the vendor's ledger infrastructure — custody of the proof layer sits with ENYAL even though content is encrypted; the paid archive call is designed to be made by the agent itself through its SDK (scoped keys with spending limits bound the exposure, but agent-initiated paid actions are exactly what our money rules gate); marketing claims on the page (proof 'no one can revoke', energy-per-archive figures) are vendor assertions not independently checkable from the site; no licence stated.
didnt: Corroboration — permanent, timestamped, independently verifiable archival of decisions and contradiction detection over the archive corroborate the anchoring our own checkpoints still lack (every checkpoint to date is unanchored) and our contradiction discipline; not adopted: hosted ledger custody, per-archive pricing and no licence (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: FairMind Project Context
licence: MIT for the repository contents (manifest and documentation, per the README License section and repository details); the FairMind service itself is proprietary, per the same section.
good: The context model is well-judged: a coding agent gets the project's needs, user stories, tasks and tests, the decisions the team recorded and how they changed over time, search over the ingested code and documents, and a write path to record what it did so the next session starts from there; Insights tools record agent activity and audits alongside the decisions; the README is candid that the repository is a manifest and guide only and that the service is proprietary.
bad: The service is hosted and proprietary — project memory (requirements, decisions, code, telemetry) lives on FairMind's platform behind an organization-issued token; the repository publishes no server code, so nothing is adoptable or auditable beyond the manifest; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated: no lane-8 disposition record backs it, so it stands as uncorroborated catalogue text, per the programme rule.
didnt: Corroboration — project memory spanning requirements, decisions with their change history, an ingested code graph and an agent-activity audit is our register-and-ledger shape in commercial form; not adopted: hosted proprietary custody, and the token is the whole perimeter (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Family Office Knowledge Graph
good: The door discipline is exemplary and mirrors our own read doors: read-only by construction, no authentication because the underlying record is public, exactly five typed tools with the same names on every node door, per-field provenance, and a published source mirror so the served surface can be inspected; the repository is explicit about what it does not carry (no orders, logs, harvest work, keys or private material).
bad: Scope is a single vertical dataset (family offices drawn from the public record) behind one vendor's door — the data's own curation is not inspectable from the repository, which mirrors the door's deploy source, not the harvesting; 0 stars and days old; of no direct use to this system beyond the pattern.
didnt: Corroboration — a read-only door whose every field carries provenance (source, reader, time, state), typed errors, and an explicit nothing-answered-from-memory rule is our read-door and citation discipline independently implemented; recorded as corroboration, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Agentic KG Holdings (operator named in the repository README)

name: FlowDot
licence: Other (NOASSERTION) — a LICENSE file is present in the repository but its terms were not exposed in the page studied, and the README's License section only points to the file.
good: Engineering seriousness shows in places: custom-node JavaScript is validated by AST parsing (not regex) against security patterns with a 100%-coverage test threshold on the validator, token scopes are picked at creation rather than all-or-nothing, educational learn:// resources scaffold the client before it invokes tools, and execution is observable (stream, cancel, retry, history and metrics).
bad: The surface is the whole platform with write and destructive reach — permanent deletes, publishing, and tools that configure OAuth/API-key credentials for other services — gated by one token; that breadth is the opposite of our least-privilege, default-deny doors; the platform itself is hosted, so workflows, apps and knowledge bases live in vendor custody; licence unresolved at source (NOASSERTION), which under our discipline means ideas only regardless.
didnt: Rejected — a 150-tool whole-platform write surface is the anti-pattern our scoped read/write doors are designed against; scope and hosted custody settle it (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Fodda Knowledge Graphs
licence: Proprietary (README License section and licence badge; repository metadata shows Other (NOASSERTION)).
good: The retrieval hygiene is better than most intelligence products: a dedicated get_evidence tool returns the source signals, articles, citations and provenance behind a trend or node, the tool table marks which tools are deterministic, the Claude connector is a scoped suite with administrative and onboarding mutators suppressed, and the privacy summary is plain that queries are logged, personal information is not sold, and queries are not used to train models.
bad: Proprietary and hosted: the graphs, the API and the curation are the vendor's, queries are logged, and even self-hosting the server code still proxies to api.fodda.ai; the catalogue's counts drift from the source (catalogue says 46 tools / 220+ graphs; the README documents a 30-tool scoped suite over 100+ datasets) — the source figures are the ones recorded here; synthetic-analyst answers are generated personas, a layer our citation discipline would not admit as evidence.
didnt: Rejected — proprietary licence and hosted custody of a commercial intelligence corpus; the get_evidence provenance tool and per-tool determinism flags were noted as corroboration of our evidence-first retrieval (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: G62 Patent Search
licence: No licence stated at source for the service (commercial developer beta, credit-priced); the worldwide front-page data it incorporates is attributed to Google Patents Public Datasets / IFI CLAIMS under CC BY 4.0.
good: The failure discipline is the best documented in this batch: every search is submitted once under a saved Idempotency-Key, the accepted response is explicitly not the result, polling respects Retry-After, and the error table tells the caller exactly what to preserve and what not to retry; results are honest research leads — ranked candidates with publication links, coverage context and the partial caveat carried through, with the underlying public datasets attributed under CC BY 4.0.
bad: Scope is patent prior-art search — a vertical research utility, not a component for this system; coverage is uneven by the vendor's own account (US/EP full text in part, worldwide front-page only, some abstracts machine-translated) and search rank establishes nothing legal; submitted searches are stored and the beta makes no confidentiality promise, so the discipline cuts both ways — queries are the user's exposure; developer beta; no licence for the service.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a patent-search utility with no place in this system; its idempotency discipline (save the operation ID before sending, never start a replacement job after an ambiguous failure, reopen a charged result free) corroborates our own no-replay-after-uncertain-failure rule and was recorded as that corroboration (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Gateco
licence: MIT (the SDK; the Gateco retrieval service it calls is a hosted commercial platform).
good: The core primitive is exactly right: Gateco sits between the agent and the vector store and evaluates policy on every retrieval, so a principal without clearance gets an empty result and a DENIED decision — the model never sees the denied chunk, only its count; access is relationship-based as well as role-based, keys carry explicit scopes with the route table published, policy and audit functions are session-only (no key route), and the audit log is exportable; sync/async client parity is enforced by a test that fails the build if the two drift.
bad: The policy engine is a hosted service — an organization's connectors, principals, policies and documents' vectors sit with Gateco, and the MIT licence covers only this SDK client; the model presumes an enterprise identity stack (Okta/Entra/IAM sync) far beyond a personal system; grounded answer synthesis is a paid tier; 0 stars, months old.
didnt: Corroboration — policy evaluated before content reaches the model, denied material surfacing as a count and a decision but never as content, and a three-state answer outcome (answered / no_access / insufficient_context) are our default-deny door and scored-abstention designs independently built; not adopted: the engine is a hosted enterprise service and the catalogue's PROMISING is recorded as corroboration, not a build (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Giant Mind
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: Two disciplines stand out: decisions are not just emphatic notes — locking a call creates a structured decision record that can supersede an earlier lock while the history and the original memory both stay; and source honesty is a product rule — an answer from memory shows the title of the memory it used so the user can open and check it; persistence itself is honest too: the connection does not save forever on its own, and save-forever is an explicit choice in Giant Mind.
bad: Hosted vendor custody of the memory, reachable today through exactly one assistant (Grok Bot) by a pasted token; the corpus is free-floating notes and decisions with no source-document layer under them; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated — no lane-8 disposition record backs it, so it stands as uncorroborated catalogue text, per the programme rule.
didnt: Corroboration — the hard distinction between a note and a locked decision (structured, replaceable, history-preserving) and answers that display the memory they rest on corroborate our decision-record and citation design; the hosted single-assistant service itself is not for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Giljo HQ
licence: Elastic License 2.0 (README badge and Edition section; repository metadata shows Other (NOASSERTION)).
good: The context-engineering shape is thoughtful: the server is passive — it stores product knowledge, assembles structured bootstrap prompts and coordinates agents, but never calls a model or spends the user's AI credits; product context is defined once and inherited by every session; the Message Hub keeps a persistent cross-session, cross-machine thread with a turn baton, and its dashboard is framed as an audit record for the human, deliberately not auto-fed back into agent context; self-hosted Community Edition keeps the database on localhost with auth on every connection and no telemetry.
bad: Licence is Elastic License 2.0 — a source-available commercial licence, so under our discipline the code is ideas-only; scope is multi-agent coding-project orchestration (missions, templates, jobs boards) rather than a knowledge record; 360 Memory entries are written automatically at project completion, where our memory writes are curated, not automatic; heavy stack for the purpose (PostgreSQL 18, Node, Vue frontend).
didnt: Corroboration — 360 Memory (every completed project deposits what was built, the decisions and the patterns into the next project's starting context) and the audit-record/context separation in the Message Hub corroborate our completion-memory and conversation-log discipline; nothing adopted, and the Elastic licence makes the code ideas-only in any case (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: ctxstore — memory that follows you across models
good: The tool surface is small and legible: five tools separating conversation context from extracted facts, preferences and decisions, with usage-versus-plan statistics exposed rather than hidden; distribution is broad (npm, pip, Docker) and the free, no-signup first run lowers the cost of trying it; the manifest states its licence plainly.
bad: The memory itself lives in the vendor's hosted tenant store — the local package is a thin client whose key is auto-provisioned against ctxstore.ai, so 'one memory in every model' means one vendor holding the memory; retrieval is semantic/vector with temporal weighting, a black box beside our inspectable lexical retrieval; facts are extracted and stored detached from any source document; 5 commits, 0 stars.
didnt: Rejected — hosted tenant custody of the memory behind a thin MIT client; the fact/decision category separation in search_facts was noted, nothing more (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Great Arrow
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial platform).
good: Several disciplines are stated as product rules: a changed fact supersedes but the old belief stays retrievable ('ask what you believed last month'), contradictions are flagged when they arrive rather than at read time, merges are undoable, every answer shows what it read, handed-off work comes back as a draft for approval, and — rare in this wave — content synced from connected tools is screened for hidden instructions before it is allowed into memory; the price cap is structural (at the limit the AI pauses; the plan price is the most you pay).
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud — the business's memory, money, meetings and tool connections (Calendar, Slack, Notion, Stripe, QuickBooks, GitHub) aggregate in one hosted workspace, and the same door that reads can take 639 kinds of action across those systems; 'newest fact wins' resolves contradiction by recency rather than by evidence, with the screening and merge logic opaque; subscription pricing; no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — contradiction-spotting on arrival with undoable merges, superseded facts kept and queryable as-of, answers that name their sources, and synced content screened for hidden instructions before it reaches memory are our supersession, citation and injection-screening designs in commercial form; the hosted custody and the 639-action write surface are not for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: HelpWell
licence: AGPL-3.0 for the open-source self-hosted edition (stated on the vendor's site); the Cloud edition is a hosted commercial service.
good: The self-updating-docs loop is the standout: the agent never guesses — it tells the customer, marks the conversation unresolved and records the gap; gaps, thumbs-down answers and the team's own replies become proposals in a single review queue; approved guidance reaches the agent immediately and article changes flow back to the repository as pull requests, so the Markdown in the repo stays the source; the open-source edition is genuinely self-hostable (own database, own model key, no account or seat count).
bad: Scope is a customer help desk and email-marketing suite, not a knowledge system for us; the AGPL-3.0 licence makes the open-source edition's code ideas-only under our discipline in any case; the Cloud edition returns custody to the vendor; the self-maintenance loop depends on the vendor's agent drafting quality, which the page asserts rather than evidences.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a SaaS help desk), with the AGPL licence settling the code question independently; its loop — an unanswered question is recorded as a gap, drafted as a fix, and published only on human approval, with a plain 'I don't know' instead of a guess — corroborates our gap-recording, abstention and approval-gate discipline and was recorded as that corroboration (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Hexa
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial platform).
good: The learning model is unusually careful: a correction is saved and shown back ('shows you what it wrote down'), then reconciled — it updates an existing rule, holds for one team, or is flagged as needing a human to settle it; scope is tiered (personal, selected people, organization, external packages) so a lesson travels exactly as far as it should; context is resolved per task and per person with the irrelevant explicitly left out; and once the AI acts in real systems, every capability is individually allow/approve/block and every outcome recorded with its authorizer.
bad: Custody is the vendor's hosted platform — the company's unwritten know-how, its rules and its corrections accumulate in HexaHQ's store; the reconciliation judgement (which version is current, where a rule applies) is the service's, taken inside its model rather than in inspectable files; no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — corrections reconciled against the existing rule corpus instead of silently overwriting it, per-task context resolved to what applies and no more, and action-level allow/approve/block policy with a full audit history are our corrections-ledger, index-first retrieval and approval-tier designs independently built; the hosted custody is not for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Husverket – Swedish Prefab Houses
licence: No licence stated at source (company-published knowledge base).
good: As a publishing pattern it is exemplary: the entire approved corpus — all 350 answers, facts and prices — is published in the open (one full-text file, structured JSON, a summary file and a questions index) with the MCP connector as a live door over the same content, so an assistant's answers can be checked against the exact approved text; the corpus is dated and the company named.
bad: Scope is one company's sales and permit knowledge — nothing transferable as a component; the approved answers are marketing-grade facts (prices 'from', ratings) whose approval is the company's own; the citation directive is a vendor instruction to agents, which our evidence-not-instructions rule treats as data; no licence stated for the published files.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a single-company customer-facing knowledge base; the shape (one canonical approved corpus, published whole in open formats beside the MCP door, answers expected to cite the source) was noted as a clean small example of the approved-corpus pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Husverket AB (company named on its own connect page)

name: Hyperresearch
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service; the page says the research stages are an open-source CLI's but names neither the CLI nor a licence).
good: The verification discipline is the strongest in this wave: a report ships with a receipt listing every claim, its quote and its verdict; quoted passages are checked to really be in the source; a critic pass asks, before writing, what source would overturn the direction and fetches those gaps first; paywalled papers are read through legal open-access copies in full, not as abstracts; the vault compounds — sources, interim notes and claims persist with quality scores, and the next question starts from the vault rather than the web; MCP scopes are read-only by default with each write or metered scope approved separately at consent.
bad: The vault and the runs live on the vendor's hosted platform — a researcher's accumulated evidence base in third-party custody; runs are metered ($9–$49 each) and starting one through MCP is paid work, gated by the separately approved runs:write scope; the benchmark table on the site is the vendor's own run of a third-party benchmark with itself first; the open-source CLI underneath is unnamed on the pages studied, so that claim is unverifiable from the source; no licence stated.
didnt: Corroboration — per-citation verdicts on a receipt, quote-integrity checking, a retraction sweep that blocks shipping, vault-first retrieval, duplicate-source collapsing and fetched content fenced as untrusted are our citation-locking, verification-gate and injection-fencing designs built as a commercial service; the catalogue's PROMISING is recorded as corroboration, not a build — hosted custody and per-run pricing settle adoption (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: inbrix
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial SaaS).
good: The autonomy model is explicit and inspectable: both guardrail scores and both thresholds are shown on the ticket itself, the three outcomes are named, anything touching money, legal matters, credentials or an angry customer goes straight to a human with a handover note, and summaries keep a case's issue, status, open point and next step attached for handoffs months later; the desk also runs fully without AI if the customer switches it off.
bad: Scope is a support helpdesk; custody of tickets, contacts and the knowledge base is the vendor's hosted platform (German hosting and a public subprocessor list soften but do not change that); the two scores are the vendor's model's judgements, with no published calibration; the catalogue name (inbrix) and the product's current name (InboxSolve) differ — the identity rests on the catalogue's own URL, inbrix.ai, serving the InboxSolve product.
didnt: Corroboration — a two-score gate (can I solve this? is it risky?) with owner-set thresholds routing each case to answer, ask-first, or hand-to-human is our scored abstention and approval-tier design in support-desk form, down to the per-ticket budget and kill switch; the helpdesk itself is out of scope and its custody is the vendor's (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: inference.sh
licence: No licence stated at source (the runtime is described as open source, with no licence named on the pages studied).
good: The skills model is genuinely well thought out: instructions are versioned, security-scanned before they circulate, fitness-ranked by use, and carry lineage, so an improvement one agent publishes reaches the next user as a better version rather than a fork; one key across hundreds of models with no per-vendor accounts is real integration value, and durable execution with persistent state and human-in-the-loop is the right shape for long agent work.
bad: The platform's centre of gravity is agent-held spending: an agent with the key runs metered apps and models and pays per run from the account's credits — standing agent spending authority, which is a rejection ground under the owner's money rules regardless of the human-in-the-loop options on some surfaces; custody of skills, agent state and the Commons workspace is the hosted platform by default; the open-source runtime claim names no licence on the pages studied.
didnt: Rejected — agent-initiated pay-per-run spending from account credits is the platform's core mechanic and a standing rejection ground here; scope (a general model/agent platform) settles the rest; the skills discipline (versioned, security-scanned, lineage-tracked, improvements published back) was noted (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: JustOnce
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: The memory model is the most principled in this wave: verbatim-first storage, full dated history with time-travel recall instead of latest-value-wins, confidence tiers so an assistant knows a verified fact from an inference, originals kept attached to the facts extracted from them, and shared-space answers attributed to the person who shared the memory; the security page posture is candid — encryption at rest is not oversold, the audit log is append-only, and the missing export feature is confessed rather than promised.
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud — a person's policies, leases, medical letters and identity documents on a small vendor's Azure tenancy, with the vendor's own AI pipeline reading real content to classify it (stated plainly on the page); the exit is the weak point the vendor itself concedes: no self-service export exists yet, so leaving depends on a manual request; retrieval is semantic, a black box beside inspectable lexical search.
didnt: Corroboration — bitemporal as-of recall, verbatim-first storage and per-fact confidence tiers are our parked bi-temporal design and our verified-vs-inferred distinction built as a consumer product, and the unbuilt export admitted in plain words is the honesty this programme rewards; not adopted: hosted custody of the most sensitive class of personal records (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Kawa Code
licence: Kawa Code Source Available License (custom source-available licence named in the README License section; repository metadata shows Other (NOASSERTION)) — personal/internal use, not open source.
good: The decision mechanics are the most developed in this wave: decisions carry reasoning, forks and abandoned approaches; the pre-edit check turns recorded reasoning into a gate at exactly the moment it matters, with three graded responses; transplanting decisions across a rewrite — classifying stack-portable vs stack-bound, re-recording with provenance cited, letting a durability rationale become a test — treats negative knowledge ('we tried X and retired it') as a first-class asset that survives the code that motivated it.
bad: Licence is a custom source-available licence (not open source) — ideas only under our discipline; the system depends on a proprietary desktop app and cloud API for storage and sync, so team memory custody sits with the vendor despite the client-side encryption of code blocks; 0 stars; the pre-edit hook's one-off force override bypasses the very check the feature exists for (acknowledged in the README, cached per session).
didnt: Corroboration — decisions recorded with their why, commits linked to intent, prior reasoning surfaced before an edit fires, and supersession (record a fork that supersedes) as the legitimate override path are our decision-record and corrections discipline built for coding teams; nothing adopted, and the custom licence makes the code ideas-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: khive
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: The capability set is coherent and honestly presented: memory, typed graph and agent task management behind one endpoint, per-account isolation, revocable keys, and usage you can see; task completion carries audit trails rather than vanishing; the Lion Studio sibling is careful to keep its data local (talking to the user's own daemon on 127.0.0.1) even though its UI is hosted.
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud — memory, graph and tasks in a hosted namespace; the memory model includes configurable decay, the designed-forgetting pole our verbatim-first record rejects; hybrid semantic retrieval is a black box; nothing inspectable as files; no licence.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody of the memory and a decay-based memory model; the GTD task layer's completion audit trails were noted, nothing more (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Kijito
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted service, free public beta).
good: The truth model is the best articulated in this wave: old and current facts are not allowed to coexist without a truth model — a correction arc is kept (believed-false, linked to its fix, dated), nothing is auto-deleted, and a memory records not just content but confidence and epistemic source; handoffs are durable (a fresh session continues from recorded constraints and open loops, not a hand-written recap), authorship stays explicit when several personas share one memory, and export as JSON is available at any time.
bad: Custody is the vendor's hosted service — the account memory lives with Kijito, and its own security framing concedes the hosted path is not operator-blind; background consolidation (strengthening what is recalled, grouping into themes, pruning) reshapes the memory between sessions, where our record changes only by explicit, logged acts; still a beta with several client integrations 'in testing'; no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — supersession that retires a belief from recall while keeping it linked and auditable, plus how-known provenance classes (observed / told / derived / speculated) with confidence, are our corrections-ledger and provenance-class designs stated almost in our own terms; not adopted: hosted custody and automatic consolidation (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Knowledge Base
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted service).
good: The basics are done cleanly: one store for notes, decisions and how-tos, organized by project yet searchable across all of them, writable and readable by the assistant in the chat the user already has, with per-project team sharing, revocable access, a full usage log and EU data residency — and it is free without a trial clock.
bad: A generic hosted notes store: the knowledge lives in B77's cloud in their structures, retrieval by meaning is an uninspectable black box, and there is no provenance, versioning or governance model beyond the usage log; one review and a small vendor; nothing here reaches what a plain-file wiki already guarantees; no licence.
didnt: Rejected — generic hosted knowledge store with vendor custody and no governance model (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Knowledge Porridge
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted service).
good: The data-minimisation is real and stated plainly: only tool calls cross to the service, never the conversation; the gaps-first map (find what the learner cannot name, then teach to it) and fixed-key grading keep the teaching honest rather than agreeable.
bad: A personal learning coach, not a knowledge system: the learning map and progress live in the vendor's hosted service, the scope is individual study, and grading against a fixed key fits set curricula, not contested or evolving material; no licence stated.
didnt: Rejected — scope and custody: a hosted personal learning coach is not a component for the wiki, and the learning record would live in the vendor's service; the tool-calls-only minimisation is noted as a good connector habit (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Korely Memory
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the client SDKs and CLI; the hosted service is expressly not open source (README).
good: The most complete bi-temporal model in the wave: valid time and knowledge time are separate named axes, supersession is a recorded link rather than an overwrite, erasure is itself auditable, and asynchronous write state is exposed honestly (ask for status instead of guessing) instead of being hidden behind a success response.
bad: The memory itself lives in a hosted EU service: extraction runs server-side and the README concedes its predicate choice is not guaranteed; the key-is-the-account model means one leaked key is the whole account, deletion included; polling is the only write-settlement signal.
didnt: Corroboration — the as_of / known_as_of split is the sharpest form yet of the bi-temporal design parked in our purpose.md Phase-2 gates, and asynchronous write status with no guessed success matches our read-back discipline; not adopted — custody is the vendor's hosted service and extraction is server-side (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Kumbuka
licence: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (AGPL-3.0) for the community services (memory, dispatch, worklist, server, console); Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0) for cimd-proxy; enterprise edition closed source — per the repository's licence statements.
good: Structural rather than promised privacy: the privileged code paths have no route to private memory at all, tenant isolation fails closed, and commissions freeze at sending with acceptance recorded as its own act — a filings discipline very close to ours; the pre-beta and no-self-host honesty is stated up front.
bad: Pre-beta and hosted-first with no self-host package; the community services are AGPL-3.0, so the code is ideas-only for us, and versioning and audit sit in the closed enterprise edition, putting two capabilities we treat as core behind the commercial tier.
didnt: Corroboration — fail-closed row-level security, private memory structurally unreachable by admin paths, and frozen commissions with acceptance-as-its-own-act independently match our default-deny and approval designs; not adopted (AGPL-3.0 community licence, hosted, pre-beta) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: LadderFlow
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial product).
good: The weekly confirm-what-it-learned review loop and approve-before-scheduling keep a human as the editor of both the memory and the output; extraction into typed idea categories (frameworks, stories, proof points) is more structured than a transcript dump.
bad: A thought-leadership content engine: the Digital Brain — the user's ideas in structured form — is custody in the vendor's cloud, the output surface is social posting, and pricing is per-seat subscription; nothing here serves a private knowledge corpus.
didnt: Rejected — scope (an interview-to-social-content product) and hosted custody of the Digital Brain; the weekly confirm-the-learning review loop is noted as a sound human-check pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: LatticeNet
licence: MIT License (MIT) — the repository states it licenses the skill instructions in the repo; the LatticeNet platform is governed separately by its terms of service.
good: Identity is anchored honestly: a named human vouches for each agent and is shown on its page, one account backs one agent by default, and the reverse captcha is a genuinely novel proof-of-agent mechanism that badges rather than blocks.
bad: A social publishing network for agents, not a knowledge system: content, identity and reach all live on the vendor's platform, the agent acts without per-post human approval by design ('you don't approve its posts'), and the onboarding material is written to recruit agents autonomously — the opposite of our approval discipline.
didnt: Rejected — scope (an agent-to-agent publishing network) and platform custody; the human-vouching identity anchor is noted as evidence of a sound trust pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: LBrain
licence: BSD 3-Clause License (BSD-3-Clause); the README notes patents pending and that the licence covers the code, not patent rights.
good: The discipline is our discipline, independently built: fail-closed session start, abstention when nothing binds, superseded material barred from governing, no-op-by-default installation, a backup before the first config write, and an unauthenticated transport refused rather than exposed.
bad: This repo is wiring, not the memory engine — the engine's own licence and behaviour are elsewhere and unstudied here; the licence carries a patents-pending qualifier; and the paste-to-agent onboarding pattern asks an agent to install software from a pasted block, a route our rules refuse regardless of the payload.
didnt: Corroboration — fail-closed session start, bind-or-abstain recall and superseded-never-governs corroborate our gate design from an independent builder; the installer is not adopted (it wires hosts to a separate engine not studied here, across harnesses we do not run in this form) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Metavolve Labs, Inc. (named in the repository licence statement)

name: LensHub
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial product, self-hosted or managed cloud).
good: Two disciplines we hold are productised here: absence reporting (the index declares its own gaps before an agent answers) and grant-by-approval shipping (an app is born with no access; each connection is an admin's decision, logged and attributable).
bad: An enterprise context platform, not a component: commercial with no licence stated, its own sync and index infrastructure across twenty third-party connectors, and a managed-cloud tier; adopting it would replace the wiki's file corpus rather than serve it.
didnt: Corroboration — not-indexed reporting and admin-approved, attributable app grants corroborate our abstention and approval designs; not adopted (commercial enterprise platform, no licence, own infrastructure) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Locul Cloud Memory
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial deployment product, sales-led).
good: The data-boundary posture is the strongest in the wave: processing inside the customer's region or premises, no outside AI provider anywhere in the data flow, isolated networks supported, and an audit trail kept on the customer's side, ready for a regulator.
bad: A deployment product for regulated firms, sold and installed through calls and certified partners: nothing here is a component we can take, its memory is one feature of a whole workspace stack, and its market (UK/EU regulated firms of 20–150 people) is not ours.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a sales-led private-AI deployment for regulated firms, not a memory component; its nothing-leaves-the-boundary posture corroborates our private-by-design stance but the product itself is not for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Lunafic
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted platform).
good: The write discipline is careful: stories are structurally read-only to agents, every write is logged and revertible (reverts logged too), guarded panels stay guarded even against agents, and expiring shown-once tokens with instant revocation are the right credential shape.
bad: A fiction roleplay platform: worlds, characters and stories are the whole domain, hosted in the vendor's service; nothing transfers to a knowledge corpus beyond the patterns.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a fiction world-building platform) and hosted custody; its revertible agent writes and structurally read-only stories are noted as sound door design (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Meeting.ai
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted service).
good: Revocation is self-service and immediate, the read-and-write scope is stated plainly rather than implied, and the never-train-on-your-meetings commitment is explicit.
bad: A meeting recording and transcription service: the corpus it builds (recordings, transcripts, who-said-what across every meeting) lives in the vendor's cloud under the account, and an agent door that can join and record meetings is a surface we have no use for.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a hosted meeting notetaker) and custody of the meeting records it accumulates (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Megastructure Arc
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial desktop app, one-time $199 licence key).
good: Local-first by construction: project state never leaves the machine by default, one-time purchase rather than subscription, and tool access governed per room rather than by each agent's say-so.
bad: A commercial desktop app for Windows and Mac only — there is no Linux build, which excludes this VM outright; it is a harness around other agents rather than a memory system, and its memory model is per-project rooms, not a governed corpus.
didnt: Rejected — scope and platform: a paid desktop harness with no Linux build; its local-SQLite posture and room-governed tools are noted, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: MemCell
good: The outcome-feedback loop is the real contribution: memory quality is driven by reported results rather than by recency or assertion, credentials sit in the OS keyring, uninstall is clean and documented, and export is a first-class command.
bad: The loop closes around a hosted account (browser approval, guest-to-account carry-over), so custody is the vendor's service behind an open CLI; hooks deliberately fail OPEN — the opposite choice from our fail-closed gates; confidence decay fades failed memories where our record keeps failures permanently; and this repository is archived, its surface frozen.
didnt: Corroboration — pre-action recall with outcome reporting and earned confidence matches the forecast-and-feedback shape of our own ledger discipline; not adopted (hosted account behind the CLI, fail-open hooks, decaying failure record, repository archived into a monorepo) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: OpenOri (copyright holder in the repository licence line)

name: Memocore
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: Project-scoped API keys and editor/viewer roles are sensibly drawn, and memory surviving a change of AI tool is the right portability instinct.
bad: A generic hosted memo store: no provenance, supersession, audit or verification story on the page, memo and storage caps sized for casual use, and the memory — including everything a team shares — lives in the vendor's cloud.
didnt: Rejected — a generic hosted memo service with vendor custody and no governance depth (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: MemoryRouter
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted commercial service).
good: The import discipline is review-first: nothing migrates without the user previewing and picking what saves, on both the prompt-profile and the full-export routes — ingest as an act of approval, not a silent sync.
bad: The portability runs into another vendor's custody: the one memory 'that follows you' lives on MemoryRouter's service at $20/month, so switching AIs is solved by adding a permanent intermediary; no export, provenance or verification story is stated on the page.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody: a subscription intermediary holding the memory it promises to make portable; its preview-and-pick import flow corroborates our ingest discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: MemQ Team Sync
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the public distribution manifests and plugin (memq-connect); the MemQ service itself is a hosted commercial service with no server source published.
good: Approved-context-only is the right default — memory holds what was approved, with checkpoints for continuity and governed retrieval rather than open recall; and the manifest repository is honest that it is distribution metadata for a hosted service, not the service.
bad: Custody is the vendor's hosted service end to end (account, API keys and billing through the vendor), the server is closed, and the public proof surface is a ring of starter and manifest repositories around a commercial endpoint.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody of the memory layer (commercial service, no server source); the approved-context posture and checkpoint continuity are noted as corroborating patterns (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Multinex AI (operator named on its GitHub organisation page)

name: MeshMarket
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the connector repository; the MeshMarket exchange and MeshTool tools are hosted services.
good: The ledger discipline is real: debit-first settlement that cannot go negative, provenance on every credit (earned vs purchased vs promotional), referral rewards only for independently transacting members ('farming signups earns exactly nothing'), and reputation that is computed, never claimed.
bad: The core mechanic is agent-held spending authority with self-onboarding: the agent mints its own key, holds a balance, rents capabilities and lists its own for sale with no human in the loop at any point — under the owner's money rules that is a standing rejection ground regardless of the sub-key caps; custody of identity, balance and the rented capabilities sits with the hosted exchange.
didnt: Rejected — agent-initiated spending and self-signup are the platform's design, not a side feature; the call-only sub-keys with allowlist and daily cap, and reliability computed from the settlement ledger rather than self-report, are noted as the well-built parts of a design we refuse (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Monolithos
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial application).
good: The constitution is our discipline stated as product law: memory changes are proposals until the owner confirms them, memory is inspectable and editable as plain files the user holds, conclusions have sources and actions leave a record — and the page scopes its own claims honestly, separating what ships today from what is in development.
bad: A commercial personal-agent application: subscription tiers meter a compute envelope, the agent roadmap (remote workspaces, goal-carrying presence) is the vendor's own product direction rather than a component, and the memory core is inseparable from the app and its hosted models; no licence.
didnt: Corroboration — propose-and-wait memory changes, owner-held Markdown/YAML memory and sourced recall are our approval and file-memory designs in consumer form; not adopted (a commercial app with metered compute, not a component) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: n3tz Atlas
licence: No licence stated at source (supervised pilot product).
good: Status before answer is exactly our lifecycle discipline: nothing is served without its approval state showing, sources remain the authority rather than being copied into a second truth, and the learning loop returns proposals for human checking instead of silently absorbing them.
bad: A consultancy-run pilot product, not a component: entry is a supervised engagement from €1,500/month with scope set in conversation, the prototype is demo-data stage, data-flow and rights architecture are defined per engagement, and there is no licence or self-host route.
didnt: Corroboration — status-before-answer, proposal-then-approval learning and decisions hardening into cited precedent independently match our claim-lifecycle and filings designs; not adopted (a pilot-stage consultancy product at €1,500/month, no licence) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: n3tz (Saarbrücken, Germany — address published on the product page)

name: naturali
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted platform).
good: Provable autonomy is genuinely engineered: one contract across every client surface, per-run receipts with cost and serving version, guardrails and human approvals inside the trace rather than beside it, and pre-ship evaluations against the owner's own cases.
bad: A hosted agent-building and operations platform: agents, knowledge, channels and traces all live in the vendor's service, priced per run with managed models drawn on a prepaid balance; the audit record itself is retained only 7–90 days depending on plan, which is short for a system whose pitch is proof.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a hosted agent platform, not a memory or knowledge component); its four-class tool-call gating (execute / guard-pass / ask a human / refuse) corroborates our tiered-approval design and is noted as such (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Naumu
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the public connector package repository; the Naumu service itself is hosted.
good: Several disciplines are done properly: a schema-violation audit as a first-class tool, deterministic filtering distinguished from ranked search, answers grounded in nodes with sources and confidence, per-tool keys with least-cost leakage, and a self-check that never prints the credential it verifies.
bad: The graph itself lives in the vendor's hosted service — the MIT repository is a connector shell (one commit; the real development is in a private monorepo), and the tool surface includes destructive graph and note operations behind the same door as reads; custody and the service's own governance are the vendor's.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody of the team graph behind a thin open connector; the schema-violation audit, permission-filtered bot tool subsets and deterministic-complete filtering are noted as sound designs (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: note1.ai
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted service).
good: The write protocol is the best in the wave: no write is replayed blind after an uncertain failure, state is read back before any claim is made, and the documentation discloses its own permission edge cases instead of hiding them.
bad: A hosted meeting-notes service: recordings, transcripts and action items accumulate in the vendor's cloud under the account, tokens 'act as you' with your exact permissions, and the one-hour upload permission outliving token revocation is a real (if honestly disclosed) revocation gap.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a hosted meeting notetaker) and custody of meeting records; its reserve-then-transfer upload protocol — frozen request identity, read-back after a lost response, idempotent completion, conflict instead of a false cancellation — is a textbook of our ambiguous-write discipline and is recorded as corroboration of it (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Nuramem
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted service).
good: Two disciplines are right: nothing is saved silently (explicit save, named destination, clarification when unclear), and the personal/team boundary is structural — team membership never copies personal memory across.
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud: the memory and the rules that govern the user's agents live on Nuramem's service across every surface, and the ask-first guarantee is only as strong as each connected agent's obedience to a remotely loaded rule set; no licence, no self-host route.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody of both memory and agent rules; the explicit-save discipline and the ask-first rules engine ('anything outside it asks you first, and you see the record') corroborate our ingest and approval designs and are recorded as such (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Obris
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the MCP server repository; the Obris service is hosted.
good: Curation is the point: knowledge enters by a human's deliberate save into a named topic rather than by ambient capture, and the connector's own data handling is minimal and stated plainly.
bad: The knowledge itself lives in the vendor's hosted account behind an API key; topics are a light organisational layer with no provenance, versioning, supersession or audit story, and the MIT licence covers only this thin connector, not the service that holds the data.
didnt: Rejected — hosted curation service behind a thin open connector; the deliberate, by-topic saving model is noted as the lightweight end of curated memory (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: OneDroid Engram
licence: No licence stated at source (service over the customer's own database; free tier for individuals and small teams).
good: Custody is answered structurally rather than by promise: the knowledge never leaves a database the customer owns and can read with plain SQL, and versioned writes with restore make agent overwrites recoverable by design.
bad: Access is still mediated by the vendor's account and service layer even though storage is the customer's database; there is no licence for the software itself, no stated export of the permission model, and the product is one layer of a two-product suite whose other half (Argus) is a separate evaluation system.
didnt: Corroboration — bring-your-own-Postgres custody plus commit-versioned memory with diff and restore is the strongest storage answer in the wave and matches our 'the data stays with you' rule; not adopted (a separate account-mediated memory service, and our corpus is files by design) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: OpenArx
good: The contribution discipline is exemplary: a claim enters the record only by passing a staged, reviewed method, with verdicts, corrections and an escalation path — and the whole infrastructure is published under Apache-2.0 as an auditable mirror precisely so agents can ground their reasoning in what was actually built.
bad: Public alpha with APIs and schemas still changing; the living system is a hosted network service (Neo4j graph, vector store, portal accounts) aimed at open scientific knowledge — a different corpus and mission from a private personal wiki — and the mirror lags whatever the service runs today.
didnt: Corroboration — the checkpoint-gated contribution door (no direct writes; publication follows staged review), typed claim relations and content-addressed provenance are the closest relatives in this wave to our compiled-wiki and claim-lifecycle design; not adopted (a scientific-knowledge network service, public alpha) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Penny
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted subscription service).
good: Accountability is engineered, not asserted: decryption is logged before it happens, the log is sealed somewhere the operator cannot quietly rewrite, unusual human access is published at once, and the honesty about what encryption does and does not prove is exact.
bad: Custody is still the vendor's infrastructure: the accountability is receipts after the fact rather than inability, the consolidation fades memory by recency and importance where our record keeps everything, and the service is a consumer subscription with no self-host route.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody; the record-before-decryption access log, sealed daily into a public tamper-evident log on a separate cloud, is the strongest accountability design in the wave and corroborates our audit stance (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Perfect Memory
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial application with a hosted relay).
good: The custody shape is correct by construction: the cloud forwards encrypted requests and never holds the data, search executes on the user's own machine, and capture pauses itself in private browsing.
bad: The source itself is continuous screen and meeting capture on the user's machine — a surveillance-shaped corpus we do not build or ingest from — and recall quality rests entirely on OCR and local indexing the page does not evidence; the relay is a vendor service even if it is content-blind.
didnt: Rejected — scope: personal screen-recall capture, whose corpus we would not hold; the relay-only bridge, under which the vendor structurally cannot read the memory it serves, is noted as the right custody shape (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Picsha AI
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted platform).
good: Isolation is enforced where it belongs — at the transport and query layer rather than by instructing the model — and the documentation discloses the weaker local package's true scope instead of letting users assume confinement it does not provide.
bad: A hosted asset-management platform for organisations' media libraries: the assets, the index and the generation pipeline are the vendor's service, the toolset reaches generative edits and face naming over people's images, and nothing here serves a text knowledge corpus.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a hosted digital-asset-management platform); its transport-layer isolation, enforced outside the model's prompts and documented with its own limits stated, is noted as honest door design (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: RCLL
good: The strongest honesty discipline in the wave: measured retrieval numbers with method and caveats, negative results published, unmeasured claims refused, mirror status and missing release stated up front — plus a genuinely structural idea, a read path that never calls a model.
bad: By its own account the fork trails its upstream by some 1,700 commits and four releases, there is no packaged release or published image (running it means building the tree), rooms are scoping rather than isolation, and its store is a Postgres/vector service — a different custody shape from our file corpus; the write path still depends on an LLM for extraction unless deliberately run in the reduced no-LLM mode.
didnt: Corroboration — rooms/halls/layers tiered recall, LLM-free reads, closets that keep source pointers, and benchmarks published with their losing arms independently match our tiered-recall and honesty standards, in a self-hosted MIT system; the FOR US verdict is recorded as uncorroborated catalogue text, and nothing was adopted this pass (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: ReasonGraph Cloud memory
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the library; the hosted cloud is a service operated by PrimAxiom.
good: Recall returns a reasoning chain with citations rather than a similarity list, superseded facts stay queryable as-of, and the local mode is a real one — the same library runs entirely on the user's machine over stdio.
bad: The intelligence is extraction-first and automatic — entities, causal edges and supersession are decided by small models at ingest rather than by a reviewing mind — and the default constructor quietly forgets (forget_after=30); the catalogue surface is the hosted EU cloud, whose extraction happens on the operator's servers.
