didnt: Corroboration — cited multi-hop chains, soft-supersession with as-of time-travel and causal tracing are strong forms of our citation and supersession design in an MIT library; not adopted (an extraction-first graph engine with a forgetting default is the opposite pole from our human-compiled files, and the named surface is a hosted cloud) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: PrimAxiom (operator of the hosted service, named in the README)

name: ResponseHub
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted SaaS).
good: Answers are held to exact-text citations rather than document-name gestures, the knowledge base is exportable without a fight, and the security posture (zero-retention AI processing, named subprocessors, pen-test report available) is disclosed in checkable terms.
bad: A vertical SaaS for vendor security reviews: the knowledge base and every answer live in the vendor's EU cloud, priced per editor seat, and the citation quality claim rests on testimonials rather than any verifiable mechanism on the page.
didnt: Rejected — scope (questionnaire automation SaaS) and hosted custody; exact-supporting-text citations are noted as the right answer standard (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Revelara
licence: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0) for the plugin repository; the Revelara service is hosted.
good: The door is read-only by construction across all 22 tools, results are organisation-scoped, and the public-incident corpus keeps links to the original reports rather than absorbing them unattributed.
bad: A hosted SRE intelligence service behind an account: the incident corpus, risk register and graph live with the vendor, the plugin repository is only the door (three commits), and the domain — production reliability — is not ours.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a hosted reliability-intelligence service); its read-only-only tool surface and an incident corpus that links back to original reports are noted as sound door design (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Reverie
good: Graph hygiene is treated as a first-class, auditable operation rather than a silent background process: merges are conservative, reversible in review via dry-run, and fully reported; the read-only query surface is enforced at the transaction layer, not by politeness.
bad: The intelligence is delegated to whichever LLM calls it — extraction, disambiguation and conflict resolution are the model's unaided judgement with no review stage; deletion is permanent with no trash or history, and the store is a Neo4j service rather than inspectable files.
didnt: Corroboration — the dream merge discipline (identity-guarded merges, nothing dropped, dry-run with a full report) and the enforced read-only query door corroborate our merge and read-door designs; not adopted (an LLM-driven Neo4j graph service) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: RFP.ai
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted platform).
good: The permission defaults are exemplary for a commercial door: read-only unless a scope is explicitly granted, deletion impossible through the surface at all, and writes both capped and audit-logged.
bad: A hosted sales-proposal platform: the knowledge base, projects and Q&A live in the vendor's service, MCP is a paid-plan feature, and approval workflows serve proposal throughput rather than a knowledge record.
didnt: Rejected — scope (RFP automation SaaS) and hosted custody; read-only-default tokens with explicit write scopes, a no-delete tool surface and a per-org write audit log are noted as sound door design (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Rippd
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted service).
good: The authorisation hygiene is careful: per-request checks rather than connect-time trust, immediate revocation, and lapse behaviour that explains itself instead of failing silently.
bad: A consumer fitness app's data door: health data (food, weight, injuries, coaching notes) sits in the vendor's service, the write surface lets an assistant alter targets and delete notes and workouts, and the domain has nothing to do with the wiki.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a fitness and nutrition app's connector); per-request authorisation checks and honestly degraded plan lapses are noted (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: RoboSystems
good: The engineering discipline is ledger-grade: dedicated per-tenant graphs that tenants can export and leave with, idempotent named writes with audit, and facts that are never stored without the rules that verify them.
bad: An accounting and financial-reporting platform at AWS scale — Dagster, OpenSearch, PostgreSQL, Valkey and a graph tier per tenant is infrastructure far beyond a personal wiki's needs, and its AI Operators spend tracked credits as part of the platform's billing design.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a financial intelligence platform); its write discipline — named operations with idempotency keys, facts that carry their own verification, and close gates that name their blockers — corroborates ours (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Salespeak Company Context
licence: No licence stated at source (hosted platform).
good: The most honest answer format in the wave: authority graded and summarised at its weakest, freshness bounded at both ends, gaps and conflicts returned as data, and the system structurally unable to settle a disagreement it should only surface.
bad: A hosted sales platform: the knowledge bank, the conflict register and the admin decisions all live in the vendor's service, answers are shaped for sales use (persona, tone, deal stage), and the verification label admits the records do not prove the answer follows from them.
didnt: Corroboration — weakest-authority summaries, not_in_kb abstention with gaps named rather than filled, and conflicts escalated to a human decider instead of being resolved by the model are our truth-aware-retrieval and corrections designs in commercial form; not adopted (a hosted sales platform) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: SessionKeeper
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial app).
good: The capture-to-wiki pipeline is well aimed at its users: record once, and summaries, a searchable campaign history and per-character memories exist without anyone taking notes.
bad: A game-night entertainment product: session recordings and the generated wiki live in the vendor's app, the 'wiki' is auto-generated colour for a campaign, and nothing in the domain touches a knowledge system we run.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a tabletop-gaming companion app) and hosted custody (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: smry Product
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the open-source reader (README licence section); the hosted product layer is a service.
good: Fetch honesty is engineered in: every attempt and its outcome is preserved as debug context, and the longer-version-wins cache rule protects content against partial extraction.
bad: The core purpose is circumventing publishers' soft paywalls — a practice we do not adopt regardless of implementation quality — and the library/monitor features that make it a 'product' live in the hosted service rather than in this open reader.
didnt: Rejected — scope and practice (a paywall-bypass reader with a hosted library layer); its parallel multi-source fetching with a per-source record of what was tried and why it failed is noted as an evidence pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Speko AI
licence: MIT License (MIT) for the MCP server repository; the Speko platform is a hosted service.
good: Least privilege is architectural rather than configurational: what a surface can do is decided by which host serves it, cannot be widened by any caller input, and the reasoning for every withheld capability is published.
bad: A hosted telephony platform: agents, calls, recordings and phone numbers live in the vendor's service on a credit ledger, and its full operational surface (the primary host) includes the very arming and deletion tools the directory hosts withhold.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a voice-AI telephony platform) and hosted custody; its per-host surface withholding — least privilege as a property of the door, with withheld tools indistinguishable from nonexistent ones — is the finest door design in the wave and corroborates our read-door discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: SPM
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial product).
good: The governing principle is exactly right and stated as a product law: refusal is a feature with reasons attached, deletion produces signed evidence rather than a shrug, and every forwarded request leaves a signed receipt.
bad: A provider-proxy product: memory sits behind the vendor's proxy and its deep review runs on the vendor's own models, the public page is a canonical statement rather than documentation (no licence, pricing, data-flow or export detail), and nothing here can be inspected the way an open repository can.
didnt: Corroboration — evidence-gated recall with stated refusal, signed deletion receipts, and state changes that keep history instead of silently overwriting are our abstention, deletion-evidence and supersession designs in their most concentrated commercial form; not adopted (a closed provider-proxy product) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Veridical Tech, Inc. (developer named on the product page)

name: Stompy – AI Memory for Claude & MCP Agents
licence: No licence stated at source (archived manifest repository with no LICENSE file; hosted service).
good: The shapes are right: context can be locked as an immutable versioned snapshot rather than merely saved, contradictions are a detection target in their own right, and the SQL door is read-only.
bad: Custody is the vendor's hosted service — the repository is an archived manifest shell with no code and no licence — and the feature claims (NLI conflict detection, immutable snapshots) rest entirely on the manifest's own text, unverifiable from this source.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody behind an archived manifest repository; immutable locked snapshots, contradiction detection and a read-only SQL door are noted as sound shapes (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Stratum MCP
licence: Business Source License 1.1 (BSL-1.1) per the README licence badge; GitHub reports Other (NOASSERTION).
good: Completion is verified rather than asserted: a step is done when its postconditions pass, failures return the exact violation, gates are real halts with bounded rounds, and every run leaves an auditable trace with revert.
bad: The licence is BSL 1.1 (source-available, reported by GitHub as Other (NOASSERTION)), so the code is ideas-only for us; it is also an execution kernel for coding-agent workflows — a different layer from a knowledge corpus — and its spec is written by the agent itself in normal use ('never shown to you'), which cuts against owner-visible process.
didnt: Corroboration — postcondition-checked step completion (the agent proposes, the server decides), human gates with bounded revision rounds, and commit/revert with a full audit trace are our verification and approval designs as an execution kernel; not adopted (BSL-1.1 licence; workflow-execution layer, not a memory component) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: SummarizeVideo.ai
licence: No licence stated at source — a hosted service; the vendor's MCP page lists the directory price as 0 USD, with volume on paid Founding Pass credits.
good: A hosted MCP server (Streamable HTTP) with three tools — summarize_video, get_summary, get_transcript — that turns a public video URL into a Markdown summary whose key points can carry [m:ss] timestamps, plus the full transcript paged in 50,000-character chunks with an explicit continuation cursor. Resubmitting the same URL and language returns the same requestID instead of starting a second summary, and its agent keys are a small study in door discipline: two scopes (Summarize and read, or Read only — a read-only key is not even offered summarize_video), expiries of 7–365 days, at most 10 active keys, shown once, revocable with effect on the next request; summaries are private to the requesting account (another account's requestID returns not found).
bad: Hosted custody throughout: videos are processed on the vendor's service and summaries live in the vendor account, and website sign-in explicitly does not work as an MCP credential (OAuth-only clients cannot connect at all). Limits are tight — 2 free summaries per rolling 24 hours or Founding Pass credits, 2 concurrent videos, public URLs only (no uploads, playlists or podcast feeds), uncaptioned videos transcribed only up to 90 minutes.
didnt: Corroboration — scoped, expiring, revocable agent keys with a read-only tier that structurally lacks the write tool corroborate our door design from the vendor side; the service itself is not adopted (hosted, metered summarisation, and the video-as-memory source class is already boarded elsewhere in this programme) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Synap Memory
licence: Apache-2.0 for the SDK repository (LICENSE file and repo sidebar); the memory engine itself is the proprietary hosted Synap Cloud.
good: Open Python + JS SDKs and 24 framework integration packages (LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, and more) over a hosted memory engine with anticipatory retrieval (context pre-fetched before the agent asks; ~15ms P50 claimed as an internal measurement), automatic cross-session entity resolution, temporal decay scoring, and retraction handling — a user saying 'ignore what I said about the budget' is processed as a retraction, not just more context. Benchmark claims are published with an open harness (LongMemEval 92.0%, LoCoMo 93.2%, gpt-5-mini answer and judge) including adapters for Mem0, Zep and Supermemory so rivals can be re-run side by side; the MCP server is a stateless adapter exposing four tools (log_exchange, check_memory_status, recall_context, list_recent_memories).
bad: The engine is hosted-only by the README's own statement — 'There's no local server to run: memory processing happens in Synap's cloud' — so every logged conversation crosses to the vendor under an API key, metered in credits (free trial 12,500 credits/month, 1 agent); the open licence covers the client SDKs, not the system that holds the memory. The repo is young (created 2026-04-10, 81 commits, no releases), and its README carries an agent-addressed install block ('Paste this into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor…') — characterised as evidence, never followed.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody: an Apache-2.0 client over a closed, credit-metered cloud engine is the custody shape our local-first design refuses, however strong the retrieval claims; retraction-as-contradiction-handling and the open, rival-rerunnable benchmark harness are noted as corroboration of direction (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Maximem (the vendor; docs at docs.maximem.ai, dashboard at synap.maximem.ai)

name: Syntology
licence: No licence stated at source — a proprietary hosted product; the graph structures public papers, citations and code.
good: A hosted knowledge graph of AI/ML research — 731,359 papers, 3,847,068 citations, 404,037 authors, 183,054 linked repos, live counts printed on the homepage — whose stated ethos is exactly a provenance discipline: 'every edge carries where it came from, every reference implementation carries a verification level, and neither is asserted without the evidence behind it actually existing on the node'; confidence is 'a recorded number, not a marketing word, and it's checked before anything gets written', extraction and ranking methods are disclosed on a methodology page, and the operator narrows its own claim — 'We don't originate the claims in this graph… we structure and verify what's already public.'
bad: A closed hosted product: the graph, its extraction pipeline and its verification levels live on syntology.ai with no open licence, no local custody and no export story visible at source; the public pages are thin (homepage plus ethos), so the verification machinery itself could not be inspected — only its stated policy.
didnt: Corroboration — per-edge provenance, per-implementation verification levels and confidence-checked-before-write are our citation-lockfile design stated as a commercial ontology's founding ethos; not adopted (closed hosted custody, research-literature scope) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Team0 Living Understanding
licence: No licence stated at source — the plugin repository's root listing carries no LICENSE file, and the Team0 application and hosted MCP service are maintained separately (closed).
good: Plugin packages for Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes and ChatGPT that load a shared, self-updating team memory ('Living Understanding') into agent turns: native runtime hooks load relevant understanding before an ordinary turn and return completed turns for 'governed learning', each host needing its own Team0 connection and host-level plugin approval; an agent's access or contributions can be stopped in Team0 under Agents.
bad: The memory itself is a hosted black box — the repo contains only plugin shells while 'the Team0 application and its hosted MCP service are maintained separately'; the runtime's after-turn hooks return completed conversation turns to the vendor service by design, which is ambient transcript egress into a memory the user cannot inspect as files; the project is embryonic (23 commits, 0 stars) and no licence is stated anywhere at source.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody plus ambient turn capture: a second brain that 'builds itself from your work' inside a vendor's closed service inverts our owner-visible, human-compiled file memory, and the plugin repo's missing licence makes even the shells ideas-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: ToothNote.ai
licence: No licence stated at source — a proprietary hosted SaaS; the MCP surface is a documented part of the paid product (Pro plan or higher, API platform enabled by the vendor).
good: The narrowest read-only door in this wave, documented for directory reviewers on a public page: exactly three tools (count_patients_seen, list_procedure_aggregates, count_letters), all read-only, idempotent and practice-scoped, every answer carrying an asOf timestamp; OAuth 2.1 + PKCE with a single scope (read:aggregates), no pasted API key on the directory path, and an explicit never-list — no patient names, charts or record identifiers, no letter bodies, no write, delete or send tools at all, with out-of-surface requests refused.
bad: Scope is one vertical SaaS (dental practice operations) behind a paid plan plus a vendor-enabled API flag ('it is not a self-serve toggle'); aggregates over a hosted practice database have no bearing on a personal knowledge OS beyond the door pattern, and the surface is built to expose counts, never content.
didnt: Corroboration — a three-tool, single-scope, aggregate-only door whose refusals are published in advance is our read-door discipline (least surface, scoped grant, timestamped answers) stated by a healthcare vendor under real privacy pressure; nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Wikinews MCP
licence: No licence stated for the server at source (a Miso product demo); the archived content is Wikinews material under CC BY 2.5, as the vendor's own FAQ states.
good: A free hosted MCP over 20,000+ Wikinews articles (2004–present) for grounded, sourced answers, installed as a plugin that also ships an open Agent Skill teaching the working discipline — search first, read the full article before quoting, and always cite the article used. The FAQ is candid about coverage (densest 2005–2010, thinner after) and about status ('not an official Wikinews service… a product demo by Miso'; sign-in by email OAuth, 30-day session, no API key).
bad: A vendor demo, not infrastructure: the archive is a fixed third-party corpus, sign-in runs through Miso, nothing at source states a licence for the server code or any continuity commitment, and coverage thins sharply after 2010 — which the vendor itself flags.
didnt: Corroboration — search-first, read-the-whole-source, cite-what-you-used is our answer discipline packaged as a consumer skill over an openly licensed corpus; not adopted (demo service, news-archive scope) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Wikipedia Trends API
licence: No licence stated in the package README as read (search-rendered PyPI page; direct PyPI open returned a client-challenge page and the catalogue GitHub repo 404s). The same vendor's MCP server is listed MIT on its Glama page — a sibling artefact whose licence is not borrowed for this package.
good: A Python client (TrendsMcpClient) for a managed trend-data service in which one API key reaches 30+ sources — Google Search/Images/News/Shopping, YouTube, TikTok, Reddit, Amazon, Wikipedia page views, news volume and sentiment, app downloads, npm, Steam — with every value normalised 0–100 so platforms compare directly; error handling is typed (status, code such as rate_limited, message), the client is stateless and thread-safe with async support, and the FAQ is plain that nothing is scraped: one authenticated REST call to the vendor's managed infrastructure, free tier 100 requests/month with no card.
bad: A thin client over a metered hosted backend: the catalogue GitHub repo (trendsapi-ai/wikipedia-trends-api) 404s, so the package page is the only first-party surface; the underlying Wikipedia pageview data is public Wikimedia data resold behind a quota, and the 'wikipedia' source is one row of a marketing-trends bundle aimed at media and investment use.
didnt: Rejected — scope and custody: a metered wrapper over public trend signals has nothing a personal knowledge OS can use, and the 0–100 normalisation that makes sources comparable also erases the raw counts a citation would need to point at (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Wikipedia Trends MCP
licence: MIT, as listed for this server on the vendor's Glama server pages (package README read in search-rendered form; the catalogue GitHub repo 404s and a direct PyPI open returned a client-challenge page).
good: The hosted MCP face of the same trend service (endpoint api.trendsmcp.ai/mcp, Bearer key): four tools — get_trends, get_growth (1W/1M/3M/6M/1Y), get_top_trends, get_ranked_trends — returning normalised 0–100 Wikipedia pageview series for any article topic, with 12+ further sources (Google, YouTube, TikTok, Reddit, Amazon, news sentiment, npm, Steam) behind the same key and connection; its FAQ argues the signal plainly (Wikipedia spikes can lead search trends by 24–72 hours on news events) and states its boundary (English Wikipedia only; multi-language on the roadmap).
bad: The same custody shape as its client package: a hosted, key-metered backend whose data derives from public Wikimedia pageview dumps; the catalogue repo (trendsmcp-ai/wikipedia-trends-mcp) 404s, leaving directory and package pages as the only surfaces; normalised scores without raw counts cannot be cited back to a checkable figure.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an attention-signal service for media/investment trend-watching; nothing in it serves a citation-locked personal wiki, and its normalised-only output is the opposite of our sourced-numbers discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: xmp4 — Semantic code knowledge for your stack
licence: Apache-2.0 for this public documentation repository (LICENSE file and repo sidebar); the server source is private (0ics-srls/lsai-xmp4) and the hosted endpoint's terms were 'TOS link pending' at source.
good: A hosted MCP server that pre-indexes 856 OSS libraries with SCIP (Sourcegraph's semantic code format) and answers signature/body/real-callers questions in ~250 tokens where grep+clone costs ~15,000 — with a published, reproducible benchmark whitepaper (Python harness; spring-boot, tokio, django, efcore) comparing itself against grep, GitMCP and Context7, and every known limitation printed verbatim in a tiers-and-quirks document ('We'd rather set expectations correctly than have a reviewer find a gap and assume the whole thing is inflated'). A privacy page states what is logged (aggregate symbol/project counts) and what is not (code contents, request bodies beyond declared parameters), with nginx access logs purged at 7 days.
bad: The engine is closed and hosted: this repo is documentation, install instructions and an issue tracker only; the index — and the aggregate query logs that decide which libraries get indexed next — live on the vendor's servers; coverage is demand-driven, and the endpoint's own terms were still pending at source. The Apache-2.0 covers the documentation, not the system.
didnt: Rejected — closed hosted engine and code-intelligence scope; its verbatim-limitations document and reproducible benchmark harness are noted as corroboration of our claims discipline (publish the gap before a reviewer finds it) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: 메모짱
licence: No licence stated at source — a proprietary hosted service (Korean consumer notes app).
good: A hosted notes/to-do app whose remote MCP connection (OAuth sign-in via Kakao/Google/Apple) is designed around reversible harm: there is no permanent-delete tool at all — deletion goes only to a trash the user can always restore; every edit keeps a change history the user can revert to, including edits the AI made; only tools approved at connect time can see the notes, per-tool permissions and recent AI activity are reviewable in settings, and the connection can be cut instantly; shared folders honour roles, so a view-only folder stays read-only through the MCP surface too.
bad: A closed hosted consumer service: notes, history and the MCP endpoint all live on memozzang.ai under social-login accounts; the connected AI acts with the user's account permissions within the approved tools, and the FAQ states plainly that note content the AI reads is passed to that AI's service; text, to-dos and tags only — photos and recordings are name-only, their bodies not editable through the surface.
didnt: Corroboration — no-permanent-delete, trash-only removal with restore, full change history with revert, and per-tool consent with an activity log are our deletion and approval discipline independently invented for a family notes app; not adopted (hosted custody, consumer-notes scope) (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: bsv.cx
licence: No licence stated at source — a hosted service; verification is free, producing proofs is per-call machine-payable (BSV or the MNEE stablecoin).
good: A timestamping and proof service whose proofs are built to outlive and out-check the vendor: content is hashed into a manifest JSON (binding the item's id, author, time and the content's SHA-256) and anchored in a Bitcoin SV OP_RETURN; verification folds a BEEF/BUMP Merkle proof against block headers the verifier holds independently — 'with no trust in bsv.cx' — and returns three honest answers, never collapsed: confirmed · rejected · inconclusive. Services include web-page capture/archive with the exact file committed on-chain, a filestamp notary (the file is hashed in the browser; only the fingerprint is sent) and batch timestamping (~1 sat/hash); the homepage answers the disappearance case plainly — the proofs 'still stand' if bsv.cx vanishes, re-verifiable with any @bsv/sdk tool.
bad: Anchoring is tied to one chain (BSV) and one vendor's format conventions (the 'bsv.cx / x1 /' OP_RETURN prefix); the stored archive copy is 'best-effort' by the vendor's own words — only the proof is forever — and the machine-payable API model invites agents to pay per call, an agent-held spending shape that requires an owner's decision, not an agent's.
didnt: Board — the trustless anchor shape for our unearned timestamp anchors: a manifest binding the content hash, an independently checkable chain anchor, three-answer verification (confirmed/rejected/inconclusive, never collapsed — the same honesty as our abstention), and proofs that survive the vendor; the chain choice and any per-call payment remain owner decisions, and nothing is adopted or paid under this pass (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Casefile
good: A self-hosted MCP server + web board giving every task an append-only case file — decisions, failed attempts, findings and open questions written as typed entries that are never edited (a correction is a new entry pointing at the old one, and 'the tracker refuses writes that would break the record'). Hand-off is a fixed read order — card, latest summary, open questions, index, then only the entries needed; closing is gated: no close without a summary and a passed verdict per check, and no starting a blocked task. Identity is per-agent and signed: OAuth sign-ins or per-agent keys (shown once, revocable, listed with issuer and last use on an Access screen), entries signed with the agent's name; it listens on localhost by default and 'assigns and schedules nothing'. The installer asks before touching other programs' config files, prints exactly what it will change, and backs each file up first.
bad: Very young and small (created 2026-09-11; 6 stars) despite 1,706 commits and 26 releases; Docker-only deployment whose hourly self-update runs through an updater service that holds the Docker socket; deliberately not an orchestrator and not a memory system — per-task work logs only, no cross-task recall — and its Network mode moves the board onto a team server, changing the custody the local default promises.
didnt: Board — the per-task append-only case file with close-gates (summary + verdict per check), corrections-as-new-entries and per-agent signed authorship is the closest external form of this programme's own coordinator/STATE.md handoff discipline, worth the ideas board as a candidate pattern for task records; nothing adopted under this pass (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Memory (official MCP servers)
licence: MIT (the License section of the server's README in the modelcontextprotocol/servers repository).
good: The MCP steering group's reference knowledge-graph memory server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory): entities with types and atomic string observations, directed active-voice relations, nine tools (create_entities, create_relations, add_observations, delete_entities, delete_observations, delete_relations, read_graph, search_nodes, open_nodes) plus the whole graph exposed as a subscribable memory://knowledge-graph resource; storage is one local JSONL file (MEMORY_FILE_PATH), and the README specifies a serious cross-process lock protocol for clients sharing one file — exclusive lock with heartbeat refresh, a single stale-lock breaker, and a write that cannot get the lock within 60 seconds fails rather than overwriting.
bad: A reference floor, not a governed memory: no provenance, no history or supersession, no citations, observations as unversioned strings, cascading deletes, substring search across names, types and observations — and the parent repo's own README warns its servers are educational reference implementations, not production solutions. This row is the mcp.so catalogue name form of a server already in this master under its repo name (modelcontextprotocol/server-memory).
didnt: Corroboration — aligned with the earlier study of the same server: the ecosystem's baseline corroborates by defining the floor our governed design is measured against, and its fail-don't-overwrite lock protocol remains the one piece of real engineering care; the earlier study's took is carried verbatim (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Memorybear
licence: Not stated in the opened sources — the evidence base is the vendor's arXiv technical reports; the MCP product is a hosted service with no licence published in the opened material.
good: A cognitive-science memory architecture published as two vendor technical reports: multimodal information perception, working-memory aggregation, long-term consolidation, memory-driven retrieval and continuous updating, with affective information structured as Emotion Memory Units in the second report (Memory Bear AI Memory Science Engine). Numbers are published, not just claimed in marketing: IEMOCAP 78.8 and CMU-MOSEI 66.7 accuracy, 68.4 accuracy on the vendor's business dataset, and 92.3% of complete-condition performance preserved under degraded multimodal input; the first report benchmarks against Mem0, MemGPT and Graphiti on accuracy, token efficiency and latency.
bad: Every number is vendor-reported in vendor-authored reports — no independent rerun or third-party evaluation surfaced; the product face (the mcp.so listing) is a single line, the system itself is hosted, and no licence is published. The second report's target is multimodal affective intelligence (emotion recognition), which sits off this wiki's axis entirely.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody on vendor-only evidence; the working-memory-to-consolidation tiering corroborates our own layered maintenance (raw record, compiled layer) from an unrelated field, and nothing else transfers (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Red Bear AI (Shanghai Shanmo Shongyang Technology Co., Ltd.; report authors Deliang Wen, Ke Sun, and Yu Wang on the second report)

name: OpenLore
licence: Not stated in the opened source.
good: Documentation served to AI agents as a virtual filesystem: an in-memory, read-only bash interpreter over SSH (lix.sh) offering the ls/cat/grep/find/tree vocabulary agents already know, keyless connections for read access, and a stated safety posture — no process execution, no network egress, no shell injection. The same content is laid out as a small filesystem (README.md, index.md, per-topic files) so an agent can pull exactly the relevant section into context instead of ingesting a whole docs site.
bad: The only opened instance is one vendor's API documentation; the catalogue line's other half — identity-scoped access and governed writing with human approval — is not exercised by this read-only instance and could not be verified anywhere. No repository, licence, pricing or product site for OpenLore itself was found.
didnt: Corroboration — the read-door-as-filesystem shape (read-only, in-memory, no egress, the agent's own shell vocabulary as the interface) matches our read-door discipline; with no source or licence exposed there is nothing adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Sensefold
licence: Proprietary hosted service; no licence published, and the vendor's own comparison records no self-host option.
good: A personal document library (full text of saved pages, threads, videos, PDFs, AI chats and notes as Markdown; notes are never rewritten on save — summary, tags, OCR and chapters are added alongside) with the strongest access engineering in this wave: OAuth 2.1 + PKCE + dynamic client registration; the connection's access tier shapes the tool list itself (a read-only connection registers only the seven read tools) with a second dispatch-layer gate (API_KEY_TIER_DENIED); version-checked writes — a stale expectedVersion is refused 409 VERSION_CONFLICT; deletes go to a recycle bin, never permanent, a repeat delete returns alreadyDeleted: true; an Activity page lists agent actions with the actor shown as AI, each openable to inspect and roll back; export is a Markdown ZIP.
bad: Hosted-only proprietary custody of the whole library, single-user, no free plan (Starter $16/mo after a 14-day trial), and by its own post: no SDK or REST API, no saved searches, email collections or automations yet, and per-account mail sending unbuilt.
didnt: Corroboration (strong) — tier-shaped tool registration, version-checked writes, soft delete and per-action rollback are our gateway discipline working in a consumer product; hosted proprietary custody decides against adoption (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: server-noonien (sequico)
good: A drop-in replacement for the official MCP memory server — the same nine tools, inputs and outputs, plus the extension operations the official nine lack (update_*, merge_entities, read_conflicts) and an import path from the official server's JSONL. The design removes the shared-file failure at the root: each node writes only its own append-only JSONL shard (single writer by design), shards merge as a CRDT LWW-Element-Set ordered by (HLC, node, sequence) — idempotent, commutative, associative, convergent — and travel either through a shared folder/S3 bucket or directly peer-to-peer via the nooniend daemon, which never authors operations, pushes on change plus periodic anti-entropy by per-shard high-water sequence, and restores a behind local shard from a peer's replica. Compaction prunes shadowed operations and physically deletes tombstones only where safe, reporting why when it keeps them. The README's comparison table and limits section are candid (eventual consistency by design; a shared area's syncer can still fork a file, and a conflict copy is just another shard to fold).
bad: MPL-2.0 places the code in the ideas-only class under our licence discipline. Substantively, multi-writer convergence is a design this wiki deliberately refuses — the completion centrepiece records multi-writer/real-time editing as rejected by design in favour of a single writer with an approval ledger; eventual consistency means a node acts on another node's writes only after an exchange. A young single-author project (TypeScript, Node >= 22, npm).
didnt: Not adopted — corroboration only: the single-writer-shard, operation-log and anti-entropy pattern validates our append-only discipline from the opposite direction, but CRDT multi-writer convergence stays outside our single-writer design and MPL-2.0 bars code reuse (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Stele
licence: Proprietary hosted service; no licence published (the FAQ states an open, SQLite-backed self-host version is planned).
good: A hosted project graph every coding agent reads before acting and writes back to: decisions, lessons, risks, goals, tasks and components with stable IDs (TASK-12, KNOW-4), atomic task claiming so two sessions never start the same job, and handoff notes left at session end. Its differentiator is a graph that maintains itself: a reversed decision is retired — still visible, still explaining itself, but no longer served as truth, with whatever replaced it served alongside carrying the reason for the change; resolved risks retire themselves; drifted entries are flagged for review and duplicates surfaced for merging; provenance walks from a decision back to the task, document, risk and person behind it. Terms are unusually fair: Free $0 forever (unlimited public projects, one private project, 500 new entries/month, 5,000 stored; reading, searching and editing are never capped), Indie $5.99/mo, Pro $12/mo, Team $20/person/mo; projects private unless published, source code stays on the user's machine, export or delete everything anytime, no training on stored content by default.
bad: The project record lives in the vendor's hosted graph — custody of exactly the layer our wiki keeps local and inspectable; the self-maintenance loop (retirements, drift flags, re-verification against live code) is described only in the vendor's own words, with no public evidence of its accuracy; entry caps on the free plan meter the record itself.
didnt: Corroboration (strong) — retire-don't-delete supersession served with its replacement and reason is our supersede-and-keep design in a commercial product, and read-before-act/write-back is our session discipline; hosted custody decides against adoption (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Tempreon
licence: Proprietary hosted service; no licence published.
good: A person-owned intelligence layer served over MCP to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and any MCP client: the memory floor is done properly (structured, searchable, exportable, with context assembly and temporal awareness), and the layer above it models how the user thinks, decides and writes — a Core Imprint built from about 15 minutes of conversation, passive Tempering at three depths (Flash same-session, Sustained multi-session, Core cross-domain synthesis) and active Honing through sharpening questions and corrections. Data terms are stated plainly: enterprise-grade isolation, complete erasure on demand, full portability, GDPR/CCPA framing; free to start.
bad: The differentiating claims are the least verifiable on the site and the riskiest custody shape in this wave: a hosted third party modelling the owner's judgment, with an Agents feature that dispatches autonomous agents in the user's voice, each with its own authority level; seven patent applications signal a closed, defended product, and paid tiers gate the depth and the agents.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted judgement-model is the inverse of our local, inspectable record, and agent dispatch under standing authority levels is a rejection ground under our approval rules; the export and erasure promises are noted (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: agentmemo
licence: Not stated in the opened sources.
good: One shared memory pool for a whole agent stack — a memory one agent stores is recallable by every other — exposed as four MCP tools (remember, recall, forget, list_conflicts): semantic recall across all stored memories, and conflict detection as a first-class tool that lists contradictions between stored memories instead of letting a later write silently win. A hosted free tier exists (50 memories, 20 recalls/month, 1 user).
bad: Hosted custody with the meter on the read side: recall itself is rationed (Starter $29/mo for 500 recalls, Team $99/mo), so the free tier is a demonstration ration; no licence is published in the opened sources; and the three-way name collision (a local PyPI library and an unrelated self-signup API share the name) makes the catalogue identity itself fragile.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody and metered recall; list_conflicts is noted as corroboration that contradiction surfacing belongs in the tool surface, not in a cleanup pass (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: ai-context-flow
licence: Not stated in the opened source (the review reports the extension was 'soon to be fully open-sourced' — a roadmap statement by the maker team, not a licence).
good: Memory buckets: isolated, project-specific memory spaces that travel with the user across AI models, with strict boundaries so personal context cannot leak into a client project; the extension sits inside the chat box (optimize the current prompt, or save this context) rather than demanding a new workflow; the maker team describes a three-tier memory (immediate conversational history verbatim, mid-term interactions as distilled semantic summaries, long-term knowledge as vectors) processed inside Trusted Execution Environments with end-to-end encryption, and the user deciding what enters memory; the free plan allows multiple buckets, each with a built-in agent for pressure-testing the saved context.
bad: The evidence is one enthusiastic review plus the comments it quotes — storage claims (TEE processing, E2E encryption) are maker statements at second hand; capturing chats from inside every AI platform via a browser extension is a broad ambient-capture surface; the MCP server that earned the catalogue line was, at review time, a roadmap item (alongside team context-sharing, an SDK and a VS Code extension), not a shipped product.
didnt: Not adopted — hosted custody plus an extension capture surface; bucket isolation corroborates per-scope separation, and the verbatim-to-distilled-to-vector tiering parallels our raw-to-compiled layering (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: lanonasis-mcp
licence: Not stated in the opened sources (proprietary hosted Memory-as-a-Service).
good: Memory-as-a-Service with the operational layer built out: memories stored with vector embeddings and searched by similarity with a configurable threshold, an explicit status field on each memory, API-key generation with usage statistics, quotas, rate-limit monitoring and rotation, npm packages for CLI, SDK and memory client, access via SDK, MCP, GitHub repositories or enterprise VPS deployment, and multi-tenant isolation with organization management on the enterprise tier; a free plan needs no credit card.
bad: Hosted custody is the product — self-hosting appears only as an enterprise deployment conversation; the README quickstart requires the user's own OpenAI API key for embeddings, adding a second custodian for the content being memorised; the tenancy and quota machinery answers a multi-customer SaaS problem that a single-owner, local-first wiki does not have.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody; usage/rotation key hygiene is noted, and nothing in the tenancy layer maps to our single-owner record (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Maximem Synap
licence: Apache-2.0 for the SDK repository (LICENSE file and repo sidebar); the memory engine itself is the proprietary hosted Synap Cloud.
good: Open Python + JS SDKs and 24 framework integration packages (LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, and more) over a hosted memory engine with anticipatory retrieval (context pre-fetched before the agent asks; ~15ms P50 claimed as an internal measurement), automatic cross-session entity resolution, temporal decay scoring, and retraction handling — a user saying 'ignore what I said about the budget' is processed as a retraction, not just more context. Benchmark claims are published with an open harness (LongMemEval 92.0%, LoCoMo 93.2%, gpt-5-mini answer and judge) including adapters for Mem0, Zep and Supermemory so rivals can be re-run side by side; the MCP server is a stateless adapter exposing four tools (log_exchange, check_memory_status, recall_context, list_recent_memories).
bad: The engine is hosted-only by the README's own statement — 'There's no local server to run: memory processing happens in Synap's cloud' — so every logged conversation crosses to the vendor under an API key, metered in credits (free trial 12,500 credits/month, 1 agent); the open licence covers the client SDKs, not the system that holds the memory. The repo is young (created 2026-04-10, 81 commits, no releases), and its README carries an agent-addressed install block ('Paste this into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor…') — characterised as evidence, never followed. This row is the Smithery catalogue name form of the product already in this master under its SDK name (Synap Memory).
didnt: Rejected — aligned with the earlier study of the same product (Synap Memory): hosted custody of every logged exchange under a closed, credit-metered cloud engine; the earlier study's took is carried verbatim (completion pass, 2026-10-21).
institution: Maximem (the vendor; docs at docs.maximem.ai, dashboard at synap.maximem.ai)

name: Memnar
licence: Not stated in the opened sources.
good: The catalogue-stated defaults are the disciplined ones: a portable personal knowledge layer serving your AI-self files and learned patterns to any MCP client, read-only by default, with a lesson saved only on an explicit ask, OAuth 2.1 for access, and EU hosting — built and dogfooded by a solo practitioner whose own consultancy runs on agents.
bad: The opened evidence is thin: one first-party post confirms the builder, the product and its EU base, but no product site, documentation, repository, pricing or licence surfaced in three searches, so every mechanism claim rests on the catalogue line alone and the custody details behind 'EU-hosted' are unexamined.
didnt: Corroboration — read-only-by-default plus a write gate that fires only on an explicit ask is our read-door discipline stated as product defaults; nothing is adoptable on this evidence weight (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: memoraeu
licence: Not stated in the opened source.
good: Zero-knowledge by construction rather than by policy: content is encrypted on the user's machine before it leaves (key derived with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 100,000 iterations to an AES-256 key, derived once at startup and held in RAM only — never written to disk, transmitted or logged), and the server stores opaque blobs plus floating-point vectors, so semantic search still works while the server cannot read the memories; the sovereignty framing is explicit about the alternative (plaintext memory on US servers, subject to the Cloud Act).
bad: The builder names the hard problem without solving it in the post: search over encrypted content still exposes the vectors, which leak structure about the memories they encode; the whole construction hangs on a human passphrase run through PBKDF2, the weak point of any such design; blob custody and service availability still sit with the vendor, and no licence, repository or independent audit appears in the opened source.
didnt: Boarded as the reference design study for the parked encrypted-sync question — client-side encryption with the server holding only opaque blobs and vectors is the shape our owner-gated device-sync gap would need; adoption itself is Tier C and untouched, and nothing was built (completion pass, 2026-10-21).

name: Memory Tool (mem0ai/mem0-memory-mcp)
good: The MCP face of the established Mem0 platform: nine memory tools (add, search, list, get, update, delete, entity and event listing) over the same ADD-only accumulation engine as the library — single-pass extraction, entity linking, parallel semantic/BM25/entity fusion with temporal ranking — distributable as a local package, a Docker HTTP endpoint, or a Smithery-hosted remote server, so the door and the library share one memory model.
bad: The README itself cautions that its headline benchmark scores reflect the managed platform, which includes proprietary optimisations not available in the open-source SDK. The MCP server wraps the hosted Mem0 API (a platform API key is required), so this face's custody is the vendor's cloud; and the project's agent-self-signup onboarding lets an agent mint a working API key with no human in the loop — an account-creation authority our rules reserve to the owner.
took: Claim-level append-only index with temporal multi-signal fusion — built in Round 3, lane TB2 — source/inspiration: Mem0
didnt: Corroboration — as the earlier study of this repo: single-pass ADD-only accumulation, entity linking and parallel semantic/BM25/entity fusion with temporal ranking confirm the direction of our claim-level append-only index; the hosted platform and its agent-self-signup onboarding are not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memsprout
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial hosted service; its site names no licence)
good: A shared team context layer with a clean three-level model (Space → Topic → Memory): personal spaces are private by default, shared spaces carry owner/editor/viewer roles that apply identically to people and to AI clients, every memory is versioned with rollback and carries a per-member provenance marker (a teammate, or an agent via MCP), and access is enforced by row-level security in Postgres itself rather than in the app layer.
bad: Hosted-only custody on the vendor's service ($10/mo individual, $15/user/mo team) with no self-host option stated; agents write back through the same MCP tools with no approval step described — the shared store is multi-writer by design, so a connected agent's writes land in the team's common brain directly.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted, multi-writer team memory is the custody and write model our single-writer, approval-gated wiki rejects by design; its role-scoped spaces, version history and per-member provenance are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memxus
good: A cross-client context layer (Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, Gemini) with per-project collections, tags and scopes, OAuth 2.1 + PKCE connect, GitHub/Notion sync into per-project collections kept tagged and separable from manually saved memories, and a written TRUST-POLICY.md stating that memory is advisory context, not instruction authority, with an explicit catalogue of what the memory layer never does.
bad: The production record lives on the vendor's infrastructure — a hosted MCP endpoint in front of a managed Supabase Postgres — with 'no local files to manage' stated as the architecture; AGPL-3.0 makes any adaptation ideas-only; the forget tool deletes permanently with no record kept.
didnt: Rejected — aligned with the earlier study of this repo: our memory has to be files the owner holds; a hosted context layer whose store is the vendor's Supabase is the wrong custody shape regardless of the governance documents around it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MiFactory agent-memory
licence: No licence found at source — no LICENSE file in the repo root listing, no README, and the Glama connector record names none (two routes)
good: A minimal persistent-memory API for agents across Claude, ChatGPT and any MCP client: exactly two tools (memory_read, memory_write) over hosted Streamable HTTP — the smallest possible read/write memory surface, with per-connector tool access control available through the Glama gateway.
bad: Embryonic: 7 commits, 0 stars, no releases, and no README or documentation at source; the directory's own scoring rates the surface thin (2 of 5 for tool count and completeness — no update, delete, list or search). The store is the vendor's hosted API, and nothing about retention, export or governance is stated anywhere opened.
didnt: Rejected — an undocumented two-tool hosted shell with no licence and no governance; nothing here is inspectable enough to board. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mymemory.dev
licence: No licence stated at source (commercial hosted service; its site names no licence)
good: A consumer second-brain (saved pages, social bookmarks, notes, PDFs, voice notes and meeting transcripts) whose assistant changes nothing silently: asked to tag, move, merge, edit or delete, it shows a card listing exactly what will change and 'nothing happens until you press Approve', every change is listed on an Assistant activity page and can be undone, answers name their source note, and its MCP server exposes a five-tool surface (save_memory, search_memories, list_spaces, get_memory_by_id, delete_memory) locally over stdio or remotely.
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud: content is stored on their infrastructure and, by its own FAQ, AI chat sends the question plus the relevant memories to a third-party model provider (OpenAI or Google Gemini); the undo window is only 15 minutes, the free plan caps at 1,000 memories, and no local-first or file-based option is offered.
didnt: Corroboration — the approve-before-change card, the complete activity list and undo confirm our approval-gated write design in consumer form; the hosted custody and third-party answer path decide against adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Omega
good: Local-first persistent memory for coding agents in a single on-device SQLite store: typed memories (decisions, lessons, error patterns, preferences) with semantic search, typed graph edges, checkpoint/resume, a reflect tool that finds contradictions and traces how a topic's decisions evolved, and a condensed five-tool surface (omega_store, omega_welcome, omega_protocol, omega_tools, omega_call) that dispatches to the full tool set to save context.
bad: The headline capabilities sit in the paid OMEGA Pro tier (multi-agent coordination, LLM routing, knowledge base, entity registry, encrypted secure profile) behind the open-source core; capture is automatic by session hook — fully supported only for Claude Code — rather than gated; and its lifecycle runs 'intelligent forgetting' (time decay, conflict resolution, deduplication by the tool's judgment, with preferences and errors exempted) rather than a written owner policy. The catalogue describes it as hosted; at source it is local-first.
didnt: Rejected — aligned with the earlier study of this repo: a competent local store whose headline capabilities are a commercial tier, with hook-driven auto-capture and tool-judged forgetting; the condensed tool surface and the contradiction-tracing reflect tool are credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: purmemo
licence: MIT for the open-source MCP wrapper (README badge and License section, via the mirror); the core memory algorithms are proprietary per the README's own contributing note — the split is recorded here
good: AI conversation memory across platforms with whole-conversation capture (save_conversation handles 100K+ characters with auto-chunking, save_with_artifacts preserves code and attachments), automatic entity extraction, natural-language recall, and OAuth 2.1 + PKCE remote connect; its v9.2.0 'living document' pattern keeps a single memory per conversation, updated under a user-chosen conversation ID instead of creating duplicates.
bad: The memory itself lives on the hosted purmemo.ai service — the open repo is only the MCP wrapper and 'core memory algorithms remain proprietary' by its own statement; the living-document model keeps only the latest version of a conversation, the inverse of an append-only verbatim record; the headline '94% memory retrieval accuracy' is a vendor claim with no methodology on the page; the free tier is 50 memories/month.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody with a proprietary core behind an open wrapper; whole-conversation capture is our shape, but single-version updating and vendor custody are not. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: remembra
good: The memory layer beneath Remembra Relay: store/recall with entity and relationship extraction, and since v0.16 a grounding rule — the memory layer keeps the exact text each fact was derived from and points the fact back to it, and by default a fact that does not match its source text is not stored (the store response lists it under dropped_facts; a flag stores it marked unverified instead). Self-hosting is free under MIT; a hosted cloud tier is also offered.
bad: The verified handoff path depends on per-client hooks (one verified client is a prerelease build; headless invocations write no handoff), the relay's facts travel to a server — self-hosted or the vendor's cloud — rather than staying in the repo they describe, and the underlying memory API's extraction (entities, relationships) is the usual LLM distillation beneath the handoff layer's rigour.
didnt: Board — aligned with the earlier study of this repo: handoffs built from the artefact, not the agent — done/not-done/failing derived from git and test runs, the departing agent's summary treated as a claim to be checked and labelled contradicted when the facts disagree, self-declared handoffs permanently labelled unchecked, and derived facts dropped by default when they fail to match their source text. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Synapse Layer
licence: Apache-2.0 for the SDK per the project's own PyPI comparison table ('Open SDK (Apache 2.0)'); the hosted Forge service behind it is the vendor's platform — recorded exactly as the project's own statement
good: Encrypted cross-agent memory with a per-memory Trust Quotient (confidence, recency and usage) ranking recall deterministically rather than by recency alone, AES-256-GCM encryption at rest with HMAC-SHA-256 integrity, and a governed handover shape: one-time, HMAC-signed, 24-hour-TTL memory packages between agent contexts whose consumption requires a stated reason (10–200 chars) recorded with the transfer.
bad: The security story is asserted, not demonstrated: a 'non-bypassable 4-layer Cognitive Security Pipeline' of trademarked layers (PII sanitization, intent validation, differential-privacy noise on embeddings, neural handover) whose zero-knowledge claim sits in tension with server-side processing of content, and differential-privacy noise on embeddings works directly against exact, verbatim recall. The memory is held by the hosted Forge service behind a token, and no evaluation or third-party verification is visible on the package pages.
didnt: Corroboration — per-memory trust scoring and reason-carrying, single-use signed handovers confirm the trust-ledger direction; the catalogue's PROMISING is not adopted as a build candidacy — hosted custody, unverifiable zero-knowledge claims and noise-added embeddings decide against. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Semantic Canvas
good: An Obsidian plugin that makes canvas layout semantic in both directions: notes gain properties from their canvas group membership and from labeled edges (semantic, i.e. typed, links), properties can be mass-edited across every note on a canvas in one command, and a note's list-type properties can be rendered back into a canvas, edited graphically, and pushed back into the notes' frontmatter.
bad: Only list-type properties can be edited — the README states it is not possible to edit Text, Number, Checkbox or Date properties — and the whole mechanism lives inside Obsidian's canvas format, so the graph it edits is an editor view rather than a portable record; the repo is a fork building on the Link Exploder work it credits.
didnt: Corroboration — typed links authored visually, with structure driving property updates, confirm the relation-typing direction our wiki took with relation maps; the plugin itself is Obsidian-bound and not adoptable into our file-based stack. The catalogue's FOR US verdict is not an adoption record (no lane-8 entry). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wordflow Tracker
good: An actively maintained Obsidian plugin (461 commits, 52 releases) that tracks focused time, edit counts and edited words per note and writes the statistics into the daily or periodic note itself — as a table, a list, or frontmatter — with file/tag/heatmap views and optional LLM-generated diff summaries via a ${diff} variable. Its collection is privacy-shaped by construction: it reads the editor's own history field, creates no extra history database and no extra data file.
bad: The statistics are transient by design — collected stats are destroyed once recorded, and the editor history itself is destroyed when the app closes — so no durable audit trail stands beneath the daily summary; the plugin is Obsidian-only, and the AI change summaries depend on an external LLM integration.
didnt: Corroboration — an activity record appended into the daily note itself, gathered without a side database, is our conversation-log/daily-log practice in miniature; not adopted (Obsidian surface — our wiki keeps its own log). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bases Chart
good: An Obsidian plugin that renders Bases data as eight chart types (bar, column, pie, doughnut, gauge, line, calendar heatmap and a KPI stat tile) from a small SQL-like query language embedded in a fenced code block, with multi-source UNION, date bucketing and relative-time functions; its worked examples include a data-quality audit — counts of notes missing tags, topics or dates — run as an ordinary query.
bad: Very young and small (23 commits, 3 stars, created 2026-04); the SQL dialect is the plugin's own subset with documented quirks (the README itself flags that month(today()) needs care with bucket formats); and it renders only inside Obsidian Bases.
didnt: Corroboration — query-driven views over note properties, with a missing-field census presented as a first-class chart, parallel our census/validator counts; not adopted (Obsidian surface). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Chat Splitter
good: An Obsidian plugin that splits long ChatGPT/Claude transcripts (paste, JSON export or ZIP archive) into one note per topic with auto-generated titles, tags, summaries and key points, plus an index (Map of Content) note with bidirectional wikilinks; topic segmentation is heuristic and fully offline (six weighted signals, no API key needed, optional local Ollama enhancement), and a preview mode lets the user rename, merge and split segments before any note is created.
bad: Zero stars and a single author at 80 commits — unproven in the field, with no evaluation of segmentation quality anywhere in the README; the split notes are derived digests of the conversation, and the full transcript itself is preserved only if the 'Keep full transcript' setting is switched on (default off).
didnt: Rejected — our ingest keeps the conversation verbatim and whole in the conversation log; deriving topic notes while the unsplit record is kept only by an opt-in setting inverts that custody, and session-transcript processing remains owner-unapproved. Its preview-before-write gate is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI for Templater
good: A small, mature Obsidian plugin (85 commits, 83 stars, 17 releases) that adds an OpenAI-compatible client to Templater — tp.ai.chat() inside a template — so note generation can call an LLM inline; it works with any OpenAI-API-compatible endpoint, including local models, and the README warns plainly that an API key is required and that, unless a local LLM is configured, the plugin makes internet requests to the OpenAI API.
bad: The README is a stub — the real documentation lives on the author's external site (tfthacker.com); generation happens at template time with the model's output landing directly in the created note, unreviewed by construction; and by default the prompt content is sent to OpenAI's API.
didnt: Rejected — fit: LLM generation inside templates, landing unreviewed in the note, is the inverse of our approval-gated, verbatim-first write path, and our stack does not run Obsidian/Templater. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Smart Templates
licence: Custom 'Smart Plugins License' — source-available per the README's License section; GitHub card reads Other (NOASSERTION). Ideas only under the programme's licence discipline.
good: Context-first prompt assembly: the current note or selection plus one or more of the user's existing templates are packaged into a ready-to-run prompt; Core is clipboard-first, so notes stay local unless the user pastes the prompt into an external chat; multiple templates can be merged in order.
bad: In-Obsidian generation is the paid Pro tier; Core only builds and copies prompts. The value is prompt packaging, not knowledge custody: no citation, verification or abstention machinery anywhere in the README.
didnt: Rejected: a custom source-available licence puts the code outside adaptation under the licence discipline, and the paid Pro gate holds the in-place generation; the context-first packaging idea is recorded here. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HandTranscriptMd
good: Handwriting drawn on an in-note canvas is saved as a standard SVG in the vault (readable without the plugin), and OCR conversion to structured Markdown uses an explicit keyword syntax (//H1, //LIST, //CHECK, //TABLE) so structure is declared by the writer, not guessed; on conversion the original SVG is archived to a dated _converted folder rather than destroyed.
bad: OCR runs through Google Gemini with the user's API key, and the README itself warns the free tier's data may be used by Google to improve models; conversion replaces the drawing block in the note (the archive is the only custody of the original); Windows/Android only.
didnt: Corroboration: an ingest path that keeps the original artefact (SVG, archived on conversion) while producing typed Markdown from it matches our raw-plus-compiled custody in miniature; nothing adopted — the wiki's own OCR queue covers the need without a Gemini dependency. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fix Math
good: One-command normalisation of LaTeX delimiters pasted from AI assistants (\(…\) → $…$, \[…\] → $$…$$) with stated safety guarantees: fenced code blocks, existing delimiters, links, wikilinks and footnotes are never touched; a selection mode limits the blast radius, and the result notice reports exactly how many formulas were converted.
bad: Deliberately narrow — a text hygiene utility, not a knowledge feature; its plain-parenthesis math detection is heuristic and can misfire on prose that merely looks mathematical, mitigated only by the undo inherent in editing.
didnt: Corroboration: ingest-time normalisation with an explicit never-touch list and a conversion count reported back is the same hygiene our own ingest applies to pasted AI output; nothing to adopt — the surface is Obsidian-editor-specific. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Attachments MD Indexer
good: Gives non-Markdown artefacts a Markdown face: canvas files become link-bearing index notes visible in the graph and to backlinks, and PDFs/images get extracted-text index files, all kept in sync automatically in one configurable folder — making attachment content searchable and reachable by Markdown-only tools.
bad: AGPL-3.0 puts the code outside adaptation under the licence discipline. PDF and image text extraction sends the files to Google's Gemini API. The sync deletes the index file when the original is deleted — deletion coupling our custody rules reject; the README itself warns to move index files out if they are meant as backups.
didnt: Rejected: AGPL-3.0 is ideas-only under the licence discipline, and the delete-with-original sync inverts our never-delete custody even though the derived-Markdown-face-for-attachments idea is sound and already our raw/compiled pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ZettelFlow
good: The strongest reflection machinery in this wave: practice loops return a note's claim blind and ask what you say now, place dated wagers on claims and ask what happened before revealing the prediction, and collide unrelated notes — all fully working with AI off; when AI is on it proposes and the user accepts, edits or rejects, with the verdict recorded. Note creation is a drawn Canvas workflow walked as a wizard with a live preview before anything is written; citations export as Markdown link-backs, Pandoc keys, BibTeX or CSL JSON, 'never a guessed field'.
bad: A very large surface (Reader, Library, dashboards, community system installs, a user-script action that runs JavaScript with vault access) — power that widens the trust surface well beyond the loops; the Script action's safety rests entirely on 'only run scripts you trust'.
didnt: Corroboration: claim-return, wager and collision loops plus AI-proposes/verdict-recorded are independent evidence that scheduled re-confrontation with one's own claims and recorded verdicts are the live frontier for knowledge systems — the direction of our claim lifecycle and trust ledger; nothing adopted directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zotero Annotations
good: Two-way sync between Zotero notes and per-paper literature notes governed by an explicit conflict table: an edited section replaces the Zotero note only when Zotero's side is unchanged; when both sides changed, nothing is overwritten and the user chooses; text outside the synced sections is never touched. Annotations are shown in place (grouped by page, drag-to-quote with a link back to the PDF page), dead links to merged or deleted items are repaired to their replacement, and each note carries an offline copy of its annotations for when Zotero is unreachable.
bad: Requires Zotero 7+ running locally with its local API enabled (10+ to send edits back), plus a companion add-on dance to obtain links; tags sync both ways without asking — an unreviewed write path, if a narrow one; very young and small (2 stars).
didnt: Corroboration: the published conflict table — never overwrite on divergence, ask the human, leave foreign text untouched — is our own sync and custody discipline implemented independently for a reference manager; recorded as design evidence, nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Frontmatter to HTML Attributes
good: A clean minimal mechanism: every frontmatter key becomes a data-* attribute on the note's HTML container (lists and objects as JSON), so metadata-driven CSS can style notes by tag or property with no build step.
bad: Presentation-layer cosmetics only: it exposes metadata to styling and does nothing for retrieval, evidence, lifecycle or correctness; attribute selectors against rendered DOM are brittle across Obsidian versions.
didnt: Rejected: no knowledge function to adopt — our Lens renders from the wiki's own data rather than scraping frontmatter into DOM attributes; recorded for completeness of the plugin survey. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mini-RAG
good: Fully local retrieval-augmented chat: Ollama or llama.cpp only, 'no data is sent to any external server'; requests are sized to the model's real context window and any notes left out are announced in the chat rather than silently dropped; the on-disk embedding cache is keyed by content hash, chunking version, provider, model and server, so edits or model changes re-embed only what changed — and the README plainly warns the cache stores note text and reconstructable vectors in unencrypted JSON, off by default.
bad: Retrieval without an evidence discipline: answers stream from retrieved excerpts with no citation requirement, no abstention when retrieval is weak, and no check that the answer matches the excerpts; desktop-only; Ollama's context is assumed to be 4,096 tokens unless configured.
didnt: Corroboration: local-only retrieval with honest truncation notices and content-hash cache invalidation matches our local-first posture, and its cache-sensitivity warning is the plain statement of storage contents our own pages aim for; the missing citation/abstention layer is exactly the gap our Ask door exists to close. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Semantic Search
good: An early (2023) Rust/WASM semantic file switcher for Obsidian: heading-delimited sections are exported to input.csv, embedded through any configured endpoint (OpenAI or a local Ollama), and queried from a modal; it also offers link recommendation from the current selection.
bad: GPL-3.0 puts the code outside adaptation under the licence discipline. The author calls it 'very much experimental... use it at your own risk'; embeddings live as CSV files in the vault root, and the README warns the API key sits in data.json where it can be committed by accident.
didnt: Rejected: GPL-3.0 is ideas-only under the licence discipline, and the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated — no lane-8 record covers this plugin; our retrieval runs through the wiki's own search and Ask machinery regardless. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Similar Notes
good: Similar notes surface at the foot of the note being written, from embeddings computed locally by default (Transformers.js ONNX models, Orama vector store, background workers, GPU with CPU fallback) with cloud providers strictly optional; the index lives in per-device IndexedDB and deliberately does not sync, so each device rebuilds its own; a scored results export (path, title, score, excerpt) lets an external agent consume the similarity search as data.
bad: Similarity is presented without provenance beyond the excerpt — no link-type or reason is recorded, so suggestions cannot be audited later; the optional OpenAI/OpenRouter routes send note content out (the README's own privacy note flags vendor retention policies); large models can crash mobile.
didnt: Corroboration: local-embeddings similar-note surfacing with a scored, machine-readable export is the plugin-ecosystem form of our neighbours/path machinery; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated — no lane-8 record covers it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vector Search
good: Minimal local semantic search: Ollama embeddings (nomic-embed-text), cosine similarity over paragraph or character chunks, results shown only above a user-set similarity threshold, and incremental index maintenance — file changes, renames and deletions are detected and the vectors updated with debouncing rather than rebuilt wholesale.
bad: Search-only: no answer layer, citations or abstention beyond the raw threshold; single embedding model and a hard Ollama dependency; operations logging goes to the developer console only; 36 commits and 3 releases — a thin maintenance base.
didnt: Corroboration: threshold-gated local embedding search with incremental updates is another independent instance of the local-first retrieval pattern this wave keeps confirming; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated — no lane-8 record covers it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Smart Second Brain
good: Hybrid keyword-plus-meaning search and a Smart Graph that groups the vault into topics from links, tags and content — both working immediately with no AI provider configured and no telemetry; an agent layer with skills, memory and MCP can be connected on top, and the README is candid that much of the code is AI-written and human-reviewed, with commits saying when an agent was involved.
bad: The agent layer reads and writes notes and draws live widgets, and the README states no approval or review gate for those writes; topic grouping is fully automatic with 'nothing to maintain', which also means nothing to correct; the daily update check is a standing network call (disclosed, and switchable off).
didnt: Corroboration: provider-free hybrid search plus automatic topic grouping corroborates our search and graph direction at plugin scale; the ungated agent write surface is the contrast case for our approval-gated writes. The catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated — no lane-8 record covers it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SystemSculpt AI
licence: MIT (plugin client); the hosted service it depends on is a paid first-party account product
good: A broad suite — vault chat streaming reasoning, citations, tool activity and approvals; transcription to Markdown/SRT; a portable semantic index; Studio visual workflows — with a genuinely detailed privacy section, and a managed-chat 'Ask Approval' mode for agent-requested vault mutations (its on-machine Codex route keeps Codex's own native approval and sandbox controls rather than overriding them).
bad: The hosted features run on a SystemSculpt account with paid plans and credit packs: prompts, selected notes, files and audio are sent to the first-party API and processed server-side through named third parties — the custody model is hosted processing of vault content, and the plugin shows license/credit purchase prompts in-product.
didnt: Rejected: hosted processing of vault content under a paid account is the custody model our local-first, owner-gated design refuses, notwithstanding the credited Ask Approval mode; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated — no lane-8 record covers it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vault LLM Assistant
licence: MIT (per the README's License section; GitHub's card reads Other (NOASSERTION))
good: Query mode answers questions over vault content 'with proper citations' and links back to the original notes; include/exclude folder scoping controls what is scanned; local models (LM Studio, Ollama) are supported alongside OpenAI, Gemini and Claude; responses can be copied as text or Markdown or saved as notes.
bad: The citation claim carries no verification, abstention or conflict machinery anywhere in the README — citations are formatting, not evidence discipline; Create mode generates whole notes on a topic with or without vault context, an unreviewed-write pattern; small and thinly maintained (41 commits, 19 stars).
didnt: Rejected: a cited-answer surface without an evidence gate is the failure mode our Ask door was built against; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated — no lane-8 record covers it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zettelkasten LLM Tools
