bad: UUID lines in notes make raw Markdown noisy for anyone outside the Logseq idiom; canonical-by-most-recently-modified can flip which copy renders when an old duplicate is merely touched; the feature surface (outline enhancements, property sync, popovers) is broad for one plugin.
didnt: Corroboration: visible-missing states with a reviewable recovery workflow corroborate our link-integrity practice; the UUID block idiom is not adopted — our wiki cites by path and line. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Minder Nexus
type: Obsidian plugin (semantic knowledge graph, bidirectional typed links)
good: The Trusted Types allowlist is the right governance for a relationship vocabulary; dead-link watching treats graph health as maintenance, not discovery; the enumeration disclosure is printed even though it is only a local scan.
bad: Four commits is nearly no development provenance for an engine that writes into other notes automatically — the inverse-link sync mutates the target note as a side effect of linking, with no review step described; typed-via-alias overloads a display syntax with semantics, which can surprise other tools.
didnt: Corroboration: typed links drawn from a user-controlled vocabulary corroborate our link-semantics direction (contrast B162's model-invented relationship labels); the automatic inverse writes are recorded against adoption, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Facet Folders
good: Virtual organisation without touching the file tree is the safe way to offer many structures over one corpus; the competitor-honesty table is the most candid positioning in this wave; type-preserving batch edits show respect for frontmatter as data.
bad: GPL-3.0 puts the code in the ideas-only class under our licence discipline; vault-wide property rename/removal sits one right-click away (field-level rather than note-level, but broad); 8 commits and 1 star.
didnt: Rejected (licence: GPL-3.0, per the README statement — ideas only, no code taken): organising by view without moving files is credited in-row — it matches our organise-only, never-move-folders instinct in spirit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bases Power Pack
type: Obsidian plugin (Bases views with write-back; open-core)
licence: MIT (source code; Premium features under a signed licence key)
good: The converter's visible-absence ethic is exactly right and quotably stated; cost-priced feature switches respect the user's machine; honest open-core gating (visible locked commands, offline unlock) beats dark-pattern trials.
bad: Write-back boards mean a drag gesture mutates notes with no review step — Undo is a partial mitigation, not a gate; the MIT-licensed repository is not the whole product (the Premium tier is key-gated), so source study covers the Lite surface plus documentation of the rest; marketing density is high.
didnt: Corroboration: the never-guess converter with in-artefact warnings corroborates our fail-visible discipline directly; the board surface is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rich Table
type: Obsidian plugin (spreadsheet tables in fenced blocks)
good: The portability cost is admitted in the project's own comparison table rather than discovered later; the read-only legacy-format option respects existing users' data; lossy operations say what they drop before you run them.
bad: AGPL-3.0 puts the code in the ideas-only class under our licence discipline; more fundamentally, the format is a plugin-locked silo — outside Obsidian the block renders as nothing, the opposite of our portable-text rule; Auto-fill overwrites existing cell content by design; the repository is a fork/template, so provenance runs through an upstream not studied here.
didnt: Rejected (licence: AGPL-3.0 — ideas only, no code taken): the format lock-in is recorded as the substantive reason it would fail our portability test under any licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Smart Related Notes
type: Obsidian plugin (semantic related notes with link-graph ranking)
good: The most measurement-honest project in this wave: numbers with baselines, intervals on small samples, unmeasured features labelled unmeasured, and killed features named; suggestions carry their reasons (the bridge note), so a human can judge rather than trust.
bad: Ranking currently scans the whole vault per query (admitted in the roadmap; a nearest-neighbour index is future work); the background reader's summaries are model-written display text (bounded, off by default, but present); model downloads run 1–5 GB; 137 commits with 85 releases is a fast-moving target.
didnt: Corroboration: measured-channel admission and cut-what-fails-measurement corroborate the evaluation discipline our own retrieval programme is judged by; nothing is adopted — our search runs over the wiki's own indexes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Semantic Backlinks
type: Obsidian plugin (semantic link suggestions and related notes)
good: Showing the matching sentence turns a similarity score into evidence a human can judge; the synced-key warning is printed in both Storage and Privacy, where users configuring sync will actually meet it; local-first defaults with cloud as the explicit opt-in.
bad: The hazard exists by design: an API key in a file that syncs by default is one toggle away from leaving the device — the warning mitigates, the architecture causes it; the OpenAI route sends note content off-device (disclosed, optional); 22 commits and 3 stars.
didnt: Corroboration: sentence-level why-previews corroborate our snippet/citation practice; the synced-data.json key is recorded as the custody anti-pattern, against this wave's SecretStorage/keychain line — nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Analogy - RAG in your vault
type: Obsidian plugin (local semantic search + MCP server)
good: The privacy engineering is the strongest in this batch: index outside the vault and never synced, snippet-only MCP exposure behind explicit configuration, exact-change preview plus backup before touching a client config, query text excluded from logs by design, and hash-verified model/runtime downloads.
bad: Licence validation phones home roughly weekly carrying a device identifier and a vault identifier, and continued full function depends on a server-provided grace window — a local-first tool with a remote kill-dim switch; a commercial-API contracts directory in the open repo signals a hosted tier behind the local story.
didnt: Corroboration: config-preview-with-backup before writing a client config, query text never logged, and path allowlists mirror our MCP door discipline (ours is read-only and licence-free); the phone-home validation is recorded against adoption, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Seeker
type: Obsidian plugin (hybrid semantic + lexical vault search; fork of Obsidian-Seek)
licence: MIT (repository code; e2e test datasets under separate LICENSE-DATA.md terms)
good: Every network fetch is enumerated in one place with a completeness claim a user can hold the author to; the WebGPU-to-CPU fallback is disclosed in the UI rather than silently degrading results; CI runs a real-Obsidian retrieval gate, so search quality is tested, not asserted.
bad: OCR on by default means extracted image text lands in a syncing vault folder unless the user intervenes; the on-device claim for diagnostic logs is contradicted by their in-vault location whenever the vault syncs; as a fork, its provenance and maintenance run through an upstream project not studied here.
didnt: Corroboration: the itemised network-use statement, surfaced hardware fallback, and retrieval-gated end-to-end tests corroborate our fetch-disclosure and evaluation habits; the fork is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Frontmatter Bootstrap
type: Obsidian plugin (frontmatter template insertion + read-only metadata health check)
good: The insertion rule is a conjunction of three conservative conditions, so the plugin structurally cannot clobber existing metadata; the health check reads without writing and refuses to judge fields against a vocabulary the user never supplied.
bad: Six commits and zero stars is minimal provenance; the fixed-name health report at the vault root can overwrite a user's own note of that name; the convention vocabulary is the plugin's own, so its health judgements only bind notes that already opted into that convention.
didnt: Corroboration: convention-without-imposition — fill only the empty, check only the opted-in, report rather than rewrite — corroborates our validator posture (our tooling likewise reports instead of rewriting owner text); nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MD Butler
good: The guardrail vocabulary is genuinely considered: protected keys, folder scoping, new-notes-only mode, and the required-vs-if-exists distinction show the author knows automation needs brakes, even where the defaults choose speed.
bad: Deleting a YAML key automatically because a condition stopped matching destroys user data as a side effect of opening or editing a note; force-apply and full-repair put vault-wide overwrites one command away; the mitigations are settings the user must discover before the automation runs, not defaults.
didnt: Corroboration: the protected-keys list and the if-exists requirement mode corroborate field-level guardrails we also insist on; the auto-remove and force-apply posture is recorded as what our review-first discipline refuses, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Foldable Frontmatter Groups
type: Obsidian plugin (frontmatter grouping, reconcile and cleanup)
good: Nearly every default points the safe way: automation off until enabled, values with data never overwritten, no background watcher, and removals logged with their values so a human can undo by hand — with the missing one-click restore admitted rather than hidden.
bad: Recovery from a bad scrub is manual re-entry from a capped log — past 500 removals the evidence itself is gone; the log's home inside the plugin folder shares the durability caveat seen across this wave; key reordering on reconcile means diffs touch notes whose values never changed.
didnt: Corroboration: insert-only-into-empty, idempotent writes, event-scoped triggers and a removal log corroborate our write-conservatism almost point for point; the plugin is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rating Filter
good: The whole design is one honest idea executed plainly: a human's quality judgement stored as ordinary frontmatter any other tool can read, with zero network surface to audit.
bad: An unnamespaced 'rating' key invites silent collisions with other plugins and the user's own schemas; fourteen commits and one star is thin provenance; a single numeric score flattens quality judgements that our citation machinery deliberately keeps separate.
didnt: Corroboration: a human quality signal kept as ordinary frontmatter corroborates our preference for plain, inspectable metadata over hidden plugin state; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agent Review
good: The most complete human/agent shared-record design in this wave: one data layer for both parties, agent capabilities bounded by their own permission mechanism instead of inheriting the human's, and broken anchors degrade to a reviewable 'orphaned' state instead of disappearing.
bad: The surface is very broad for 26 commits and zero stars, so the governance machinery is more designed than battle-tested; the review corpus lives in a dot-folder inside the vault, so it syncs wherever the vault syncs; the in-vault API means any other plugin could in principle call the same surface.
didnt: Corroboration: a shared human/agent review layer with separately gated agent deletion, idempotent agent commands, and orphaned-never-deleted anchors corroborates our filings and door architecture directly; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WhatsApp Local Sync
type: Obsidian plugin (read-only local WhatsApp chat mirror)
good: Copy-then-read is the correct way to touch another app's live database, and the WAL freshness lag is disclosed with its remedy instead of presenting the mirror as real-time; the sensitivity warning about plaintext transcripts is printed where the user will meet it.
bad: Two commits is near-zero provenance for a tool reading a private chat database; Full Disk Access is a broad macOS grant for one plugin's host app; the product makes plaintext copies of private conversations one click away, and the reset path can silently duplicate recent messages (disclosed, but the failure mode is data-shaped).
didnt: Corroboration: read-only temp-copy source access and row-id cursor dedup corroborate our ingest shape for chat records; not adopted — our messaging routes are the connected ones, and mirroring private chats into a vault is the owner's call, not a default. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: X Bookmarks
type: Obsidian plugin (X bookmarks sync via private web API)
good: Existing notes are never rewritten, so the human's annotations outrank the machine's re-render — the correct precedence, chosen deliberately after another tool got it wrong; failures announce themselves with a cause instead of dying silently, and the test suite never touches the live service.
bad: The whole tool rides an unofficial private API, so account risk is inherent (disclosed, but real); the session cookie's home in data.json means vault sync can carry a live credential off-device, and unlike the wave's better examples no warning is printed for that; a terms-of-service grey zone is the foundation, not an edge case.
didnt: Corroboration: skip-existing/never-overwrite dedup and loud, named failure corroborate our ingest discipline; the cookie-in-data.json custody and private-API basis are recorded against adoption, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Starred News Sync
good: Dedup identity survives renames because it lives in frontmatter, and the URL-normalization rules are written down instead of being folklore; the fetch pipeline treats fetched HTML as hostile (sanitized, host-restricted, size-capped) and discloses even the IP/user-agent residue of the optional image mode.
bad: Reader credentials sit in the plugin's data file, the syncing-file class (stated, but not warned about in sync terms); five provider dialects across two protocols is a wide compatibility surface for 21 commits, and the README concedes compatibility 'depends on the exact API variant'; embedding raw API payloads in notes is possible via the debug view.
didnt: Corroboration: hash-keyed rename-safe dedup, skip-existing imports, and a hardened article-fetch path corroborate our ingest discipline; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Grimmory Sync
type: Obsidian plugin (book highlights sync from self-hosted Grimmory)
good: The rewrite boundary is the note's own markers, so the user's additions and frontmatter are structurally out of reach; the login password is exchanged once for a token and never persisted — the credential pattern the rest of this wave should copy.
bad: A single-purpose mirror of one niche self-hosted application; the managed zone is erasable by hand (documented as the opt-out, so a feature, but accidental marker deletion silently ends sync for that book); zero stars and a pending manual review mean little external validation yet.
didnt: Corroboration: managed-zone containment (rewrite only what the tool owns, preserve everything the user added) and a password that is never stored corroborate our ingest and custody rules; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tagged Sync for reMarkable
type: Obsidian plugin (reMarkable notebook/PDF sync with local transcription; freemium)
licence: Apache-2.0 for everything except pro/; pro/ under PolyForm Strict 1.0.0 (noncommercial, no modification/redistribution; commercial use via LICENSE-COMMERCIAL.md) — split stated at the head of the LICENSE file; registry card NOASSERTION
good: Direction and safety are designed in, not configured in: the tablet is read-only to the plugin, user edits are never silently overwritten, and handwriting stays on the user's machine unless they explicitly choose a cloud backend with their own key; the split licence is disclosed at the head of the LICENSE file itself.
bad: The split licence means the shipped binary is not fully open — the Pro code is source-visible under PolyForm Strict, ideas-only under our discipline; free tier syncs exactly one tag, a tight funnel into the paid tier; desktop-only, and transcription quality outside macOS depends on infrastructure the user must run themselves.
didnt: Corroboration: one-way-by-design transfer, never-silently-overwrite, never-delete, and local-by-default transcription corroborate our sync ethics strongly; the free core is Apache-2.0 but the PolyForm Strict pro/ parts are ideas-only, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Postgres Sync
type: Obsidian plugin (vault sync to self-hosted Postgres/pgvector via PostgREST)
good: The limits are printed where a user will meet them before adopting: the default-key warning, the HTTP exposure warning, the silent-truncation footgun, and an unvarnished statement of last-write-wins with its intended scope (one person, a few devices).
bad: Last-write-wins is exactly the silent-overwrite posture our review-first discipline refuses — simultaneous offline edits lose one side by design; operating Postgres + PostgREST + an embedding server is a heavy stack for note sync; seven commits is thin provenance; the API key lives in per-device plugin settings.
didnt: Corroboration: a self-hosted store whose notes double as a queryable semantic index corroborates our local-first custody direction, and the LWW model is stated honestly enough to judge; LWW itself is recorded against adoption for our wiki, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Qdrant Sync
type: Obsidian plugin (vault sync to self-hosted Qdrant)
good: The intended scope is stated as plainly as in the sibling — one person, a few devices, no collaboration pretence — and reusing the sync store as the search index keeps custody in one self-hosted place.
bad: Last-write-wins silent overwrite, as with its sibling; the docs omit the transport warning and edge-case handling the sibling includes, so the safety story here rests on fewer printed guarantees; ten commits and zero stars; a public-URL vector database holding every note is an exposure the README treats as a setup step rather than a risk.
didnt: Corroboration: a self-hosted vector store doubling as the sync target corroborates the local-first, queryable-custody direction; the LWW model and thinner safety documentation are recorded against adoption, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CoNote Git
good: The sharing boundary is structural — a folder per repo, the rest of the vault untracked and private — and authentication uses the platform's device flow instead of asking users to mint and paste tokens; conflicts are resolved in a purpose-built modal, never as markers inside someone's notes.
bad: Auto-commit after 10 seconds of inactivity is the automatic-writing pole: half-finished edits become permanent history on a timer, and pulls merge silently every 30 seconds; the planned agent push/pull MCP door is exactly the kind of write channel our tiers gate, and it is an aspiration in a README, not a shipped, auditable mechanism; twenty commits.
didnt: Corroboration: folder-scoped sharing boundaries, device-flow authentication with no pasted tokens, and modal conflicts instead of in-note markers corroborate pieces of our collaboration shape; the auto-commit cadence and silent merges are recorded against it, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notion Vault Sync
type: Obsidian plugin (two-way vault sync with Notion)
good: The changes list with per-file push and the pull-rollback history are real review machinery around a two-way sync, and the overwrite direction is disclosed in the README rather than discovered in use.
bad: Pulling makes a hosted third party the source of truth for the vault — the exact custody direction our wiki refuses; the integration token sits in the vault's data.json where vault sync can carry it, unflagged; everything except Notion-side deletions propagates automatically.
didnt: Rejected: a hosted third party in the truth path is incompatible with our custody rules; its changes-list and pull-rollback mechanics corroborate review-before-overwrite as a pattern, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: N2O Sync Lite
type: Obsidian plugin (one-way Notion import, read-only from Notion)
good: The conflict-beside rule is the correct failure shape for an importer: divergence is preserved as a visible sibling file, never resolved by silently overwriting the user's edits.
bad: One commit and a 100-page free cap make it a funnel for the author's paid tools rather than a maintained importer; no visible development history, tests or release cadence to judge.
didnt: Corroboration: one-way pull plus conflict-beside corroborates our visible-conflict rule in importer form; the project itself is too thin to adopt, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Property Kanban
good: The truth/derived asymmetry is designed, not accidental: one field is canonical, the reverse index is explicitly derived and rebuildable, cycles are prevented structurally, and deletes are recoverable by construction.
bad: The model is one vault's frontmatter convention — the truth claim holds only while every writer respects it; 26 commits is a young project, and the board quietly becomes a second writer of the same fields it claims merely to view.
didnt: Corroboration: a canonical truth field with a derived, rebuildable reverse view is our truth/derived discipline in plugin form; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PrimeTask
type: Obsidian plugin (companion bridge to the PrimeTask desktop app)
good: Explicit-promotion-only plus origin provenance on every promoted item is the approval-gated write pattern done as a product rule, and approving the connecting build by code comparison inside the receiving app is a genuinely careful authorization shape.
bad: The plugin is a satellite of a proprietary desktop app — the vault side is open, the receiving side is a black box; the same-machine local-port coupling and two-way property sync round-tripping are a wide trust surface for a task list.
didnt: Corroboration: explicit promotion, origin provenance and approve-the-build authorization corroborate our approval-gated write pattern in consumer form; the proprietary companion is not adopted, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Token Count
good: Context cost made visible where the writing happens — a live, provider-accurate token count turns an invisible budget into a number the writer can steer by.
bad: Trivial scope and thin provenance (10 commits, one star); a desktop-only status-bar gadget with a one-time network fetch for one provider's vocabulary.
didnt: Corroboration: an always-visible context-budget number corroborates our context-budget discipline in miniature; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Unhidden
good: Visibility without modification is the right shape: the files on disk are untouched, the patch surface is guarded and reversed on unload, and the reliance on undocumented internals is disclosed in the README rather than hidden.
bad: Patching undocumented adapter methods means any Obsidian update can break it silently or loudly; three commits is minimal provenance for code that rewrites how the host app sees the filesystem.
didnt: Corroboration: index-layer visibility with the underlying files untouched, plus reversible guarded patching, matches our read-door posture; the plugin is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Auto-tagging family (grouped: Smart Tagger, Auto MOC and AI Tagger)
good: Preview-before-apply as the default, with the vault's existing vocabulary (and its casing) winning over the model's inventions, is the correct shape for machine-proposed metadata.
bad: Note content leaves the vault to a cloud provider by design, keys sit in the vault's data file, and the auto-apply switch removes the review step that makes the design safe; tags are flat labels carrying no provenance.
didnt: Corroboration: review-before-apply plus existing-vocabulary-wins corroborates our proposal discipline for derived metadata; the family is judged on the named repo, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Synapse
type: Obsidian plugin (AI enrichment engine with proposal review)
good: Proposal-first with a staleness re-check (the note changed since this was proposed — ask again), byte-exact frontmatter preservation, whole-run undo and checkpointed resumable scans is the most complete review machinery in this wave, documented with unusual candour about its own cascades.
bad: AGPL-3.0 puts the code off-limits for adaptation; the cascade surface is large — many enrichment cascades default ON, so one command can trigger chains a user did not individually ask for; several action types bypass proposals entirely, and note content goes to cloud providers unless Ollama is used.
didnt: Corroboration: the proposal/staleness/undo machinery corroborates our review-first write discipline at product scale, and its whole-run undo and scan checkpointing are noted as design details worth remembering; AGPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Clipper variants (grouped: Easy Web Clipper, Ishibashi Web Clipper V2, Linkhaven, Star Gate)
good: Capture with zero external dependency and provenance frontmatter written at clip time (source, author, date) is the ingest-capture pattern in its simplest honest form.
bad: Readability extraction is imperfect on unusual page structures (its own FAQ concedes manual cleanup), JS-rendered and login-gated pages are out of reach, and images are not localized, so clipped notes can silently lose their pictures.
didnt: Corroboration: in-app clipping into frontmatter-carrying raw records corroborates our ingest capture shape; the group is judged on the named repo, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Third-party cloud sync/RAG (grouped: Knowz AI Sync, mybrain.ai, Syncidian, Rootr Sync)
type: Obsidian plugin (hosted cloud sync + RAG platform bridge, grouped)
good: The safeguard set is the best in this group: first-sync consent preview, conflict-beside with notice, state advancing only on server confirmation, and an explicit refusal to interpret an empty read as mass deletion — all disclosed in plain language.
bad: The corpus itself moves to a proprietary hosted platform for indexing and answering — custody of the primary knowledge leaves the user's machine by design; two-way sync with five-minute auto-pull runs by default once connected; the API key lives in plaintext inside the vault.
didnt: Rejected: a hosted third party holding the corpus for retrieval is incompatible with our custody rules, however careful the sync mechanics; its conflict-beside, consent-preview and empty-read-refusal safeguards corroborate our own, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Generation gadgets (grouped: Research Paper, Literature Review Synthesizer, Trending Digest, Chew It, Ask Any AI)
good: Evidence first, generation second: the human selects the sources before anything is written, DOIs are verified against Crossref, and machine synthesis is labelled as machine synthesis inside the artefact itself.
bad: The generated brief lands inside the vault in paper format, where a later reader can mistake labelled synthesis for scholarship; relevance scores are the model's own; provider keys live in plugin settings.
didnt: Corroboration: traceable sources, DOI verification and labelled synthesis corroborate our citation-truth discipline; the group is judged on the named repo, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gemma 4 E4B LLM Wiki
good: The closest architectural sibling to our own system in the entire catalogue, arrived at independently: schema-as-rules, append-only operations log, preview-before-write, plugin-listed sources instead of model-invented citations, and abstention when the notes have nothing — each one a load-bearing choice we also made.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us; a 4B local model is weak at open-world knowledge (the README says so itself); desktop-only with a ~3 GB model that sync tools will happily replicate to every machine unless excluded.
didnt: Corroboration: an independent implementation converging on our schema/log/preview/abstention architecture is the strongest external corroboration in this wave; GPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sync and MCP
type: Obsidian plugin (E2E-encrypted sync + rule-scoped MCP access)
good: Off-by-default, rule-scoped agent access with a staleness check before any suggested edit is applied is our MCP-door posture; stating the plaintext-for-AI trade-off in the README's privacy model is the honest way to offer it.
bad: GPL-3.0 (ideas only for us); the AI-readable copy of chosen notes sits in plaintext on a server by design; 16 commits with a companion backend to operate is a young, heavy stack.
didnt: Corroboration: rule-scoped, off-by-default assistant access plus never-overwrite conflict handling corroborates our door discipline; GPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Typed Graph
type: Obsidian plugin (typed property graph + Cypher queries + read-only sidecar)
good: Relations as first-class data — typed, signed, property-carrying edges with stable ids and schema notes — plus a read-only sidecar/MCP surface for agents is the most complete graph layer in this wave, and its lossy exports come with a report instead of silence.
bad: A large surface (plugin, CLI, sidecar, query engine) for one author; the edge syntax is a private dialect that lives inside note bodies, so the graph's value is locked to tools that speak it; the sidecar features need a headless service the mobile app cannot host.
didnt: Board: boarded as the reference design for edge properties and signed/negative relations, which our link typing does not yet carry; the read-only sidecar corroborates our agent-door shape, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Literature Graph
type: Obsidian plugin (citation graph over literature notes)
good: Match-or-nothing linking is the right citation discipline: an ambiguous reference-list entry is left unlinked rather than attached to a plausible wrong work, and the graph is derived from the notes read-only, with external data cached and the network switchable off.
bad: Zero stars and a single author for a parser that must survive arbitrary PDF-conversion damage; the conservative matcher will under-link real citations whose titles were mangled, and the meaning-map machinery is heavy for a citation panel.
didnt: Corroboration: conservative match-or-nothing reference linking, read-without-modifying derivation and local-only computation corroborate our citation discipline; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Activity Timeline
type: Obsidian plugin (vault activity timeline from live edits + git history)
good: An append-only event log (events.jsonl) rebuilt from two independent sources with the weaker source's entries labelled as such is our own log discipline; the AI-authorship and no-audit disclosures are a candour standard most READMEs in this wave do not meet.
bad: Twelve commits and an explicitly unaudited codebase that holds the vault's note text in memory (capped at 80 MB) to diff edits; without git there is no history before installation day.
didnt: Corroboration: dual-source event reconstruction with provenance labels on the weaker source corroborates our conversation-log practice; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Stateful Git Sync
good: The most rigorous sync semantics in the wave: verified baselines, tombstones with identity, explicit conflict choice, and read-back-before-success — completion means the verified state was re-read and matched, not that an upload returned OK.
bad: Eighteen commits and zero stars for a protocol this intricate, and the correctness burden sits on state files the user must preserve across upgrades (data.json, sync-state.json, .sync-history/); GitHub is the transport, so custody rides on one hosted forge.
didnt: Board: boarded as the reference protocol design for verified-baseline sync — tombstones, file identity and read-back-verified completion speak directly to our owner-gated device-sync gap; nothing is built or adopted under this pass. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Linten
licence: Conflict at source: GitHub card reads MIT; the README licence section declares proprietary Loopstates Client License terms (source-available for evaluation only) — recorded as a conflict and treated as proprietary, ideas only
good: Machine-readable-manifest validation with live link-health probing and context-budget gauges is a real tooling idea for LLM-facing corpora, and the local/cloud split is at least documented in the README.
bad: The licence contradicts itself between the registry card and the README — a user relying on the card would believe they hold MIT rights the author simultaneously disclaims; core audits depend on the vendor's cloud service, so the tool stops working if the service does.
didnt: Rejected: a self-contradictory licence at source (card MIT vs README proprietary) fails our licence discipline outright, and the cloud-dependent core is recorded against it; nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI Reading Highlights
type: Obsidian plugin (LLM semantic highlighting, render-layer only)
good: Verbatim-anchor-or-drop is exactly the right contract for model output over a record: what the model cannot tie to the actual text simply never appears, and the underlying note is structurally untouchable.
bad: Block text leaves to a configured endpoint by design (local Ollama is an option, not the default story); 35 commits is young; highlights inherit the model's judgement of what matters, with no provenance beyond the anchor.
didnt: Corroboration: unanchorable model output being dropped rather than rendered, over files the tool cannot modify, corroborates our anchoring discipline; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Refwright
type: Obsidian plugin (local-first reference manager; notes as the database)
good: Retraction checking and pre-submission reference verification treat citations as claims that can go stale — the scholarly end of citation truth — and the retrieval numbers are measured on a named benchmark instead of asserted; notes-as-database keeps custody where it belongs.
bad: A very wide surface (import, summary, screening/PRISMA, chat, MCP editing) for one author; the hosted cross-encoder reranker is a paid per-search dependency inside a local-first story; AI summaries sit in the same notes as the verified metadata, separated by section discipline rather than by file.
didnt: Board: boarded as the reference design for retraction/status checking and pre-submission reference verification — our scholarly citation truth-checking gap; its notes-as-database shape and measured retrieval corroborate our citation machinery, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Prism
type: Obsidian plugin (sandboxed interactive visualizations for notes)
good: Agent-written executable content confined to a no-network sandbox, plus a render-verify loop whose errors carry line numbers and exit codes, is verification built into the tooling rather than left to the agent's honesty.
bad: Arbitrary HTML/JS in notes is inherently a sharp edge — the sandbox is the only thing between a pasted block and the vault's rendering context; write-back widgets widen that surface; one author maintains the renderer, the CLI and the skill.
didnt: Corroboration: sandboxed-by-default rendering and a machine-checkable render loop corroborate our verify-before-claim discipline for agent output; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tapedeck
good: The import discipline is careful: explicit selection, no history sweep on enablement, session-id dedup that preserves user edits, and a title extractor that knows the difference between what the user typed and what the harness injected.
bad: It normalizes keeping full agent transcripts — including tool outputs and file contents — as vault notes, a corpus whose sensitivity the README's privacy section only partly addresses; transcripts are other tools' formats, so parsers chase three vendors' changing layouts.
didnt: Corroboration: its explicit-selection, no-sweep import discipline corroborates ingest care; session-transcript ingest into our own wiki is unapproved by the owner (our conversation record is the CONVERSATION-LOG), so the capability class stays owner-gated for us and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tahoe Intelligence
type: Obsidian plugin (on-device AI: Apple Intelligence / Ollama)
good: Review-before-change as the stated product law, existing-values-only property filling, and dates computed in code rather than sampled from the model are three of our own rules arrived at independently; on-device processing makes the privacy claim architectural.
bad: Four commits is near-zero provenance for a suite this broad, and the Apple Intelligence path is Mac-only with an Xcode-built helper most users cannot audit; the meaning index depends on macOS text embeddings even when Ollama supplies the model.
didnt: Corroboration: review-before-change, vocabulary-constrained metadata and code-computed dates corroborate our write discipline; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Clip Tidy
type: Obsidian plugin (AI organization of clipped notes)
good: Confidence-gated automation with a human queue for the uncertain cases, undo that refuses on staleness, and an exact payload disclosure is the careful shape for machine filing; the uncalibrated-confidence admission is the honest sentence most such tools omit.
bad: Above-threshold moves happen automatically once enabled — our gates apply nothing at any confidence without review; the UNENCRYPTED API key and complete before/after note backups both live in data.json inside the vault (disclosed, with a never-publish warning); four commits, Chinese-only UI.
didnt: Corroboration: the review queue, staleness-refusing undo and payload enumeration corroborate our gating; the auto-apply-above-threshold pole is recorded as the contrast, and nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Citation Links
type: Obsidian plugin (citekey wikilinks rendered as APA citations)
good: Derived rendering over canonical source: the note keeps a plain link any tool can read, the citation exists only at render time, and an unresolvable key advertises itself in red instead of quietly formatting a guess.
bad: APA 7 with the US locale is the only style — a deliberate narrowing, but a hard one; it renders nothing at all until the CSL JSON folder is configured, and desktop-only.
didnt: Corroboration: render-time citation formatting over untouched source links, with loud unknown-key failure, corroborates our cite-layer design (source canonical, rendering derived); nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Citation Suite
type: Obsidian plugin (Pandoc-style citing from Zotero or vault files)
good: Preview fidelity to the export pipeline and always-on unknown-key flagging treat the citation as a checkable claim rather than decoration; sourcing the bibliography from vault files keeps a no-Zotero route open.
bad: AGPL-3.0 puts the code off-limits for adaptation; the Zotero route depends on Zotero's local app-communication setting, and the feature breadth (footnotes automation, style resolution) is a lot of surface over the note text.
didnt: Corroboration: export-faithful preview and visible unknown-key marking corroborate our citation discipline; AGPL-3.0 makes it ideas-only, and nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CMDS Zotero
good: Identity separated from display key, a read-only source, full-refresh-with-hashes instead of cursor trust, and fingerprint-gated migration with refusal-on-change rollback — verification treated as the product, not a feature.
bad: The machinery is heavy: a running Zotero + Better BibTeX with specific RPC contracts ('version numbers alone do not establish compatibility'), a background-refreshed index inside the vault, and an agent CLI surface that reaches the plugin through the Obsidian CLI — breadth that demands the very diagnostics it ships.
didnt: Corroboration: verified-identity indexing, read-only source custody and fingerprint-checked change application corroborate our verification machinery point for point; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mendeley Integration
type: Obsidian plugin (Mendeley library sync into reading notes)
good: Managed-region containment plus never-delete, with the unencrypted-credential fact printed in the security section rather than discovered, is the honest minimum for a sync importer — and it is met.
bad: Nine commits and MVP scope; the upstream is Elsevier's hosted Mendeley, so the library of record lives with a publisher platform; the OAuth secret sits in a syncing file, mitigated by a warning rather than by storage.
didnt: Corroboration: delimited managed-region writes and the never-delete rule corroborate our ingest containment (the same marker pattern as B164's Grimmory Sync); nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zotero Annotation Citations
type: Obsidian plugin (Zotero annotation links to Pandoc citations)
good: Citation links at annotation granularity — the claim points at the exact highlighted passage, not just the paper — with the two resolution routes' certainty levels kept separate and ambiguity surfaced as a Notice instead of a guess.
bad: A narrow single-purpose transform riding Zotero's drag-and-drop formats; the .bib route's surname+year matching is exactly as fragile as the README admits; desktop-only.
didnt: Corroboration: annotation-level citation links, ambiguity-surfaced-never-guessed and unresolved-left-untouched corroborate our citation granularity and ambiguity discipline; nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Literature Library
good: One folder per paper holding the PDF, OCR text, translation, notes and metadata as ordinary files — the library is the filesystem, not a database. Metadata lookup goes to Crossref/arXiv, and a per-feature network table in the README states exactly what is sent where: the identifier or query to Crossref/arXiv, the file itself to a user-configured OCR service, text chunks to a user-configured translation service; credentials are held in Obsidian Secret Storage rather than in the vault.
bad: Automatic metadata recognition after import is on by default (the README names the off-switch), and importing moves files into the paper folder — automatic reorganization as a default. The shipped source is JavaScript recovered from the installed build because the original TypeScript project was unavailable, a provenance caveat the README discloses honestly; 3 commits and no releases is early-stage.
didnt: Corroboration (weak): one ordinary-files folder per paper plus a per-feature table stating exactly what data goes to which remote service is the data-flow disclosure discipline we require of ourselves, independently implemented; the default-on automatic recognition and file-moving are recorded as the automatic-writing pole we refuse by default. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Literature Database
good: A Zotero-style literature manager whose library stays in Markdown alongside the original PDFs, and deleted papers are recoverable from Trash rather than destroyed. Its AI organization flow is reviewable before it lands: every suggestion is editable before applying, the batch plan is confirmed first, and an existing taxonomy is reused and merged rather than replaced wholesale.
bad: AI organization via DeepSeek is included and enabled by default, and starting a task sends selected PDF text plus the taxonomy to DeepSeek — a corpus-adjacent payload leaving the machine on a default-on path, mitigated by the confirm-first batch plan but recorded against it. AGPL-3.0-only confines any use to ideas.
didnt: Corroboration: Markdown-plus-PDF custody with Trash recovery, and an AI organizer whose suggestions are editable and whose batch plan is confirmed before anything is applied, corroborate our review-first discipline; the default-on DeepSeek text upload is recorded as the contrast. AGPL-3.0, so ideas only in any case; nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Paperless Sync
good: The cleanest one-way sync contract in this wave: the Paperless-ngx source is strictly read-only (GET requests only; nothing in Paperless-ngx is ever changed and no note is ever deleted); only paperless_* properties are managed, so user text and user-added properties are never overwritten; notes are matched by paperless_id, not path, so renames are safe; a deleted document flags its note paperless_missing: true instead of deleting it; document text stays out of the vault by default (opt-in per tag or all); a skip-tag beats an include-tag; if the API user may not read tags the sync stops instead of guessing; the token lives in Obsidian secret storage, never in the vault; and a sync that finds nothing new writes nothing.
bad: The guarantees rest on the README's own account of the sync engine rather than on an independently audited test suite visible on the page, and the value is only realised against a running Paperless-ngx instance, which we do not operate.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): a read-only source, a managed-property scope that never touches user text, identity-keyed matching, a missing-flag instead of deletion, stop-rather-than-guess on missing permissions, and a no-op sync writing nothing together corroborate our ingest discipline almost clause for clause. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Super Useful SQL
good: Read-only SQL over SQLite databases outside the vault, enforced mechanically rather than by parsing the SQL: a readOnly connection open, PRAGMA query_only = 1, an SQLite authorizer allow-list, single-statement prepare, a VACUUM/ATTACH text guard and a function deny-list — and if node:sqlite is unavailable the plugin refuses to run at all rather than silently degrading to an unchecked path. No subprocess or shell is spawned; only user-registered absolute paths are opened; and the AI-assistant instruction block is written into a note only on an explicit button press, inside markers so re-running replaces rather than duplicates.
bad: The README admits there is no query timeout, so a pathological query blocks the UI; 4 commits is very early, and the enforcement layers are the author's own account of them.
didnt: Corroboration: defence-in-depth read-only enforcement with refusal-instead-of-degradation, an explicit-path allow-list, and a marker-bounded, button-gated write of assistant instructions corroborate both our read-door design and the managed-region write rule. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tag Graph
good: A Bases graph view where tags, folders and properties are hubs, and the graph is a working surface: drag a note onto a tag to tag it, drag a tag onto another to merge it across notes. The safety shape is the study point: every edit shows a notice with Undo, and undo proceeds only if the files are still exactly as the edit left them — an integrity check before reversing, not a blind restore; confirmations are on by default before multi-note changes and before file moves; folder-moving by drag is off by default; look-alike tags (#jounral vs #journal) are detected with Merge buttons; and renames touch only the exact tag, never its subtags (#todo/sub is not #todo).
bad: Bulk tag surgery across many notes is powerful enough that the defaults carry the safety, and the undo integrity check means an undo can legitimately refuse after any intervening edit — correct behaviour, but a user expecting unconditional undo will be surprised; the graph view itself is presentation, not knowledge structure.
didnt: Corroboration: an undo that verifies the files are unchanged since the edit before reversing, confirmations on by default for bulk changes, and exact-scope renames corroborate our verify-before-write and no-silent-bulk-change rules. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Base Diagram
good: A read-only relationship diagram over one folder whose README states the custody rule outright: 'Your notes stay the single source of truth. Base Diagram never stores your content anywhere else — it only reads what's already in your frontmatter.' Link-type properties become typed arrows; layout is manual by design, because an automatic reshuffle would destroy a human-meaningful arrangement, and positions are saved per folder. Known limitations (one folder at a time, straight crossing lines, no cardinality notation) are stated on the page rather than discovered by users.
bad: One folder at a time and no cardinality notation bound its use for large relationship maps, and a per-folder saved layout is presentation state that must not be mistaken for structure in the notes themselves.
didnt: Corroboration: a derived view that reads the notes as the single source of truth, stores no content of its own, and refuses automatic rearrangement of a human-meaningful layout corroborates our derived-view discipline. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Canvas Kanban Sync
good: Dragging a card between Canvas groups writes the group name to the note's Status property and records StartedAt/ModifiedAt/CompletedAt automatically; an elapsed-days badge surfaces stalled tasks; and the frontmatter is explicitly designed as data for AI agents to read — the author runs Claude scheduled tasks over it for daily summaries, a worked example of notes-as-agent-readable state. Archive removes only the card's Canvas placement, leaving the note and its Status untouched, and automatic archive is off by default; the bundled tutorial canvas is fully self-contained ('delete the folder — no trace left'), and even the demo GIF's shortened timing is disclosed in its caption.
bad: The property display relies on Obsidian's internal DOM, which the README discloses can break on an Obsidian update; board state lives partly in the Canvas file, so the board and the notes can drift if either is edited outside the plugin.
didnt: Corroboration: status and lifecycle timestamps written into ordinary frontmatter that agents can read, archive that removes placement rather than data, and honest disclosure of a fragile DOM dependency corroborate our notes-as-data and disclosure disciplines. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kanbase
good: Kanban as a Bases view whose README states the custody rule plainly: 'Markdown-Native Data: card moves and edits update ordinary Markdown files and frontmatter; Kanbase does not maintain a separate task database.' Manual card order is stored as an explicit kanban_order frontmatter property rather than hidden view state; WIP limits and board-specific default properties for new cards are supported; and the page credits its derivation from Base Board with attribution to the original author — provenance stated, not laundered.
bad: Board semantics ride entirely on frontmatter conventions, so a property rename outside the plugin silently re-buckets cards; and as a Bases view it inherits Bases' own limits rather than defining a task model of its own.
didnt: Corroboration: a board that is a derived view over ordinary Markdown with order made explicit in frontmatter and no shadow database is the third independent instance of the pattern in this catalogue (after Property Kanban and Base Diagram), and its stated derivation corroborates our attribution discipline. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PDF Report Exporter
good: Polished templated PDF reports (cover, header/footer, clickable TOC, styled tables and callouts, vector Mermaid) produced entirely offline with bundled fonts, no network requests — and the load-bearing machinery is its Confidential passages system: passages marked by audience or TLP level are removed before rendering — 'never hidden under a black box: the text is not in the file at all, nor in its table of contents, links or metadata'; a multi-level passage leaves only in a version that keeps all its levels; scopes cover whole notes, sections, callouts and phrases; an optional export log records counts of what was removed, never the removed text; and the system fails closed — an unknown level or a malformed marked phrase stops the export with a message rather than letting the passage through, restricted passages are visibly labelled in the full version for reviewers, and an unrecognised TLP value raises a warning instead of applying silently.
bad: The guarantee is only as strong as the marking: an unmarked confidential passage exports in full, and the README's own model puts correct audience/TLP labelling on the author; a missing image is flagged rather than failing the export, which is the right call for reports but means output completeness is a human check.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): removal-before-render (never visual hiding), fail-closed on unknown levels or malformed markers, and an audit log that records removal counts and never removed content is our public/private separation discipline in export form, independently implemented. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bookmarks Sync
good: Imports Safari, Chrome-family and Firefox bookmarks as individual Markdown notes from user templates, 100% offline with no telemetry. The safety shape is the study point: automatic sync stays disabled until one manual sync has completed successfully, 'to prevent accidental imports'; the default mode syncs only new bookmarks and existing notes are never modified; URL-based indexing dedups, so one note exists per URL even if it is filed in several folders; notes are tracked by URL mapping in data.json, so renames and moves keep the association and a note deleted in the vault is recreated rather than resurrected wrongly; browser-side deletions remove only notes the plugin created and tracks; the Firefox places.sqlite database is read from a temporary copy taken together with its -wal file; and a user-picked Safari plist is held in memory for the session only, never persisted.
bad: The URL-to-note association lives in the plugin's data.json, so losing that file breaks rename tracking (deleted notes then return as duplicates of new ones); and browser bookmark stores are read at file level, which depends on each browser's on-disk layout staying stable.
didnt: Corroboration: manual-first gating before any automation, a new-only default that never modifies existing notes, copy-then-read of a live database, and deletion confined to records the tool itself created and tracks corroborate our ingest discipline clause for clause. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dependent Properties
good: A linked source note is declared canonical and configured properties are copied from it into dependent notes — forward when the link is set or changed, and in reverse when the source changes, via backlinks, debounced so edits do not thrash. Fresh installs start with no rules; the bulk 'Sync all matching files' command asks for confirmation before scanning; automatic sync reacts to metadata changes only and never scans the vault on startup or in the background; there is no network access. The README's permissions section states these limits as guarantees rather than leaving them to be inferred.
bad: Inheritance is by materialized copies: the duplicated values are real frontmatter in each dependent note and can be edited independently, so the notes can drift from the canonical source until the next sync event reconciles them — the copy model trades the derived-view purity of Property Kanban or Kanbase for local queryability, and the README does not describe a drift report.
didnt: Corroboration: a declared single source of truth with explicitly-scoped, confirmation-gated propagation corroborates our truth/derived discipline, and the materialized-copy drift risk is recorded as the cost of the alternative design. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Auto Move File
good: Rule-based moving and copying of notes by frontmatter property or filename, with a more careful rule vocabulary than most automation plugins: per-rule exact or fuzzy matching (fuzzy is contains-matching and regex-compatible, with invalid regexes falling back to contains 'so it never errors out'), trigger values plus blocking values that veto a move, rule-order or property-value-order priority, watch-folder and scan-scope limits, a configurable delay, folder-archive and copy modes, and a real-time monitoring toggle whose off state means manual triggering only — the FAQ's own answer to 'how do I only trigger manually'.
bad: With monitoring on, files move automatically the moment a property changes — relocation as a side effect of an edit, with no review queue, undo or move log described in the README; fuzzy filename matching widens the blast radius of a loosely written rule, and the never-errors-out regex fallback can silently change what a rule matches.
didnt: Corroboration: the explicit rule vocabulary (trigger plus blocking values, exact-before-fuzzy modes, declared priority) is inspectable and credited; the real-time auto-move default is recorded as the automatic-writing pole our review-first discipline refuses. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Excel Template Export
good: Fills the user's own formatted Excel templates (colours, column widths, merged cells, logos and formulas preserved) with properties from notes and their linked relations, and the export is previewed inside Obsidian, file by file and sheet by sheet, before anything is written — the .xlsx files are written only on confirming Export, preview-before-export defaults to true, and overwrite defaults to 'ask'. Its filter language is specified like a contract: missing fields make comparisons false rather than matching vacuously, dates are interpreted in local time with no timezone shift, and after export a notice reports generated files and warnings with a detail view of unresolved data and broken links — a missing datum never cancels the export, it is surfaced for review, and a Revisar (review) step lists cells that find no data. Fully offline: no network requests, reads and writes only inside the vault.
bad: The interface is currently in Spanish only, which the README states upfront but which bounds its audience today; template definitions live in the plugin's data.json rather than in notes, so the mapping is not itself vault data; 9 commits and no stars is very early.
didnt: Corroboration: preview-before-write with an ask-default overwrite rule, a filter semantics in which missing data fails closed instead of matching, and a post-export review list of unresolved cells corroborate our review-first export discipline. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Hugo Exporter
good: Exports notes to Hugo page bundles behind a genuine publish-review gate: an AI review (configurable OpenAI-compatible endpoint) reads the final exported Markdown — not the source note — for sensitive topics, PII and location data, and presents findings in an editable review table where only suggestions explicitly marked Replace are applied; ignored or untouched findings preserve the original text and the source note is never changed. Referenced images have their privacy metadata stripped locally before SHA-256-based naming and copying, and that cleaning runs even when AI review is disabled; if cleaning fails, the original image is kept only after a prominent warning and explicit confirmation. Writes are failure-safe: index.md is published only after all assets are ready, an incomplete export is removed after a filesystem error, existing export directories are never overwritten (a numbered directory is created instead), and output paths are validated — an absolute Hugo path is required and the relative content path is confined to the project, with .. escapes rejected. API keys are referenced through Obsidian SecretStorage, never stored in data.json, and release assets are built by GitHub Actions with artifact attestations.
bad: With AI review enabled (the default), the complete final Markdown of the note leaves the machine to the configured endpoint — the README states this plainly in its privacy section and the provider's own retention and billing policies apply, but it is a real disclosure on a default-on path; the review is only as good as the configured model, and a clean review is not a guarantee, which the table-presentation mitigates but cannot remove.
didnt: Board: the publish-review gate is a reference design for our own public/private boundary — review the final exported copy only, apply only explicitly-marked fixes, never modify the source, strip image metadata locally with a loud fail (warning plus confirmation, never silent pass-through), and write failure-safely without overwriting prior exports. Nothing adopted yet; boarded as the reference for any future publish-side review step. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Player Facing Notes
good: Audience-filtered publication done at the right layer: blocks flagged with ::pf … ::/pf markers (or a whole-note pfn property) sync into clean copies in a mirror folder with publish: true, while master notes keep publish: false — 'Because filtering happens before upload, players cannot recover DM text from page source — unlike CSS/publish.js hiding, which only hides content client-side.' Copies are tracked by a pfn-source property rather than by path, so they can be rearranged freely; frontmatter the user adds to a copy survives syncs because only publish and pfn-source are managed; notes inside the player folder without pfn-source are never touched or pruned; stale copies are pruned automatically; and wikilinks to DM-only notes are flattened to plain text 'so the link target's existence doesn't leak' — non-disclosure of even the existence of the private material.
bad: The audience boundary rests on authors flagging correctly — an unclosed ::pf marker flags everything to the end of the note, which fails open toward publishing rather than closed; auto-sync on save is available, so a mis-flagged block can reach the publish folder without a review step.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): pre-upload filtered copies instead of client-side hiding, existence-non-leaking link flattening, and a two-property managed scope on generated copies corroborate our public/private separation and managed-region disciplines — the second independent instance in this batch alongside PDF Report Exporter's removal-before-render. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Private Quartz Publish
good: Opt-in publishing engineered around non-disclosure: the plugin makes zero network calls and only edits frontmatter (publish: true plus a cryptographically random 10-character base62 slug, ~60 bits); a server-side stager copies only flagged notes into a separate content directory, Quartz never sees the raw vault, and the vault is bind-mounted into the stager read-only. Wikilinks to unpublished notes are stripped to plain text before staging so an unpublished name never reaches the public HTML; images and PDFs are renamed to SHA-256 content hashes so they cannot be enumerated by filename; there is no sitemap, RSS, index or search, so the public surface cannot be enumerated; an ExplicitPublish filter drops any stray file at render time as a second line of defence; rotating a URL makes the old one 404; folder bundles write folder_slug into each child note's frontmatter so publish state survives sync mechanisms that exclude plugin data files; and unpublishing retains the slug so a re-publish restores the same URL.
bad: Capability URLs are bearer secrets in practice: anyone holding a link holds the note, rotation is the only remedy, and the ~60-bit slug space is a deliberate trade of strength for short URLs; the system also depends on the user's own vault sync faithfully replicating frontmatter to the server, so a sync that drops the publish flag fails silent toward not publishing.
didnt: Board: the capability-URL sharing pattern — opt-in staging of only flagged files, unguessable non-enumerable URLs, unpublished names stripped before staging, hash-renamed embeds, and rotation that 404s the old URL — is the reference design for sharing individual wiki pages without exposing the corpus or its structure. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Promptuary
good: A reading-to-revision pipeline whose custody rules are the study point: highlights and review comments live in sidecar JSON under .promptuary/ so the original Markdown is never modified; comments are exported as a Markdown instruction file any external AI can execute (or copied as a prompt, or run through a local agent CLI, or a BYOK API call); and after the AI edits, the plugin presents a diff preview with Accept All, Accept by Chunk, or Rollback before anything is final. Accepted edits trigger automatic re-anchoring of the remaining annotations (an LCS diff mapping with a fuzzy-locate fallback), executed comments are removed, and a baselineHash detects document drift; API keys are stored locally only.
bad: The one-click CLI and direct-API paths hand the note and its comments to an external agent or model — the corpus leaves to whichever tool the user configured (the API path shows a privacy confirmation first, and keys stay local, but the execution itself is delegated wholesale); the diff gate is desktop-only, so mobile exports have no equivalent review step.
didnt: Corroboration: annotations held in sidecars so sources stay untouched, revisions handed to an agent as an explicit instruction file, and the agent's edits landing only through a diff preview with per-chunk acceptance or rollback is our approval-gated write pattern in editor form. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Revision Session Marks
good: Saves a writing baseline and turns later edits into a separate CriticMarkup review note — and before writing anything it verifies the marked text both ways: accepting the marks must reproduce the current text and rejecting them must reproduce the baseline, with both passed checks shown in the dialog. Unsupported input (existing CriticMarkup, links, code, frontmatter, headings, lists, tables) is rejected with the offending structure identified and the baseline kept — fail-closed, no partial output; size and diff limits (100 KB, one second, 1,000 token edits) mean a stopped comparison creates no review; folder reviews check every input before the first output and move partial outputs to trash if a later write fails. The payment/network section is exemplary: no network requests at all until the user signs in, a GitHub device flow with read:user scope only, no note content ever sent, the token held in secret storage.
bad: The plain-prose-only scope excludes exactly the structured notes (frontmatter, links, headings, lists) that dominate a real vault, so the verified-review guarantee covers a narrow slice of writing; after an update the plugin opens a What's new tab that suggests the publisher's other plugins — disclosed, data-free and turn-off-able, but promotional surface inside a review tool; Pro features ride on a GitHub Sponsors check.
didnt: Corroboration: a change representation that is verified in both directions before it is written, fail-closed rejection of unsupported input with the baseline preserved, and batch outputs pre-checked with partial results trashed on failure corroborate our verify-before-writing discipline almost clause for clause. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sync Witness
good: A watchman for the failure mode sync tools never report: it keeps a local record (path, size, SHA-256, modification time) of every vault file plus byte copies stored in Obsidian's app storage outside the vault, so the sync tool under suspicion cannot delete the evidence. When files vanish, are emptied, roll back to an earlier version, or suffer a large unexplained cut outside Obsidian, related changes are batched into one incident with one alert; restore writes the exact bytes back and re-checks the hash afterwards, and if the path has been retaken the copy returns beside it as 'name (restored).ext' rather than overwriting the newer file. The user's own edits, deletions, renames and typing stay quiet, and the limits are quantified with unusual precision: rollback recognition windows, cut thresholds (a removal exceeding additions by a quarter of the note or ten lines), and the different treatment of in-Obsidian sync plugins.
bad: Desktop only, tested on one Obsidian version on Linux; copies are bounded (10 MB per note, 1 GB of attachments), so the largest files are watched but not restorable; and it can only protect states it has itself recorded — loss before the first record, or a same-size line-swap that matches no earlier version and stays under the cut thresholds, passes silently, as its own limits section concedes.
didnt: Board: a silent-loss witness — hash records plus out-of-vault copies, one alert per incident, restore verified by re-hashing, non-destructive restore-as-sibling on path collision — is the reference design for detecting the sync removals and rollbacks our own multi-device and agent workflows risk. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Unread Changes
good: Unread-message awareness for shared vaults: notes changed by another device, a collaborator or an automation get an unread dot (with folder counts), an inbox entry with attribution and a plain-English summary when available, and a banner linking to the note's changelog and diff; per-write changelog notes carry attribution and exact diffs. Read state syncs across devices without modifying note content — the README stresses notes are never modified to display the banner — and your own edits never alert on the device that made them; read-marking can be manual, instant, or after a configurable dwell.
bad: Attribution is only as trustworthy as the device-name setting each device declares for itself, and the awareness layer depends on an external sync service actually delivering the read-state and changelog files between devices; sectioned inbox views and urgency colours are still in development, as the README states.
didnt: Corroboration: change-awareness with attribution and exact diffs for a vault edited by several hands and automations, delivered without ever modifying the notes being reported on, corroborates the visibility our multi-agent filings workflow needs. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nanalStamp
good: Tamper-evident note sealing with a privacy model worth the study: the SHA-256 of a settled note is computed on-device and only that hash, a hash of the file path, a timestamp and the API key ever leave for sealing — content and readable filenames never do. The server chains entries (each binding user, sequence, previous hash, content hash, path hash and receipt time, Ed25519-signed) and anchors the chain head into Bitcoin via OpenTimestamps, so proof of existence and of an unbroken day-by-day edit history is verifiable independently of the service, with standard tools. A full host table states every endpoint, when it is contacted and exactly what is sent; a 'What this proof is (and isn't)' section states plainly that it is not a government-accredited timestamp; content upload happens only for explicitly enabled storage features.
bad: The continuity proof is only as durable as the service's chain: independent verification covers the Bitcoin anchor, but day-to-day entry integrity leans on the server's signed chain, and the optional paid original-file storage is encrypted with keys the service manages so it can restore files — a custody caveat the README's own table states. GPL-3.0 confines any use to ideas.
didnt: Board (GPL-3.0, ideas only): hash-only sealing with path commitment and an independently verifiable Bitcoin anchor is the reference for earning the timestamp anchors our checkpoints have not yet earned, and its published host table plus is/isn't proof statement is the disclosure standard such a feature should meet. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Git Changelog
good: Turns the vault's git history into sidebar changelogs (vault-wide and per-file, with renames/moves detected separately and line counts per file) and, more importantly, into a review checkpoint discipline: 'Show vault changes since the last checkpoint' compares the present against the last checkpoint, where a checkpoint is created by running the command and approving the shown changes — the baseline moves only when a human has reviewed what changed. Its Data Loss Monitoring section names the causes plainly (sync conflicts, faulty plugins, faulty scripts, and 'AI Tools: they have a tendency to overwrite or delete random content') and recommends pairing the checkpoint reviews with frequent auto-commits and periodic git fsck integrity checks.
bad: Detection is interval-relative: text added and lost inside the same interval nets to zero in the counts, so loss shows only as missing expected additions — a subtle signal the README has to teach; coverage depends on a frequent auto-commit interval the user must configure in a separate plugin, and uncommitted work is invisible to it; rename detection is content-similarity heuristics with false positives and misses, tunable but not exact.
didnt: Corroboration: a checkpoint defined by changes the user has reviewed and approved, over the same git history our wiki already keeps, corroborates the verified-baseline pattern from the review side — surveillance between approved baselines rather than after-the-fact diffing. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cloudflare Vault Backup
good: One-way backup to the user's own Cloudflare R2 bucket with storage engineering worth studying: file contents live in content-addressed blobs named by SHA-256 and each snapshot is a JSON manifest mapping paths to hash, size and modification time, so unchanged files are stored once and a one-note backup uploads one blob and one manifest; vault paths never appear in object keys. A conditional-write run lock with refresh and expiry stops one device's cleanup deleting a blob another device is about to reference, and pruning deletes only blobs no kept manifest references and only after a 24-hour grace period protecting in-flight uploads. Restore verifies every download against its hash before writing, offers restore-as-copy or restore-into-a-folder, requires typing 'restore' plus a fresh backup before an in-place overwrite, and never deletes files; configuration-folder restores get an extra confirmation and executable-hook paths are never restored. Credentials and the encryption passphrase live in Obsidian secret storage — data.json holds only the names of the secrets — and an older version that cannot read a snapshot 'fails with an error and changes nothing'.
bad: The destination is the user's own Cloudflare account, so the corpus still leaves the device to a third-party cloud — to infrastructure the user owns and keys they hold, but not local custody; with encryption off the bucket holds plaintext notes and full path manifests, and even with encryption on, object sizes, snapshot times, blob counts and the never-encrypted vault.json metadata remain visible to anyone who can list the bucket, as the README itself enumerates; R2 may require a payment method beyond the free tier.
didnt: Board: content-addressed blobs plus per-snapshot manifests, hash-verified restores that never delete, grace-period pruning, and an explicit statement of what stays visible even encrypted form a reference design for backup integrity well beyond a nightly zip. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Encrypted self-hosted sync family (grouped: LiteSync, MDSync, oVaultd Sync, Selfsync)
good: Judged on LiteSync, the repo the grouped entry names: self-hosted end-to-end encrypted sync (PBKDF2 at 600k iterations plus AES-256-GCM; the server stores only ciphertext) with per-file revisions, SHA-256 and a global change sequence; diff3 three-way merge for Markdown with unresolvable overlaps keeping both versions; immutable server-side version history; deletions that go to trash on every platform and are never permanent ('if trashing fails the file is kept and flagged'); per-device revocable tokens, the root token exchanged away on first sync and never kept on devices; QR pairing packages encrypted on-device, single-use with a five-minute expiry, the key carried only in the link fragment; and an onboarding wizard that forces an explicit restore-or-merge choice while verifying the server's stable vault identity so a reinstalled server cannot silently clobber notes. Its threat table is the standout: rollback, replay, metadata-fork and downgrade attacks each marked detected, via device-signed checkpoints under which a fork stops sync instead of picking a side and a trust anchor that only moves forward — and the one undetectable attack (withholding a never-seen file) admitted as structural, in writing.
bad: The admitted structural gap is real: a server can withhold a file a device has never seen, and no local anchor can prove the set complete; path/filename encryption is still release-candidate with an irreversible erasure step the README warns against on a sole real vault; and the whole design requires running and maintaining one's own server, with multi-user isolation enforced by the server operator's honesty about usernames and usage, which the admin can see.
didnt: Board: for the owner-gated encrypted device-sync gap, LiteSync's construction — publish expectations before trusting, device-signed forward-only checkpoints, fork-stops-sync, per-device revocable credentials, trash-only deletion, and a threat table that admits its structural gap — is the strongest reference design in this catalogue. Judged on LiteSync as the named repo of the grouped entry; nothing built, the gap itself being owner-gated. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Central Vault Sync
good: Revision-safe sync against a self-hosted authoritative server whose safety properties read like a protocol contract: every accepted mutation receives a stable entry identity, a revision, a content hash and an ordered journal sequence; a stale server revision is never silently overwritten; durable local operations are published before newer remote bytes are pulled, and queue markers, blob-reference operations, cursor and apply intents are persisted before work is acknowledged — write-ahead, not best-effort.
