Three-way merge is used only for independent UTF-8 text edits; overlaps and binary divergence become conflict copies; every upload and download is verified by SHA-256 and byte length; echo suppression matches expected path and hash rather than a timer; and a remote replacement, rename or deletion is deferred while the affected path has durable local work or an unsaved open editor. Canonical server bytes stay unchanged until an explicit resolution in a base/server/client comparison; credentials live in SecretStorage and pairing uses a ten-minute one-use code.
bad: The authoritative-server model concentrates trust and availability in the WebObsidian server — a design trade the README states by construction rather than discussing; it is a community-review release not yet in the Community Plugins directory; and mobile sync while the OS has the app suspended is explicitly not promised, catch-up happening on load, focus or manual sync.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): write-ahead apply intents, publish-before-pull, deferral of remote writes over paths with local work, hash-verified transfers and conflicts resolved explicitly against canonical bytes corroborate the verified-baseline sync protocol Stateful Git Sync boarded in B166, here from the authoritative-server side. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CopyGuard
good: Conflict-copy cleanup built as a two-step, review-first process: it finds sync-conflict copies across Dropbox, Obsidian Sync, Proton Drive, Syncthing and Nextcloud naming patterns in eight languages (plus empty files and temp leftovers), lists them even when the original is missing, badges copies whose bytes are identical to the original, and offers a Compare view — but it never merges and never deletes on scan. The user reviews and moves only approved files into a dedicated trash-box folder; deletion is a separate second step, and the startup prompt's default is to keep. Restore returns an indexed file to its original path and fails rather than overwriting if something occupies that path; .icloud placeholders and currently open files are skipped.
bad: Detection is name-pattern based across sync tools and languages, so an unusually named conflict copy can be missed and a legitimately named file can be flagged — the disclaimer concedes detection can be wrong; and because moves and deletions themselves sync, a mistaken quarantine propagates to other devices, which the disclaimer also states.
didnt: Corroboration: find, review, quarantine, and only then delete as separate confirmed steps — with a restore that refuses to overwrite and a default of keeping — is our two-step deletion discipline in plugin form. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Safe Attachment Trash
good: Unused-attachment cleanup with the safety model stated as the headline: 'A scan never moves or deletes anything. It only creates a review list.' The reference check is thorough — Markdown links and embeds, resolved internal links, frontmatter properties in single and list form, Canvas files, and attachment paths stored in .base files — and selected files are re-scanned immediately before moving, so a file that became referenced after the original scan is skipped. Intentional standalone files can be protected ('Never suggest') and stay in place, excluded from future scans; a minimum file age keeps just-added files out of the list; original paths are stored so trashed files restore to their remembered folders; permanent deletion always requires confirmation; and the tool is fully local with no account, telemetry or network requests.
bad: 'Unused' is bounded by the reference classes the scanner knows — a reference form it does not parse (a plugin-specific path, a raw HTML embed) can mark a live file as unused, which is why the review list and the re-check carry the safety; restore-conflict handling includes an overwrite option that a careless click could choose.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): a read-only scan producing a review list, protected files excluded by declaration, a re-check at the moment of action, restore from remembered paths, and confirmation-gated permanent deletion is precisely the list-first, nothing-without-approval cleanup discipline the owner requires of us. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dataview Serializer
good: Materializes Dataview queries into plain Markdown written into the notes themselves, which buys three concrete things a live query cannot: the generated links are real links that appear on the graph, the content renders on Obsidian Publish (where Dataview does not run), and the results are ordinary text — greppable, diffable and version-controllable. It is the most mature project in this batch (294 commits, 168 stars, 69 releases), and the catalogue description records that it keeps the rendered representation up to date rather than serializing once and abandoning it.
bad: A materialized result is a snapshot: between serializations the written Markdown can drift from what the live query would return today, so freshness depends on re-running the serializer, and the plugin is useless without the Dataview plugin installed; the README itself carries almost no mechanics, deferring to external documentation, so the behavioural detail rests on the catalogue description and the documented model rather than on this page.
didnt: Corroboration: static materialization of live queries into ordinary Markdown — real links, publishable output, no runtime dependency at read time — corroborates our derived-representation discipline (the Lens is a built static site over the wiki on the same principle), with the snapshot-staleness cost recorded. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pressroom
good: Per-note publishing to Quartz 5 sites in GitHub repositories with the separation rules made explicit: your notes are never modified — no frontmatter or markers are added, the published copy is generated separately; the published copy keeps only an allow-list of frontmatter properties (title, tags, date, description by default), and 'everything else, such as private notes to yourself, is removed'; excluded folders are never published and never pulled in by links; links to unpublished notes become plain text by default, and an 'Isolate this site' option flattens cross-site links to plain text 'so visitors cannot tell the sites belong to the same person'. The GitHub token is a fine-grained Contents read/write token held in Obsidian secret storage; Test connection checks everything 'without writing anything'; the management panel shows per-site status (Synced / Modified / Moved / Source deleted); bulk actions show the affected list first, ask for confirmation, and then make a single commit; and when a note is unpublished, links to it are turned back into plain text so no dead links are left behind.
bad: The per-site manifest stored in each site repository records where every published note lives in the vault, so a public site repository leaks the vault's folder structure — the README recommends keeping site repositories private for exactly this reason; and the GitHub token it holds is Contents read-and-write on the site repositories, a real write credential whose compromise would expose every connected site.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): an allow-list that strips everything not named, a source the publisher never modifies, links flattened when their targets are not public, cross-site identity isolation, and bulk actions that preview and confirm before a single commit corroborate our public/private separation and review-first disciplines. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MemVector Knowledge Engine
good: A local-first knowledge engine built on human-declared structure rather than inferred links: the user declares typed, weighted relations between notes (17 canonical types — IMPLIES, REQUIRES, CONFLICTS_WITH, REFUTES, GENERALIZES and kin), and every relation is stored as a plain Markdown note in the vault carrying its type, an optional reason in plain text, and wikilinks to both notes — 'readable, editable, searchable, version-controlled', not a black box. The vocabulary itself is data (a JSON file in the vault; weights and repulsion are per-type settings, presets ship for STEM, Law, Medicine and Philosophy, and edge labels are plain strings so vocabulary changes never break existing edges). Declared relations win over semantic similarity — 'similarity fills the gaps' — and its hybrid GraphRAG synthesis enriches a query with two independent lookups, vector-similar notes and graph-hop neighbours, on the stated ground that neither alone covers both. Embeddings and graph live in one local SQLite file; Ollama works with no API key; provider keys sit in Obsidian Secret Storage; optional writes through the Jovian write gate (per-note lock, stale check, journal of every write) are off by default; and its CLI search is reads-only.
bad: Pre-1.0 and self-described as early-stage with rough edges; the graph also lives in a SQLite database inside the vault, so the Markdown relation notes and the database are two representations that must stay in step; and a hand-declared graph scales with the author's discipline — on a large vault the declared structure will cover a fraction of the notes, leaving the canvas mostly similarity-driven despite the precedence rule.
didnt: Corroboration: typed relations stored as ordinary reason-carrying Markdown notes, with human-declared structure outranking embedding similarity and the AI confined to on-request synthesis, corroborate our typed-edge direction (boarded in B165 via Typed Graph) and the claims-with-reasons model; the catalogue's existing verdict for this entry is not repeated, there being no lane-8 record for it. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Proxima
good: Local-first semantic retrieval with two design decisions worth the study: chunking is meaning-aware — notes split on Markdown structure and sentence/paragraph boundaries rather than fixed overlapping windows, and every chunk carries its note title and section heading so the embedding knows where the text lives, not just what it says; and retrieval is a two-stage funnel, dense vector recall refined by an on-device cross-encoder reranker for precision. Explicit wikilinks and backlinks are displayed alongside semantic matches as badges and an orbit ring, so declared structure and inferred similarity stay visibly distinct rather than blended. Everything runs on-device (WebGPU/WASM); the only network access is a one-time model download from Hugging Face; notes are never transmitted or modified.
bad: Similarity has no notion of time or supersession: a stale note and its replacement rank purely on meaning, so the tool cannot prefer the current truth — the exact weakness our truth-aware retrieval work targets; the index lives in the plugin folder rather than in inspectable vault files; and desktop-only WebGPU/WASM inference bounds where it can run.
didnt: Corroboration: structure-aware chunking carrying its own location context, a recall-then-rerank funnel, and declared links kept visibly distinct from inferred similarity corroborate our retrieval design, with the no-supersession limit recorded as the contrast against our truth-aware gap. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agentic Vault
good: Git-backed sync for an AI-configuration folder (system prompts, rules, skills) defended in three layers the README names plainly: a default-deny whitelist means the entire AI-Brain folder is blocked from syncing except known safe text formats; any additional folder must be explicitly approved in the Setup Wizard ('the system will never silently sync unapproved files'); and a content-based secret scanner reads the changed files before every commit and blocks the commit on AWS keys, Slack tokens, private keys or generic secret patterns. Merge conflicts are handled Dropbox-style — the remote version is kept and local edits are preserved side-by-side as .conflict-local copies, so no file is left containing conflict markers. A setup wizard symlinks OS-level agent config directories (Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and others) into the vault and backs up existing local configs first.
bad: The limitations section concedes the inbound path is unscanned — files pulled from the remote are not inspected, so a compromised remote delivers content without warning — and that pattern scanning is heuristic with false positives that block the whole sync; the auto-sync itself (background pull, commit, push) moves the vault without a review step, and the scanner can be disabled outright, leaving the whitelist as the only layer.
didnt: Corroboration: a default-deny allow-list plus a content scanner gating every commit corroborates our leak-lint discipline; the background auto-sync and the admitted unscanned inbound path are recorded as the contrast our pull-and-verify posture refuses. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI Session Atlas
good: A session-transcript catalogue built with more care than its category usually gets: it indexes Claude Code and Codex transcripts into one searchable catalog with live session cards and token/cost statistics, runs entirely locally (a small server on 127.0.0.1, optional AI features off by default), opens Codex's state database read-only, and states that existing Codex session files are never written. Its cross-agent resume copies a conversation word-for-word with tool calls reduced to short lines, never copies thinking, reasoning or encrypted content, discloses truncation in the new session's first message when the history exceeds its budget, and does not double-count copied messages in search or statistics; deleting a session requires a confirmation listing every file.
bad: The tool's entire premise is ingesting agent session transcripts, which for our wiki is a category the owner has not approved (recorded in-row, per the standing session-transcript position); it is also macOS-only, and its live-card features depend on reading terminal screens and process tables, a fragile integration surface.
didnt: Rejected: session-transcript ingest is unapproved by the owner, so the capability itself is not for us regardless of implementation quality; the tool's own safeguards — read-only source handling, never writing the other agent's files, verbatim-with-disclosed-truncation handoffs, and no double counting — are recorded as the standard such a tool would have to meet if the owner ever approves the category. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PKM Assistant
good: Agents that live in the vault under a transparency rule stated as the product's thesis: 'There is no magic here. Your agent is a prompt. Here is what it is made of.' A Prompt Inspector shows every section of the system prompt with token counts, all editable; skills are Markdown files; agent-to-agent mail is plain Markdown stored in the vault; persistent memory is inspectable notes (brain index, durable memory, session archive, cascading summaries). Autonomy is tiered (YOLO / Ask at the edge / Ask about everything) with per-tool approval notifications; a strict path sanitizer rejects traversal including encoded forms, null bytes and zero-width unicode; executable custom JavaScript tools were removed in v2.2 in favour of external MCP servers the user explicitly configures; and the README enumerates 'what the plugin does outside your vault' as a complete list — processes spawned only for user-added servers, one outside file read only on an explicit import click, clipboard only on explicit copy actions.
bad: API keys are stored in a settings file inside the vault itself, with the README's own warning to treat the vault folder as sensitive if it is synced or shared — weaker custody than secret storage; agents with note-writing tools plus a YOLO autonomy level concentrate a great deal of trust in the per-agent toggles; and the author states plainly that it is a solo early-days project with rough edges. GPL-3.0 confines any use to ideas.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): total prompt transparency, plain-file agent mail, tiered autonomy with per-tool approvals, and an enumerated complete list of outside-the-vault actions corroborate our transparency and approval disciplines; keys-in-vault-settings is recorded as the custody weakness. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Note Improver
good: The reviewed-edit pattern at its smallest scale: an LLM (Groq cloud or local Ollama) proposes a clearer version of the active note, every proposed change is displayed with a Before/After preview, and the user accepts all, accepts a selection, or rejects everything — the note is modified only after that choice. When changes are applied, the original is first saved as a timestamped backup in a backups/ folder at the vault root. The API key sits in Obsidian SecretStorage with data.json holding only the secret's identifier; the privacy section states per provider exactly what leaves the machine (the complete note to Groq; nothing remote under Ollama); and the README closes the loop honestly: 'LLM-generated output can contain errors, so review all proposed changes before accepting them.'
bad: One headline behaviour is that the model 'fills in essential missing information' — invented content entering a note, which is precisely what the review gate must catch and what a tired reviewer will eventually wave through; with the cloud provider the complete note leaves the machine for a formatting pass; and the backups folder grows without bound since backups are never deleted automatically.
didnt: Corroboration: per-change preview with selective acceptance and an automatic pre-apply backup is the reviewed-edit pattern at gadget scale (kin to Promptuary and Review Edit in this batch); the fill-in-missing-information behaviour is recorded as the risk that makes the gate necessary. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mdfit - Fit Any Markdown
good: Paste-time normalization of LLM output is genuinely careful in one respect: a protection layer guarantees code blocks, inline code and math are never touched, so examples inside the converted text stay byte-identical; tables and task lists are recovered from chat-app HTML, math delimiters are converted to renderable form, and CJK/Latin spacing and zero-width junk are cleaned.
bad: Stripping citations is a headline feature: pasted research loses its source pointers at the exact moment it enters the vault, irreversibly and silently — the opposite of provenance discipline; heading 'promotion' also rewrites the author's structure on paste, and the conversion happens automatically the moment text lands, with no preview of what was changed.
didnt: Rejected: a tool that deletes citation markers from incoming text destroys provenance by design and cannot be corroborated by a system whose core discipline is citation integrity; its byte-identical protection of code and math regions is credited in-row as the one sound rule. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Antinomia
good: Personal Tension Management: a vault layer for what does not add up, organized in six frontmatter types — tension (two positions in contradiction), substrate (raw material), principle (an operational IF/THEN rule carrying its origin_tension, grey zone and presuppositions), defeated (a belief proven false, kept as historical memory with its replaced_by), presupposition (an implicit assumption a principle rests on, mapped into a first-class note that can be challenged) and meta_note. The design invariant is that a note's layer lives exclusively in its frontmatter and files never move when the layer changes. Its AI Contradiction Hunter scans open tensions and substrates and proposes contradictory pairs with confidence ratings under an explicit constraint — 'it identifies, it does not resolve' — and the README's status banner states the epistemic limit in plain words: 'Antinomia is not a decision-support system. The pairs the Contradiction Hunter proposes are prompts for thinking, not truths on which to base real decisions... Use Antinomia as a reflective practice.' No autonomous network requests; AI features fire only on explicit invocation to the configured backend.
bad: API keys are stored in plain text in the plugin's data.json inside the vault, with the README's own warning that the file — and the keys — travel with any synced vault; and the Hunter's contradiction pairs are model judgements whose confidence ratings are uncalibrated, which the not-a-decision-support banner implicitly concedes.
didnt: Board: a first-class contradiction layer — tensions as typed notes, defeated beliefs preserved with their replacements, presuppositions surfaced as challengeable notes, and an AI hunter constrained to identify and never resolve — is the reference design for the contradiction half of truth-aware knowledge work, the side our supersession work does not cover. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Review Edit
good: Per-hunk review of changes against automatic snapshots, built explicitly for the AI-edit case: whenever editing pauses past a session threshold the pre-edit content is snapshotted, and this works for edits made by external tools and scripts while Obsidian runs — 'ideal for reviewing AI edits' — with a whole-vault baseline taken on first launch. Review renders a git-style inline diff in the editor with a pending-hunk counter and navigation; each hunk is kept or reverted individually; the editor is read-only during review and the mode exits automatically if the file changes externally; snapshots are stored locally in IndexedDB, never leave the machine, and are pruned after a configurable retention (30 days by default); core File Recovery snapshots are used as an additional source when available, and identical snapshots are hidden from the picker.
bad: Edits made while Obsidian is not running have no pre-edit snapshot, so the review falls back to the last stored state and cannot show exactly what the outside change did; snapshots live in the device's IndexedDB rather than in portable files, and reading the core File Recovery store depends on that plugin's internal database structure (the README isolates the dependency to one source file, but it remains a dependency on an internal).
didnt: Corroboration: automatic pre-edit baselines that capture external and agent edits, with per-hunk keep/revert review, is the reviewed-edit pattern purpose-built for AI changes — the diff-level counterpart to Promptuary's and Note Improver's whole-note gates in this batch. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Annoteca
good: Categorized inline feedback engineered as a human-agent protocol: comments live in the file as plain HTML markers with typed categories (Tone, Clarify, Cut, Expand, Tighten, Source needed and custom sets), anchored to exact passages with closing markers, threaded replies signed with author and date — 'readable by humans, by grep, and by any AI assistant: the file is the API'. The AI revision flow is the study point: when an assistant rewrites a passage it marks the comment addressed and keeps the original text verbatim inside the marker; the human then accepts (resolve), revises (reopen) or rejects — and reject restores the original prose automatically. Agent behaviour is governed per category: an agent may act on a comment, only reply, or skip it entirely ('Note to self' ships set to Skip, so a personal reminder is not treated as a request), and the choice is written into an exported, versioned AI skill file that teaches assistants the format and vocabulary, with a staleness warning when the plugin updates. If another tool rewrites a note and drops a comment, Annoteca offers to restore it; resolving keeps a dimmed record by default, with resolve-and-remove available.
bad: Comments embedded in the prose file travel everywhere the file travels — including into exports and shares unless stripped — and a long thread makes the raw file noisy to read outside Obsidian; the accept/revise/reject discipline also depends on the assistant honouring the exported skill's protocol, which is a convention, not an enforcement.
didnt: Board: the revision protocol — typed comments as plain in-file records any agent can work, AI responses that keep the original verbatim, human accept/revise/reject with reject restoring the original, and per-category rules for what an agent may touch — is a reference design for human-agent revision on shared documents. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Claude Vault Citations
good: Vault question-answering that takes citations out of the model's discretion: retrieval is BM25 with a title boost, candidate notes are chunked into paragraph blocks (code fences kept intact), and the top notes are sent to Claude as document blocks with the native Citations API enabled, so cited_text is guaranteed to come from the user's notes rather than being an attribution the model composed; each citation renders as a clickable pill that jumps to the source note at the cited paragraph. Only the top-ranked notes for a question leave the vault, and prompt caching keeps follow-up questions in a session cheaper.
bad: A citation guarantees the passage exists in a sent note, not that the claim follows from it — support is still the model's word; retrieval is BM25-only with the top notes always sent, and there is no abstention path when the vault does not contain an answer, the gap our scored abstention gate exists to close; the API key is stored in the vault's plugin data.json, and at 2 commits with a placeholder screenshot this is a sketch, not a hardened tool.
didnt: Corroboration: provider-native citations whose cited text is guaranteed drawn from the user's own notes, at paragraph granularity with jump-to-passage links, corroborate the citation-integrity direction; the missing abstention path and the existence-not-support limit are recorded against our standard. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI Term Research
good: Term research whose citation hygiene is the study point: links in a provider's report that do not appear in the verified source metadata are de-linked and written into a 'to verify and uncertainty' section; if a search returns no verifiable URL at all, the search fails rather than presenting unsourced content as a researched result; deep research runs a multi-round query plan, cross-checks sources, and collects conflicts and to-verify items explicitly; classification confidence below 60% files the result under 'Other' and prompts for human confirmation before saving. The save flow always shows the full target path, classification, filename and the wikilink replacement diff, together with warnings for incomplete citations, source conflicts and provider warnings; no path ever auto-overwrites — an existing target offers open existing, append (an atomic read-modify-write preserving the old content), save a copy under a fresh name, or cancel — and the original term is replaced by a wikilink only after a successful create and only if the selection is still unchanged. Only the selected term is sent by default (paragraph context is opt-in), keys live in SecretStorage and never enter prompts, logs or data.json, and the README states plainly that all facts and citations still require human verification.
bad: The README concedes that end-to-end verification against real providers, networks and quotas must be performed manually by the user — the automated tests cover isolated fixtures and a synthetic vault only; cancellation stops local orchestration and blocks writes but cannot guarantee an in-flight request stops or goes unbilled; and at 4 commits the verification machinery is young.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): unverified citations de-linked and quarantined, a search that fails rather than fabricating, confidence-gated filing with human confirmation, and saves that can never silently overwrite corroborate our citation-integrity and review-first disciplines in research form. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: eBrain Gardener
licence: Licence conflict at source: GitHub licence card reads AGPL-3.0; the README's closing licence section reads MIT
good: A PROCESS → TRIAGE → PUBLISH pipeline for a digital-garden inbox whose scoring is published rather than vibes: score = name_quality (×0.4) + frontmatter_completeness (×0.3) + maturity (×0.3), with maturity banded by word count (STUB/SEED/BUDDING/EVERGREEN) and notes at 0.7 or above surfaced as ready. The Process command has the LLM suggest frontmatter and wikilinks and presents them in a diff modal for acceptance before anything is written; the Publish command enriches the note and sets published: true behind an approval gate; outbound requests happen only on an explicit Process or Publish command and only to the configured provider, with a fully local Ollama option.
bad: The licence is in conflict at source — the GitHub licence card reads AGPL-3.0 while the README's closing section claims MIT — recorded here as a conflict, not resolved in either direction; maturity scoring is word count, a proxy that rates length rather than quality; the API key is stored in data.json with a warning to exclude it from sync; and wikilink validation against real vault files is still on the roadmap, so suggested links can point at notes that do not exist.
didnt: Corroboration: a published triage scoring formula, LLM enrichment accepted only through a diff modal, and an approval-gated publish step corroborate our ingest-triage discipline; the licence conflict is recorded as found and, AGPL-3.0 being one of the two claims, any use would be ideas-only in any case. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jemz Vault Assistant
good: Capture, triage and vault health under one fix discipline stated as a guarantee: 'Nothing is ever changed without your review.' Eight health checks (broken links, orphans, empty notes, unused attachments, duplicate titles, look-alike tag inconsistencies, missing required metadata, large files — with unparseable-frontmatter notes reported separately because their fix is different) feed a single fix path: select issues, a preview modal lists the exact files and edits, a timestamped backup is written, and only then are changes applied; a file that changed between preview and apply is skipped rather than overwritten; deletion moves files to trash and permanent deletion needs a second, separately worded confirmation; 'Restore last fix backup' undoes the most recent batch, and an action log records the last 100 things the plugin did. The inbox triage mode walks items one at a time by keyboard (delete asks first) and ends with a summary; tag-merge suggestions require both a small edit distance and a shared three-character opening, and merging is never automatic. Its privacy section enumerates exactly what it reads (every file's path and metadata, note contents lazily and only when a scan/search/preview needs them, attachment bytes never) and states there are no network requests ever.
bad: The health score compresses eight unlike problem classes into one 0–100 number whose weights are configurable opinion; undo covers only the most recent fix batch (the last ten backups are kept, but restore is framed around the last fix); and the whole-vault enumeration it honestly declares is the unavoidable cost of its health checks.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): preview the exact edits, back up, apply only to files unchanged since preview, delete in two stages, and keep an undo for the last batch is our review-first fix discipline end to end; the one-at-a-time triage mode likewise matches how our own queues are worked. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vault Triage
good: A review queue for vault decay rather than a flag dump: it scans for stale, thin, orphaned and metadata-broken notes and draft markers (TODO, FIXME, WIP and custom markers), shows why each note was flagged, and lets the user work through them one at a time or in batches, with ignore, exclude and mark-reviewed states so a finding once judged stops nagging. The free tier carries real scanning and one-at-a-time cleanup; thresholds, required properties and exclusions are configurable. Its Pro licence is verified offline with Ed25519 — a one-time payment, no account, no server, no always-online check — and the plugin is fully local with no telemetry.
bad: The free tier is deliberately bounded — bulk actions, saved audits, custom rules and report export sit behind the Pro payment, so the review-queue discipline scales only for paying users (the split is disclosed in a plain comparison table); and its detectors are threshold proxies (untouched-days, minimum length, marker strings) whose false positives the user must absorb through the ignore controls.
didnt: Corroboration: scan, show why each note was flagged, and work a one-at-a-time queue with ignore and mark-reviewed states corroborates the triage pattern our own lint and cleanup queues follow (kin to Jemz Vault Assistant's health flow in this batch). Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Knowledge Forge
good: A typed knowledge graph extracted from the vault under a provenance rule with teeth: subject-predicate-object triples are parsed from frontmatter, Breadcrumbs-style Connections fields and wikilinks; nodes are typed by folder-to-fileClass mapping; every triple carries provenance — source, confidence, timestamp and lineage — and the schema validator reports missing provenance and malformed source_ids as violations alongside missing fileClass and broken source links. GraphRAG prompts are built from a k-hop subgraph of typed triples serialized as bullet facts with a 'say so if facts don't support' guard, and competency questions are tracked and checked against whether the current schema can answer them. The edge vocabulary uses declared inverse and symmetric pairs (requires↔enables, up↔down, next↔prev, related_to symmetric); exports go to Neo4j Cypher MERGE statements or Dataview templates; everything is local-first with no network requests, and the permissions section enumerates the vault enumeration, read/write and clipboard capabilities it uses.
bad: At 6 commits this is a young implementation of an ambitious model; extraction reads conventions — frontmatter, Connections sections, wikilinks — rather than prose, so facts a note states only in running text are invisible to the graph; and its abstention guard is a prompt instruction to the model, not a scored, thresholded gate of the kind our Ask door enforces.
didnt: Board: provenance enforced as a schema rule (missing provenance is a validation failure, not a style lapse) and competency questions tracked against what the schema can actually answer form the reference for claim-level provenance in our typed-edge direction, alongside Typed Graph (B165) and MemVector (B168). Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ThirdBrain
good: A proposition graph with unusually strict grounding: atomic propositions are extracted with a source_span anchor back to originals preserved verbatim in raw/, edges are restricted to ten typed relations on four axes, and every edge must cite its axiom_basis. Contradictions become problem nodes with an open-to-resolved lifecycle; resolution offers only reclassifying the edge, adding a higher premise, or discarding one side, and records how the problem was resolved. Question answering cites only existing nodes, displays invented nodes struck through with a warning, and requires a no-basis answer when the graph supplies none; before a user-initiated AI operation, a cost preflight shows estimated calls, tokens, cost and time and waits for confirmation.
bad: Proposition extraction, edge classification and the 75% auto-link threshold remain model judgements; a confidence score is not proof that a proposition or relation is correct. The cost gate can be switched off, and the README's small automatic calls when a panel opens are outside the gate, so the protection is a default rather than an invariant.
didnt: Board: source-anchored propositions, typed edges that must carry their grounds, contradictions promoted to lifecycle-bearing problem nodes with the resolution recorded, existence-checked citations with forced no-basis answers, and a pre-operation AI cost gate form the closest full architectural sibling in this wave and a reference design for truth-aware knowledge work. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Relation Sync
good: Keeps declared inverse frontmatter relations consistent while changing frontmatter only, never note bodies, and never creating missing notes. New installations start with automatic sync paused; first use previews exactly which note and property will change, including missing or excluded targets, and vault-wide sync is idempotent on already consistent notes. Existing synonyms are recognised and preserved instead of duplicating an inverse, custom pairs are validated before saving, and ambiguous terms are not inferred from names or note contents. A relations panel exposes present, missing and excluded inverses, and undo previews the latest recorded write batch before reversing it.
bad: The recent-sync log holds at most 200 changes for the current session only; restarting Obsidian or disabling the plugin clears that history, and the README states plainly that undo is not a backup. Targets must be existing Markdown notes, and relation meaning still depends on the user declaring the pair correctly.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): paused-by-default automation, preview before apply, idempotent reconciliation, refusal to infer ambiguous relations, and a previewed undo corroborate our write discipline; mechanically maintained inverse pairs are the operational counterpart to declared inverse relations in typed graph vocabularies. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Not Submodules
good: Replaces submodules with plain nested Git repositories discovered by scanning the vault for .git entries. Identity comes from the origin remote rather than the folder: locations sharing an origin are grouped as one repository however they are named or placed, and a rename or an SSH-to-HTTPS respelling of the remote is recognised as the same location rather than a deletion. A self-maintaining POSIX pre-commit hook keeps a managed block in .gitignore synchronised, while the hook installer refuses to overwrite a hook it did not install; nested entries are classified as original clones, worktrees or real submodules, with the submodule section read-only. Migration from the older naming-convention system carries registrations forward.
bad: Refresh is manual only, so the view can be stale until the user asks for a rescan. It is desktop-only because it shells out to local Git, and the nested repositories remain separate histories and remotes whose divergence the plugin surfaces but cannot remove.
didnt: Corroboration: identity settled from the origin remote rather than a path or name, a managed region inside .gitignore, refusal to overwrite a foreign hook, and manual-only scanning corroborate our identity, managed-region and no-surprise-automation disciplines. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Folder Git
good: Provides VS Code-style source control separately for each vault folder, with independent GitHub or Forgejo/Gitea remotes, branches, commit schedules and push settings. Discarding always asks for confirmation, merge conflicts are resolved per file, amend and undo warn when a commit was already pushed, and restoring a historical version leaves it unstaged for review. Its credential handling is unusually explicit: tokens travel only in an Authorization header to the configured host, are passed to Git through environment variables and a command-line credential helper rather than written into .git/config or a remote URL, host matching is exact, and GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 makes Git fail rather than prompt. When the vault root is itself a repository, the plugin adds its own data file to .gitignore and warns if that file is already committed.
bad: The central weakness is stated in the README: access tokens are saved unencrypted in the plugin's data.json, so anything that copies that file copies the tokens. The token also sits in the Git process environment, readable by other programs running as the same user; a user-configured plain-HTTP Forgejo instance is the one exception to the no-token-over-HTTP rule and triggers a warning.
didnt: Corroboration: exact-host token delivery, environment-only handoff to Git, self-exclusion of the secret-bearing settings file, pushed-state warnings and confirmations around destructive history operations corroborate our credential and write disciplines; unencrypted token storage at rest is recorded as the residual risk. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WebDAV PQC Sync
good: Bidirectional end-to-end encrypted sync to any WebDAV server using ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation with a fresh per-file AES-256-GCM key. File contents, filenames and folder names are encrypted, with the hierarchy mapped to an equal-depth encrypted path so the server sees random names and binary payloads; the secret key never leaves the device. ETag-based incremental transfer, a local journal for crash-safe operation, dated conflict copies for both-sides-changed files, and chunked transfer for large files make the sync mechanics concrete.
bad: Version 2 was a breaking replacement of the earlier RSA/OpenPGP design: old keys, the old passphrase and all previously encrypted remote data were invalidated, requiring a new key pair and a fresh or emptied remote. Its own security table records that v2 removed passphrase protection, so keys are raw with no encryption at rest, and both keys must be stored because a Kyber public key cannot be derived from the secret key; device migration exports the configuration including those keys.
didnt: Corroboration: post-quantum end-to-end encryption covering names and structure as well as contents, plus a crash-safe journal and keep-both conflict copies, is another concrete instance for the owner-gated encrypted device-sync gap; the unencrypted-at-rest key regression and break-everything upgrade are recorded against it. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: S3 Sync + Backup
good: The most engineered sync design in this batch: three-way reconciliation compares local state, remote state and per-file SHA-256 baselines held in a local IndexedDB journal, with no cloud manifest required, and a destination fingerprint detects reconnecting to a different bucket or prefix. Both-sides-changed files produce LOCAL_ and REMOTE_ copies rather than a silent winner; optional end-to-end encryption uses XSalsa20-Poly1305 with Argon2id, and scheduled full-vault snapshots can be downloaded as ZIP files. Its own settings directory is hardcoded-excluded from sync so credentials and a saved passphrase cannot leak to S3, and the README enumerates reads, writes, off-device traffic and exclusions in detail.
bad: S3 credentials and the optional remembered passphrase are stored in Obsidian's data.json, protected from sync by the hard exclusion rather than by a separate secret store. Even with encryption enabled, every backup manifest remains plaintext JSON containing file paths, sizes, SHA-256 checksums, the encryption flag and the originating device ID; other .obsidian configuration files are also in sync scope by default unless the user excludes them. A lost encryption passphrase has no recovery, and restoring a backup is a manual download, extract and copy-back process.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): baseline-based three-way reconciliation without a cloud manifest, a destination fingerprint, keep-both conflicts, last-writer device attribution, extensive tests and a hardcoded exclusion for its own credential-bearing settings corroborate the integrity and leak-prevention side of our sync discipline; the plaintext backup manifest is the recorded residual metadata exposure. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NoteFlare
good: Publishes selected folders, selected files or the whole vault as one or more digital gardens through Cloudflare Workers by direct API upload or through Cloudflare Pages using Git, resolving wikilinks and images during packaging. A separate local-authoritative backup can sync the vault root to a private GitHub repository on a schedule or after edits, and multiple sites can keep independent scopes and domains. API tokens are stored through the operating system's native keychain rather than in vault settings.
bad: The one-click pitch explicitly treats the absence of GitHub App authorisation, webhooks and manual approval steps as the feature, while whole-vault publishing is an offered scope and the README describes no publish-review gate for what is about to become public. Automatic backup after edits likewise writes in the background. At 25 commits and one star it is also a young implementation.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): native-keychain token storage and independently scoped multi-site publishing are the creditable parts; the no-approval-steps framing for a public publish path is the contrast case against our gated publish discipline. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Enveloppe
good: A mature opt-in publisher: only notes whose frontmatter carries share: true are uploaded, converted copies go to a vault-named branch in the target GitHub repository, wikilinks are converted, Dataview queries are resolved at publish time, and removing depublished or deleted files is a separate explicit purge command. It supports the user's choice of Jekyll, MkDocs, Hugo or custom templates rather than imposing one site generator. The README is candid about the boundary: it warns users not to use the plugin to sync or save the vault and not to open the converted repository files in Obsidian.
bad: The branch's pull request is automatically merged by default; the user can disable that behaviour, but unless they do, the review step is a formality. The README also warns that frequent pushes can leave the branch unmerged because of conflicts, and conversion is deliberately one-way rather than a backup or round-trip representation of the vault.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): an explicit per-note share flag, converted copies rather than modified sources, a separate purge operation and a plain not-a-backup warning corroborate our publish discipline at production scale; the auto-merge default is recorded as the softening of that review step. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AgentBoard
good: A two-way board over one Markdown todo file whose file-format contract protects human edits from the agent that maintains the file. Board edits stamp a task UsrEdit:Y; the companion agent skill is forbidden to emit that flag and must not overwrite the urgency, importance, effort, due date or critical values of a task carrying it. Derived fields are kept mechanically consistent (Total equals Urgency plus Importance, and Critical follows a stated threshold), parent tasks and subtasks stay together through reordering, block order and formatting are preserved so diffs stay clean, and the plugin never rewrites the file's Last updated on line because that line belongs to the agent.
bad: The protection is a format convention the external agent is instructed to honour, not an enforcement mechanism inside the plugin; a writer that ignores the contract can still rewrite the shared file. The model is deliberately narrow: one configured todo file, one level of subtasks, and subjective one-to-three urgency and importance scores whose derived critical threshold is necessarily crude.
didnt: Board: a machine-owned flag inside a human-and-agent shared file, with the other writer required to treat flagged values as the user's and leave them alone, plus derived-field consistency and diff-preserving formatting, is our managed-region and single-writer discipline proved in miniature. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ingester
good: A deliberately small bridge from clipping to ingest: the Web Clipper saves an article into a watched folder such as raw/clippings/, the plugin detects the new file, opens a tmux window and runs the user's Claude Code /ingest skill against that path. Its disclosures are complete for a tool of this kind: an Anthropic account is required, the plugin itself makes no network requests while the invoked Claude Code session connects to Anthropic, external programs are executed through child_process, and the tool is desktop-only.
bad: Auto-ingest defaults to true, so a file landing in the folder triggers an unattended agent run with no per-item confirmation, preview or cost gate described. It also depends on Claude Code, tmux and zsh being installed and correctly configured, and the spawned session operates over the vault directory.
didnt: Rejected: unattended, folder-triggered agent writes into a wiki are the automatic-writing pole our approval discipline refuses, even though the ingest pipeline shape resembles ours; the complete disclosures section is credited as the honest minimum for such a tool. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Active Note
good: Externalises one narrow piece of Obsidian UI state into an inspectable JSON pointer file: the vault-relative path of the active note and, only when text is selected, the selected text with its one-indexed start and end lines. Any external tool can read that file without an Obsidian-specific API, writes are event-driven and debounced to avoid excessive file churn, and the pointer path is configurable. The narrow schema makes exactly what context is being shared easy to audit.
bad: Selected text is written in plaintext to .obsidian/active-note.json, where any local process able to read the vault configuration area can see it; the README describes no access control, encryption or retention rule for that selection. At 11 commits and no stars it is a small utility, and resolving the @. shorthand depends on the external agent being configured to understand the convention.
didnt: Corroboration: a tiny, explicit and inspectable context pointer is the deliberate-handoff alternative to ambient capture, with the shared context visible in one file; the plaintext persistence of selected text is recorded as the exposure that bounds the pattern. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MCP REST
good: A thin, zero-npm-dependency MCP wrapper over the local Obsidian REST API, defaulting to 127.0.0.1 and requiring a bearer API key for the vault tools. Its patch operation can target a heading, block or frontmatter section, or perform a precise search-replace, rather than forcing whole-file rewrites; search supports full text, Dataview DQL or JsonLogic and optional semantic search. The README states that the server communicates only with the local REST API, with its fetch tool making outbound requests only when explicitly invoked, and the repository carries 28 tests.
bad: One bearer key unlocks a broad write surface: create or overwrite files, append, patch, execute templates and delete either the active file or an arbitrary vault file. The README describes no per-tool scopes, path allowlist, approval or elicitation step, or audit log separating read tools from destructive ones; the unauthenticated server-info tool and the general-purpose fetch tool widen that surface further.
didnt: Rejected: a single-key, full-CRUD and delete-capable vault door without described scoping or approval gating is the opposite shape from our default-deny, read-first door and approval-gated writes; its loopback-only transport and precise patch targeting are credited in the row. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Advanced Metadata Cache
good: Maintains the indexes Obsidian otherwise rebuilds by scanning the vault: backlinks, note names and aliases, frontmatter titles and per-heading created/modified/seen times, each as an independently switchable module. Core lookups keep Obsidian's own signatures and answers while adding fast, safe and original modes: fast reads the cache, safe waits for pending changes to settle, and original bypasses the cache for comparison. Name lookup deliberately returns an unranked list when several notes share a name or alias rather than guessing which one was meant. Heading times are never written into notes, unseen events remain null rather than being guessed, and the cross-plugin API is published with a hand-written declaration file and a versioned argument-and-result contract.
bad: Answering core calls from its cache requires replacing the built-in metadata-cache methods while a module is enabled, which is a compatibility surface against Obsidian internals and other plugins. Fast answers can be a moment behind a change Obsidian has not finished processing; heading identity is inferred by comparing successive versions, and the README concedes that two identical headings swapping places keep each other's history. Heading times are also only what the current device saw, with changes arriving from another device stamped when they arrive here.
didnt: Corroboration: maintained indexes with explicit fast, safe and original answers, ambiguity returned unranked instead of resolved by guesswork, and unknown times kept null corroborate our index-first retrieval and honest-unknown disciplines. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Scientific Article Card
good: Turns a PMID, PMCID, DOI, arXiv ID or article URL into a plain-YAML metadata card using scholarly sources rather than a generic web preview, with identifiers, citation fields, abstract and keywords preserved as editable data. A paper note uses the paper's metadata as properties while keeping the user's status, rating, tags and writing separate; an existing note with the same DOI or PMID is reused instead of duplicated. Refresh updates only fetched properties, an empty result keeps the old value, and it never overwrites the user's fields or note text. Network requests happen only when an identifier is converted, every destination is listed, the plugin states that it never accesses the clipboard, and releases carry GitHub artifact attestations.
bad: Some publishers, including Elsevier and ScienceDirect, block automated page requests, and first-figure preview images are often unavailable outside open-access PubMed Central. To avoid listing the whole vault, paper-note discovery searches only the reading list's paper links and the papers folder, so a note kept in another project folder can be missed and a duplicate created unless a dedicated papers folder is used. The card verifies and organises bibliographic metadata; it does not verify the article's own claims.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): identifier-keyed deduplication, fetched metadata kept apart from the user's own fields, a refresh that cannot overwrite user writing, explicit network destinations and signed release artefacts corroborate our citation and provenance hygiene for paper ingest. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Better Pandoc Reference List
good: A maintained fork that renders Pandoc citekeys in notes as formatted citations and a sidebar reference list using the selected CSL style. It can read the library directly from the locally running Zotero application without requiring Better BibTeX, falls back to Better BibTeX or a Pandoc-readable bibliography file, and downloads only changed references after the first import. Its cache lives outside the vault, the plugin keeps working from that cache when Zotero is closed, and a failed update never empties the bibliography.
bad: A reference with no Citation Key cannot be cited and is not listed, and new references require Zotero to be running with local application communication enabled. The cache is per-device and is not synced, downloaded citation styles and languages are stored in a hidden .pandoc folder inside the vault, and the project inherits the maintenance risk of forking an unmaintained original.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): incremental bibliography updates, an outside-vault cache, and degradation that preserves the last good bibliography instead of emptying it corroborate our citation tooling's fail-safe direction. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Project Planner
good: Turns tasks already in the vault into a dependency graph, a Gantt chart with a computed critical path, a board and time-and-materials costing, with every task, date, dependency, person and cost read from and written back to plain Markdown in the syntax style each line already uses. Its honesty rules are the study point: inferred dates are drawn dashed and stay out of notes until accepted; schedule warnings judge only dates the user actually wrote; people with no rate are listed as unpriced rather than costed at zero; allocation shares that do not total 100% are used exactly as written rather than scaled; and one shared undo history spans all views, with optimistic writes rolled back when a vault write fails.
bad: Dataview is a hard requirement and the views refuse to render without it. The planning surface is very large, and two automatic behaviours need watching: deleting a task in a chain hands its blockers to its dependents (chain healing rewrites other tasks' metadata), and people are matched by name meaning, so near-identical names can be treated as one person.
didnt: Board: dependency-first planning over plain Markdown in which inferred dates stay visible suggestions until accepted, costs resting on guessed dates are counted separately, unpriced people are reported rather than costed as free, and allocation shares are never silently rescaled is a reference design for honest planning arithmetic. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Task Center
good: Collects checkbox tasks scattered across the vault into Today, Week, Month, TODO, Unscheduled, Completed and Dropped views, with custom filter tabs, drag-to-schedule, and estimated-versus-actual time tracking, while tasks stay as plain Markdown in their original notes and no database or new format is introduced. Its agent-facing CLI is designed for reliability: every task has a fixed path-and-line id, running the same command twice gives the same result, completing an already completed task returns unchanged instead of writing again, and every change prints the before line and the after line so the edit can be checked. Fields and tags the plugin does not know are left exactly as they are.
bad: The fixed task id is a file path plus line number; if the line moves, recovery falls back to matching by title, which can collide when titles repeat. The same CLI that makes agent use reliable also gives an agent read and update access to tasks with no approval step described, and the plugin depends on Tasks or Dataview plus the Daily Notes core plugin.
didnt: Corroboration: plain-Markdown tasks with no database, idempotent agent commands whose repeat runs report unchanged instead of rewriting, and a printed before-and-after line for every change corroborate our agent-operation discipline; the line-number identity is recorded as the fragile part. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Atoms
good: A capture-first filing loop with strict non-negotiables: thoughts are dumped as daily-note bullets with no filing decisions, and later classification creates flat atom notes whose body is the original capture text verbatim, with title, tags and reason-bearing links added around it. Existing atom files are never overwritten on a title collision, and the model never rewrites hand-authored bullets. Automatic filing is off by default, requires a one-time privacy acknowledgement, only files captures from the day it was enabled forward, and never processes today's daily note; older history is an attended backfill that is priced before it runs. The Anthropic key lives in SecretStorage, never in data.json, and the README enumerates exactly what each classify run sends.
bad: Filing is impossible without a paid AI route, either the user's Anthropic bill or the Atoms Plus subscription, and each classify run sends capture text plus vault note titles, tags and person-hub titles to that service. The atom-versus-noise classification and the suggested titles, tags and links are model judgements, and the optional Ask mirror keeps a cloud copy of the filed atoms so external chatbots can search them.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): verbatim capture bodies that the model may never rewrite, collision protection for existing notes, automatic filing bounded by an acknowledgement, a start date and a never-today rule, a backfill priced before it runs, and keys in SecretStorage corroborate our capture and custody disciplines; the paid cloud classification dependency is recorded against it. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Reading Inbox Synthesizer
good: Turns a web-clippings backlog into reading memory: a sync extracts a summary, key claims and topics for each clipping, and a generated Reading Synthesis note shows the inbox at a glance, themes shared across two or more clippings with both the consensus and the tension between sources, the current week's saves, and stale items past a threshold, oldest first. Syncing is incremental so unchanged clippings are never reprocessed, and generating the report makes no LLM call, so it stays free and unlimited. The free tier's accounting is careful: a sync use is reserved before the request and refunded if the sync does not complete, and the Pro licence is verified offline with no account or server-side usage record.
bad: Summaries, key claims and topics are produced by the configured external AI provider, and the README describes no citation or verification step tying a generated claim back to the clipping it came from. The API key is stored in Obsidian's local data storage without the stronger SecretStorage treatment named by peer plugins, and the free tier's ten lifetime syncs are tracked in local plugin data that the README concedes can be reset by removing that data.
didnt: Corroboration: incremental processing that never reprocesses unchanged clippings, a failed sync refunding its reserved allowance, themes that report tension between sources rather than only consensus, and a report built from already-synced data with no further model call corroborate our ingest accounting; the unverified generated claims are recorded as the contrast. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Copy for Email and Chat
good: Copies a selection or a whole note as email-ready rich text by attacking the actual failure mode: instead of classes and style blocks that mail clients strip, every style is inlined on every element, while Mermaid diagrams, charts, math and SVGs are rasterised to embedded PNGs and vault images are embedded as data URIs. The same copy operation also writes a chat-ready plain-text flavour in which structure survives through configurable glyphs for headings, emphasis, lists and quotes, so pasting into Slack, WeChat or iMessage yields structured text instead of raw Markdown. Frontmatter is excluded from the copied note.
bad: The fixed light palette overrides the author's theme so output stays readable in a white email body, which changes appearance by design. Data-URI images may not display while composing in classic Outlook for Windows, diagrams and math degrade to a placeholder on mobile, internal links and tags are flattened to plain text, and tables in the chat flavour remain pipe-separated rows that cannot align in proportional fonts.
didnt: Corroboration: a derived, destination-specific copy produced at the clipboard while the source note stays untouched, with its rendering losses enumerated in the README, is the export-side form of our source-versus-derived discipline. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Deep Research Formatter
good: The cleanup itself is narrowly and conservatively engineered: it touches only Deep Research marker wrappers, applies minimal whitespace cleanup afterwards, preserves YAML frontmatter, fenced code blocks and inline code, and does nothing at all when no markers are found. The command-line mode recursively formats a vault directory, skips .obsidian, .git and node_modules, rewrites only files whose content actually changes, prints scanned, updated and failed counts with marker totals, and uses distinct exit codes for invalid arguments and processing failures.
bad: Removing citations is the product: cite markers and exported citation blocks are deleted entirely, and entity and URL markers are reduced to their readable labels, so the link targets and the claim-to-source mapping leave the document at the moment it enters the vault. Unknown marker types are best-effort and otherwise removed, and both the note command and the recursive CLI rewrite files in place with no preview or backup described.
didnt: Rejected: a formatter whose headline operation deletes citation markers and citation blocks destroys provenance by design, the same ground as mdfit in B169; its preservation of frontmatter and code regions is credited in the row as the one sound rule. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Advanced Copy
good: Copies a page or selection through user-defined template profiles that transform Markdown element by element into HTML, Anki cards or any custom format, with variables such as heading level, element content, filename and date available to the templates. One documented use case is copying content together with a source reference to the original note, so the detached copy can carry its provenance with it. The source note is never modified; the transformation exists only on the clipboard.
bad: The transformation is only as trustworthy as the hand-built profile: templates are configured element by element, a source reference appears only if the chosen profile includes one, and the copied result is a detached rendering that can drift from the note without any marker of which version produced it. Enabling or disabling per-profile commands requires an Obsidian restart.
didnt: Corroboration: clipboard-only derived output under explicit user-chosen profiles, with a source reference available as a first-class template ingredient, corroborates the clipboard-as-gate pattern filed with Briefmaker and Simple exporter in B158. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Flint Chart
good: Renders charts from semantic specifications rather than rendering configuration: the author states what each column means and which chart is wanted, and scales, axes, aggregation, number formats, layout and colour are derived. Explicit semantic-type annotations always win over the plugin's inference from names and values. A chart block can point at a Markdown table in a note so the table remains the thing the user edits and the chart follows it; the create-from-table command draws every suggested chart once before showing it, so what is offered is known to render; an unsupported encoding channel is reported with the channels the chart does accept instead of drawing nothing; and PNG export never overwrites an existing file. Unsupported theme specifications are announced rather than silently ignored.
bad: When semantic types are not annotated, they are inferred from column names and values, so a misleadingly named column can be given the wrong meaning and a confidently wrong chart. The bundle is about 1.3 MB because narrowing ECharts would cost most chart types, Flint's own theme presets are unavailable on the ECharts backend, and at 18 commits the plugin is young.
didnt: Board: semantic-typed chart specifications in which explicit meaning annotations outrank inference, the maintained table stays the editable source while the chart follows it, and machine suggestions are rendered before they are offered form a reference for the table-and-image side of our evaluation work. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BibTeX Manager
good: Creates a literature note from a pasted BibTeX entry using customisable templates, formats the entry as a reference list inside the note while keeping the original BibTeX entry itself unmodified, inserts citations directly into notes, and can fetch entries from remote sources such as arXiv and Google Books. It runs on desktop and mobile with no external service dependencies, accepting entries from Zotero, Mendeley or any other reference manager.
bad: The README is feature-level: it describes no deduplication, update or conflict behaviour for entries that change in the reference manager, and no verification of fetched entries against a second source, so a literature note is only as accurate as the single BibTeX record it was pasted or fetched from. Custom templates must be configured by path before note generation is useful.
didnt: Corroboration: the original BibTeX entry is kept unmodified while the formatted reference list is a derived rendering of it, which is our source-versus-derived separation inside a single note. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Literature Feed
good: A literature pipeline built around human selection and measured search quality. OpenAlex scans fill a weekly reading-inbox note with deduplicated papers ranked by tier; only papers the user ticks are ever sent to Zotero, a failed feed does not move the last-scan date or block other feeds, and dismissed papers record their reason and leave the waiting counts. A local ledger tracks what each search listed, dropped and eventually had ticked, sent or read, and its effectiveness report offers rule-change suggestions that change nothing by themselves. Literature reviews are reproducible: the note records the run time, window, exact search definitions, ranking rules, the prompt's length and SHA-256 hash and the cost, keeps the prompt and the pasted answer verbatim, and can repeat the review and diff what changed. Its DOI finder checks each Crossref result on title, first author, year, volume and first page and routes mismatches to a human as Check rather than Found, and OpenAlex spending is estimated before a run and stopped at a per-review limit.
bad: The catalogue description promises a working weekly feed, but the source's own status banner says the plugin is under development, the weekly schedule is not built yet and it is not in the community store, at 10 commits. Its effectiveness and identity machinery has admitted soft spots: authors are matched by family name and first initial, so two people sharing both count as one, and the citation network is only as complete as OpenAlex's reference lists, which the README concedes are incomplete for some works. The full workflow also leans on OpenAlex and Zotero API keys, Zotero and the author's Lab Kit conventions.
didnt: Board: a literature pipeline in which only human-ticked papers cross into Zotero, search quality is measured from recorded outcomes in a local ledger whose suggestions change nothing by themselves, and every review preserves its exact prompt, prompt hash, cost and verbatim answer is a reference design for reproducible literature work and for the scholarly side of our citation programme. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Nope
good: Exports modular Obsidian notes to publication-ready PDFs through a Docker-based Pandoc and LaTeX pipeline, so no local TeX installation is needed. The authoring model is atomic: chapters, theorems, tables, glossary entries and diagrams live in their own notes and are embedded into a main document, cross-references number themselves, and glossaries and bibliographies build themselves, with branding taken from a note. The settings page runs preflight checks that pinpoint what is missing, and the documentation site shows the Markdown source beside the exported PDF, built by the pipeline itself.
bad: The README's own banner says the plugin is still in early development, is not stable yet and may have breaking changes. Only Linux and macOS are tested, Windows is experimental and untested, and the no-local-TeX benefit is bought with a Docker dependency and a first export that pulls the pipeline image for one to three minutes.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): modular source notes assembled into a derived publication whose references, glossary and bibliography are built by the pipeline, with preflight checks before export, corroborates our documents-as-derived-artefacts practice; the Docker pipeline is not our PDF route. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bases Chart Views
good: Adds chart views to Obsidian Bases in two modes. The curated Data Charts give scatter, line, bar and pie views purpose-built controls: multiple Y properties each with its own aggregation, grouping through the native Bases group menu, synced axes, and click-through from a chart element to the source files behind it in a searchable data table. The AI Chart mode accepts a full ECharts configuration for the wider chart family. The plugin is a from-scratch rewrite of an earlier fork, with tests and responsive light and dark layouts.
bad: The curated Data Charts cover only scatter, line, bar and pie, and the line chart offers filling gaps with zero as a display choice. The AI Chart path depends on Claudian, has the AI write the complete ECharts configuration directly into the .base file with no review step described, and renders that saved configuration independently of the Bases query, so the picture can drift from the data it claims to show.
didnt: Rejected: the AI chart path rests on Claudian, which our stack has already rejected, and on an agent writing configuration directly into a vault file without a review gate; the curated Data Charts' per-property aggregation and click-through to source files are credited in the row. GPL-3.0 would confine any use to ideas in any case. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Smart Relations
good: Builds six local indexes over the vault (UUID identity, stemmed terms, tag co-occurrence, character trigrams, a bidirectional relation graph and per-document statistics) and ranks related notes from four published signals: BM25, tag Jaccard similarity, vocabulary overlap and graph proximity, combined with configurable weights and shown to the user as a per-signal breakdown rather than a single opaque number. Identity is a stable frontmatter UUID that survives renames; the auto-add-IDs option that writes those ids into notes is disabled by default precisely because it modifies files. Duplicate ids are flagged, dangling references are logged rather than crashing, a corrupted index is rebuilt, and the whole system runs offline with zero external API calls.
bad: Despite the vectorisation framing, there are no embeddings: the ranking is lexical and graph-based, with English Porter stemming and an English stopword list, so non-English and genuinely semantic matches are out of reach. Notes without a frontmatter id are skipped from indexing entirely, duplicate ids keep the first occurrence, tokenisation is capped, and min-max normalisation means a note's combined score shifts with the rest of the corpus. Similarity also carries no notion of supersession or truth.
didnt: Corroboration: fully local, deterministic retrieval whose combined score can be opened into its four signals, over notes with stable rename-proof identities and an auto-identity writer that is off by default because it modifies files, corroborates our inspectable-retrieval and identity disciplines; the lexical-not-semantic limit and the absence of any truth or supersession notion are recorded. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Authorship Tracker
good: Stamps lightweight provenance onto notes in a mixed human, AI and automation vault: created_by, last_modified_by and edit_count frontmatter plus a content_origin field whose suggested values separate primary sources, human-authored text, AI-derived and AI-generated content for citation decisions, and a daily JSONL log with section-level summaries of what changed. It deliberately reacts only to the user's own typing in the editor, so external writers cannot trigger false attribution, while configured auto-import folders stamp incoming files with their source and trust level. The no-network property is enforced by lint rules rather than left to review, there are no runtime dependencies, and the README is candid that the log itself contains note paths and heading text and travels wherever the vault travels. User-supplied filename regexes are screened against adversarial inputs and rejected when measurably slow rather than downgraded to matching everything.
bad: Attribution is prospective only, with no retroactive pass over existing notes. External filesystem edits are not detected at all unless they land in a configured auto-import folder, and the external-writer contract is best-effort declared provenance that the README itself says is not identity verification or tamper-evident auditing; the content_origin vocabulary is a convention, not enforced, and author identity is simply the configured name string.
didnt: Board: note-level provenance fields with a trust vocabulary, a daily human-readable change log, and an external-writer contract that states its own non-verification limits in the open form a reference design for authorship provenance in human-and-agent vaults, the consumer-scale counterpart to our filings discipline. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Authorship
good: Tracks authorship inside the text rather than per note: CodeMirror transaction events distinguish typed from pasted text, selections can be marked manually as AI, Self or Reference, and the editor visually separates the three. The annotations persist at the end of the Markdown file in the open Markdown Annotations format as grapheme-cluster ranges, and a SHA-256 hash validates the file on reopening so modification outside Obsidian is detected. Everything is local with zero network calls, and per-author character percentages appear in the status bar.
bad: At five commits this is a sketch of the idea. Pasted text has no intrinsic author, so classification falls back to a configurable default paste source that can mislabel it; authorship ranges are grapheme offsets into the text, so an external edit can shift what the ranges point at, and the SHA-256 check detects that the file changed without repairing the attribution. AI text typed or written by an external tool is outside the editor-transaction view unless marked by hand.
didnt: Corroboration: range-level authorship provenance in an open annotation format, with a hash that detects out-of-band modification instead of silently trusting stale ranges, corroborates provenance at a finer grain than Authorship Tracker's note-level fields in this batch; the fragility of offset ranges is recorded. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI Scheduler
licence: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 (custom licence, settled from the README badge and License section; GitHub card shows Other (NOASSERTION))
good: A scheduling and execution layer that drives an already-configured AI backend plugin rather than calling providers itself: cron, interval, event and chained triggers, variables filled per run, retries and time limits, run history, and vault-synced schedule notes editable from either the dashboard or the note.
