Its restraint points are real: approval mode is on by default so changes to existing notes wait as diffs in an Awaiting approval list, prompts can be previewed exactly as they will be sent, follow-up tasks an AI proposes are created disabled for human review, a per-device setting makes a synced vault run each task once, and the Privacy section states no telemetry and no third-party servers.
bad: The execution model is unattended by design — tasks run 'while you work or sleep' — and approval covers only changes to notes that already exist: new notes are created immediately with no gate, so a scheduled agent can fill the vault unreviewed. Two of its three backends are Claudian and Oh My Claudian, and Claudian is a component the owner has already rejected. Calendar add-ons widen the surface: Google sign-in asks for calendar scopes through the user's own Cloud project, Outlook's permission is Calendars.ReadWrite because Microsoft offers nothing narrower, and private calendar links are bearer-equivalent secrets the README itself warns about.
didnt: Rejected: unattended scheduled AI execution whose approval gate covers only edits to existing notes, built primarily on the owner-rejected Claudian backend, under a noncommercial custom licence that is ideas-only in any case. Its approval-diff list, prompt preview and created-disabled follow-ups are credited as the right instincts. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OKF Enforcer
good: Validates a Markdown vault against the Open Knowledge Format with the spec's own discipline: hard rules (parseable frontmatter, non-empty type, index/log structure) are errors, recommended fields are toggleable warnings, and permissive rules are respected so broken links and missing optional fields never fail a bundle. The v0.2 layer checks provenance and trust families (generated/verified, status, stale_after with passed-date detection, sources with credibility signals), derives a per-note trust tier, and validates Attested Computation concepts. Index generation is additive — it appends missing entries, corrects wrong paths, drops entries for notes that are gone, and preserves the author's prose, ordering and edited descriptions — and a report-only mode serves vaults that keep indexes by hand. Auto-fix inserts missing frontmatter without ever overwriting values already set, and the v0.1 to v0.2 migration can be kept behind its explicit command.
bad: It enforces one specific external format (OKF v0.2, with an opt-in beta Portent layer whose spec is pre-1.0 and may change), so adopting its checks means adopting that format's vocabulary and lifecycle model. The default posture writes an index.md into every folder as notes change, which is a standing automatic write across the vault; the auto-migrate-on-fix default likewise lets ordinary fixes rewrite a legacy timestamp and citations block. The catalogue described this as OKF v0.1; the source is v0.2 throughout, so the catalogue version claim does not hold.
didnt: Board: spec-faithful conformance checking that separates errors from warnings exactly where the format does, additive index maintenance that preserves human prose and ordering, a report-only mode for hand-kept indexes, and auto-fix that never overwrites a set value together form a reference design for a wiki validator. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Propsec
good: Schema enforcement for Obsidian properties that is validation-only by stance: 'Your notes are untouched, but your vault's consistency becomes easier to manage.' Schemas are picked by rule expressions over folder, tags and properties; fields carry primitive, custom reusable and union types; flags distinguish a hard required key from a soft warn, and a unique flag catches duplicate values for a field across notes. Rules are written in a small CEL-derived expression language that can compare fields against each other, with editor helpers for common constraints. Violations surface in the status bar and sidebar rather than being silently repaired.
bad: It reports drift but never repairs it, so a vault can accumulate known violations with no assisted path back to conformance. The rule language is a second syntax to learn and maintain alongside the schemas themselves, and schema definitions live in plugin settings rather than in portable files beside the notes they govern. There is no notion of provenance, lifecycle or supersession in the schema model — it checks shape, not truth.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): independent evidence that property-schema validation with required-versus-warn severity and cross-note uniqueness is a live, wanted capability, done here as pure read-only checking that never writes the notes it judges. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Rollup to PDF
good: Compiles a whole tree of wiki-linked notes into one typeset PDF through Pandoc: only line-leading arrow links expand, so cross-links are never pulled in by accident; linked pages nest one heading level below their link, cycles render as a visible 'see X' reference instead of recursing forever, and an appendix mode moves detail out of the body into numbered appendices. Failure is surfaced, not hidden: an embed whose target is missing or in a format LaTeX cannot draw degrades to a visible marker rather than failing the render, and when CJK glyphs would be silently dropped by the LaTeX engine the completion notice lists the lost characters. The test suite runs the real shipped walker against an edge-case vault rather than a second copy of the logic.
bad: The expansion model imposes strict authoring rules (no H1s, arrows only at line start, consistent chapter heading levels) that an existing vault will not satisfy by accident, so adoption means reformatting content to the tool. It is desktop-only and depends on a local Pandoc plus XeLaTeX toolchain with the right packages, which is a heavy prerequisite chain. Output is a rendered document only — nothing in the model carries provenance or links back from a PDF passage to its source note beyond the section structure.
didnt: Corroboration: a working note-tree-to-PDF compiler whose degradation rules (visible markers, reported glyph loss, cycles as references) corroborate the completion programme's own export honesty requirements. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pandoc Reference List
good: The original sidebar reference list for Pandoc citekeys: for each citekey in the active document it shows the formatted reference in the sidebar, driven by the user's own bibliography file and an optional CSL style, requiring Pandoc 2.11 or newer. Its longevity is the evidence — 276 stars and 61 releases since 2022 made it the reference implementation that later forks, including the maintained Better Pandoc Reference List studied in B170, measure themselves against.
bad: The repository now sits under GitHub's community-archive organisation and the README carries no maintenance commitment; the maintained line of development is the fork, not this repo. The README is minimal — setup steps only, with no statement of failure behaviour when the bibliography or a citekey is missing, and no local-Zotero path (a bibliography file must be supplied and kept current by something else). GPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only under the licence discipline in any case.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): the archived original of the citekey-sidebar pattern, recorded so the catalogue line resolves to a studied source; the live implementation line is its maintained fork. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Local Zotero Mirror
good: Mirrors a Zotero library into local Markdown with the two protections that matter: one canonical note per Zotero item, and user-written sections outside the plugin's managed blocks are preserved across regenerations, while Zotero native notes migrate into a protected block of their own. Collection index notes are regenerated to link the canonical notes, source tags are converted to Obsidian-safe zotero/ tags while the originals are kept verbatim in a zotero_tags property, and the mirror writes a local full-text search index so the Zotero side can find the Obsidian notes. Pandoc-style citations in a note render as APA references in reading mode with a virtual References block built from the citekeys actually used.
bad: It is only half of a pair: mirroring depends on the companion Zotero-side plugin Local Zotero Bridge, so the system has two moving parts and two failure surfaces, and the README states no behaviour for when the bridge is absent or the two sides disagree. The project is young (16 commits, 2 stars) and distributed via BRAT rather than the community store, and the README describes no conflict rule for a canonical note edited on both sides between syncs beyond the managed-block boundary.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): the managed-block contract — machine-regenerated regions fenced off from preserved human writing inside the same note — is the same preservation shape the wiki's own generated pages need, demonstrated here against a live external library. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kandyban
good: A non-destructive Kanban and list view over Markdown project files that lead with bold-key metadata: dragging a card or picking an enum writes only the leading field value, and annotations attached to that value (for example 'done (merged 2026-05-19, PR #29)') are preserved byte-identical, with everything outside the field untouched. It is explicit that the board reflects what is written in the file and never infers progress — if work started without the status being written, the card stays where the file says. It reads both the current and legacy item conventions, canonicalises milestone values, populates filters from values actually present, and carries a documented section on cache staleness with a manual rescan command.
bad: It is built against one project's convention — SweetClaude's issue and milestone files, its mode field, its phase file — so the board is a companion to that framework rather than a general vault tool, and its README carries a pre-alpha status badge. In the project-root layout, external edits to the dot-folder files do not reach the board until a manual rescan, and click-to-open degrades to the OS default app unless a separate dotfile-indexing plugin is installed. Desktop-oriented despite declaring itself not desktop-only.
didnt: Corroboration: field-scoped writes that preserve attached annotations byte-identical, plus a board that refuses to infer state the file does not state, corroborate the write-discipline the wiki's own boards follow. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Smart tasks-kanban
good: Turns selected columns of an existing Kanban board into live views over vault-wide Tasks queries: a frontmatter block names each smart column and its source bucket (due/scheduled/start/created windows or a tag), and the plugin fills the column automatically. Completion is written back to the task's source note with the Tasks completion date, dragging a card back out undoes it, completing a recurring task generates the next instance in the source note, and cards completed on earlier days are auto-archived into Kanban's native archive. Its README includes an unusually honest comparison table that names richer rivals and says when to choose them instead.
bad: Smart columns are rewritten by the plugin on every refresh — the README warns not to edit cards inside them manually — so hand edits in those columns are disposable by design. The write-back chain depends on the card keeping its source link; turning that display option off silently disables write-back and drag-out undo. It requires both the Kanban and Tasks plugins as hard dependencies, and the project is days old at study time (11 commits, created 2026-10-16) with a maintainer note conceding a README screenshot is still owed for directory review.
didnt: Corroboration: query-filled board columns whose every state change is written back to the task's source line — the board as a view, never a second copy — corroborate the derived-view discipline used by the wiki's own task surfaces. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tasks Map
good: Visualises tasks as an interactive dependency graph from two sources at once: inline checkbox tasks read through Dataview, and whole-note tasks declared by frontmatter. Edges come from explicit syntax — id/blocked emoji markers inline, or blockedBy/dependsOn fields on note-tasks — so the graph shows declared dependencies rather than guessed ones. Tasks can be completed from the graph, filtered by tag, and the project is actively engineered: 729 commits, 159 releases, a test suite and full documentation site. This is also the original that B171's Project Planner forked from, with the original copyright retained there.
bad: It is pre-v1.0 and the README warns plainly that interfaces — embed format, filter field names, settings — may change between releases, which is a real cost at 159 releases of churn. Dataview and Tasks are both hard requirements. The graph is a task-dependency view only: edges mean blocked-by, and there is no provenance, evidence or supersession relation in the model.
didnt: Corroboration: declared-dependency edges drawn from two task representations at once corroborate the typed-edge discipline; the fork studied in B171 shows the same codebase carrying a planning layer when dates and costs are added honestly. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RSS Importer
good: An importer with a human in the loop: feeds resolve to a preview before being saved, and importing opens a three-state window (imported / dismissed / available) where the user ticks items — nothing is pulled in automatically. Every imported note carries a stable identity in its frontmatter, so moving or renaming notes never produces duplicates on the next import. The README's Permissions and access section is exemplary: it enumerates exactly three disclosed capabilities (optional media writes outside the vault, vault enumeration for dedup, write-only clipboard for the debug log), what each is for, and what each never does, backed by PRIVACY.md and SECURITY.md files in the repo. Cleanup rules match by link target and structure rather than wording, and the README warns plainly that the cleanup command rewrites notes and to keep backups.
bad: It writes and can rewrite vault notes at scale, so a wrong cleanup rule re-applied over existing notes is a bulk-edit risk the backup warning exists for. The source tree includes a paywall detector, and the README does not state what the plugin does when an item is detected as paywalled — the boundary of that behaviour is not described at source. Desktop-only, and media downloads can place files outside the vault when the user enables that setting.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): user-ticked import with stable note identity and a capability-by-capability permissions disclosure corroborate the ingest discipline — and its disclosure section is a model worth matching when the wiki documents its own tools. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graph Heatmap
good: Colours graph nodes by a chosen metric — last modified, created, total connections, backlinks, outgoing links, word count or file size — with focus modes that isolate orphans, hubs, the stale tail or stubs, which makes it a practical vault-hygiene lens: the README's recommended combinations are explicitly cleanup lists (unlinked notes coloured by staleness; shortest notes for expansion or deletion). A recent-edit halo blends notes touched in the last 24 hours toward a marker colour regardless of metric. The How it works section is candid about the mechanism, naming the exact renderer field it writes and the events it hooks.
bad: It depends on undocumented Obsidian renderer internals, and by its own account the failure mode is silent: if the renderer's shape changes, colours simply stop updating until the plugin is patched. Colouring is a relative rank across the vault by default, so the same note changes colour as the vault changes around it — a view state, not a recorded property. It reads structure and timestamps only; nothing about a note's content, evidence or status feeds the metric.
didnt: Corroboration: metric-coloured graph views with orphan/stale/stub isolation corroborate graph-based hygiene reporting; recorded with its silent-degradation dependency on undocumented internals stated. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Properties to Graph
good: Adds the grouping the graph view lacks: chosen frontmatter properties contribute one virtual node per unique value, in a per-property colour, so notes cluster by property as well as by link or tag. Clicking a property node filters like a tag, shift-clicking folds its notes away, display names can be renamed from the graph's own Filters panel, and node sizing can reflect group size. The README credits the graph-injection approach it was inspired by and notes the codebase was since rewritten independently around properties.
bad: The README's own Notes section concedes the plugin relies on Obsidian's internal Graph View renderer APIs, which are not part of the public types and can change between releases — the same fragility class as Graph Heatmap in this batch. The project is small and young (19 commits, 1 star), and virtual nodes are a display construct only: nothing is written to the vault, so the grouping exists only while the plugin renders it.
didnt: Corroboration: property values as first-class graph nodes corroborate the wiki's own property-driven navigation; the value here is the interaction pattern, not a data model. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graph Edge Notes
good: Overlays short relationship labels on graph edges, read from a relations list in frontmatter where each entry carries a label and optional detail text shown on hover — so an edge can say 'limited-open' instead of merely existing. It accepts both its compact string encoding and object-style YAML when reading, the property name is configurable, and a command creates a relation for the current note. The README states its central limitation in its own section rather than burying it.
bad: That limitation is structural: the plugin annotates edges that already exist and creates none, so the two notes must be linked somewhere in the body for a labelled relation to render — the frontmatter relation alone draws nothing. The editor saves relations in a string-encoded micro-format that is awkward to hand-edit or validate, and the project is at sketch scale (3 commits). Labels are display text with no typed vocabulary, evidence or direction semantics beyond the string the author typed.
didnt: Corroboration: labelled edges corroborate the demand for typed relationships in graph views, and its stated limitation — annotation without edge creation — is a useful boundary marker for what an edge layer must do to count as a relation system. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Better Backlinks
good: Rebuilds backlinks as context: one card per linking note showing the whole block around the link (the full section for a heading link, the whole top-level list item with its nesting, the property row for a frontmatter link), with duplicate blocks merged and every link highlighted. Beyond links, it finds title matches and unlinked mentions with careful matching — whole words, any case, and text inside links, tags, properties, code, URLs, comments and math excluded — and each mention carries a one-click Link action that preserves the author's original wording as the display text when the casing differs. The README states the write surface precisely: apart from Link on mentions and ticking a checkbox in an excerpt, those are the only changes the plugin makes to notes. Creation dates prefer a note's created property over file dates, with the reason given (file dates change on sync, copy or restore).
bad: Finding mentions means reading every note, and the README concedes the mentions group fills in over a second or so in a large vault — the cost of whole-vault matching on every note open. One-click linking makes bulk link creation easy enough that a wrong whole-word match can be linked before it is read closely, and title matches are substring-based, so short common names will gather noise despite the whole-word rule. It is a reading and linking aid only: nothing records why a link was made or what relation it asserts.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): whole-block backlink context plus exclusion-disciplined unlinked-mention detection with a precisely stated write surface corroborates the link-integrity tooling direction; its created-property-over-file-date rule matches the wiki's own dating caution. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Auto Linker
licence: GPL-3.0 (ideas only; settled from the README License section, which links GPL-3.0-only — the GitHub card shows Other (NOASSERTION))
good: Auto-linking with the restraint the name usually lacks: it always suggests and never links on its own. Candidates pass an eleven-step pipeline the README publishes in full — tokenisation, skip zones for existing links/tags/code, phrase lookup, a reject and self-link filter, then lexical, significance (IDF-graded rather than a hard stop-word list), capitalisation, PageRank importance and learned-preference signals renormalised to one confidence score, with a user-controlled threshold and per-signal weight sliders. Rejections are remembered per-note or vault-wide, aliases are learned from links the user actually makes, and the optional semantic tier is off by default, runs an on-device model, and is honestly bounded: it re-ranks literal candidates and cannot surface a note sharing no word with the text. Privacy is all-local; the only network event is the optional one-time model download.
bad: GPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only under the licence discipline. A scored suggestion engine still puts plausible-but-wrong links one click away, and its learned-preference and learned-alias features compound past accepts — a bad early accept teaches the ranker. The README discloses the software was vibe-coded, and the confidence model's many interacting signals (including PageRank over the link graph) make individual suggestions hard to explain beyond the pipeline description.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): suggest-never-insert linking with a published scoring pipeline, reject memory and an honestly bounded semantic tier corroborates the human-gated linking discipline; the mechanism is recorded, the code is not usable. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Side Comments origin
good: Sidebar annotation that never touches the note's syntax: comments are standalone Markdown records stored per note as JSON, while the note keeps only a visual mark. Anchoring is engineered rather than positional: an annotation is relocated using document position, absolute offset, the selected text and its SHA-256 hash, heading path, occurrence index and surrounding context, and it becomes orphaned only when the text can no longer be found reliably — orphans are counted in settings with batch cleanup rather than vanishing. The Data and Privacy section states where every artefact lives (data, attachments, backups, all inside the vault), that clipboard access happens only on explicit paste or copy, and that the code makes no network requests. Exports include a Markdown summary, a precise callout backlink, and a .docx export preserving annotations as native Word comments.
bad: The annotation layer lives outside the notes as per-note JSON in a plugin data folder, so comments do not travel with a note copied on its own, and the export and backup routes are the only bridges back to portable form. Version 1.0.4 has no semantic categories and no resolved state — styles are visual only — so the layer cannot express the difference between a question, a task and a settled decision. The interface (commands, settings, most text) is currently in Simplified Chinese, which the README states plainly. GPL-3.0 keeps it ideas-only under the licence discipline in any case.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): hash-and-context anchored comments kept outside the annotated text, with orphans surfaced rather than silently dropped, corroborate the annotation-layer design; the format is recorded, the code is not usable. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agentNote
good: A local-first bridge that lets the user hand chosen material — a note, a folder, a passage — to agents such as Claude Code, Codex and WorkBuddy running on the same computer, and have results written back as ordinary Markdown notes, so knowledge outlasts the conversation and survives changing agents. Sharing is explicitly user-directed ('You direct the context'), nothing asks for a cloud account or a vault move, and files and activity records stay in the vault. Its knowledge profile records which documents were read or developed, which agents used them and when — with the honest caveat that activity values describe recorded actions, not a judgment of the work's quality.
bad: The trust boundary is the user's selection discipline: once material is shared, the README itself notes it 'is still processed according to that agent and its provider', so the local-first framing ends at the handoff. The README sections read describe the sharing model and the reuse profile but do not set out how the local service authenticates the agents that connect to it, so that property cannot be confirmed from the source's own top-level documentation. The reuse profile also only ever sees what passes through this one bridge — work done with the same notes outside it is invisible to the record.
didnt: Corroboration: user-directed context sharing with results returned as ordinary notes, plus a local reuse record, corroborates the agent-door pattern the wiki's own gateway implements with stricter scoping. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI Knowledge Workflow
good: Project knowledge and task workflow management in ordinary Markdown that runs fully without AI: manual mode is the default and creating, moving, completing and reopening tasks needs no AI service, API key or other plugin. Vault initialisation is previewed before confirmation and adds only missing files — it never overwrites existing content — including three companion skills (project onboarding, task management, weekly summaries) placed under .agents/skills, and re-running it adds what is missing without silently updating what exists. Task status lives in each task's YAML status field as the single source the board synchronises from, completing stamps completed_at and reopening clears it. The Privacy section is candid: no telemetry, no direct model calls, no self-updating, and an explicit statement that initialisation downloads and executes nothing.
bad: It prescribes a fixed vault layout (numbered task/workflow/project/inbox/template folders, a rules folder, per-project AGENTS.md/index.md/links.md), so adoption means conforming an existing vault to its structure. The interface is primarily Chinese, and the README's own validation record says real-device validation on Windows and Linux is still pending. When a user does configure a CLI, the privacy section concedes commands run with the user's full file permissions and are not confined to the vault, and project paths may point outside it — safe only under the configure-only-what-you-trust rule it states.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): preview-then-confirm initialisation that never overwrites, manual-by-default operation, and a privacy section that states the unconfined-CLI risk in plain terms corroborate the wiki's own scaffolding and disclosure discipline. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Context Anywhere AI Bridge
licence: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 (custom licence, settled from the README License section; GitHub card shows Other (NOASSERTION))
good: A complete self-hosted workflow for making a vault remotely readable by any MCP-capable AI: an Obsidian plugin mirrors eligible content one-way by default to the user's own Cloudflare R2 bucket behind a Worker, and AI clients reach it through an MCP endpoint gated by OAuth that issues a read-only access token — search, read note, recent notes, list and read allowed attachments — while the write token never leaves the plugin side. The scoping discipline is explicit: chosen folders only, configuration paths and key-bearing settings always excluded, unreferenced attachments not mirrored, two-way sync deliberately off by default, and when it is on, the losing copy is preserved in a visible conflicts folder rather than discarded. AI write-back is deliberately indirect — the AI returns an obsidian:// URL and the local app performs the write, so the MCP client has no direct write access. Token lifetimes, rotation behaviour and running costs are all documented at source.
bad: The mirror is unencrypted at rest in the R2 bucket — the README's own advice is to mirror only folders the user is 'comfortable exposing to AI', which for a private wiki is the whole decision, not a detail. Credential lifetimes are long: refresh credentials run 365 days, and rotating the read key does not revoke already-issued OAuth grants — both stated at source. Two-way sync resolves conflicts by later modification time (device clocks become a correctness input), and setup is a nine-step deployment across Cloudflare resources, secrets and per-device configuration. PolyForm Noncommercial keeps it ideas-only under the licence discipline in any case.
didnt: Board: a complete self-hosted reference for the hosted-door pattern — scoped unencrypted mirror, read-only OAuth-brokered MCP access, no direct AI write path — recorded as design evidence for the owner's still-open hosted-door decision, which this study does not take. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Archivist
good: Versioned vault backup to Dropbox built like a backup system rather than a file copy: content-addressed SHA-256 blobs mean identical files are stored once and a rename costs no new bytes, per-snapshot manifests give file-level history and one-click restore, and hierarchical retention (frequent recent snapshots, daily for a month, monthly for years) is guarded by an always-keep safety floor. Pruning is inspectable — a dry-run preview command shows what retention would delete before the real run. Token custody is documented to an unusual standard: tokens live in Obsidian's encrypted secret store, never in data.json or plaintext, with per-OS explanation of where the master key lives and where the protection is real versus obfuscation, plus the legacy plaintext file is migrated and deleted on upgrade. Dropbox access is an app folder under four enumerated least-privilege scopes, exactly three network hosts are declared, and a zero-dependency standalone restore CLI ships in every release so recovery survives the plugin itself breaking.
bad: It is explicitly pre-1.0 and the README urges keeping a second independent backup alongside it — the correct advice, and an admission that this cannot yet be the only copy. Backups are content-addressed blobs plus manifests, so the Dropbox folder is not human-browsable; recovery depends on the plugin or its CLI. The token section concedes a structural limit it cannot fix: Obsidian does not isolate secrets per plugin, so any other installed plugin can read the stored token through the same secret store. Dropbox itself is a third-party dependency — the backup leaves the user's own machines by design.
didnt: Board: content-addressed versioned backup with hierarchical retention guarded by a safety floor, previewable pruning, secret-store token custody with a fully stated threat model and a break-glass restore path independent of the plugin is a reference design for the wiki's own backup layer. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ztsd Vault Backup
good: Whole-vault backup with the two safety properties that matter most, stated as design: every archive (tar + Zstandard, built fully in-process with no shell commands or external binaries) carries a sidecar SHA-256 checksum that is validated before any restore is attempted, and restoration never overwrites the live vault — the snapshot extracts into a dedicated timestamped folder in the recovery directory so files can be reviewed and merged by hand. The safety section enumerates the reasoning (no destructive overwrites, no shell spawning so no command-injection or path-with-spaces failures, cache and trash folders excluded), and backups are manual or on demand from settings, keeping the user in the loop.
bad: Two catalogue claims do not survive the source: the catalogue described GFS time-tiered retention, but the README's pruning is a simple maximum-count limit (keep the last N archives) with no grandfather-father-son tiers; and the catalogue name spells it 'Ztsd' where the plugin itself is 'Zstd Backup'. Backups are whole-vault archives, so there is no per-file history or incremental restore granularity, and excluding .obsidian means plugin configuration is outside the backup by design. Local-only: the archive protects against vault corruption, not loss of the machine holding both vault and backups.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): checksum-verified, non-destructive restore into a separate recovery folder corroborates the restore discipline the wiki requires of any backup route; the catalogue's retention claim is corrected in-row. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gitbin
good: Git-based vault sync that keeps readable files in the user's own repository (several vaults can share one repo, each in its own folder), works offline and syncs on reconnect, keeps credentials in Obsidian's secret storage, and offers a review surface to browse sync history and compare local, remote and merged files. Hidden configuration folders stay local, on-demand download keeps large vaults light on small devices, and a phone can be set up by scanning from an existing device.
bad: The core mechanism is the problem: concurrent text edits are merged automatically by CRDT, so two devices' competing edits to the same passage resolve without either writer — or any reviewer — ever seeing a conflict or making a decision; that is exactly the silent auto-resolution the owner's design rejects (multi-writer automatic merging is a rejected-by-design capability in the wiki's own gap map). Attachments resolve as whole competing versions with no merge at all. The README's own warning adds that symlinked files or folders may cause sync to read or modify files outside the vault, and mobile support is experimental and untested on physical devices. The project is also very young (19 commits, created 2026-10-05).
didnt: Rejected: automatic CRDT merging of concurrent edits removes the human-visible conflict step the wiki's custody model depends on. Its credential storage, history review view and candid symlink warning are credited in-row. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Selective Publisher
good: Selective publishing to a Git repository with a real review step: notes and attachments are filtered by a composable criteria tree (tag including hierarchical subtags, frontmatter key/value with regex, folder, title, path and body-content regex, combined with AND/OR/NOT), and before anything moves, a preview modal lists the matching files with their status against the target repository — new, modified, deleted, unmodified. The user can then commit locally only, or commit and push. The developer-policy disclosures are stated in the README: network use is only the Git remote sync, and the out-of-vault file access is exactly the target repository directory and the git command.
bad: The preview is a setting, and the README documents turning 'Show preview before publishing' off — at which point publishing becomes one click from ribbon to push. Criteria include full-body regex content matching, so a note can be selected for publication by text deep inside it that the author may not associate with the publishing rule. It drives a local Git clone with the user's own Git credentials, so its safety inherits whatever that clone and its remote allow, and the README's own related-projects section concedes richer rivals (Enveloppe, Quartz Syncer, Digital Garden) exceed it in link and frontmatter processing.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): criterion-tree selection plus a status preview before any commit corroborates the publish-gate pattern used by the wiki's own staging flows. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wiki-platform bridges (grouped: GitHub Wiki, XWiki Publisher, Vault to Notion)
good: The named bridge syncs a vault folder to a GitHub repository's wiki (the .wiki.git repo), so wiki pages can be edited as ordinary Obsidian notes. Its network behaviour is disclosed with unusual precision: exactly four user-controlled triggers (manual sync, sync on startup, debounced auto-sync on file change inside the wiki folder, and an opt-in periodic timer that defaults to off), no telemetry, and no destination other than the configured wiki repository. Top-level files in the folder map to wiki pages, and the plugin is mobile-compatible.
bad: The recommended sign-in routes through an OAuth App owned by the plugin author and requests GitHub's full repo scope — far broader than one wiki repository — and the README notes signing out removes the token from the device only, leaving the grant live until revoked in GitHub settings. A pasted classic PAT carries the same broad scope. GitHub wikis are a flat page namespace, so a folder of notes maps onto a platform with no folder structure, no review flow and public-by-default visibility on public repos. The named repo is small and young (14 commits, 2 stars).
didnt: Corroboration: an enumerated-trigger network disclosure and a folder-scoped bridge to an external wiki platform corroborate the bridge pattern; judged on the named repo, with the group's other two bridges not separately opened. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Charts for Bases
good: A chart layout for Obsidian Bases built with pure SVG and zero dependencies — the rendering is entirely its own code, so there is no chart-library supply chain and no AI generation step anywhere in the path: the chart shows the notes the Bases query returns, aggregated by the chosen X-axis property, optionally split into series by a second property, with reference lines, value labels and legend placement configurable. It is the most actively maintained of the three Bases-chart implementations catalogued (110 commits, 29 releases), and its documentation is a downloadable sandbox vault where every layout and option is demonstrated as live notes.
bad: It is a rendering layer only: charts are computed from whatever the Bases query returns, with no validation of the underlying values, so a miscategorised property produces a confident wrong chart. Aggregation by category can hide row-level detail behind sums, and the README is brief — configuration is documented mainly through the sandbox vault rather than in text. As the third Bases-chart implementation in this catalogue, it also shows the category is crowded with overlapping small projects.
didnt: Corroboration: a dependency-free, query-faithful chart view corroborates the Bases visualisation layer; its lack of any AI generation path is the relevant contrast with the rejected entry in B171. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Claude Sync
good: What it does, it does simply: it polls a watched folder (default ~/Downloads/Claude Exports, paired with a companion Chrome extension) and imports new Markdown files into a vault folder, preserving the subdirectory structure, skipping files that already exist in the vault so nothing is duplicated, with a manual sync command alongside the automatic polling.
bad: The premise is the ground for rejection: session-transcript ingest is unapproved by the owner, and this automates it end-to-end. The defaults make it worse — 'Delete after import' is Enabled by default, so the original export files are removed once copied, destroying the untouched source a real ingest must preserve; and re-import requires deleting the vault copy first, so there is no update or supersession path, only first-copy-wins. The repo is minimal (2 commits, a prebuilt main.js with no source), so the behaviour cannot be audited beyond the README's description.
didnt: Rejected: automatic Claude chat-export import is session-transcript ingest, which the owner has not approved (same ground as Tapedeck in B166 and AI Session Atlas in B169), and its delete-after-import default would destroy source exports. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Aegis Note Locker
good: Focused local encryption: protect a note body or selected top-level frontmatter values with password-derived, authenticated encryption, the password held only in session memory with timeout controls, batch locking, encrypted backup export and recovery of the last supported operation. The README is candid about the central limitation — unlocking can leave plaintext on disk and clearing the session does not re-encrypt it — rather than claiming the note is never exposed.
bad: The business model is the disqualifier: encryption operations are metered through a connected account — five lifetime operations free, then paid packs (50 operations for $2 up to 1,200 for $14) — so protecting one's own notes becomes a per-action purchase tied to an external account, and basic usage events are sent to a third-party domain (atcdn.cyou) even though note contents are not. Under the owner's money rules, a tool that charges per protection operation and phones home usage events is not an acceptable custody layer. The README also concedes the protection is porous in use: unlocking can leave plaintext on disk, and clearing the password session does not re-encrypt it.
didnt: Rejected: metered, account-connected pricing for the act of encrypting one's own notes, with usage-event telemetry, fails the owner's money and custody rules regardless of the local cryptography, whose honest plaintext caveat is credited in-row. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: age encryption family (grouped: AGE Crypto, Age Encrypt, Halfday Rune)
good: Note and selection encryption in the age format (X25519) via a bundled TypeScript implementation — an earlier version shelled out to the age CLI; the bundled form runs on desktop and mobile with no external binaries. Key hygiene is the study point: each device generates its own local identity key, the identity is deliberately not stored in Obsidian plugin data (so it does not sync), public recipients sync instead, and one encrypted block can be addressed to every listed device's recipient so each opens it with its own key. The Security section states the failure modes plainly — back up each identity, a shared private key is compromised and must be rotated, ciphertext changes on every encryption, which is normal for age.
bad: Key loss is total: a note encrypted only to a lost device identity cannot be decrypted with a newly generated key, so the per-device model multiplies the number of keys whose backup is critical. After decryption the editor holds plaintext until the user re-encrypts, and armored blocks break if stored inside Markdown tables (Obsidian converts their newlines), both stated at source. The recipient list lives in synced plugin data while identities stay local, so a mis-synced recipient list can produce blocks a device cannot open. GPL-3.0 keeps the family ideas-only under the licence discipline in any case.
didnt: Corroboration (GPL-3.0, ideas only): per-device age identities kept out of synced data, with multi-recipient blocks and plainly stated loss semantics, corroborate the age-based encryption direction the wiki's own sealed-backup thinking uses; judged on the named repo. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CipherLink
good: Encrypted notes that keep the graph alive: each secure note is a public Markdown envelope holding only metadata the user explicitly chooses to expose (title, aliases, tags, status, relationship links) plus an encrypted body stored as a separate age object, so native search, tags, backlinks and Graph view keep working while the body stays ciphertext. Decrypted text is edited in an in-memory secure editor and is never inserted into the outer document, written to temporary files, plugin data or logs; the unlock password is never saved and the age identity is stored only in passphrase-protected form. An optional gateway mode can hold authoritative encrypted versions with conflict control and audit, but standalone use needs no server, and the privacy section states standalone mode makes no network requests at all.
bad: The envelope is a deliberate exposure: titles, aliases, tags, status and chosen relationship links are readable by sync software, other plugins and local AI tools, so the metadata itself must be treated as public — the graph survives precisely because the structure leaks. The README concedes it cannot isolate plaintext from a malicious plugin in the same Obsidian process, gateway deployment acceptance is still pending, mobile acceptance is explicitly deferred and untested, and losing both the identity package and its password makes standalone notes unrecoverable. The project is young (16 commits, version 0.1.1).
didnt: Board: the envelope/object split — only explicitly chosen metadata public, bodies as age objects, plaintext never persisted — is a reference design for encrypted notes inside a working graph, with its exposures stated by its own author. Nothing adopted yet. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cloud KMS Encryption
good: Transparent encryption of secret blocks inside notes and of whole binary files, using envelope encryption: each block or file gets a unique AES-256-GCM data key wrapped by an AWS KMS master key, the encryption context is bound to vault name, file path and format version, data keys are zeroed after use, and decrypted content exists only in process memory — never on disk. Identity is the AWS credential chain (SSO, IAM role) rather than a plugin password, so every key use is logged in CloudTrail and access is managed with IAM policy, including multi-account patterns the README documents. The release engineering is verifiable: SLSA provenance, cosign signatures and an SBOM ship with each release, a pre-commit hook guards against plaintext leaks to Git, key rotation tooling is provided, and a CLI can decrypt without Obsidian — so the vault is never hostage to the plugin.
bad: One behaviour cuts against the headline: the README's own behaviour table says that if KMS is unavailable on save, the file is saved as-is with an error shown — for a marked secret block, that means plaintext reaches disk precisely when the key service fails. Transparency is achieved by monkey-patching the vault adapter, which the README lists as a known limitation and which couples the vault's every read and write to the plugin's health. The model also requires an AWS account and working credentials on every device, so vault access inherits AWS availability and IAM correctness; a lost or mis-scoped KMS key makes the ciphertext permanent.
didnt: Corroboration (strong): envelope-encrypted secret blocks with context binding, audited key access, verifiable releases and an Obsidian-free decryption path corroborate the sealed-content design space; the plaintext-on-KMS-failure save behaviour is recorded as its sharpest defect. Nothing adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Environment Keys
good: Secrets-by-reference done thoroughly: tokens sit encrypted under a master password inside the vault, notes carry only a key such as {{basic:JIRA_ACME}}, and the plugin substitutes the real value at the last moment, only for hosts on that variable's allow-list, masking the value again in responses. An agent may ask for a new variable but only opens a form for the human to type the value into — the tool rejects a value argument outright — and requests to unlisted hosts wait for the owner's approval; everything runs as a local MCP server with no external service.
bad: Brand new and unproven: created 2026-09-23, 0 stars, single author, and the v2.0 form depends on a companion AI Ecosystem plugin (standalone transition mode is a compatibility bridge). Desktop only, since it needs Node APIs for its local server. The substitution proxy is itself a privileged position — every allowed request passes through the plugin with the real credential in hand at send time.
didnt: Board — the secrets-by-reference vault pattern (name-only references in files, host allow-lists, human-types-the-value creation, refusal-inclusive behaviour) for the gateway credential-design shelf, alongside the AgentPlaybooks row boarded in B142; the consumer form of the rule that agents use credentials without ever seeing them. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Markdown Password
good: A minimal, standard-shaped version of the same idea: typing [|secret|] auto-encrypts it to a [|vault:id|] placeholder, so Markdown files stay clean and sync-safe while the ciphertext lives in a separate vault.json; the master key and decrypted vault key exist only in RAM, and the README states its cryptography plainly (AES-256-GCM, PBKDF2-SHA-256, 100k iterations).
bad: Very small — 8 commits, 3 stars, one release, community listing still 'coming soon'. There is no recovery: lose the master key and the secrets are gone, by its own warning. The stated footgun matters: text typed in the bracket syntax while the vault is locked remains plain text and unprotected, and the README's audit-trail claim ('modifications can be tracked via logs') is asserted rather than demonstrated.
didnt: Corroboration — placeholder-only secrets inside files with a decoupled encrypted store and zero-persistence keys confirm the vault-reference design from the minimal end; gadget scale beside Environment Keys' fuller pattern in this same batch. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CMDS Share
good: Note publishing with the governance stated per backend rather than implied: shares can carry expiry, view counts and revoke/restore where the chosen host enforces them, unsharing is done by unchecking a property in the note itself, and the reader experience (contents, themes, Bases, canvases) is unusually complete. The README's privacy section says plainly which guarantees each host does and does not provide.
bad: The default backend is GitHub Pages, which publishes into a public repository — the opposite default from a private wiki. Even encrypted shares upload images and drawing fonts unencrypted (stated in its own limits), a shared Base publishes every row its filters match, and the managed CMDSPACE instance is invite-only, so the governance features depend on a host most users do not have.
didnt: Corroboration — per-backend governance honesty (expiry, view counts, revocation named as host-dependent, never universal) and unshare-from-the-source-property are the publish-surface manners our Lens already follows; the public-by-default posture is recorded against it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Encrypted note sharing (grouped: Share Note, QuickShare)
good: The mature end of encrypted note sharing (729 stars, 509 commits): notes are encrypted by default with the decryption key carried only in the share link's # fragment, so the hosting server never holds it; the full theme and rendered content travel with the note, the server is self-hostable via a published Docker image, and the README carries a proper Disclosures section (network requests, base64 use, clipboard) written for Obsidian's plugin scorecard.
bad: Encryption covers note text only — attachments are stored unencrypted, stated plainly in its own Encryption section, so an illustrated note leaks its images. Encryption is per-note optional via frontmatter checkboxes (share_unencrypted), so a single property can silently downgrade a share, and the default route is the vendor's note.sx server rather than the user's own host.
didnt: Corroboration — key-in-fragment encrypted sharing with a self-hostable server and printed disclosures is the reference shape for sharing anything out of a private corpus; the unencrypted-attachments caveat is recorded as the standing warning for our own exports. Grouped entry judged on Share Note, the repo the catalogue names. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VaultPack
good: Exports selected notes and Bases views into a self-contained, zero-dependency static site in five modes — plain folder, AES-256 encrypted ZIP, public web, link-only (unguessable folder name, noindex), and a PHP password gate for shared hosting — and labels each mode's protection honestly ('link-only reduces discoverability; it is not access control'). Exports never modify notes, land in brand-new timestamped folders, and use opaque hashed filenames so titles never leak into URLs; a self-check page verifies the host actually blocks the private folder before a password-mode link is shared.
bad: Very young: created 2026-07-04, 19 commits, 3 stars, single author. Desktop only (needs the desktop rendering pipeline), and password mode does not encrypt files at rest nor protect content from the hosting provider — stated by the README itself, but it caps what the strongest web mode can promise.
didnt: Board — mode-labelled export packaging (each output mode printed with what it does NOT protect, plus a verify-the-host self-check before sharing) for the preservation/delivery shelf; the honest-labelling discipline matches our own bag and export practice. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mq
good: Brings mq — a jq-like query language over Markdown node trees — into Obsidian fully client-side via WebAssembly: live query blocks scoped by file/folder/tag, structural selectors (.h1, .todo, .link) that text search cannot express, and vault-wide transforms whose default is a non-destructive report note. The destructive in-place mode asks for confirmation and states how many notes will be affected before touching anything — preview predicts apply.
bad: Tiny and young: 3 stars, 34 commits, not yet on the Community Plugins list (manual install only), single author. Nothing leaves the device, but the in-place overwrite mode exists at all, gated only by a confirmation dialog; the query language is one more syntax to learn beside Dataview's.
didnt: Corroboration — structural queries over the Markdown tree (headings, tasks, links as addressable nodes) confirm the query-over-plain-files direction from a second engine beside CFR Js in this batch, and its confirmation-with-affected-count before bulk writes is our preview-gate shape in miniature. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Graphnosis
good: The plugin half is thoughtfully scoped: local-only by design (talks to a sidecar on localhost, AES-256-GCM encryption at rest), recall with an explicit per-query token budget (100–8,000), engram routing so topics land in separate memory graphs, and a status-bar vitality signal. Its README warns in a highlighted box that the first vault-sync enable imports the whole vault.
bad: The plugin is a thin bridge (9 commits, 0 stars) — the actual memory engine is the separate Graphnosis desktop app and SDK, outside this repo and its Apache-2.0 licence, so the system's custody and behaviour cannot be judged from the opened source. Vault sync pushes modified notes automatically on save once enabled, and catch-up sync imports everything edited anywhere — an ingest posture with no per-item approval, against our gated ingest.
didnt: Rejected — a thin plugin over an external app's opaque 'cortex' means the files stop being the memory, and automatic on-save push plus bulk first import run directly against approval-gated ingest; token-budgeted recall is noted as a commonplace, not a take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ferry
good: Store-and-forward vault transfer with the full safety set our own filings discipline uses: delta parcels (an encrypted zip with a manifest and only changed files, measured against remembered exchange state), a preview with counts before every apply, a snapshot of everything the apply would overwrite, one-command undo of the last unpack, conflicts landing beside the original as named conflict copies — never silently overwritten — and deletions that need an explicit tick every time and go to the trash. One owner per folder, named by a marker, removes merge arbitration entirely, and a 'What Ferry is not' section bounds the claims.
bad: Brand new: created 2026-10-01, 15 commits, 0 stars, single author, untested at any scale. Strictly two-party and manual — the parcel travels by email/USB by hand, the passphrase is shared out-of-band, and the README itself says it is not a backup; state divergence (a lost parcel resent wrongly) is handled by instruction ('resend the same file') rather than machinery.
didnt: Board — the parcel discipline (delta against remembered state, preview-predicts-apply, snapshot-before-write, conflict copies, deletion tick, one-owner folders) as the consumer reference design for agent-filings transport between our own trees. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TaskNotes
good: The mature proof of one-file-per-task: each task is a Markdown note with structured frontmatter, every view (list, kanban, calendar, agenda) is a plain-text Bases query over those files, and there is no plugin database — data stays portable and scriptable. Recurrence is handled properly (RRULE with per-instance completion tracking and optional materialised occurrence notes that inherit planning metadata but not completion history), and computed fields like urgency score live in the .base files where anyone can read them.
bad: Scope is task management, not knowledge memory — nothing here speaks to citation, provenance or retrieval quality. The surface is very large (calendar sync, Pomodoro, webhooks, HTTP API), and a hosted web/iPhone beta (app.tasknotes.dev) now sits beside the local files, so the product's centre of gravity is drifting toward a service.
didnt: Corroboration — one note per tracked item with frontmatter state and file-based views is our tracked-items shape validated at consumer scale (2,223 stars); our tracking lives in the wiki and goals system, so nothing transfers directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Task Vault
good: The closest consumer relative of our delegation discipline in this whole wave: one file per task with a stable UUID, an explicit state machine with legal transitions only, an append-only execution log whose typed entries (decision / comment / blocker) are the memory of the task, and a hard review gate — agents may deliver only to `review`, confirming `done` stays a human act, and an agent may mark done only when carrying a verifiable in-chat approval citation. Its agent API is off by default, localhost-only, per-agent tokened, and routes every write through the state machine and the gate; a Permissions & capabilities section discloses its shell hooks and filesystem access before any scanner flags them.
bad: Brand new and unadopted: created 2026-08-19, 0 stars, community-market listing still pending review, single author. The dispatch/terminal hooks are arbitrary user-configured shell commands (empty by default, but the capability is the risk), and the Apple Reminders sync is a DIY macOS cron script against a hard-coded list name.
didnt: Board — the review-gate pattern stated as a product rule (agents deliver to review, never done; done requires a verifiable approval citation; append-only typed execution log as the record) as the reference design for task-tracking inside our agent team; it corroborates the delegation tiers from the consumer side. Catalogue says 7-state; the source README documents eight states. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Render API
good: Functionally generous: a zero-dependency local REST API plus an MCP stdio bridge exposing rendered vault content — Dataview DQL results, file rendering through the full Obsidian pipeline, HTML/text/JSON output — with a health endpoint and a detailed permissions explanation written for the community-market review.
bad: The door is ungated by our standards, and its own README contradicts itself about the exposure: the Permissions block says the server binds 0.0.0.0 while the FAQ claims it binds only to 127.0.0.1. Authentication is optional (an empty API key means no auth), CORS defaults to *, and the DataviewJS endpoint executes arbitrary JavaScript through the API — code execution as a feature, behind that optional auth.
didnt: Rejected — arbitrary-code execution over an optionally-authenticated endpoint, with a bind-address contradiction between its own permissions disclosure and its FAQ, is the exact door shape our gateway's default-deny and scoped-token design refuses; rendered-content access is already served by our read-only MCP door. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GitHub Tasks
good: Ingest manners worth naming: setup instructs a fine-grained PAT with read-only access to issues, metadata and pull requests, scoped to chosen repos and dedicated to this plugin; imported tasks carry a source id tag (^gh-#######), closed items arrive marked completed, and refresh updates status without overwriting the user's local edits to a task.
bad: One-way only, by its own Usage Notes: completing a task in Obsidian never updates GitHub, so the two records diverge by design. Duplication is a documented behaviour (PRs both opened by and assigned to you appear twice; changing the target note path duplicates everything), and identity rests on a tag the user can edit or delete, after which sync breaks and duplicates accumulate.
didnt: Corroboration — read-only scoped tokens, source-id carriage and non-overwriting refresh are the ingest manners our own external mirrors follow; the one-way divergence is recorded as the accepted cost of a mirror, not a sync. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agile Task Notes
good: Does one job directly: pulls Jira or Azure DevOps tasks assigned to you into per-task notes with starter content, generates a local sprint kanban, and refreshes on an interval or on demand — the Azure DevOps half is at least aimed at the tracker our own team uses.
bad: Two disqualifying behaviours, both stated in its own README: the API key/PAT is stored in plain-text settings ('put your API key in at your own risk'), and the generated kanban board is destroyed and replaced on every update, deleting any manual changes with it; the README further advises backing up task notes because bugs in the code could remove them.
didnt: Rejected — plaintext credential storage and regenerate-by-destruction of a user-edited artefact run against both our credential custody and our never-discard rules; kept as the cautionary record for tracker-to-notes imports. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Completed Tasks to Notes
good: Turns a checked task into a first-class, citable note: the generated note carries topic (nearest heading), completion date, full heading path and a source link back to the original note and heading, with indented context and links preserved. The safety discipline is the point — the original task is removed only after the new note has been created and verified, tasks edited mid-conversion are left untouched, and filename collisions get numeric suffixes instead of overwrites.
bad: New and tiny: created 2026-07-31, 19 commits, 0 stars, single author, shipped partly as a compiled main.js at repo root. Note identity is weak — filename is completion date plus a 40-character slug of the task text — and the optional regex cleanup presets can strip formatting (links, callouts, comments) from the generated record, trading fidelity for tidiness.
didnt: Corroboration — verify-before-delete conversion with a source backlink is our completion-record shape (a finished item becomes a standalone, linked, searchable record; nothing is removed until its replacement is verified). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CFR Js
good: A from-scratch, Dataview-compatible query engine (TABLE/LIST/TASK blocks, inline expressions, a JavaScript API) built explicitly for performance on large vaults: incremental tag/folder/link indexes so FROM never scans the vault, per-version shared page rows, dependency-tracked view refresh, and a published benchmark harness (10,000-note generated vault). Its Differences from Dataview and Security sections are candid, including that JavaScript execution can be turned off entirely, leaving the safe query subset.
bad: Days old and unproven: 4 commits, 0 stars, single author; the performance claims rest on the author's own bench harness, not independent measurement. The cfrjs blocks and inline $= expressions execute JavaScript written in notes with the same permissions as Obsidian itself (stated in its Security section) — the off switch mitigates, but the default posture executes note code; CALENDAR views and recursive subtask completion are not implemented.
didnt: Corroboration — a second independent structural-query engine in the same batch as mq confirms query-over-plain-files as commodity capability; its benchmark-harness honesty (claims tied to a reproducible generator) is noted for our own evaluation pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bases Serializer
good: Freezes a dynamic Bases view into real static Markdown — links become real links visible to Graph, Search and Publish — wrapped in sentinel comments keyed to the view, so re-running refreshes only that block in place and everything else in the note is untouched. A Freeze mode drops plain Markdown with no markers for a final baked note. Read-only with respect to the queried notes; pure logic (sentinels, rendering) is separated from Obsidian imports and unit-tested; the AI-assisted authorship is disclosed in the README with an Assisted-by git trailer convention.
bad: Brand new (created 2026-10-12, days before this study) with 0 stars and one release; requires Obsidian 1.10+ with the public Bases API and cannot serialize the built-in Table/Cards views because QueryController is opaque. The frozen output is a copy that can go stale, and the optional auto-serialize mode rewrites it on data change (debounced), so a snapshot can drift without a human re-checking it.
didnt: Corroboration — sentinel-keyed managed regions refreshed in place, with the source of truth (the base query) kept beside its snapshot, is our derived-view discipline again; alongside Bases Serializer in the same wave, TaskNotes and GitHub Tasks corroborate the one-note-per-task plus generated-view pattern. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Almagest
good: An independent LLM wiki converging on our core shape: dropped-in sources become watched ingest tasks whose change logs can be approved, cancelled, edited and questioned; every agent change to the knowledge base gets a dedicated changes page with an approve or deny path; a human wiki-view (home, timeline, library) is generated over a tool/ core where agents work via MCP; a Librarian checks material out into copies with a ledger and proposes edits back as one change on Return; Safe delete moves unlinked pages to a trash folder and shows the links when something does link; journals stay in place even after ingest. The Disclosures section is exemplary — external binary, files read outside the vault, clipboard behaviour, no telemetry, all stated.
bad: The plugin is only the interface: the real system is the separate Almagest agent plugin and binary, installed through the Claude Code marketplace, so the approval machinery cannot be judged from this repo alone. Created 2026-10-07 with 0 stars — days old and unproven. Agent terminal handling is macOS-centric (custom command needed elsewhere), the binary also takes 'quiet snapshots', and its approve/reject surface lives inside the app, the opposite of our owner's ruling that approvals happen in chat, not in a portal.
didnt: Corroboration (strong) — a from-scratch LLM wiki independently arriving at ingest tasks, change pages, approve-everything gating, checkout ledgers and safe delete validates our architecture choices; the in-app approval surface is noted as a deliberate difference, not a model. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AI Co-Editor
good: A review layer, not an AI: when a connected agent edits a note, the edit becomes a proposal rendered in the note itself — struck deletions, green insertions, accept/reject per change — with per-author colours, an audit note of who changed what and when, a snapshot kept before every external edit, %%protect%% sections no collaborator can change, and per-folder modes (approval everywhere, auto-merge in scratch, off). Concurrent edits are three-way merged at word level with conflicts keeping the user's version, proposals survive Obsidian being closed, and the plugin itself makes no network requests.
bad: The premise is live multi-AI co-editing of the same notes — the multi-writer direction our system rejects by design in favour of a single writer with gated proposals. Young and small (3 stars, created 2026-07-07); the Claude/Perplexity bridges are separate scripts needing API keys in the environment, and tools that edit files directly are picked up only by watching the vault, so attribution depends on a collaborator marker file the tool must write voluntarily.
didnt: Corroboration — per-word attribution, protected sections, snapshots before external edits and proposals that wait for a human decision corroborate our editor's review mechanics; the live co-editing premise itself stays rejected by design. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Agent Annotations
good: Turns reading into a work queue for an agent: select a passage, write the change you want, keep reading; the annotations wait in a pane as this round's pending list, each anchored with the selected text plus heading path and ~40 characters of prefix/suffix context. The handover protocol for the consuming skill is the careful part: answer every row, delete an id only after it succeeds, leave failures in place, and if the process crashes before write-back leave the file untouched — a crash-safe, no-silent-loss queue contract, with outcomes reported in chat rather than written back into the queue file.
bad: The queue lives in plugin state under .obsidian/, not in the notes or git, so the record of what was asked is not part of the vault's own history. Very young (14 commits, 0 stars, created 2026-09-07), and the flow depends on the user installing the companion skill into each agent's skills directory by hand.
didnt: Board — the answer-every-row, delete-only-on-success, crash-leaves-the-file-untouched queue protocol is a filings/ask-queue processing contract worth boarding for our own agent queues. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obelisk
good: Inline comments and suggested edits anchored the way our citation discipline anchors claims: by the quoted text itself. The README states the rule outright — a line number is never an anchor, because a model asked for one produces a plausible wrong number that attaches a comment to the wrong paragraph without looking like an error. A suggestion applies only if the anchored text is unchanged, detaches (flagged, never silently moved or dropped) when its passage is edited, and reattaches if the text returns. Agent writes are frontmatter-only, leave the body byte-identical, re-read the file first and refuse if it changed underneath; model comments are badged with an origin and a shared review-pass id; the MCP server is stdio, spawned per session, no port and no daemon.
bad: The author says it plainly: 'Early... None of it has been exercised against a large vault' (2 stars, created 2026-08-31). Storing every comment thread in the note's own frontmatter makes the metadata block grow with review history and puts the review record inside the file it reviews.
didnt: Corroboration (strong) — quote-as-anchor, refuse-to-apply-on-change, re-read-before-write and run-badged agent review passes are our anchoring and write discipline arrived at independently. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Redline
good: PR-style review for vault documents with the protocol-based design our sidecars use: comments live in a documented plain-Markdown .review.md sidecar, so any tool — a script, an AI assistant, a coworker — can read the open comments, edit the source and flip the status, with no binding to a specific downstream tool. Anchors use Obsidian's native ^blockref markers and survive reflow; an anchor whose block was edited away is flagged stale with one-click reattach from saved context; a cross-doc dashboard lists every reviewed document with open/stale/overdue counts; renaming, moving or deleting a source mirrors onto its sidecar.
bad: The 'source document stays clean' pitch is only half true: anchoring injects ^blockref markers into the source itself — the sidecar is clean, the source gains markup. Small and young (3 stars, created 2026-05-18), and the README states the UI components are verified manually, with automated tests covering only the parser and block-id logic.
didnt: Corroboration — documented sidecar review files, stale-anchor detection with reattach, and a vault-wide review dashboard corroborate our review-surface design; the anchor-injection caveat is recorded against it. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Sidemark
good: Comments and suggested edits in sidecars following MRSF, an open specification other tools already read and write (VS Code extension, CLI, MCP server), so the review record is not one plugin's private format. Anchoring follows the W3C TextQuoteSelector pattern and keeps both the reviewer's original selected_text and the current anchored_text, so drift is shown rather than hidden; orphaned comments get a re-anchor flow. Two abstention-grade rules: the plugin never rewrites a sidecar it cannot fully parse (it shows the error and leaves the file alone), and accepting a suggestion is refused — HTTP 409 over its REST surface, changing nothing — when the passage cannot be found, appears more than once, or has changed since the suggestion was made; comment edits support an expected_text optimistic guard the same way. Its deliberate divergences from the spec are documented in a table.
bad: Young and little-used (2 stars, created 2026-09-16), and an acknowledged fork that changes where Tandem Comments stores its data rather than a new model. Read/unread state is kept in per-device plugin settings, not the sidecar, and the README documents a wart: undoing an accepted suggestion restores the note's text but leaves the suggestion marked accepted until it is manually reopened.
didnt: Board — the MRSF-style open sidecar spec, selected-vs-anchored drift fields, refuse-to-write-what-you-cannot-parse and 409-on-changed-passage guards are boardable for our review and claim sidecars. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Annotex
good: Publishes a note to a self-hosted server you run, where invited colleagues comment inline on the rendered text; a stable document id in frontmatter keeps the same comment thread across renames and re-publishing, and comments survive edits by re-anchoring on quoted text. The discussion is mirrored back into the vault as a sidecar JSON beside the note, refreshed on open and publish, so it versions and backs up with the note instead of living only on the server. Token hygiene is right: a publish token scoped to publishing only is preferred over the master admin token, and the network disclosure lists exactly the two endpoints used and states there is no telemetry.
bad: The author states the asymmetry plainly: the vault sidecar is a one-way mirror — the server stays the live hub and the copy is not yet re-imported to rebuild the server from the vault. Rendering flattens wikilinks to display text and drops embeds. Twelve commits, 0 stars, v0.2 — a sketch of the pattern, not a proven system.
didnt: Corroboration — a hosted annotation layer whose record is mirrored back into the vault, with a scoped publish-only token, corroborates our hosted-surface and credential-scoping instincts; the one-way mirror is the gap to avoid. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Git History Reviewer
good: Lets a meticulous vault owner walk every commit, read each diff, tick off files as reviewed, and approve commits — with the review state engineered so it can never pollute the history it reviews: approvals are keyed by commit hash in a data file the plugin auto-adds to .gitignore (untracking it if it was somehow tracked), and a status pill continuously verifies the exclusion with git check-ignore, turning orange with a one-click fix if the protection ever lapses. The multi-device section states its own failure modes plainly — state is read once at startup and sync is whole-file last-writer-wins — instead of hiding them.
bad: Nine commits and 0 stars; desktop-only because it shells out to git. The documented sync caveats cut deep in practice: review on a second device without reloading first and your next tick writes older state back over the synced file, silently losing approvals — mitigated by instructions, not by the design.
didnt: Board — hash-keyed review state kept out of the history it reviews, plus a live guard that verifies the exclusion is actually in force, is directly applicable to our checkpoint and review bookkeeping. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GitHub Review
good: Reviews GitHub issues and PRs from inside Obsidian without forking the source of truth: every comment, close and review writes straight back to GitHub, approvals use GitHub's native PR review so branch protection recognises them, and nothing is stored locally. The AI-context door is designed the safe way — a read-only stdio MCP server, spawned on demand, that exposes only the item you have open and holds no token at all ('your GitHub token never leaves the plugin'). The token guidance is a fine-grained PAT with an explicit minimal permission table (Contents read; PRs and Issues read/write; Metadata read).
bad: Against its own good design, the fine-grained PAT is stored in plaintext in the vault's data.json — the README warns about it in bold, but a synced vault still carries a write-capable token in clear text, where the secrets-by-reference pattern elsewhere in this wave exists precisely to avoid that. The plugin also auto-writes the vault's .claude/mcp.json to register itself, a convenience that mutates agent configuration unasked, and its named AI client is Claudian, which the owner has rejected; 13 commits, 2 stars.
didnt: Corroboration — native-review passthrough (never fork the source of truth) and a tokenless, read-only, on-demand MCP context door corroborate our gateway instincts; the plaintext token storage and auto-registration are recorded as anti-patterns. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Research Source Review
good: Built for exactly our citation problem: when a conclusion depends on a passage in another note, pin the approved text; a scan compares the current passage literally and shows both versions side by side. Approval is guarded the way our re-verification is — it re-reads the source and stops if the text differs from the passage you were shown, rejects approval when the saved baseline changed during another review, and a missing block or missing source keeps the baseline and offers no approval button at all.
