The honesty is thorough: the FAQ states the comparison detects a literal text change only, not whether a claim is correct, and a 'What did you not test?' section lists phones, Linux, large vaults and concurrent sync writes. Its GitHub token is held in Obsidian's secret storage, not settings.
bad: Two commits, created 2026-10-14 — a week old at study time and essentially unproven. Scope is narrow by design: Markdown paragraph blocks with explicit IDs only (no headings, lists, tables, PDFs or images), and ambiguous duplicate IDs are ineligible. Grouping and dated reports are paywalled behind a GitHub Sponsors Pro tier, and the settings open a promotional What's-new tab suggesting the author's other plugins (an off-switch exists).
didnt: Board — approve-against-a-fresh-read with stop-on-mismatch, and no approval path at all when the source is missing, is our citation re-verification discipline in plugin form and worth boarding for the claim lifecycle. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Permanent Ink
good: An editor built on never erasing: in restricted mode Backspace and Delete strike words through instead of deleting them, Undo and Cut are blocked, and new text can only be added at the end, so the document keeps a visible record of how the thinking evolved — the append-only, history-preserving instinct of our logs and corrections ledger applied at keystroke level. Highlights and strikethroughs carry comments, and longer asides live as ordinary Markdown files pinned into the text and tied by a property, so they survive renames and moves. Its debt to the annotations plugin it grew from is credited, with the original MIT notice kept in NOTICE.md.
bad: It is a personal writing-discipline tool, not a knowledge system: nothing here manages sources, claims or retrieval. Blocking Undo and Cut is hostile as a default for real editing work, and the whole mode is a per-note opt-in a writer must choose to suffer. Two stars, 20 commits — a niche experiment.
didnt: Corroboration — write-forward, strike-don't-erase editing echoes our append-only conversation log and never-delete-a-correction rule at editor scale. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Preserve Frontmatter Formatting
good: Fixes a real corruption vector: Obsidian rewrites a note's whole frontmatter block whenever any plugin touches one property — comments, quoting, blank lines and inline lists are destroyed, even by a plugin that only read the properties. This plugin splices only the changed property, leaves every other line byte-identical, and writes nothing at all for a no-op change; it covers other plugins without their cooperation. Its fallback rule is the discipline we want in our own writers: when it cannot prove a change can be spliced faithfully (YAML anchors and aliases), it falls back to Obsidian's own rewrite for that change — never making a note worse than the platform would. The limits are stated in a dedicated 'deliberately does not do' section, and the documentation is a runnable demo vault.
bad: To reach the formatting before it is lost it replaces processFrontMatter() rather than wrapping it, so another plugin that patched the same method earlier is silently not called for Markdown files — a load-order side effect on other plugins. A value that does change comes back in default style (a changed quoted string returns unquoted), and comment survival beside a rewritten property is bounded by the yaml library's admittedly unstable comment handling.
didnt: Board — minimal-diff writes, no-op-writes-nothing, and fall-back-when-unprovable are directly boardable write discipline for our frontmatter and schema-migration tooling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OpenContent
good: A workbench for sourced writing built on the same skeleton as our claim system: Material → Knowledge → Claim/Evidence → Artifact → an independent five-axis Critic → a human APPROVED decision, with drafts and review records as Markdown in the vault and a kernel holding state and gates. Evidence discipline is strict in the way ours is: a quotation must be a locatable verbatim slice of the material, and a draft that alters a number or a negation or invents a source is rejected, not quietly 'fixed' into different evidence; an invalid Knowledge ID is never rebound to another item. Approval binds the current text and its dependency versions, so changing the text, the material or the shared charter invalidates the old approval, and an unapproved draft can be copied for preview but never exported as a finished work. The disclosures are unusually complete, including that the local CLI processes are not a sandbox.
bad: Verified only on Windows desktop (Obsidian 1.13.7) and the README states three symbolic-link tests still fail there on permissions; the community download deliberately excludes the Python kernel, so full use means hand-installing Python 3.12+, dependencies and an authenticated Codex or Claude CLI — a heavy, fragile setup. Zero stars, 20 commits, and the package also carries channel machinery (WeChat drafts, Qimao market rankings) well beyond its evidence core.
didnt: Board — verbatim-quote evidence binding with reject-don't-repair, approval that dies when its inputs change, and kernel-as-authority over the rendering surface are a direct parallel to our claim, citation and approval model, and one of the strongest finds in this batch. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vault MCP Connector
good: The hosted-door design our own gateway has not yet built, done carefully in its default paths: hosted clients see only an allowlisted derived index approved by the plugin; write tools are disabled by default and, when enabled, only queue proposals — a proposal for an existing note must carry the current content hash, stale hashes and non-indexed notes are refused before storage, and the plugin still re-checks the live file hash, shows a diff, backs up, audits and requires approval before applying. Denied paths stay unavailable even if a client guesses an id or exact path; fetched content is labelled to the client as untrusted reference material; local filesystem access is off by default, time-boxed per session, gated by an exact user-intent phrase per call, and the hosted bridge must be re-armed every session, resetting to Off on reload.
bad: The same product ships a 'GOD mode' one selector away: direct read/write/create/move/delete across the entire local filesystem with — in its own words — no proposal and no additional approval, which negates the careful proposal machinery for anyone who flips it. MCP and sync tokens are stored in the vault's plugin data; it is a public alpha (0 stars) whose default hosted server is the author's own Vercel deployment, so the default path trusts a third party's server with the approved index.
didnt: Board — the allowlist-only index, hash-carrying write proposals with live re-check, diff, backup and audit before apply, and session-only arming are boardable design evidence for the hosted door; the door itself remains an owner-gated decision, and GOD mode is recorded as the anti-pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Koda
good: The write rule is stated as unbypassable and it is the right shape: the agent writes freely only inside its own folder; anything else — writing, moving, editing the note you are in — opens a dialog showing the full text or a line diff first, and deleting and writing skills always ask. Everything that steers it (instructions, memory, skills) is a Markdown note the owner can read and edit; every tool call appears in the chat so an answer shows which notes it rests on; it runs against a local model by default so notes need not leave the machine; long conversations compact old tool results before touching the user's own messages.
bad: AGPL-3.0-or-later, which settles the disposition before the design is weighed: nothing here can be adapted, only learned from. Beyond the licence, other plugins can lend Koda their tools (each toggleable, but a supply-chain surface inside the approval loop), and while local models are the default story, a hosted endpoint with an API key sends note content to that provider.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0-or-later places it in the ideas-only class under licence discipline, and its one transferable idea (an approval dialog no tool can bypass) is already our gateway's core rule. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Convert to Markdown
good: Converts PDFs, Office files, ebooks, email, notebooks, subtitles, spreadsheets and images to Markdown entirely on the machine — deterministic structural parsing (the same file always produces byte-identical output), local Tesseract OCR for pixels, no LLM, no API key, nothing uploaded. The provenance discipline is the standout: coverage is written into the frontmatter as fractions (pages_converted: 40/40); anything dropped is named in a callout, never merely counted ('3 items skipped tells you nothing you can act on'); invoice and statement fields are labelled missing_fields, guessed_fields, ocr_fields or ambiguous_fields, and the figures are cross-checked against each other with any mismatch stated with both numbers. OCR reports its confidence and which pages it touched; conversion never overwrites an existing note.
bad: Desktop-only (Node zlib). The 'fully offline' headline has one disclosed exception: the OCR engine downloads the first time an image or scanned PDF is converted, unless supplied from the vault. Five stars and created 2026-08-01 — young, and the financial-document extraction is heuristic label-matching that the README itself bounds.
didnt: Board — coverage fractions in the record, named-not-counted drops, and guessed/OCR/ambiguous field labelling with cross-checked figures are ingest-provenance discipline worth boarding for our own conversion and OCR queue. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vaire
type: Obsidian plugin over the vaire CLI (dezemand)
good: Knowledge packages with typed references ([[type:id]], cross-package [[@pkg/type:id]]) and, most valuably, loose ends: a [[?type: descriptor]] reference records an unresolved mention in the text itself and can later be resolved to a real node while keeping the author's original wording as the display text. Renaming a node — where an address is its identity — offers two strategies side by side: tombstone (the default, called release-safe; the old file becomes a redirect with superseded_by set so the old address keeps resolving) and rewrite-in-place, which the dialog flags in red as a MAJOR change and lists the backlinks that will dangle. Dependency packages open read-only; a lockfile can be reproduced exactly and verified against its checksums; a frozen mode refuses anything not already in the store; the access section states plainly that the plugin never writes outside the vault.
bad: The plugin is a shell: every graph-shaped question is answered by spawning the external vaire CLI, so the system's real behaviour and terms live in that separate project, which this row does not judge. Six commits and 0 stars — the surface is freshly built; desktop-only.
didnt: Board — tombstone-by-default renaming with a resolving redirect, and first-class loose-end references that resolve without losing the author's wording, are boardable for our page-identity machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wasl
good: Unlinked mentions for Arabic, where Obsidian's literal matching fails: mentions are caught through prefixes, diacritics, tatweel, a dropped initial hamza and Persian letter variants, each suggestion shows its sentence and the reason it matched, weaker matches are folded into a separate 'possible' section, and nothing is written before a previewed, per-mention confirmation — never a bulk link pass, with an undo for the last link. The written link preserves the author's exact word as display text so a later rename cannot silently change their sentence. The matching limits are argued from the language itself (no stemming, because conflating 'writing' with 'book' makes a wrong link worse than a missed one), and the measurement section is a model of honesty: locked test cases, a run that fell below the author's own threshold reported as such, and daily-use confidence explicitly labelled an impression, not a measurement.
bad: Scope is deliberately narrow: existing titles and aliases only, no roots, plurals or synonyms (the author argues the trade-off rather than hiding it), tanwin is out of the rules, and Android is untested — 'no promise', by the README's own words. One star, created 2026-10-08; the headline corpus figure (~41% of correct mentions) comes from a private novel text that cannot be re-run from the repo.
didnt: Corroboration — script-aware mention detection with reason-carrying, one-at-a-time confirmed suggestions and below-threshold results reported rather than buried corroborates our linking and measurement honesty; the non-Latin handling is the part our i18n corpus work should note. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: graphology
type: npm library — graph data structure specification and reference implementation
good: A specification plus reference implementation for a robust, multipurpose JavaScript graph object — many graph kinds (directed, undirected, mixed, multi-graphs) under one unified interface — and by the npm page's own figures the ecosystem's centre of gravity: version 0.26.0 with 617,689 weekly downloads, far beyond anything else in this batch. A stable, shared graph vocabulary is what lets independent tools exchange graph data without bespoke converters.
bad: It is a data-structure library, not a knowledge system: no persistence, no vault or document semantics, nothing about provenance or review. The npm README is a stub that defers to external documentation, so the page alone cannot support claims about the wider graphology ecosystem packages.
didnt: Corroboration — the standard unified graph model in the JavaScript ecosystem is context for our graph layer's data shapes; our own graph work is not built on it. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @portaljs/remark-wiki-link
good: A remark plugin that parses and renders Obsidian-style wiki links for static publishing: internal links, aliases, heading fragments and embeds, with the three Obsidian path formats (raw, absolute, short) handled explicitly — short paths resolve against a caller-supplied permalink list. Unresolved links are marked, not hidden: the node carries data.exists and a 'new' class so a rendered page can show a link whose target does not exist yet, which is the honest treatment our own renderer aims for.
bad: Note embeds (![[Embed note]]) and audio/video embeds are still on the unchecked future list, so Obsidian content using them renders incompletely; unsupported image formats degrade to showing the raw link string. Ninety weekly downloads — a niche package, and its short-path resolution depends on the caller supplying an accurate permalink list.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent wikilink implementation that marks unresolved links as new instead of dropping or inventing them corroborates our renderer's stance. Nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mdx-wikilink-plus
licence: BSD (PyPI registry record: licence field 'BSD License' and OSI BSD classifier; the catalogue's 'not stated' is corrected at source)
good: Converts Obsidian-style [[wikilinks]] (and the ![[...]] image form, with optional labels after |) into relative links while Python-Markdown renders: base_url/end_url/whitespace/case handling is configurable per instance, a build_url callable and Markdown metadata can override link construction, and page labels are auto-derived from the target path when none is given. Version 1.4.1; author Md. Jahidul Hamid (neurobin).
bad: Unmaintained: the latest release is 1.4.1 of 26 Jul 2022, and the version history is five releases across 2019-2022. It rewrites links at render time only — nothing checks that a wikilink target exists — and it explicitly cannot be combined with Python-Markdown's stock wikilinks extension, nor do its URL configuration options apply to absolute URLs.
didnt: Rejected — stale since 2022 and render-time only: it rewrites wikilinks while converting to HTML but never verifies that a target exists, which is the property a citation-bearing corpus actually needs from its link layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pybtex
licence: MIT (settled at source: the PyPI registry record carries SPDX license_expression 'MIT'; the catalogue's 'not stated' was wrong)
good: A BibTeX-compatible bibliography processor in pure Python (author Andrey Golovizin; repository on Codeberg): reads BibTeX, BibTeXML and its own YAML format, writes LaTeX, HTML, Markdown and plain text, and accepts styles both as classic .bst files and as styles written in Python. Actively maintained — version 0.26.1 of Apr 2026; Python >=3.8.
bad: Its classifiers still declare Development Status '4 - Beta' after two decades of releases, and the workflow is the LaTeX one (it processes the .aux file of a document being typeset): it formats bibliographies — it does not retrieve, resolve or verify the works being cited.
didnt: Corroboration — a maintained, MIT, local bibliography engine exists off the shelf for the formatting side of a citation pipeline; the open problem stays verification of the cited record, which pybtex does not attempt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pybib
licence: BSD-3-Clause (PyPI registry record: SPDX license_expression and OSI classifier)
good: A small command-line tool (author Jonathan Gilchrist) that turns identifiers into BibTeX at the shell: 'bib get <doi>' fetches the entry for a DOI and 'bib search' finds one by author/title fragment, printing BibTeX designed to pipe into bibtool and a reference manager. Version 2.3.2.
bad: The record is thin: the README documents the two commands and little else — no stated lookup backend, error behaviour or offline mode — and a fetched entry is metadata as served by the resolver, with no check that the DOI resolves to the work the author meant to cite. (Studied from PyPI's registry JSON record for the package; the project page itself served a client challenge to this reader.)
didnt: Corroboration — DOI-keyed retrieval is the right join key for citation truth-checking, and pybib shows how small the fetch half is; the check half is what nobody here ships. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bibcites
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: OSI MIT classifier)
good: Annotates a .bib file: for each entry with a DOI it queries the open OpenCitations index and writes the incoming-citation count into the entry's addendum field ('Cited by N in OpenCitations'), with type include/exclude filters, configurable batch sizes and deterministic sorted output. Author Mathieu Daeron; version 2.0.1 of Mar 2025; Python >=3.11.
bad: A citation count is decoration, not evidence: it says nothing about whether the citing works support the claim being made. The tool also depends on a live external API at run time, and its own release history shows fragility — version 2.0.0 was yanked from PyPI over an API-key problem and replaced by 2.0.1.
didnt: Corroboration — the open OpenCitations graph is exactly the substrate a citation truth-checking layer would build on; bibcites itself only stamps counts into bibliographies. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: citeable
licence: BSD-3-Clause (README 'Licence' section of the registry record; the record's free-text licence field itself is empty)
good: Zero-dependency library for declaring software citations as data: structured citation objects validated at construction time (missing fields are named in the error), deterministic citekey generation with automatic letter-suffix collision resolution so independently authored plugins can contribute citations that merge without key clashes, value-based deduplication, and BibTeX export (write_bibtex). The current release (2026.10.15) ships with provenance attestations; Python >=3.11.
bad: Its world is one ecosystem — it exists to collect the citations of cogent3 applications and their plugins — and it validates the shape of a citation, never the truth of the cited record: nothing is retrieved, resolved or checked against the work itself.
didnt: Corroboration — validated citation objects with collision-safe keys assembled from many contributors confirm the citekey-note design direction; assembly-time dedup across independent contributors is the detail worth remembering. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pymarkdown
type: PyPI package — literate Markdown code evaluator (abandoned)
licence: Conflict recorded at source: the PyPI registry record's licence field says 'BSD License', while GitHub's licence detection on the repository reports its LICENSE.txt as Other (NOASSERTION); the licence file itself was not opened this pass, so neither statement is borrowed over the other
good: Matthew Rocklin's 2015 literate-programming microtool: it parses a Markdown document with doctest, executes the code segments sequentially with shared state, and emits a corrected document with computed results inlined — including __repr_html__ rendering for pandas DataFrames and matplotlib/Bokeh figures. Studied from the repository README (the PyPI record's own description is literally 'UNKNOWN').
bad: Abandoned on arrival: created 2015-04-05 as a self-described 'single-weekend project', five PyPI releases all on that one day, and the README opens with 'You should not use this project. You should use knitpy' and its Support section states 'There is none!'. Executing arbitrary document code with exec is also the opposite of a safe ingest path.
didnt: Rejected — an abandoned 2015 weekend project whose own README redirects users elsewhere; the evaluated-documents idea lives on in maintained tools, not here. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mdformat
licence: MIT (settled at source: the PyPI registry record carries SPDX license_expression 'MIT'; the catalogue's 'not stated' was wrong)
good: An opinionated Markdown formatter (maintainer hukkin) with a CLI and a Python API: it formats to CommonMark and validates its own work by checking that the rendered HTML is unchanged, offers a --check mode for CI, wraps prose to a configurable width, and extends via plugins (GFM, front matter, footnotes, MyST, code-block formatters) installed with pipx inject. Built on markdown-it-py with a single direct dependency; version 1.0.0 of Oct 2025; Python >=3.10.
bad: CommonMark-only by design: confronted with Obsidian-, MkDocs- or Hugo-flavoured syntax it backslash-escapes the unfamiliar constructs to protect rendering rather than preserving their meaning, so a vault-flavoured corpus needs its plugin set and still negotiates with an opinionated, take-it-or-leave-it style.
didnt: Corroboration — a formatter that proves its edits render-identical is the right shape for mechanical corpus hygiene; not adopted in-tree, because our pages carry wikilink and frontmatter conventions outside CommonMark that mdformat escapes instead of understanding. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: flake8-markdown
good: Runs real flake8 over the Python and pycon code blocks inside Markdown files (author John Franey), as a CLI ('flake8-markdown <file>') and as a pre-commit hook, so the code samples inside documentation are held to the same lint standard as the codebase. Version 0.6.0; requires flake8 >=5.
bad: Narrow and slow-moving: it speaks only Python (nothing for prose, links or other languages), and its README's own version history stops at 0.5.0 (Sep 2023) although 0.6.0 is the latest release — a single-maintainer cadence. (The registry JSON endpoint served a client challenge to this reader; this row is studied from the fully rendered PyPI project page.)
didnt: Corroboration — linting the code inside the notes is a real, cheap hygiene check class; a prose-and-citation corpus keeps it as a pattern rather than a dependency. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markdownlint-rs
licence: The Unlicense (PyPI registry record licence field and the README's License section agree)
good: A Rust reimplementation of the markdownlint rule set (the mdlint project, distributed through PyPI as prebuilt wheels): check, format (auto-fix where a rule supports it) and migrate commands — the last converts markdownlint-cli2 configuration — over rules MD001-MD060+, with TOML configuration discovered by walking up directories, JSON output, and every deliberate divergence from the upstream defaults tabulated with its reason (e.g. a 120-column default instead of 80). Version 0.3.24; Python >=3.10 for the wrapper package.
bad: Pre-1.0 (0.3.x) and proudly opinionated: because its defaults deliberately differ from canonical markdownlint, its verdicts are not interchangeable with the reference implementation's. And like every linter here it judges shape only — MD042 flags an empty link; nothing checks that a real link still points at what the text claims.
didnt: Corroboration — its per-rule divergence table, each change from upstream stated with a reason, is the honest way to fork a rule set (the same discipline as our renderer's pinned CommonMark divergences); the rule set itself is commodity. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linkcheckmd
type: PyPI package — asyncio Markdown link checker
licence: MIT (the repository named in the PyPI record carries a LICENSE.txt that GitHub's licence detection reads as MIT; the PyPI registry record itself leaves its licence field empty)
good: An asyncio/aiohttp link checker (Michael Hirsch, scivision) that reads Markdown files directly — the static site generator does not have to be running — checks local and remote links at a claimed 10,000 files per second, prints each missing link with its file, and exits with code 22 when any are missing; usable as a library (linkcheckmd.check_links), a CLI, a pre-commit hook or a CI step.
bad: Ageing: the latest PyPI release is 1.4.0 of Feb 2021, and the README itself warns that strict anti-leeching sites produce false positives. It tests whether a link resolves today, not whether the target still says what the citing page claims — liveness, not truth.
didnt: Corroboration — exit-code link liveness over raw Markdown files is the cheap outer ring of link hygiene; the unsolved ring remains target-content drift, which this class of tool does not see. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: md-link-checker
type: PyPI package — Markdown link checker (URLs, sections, paths)
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later (settled at source: the registry record carries SPDX license_expression 'GPL-3.0-or-later' and the README's License section states GPL v3 or later; the catalogue's 'not stated' was wrong)
good: Checks all three link classes in Markdown files — remote URLs, in-document section references, and relative path links — where most checkers in this wave do URLs only (author Mark Blakeney, bulletmark). URLs are deduplicated across all input files before fetching and checked up to 10 in parallel, and the tool is built for one-shot runs via uvx as well as installed use; version 1.10, current (2025 copyright).
bad: GPL-3.0-or-later puts the code itself off-limits under this programme's licence discipline. Its URL checks are live network fetches, which its README admits are slow, and its section/path checks validate that a target exists, not that it still supports the sentence linking to it.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0-or-later is ideas-only here; the idea worth keeping is the three-class coverage (URL + section anchor + relative path) as the checklist shape for link linting. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: py-obsidianmd
type: PyPI package — Obsidian vault batch-metadata library
licence: Conflict recorded at source: the PyPI record's licence field and OSI classifier say MIT, while the README's own License section links its LICENSE.txt as 'BSD 3' — the two statements are recorded as found, neither borrowed over the other
good: A library for batch surgery on an Obsidian vault's metadata (Selim Raboudi): load a vault as a Notes collection, filter notes by metadata, and rewrite in bulk — moving metadata between frontmatter and inline forms, regrouping inline metadata into callouts, adding and removing keys across every note — with a documented API, an example vault to rehearse on, and a single dependency (python-frontmatter). Version 0.1.7.
bad: The README's own warning is to back up the vault before use: the writes are bulk and in place, with no dry-run, diff or approval step visible. It is also stale — 0.1.7 of Dec 2022 is the latest of five releases — pre-1.0, and its licence is stated inconsistently at source (see the licence field).
didnt: Rejected — bulk metadata rewriting without a preview-and-approve gate is the opposite of this corpus's write discipline, and the project is stale with an unsettled licence; the frontmatter-versus-inline metadata duality it manipulates is, though, a real phenomenon of Obsidian-flavoured corpora. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markdown-it-py
type: PyPI package — CommonMark parser (Python port of markdown-it)
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: OSI MIT classifier; the record's free-text licence field is empty)
good: The Python port of markdown-it (Executable Books project; Chris Sewell): a CommonMark-spec parser whose rules are configurable and replaceable, with a plugin architecture (front matter, footnotes and the mdit-py-plugins family), token-stream access for tools that need structure rather than HTML, a command-line interface, documented security configuration, and membership of Google's Assured Open Source Software programme. It is the parser underneath mdformat (this same batch). Production/Stable, version 4.2.0; Python >=3.10.
bad: A parser is a component, not a knowledge system: it turns Markdown into tokens and HTML and knows nothing about whether a link target exists, a citation is real, or a newer page supersedes an older one. A corpus with its own pinned rendering divergences also cannot swap parsers for free.
didnt: Corroboration — this is the reference CommonMark engine of the Python documentation stack, i.e. the commodity layer our own renderer is measured against; everything this programme cares about sits above it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: python-frontmatter
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: license_expression 'MIT', LICENSE file shipped)
good: A small, Production/Stable parser for posts with YAML, JSON or TOML front matter: load a Markdown post, read or edit its metadata, and dump it back with the body intact (round-trip preserved). Repository eyeseast/python-frontmatter; version 1.3.0.
bad: Parsing only: it preserves and rewrites front matter faithfully but validates nothing about the values — no schema, no lifecycle semantics, no check that a metadata key means what a corpus convention says it means.
didnt: Corroboration — front-matter parsing with faithful round-trip is the commodity substrate our pages' metadata rides on; the semantics above it (lifecycle states, citation locks) are ours to enforce, and this library confirms they are not available off the shelf. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mdutils
licence: MIT (PyPI record: licence field and OSI MIT classifier, LICENSE.txt shipped)
good: Convenience helpers for creating Markdown files while Python code executes (maintainer Didac Coll): write, read and append to .md files, and build headers, tables, tables of contents, links, lists and images programmatically instead of hand-writing markup. Version 1.8.1.
bad: Generation only, from a single maintainer: it creates Markdown files from code but reads nothing back semantically — no parsing of an existing corpus, no link-target or citation awareness — so it can produce a document, never check one.
didnt: Corroboration — programmatic Markdown generation is a solved commodity; our generator stays in-tree because it must emit this corpus's own conventions (front matter, wikilinks, citation locks), which a generic helper knows nothing about. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fastmcp
good: The full-featured MCP framework from PrefectHQ: build servers, clients and apps from decorated Python functions, with tool schemas and validation generated from type hints. Its own page records that FastMCP 1.0 was incorporated into the official MCP Python SDK in 2024. Current release 4.1.3.
bad: A framework dependency with a commercial gravity well: the README pitches Prefect Horizon, the vendor's hosted gateway, alongside the library, and adopting the framework means tracking its fast release train (the catalogue's version was stale within this pass) rather than owning a small door outright.
didnt: Corroboration — decorator-to-schema tool generation is the ergonomic pole of MCP authoring, and the official SDK's absorption of this project's 1.0 confirms where the protocol's centre of mass sits; our doors stay hand-rolled standard-library code by deliberate choice, so the framework is evidence, not a dependency. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp
type: PyPI package — official MCP Python SDK
good: The official Model Context Protocol Python SDK (author: Model Context Protocol, a Series of LF Projects, LLC): servers and clients over stdio, Streamable HTTP and SSE, tool definitions generated from Python type hints, plus a CLI and the MCP Inspector. Version 2.3.0.
bad: A heavy dependency tree (Starlette/Uvicorn/Pydantic/httpx and more) for what a small read door does with the standard library alone, and the SDK's surface moves with the specification — a versioned chase that a hand-rolled local door deliberately avoids.
didnt: Corroboration — this is the reference implementation our hand-rolled stdio doors are measured against; the protocol is the standard worth matching, the dependency is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vscotero
licence: no licence stated at source (the PyPI record names none; the repository's licence card reads Other (NOASSERTION) and its root LICENSE file is empty — 0 bytes)
good: Generates Markdown literature notes in a VS Code workspace from a Zotero auto-exported BibTeX file plus the PDF annotations stored in zotero.sqlite, grouping a paper's highlights by annotation colour — so marginalia become structured notes instead of staying trapped inside PDFs. Version 0.3.0.
bad: Unfinished by its own account: the repository TODO list still opens with 'fix the config system', 'confirmation prompt before deletion', 'error handling' and 'better tests'; 41 commits and 0 stars; and there is no licence — the root LICENSE file is empty (0 bytes), so the code is all-rights-reserved in practice.
didnt: Rejected — no licence at source (an empty LICENSE file) makes the code unusable under this programme's licence discipline, and the author's own TODO list concedes the config system, deletion confirmation, error handling and tests are unfinished; the annotation-colour-to-note-structure idea is noted as an idea only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: oarepo-citations
licence: MIT (settled via the repository named in the PyPI record: oarepo/oarepo-citations carries a root LICENSE read as MIT; the PyPI record itself names no licence)
good: Citation-style rendering for the OARepo/Invenio repository ecosystem: renders a record's citation in ISO 690, APA, Harvard, MLA, Vancouver, Chicago, IEEE or BibTeX form, delivered as dropdown and modal UI components. Version 1.0.2.
bad: Formatting only, and only inside one stack: its runtime dependencies are oarepo-runtime and oarepo-ui, so it renders inside the OARepo/Invenio platform and nowhere else — and a style-correct rendering says nothing about whether the cited work exists or supports the claim being made.
didnt: Corroboration — multi-style citation rendering is a commodity component inside repository platforms; the open problem stays verification of the cited record, which no renderer in this wave attempts. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: CESNET (the README's License section: part of the OARepo ecosystem developed by CESNET)

name: word2Tex
licence: MIT (PyPI record: licence field and OSI MIT classifier)
good: Moves manuscripts from Word to LaTeX: its cite2Tex function converts author-year citations into \cite{} keys resolved against a provided .bib file and notifies the user which citations are missing from that bibliography, while fixBibTex normalises EndNote-exported identifiers to AuthorYear form; output always goes to a new file 'to avoid dataloss'. Version 0.0.17.
bad: Narrow and ageing: its classifiers target Python 3.6/3.7 and the version is 0.0.17, and the missing-citation report is only as good as the .bib supplied — a key present in the bibliography is not thereby verified against the work itself.
didnt: Corroboration — reporting which citations in a manuscript have no bibliography entry is the smallest honest form of citation checking, and it is the check half of this wave's citation tooling that actually touches truth; the full check (does the entry resolve to the claimed work) remains unbuilt everywhere here. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: know-do-graph
type: PyPI package — wiki-style knowledge graph store
licence: no licence stated at source (three routes: the PyPI registry record names none, the full README carries no licence section, and a web search surfaced only the PyPI page itself — no repository found)
good: Wiki-style knowledge entries with typed edges and [[wikilinks]], stored in a SQLite database: entries are disabled instead of deleted, keyword search degrades gracefully when embeddings are unavailable, and built-in chat agents answer over — and can edit — the graph. Version 0.1.9.
bad: The SQLite database is the source of truth — the inversion of files-as-truth — and its built-in chat agents include a graph-editing agent with no approval gate described at source. No licence is stated at source after three routes (registry record, full README, web search), so the code is all-rights-reserved in practice.
didnt: Rejected — a database-as-truth custody model with an ungated graph-editing agent is the inverse of this system's files-as-truth, approval-gated design, and with no licence at source the code is ideas-only regardless of fit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markdowncore-ai
type: PyPI package — local Markdown knowledge-base engine (mdcore)
licence: MIT (settled at source: the PyPI registry record carries SPDX license_expression 'MIT' with a LICENSE file shipped; the catalogue's 'not stated' is corrected at source)
good: A local, LLM-agnostic engine ('mdcore') for a personal Markdown knowledge base: it indexes Markdown, PDF, DOCX and TXT files; its search synthesises a cited briefing into an output folder (with a --raw mode that makes zero LLM calls); and its ingest classifies and routes new material, detects conflicts with existing notes, generates a proposal and writes only after explicit approval — with a delta-scan index that asks for confirmation and a printed account of exactly where LLM calls happen. Retrieval is a BM25 pre-filter (rank-bm25) under vector search. Version 1.1.5.
bad: Beta and single-author (Piyush Tyagi), with version drift inside its own record (release 1.1.5, README header 1.1.4). The synthesised briefing is LLM prose over retrieved chunks: citations point at chunks, and nothing locks a briefing to the vault text it was drawn from, so later edits silently desynchronise the two; the stack is heavy (ChromaDB, LangChain, unstructured, FastAPI), its own observability note concedes 'No eval framework — tracing only', and an optional aggregator backend pools free-tier API keys via llm-keypool — a key-pooling posture recorded here and not followed.
didnt: Corroboration — proposal-then-approval ingest with conflict detection against the existing vault is this system's gateway discipline independently built for a personal Markdown base; its unlocked synthesis is exactly the failure our citation lockfile exists to prevent. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-kasten
type: PyPI package — CLI Zettelkasten for LLM agents (kasten)
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: SPDX license_expression 'MIT', LICENSE file shipped; README badge and License section agree)
good: A CLI Zettelkasten for LLM coding agents, explicitly inspired by Karpathy's approach to LLM-maintained personal knowledge bases: plain Markdown notes with YAML frontmatter are declared the source of truth ('Files outlast tools'), indexed by a rebuildable SQLite FTS5 index with [[wiki-link]] backlinks, broken-link and orphan detection, and hub ranking; an optional MCP face exposes exactly 8 read-only tools, every CLI command returns structured JSON, and notes move through a named lifecycle — draft, review, evergreen, stale, deprecated, archive. Version 0.2.0.
bad: Alpha (Development Status 3) from a single author, with both releases uploaded on one day (2026-04-07 in the record). Its repair command auto-promotes notes by word-count heuristics (50+ words to review, 100+ plus links to evergreen) and auto-fills missing tags and summaries — lifecycle movement without a human verdict — and init auto-injects usage docs into CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and sibling agent-config files (recorded as found; not a posture taken here).
didnt: Corroboration — files-as-truth with a rebuildable index, a read-only MCP verb set and a named lifecycle are this system's architecture independently arrived at from the same Karpathy starting point; its auto-promotion by word count marks exactly where our lifecycle requires a verdict instead of a heuristic. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: synto
type: PyPI package — notes-to-wiki compiler (Karpathy LLM Wiki implementation)
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: OSI MIT classifier)
good: The closest full relative in this wave: an explicit implementation of Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern (author kytmanov) in which raw notes are never modified, a local LLM extracts concepts and compiles one cross-linked article per concept, and drafts wait in wiki/.drafts/ behind a three-state lifecycle (draft, verified, published). Rejection reasons are stored and injected into the next compile of that concept — five rejections auto-block it — hand-edits to published articles are protected by a SHA-256 content hash, concept identity is a stable entity_id under aliases, homonyms and senses (with merge candidates surfaced for a human decision instead of silently absorbed, and denial tombstones stopping a removed alias from re-attaching), extracted relations must be backed by a verbatim quote and may only join concepts the vault already knows, and an MCP server exposes the published wiki with drafts hidden by default. Version 0.8.0.
bad: Its own README names the cracks: the concept keep command 'updates the state DB directly; it does not auto-commit and is not reversible with synto undo', relations from a deleted source 'are not garbage-collected yet', and state lives in a gitignored SQLite state.db, so files and database can split — 'git revert on a curation commit will not restore the database'. Draft confidence scores are model-assigned (0-1) and approve --min-confidence can publish in bulk, a bulk-approval path this programme's one-by-one ruling discipline would not take; hand-edit protection is hash detection, not citation locking, so a compiled article can still drift from its sources between compiles.
didnt: Board — two mechanisms this system does not have in this form: the rejection-feedback loop (a rejection reason is stored and injected into the next compile of that concept, with repeated rejections auto-blocking it) and alias denial tombstones (a detached alias is tombstoned so re-ingest cannot silently re-attach it). The rest is the wave's strongest corroboration of the raw/wiki/drafts shape. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rank-bm25
good: A tiny, numpy-only implementation of the BM25 ranking family — Okapi BM25, BM25L and BM25+ — taken from the survey paper it cites, which benchmarks the variants against each other; scoring a query and retrieving the top-n documents take a handful of lines, and the package is archived with a Zenodo DOI. Version 0.2.2.
bad: It does no tokenisation or preprocessing at all — by its own warning the caller must apply identical preprocessing to corpus and query for the comparison to be apples-to-apples — two of its five listed variants (BM25-Adpt, BM25T) remain unimplemented, and the last release is 0.2.2 of Feb 2022: unmaintained since.
didnt: Corroboration — lexical BM25 remains the honest baseline layer beneath semantic retrieval (this batch's own markdowncore-ai uses it as the pre-filter in front of vector search); the programme's retrieval work treats it as the floor any semantic layer must beat, not a component to adopt. The catalogue's ALREADY HAVE tag is not repeated: no lane-8 record covers this package. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: my-llm-wiki
licence: MIT (settled at source: the PyPI registry record carries SPDX license_expression 'MIT' with a LICENSE file shipped, and the README's License section agrees; the catalogue's 'not stated' is corrected at source)
good: Implements all three layers of Karpathy's LLM Wiki concept as described at source — raw files never modified, a compiled wiki with cross-references, and a schema that tells the LLM how to maintain it — over code (tree-sitter AST extraction for 19 languages, with typed extends/implements edges, signatures, doc comments and a call graph), Markdown, and documents via Docling (PDF/DOCX/PPTX/HTML/EPUB with layout-aware extraction; scanned PDFs auto-OCR). Re-runs skip unchanged files via a SHA256 cache, the output is a drop-in Obsidian vault, and agent sessions can write back so the graph compounds over time. Version 0.9.0.
bad: Beta and single-author. Compilation is automatic on re-run and the README describes no review or approval state for compiled pages, while session write-back compounds the graph without a stated gate; the graph itself is extraction-derived structure (AST edges, wikilinks), not verified claims, so 'compile once, query forever' inherits whatever the extractor asserted. No evaluation is described on the page.
didnt: Corroboration — the three-layer shape with hash-skipped re-runs is this programme's ingest architecture independently implemented, down to the SHA-256 change detection our citation lockfile also uses; the difference is the gate — its compile is automatic, ours is reviewed before anything becomes the record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-llm-wiki
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: OSI MIT classifier)
good: Synto's predecessor by the same author, and the pattern's earlier full form: raw notes are never modified, a local LLM (Ollama by default) compiles one article per concept into an Obsidian vault, drafts wait for interactive review, rejection feedback is stored and injected into the next compile of that concept (five rejections without an approval auto-block it), hand-edits are detected and never overwritten, and every automatic action commits with an [olw] prefix with an undo for the last one. Query synthesis pages store their source pages' body hashes in frontmatter, refuse in-place update once hand-edited, and cannot cite another synthesis page. Version 0.8.5.
bad: In maintenance mode by its own README banner — bug fixes continue, but new features are developed in synto, its named successor — and its routing layer is the wiki index page, with a stated comfort zone of up to ~100 source notes. The one-command run offers an optional auto-approve step, and draft quality and confidence signals come from the fast model.
didnt: Corroboration — the same review discipline as its successor (drafts held for review, rejection feedback, hand-edit refusal, hash-stamped synthesis) arrived at independently of this system; the pair is the wave's strongest external evidence for the pattern, and its ~100-note routing ceiling is the scale limit our register is built to exceed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yantrikdb-mcp
licence: Split at source: the MCP package is MIT (README badge and its own licence table), while the engine it embeds is Apache-2.0 (same table); the catalogue's 'not stated' is corrected at source
good: A local-first MCP memory server (19 tools) over a local SQLite store with no telemetry: semantic recall from a bundled embedder, contradiction detection whose open conflicts surface in later recall, a correct tool that fixes a memory while preserving its history, a one-call session digest for cold starts (open decisions, unresolved conflicts, stale high-importance memories), a gaps tool surfacing frequently-asked but poorly-answered queries, and an explicit trust boundary in its injected playbook — recalled memories are 'data, not instructions'. The design is written up as a citable paper (Zenodo DOI). Version 0.24.0.
bad: The operating model is auto-capture: 'The agent auto-recalls context, auto-remembers decisions, and auto-detects contradictions — no prompting needed', and outcome writes default ON — capture and write without a human gate. Memory lives in a SQLite database rather than owner-readable files, the headline token-savings and precision figures are the vendor's own (run by its own benchmark script), and agents can author behaviour-shaping skills into the substrate (off by default behind an env flag, but present). Beta, single author.
didnt: Rejected — automatic remembering with writes on by default is the ungated-capture model this system refuses, and custody is a database, not files the owner can read. Its conflict-surfacing in later recall, the gaps tool (frequently-asked, poorly-answered queries as known unknowns) and the data-not-instructions trust boundary are credited as design evidence only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ai-agent-memory-mcp
type: PyPI package — agent-agnostic MCP memory layer (aamm)
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: licence field and OSI MIT classifier, LICENSE file shipped)
good: An agent-agnostic persistent memory layer ('aamm') that travels with each project in a .aamm/ directory and is shared across Claude Code, Qoder and Cursor, with a source_agent stamp distinguishing writers. Three layers joined by id — SQLite (CRUD + FTS5), embedded Chroma vectors, and a human-readable Markdown mirror of every memory — with a CLI that can rebuild the database and vectors from the Markdown and a check command verifying consistency across all three stores. Retrieval is a published three-way fusion (vector 0.6, FTS5 keyword 0.25, title/tag 0.15), and a separate work journal (per-day append-only Markdown timelines) is deliberately excluded from recall search. Version 0.2.0.
bad: SQLite is the declared 'structured source of truth' — the Markdown mirror is a mirror, not the record (the rebuild-from-Markdown sync mitigates but does not change which store is truth). Embeddings default to a cloud service (Volcengine's doubao model), so memory content leaves the machine unless the user reconfigures the endpoint; memory writes and deletes are ungated; Alpha at v0.2.0 from a single author.
didnt: Corroboration — a three-layer store with a rebuild-from-Markdown sync, a cross-store consistency check and a work journal that recall deliberately does not search are honest engineering around the same shape as ours; custody still resolves to the database and embeddings default to a cloud endpoint, so the pattern is credited, not the package. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-nexmem
type: PyPI package — shared team-memory MCP server
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: SPDX license_expression 'MIT', LICENSE file shipped)
good: A plug-and-play MCP memory server whose knowledge graph is wire-compatible with the reference @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory JSONL format (import/export included), with five pluggable storage backends (JSONL by default, SQLite, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Redis) behind a StorageAdapter interface, namespace isolation between self and team graphs, atomic operations (insert-on-conflict, atomic appends) so simultaneous writers never overwrite each other, and a NEXMEM_READ_ONLY mode that disables the write tools. Version 0.3.0.
bad: It is a multi-writer system by design: in team mode every member's agent writes into one shared graph, the only boundary is a shared team-name string, and the server's built-in instructions make the agent 'write proactively — saves useful discoveries without being asked'. There is no per-item provenance, review or approval path, and deletes are ordinary tools. Alpha at v0.3.0.
didnt: Rejected — shared multi-writer memory with proactive ungated writes is the model this system rejects by design (single writer, approval-gated); its atomic-operation discipline and reference-format compatibility are noted as engineering evidence only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memorygraphMCP
type: PyPI package — graph-based MCP memory server
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: OSI MIT classifier, LICENSE file shipped)
good: A graph-based MCP memory server for coding agents: memories carry typed relationships in seven categories (causal, solution, context, learning — including CONTRADICTS and CONFIRMS — similarity, workflow, and quality, including SUPERSEDED_BY and DEPRECATED_BY), so a query returns the full causal chain rather than isolated hits; session briefings, fuzzy recall with relationship context, two tool profiles (core 9 tools, extended 12), and a choice of backends (SQLite by default, FalkorDBLite, LadybugDB, Neo4j, Turso). Its best-practices section is unusually honest that the server itself stores nothing automatically: 'You control what gets stored — nothing is saved without explicit instruction'. Version 0.12.4.
bad: The recommended setup pastes an agent-addressed protocol block into the user's own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md ('Do NOT wait to be asked. Memory storage is automatic.') — characterised here as evidence, never followed — and importance is an agent-assigned 0.3-1.0 float with no verification behind it. Custody is a graph database, and the Production/Stable classifier sits on a v0.12.4 from a single maintainer.
didnt: Corroboration — typed causal and supersession chains over memories are the graph form of our claim lifecycle, and its own documentation concedes the honest default (nothing stored without explicit instruction); the auto-storage protocol it recommends pasting into agent configuration is the part not taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: breathing-memory
type: PyPI package — local Codex memory manager (MCP server + core API)
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: SPDX license_expression 'MIT', LICENSE file shipped)
good: A local memory manager for Codex with a stable stdio MCP server (built on the official SDK) plus a typed in-process core API: memory is stored per-project in SQLite under the user app-data directory, organised around anchors and fragments, with text-first retrieval today. Capture is explicit by design — 'Breathing Memory does not auto-capture the full client conversation by itself. The consuming runtime must call it explicitly' — maintenance runs as a working/holding compression pass through a separate coding-agent backend so it does not pollute the live conversation, and a doctor command inspects installation, project identity, database path and effective retrieval mode. Runtime behaviour is specified in a normative spec.md with a separate design-rationale document. Version 0.7.1.
bad: Custody is SQLite under the user app-data directory, the supported client list is Codex plus in-process Python only, and installation writes a managed block into the repository's AGENTS.md and registers the server into Codex configuration (self-installing guidance — recorded as found, not a posture taken here). Older unpinned databases are not auto-migrated, by its own note. Alpha at v0.7.1.
didnt: Corroboration — explicit-capture-only memory with a normative spec and a published design rationale is the honest end of this wave's design space; its storage still resolves to SQLite and its install writes itself into agent configuration, so the pattern is credited, not the package. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mem0-agent-memory
type: PyPI package — third-party MCP wrapper for Mem0
licence: MIT (PyPI registry record: licence field and OSI MIT classifier, LICENSE file shipped)
good: A third-party MCP server wrapping Mem0 (author Arunkumar Selvam) with a wide backend matrix — FAISS local, Qdrant embedded or server, OpenSearch, or the Mem0 Platform cloud — and LLM providers spanning AWS Bedrock, Ollama and LM Studio; full CRUD with change history, metadata filtering, document ingestion (PDF/DOCX/Markdown/text), session partitioning by run_id, an export/import pair, and compact response modes that cut per-memory token cost by a stated ~55%. Version 1.3.2.
bad: The MCP surface exposes permanent destructive operations — delete_all_memories and a reset_memory tool described as 'Reset entire memory store (destructive)' — with no approval mechanism described (bulk delete's dry-run is the one mitigation). LLM fact-extraction inference defaults ON, memory quality therefore depends on the configured cloud or local LLM, and one supported backend is the vendor's hosted Mem0 Platform. The Production/Stable classifier sits on a wrapper whose core behaviour is inherited from the platform it wraps.

type: PyPI package — wikilink extension for Python-Markdown (fork)
licence: BSD (the package metadata's licence field states 'BSD' and the classifier records BSD License; the clause count is not pinned in this record and is not borrowed from the parent package)
good: A small Python-Markdown extension (classified Production/Stable) converting [[wikilinks]] to relative links, with explicit labels, the GitHub image variant, alt text, and a configurable build_url callable plus metadata-driven configuration — the render-time wikilink function in its commodity form.
bad: A single release from July 2022 whose README is the upstream project's near-verbatim, so the fork's own delta is not documented at source. It converts syntax at render time only — no link validation, no existence checking, nothing about the target's state.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and staleness: our Lens renders wikilinks natively, and the parent package (mdx-wikilink-plus) was already studied in B198; a render-time converter adds nothing the stack lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hugo-theme-academic-cv
type: GitHub project — Hugo academic portfolio/CV site template (HugoBlox)
licence: MIT (repository details record MIT License with a root LICENSE.md; catalogue MIT confirmed)
good: A mature academic-portfolio template (5,079 stars, 6,422 forks, created 2017): BibTeX/DOI auto-import generates publication pages with proper citations and metadata, Jupyter and RMarkdown notebooks publish as posts, LaTeX math and reveal.js Markdown slides are built in, and every file stays plain Markdown — 'No database, no lock-in, take your content anywhere' — hostable free on GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare.
bad: It is a public-portfolio website template, not a knowledge system: no ingest discipline, retrieval, citation verification or memory machinery, and its direction is public self-presentation — the opposite custody direction from a private wiki. The README is marketing-led (a testimonial's 'My citations went up 3x' is a testimonial, not a measurement) with a premium tier upsell.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an academic CV/portfolio site template, not a wiki feature source (the catalogue's own verdict); its BibTeX-driven publication-page generation corroborates a mechanism our scholarly corpus work already has by other means. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: digital-gardeners
type: GitHub repository — curated digital-gardening resource list that doubles as the code for the author's own Next.js garden site
good: A genuinely useful map of the digital-gardening field in one repo: an annotated tool directory (TiddlyWiki, Roam, Obsidian Publish, Foam and more), starter templates, how-to guides, essays on gardening theory, and a directory of real practitioners' gardens — and the repo doubles as the code for the author's own working Next.js garden, so the collection is itself a practised example. Mature and stable (4,800+ stars, created 2020).
bad: It is a bibliography and a website, not knowledge software: no capture, no retrieval, no linking machinery of its own, and no citation or verification discipline — everything it recommends still has to be evaluated tool by tool. The catalogue's own verdict was NOT FOR US (resource list).
didnt: Rejected — a curated link list and content site, not a knowledge system; nothing in it operates on a corpus, so there is nothing to adopt or build from (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: knowledge-garden
type: GitHub repository — one person's complete Obsidian vault published whole as a template/content snapshot
good: A real, lived-in vault published end to end: Atlas/Calendar/Cards/Sources/Spaces folders under an ACCESS organisation scheme, Zettelkasten practice, a working published site (garden.oldwinter.top), and v2.0 notes on AI-era workflows using multiple models — a concrete reference for vault organisation. It is also honest about its limits: the README states plainly that it is a personal notebook which cannot accept others' notes.
bad: It is content, not a tool: a snapshot of one person's notes with no ingest, search, citation or maintenance machinery beyond Obsidian itself, and by the author's own account no path for anyone else to adopt it as a system. The vault ships agent instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md) — recorded here as a fact of the artefact, not followed.
didnt: Rejected — a personal vault snapshot, not reusable knowledge software; its organisation ideas are already covered by our own schema practice (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obsidian-Templates
type: Documentation/template pack — a complete Zettelkasten template system for Obsidian (Markdown guides, editor snippets, worked examples)
licence: CONFLICT AT SOURCE: MIT per the repository metadata and the root LICENSE.md; CC BY-SA 4.0 per the README's own licence section (© 2022-25 Edmund Gröpl) — recorded as a conflict, neither side borrowed
good: A thorough, worked Zettelkasten method for Obsidian: five note types (permanent, fleeting, project, literature, hub) with copy-paste examples, reusable editor snippets, and plain-language guides to ontology, linking and tagging — method documentation a vault owner can actually follow, maintained over 584 commits and 12 releases.
bad: It is guidance and templates, not software — no code operates on a corpus, and adopting it means adopting Obsidian plus one author's method wholesale. Its licence is contradictory at source (MIT in the metadata and LICENSE.md; CC BY-SA 4.0 in the README), so even the documentation could not be adapted without first resolving which licence governs. The catalogue's verdict was NOT FOR US.
didnt: Rejected — an Obsidian method/template pack, not knowledge software; and its licence conflict (MIT vs CC BY-SA 4.0 at source) bars adaptation in any case (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-mind
type: Obsidian vault template — a lifecycle-hook harness that gives AI coding agents persistent, self-organising memory inside a vault
licence: MIT (repo sidebar + root LICENSE + README badge)
good: The hook-owned environment is the most disciplined agent-memory design in this batch: five lifecycle hooks (session start, prompt submit, post-tool-use, pre-compact, stop) set up and police the agent's context deterministically instead of by prompt pleading; the session-start injection runs under an explicit byte budget with an injection-size meter; and when the budget overflows, sections degrade to named pointers rather than vanishing — the README's line that 'a silent loss is worse than the bloat' matches hard-won compaction experience. Search is fully local (QMD with three small local models over an MCP server, grep fallback), memory lives in git-tracked vault notes under a tiered-loading scheme, and the whole contract is visible in the repo.
bad: The agent files, links and reorganises notes autonomously — no approval gate, no citation discipline, no claim verification — so memory quality rests entirely on the agent's own drift checklist. Its pre-compact hook works by backing up the session transcript, the session-transcript substrate the owner has not approved. The stack is brittle at the edges: it requires the Obsidian 1.12+ CLI and runs its hooks through a Node 22 experimental type-stripping flag.
didnt: Corroboration — its deterministic hook-owned context, budgeted injection and degrade-to-named-pointers rule converge with our checkpoint/compaction design and confirm it from an independent build; the ungated auto-filing is the contrast, not a model (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mindwtr
type: Cross-platform GTD task manager (Tauri desktop + React Native mobile), local-first and offline
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE / GitHub sidebar; site FAQ agrees)
good: A complete, disciplined GTD implementation: the full capture-to-review workflow, entirely offline with no account, data in a local SQLite store with plain JSON/TOML export, sync only through channels the user picks (iCloud Drive, Dropbox, WebDAV, Git), optional bring-your-own-key AI assistance that is off by default, natural-language task entry, and a long release history (137 releases) behind a claimed ~30,000 users.
bad: It is a task manager, not knowledge tooling — tasks, contexts and weekly reviews, with no notes corpus, linking, citation or retrieval machinery to learn from. AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline regardless.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a GTD task manager, not a knowledge system (the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict agreed); AGPL-3.0 bars code adoption in any case (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: note-gen
type: Tauri desktop Markdown notes app — capture-first records that an AI organises into structured notes, with RAG chat and MCP support
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE / GitHub sidebar; README License section agrees)
good: The capture model is genuinely thoughtful: everything (text, voice, screenshots, links, files, todos) lands first as unorganised records, and only records the user selects are AI-organised into structured notes that stay plain Markdown files on disk. Sync is unusually well engineered for its class — multi-backend (GitHub, Gitee, GitLab, Gitea, S3, WebDAV) with a push queue, remote-version checks and explicit conflict handling rather than silent overwrites — and the app is large and active (12,900 stars, 168 releases), with RAG chat and MCP support.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline. The organising step is LLM restructuring of the user's records with no citation discipline — nothing ties a generated note back to the records it came from — and write access runs both ways (sync pushes, an MCP surface) without an approval gate. The catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict stands.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 (ideas only), and its AI organisation has no provenance or citation machinery to adopt; the catalogue verdict agreed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OB1 (Open Brain)
type: Self-hosted shared AI memory infrastructure — one Supabase Postgres database (pgvector) behind an AI gateway, capture bots and an MCP server
licence: FSL-1.1-MIT (Functional Source License, per the README License section and root LICENSE.md; GitHub metadata reports Other/NOASSERTION) — source-available, not open source at grant; converts to MIT at a later date, so ideas-only under our licence discipline
good: A coherent answer to 'one memory every AI can use': captures from Slack, Discord, email and voice land in a single pgvector thoughts table that any MCP client can read, row-level security keeps users' thoughts apart in a shared deployment, and the repo teaches extension through a six-step learning path plus recipes for importing ChatGPT, Gmail, Obsidian, X and Google Takeout histories. Its optional Agent Memory sidecar (provenance, review, recall-trace and audit schemas) shows the author reaching for the same trust machinery we run.
bad: Custody is the deal-breaker: memory lives as rows in a hosted Postgres, not as a plain-file corpus under git, and every connected AI can write as well as read — the ungated multi-writer shared-memory model rejected by design in our system. There is no citation locking and no scored abstention, and the FSL-1.1-MIT licence makes the code ideas-only in any case.
didnt: Rejected — database-custodied, multi-writer shared memory is the architecture our file-corpus design exists to avoid (the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict agreed); FSL-1.1-MIT is ideas-only in any case (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memex (AI journal)
type: Mobile AI journal (Flutter, iOS/Android) — captured fragments auto-organised by a multi-agent system into timeline and knowledge cards
good: The storage layering is the best idea in the app: raw facts stay Markdown files, derived cards are YAML, event logs are JSONL, and SQLite is only a rebuildable cache — the derived layers can be regenerated from the facts, which is our own raw/compiled split in miniature. Capture is broad (text, photos, voice memos), models are bring-your-own and called directly from the device, custom agents run on the Agent Skills standard with per-agent models and scoped working directories, and one-click Markdown export keeps the exit open.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline. A multi-agent system organises captures into cards and insights automatically, with no approval gate and no citation discipline, and the surface is a phone journal with AI companion characters — not a desktop, git-backed knowledge corpus. The catalogue's verdict was NOT FOR US.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 (ideas only) and scope: an auto-organising phone journal, not corpus tooling; its facts-to-cards layering is noted as corroboration of our raw/compiled split, nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-llm-wiki-local
type: Local CLI (the olw tool) — compiles raw Markdown notes into a linked Obsidian wiki with a local LLM (Ollama by default); the source repo behind the PyPI package obsidian-llm-wiki
licence: MIT (repo sidebar + root LICENSE; PyPI classifier agrees)
good: The review discipline is the strongest in the Obsidian wiki family: compiled articles land as drafts in wiki/.drafts for interactive review, rejection feedback is stored and injected into the next compile (five rejections auto-block a concept), hand-edited articles are detected and never overwritten, and query answers route through wiki/index.md with no embeddings or vector database. It is git-aware ([olw]-prefixed commits, olw undo), 100% local with Ollama by default, and honest about its ceiling (the index-routing approach works well 'up to ~100 source notes').
bad: Now in maintenance mode — the README banner sends new development to its successor Synto (boarded in B199) — so this exact tool is a dead end for adoption. There is no citation lockfile and no scored abstention; inline source citations exist only as an experimental toggle, and the no-embeddings routing it is proud of is also its stated scaling limit.
didnt: Corroboration — the same review discipline as its successor (drafts held for review, rejection feedback, hand-edit protection), confirmed again at the repo itself; the earlier study of this project under its package name stands, and new development has moved to Synto (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: open-notebook
type: Self-hosted NotebookLM alternative — multi-model research notebooks (Next.js frontend, Python API, SurrealDB), deployed via Docker
good: A full-featured, genuinely self-hosted NotebookLM alternative: 20+ model providers including local Ollama, multimodal sources (PDF, video, audio, web pages, Office documents), full-text and vector search, answers that cite the sources, notes and insights they used, fine-grained control over exactly what context each chat sees, a complete REST API, and multi-speaker podcast generation — at serious scale (40,000 stars) under MIT.
bad: Custody is a SurrealDB database behind a Docker stack, not a plain-file git corpus, and the product shape is a NotebookLM-style research Q&A surface — sources in, chat and podcasts out — with no claim tracking, no citation locking and no approval-gated writes. By default the UI and API publish on all network interfaces with no password set, a deployment footgun the README itself has to warn about. The catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict stands.
didnt: Rejected — a database-custodied research notebook duplicating a Q&A surface we deliberately do not build; nothing in its architecture serves the file corpus (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: fsnotes
type: Native macOS/iOS Markdown notes app (Swift) — plain-file notes with fast search, note encryption and optional Git backups
licence: MIT (repo sidebar + root LICENSE; README states 'released under the MIT license')
good: File-first custody done right by a notes app: every note is a portable Markdown or plain-text file, explicitly 'not a proprietary database', search stays smooth across collections of 10,000+ notes, folders are ordinary folders openable in external editors, sync is the user's own iCloud Drive or Dropbox with optional Git backups, and private notes can be protected with AES-256 encryption, with tags and [[links]] for connection. A long-lived project (342 releases since 2017) under MIT.
bad: It is a single-user editor for Apple platforms only — no ingest pipeline, no linking beyond tags and [[links]], no citation, claim or verification machinery, and no agent surface at all; nothing in it operates on a corpus the way our system must. The catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict stands.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a personal Apple-platform note editor, not knowledge-system infrastructure (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: massCode
type: Local-first developer workspace (Electron) — code snippets, notes, HTTP client, math notebook and dev tools in one app over a plain-Markdown vault
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE / GitHub sidebar; README License section agrees)
good: The vault design is sound: snippets, notes and HTTP requests all live as plain Markdown files with frontmatter — git-friendly, syncable through any file channel, and watched for external changes in real time. Around it sits a broad, mature app: a multi-language snippet library, a full HTTP/GraphQL/WebSocket client, a notes graph and mindmaps, preview-first imports, an MCP server whose writes protect against overwriting newer changes, and an AI assistant that can preview edits before applying them and undo changes that support it.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline. And the centre of gravity is a developer's snippet-and-API workbench — notes are one module among five — with no citation, claim or verification machinery; the catalogue's description of it as a snippet manager is dated, but its NOT FOR US verdict stands for our corpus.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 (ideas only) and scope: a developer workspace whose notes module is not corpus infrastructure (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Laverna
good: A privacy-first Evernote alternative from 2014: Markdown editing with three modes, offline note management, secure client-side encryption (SJCL implementing AES, code paths named in the README's Security section), no registration, and synchronisation with Dropbox or RemoteStorage rather than a vendor account.
bad: Notes live in browser databases (IndexedDB/localStorage), not in files a user can keep custody of or grep; the stack is legacy (Marionette.js, Bower, Gulp, Travis CI), and the catalogue's last-activity signal is May 2021 — the project is effectively unmaintained. MPL-2.0 code is ideas-only for our stack in any case.
didnt: Rejected — unmaintained since 2021, browser-database custody instead of plain files, and no retrieval or citation machinery; MPL-2.0 makes its code ideas-only for us regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rnote
good: A polished vector-based drawing and handwriting app in Rust/GTK4: pressure-sensitive stylus input with configurable strokes, an infinite canvas, PDF/picture import, export to SVG/PDF/Xopp, autosave, tabbed documents, and a CLI for basic automation of its files.
bad: Its own README warns the native .rnote file format is still unstable and has already broken compatibility across four major versions; X11 is unsupported with unreliable stylus/touch input; the medium is handwriting on a canvas, not text knowledge, and GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — a handwriting/drawing canvas, not text knowledge tooling; GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MiaoYan
good: A native Swift Mac app whose notes are plain Markdown files in a folder the user chooses, with no data collection: wikilinks, LaTeX, Mermaid, version history and split edit/preview built in, a small CLI (open/new/search/list/cat), and sync deliberately delegated to whatever cloud-drive folder the user points it at rather than an account of its own.
bad: It is a single-platform writing app (macOS 12+; the App Store build extends to iPhone/iPad over the same iCloud folder) with no plugin system and no retrieval, linking-graph or verification machinery beyond wikilinks — an editor surface, not knowledge infrastructure.
didnt: Rejected — a single-platform personal writing app; its folder-of-Markdown custody matches our substrate, but there is no retrieval or verification machinery here that our editor and Lens do not already cover (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GitJournal
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo metadata and LICENSE file; the README's License section states the principal author's code is AGPL, other contributors' code is Apache-2.0, and documentation/translations are CC BY 4.0)
good: Mobile-first capture with the right custody model: notes are stored as standardised Markdown with optional YAML headers inside a Git repository of the user's choice (GitHub, GitLab or a custom/self-hosted provider), focused on privacy and data portability, with migration paths from Google Keep, Day One, Narrate and Simplenote.
bad: It is a capture client only — no retrieval, linking-graph or citation machinery over the repo it writes to — and the AGPL-3.0 terms on the principal author's code bar adoption for us (the split licensing, AGPL for one author and Apache-2.0 for other contributors, exists so it can ship on the Apple App Store).
didnt: Corroboration — a phone writing plain Markdown into the owner's own Git repository is our custody model at the capture edge, independently built; the app itself is only a capture client and its AGPL code is ideas-only for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Alexandrie
good: A capable self-hosted team knowledge base: an extended CodeMirror Markdown engine (LaTeX, diagrams, snippets, speech-to-text), multi-tenant Teams/Workspaces with a 5-level access model, OIDC SSO, an offline-first PWA, full-text indexing with a command centre, integrated Kanban, S3-compatible asset storage and full ZIP import/export of nodes or whole platform states, deployable in one Docker command.
bad: It is a multi-tenant application on its own backend store (Go backend plus database), not a folder of Markdown files a person keeps custody of; its centre of gravity is team workspaces, permissions and tenancy — the multi-writer team model our single-writer design rejects — and it documents no citation or verification discipline.
