didnt: Rejected — a multi-tenant team workspace on its own application store; nothing Markdown-file-native for a personal local-first wiki to take (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Butterfly
licence: AGPL-3.0 for the code (README License section: the api/ files are Apache-2.0 and images/docs are CC-BY-SA-4.0)
good: A genuinely local-first infinite-canvas notes app (Flutter, every platform plus web): handwriting, text, Markdown, shapes, images and PDFs on one endless workspace, files stored locally in a directory the user chooses or via WebDAV/Nextcloud, no required account or cloud, flexible export (PDF, SVG, images, portable Butterfly files), and experimental end-to-end-encrypted collaboration.
bad: The medium is a handwriting/drawing canvas — spatial ink, not text knowledge — so nothing in it operates on a corpus of Markdown; collaboration is flagged experimental, and the AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — a drawing/handwriting canvas, not text knowledge tooling; AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: org-roam-ui
good: A well-liked graph frontend for org-roam: an interactive 2D/3D node graph with local and global views, note previews, filters, theme syncing with Emacs, follow-mode that tracks your position in Emacs, and click-through to open notes in the editor — served locally side-by-side with Emacs.
bad: Its own Disclaimers call it alpha software that may break and whose development may stop any day; it only works with org-roam v2 inside Emacs, and its FAQ documents real graph performance limits (large networks over ~2k nodes slow down, with a list of effects to disable). GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — an Emacs/org-roam substrate graph viewer; our Lens already provides the reading and graph surface over our own files, and GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yarle
good: The reference Evernote exit tool: converts .enex exports to Markdown while preserving the metadata that migrations usually lose — original creation/modification times (including file timestamps), tags, GPS location, notebook name and source URL — plus internal note links, attachments in a resources folder, and user-defined output templates with target formats for Obsidian, Logseq, Tana and Heptabase; runs as a desktop app or CLI.
bad: It is a one-way, one-source migration utility: nothing retrieves, verifies or maintains the corpus after conversion, target-specific conversions carry their own stated limitations, and Evernote is not a source our ingest takes in the first place.
didnt: Rejected — a one-way Evernote migration tool; its metadata-preservation discipline (original timestamps, tags and source URL carried into the Markdown) is the right bar for any migration ingest, but there is no Evernote corpus in our pipeline and our converters cover the formats we do take (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rocketnotes
good: A Markdown notes app with the AI layer integrated rather than bolted on: chat with your documents, copilot-style text completion, semantic plus keyword search, multi-LLM support (OpenAI, Anthropic, Together, Ollama), voice-to-text, a Zettelkasten inbox, an MCP server integration exposing the knowledge base to other LLM apps, and a fully local Docker mode running on Ollama.
bad: Documents live in the app's own cloud-shaped store (DynamoDB and S3; ChromaDB only in local mode), not in files the user keeps; its headline Zettelkasten feature is agentic archiving — an AI agent files inbox snippets into existing documents with no approval gate — and chat answers are synthesised from retrieved text with no citation locking or abstention discipline.
didnt: Rejected — an editor-with-chat over a DynamoDB/S3 store whose agent files notes into documents ungated; that autonomy is exactly what our approval-gated write discipline refuses (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: org-roam (rudimentary Roam replica)
licence: GPL-3.0 (README License section: GNU General Public License, Version 3, or later)
good: The mature plain-text Zettelkasten inside Emacs/Org-mode: non-hierarchical note-taking with backlinks, a built-in graph visualisation, offline editing entirely under the user's control, GPG encryption of notes, and the whole Emacs ecosystem to extend it — lasting notes in plain text, as its README puts it.
bad: The substrate is Emacs and Org-mode with a SQLite cache (emacsql) — a different text format and editor world from our Markdown files — and there is no citation, verification or agent-door machinery; GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — an Emacs/Org-mode substrate; its plain-text backlinked-Zettelkasten model corroborates the family our wiki belongs to, but there is nothing portable to take and GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lobehub
licence: LobeHub Community License (custom licence, repo metadata Other/NOASSERTION, settled by opening the root LICENSE file: based on Apache-2.0 with additional conditions — developing and distributing a derivative work requires a commercial licence from the producer, and the producer reserves the right to adjust the agreement)
good: A very large, actively developed agent platform (83k stars): it has pivoted from chat UI to a 'Chief Agent Operator' that hires, schedules and reports on teams of agents, with agent groups for parallel collaboration, scheduled runs, a 10,000+ skills/MCP plugin ecosystem, self-hosting via Vercel or Docker, and a stated commitment to white-box, structured, editable personal memory.
bad: It is an agent-operations platform, not knowledge tooling for a personal wiki: memory is one feature inside a team-agent work OS, custody runs through its own app/database deployments, and the custom Community License reserves derivative distribution to a commercial licence and lets the producer tighten terms — the opposite of the permissive terms our adaptations require.
took: Nothing taken. Lane 8 records LobeHub only as one name in the Round-3 Tier B bundle bullet of research candidates (boarded, Waiting, with its licence then unverified); no build or adoption followed.
didnt: Rejected — an agent-operator platform, not knowledge tooling for the wiki, and its custom Community License makes its code ideas-only for us in any case; this study also settles the licence the Round-3 bundle bullet left unverified (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Langchain-Chatchat
good: A pioneering, very widely used offline RAG and agent application (38.7k stars): a fully open-model stack (ChatGLM, Qwen, Llama via Xinference/Ollama/LocalAI/FastChat) that can run entirely offline, with knowledge-base, file (BM25+KNN), database, arXiv and web-search chat modes, local knowledge-base management and a Streamlit WebUI — proof at scale that local knowledge Q&A is a real category.
bad: Its answer path is the classic top-k pattern its README diagrams — chunks matched by vector similarity are pasted into a prompt and the model generates — with no citation locking, no supersession awareness and no abstention when the base has nothing; deployment is heavy (the model framework must run separately, and the docs warn the two belong in different virtual environments).
didnt: Rejected — a RAG product whose answers rest on retrieved chunks without citation locking or abstention; the category is covered by our Ask door with a stronger verification discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yuxi
good: A complete self-hosted enterprise knowledge-agent platform: unified RAG (multi-format parsing with MinerU/PaddleOCR, embedding/rerank, retrieval testing and a built-in RAG evaluation workbench), a knowledge graph extracted into Neo4j, LangGraph multi-agent orchestration with sub-agents, MCP/Skills, sandbox workspaces with file artefacts — and, to its credit, human-approval cards that pop up and wait before an agent modifies files or calls high-risk external interfaces.
bad: It is enterprise multi-tenant infrastructure: knowledge lives in Milvus vectors, a Neo4j graph and PostgreSQL behind a FastAPI/Vue stack — nothing is a folder of files a person keeps — and upgrades between minor versions already require downtime, backup and migration windows; the scale and store are the opposite of a personal files-first wiki.
didnt: Rejected — an enterprise multi-tenant platform on Milvus/Neo4j/PostgreSQL, the wrong scale and store for us; its in-conversation human-approval card for file changes and high-risk calls is the platform form of our own gate, credited as corroboration of that pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: eleventy-garden
good: A friendly Eleventy starter for a personal mind garden: double-bracket links, displayed backlinks with hovercards, notes dropped into a folder and published as a static site to Netlify/Vercel — the lightweight end of the digital-garden publishing pattern, done cleanly.
bad: It is a starter template, not a system: 140 commits, no retrieval, no ingest, no verification machinery, and its own maintainer notes in the README that the project is not built for himself and feedback must come from users; garden publishing is a solved surface in our stack.
didnt: Rejected — a starter template; the garden-publishing pattern sits with our Lens/portal and the public edition's machinery, which go well past a static starter (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: digital-garden-hugo-theme
good: A Hugo theme for a personal digital garden (apvarun/digital-garden-hugo-theme, 299 stars, 113 commits): multi-column responsive layout, portfolio showcase layout, code highlighting, light/dark mode, KaTeX math, SEO/Twitter Cards/Open Graph, sitemap and RSS out of the box, newsletter hooks (Substack/Buttondown/Revue), and claimed perfect Lighthouse performance; installs as a theme clone or git submodule into an existing Hugo site (min Hugo 0.82.1).
bad: It is presentation only: a theme contributes no capture, linking discipline beyond Hugo defaults, search, retrieval, citation or verification machinery, and the garden it renders is whatever the underlying Hugo content already is. Two releases and a small commit history; garden-publishing needs of this shape are already covered by our Lens/portal and public machinery.
didnt: Rejected — a Hugo presentation theme; the digital-garden publishing pattern is already covered by our portal/Lens stack and a theme adds no knowledge machinery (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bangle.io
licence: No licence — no LICENSE file in the repo root listing, no licence shown in the repo metadata, and no licence statement in the README as opened (ideas only)
good: A web-only WYSIWYG note-taking app (bangle-io/bangle-io, 1,236 stars, 1,233 commits) that stores notes locally in human-readable Markdown with no data lock-in and no Electron; rich-text editing via its sister bangle.dev editor, an extension architecture, and a performance claim of handling thousands of notes (its README demos a 10,000-Markdown-file project). Local-first file storage is the right custody shape.
bad: Browser-only surface with zero tagged releases, a default branch that is itself an in-flight work branch, and no search/retrieval, citation, provenance or verification machinery beyond editing; and with no licence anywhere in the repo as opened, nothing in it may be reused regardless.
didnt: Rejected — an unlicensed browser editor over local Markdown files; local-file custody corroborates our store, but there is no retrieval or verification layer to learn from and no licence to reuse under (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Relatrix
licence: No licence — no LICENSE file in the repo root listing and no licence statement in the README as opened (ideas only)
good: Relatrix (saad-ibra/gray-matter) is a reflection-first Android knowledge app: resources (links, PDFs, Markdown, any file) live under Topics, and every resource accumulates a timeline of typed cards — Opinions are timestamped personal reflections carrying a confidence score, PDF cards anchor annotations/bookmarks/lookups to specific passages — with [[wiki-links]], tags, full-text offline search and a physics-simulated 3D graph of the links; all data stays offline in a SQLCipher-encrypted database. Timestamped, confidence-scored reflection cards anchored to source passages are a genuinely thoughtful evidence habit.
bad: The store is an encrypted app database on Android, not files a person or another tool can read; there is no licence in the repo as opened, so the code is ideas-only in any case; and the 3D graph is a discovery novelty layered on a small, very new project (56 stars, repo created 2026-03) with iOS still in development.
didnt: Rejected — an Android app on an encrypted database with no licence; its confidence-scored, passage-anchored reflection cards corroborate our claim-confidence and citation habits, but nothing here is adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: note-cli
licence: BSD-3-Clause (README LICENSE section and root LICENSE.txt; repo metadata card shows NOASSERTION, so the licence rests on those statements as opened)
good: Note-CLI (yuis-ice/note-cli) indexes chunks of a single Markdown file into a SQLite database and searches them with PCRE regular expressions or raw SQL, by header, content or whole note, emitting JSON/Markdown/HTML — built by an author who quit Evernote over its weak search (no regex, poor special-character handling). Regex-plus-SQL querying over plain Markdown is a power-user retrieval idea worth noting.
bad: A single-file, single-user model with a hard system dependency on sqlite3-pcre, nine commits total since 2021 and no releases — unmaintained; no links, no citations, no multi-file corpus handling, so it does not scale to a wiki-sized tree, and our own search tooling already covers the ground more safely.
didnt: Rejected — an unmaintained single-file Markdown indexer; regex/SQL search over Markdown is credited, but the model and maintenance state rule it out (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: getstreamline (Streamline)
good: Streamline (akaalias/Streamline) is a stream-of-consciousness writer for Obsidian vaults: a deliberately distraction-free, standalone macOS app for morning-pages-style flow writing that saves into the vault, lowering the friction of daily capture to nearly zero. Frictionless stream capture is the right instinct for the flow side of a knowledge system.
bad: It is a GPL-3.0 macOS-only standalone app (an Xcode project, 39 stars, no releases) for one narrow capture ritual; it contributes no organisation, linking, retrieval or verification machinery, and capture into our wiki already happens in chat and the editor without a separate single-purpose app.
didnt: Rejected — a GPL macOS flow-writing app for Obsidian vaults; the low-friction capture instinct is credited, the tool itself is out of scope (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mindforger
good: MindForger (dvorka/mindforger, 2,723 stars, 17 releases) is a human-mind-inspired personal knowledge tool: a Markdown editor/IDE with notebooks and outlines, associations and memory features, stencil/template support and broad platform packaging (Debian/Fedora/Flatpak/Snap/macOS/Windows/WSL, Docker, tarballs), privacy-respecting and local. Its longevity and packaging discipline are respectable.
bad: A GPL-2.0 Qt desktop application for one person's notebook; its knowledge model lives inside the app rather than in an inspectable file corpus with citations, there is no web/portal or agent surface, and the author's own README frames it as a personal tool maintained to personal taste ('IAGNI') — nothing our file-native system can build on.
didnt: Rejected — a GPL desktop thinking notebook; a personal app model with no file-corpus, citation or agent machinery for us (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Leo editor
licence: MIT (root LICENSE file opened directly, settling the repo metadata's NOASSERTION card; portions of the pygments interface are Modified BSD per the same file)
good: Leo (leo-editor/leo-editor, 1,611 stars, 66 releases, ~39,800 commits) is an outline-oriented editor in 100% Python built on two powerful ideas: clones, where one node lives in several outline places with a single source, and @file nodes that keep an outline and external source files in two-way sync — an outline becomes a structured view over plain files rather than a database. Actively maintained for decades (6.8.10 current) with a scripting API, themes and a Leo server.
bad: It is a desktop outliner/IDE (Qt) whose unit is the outline node, not the cited wiki page: no citation, provenance, abstention or approval machinery, and adopting its outline-over-files model would mean replacing our page/file conventions with Leo's .leo document format for the working surface.
didnt: Corroboration — clones and @file synchronisation are independent, decades-old confirmation of the single-source, file-as-truth discipline our wiki is built on; the outliner itself is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cotoami Remake
good: Cotoami Remake (cotoami/cotoami-remake, Apache-2.0) rebuilds Cotoami as a local-first Tauri desktop app around Cotos (units of information) linked by Itos, held in Cotonomas that keep a chat-like flow timeline and a pinned, hierarchically organised stock side by side; its Knowledge Growth Cycle — post, connect, then promote a well-connected Coto into a Cotonoma of its own — is a real discovery discipline. It adds an offline built-in world map for geolocated notes, networked SQLite databases whose graphs merge with granular per-node permissions (posting-only by default), and a WebAssembly plugin system.
bad: The store is a SQLite database inside the app, not readable files; collaboration is real-time multi-writer graph merging — a model our approval-gated, single-writer design rejects by design; and there is no citation, provenance or abstention layer. Small project (46 stars) despite deep commit history.
didnt: Corroboration — the flow-to-stock promotion cycle independently mirrors our capture-now, compile-and-promote-later ingest discipline; the database store and real-time multi-writer networking are not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GNU Hyperbole
good: GNU Hyperbole (rswgnu/hyperbole, 9.3.0) is an Emacs information manager whose implicit buttons automatically recognise dozens of patterns in any buffer — URLs, email addresses, grep output, backtraces, Org/Markdown links, key sequences — and activate them with one key, no markup required; it adds the Koutliner (auto-renumbering outlines with permanent per-node anchors), HyRolo hierarchical records, HyWiki zero-markup hypertext and window management, all as one installable package with a full reference manual.
bad: GPL-3.0 and wholly Emacs-bound: the value exists only inside Emacs buffers, its link model is button types in Lisp rather than an inspectable file corpus, and there is no citation, provenance or agent surface — the substrate mismatch that rules out the whole Emacs family for our file-native stack.
didnt: Rejected — a GPL Emacs substrate tool; implicit-pattern linking is clever and credited, but nothing transfers to a file-native wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Pepperminty Wiki
good: Pepperminty Wiki (sbrl/Pepperminty-Wiki, 207 stars, 62 releases since 2014) is a complete wiki engine contained in a single PHP file — 'a wiki in a box' — with file uploads, page revision history with revert, page tags, a dynamic help page, themes and a modular architecture packed into the one deployable file, runnable on any PHP web server with no database ceremony.
bad: MPL-2.0, so ideas-only under our licence discipline; and functionally it is a small conventional web wiki — pages live behind the PHP app rather than in an inspectable file corpus with citations, and there is no retrieval-verification, provenance or agent machinery. The single-file trick is deployment elegance our static portal does not need.
didnt: Rejected — an MPL single-file PHP wiki; charming packaging, but a conventional app-store wiki with no citation or verification layer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wikimd
good: wikmd (Linbreux/wikmd — the project spells itself without the second 'i'; 424 stars, 30 releases, 537 commits) is a Python file-based wiki that deliberately stores everything as readable files instead of a database, converting Markdown to HTML for the browser, with git support for version control, a knowledge-graph view, a plugin system (drawio, alerts, embedded pages, swagger, plantuml), image handling, LaTeX math, code highlighting, search, a CodeMirror editor and password protection. File-based custody plus git is the right base shape.
bad: It is a minimal personal wiki: the knowledge graph is labelled beta, there is no citation, provenance, abstention or approval machinery, and its editing/search surface is well inside what our own editor, Lens and Ask stack already do over the same file-native base.
didnt: Rejected — a minimal MIT file wiki whose file-plus-git custody corroborates our base, but functionally a subset of our existing stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Cowyo
licence: MIT (README License section; no LICENSE file in the root listing and no licence in the repo metadata)
good: A self-contained Go wiki/scratchpad server (578 commits): autosaving pages with real-time co-editing, browser-side end-to-end-encrypted private pages whose 256-bit key lives only in the URL fragment (the server stores ciphertext plus a hash of the write capability), password-encrypted blocks, page locking, self-destructing pages, and a plain curl API with a versioned page-control endpoint.
bad: Pages are stored in SQLite by default (PostgreSQL optional) — a database-backed scratchpad, not plain files — and multi-writer real-time editing is the centre of the design; the README's own E2EE threat-model notes concede that configured AdSense/Umami scripts also run on private pages and can access the URL fragment and decrypted content, and a lost private key is unrecoverable by construction.
didnt: Rejected — fit and custody: a database-backed, multi-writer shared scratchpad is the opposite custody shape from our single-writer plain-file wiki; its link-as-capability E2EE page is a neat trick, but keys-in-URLs and a database store are not a model we would take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Instiki
licence: Ruby licence (README License section states the licence is 'same as Ruby's'; no LICENSE file at the root)
good: A long-lived Rails wiki (repo created 2009, 2,389 commits) focused on portability and stability: near-one-step setup on any Ruby platform, per-page revisions with rollback and author attribution, regular-expression search, multiple webs with password protection, export of the whole wiki to HTML or markup in a zip, PDF export and math typesetting.
bad: Content lives in a Rails database (SQLite by default, MySQL/PostgreSQL and others supported) rather than plain files, and the feature set is a legacy one — the README documents no graph, no full-text search depth and no AI/programmatic access layer; running it still assumes a local Ruby 3.2+ toolchain.
didnt: Rejected — fit and maturity: a legacy database-backed Rails wiki; everything it does well (easy setup, revisions, export) our plain-file stack already does without the database. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ADR Manager
good: A web-based application for creating and managing architectural decision records in Markdown (MADR): a form editor (basic and advanced modes) that keeps decision records in a consistent template while each decision stays a separate file, aimed at people who do not work in git directly.
bad: The README states it currently only supports MADRs stored in the folder docs/adr in GitHub repositories, and the tool needs a GitHub OAuth connection to do anything at all; work in progress is kept in browser local storage and is lost when the user disconnects or clears it.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a GitHub-bound web UI for what our decision records already do in plain markdown, with rulings given in chat and the format fixed by our schema; its one idea, a format-enforcing editor, is already covered. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: University of Stuttgart, Institute of Software Engineering (started as an undergraduate research project there, per the README's Project Context; submitted to the ICSE Score Contest 2021)

name: adr-viewer
good: A small Python tool (installable from PyPI or Homebrew) that turns a directory of Architecture Decision Records into an easy-to-navigate web page — either a generated static index.html or a local server — with Mermaid diagram rendering inside records and accessibility checking (pa11y) in its own tooling.
bad: It is view-only: it renders and lists records but writes nothing, and adds no search, cross-linking or verification beyond the record files themselves; it is small single-maintainer scale (111 commits).
didnt: Corroboration — decisions kept as plain files and surfaced as one readable static view is the same shape as our index/log plus Lens; it covers a job already covered. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: e-adr (Embedded ADR)
licence: EPL (Eclipse Public License — the project page's licence badge reads 'license-EPL'; weak copyleft, ideas only for us)
good: Java annotations that narrow the gap between architects and developers: @ADR(n) links a class to a decision record stored in docs/adr/, and @MADR can embed the full decision (context, alternatives, chosen alternative, justification, related decisions) directly in the code; the library is published on Maven Central (io.github.adr:e-adr) and supports both MADR and Y-Statement formats.
bad: It is Java/JVM-only and research-grade — the page's own linked paper notes that auto completion requires an external tool — and the embedding mode duplicates decision content into source code, where it can drift from the record files in docs/adr/ that remain the convention.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a Java-code annotation scheme; our claims and decision links live in the pages themselves, and EPL code would be ideas-only for us in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Structurizr Lite
licence: Apache-2.0 (the Structurizr open-source codebase; Lite is described in its official docs as the free and open source version — settled search-rendered)
good: A free local tool that works directly off the filesystem on a text workspace (DSL or JSON): view and edit C4 architecture diagrams, read the workspace's documentation, and browse its architecture decision records with list, detail and search, as a single-person authoring/staging environment for the wider Structurizr family.
bad: It is an architecture-modelling tool, not a knowledge system — the ADR browsing is one view inside a C4 workspace — and the official docs warn it is designed for a single person only: concurrent access to one instance or several instances on one folder can corrupt the workspace, with collaboration deliberately reserved to the cloud service and on-premises editions.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an architecture workspace viewer whose only overlap with us, a browsable list of markdown decision records, is already covered by our index and log. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: release-please
good: Google's release automation: it parses Conventional Commit messages in the git history (fix: = patch, feat: = minor, breaking = major), generates the changelog and version bumps, and maintains a standing Release PR that accumulates changes until it is merged — at which point it updates the changelog and version files, tags the commit and creates the GitHub release; a manifest mode handles monorepos with many packages.
bad: The flow is GitHub-specific end to end (Release PRs, the GitHub API, GitHub releases), it expressly does not handle publication to package managers or complex branch management, and the changelog is only as truthful as the conventional-commit discipline of every merged commit.
didnt: Rejected — fit: GitHub-bound release-PR automation for versioned packages; our wiki publishes no packages and its canonical store is Azure, and the portable fragment idea the catalogue flagged (per-change changelog fragments assembled at release) needs no GitHub machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Release Drafter
good: A GitHub Action that drafts the next release's notes incrementally as pull requests merge: merged PRs are categorised by labels or titles into a configurable template, the next version is resolved from the labels, an autolabeler can label PRs from their titles and paths, and a read-only check action validates PRs against the configuration; a CLI/programmatic package extends it beyond Actions to GitHub Enterprise, Gitea, Forgejo and GitLab.
bad: It is centred on GitHub's pull-request and label workflow (the action runs with contents: write on the repo) while our canonical store is Azure rather than GitHub PRs, and the drafted notes can only be as accurate as PR titles and labels — the summary is derived from metadata, not from the change record itself.
didnt: Rejected — fit: platform-bound release-notes drafting; our append-only log and checkpoint record already keep the running account that such drafting would only summarise. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: semantic-release
good: Automates the whole package release workflow from commit messages: determines the next Semantic Versioning number from Conventional Commits (Angular convention by default), generates release notes, creates the git tag and publishes the package, all inside CI after a successful build. A plugin architecture and shareable configurations let it support any package manager or language and multiple distribution channels, and it supports npm package provenance via signed attestations on GitHub Actions. Very mature: 2,229 commits, 458 releases, 24,121 stars.
bad: It is release machinery for software packages, not a knowledge artefact: it requires a hosted git repository, a CI service with securely stored credentials, Node.js, and a formalised commit-message convention, so output quality is bounded by commit-message discipline. The README documents no knowledge-log, citation or provenance function.
didnt: Rejected — scope: fully automated versioning and changelog generation for published software packages; our wiki is a knowledge log whose changes are recorded in its own append-only log, and no package-publishing pipeline is missing from our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: scriv
good: Manages a directory of small changelog fragments (changelog.d): `scriv create` makes a timestamped fragment file to commit alongside the change, `scriv collect` aggregates the fragments into a new CHANGELOG entry at release time, and `scriv github-release` can publish changelog entries as GitHub releases — even for changelog files not created by scriv. The fragment pattern removes the merge conflicts of one shared changelog file edited by everyone.
bad: It solves a software-changelog problem only: fragments are free-text release notes with no citation, provenance or verification machinery, and it is a single-maintainer Python tool (Ned Batchelder; 305 stars). The same fragment pattern is already represented in this catalogue by Changie, so scriv adds no new mechanism.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and scope: the fragment-collection pattern is already carried by Changie in this wave, and neither tool addresses a gap in our citation-locked, approval-gated wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: towncrier
good: Produces a useful, summarized news file from per-change 'news fragments' written for end users rather than read from git history, categorised by fragment type and rendered through templates, avoiding the merge conflicts of a single shared changelog file. It is the original of the fragment family, used by Twisted, pytest, pip, BuildBot and attrs, and usable with any project type as long as Python-specific affordances are avoided.
bad: Pure changelog tooling for software projects: no provenance, citation or custody features, and its own Philosophy section says it works best in a development system where all merges involve closing an issue. It duplicates the fragment pattern already represented by Changie and scriv in this catalogue.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and scope: a third representative of the news-fragment family in one catalogue wave; the pattern is noted, but our wiki's change history is its verbatim conversation log, not generated release notes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notra
licence: Proprietary (commercial SaaS; the vendor's own guide states it is not open source)
good: Connects to a GitHub repository and uses AI to turn commits and pull requests into technical changelogs, then reuses the changelog as source material for blog posts and social-media updates — the differentiator its own guide claims over tools that stop at the changelog. Setup is low-friction: connect GitHub and select repositories, with no configuration files or commit-message conventions required, plus a rich-text editor and scheduling so generated content can be reviewed before publishing. The vendor's guide prices it at Basic $20/month and Pro $50/month.
bad: Hosted and closed: all generation happens on the vendor's service over your repository contents, and a subscription is required. The vendor's own guide states it is currently GitHub-only (Linear and Slack integrations 'coming soon') and that output quality depends on how detailed the PR descriptions are; there is no self-hosted or local-first option.
didnt: Rejected — hosted commercial content generator: it rewrites engineering activity into marketing prose on a vendor platform, the opposite direction from our verbatim record, and our change notes are not a marketing surface. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AnnounceKit
good: Write-once announcement publishing: one post goes out to 10+ in-app widget display modes, a standalone changelog page, automated email digests, Slack channels and RSS/Atom/JSON feeds, with attention 'boosters' (modal overlays, top/bottom bars with countdowns, full-page takeovers), audience segmentation by role, plan, location or custom property, post scheduling and expiry dates, custom labels, and a GraphQL API plus 11 webhook events for automation. Modular pricing starts at $49/month billed annually ($59 monthly) for the Changelog product with 10,000 MAU included, no per-seat fees and a 15-day free trial.
bad: A hosted marketing surface at stacking subscription prices (Changelog $59/mo, Knowledge Base $69/mo, In-app Notifications $99/mo, Enterprise from $799/mo); segmentation is gated to the Growth plan and above, and all announcement content and audience data live on the vendor's platform. It publishes announcements about a product — it keeps no verifiable record of its own.
didnt: Rejected — hosted SaaS announcement surface; our system publishes through its own portal (the Lens) and its record stays in owner custody, not on a vendor's changelog page. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ZotFile
good: Zotero plugin that manages attachments end to end: automatically renames, moves and attaches PDFs (or other files) to Zotero items, syncs PDFs from the library to a mobile PDF reader (e.g. a tablet) and back, and extracts annotations and highlighted text from PDF files. Long-lived and widely used: 1,119 commits, 4,380 stars, 33 releases since 2011, by the same author as Beaver.
bad: The README states plainly that ZotFile 'is currently not actively developed and maintained', that updates are 'extremely rare' and that the maintainer will mostly not respond to issues and pull requests; its installation instructions target Zotero 5 (and 4.x), and annotation extraction is bounded by what pdf.js can copy out of a file. GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us in any case.
didnt: Rejected — unmaintained Zotero attachment plumbing (GPL-3.0, ideas only) for a reference manager our stack does not run; the annotation-extraction pattern is already covered by the Zotero-integration study elsewhere in this survey. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mdnotes
good: Zotero plugin that exports item metadata and notes as Markdown files whose names follow a citekey-based naming convention, creates a Markdown file for your own notes per item, and batch-exports metadata, notes and ZotFile-extracted annotations together — the Zotero-to-Markdown bridge pattern, aimed at feeding tools such as Obsidian. 1,399 stars, 20 releases.
bad: The repository is archived and the README states the plugin 'is not compatible with Zotero 7' and that the author no longer has time to maintain or update it, pointing users to alternatives; it was tested against Zotero v5.0.89 and recommends ZotFile and Better BibTeX also be installed, untested without them. A dead export shim, and GPL-3.0 besides.
didnt: Rejected — archived, Zotero-7-incompatible export shim (GPL-3.0, ideas only); the one convention it carried, citekey-to-note-name, is already represented by Better BibTeX in this survey. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Beaver
licence: no licence stated at source (the frontend is described as open source on GitHub, but no licence name is stated in the sources read; the service itself is a commercial cloud product)
good: AI research-assistant panel inside Zotero (opens with Cmd/Ctrl+J) that recognises the current reading context down to the page just opened: it explains highlighted PDF text, answers natural-language questions across the whole library, fills in missing DOIs, and can automatically sort new entries into collections. The free version allows unlimited use with your own API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek and custom endpoints), a Plus tier ($10/month) adds monthly credits, external-database search and batch PDF processing, and it also offers an MCP server for connecting external AI tools. Built by Joscha Legewie, the ZotFile author.
bad: Beta software — its own forum announcement warns 'you might run into bugs' — whose cloud features require an internet connection and an account, with library content processed through third-party LLM APIs, and local storage described as still being developed. Its automatic sorting of entries into collections is precisely the ungated auto-organisation pattern our owner rejected as auto-discovery, and it lives inside Zotero, which is not our store.
didnt: Rejected — AI layer inside Zotero with cloud custody and auto-sorting (the rejected auto-discovery pattern); our answers are grounded in our own citation-locked pages, not in a reference manager's library. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-actions-tags (Actions and Tags for Zotero)
good: Mature workflow-automation plugin for Zotero (2,852 stars, 311 commits, 107 releases): user-defined actions triggered by Zotero events (item created, file opened or closed, annotation or note created, startup) or by shortcuts and menus, performing tag operations (add, remove, toggle), chaining other actions, or running custom scripts; a worked 'unread' tag lifecycle example ships in the README. Community action scripts are shared through its discussions and, per the README, manually reviewed by the maintainer.
bad: The automation exists only inside the Zotero client, and its most powerful operation, customScript, executes arbitrary user-supplied code with full Zotero-client privileges — the README itself warns a script 'can do anything that you can do in the Zotero client' and may cause data loss if used improperly. AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us regardless.
didnt: Rejected — event-triggered automation confined to Zotero (AGPL-3.0, ideas only); our trigger-and-action needs run in our own tooling, and arbitrary-script execution inside the store is the opposite of our gated-write design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jasminum
good: Zotero add-on for Chinese-language scholarship (7,311 stars, 92 releases, Zotero 8/9 target badges): retrieves metadata for Chinese PDFs from CNKI with a manual pick among multiple matches, downloads community Chinese translators and citation styles, splits and merges Chinese author names, matches manually downloaded attachments to items by title/filename similarity, and adds a PDF outline/bookmark editor in the reader sidebar.
bad: Single-source by design: the README states metadata retrieval currently supports only CNKI, with other sources merely under consideration, so its value is confined to Chinese-language corpora served by that one database; the documentation is primarily in Chinese. AGPL-3.0 keeps the code ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — locale-specific CNKI metadata fetcher (AGPL-3.0, ideas only); our corpus is not CNKI-centred and Zotero is not our store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-pdf2zh
good: Brings the PDF2zh and PDF2zh_next (PDFMathTranslate) engines inside Zotero: layout- and formula-preserving PDF translation with bilingual dual output, cropped single-column reading versions, batch translation, and a wide choice of translation services — free routes (Bing/Google, a free SiliconFlow tier) or the user's own LLM API keys. Actively developed (628 commits, 61 releases, supports Zotero 7–10) and the translation server runs locally by default (127.0.0.1, port 8890), so documents need not leave the machine for locally run engines.
bad: Heavy moving parts: it requires a separately installed, continuously running Python server (uv/conda environment) beside Zotero, most quality translation routes need the user's own paid API keys, and the README announces a full rewrite in progress with contributions paused and current-version support deferred. It translates reference PDFs — a reading aid, not a knowledge-base feature — and AGPL-3.0 applies.
didnt: Rejected — PDF translation is a reading workflow outside our wiki's scope (AGPL-3.0, ideas only); our pages cite sources in their original language, with the citation lock holding the exact wording. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-shortdoi
good: Small, focused DOI-hygiene extension (1,631 stars, 24 releases since 2017): fetches long DOIs via the CrossRef API, looks up shortDOIs via shortdoi.org, verifies that stored DOIs are valid, marks invalid ones, and strips stray prefixes (doi:, https://doi.org/, publisher URLs) from the DOI field — applied across a selection of items in one action.
bad: A metadata micro-fix inside Zotero only: it cleans one identifier field, depends on two external services (CrossRef and shortdoi.org), and offers nothing for citation provenance in a document store. MPL-2.0 puts its code in the ideas-only class for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — single-field DOI cleanup inside a reference manager we do not run (MPL-2.0, ideas only); our citation lockfile verifies citations against our own recorded sources, not a Zotero library. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-reference
good: Reader-side reference panel for Zotero (2,829 stars, 70 releases): parses the open PDF's reference list, or fetches references from Crossref, Semantic Scholar, readpaper or arXiv sources, and lets each reference be copied with its identifier, edited, or added to the library with bidirectional relations to the citing item; related-item recommendations come from the ReadCube API and Unpaywall is among its APIs. It produces no data of its own — in the author's words it is 'just a porter' of data from its sources.
bad: The panel lives inside Zotero's reader and depends on a shifting set of third-party APIs (Crossref, Semantic Scholar, readpaper, ReadCube, Unpaywall) whose availability governs its sources; the README notes its auto-association feature is incompatible with the sci-hub plugin, and its TODO list records open questions about Chinese-reference handling and per-journal strategies. AGPL-3.0, ideas only.
didnt: Rejected — in-reader reference list inside Zotero (AGPL-3.0, ideas only); our citations live as locked claims in page text under a machine-checked lockfile, not in a PDF side panel. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-citation
licence: AGPL-3.0-or-later (README License section; repository metadata shows AGPL-3.0)
good: Makes Zotero's Word citations visible and easier to drive: it mirrors each Word citation session into a temporary collection, adds a Citation column showing the in-text citation text for each item, inserts citations from Zotero with an apostrophe keystroke or drag-and-drop, and delegates all styling and field writing to Zotero's native Word integration instead of pasting static text. Its README documents its own mechanics (session polling, document-name matching, citation-window handling) in unusual depth. 1,288 stars, 44 releases.
bad: It targets desktop Microsoft Word on Windows and macOS only — not Word for the web, WPS or LibreOffice — and the README concedes it rests on internal Zotero session data and citation-window contracts that 'are not stable public APIs', so Zotero or Word upgrades may require adaptation; its own runtime test uses a fixture document backend and 'does not verify real Word writes'. AGPL-3.0-or-later besides.
didnt: Rejected — Word-side citation ergonomics for a word-processor workflow we do not use (AGPL-3.0, ideas only); our citations are inserted and locked in wiki pages directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-attanger
good: The maintained successor pattern to ZotFile (1,385 stars, 52 releases, Zotero 7–10): organizes attachments in three work modes (Zotero storage only, external linked files, or storage plus an organized external copy), renames with Zotero's native filename templates — optionally re-renaming when titles, authors, year or Better BibTeX keys change — builds subfolder layouts from collections, years or template variables, matches files in a download folder to items, and guarantees existing files are never overwritten while moves preserve annotations, notes, tags, relations and the full-text index.
bad: File management inside Zotero only, and one default cuts against careful custody: the README's settings reference states that 'delete the file from the download folder after attaching or matching it' is on by default — deletion as a default behaviour, even if scoped to the download folder and successful matches. AGPL-3.0 keeps its code ideas-only in any case.
didnt: Rejected — attachment housekeeping for Zotero (AGPL-3.0, ideas only), with delete-after-attach enabled by default; our files stay in the wiki tree under their own naming and custody rules, and nothing is deleted without the owner's approval. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-arxiv-daily
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file; README License section: 'Distributed under the AGPLv3 License'; the catalogue's 'not stated' settled at source)
good: A standalone Python tool (not itself a Zotero plugin) run as a forked GitHub Actions workflow at zero cost: it reads the user's Zotero library via API, fetches the previous day's papers from arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv and ChemRxiv, scores each paper by embedding similarity of its abstract against the library (recent additions weighted higher), and emails a relevance-sorted digest with LLM-generated TL;DRs, author affiliations and PDF/code links, with glob patterns to ignore unwanted library papers.
bad: The README's own Limitations section concedes the recommendation algorithm 'is very simple, it may not accurately reflect your interest', and a high MAX_PAPER_NUM can exceed GitHub Actions runner quotas; deployment also requires the user's Zotero API key, SMTP password and an LLM API key stored as repo secrets, and fork owners are told to keep merging upstream updates to receive fixes. Its whole purpose is an automated recommendation feed — the auto-discovery pattern.
didnt: Rejected — a daily recommendation feed drawn from the user's library is the auto-discovery pattern the owner has rejected in any form, and AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack regardless. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotmoov
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file / GitHub licence metadata; the catalogue's 'not stated' settled at source)
good: A Zotero 7 plugin for attachment management: it automatically moves or copies imported attachments into a custom directory as linked attachments, offers right-click manual move/copy to and from that directory, automatically deletes linked attachments from the computer when they are deleted in Zotero, can attach the last-modified file in a source folder to an item, and documents a migration path from ZotFile that preserves existing linked files.
bad: Attachment plumbing only — it decides where Zotero's files sit, not anything about knowledge. Zotero does not support linked files for group libraries, so moves work only in the personal library; copied files are no longer tracked by Zotero and are not easily reimported; and the README repeatedly urges a full local backup before use because it rewrites where a library's files live.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and a Zotero attachment mover has no counterpart in a plain-file markdown wiki whose files already live where the owner put them. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ethereal Style
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file / GitHub licence metadata; the catalogue's 'not stated' settled at source)
good: A popular Zotero plugin that adds reading-centred columns to the library view — the title background visualises per-page reading-time distribution, with annotation-progress, read/unread and star-rating columns, and publication-rank tags drawn from dozens of journal lists (JCR quartiles, CSSCI, CCF and many university lists) — plus nested tags, quick item-type filtering, view groups, an Obsidian-style graph view of related items, and custom PDF styles including dark modes.
bad: It is a presentation layer over Zotero's UI with no knowledge mechanism of its own; the documentation is primarily Chinese with video tutorials, the publication-rank datasets it ships are 2021–2022 lists, and its own TODO list leaves settings/theme sync and theme switching unimplemented.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and a Zotero interface theme, however polished, adds nothing to a citation-locked markdown wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-night
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file / GitHub licence metadata; the catalogue's 'not stated' settled at source)
good: A Zotero 6 plugin providing a Nord-based dark theme for the whole Zotero UI plus dark-mode PDF reading with two filters (a very dark one, and one matching the UI background colour) and a quick toggle between them, together with small UI improvements such as a cleaner tab bar, subtle animations and border removal.
bad: The README's top note states development of the plugin has ceased because Zotero 7 introduced its own native dark mode, so it targets a superseded Zotero generation; its own Limitations section admits popup menus lack proper styling on some platforms and that the CSS-filter approach to darkening PDFs 'is rather slow'.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and a dark theme for Zotero 6, a version whose own successor made it obsolete, has no bearing on our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zotero Add-ons Market
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file / GitHub licence metadata; the catalogue's 'not stated' settled at source)
good: A Zotero plugin that lets users browse, install and review other plugins from inside Zotero instead of hunting .xpi files by hand; its catalogue is fed by a companion scraper project with several selectable data sources (GitHub, Gitee, jsDelivr and gh-proxy mirrors), and custom sources in the same data format are supported.
bad: It is a storefront, not a knowledge feature: the catalogue depends entirely on an external scraper dataset and third-party proxy mirrors, and one-click in-app installation of community plugins widens the user's code-trust surface rather than adding any capability to the library itself.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and a plugin marketplace is distribution plumbing, not a feature our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Docs (LaSuite Docs)
licence: MIT (repo LICENSE file and README License section), with a split recorded: some advanced features (for example PDF export) rely on GPL-licensed BlockNote XL packages that are not MIT-compatible, and a PUBLISH_AS_MIT=true build excludes them
good: Government-built collaborative editor (Django + React on BlockNote/Yjs): real-time co-editing with live cursors, presence and comments, cleanly structured documents and sub-documents with searchable hierarchy, offline editing, granular access control, a presentation mode, import from .docx and .md and export to .docx/.odt/.pdf, optional model-agnostic AI writing helpers, and self-hosting on Kubernetes or Docker Compose with full data ownership.
bad: Its core model is real-time multi-writer collaboration served from a Django database with S3-compatible storage — content does not live as plain files in the owner's custody, and the README documents no citation locking, abstention or approval gating; it is also a substantial platform to run (database, object storage, collaboration server) for what is, to us, a document surface.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a multi-writer real-time collaboration platform is the design our single-writer, approval-gated, plain-file wiki deliberately is not, and adopting it would replace our file custody rather than complement it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: French DINUM and German ZenDiS governments (a joint La Suite numérique initiative)

name: draw.io
licence: Apache-2.0 for the source code (repo LICENSE file and README License section), with extra custom terms over the icon sets, stencil libraries and diagram templates (barred from use in, or distribution for use with, Atlassian products without written permission); end-user diagram output carries no copyright claim and is unrestricted
good: A mature, widely deployed JavaScript client-side diagram editor for flowcharts, UML, ER, network and general diagramming and whiteboarding, runnable in the browser, as a desktop app, via a Docker image or packaged .war files, jointly developed by draw.io Ltd and draw.io AG with a production deployment at app.diagrams.net.
bad: The README states this repository is a test version of draw.io for evaluating and trying it out, with a paid production version available for production deployments, and that pull requests are not accepted (development is core-team only); its stated scope is diagramming only — expressly not an SVG editor, and this version has no real-time collaborative editing.
didnt: Rejected — scope: diagrams are attachments in our system, not a knowledge mechanism, and the diagram-editor class was already covered in the catalogue's earlier waves (Excalidraw); the test-version/paid-production split is a further reason nothing here is adoptable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jotty
type: GitHub project — self-hosted notes and checklists app
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file and GitHub metadata; the catalogue agrees)
good: A self-hosted checklists-and-notes app (jotty·page) that needs no database: checklists and notes are stored as Markdown and JSON files in a single data directory. It offers Kanban boards and time tracking for task projects, a TipTap WYSIWYG editor with GitHub-flavored Markdown plus wikilinks and a 'brain view', sharing including public links, PGP encryption of notes, a REST API, OIDC single sign-on and MFA, and the repo ships an MCP server (mcp-server directory with its own compose file).
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us. It is a multi-user server product (user management, sharing, SSO) aimed well beyond a single-owner wiki, and the README states the PWA has only partial offline caching with no offline create/update/delete support. The project is also young — created in August 2025 — despite its fast release cadence (62 releases).
didnt: Rejected — licence and scope: AGPL-3.0 is ideas-only under our licence discipline, and its multi-user checklist/productivity surface adds no capability our wiki lacks; its wikilink brain view merely corroborates the graph direction we already have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Livebook
type: GitHub project — interactive Elixir code notebooks
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo LICENSE file and GitHub metadata; the catalogue agrees)
good: A web app for interactive, collaborative Elixir code notebooks: Markdown cells plus code cells evaluated on demand, Kino interactive outputs (Vega-Lite charts, tables, maps), Smart cells for tasks like database queries, and reproducibility by construction — execution runs in a predictable order down to package management and the notebook annotates which parts are stale. Notebooks are stored in .livemd, a Markdown subset with Mermaid diagrams and KaTeX math, so they are shareable and play well with version control.
bad: Livebook exists to execute code, and its own README security section states that anyone with access to an instance can access any file and execute any code on the host machine; it binds to localhost and uses a boot token for that reason. It requires the Elixir/Erlang stack, and its real-time multi-user editing is a collaboration model our design rejects; above all it serves code and data workflows, not prose knowledge.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a first-rate computational notebook system (Apache-2.0), but our corpus is prose knowledge under citation locking, not runnable code; the one transferable trait, notebooks as plain versionable Markdown files, is a custody shape we already have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Neverkin
type: GitHub project — collaborative worldbuilding and writing app
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file and GitHub metadata; the catalogue agrees)
good: An open-source collaborative writing and worldbuilding app for storytellers, DMs and novelists: wiki and character pages, relations through @mentions, an interactive mindmap, multi-track timelines, custom calendars and real-time collaboration, with a desktop app and self-hosting. It is actively developed — 2,248 commits and 416 releases — on a documented microservice architecture.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us. The domain is fiction and tabletop-session planning, and the deployment shape is heavy for a personal knowledge base — Docker Swarm microservices over PostgreSQL and Redis — with content held in its database rather than plain owner-readable files. Its audience is also small (17 stars).
didnt: Rejected — scope and licence: a fiction-worldbuilding niche under GPL-3.0; nothing in its timelines-and-calendars surface answers a need of a citation-locked personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Note Mark
type: GitHub project — minimal web Markdown notes app
licence: AGPL-3.0 for the code (LICENSE.txt and README License section; the project's icon/mark is separately all-rights-reserved — split recorded; the catalogue agrees on AGPL-3.0)
good: A lightweight, minimal web-based Markdown notes app: GitHub-flavored Markdown, data stored in a standard file/folder system, note sharing, friendly URLs, rendered and plain views of a note, asset uploads and attachments, OIDC single sign-on, and a fast editor with shortcuts. It is steadily maintained (708 commits, 50 releases) and explicitly designed so the owner always owns and can transfer their notes.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us. Minimalism is the design goal, so the README shows no graph, linking, search or verification machinery beyond the basics, and it is a single-maintainer project.
didnt: Rejected — licence and duplication: an AGPL-3.0 minimal editor whose file/folder storage matches what we have and whose feature set stops well short of it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Overleaf
type: GitHub project — collaborative LaTeX editor (Community Edition)
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file and README License section; the catalogue agrees)
good: The open-source real-time collaborative LaTeX editor behind overleaf.com, self-hostable as the Community Edition: a complete TeX Live-based compile toolchain in its Docker images and a codebase matured over a decade (28,830 commits since 2014, about 18,000 stars).
bad: The README's own caution states the Community Edition is only for environments where all users are trusted: without sandboxed compiles, users have full read and write access to the container's filesystem, network and environment variables during compiles, and features such as SSO and tracked changes sit in the paid Server Pro. AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us, and LaTeX authoring is document production, not knowledge management.
didnt: Rejected — scope and licence: an AGPL-3.0 LaTeX authoring platform; nothing in it serves a prose knowledge wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Plainpad
licence: GPL-3.0 for the code, CC BY 3.0 for content (README License section; GitHub metadata GPL-3.0; the catalogue agrees)
good: A self-hosted note-taking application (Laravel/PHP + React PWA) designed around simplicity and stability: run it on your own server with a single docker compose command and own your data at no cost. It has 447 commits and 11 releases since 2019.
bad: The README documents almost nothing beyond setup — no feature surface is visible at the source — and the app is database-backed (its own demo seeder populates the database with notes) rather than plain-file based. GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — licence and fit: a GPL-3.0, database-held notes PWA whose own README shows no capability beyond generic note-taking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: plumio
type: GitHub project — self-hosted Markdown notes server
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file and README License section; the catalogue agrees)
good: A self-hosted Markdown editor with live preview, end-to-end document encryption, multi-user and multi-organization support, webhooks firing on document creation/updates/deletions/moves, API-key management for programmatic access, and an optional automated daily backup system with retention management, plus an unsigned desktop app for Windows and macOS.
bad: The project was created in January 2026 and is very young, with a small community (138 stars), and its desktop app is unsigned — the README itself walks users through bypassing OS warnings. AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us, and the encrypted multi-organization server model is a team shape a single-owner wiki does not need.
didnt: Rejected — licence and scope: an AGPL-3.0 multi-user encrypted notes server; its webhook-on-document-events and backup-retention touches are design colour we already match or exceed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TriliumNext Notes
type: GitHub project — hierarchical personal knowledge base (community continuation of Trilium)
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE file and GitHub metadata; the catalogue agrees)
good: The community-maintained continuation of Trilium: a hierarchical personal knowledge base whose notes sit in an arbitrarily deep tree with cloning (one note in several places), seamless note versioning, attributes usable for organisation, querying and scripting, relation maps and note/link maps, per-note encryption, synchronisation with a self-hosted sync server, a REST API for automation, and stated scaling past 100,000 notes. It is a very large, active codebase (41,964 commits, 356 releases, about 38,000 stars).
bad: Notes live in Trilium's own database rather than plain Markdown files, so the corpus is not directly readable or greppable outside the app. AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us, and the README warns the fork's incremented sync versions break direct migration from zadam/trilium databases after v0.90.4.
took: Relation maps + note hoisting — built in Round 3, lane TB4/TB5 (compound bullet) — source/inspiration: Trilium (idea only, as recorded in lane 8).
didnt: Corroboration — the living continuation of the Trilium line whose relation-maps and note-hoisting ideas our Round 3 build already took (idea only, AGPL-3.0); the application itself, a database-backed hierarchical notes system, is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Turtl
type: GitHub organisation — private encrypted personal database and notes
licence: GPL-3.0 for the apps and core libraries, AGPL-3.0 for the server (per-repo licences on the organisation page; the catalogue's GPL-3.0 covers the app side — split recorded)
good: A private personal database for notes, bookmarks and passwords built around an embeddable core library that manages the cryptography, peer-to-peer syncing and data models, with a self-hostable server and desktop/mobile clients — owner-held, encrypted custody by design.
bad: The organisation page shows a largely dormant project: the main app interface was last updated in November 2023, the server in March 2024 and the core in September 2024, and one of its p2p libraries is archived. Content sits inside its own encrypted store rather than readable files, and the GPL/AGPL licensing is ideas-only for us in any case.
didnt: Rejected — a dormant encrypted silo: its custody instinct matches ours, but a stalled, database-and-crypto-bound store is the opposite of a living plain-file wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dokieli
type: project — clientside editor for decentralised scholarly publishing and annotation (dokieli/dokieli)
licence: Apache-2.0 for the source code (repository details, root LICENSE and the README License section); images and other media assets are CC BY 4.0 per the same section
good: A clientside editor for decentralised article publishing, annotations and social interactions, built entirely on open standards: in-browser authoring with RDFa semantic enrichment, W3C Web Annotation modelling, Solid/Linked Data Platform storage, WebID identity, Linked Data Notifications and ActivityPub sharing, versioning with immutable resources, URI fragments assignable to any unit of significance, automated references and citations, content negotiation (Turtle, JSON-LD, RDF/XML) and scholarly print views (ACM, LNCS). Long-lived and still developed: 6,257 commits since 2013, currently supported by NLnet.
bad: The price of the standards purity is the full W3C/Solid spec stack — WebID, Web Access Control, LDP, ODRL, SPARQL vocabularies — a far heavier apparatus than our plain-Markdown corpus with a citation lockfile, and there are no releases or tags despite the commit count. Annotations live in the decentralised-web model rather than being filed into an owner-held corpus, and there is no abstention, approval-gating or verification machinery.
didnt: Rejected — scope and weight: a decentralised-publishing editor on the Solid/W3C stack, where our ingest files quotes and sources directly into Markdown pages under a citation lockfile. Its fragment-level anchoring and robust-links citation practice corroborate our anchoring instincts from the standards side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: R&D support acknowledged in the README from MIT, Qatar Computing Research Institute, University of Bonn, Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft and TIB Hannover; currently supported by NLnet

name: Apache Annotator
type: project — W3C Web Annotation library toolkit for browsers and servers (apache/incubator-annotator)
licence: Apache-2.0 (repository details, root LICENSE file and the README License section)
good: The Apache Software Foundation's annotation-enabling libraries: code for identifying textual fragments in browser environments following the W3C Web Annotation model — the spec-grade selector machinery an annotator is built from — with a test suite, typedoc API documentation and a demo application.
bad: The repository is archived and the project still carries its incubating disclaimer: maintenance has stopped at one release. It is also plumbing, not an annotator — no storage, interface or corpus of its own — so there is nothing end-user-facing to take even if it were live.
didnt: Rejected — a library for building annotators rather than an annotator, and an archived one; our highlights live as verbatim quotes filed in Markdown pages with line-level citations, so DOM-selector machinery has no surface in our stack to attach to. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Apache Software Foundation (incubating project)

name: Hypothes.is-class web annotator (unnamed in listing)
type: project — open-source webpage annotator with real-time collaboration and an MCP agent work queue (MarkLayer, thevrus/MarkLayer)
licence: Apache-2.0 (repository details, root LICENSE file and the README License section)
good: Paste any public URL and get a collaborative review board on the live page: pen/highlighter/shapes, text-selection highlights, threaded comments pinned to elements, real-time cursors and drawing over WebSocket, shareable by a single link with no account or extension needed. Every share link is also a remote MCP server, so an AI agent can watch annotations and work them as a queue (acknowledge, fix, resolve, reply), and element inspection packages a stable selector, computed styles, layout and framework component info as an agent-ready Markdown snapshot. Self-hostable (Cloudflare Workers/D1/R2), with drafts persisting locally.
bad: The access model is the flaw: the share id is itself the access token, rooms can be minted by one unauthenticated POST, and anyone holding the link holds the board. Custody is hosted and ephemeral by design — shared boards expire 90 days after their last view — the opposite of a durable owner-held record. The project is young and small (38 stars, created March 2026, no releases), and its MCP door has an agent acting on third-party feedback with no human approval gate described.
didnt: Rejected — the link-as-bearer-token access model and 90-day expiring hosted boards are the custody and gating anti-patterns for our system (owner-held files, named scoped identities, approval-gated writes). The one transferable idea — attaching an element-context snapshot (selector, styles, layout) to each annotation so feedback arrives self-locating — is noted here. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docusaurus
licence: MIT (repository details and root LICENSE; the README License section states the code is MIT licensed and the documentation is Creative Commons licensed)
good: Meta-maintained generator for building, deploying and maintaining open source project websites easily, shipping the key pages (home, docs section, blog) out of the box, with localization support via Crowdin and deep customisation. Large, actively maintained ecosystem (66,552 stars, 157 releases).
bad: A heavyweight React/Node.js website stack: getting started is via npm init and a JavaScript toolchain, and the customisation model is React components rather than plain Markdown processing. The README describes a project-website tool, with no knowledge-layer, citation or retrieval features.
didnt: Rejected — capable docs SSG but it duplicates the static publishing layer we already run (Lens on Azure Static Web Apps) and adds a React build chain with no knowledge features. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Meta

name: docsify
licence: MIT (repository details, root LICENSE and the README License section)
good: Turns one or more Markdown files into a website with no build process required: simple and lightweight, with a smart full-text search plugin, multiple themes, a plugin API and emoji support. Deployable from a single index.html on GitHub Pages or any static host.
bad: By design there are no statically built HTML files — pages render in the browser at runtime, so output depends on JavaScript/CDN delivery rather than a build-time artifact that can be validated or citation-checked. Core search is a plugin, and the README lists no versioning or offline guarantees.
didnt: Rejected — runtime-rendered docs conflict with our build-time validated, static, citation-locked publishing model; the catalogue's FOR-US note reached only for the no-build render idea, and runtime rendering is precisely what our model refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: storybook
type: project — UI component workshop and documentation tool (storybookjs/storybook)
licence: MIT (repository details, root LICENSE and the README License section)
good: The industry-standard frontend workshop: build, document and test UI components and pages in isolation across React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, web components and more, with a large addon ecosystem (docs pages generated from components, accessibility testing, actions, viewports, interaction tests) and very deep maintenance (91,337 stars, 1,858 releases). Its docs addon is the reference example of documentation generated alongside the components it describes.
bad: Scope: it is frontend component tooling carried by a heavy Node monorepo toolchain. Its 'documentation' is component stories and API pages — there is no ingest, citation, retrieval, provenance or memory machinery, and nothing knowledge-shaped for a wiki to borrow as a component.
didnt: Rejected — UI component tooling (the catalogue's own verdict); massively successful in its own category, but our wiki and Lens have no component-story surface and no gap it fills. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: the-art-of-command-line
type: project — single-page command-line fluency guide; a content document, not software (jlevy/the-art-of-command-line)
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 per the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 badge the README carries; repository metadata records no licence and there is no root LICENSE file, so the licence rests on the README badge, recorded exactly as such
good: Command-line fluency compressed into one page with unusual editorial discipline — breadth, specificity and brevity as stated goals: Bash basics, everyday use, file and data processing, system debugging, one-liners, and macOS/Windows sections, every tip a concrete example. Community-maintained since 2015, translated into more than eighteen languages, and one of the most-starred documentation repositories on GitHub (162,579 stars).
bad: It is a content document, not a tool: there is nothing to integrate, no releases, and the author states at the top that he is planning a revision and looking for a co-author because it 'could be broader and a bit deeper'. Its tips are also generic public guidance with no provenance or verification apparatus.
didnt: Rejected — a content document, not software for our stack (the catalogue's own verdict); a good human reference that needs no place in our machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tldr
type: project — community-maintained cheatsheet corpus for console commands (tldr-pages/tldr)
licence: CC BY 4.0 per the README's licence badge; repository metadata records Other (NOASSERTION) with a root LICENSE.md — the badge/metadata mismatch is recorded as found, neither side borrowed or silently resolved
good: A community-maintained corpus of example-first help pages for command-line tools — simpler, practical complements to man pages — spanning Linux, macOS, Windows, the BSDs, Android and more, translated into dozens of languages (24,423 commits, 64,012 stars). Access is multiply redundant: official Python, Rust and Node.js clients, an offline-capable web client (PWA), and PDF editions.
bad: It is a content corpus, not software for our stack: the pages are usage examples with no provenance, citation or verification machinery behind them, and coverage/quality rests entirely on community contribution. The README itself notes the Node.js client 'has fallen behind in updates'.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a cheatsheet corpus (the catalogue's own verdict). Its one-page-per-tool, examples-first discipline corroborates concise operator documentation from the consumer side, but there is no component here for our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docz
good: Documentation sites from MDX files with live reloading and interactive components — Playground renders live component examples and Props documents their APIs inline — themed through Gatsby theme shadowing, building to static assets deployable on any static host. Widely adopted in its day (23,567 stars, 127 releases) with a long example gallery.
bad: The repository is archived: development has ended. Even in its prime the model was a React/Gatsby/MDX build chain aimed at documenting React components — a heavyweight toolchain next to our static Lens, and the catalogue's own note that the chain is heavier than our publishing route understates that it is now unmaintained.
didnt: Rejected — archived, and React-component documentation scope; our Lens publishes the wiki from plain Markdown without an MDX/Gatsby chain, and an unmaintained generator is not a candidate in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PaperMemory
licence: MIT (repository details and root LICENSE file)
good: A browser extension that acts as an automatic reference manager: it detects and records papers as you open them across some thirty-five venues (arXiv, OpenReview, ACL, PMLR, Nature, IEEE and more), matches preprints to their published versions using DBLP, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall, discovers code repositories via the PapersWithCode API, and produces BibTeX citations and Markdown links, renames PDF tabs and downloads with the paper's title, and exports the whole memory as JSON or .bib. Data is stored locally by default, with optional sync via GitHub Gists; 41 releases show sustained maintenance.
bad: Capture lives in the browser and records metadata, tags and comments — not the source itself preserved under citation discipline — and its matching depends on external APIs outside the user's control. It is a single-maintainer project whose own Todo asks for many more tests, and venue coverage is weighted to machine-learning and science publishing.
didnt: Rejected — browser-side paper capture duplicates what our ingest already does with stronger custody: the source is filed raw, compiled into the wiki and citation-locked. Its preprint-to-publication matching across DBLP, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall corroborates, from the consumer side, the scholarly citation truth-checking direction on our gap list. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: academic-file-converter
licence: MIT (per the SourceForge project page; the repo itself was not opened this pass — verification level search-rendered)
good: Converts a reference-manager BibTeX export into Markdown publication pages for a website or book, and Jupyter notebooks into blog posts or book chapters; 100% Python with no Pandoc dependency, compatible with static generators (Hugo, Astro, Gatsby, Next) and automatable via a GitHub Action.
bad: The SourceForge mirror was last updated ~891 days before this pass and its support page states the project has not indicated a support channel. The tool is a one-way publishing converter: it performs no verification of citations against their sources, and output fidelity is whatever the BibTeX or notebook input carries.
didnt: Board — the BibTeX-publications-to-Markdown and notebook-to-chapter conversion pattern as a sources-page generator candidate for the wiki's source records. The catalogue's FOR US verdict is not repeated as programme evidence (no lane-8 record exists); this is the completion pass's own judgement from the feature list. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DocsAgent
licence: no licence file at the repository root; licence name not settled at source in this pass (the README carries a License section whose text the routes used did not retrieve)
