good: Local-first MCP server giving agents search, read and write access to Zotero, Obsidian and Apple Notes through a resident C++ BM25 + passage-ranking core (~15 ms over 1,000+ PDFs, 160-227 MB for a 1,500-paper library); 8 MCP tools (5 read, 3 write) with JSON-schema-validated arguments, token budgets, result dedup and a three-layer write safety gate; stdio and Streamable HTTP transports, the latter with origin checks, API-key / OAuth 2.0 introspection and per-request RBAC; feature-equal TypeScript and Python shells over one JSON-RPC contract.
bad: Embryonic: 19 commits and zero releases at this pass, created April 2026. The repo root carries no LICENSE file (root listing checked) and the README's License section text was not retrievable through the routes used, so the licence is not settled at source here. Apple Notes support is macOS-only, and the write tools act inside other applications' stores rather than over a file corpus the user owns outright.
didnt: Corroboration — a local-first MCP door with fused multi-source BM25 retrieval and a layered write-safety gate over an existing personal store is our gateway / MCP-read pattern stated as a product. Not adopted: our store is the wiki itself rather than Zotero/Obsidian/Apple Notes, and the project is embryonic with an unsettled licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mind-elixir-core
licence: MIT (per the project's own guide/materials; verification level search-rendered)
good: Framework-agnostic JavaScript mind-map core usable with any frontend framework: interactive editing with drag-and-drop and node editing, multi-node bulk operations, undo/redo, custom node connections and summarisation, operation guards (before-hooks that can veto an edit), Markdown import/export of map data, and SVG/PNG/HTML export; lightweight, mobile-friendly and plugin-extensible.
bad: It is an embeddable editor core, not an application or a knowledge store: a host app must supply persistence and semantics, and the unit of work is a single map document rather than a graph of interlinked pages. Nothing in the material read addresses citations, retrieval or write gating.
didnt: Rejected — an embeddable mind-map editor core; our graph needs are view-side renderings of the wiki's link structure and are already served, and a map document is not a knowledge store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SimpleMindMap
licence: MIT, with additional README-stated commercial-use attribution conditions (the source must be indicated inside the application; removal of the notice is available by paid arrangement with the author)
good: A full mind-map library plus web app: many layouts (logical structure, organisation chart, timeline, fishbone, catalogue), rich node content (rich text, images, icons, hyperlinks, notes, tags, summaries, KaTeX formulas), import/export across JSON, Markdown, XMind, PNG/SVG/PDF and TXT, search/replace, a presentation mode, and a plugin architecture that includes real-time multi-user collaboration via Yjs + WebRTC.
bad: The licence is MIT but the README adds commercial-use conditions beyond stock MIT (retain the project's copyright notices and indicate the source in the application; removal is a paid arrangement). Its collaboration plugin is real-time multi-writer editing — a design our system rejects — and maps persist as the library's own JSON documents, not as interlinked citable pages.
didnt: Rejected — a mind-map editor/app whose maps are attachments, not a knowledge store; its real-time multi-writer collaboration is rejected by design in our system, and the non-stock licence rider adds friction to any reuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tmmpr
licence: MIT (per the LinuxLinks review; verification level search-rendered)
good: Terminal mind mapper written in Rust: notes placed on an infinite canvas with visual, colour-customisable connections, vim-inspired modal navigation (normal, visual, move, connection and edit modes), configurable auto-save intervals and an automatic backup system.
bad: A single-user terminal novelty: the review documents no Markdown or other-format import/export, no linking model beyond canvas connections, and no retrieval or provenance machinery; maps live in the app's own canvas rather than in interlinked text files.
didnt: Rejected — a terminal mind-mapping novelty with no interop with a Markdown wiki and no knowledge capability our system lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mindolph
licence: GPL-3.0 (per AlternativeTo's listing of the project; not stated in the README material read)
good: Open-source desktop PKM for all desktop platforms: local workspaces with full user control of files, tabbed editing of Mind Map (.mmd), Markdown, PlantUML, CSV and plain-text files, GenAI generate/summarise support across many providers (OpenAI, Qwen, Ollama, Gemini, Hugging Face, ChatGLM, DeepSeek, Moonshot), mind-map import from Freemind/Mindmup/XMind/Coggle/Novamind and export to Freemind/Markdown/images/AsciiDoc, plus outline view, snippets and folder text search.
bad: GPL-3.0, so its code is ideas-only for our stack. It is a desktop suite organised around its own workspace model rather than a plain interlinked file corpus with citation machinery, and its GenAI features send content to third-party LLM APIs by provider (Ollama excepted); the README documents no provenance, abstention or approval gating.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 desktop suite with its own store and provider-egress AI features; no portable capability our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-TagsRoutes
good: Obsidian plugin rendering files and tags as nodes in one 3D graph (file-to-file, file-to-tag and tag-to-tag links), with node sizing by link count and tag frequency, tag queries that surface the paragraph context around a tag (including time-based tags), paragraph-level deep links, orphan-file and orphan-Excalidraw linking for review, path filters, a vault-growth time-lapse animation, and click-to-focus synchronisation between the graph and the editor.
bad: Obsidian-only: it visualises a vault inside one host app and offers nothing portable to a file-based wiki with its own Lens. A small single-author project (102 stars), and the graph is presentation only — no provenance, citation or write-gating semantics.
didnt: Rejected — an Obsidian-bound visualisation plugin; our graph views are served by the Lens over the wiki's own link structure, and tag/orphan review already exists in our lint machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markmap (editor/skill family)
good: Parses plain Markdown — headings and lists — and renders it as an interactive, collapsible mind map with links, text formatting, code and KaTeX preserved; usable as a library (markmap-lib / markmap-view), as a CLI producing standalone interactive HTML or SVG, and through a wide editor and skill family, all from the same plain-text source with no proprietary map format. The family's MCP server (jinzcdev/markmap-mcp-server) was studied separately in an earlier batch.
bad: Pure rendering: the map reflects heading hierarchy only, so cross-page wikilink structure, citations and provenance do not appear in it. The family is fragmented across many repositories and packages that must be tracked separately, and a rendered map is a view, never a store.
didnt: Board — outline-to-mindmap rendering of a wiki page's own headings as a cheap Lens view: the input is just the page's Markdown, the family is MIT, and no new store or format is introduced. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Journiv
licence: not settled at source — repository metadata is Other (NOASSERTION) and the author describes a 'source available' project, while the SourceForge mirror claims MIT; conflict recorded, neither claim borrowed
good: Self-hosted private journaling web app (Docker, SQLite or PostgreSQL): prompt-based journaling, mood tracking with analytics, 'On This Day' memories, media uploads, advanced search, multiple journals and streak/word statistics, with data kept on the user's own infrastructure.
bad: Beta software whose README warns breaking changes may still occur and urges regular backups; entries live in the app's own database rather than in plain files. Licence conflict at source: the repository itself is detected as Other (NOASSERTION), its README says only 'licensed under the terms specified in the LICENSE file' and its disclaimer calls Journiv a 'personal source available project', while the SourceForge mirror claims MIT — the MIT claim is not adopted and the licence is not settled as MIT.
didnt: Rejected — a journaling app with its own database store and beta stability; the daily record in our system is the wiki log and conversation log in plain files, and the unsettled licence bars reuse in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linked
good: Distraction-free daily journal Electron app: write freely per day, search across all days, text styles with todo, list and code blocks, keyboard-first navigation, dark/light modes and multi-language support; entries are kept as the user's own files under ~/Documents/linked rather than in a cloud account.
bad: GPL-3.0. The README's own Upcoming list shows the knowledge-relevant features still missing — linking days together for references, a month overview and cross-device sync are unbuilt — so it is a day-per-page notebook with no interlinking, retrieval or provenance machinery.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 journaling app; daily notes already live in the wiki log, and its plain-file custody stance is one we already practise. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zotero-format-metadata
good: A mature Zotero metadata linter: 70+ validate/correct/require rules covering title rich text and sentence case, journal abbreviations from a built-in ~96,000-entry JabRef dataset (with ISO 4 inference as fallback), language detection, university-place lookup, normalised dates/DOIs/pages/volumes, duplicate detection on import, and one-click metadata completion via DOI/ArXiv through the CrossRef and Semantic Scholar APIs.
bad: AGPL-3.0 with an unusually aggressive NOTICE: the project asserts that code, rules or strings copied, paraphrased, translated or AI-regenerated into another plugin make that work a derivative that must itself be AGPL — so even its rule designs must be re-derived independently, never adapted. It is Zotero-internal housekeeping (with a substantial GB/T 7714 and Chinese-library orientation) and does nothing outside Zotero's own database.
didnt: Board — the import-time bibliographic lint pattern (validate and correct citation fields against authority datasets at ingest) as an idea for our citation checks, re-derived independently; the code and rule texts are AGPL-3.0 and the project's NOTICE claims even paraphrase as derivative, so nothing is adapted from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vimwiki
good: A personal wiki that is nothing but interlinked plain-text files: three markup syntaxes (its own, Markdown, MediaWiki), link creation and navigation inside Vim, full-wiki search, tagging, outlined notes and task lists, auto-formatted tables, diary support and export of the whole wiki to HTML — one of the oldest plain-file wiki designs still in use.
bad: Bound entirely to Vim/Vimscript — there is no standalone renderer, API or agent surface, so it can serve only a human sitting in that editor. Its README is candid that VimWiki 'has a lot of users but only very few recurring developers'.
didnt: Corroboration — interlinked plain-text files with an index page as the durable substrate, navigable without any database or service, is exactly our wiki's base design; nothing is taken, since the implementation is editor-bound Vimscript. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AnkiDroid
licence: GPL-3.0 for the app with AGPL-3.0 components (F-Droid metadata lists AGPL-3.0-or-later) — licence split recorded at source
good: The Anki spaced-repetition system on Android: text, image, audio, video and LaTeX/MathJax cards, more than 6,000 premade decks, detailed statistics, a card browser and editor, whiteboard and write-answer modes, full backups and collection import, with optional sync to desktop Anki.
bad: An Android review client, not knowledge machinery: it has no authoring model, citation or provenance surface for a wiki. Licence split at source — the app is GPL-3.0 (per the project wiki) with AGPL-3.0 components (the bundled Anki backend), while F-Droid's metadata lists AGPL-3.0-or-later; and its default sync target, AnkiWeb, is a non-libre service (the self-hosted sync server is unofficial).
didnt: Rejected — a flashcard review client; spaced repetition is a study-delivery tool, not a wiki feature, and the GPL/AGPL licensing makes its code ideas-only regardless. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LibreLingo
good: Community-owned language-learning platform built as a modular monorepo (Next.js web app plus Python YAML course loader, JSON export and shared types/utils packages): course content is authored as YAML files decoupled from the software, so courses can be reused in other formats; interactive exercises, spaced repetition, progress saving and cross-device sync form the stated feature set, with 90+ contributors.
bad: AGPL-3.0. Maturity is early and the project's own roadmap shows alpha-stage gaps (course progress sync and a contributor course editor unfinished, only the Spanish demo course substantially built), and LinuxLinks lists the project website as abandoned.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 language-learning platform, out of scope for a knowledge OS; its one transferable pattern, course content as plain YAML decoupled from the delivery app, is a files-first stance we already practise. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PageLM
licence: CaviraOSS Community License (custom; GitHub metadata Other/NOASSERTION)
good: Community-driven NotebookLM-style education platform (2,036 stars) that turns uploaded study materials (PDF, DOCX, Markdown, TXT) into interactive resources: quizzes with hints and scoring, non-overlapping flashcards, Cornell-style SmartNotes and AI podcasts, plus contextual chat over the uploads, voice transcription, a homework planner and an exam simulator. It is multi-provider by design (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Grok, local Ollama, OpenRouter and more), with WebSocket streaming, file-based persistent storage for generated content and Docker deployment.
bad: A study-content generator, not knowledge machinery: the generated artefacts are the product, and the README documents no citation locking, provenance or verification of generated content against its sources. Zero releases despite the feature breadth. The custom Community License allows personal/educational use but requires prior written permission for commercial use or resale, so its code is ideas-only for our stack (a SourceForge mirror page claiming 'MIT License' is contradicted by the repo's own LICENSE.md).
didnt: Rejected — scope (an AI study-content generator over uploads; the RAG-product family our wiki is not) and licence (custom CaviraOSS Community License, commercial use by permission only). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: scholarsome
good: Self-hostable web-based flashcard studying system (NestJS/Angular/Prisma monorepo) built as a no-paywall alternative to the large study sites: create and share study sets, import and export sets to and from Anki, Quizlet and CSV, LaTeX expressions in cards, quizzes in fill-in-the-blank, true/false and multiple-choice forms, set editing and visibility controls, with data kept on the user's own server.
bad: By its own README the spaced repetition system is still listed under 'Features coming soon', alongside interactive study games, persistence of quiz results and a user-accessible API — the core retention mechanism of a flashcard system is unbuilt — and the Design Philosophy section states plainly that 'Scholarsome is far from complete'. AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack in any case.
didnt: Rejected — a flashcard study app (retention tooling is outside the wiki's scope) whose own README lists spaced repetition as not yet implemented; AGPL-3.0, so ideas-only regardless. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mnemosyne
licence: AGPL-3.0 with an additional provision (the name 'Mnemosyne' must be clearly visible in derived works); the openSM2sync component is LGPL-3.0
good: Long-running spaced-repetition flashcard program that doubles as a research project into long-term memory (2,847 commits, active since 2017): rich-media flashcards (images, video, audio), bi-directional syncing between devices, clients for Windows/Mac/Linux and Android, powerful card types, several learning schedulers plus a cramming scheduler that leaves the regular schedule untouched, learning-process visualisation, an extensive plugin architecture, and an optional anonymised learning-data upload (off by default) feeding the research side.
bad: A desktop SRS application, not knowledge machinery — flashcard retention scheduling sits outside the wiki's scope. Its built-in review webserver 'does not implement any security features so far' by the README's own admission. The licence is split and encumbered (AGPL-3.0 plus a naming-visibility provision for the main code, LGPL-3.0 for openSM2sync), so the code is ideas-only regardless of fit.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a flashcard SRS program; retention tooling is not a wiki capability, and AGPL-3.0 (with an extra naming provision) makes its code ideas-only. It stands in this batch only as the mature contrast class to the FSRS scheduling line. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: carden
good: Chrome extension that turns reading into flashcards in context: SM-2 spaced repetition, decks, points-and-levelling gamification, in-depth stats with charts, import/export as .txt and .csv, and claimed cross-compatibility with Anki, Quizlet and Brainscape; it can be self-hosted from the repo's own PHP/MySQL server folder instead of using the Chrome Store build.
bad: Effectively stale: 21 commits in total, no releases, and last updated June 2022, matching the catalogue's signal. Self-hosting is a manual multi-step process (edit POST URLs and CORS allow-origins across the JavaScript/PHP files, hand-edit database credentials), the hosted version monetises through a yearly ExtensionPay subscription, and the whole thing is a browser flashcard toy rather than knowledge machinery.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a gamified flashcard extension; retention tooling is outside the wiki) and maturity (21 commits, untouched since 2022). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FSRS (DSR-model algorithm)
good: The reference Rust implementation of FSRS, the Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler built on the DSR (Difficulty, Stability, Retrievability) model that descends from MaiMemo's DHP model: a scheduler plus a parameter optimizer that fits the algorithm's weights to the learner's own review history, simulation capabilities, SM-2 migration helpers, a single-user Cost ADR policy optimizer that trades study time against retention, and C, Python, Node, Dart and PHP bindings; actively released (73 releases).
bad: It is a card-scheduling algorithm library, not a knowledge system: its entire domain is flashcard review intervals, and the README's own Q&A splits scheduling-only users off to the lighter per-language [lang]-fsrs crates. Nothing in it addresses knowledge content, citation or provenance — any use in a wiki is by analogy to its scheduling mathematics, not by adopting the crate.
took: Per-claim re-verification scheduling (from each claim's verification history) — built 2026-10-20 — source/inspiration: FSRS-6 / DSR model (lane-8 record); the standing reverify batch runs on that FSRS schedule in the nightly sweep. The fsrs-rs code itself was not adopted.
didnt: Corroboration — the DSR model is the recorded inspiration for our built per-claim re-verification scheduling: a claim's next check is scheduled from its verification history exactly as FSRS schedules a card from its review history. The Rust crate itself is not part of our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: KAG
good: Logical-form-guided reasoning and retrieval framework over the OpenSPG engine, aimed at factual Q&A over professional domain knowledge bases: a knowledge-and-chunk mutual indexing representation that cross-indexes graph structure with the original text blocks, schema-constrained knowledge construction alongside schema-free extraction, knowledge alignment to reduce OpenIE noise, and a hybrid solver whose planning, reasoning and retrieval operators mix exact-match retrieval, text retrieval, KG reasoning and numerical calculation for multi-hop questions.
bad: Platform-scale enterprise machinery: it presupposes the OpenSPG engine and Docker-deployed services and targets vertical-domain knowledge bases built by teams, and the README's architecture section notes the third component (kag-model) will only be open-sourced gradually — the released system is the builder and solver only. Its operating scale is far beyond a personal wiki's.
took: Mutual indexing with logical-form retrieval — built in Round 3, lane TB7 — source/inspiration: KAG (lane-8 record). The KAG framework itself was not adopted.
didnt: Corroboration — its mutual indexing of graph structure and original text, resolved into logical-form-guided retrieval, is the design our Round 3 TB7 build recorded as its inspiration; the framework itself is enterprise platform machinery we do not run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Material for MkDocs
good: The dominant MkDocs theme and documentation framework (27,582 stars, 449 releases): turns plain Markdown into a professional static site in minutes — searchable, responsive on all devices, available in more than 60 languages, heavily customisable (colours, fonts, icons, logo) — with a deep bench of bundled extras including built-in plugins, social cards, annotations and search, installed with one pip command and a two-line theme declaration.
bad: It is a presentation layer: adopting it would replace the Lens's own rendering and look wholesale rather than add a capability, and its depth is documentation-site chrome (navigation, search, social cards), not knowledge machinery — the README shows no citation, provenance or verification features.
didnt: Rejected — as a theme it replaces the Lens look rather than adding a capability; the stealable part is its bundled-extras feature checklist, which is recorded in this row rather than taken as code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-macros
licence: MIT (per the README licence badge and the root LICENSE.md; GitHub's metadata shows Other/NOASSERTION)
good: General-purpose MkDocs plugin (410 stars, used by more than 2,000 repositories) that transforms Markdown pages into Jinja2 templates: variables definable in the config file, external YAML files, a Python main module or page front matter; user-defined macros and filters callable inline in prose; Jinja conditions and loops in pages — which is also what makes build-time inclusion/transclusion of external files into a page possible — plus 'pluglets', reusable macro modules distributed as ordinary Python packages.
bad: Undefined variables are printed into the page as-is by default (strict failure is an opt-in setting), so template errors can ship silently; macros execute arbitrary Python at build time, a trust surface a documentation build must accept deliberately; and the mechanism is bound to the MkDocs build pipeline, which our Lens does not use.
didnt: Board — build-time transclusion: including external files into a rendered page at build time is the TiddlyWiki transclusion pattern translated to a static build, and it is the idea worth carrying to the Lens backlog; the plugin itself is MkDocs-bound and our renderer is custom. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocstrings
good: Automatic documentation from source code for MkDocs: language handlers (Python, C, Crystal, TypeScript, MATLAB, VBA, shell scripts, GitHub Actions) collect and render docstrings inline anywhere in a Markdown page via a simple '::: identifier' directive with YAML options, with cross-references to headings across pages and across sites through intersphinx-style inventories, and global plus per-directive configuration with reasonable defaults.
bad: Its subject is code APIs, not knowledge pages: the base package deliberately ships no language support of its own (each handler is a separate install), and nothing in it addresses prose knowledge, citation or provenance. Generated reference pages are only as current as the build that produced them.
didnt: Rejected — scope: docstring-driven code-API documentation, not a knowledge-page capability our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized
good: MkDocs plugin that displays each page's last git modification date, localised with babel and timeago.js in several formats (datetime, date, ISO, relative 'time ago'), integrating with the Material theme's page footer; mature and actively maintained (476 commits, 60 releases).
bad: It needs the last commit that touched each file, so CI builds must be reconfigured to fetch full history (the README spells out fetch-depth 0 for GitHub Actions and the equivalents for GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps), which costs build time on large repositories. A git modification date is also only a change date — it says nothing about whether the page's claims were re-verified then.
didnt: Board — deriving per-page dates from git history rather than hand-maintaining them is the pattern worth taking for Lens page furniture; the caveat recorded here is that for our pages the date that matters is 'last verified', and a commit date alone would overstate freshness. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-awesome-pages
good: MkDocs plugin (627 stars, 33 releases) that gives full control over the navigation structure without hand-writing the entire nav: reorder items or use extensive sorting options, add sections and external links, customise section and page titles, hide pages or whole sections from the nav while leaving them reachable by URL, and match files with glob patterns.
bad: Pure navigation management inside MkDocs's nav model. Our wiki's navigation is deliberately the hand-maintained index.md, so there is no nav pipeline for it to plug into; the project has also renamed itself (Awesome Nav) since the catalogue entry was written.
didnt: Rejected — navigation management only; our index.md is the nav, deliberately, and the plugin is MkDocs-bound. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-redirects
good: MkDocs plugin maintained under the mkdocs organisation that creates redirect stub HTML files for moved or renamed pages from a declarative redirect_maps table in mkdocs.yml (old Markdown path → new Markdown path or external URL), handling directory-URL conventions during the build and warning when a redirect target does not actually exist — so previously published links keep working after a rename.
bad: The map is hand-maintained in central config and only covers renames the author remembers to declare; the plugin is bound to the MkDocs build, and a stub preserves the old URL without recording why the page moved.
didnt: Board — redirect stubs for renamed pages: renamed wiki pages currently break old links, and a declared old→new map rendered as redirect stubs is the known pain-point pattern worth carrying to the Lens backlog; the plugin itself is MkDocs-bound. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-minify
good: MkDocs plugin that minifies a page's HTML before it is written to disk (via htmlmin2) and can also minify JS (jsmin) and CSS (csscompressor), with glob support for selecting asset files and a cache_safe option that adds a hash to JS/CSS filenames so browsers always load the latest version.
bad: Build hygiene only, and opt-in at that: every minification defaults to False, and JS/CSS minification requires hand-listing the files or globs to process. It adds no reader-facing or knowledge capability whatsoever.
didnt: Rejected — output minification is build hygiene, not a capability gap in our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-newsletter
licence: GPL-3.0-only (PyPI record licence field, GPLv3 classifier and README License section agree)
good: MkDocs plugin by Lyz that automatically creates daily, weekly, monthly and yearly newsletter articles from a project's git commit messages, grouping changes by category, subcategory and file in navigation order, and publishing RSS feeds per newsletter type.
bad: It only includes changes it judges 'interesting' and assumes semantic-versioning commit discipline, so the newsletter is only as good as the commit hygiene behind it; it also needs a chain of companion MkDocs plugins to work.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under licence discipline, and the scope is an email/newsletter publishing channel we do not use; our conversation log is already the chronological record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-blogging-plugin
licence: MIT (PyPI record licence field and classifier agree)
good: MkDocs plugin that generates a blog index page listing selected pages sorted by creation or revision time taken from the git log, with tags, category-level configuration and template customisation.
bad: The README states only the Material theme is adapted so far, and MkDocs' navigation.instant feature cannot be enabled when blog paging is on — a narrow, theme-bound listing feature.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a blog listing plugin for MkDocs sites; our reader is the Lens, not MkDocs, and our log is already chronological. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-swagger-ui-tag
licence: MIT (PyPI record license_expression, classifier and README License section agree)
good: MkDocs plugin adding a <swagger-ui> Markdown tag that embeds Swagger UI in a docs page; all Swagger UI assets are served as static files (no CDN, so it works on intranets), multiple UIs per page and multiple OpenAPI specs with a top-bar selector are supported, with initOAuth support and dark-mode sync with the Material theme.
bad: API-documentation scope only; the default validatorUrl points at swagger.io's online validator (an external call unless explicitly set to none), and embedding is iframe-based.
didnt: Rejected — scope: embedding interactive API docs in MkDocs pages; our wiki publishes no OpenAPI documentation. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mkdocs-jupyter
licence: Apache-2.0 (PyPI record licence field and the bundled LICENSE.txt agree)
good: MkDocs plugin that treats .ipynb notebooks and .py scripts (via jupytext) as first-class navigation pages, with optional notebook execution before conversion, ipywidgets support, a table of contents, optional source download, and content-hash caching of conversions.
bad: The README states Markdown/Material features such as admonitions do not work inside notebooks because of the nbconvert conversion path, and notebook styling is 'not always possible' across themes — it is mostly tested against Material.
didnt: Rejected — scope: notebook embedding in MkDocs sites; we publish no Jupyter notebooks in the wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Entangled
licence: Apache-2.0 (project site License section and PyPI README licence statement agree)
good: Literate-programming tool from the Netherlands eScience Center: two-way synchronisation between Markdown documentation and source code (tangling in both directions via a watch daemon), cross-referenced named code blocks assembled into target files, an MkDocs plugin, and a REPL-session hook that evaluates REPL commands into the documentation.
bad: Its own README states the minuses plainly: 'not intended for scientific use: numbering and referencing equations, figures and tables is hard to setup', and the documentation is 'hard if you want specifics'.
didnt: Rejected — scope: literate programming for code projects, keeping docs and code in sync; our wiki's sources are records and citations, not runnable code awaiting tangling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Netherlands eScience Center

name: tiddlyroam
licence: BSD-2-Clause (repo metadata, LICENSE file and README License section agree)
good: A free Roam Research alternative built on TiddlyWiki: bi-directional links and interactive graph maps (built on the TiddlyMaps and TiddlyBlink plugins), distributed as a single tiddlyroam.html file run through TiddlyDesktop.
bad: A very small surface — 11 commits and 2 releases; the edition is essentially backlinks plus a graph view layered on stock TiddlyWiki, and easy saving depends on TiddlyDesktop.
didnt: Rejected — a TiddlyWiki flavour; the bidirectional-link and graph pattern is already carried by the TiddlyWiki deep dive and by our own wiki's links, with no citation or custody machinery added. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jimmy
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo metadata and the root licence file agree)
good: Standalone, offline, cross-platform converter that turns notes from 40+ apps (including TiddlyWiki, Evernote, Notion, Joplin and Google Keep) and many document formats into Markdown plus front matter through a two-stage intermediate format, preserving resources, tags and note links where possible; full CLI plus a beta TUI subset, and it states no AI is used in conversion.
bad: Preservation is explicitly 'when possible' — the README itself warns 'Make sure your data is converted properly' — and the TUI is beta with only a feature subset of the CLI.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only under licence discipline (the two-stage intermediate-format pipeline is the idea), and our ingest converters are directed per-source with verbatim raw preservation rather than a generic migration tool. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tiddlyhost
licence: Conflict recorded: README License section states 'It uses a BSD license. See LICENSE.md' and a root LICENSE.md exists (exact BSD variant not read), while GitHub repo metadata reports Other (NOASSERTION) — the two are recorded as found, not silently resolved.
good: Rails hosting service for TiddlyWiki, successor to Tiddlyspot: secure SSL hosting, password recovery, TiddlyWiki5 support, upload of existing wiki files, private or public sites, a searchable Hub of hosted wikis, open-source code that is self-hostable via Docker, and active development (1,652 commits).
bad: It is a hosted platform: on the hosted service, custody of the wikis sits with the operator, and backups require the user's own manual actions — the opposite of our owner-custody model.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted platform for wikis, excluded by our no-hosted, local-first custody posture for the private wiki regardless of the self-host option. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tidme / TiddlyMemo
licence: Split recorded per distribution, neither borrowed for the other: Tidme is Apache-2.0 (repo metadata + LICENSE); TiddlyMemo is MIT (repo metadata + LICENSE + its npm package record).
good: Two sibling TiddlyWiki distributions by oflg implementing incremental learning inside the wiki: SuperMemo-style incremental reading, LingQ-style language annotation, and Anki-style memory notes and flashcards (Tidme is the current successor edition; TiddlyMemo the archived plugin/edition).
bad: TiddlyMemo is archived and superseded, and both distributions are dormant on the catalogue's own signals (TiddlyMemo Oct 19, 2023; Tidme Mar 4, 2024); the scope is a spaced-repetition learning layer, not knowledge-OS machinery.
didnt: Rejected — SRS-flavoured TiddlyWiki distributions, dormant, and a learning-scheduler scope our system does not carry. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Modern.TiddlyDev
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: One-click development environment/template for TiddlyWiki plugin authors on a modern front-end stack: a dev-mode page server that auto-detects plugin file changes and syncs them to the browser for WYSIWYG development, one-click plugin building and plugin-library generation, built-in GitHub Pages and GitHub Release publishing scripts, TypeScript tailoring (tw5-typed annotations, multi-entry esbuild incremental builds, sourcemaps, automatic hash-check signatures for generated plugins) and Playwright E2E tests.
bad: Scope-bound: it is a template and toolchain for building TiddlyWiki plugins, carrying a heavy modern JS toolchain (pnpm, esbuild, Tailwind, Playwright) for that one ecosystem; it offers nothing to a system that does not develop TiddlyWiki plugins.
didnt: Rejected — scope: developer tooling for building TiddlyWiki plugins; we build no TiddlyWiki plugins. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tiddlywiki-ipfs
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later (LICENSE file and README License section; repo metadata shows GPL-3.0)
good: TiddlyWiki plugin that stores and retrieves wikis and attachments on IPFS, with compression, encrypt/decrypt/sign support (including Ethereum/SHA-3), IPNS key publishing, and MetaMask wallet and ENS publishing support.
bad: The repo is archived, and the working setup demands a heavy prerequisite stack: a local IPFS node or IPFS Companion, MetaMask for .eth resolution, and an Ethereum wallet for ENS updates.
didnt: Rejected — GPL code is ideas-only under licence discipline, the project is archived, and decentralised IPFS hosting runs against our Azure-canonical, owner-only custody design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: VitePress
licence: MIT (repo metadata, LICENSE file and README License section agree)
good: Vue-powered static site generator built on Vite, the spiritual successor to VuePress and the generator behind the Vue and Vite official docs: near-instant dev-server start and hot reload, Vue components usable directly in Markdown, and a clean default documentation theme.
bad: A documentation SSG only: the source shows no knowledge-management machinery — no citation locking, provenance, abstention or gated writes — and it binds a site to the Vue/Vite ecosystem with a deliberately minimal theming surface.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a docs theme/generator for software projects; our renderer is the Lens and VitePress adds nothing beyond the Docusaurus-class features already surveyed. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Starlight (Astro)
licence: MIT (repo metadata, LICENSE file and README License section agree)
good: Astro's purpose-built documentation framework: built-in site navigation, search, internationalisation, SEO, readable typography, code highlighting and dark mode out of the box; Markdown, Markdoc and MDX authoring with TypeScript-type-safe frontmatter validation; framework-agnostic UI components (React, Vue, Svelte, Solid) on Astro's performance model.
bad: A documentation-site framework only: the source shows no citation, provenance or approval-gate machinery, and adopting it would bind the reader to the Astro ecosystem — a second rendering stack beside the Lens.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a docs theme/framework; the Lens is already our purpose-built reader. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Docsy (Hugo theme)
licence: Apache-2.0 for code, CC-BY-4.0 for documentation (repo metadata and README Licenses line agree)
good: A Hugo theme purpose-built for technical documentation sets, now a Linux Foundation project: documentation best practices built in (autogenerated site navigation, layouts optimised per content type, feedback/contribution links, internationalisation on Hugo's multi-language support), shipped with a full example site and user guide in the same monorepo.
bad: Its own user guide states what Docsy does not provide: no source hosting or management, no site deployment, and it does not generate the HTML — that is Hugo's job. It is a theme layer bound to the Hugo ecosystem.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a project-documentation theme for Hugo sites; our reader is the Lens and we run no Hugo stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Nextra
good: MDX documentation framework on Next.js: build-time full-text search via Pagefind with zero configuration, Shiki build-time syntax highlighting, file-system routing, folder-based i18n, automatic conversion of Markdown links and images to Next.js Link/Image, and last-git-edit-time stamps.
bad: Wholly inside the Next.js/React ecosystem — MDX components-in-Markdown and a Node build chain to publish what is a static docs site; a presentation framework only, with no knowledge features (no backlink graph, queries over the corpus, or citation machinery).
didnt: Rejected — React/Next.js docs framework; our portal renders plain Markdown without a framework build chain, and MDX component embedding works against file purity (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Jekyll
good: The original blog-aware static site generator: transforms plain text into static websites and blogs with no database, with permalinks, categories, pages, posts and custom layouts as first-class citizens, free hosting via GitHub Pages, and a very large theme and plugin ecosystem built over two decades.
bad: Ruby/gem toolchain (bundler) in a Node/Python estate; a blog-centric data model of dated posts rather than a knowledge graph; Liquid templating; no search, linking intelligence or citation support of its own.
didnt: Rejected — legacy blog SSG on a Ruby stack we do not run; the Lens already renders the wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Zola
good: A single Rust executable with no dependencies: Sass compilation, syntax highlighting, table of contents and a search index all built in; the average site renders in under a second; augmented Markdown with internal links; fully static output with no server or database to run.
bad: The repo's LICENSE file is the EUPL-1.2, a copyleft licence, so its code is ideas-only under our licence discipline; Tera templating is its own dialect; still a presentation-layer SSG — no backlinks-as-data, corpus queries or citation support.
didnt: Rejected — EUPL-1.2 copyleft makes the code ideas-only, and it is a presentation SSG with no knowledge features (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Eleventy
good: Fastest-in-class builds (the project's own published benchmark builds 4,000 Markdown files in 1.93s against Astro 22.90s and Gatsby 29.05s); zero client-side JavaScript by default and no injected markup; a dozen-plus independent template languages usable together in one project; no telemetry; 227 releases since December 2017 of which only three required developer intervention — content stays decoupled from the tool.
bad: Mid-rebrand at study time: the project renamed Eleventy to Build Awesome in March 2026, the package moved to the @awesome.me npm scope, and v4.0.0-alpha is in development, so names and docs are in motion; still a generic SSG with no knowledge graph, backlinks-as-data or citation support.
didnt: Rejected — a strong generic SSG, but the Lens already meets our rendering need and a rebrand-in-flight dependency buys nothing (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Gatsby
good: React-based framework with a unified GraphQL data layer that integrates content, APIs and services into one model, with SSR, deferred static generation and cloud functions for flexibility beyond pure static output, and a very large plugin ecosystem.
bad: The heaviest machinery in this set — a GraphQL data layer and the React runtime to produce static pages, with build times at the slow end of the field (29.05s for 4,000 files in Build Awesome's published comparison); stewardship in transition — the project's own homepage now leads with Gatsby Cloud and Netlify Cloud uniting and migration paths to Netlify.
didnt: Rejected — heavy React/GraphQL data-layer SSG in corporate transition; the wrong weight class for a plain-Markdown wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Read the Docs
good: Documentation hosting done as docs-as-code: connect a Git repository and it runs the builds, gives every pull request a preview build with a visual diff against production, builds multiple versions from branches and tags, and adds search, authentication and SSO; supports Sphinx, MkDocs, Docusaurus and more; free for open source since 2010, and now advertising llms.txt and Markdown content negotiation for AI tools.
bad: It is a hosted platform — our wiki is owner-only private material that stays in our own custody, and self-hosting the full platform is exactly the operations burden the service exists to sell relief from.
didnt: Rejected — a hosting platform; private-wiki custody rules keep the wiki on our own static pipeline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Textus
good: WYSIWYG Markdown editor (Tauri/Rust and React) whose AI edits arrive as proposals, each with a reason, acceptable whole or sentence by sentence; documents are plain .md files kept wherever the user chooses; no account, analytics or telemetry; the editor works fully offline and without AI, and Textus AI takes 20+ providers or a local Ollama model; exports to PDF, Word and HTML.
bad: A writer's editor, not a knowledge system — the README shows no vault-wide linking, graph, query or citation machinery; very young (created July 2026) and single-studio, with iPhone/iPad still listed as coming; its style-learning memory is an opaque convenience a citation-grounded system would not import.
didnt: Corroboration — AI edits delivered as reasoned proposals, accepted whole or sentence by sentence, independently confirm our approval-gated write pattern at editor scale (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: libreta
good: Genuinely local-first (no accounts, cloud or tracking) with rich note furniture: folders and subfolders, smart folders by rules, checklists, tables, attachments of any type, hand drawing and document scanning; accent-insensitive, typo-tolerant search with field filters; [[links]] with a mentions/backlinks view; per-note version history with restore; password-locked notes encrypted with AES-256-GCM; automatic dated .tar.gz backups; broad import (Markdown folders, Joplin, Obsidian, Bear, Notion, Evernote .enex) and export to PDF/HTML/Markdown.
bad: Notes are stored as JSON files in a user folder — Markdown is an import/export format, not the storage format, so the corpus is not plain-text-native; a brand-new, single-author-scale project (repo created 2026-10-19, 0 stars); the Windows installer is unsigned (the README itself warns of the SmartScreen prompt); no real-time collaboration — a shared folder is last-save-wins.
didnt: Rejected — JSON-file storage breaks the plain-Markdown corpus rule, and the project is days old (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: IncarnaMind
good: The closest design relative in this batch: draft checking sentence by sentence and figure by figure, returning supported, unsupported or contradicted with the exact page one click away; answers cite the page and carry the quote, which is checked against the source (a green mark if present, amber if not), and exports mark a citation that failed the check as [unverified]; reads PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, CSV, Markdown and text files in place, never moving or changing them; discovers sources via OpenAlex, arXiv and PubMed and imports Zotero/CSL/BibTeX/RIS; MCP connectors and skills whose tools could change something run only after the user says yes (allow once, always, or deny — revocable); meeting recording with on-device transcription saved as a citable document.
bad: Not yet released — the README states there are no installers yet and it runs from source, despite the mature commit history; its own honesty caveat cuts deep: a found quote means the quoted words are in the named place, not that they prove the sentence, so its checking is lexical rather than semantic; with a cloud model, the question and the passages found still go to that provider.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent implementation of quote-checked citations, supported/unsupported/contradicted claim checking, in-place source custody and ask-first tool permissions confirms our citation-lockfile and approval-gate design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: keep-the-why
good: Preserves the why of a codebase — architecture decisions, rejected alternatives, workarounds, incident learnings, operational constraints — as plain Markdown in a context/ folder inside the repo, so Git provides the storage, history, review and distribution; four operating modes (continuous capture, retrospective recovery from history/issues/code, knowledge-transfer interview, and maintenance that resolves contradictions and marks superseded entries); unattended agents write entries flagged pending-confirmation instead of asking into the void; a published controlled experiment (twenty fresh agent sessions asked to simplify a retry wrapper: without a recorded reason 7 of 10 re-proposed the already-rejected change, with one context/ entry 0 of 10 did); SKILL.md format installable across 70+ agents, with a structural linter (keep-the-why-lint) for CI.
bad: Built for code repositories — the memory lives beside code and assumes Git review culture, so it transfers to a personal wiki by pattern, not directly; capture depends on the agent noticing rationale, and its evals are tracked against one agent (Claude Code) with stated caveats; a skill cannot load itself, so autostart needs hooks or entry-point sections measured per agent; the install notes warn that the main branch is active development, not guaranteed release-ready.
didnt: Corroboration — its controlled promotion (append-only raw capture, review as the promotion boundary, one canonical current-state surface), pending-confirmation flags for unattended writes and superseded-entry marking independently match our ingest/promotion and corrections-ledger discipline (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: foliole
good: Incremental reading as the native workflow — extract passages and create cloze deletions without leaving the reading flow, scheduled by an integrated FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler); local-first with no account system and no central cloud sync (devices sync over the local network); indexes external folders in place without copying or moving the originals; open data via a SQLite store with a Markdown mirror; command-line and agent workflows, and publishing of evolving topics to the user's own site, WordPress or Discourse.
bad: Alpha software — the README labels the macOS/Windows/Linux builds alpha or experimental and mobile builds still expected; the primary store is a SQLite database, so Markdown is a mirror rather than the source of truth; its scheduling serves memorisation, not verification.
didnt: Board — FSRS-style spaced scheduling applied to our reverify/review queue, so pages and citations come due for re-checking on a forgetting-curve cadence instead of sitting on a flat list (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: light-note
good: One account workspace unifying bookmarks (auto-fetched title, description and icon), notes (rich-text and Markdown dual-mode editing), cloud files and todos, tied together by unified tags and cross-module search; per-module AI assistance scoped to the current resource (summarise, generate, break down, organise); a free hosted tier with mobile access.
bad: A hosted cloud service first — the author's own deployment (the README names its Huawei Cloud / Nginx / MySQL / object-storage stack), with notes and files living server-side, the opposite custody model from local-first files; the README itself states no one-click self-hosting is offered, the full environment needing database, object storage, cache, mail and third-party AI services; zero tagged releases in two years.
didnt: Rejected — hosted, account-and-server-centric platform; custody and self-hosting both fail our local-first rule (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Noto
good: Byte-exact saving as the central design property: the file is parsed into blocks, each block's exact source bytes are recorded with its origin and hash, and on save every untouched block is written back exactly — line endings and whitespace preserved — so opening and saving without edits leaves the file identical to the byte; the same block record detects an external change, refuses the save and offers a copy instead; performance is published as measured tables from the packaged build, and a 237-test packaged suite is run on macOS, Windows and Linux.
bad: AGPL-3.0 copyleft, so its code is ideas-only under our licence discipline; pre-1.0 and single-author scale (v0.0.3 of 2026-10-17 is the first release outside alpha; 3 stars), unsigned by choice on all platforms; content search scans the folder on demand (about 1.3s cold over its own 7,066-note test vault) rather than keeping an index, a design that caps out at personal-vault scale.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 copyleft keeps the code ideas-only and it is a young WYSIWYG editor; the byte-exact block-hash round-trip is recorded as design evidence only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lanternote
good: Built for very large plain-Markdown folders and measured on a real one (190,522 notes, 2.49M links, 728 MB: reopen about 1–2s, full-text search 20–130 ms, live query about 0.1s); everything is plain .md in a folder the user chooses, offline, with no account, telemetry or update check; galaxy view and link graph, live queries in the Dataview query language, tasks and calendars collected from all notes, Kanban boards and JSON Canvas canvases stored as plain Markdown, unlinked mentions and version history; a built-in MCP server (search, read, query, tasks, plus a verify_quote tool that checks a quotation and its numbers against the note before citing) that is read-only unless the user turns on AI edits, with every AI change logged and reversible.
bad: Young and small: the app is not code-signed yet (SmartScreen and Gatekeeper warnings; macOS and Linux builds are new); stated ceilings — a 1,000,000-file limit, and beyond 1.5 GB of text the search covers only part of the folder and says so; when an AI assistant is connected, the notes it reads are sent to that provider, as its own Privacy section states.
didnt: Corroboration — read-only-by-default MCP access, logged and reversible AI edits, and a verify-before-citing quote check over a plain-files corpus confirm our door and editor design at vault scale (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Bower
licence: FSL-1.1-MIT (Functional Source License 1.1, MIT Future License) per the repo LICENSE file and README badge; GitHub repo metadata shows NOASSERTION and the catalogue stated no licence — the LICENSE file governs: fair-source terms, each version converting to MIT two years after publication, competing hosted offerings prohibited
good: A self-filing second brain over the user's own Google Drive: captures (files, links, text) land in an inbox, and on the owner's 'Tidy up' tap a headless Claude with every tool turned off proposes a name and PARA folder for each item while plain code performs every write, each write re-checking the file is still as it was read; near-duplicates become a question to the owner rather than a guess, notes keep a rewritten 'Current state' section with two-way links, and nothing is ever hard-deleted — moves go to the Drive Bin.
bad: The filing decisions themselves are the model's: the owner taps once and Claude names and files everything — the auto-organise pattern our ingest rules reject; the store is Google Drive behind a Cloudflare Worker and a GitHub Actions runner, so custody is a chain of third-party services plus a Claude plan, and photos and scanned PDFs are not read at all, only filed by the user's caption.
didnt: Rejected — self-filing auto-organisation (our pattern is directed ingest with a human ruling) and Google Drive custody; its propose-then-checked-write split corroborates our approval-gated writes, but the gate here is one tap for a whole inbox, not a ruling per item. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Third Brain
licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file, full text; README Licence section and repo metadata agree)
good: Local-first capture layer that turns Outlook/Gmail mail, Teams chats and meetings, and Claude.ai/ChatGPT conversations into short, sourced Markdown notes in the user's own Obsidian vault, with a pre-AI safety pass that blocks passwords, one-time codes, and card, bank and ID numbers before any model sees the text; the vault is backed up to a private GitHub repo and served to AI clients through a local search + MCP server (GBrain: keyword plus local Ollama embeddings), with remote access off unless the owner turns it on.
bad: It is a sync-everything engine on a 15-minute schedule — the undirected ingest our rules reject, and chat-transcript ingest specifically is unapproved; the Claude.ai/ChatGPT connectors ride those sites' unofficial web APIs ('can break when the sites change... use them at your own risk', per its own README); early preview, Windows-only, a Microsoft 365 sign-in is required even for Gmail, the installer is not code-signed, and the notes are model-written distillations, not verbatim records.
didnt: Rejected — sync-everything ingest including chat transcripts (unapproved), built on unofficial web APIs; its credential/secret pre-filter, applied before any AI sees text, is recorded as corroboration of our write-time secret blocking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: OSS Malaysia

name: Seahorse
licence: MIT (LICENSE file; README License section agrees)
good: A Telegram/Obsidian capture agent that keeps every message verbatim as an 'engram' before organising it into four areas (Intention, Memory, Knowledge, Identity) as plain Markdown in the user's own private Git repository; it plans the week around free hours, rolls undone tasks to the next free day, and answers questions from the notes — capture itself is lossless even though the organisation layered over it is the agent's.
bad: The agent maintains a self-model of the owner — an Identity area of inferred profile, routine, patterns and tastes — and rewrites existing notes when a new fact arrives ('a new fact changes old notes'), with no approval gate on the reorganisation; it is proactive by design ('talks to you first', suggests content it thinks you would like), needs an always-on server plus a Claude or ChatGPT subscription, and is a single-author project with 0 stars.
didnt: Rejected — agent-maintained self-model with auto-inference about the owner, and ungated rewriting of existing notes, are out of bounds under our custody rules; the verbatim engram (each message kept exactly as sent, organisation layered over it) is recorded as corroboration of capture-first design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Dotflowy
licence: O'Saasy License Agreement (custom licence, repo LICENSE file: MIT-like terms plus a prohibition on offering the software as a competing hosted/SaaS product); repo metadata shows NOASSERTION and the catalogue stated no licence — recorded as a conflict, the LICENSE file governs
good: A fast browser outliner (Workflowy alternative): one nested outline of bullets, tasks, paragraphs and embeds with zoom and drag, node mirroring so a single node lives in several places and edits update both, OPML import from Workflowy plus OPML/Markdown export, and an MCP/CLI surface where agent changes appear live with attribution and text marked as spoilers is redacted before it reaches agents, not merely hidden.
bad: It is a hosted product, not a local tool: outlines live in the vendor's Cloudflare Durable Objects behind an account, the free tier caps at 10,000 nodes, MCP/CLI agent access sits in the paid tiers, sharing and collaboration are not available yet, and the custom O'Saasy licence — despite the 'open-source alternative' framing — reserves competing hosted use to the copyright holder.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody and a custom licence (ideas-only under our discipline); an outliner app, and outlining already lives inside our pages. Node mirroring and agent-change attribution are noted as design observations only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: logseq-cli
good: A CLI that lets an agent write into a file-based Logseq graph through the running app instead of guessing at the files: every write is verified against Logseq before success is reported ('writes are verified, not assumed'), --dry-run previews any write, --expect-hash refuses a change when the block moved since it was read, a read_only config switches all writes off before the first request, the block being typed in and blocks others reference are protected from overwrite/deletion, and reads are bounded to a caller-set size with every cut announced.
bad: There is no undo — a deletion is final; it works only while Logseq runs with its HTTP API server on and a bearer token in the environment, the README itself concedes the safety switches bind a careless agent rather than a determined one, and it covers only Markdown graphs (Logseq 0.10.x / OG), not the DB version; a 0-star single-author 2026 project.
didnt: Board — the agent-CLI write discipline as a pattern for our own tooling: writes verified not assumed, hash preconditions on edits, dry-run on every write command, a read-only mode checked before the first request, and bounded reads that state what they left out. The tool itself drives Logseq, which is not our substrate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zettelbranch
good: A browser extension that branches any claude.ai conversation from a chosen message into a new chat carrying the conversation so far, naming branches with Luhmann-style addresses (sky/1a1) shown in the sidebar so a conversation tree stays navigable; its trust posture is unusually strict — no permissions, no background script, no conversation content stored or sent anywhere, writes only on click with the user pressing Send, and an AUDIT.md whose never-does claims are checkable with supplied grep commands.
bad: It depends on claude.ai's undocumented web interface, which the README says to expect to break ('one of these updates will break it, probably soon'); images, files and artifacts are not copied into branches (placeholders only), Chrome installation needs developer mode, and it is an early v0.2.2 single-author project.
didnt: Rejected — a chat-branching extension over a third-party chat UI; our conversation log is a single verbatim, append-only record by design, and tooling premised on a chat service's undocumented internals is too fragile to build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Obsidian-ZettelFlow
licence: MIT (LICENSE file; repo metadata agrees; agrees with the standing master row 'ZettelFlow')
good: Re-study agrees with the standing master row: an Obsidian plugin whose practice loops return a note's claim blind and ask what you say now, place dated wagers on claims and reveal the prediction only after asking what happened, and collide unrelated notes — all fully working with AI off; when AI is on it proposes and the user accepts, edits or rejects, with the verdict recorded; note creation is a drawn Canvas workflow walked as a wizard with live preview, and citations export as Markdown link-backs, Pandoc keys, BibTeX or CSL JSON, never a guessed field.
bad: A very large surface (Reader, Library, dashboards, community system installs, a user-script action that runs JavaScript with vault access) — power that widens the trust surface well beyond the loops, exactly as the standing row records; it is bound to Obsidian, which is not our substrate.
didnt: Corroboration — this listing is the same project as the standing master row 'ZettelFlow' (rafaelgb/Obsidian-ZettelFlow); re-studied at source and in agreement with that row: claim-return, wager and collision loops plus AI-proposes/verdict-recorded are independent evidence that scheduled re-confrontation with one's own claims and recorded verdicts are the live frontier for knowledge systems — the direction of our claim lifecycle and trust ledger; nothing adopted directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vault-cortex
licence: MIT (LICENSE file ships in the repository; agrees with the standing master row 'aliasunder/vault-cortex')
good: Re-study agrees with the standing master row: a standalone MCP server over an Obsidian vault the owner keeps as plain Markdown — hybrid search, structured append-only dated memory that shows how a view evolved, tasks and link-graph health, reachable from a phone under OAuth 2.1 while the vault itself never stops being a folder of files; a heavily shipped, field stress-tested project (its repo runs gitleaks, Trivy and OpenSSF Scorecard CI).
bad: Remote mode rents back your own vault, as the standing row records: it needs a paid Obsidian Sync subscription and a hosted copy on Railway/Render or a VPS you maintain, and its setup asks for your Obsidian account credentials (the server keeps the Sync token) — a custody step the convenience does not erase; there is no citation or abstention machinery in anything the source shows.
didnt: Corroboration — this listing is the same project as the standing master row 'aliasunder/vault-cortex'; re-studied and in agreement: a disposable server over owner-held plain Markdown with append-only dated memory corroborates our files-first substrate bet, productised for Obsidian users. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: carnet
licence: AGPL-3.0-only (LICENSE file, full text; README badge and License section agree) — the catalogue stated no licence
good: Mobile-first knowledge capture for Obsidian with a save-first rule — the file lands instantly and LLM enrichment patches afterwards — across six modes (idea, note, voice journal, business-card OCR into a People note, photo, audio memo), an offline on-device queue drained on reconnect, everything written as plain Markdown into the user's own folders and synced device-to-workstation by Syncthing peer-to-peer, with API keys held in the OS secure keystore.
bad: AGPL-3.0-only, so its code is ideas-only for us; every capture is routed through an external LLM service (an OmniRoute endpoint and API key are required for the enrichment), it is an Android front-end for Obsidian rather than a substrate we run, and its two distribution channels (GitHub APK, planned Play build) cannot upgrade each other.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0-only and an Obsidian mobile capture front-end; its save-first ordering (the record lands before any enrichment touches it) is noted as corroboration of capture-before-processing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Caldera
licence: MIT for the core and plugin packages (root LICENSE file, MIT, copyright mjonesone, LLC; the open protocol spec is CC-BY-4.0 per the README's package table) — the catalogue stated no licence
good: A social layer for Obsidian with careful defaults: nothing leaves the vault unless a section is switched on, a note is marked caldera: public, or a card is shared with a named friend; every publish can be previewed first; sharing uses end-to-end encrypted cards over a signed-envelope protocol with Ed25519/X25519 identity — keys, not accounts — and the plugin discloses its network use (the configured hub only, on publish, sync or action; no telemetry).
bad: Its purpose is publication and social mechanics — a living profile generated from your vault, friends between vaults, asks and offers, help credits and positive-only 'gravity' — run through a hosted hub (caldera.social); that is the opposite direction from our private-by-design wiki, and it is a young single-vendor project (mjonesone, LLC).
didnt: Rejected — a social/sharing layer; our wiki is private by design and publication is an owner-gated act, not a substrate feature. Its preview-before-publish and per-note opt-in are noted as the least-bad form of the pattern. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Moss
good: One person's technical digital garden run as a real system: a component lab with live previews and copyable code, a manual of guides, a log (bitácora) recording learnings, decisions and errors, ordered learning routes through the material with progress tracking, project pages that document each decision together with the alternative discarded and the lesson taken, and global search across all of it; the template is enforced — the site tests fail if a project page's documented-version or last-review frontmatter is missing.
bad: It is a personal content site, not a reusable tool: nothing in the repo is machinery another knowledge system could adopt, route progress is kept only in the visitor's browser storage, and the content is a single author's Spanish-language portfolio.
didnt: Rejected — a personal site, not a tool (scope), as the catalogue judged; its project-page discipline (decision, discarded alternative, lesson, with missing review fields failing the build's tests) is a documentation habit worth noting, not a build. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Xanadu implementation (unnamed repo in listing)
licence: Apache-2.0 as stated in the repo's own description, its README disclaimer and its LICENSE file — recorded with the formal conflict that the LICENSE file carries only the short Apache appendix notice rather than the full text and GitHub's repo metadata shows NOASSERTION; the catalogue likewise carried Apache-2.0 'as stated in its listing text'
good: A working Rust/TypeScript implementation of the Xanadu document model: real transclusion (a passage appears live in another document as a window onto the source, updating with it, provenance traced back), typed links (Comment, Reference, Disagreement, Quotation, See Also, Web) visible from both ends, per-author attribution with Ed25519 span signing and a tamper-evident chained audit log whose full verification distinguishes a warning from a tampering verdict, every version addressable and comparable, and links that survive edits because positions are tumbler addresses, not offsets.
bad: Its centre is real-time multi-writer CRDT collaboration, shared public docuverses and cross-server federation — the multi-writer/real-time direction our design rejects by decision; it is a large surface (a 140+ operation WebSocket API) from a single author pursuing a heritage design, not a component a personal wiki can lift.
didnt: Board — as a design reference only, as the catalogue judged: transclusion-with-provenance and character-level signed attribution are the intellectual source of the include pattern; nothing to run, and the multi-writer CRDT core is not for us. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PersonalClaw
licence: MIT (LICENSE file and README badge; the catalogue's 'MIT as stated in its listing text' is confirmed at source)
good: A self-hosted personal agent OS: chat, autonomous goal loops under a deterministic supervisor the owner can pause, nudge or stop, long-term memory, a knowledge base, skills and scheduled automation behind one gateway process, with every vendor a removable app, a permission-gated and scanner-gated app platform, approvals and guardrails in the context engine, no analytics, all state under one ~/.personalclaw home, and graceful degradation to local-only operation.
bad: Pre-1.0 (v0.2.4) with an explicit clean-break doctrine: breaking changes arrive with no automatic migration of sessions, memory or knowledge data, and the README itself warns 'Don't make this your only system of record yet' — disqualifying custody terms for a memory system today; it is also an agent platform, not a wiki feature source.
didnt: Rejected — an agent platform, not a wiki feature source, and its pre-1.0 clean-break data policy contradicts durability-first custody; its permission-gated, scanner-gated app platform is noted as a design observation only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ntropy
licence: MPL-2.0 (LICENSE file carries the full Mozilla Public License 2.0 text; repo metadata agrees) — the catalogue stated no licence
good: An opinionated Markdown note-taking CLI with no database: notes are plain files whose identity is a stable ULID rather than a title, filing is frontmatter metadata, and any hierarchy is a derived projection of that metadata materialised as browsable filesystem views; a real query language, fuzzy full-text search, editor-native link and tag completion over LSP, PDF and website export, and the design recorded as ADRs — with the documentation itself kept as a vault the tool exports as its own website.
bad: MPL-2.0, so its code is ideas-only for our stack; metadata-as-filing is the opposite of our deliberate folders + index choice; macOS and Linux only (Windows expressly unsupported), and a single-author, heavily opinionated tool.
didnt: Rejected — the filing model contradicts a deliberate design decision (our filing is folders + index), and MPL-2.0 is ideas-only; hierarchy-as-derived-projection over flat storage is the one transferable idea, already present in our derived views. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: biblical-word-root-lookup
licence: MIT for the code (repo LICENSE file; GitHub repo metadata shows NOASSERTION — a detection discrepancy recorded, not resolved); the bundled Strong's data is CC-BY-SA (Open Scriptures) per the README's Data and licences section — the catalogue stated no licence
good: A Claude skill for Bible word studies with bundled, offline Strong's Hebrew and Greek data: it returns the Strong's number and definition, the root chain and same-root words, and for Hebrew the entry number in Benner's Lexicon so the owner checks the printed book beside it; claims are labelled by source, the transcription's uncertainty is disclosed in the open (spot-checked, not proofread row by row; the least-sure rows are listed in SOURCES.md), and its best rule is that the user's own reading is the authority — 'The skill never writes your meaning for you', it only builds the note skeleton.
bad: A single-domain skill, not knowledge-system machinery; it requires the owner's own copy of Benner's Lexicon (entry text is not included), about a third of Hebrew Strong's numbers have no Benner row, and verse lookups need web access.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a domain skill for Bible study, not a tool for our system; its authority rule (the human's reading governs, sources labelled, uncertainty disclosed) is recorded as corroboration of our verification posture. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bloglite
good: Self-hostable Rust (micro)blogging service with a footprint of only a few MB of memory: Markdown posts with built-in syntax highlighting and LaTeX math display, publishing and editing from desktop or mobile, file/image uploads, and an automatic backup path — an API download exports the whole site as plain text files (all.tar.xz) that can be committed to git, with an optional token-triggered backup workflow on GitHub or Forgejo. Actively developed (452 commits, 29 releases since April 2025).
bad: A public publishing timeline, not a knowledge store: content lives in a SQLite database behind a single-admin env-password model, and the README documents no citation, provenance or verification machinery — retrieval is the built-in search or, as the README itself suggests, Google. Nothing in it addresses a personal wiki's organisation or trust problems.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a self-hosted microblog publishing service; its plain-text backup-to-git pattern is sound but already our practice via the wiki repo itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FlatPress
good: Mature flat-file PHP blogging engine (since 2013, 3,491 commits, 21 releases): no database — all data in files, so backup is a file copy; a plugin system with widget support, Smarty-powered themes, comments with spam protection, 17 interface languages, and PHPStan plus CodeQL checks running in GitHub Actions on every change.
bad: GPL-2.0, so its code is ideas-only for our stack. It is a blog publishing engine: no knowledge organisation, citation or provenance machinery, and it requires operating a PHP web server (PHP 7.2–8.5) as a public surface.
didnt: Rejected — scope (flat-file blog engine; the files-as-truth pattern it shares with us is already our substrate) and licence (GPL-2.0, ideas only). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HTMLy
licence: GPL-2.0 (repo metadata and LICENSE.txt; README Copyright/License section says GPL version 2.0 or later)
good: Databaseless flat-file PHP blogging platform/CMS (1,367 stars, 74 releases since 2013): content stored as files and found by a date/type/category/tag/author lookup the README says stays fast with ten thousand posts and hundreds of tags; Markdown content, an online installer, and a backup feature (PHP-ZIP).
bad: GPL-2.0 family, so its code is ideas-only for our stack. Scope is a blog CMS — a publishing surface with roles and a dashboard, no citation/provenance machinery; the README also leaves a manual security chore to the operator (the installer tries to delete itself and the user must verify install.php is gone).
didnt: Rejected — scope (flat-file blog CMS) and licence (GPL-2.0, ideas only). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ech0
licence: AGPL-3.0 (README: AGPL-3.0-or-later; a COMMERCIAL.md alongside the LICENSE offers commercial terms)
good: Fast-moving self-hosted personal microblog/timeline (Go + Vue, 2,767 commits and 257 releases in its first year): Markdown writing with tags, portable content capsules that export everything you have written as a self-contained package importable into another instance or compilable into a static site, snapshot/capsule backup via Web, CLI and TUI, S3-compatible storage, passkey/OAuth2 login with scoped revocable API tokens, a built-in MCP server exposing near-complete product features over Streamable HTTP with scoped JWT, and an AI Copilot doing vector-RAG Q&A over your own posts.
bad: AGPL-3.0-or-later, so its code is ideas-only for our stack. By its own README it is the wrong shape for us: 'Probably not for you if you need a bi-directional knowledge base workflow (for example Obsidian-style PKM)' — it is a social publishing timeline, and its Copilot's RAG answers carry no citation locking, provenance or abstention machinery.
didnt: Corroboration — its portable content capsules (export everything as one self-contained, re-importable package) corroborate our whole-corpus portable export and preservation practice; the platform itself is out of scope (microblog publishing) and AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Known
licence: Apache-2.0 (README Copyright and License section and root LICENSE file; repo metadata reports Other/NOASSERTION — the README statement governs)
good: Long-lived PHP IndieWeb social publishing platform (9,072 commits since 2013, 29 releases): publish once and syndicate via Webmention/ActivityPub, with federation, syndication and update/delete propagation moved into a documented asynchronous event queue (background worker under systemd or cron) so page saves no longer lose work to a timeout. Plugin architecture, composer install, active development on PHP 8.3+.
bad: A social publishing platform, not knowledge machinery — no citation, provenance or memory layer. Operationally heavy for its purpose: a database backend plus a permanently running queue worker are required for ActivityPub (the README warns queued events sit unprocessed if the worker dies), and the project's own naming is confusing (the product is Known, the repo and code are Idno).
didnt: Rejected — scope: an IndieWeb social publishing platform; its async-queue-for-federation design is ordinary infrastructure and nothing in it fills a gap in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FreshRSS
good: Mature multi-user self-hosted RSS aggregator (16,378 stars, 72 releases since 2012): WebSub instant push notifications from compatible sources, native XPath web scraping and JSON support for sites without feeds, resharing selections of articles by HTML, RSS and OPML, custom tags, an API for mobile clients plus a CLI, Google Reader and Fever API compatibility, extensions, 20+ languages, and light enough to run on a Raspberry Pi 1 with 150 feeds.
