bad: AGPL-3.0, so its code is ideas-only for our stack. It is a reading inbox: articles flow through for consumption, with no citation locking, provenance or durable knowledge layer, and running it means operating a PHP 8.1+ application with PostgreSQL/SQLite/MySQL behind a web server.
didnt: Rejected — scope (a feed aggregator; subscription reading is an input channel, and WebSub push is a feed-ingest pattern our capture survey already covers) and licence (AGPL-3.0, ideas only). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Miniflux
good: Minimalist opinionated feed reader in Go (9,812 stars, 83 releases): a single statically compiled binary using a couple of MB of memory, Atom/RSS/JSON Feed support, OPML import/export, Postgres full-text search, strong privacy hygiene (pixel-tracker removal, tracking-parameter stripping, media proxy, strict CSP/Trusted Types, sanitised rendering), a local Readability extractor with custom scraper and rewrite rules, Fever/Google Reader API compatibility, 25+ save-to integrations, webhooks, and passkey/OIDC/reverse-proxy authentication; the README credits a comprehensive unit + integration test suite.
bad: Scope is a reading inbox, deliberately feature-limited ('opinionated' is its own framing): articles are consumed, not compiled into a cited knowledge base, and there is no provenance or citation machinery. It works only with PostgreSQL, which is a real dependency for a personal tool.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an excellent feed reader, but feed reading is an input channel to our wiki, not a wiki capability; nothing in it fills a gap in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CommaFeed
good: Google Reader-inspired self-hosted RSS reader (Quarkus + React/TypeScript, 6,343 commits since 2013) that compiles to native code for fast startup and low memory, scales to thousands of users and millions of feeds, and offers four layouts, OPML import/export, a REST API, Fever and Google Reader APIs for mobile apps, rule-based auto-mark-as-read, push notifications, custom CSS/JS, 25+ languages, and SSRF protection that blocks local addresses when adding feeds by default. Runs on H2/PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB.
bad: Scope is a feed reader — a consumption inbox with no knowledge compilation, citation or provenance layer. The free public instance carries limitations versus self-hosting (per its own docs), and self-hosting means running a Java/Quarkus service.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a feed reader; its SSRF-blocking feed fetcher is good hygiene for an ingest channel but not a capability our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NewsBlur
good: Full-featured personal news reader and social news network (21,895 commits since 2009): real-time RSS, an 'intelligence' trainer whose like/dislike classifiers highlight and hide stories, full-text search, story tagging and saved searches, shared stories on a public blurblog, a Track Changes feature showing how a story evolved since first published, email newsletters delivered as feeds, native iOS/Android apps, and a built-in MCP server exposing feeds, stories and classifiers to AI agents (read, save, subscribe, train, discover).
bad: Hosted-service-first: the free hosted tier is capped at 64 sites with premium plans behind the rest, and the README states the MCP server requires a premium subscription on the hosted service. Self-hosting the repo means operating a heavy stack — Django with PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Celery and Node services. It remains a reading product: no citation locking or knowledge-compilation layer.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a news reader/social service, not knowledge machinery; its story change-tracking and agent-facing feed MCP door were noted, but neither fills a gap in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tiny Tiny RSS
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo metadata and root COPYING; README License section: version 3 or any later version)
good: Flexible web-based RSS/Atom reader and aggregator with a long lineage (12,998 commits carried into this repo): plugin and theme systems, multi-user support, Docker images for linux/amd64 and arm64 published to Docker Hub and GHCR as drop-in replacements for the old images, and documentation recreated in a companion repo after the original project's retirement.
bad: GPL-3.0, so its code is ideas-only for our stack. Continuity risk is stated in its own README: the original project was retired on 2025-11-01 and development now rests on a continuation fork by one long-time contributor. Scope is a feed reader — no knowledge or citation layer.
didnt: Rejected — scope (feed reader/aggregator) and licence (GPL-3.0, ideas only); the fork-continuation is recorded as the project's current custody state. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Selfoss
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo metadata; README Credits state GPL version 3 or later for the source as a whole, with some parts version-3-only and the bundled package possibly v3-only — split recorded as found, not resolved)
good: Multipurpose PHP RSS reader and mashup aggregator (since 2011, 3,046 commits): follows websites, social networks and other platforms in one place, supports OPML import, runs basically anywhere PHP runs, and works with SQLite out of the box (database tables created automatically).
bad: GPL-3.0 family with the unresolved version split recorded in the evidence, so its code is ideas-only regardless. Maintenance is thin by its own Status section: maintained by one person in his free time, with maintenance prioritised over new features. Scope is a feed reader — no knowledge or citation machinery.
didnt: Rejected — scope (feed reader/mashup aggregator) and licence (GPL-3.0 family, ideas only, with the v3-only parts split noted). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Yarr
good: Deliberately tiny web-based feed aggregator in Go (4,068 stars): a single binary with no dependencies, cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux), usable as a desktop app or a personal server, storing to SQLite or Postgres.
bad: Minimal by design to the point of thinness at source: the README is a five-bullet list with documentation off-repo, and the tool is a reading inbox only — no search/organisation story, citation or provenance machinery visible, and a small single-author maintenance footprint (1,272 commits, 15 releases since 2020).
didnt: Rejected — scope: a minimal feed aggregator; the single-binary discipline is admirable but it is an input channel, not a wiki capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RSSHub
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo metadata, root LICENSE and README Author section; the catalogue's 'MIT' is contradicted at the primary source and the source governs)
good: The world's largest feed-generation network (46,603 stars, 20,026 commits, 5,000+ public instances): thousands of community-maintained routes generate RSS feeds for websites, social platforms and universities that lack them, with companion discovery tools (RSSHub Radar browser extension, RSSBud/RSSAid mobile apps) and one-click deployment options.
bad: AGPL-3.0, so its code is ideas-only for our stack — and the catalogue's MIT label for it is wrong at source. It is feed-generation plumbing, not a reader or a knowledge tool: routes scrape third-party sites, so the model carries a permanent route-maintenance load borne by a large standing contributor community, and its README carries paid promotion for a residential proxy scraping service.
didnt: Rejected — scope (feed-generation infrastructure, not a wiki feature) and licence (AGPL-3.0, ideas only; catalogue MIT label corrected at source). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RSS-Bridge
good: PHP web application that generates RSS/Atom/JSON feeds for websites that don't have one, via 447 small 'bridge' scraper modules (social platforms, video, forums) plus generic CssSelector and XPath bridges and utility bridges (FeedMerge, Filter, FeedReducer). Minimal requirements — PHP 7.4+, unzips onto shared hosting — with an officially hosted public instance and thorough installation documentation for many hosts.
bad: Feed-generation plumbing, not a reader or knowledge tool. Per-site scraping is brittle by construction — the README's very long how-to and troubleshooting sections (access denied, cache and database errors, per-bridge fixes) are the standing cost of the model — and an instance is only as trustworthy as whoever runs it, since bridges fetch and re-serve third-party content.
didnt: Rejected — scope: feed-generation plumbing of the same family as RSSHub; it could feed an ingest channel but is infrastructure, not a wiki feature. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: TinyFeed
good: Dead-simple Go CLI that generates a single static HTML page from a list of RSS, Atom or JSON feeds (via the gofeed library): no database, no config file, customisable with external stylesheets and templates, light/dark themes, an accessible lightweight page, and a daemon mode to regenerate the output periodically under cron/systemd — a personal 'planet' page in minutes.
bad: A presentation surface only: one generated page with no search, organisation, persistence or provenance model — at wiki scale it is a toy, and it keeps nothing; when the page regenerates, yesterday's aggregation is gone unless something else archived it.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a feed-to-static-page generator; a pleasant publishing toy, not knowledge machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GithubStarsManager
good: Local-first manager for GitHub stars, forks and gists: it syncs a starred collection and enriches it with AI summaries, tags and auto-categorisation (with locked categories the AI will not overwrite), natural-language and vector semantic search including a 'find similar repositories' neighbourhood, release tracking with asset filters and one-click downloads, and a repository Q&A assistant whose answers are pinned to a specific commit and show read-only evidence with traceable sources; a read-only MCP server exposes the enriched stars to agents.
bad: Its scope is GitHub-stars triage only — it organises starred repositories, not knowledge, and has no citation locking or abstention discipline of its own: its Q&A carries an early-access notice that it may fail or return incomplete evidence and does not index the whole repository. Semantic search runs on Cloudflare Vectorize and the AI features need the user's GitHub token plus AI provider keys, so the enrichment path is cloud-bound.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an AI stars-triage tool, not a wiki feature; its commit-pinned Q&A with traceable sources corroborates our citation practice, but there is no missing capability to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: faved
good: Private bookmark manager built for large collections: customisable nested tags with colour/description, tag rollup into child tags and pinned tags, automatic fetching of titles/descriptions/preview images, duplicate detection, instant search with bulk actions, a PWA with light/dark mode, a Chrome extension, bookmarklet and Apple Shortcuts integration, and import from Chrome/Safari/Firefox/Edge and Raindrop.io/Pocket preserving folder structure as nested tags; self-hosted with all data stored locally on PHP 8/SQLite.
bad: Features the README itself flags as unfinished: automated tagging is only planned and tag icons are 'coming soon'. It is a young project (repo created 2025-06) and a bookmark manager only — no page-content archiving, citation or knowledge-synthesis features are documented.
didnt: Board — nested tags with rollup (a parent tag automatically including its children's items) as a taxonomy idea for wiki topic pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Anchr
good: Self-hosted toolbox for small internet tasks: searchable bookmark collections organised into categories, a link shortener whose links are checked against Google's Safe Browsing API, client-side-encrypted image uploads, OAuth2 login, a Telegram bot, Chrome/Firefox extensions and Prometheus metrics; also offered as a hosted GDPR-compliant service at Anchr.io.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack. The README's own Project History calls it mostly feature-complete, with origins in 2014 and parts still on ES5-era tooling (Grunt/Bower) — and it is a bookmarks/shortlinks/images toolbox with no knowledge, citation or provenance features.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence and scope: a bookmark toolbox with no knowledge features; nothing in it is missing from our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tirth8205/code-review-graph
good: Local-first code intelligence graph for MCP and CLI: Tree-sitter parses a codebase into a persistent SQLite graph of functions, classes, imports and call/test edges, kept current by incremental SHA-256-diff updates via hooks, so AI coding tools read only the files a change touches; blast-radius analysis traces callers, dependents and tests, published benchmarks (pinned SHAs, deterministic reruns) report ~63x median per-question token reduction across six repositories, and a GitHub Action posts risk-scored PR reviews.
bad: It is a code-review tool for source code, not a knowledge store: nothing in it manages documents, citations or memory. Its benchmark ground truth is graph-derived and its own (0.69 average impact F1), the project is very young (created February 2026), and its install step writes MCP entries, hooks and instruction files into up to sixteen different AI tools — an agent-surface modification pattern we record as evidence and would never adopt.
didnt: Rejected — scope: code intelligence for coding agents, not a wiki feature; its persistent graph map with hash-diff incremental updates corroborates index-first, read-only-what-matters retrieval, but there is no component to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vesoft-inc/nebula
good: NebulaGraph: a mature distributed graph database (in development since 2018) with storage/compute separation, horizontal scalability, strong consistency via RAFT, an OpenCypher-compatible query language, role-based access control and built-in graph analytics algorithms; Apache-2.0, with a large production user base across social, recommendation, security and knowledge-graph workloads.
bad: It is enterprise infrastructure: a distributed C++ database cluster whose operational weight — multiple services, a RAFT quorum, dedicated operations — is wildly disproportionate to a personal single-writer wiki whose corpus lives in files. Nothing in it addresses citation, provenance or approval-gated writing.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scale: a distributed graph database answers a problem our files-first wiki does not have, at an operational cost we will not carry. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: adongwanai/AgentGuide
good: A systematic Chinese-language AI-agent learning and job-hunting guide: structured paths for algorithm and engineering roles covering agent harnesses, context engineering, advanced RAG/GraphRAG, evaluation and post-training, a 1,500+ question interview bank and resume-ready project walkthroughs, all organised as what to learn, in what order, and how it is examined.
bad: It is a tutorial and career guide, not software: there is no runnable component and no evaluation harness of its own to reuse, and no licence is stated anywhere at the source, so its content is all-rights-reserved and cannot be reused. Its centre of gravity is interview preparation, not knowledge-system design.
didnt: Rejected — a tutorial/career guide with no licence and no component; nothing in it is a missing capability for our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FalkorDB/FalkorDB
licence: SSPLv1 (per the README License statement and root LICENSE file; GitHub repo metadata reads Other (NOASSERTION) — conflict recorded, the repo's own files govern)
good: A multi-tenant graph database built on GraphBLAS sparse matrices: the adjacency matrix is a sparse matrix and queries execute as linear algebra, giving very low-latency property-graph traversals with OpenCypher support; it ships as a Redis module with official clients in six languages and is aimed squarely at knowledge graphs for LLM GraphRAG and agent memory.
bad: Licence conflict at source, recorded as found: the README states the project is licensed under the Server Side Public License v1 (SSPLv1) while GitHub's metadata detects only Other (NOASSERTION) — either way it is source-available rather than open source, so its code is ideas-only for us. It is also a database engine: adopting it would mean running Redis-module infrastructure to hold a graph our wiki keeps in files.
took: Sparse-matrix / CSR graph representation (regional-scene machinery) — built in Round 3, lane TB7 — source/inspiration: FalkorDB (idea only, as recorded)
didnt: Rejected — the database itself: SSPLv1 licence and Redis-module infrastructure far beyond a personal wiki's needs; its sparse-matrix representation was taken as an idea only (see took). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: deeplethe/utopia
good: An enterprise 'world model' on one Rust binary plus Postgres/pgvector whose base layer is a bitemporal knowledge graph: every fact carries when it held and where it was said, a correction closes the old version and links the new one to it instead of overwriting, and the two clocks (true in the world vs learned by the system) stay separate. Around it sit ontology starter packs, three kinds of conflict detection with explicit choices, a human review queue for low-confidence extractions and suspected duplicates, an append-only decision ledger, and MCP access where anything an agent wants to record goes to a person first.
bad: It is at v0.1 (release candidates) and its own Status section warns the schema evolves between versions with forward-only migrations and no rollback. It is also enterprise multi-user platform scope — ontology workbench, mounted-warehouse querying, role systems — far beyond a personal wiki, on a Postgres platform we do not run.
didnt: Corroboration — its bitemporal facts, correction-by-closing, review queue and append-only decision ledger independently confirm the design directions in our parked Phase-2 questions (bi-temporal fields remain an owner decision; nothing is decided or built from this). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neo4j-labs/llm-graph-builder
good: Neo4j Labs' reference GraphRAG builder: it turns unstructured sources (local files, S3, GCS, web pages, YouTube, Wikipedia) into a Neo4j knowledge graph with LLM extraction under a user-defined or free schema, duplicate-node detection over node pairs, graph visualisation in Neo4j Bloom, and chat over the graph in hybrid modes (vector, graph, fulltext and combinations) that returns source metadata with its answers; many LLM providers are supported including local Ollama, and token usage is tracked per user.
bad: It hard-requires Neo4j 5.23+ with APOC — a graph-database platform dependency our files-first wiki does not carry — and several headline providers are cloud APIs, so extraction sends content out by default. Extraction quality is entirely LLM-bound: there is no citation locking, no verification of extracted facts against their source sentences, and no abstention when the graph has nothing.
didnt: Board — schema-guided extraction with duplicate-node detection and hybrid vector+graph+fulltext chat modes as reference design for our graph/retrieval layer; the Neo4j dependency itself is not taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Neo4j Labs

name: memgraph/memgraph
licence: BSL (Community) / MEL (Enterprise) per the README License section; repo metadata reads Other (NOASSERTION) — recorded as found
good: A high-performance in-memory graph database in C++: sub-millisecond multi-hop traversals, full Cypher compatibility, ACID with Raft-based high availability, and built-in vector and text indexes so hybrid graph retrieval runs as a single atomic query; the MAGE library ships 40+ graph algorithms and the AI Toolkit adds framework integrations and an MCP server for GraphRAG and agent-memory workloads.
bad: Licence split at source: the README's License section states Memgraph Community is under the BSL and Enterprise under the proprietary MEL, while repo metadata detects no standard licence (Other/NOASSERTION) — BSL is source-available, not open source, so the code is ideas-only for us. It is also an enterprise in-memory engine: RAM-resident infrastructure with HA, multi-tenancy and SSO machinery a personal wiki does not need.
didnt: Rejected — BSL source-available licence and enterprise database scope; its single-query atomic GraphRAG pattern is noted, but there is no component we can or should take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: 1517005260/graph-rag-agent
good: A hand-built fusion of GraphRAG, LightRAG and Neo4j llm-graph-builder patterns: multi-format document ingestion, LLM entity/relation extraction with disambiguation and alignment, incremental graph updates, community detection and summaries, local/global/hybrid search plus DeepSearch-style multi-step reasoning with an evidence chain recorded for each step, a Plan-Execute-Report multi-agent mode, and a self-built GraphRAG evaluation framework with 20+ metrics.
bad: A single-author learning project (its own framing is 'patchwork RAG'): no releases, Chinese-language documentation, and a hard Neo4j + LLM-API stack; its evaluation framework is self-built and self-run, with no external benchmark or independent verification visible at the source. Every architectural ingredient re-implements a system we already track at its origin.
didnt: Rejected — a derivative fusion of GraphRAG, LightRAG and llm-graph-builder, all studied at their own sources (llm-graph-builder sits in this same batch); its evidence-chain tracking corroborates our citation practice, but there is nothing missing to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: raphaelmansuy/edgequake
good: EdgeQuake productionises the LightRAG algorithm in Rust: one binary over a single Postgres (pgvector + Apache AGE), documents become entities and relationships, and answers come back with sources across naive/local/global/hybrid modes, with any LLM from cloud APIs to fully local Ollama. Its engineering discipline is unusually explicit: the API never migrates the database (migration is a separate, replay-tested command), fail-closed multi-tenant isolation, connection keys encrypted and write-only, an MCP server, and published benchmarks that report a statistical tie with LightRAG rather than a win.
bad: Young and fast-moving (created December 2025, at version 0.36 within the year) and a multi-tenant production platform — auth, SSO, workspaces, audit logging — whose weight a personal single-user wiki does not need; by its own published numbers its evidence recall (0.932) trails LightRAG's (0.949), and it still requires running Postgres with two extensions.
didnt: Board — the explicit, replay-tested migration discipline (the serving process never migrates its own store) and single-datastore GraphRAG packaging as reference ideas for our retrieval layer; the platform itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OnlyTerp/hermes-optimization-guide
good: A community operations guide for Nous Research's Hermes Agent — setup, migration, memory (including a LightRAG chapter), messaging and skill creation — whose claims are measured on a real install, e.g. the fixed per-call prompt prefix (~13,000 tokens, three quarters of it tool schemas) and the per-call cost of a 32 KB AGENTS.md (+8,600 tokens). Its drift guard is the standout practice: CI installs the pinned upstream release, captures its real command tree, config schema and docs pages, and fails if the guide mentions anything that does not exist.
bad: It is documentation for a different agent platform: there is no software component to adopt, and its settings, token figures and fixes are Hermes-specific and expire with each upstream release (the guide itself must be re-pinned and re-verified continuously). Nothing in it addresses knowledge custody, citation or provenance.
didnt: Corroboration — its drift guard, which mechanically checks every guide claim against the pinned upstream release and fails CI on drift, independently confirms our verify-against-the-source discipline; the guide itself targets another platform and nothing is taken from it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: LeDat98/NexusRAG
licence: MIT (stated in the README badge only; no LICENSE file at the repo root and no licence detected in repo metadata)
good: A hybrid RAG build that preserves structure end-to-end: Docling/Marker parsing keeps headings and page boundaries, images and tables are captioned by an LLM and embedded into their page's chunks so they become searchable, and retrieval runs vector over-fetch, LightRAG knowledge-graph lookup and cross-encoder reranking in parallel. Answers carry inline citations with page number and heading path that click through to the exact place in a document viewer, and an MCP server exposes the pipeline.
bad: Very early: 46 commits, no releases, a single-author project created in March 2026. Its licence rests only on a README badge (MIT) with no LICENSE file at the root. Grounding is by instruction — the model is told to cite only supporting sources, under generated 4-character IDs — with no verification that a citation actually supports its claim and no abstention path; the default knowledge-graph embeddings route through Gemini's cloud API.
didnt: Rejected — an early-stage assembly (46 commits, no releases) of components we track at their sources (Docling, LightRAG, bge rerankers); its page-aware citation design corroborates our citation practice, but there is nothing missing to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: skygazer42/GustoBot
good: Three-layer LangGraph multi-agent customer-service system over a Chinese-recipe knowledge graph: intent routing into GraphRAG and knowledge-base subgraphs, Text2SQL/Text2Cypher against MySQL/Neo4j, LightRAG local/global/hybrid community search, Milvus + PostgreSQL pgvector retrieval with a dual-threshold reranker, and a structured-data-first, vector-second, external-search-last fallback order; answers carry source labels and a guardrails node refuses out-of-domain queries.
bad: The corpus is one recipe dataset and the stack is heavy (Neo4j, Milvus, MySQL, Redis, Docker Compose, external reranker/search APIs); the README itself notes some bundled historical texts and sample records have no verifiable upstream provenance. Its guardrail refusal is scope-checking, not scored abstention, and there is no citation locking or approval-gated write path.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a vertical customer-service bot assembled from other RAG frameworks; its guardrail-refusal and fallback-ordering patterns confirm our abstention design, but there is nothing here our stack lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: skygazer42/pokemon-chat
good: The same author's transferable domain-assistant template applied to Pokémon: LangGraph supervisor/worker multi-agent orchestration (RAG/Web/Graph/Stats/MCP workers), LightRAG knowledge-graph retrieval hybridised with Milvus vectors and BM25, Self-RAG/CRAG/HyDE techniques, a fine-tuned domain model, a knowledge-base workbench with batch import and chunk management, and rule-first routing that answers deterministic questions from local data without an LLM call.
bad: A fan-domain showcase: the knowledge graph is scraped Pokémon data, the full system needs Neo4j/MySQL/Milvus infrastructure plus LLM API keys, and its own changelog records repeated agent-mode crash and race-condition fixes — breadth over verifiable depth; no citation locking, abstention scoring or gated writes.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a themed instance of the GustoBot template; it confirms the template transfers across domains but offers nothing our wiki design is missing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: NanGePlus/LightRAGTest
good: A worked head-to-head of LightRAG and Microsoft GraphRAG on the same corpus (the first nine chapters of Journey to the West): index build time, number of model requests, token cost in money, and retrieval quality across naive/local/global/hybrid and DRIFT modes, with stated model configuration (gpt-4o-mini / gpt-4o, text-embedding-3-small), a results file, and incremental-index plus Neo4j graph-visualisation comparisons.
bad: A tutorial/share artefact rather than maintained software: 20 commits, no releases, a single small corpus, and November-2024 versions (GraphRAG 0.5.0) whose numbers do not transfer to current releases; no licence file or licence statement anywhere at the source.
didnt: Rejected — a dated one-off comparison on one small corpus; its cost-and-quality comparison method is sound, but our evaluation machinery already measures our own stack directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: charan820/PhantomCrowd-Simulacra
licence: MIT (licence conflict recorded: the README embeds the full MIT text and points to a LICENSE file, but no LICENSE file appears in the repository root listing — the README statement governs as found)
good: Multi-agent social-propagation simulator ('EchoHerd' in its own README): persona agents with personality, attention-span and memory-decay parameters react to a seed message over a LightRAG in-memory graph, producing drift and decay analysis of how a message mutates across communities; runs fully locally on Ollama models, with export and replay of simulation runs as JSON/CSV/GIF.
bad: Identity discrepancy at source: the repo is named PhantomCrowd-Simulacra / 'AI Marketing Simulator' while the README presents a different product name, EchoHerd. The repository root holds only a README, an index.html and two SVG files — no engine code is present at the source to back the feature claims — and the README's own disclaimer states outputs cannot predict real-world behaviour.
didnt: Rejected — scope (marketing simulation) and evidence: the claims at source are not backed by code in the repo, so there is nothing verifiable to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PromtEngineer/localGPT
good: Mature local-first document-intelligence platform (22,193 stars, 378 commits): hybrid dense-vector + full-text search over LanceDB fused by reciprocal rank fusion with a calibrated cross-encoder reranker, query decomposition, per-query routing between RAG and direct answering, source attribution returning the grounding chunks, Docling parsing with OCR fallback, and an eval folder whose measured ablation decisions determine which components ship enabled.
bad: A chat-over-documents product, not a knowledge store: no citation locking, provenance model or approval-gated writes; its optional answer-verification pass ships off by default because the project's own ablation measured it annotating confidence without changing any verdict; it also requires Ollama, 8–16 GB RAM and local model management.
didnt: Corroboration — its fully-local custody, source-attributed answers and evaluation-gated defaults confirm our design choices; nothing taken, as our wiki is the store, not a document-chat front end. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BruceMacD/chatd
good: Electron desktop app that bundles the whole local stack: it packages an Ollama runner (or reuses an already-running one) with Mistral-7B so a non-technical user installs a single executable and chats with documents with no data leaving the machine; six releases across macOS, Windows and Linux.
bad: A minimal single-purpose chat front end (97 commits): the README documents no citation, provenance or evaluation machinery, custom model choice is a manual advanced setup, and the Windows build is unsigned; there is no knowledge organisation beyond the chat session.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a document-chat desktop app; its bundled-runner, zero-cloud custody matches our local-first posture, but there is no mechanism here our store lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: marella/chatdocs
good: Offline chat-with-documents CLI and web UI in the PrivateGPT lineage: pip-installable, downloads GGML/GGUF or Transformers models once and then runs fully offline across a wide format list (PDF, DOCX, EPUB, EML, ODT, PPTX, Markdown and more), with Chroma storage and a single YAML configuration file.
bad: A 2023-era artefact (36 commits; the catalogue notes it was last updated in 2023): default models are GGML-generation (Wizard-Vicuna-7B class), changing the embedding model requires deleting and rebuilding the whole database, and the README documents no citation or source-grounding machinery.
didnt: Rejected — dated scope: an early offline doc-chat tool whose approach our retrieval stack has long superseded. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: theaiautomators/insights-lm-public
good: Self-hosted NotebookLM alternative (Supabase + n8n + React): upload documents and chat with answers grounded exclusively in the provided sources, with verifiable citations that jump directly to the source passage, plus NotebookLM-style audio-overview (podcast) generation; ships as a GitHub template with a no-code setup path.
bad: This public version is not local: its README states it relies on cloud AI services (OpenAI, Gemini), and the stack is heavy and credential-sprawling (Supabase project, n8n workflows and webhook secrets, edge-function JWT workarounds); its citations are passage links with no locking, verification or abstention, and the backend automation runs on n8n's Sustainable Use License, which the README itself flags.
didnt: Corroboration — source-grounded answers with jump-to-source citations in a mainstream NotebookLM clone confirm the pattern our citation lockfile hardens; nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PromtEngineer/localGPT-Vision
good: Vision-first RAG over documents: pages are embedded as images with ColPali/ColQwen (via Byaldi) so layout, tables and figures are retrievable without OCR or chunking, retrieved pages are passed to a vision-language model (Qwen2-VL, Llama-3.2-Vision, Pixtral, Molmo, or proprietary Gemini/GPT-4o), and indexes and sessions persist on disk.
bad: No licence file and no licence statement anywhere at the source, so the code stands all-rights-reserved; a 24-commit demo whose README concedes answer quality depends heavily on the chosen VLM and image resolution, and two of its supported backends are proprietary cloud APIs, breaking the local claim.
didnt: Board — ColPali-style page-image retrieval for our open table/image evidence gap: retrieving the page as an image rather than as extracted text is a candidate route for figure- and table-heavy sources; the code itself is ideas-only (no licence at source). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: supabase-community/chatgpt-your-files
good: Supabase community workshop repo that builds a document-chat MVP step by step with git-tag checkpoints: storage buckets guarded by row-level-security policies scoped per owner, pgvector embeddings generated by edge functions, and GPT chat over the stored documents, with a recorded two-hour walkthrough video.
bad: By its own framing a workshop MVP (57 commits): documents and embeddings live in Supabase/Postgres and answers come from OpenAI's cloud models — hosted custody, not local files; the README documents no citation or provenance machinery, and no licence file or licence statement appears at the source.
didnt: Rejected — a teaching artefact for a hosted stack; its row-level-security discipline is sound but belongs to a custody model opposite to our local-first files. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: run-llama/voice-chat-pdf
good: LlamaIndex/Next.js example extending OpenAI's realtime console with a simple LlamaIndexTS RAG layer: embed a folder of PDFs once, then hold a spoken, interruptible conversation (push-to-talk or voice-activity detection) with the documents through the OpenAI Realtime API via a relay server.
bad: An example, not a product: it requires an OpenAI API key with Realtime API access (cloud voice and embeddings), ships a single sample PDF, and the README itself flags a known defect — the console prompts for the API key again on startup, marked 'this needs to be fixed'.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a vendor demo of realtime voice over a toy corpus; voice is an interface choice, not a capability our store is missing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: theaiautomators/insights-lm-local-package
good: The fully-local packaging of InsightsLM: the same source-grounded chat with jump-to-source verifiable citations and audio overviews, re-architected to run entirely in local Docker containers — Ollama (Qwen3) for inference and embeddings, Whisper for transcription, Coqui TTS for podcast generation, local Supabase — so no data leaves the machine.
bad: Not a standalone codebase: the repo (12 commits) is an overlay of .copy files and instructions pasted into a different base repository (Cole Medin's local-ai-packaged) through an 11-step manual assembly, and its automation layer is n8n under the Sustainable Use License, which the README flags as restricting commercial SaaS use.
didnt: Corroboration — a fully-local, citation-grounded NotebookLM variant confirms both our local-first custody and our source-grounding design; nothing taken, as it is packaging over other projects rather than new machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: weike-zhang/architecture-canvas
good: Local workspace that turns uploaded documents (text, Office formats, PDF, images) into editable Excalidraw architecture diagrams through conversation: AI-proposed changes are listed first and take effect only when the user applies them (fixed components keep their positions), read failures are reported honestly rather than faked (an OCR failure prompts instead of pretending the file was read), its MCP server reads files only under an explicitly authorised --root (without one it is render-only), and API keys live only in process memory.
bad: Brand-new alpha (created 2026-10-03, 2 commits, single author): scope is deliberately narrow — layered/module diagrams of at most about 22 components, no sequence or ER diagrams — per-session limits (20 files, 25 MB, 100 PDF pages) are stated in its own current-boundaries section, and model output is stated to need human checking.
didnt: Board — the propose-then-confirm edit loop over a generated artefact, plus read-failure honesty and a root-confined MCP door, are patterns worth the ideas board for our editor and Lens surfaces. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Addepto/graph_builder
good: ContextClue Graph Builder: extracts structured knowledge graphs from documents and tables — configurable headers, entity labels and relationship types turn PDFs and tabular files (worked example: a coffee-machine specification PDF) into a queryable entity graph, served through a FastAPI REST API with Docker deployment, aimed at digital-twin, MRO and knowledge-assistant use cases.
bad: By the README's own important-notes section, graphs live only in runtime memory and are lost on every API restart, so they must be rebuilt — the inverse of a durable knowledge store; chunking/embeddings, graph-database persistence and visualisation are roadmap items rather than present features; 26 commits.
didnt: Rejected — its extraction output is runtime-only and rebuilt on restart, against our files-are-truth durability; the table-to-graph extraction itself is generic and already covered by our ingest. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: FabioYanezRomero/Knowledge-Graph-Builder
good: Modular Python pipeline (KGB) that extracts source-grounded triples via langextract — each triple carries character positions in the original text — from JSONL/JSON/CSV input, with pluggable LLM backends (Gemini API, local Ollama, LM Studio), per-domain prompt/schema constraints, YAML-orchestrated pipeline steps, GraphML output and interactive Cytoscape.js visualisations. Every triple is origin-tagged explicit (extracted) or contextual (generated by the connectivity-augmentation step), so inferred edges are never passed off as extracted ones.
bad: Young single-author project (created September 2025, 67 commits, no releases) built around specific datasets (the worked examples are UK Supreme Court legal texts); the augmentation step deliberately invents bridging triples by LLM inference, and there is no human review or approval gate before they enter the graph. README documents no evaluation of extraction accuracy.
didnt: Corroboration — its per-triple origin tag (explicit extracted vs contextual inferred, with source character positions for the extracted ones) independently matches our extracted-vs-inferred provenance discipline; the unreviewed augmentation step is the part our approval gate exists to refuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: elbruno/graphify-dotnet
good: A .NET 10 port of graphify: reads code, docs and media files, extracts concepts and relationships via tree-sitter AST parsing plus optional AI semantic analysis (Azure OpenAI, Ollama, GitHub Copilot SDK, or AST-only with zero config), applies community detection, and exports interactive HTML, JSON, SVG, Neo4j Cypher, Obsidian vault and wiki formats; ships as a dotnet global tool with three NuGet packages and CI/publish workflows.
bad: A port of an already-studied project into a stack we do not run (.NET 10 / Copilot SDK); its graph is a codebase structure graph (classes, functions, imports), not a knowledge graph over documents, and the AI semantic layer adds inferred relationships with no provenance or approval distinction visible in the README.
didnt: Rejected — a .NET re-implementation of Graphify (already studied in its original form) aimed at codebase graphs; neither the runtime nor the code-structure graph model fits our Markdown-wiki knowledge layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tao-pr/vor-knowledge-graph
licence: GPL-3.0 (stated in the README's Licence section as 'GNU 3 public licence'; no LICENSE file at root and no licence detected in GitHub's repo metadata)
good: End-to-end open-knowledge mining pipeline from 2016: endlessly crawls Wikipedia from a seed page, stores raw text in MongoDB, builds a topic/keyword graph in OrientDB, trains a Word2Vec model over the crawl and generates a frequency-weighted inverted topic index, with Sigma.js visualisation of the resulting graphs.
bad: Archived and unmaintained, GPL-3.0, and built on a dead stack (OrientDB plus MongoDB, Python/Node scripts run by hand with the database root password passed on the command line). The crawler runs until manually killed, and graph edges are keyword co-occurrence, not sourced claims — no provenance, citations or review step.
didnt: Rejected — archived GPL-3.0 project on a defunct database stack; its crawl-everything, edge-by-co-occurrence model is the opposite of our curated, citation-locked ingest. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nik21hil/auto-audience-generator
good: Streamlit tool that builds a knowledge graph from user/product/content CSVs, turns a natural-language prompt ('find crypto enthusiasts') into executable logical audience rules (AND/OR/nested) via an LLM on OpenRouter, expands keywords semantically with embeddings ('crypto' to 'blockchain'), evaluates the rules on the graph and visualises the matched user-item subgraph.
bad: A marketing-segmentation demo over bundled sample CSVs (users, products, orders, streaming): the LLM-generated filtering rules are executed with no human review or confidence scoring — rule confidence and prompt follow-ups sit in its own Planned Enhancements table — and it requires an OpenRouter API key held in Streamlit secrets. No evaluation of rule correctness is documented.
didnt: Rejected — scope and gating: ad-tech audience targeting over behavioural user data is outside a personal knowledge wiki, and its unreviewed LLM-generated rules executing directly on the graph is precisely the ungated-write pattern our approval design refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kingwingfly/knowledge_graph_builder_and_consultant
good: A chained scholarly-graph toolchain: parses literature metadata exported from CNKI, extracts author-cooperation relations, extends records by crawling Baidu Baike, runs LTP-based segmentation and triple extraction behind a Flask service, loads everything into Neo4j and serves a small web Q&A system over the graph.
bad: A 13-commit 2022 coursework-style project bound to two specific Chinese sources (CNKI exports and Baidu Baike crawling, with hand-edited credentials in the Neo4j builder script and model files downloaded manually); documentation exists only as brief Chinese README notes, there are no tests, releases or maintenance since, and the crawled extension data enters the graph with no provenance or verification step.
didnt: Rejected — a dated, single-purpose CNKI/Baidu pipeline; nothing in its extraction or query layer improves on our ingest, and its crawl-and-load flow carries no source verification. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: blacksmithop/LLM-Graph-Builder
good: Takes uploaded documents (positioned around Excel files), extracts entities and relationships with a configurable LLM (Azure OpenAI, Ollama or a custom provider), creates a vector index and populates a Neo4j (DozerDB) graph, then offers a Streamlit QA chatbot that constructs Cypher from the graph schema and retrieves related nodes to answer.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source, so the code is all-rights-reserved by default. It is a small single-author project (23 stars, no releases) hard-coupled to Neo4j/DozerDB with configuration done by editing FILE_PATH and prompt_version in the source files; the README documents no provenance for extracted entities, no evaluation, and no review step before graph writes.
didnt: Rejected — no licence at source (ideas only at most), and a Neo4j-coupled demo pipeline whose extraction writes carry no citation grounding or approval gate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RhythmSyed/KnowledgeGraph_Builder
good: An unsupervised end-to-end research pipeline that constructs RDF-triple knowledge graphs from unstructured text: spaCy and Stanford CoreNLP plus neural coreference and sentence-transformers perform NER, coreference resolution, relation extraction and entity linking, aimed at automated ontology construction and taxonomy expansion; ships evaluation notebooks for each stage (NER, coreference, relation extraction, entity linking) and an accompanying paper PDF.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source. It is a 2020-era research prototype (Python 3.7, a manual CoreNLP 4.2.0 download placed in the repo root, conda environment, no releases) whose output is a flat triples CSV; extracted triples are not grounded back to source spans, and there is no human review, confidence handling or maintenance since.
didnt: Rejected — unlicenced, unmaintained research code from 2020; its classical NLP extraction chain predates the LLM extraction our ingest already uses and offers no provenance mechanism to borrow. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: modelscope/ms-swift
good: ModelScope's SWIFT framework: full-pipeline training, inference, evaluation, quantisation and deployment for 600+ text LLMs and 400+ multimodal models, spanning CPT/SFT, preference methods (DPO, KTO, SimPO, ORPO), the GRPO RL family, Megatron parallelism, and — the part that landed it in this catalogue wave — embedding, reranker and sequence-classification training tasks with built-in datasets and vLLM/SGLang/LMDeploy serving.
bad: It is GPU training infrastructure, not a knowledge system: using it means running multi-GPU fine-tuning jobs (DeepSpeed/FSDP/Megatron, CUDA/ROCm/NPU hardware matrices) to produce models, and the embedding/reranker support is one training task family among hundreds. Nothing in it manages, cites or retrieves over a document corpus.
didnt: Rejected — scope: our system consumes finished models behind its Ask door; it does not fine-tune LLMs, embedders or rerankers, and standing up a training framework to do so is outside the wiki's design and hardware. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: ModelScope community (Alibaba)

name: SylphAI-Inc/AdalFlow
good: PyTorch-like library for building LLM applications (chatbots, RAG, agents) as differentiable graphs, with a unified auto-optimisation framework — textual gradients (LLM-AutoDiff) and few-shot bootstrap — that tunes prompts and pipeline parameters against a task metric instead of by hand; model-agnostic components include retrievers and rerankers, with tracing and human-in-the-loop support in the open-source SDK.
bad: A general application framework: adopting it would mean rebuilding our hand-rolled Ask pipeline inside its component model, and its optimisation loop tunes for benchmark accuracy — it has no notion of citation locking, provenance, or abstention, and optimised prompts can drift away from evidence discipline unless the metric encodes it.
didnt: Board — the idea worth keeping is metric-driven auto-optimisation of the Ask door's prompts (textual-gradient style iteration scored on our golden set, where the score already includes abstention and citation checks), as a future evaluation experiment; the framework itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: netease-youdao/BCEmbedding
good: Bilingual (Chinese/English) two-stage retrieval models built for RAG: a 279M embedding model specialised for monolingual and crosslingual retrieval without query instructions, plus a 279M reranker (adding Japanese and Korean) that handles passages beyond 512 tokens up to 32k and returns meaningful relevance scores usable for thresholding low-quality passages; published MTEB and LlamaIndex RAG evaluations, LangChain/LlamaIndex integrations, and production use inside Youdao products.
bad: A single model generation from January 2024 (base size only, no larger variants, repo news stops in February 2024) in a fast-moving model class; coverage is EN/ZH-centred, and the repo is a model release with usage code rather than a maintained retrieval system — no releases or tags in two years.
didnt: Board — the bce-embedding/bce-reranker pair as a candidate bilingual embedding+reranker set for the wiki's retrieval evaluation bench, notable because its reranker emits calibrated relevance scores, the property our abstention thresholding depends on; vintage noted, to be benchmarked against current models before any adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: NetEase Youdao

name: AnswerDotAI/rerankers
good: A lightweight, dependency-free-by-default Python library giving one unified rank() API over essentially every reranking family: cross-encoders, T5 rankers, ColBERT/late-interaction (incl. PyLate), FlashRank ONNX models, LLM listwise rankers (RankGPT, RankLLM) and hosted API rerankers (Cohere, Jina, Voyage, MixedBread, Pinecone), all returning a common RankedResults with scores, document metadata and top_k; ships consistency notebooks checking implementations against published SciFact numbers.
bad: Deliberately a thin unification layer: it adds no retrieval, indexing or evaluation of its own, several wrapped families are only partially fledged (its own feature table marks RankLLM/RankZephyr support partial and untested in places), hosted API rankers require vendor keys, and the README still describes the library as a beta release.
didnt: Board — a unified reranker interface is the right shape for our Ask door's rerank stage: it would let reranker choice (local cross-encoder vs ColBERT vs API) be swapped and benchmarked on the golden set instead of hard-wired; candidate for the retrieval evaluation queue, not yet adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Answer.AI

name: NovaSearch-Team/RAG-Retrieval
good: End-to-end code for fine-tuning and distilling RAG retrieval models — BERT- and LLM-based embedders, ColBERT late-interaction models and rerankers — with MRL loss, Stella/Jasper distillation of large models into small ones, DeepSpeed/FSDP multi-GPU training, published MTEB reranking results for its recipes, and a lightweight rag-retrieval inference package giving a unified call interface over reranker models with long-document handling.
bad: A model-training codebase (like ms-swift, its value is producing better retrievers, which requires GPU training runs and training data we do not have); the published gains from its own fine-tuning tables are marginal on general data (+0.29 to +0.66 points, by its own note), and its inference library overlaps the rerankers unification idea with a narrower model set.
didnt: Rejected — scope: we run off-the-shelf retrieval models and evaluate them; we do not fine-tune or distil retrievers, and its inference wrapper duplicates the boarded rerankers idea with less coverage. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: anush008/fastembed-rs
good: Rust port of FastEmbed for fully local inference: ONNX (via ort) dense text embedding across a wide model list (BGE, E5, GTE, Nomic, Qwen3, EmbeddingGemma, incl. quantised variants), SPLADE/BGE-M3 sparse embeddings, CLIP image embedding and BGE/Jina rerankers, with synchronous no-Tokio usage, local user-defined model files, and built-in cosine/top_k similarity helpers; actively released (106 releases) as a crates.io library.
bad: An inference library only — no index, store or query layer beyond in-memory top_k (its README points larger corpora to an external engine such as Qdrant); some headline models sit behind alternate candle-backend feature flags (Qwen3, Nomic v2 MoE), and model weights are downloaded from HuggingFace at first use rather than vendored.
didnt: Board — a single local library covering embedding and reranking is a candidate inference layer if the wiki tooling ever needs local vectors without a Python service (e.g. for the Lens or a native helper); boarded as a candidate for the retrieval stack evaluation, not adopted today. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shibing624/ChatPDF
good: A dependency-light, natively implemented local RAG chat over PDF/docx/markdown/txt files: local or API LLMs (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Ollama), pluggable embeddings, hybrid retrieval weighting BM25 literal matching (jieba-segmented) with vector similarity, a reranker stage that prunes the candidate set, context expansion around hit chunks, Chinese/English mixed-document chunking, a lightweight GraphRAG local mode, and a Gradio streaming web UI — all without a third-party agent framework.
bad: A single-user demo application (rag.py / webui.py scripts, 131 commits from one author): answers are generated from retrieved chunks with bracketed chunk numbers, but there is no citation locking to source files, no abstention when retrieval is weak, no persistent curated knowledge layer, and its accuracy claims are asserted in the README without a published evaluation.
didnt: Corroboration — its retrieval shape (BM25 + vector weighting, reranker pruning, context expansion, fully local models) independently matches the hybrid retrieval design our Ask door uses; as a chat-over-files demo without citation locking or abstention it also marks the line between a RAG demo and a knowledge system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: CodeBendKit/codeseek
good: Rust code-intelligence CLI for coding agents: tree-sitter AST parsing across 7 languages builds call graphs plus a hybrid search index — dense vectors (LanceDB), BM25 (Tantivy) and graph name search fused by reciprocal rank fusion, then cross-encoder reranking (Qwen3-Reranker) — with MD5-incremental re-indexing, git-hook auto-indexing, graceful fallback to graph name search when the embedding/reranker APIs are unavailable, and native MCP tool registration for Claude Code and Codex.
bad: Scoped to source code, not documents: it indexes functions and call graphs for coding agents, depends on external API-hosted embedding and reranker models (its config holds API tokens for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint), and is a very young project (created June 2026, 122 commits). Its scores are relevance ranks with no provenance or citation discipline.
didnt: Corroboration — its pipeline (dense + sparse + graph signals, RRF fusion, cross-encoder rerank, and a designed fallback when models are unavailable) is the hybrid-retrieval pattern stated cleanly in another domain; the tool itself serves codebase navigation, which our wiki does not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HelixDB/helix-db
good: An OLTP graph database in Rust that unifies a labelled property graph, native vector search (ANN prefiltered by graph traversal) and BM25 full-text search in one transactional engine built on object storage, with SDKs for Rust, TypeScript, Python and Go, an embedded mode, and Cypher support in source builds; very actively developed (4,258 commits, 192 releases).
bad: Young and fast-moving: created 2024-11 and already on a v3 SDK/wire generation with uneven SDK maturity (Rust crate 3.0.0 vs Python SDK 0.3.4); local data lives in memory by default and the durability story is object-storage/server-centric with a managed Helix Cloud tier — the corpus would live in a database, not inspectable plain files.
didnt: Corroboration — graph + vector + BM25 unified retrieval over one store confirms our hybrid-retrieval direction; the engine itself is a server/object-storage database rather than a files-first substrate, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JanusGraph/janusgraph
licence: Apache-2.0 for code (APACHE-2.0.txt at repo root) with documentation under CC-BY-4.0 (CC-BY-4.0.txt); repo metadata reports Other (NOASSERTION) — split recorded as found
good: A distributed graph database built for billions of vertices and edges across a cluster, with pluggable storage backends (Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable, BerkeleyJE, Scylla) and pluggable index backends (Elasticsearch, Solr, Lucene), queried via Gremlin/Apache TinkerPop; long production history (Airbnb, eBay, Netflix, Uber listed as users).
bad: Cluster-scale operational weight: it needs an external storage backend and usually a separate index backend, and is designed for thousands of concurrent users; graph data lives inside those backends, not in inspectable files — the opposite end of the scale spectrum from a personal wiki.
didnt: Rejected — scale and operational model contradict a personal single-writer wiki; the pluggable index-backend split (a replaceable Lucene/ES index over a durable store) is the one transferable idea and is already our architecture. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: orientechnologies/orientdb
good: A mature multi-model DBMS (since 2012, 27,249 commits) combining native graph, document, full-text and geospatial models in one engine, with an SQL dialect, ACID transactions, schema-less/schema-full/schema-mixed modes and role/predicate security.
bad: Its distributed mode is Multi-Master — multi-writer by design, which our single-writer custody rule rejects outright; and it is a Java server DBMS whose store is opaque database files rather than plain, greppable text.
didnt: Rejected — the multi-master multi-writer model contradicts our custody design; multi-model-in-one-engine is noted as corroboration of the unified-store instinct only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: apache/age
good: A graph database delivered as a PostgreSQL extension: one storage handles relational and graph data, with ANSI SQL and openCypher hybrid querying in the same query, multiple graphs per database, property indexes, and all of PostgreSQL's transaction machinery underneath.
bad: Requires running PostgreSQL (versions 11–18) and loading the extension on every connection; the README itself documents transactional-visibility gotchas for non-autocommit clients (graphs created but invisible until commit); graph data lives in database tables, not files.
didnt: Corroboration — hybrid SQL+Cypher over a single store confirms our single-substrate instinct (plain files plus derived indexes); the extension itself is not adopted, as no database server belongs in our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cozodb/cozo
good: An embeddable, transactional relational-graph-vector database queried in Datalog: recursion and composable rules are first-class, HNSW vector search and full-text search live inside the query language, MVCC protects concurrent writes, and time travel is supported per-relation on an opt-in basis so history costs are paid only where wanted.
bad: MPL-2.0 copyleft keeps its code ideas-only for us; Datalog is a further query paradigm to learn and staff; storage is an embedded engine's own format (RocksDB and other backends), not human-readable files.
didnt: Board — opt-in per-relation time travel (pay the history cost only where a relation wants it) and composable Datalog-style rules as ideas for our query layer; MPL-2.0, so ideas only, no code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kuzudb/kuzu
good: An embedded, serverless property-graph database built for analytical speed: columnar disk storage, Cypher, native full-text search and vector indexes, serializable ACID transactions, multi-core vectorized query processing and a Wasm build.
bad: The repository is archived — the README announces the team is archiving KuzuDB and moving to something new, and the official extension server has been shut down (extensions must be self-hosted or taken from the final 0.11.3 bundle); adopting an archived engine would strand our substrate.
didnt: Rejected — archived upstream; its embedded graph + full-text + vector in one engine is corroboration of the unified-engine direction, recorded as such. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: terminusdb/terminusdb
good: A knowledge-graph database with git-like version control as its core model: every update is a commit, with branch, merge, diff, JSON diff-and-patch, push/pull/clone between nodes, time-travel queries at any historical commit, schema constraints, and a WOQL Datalog engine — a database designed as a system of record.
bad: It is a server (Docker/Prolog stack) with a collaboration-first model and an Enterprise tier holding clustering and backup/restore features; documents live inside the database rather than as plain files, and running it means operating that server.
didnt: Corroboration — the strongest external confirmation in this wave that version-control semantics (commit, branch, diff, time-travel) belong at the centre of a knowledge store, which is the design our git-backed wiki already implements with plain files; the server itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: apache/hugegraph
good: A graph database engineered for more than 10 billion vertices and edges, with Gremlin and openCypher query, schema/index management, pluggable backends (embedded RocksDB standalone; Raft-based PD + HStore distributed), and Flink/Spark/HDFS integration.
bad: Built for clusters up to a stated 1000 TB data scale: a Java 17 server with separate PD/Store nodes in distributed mode, and its own README warns authentication must be explicitly enabled before production exposure — operational weight utterly out of proportion to a personal corpus.
didnt: Rejected — scale and scope: a big-data cluster database has nothing to offer a single-user file-based wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: JaidedAI/EasyOCR
good: Ready-to-use local OCR for 80+ languages and scripts (Latin, Chinese, Arabic, Devanagari, Cyrillic and more) on PyTorch: readtext returns bounding boxes, text and a confidence level per span, runs CPU-only if needed, and models can be pre-downloaded for offline use; 30,092 stars.
bad: Heavyweight PyTorch dependency with model weights auto-downloaded on first use; handwriting support is still on the roadmap rather than shipped; release cadence is slow (latest release v1.7.2, September 2024).
didnt: Board — candidate engine for our open OCR queue (ocr-0001): local execution plus a confidence score on every span fits our never-trust-unverified-OCR posture; to be trialled against the queued item, not yet adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RaRe-Technologies/gensim
good: The classic Python topic-modelling and document-similarity library: memory-independent streaming algorithms that process corpora larger than RAM (online LSA/LDA, Random Projections, HDP, word2vec), multicore implementations, and extensive documentation, in continuous use since 2011.
bad: LGPL-2.1 copyleft makes its code ideas-only for us; the README declares stable maintenance mode with no new features accepted; and its vector-space methods predate the embedding-retrieval stack we already evaluate against.
didnt: Rejected — LGPL-2.1 licence (ideas only) and a maintenance-mode upstream; its streaming, out-of-core corpus-processing discipline is noted as an idea, nothing more. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Unstructured-IO/unstructured
good: Open-source document ETL: partitions PDFs, HTML, Word/Office documents, email and images into typed structured elements for LLM pipelines, runs locally as a library, and — unusually — the vendor publishes its own accuracy table, including a 'tokens added' (invented content) metric for the OSS tier.
bad: By the vendor's own published table the open-source library is the weaker tier (text accuracy 0.715, tokens added 0.119) against its paid Transform API (0.878 accuracy, 58% less invented content, 2x table accuracy); full local use also pulls heavy system dependencies (poppler, tesseract, LibreOffice).
didnt: Board — candidate partitioner for our document-ingest path, with its own published table as the caution: any use must measure invented content ('tokens added') against the source before output is trusted; the paid API tier is not used. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: apache/lucene
good: The reference full-text search library: a high-performance, full-featured Java text search engine (inverted indexing, BM25 ranking) with 39,665 commits of history, sitting underneath Solr, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and index backends such as JanusGraph's — the standing proof of the durable-store-plus-replaceable-index architecture.
bad: It is a Java library, not a store or an application: adopting it means building and running a JVM service around it, and its power is aimed at search-cluster scale far beyond a personal wiki, which far lighter embedded indexes already serve.
didnt: Corroboration — Lucene confirms that a separate, rebuildable index layer over a durable store is the right architecture, which our files-plus-derived-index design mirrors; the library itself is not adopted (JVM weight, scope). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: langroid/langroid
good: A principled Python framework for multi-agent LLM applications from CMU and UW-Madison researchers: Agents equipped with LLMs, vector stores and tools are wrapped in Tasks and collaborate by message exchange (actor-model inspired), with an MCP tool adapter, support for practically any LLM including local models, and a very active release cadence (598 releases).
bad: A general agent framework, not a knowledge store — it carries no custody, provenance or citation model of its own; contributions are by invitation only; and its centre of gravity is LLM API providers rather than local-first files.
didnt: Corroboration — its Agent/Task message-passing decomposition parallels our coordinator/lane working pattern; not adopted, as orchestration here is runtime-provided and Langroid offers no memory substrate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Carnegie Mellon University and University of Wisconsin-Madison (per README: 'from CMU and UW-Madison researchers')

name: embeddings-benchmark/mteb
good: The standard evaluation toolbox for text embeddings and retrieval: hundreds of versioned tasks across classification, clustering, retrieval, reranking, bitext mining and STS, expanded multilingual/multimodal by MMTEB, with a public leaderboard and reproducible task/benchmark definitions any model can be run against.
bad: Its scores are leaderboard-shaped — rankings move with task selection, and it evaluates embedding models against fixed datasets, not a living corpus where newer pages supersede older ones (our truth-aware retrieval problem); running full benchmarks is dataset- and compute-heavy.
didnt: Board — the task taxonomy and versioned-benchmark discipline as a reference for extending our own retrieval evaluation, including the supersession slice our battery measures and MTEB does not; the framework itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ashvardanian/StringZilla
good: SIMD/SWAR-accelerated string primitives for C, C++, Python, Rust, JS, Go, Swift, C# and Java — substring and set search, hashing (including SHA-256 and MinHash/rolling fingerprints), edit distances, sorting, and Unicode case-folding/segmentation — with published per-operation benchmarks, named hardware and methodology links.
bad: A low-level primitives library only: no storage, indexing or retrieval semantics, and the headline speed multipliers are the author's own runs on named hardware — the README itself cautions they are 'a first impression, not a benchmark suite' and will not reproduce exactly.
didnt: Corroboration — MinHash/rolling fingerprints and fast edit distance are the right primitives for near-duplicate and drift detection at scale; at our corpus size the standard library suffices, so nothing is adopted now. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Readflow
licence: Licence split recorded: code AGPL-3.0; artwork CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (some avatar art CC BY 4.0)
good: Self-hosted news / read-it-later reader (475 stars, 687 commits, 7 releases): article export to HTML/PDF/EPUB/ZIP, categories with scripting-engine classification, incoming and outgoing webhooks, PWA with offline reading, no ads or trackers. Its readflow-ctl companion ships a read-only MCP server (list/get articles and categories).
bad: Requires a PostgreSQL database to run; scope is feed reading only. The code licence is AGPL-3.0, which is ideas-only under our licence discipline.
didnt: Rejected — a feed reader outside the wiki's scope, and AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us; its read-only MCP door corroborates our own read-door design but nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Goeland
good: Mature feed-to-email digest tool (205 stars, 657 commits, 55 releases, self-described stable/production): RSS/Atom/JSON plus Imgur and Miniflux sources, full-text extraction, 20+ composable filters, built-in cron scheduler, Docker deployment, zero cloud dependency.
bad: Email-digest plumbing only — it produces digests, not a knowledge store; SMTP credentials sit in its own config file.
didnt: Rejected — digest plumbing outside the wiki's scope; our ingest works from sources directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: reader (lemon24)
good: Well-engineered Python feed-reader library (558 stars, 2,862 commits, 92 releases): framework-free 'fat model' design, Atom/RSS/JSON feed support, full-text search, OPML import/export, tags and arbitrary entry metadata, a plugin system and a stable typed API; optional Flask/htmx web app and CLI on top.
bad: A library, not an application — adopting it means building our own app around it; its domain is feeds only.
didnt: Rejected — a feed-domain library outside the wiki's scope; nothing in our ingest needs a feed-reader core. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PromptDirector
licence: Apache-2.0 (root LICENSE + NOTICE); split noted — the README states the code licence grants no rights to the third-party case media bundled with it
good: Chrome extension that saves AI-generated images/videos together with their public prompts from 20+ sites (Midjourney, Jimeng, Higgsfield, X and others) into a local-first, account-free library; a local MCP server lets agents search and read the library; ships 1,000+ curated case packs; actively released (49 releases).
bad: The local MCP also lets agents save back into the library — an agent write path with no approval gate. The library lives in browser storage; capture depends on each site's layout and login state (the README itself advises preview-before-save); a three-month-old single-author project (created 2026-07-19, 16 stars).
didnt: Rejected — a prompt-asset library for image generation, outside the wiki's scope, and its agent save-back write path runs against our approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: qiaomu-clipper
licence: MIT (upstream Obsidian Web Clipper MIT retained); split noted — the bundled Zhuque Fangsong font is SIL OFL 1.1
good: User-initiated clipping of pages, video and podcasts into Obsidian as editable Markdown: official captions preferred, timestamped transcripts, local ASR options (MLX Whisper, faster-whisper) or bring-your-own cloud ASR; an optional native helper writes into the vault with destination validation (per the audit); substantial test suites (935 TypeScript + 172 Python tests, per the audit).
bad: The README carries an agent-addressed install prompt — characterised here as evidence only, never followed. Its AI answers are not claim-level citations; cloud routes send content/audio to the chosen provider; broad host permissions plus a cookie handoff to the helper for yt-dlp (per its privacy notice as audited); project created 2026-10-02 and its own security file notes no independent security audit (per the audit).
didnt: Rejected — another Obsidian clipper variant; wave 1 already covered this pattern and our ingest does not route through a browser clipper. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: page2ai-extension
good: One-click conversion of any webpage to clean, LLM-ready Markdown, 100% local in the extension: minimal permissions (activeTab only, no host_permissions, no <all_urls>), hidden-tab code capture, profile-aware extraction, a client-rendered-page readiness gate, an extraction quality gate with automatic fallback, rich YAML frontmatter (OpenGraph, Twitter Card, JSON-LD), opt-in PII masking; listed on both the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons; the same engine is published as the @page2ai/core library and a local @page2ai/mcp server.
bad: Zero stars and created 2026-07-21 — a three-month-old single-author project. The same engine is also offered as a hosted remote MCP endpoint (on Vercel) whose server-side fetching carries a different privacy posture from the local extension. Output goes to the clipboard; there is no library or preservation layer.
didnt: Rejected — another page-to-Markdown clipper variant (wave 1 covered the pattern); its least-privilege permission stance corroborates our door design but nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markClipper (Heros Suite)
licence: MIT as stated in the README (badge and text); no LICENSE file is present in the repository root, so the licence rests on the README statement
good: Manifest V3 side-panel clipper in vanilla JavaScript with zero dependencies: six capture modes (article, full page, selection, bookmark, link, image, screenshot), a Photo Lab harvesting up to 250 images per page with hi-res srcset resolution and dedupe, a local library with search/tags/stars, four export formats plus JSON backup/restore, CSP script-src 'self', no accounts, cloud or telemetry.
bad: The repository was created 2026-10-18 with a single commit and zero stars — days old, and its claims ('90+ features, every one implemented') are unverified beyond its own README. The library lives in chrome.storage.local (quota-bound browser storage), not in plain files in a folder the user controls; the catalogue's 'markdown/astro website' gallery phrase was not confirmed in the README.
didnt: Rejected — another clipper variant (wave 1 covered the pattern), days old and unverified; our capture path is our own ingest, not a browser panel. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jotdrop
good: Capture trio for Obsidian — Obsidian plugin, Android app and Chrome clipper (23 stars, 113 commits, 69 releases, created 2026-05-09): fully offline, plain Markdown clips, refcount-aware delete, a never-lose-a-clip fallback, and a Syncthing handshake between the surfaces.
bad: Small young project; the README still lists the open known issue 'bulk delete while a sync peer is offline', and an ML Kit diagnostics note remains in the capture path.
didnt: Corroboration: its capture rules — plain files, refcount-aware delete, fallback so nothing captured is lost — corroborate our ingest discipline; quick capture is not a gap in our system, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WordyMe
licence: AGPL-3.0 (open-core; a PRO enterprise version is announced)
good: Lightweight self-hosted personal wiki (54 stars, 326 commits, 15 releases): one Docker container light enough for a Raspberry Pi, a Lexical rich-text editor with Mermaid diagrams and KaTeX math, documents organised into spaces with revision history and real-time updates; ships an MCP server through which Claude can search, read and write notes as the user's own account, every change saved as a restorable revision.
bad: AGPL-3.0 is ideas-only under our licence discipline. Content is stored in a libSQL database rather than plain files in git; real-time multi-user editing is the multi-writer pattern rejected by design in our system; its MCP writes as the account with no approval gate (revisions are restorable, but writes are unconditional).
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 ideas-only, and a database-backed rich-text application rather than a plain-file wiki; its revision-per-change habit corroborates our checkpointing but nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: xlog
good: Git-native Go static site generator for digital gardens and personal wikis (233 stars, 1,287 commits, 93 releases): works directly in any Markdown directory, converts mentions into links, generates automatic backlinks, hashtags, full-text search, a live-preview server and 37 built-in extensions.
bad: A publishing/rendering layer over Markdown directories — it has no capture, citation or approval machinery of its own.
didnt: Board — automatic implicit-link surfacing (mention-to-link conversion plus automatic backlinks) as a feature idea for the wiki traverse/Lens layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: link (Local personal memory for LLM agents)
good: Local Markdown memory layer for agents built explicitly on Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern (216 stars, 868 commits, 13 releases): raw sources become an inspectable wiki; writes are review-gated — agents propose, the user approves, and even automatic session hooks capture proposals, never facts; no LLM sits in the memory layer, so ingest and recall are deterministic; CI blocks outbound network code in the runtime. Measured, not asserted: LoCoMo end-to-end QA 84.8%, LongMemEval evidence retrieval 99.4%, an 18-case memory-poisoning adversarial benchmark with zero attacks reaching the inbox unlabeled, and point-in-time recall reconstructed from dated files and their supersede lineage. Sync moves reviewed memory through a git remote the user controls, with secret scanning before anything leaves; a local ledger records which memories were actually retrieved.
bad: Single-author project created 2026-04-10; the headline benchmarks are self-published (own harness and judges — losing experiments are disclosed, which softens but does not remove this). Its session hooks capture session context as proposals — session-transcript ingest is unapproved in our system even in proposal-gated form — and 'lnk setup' auto-detects installed agents and wires them in one command, an auto-discovery pattern.
didnt: Corroboration — its review-gated writes, deterministic no-LLM memory layer, supersede-lineage point-in-time recall and published adversarial-poisoning benchmark corroborate our approval-gated writes, abstention battery and supersession design; our own implementations already exist, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: til
