licence: LICENCE CONFLICT recorded as found: repository metadata / LICENSE detection shows CC0-1.0 while the README badge states 'License: MIT' — the root LICENSE file governs, so the row rests on CC0-1.0
good: A well-kept personal TIL ('today I learned') content collection (87 stars, 478 commits): short notes organised by category at the intersection of tech and life, rendered as a VitePress site — a clean example of the plain-Markdown personal-wiki content pattern.
bad: It is a content repository, not software — there is nothing to adopt, integrate or run. Its licence signals conflict (recorded above).
didnt: Rejected — a personal content repository rather than a tool; nothing to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Kompl
good: Self-organising, compounding LLM-wiki (79 stars, 340 commits, 8 releases): on ingest it extracts entities, concepts, claims and contradictions (local spaCy NLP plus one LLM call), resolves entities through a cascade, cites sources from its claims, surfaces disagreements on comparison pages with provenance, and archives the previous version of every page it rewrites via outbox commits. Its MCP server is read-only (search_wiki, read_page, list_pages, wiki_stats).
bad: It rewrites and updates existing pages automatically on ingest — 'organizes and updates itself... zero upkeep' — with no human approval gate, the self-organising pattern the owner has rejected. It requires a Firecrawl API key (hosted scraping egress) plus a Gemini or DeepSeek key; the stack is heavy (app + NLP service + n8n containers, ~5 GB disk / 4 GB RAM); single-tenant with no multi-user authentication, and the README warns against exposing it publicly; 38 open issues.
didnt: Rejected — automatic self-organisation and page rewriting without an approval gate is the owner-rejected auto-discovery pattern, and the LLM-wiki family is already covered; its read-only MCP door and claim-citation habits corroborate our design at most. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shiori
good: Single-binary Pocket-style bookmark manager (11,679 stars, 677 commits, 32 releases) with CLI and web interfaces: imports/exports Netscape bookmark files and Pocket exports, runs on SQLite/PostgreSQL/MariaDB/MySQL, and by default parses readable content from each saved page into an offline archive.
bad: Its browser extension is explicitly labelled BETA; as a bookmark manager it duplicates what our wiki's capture layer already does.
didnt: Corroboration — its default behaviour of parsing readable content and keeping an offline archive of every saved page confirms our preserve-the-source capture rule; the manager itself is a duplicate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: castorini/rank_llm
good: A reproducible IR reranking toolkit from the Castorini group: pointwise (MonoT5, MonoELECTRA), pairwise (DuoT5) and listwise (RankZephyr, RankGPT/RankGemini variants) rerankers under one interface, two-click reproduction (2CR) commands for the DL19-DL23 benchmarks, trec_eval evaluation with aggregated results shipped in the repo, invocation-history error analysis, a canonical rank-llm CLI plus HTTP and MCP serving, and training support; the resource paper was accepted to SIGIR 2025.
bad: Benchmark-research scope (TREC / MS MARCO), not a knowledge store: nothing here holds a corpus with citations or provenance. The optional stacks are heavyweight (Java 21 for the Pyserini retrieval extra, CUDA PyTorch and vLLM for local models) and the hosted rerankers require third-party API keys.
didnt: Board — its reproducible-reranking discipline (2CR commands, in-repo aggregated trec_eval results, invocation error analysis) is candidate machinery for measuring our own retrieval quality, the truth-aware retrieval gap included; the toolkit itself is IR-research scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Marker-Inc-Korea/RAGchain

didnt: Rejected — archived at source and unstable by its own acknowledgement; its multi-retriever Linker split and time-aware RAG are noted as ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: langchain-ai/langchain

bad: A general application framework, not a knowledge store — it holds no corpus, citations or provenance of its own. The surface is enormous and fast-moving (17,046 commits, 1,396 releases), and the production observability/deployment pieces live in separate LangChain products; adopting it would replace our purpose-built file-first machinery with framework abstractions.
didnt: Rejected — scope and duplication: framework generality against our purpose-built, file-first stack; the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict stands on the source evidence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

The default install path steers the user to sign in to the hosted claude-mem observer (account, trial, cloud sync at cmem.ai); the purely local provider is opt-in.
took: 3-layer progressive-disclosure retrieval — built in Round 3, lane TA1 — source/inspiration: claude-mem

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: infiniflow/ragflow

name: meilisearch/meilisearch

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 licence, and a general-purpose search server adds operational weight our file-first retrieval does not need; its scoped-API-key and typo-tolerance patterns are noted as design references only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

good: Open-source workplace context layer: 50+ connectors (Slack, Drive, GitHub, Microsoft 365, Jira and more) feeding a permission-aware workspace whose access is resolved at query time against the source system's own permissions, grounded answers with block-level citations to the original documents, knowledge-graph retrieval, an MCP server and Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs, fully self-hostable with any LLM provider.
bad: An enterprise multi-tenant platform — a heavy multi-service Docker/Kubernetes stack (graph DB, message broker, KV store) built for company workforces, including no-code agents that execute actions across enterprise tools; its citations are block references with no citation locking, supersession or abstention discipline, and nothing about it is personal-scale.
didnt: Corroboration — permission-resolved-at-query-time cited retrieval over connected sources is the same category our gateway and Ask door implement at personal scale; the platform itself is enterprise weight we will never run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pingcap/autoflow
good: Graph RAG conversational knowledge base built on TiDB Serverless vector storage with LlamaIndex and DSPy: a Perplexity-style conversational search page with a built-in website crawler that scrapes sitemap URLs, plus an embeddable JavaScript snippet that drops the conversational search window into an existing website.
bad: Its README warns AutoFlow 'is still in the early stages of development'; the design hard-depends on PingCAP's TiDB for vectors, chat history and analytics, and it is aimed at public documentation-site Q&A, with no abstention, citation-locking or private-corpus custody story.
didnt: Rejected — vendor-bound (TiDB) and early-stage, aimed at public documentation chat rather than a private cited corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: OSU-NLP-Group/HippoRAG
good: Neurobiologically inspired long-term-memory RAG framework (HippoRAG, NeurIPS '24; HippoRAG 2, ICML '25): an OpenIE knowledge graph plus Personalized PageRank retrieval that the papers' evaluations, reproduced in the repo, show improving multi-hop associativity and sense-making over GraphRAG, RAPTOR and LightRAG at lower offline indexing cost; persisted indexes are bound to the endpoint, model and component identity that produced them and a mismatched index is rejected rather than mixed silently; ships an MCP server face exposing retrieve, rag_qa, index and delete tools.
bad: Research code (a single release tag) whose graph facts come from LLM OpenIE extraction — extraction errors enter the graph unchallenged, with no citation locking back to source lines and no abstention scoring; local deployment is vLLM/GPU-oriented and index migration means re-indexing into a fresh directory.
didnt: Board — the index-identity binding (an index records the model and endpoint identity that produced it and refuses silent mixing when that identity changes) as a candidate discipline for our retrieval indexes; its PPR-over-OpenIE-graph retrieval itself corroborates graph-mediated multi-hop retrieval. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Ohio State University (OSU NLP Group)

name: promptfoo/promptfoo
good: CLI and library for evaluating and red-teaming LLM applications: declarative configuration test matrices across prompts, models and RAG pipelines, red-teaming and vulnerability scanning, pull-request code scanning, CI/CD integration, and evals that run 100% locally so prompts never leave the machine; battle-tested at scale (26k stars, 430 releases).
bad: A general LLM-app test harness with a Node toolchain and its own assertion and judge model — adopting it would duplicate our bespoke golden-set and abstention batteries rather than extend them, and its red-teaming is application-security oriented, not corpus-truth oriented.
didnt: Board — declarative eval configurations gated in CI as a candidate shape for presenting our golden and abstention batteries; the tool itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: langfuse/langfuse
licence: MIT for the core (root LICENSE file, 'MIT Expat' grant); the ee/, web/src/ee/ and worker/src/ee/ directories are under the separate enterprise licence in ee/LICENSE — split as stated in the root LICENSE file
good: Open-source LLM engineering platform: end-to-end observability tracing LLM calls, retrieval, embeddings and agent actions, prompt management with version control, evaluations spanning LLM-as-a-judge, code evaluators, user feedback and manual labelling, and datasets for test sets and benchmarks; self-hostable in minutes (ClickHouse-backed) with typed Python and JS/TS SDKs and broad framework integrations.
bad: A team platform, not a library — self-hosting means running its web, worker and ClickHouse stack, and the enterprise features sit outside the MIT grant in the ee/ directories; its evaluation model centres on scores attached to traces, not source-grounded citation truth.
didnt: Rejected — platform weight and scope: team LLMOps telemetry for production applications; our gateway ledger and Ask batteries already cover our observability needs at file scale. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mlflow/mlflow
good: The largest open-source AI engineering platform (maintained since 2018, over 60 million monthly downloads per its README): experiment tracking, a model registry, OpenTelemetry-based observability for agents and LLM applications, systematic evaluation with 50+ built-in metrics and LLM judges, prompt versioning with lineage and automatic prompt optimization, and an AI gateway for routing, rate limits, fallbacks and cost control across providers.
bad: A production team platform — tracking server, model registry and gateway — orders of magnitude beyond a personal wiki's needs; its evaluation centres on production quality metrics and LLM judges rather than corpus citation truth.
didnt: Rejected — scope and weight: production ML and LLM lifecycle infrastructure, nothing our system lacks at personal scale. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: elastic/elasticsearch
licence: Triple licence per the root LICENSE.txt — AGPLv3-only / SSPL v1 / Elastic License 2.0 by default; x-pack code solely under Elastic License 2.0; some files under Apache-2.0-compatible licences as noted in their headers
good: The reference distributed search and analytics engine: near-real-time full-text and vector search over massive datasets on Lucene, hybrid retrieval positioned for RAG workloads, aggregations, geospatial and log/metric analytics, and a mature REST API and client ecosystem, battle-tested since 2010 (78k stars).
bad: A JVM cluster to operate — heavy memory and operations footprint, feature tiers gated behind Elastic subscription licences (its own local setup reverts from a one-month trial to Basic), and a source-available/copyleft triple licence that is ideas-only under our discipline; absurd overkill for a file-scale personal corpus.
didnt: Rejected — operational weight and licence: a production search cluster where our corpus needs an embedded index at most. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: searxng/searxng
good: Privacy-respecting metasearch engine that aggregates results from dozens of search services and databases while neither tracking nor profiling its users; self-hostable, actively developed (38.7k stars, ~9,800 commits), with per-engine configuration and a JSON API other tools can consume.
bad: AGPL-3.0 — its code is ideas-only for us. It searches the public web through upstream engines whose rate limits, blocking and result quality it inherits, and it is a web-search service, not a search engine over the owner's own corpus.
took: The SearXNG pattern is recorded in lane-8 dispositions as the source/inspiration for the Round 3 lane TB8 build 'Low-confidence web expansion (seam off)'.
didnt: Corroboration — the metasearch-aggregation pattern behind our built low-confidence web expansion seam (off by default); the AGPL code itself is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: qdrant/qdrant
good: Production vector database written in Rust: dense, sparse and multi-vector search, rich payload filtering with should/must/must_not conditions, hybrid queries merged by RRF or DBSF fusion, quantization cutting RAM usage by up to 97%, write-ahead logging, REST and gRPC APIs, distributed sharding and replication, and Qdrant Edge, a lightweight in-process variant for edge and offline use.
bad: Massive-scale infrastructure — a server database to deploy and operate (or a managed cloud account) to solve what is at our scale an in-process index problem; similarity ranking alone says nothing about citation truth or supersession, which is where our retrieval gap actually sits.
didnt: Rejected — scale mismatch: massive-scale vector infrastructure for a personal corpus whose open problem is truth-aware ranking, not approximate-nearest-neighbour throughput. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: valeriansaliou/sonic
good: Featherweight search backend in Rust (about 30MB RAM, microsecond-range query responses on its published benchmarks): an identifier index that stores words rather than documents, so queries return object IDs to resolve against the owning store, with query typo correction, real-time autocomplete via its suggest operation, stop-word handling across 80+ languages, live push/pop index updates and a simple TCP protocol (Sonic Channel) with client libraries in many languages.
bad: Identifier-only by design — no document storage, no phrase or field semantics, and relevance comes from a word graph rather than ranked full-text retrieval; it is a separate server process to run, and MPL-2.0 puts its code in ideas-only territory under our licence discipline.
didnt: Board — the identifier-index shape (the index holds words to IDs only while documents stay in their owning store) as a lightweight Lens search-backend pattern; ideas only, MPL-2.0. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: quickwit-oss/tantivy
good: Lucene-inspired full-text search engine library written in Rust: BM25 scoring, natural query language with phrase and range queries, faceted search, fast fields and aggregations, incremental multithreaded indexing over an mmap directory, startup under 10ms, configurable tokenizers including Chinese (jieba, cang-jie), Japanese and Korean support, and Python bindings via tantivy-py; its published benchmark puts it at roughly 2x Lucene's search latency.
bad: A library, not a server — distributed search is an explicitly stated non-feature (its sibling Quickwit covers that), documents are immutable so an edit is a delete plus reindex, and adopting it means carrying a Rust component or its Python binding in a Python-first stack.
took: Named in the Round-3 research candidates bundle boarded Tier B (Waiting) in lane-8 dispositions; nothing built from it.
didnt: Board — already boarded via the Round-3 research candidates bundle (Tier B, Waiting): an embeddable BM25 library remains the candidate engine if Lens search ever outgrows its current ranker. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: opensearch-project/OpenSearch
good: An enterprise-grade open-source distributed search and observability suite (the community fork line of Elasticsearch): RESTful full-text search and analytics at cluster scale, 61,574 commits and 72 releases under the Linux Foundation's OpenSearch project, with a large plugin/module ecosystem.
bad: It is a heavyweight Java server cluster — distribution, modules, QA and benchmarking trees fill the repo — built for enterprise log/search infrastructure. Running it to search a personal wiki's files would invert our custody model: the index lives in a managed cluster, not in inspectable files, and its observability half is out of scope entirely.
didnt: Rejected — scale and scope: a distributed enterprise search server is not a component a local-first personal wiki can or should run; our search stays file-derived and statically served (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nextapps-de/flexsearch
good: A next-generation full-text search library for browser and Node.js: multi-field document search, context and phonetic/fuzzy search, partial matching, tag search, suggestions and highlighting, with v0.8 persistent prebuilt indexes portable across InMemory, IndexedDB, SQLite, Postgres, Redis, MongoDB and ClickHouse backends, worker-parallel indexing, and charset encoders spanning Latin, CJK, Hindi, Arabic, Cyrillic, Greek and Hebrew.
bad: Relevance is purely lexical: it returns ranked hits with no citation binding, abstention, or provenance. Its headline speed claims (up to 1,000,000x) rest on the project's own published benchmark pages, not an independent evaluation, and maintenance is a single small vendor (NextApps) sustained by donations and sponsors.
didnt: Corroboration — an embeddable, prebuilt-index full-text library that runs entirely client-side is exactly the shape our static Lens search needs; FlexSearch corroborates that design choice, though nothing was adopted (no lane-8 record) (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: searx/searx
good: A privacy-respecting, hackable metasearch engine: it aggregates upstream search engines without tracking users, is self-hostable, and deliberately refuses engine metrics that could leak what users search — privacy treated as a design constraint even at the cost of worse bug reports, as its own FAQ explains.
bad: The README states plainly that searx is no longer maintained — the maintainer has shifted focus to a new tool (Hister) — and its own announcement lists the metasearch model's inherent limits: results only as good as upstream engines expose, partial privacy because requests still leave the machine, and no persistent memory. AGPL-3.0 also makes its code ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — unmaintained at source and AGPL-3.0 (ideas only). The related pattern our programme did build from (Round 3, lane TB8) was the SearXNG fork's, recorded in lane 8 under that name; it is not evidence about this repo and is not borrowed onto this row (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: manticoresoftware/manticoresearch
good: A fast, SQL-first open-source search database (the Sphinx-lineage engine): full-text, vector and hybrid search in one query, real-time indexing, auto-embeddings with automatic chunking, conversational search via CALL CHAT, row-wise and columnar storage, Galera multi-master replication, and a small ~40 MB footprint, with published reproducible benchmark dashboards against MySQL, Typesense, Elasticsearch and ClickHouse.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us, and it is a server database: adopting it would mean running and administering a search daemon with its own storage, replication and auth surface to answer questions over a file corpus that our static index already serves. Its speed figures are the vendor's own benchmark dashboard.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 (ideas only) and server-database scope; hybrid full-text+vector in a single SQL query is noted as the pattern, nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zaidmukaddam/scira
good: An AI search engine (formerly MiniPerplx) that plans a question into sub-tasks, retrieves from live sources, and returns grounded answers with inline citations the reader can click to audit; 17 search modes and 28 tools spanning web, academic, GitHub, Reddit, X, finance and media, built on the Vercel AI SDK with Exa/Firecrawl/Tavily retrieval.
bad: Its answers ride on a stack of third-party paid APIs (OpenAI and Anthropic keys are required even to self-host, plus Exa for search), several modes (Connectors, Memory, Voice, XQL) are Pro-tier on the hosted product, and its citations are presentation links — nothing verifies a cited source still says what the answer claims, and there is no abstention when evidence is thin. AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only regardless.
didnt: Corroboration — a popular open AI-search product treating click-to-audit inline citations as the core trust feature corroborates our citation-first answer design; our lockfile goes further than display citations, and AGPL keeps this ideas-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: quickwit-oss/quickwit
good: A cloud-native Rust search engine built to search directly on object storage (S3/Azure Blob/GCS) with sub-second latency: full-text search and aggregations, an Elasticsearch-compatible API, OTEL-native log and trace ingest, schemaless or strict-schema indexing, decoupled stateless indexers and searchers, and multi-tenancy with retention policies.
bad: Its entire design centre is observability — logs, traces, and soon metrics — at cloud scale, with Kafka/Kinesis/Pulsar ingest and Kubernetes deployment. None of that maps onto a personal knowledge corpus: it indexes event streams into cloud buckets, not cited files under the owner's custody.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an observability search engine for cloud log infrastructure, however good, is not a component of a local-first personal wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: benbusby/whoogle-search
good: A self-hosted, ad-free metasearch front-end for Google results: no JavaScript, cookies, AMP links or IP tracking, Tor/proxy support, custom bangs, JSON result output, and one-click Docker deployment — for years the lightest way to get private web search on your own machine.
bad: The repository is archived and its README carries a dated notice (24 Jul 2026): Whoogle no longer returns search results at all, because Google closed the no-JavaScript query route it was built on and the Custom Search BYOK fallback is 'no longer a workable alternative either' — no further commits, releases, fixes or support. The code remains only as a reference record.
didnt: Rejected — dead at the source: the upstream door it depended on was closed by Google and the project has ended; recorded as the cautionary case for building on a single third-party's tolerated access route (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: volcengine/OpenViking
good: An open-source context database for AI agents that unifies memory, knowledge RAG and skills as one inspectable virtual filesystem (viking://): agents navigate it with ls/tree/read/grep, every directory carries generated L0 abstract and L1 overview summaries so relevance is judged before full L2 content is read, sessions are committed into inspectable/editable Markdown memories, and retrieval can be scoped to a subtree instead of a flat vector pool. Published LoCoMo and tau2-bench evaluations report large accuracy and token gains over native agent memory.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us. Its capture substrate is session archiving — committing conversations and extracting memories automatically — the session-transcript ingest pattern the owner has not approved. The README is also an agent-addressed surface: 'let your agent deploy it' blocks and curl|bash installers instruct an agent to install and wire the server (characterised here as evidence, never followed). Its benchmark numbers were measured with the vendor's own Doubao models, and a hosted Volcengine edition plus commercial tiers sit behind the open repo.
took: L0/L1/L2 tiered reading — built in Round 3, lane TB2 — source/inspiration: OpenViking (idea only, as recorded in lane 8); OpenViking is also one of the six memory-and-retrieval designs (Tier B, lane TB2) recorded as built in Round 3.
didnt: Corroboration — the L0/L1/L2 tiered-reading design our index-first protocol took from it in Round 3 is corroborated at source: summary-before-source, directory-scoped search, and memory as files a human can open and edit; AGPL-3.0 keeps the code itself ideas-only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Volcengine

name: VectifyAI/PageIndex
good: A vectorless, reasoning-based RAG engine for long professional documents: instead of chunking into a vector store it builds a hierarchical tree index of each document and lets an LLM reason its way down the tree, returning traceable, explainable retrieval tied to explicit references. Local mode runs with the user's own model key, indexing cost is published at roughly $0.001/page, and benchmark methodology (62 lookup questions over 34 PDFs from MMLongBench-Doc-V2, runner and data in a public benchmark repo) is unusually inspectable.
bad: Retrieval quality rides on the chat model chosen — the README itself advises using the best model affordable — and its headline 98.7% FinanceBench figure is vendor-reported. The open local mode is the reduced product: block-level citations, OCR/image understanding, metadata, folders and the MCP server are Cloud-only, moving custody of the index to the vendor.
didnt: Corroboration — tree-index, reasoning-over-structure retrieval with results traceable to explicit references is the document-scale form of our index-first protocol, and it corroborates that design; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is not repeated, as no lane-8 record or master row supports it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: langchain4j/langchain4j
good: An idiomatic Java library for LLM applications on the JVM: unified APIs over 20+ LLM providers and 30+ embedding stores, tool calling with MCP support, chat memory, agents and RAG patterns, and first-class Quarkus/Spring Boot/Helidon/Micronaut integrations across a very large module tree (4,210 commits, 91 releases).
bad: It is an enterprise Java framework — our system is Python tooling over Markdown files, with no JVM anywhere in the stack. Its breadth is provider plumbing for application developers; it contains no knowledge-custody, citation or governance machinery of its own, and adopting any of it would mean adopting a second runtime for no capability we lack.
didnt: Rejected — stack and scope: a JVM application framework is not a component of our file-based knowledge system (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: oramasearch/orama
good: A complete search engine in a tiny TypeScript package (core under 2kb) that runs in the browser, on a server or at the edge: full-text (BM25, typo tolerance, stemming/tokenisation in 30 languages), vector and hybrid search, facets, filters, geosearch and a plugin system including data persistence and embeddings; 161 releases show sustained maintenance.
bad: It is a search primitive, not a knowledge system: no citations, abstention, provenance or write governance, and its RAG/answer-session path is built around calling OpenAI from the client via a secure-proxy plugin. Repo licence metadata reads Other (NOASSERTION); the licence is settled as Apache-2.0 only by opening LICENSE.md itself, which agrees with the README's License section.
didnt: Corroboration — a sub-2kb embeddable full-text/vector/hybrid engine that runs entirely in the browser corroborates the client-side search shape our static Lens uses; nothing adopted (no lane-8 record) (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: oceanbase/oceanbase
good: A distributed relational database developed by Ant Group: Paxos-based consistency with RPO=0 and RTO under 8 seconds, transparent scaling (clusters of 1,500 nodes, petabytes, a trillion rows), HTAP real-time analytics on the same engine, MySQL compatibility, and published TPC-C/TPC-H benchmark results, with vector/full-text features added for AI workloads.
bad: This is planet-scale financial infrastructure — a common-server-cluster database whose smallest sensible deployment is already far beyond a personal wiki's needs, and whose search features are table features inside a distributed RDBMS, not a knowledge layer. Nothing in it addresses citations, abstention or owner-custodied files.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a distributed enterprise database is not a substrate for a local-first personal knowledge system (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Ant Group

name: surrealdb/surrealdb
licence: BSL 1.1 (Business Source License 1.1 — source-available, not open source; converts to Apache-2.0 on the Change Date, 2030-01-01)
good: A multi-model database in a single Rust binary — document, graph, relational, time-series, geospatial and key-value models with full-text/vector/hybrid retrieval in one engine, SurrealQL, ACID transactions, realtime live queries, row-level permission-based access control, an MCP server for agent integration, and embedded, browser (WASM), single-node or distributed deployment from the same binary.
bad: The licence is the blocker and is recorded exactly as found: repo metadata says Other (NOASSERTION), and the root LICENSE is Business Source License 1.1 — source-available, expressly not an open-source licence, with an Additional Use Grant that forbids offering the work as a database service to third parties; it converts to Apache-2.0 only on 2030-01-01. Its realtime multi-writer collaborative model is also the multi-writer design our single-writer wiki rejects by design.
didnt: Rejected — BSL 1.1 is source-available, ideas-only under our licence discipline, and a realtime multi-writer database is the wrong custody model for a single-writer, file-as-truth wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neo4j/neo4j
licence: GPL-3.0 (Community Edition; Enterprise Edition is closed-source under a commercial licence, per the README's Licensing section)
good: The reference native graph database: a high-performance graph store with the Cypher query language, ACID transactions, and a flexible node/relationship model, matured over 86,800 commits since 2012, with a full tooling ecosystem (Desktop, Aura managed service, graph data science and visualisation tools).
bad: Community Edition is GPL-3.0 — ideas-only for us — and the features that make it enterprise-complete sit in the closed Enterprise Edition. Architecturally it is a server database that would take custody of the graph; our wikilink/claims graph is a derived view rebuilt from files, so the files stay the truth and no database needs to be run, backed up or trusted.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 (ideas only) and database custody of what must remain a file-derived view; Cypher-style graph querying over our pages is already served by derived indexes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: arangodb/arangodb
licence: BSL 1.1 (Business Source License 1.1 — source-available, not open source; converts to Apache-2.0 four years after each version's release date)
good: A native multi-model database — documents, graphs and key-values in one engine with the AQL query language, an integrated search engine (ArangoSearch) for ranked full-text, horizontal sharding, replication with automatic failover, hot backups, and a free Community Edition alongside the Enterprise tier, written in C++ for large datasets (54,905 commits since 2011).
bad: Licence history recorded as found: long Apache-2.0, the current root LICENSE (devel branch) is Business Source License 1.1 for 'ArangoDB Self Managed' (March 2024) — internal production use is granted but offering it as a database service to third parties is barred until the change date converts it to Apache-2.0; the README also reserves headline scalability/security features (SmartGraphs, Encryption 360, detailed auditing) to the commercial Enterprise Edition. It is a server database with cluster operations our file corpus does not need.
didnt: Rejected — BSL 1.1 is source-available, ideas-only under our licence discipline, and a multi-model server database is the wrong substrate for file-as-truth custody (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Glass Keep
good: Keep-style notes (Markdown, checklists, images, tag chips) in a single Docker image (Express + SQLite) with multi-user auth, real-time collaboration guarded by revision checks that reject stale saves, a local server-side AI assistant (Qwen + llama.cpp) that answers from the user's notes with clickable source-note links, Google Keep Takeout import, JSON export/import, and Tauri desktop/mobile clients plus a PWA.
bad: Notes live in the server's SQLite database rather than plain files on disk, so custody and greppability are weaker than a files-first vault; the clients are useless without the server running; backup sync via export/import is manual; the collaboration model is multi-writer, the opposite of our single-writer rule.
didnt: Rejected - a sticky-notes web service with database custody and multi-writer collaboration; its one strong idea, answers that link back to the source note, is already our citation discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Notus
good: Local-first Markdown workspace where files are the single source of truth (SQLite holds only the index, conversations and task state); hybrid retrieval (vector + FTS5 + title/path ranking + segment aggregation + reranking) with traceable citations; agent file writes go through Markdown diffs with manual confirmation or auto-apply, previews are compared against the current file version before applying so a stale preview is returned instead of overwriting, rollback is offered, and no delete tool exists; MCP client and server faces; secrets kept out of listings and logs; external Skill/MCP content treated as untrusted task material, and MCP writes verify a note hash.
bad: Very young and small (34 commits, 18 stars, single author, created 2026-04-19); AI answers depend on user-configured cloud model and search providers (Firecrawl, Tavily, Exa); it is an Electron/Next.js notes app, not a substrate we would adopt; an auto-apply write mode exists, weaker than our approval gate.
didnt: Corroboration - its reviewable diff writes, compare-at-write stale-preview rejection, no-delete tool surface and cited answers independently match our gateway and editor design, so nothing needed taking. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Panda Note
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later (upstream Zed licensing per the README License section, primarily GPL-3.0-or-later with Apache-2.0 components where marked; repo metadata shows Other/NOASSERTION)
good: A real native editor kernel (Zed's: Vim, multicursor, IME, find/replace) under a three-pane notes shell; Markdown source is canonical (no WYSIWYG transformation); syncs through the user's own panda-server, which also exposes HTTP and MCP surfaces for agent access; a documented upstream-sync branch pipeline keeps the fork current with Zed.
bad: It is a fork of an entire IDE (40,507 commits, almost all upstream Zed), so the notes product is a thin shell on a huge codebase; 7 stars, no CI packaging, and the build bar is 'the same as building Zed'; no multimedia embeds yet; the inherited licence is primarily GPL-3.0-or-later.
didnt: Rejected - an editor fork, not knowledge machinery; GPL-3.0-or-later makes it ideas-only in any case, and our editing surface already exists. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HahaNote
good: File-based end-to-end-encrypted note sync (Argon2id key derivation, XChaCha20-Poly1305; only ciphertext touches the remote) to Dropbox, WebDAV, GitHub or other git platforms; notes stay editable in any editor and sync offline-first; immutable per-file version history that is never auto-deleted, with restore and cross-device conflict handling; Windows, Linux and Android clients.
bad: GPL-3.0, so the code is ideas-only for us; the encrypted-store model conflicts with our agent-readable plain-text vault - an agent could not read or cite notes without the key; a single-author project (33 stars) whose README says macOS/iOS support waits on the author's hardware and donations; the repo also carries a paid-tier buy_vip.md and a deprecated paid privacy policy.
didnt: Rejected - GPL-3.0, and an encrypted store our citation machinery cannot read; our sync custody is git itself. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Concrete
good: Local-first STEM learning workspace (Electron) that keeps notes as ordinary Markdown files; quiz generation (multiple-choice, cloze, code) and tutor explanations grounded in the currently open note; Codex/Claude agent workflows that inspect and edit vault files; sandboxed code execution; learning-progress tracking; no account or hosted backend for core workflows.
bad: The README's own Project status calls it experimental with file formats still evolving; single author, 9 stars, created 2026-09-13; it is a study app for STEM students, not knowledge infrastructure; by default it stores agent trajectories as JSONL outside the vault 'for later analysis and potential RL fine-tuning', a session-record reuse posture our owner has not approved.
didnt: Rejected - a single-author experimental study app; its grounded-in-the-open-note quizzing is a teaching feature, and our homeschool and wiki systems already cover their own ground. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: UniNotes
good: A complete, conventional full-stack build (Django): students can discover, purchase and access revision notes by subject with Stripe checkout, and keep private per-user revision notes with ownership and privacy rules spelled out in user stories; file uploads for note documents; the README honestly documents its planning phases and deployment bugs.
bad: It is a university coursework project (0 stars, created 2026-10-01) whose README is an assignment document - user stories, sprint plan, bug diary - not a maintained product; the concept is a notes marketplace with payments, the opposite direction from a private family vault.
didnt: Rejected - a coursework notes marketplace; nothing in it speaks to our wiki's machinery or custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Tisty
good: Tasks and Markdown documents live as plain files on disk (no database, no account, no server, no telemetry); finishing a task archives it with its description, journal, steps and attachments - 'an archive that keeps what each task taught you' - searchable years later; deliberately one-person (no assignees, boards or sprints); an MCP endpoint lets the user's own assistant create tasks and close them with a journal entry; two-machine sync is just a folder the user already syncs; no AI inside by design.
bad: AGPL-3.0, so the code is ideas-only; 4 stars and one author; Windows/macOS only, with no Linux build, which is where our machinery runs; its no-AI-inside stance means the agent value depends entirely on the external MCP door.
didnt: Boarded as a practice, not software - the task-to-lesson archive (every closed task leaves a searchable Markdown lesson note) is a habit worth adopting in our own tracking; the AGPL-3.0 code itself is ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Lararium
good: A self-hosted personal agent daemon with plain-file memory (Penatus spec); a separate custody daemon seals credentials at rest and injects them only at the network boundary after a policy check (auto/ask/deny), with secrets referenced as ${env:...}/${vault:...} and stripped from results and logs; an append-only audit chain and per-session event logs; agent code runs in kernel sandbox cells (systemd-nspawn + cgroup2 + overlayfs) with fail-closed networking; approval cards fan out to web, Telegram and Android with one answer settling everywhere; standing MCP approvals are bound to tool-definition fingerprints, so a schema change revokes them.
bad: Public beta v1.0.0-beta1 whose README says 'Not fit for production or multi-tenant use'; 2 stars, created 2026-09-28; Linux-only and heavy (three daemons plus kernel sandboxing) for a single-user vault; AGPL-3.0-only makes the code ideas-only for us.
didnt: Corroboration - its vault-by-reference credential custody, policy gate at the network boundary, fingerprint-bound standing approvals and approval fan-out independently match our gateway and vault design; AGPL-3.0-only, so nothing was taken as code. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Emanote
licence: AGPL-3.0-or-later (README SPDX statement and AGPL badge; repo metadata shows Other/NOASSERTION; default config/templates are CC0-1.0 OR AGPL-3.0-or-later, bundled Stork search Apache-2.0, Tailwind CSS MIT)
good: Renders a structured website (personal page, blog, wiki, Zettelkasten, knowledge base) from future-proof plain-text notes with live preview that updates in real time; Pandoc-based parsing handles Markdown and org-mode; a mature single-author Haskell project (965 stars, running since 2021).
bad: It is a static viewer/generator only - no capture, editing, validation or question-answering machinery; the Haskell-plus-Nix toolchain is a high bar for adoption or contribution; AGPL-3.0-or-later makes the code ideas-only.
didnt: Rejected - a publishing view over notes, which our Lens already provides, under AGPL-3.0-or-later; nothing it does is missing from our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PlainApp
good: Manages an Android phone from a desktop browser entirely on the local network - files, media, contacts, SMS, calls, screen mirroring - with TLS + XChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, no account and no cloud; built-in Markdown notes and an RSS reader; mature and popular (7,003 stars, 67 releases, F-Droid and Play distribution).
bad: It is phone-management software, not knowledge tooling - the Markdown notes are one minor built-in among many device features; AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only; nothing in it addresses vault custody, citation or retrieval.
didnt: Rejected - out of scope: a phone manager whose notes feature is incidental. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cheat-sheets
good: A personal operations knowledge base kept as plain Markdown in git, organised by domain (cloud, infra, linux, macos, tools, windows), free for reuse under MIT and heavily forked (1,441 forks) - evidence that the plain-repo personal knowledge-base pattern works at community scale.
bad: It is a content collection, not software: no retrieval, citation, validation or freshness machinery; accuracy rests on one author, whose README warns that products change and the sheets will not always be current; the content domain is one person's IT and homelab practice.
didnt: Rejected - a content exemplar with no mechanism to adopt; the pattern it proves (a personal knowledge base as plain Markdown in git) is the one our wiki already runs, with validation and citations on top. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Ghost
good: A mature headless Node.js publishing platform (55,584 stars, 1,013 releases) with memberships, paid subscriptions, newsletters, themes and a full API - proof that a Markdown-centred publisher can run a real business.
bad: It is a publishing business platform with its own content store and member/payment machinery; adopting it would move custody out of the wiki's plain files; the vendor's hosted Ghost(Pro) is the path the project steers users towards.
didnt: Rejected - scope: it publishes for audiences and members, while our Lens already publishes the wiki for its owner; nothing to take in this pass. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WriteFreely
good: A minimalist Markdown publishing platform in Go - single binary, SQLite or MySQL/MariaDB storage, multiple blogs per instance, private-by-default reading, ActivityPub federation, 20+ languages; clean, focused engineering from the Write.as team.
bad: A federated blog server: its centre of gravity is public writing and federation, not private knowledge custody; no retrieval, citation or validation machinery; AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only.
didnt: Rejected - a blog host, not a knowledge system; AGPL-3.0 in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Haven
good: A private blogging app for friends and family (Ruby on Rails): invite-only accounts with no self-signup, Markdown editing with live preview, a built-in RSS reader and private RSS feeds, media support, and a deliberate low-bandwidth, no-JavaScript-framework design.
bad: A blog plus feed reader for a small social circle - no knowledge machinery (no link graph, retrieval, citation or validation); its deployment is a database-backed Rails app, not plain-file vault custody.
didnt: Rejected - scope: private blogging for friends and family, a job our wiki does not have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Mataroa
licence: AGPL-3.0 (CONFLICT recorded: the catalogue line said MIT; repo metadata, the root LICENSE file and the README License section all state AGPL-3.0 - the source governs)
good: A clean minimalist blogging platform (Django): subdomain blogs, newsletters, post-by-email, generous exports including Hugo/Zola/epub bases kept in the repo, and billing/moderation handled in the open codebase.
bad: A hosted-style multi-blog service ('naked blogging platform') aimed at public writers; no knowledge machinery; and the licence is AGPL-3.0, not the MIT the catalogue claimed - the conflict is recorded in the licence field rather than silently resolved.
didnt: Rejected - scope (a minimalist blog host) and AGPL-3.0 ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: matplotlib/matplotlib
licence: Matplotlib License (custom, PSF-derived permissive licence; text in the repo's LICENSE/LICENSE file, GitHub classifies it as Other)
good: The standard Python plotting library: a comprehensive library for static, animated and interactive visualizations producing publication-quality figures across hardcopy formats and GUI toolkits (Qt, GTK, Tk, wx), usable from scripts, IPython shells and web servers — 55,567 commits, 103 releases, NumFOCUS-sponsored, with ready-made CITATION.cff citation entries.
bad: It is a general-purpose charting library, not knowledge machinery: no documents, retrieval, citation binding or provenance. Its low-level API is famously verbose, and nothing in it speaks to a personal wiki's needs beyond rendering a chart.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a plotting library is a dependency of data work, not a component of a local-first knowledge OS; our reporting renders through its own document stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RDFLib/rdflib
good: A mature pure-Python RDF toolkit: parsers and serializers for RDF/XML, Turtle, N-Triples, N-Quads, TriG, TriX, JSON-LD and more, a Graph interface over pluggable stores (in-memory, Berkeley DB, remote SPARQL endpoints) and a built-in SPARQL 1.1 query/update implementation, maintained since 2012 with 22 releases.
bad: It is a library, not a system: no ingest, no documents, no human-facing wiki. Its in-memory/Berkeley stores are not plain inspectable files, and adopting the RDF stack wholesale would replace our Markdown-and-citation substrate with a triple-store model our design deliberately avoids.
didnt: Board — a standards-based RDF/Turtle export of the compiled wiki graph (claims and citations as triples) as an interchange idea, using this BSD-3 library's serializer family as the reference; nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: digitalbazaar/jsonld.js
licence: BSD-3-Clause (root LICENSE file is the New BSD 3-clause text; repo metadata says Other/NOASSERTION — settled by opening the licence file itself)
good: Digital Bazaar's reference-grade JavaScript implementation of the JSON-LD specifications: compact, expand, flatten, frame, canonize (RDF dataset canonicalization for hashing/signing) and toRDF/fromRDF, running in Node and the browser, with a safe mode that fails on lossy constructs — the machinery behind verifiable-credential linked data.
bad: A single-format processor only: no storage, retrieval or documents, and its conformance target is still largely the 1.0/1.1 drafts the README lists. JSON-LD contexts are also a web-facing concern; our corpus is local files whose semantics live in our own schema, not in dereferenceable contexts.
didnt: Board — JSON-LD as an export/context idea for the wiki's structured metadata (its canonize step is the interesting half: a canonical form that can be hashed, kin to our citation lockfile); the library itself not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: linkml/linkml
good: A linked-data modeling language with a serious toolchain: schemas authored in YAML following object-oriented and ontological principles, convertible to JSON Schema, RDF/OWL, SHACL/ShEx and code, with 170 releases and an active standards-oriented community (json-ld-context, data-dictionary and schema topics throughout).
bad: It is a schema-engineering framework aimed at data-sharing consortia, not a knowledge base: no pages, no retrieval, no human workflow. Its full metamodel is a large dependency to carry for a personal wiki whose schema is a single AGENTS.md constitution evolved by hand.
didnt: Board — the YAML-schema-with-generators pattern as an idea for our own page-schema discipline (one authored model, several derived checkers); the framework itself not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SemanticMediaWiki/Semantic-MediaWiki
licence: GPL-2.0-or-later (README License section and COPYING file; repo metadata says Other/NOASSERTION — settled by opening the README's License section; the batch URL's hyphenated repo name 404s, the live repo is SemanticMediaWiki/SemanticMediaWiki)
good: The original semantic wiki, maintained since 2005: a MediaWiki extension that lets a wiki store and query structured data inside its pages, display results as maps/calendars/graphs, and export via RDF/CSV — 15,045 commits, 81 releases, with SQL/SPARQL/Elasticsearch store backends and a large spinoff-extension ecosystem.
bad: It is an extension to a PHP web application with a database: multi-writer server custody, the opposite of plain Markdown files under one owner's control, and its in-page annotation model mixes prose and data in the same wikitext rather than keeping a verbatim layer and a compiled layer apart. GPL-2.0-or-later code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Corroboration — pages carrying queryable structured data with export is the semantic-wiki pattern our compiled layer implements over files; SMW is its two-decade proof of demand, while its server/database custody and GPL code are not taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dbpedia-spotlight/dbpedia-spotlight
licence: Apache-2.0 for the project's original code (per its own licenses page, search-rendered evidence; parts use LingPipe under a royalty-free licence and some modules depend on GPL/LGPL code, as the same page states)
good: A research-grade entity linker (I-Semantics 2011 paper): it automatically annotates mentions of DBpedia resources in text, with configurable disambiguation by prominence, topical pertinence and confidence, exposed as a web demo, a RESTful service returning XML/JSON/RDF, and Java/Scala annotation and indexing APIs over a Lucene index of ~3.5M entities.
bad: It links only to DBpedia/Wikipedia entities, depends on multi-gigabyte external datasets that cannot ship with the code, and is a heavyweight Java/Scala server; the catalogue record's last update is March 2018 and the search-rendered evidence shows a project in maintenance stasis. Verification level: search-rendered — the repo page itself could not be opened this pass (fetch-service 429).
didnt: Rejected — an entity linker bound to one external corpus (DBpedia) with server-scale data dependencies; our entity pages are owner-curated records, and automatic mention-linking against Wikipedia is not a missing capability (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: iamgio/quarkdown
good: A Markdown-based typesetting system with real ambition: a Turing-complete extension of CommonMark/GFM (functions, variables, a standard library with layout, math, conditionals and loops) compiling one source to paged HTML, slides, docs sites, PDF, GFM or plain text, with live preview, editor extensions and fast whole-wiki compiles (its own 100+ page wiki in ~2 seconds).
bad: It replaces the corpus format itself: documents become .qd sources in a dialect only this Kotlin compiler renders, so adopting it would move the wiki's plain-Markdown files into a single-vendor language. PDF export needs a Chromium-family browser, and GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — a typesetting compiler duplicating our document/PDF rendering stack, bought at the price of a proprietary-feeling dialect over plain Markdown; GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only in any case (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: silverbulletmd/silverbullet
good: A self-hosted, browser-based personal knowledge database with the right substrate: content kept as a collection of Markdown pages (a Space) with wiki-style bi-directional linking, a built-in object database and query language (SLIQ), tasks, outlining and a fully integrated Space Lua scripting environment for commands, templates and widgets — a single Rust binary serving the space.
bad: It is an application server you run and live inside, whose programmable surface (Lua plugs executing in the space) is a trust model our approval-gated, agent-mediated design does not share; and it offers no citation locking, abstention or verification machinery. The catalogue called it ALREADY HAVE, but no lane-8 record or master row backs that verdict, so it is not repeated here.
didnt: Corroboration — a Markdown-file space with an object/query layer over the pages is close kin to our files-plus-compiled-layer design, independently built and MIT-licensed; nothing was adopted (no lane-8 record) (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: athensresearch/athens
licence: EPL-1.0 (root LICENSE file: 'Source code distributed under the Eclipse Public License - v 1.0'; images in the same file are CC BY-SA 3.0; repo metadata says Other/NOASSERTION — settled by opening the licence file itself)
good: A YC W21-backed open-source collaborative knowledge graph: a Roam-style block/outliner graph for teams to capture and synthesize knowledge together, built on a graph database (Clojure/ClojureScript), with a desktop app and a browser demo — 4,647 commits and 114 releases at its peak.
bad: Dead: the README's own headline says Athens is no longer actively maintained (last catalogue activity February 2023), and data rescue depends on an unofficial community export tool. Its custody model was a graph database for collaborative editing — the multi-writer model our single-writer design rejects — with no citation or verification discipline.
didnt: Rejected — an unmaintained collaborative graph-database outliner; its shutdown is itself the custody cautionary record for database-held notes versus plain files (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GitJournal/GitJournal
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo metadata and LICENSE file; the README's License section states the principal author's code is AGPL, other contributors' code is Apache-2.0, and documentation/translations are CC BY 4.0)
good: Mobile-first capture with the right custody model: notes are stored as standardised Markdown with optional YAML headers inside a Git repository of the user's choice (GitHub, GitLab or a custom/self-hosted provider), focused on privacy and data portability, with migration paths from Google Keep, Day One, Narrate and Simplenote.
bad: It is a capture client only — no retrieval, linking-graph or citation machinery over the repo it writes to — and the AGPL-3.0 terms on the principal author's code bar adoption for us (the split licensing, AGPL for one author and Apache-2.0 for other contributors, exists so it can ship on the Apple App Store).
didnt: Corroboration — a phone writing plain Markdown into the owner's own Git repository is our custody model at the capture edge, independently built; the app itself is only a capture client and its AGPL code is ideas-only for us. Agreeing re-study of the standing master row 'GitJournal' (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Smaug6739/Alexandrie
good: A capable self-hosted team knowledge base: an extended CodeMirror Markdown engine (LaTeX, diagrams, snippets, speech-to-text), multi-tenant Teams/Workspaces with a 5-level access model, OIDC SSO, an offline-first PWA, full-text indexing with a command centre, integrated Kanban, S3-compatible asset storage and full ZIP import/export of nodes or whole platform states, deployable in one Docker command.
bad: It is a multi-tenant application on its own backend store (Go backend plus database), not a folder of Markdown files a person keeps custody of; its centre of gravity is team workspaces, permissions and tenancy — the multi-writer team model our single-writer design rejects — and it documents no citation or verification discipline.
didnt: Rejected — a multi-tenant team workspace on its own application store; nothing Markdown-file-native for a personal local-first wiki to take. Agreeing re-study of the standing master row 'Alexandrie' (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: freeplane/freeplane
good: A long-lived (since 2012, 19,601 commits) free mind-mapping and knowledge-organisation application: concept/information mapping with outlining, formulas, LaTeX, Markdown and scripting plugins, running anywhere Java runs, even from a USB drive — a robust, feature-deep desktop tool for structuring ideas visually.
bad: A desktop GUI application whose native artefact is the mind-map file, not a corpus of linked Markdown pages: no text-first ingest, retrieval or citation machinery, and its Java/Swing desktop model has no place in a headless, agent-operated wiki. GPL-2.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — a mind-mapping desktop application; visual mapping is a presentation of knowledge, not the file-based memory substrate we operate (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: zmister2016/mrDoc
good: Self-hosted Python/Django document and knowledge-base system for individuals and small-to-medium teams: Markdown, rich-text and spreadsheet editing with hierarchy, tags, templates, versions and recycle bin, public/private/access-code permissions, AI Q&A and writing over its own documents, full-text search, and PDF/EPUB publishing. It ships web, browser-extension, desktop, mobile and Obsidian-sync clients and deploys from a single Docker Compose setup with data staying on the user's infrastructure.
bad: The README splits an Open Source Edition from a Professional Edition sold on a one-time licence, so the full feature set is not in the open repo. The GPL-3.0 licence is paired with a requirement to retain MrDoc copyright notices, with removal expressly prohibited. It is a server-side document portal, not a local-first file wiki.
didnt: Rejected — a server document portal duplicating our wiki/portal stack, and GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us. Agreeing re-study of the standing master row 'zmister2016/MrDoc' (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kepano/obsidian-skills
good: Steph Ango's (kepano) agent-skills pack for Obsidian, following the open Agent Skills specification so any compatible agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) can use it: skills that teach an agent Obsidian Flavored Markdown (wikilinks, embeds, callouts, properties), Bases, JSON Canvas and the Obsidian CLI, plus Defuddle web-to-Markdown extraction and Knap template rendering — 49,889 stars within months of its January 2026 creation.
bad: It is a set of instructions for agents working in someone else's app: it presumes an Obsidian vault and the Obsidian CLI, ships no verification, citation or approval machinery of its own, and its correctness rests entirely on the host model's compliance with the skill text. Very young (49 commits, no releases).
didnt: Board — the pattern, not the pack: a SKILL.md that teaches an agent an open file format (Markdown/Bases/JSON Canvas) is the distribution shape our own read door already uses, and this repo's six-skill decomposition is boarded as a reference for packaging format skills for our wiki's doors (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: PDFMathTranslate/PDFMathTranslate
good: Layout-preserving translation of scientific PDFs (pdf2zh): formulas, charts, tables of contents and annotations survive translation into mono- and bilingual PDFs, across many translation services (Google, DeepL, Ollama, OpenAI and more), with CLI, GUI, Docker, MCP and Zotero-plugin faces and experimental OCR for scanned pages — an EMNLP 2025 demo paper's system, 37,737 stars.
bad: Translation quality is bounded by whichever external service is configured, the layout pipeline is a heavy ONNX/YOLO dependency chain, and the project has already forked its 2.0 line into a separate repository (PDFMathTranslate-next), splitting maintenance. AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Board — layout-preserving bilingual output for ingested papers as an idea for the scholarly ingest queue (a translated paper that keeps its formulas and layout is the form a citation-checked corpus wants); AGPL code itself ideas-only, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: W (wcms)
good: Lightweight flat-file wiki/CMS in PHP with no database manager: multi-user page creation in Markdown/HTML/CSS/JS, a media manager, a link-graph view, geolocation maps and LDAP authentication (both marked beta), a URL-based command interface, and full function even without JavaScript; actively maintained (1,485 commits, 54 releases).
bad: Self-described as an experimental tool aimed at artists and experimental projects — per-page styling and website-architecture freedom are the design centre, not knowledge machinery: the README documents no citation, provenance or approval-gating features, its API is explicitly experimental (v0), and the team is the creator, his brother and one later contributor. AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 licence and an experimental art/website CMS; its flat-file multi-user pattern is one we already have, and it offers no knowledge capability our wiki lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: WiKiss
licence: GPL-2.0 (GNU GPLv2, stated on the project site)
good: Minimal PHP wiki engine (its name contracts Wiki with the KISS principle, 'Keep It Short and Simple'): requires only PHP and, per its site, installs and configures in about two minutes; simplified syntax, page history with differences shown between versions, password protection, an automatic table of contents, built-in search, extension by plugins (table management, RSS feed generation and more), easy theming, and XHTML 1.0 Transitional compliance.
bad: A legacy, deliberately feature-minimal wiki: the current version presented on its own site is 0.3, it is a derivative of TigerWiki (whose development the site states is now stopped), protection is a simple password rather than user accounts, and the site documents no citation, provenance or approval-gating features. GPL-2.0 copyleft makes its code ideas-only for our stack.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-2.0 legacy minimal PHP wiki: deliberately feature-minimal under its own KISS principle, with no citation, provenance or approval machinery, and its simple-wiki pattern is already covered by our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch
licence: Apache-2.0 (settled by opening the root LICENSE.txt, which is the Apache License 2.0 text, copyright Sebastian Raschka; repo metadata shows Other/NOASSERTION. The licence text's Source definition expressly excludes books and related images.)
good: The official code companion to the book Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch): it builds a GPT-like LLM in pure PyTorch step by step - tokenization and BPE, attention mechanisms, the GPT architecture, pretraining, then finetuning for classification and instruction following - with exercises, solutions, and a large bonus tree of from-scratch implementations (Llama, Qwen3, Gemma variants, KV cache, MoE, DPO). Designed to run on conventional laptops, CI-tested on Linux/Windows/macOS, 1,077 commits.
bad: It is teaching code frozen to a print book: the README states contributions that would extend the main chapter code cannot be accepted, because they would deviate from the physical book. The models produced are small educational artefacts, not production models, and nothing in the repo addresses retrieval, citation, or record-keeping.
didnt: Rejected - scope: an LLM-internals textbook companion; it teaches how models work but offers no mechanism a personal knowledge OS lacks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: GokuMohandas/Made-With-ML
licence: MIT (repo metadata; LICENSE file at root)
good: A complete MLOps course-as-code: design, develop, deploy and iterate on a production-grade ML application, with first-principles lessons wired to working scripts - Ray for scaled training/tuning/serving, MLflow experiment tracking, evaluation on a holdout set, testing, CI/CD and continual learning - around a worked text-classification system. 49,792 stars and a 40K+ learner community.
bad: Courseware built around the Anyscale/Ray production stack (hosted Anyscale workspaces and paid live cohorts are the pushed route), and the current main holds only 19 commits as a course snapshot. Its subject is ML product engineering - training and serving models - not knowledge management, retrieval quality, or cited answers.
didnt: Rejected - scope: production-ML training material; its testing/evaluation habits are generic engineering practice our pytest-based stack already follows (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hankcs/HanLP
licence: Apache-2.0 for the source code (repo metadata and root LICENSE); the README's License section treats the pretrained models separately from the source code, so model terms are not the code licence and were not borrowed from it
good: A production-oriented multilingual NLP toolkit built on PyTorch and TensorFlow 2.x: word segmentation, POS tagging, NER, dependency and constituency parsing, semantic dependency parsing, SRL, coreference, semantic similarity, keyword extraction, summarization and classification - 10 joint tasks over 130 languages - offered as a lightweight RESTful API and a heavyweight native API, with tooling to train custom domain models. 36,519 stars, 1,812 commits, 62 releases since 2014.
bad: Centred on Chinese NLP and heavy deep-learning runtimes: the native API README specifies Python 3.6-3.10 and recommends GPU/TPU for volume work; the lightweight RESTful route is a hosted service whose anonymous quota is small (a free API key is recommended); and the pretrained models sit under separate terms from the Apache-2.0 code, so each model needs its own check.
didnt: Corroboration - a mature deterministic multilingual preprocessing stack exists if CJK/multilingual ingest ever needs real tokenization and parsing locally; no build now (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: explosion/spaCy
good: Industrial-strength NLP in Python/Cython: linguistically-motivated tokenization and trainable pipelines for 70+ languages - tagging, parsing, NER, text classification, entity linking, lemmatization - with pretrained pipelines, multi-task learning over transformer models, a production-ready training system, easy model packaging, and an extensive test suite. 33,981 stars, 16,328 commits, 138 releases; v3.8 current.
bad: A component library, not a knowledge system: value only arrives after downloading or training per-language pipelines matched to the installed version, and the README's install section bounds Python to >=3.7,<3.13. It does no retrieval, citation, or storage on its own.
didnt: Corroboration - aligned with the earlier Tier 1 spaCy study: the mature default if deterministic preprocessing is ever needed locally; no build now (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: huggingface/datasets
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata; LICENSE at root) - this covers the library only, not the datasets it loads
good: One-line dataloaders for the Hugging Face hub's public datasets (text in 467 languages and dialects, image, audio, video, PDF, 3D medical, agent traces) plus fast, reproducible preprocessing of local files in many formats. Apache Arrow memory-mapped storage removes RAM limits, streaming mode iterates without downloading, processing results are cached, and there is built-in FAISS/Elasticsearch indexing and conversion to NumPy/Pandas/Polars/PyTorch/TensorFlow/JAX/Spark. 22,080 stars, 4,395 commits, 123 releases.
bad: The Apache-2.0 licence covers the library only: each hub dataset's licence, description and citation are controlled by its own owner (per the README's Disclaimers), so every dataset needs its own licence check, and reproducibility requires pinning dataset revisions. It is ML data plumbing for training and evaluation, not a knowledge system.
didnt: Rejected - scope: dataset loading for model training/evaluation; our corpus is the owner's own files under citation locks, not hub datasets (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: QwenLM/Qwen
licence: Code/weights split, recorded as found: the repo's own License Agreement states the source code at QwenLM/Qwen is Apache 2.0 (licence at the root directory), while model weights carry per-model agreements - Qwen-72B, Qwen-14B and Qwen-7B under the Tongyi Qianwen LICENSE AGREEMENT, with commercial use requiring an application form. Neither side was borrowed for the other.
good: The official Alibaba Cloud repository for the Qwen (Tongyi Qianwen) large-language-model family: pretrained and chat models with the Qwen Technical Report (arXiv:2309.16609) as its citation anchor, and - per the repo's License Agreement - code and model weights free for researchers and developers to use, with many variants of the family distributed as open weights.
bad: The licence split (above) means no single licence covers the repo's contents - each model's agreement must be checked before use. The repo is also the first-generation family home while the line has moved on to successor generations (Qwen2/Qwen3), and as a vendor model-release repo it offers the knowledge layer nothing: no retrieval, citation, or custody machinery.
didnt: Rejected - a vendor model family's release repo; which models answer is a model-router matter (owner-gated), not a gap in the knowledge layer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RasaHQ/rasa
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata; README License section, copyright Rasa Technologies GmbH)
good: A mature open-source ML framework for automating text- and voice-based conversations: NLU plus dialogue management that handles layered conversations with back-and-forth, and connectors to Facebook Messenger, Slack, Webex, Microsoft Bot Framework, Rocket.Chat, Mattermost, Telegram, Twilio and custom channels. 32,386 commits and 254 releases since 2016.
bad: The README itself declares Rasa Open Source to be in maintenance mode and labels the framework below it 'Legacy', steering builders to the hosted Hello Rasa playground and the CALM engine on the commercial Rasa Platform; its intent-training paradigm is the one its own successor abandoned ('We have moved beyond intents').
didnt: Rejected - a maintenance-mode chatbot framework; dialogue bots are not a gap in a cited personal record, and its future is a hosted platform (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: camel-ai/camel
good: A multi-agent framework from a 100+-researcher open-source collective, built to find the scaling laws of agents: role-playing agent societies with stateful memory, toolkits, data loaders, retrievers, benchmarks and human-in-the-loop modules, under stated design principles (evolvability, scalability, statefulness, code-as-prompt), used for data generation, task automation and world simulation. 17,947 stars, 2,312 commits, 213 releases.
bad: Its centre of gravity is research at scale - simulating up to 1M agents - and its agents run on external model APIs (keys supplied via .env). Its memory module is agent state management for multi-step interaction, not an owner-visible, cited record; nothing in the source shows citation locking, scored abstention, or approval-gated writes.
didnt: Rejected - scope/duplication: our agent team already coordinates through the wiki's filing, approval and custody machinery; a general agent-society framework adds no missing mechanism (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: google-research/bert
good: The original BERT release from Google Research: TensorFlow code and pretrained models for bidirectional pretraining, with fine-tuning recipes for sentence classification and SQuAD, feature extraction, multilingual models covering 104 languages, and 24 smaller models (down to BERT-Tiny) aimed at restricted-compute settings and distillation. 40,039 stars; its SQuAD v1.1 and GLUE numbers defined the 2018 state of the art.
bad: The repository is an archived public archive - unmaintained TensorFlow-era code, no releases, and its README news ends in March 2020. BERT itself is a 2018 encoder long superseded as a default embedding/retrieval model, and the repo is a model artefact, not maintained machinery.
didnt: Rejected - an archived model artefact; embedding-retrieval design questions are already covered by the ColBERT-line records in this programme (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Google Research

name: xtekky/gpt4free
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo metadata; LICENSE at root) - copyleft, so its code is ideas-only for us in any case
good: A community aggregator that puts many LLM and media providers behind OpenAI-compatible APIs, with Python and JavaScript clients, a local web GUI, CLI, Docker images (full and slim), and an MCP server offering web search, scraping and image generation. Actively maintained at scale: 66,918 stars, 4,739 commits, 565 releases.
bad: The premise is free access to third-party providers: the repo's topics include reverse-engineering, several provider adapters need browser automation with cookie/HAR files harvested from logged-in sessions, and the repo carries a LEGAL_NOTICE.md and a security/privacy and takedown policy - providers break or are taken down without notice, so any route through it is fragile by construction.
didnt: Rejected - grey-area provider access is not a legitimate sourcing route for this system (our sourcing runs on official, genuinely free tiers), and GPL-3.0 bars code adoption regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wechaty/wechaty
good: A conversational RPA SDK for chatbot makers: write a bot once (TypeScript/JavaScript first-class, with Python, Go, Java and other bindings) and run it across WeChat, WhatsApp, QQ and more by swapping 'puppet' protocol providers; a six-line bot logs in and answers messages. 23,393 stars and 7,104 commits since 2016, with plugins, Docker images and a large examples ecosystem.
bad: Platform access rides on unofficial protocol puppets - web, iPad and Windows protocol hooks, several already marked DEPRECATED in the README's own provider table - and login is by QR-scanning a personal account, so platform-ToS and account risk are structural, not incidental. The README's release history also stops at v1.11 (Nov 2021).
didnt: Rejected - scope plus custody: our messaging runs through connected official connectors; unofficial-protocol automation over personal accounts is the opposite direction (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: neo4j/neo4j-graphrag-python
licence: Apache-2.0 (settled by opening the root LICENSE.txt: 'Unless stated otherwise, this software is distributed under the terms of the Apache License 2.0', with the full text in LICENSE.APACHE2.txt and marked parts under the Python Software Foundation License v2 per LICENSE.PYTHON.txt; repo metadata shows Other/NOASSERTION)
good: Neo4j's official first-party GraphRAG library for Python, with long-term vendor support stated: knowledge-graph construction pipelines (a customizable Pipeline and the streamlined SimpleKGPipeline, over text and PDFs), vector index creation/upsert, a retriever family including hybrid and Text2Cypher retrieval, and pluggable LLM/embedder providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, Mistral, Bedrock, Vertex AI, Gemini, Ollama). 548 commits, 38 releases, Python 3.10-3.14 supported.
bad: It presupposes a running Neo4j instance (with the APOC library installed for KG construction) and at least one external LLM provider for RAG and the KG builder. The KG-construction pipelines live in an experimental namespace the README warns may change without notice or be removed, and which is not recommended for production use.
didnt: Rejected - a graph-database server dependency inverts our files-first custody, and its graph/retrieval patterns are already represented in file form; the Tier 1 patterns took came from the separate Neo4j LLM Graph Builder, not this library (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vibrantlabsai/ragas
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata; LICENSE at root and README licence badge)
good: An LLM-application evaluation toolkit: objective metrics (LLM-based and traditional, including faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall), production-aligned synthetic test-set generation, aspect-critique discrete metrics that return a score with its reason, integrations with LLM frameworks and observability tools, and feedback loops that fold production data back into evaluation. 16,110 stars, 89 releases; quickstart templates for RAG evaluation.
bad: Its headline metrics are LLM-judged (the quickstart runs through an OpenAI API key), so scores inherit judge-model cost and variance rather than being deterministic. The README also discloses that the library collects anonymized usage analytics by default, with opt-out only via the RAGAS_DO_NOT_TRACK environment variable.
took: The metric definitions as the scoring rubric for the Ask door and search tuning, and RAGAS-style generation to grow the 15-question golden set. Verdict recorded: "FOR US — Apache-2.0, copyable.". Additionally: Survey wave 2: "RAGAS's faithfulness rubric and DeepEval's pytest-style tests give the Ask door and Lens search a regression harness shape". Additionally: Built (marathon records): Standing quality gates
didnt: Adopt/build - aligned with the earlier Tier 1 RAGAS study: standing quality gates built in Round 3 (lane TB6, source Ragas/UpTrain) use RAGAS's metric definitions as the scoring rubric for the Ask door and search tuning, with its LLM-judged metrics treated as a rubric and harness shape, not a sole judge (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: confident-ai/deepeval
good: Pytest-style unit testing for LLM systems: G-Eval, a DAG metric (deterministic decision-tree judge), RAG metrics (faithfulness, contextual recall/precision/relevancy), agent, multi-turn, voice and MCP metrics, synthetic dataset generation, prompt optimization, benchmarking, and CI/CD integration - with metrics that can run on local models. 19,021 stars, 10,438 commits, 64 releases.
bad: Its headline metrics are LLM-as-a-judge based (G-Eval and the DAG judge), so scores inherit judge-model cost and variance rather than being deterministic. The README 'highly recommends' creating a Confident AI account and states that once logged in all test cases are automatically logged to that cloud platform, which cuts against local-first custody unless the integration is deliberately avoided.
took: The pytest-shaped eval suite as the natural harness for wiki search + Ask regression tests (the wiki's stack is already Python/pytest). Verdict recorded: "FOR US".
