didnt: Adopt/build - aligned with the earlier Tier 1 DeepEval study: the pytest-shaped eval suite as the harness for wiki search and Ask regression tests, because the wiki stack is already Python/pytest and its RAG metrics map onto our cited-answer checks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SSDEVIL108/LLM-Guided-Crawler-Secret-Hunter
licence: MIT (repo metadata reads Other/NOASSERTION; settled by opening the root LICENSE file itself — MIT License text — agreeing with the README License section)
good: A web reconnaissance crawler with one sound design choice: links and script sources are extracted deterministically with BeautifulSoup before any LLM sees the page, then code snippets are audited in parallel across multiple models and assembled into an in-memory knowledge graph (pages → scripts → findings) with staging/debug-flag/API-endpoint leak detection, live Markdown reporting, and resume-from-report so an interrupted scan does not re-crawl.
bad: Seven commits and a single crawler.py script, created 2026-07 — a brand-new single-author tool. It is offensive bug-bounty tooling aimed at third-party sites, needs an NVIDIA NIM or OpenAI API key, and its 'Deterministic 0% Hallucination Extraction' headline is a README claim with no evaluation or tests in the repo.
didnt: Rejected — scope and posture: offensive reconnaissance against other people's sites; our ingest reads only sources the owner directs, and there is nothing in a 7-commit single-script crawler that our pipeline lacks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Black-Tusk-Data/minikg
licence: no licence stated at source (no licence in repo metadata, no LICENSE file at root, none declared in setup.py, no licence section in the README)
good: A deliberately small, hackable LLM-powered knowledge-graph builder/retriever: the README walks a complete worked example — Meta earnings-call transcripts converted from PDF to text and committed, a graph built over them, community visualisation, and a query script — with a companion article explaining the GraphRAG design choices.
bad: Its own README frames it 'for instructive use' and quick POCs; building requires OpenAI and Jina AI API keys, and with no licence stated anywhere the code is all-rights-reserved — ideas only at best.
didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at source, and an instructive proof-of-concept whose hosted-API extraction offers nothing our compile pipeline lacks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gauravmanandhar/legal-graphify-skill
licence: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual-licensed — LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT files at root; the README License section states 'Dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 or MIT', badges agree)
good: An agent skill that turns a folder of legal documents into a clause-level knowledge graph: obligations, prohibitions, permissions, definitions and penalties extracted with citations, cross-document conflict detection, compliance-chain tracing, and incremental updates that re-extract only changed files — with every node and relationship tagged EXTRACTED (explicit in the text), INFERRED (derived by convention) or AMBIGUOUS, so stated text is never confused with interpretation. Processing is local through the user's own agent.
bad: Three commits, created 2026-07-30 — brand new and single-author. Its benchmark table (94% clause recall, 89% conflict detection) is printed in the README with no dataset or methodology, and the headless extraction mode requires a hosted LLM API key (Gemini/Anthropic/OpenAI).
didnt: Board — the EXTRACTED / INFERRED / AMBIGUOUS confidence tag carried on every extracted node, for the ideas board: a three-way provenance label that separates what a source states from what the compiler inferred and what is genuinely unclear — a stricter discipline than a binary cited/uncited split, worth weighing for our compiled pages. The legal-domain skill itself is out of scope (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: uilab-vtt/knowledge-graph-builder
good: A complete scripted pipeline for building a knowledge graph over video content: initialise the database, add label data as JSONL via stdin, merge similar items, and dump the graph as JSONL — with test input/output fixtures committed alongside the code.
bad: Research code from 2018 (34 commits, no releases) for video-event understanding; its input format is defined by a separate knowledge-graph-input repository, and it has nothing to say about documents, retrieval or question answering.
didnt: Rejected — a 2018 video-understanding research prototype: wrong domain, long stale, nothing transferable to a document wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: uilab-vtt (README acknowledgements cite an IITP grant funded by the Korea government, MSIT)

name: DataScienceLabFHSWF/KnowledgeGraphBuilder
good: Ontology-guided KG extraction with the trust machinery done properly: entities and relations are extracted from documents under an OWL ontology, extracted facts carry provenance verification (a TextAligner checks them against the source text), the assembled graph is validated against SHACL shapes generated from the ontology, and results are served as evidence-backed facts. Its published evaluation is unusually honest — the README states plainly that the scores are not held-out or independently reviewed and that corpus counts measure output, not accuracy.
bad: Heavy infrastructure for a personal system — Neo4j plus Qdrant plus Docker, as one of a three-repository research ecosystem. The README itself warns the extraction POST endpoint is currently unauthenticated and run state is in memory, so jobs are lost on restart; created 2026-01 with 5 stars, it is a young research system.
didnt: Corroboration — an academic lab independently building to our core discipline: an extracted fact is only trusted once it is verified against the source text, and the compiled graph must pass schema validation before it is believed — our citation lockfile and validator restated in ontology dress (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Data Science Lab, South Westphalia University of Applied Sciences (FH SWF)

name: hnagnurtme/NavNexus
good: A multilingual knowledge-graph platform built for the Naver Vietnam AI Hackathon 2025: an 'Integrity Engine' harmonises research terms across languages into unified entities, a Discovery Map visualises the Neo4j graph, natural-language queries run as semantic inference over the graph, and a Recommendation Assistant detects knowledge gaps (orphan nodes, broken bridges) and suggests further searches.
bad: A hackathon build on a heavy stack (ASP.NET Core 8, Neo4j, Qdrant, RabbitMQ, Docker Compose) hard-wired to Naver's HyperCLOVA X and Papago APIs and Naver Object Storage — vendor-locked, with no path to run it outside that ecosystem.
didnt: Rejected — a hackathon prototype locked to Naver APIs and a server stack we do not run; the gap-detection idea is already covered by our own weeding/backlog machinery (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hanxiao/pi-kg
licence: MIT (stated in the README's License section only; no LICENSE file at root and no licence shown in repo metadata)
good: A clean controlled experiment in prompt-driven knowledge-graph construction: a minimal agent harness builds a canonical KG from a corpus driven entirely by a system prompt, run as an A/B test — variant A spells out the workflow steps, variant B defines only the required outcome and quality bars. Judgement metrics are published in the README, including groundedness defined as the fraction of facts whose evidence span is a verbatim substring of its source document, plus duplicate-node/edge rates and cross-document entity connectivity; output is canonical KG.jsonl with dedup done by the agent itself using embedding tools.
bad: Six commits — a single experiment, tied to one local model build (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP) on one NVIDIA L4 with a context-window coupling the README warns about. The graph is a downstream artefact for mining hard eval questions; there is no custody, editing, retrieval or QA surface.
didnt: Board — two evaluation ideas for the ideas board: (1) the steps-vs-outcome system-prompt A/B as a cheap, honest way to test compile-prompt designs before adopting one, and (2) groundedness measured as verbatim-substring evidence coverage — a mechanical check on extracted claims in the same spirit as our citation lockfile (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Galbaz1/knowledge_graph_builder
licence: no licence stated at source (no licence in repo metadata, no licence file in the root listing, and the repo has no README to state one)
good: A minimal, inspectable worked example of chunk-to-KG extraction: one build_kg.py script using Instructor structured output over GPT-4 with Graphviz rendering, with the sample business-plan inputs and each iteration's graph output committed so the whole process can be read end to end.
bad: A 2023 demo (8 commits): the committed sample texts and PNG outputs are the substance; there is no README, no licence, no tests and no reuse path, and extraction hard-depends on GPT-4.
didnt: Rejected — a toy demo with no licence stated and nothing our extraction pipeline lacks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: iamaziz/paperQA_KG
licence: no licence stated at source (no licence in repo metadata, no licence file in the root listing, no licence statement in the README)
good: A small LangChain/OpenAI demo combining two things in one app: question answering over scientific papers and a knowledge-graph builder/visualiser over the same literature.
bad: By its own README TODO it works only on abstracts, not full papers, and entity/relationship resolution plus aggregation into a real graph database are listed as unimplemented future work. A 2023 demo (22 commits) with no licence anywhere.
didnt: Rejected — an abstracts-only demo whose own TODO lists the missing substance, with no licence stated at source (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DEEP-PolyU/Awesome-GraphRAG
good: The companion repository to a published GraphRAG survey (arXiv:2506.08938): a maintained taxonomy of GraphRAG research — papers, benchmarks and open-source projects organised by knowledge organisation, retrieval and integration — plus the lab's own GraphRAG Benchmark, at 2,679 stars with dated research news running through 2026 (ICLR/ACL/KDD acceptances in the area).
bad: It is a bibliography, not a system: nothing in the repo runs, and coverage depends on community pull requests and the maintaining lab's own interests.
didnt: Board — as a standing landscape source for the weekly research watch: its benchmark list and taxonomy are the fastest maintained map of GraphRAG movement, worth consulting when retrieval work is planned (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: DEEP Lab, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU)

name: dendronhq/dendron
good: A mature local-first Markdown PKM built into VS Code (6,380 commits, 7,468 stars) organised around gradual structure: hierarchical dot-named notes, note schemas that enforce consistency and apply templates on creation, a unified lookup for finding and creating notes, backlinks and graph navigation, refactoring that renames notes and sections without breaking links, and git-backed vaults that publish with per-vault/per-hierarchy/per-note permissions — retrieval designed to work as well at ten thousand notes as at ten.
bad: The README's own banner states Dendron is in maintenance only and active development has ceased. It is also a human editor tool: no agent memory, compilation, provenance or question-answering layer — the structure serves the writer, not a machine reader.
didnt: Corroboration — its schemas, hierarchical naming and gradual-structure discipline independently validate our page conventions (frontmatter schema, hierarchical index, rename-with-link-repair) in a human PKM proven at scale; nothing taken because the tool itself is editor-bound and no longer developed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: org-roam/org-roam-ui
good: A well-liked graphical frontend for org-roam (2,288 stars): an interactive 2D/3D node graph with local and global views, note previews, filters, theme syncing with Emacs, and a follow-mode that tracks your position in the editor — served locally, side-by-side with Emacs.
bad: Its own Disclaimers call it alpha software that may break and whose development may stop any day; it only works with org-roam v2 inside Emacs, and its FAQ documents real graph performance limits (networks over ~2k nodes slow down, with a list of effects to disable). GPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — an Emacs/org-roam substrate graph viewer; our Lens already provides the reading and graph surface over our own files, and GPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us regardless (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: akosbalasko/yarle
good: The reference Evernote exit tool (1,814 stars, 150 releases): converts .enex exports to Markdown while preserving the metadata migrations usually lose — original creation/modification times (including the files' own timestamps), tags, GPS location, notebook name and source URL — plus internal note links, attachments in a resources folder, and user-defined templates with target formats for Obsidian, Logseq, Tana and Heptabase; runs as a desktop app or CLI.
bad: It is a one-way, one-source migration utility: nothing retrieves, verifies or maintains the corpus after conversion, target-specific conversions carry their own stated limitations, and Evernote is not a source our ingest takes in the first place.
didnt: Rejected — a one-way Evernote migration tool; its metadata-preservation discipline (original timestamps, tags and source URL carried into the Markdown) is the right bar for any migration ingest, but there is no Evernote corpus in our pipeline and our converters cover the formats we do take (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: iwe-org/iwe
good: A Rust Markdown knowledge-graph toolkit (1,790 stars, 368 commits, 116 releases) built on exactly our premise — your notes are your agent's memory, kept as ordinary Markdown in a folder you own: an LSP gives editors link autocomplete, backlinks and safe renaming; a CLI searches and reorganises notes; an MCP server (iwec) lets Claude/Codex and other MCP agents read and write the same documents; and in its Mac app each agent run is a single undo step. Memory the owner can read, correct or delete is a stated design goal.
bad: The memory is navigation-shaped, not truth-shaped: nothing at source describes citation locking, provenance, abstention or an approval gate — connected agents write to the shared notes directly, bounded mainly by undo. Much of the surface (Mac app, docs, guides) is documented off-repo at iwe.md, so several claims rest on the project's own site rather than this repository.
didnt: Corroboration — one of the closest living relatives of our design (shared human/agent Markdown memory in owner-held files, an MCP door, memory the owner can inspect and correct) confirms the architecture from the market side; the difference is the trust machinery it does not describe and we built — citation locking, scored abstention, approval-gated writes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: circlemind-ai/fast-graphrag
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file; README badge agrees)
good: A streamlined, promptable GraphRAG framework built on nano-graphrag: it extracts a domain-tuned knowledge graph from raw text and explores it with personalised PageRank for retrieval, supports incremental updates as data changes, is fully asynchronous and typed, and can include references to the information used in an answer (with_references=True). The README's worked example claims a 6x cost saving over Microsoft's graphrag on The Wizard of Oz ($0.08 vs $0.48).
bad: Extraction and querying are LLM-driven (the quickstart requires an OpenAI API key), so graph quality rides on the model and on the domain prompt the user writes; its only cost evidence is the vendor's own single-book example, and the project steers users toward Circlemind's metered managed service ('first 100 requests free every month'). Nothing in the design binds an answer to a checked source version — no citation locking, and no abstention when the graph lacks the answer.
didnt: Corroboration — PageRank graph exploration over an interpretable, human-navigable knowledge graph with an optional references-in-answer mode corroborates graph-assisted cited retrieval; not adopted, as LLM-API extraction with no provenance or supersession discipline is not our file-first design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gollum/gollum
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file)
good: The wiki is simply a Git repository of human-editable markup files: pages in many markups (Markdown flavours, AsciiDoc, Org, RDoc and more via github-markup), editable in any editor or the built-in local web frontend, with every version displayable and revertible, GitHub/GitLab wiki compatibility, BibTeX and citation support, CriticMarkup annotations, diagrams, macros and redirects. Mature and heavily used: created 2010, 14,334 stars, 2,576 commits.
bad: It is a rendering and editing layer only — no search or retrieval machinery beyond page lookup, no citation locking, no abstention; web edits commit straight to Git with no approval gate, and the stack is Ruby/JRuby, foreign to our tooling.
didnt: Corroboration — a wiki whose store is a plain Git repository of human-editable files, with citation support and full version history, is the substrate our own wiki already stands on; not adopted as a component (we have our own Lens and editor). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: blacksmithgu/datacore
good: A re-imagining of Dataview as an Obsidian plugin: an index over Markdown files supporting live-updating views and metadata queries at section and block granularity (indexing attachments, PDFs and images too), a React-based JavaScript API with stateful views, WYSIWYG table views with live editing, working embeds, and a claimed 2–10x query and rendering performance improvement over Dataview.
bad: Self-described work-in-progress from a single maintainer lineage, and it is an Obsidian plugin — its index lives inside a host application our system deliberately does not depend on; live in-view editing writes metadata directly, with no approval gate or provenance discipline.
didnt: Corroboration — a live index over plain Markdown files with block-level query granularity corroborates our index-first retrieval over the same substrate; not adopted (Obsidian-bound, work-in-progress). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: toeverything/AFFiNE
licence: Split at source: most of the repo is MIT (root LICENSE directs to LICENSE-MIT), but content under packages/backend and packages/common/native is carved out under a separate licence defined in packages/backend/server/LICENSE, and an Enterprise Edition is separate again; repo metadata reads Other (NOASSERTION) — settled by opening the root LICENSE file itself.
good: A local-first, self-hostable workspace (73,736 stars, 11,533 commits) that hyper-merges documents, an edgeless whiteboard canvas and multi-view databases into one block model, with CRDT-based real-time collaboration and sync across web and cross-platform clients, and an integrated multimodal AI assistant.
bad: Its centre of gravity is real-time multi-writer CRDT collaboration — the model our single-writer, approval-gated design rejects by design; documents live in its OctoBase database rather than as plain human-editable files we could keep custody of, the licence is split with a backend carve-out and a commercial enterprise tier, and the monorepo's scope dwarfs a personal knowledge system.
didnt: Rejected — a multi-writer collaboration platform with database custody and a split licence; its local-first claim is credited, but the sync model and scope are the opposite of our design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docmost/docmost
licence: AGPL-3.0 (core, per repo metadata and the README License section; the directories apps/server/src/ee, apps/client/src/ee and packages/ee are under the Docmost Enterprise licence)
good: An open-source collaborative wiki and documentation platform positioned as a Confluence/Notion alternative (22,060 stars): real-time collaboration, diagrams (Draw.io, Excalidraw, Mermaid), spaces, permissions management, groups, comments, page history, search, file attachments and embeds, with translations in 10+ languages.
bad: The core is AGPL-3.0 while enterprise features sit under a separate Docmost Enterprise licence in dedicated directories, so the open edition is deliberately split from the commercial one; the README documents no flat-file/plain-Markdown storage — content lives inside the application, not as files we could keep custody of — and real-time multi-writer editing is the collaboration model our design refuses.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only for our stack, and its database-backed team-collaboration scope does not fit a personal local-first LLM wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: suitenumerique/docs
licence: MIT (repo metadata, root LICENSE and README License section agree); the README warns that some advanced features (e.g. PDF export) rely on GPL-licensed BlockNote XL packages that are not MIT-compatible, excludable by building with PUBLISH_AS_MIT=true
good: A web-native collaborative text editor built to scale (Django + React, Yjs): cleanly structured documents and sub-documents, live cursors and presence, comments and sharing, granular access control, offline editing, import/export across .docx/.md/.odt/.pdf, a delimiter-based presentation mode, and optional model- and gateway-agnostic AI helpers, including a toolbar where the user accepts, rejects and iterates AI feedback; self-hostable via Kubernetes or Docker Compose.
bad: It is a real-time multi-writer team editor — the collaboration model our single-writer, approval-gated design rejects by design; content custody sits in its server stack (Django, databases, S3-compatible storage), not plain files; and the full feature set is not all MIT, since GPL BlockNote XL packages ride along unless explicitly built out.
didnt: Rejected — government-backed and genuinely well-built, but a multi-writer collaboration server with server-side custody; nothing in it answers a personal wiki's citation and abstention needs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: DINUM (French government) and ZenDiS (German government) joint initiative, per the README Credits section

name: RagView/RagView
licence: no licence stated at source (the repo root contains only README.md — no LICENSE file; the README FAQ states RagView 'currently has no open source plan')
good: A unified RAG evaluation platform built on an honest premise — 'every SOTA result is only valid on its own dataset': users upload their own document set and test set (questions, source passages, reference answers) and benchmark RAG solutions apples-to-apples on answer accuracy, context precision, context recall, latency and token consumption, with per-query and per-metric drill-down into how each score was computed.
bad: The platform itself is a closed hosted service: the GitHub repo is a README only (18 commits, no code, no licence), evaluation runs consume purchasable 'evaluation counts', its own FAQ lists only three RAG solutions actually integrated (R2R, LangFlow, DocsGPT), documents are PDF-only, and the corpus must be uploaded to ragview.ai — custody leaves the user's hands.
didnt: Board — evaluating retrieval on your OWN dataset with context precision and recall as first-class metrics, as a candidate discipline for our golden-set evaluation; the hosted metered service itself is rejected (closed, no licence, corpus custody surrendered). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: BukeLy/rag-api
licence: MIT per the README License section and licence badge; the README links a LICENSE file, but no LICENSE file appears in the root listing as opened — recorded as found
good: An enterprise-grade multi-tenant RAG API service built on LightRAG/RAG-Anything: multimodal document parsing (PDF, Word, Excel, PPT and images with OCR, table and formula extraction) with complexity-scored automatic parser selection across DeepSeek-OCR, MinerU and Docling, five query modes from naive vector to full hybrid graph retrieval, complete tenant isolation with per-tenant instances and API keys, batch upload of up to 100 files with async progress, and one-click Docker deployment.
bad: A brand-new project (created October 2025, 65 stars, no releases) whose scope is multi-tenant enterprise serving — the opposite of a personal wiki; it requires external LLM and embedding API keys and a stack of databases (Qdrant, Memgraph, DragonflyDB/Redis), and its answers carry no citation locking or abstention discipline.
didnt: Board — complexity-scored parser auto-selection (routing each document to DeepSeek-OCR, MinerU or Docling by scored difficulty) as a candidate for our document/OCR ingest queue; the multi-tenant API service itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MegaGrindStone/go-light-rag
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file)
good: A Go library implementation of LightRAG with clean interface separation — GraphStorage, VectorStorage and KeyValueStorage interfaces with pluggable implementations (Neo4j, ChromeM/Milvus, BoltDB/Redis) and pluggable LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, OpenRouter) — and a deliberate design that returns raw retrieved context (sources with relevance scores) to the caller instead of imposing prompt templates; tests and benchmarks against a NaiveRAG baseline are included.
bad: The repository is archived — a public archive, unmaintained; it is a derivative port of the already-studied LightRAG pattern rather than a new mechanism, its provided storage implementations lean on external database servers (Neo4j, Milvus), and it is a Go library, the wrong stack for our Python and file tooling.
didnt: Rejected — an archived derivative implementation of the LightRAG pattern we have already studied at source; maturity (archived) and stack rule it out. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ZB052-A/LightRAG-Deepseek-Test
licence: no licence stated at source (no LICENSE file in the root listing, no licence in repo metadata, no licence section in the README)
good: A worked example of wiring LightRAG to the DeepSeek API (with SiliconCloud embeddings): a vendored LightRAG tree offering many knowledge-graph backends (Neo4j, Postgres, Mongo, Milvus, Chroma and more), a FastAPI server entry point, and test texts in English and Chinese (a Gutenberg book and a Ming-history chapter).
bad: It is a personal test harness, not a system: 5 commits, no releases, the LightRAG code is vendored in wholesale with no licence stated anywhere in the repo, it needs DeepSeek and SiliconCloud API keys, and the README documents no evaluation results — nothing original to learn beyond the wiring.
didnt: Rejected — a throwaway experiment around an already-studied engine; no licence at source (ideas-only at best) and no mechanism of its own. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Fractera/Agentic-Engineering-Infrastructure
licence: PolyForm Small Business License 1.0.0 (source-available) — settled by opening the root LICENSE file itself (repo metadata reads Other/NOASSERTION; the README's own License section calls it 'Open Code (source-available)', which contradicts the repo description's 'Fully open-source' claim — the conflict is recorded as found, the licence file governs)
good: A self-hosted agent-engineering substrate: it provisions a private VPS end-to-end (Nginx routing, automated HTTPS, databases, multi-role auth, local media storage) in minutes, deploys a large pre-built Next.js boilerplate (~50,000 lines) so agents work against a fixed architecture instead of re-deriving it, assembles changes through deterministic atomic MCP commands rather than free-form file rewriting, and keeps code and data on the owner's own server with a local SQLite WAL store and a LightRAG memory layer.
bad: The README is marketing-led: headline claims (90–94% token savings, 'zero-token overhead', 'infinite scale') are asserted, not evidenced; the product's core act — autonomous agent teams deploying and modifying production infrastructure — is ungated autonomy of exactly the kind our approval-gated design refuses; the repo has no releases, and the licence is source-available PolyForm, not open source as the description claims.
didnt: Rejected — autonomous DevOps-by-agents scope and a source-available licence (ideas-only); its deterministic MCP-first assembly stance is noted as corroborating our preference for constrained tool surfaces over free-form file access, nothing more. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: olafgeibig/knowledge-mcp
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file)
good: A locally running MCP server that turns curated document collections into named knowledge bases agents can consult during reasoning: a CLI creates, deletes and manages bases and documents, LightRAG builds hybrid vector+graph indexes over PDF/Text/Markdown/DOCX with file-based storage by default, per-base configuration sets query mode, top_k, token limits and even a custom response-format user prompt, and several LLM/embedding providers are supported including local Ollama and Hugging Face.
bad: A small single-author project (64 commits, 59 stars); the MCP surface is search-only retrieval with no citation locking, no scored abstention and no provenance on what it returns, knowledge-base mutation happens out-of-band through the CLI, and the documented defaults assume an OpenAI API key.
didnt: Corroboration — a local MCP read door over personal knowledge bases, managed by CLI and queried by agents, is the same shape as our own MCP door; its LLM-extracted graph custody is not our verbatim-file custody, so the engine is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: HerSophia/LightRAGforSillyTavern
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file)
good: A LightRAG fork that wraps the engine in an OpenAI-standard response API (with prefill support) so any compatible chat frontend — built for SillyTavern role-play users — can consume it, adding multi-file graph build and insert, hot model switching with automatic model-name and max-token filling, a keyword trick that keeps highly relevant entities and relations in the prompt, incremental extraction that feeds already-known entity names back to the model, and a Gradio management frontend for documents and graphs.
bad: Scope is role-play chat memory, not knowledge work; it is a student-maintained fork developed in sync with another repository, the authors themselves warn it inevitably has bugs and that its features are poorly decoupled, setup is Windows .bat-centric, and an .env file — the very file the README tells users to fill with their API settings — sits committed in the repo root listing.
didnt: Rejected — a role-play-chat fork of an already-studied engine; self-declared immaturity and scope rule it out. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Shen-An/policyflow-ai
licence: MIT per the README's own licence section (final section: 'MIT'); no LICENSE file appears in the root listing as opened — recorded as found
good: An enterprise policy-Q&A assistant whose two public promises are exactly evidence and approval: answers must carry evidence, with a hard refusal when no reliable evidence exists, and untrusted answers explicitly labelled as model reference; high-impact actions run as sandbox draft → human approval (fresh RBAC re-check, action digest, expected version) → at-most-once commit, and official policy originals are never rewritten. Around that core: BM25 + LightRAG hybrid retrieval under a single LangGraph orchestration shared by chat and evaluation, versioned materials in SHA-256 object storage, tiered memory that is explicitly non-authoritative ('memory may not override this turn's retrieval evidence'), a golden-set evaluation centre (Hit@1/5/10, MRR, negative-sample gating), and an unusually honest README that marks everything not actually run locally as [~] and states that skip does not equal pass.
bad: It is an enterprise multi-tenant platform — PostgreSQL with row-level security, Milvus, MinIO, Redis and RabbitMQ — far beyond a personal wiki's scale, from a single author with no releases; its Stage 10 acceptance is still in progress, and several guarantees are honestly marked unproven locally (gVisor sandbox isolation never ran a real pod, the signed Electron build never ran, the 1000-session load soak is untested), while knowledge-base deletion is physical across objects, vectors and SQL rows.
didnt: Corroboration — the closest design relative in this batch: an evidence gate with hard abstention, approval-gated at-most-once writes over sandboxed drafts, versioned evidence, and memory that may never override sourced evidence independently mirror our citation-locking, abstention and approval-gate invariants. Not adopted (enterprise multi-tenant scope and stack). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: castorini/pyserini
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata licence card and root LICENSE.txt; agrees with the Tier-1 'Pyserini' study's verified Apache-2.0 and with the catalogue line)
good: A mature, actively maintained toolkit for reproducible first-stage retrieval research (Castorini group, University of Waterloo; 2,171 stars, 57 releases, v2.4.0 in August 2026): sparse retrieval (Lucene BM25 plus learned sparse models) via Anserini, dense retrieval via Faiss, and hybrid sparse-dense fusion, shipped as a standard Python package with queries, relevance judgments, evaluation scripts, and prebuilt indexes whose MD5 checksums are printed in the README. Its reproducibility discipline is the real strength — published reproduction matrices per corpus (experimental condition x query set) and 'two-click reproductions' of published runs — and it now also exposes a REST API and an MCP server.
bad: The stack is heavy exactly as the Tier-1 study recorded: it requires Java 21 (via Anserini/Lucene) and Python 3.12, a pip install pulls in PyTorch, Transformers and ONNX Runtime, and the right Faiss variant (cpu/gpu) must be installed by hand because it is deliberately not a declared dependency. It is oriented to public IR test collections (MS MARCO, BEIR, Mr.TyDi) and their multi-GB prebuilt indexes, not to a personal corpus, and it is a first-stage retriever only — no citation, custody, or answer layer.
took: The reproducibility practices only: checksum the projection the benchmark ran against, and publish a condition × metric matrix whenever the search recipe changes. Verdict recorded: "PROMISING — copy the reproducibility practices; do not adopt the stack."
didnt: Rejected — the stack itself, aligning with the Tier-1 'Pyserini' study of the same repo (second-name form): Java/Lucene + PyTorch is far too heavy for our pipeline, and a benchmark-first-stage retriever for public test collections is not a component our local-first wiki lacks; what that study took (the reproducibility practices, carried verbatim in took) remains the programme's only take from Pyserini (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy
good: The leading open-source Notion alternative at real scale (77,636 stars, 152 releases): documents, wikis, databases and Kanban project tracking plus AI in one cross-platform Flutter/Rust workspace, self-hostable, built on the stated mission of 100% user control of data with native performance.
bad: It is a multi-writer team collaboration workspace — the shape our single-writer design rejects — with custody inside the app's own workspace rather than a plain-file git corpus, and no citation locking, claim tracking or abstention machinery; AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 (ideas only) and scope: a collaborative team workspace, not personal knowledge-OS infrastructure (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: laurent22/joplin
licence: AGPL-3.0-or-later (root LICENSE file, opened directly; the GitHub metadata card reads Other/NOASSERTION because directories carrying their own LICENSE file — e.g. packages/server — override the default)
good: Offline-first Markdown notes on every platform with end-to-end-encrypted sync (Nextcloud, Dropbox, OneDrive or Joplin Cloud), Evernote import preserving formatted content, resources and full metadata, full-text search, a plugin system and a web clipper — a very mature project (56,828 stars, 423 releases since 2017).
bad: A personal notes application: notes live in the app's own database/sync model rather than an owner-greppable plain-file corpus, and there is no citation, claim, verification or agent machinery; AGPL-3.0-or-later makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline.
took: Listed as the Note Overview pattern in Live queries harvest.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0-or-later (ideas only) and scope: a notes app, not corpus infrastructure; this pass settles at the LICENSE file the licence the Tier 1 record left unverified (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: logseq/logseq
good: Privacy-first, local-first knowledge management on plain Markdown/Org files: an outliner with a graph model over files, PDF annotation, task management, queries and a plugin API, at large scale (45,326 stars) with longevity and user control as stated values.
bad: The new Database version is in beta with the README itself warning that 'data loss is possible', and it moves graphs toward a SQLite database plus real-time collaboration (RTC, in alpha) — away from the plain-file single-writer model; there is no citation locking or abstention, and AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only.
didnt: Corroboration — its file-based outliner graph corroborates our plain-file substrate, while its DB/RTC direction is the path we decline; code AGPL, not taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lfnovo/open-notebook
good: A full-featured, genuinely self-hosted NotebookLM alternative: 20+ model providers including local Ollama, multimodal sources (PDF, video, audio, web pages, Office documents), full-text and vector search, answers that cite the sources, notes and insights they used, fine-grained control over exactly what context each chat sees, a complete REST API, and multi-speaker podcast generation — at serious scale (40,438 stars) under MIT.
bad: Custody is a SurrealDB database behind a Docker stack, not a plain-file git corpus, and the product shape is a NotebookLM-style research Q&A surface — sources in, chat and podcasts out — with no claim tracking, no citation locking and no approval-gated writes. By default the UI and API publish on all network interfaces with no password set, a deployment footgun the README itself has to warn about. The catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is corroborated by no lane-8 record and is not repeated.
didnt: Rejected — a database-custodied research notebook duplicating a Q&A surface we deliberately do not build; nothing in its architecture serves the file corpus (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: streetwriters/notesnook
good: Fully open-source, zero-knowledge note-taking: everything is encrypted on the device with XChaCha20-Poly1305 and Argon2, across web, desktop and mobile clients plus a web clipper, with self-hostable sync and a public page for verifying the encryption claims yourself; mature at 14,808 stars and 398 releases.
bad: A consumer notes app whose encrypted-at-rest custody makes the corpus opaque to a citation/verification pipeline that must read what it cites; no claim, citation or abstention machinery; GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 (ideas only) and scope: an encrypted notes app whose custody model hides the corpus from verification tooling; the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict is corroborated by no lane-8 record and is not repeated (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: xwmx/nb
good: Plain-text note-taking, bookmarking and archiving in a single portable script: notes as files with [[links]], nested tags, full search, Pandoc conversion and optional password-encrypted notes — and notebooks are Git repositories, with versioning, sync, revision history and documented sync-conflict handling, plus published file-format specifications for bookmarks and todos (8,453 stars, developed since 2016).
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline; it is a personal CLI notebook with no ingest pipeline, citation/claim machinery or agent surface, and the single-script Bash architecture is a deliberate constraint rather than a platform.
took: Ideas only: the bookmark/todo file-format specs as a model for making the wiki's own capture formats explicit and tool-agnostic.

name: glushchenko/fsnotes

A long-lived project (342 releases since 2017) under MIT.

name: jrnl-org/jrnl
licence: GPL-3.0 (search-rendered: the LinuxLinks jrnl listing states GNU General Public License v3.0; the Tier 1 record had the exact licence unconfirmed and treated it as ideas only)
good: One-command, natural-language journaling from the terminal into plain-text files the site promises will 'still be readable in 50 years', with AES-encrypted journals, several journals for different parts of life, and sync through ordinary file tools such as Dropbox rather than a proprietary cloud.
bad: A personal journal CLI: entries are diary text, not a linked or cited corpus, and there is no verification, claim or agent machinery; GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline.

name: massCodeIO/massCode
licence: AGPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE / GitHub sidebar; README License section agrees)
good: The vault design is sound: snippets, notes and HTTP requests all live as plain Markdown files with frontmatter — git-friendly, syncable through any file channel, and watched for external changes in real time. Around it sits a broad, mature app: a multi-language snippet library, a full HTTP/GraphQL/WebSocket client, a notes graph and mindmaps, preview-first imports, an MCP server whose writes protect against overwriting newer changes, and an AI assistant that can preview edits before applying them and undo changes that support it.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline. And the centre of gravity is a developer's snippet-and-API workbench — notes are one module among five — with no citation, claim or verification machinery; the catalogue's description of it as a snippet manager is dated, but its NOT FOR US verdict stands for our corpus.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 (ideas only) and scope: a developer workspace whose notes module is not corpus infrastructure (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: codexu/note-gen
licence: GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE / GitHub sidebar; README License section agrees)
good: The capture model is genuinely thoughtful: everything (text, voice, screenshots, links, files, todos) lands first as unorganised records, and only records the user selects are AI-organised into structured notes that stay plain Markdown files on disk. Sync is unusually well engineered for its class — multi-backend (GitHub, Gitee, GitLab, Gitea, S3, WebDAV) with a push queue, remote-version checks and explicit conflict handling rather than silent overwrites — and the app is large and active (12,905 stars, 168 releases), with RAG chat and MCP support.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline. The organising step is LLM restructuring of the user's records with no citation discipline — nothing ties a generated note back to the records it came from — and write access runs both ways (sync pushes, an MCP surface) without an approval gate. The catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict stands.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 (ideas only), and its AI organisation has no provenance or citation machinery to adopt; the catalogue verdict agreed (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: laverna/laverna
good: A web-based Markdown note app with secure client-side encryption (SJCL/AES), offline use with no registration, three editing modes, and synchronisation via Dropbox or RemoteStorage; 9,166 stars.
bad: Custody is browser databases (indexedDB/localStorage), not plain files; the stack is dated (Marionette/Bower/Gulp-era) and the catalogue's own signal — last update May 2021 — shows the project unmaintained; MPL-2.0 is ideas-only under our licence discipline.
didnt: Rejected — MPL-2.0 (ideas only), unmaintained, and browser-database custody instead of plain files; agrees with the standing master row 'Laverna' (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: foambubble/foam
licence: MIT (README License section: 'Foam is licensed under the MIT license'; the GitHub metadata card reads Other/NOASSERTION)
good: Personal knowledge management as a VS Code extension over plain Markdown files in a Git repository you own: wikilinks with autocompletion that sync on file rename, note sections and embeds, backlinks, tag, orphans and placeholder panels, a graph view, templates and daily notes, and generated Markdown references so notes stay navigable on GitHub itself; 17,461 stars.
bad: The README itself demands a 'high tolerance for alpha-grade software' — Foam is still a work in progress whose features 'might break' — and it is an editor layer only, bound to VS Code, with no ingest pipeline, citation locking or abstention machinery.

bad: A distributed OLAP platform — frontends, backends, streaming ingestion, cluster operations — built for customer-facing analytics at data-warehouse scale; operating it is a data-platform commitment orders of magnitude beyond a personal file corpus's retrieval needs, and none of it is knowledge-OS machinery.

name: tensorchord/VectorChord

good: PostgreSQL-native vector search engineered for cost: RaBitQ 4/8-bit quantization with autonomous reranking (the README claims <1% recall loss at RaBitQ8), full pgvector type/syntax compatibility, and very fast index builds, with vendor figures of 100M vectors hosted on a single small instance.
bad: Billion-scale database engineering for a problem our corpus does not have: it requires running PostgreSQL with a native extension, its headline numbers are the vendor's own cost comparisons, and the dual AGPLv3/ELv2 licensing makes the code ideas-only under our discipline.

name: huggingface/transformers
good: The model-definition framework for state-of-the-art ML: one agreed definition for hundreds of architectures across text, vision, audio and multimodal models, compatible with the major training frameworks and inference engines, over a million pretrained checkpoints on the Hub, and a simple three-class Pipeline API (167,960 stars).
bad: A heavyweight ML library (Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.6+), not knowledge-system software: the README itself warns it 'is not a modular toolbox of building blocks for neural nets' and that its training API is optimised for its own PyTorch models only.
didnt: Corroboration — Transformers is the standard model layer that local embedding/inference work across this survey presupposes; nothing in it is wiki machinery to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: markedjs/marked
licence: MIT — repo metadata reads Other (NOASSERTION); settled from the README License section, which states MIT under both the MarkedJS (2018+) and original Christopher Jeffrey (2011-2018) copyright lines, with a LICENSE file at root
good: A fast, low-level Markdown parser and compiler implementing the CommonMark/GFM flavours, easily adaptable with custom extensions, running in the browser, on a server, or from a CLI — 37,254 stars, 3,885 commits, 185 releases.
bad: The README itself warns that Marked does not sanitize the output HTML, so every consumer must bolt on a sanitizer (DOMPurify, sanitize-html or insane) against XSS; only current and LTS Node.js versions are supported. It is a plain parser — no citation, provenance or validation machinery.
didnt: Rejected — a commodity Markdown parser; our publishing pipeline renders through its own pinned renderer with its divergences recorded, and Marked offers no citation locking, abstention or evidence machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docsifyjs/docsify
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: Turns one or more Markdown files into a documentation website with no build process required: simple and lightweight runtime rendering with a smart full-text search plugin, multiple themes and a useful plugin API — 31,553 stars, maintained since 2016.
bad: There are deliberately no statically built HTML files — pages render at runtime in the visitor's browser, so nothing is validated at build time and rendering/search depend on client-side JavaScript and CDN availability. Runtime rendering is the opposite of a build-time checked, static publishing model.
didnt: Rejected — runtime-rendered docs conflict with our build-time validated, static, citation-locked publishing model; the catalogue's FOR-US note reached only for the no-build render idea, and runtime rendering is precisely what our model refuses. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: truera/trulens
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: Evaluation and tracking for LLM experiments and AI agents: OpenTelemetry-native tracing records latency, inputs, outputs, tokens and cost per step; LLM-judge feedback functions include the RAG Triad (context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance) plus seven purpose-built agentic evaluators, and the judges are themselves graded against human annotations (groundedness F1 0.81 on LLM-AggreFact, as reported in the README).

didnt: Corroboration — the context-relevance / groundedness / answer-relevance triad independently confirms the three-legged scoring shape of our own retrieval evaluation, while our scored abstention and citation locking go further than LLM-judge scores. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

bad: Its scope is building and versioning cloud infrastructure — nothing to do with knowledge management — and this repo is Terraform core only, providers living elsewhere. name: AykutSarac/jsoncrack.com

bad: It renders data documents, not sourced knowledge: the graph is a document tree, large inputs run into a configurable node limit (NEXT_PUBLIC_NODE_LIMIT), and the project's commercial energy goes to its ToDiagram sibling. There is no provenance, citation or persistence model.

name: xyflow/xyflow
licence: MIT (repo metadata, root LICENSE file and README License section agree)
good: React Flow and Svelte Flow: powerful, mature libraries for building node-based UIs with React or Svelte — custom nodes and edges, minimap, controls and background components, state hooks, ready out of the box and deeply customisable (38,740 stars, 395 releases).
bad: A pure UI layer: it renders and edits node diagrams but supplies no graph semantics, no knowledge-graph layout intelligence, no provenance and no persistence. Its maintenance is sponsorship-funded, with commercial users steered to the paid React Flow Pro offering.

name: grobidOrg/grobid
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: Production-grade machine-learning extraction from scholarly PDFs into structured XML/TEI: header metadata, reference extraction and parsing (around .87 F1 on an independent PubMed Central set, around .90 on bioRxiv, as reported), citation-context recognition and resolution (.76–.91 F1), full-text structuring with PDF coordinates, and consolidation of extracted references against CrossRef/biblio-glutton (above 0.95 F1, as reported) — deployed by Semantic Scholar, ResearchGate, HAL and others, with Docker images and Python/Java/Node clients.
