name: chroma-core/chroma
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: Open-source search infrastructure for AI: an embeddable vector database whose core API is four functions, handling tokenisation, embedding and indexing automatically, with metadata and document filtering, in-memory prototyping or persistent local deployment, and a Rust core — 29,545 stars.
bad: Similarity search only: no citation binding, supersession or abstention semantics, and adopting it makes a database the truth store next to the files. Releases churn weekly and the vendor's visible energy is split toward the hosted Chroma Cloud service.
didnt: Rejected — a vector store duplicates the embedding retrieval our stack already covers and would tie the wiki's custody to a database we do not run; the separate chroma-mcp server was rejected on the same ground in its own row. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cytoscape/cytoscape.js
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: A fully featured graph-theory library: a headless graph model with analysis algorithms plus an optional interactive renderer, usable server-side in Node.js or in a rich browser UI, with a large extension ecosystem and an academic maintenance record running since 2011 (11,249 stars, 175 releases; Bioinformatics papers in 2016 and 2023).
bad: Visualisation and analysis only: it defines no provenance, citation or persistence semantics, so every piece of knowledge meaning must be built on top of it. The default development branch is literally named 'unstable', with feature releases monthly and patches weekly.
didnt: Board — a candidate graph library for Lens relation views: its headless model fits our build-time static pipeline (analysis at build time, rendering in the page) better than editor-first libraries. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: University of Toronto (created there, per the README; Bader Lab)

name: KnowledgeXLab/RAKG
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: A document-level retrieval-augmented knowledge graph construction framework: documents are segmented and vectorised, preliminary entities extracted and disambiguated, then Corpus Retrospective Retrieval and Graph Structure Retrieval feed an LLM that builds relation networks per entity and merges them into the graph — with LLM, MINE and Ideal-KG evaluation suites and a 2025 paper.
bad: A research prototype: 13 commits and no releases, expecting a 72B-class main model (Qwen2.5-72B in its own configuration). The newly built graph is merged automatically — extracted triples carry no per-triple source citation and pass no human approval gate.
didnt: Rejected — automatic LLM graph construction without source-locked provenance or approval gates contradicts our ingest discipline, and the prototype's maturity (13 commits, no releases) offers nothing solid to build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Nankai University (contact address in the README; arXiv:2504.09823)

name: tomasonjo/diffbot-kg-chatbot
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: A compact end-to-end reference pipeline: news articles are extracted into a Neo4j knowledge graph via Diffbot (news retrieval, graph extraction from text, entity enrichment), analysed through visualisations, and questioned through an LLM chat interface — the whole demo in 97 commits with a docker-compose setup.
bad: A demo, not a product (no releases): extraction is a commercial black-box API (Diffbot), storage is Neo4j and chat is OpenAI, so custody and correctness sit with three vendors, and no step verifies an extracted fact back against its source text.
didnt: Rejected — a vendor-dependent demo; our ingest keeps extraction inside our own governed pipeline with the sources preserved on disk. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: SDM-TIB/SDM-RDFizer
licence: Apache-2.0 (repo metadata, root LICENSE file and README License section agree)
good: An interpreter of declarative RML mapping rules that transforms heterogeneous data (CSV, JSON, RDB, XML) into RDF knowledge graphs, with optimised data structures and a TriplesMap planning module; its published evaluations complete testbeds where RMLMapper and RocketRML time out, and it has built knowledge graphs at billion-triple scale in EU H2020 projects (iASiS: 1.2B triples from 40+ sources) — 170 releases since 2018.
bad: It belongs to the RDF/SPARQL world: every source needs hand-authored RML mappings and the output is a triple store, not sourced, human-readable pages; nothing in the engine checks a generated triple back against a citable source passage.
didnt: Corroboration — its mapping-rules-as-checked-artefacts approach independently confirms our design choice that ingest transforms are explicit, reviewable rules rather than model improvisation; the engine itself is not adopted (RDF stack mismatch). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: TIB — Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology (Scientific Data Management Group)

name: zjunlp/Generative_KG_Construction_Papers
licence: MIT (repo metadata and root LICENSE file agree)
good: The companion repository to the EMNLP 2022 review 'Generative Knowledge Graph Construction: A Review': a detailed taxonomy of generative KGC methods in five paradigms (copy-based, structure-linearized, label-based, indice-based, blank-based sequences) with the advantages and weaknesses of each, plus a survey-paper list and a timeline of the field.
bad: A bibliography, not software: there is no code, test suite or evaluation harness to run, and the survey freezes the field at 2022 — before LLM-agent extraction practice — so its map no longer covers the methods that matter now.
didnt: Rejected — a reading list; useful as literature orientation only, with nothing buildable, and its coverage is superseded by our own deep-study register. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Zhejiang University (NLP lab, zjunlp; review authors Ye, Zhang, Chen & Chen)

name: dstlry/dstlr
licence: no licence stated at source — no LICENSE file in the root listing and no licence statement in the README, so the code is all-rights-reserved by default and ideas-only
good: An end-to-end platform for scalable knowledge graph construction from unstructured text (Spark/CoreNLP): mention and relation extraction, linking to Wikidata entities, and enrichment with Wikidata facts — its demo distils ~600K Washington Post documents into ~97M triples — and its data-cleaning queries align extracted relations against Wikidata ground truth to surface supporting, inconsistent and missing information.
bad: Archived and unmaintained on a 2019 stack (the README itself documents a Spark/CoreNLP protobuf-jar workaround), it carries no licence at all, and running it needs a Spark cluster, SolrCloud and Neo4j.
didnt: Board — the supporting / inconsistent / missing-fact alignment queries are a design pattern for our contradiction and reverify machinery (check extracted claims against a ground truth and queue the mismatches); the code itself is ideas-only (no licence, archived). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: peng-gao-lab/ctinexus
licence: MIT (repo metadata, LICENSE.txt and README License section agree)
good: A framework for automatic cyber threat intelligence knowledge graph construction using optimised in-context learning: entity and relationship extraction from unstructured CTI text with minimal training data, hierarchical entity alignment (typing plus merging with IOC protection), link prediction, and interactive graph visualisation — packaged as a pip library, CLI, Gradio web UI and Docker image, with a Euro S&P 2025 paper behind it.
bad: Domain-locked to cyber threat intelligence, and its link-prediction stage predicts and adds missing relationships into the same graph as the extracted ones, so model-inferred edges are not kept visibly separate from sourced facts; extraction quality rests entirely on whichever LLM provider the user plugs in.
didnt: Rejected — out of domain (cyber threat intelligence), and writing predicted links into the graph as facts breaks our extracted-vs-inferred separation, under which inferred material stays labelled and is never silently promoted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Virginia Tech (Peng Gao Lab; author addresses in the README)

name: awslabs/unified-kg-rag-on-aws
good: AWS-native knowledge-graph RAG framework reimplementing Microsoft GraphRAG community summarization and LightRAG dual-level keyword search on one shared stack (Bedrock, Neptune, OpenSearch); triple-hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector + graph traversal fused with RRF and a Bedrock reranker); incremental indexing via a document-status registry; multilingual support; every answer returns the sources actually placed in the model's context; prompt tuning, RAGAS-style evaluation and graph visualization included; a local mode exists (embedded SQLite stores, Ollama).
bad: Hard AWS coupling — the CDK stack (Bedrock/Neptune/OpenSearch) bills hourly and custody sits in cloud services; the README's own Security & Disclaimer section calls it a reference framework provided for educational and illustrative purposes that should not be deployed to a production environment without additional security testing; local mode is dev/eval only (~100,000 documents per index, container stores with no authentication or TLS, small local models extract weaker graphs); brand-new project (created July 2026), 36 stars, no releases.
didnt: Rejected — cloud-service custody and hourly-billed infrastructure are the opposite of our local-first, owner-visible design, and the GraphRAG/LightRAG methodology ideas were already taken into our system through the lane-8 GraphRAG build (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Hastur-HP/The-Brain
good: Multimodal RAG dashboard with an interactive 3D knowledge graph built on LightRAG/RAG-Anything with Neo4j and NanoVectorDB; MinerU parsing handles PDF layout, OCR, tables and equations; can run fully offline via Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible API; the live query log shows which graph entities and chunks the model retrieved; pause-queue and failed-upload tracking.
bad: Very young single-author project (31 commits, 33 stars, created March 2026); heavy Docker stack (Neo4j 5 + APOC, host networking) plus large model downloads (the reranker is auto-downloaded at first start); no citation locking, abstention scoring, or approval-gated writes anywhere in the README; graph data lives in Docker volumes/Neo4j rather than owner-visible files.
didnt: Rejected — an immature presentation layer over LightRAG; its value is dashboard display, not the provenance machinery (citation locking, scored abstention, approval-gated writes) our system is built around (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nashsu/llm_wiki
licence: GPL-3.0 (root LICENSE file is the full GPL v3 text, 'LLM Wiki — Copyright (C) 2024-2026 Yong Su'; the README License section agrees; GitHub's metadata card reads Other/NOASSERTION, settled by opening the licence file itself)
good: Cross-platform desktop implementation of Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern: three-layer raw → wiki → schema structure with index.md/log.md, [[wikilinks]] and YAML frontmatter, Obsidian-compatible; two-step chain-of-thought ingest with sources: [] traceability in frontmatter and a SHA256 incremental cache; purpose.md; a 4-signal knowledge-graph relevance model with Louvain community detection and graph insights; an async human-in-the-loop Review system; a local HTTP API at 127.0.0.1:19828 (token-protected) plus a bundled MCP server and an agent skill; source-folder auto-watch; Deep Research via Tavily/SerpApi/SearXNG.
bad: GPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us; the LLM builds and maintains the wiki automatically behind a review queue, whereas our design is approval-gated writes with a citation lockfile and scored abstention — neither a citation lockfile nor abstention scoring appears in its README; custody sits inside the desktop app's own project format (.llm-wiki/ state) rather than a plain owner-controlled tree.
didnt: Corroboration — a popular independent implementation (20,865 stars) of the same Karpathy pattern confirms the persistent compiled-wiki design, purpose.md and review-queue ideas our system is built on; the code is GPL-3.0 so it is ideas-only, and our custody, citation-locking and abstention machinery go beyond it (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: olivernn/lunr.js
good: Tiny client-side full-text search library for the browser: indexes JSON documents and returns scored results with match metadata, works fully offline with no server or network; full-text search for 14 languages, query-time and index-time boosting, field-scoped search, fuzzy matching with wildcards and edit distance.
bad: Lexical only — no vector or semantic search; maintenance visibly stale (the README build badge points at the defunct travis-ci.org; the catalogue topic listing was last updated Jul 31 2024); the index lives in page memory or serialized JSON with no persistence or incremental-update story of its own.
didnt: Corroboration — a small embeddable in-browser lexical engine over a static corpus is the same shape our static Lens search uses; it confirms the approach without offering anything our current search lacks (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: unum-cloud/USearch
good: Single-header C++11 HNSW similarity-search engine with native bindings for 10+ languages (Python, JS, Rust, Go, Swift, C#, Java and more); user-defined metrics with JIT compilation; half- and quarter-precision dtypes; indexes can be viewed and served from disk without loading into RAM; filtering predicates during traversal; used inside ClickHouse and DuckDB per its README; BENCHMARKS.md and CITATION.cff in tree.
bad: A low-level ANN component, not a knowledge system — no text pipeline, citations, or governance; its headline '10x faster than FAISS' figures are the vendor's own benchmarks; at personal-wiki corpus scale its performance engineering is unnecessary.
didnt: Board — a candidate embeddable ANN layer if our retrieval ever adds a vector stage: permissively licensed, disk-servable and language-portable, so it can be evaluated then without redesign (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: teamtnt/tntsearch
good: Fully-featured full-text search engine written entirely in PHP; the index is stored in SQLite (default), MySQL or Redis and can be updated on the fly without reindexing; BM25/TF-IDF ranking, boolean, fuzzy and prefix (search-as-you-type) modes, stemming for many languages, custom tokenizers, highlighting/snippets, geo search and text classification; Laravel Scout integration.
bad: PHP stack — nothing else in our system is PHP; lexical only; search() returns document IDs rather than documents, so the caller must fetch the rows and preserve order itself; stemmer and tokenizer choices are baked in at index time.
didnt: Rejected — wrong stack and wrong layer: a server-side PHP search engine for web applications, while our lexical-search needs are already met inside our own tooling (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: seekstorm/seekstorm
good: Rust search engine offered as both an in-process library and a multi-tenancy server; native hybrid search — a BM25F/BM25F_Proximity inverted index plus IVF ANN behind one query planner, fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, with field filters active during vector search; embedded Model2Vec inference or bring-your-own embeddings; true real-time indexing (documents searchable before commit); the same binary index is portable across library, server and cloud; ships a stdio MCP server that embeds the engine directly (no server process or network needed) exposing lexical, vector and hybrid search plus indexing tools.
bad: Single-author bootstrapped project (Wolf Garbe; 'Independent & bootstrapped, no VC' per the README); all latency claims (e.g. 306 µs average lexical latency, 8x lower than Lucene) are the author's own benchmarks; designed for billion-scale corpora far beyond a personal wiki; a search component, not a knowledge layer — no citations, abstention, or write governance.
didnt: Board — the stdio-MCP-embedded hybrid engine is a candidate pattern for a future vector/hybrid stage of our read door; the engine itself is not needed at our corpus scale (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: asg017/sqlite-vec
licence: Apache-2.0 OR MIT (dual-licensed as found: the repository root carries both LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT; the GitHub metadata card reads Apache-2.0; the catalogue line likewise said 'Apache-2.0 / MIT' — recorded as found, neither side suppressed)
good: Extremely small pure-C SQLite extension with no dependencies that runs anywhere SQLite runs, including the browser via WASM; vec0 virtual tables store float, int8 and binary vectors with metadata, auxiliary and partition-key columns; KNN queries written in plain SQL; bindings and packages for Python, Node, Ruby, Go, Rust, Datasette and sqlite-utils; sponsored as a Mozilla Builders project (plus Fly.io, Turso, SQLite Cloud, Shinkai).
bad: The README states plainly that sqlite-vec is pre-v1, so breaking changes are expected; positioned as 'fast enough' small-scale search — the headline design is brute-force-class at small scale; a storage component only, with no retrieval governance, citations, or abstention.
didnt: Board — the leading candidate for a local vector stage inside our existing SQLite-shaped tooling if Ask/Lens retrieval adds embeddings: embeddable, dependency-free and local-first, matching the catalogue's FOR US verdict (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: firecrawl/firecrawl
good: Web data API for AI agents: Search, Scrape and Interact endpoints plus Parse, Agent, Crawl, Map, Batch Scrape and Monitor; LLM-ready output (clean Markdown, structured JSON, screenshots); handles rotating proxies and JS-heavy pages (vendor claims 96% web coverage at P95 3.4s); SDKs for Python, Node, Go, Java, Elixir, Rust, Ruby, .NET and PHP; an MCP server (firecrawl-mcp); a SELF_HOST.md self-hosting route exists.
bad: AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us; the product's primary route is the hosted, metered service at firecrawl.dev gated by an API key — the MCP server likewise requires FIRECRAWL_API_KEY — which is the opposite custody shape from our local-first design; the reliability claims rest on the hosted proxy/orchestration layer, not on anything the self-hosted code guarantees; the README contains an 'Agent Onboarding' section instructing AI agents to fetch a skill file in order to sign up their user and obtain an API key — an embedded sign-up funnel, recorded here as evidence and not followed.
didnt: Rejected — AGPL-3.0 code is ideas-only, and a hosted API-key extraction service contradicts local-first custody; our ingest fetches sources directly, matching the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docling-project/docling
licence: MIT (codebase; the README License section notes that individual models carry the licences found in their original packages)
good: Deep document parsing for generative AI: many formats (PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML, EPUB, Apple Pages/Numbers/Keynote, email EML/MSG, images, LaTeX, plain text, audio and video with ASR, ODF, XBRL, JATS/USPTO XML) with advanced PDF understanding — page layout, reading order, table structure, code, formulas, image classification; a unified, expressive DoclingDocument representation with exports to Markdown, HTML, WebVTT, DocLang, DocTags and lossless JSON; extensive OCR and Visual Language Model support (e.g. GraniteDocling); local execution for sensitive data and air-gapped environments; CLI, Python API, an MCP server and a docling-serve API server; integrations for LangChain, LlamaIndex, Crew AI and Haystack; a published technical report (arXiv 2408.09869).
bad: A heavy ML pipeline — the bundled models carry their own licences, which the README's License section says must be checked in the original packages; metadata extraction (title, authors, references, language) is still listed under 'Coming soon'; it is a parser, not a knowledge system: no retrieval governance, citation locking, or abstention.
took: Structured ingest — built in Round 3, lane TB7 — source/inspiration: Docling
didnt: Corroboration — the lane-8 record already credits Docling as source/inspiration for our built Round 3 structured-ingest item (lane TB7), and this firsthand study confirms that choice: MIT-licensed, locally runnable, structure-preserving parsing; the parser itself remains a candidate component for the document/OCR queue rather than something to rebuild (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: IBM Research Zurich (project origin, per the README); hosted as a project in the LF AI & Data Foundation

name: Textualize/rich
good: Mature Python library for terminal output: styled text, tables, progress bars, trees, columns, syntax highlighting, readable tracebacks, a logging handler, an inspect function and Markdown rendering to the terminal, all out of the box; works on Linux, macOS and Windows and inside Jupyter notebooks.
bad: Purely presentational — no knowledge, retrieval, citation, or storage function of any kind; true colour and emoji degrade on classic terminals (16 colours, per its own Compatibility section); terminal chrome is not a surface our system ships — our outputs are the Lens portal and generated artefacts.
didnt: Rejected — a presentation-only library; nothing in it serves the knowledge layer, matching the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: prettier/prettier
good: The standard opinionated code formatter: parses code and re-prints it under its own rules (maximum line length, wrapping when necessary) for JavaScript, TypeScript, Flow, JSX, JSON, CSS/SCSS/Less, HTML, Vue, Angular, GraphQL, Markdown and YAML; runs in editors on save, in pre-commit hooks, and in CI environments, removing style disputes mechanically.
bad: It formats code style, not knowledge; for Markdown its wholesale re-printing would fight our wiki's own conventions — YAML frontmatter, citation markers and [[wikilinks]] are semantic conventions a generic formatter does not know — and a tool that rewrites files wholesale is the opposite of our diff-disciplined, approval-gated editing.
didnt: Rejected — a code-style formatter has no role in a knowledge system whose files are edited under citation and approval discipline, matching the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jekyll/jekyll
good: The canonical blog-aware static site generator (Ruby, since 2008; the engine behind GitHub Pages): takes Markdown content plus Liquid templates and YAML front matter and emits a complete static website with no database — a file-based CMS whose stated philosophy is 'Jekyll does what you tell it to do — no more, no less'; plugin system, permalink control and a large theme ecosystem.
bad: Ruby stack, which nothing else in our system uses; a site generator, not a knowledge system — no retrieval, citation, or write governance; our Lens is already a purpose-built static portal over the wiki, so adopting Jekyll would replace working machinery with a generic blog engine.
didnt: Corroboration — seventeen years of production use prove that plain Markdown files with YAML front matter compile into a durable static site, the same bet our Lens makes; nothing to adopt (Ruby stack, and our renderer already exists), matching the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict in substance (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jgm/pandoc
licence: GPL-2.0-or-later (repository metadata card: GPL-2.0; README License section: 'Released under the GPL, version 2 or greater', © 2006-2024 John MacFarlane)
good: The universal markup converter (Haskell library plus command-line tool): roughly 60 input formats and 80 output formats — Markdown dialects (CommonMark, GFM, Pandoc's Markdown), docx, EPUB, LaTeX, HTML, JATS, MediaWiki, Org, Typst and more — through a modular reader/AST/writer architecture with Lua filters and custom readers and writers; built-in citation processing (BibTeX, BibLaTeX, CSL JSON inputs); PDF output via LaTeX, Groff ms, or HTML.
bad: GPL-2.0-or-later makes the code ideas-only for us; conversions are lossy by design — the README warns its intermediate representation is less expressive than many of the formats it converts between, so formatting details are not preserved and complex tables may not fit its simple document model; a Haskell toolchain is a heavy dependency for a conversion utility.
didnt: Rejected — GPL licensing bars code adoption, and our conversion needs are covered by the boarded MIT-licensed options (markitdown, Docling) whose terms permit adoption; pandoc's reader/writer AST architecture remains a useful reference idea only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kg-construct/awesome-kgc-tools
good: A curated taxonomy of knowledge-graph-construction tooling: RML/R2RML materializers (Morph-KGC, RMLMapper, SDM-RDFizer), virtual knowledge-graph access (Ontop), mapping specifications, editors and translators, end-to-end pipelines, and KGC evaluation benchmarks (KROWN, GTFS-Madrid-Bench). As a map of the declarative-mapping corner of the KG world it is well organised.
bad: The repository is a link list only — its root holds a single README.md, with no code, no tests and no releases of its own. Its scope is RDF/RML-centric, and no licence is stated at source, so even the list text is reuse-restricted by default.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a catalogue of RDF mapping tools is a reference list, not a component; nothing in it serves a files-as-truth personal wiki, and with no licence stated it is ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: seukgcode/MELBench
good: Three documented multimodal entity-linking datasets — Weibo-MEL (25,602 samples), Wikidata-MEL (18,880) and Richpedia-MEL (17,806) — built through a documented five-stage construction pipeline, with baseline experiments showing the three datasets are distinguishable in difficulty. A clean, citable benchmark artefact.
bad: A dataset-only research artefact of 2021 vintage (12 commits, a single release): the repository carries code and documentation, while the bulk visual and knowledge-graph resources live off-repo on Baidu Cloud Disk, so the repo alone is not self-contained.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a social-media/encyclopedia multimodal entity-linking benchmark measures a capability our citation-locked, text-corpus wiki does not perform; no fit despite the clean MIT licence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Wings-Of-Disaster/VaLiK
good: An annotation-free multimodal knowledge-graph construction pipeline: a VLM converts images to text (Chain-of-Evidence style), cross-modal similarity verification prunes bad extractions, and a LightRAG-based stage builds the graph. The README reports state-of-the-art gains on CrisisMMD classification and ScienceQA (Qwen2.5-72B enhanced) with a compact 489 MB graph store.
bad: Paper-companion research code — 25 commits, no releases — that recommends 32B–72B vision-language models, far beyond our local scale. No licence is stated at source, so the code is ideas-only regardless of fit.
didnt: Rejected — scope and licence: automatic multimodal KG construction from images is outside our text-corpus wiki's work, the compute expectations overshoot our hardware, and the unlicensed code cannot be adapted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ItzCrazyKns/Vane
good: A privacy-focused, self-hosted AI answering engine (the former Perplexica): SearXNG web search with cited sources, local Ollama or cloud LLMs, Speed/Balanced/Quality search modes, file uploads, domain-limited search, locally kept search history, a developer API, and one-command Docker deployment with SearXNG bundled. Mature and very widely adopted.
bad: Its answers cite live web results, not a locked personal corpus: there is no scored abstention when evidence is thin and no approval-gated write path into a durable store. Authentication is still listed as an upcoming feature in its own README.
didnt: Corroboration — cited, self-hosted answering over retrieved sources is the mainstream expectation, and Vane is its most popular open form; our differentiator is exactly what it lacks — a locked corpus with a citation lockfile, scored abstention and approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: lancedb/lancedb
good: An embedded, in-process vector database on the Lance columnar format: vector, full-text and SQL search over multimodal data in one local library, with zero-copy automatic dataset versioning and Python/TypeScript/Rust SDKs — no server to deploy or operate.
bad: The store of record is still a binary columnar dataset rather than owner-readable plain files, and the framing targets petabyte-scale ML workloads. Its versioning versions datasets, not claims — there is no supersession semantics for a corpus whose newer pages override older ones.
didnt: Board — the embedded, file-resident, automatically versioned index is the right shape for a dense-vector layer beside (never instead of) the plain-file index; board for a trial alongside the other retrieval candidates. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: goniszewski/grimoire
good: A local-first bookmark manager with serious custody engineering: content extraction for pages, PDFs, GitHub repos and YouTube transcripts; SQLite FTS5 plus semantic and hybrid search; a durable job queue where a failed pipeline step keeps the bookmark usable with retry controls; a loopback-only daemon (127.0.0.1) with public exposure explicitly unsupported; MCP capture endpoints requiring bearer tokens; and checksummed encrypted backups whose restores verify checksums and keep pre-restore rollback copies.
bad: Its store of record is a SQLite database, not owner-readable plain files. The optional AI enrichment (summary, tags, category) runs automatically inside the ingest pipeline rather than behind an approval gate, and the scope is bookmarks only.
didnt: Corroboration — local-first custody, a token-gated capture door, verify-before-restore backups and failure-tolerant ingest queues are our own design patterns confirmed in the wild; the divergence is its database-as-truth store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: uptrain-ai/uptrain
good: An open-source LLM-application evaluation toolkit with 20+ preconfigured checks — factual accuracy, context relevance/utilization/conciseness, response completeness, code hallucination, prompt-injection and jailbreak detection, plus custom guideline and prompt-based evaluators — with root-cause analysis on failures. Evaluations run locally and results stay in a locally hosted dashboard; data leaves the machine only for the LLM grading calls themselves.
bad: The grading is itself LLM-judged — an LLM scores factual accuracy — so there is no deterministic or citation-locked verdict behind the numbers. It is aimed at production LLM applications, and its dashboard is still labelled Beta in its own README.
took: Recorded in lanes/lane8-dispositions.md as a source/inspiration (with Ragas) for the standing quality gates built in Round 3, lane TB6.
didnt: Corroboration — preconfigured, always-on evaluation checks with failure root-cause analysis are the shape our standing quality gates took; its judge-graded scores are the contrast with our mechanical, citation-locked checks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: tensorzero/tensorzero
good: One self-hosted Rust stack unifying an LLM gateway (unified API over every major provider, <1ms p99 latency overhead claimed), observability with inferences and feedback stored in your own database, evaluations powered by heuristics and LLM judges framed as unit and integration tests, and experimentation with A/B testing, routing and fallbacks.
bad: The repository is archived at source, so the project is unmaintained as opened. Its scope is industrial LLMOps (10k+ QPS, Fortune-10 framing), and its paid Autopilot layer optimizes prompts and models autonomously — the pattern our approval gates exist to restrain.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and fit: archived upstream and built for production LLMOps at industrial scale; its evaluations-as-unit-tests framing is already embodied in our own gates machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: evidentlyai/evidently
good: A Python evaluation and monitoring framework with 100+ built-in metrics: data-quality checks, distribution drift with 20+ statistical tests, ranking metrics (NDCG, MAP, MRR, Hit Rate) and LLM judges. Any Report becomes a Test Suite by adding pass/fail conditions — CI-friendly regression checking — with conditions auto-generatable from a reference dataset, and results exportable as JSON, HTML or dict.
bad: The framing is pandas-and-production-pipeline monitoring, not a personal corpus. Its LLM-judge evaluators inherit judge-dependence, and several operational features (alerting, dataset and user management, no-code evals) sit in Evidently Cloud rather than the open-source library.
didnt: Board — the deterministic drift/data-quality metrics and the ranking test-suite machinery are a concrete candidate layer for corpus-quality checks beyond our abstention battery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: helicone/helicone
good: One-line-of-code LLM observability: proxy logging of cost, latency and traces, an AI gateway with intelligent routing and automatic fallbacks across 100+ models, and prompt versioning driven by production data. Self-hosting via docker-compose is documented for those who want the data at home.
bad: The default quick start routes your prompts through Helicone's hosted gateway — a custody inversion for a private corpus. The self-host is a five-service stack (web, worker, log server, Supabase, ClickHouse, plus MinIO), and what it observes is outbound API traffic, not the truth state of a knowledge base.
didnt: Rejected — the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict stands at source: hosted-gateway custody by default and team-production scope do not fit a local-first personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yichuan-w/LEANN
good: A low-storage vector index built on graph-based selective recomputation with high-degree-preserving pruning: it stores only a compact graph and recomputes embeddings on demand, indexing 60 million chunks in 6 GB instead of 201 GB (~97% saving) at no reported accuracy loss. Fully local with zero telemetry, personal-data-first (files, email, browser and chat histories), with reproducible benchmarks, an MCP semantic-search service for coding agents, and a ContextBench comparison showing 2.1x BM25's initial relevant-code recall.
bad: Recomputation trades query latency for the storage saving, and the native DiskANN/HNSW build chain is heavy — MKL, Boost and Protobuf with per-OS toolchain notes in its own install documentation. The index remains a derived artifact with no notion of claim supersession: it can rank by similarity, not by which page is currently true.
didnt: Board — the strongest dense-retrieval candidate yet for our scale: MIT, fully local and storage-light; board for a trial as the dense layer underneath the citation-lock and abstention machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: labring/FastGPT

bad: A multi-service application platform whose store of record is its own database rather than owner-readable files. Its custom licence bars SaaS provision and reserves commercial terms, which makes the code ideas-only under our discipline; the README's self-host quick start even ships a default root password (1234).
didnt: Rejected — the catalogue's NOT FOR US verdict stands: custom source-available licence and platform scope; its chunk-editing and call-chain-logging ideas need no adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: AmenRa/ranx

Small, pure-Python and Numba-accelerated.
bad: It evaluates runs against labelled qrels, so it can only speak as well as the golden set behind it — ours is 15 questions — and it measures ranking quality only: nothing about whether the top-ranked page is the currently true one.
didnt: Board — ranx is the measurement layer our retrieval work needs: coverage@10 and the supersession slice are exactly its NDCG/MAP-plus-significance-test shape, and its RRF fusion is the standard way to combine lexical and dense runs; MIT and dependency-light. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ThilinaRajapakse/simpletransformers

bad: It is a model-training library, not a knowledge system: use means a Conda/PyTorch (ideally CUDA) training stack, and the documentation has moved off-repo to an external site. It offers nothing for citation, custody or abstention — our system consumes pretrained models and trains none.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a fine-tuning/training wrapper; no component our knowledge OS lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MiroMindAI/MiroThinker
good: An open deep-research agent family built on 'interactive scaling' — training the agent for deeper, more frequent environment interaction: 256K context, up to 300–600 tool calls per task, models at 30B–235B, a comprehensive benchmark suite (BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, GAIA, HLE, FutureX) and trace collection for long-chain tasks, with step-verifiable reasoning claimed for the proprietary H1 line.

good: An autonomous deep-research agent: planner agents generate research questions, execution agents gather and source-track material, a publisher aggregates cited reports from 20+ sources; it also researches local documents, ships an MCP client and server, does recursive breadth/depth 'Deep Research', and benchmarks its context filtering by replaying the same scraped sources with only the filter changed (usefulness-scored Jev kept 73% relevant passages vs 46% for embeddings).

didnt: Board — the replay-benchmarked, usefulness-scored context filter (score passages by usefulness to the question, not embedding similarity) as candidate machinery for our open sentence-level evidence-scoring gap; the agent itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: apache/seatunnel

bad: Enterprise ETL infrastructure: JVM clusters with Kubernetes deployment, built to move data between databases and warehouses. Nothing in it addresses a personal, human-readable file corpus, and its scale assumptions invert ours.

name: lancedb/lance

Our corpus is human-readable Markdown under git; moving it into a table format would break the file custody and direct inspectability the whole system rests on. Its zero-copy versioning is, however, the same instinct as our git-versioned pages.
didnt: Rejected — format and scope: a multimodal ML lakehouse format; versioning corroborates our git approach but the format itself is not adoptable for a text corpus. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: KevinMusgrave/pytorch-metric-learning

bad: A training-side library: it exists to train embedding models, predominantly for computer vision. Our system consumes pretrained embeddings and trains nothing, so there is no place for it in the stack.
didnt: Rejected — scope: embedding-model training machinery we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: brianpetro/obsidian-smart-connections

good: An Obsidian plugin that surfaces semantically related notes and excerpts while you write: a bundled local embedding model gives zero-setup, no-API-key, offline-by-default semantic search over the vault, a Connections view (graph + list) with hide/pin feedback, a Lookup view for ad-hoc semantic search, and Smart Context assembly of connected notes into a prompt-ready bundle.

bad: A production inference server: per-backend Docker/GPU images (CUDA, ROCm, Intel, ARM) and server operations are its world, and supported model architectures are a bounded list. A personal wiki's embedding work is batch-scale; running a serving tier for it is operational weight without a present need.
didnt: Board — TEI as the reference option for air-gapped, self-hosted embedding + reranker serving (Apache-2.0) if our semantic layer ever outgrows batch embedding; not deployed now. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: supabase/supabase
good: The Postgres development platform: a dedicated Postgres database with authentication (JWT-based GoTrue), auto-generated REST (PostgREST) and GraphQL (pg_graphql) APIs, realtime subscriptions over websockets, database and edge functions, S3-backed file storage with Postgres-managed permissions, and an AI/vector toolkit (pgvector) — Firebase's feature set rebuilt on enterprise-grade open-source tools, hosted or self-hosted, with modular client libraries across a dozen languages.
bad: It is application-backend infrastructure, not a knowledge system: adopting it means running (or trusting the hosted version of) a Postgres-centred service stack as the data's home, which inverts our plain-file custody model, and nothing in it provides citation locking, scored abstention or approval-gated writes.
didnt: Rejected — scope and custody: a hosted/self-hosted app backend platform; our corpus stays in human-readable files under git, and Supabase answers a database-serving need we do not have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: RyanCodrai/turbovec
good: An in-process vector index in Rust with Python bindings, built on Google Research's TurboQuant: it stores each vector at 2 or 4 bits per dimension (7.8–15.5x smaller than float32) and searches the compressed form directly with SIMD kernels — 4.4x FAISS FastScan at 4-bit at matching recall — with no training step, microsecond add/remove, allowlist-filtered search, stable caller-owned uint64 ids (IdMapIndex), and incremental, crash-safe sync() persistence to a single file; fully local, with drop-in LangChain/LlamaIndex/Haystack integrations.
bad: Very young and single-author: created 2026-03-26, 376 commits and zero releases (tags only), so the API and file format carry no stability track record. Quantization is lossy by design — the top result matches float ground truth 96–98% of the time at 4-bit and less on low-dimensional embeddings (GloVe d=200 recall@1: 0.86 at 4-bit, 0.57 at 2-bit) — and it scans every vector, so cost grows linearly with corpus size; it is a library, not a server.
didnt: Board — a local-first, single-file, incrementally synced quantized vector index (MIT) as a candidate embedding store for our semantic layer: its allowlist-filtered search and stable-id map fit approval-gated retrieval unusually well; too young (no releases yet) to adopt today. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: d3/d3

bad: It is deliberately low-level — the README sells flexibility, not ready-made charts — so every visualization is hand-built code, and the documentation, examples and community resources live off-repo (d3js.org, Observable). It is a browser rendering library only: no data model, storage, or knowledge semantics of any kind.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a general-purpose browser visualization library, not a knowledge or memory component; our portal renders pages and has no charting requirement this fills. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

bad: It is infrastructure monitoring, a different domain entirely from knowledge work, and a very large system (23,838 commits) whose dashboard UI is not under the agent's GPL (NCUL1) and whose Cloud tier is a commercial service. GPL-3.0 code would in any case be ideas-only for us.
didnt: Rejected — scope and licence: a GPL-3.0 infrastructure monitoring platform with a non-GPL UI; nothing in its metric-collection domain maps to a personal knowledge system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

bad: An enormous observability monolith (74,866 commits, Go + TypeScript) aimed at operational metrics and logs, not documents or knowledge; AGPL-3.0 makes its code ideas-only for us, and running it means operating a metrics stack our file-based system deliberately does not have.

name: apache/superset

bad: It is an enterprise BI platform over SQL datastores — a heavy Flask/React monolith (23,908 commits) deployed via Docker/Helm against a metadata database — whose entire model is tables and dashboards, not documents, citations or memory; operating it would dwarf the system it served.

name: apache/echarts

good: An easy-to-use open-source BI and embedded-analytics tool: set up in minutes, lets anyone ask questions of data without SQL while keeping a full SQL editor, an AI assistant (Metabot), interactive dashboards with alerts and scheduled subscriptions, content curation with Git versioning, embedding components, and granular permissions for internal and embedded use.
bad: A business-intelligence product over company databases — a 45,836-commit Clojure/JavaScript monolith whose README's easiest path is a paid Metabase Cloud trial; the open-source half is AGPL (ideas-only for us) and the rest is commercial, and its question-answering is over tables, with no citation or provenance discipline for knowledge.

name: pixijs/pixijs
good: The HTML5 creation engine: a fast, lightweight 2D rendering library with WebGL and WebGPU renderers, an asset loader, flexible text rendering, primitive and SVG drawing, dynamic textures, masking, filters and advanced blend modes, working across devices for rich interactive graphics and cross-platform apps.
bad: A games-and-graphics rendering engine — it draws sprites and scenes and knows nothing of data, text or knowledge; the README itself documents TypeScript/WebGPU type friction (its types depend on @webgpu/types or @types/web depending on TS version), and everything above the renderer (apps, content, semantics) is the embedder's problem.

name: gradio-app/gradio
good: An open-source Python package for building a demo or web app around any ML model, API or Python function in a few lines — no JavaScript, CSS or hosting experience needed — with 30+ built-in components, gr.Blocks for custom layouts and data flows, gr.ChatInterface for chatbots, one-parameter public share links, Hugging Face Spaces hosting, and a server mode with MCP support.

didnt: Rejected — scope: an Apache-2.0 ML demo/app UI framework; our portal is a static, owner-gated site of record, not a function-demo surface, and its hosted sharing cuts against our custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

good: A flexible backend that wraps any SQL database (Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, MS SQL, SQLite, OracleDB, CockroachDB and more) with automatically generated REST and GraphQL APIs and a visual Studio, fully extensible via custom endpoints, hooks and modules — and notably, a native MCP server through which AI agents work on live data under the same policy-based, field-level access control as human users, governed by default with no special cases.

(completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: reflex-dev/reflex
good: A library for building full-stack web apps in pure Python — frontend and backend in one language, no JavaScript to learn — that is easy to start yet scales to complex apps, with fast refresh during development, deploy-in-seconds tooling, an AI Builder, and an Agent Toolkit connecting MCP and Skills to coding assistants.

name: plotly/dash

name: Sinaptik-AI/pandas-ai
licence: MIT (expat) — README License section: 'PandasAI is available under the MIT expat license, except for the pandasai/ee directory of this repository, which has its own license' (repo metadata NOASSERTION; root LICENSE file present, ee/ directory at root)
good: A Python library that makes data conversational: ask questions of databases and datalakes (SQL, CSV, parquet) or multiple DataFrames in natural language using LLMs and RAG, get answers and generated charts back, with an optional Docker sandbox extension for isolated code execution.
bad: Its mechanism is LLM-generated code executed against your data — the Docker sandbox is an optional add-on rather than the default path the README demonstrates — and its worked examples return bare values ('Olivia gets paid the most.') with no citation, provenance or abstention mechanism documented; the README also pins Python 3.8+ to <=3.11, and the enterprise ee/ subtree sits under a separate licence.

name: vanna-ai/vanna
good: Vanna 2.0 turns natural-language questions into SQL and answers via agentic retrieval, with a security model that is user-aware at every layer: identity flows through system prompts, tool execution and SQL filtering, queries are automatically filtered per user permissions with row-level security, every query is audit-logged per user, and tools declare access groups that are checked before execution; it streams tables, charts (Plotly) and summaries to a pre-built web component and works with any LLM and most SQL databases.
bad: The repository is archived as opened (GitHub marks it a public archive), so it is a finished artefact, not a maintained dependency; 2.0 is a complete rewrite that breaks the 0.x API (a migration guide and legacy adapter are provided); and it answers over SQL databases — the generated SQL is by default shown only to admin users, so ordinary users get results without the query that produced them.
didnt: Corroboration — its user-aware tool permissions, group-checked tool access and per-user audit logs independently confirm our gateway's scoped-access-plus-ledger design for agent doors (evidence only: the repo is archived and its text-to-SQL domain is not ours, so nothing is adopted). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: streamlit/streamlit
good: Streamlit turns plain Python scripts into interactive web apps in minutes rather than weeks: a simple, Pythonic API for dashboards, reports and chat apps, with input widgets, dataframes, charts, layouts and multi-page apps, live editing that updates the app as the script changes, a community Components ecosystem that extends it, and a free Community Cloud for deploying and sharing apps.
bad: It is a data-app UI framework only — it renders widgets and charts over Python state and provides no storage, retrieval, citation or memory model, so everything knowledge-shaped would still be ours to build; its sharing story runs through the vendor's hosted Community Cloud, a custody posture opposite to our local-first, owner-only doors; and the repo states that pull requests from outside the maintainer team are currently paused.
didnt: Rejected — scope: an Apache-2.0 Python framework for building and sharing data apps; our portal is a static, owner-gated site generated by our own tooling, and Streamlit offers no citation, provenance or memory layer a knowledge system could take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidianmd/obsidian-releases
licence: No licence stated at source (no LICENSE file in the repo root and no licence shown in repo metadata)
good: The official distribution point for a major notes app: it hosts Obsidian's public releases (173 releases) and the community plugin and theme directories as plain JSON files (community-plugins.json, community-css-themes.json, plugin stats and deprecation lists), and its README documents exactly how Obsidian pulls a plugin's manifest.json and README from the author's own repo and fetches the release files from GitHub releases — a directory-as-data model at real scale (22,462 stars, 9,984 commits).
bad: It contains no application source at all — the README states plainly that Obsidian is not open source and this repo does not contain its code — and the repo accepts no issues, routing all questions elsewhere. It is a release/directory host for a proprietary app, and no licence is stated for the directory data itself.
didnt: Rejected — scope and licence: a distribution directory for a proprietary app we do not use, with no licence stated for its data; our wiki's own registry and release discipline live in its files and git history (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jackyzha0/quartz
good: A fast, batteries-included static-site generator that transforms Markdown content into fully functional websites, aimed at publishing a digital garden and notes as a website for free. Adoption and maturity are strong on the opened page: 13,432 stars, 4,129 forks and 1,927 commits, with Obsidian/digital-garden/networked-thought topics and a Docker file and default YAML configuration in the repo; the complete garden-publishing feature set — wikilink/backlink resolution, local graph, full-text search, tag pages, and Obsidian-flavoured markdown in a build-time static site — is recorded in the Tier 1 Quartz study this row re-opens and agrees with.
bad: The fetched README is minimal — it points to external documentation for features and setup, so the opened page itself does not evidence its wikilink, backlink, graph or search behaviour. The current default branch is v5 while the catalogue-era tooling targeted earlier Quartz versions, so version-specific behaviour would need re-checking before any reuse.
took: The benchmark for any public or read-only view of the wiki; patterns copyable (MIT), and its component model is the reference if the Lens ever rebuilds. Additionally: Built (marathon records): Per-page link-health in the Lens inspector (data)
didnt: Adopt/build — per-page link-health in the Lens inspector, built in Round 3, lane TA7, source Quartz / LeafWiki as recorded in lane8-dispositions.md; Quartz (MIT) also stands as the benchmark and component-model reference for any public or read-only view of the wiki and for a future Lens rebuild, rather than as a publisher we run (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: Vinzent03/obsidian-git
good: Full Git version control inside Obsidian: scheduled automatic commit-and-sync (commit, pull, push), auto-pull on startup, a source-control view for staging/committing/diffing, history and side-by-side diff views, in-editor conflict resolution (ours/theirs/both/base), editor change signs, submodule support, and GitHub integration — mature at 12,148 stars, 1,113 commits and 154 releases.
bad: The README itself warns the mobile implementation is 'highly unstable' and 'very unstable' (no SSH auth, repo-size limits from memory, no rebase or submodules, possible crashes on clone/pull), Snap installs are unsupported and Flatpak not recommended on Linux, and on desktop the plugin needs shell execution and direct filesystem access, which the community scorecard flags.
didnt: Corroboration — a vault whose every change is a git commit, with automatic sync and in-editor history/diff, is our wiki's custody model (git is the memory's version history) working at consumer scale; not used as a component because our wiki is versioned with git directly, not through an Obsidian plugin (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kepano/obsidian-minimal
good: A highly polished Obsidian theme: distraction-free design with deep customisation via companion plugins (Minimal Theme Settings, Hider, Style Settings), preset and custom colour schemes, focus mode, and CSS helper classes that turn Dataview tables into cards, image grids and controlled-width embeds — winner of Obsidian's official Best Theme award, with 244 releases keeping it current with the app.
bad: It is purely presentational CSS for one proprietary app. The README's own Disclaimer states it is provided as-is, designed for the author's personal use on macOS, not thoroughly tested across operating systems and use cases, and that it modifies significant parts of the Obsidian interface so it may break with future updates or conflict with other custom CSS.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a cosmetic theme layer for an app our system does not run; it touches no question of custody, citation, retrieval or writing that our wiki machinery answers (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidianmd/obsidian-clipper
licence: MIT (source code; the README's License section excludes trademarks, icons, marketing copy and other marketing assets)
good: The official Web Clipper for Obsidian: highlight and capture web pages from Chrome/Chromium, Firefox, Safari and Edge, saving them as durable Markdown files that can be read offline and preserved long-term, with templates, variables and filters shaping each capture; extraction/conversion uses the defuddle library and DOMPurify sanitisation, and the extension is actively released (68 releases since Aug 2024).
bad: It writes into Obsidian vaults specifically, so its capture target and template model are that app's. Several headline conveniences are still roadmap items on the opened page (annotate highlights, a template directory, syncing settings across browsers), and the actual user documentation for highlighting/templates lives outside the repo on the Obsidian Help site.
didnt: Corroboration — capture the web into durable, local, plain Markdown files you own is exactly our ingest-to-files principle in browser form; our own ingest runs through directed chat and wiki routes rather than a browser clipper, so the extension itself is not part of our stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: MoMoM101/RAG-ReActAgent
good: A local-first document-QA system with serious honesty machinery: hybrid retrieval (Qdrant semantic + SQLite BM25 fused by weighted RRF, optional cross-encoder reranker), a self-built ReAct tool loop, persistent resumable ingest tasks, and post-answer verification that checks citations exist (phantom citations are detected and repaired), that citation placement and numeric claims match the evidence, and that the system refuses when evidence is insufficient — all with data stored locally by default and JWT auth.
bad: It is a beta (v0.2.1-beta) from a single developer (the README's origin statement discloses AI-assisted development and one public snapshot in July 2026; 84 commits, 0 forks). Its headline metrics (100% faithfulness, 99.62% citation precision on 93 controlled questions) come from a synthetic benchmark that the README's own limitations section admits includes the development subset, has no strictly isolated held-out test, and uses hand-written synthetic corpora rather than real documents; the stack (Qdrant, FastAPI, React) is heavy for what it proves.
didnt: Corroboration — its post-answer citation verification, phantom-citation detection and refusal-on-insufficient-evidence independently implement the honesty goals our citation lockfile and scored abstention meet by construction; the beta document-QA app itself is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: scientist-labs/red-candle
good: A Ruby gem that runs language models entirely locally via Rust's Candle framework (Metal/CUDA acceleration): LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, Phi, incl. GGUF quantised models), embeddings, document rerankers, tokenizers, NER and vision-language models directly from Ruby with no Python, no APIs and no external services, so data never leaves the machine.
bad: It serves the Ruby ecosystem only — our tooling is Python — and carries real format limits stated in its README: embedding and reranker models are safetensors-only, a known Phi-3/Phi-4 GGUF KV-cache defect requires recreating the model per generation, gated Hugging Face models need a login/terms step, and local models run from ~100MB to several GB of cache.
didnt: Rejected — stack and scope: local-inference plumbing for Ruby applications; it confirms local reranking is commodity machinery, but our retrieval runs in Python over our own files and needs no Ruby inference layer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jina-ai/mlx-retrieval
licence: Apache-2.0 (the README's License section states the code is Apache-2.0; the bundled example model gemma-3-270m-mlx is a third-party asset under Gemma terms and is not covered by it)
good: Training code for retrieval models on Apple Silicon with MLX: full/partial LoRA training of embedding and reranker models with InfoNCE/NT-Xent losses and hard-negative mining, gradient accumulation, MTEB evaluation integration, W&B logging and a post-training distillation script — its README reports ~4,000–5,000 tokens/sec training gemma-3-270m on an M3 Ultra.
bad: The README states the project is primarily for educational purposes and currently tested on a single 270M model, with a single-LoRA retrieval configuration rather than task-specific adapters; the repo is thin (16 commits, no releases) and Apple-Silicon-only, and its example model files are excluded from the project's Apache licence (Gemma terms apply instead).
didnt: Rejected — scope and platform: model-training code for Apple hardware; we consume retrieval over our files, we do not train embedders or rerankers on MLX (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: notadev-iamaura/OneRAG
good: A configurable RAG backend (FastAPI) whose components swap by one line of config: six vector DBs (Weaviate, Pinecone, Qdrant, ChromaDB, pgvector, MongoDB), five LLM providers, six rerankers, hybrid Dense+BM25 search, GraphRAG and PII masking options, an OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions API, and a fully offline mode using a local Ollama LLM; the repo header claims 2,100+ tests with CI gates.
bad: The repo was created in January 2026 and has a single release, so its 'production-ready' framing is the project's own claim at an early stage. Its architecture is centred on vector databases and provider LLM keys (the full server quick-start needs a Google API key), which inverts our files-first custody, and the documented pipeline (route, expand, retrieve, cache, rerank, generate, PII-mask) shows no citation-locking or abstention machinery.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and scope: a generic, young RAG framework built around vector stores; our Ask door already answers from the wiki's own files with citation locking and scored abstention, which this does not offer (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: allenai/s2search
good: The Semantic Scholar search reranker from the Allen Institute: given a plain-text query and academic documents (title, abstract, venue, authors, year, citation counts), its fast model+featurisation scores each document's match, using citation features such as n_citations and n_key_citations — the reranking stage of a scholarly search pipeline, usable standalone when the document set is small enough to skip a first-stage ranker.
bad: The repo has 2 commits and dates from 2020, with a Python 3.7/conda-era install; its model artifacts are a 10GB compressed (17GB uncompressed) S3 download and the README warns the example needs more than 17GB of RAM for the kenlm models. It is only the reranking stage, and its required fields are Semantic Scholar-specific.
didnt: Rejected — maturity and scope: a frozen 2020 scholarly reranker with a 17GB in-memory footprint, tied to Semantic Scholar's feature set; our corpus is a personal wiki, not an academic index, and our retrieval is file-derived (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Allen Institute for AI (AI2)

name: tanaos/artifex
good: A Python library for task-specific small language models that run on CPU (~100M parameters): pre-trained models for guardrails, intent classification, reranking, sentiment, emotion, NER, PII anonymisation, spam, topic classification and summarisation — and, distinctively, fine-tuning APIs that generate synthetic training data on the fly from your instructions, so a custom guardrail or reranker can be trained with no labelled data, kept local forever, with built-in local evaluation and monitoring.
bad: The repo was created in September 2025, and the effectiveness of instruction-only fine-tuning rests on synthetically generated data whose quality the page does not evidence independently. Most tasks are English-only, and the README's Enterprise section reserves higher-performance models, more languages and models trained on far more data for paying customers.
didnt: Board — the instruction-only fine-tuning pattern for tiny CPU task models: a local guardrail or reranker trained from a behaviour description with synthetic data and local evaluation is a candidate technique for our evaluation machinery (in the line of the task-specific evaluators boarded earlier in this programme); the library itself is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: noamschwartz/atlas-memory-demo
good: A research demo of agent memory on Elasticsearch with a thoughtful shape: three memory types (episodic, semantic, procedural) in three indices, hybrid BM25 + Jina v5 dense recall fused by RRF with a reranker, supersession and decay, per-user document-level-security isolation, the same memory layer exposed as an MCP server (recall_memory / write_memory / forget_memory), and an inline memory inspector showing exactly which documents were retrieved and written on each turn.
bad: It is a demo: 18 commits, no releases, seeded with three synthetic users, and it cannot run without an Elasticsearch cluster plus Kibana and the Elastic Inference Service (hosted Elastic custody or a self-hosted cluster). Its agent recalls and writes memory on every turn with no approval gate on writes.
didnt: Corroboration — the inline memory inspector (owner can see exactly what was retrieved and written) and the episodic/semantic/procedural split corroborate our owner-visible, file-based memory design; the demo itself is not adopted, since hosted Elastic custody and ungated write-on-every-turn are the opposite of our approval-gated writes (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: DataArcTech/RagVL
good: The official PyTorch implementation of the paper 'MLLM Is a Strong Reranker' (arXiv:2407.21439): it uses a multimodal LLM as the reranker for multimodal RAG, with knowledge-enhanced reranking and noise-injected training so the generator stays reliable when retrieval returns noisy passages, with full training/evaluation pipelines for WebQA and MultimodalQA across LLaVA, Qwen-VL, mPLUG-Owl2 and InternVL2 backbones.
bad: It is research code: datasets and checkpoints are downloaded from Google Drive and reassembled by hand into the tree, training means GPU fine-tuning of vision models up to 13B, there are no releases, and the README's updates stop in September 2024. Its multimodal image-text scope is far beyond a text wiki's needs.
didnt: Rejected — scope: multimodal RAG research code for training vision-language rerankers; the noise-robustness finding is noted, but nothing here transfers to our text-first, file-based retrieval (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: luyug/Reranker
good: A lightweight package for training and deploying deep language model rerankers in IR, QA and NLP pipelines, built as a thin wrapper over Hugging Face — its model subclasses PreTrainedModel and its trainer subclasses the HF Trainer, so pretrained models such as BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA drop in with familiar interfaces and checkpoint interoperability. Training follows the authors' ECIR 2021 localized contrastive estimation (LCE) loss, and the README records two submissions to the MS MARCO document leaderboard that each took 1st place; GPU memory optimisations (Loss Parallelism and Gradient Cache), distributed data parallel and automatic mixed precision support larger-scale training.
bad: Effectively frozen: created in January 2021 with only 7 commits and no releases, and tested only against 2021-era dependencies (torch 1.6.0, transformers 4.2.0, datasets 1.1.3). Parts are unfinished on the page itself — the Gradient Cache is marked experimental and several sections say detailed instructions are 'to be added' — and it is reranker training/inference machinery only, with no retrieval, storage or answer layer of its own.
didnt: Rejected — scope and maturity: reranker training and deployment machinery for IR pipelines; our retrieval is file-derived over the wiki's own pages with citation locking and scored abstention, and we do not train rerankers. The codebase is also a frozen 2021 snapshot (7 commits, no releases, 2021-era pinned dependencies) (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Carnegie Mellon University (author contact [email redacted]; ECIR 2021 paper with Zhuyun Dai and Jamie Callan)

name: shell-nlp/gpt_server
good: An open-source framework for production-grade deployment of LLMs, embedding, reranker, ASR, TTS, text-to-image, image-editing and text-to-video models behind one OpenAI-spec API server built on FastChat: chat, embedding, rerank (/v1/rerank, plus a Cohere-style variant), text-moderation, ASR and TTS endpoints, four inference backends (HF, vLLM, LMDeploy, SGLang) with several models sharing a single port under automatic model scheduling, Responses API support, and Docker deployment — substantially built out at 558 commits and 32 releases.
bad: The README's own notice states the repository has not been maintained since 2026-05-09 — no new features, bug fixes or security updates — because vLLM/SGLang/LMDeploy dependency conflicts made the environment too costly to keep compatible, and it directs users to migrate to the official backend images or other routers. It is a single-maintainer project, its optional visual server UI is self-described as buggy and deprecated, and the primary documentation is in Chinese with detailed configuration docs hosted off-repo.
didnt: Rejected — scope and maintenance: a GPU model-serving framework for production LLM deployment; our system answers from its own local files and does not serve models, and the project is declared unmaintained at source with migration away from it recommended (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bibliojson
type: npm package — JSON bibliography format and converter library
licence: LGPL-3.0 (registry license field and README licence badge agree; copyleft, so ideas-only under our licence discipline)
good: A JSON-based bibliography format built for lossless round-trips: importers and exporters for BibLaTeX, CSL-JSON, RIS, ENW, EndNote XML and Citavi, and it can even extract citation data from DOCX/ODT files. It deliberately preserves BibLaTeX-specific detail — name particles, date granularity as EDTF strings, rich-text marks — that CSL-JSON would drop on conversion.
bad: LGPL-3.0 copyleft makes the code itself ideas-only for us. It is a small, niche package (catalogue signal ~3,210 downloads/month) from the Fidus Writer ecosystem, and honouring its full BibLaTeX field model is a large specification surface for a single-purpose converter.
didnt: Board — the lossless, BibLaTeX-preserving JSON interchange design as a reference for citation import/export in our citation layer; the code is LGPL-3.0, so ideas only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: graphology-communities-louvain
type: npm package — Louvain community detection for graphology
good: Implements the Louvain modularity algorithm for graphology with the relevant modularity computations for undirected and directed graphs, weighted edges, a resolution parameter, and a detailed mode returning the partition, community count, dendrogram and final modularity; grounded in the cited Newman/Blondel/Dugué literature in its README.
bad: It cannot process true mixed graphs — the README requires casting to directed or undirected first — and runtime is bounded by edge count, so multi-graphs may need simplifying before use. The registry record was last modified 2024-12, a slow release cadence.
didnt: Board — Louvain clustering of the wiki link graph as a candidate topic/neighbourhood discovery signal for the Lens. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: graphology-metrics
type: npm package — graph metrics library for graphology
good: A broad metric suite for graphology graphs: density, diameter and modularity at graph level; eccentricity and weighted degree per node; disparity, Simmelian strength and chi/G-square per edge; betweenness, closeness, eigenvector, HITS and PageRank centralities; plus layout-quality measures such as stress and neighbourhood preservation. Actively maintained (registry record modified 2026-09).
bad: A pure computation layer — no storage, layout or rendering — so it only has value inside a graphology-based pipeline, and several metrics (diameter, betweenness) are expensive on large graphs.
didnt: Corroboration — PageRank/centrality and modularity over a link graph are the standard toolkit behind page-importance ranking signals, confirming that part of our design direction. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cytoscape
type: npm package — graph theory library for analysis and visualisation (Cytoscape.js)
good: A fully featured graph theory library: a graph model plus an optional interactive renderer, usable headless in Node or in the browser, with zero runtime dependencies, 70+ extensions, and active maintenance (registry record modified 2026-10; latest 3.34.4).
bad: The API surface is large and renderer/browser-oriented; interactive visualisation is not something our read-mostly, text-first Lens currently needs, and its analysis functions overlap what graphology already offers.
didnt: Board — candidate renderer if a Lens link-graph view is ever built; not needed by the current portal. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: University of Toronto (per README: created there; Bader Lab)

name: sigma
type: npm package — WebGL graph visualisation library (Sigma.js)
good: A WebGL renderer aimed at visualising graphs of thousands of nodes and edges, built on top of graphology, with a companion package family (node image/border/piechart programs, image export, map layers). Actively maintained — v4.0.3, registry record modified 2026-10.
bad: Rendering only: the graph model lives in graphology and layouts in separate packages, so sigma is never a standalone choice; it also requires WebGL, excluding the simplest static-page contexts.
didnt: Board — the WebGL half of a possible graphology + sigma Lens graph view for large wiki graphs. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)
institution: Sciences Po médialab (initial support and co-development, per README) and OuestWare

name: dagre
type: npm package — directed graph layout library
licence: MIT (registry license field and README License section agree)
good: A small client-side library that lays out directed graphs (Sugiyama-style) with a tiny API; it has a long deployment history as the layout engine behind many diagramming tools.
bad: Unmaintained: the registry record was last modified in 2022-06 and the latest release is 0.8.5; the README is minimal and defers to an external wiki; it depends on lodash and graphlib.
didnt: Rejected — stale since 2022; directed-layout needs are better served by maintained engines such as Graphviz WASM or ELK. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @hpcc-js/wasm-graphviz
type: npm package — WebAssembly wrapper for Graphviz
good: The real Graphviz C library compiled to WebAssembly: DOT parsing and layout to SVG inside a browser or Node with no native binary to install, plus programmatic graph construction, parsing existing DOT into a mutable graph, and re-layout after mutation. Very actively maintained (registry record modified 2026-10-21; latest 1.30.0).
bad: Carries a WASM payload and a manual memory discipline — graph objects must be delete()d or scoped with `using`; it is layout only, with no interactivity and no graph model beyond DOT semantics.
didnt: Board — server-free DOT layout for rendering wiki structure and dependency diagrams in the Lens without installing native Graphviz. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: yjs
type: npm package — CRDT framework for collaborative editing
good: A mature CRDT framework: shared Map/Array/text types whose changes distribute to peers and merge without conflicts, with offline editing, version snapshots, undo/redo and shared cursors; network-agnostic and editor-agnostic, and proven in production knowledge tools (the README lists AFFiNE and GitBook among its users).
bad: Its whole premise — many simultaneous writers merging automatically — inverts our single-writer, approval-gated custody model, and the providers, persistence and awareness plumbing would all have to be built and hosted by us.
didnt: Rejected — real-time multi-writer editing is rejected by design in our system, which uses approval-gated writes with a trust ledger instead; a CRDT sync layer would undo that custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: diff-match-patch
type: npm package — text diff, patch and fuzzy match library (Google's algorithms)
good: Google's battle-tested diff/match/patch algorithms: Myers diff with semantic and efficiency cleanup passes, fuzzy patch application and fuzzy text search, with configurable timeout and edit-cost knobs; zero dependencies and an enormous installed base.
bad: The npm package is a thin repackage of Google's library and is stale — registry record last modified 2022-06, version 1.0.5 — and the README itself notes diff computation can be slow on large unrelated texts, which is why the timeout knobs exist.
didnt: Corroboration — its semantic-cleanup pass, which rewrites an optimal but unreadable diff into a human-intelligible one, confirms our design point that change detection must optimise for human review, not just minimal edit scripts. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: jsondiffpatch
type: npm package — JSON diff and patch library
good: Deep-diffs JavaScript objects and arrays into a compact JSON delta that can patch, be reversed, and unpatch (revert); it can also generate and apply RFC 6902 patches and render annotated HTML deltas, in about 16 KB minified+gzipped. Maintained — registry record modified 2026-05, latest 0.7.6.
bad: Matching objects inside arrays requires a user-supplied objectHash function or it falls back to positional matching; current builds are ESM-only, and long-string text diffing is delegated to a diff-match-patch fork.
didnt: Board — reversible JSON deltas as a candidate format for structured-record change tracking (registers, manifests) where an auditable undo matters. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: diff
type: npm package — JavaScript text differencing library (jsdiff)
licence: BSD-3-Clause (registry license field and repo LICENSE/sidebar agree)
good: Myers-algorithm differencing at character, word, line, sentence and JSON token granularities, with unified-patch creation, parsing and application — including multi-file git patches with renames and mode changes. Zero dependencies and the de-facto JS text-diff standard (catalogue signal ~599M downloads/month), actively maintained at v9.0.0.
bad: A text-first model: its JSON support is a line diff over pretty-printed serialisation, not a structural delta; the README documents deliberate deviations from the published Myers algorithm and naive sentence tokenisation (full stops only).
didnt: Corroboration — token-level diffing with unified-patch interchange is exactly the substrate our git-based change detection already assumes; it adds no capability we lack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rfc6902
good: A complete implementation of RFC 6902 (JSON Patch) and RFC 6901 (JSON Pointer): createPatch diffs two objects into patch operations and applyPatch applies them, returning a per-operation result list with descriptive errors. Zero dependencies and maintained (registry record modified 2026-07; latest 5.3.0).
bad: The README is candid that createPatch is not optimal — it emits only add/remove/replace (no move/copy) and does not search for the minimal patch — and applyPatch mutates the target object in place.
didnt: Corroboration — JSON Patch is the standard vocabulary for expressing a proposed change as a list of operations, the same shape as our approval-gated write proposals. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: git-diff
type: npm package — wrapper returning git diff output for two strings
good: Returns authentic git diff output for two strings by shelling out to the real git binary (via printf), with colour, word-diff and arbitrary git-flag options; if git or printf is unavailable it falls back to the jsdiff package to produce a close approximation.
bad: A thin wrapper whose real work is done by git itself or by jsdiff; shelling out through shelljs is platform-dependent and heavy, and its dependency pins are old (diff ^3.5.0, chalk ^2.3.2).
didnt: Rejected — our tooling invokes git directly; an extra shell wrapper adds failure modes without adding any capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: diff2html
