good: Generates pretty HTML from git or unified diffs: line-by-line and side-by-side views with old/new line numbers, GitHub-like styling, syntax highlighting and line-similarity matching. Maintained — v3.4.56, registry record modified 2026-01.
bad: Presentation only — it renders diffs produced elsewhere and computes nothing itself — and its own troubleshooting section flags out-of-memory or slow execution on very large diffs.
didnt: Board — candidate renderer for the human review step of approval-gated writes in the Lens, where a proposed change is read before it is ruled on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: conventional-changelog
type: npm package — changelog generator from git metadata
licence: MIT (registry license field and README License section agree)
good: Generates a human changelog from git history by parsing conventional-commit messages, with a preset ecosystem (angular and others), both a CLI and a JS API, and non-destructive prepends to existing changelogs. Actively maintained — v8.1.3, registry record modified 2026-08.
bad: Output quality depends entirely on disciplined conventional-commit messages, which our gateway-trailer commit style (Agent:/Session:/Sources:/Operation:) does not follow; the package is ESM-only.
didnt: Corroboration — machine-readable commit conventions feeding an automatically generated change log confirms our own commit-trailer discipline; the angular preset itself does not fit our trailers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: auto-changelog
good: Generates a changelog from git tags and commit history behind a single command, with compact, keepachangelog and JSON templates, commit/issue/merge link generation for GitHub/GitLab/BitBucket/Azure DevOps remotes, monorepo autodetection, a plugin system, and deliberately hardened handling of untrusted in-repo config (options that could load code or write outside the repo are refused from config files).
bad: It only works as well as the repo's discipline: semver tags are an absolute requirement (git 1.7.2+), and useful output depends on merge/issue conventions in commit messages. It is a release-engineering utility — nothing in it touches retrieval, citation or knowledge custody.
didnt: Rejected — mature and well-built, but release tooling peripheral to the knowledge OS; our repos' history is governed by the wiki's own log discipline, and nothing here serves citation, retrieval or write-gating. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: standard-version
good: One command bumps the semver version from Conventional Commits history, generates the changelog (via conventional-changelog), commits and tags; lifecycle scripts and custom updaters let it version files beyond package.json.
bad: Deprecated at source: the README's own head notice declares standard-version deprecated and recommends release-please instead, and the registry time record shows the last publish was 2022-05-15 — unmaintained for years.
didnt: Rejected — deprecated by its own README and unmaintained since 2022; in any case release versioning sits outside the knowledge-OS core. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @commitlint/cli
type: npm package — commit-message linter (CLI of the commitlint monorepo)
good: Lints commit messages against the Conventional Commits format with a rule system, shareable configurations published via npm (config-conventional, config-angular, lerna/nx scope configs), local (husky) and CI setups, and programmatic API packages (lint, load, read, format). Actively maintained — registry latest 21.2.4 of 2026-10-18; the repo shows 192 releases and is not archived.
bad: The project is unsponsored and its README states plainly that patch versions for older releases cannot be promised in a timely manner. It requires Node.js LTS >= 22.12.0 and git >= 2.13.2, and the npm registry README is a stub — the substance lives in the repo and docs site.
didnt: Board — a commit-message lint gate (conventional format plus our required trailers, e.g. the no-Claude-co-author rule) for the wiki and WikiCitadel repos is worth weighing as governance tooling. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pdfjs-dist
good: Mozilla's web-standards platform for parsing and rendering PDFs, shipped as a pre-built generic build usable in browsers and Node; actively released (6.4.299 of 2026-10-03 per the registry record) and the de-facto in-browser PDF engine.
bad: This package is a build artifact: its README carries no API documentation and points to the pdf.js repo and wiki, and environments without the latest JavaScript features must use the separate legacy/ build. It parses and renders PDFs but performs no knowledge-level extraction, citation or indexing itself.
didnt: Corroboration — a mature Apache-2.0 commodity engine already covers PDF rendering, so there is nothing to build; our corpus's PDF needs are ingest-side and served by our own pipeline choices. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @safetnsr/md-kit
type: npm package — markdown link checker CLI
good: Zero-dependency CLI that finds broken [[wikilinks]] and dead relative links in any markdown workspace and suggests fixes; fix (dry-run/--apply/--patch), mv (moves a file and rewrites incoming links) and watch commands, CI-friendly exit codes, a documented --json agent interface, and an event-driven pipe mode matching on path/frontmatter/tags with multi-step pipelines.
bad: Very young and unproven: created 2026-02-28 per the registry record, v0.6.0, single maintainer, and the catalogue signal was ~10 downloads/month. Its wikilink check strips headings and verifies only that the target file exists, not anchors; pipe mode executes shell commands and webhooks from a config file, which demands trust in the workspace.
didnt: Board — its fix --patch flow (proposed link fixes written to a review file rather than applied) is a pattern our surfacing-only lint lanes could adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @vaultctl/core
type: npm package — Obsidian vault core library (TypeScript)
good: Pure-TypeScript library for structured vault operations: frontmatter parse/serialize, wikilink extraction and resolution, tag operations validated on write, filtered search, template rendering, health checks (broken-links, orphans, stale, frontmatter) and a safeJoin helper with path-traversal protection.
bad: Brand new and tiny: created 2026-02-15 per the registry record, v0.5.0, single maintainer, catalogue signal ~21 downloads/month. It is shaped for Obsidian vaults, and its health-check set is a small subset of what our validator and lint lanes already run.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent vault core converging on the same health-check set (broken links, orphans, staleness, frontmatter) as our lint lanes confirms that design; nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @idan_ariav/qvoid
type: npm package — unresolved-wikilink indexer with MCP server
good: Indexes the unresolved wikilinks of an Obsidian-style vault with origin file, surrounding sentence and inline semantic annotations (Supports::, Related::), classifies each target (idea/person/date/file/template/unknown) with a two-pass heuristic, and uses local ONNX embeddings (bge-small-en-v1.5) to cluster near-duplicate targets and suggest canonical names; ships an MCP server, runs incrementally, and is fully offline with no telemetry.
bad: Young and single-author: created 2026-04-20 per the registry record, v0.6.0, catalogue signal ~21 downloads/month. Classification leans on title heuristics its own methodology calls medium-confidence, the embed step downloads a ~25 MB model, and it is oriented to Obsidian vaults rather than a governed git corpus.
didnt: Board — an unresolved-link index carrying occurrence counts, sentence context and near-duplicate clustering would strengthen our missing-links lint lane beyond a flat list. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: glovrex-cli
good: Turns an Obsidian vault into a portable knowledge graph (JSON/GraphML/markdown) with Obsidian-faithful resolution — wikilinks with heading/block anchors and aliases, embeds as their own edge type, frontmatter aliases, nested tags — keeps unresolved links as visible edges instead of dropping them, and exports markdown byte-for-byte so round-tripping is lossless. A decision hook records why a change was made against the HEAD commit and later outcomes against the decision, in the same graph.
bad: Extremely young: created 2026-07-09 per the registry record, v0.2.0, single maintainer, catalogue signal ~19 downloads/month. .canvas files are explicitly out of scope, and the decision feature is an MVP (reading the 'why' from diffs is listed as not built yet).
didnt: Board — decision-to-commit-to-outcome edges, where a decision with no recorded outcome stays visible as a gap, is a graph idea our decisions register does not yet express. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @wiki-nexus/core
type: npm package — markdown-wiki indexing engine (SQLite graph)
good: Parses markdown wikis (frontmatter, [[wikilinks]], heading hierarchy) into a relational knowledge graph in SQLite (pages, edges, tags, sources), clusters pages into topic communities with Louvain detection, traces knowledge flows from source documents through derived pages, analyzes impact (blast radius), staleness, orphans and broken links, and searches via BM25 (FTS5), embeddings and hybrid RRF fusion.
bad: Embryonic: v0.1.1 from a single publish day in April 2026 with no later modification in the registry record, catalogue signal ~6 downloads/month. It expects a flat wiki/pages/ layout and its own frontmatter conventions, and its SQLite graph duplicates the git source of truth rather than governing it.
didnt: Corroboration — independent convergence on our architecture (source-to-derived tracing, staleness/orphan analysis, hybrid search); far below our maturity, nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidiary
type: npm package — isomorphic Obsidian vault parser/renderer core
good: An isomorphic vault core (nothing imports node:*) that runs the identical code at build time and in the browser: Obsidian-faithful link resolution including folder proximity, transclusion with cycle/depth guards, callouts, .canvas files as first-class notes, backlinks and unresolved-link tracking. GitHub reads are pinned to a resolved commit SHA so a multi-file read never mixes revisions, the force layout is deterministic (no Math.random), and search reports why each result matched (title, alias, heading, tag or body).
bad: Embryonic: v0.1.2 of August 2026 per the registry record, single maintainer, catalogue signal ~44 downloads/month. It is a publishing renderer for Obsidian vaults — it has no governance, approval or citation machinery of its own.
didnt: Corroboration — SHA-pinned reads and why-it-matched search results independently confirm our custody and evidence-packing choices; nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @petroglyph/core
good: Core library for PKM systems with a filesystem abstraction, Obsidian-style note resolution (by path, wikilink or name, with nearest-note disambiguation), Zod-schema-typed frontmatter notes, an auto-refreshing index on file create/delete, and first-class Files, Bases and Canvases collections.
bad: Published in a single burst on 2025-12-30/31 and untouched since per the registry time record; v0.2.1, single maintainer, catalogue signal ~11 downloads/month. The README is a sketch — the full API reference lives in the repo docs — and everything is Obsidian-shaped.
didnt: Rejected — stalled since December 2025 and embryonic; its vault-core functions duplicate our own stack, and typed frontmatter is already our schema's territory. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @petroglyph/renderer
good: Markdown renderers for Petroglyph built as remark/rehype plugins: wikilinks resolved with nearest-neighbour logic, embeds, callouts converted to styled HTML, syntax highlighting and GFM, behind a pluggable renderer interface with a raw-content renderer as an escape hatch and separate entry points per renderer.
bad: Same stalled December 2025 burst as @petroglyph/core: created and last modified 2025-12-30 per the registry record, v0.2.0, single maintainer, catalogue signal ~13 downloads/month. It is rendering only — no corpus governance, validation or custody.
didnt: Rejected — stalled and embryonic, and our Lens renderer already does this job under our own pinned rules. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: margins
type: npm package — local markdown-folder browser/editor server
good: Opens any folder of markdown in the browser from the terminal with no vault, config or account: folder tree, GFM rendering, GitHub-style relative links and Obsidian-style [[wikilinks]] with deterministic resolution (own folder, then shallowest, then alphabetical), backlinks shown with the linking line, edit with live preview, full-folder search, and live reload when files change in another editor. Its safety model is serious: DOMPurify sanitisation plus a strict CSP, path/symlink confinement to the folder, .git and node_modules never opened or written, 127.0.0.1-only with DNS-rebinding defence, and saves checked by content hash so a file changed on disk is never silently overwritten (409). The server itself uses no packages; 90 tests.
bad: Deliberately small, per its own 'what it does not do': no graph view, plugins, sync, database or on-disk index — search and backlinks rescan files each time and it stops at 20,000 files; embeds render as links rather than inlined content, and code blocks are not syntax-highlighted yet. Young (September 2026) and single-author, though actively developed (v0.3.0 published 2026-10-21 per the registry record).
didnt: Corroboration — its sanitise-and-confine safety model, hash-checked saves and deterministic link resolution confirm the discipline our own Lens and editor are built under; a local reader is a different shape from the owner-only Lens, nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wikimoth-mcp
type: npm package — npx launcher for the WikiMoth MCP server
good: A thin zero-dependency npx launcher that spawns the Python WikiMoth MCP stdio server for any MCP client: careful vault resolution (--vault flag, WIKIMOTH_VAULT env, cwd fallback) injected as an absolute path with diagnostics on stderr only, and self-healing via uvx when no Python with wikimoth is found. The server it launches offers deterministic, token-minimal recall over a [[wikilink]] vault with no LLM call in the retrieval loop, plus memory-hygiene tools (list_conflicts, list_lint, list_duplicates, list_fading, supersede).
bad: The npm package contains no engine — it is a launcher for the Python wikimoth package, so the registry record alone cannot evidence the engine's behaviour, and it imposes a two-runtime dependency (Node plus Python 3.10+ or uv; the first uvx run downloads WikiMoth and may exceed strict client startup timeouts). July 2026, single maintainer, catalogue signal ~123 downloads/month.
didnt: Corroboration — deterministic no-LLM retrieval with conflict, duplicate, fading and supersede hygiene tools converges with our Ask, lint-lane and supersession design; nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-llmwiki-mcp
type: npm package — read-only MCP server over an LLM-wiki vault
good: A read-only MCP server over an Obsidian LLM-wiki vault exposing four stdio tools (wiki_expand, wiki_pack, wiki_read_page, wiki_search): lexical seeds feed 1-hop graph expansion over [[wikilinks]] and relation lines, with optional BM25 rerank, returning compact claim packs whose headers carry type, confidence and status. Retrieval is deterministic and held byte-identical to a Python reference implementation by parity tests; the server makes no LLM calls, opens no network connections and contains no filesystem write APIs (CI enforces an fs allowlist), enforces realpath/O_NOFOLLOW path containment, and its answer conventions forbid answering from a stale page — the agent is sent to the superseded_by replacement instead.
bad: Hard-wired to one vault schema (wiki/L1-working, L2-episodic, L3-semantic, L4-procedural, moc) that is not ours; duplicate slugs are silently resolved by sorted walk order; there is deliberately no Unicode normalization, so NFD/NFC filename mismatches fail; pages reachable only through symlinks are invisible; stdio only with no authentication. v0.1.1 of September 2026, single author, catalogue signal ~93 downloads/month.
didnt: Corroboration — the closest external parallel to our MCP read door (read-only verbs, claim packs, supersession-following, containment) built independently; our door already serves our schema with eight verbs, nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @kipachu/omem
good: Obsidian-vault-first memory for AI agents: it indexes vault Markdown in SQLite and fuses keyword, vector (local embeddings after a one-time ~30 MB model download) and wikilink-graph search, served over an MCP server (stdio or HTTP) with optional git auto-sync. Writes are disciplined: note updates carry an expectedHash so stale writes are rejected, superseded notes are archived rather than deleted, and a shared skills store follows the Agent Skills format.
bad: Very young and pre-1.0: first published 2026-07 per the registry record, latest v0.11.2, single maintainer. The README itself warns the HTTP endpoint is open unless OMEM_HTTP_TOKEN is set. Retrieval returns budgeted context with no citation locking and no evidence grading or abstention scoring documented.
didnt: Corroboration — vault-first Markdown memory with hash-checked writes and supersede-don't-delete independently matches our wiki custody rules; nothing in it clears our citation-locking or abstention bar for adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nexus-canon
good: Portable agent memory held in a git repo the user owns: sessions are stored once in a provider-neutral, lossless, append-only canonical format with provenance recorded, translated at the edges for each harness, and pulled back out anywhere; capability artifacts and project knowledge graphs (session-to-file edges plus code graphs, every edge confidence-tagged) ride the same store. The package is dependency-free Node built-ins.
bad: Its core pipeline is automatic capture and sync of harness session files (a watcher daemon runs sync-translate-graph on every change) — the session-transcript ingest pattern our programme has not approved. First published 2026-08 per the registry record, from a single small vendor, and its canonical line is session history rather than evidence-graded knowledge.
didnt: Board — the append-only canon plus provenance contract (store once, translate at the edge, never rewrite the canonical line) is worth keeping on the ideas board, separated from its session auto-capture, which we reject. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: scholar-feed-mcp
good: MCP paper search with ranking and citation tracking: 600k+ CS/AI/ML papers sortable by relevance, proven citation count or rising impact, citation lineage traced forward and backward across a claimed 22M+ edges, with full-text and BibTeX export; the index is updated daily and no API key is required to start.
bad: It is a client for the hosted scholarfeed.org service: anonymous access is capped at 200 calls/month (500/month with a free account key), coverage is arXiv CS/AI/ML only, and each paper's summary and novelty score are LLM-generated by the service rather than source-verified.
didnt: Rejected — a metered hosted index with quotas and service-generated summaries conflicts with our read-the-primary-source rule; the deep-study programme opens papers at their own venues instead. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-zotero
good: Gives an agent four actions over a local Zotero library through Better BibTeX's JSON-RPC server: full-text search returning cite keys, BibTeX export for chosen keys, full metadata/notes/PDF annotations per item, and collection membership; an offline .bib fallback (BIBTEX_PATH) covers times when Zotero is not running.
bad: Built only for the pi agent harness and published out of a subdirectory of a personal dotfiles repository; it requires desktop Zotero with the Better BibTeX plugin running on localhost:23119, and has a single v0.1.0 release.
didnt: Rejected — fit: harness-specific and dependent on a running desktop Zotero, which our wiki pipeline does not use. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bibtex-mcp
good: Fetches BibTeX through Google Scholar's own visible citation-export flow (per-result Scholar id, citation dialog, signed scholar.bib link) and ranks archival journal/conference/publisher records above preprints, following 'All versions' clusters to find the archival version; the README is candid about accuracy limits and ships a deterministic fixture-based stress test.
bad: It works by reverse-engineering Scholar's undocumented HTML flow — fragile by construction — and the README concedes Scholar's exported metadata can be duplicated, incomplete or venue-variant; it states it does not bypass CAPTCHA or rate limits, so the route can close at any time. Single tool, v0.1.0, single maintainer.
didnt: Rejected — citation truth in our system must rest on primary records (Crossref, DOI, publisher pages); a Scholar-scraping route is the opposite direction, however honest its caveats. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: citation-finder-ai-mcp
good: Four MCP tools from MEOK AI Labs: format a citation in APA/MLA/Chicago and other styles, generate a BibTeX entry, parse raw citation text into structured fields, and validate a DOI.
bad: The formatters generate entries purely from caller-supplied title/authors/year/journal with no lookup against any source record — the tool manufactures the citation rather than verifying it. The npm package's own README installs a Python server via pip, and use is metered: free tier 30 calls/day with a paid upgrade at meok.ai.
didnt: Rejected — generating BibTeX from unverified inputs is exactly the failure our citation lockfile exists to prevent; the metered hosted tier is a second disqualifier. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @dpm-tools/mcp-citations
good: Six MCP tools over CrossRef (~120M DOIs) and OpenCitations: DOI metadata lookup, formatting in BibTeX/APA/MLA/Chicago/Harvard, CrossRef search with year range, batch bibliography from up to 20 DOIs, DOI extraction from text, and citation counts; all sources are free public APIs and no API key is required.
bad: A thin wrapper over free APIs our programme can call directly; it formats and fetches metadata but never checks that a cited work supports the claim being made. v0.1.0, single release.
didnt: Corroboration — DOI/CrossRef-first metadata is the same ground-truth route our citation lockfile uses; the wrapper itself adds nothing we lack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-lit-search
good: Merged keyword search across Crossref, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, deduplicated by DOI, returning title/authors/year/venue/citation counts with year filters and citation/date/relevance sorting; batch BibTeX generation reports failed DOIs separately instead of dropping them silently; related works via OpenAlex. All data sources are free public APIs with no key required, behind a polite mailto User-Agent.
bad: Search and formatting only — it performs no field-level or claim-level verification of the records it returns. First published 2026-08 per the registry record; its default citation style (GB/T 7714) targets Chinese theses, and the MCP form lives in a separate companion package.
didnt: Corroboration — multi-source DOI-deduplicated search with failures surfaced separately matches our evidence discipline; the deep-study programme already queries these same APIs directly. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: bibverify-opencode
good: A BibTeX citation metadata verifier: each entry's fields (title, authors, year, journal, volume, number, pages, DOI, publisher) are compared against real records through a staged lookup — DOI to CrossRef, title search in CrossRef, DOI to OpenAlex, title search in OpenAlex — returning scored verdicts (PASS at 85%+, WARN 55–85%, FAIL below 55%) and an explicit NOT FOUND state when no route finds the paper.
bad: Packaged as an OpenCode plugin over a Python runtime whose README install line still carries a YOUR_USERNAME placeholder, and the registry record names no repository or homepage to inspect. Verification covers metadata match only — not whether the paper actually supports the citing claim.
didnt: Board — its staged CrossRef/OpenAlex lookup with cannot-determine as a first-class verdict and field-level scoring is direct design evidence for our honestly-open scholarly citation truth-checking gap. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @ephremyuan/citeagent
good: An OpenCode plugin ('CiteAgent') with 25+ native TypeScript tools: BM25 corpus search, Merkle proof verification of ingested documents, exact passage retrieval for claim-to-evidence audits (cite_node_lookup), an argument graph over claims and contradictions, opt-in DOI/title existence checks through Crossref, CSL rendering, and a 4-tier persistent memory — with a separate hidden verifier subagent that independently audits the Merkle proofs.
bad: Bound to the OpenCode host and pre-1.0 (v0.5.0); document ingestion and OCR depend on optional sidecars (the citeindex CLI, tesseract); the breadth of the claims rests on the README alone.
didnt: Corroboration — Merkle-verified retrieval, claim-to-evidence passage lookup and an independent verifier subagent mirror our citation-lockfile and audit design from an independent project. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @getlore/cli
good: A shared human+agent knowledge substrate ('Lore') built on three primitives — sources as eternal evidence with citations, briefs as versioned, staleness-aware living synthesis per project, and procedures — served identically over MCP (9 tools), CLI and TUI. Working-copy edits in repo-attached .lore/ folders stay proposals until reviewed: changes are applied, discarded or LLM-merge-resolved explicitly, and sync is hash-deduplicated across machines; search is hybrid semantic+keyword with reciprocal rank fusion.
bad: It is an account product: setup requires login (email OTP) and API keys, multi-tenant isolation runs on Postgres row-level security, and canonical truth lives in the Lore service rather than in files the user solely holds — custody is hosted, not local-first. Entity briefs are gated behind a feature flag and much of the stated thesis (scope layers, synthesis cascade) is listed as direction, not shipped.
didnt: Corroboration — sources/briefs/proposals-until-approved independently validates our compiled-wiki plus approval-gated-write architecture; its hosted account custody is exactly where we deliberately differ. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @publisle/research
good: The research profile of the Publisle portable semantic-document standard: it adds citations, publisher templates and LaTeX, JATS and PDF export to Markdown/typed-JSON documents compiled into static articles with optional interactive islands. The monorepo is actively developed (190 commits, 5 releases, dedicated research and PDF-UA test configurations).
bad: In beta by its own badge and README, with 2 stars and a repo created 2026-09; requires Node.js 24+; PDF tooling is installed separately, and the README itself cautions that template availability does not imply journal acceptance or PDF/UA certification. It is article-publishing tooling, not knowledge memory.
didnt: Rejected — scope: a publishing/export standard; our report pipeline already produces PDFs (weasyprint route) and the wiki is the memory layer, not a journal typesetter. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @aimform/knowledge
good: Provider-neutral contracts for evidence-backed memory: validated Spaces Collections as the stable model behind persistence, retrieval and generation; an evidence-backed SynthesizedLearning read model (conclusion, reuse guidance, contributor, attachments, Skill lineage); exact citation-range verification; Accuracy 0–5 policies; deny-by-default promotion rules; append-only ontology expansion; and YAML-compatible OKF projection/import in which OKF stays an interchange projection while authoritative records remain in Collections.
bad: A contracts/model package for the Aimform platform: v0.1.0, a single release (2026-10), and the registry record names no repository or homepage, so the implementation behind the contracts cannot be inspected from the record.
didnt: Corroboration — deny-by-default promotion, exact citation-range verification and accuracy scoring state our approval gates and citation discipline in another project's contract language. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: smartware
good: A local-first, user-owned memory protocol with a TypeScript reference implementation: observations are append-only and chained with SHA-256 integrity metadata; derived claims keep claim-level provenance (source observations, author, extraction method, epistemic status, revision history); memory is bitemporal (valid time and transaction time); retrieval is policy-first — scope, grants, sensitivity, lifecycle and currentness resolve before any semantic search — with freshness-bound indexes that cannot silently participate when stale, deterministic fallback to canonical retrieval, and fail-closed activation of new memory behaviour until held-out evidence passes explicit quality, safety, latency and cost gates. The README reports a 493-test protocol suite and a deterministic retrieval kernel at Hit@1 1.0 with zero forbidden hits.
bad: Beta software by its own status section (the 0.6.x line; package v0.8.0), first published 2026-08 per the registry record; the full protocol-plus-tenant ecosystem (Pods, connector runtime, MCP server packs, per-tenant provisioning) is far heavier than a personal wiki needs, and semantic retrieval remains opt-in and gated off by default.
didnt: Corroboration — evidence-before-inference, claim-level provenance and fail-closed activation independently match our design; its bitemporal model is recorded here as evidence for the owner's gated bi-temporal-fields decision, not adopted by this pass. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @happyvertical/smrt-facts
good: A fact store with provenance and confidence scoring for the SMRT framework: facts are linked to sources carrying per-source credibility (0–1) and to subjects, confidence is recomputed from source volume, credibility, recency and corroboration, and facts evolve through parent–child chains in which a correction or contradiction branch marks the predecessor superseded, with full evolution-chain/tree traversal. Ingest runs 3-zone semantic reconciliation: at 0.85+ similarity an active fact is auto-merged, between 0.60–0.85 a typed decision or AI disambiguation is gated at a conservative 0.75 merge threshold, and below that a new fact is created — uncertainty branches instead of forcing a merge.
bad: Bound to the SMRT framework's ORM/Postgres stack and optional multi-tenancy machinery; the middle reconciliation zone leans on AI disambiguation; and the confidence formula's recency term decays over 10 days, an arbitrary fit for durable knowledge. Fact statuses and merges are database state, not files under the user's sole custody.
didnt: Board — evolution chains with superseded predecessors plus thresholded, uncertainty-branching reconciliation are concrete design evidence for our truth-aware retrieval (supersession) gap, the sharpest open gap in the report's centrepiece. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @agentproto/knowledge
licence: Apache-2.0 — registry license field and the repo LICENSE file agree; CONFLICT AT SOURCE: the registry README's own License section states 'MIT — see LICENSE', contradicting both the metadata and the LICENSE file it points to. Recorded as found; neither side borrowed.
good: AIP-10 KNOWLEDGE.md reference implementation: a filesystem-first knowledge-base format where an LLM curates, links, and lints a markdown wiki layered on top of immutable raw sources, so agent knowledge becomes a compounding artifact instead of a per-query retrieval miss; spec published at agentproto.sh/docs/aip-10.
bad: Self-described '0.1.0-alpha' scaffold: the README states the build() and validate() bodies are TODOs, so the reference implementation is not yet functional; the registry README is a stub (669 chars) with the substance living in the external spec; v0.1.5, first published 2026-06.
didnt: Corroboration — an external spec independently fixing our exact architecture (LLM-curated markdown wiki over immutable raw sources, with lint) confirms the design; the code is an alpha scaffold with TODO bodies, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @agentproto/adapter-knowledge-corpus
good: An IKnowledgeProvider adapter over an AIP-10 corpus workspace that delegates vector/graph queries to any backing engine and hydrates every hit with canonical provenance — entryPath, sourceIds, sourceHashes, kind, status, qualityScore, riskScore and a live temporal-decay score; it enforces the corpus access policy (silently filtering invisible hits, failing closed on unverifiable provenance), architecturally rejects agent-side ingest()/deleteSource() so writes land only via a privileged writer at the end of a candidate-review lifecycle, and supersede() flips an entry to deprecated with a supersededBy link plus a compare-and-swap attestation.
bad: One composition layer inside a large, young protocol ecosystem (@agentproto/knowledge-engine, @agentproto/corpus, AIP-10/AIP-18) — it does nothing without adopting that stack; pre-1.0 (v0.4.3, first published 2026-07); its provenance is entry/source-hash metadata, not citation-locked page evidence.
didnt: Corroboration — provenance-hydrated hits, fail-closed visibility, supersession-with-attestation, and write-gating behind a review lifecycle independently confirm our citation, provenance and approval-gated-write design; ecosystem-bound, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @kindgi/crypto
good: Focused cryptographic primitives with zero runtime dependencies beyond Node built-ins: Ed25519 signatures for asymmetric use (signed audit bundles, provenance exports, deployment attestations) and HMAC-SHA256 for symmetric use (webhook payloads, incl. Standard Webhooks signatures, with timing-safe verification); keys move as raw bytes end-to-end with PEM/base64 serializers, typed Result errors for caller-recoverable failures, and a caller-provided SigningKeyBinding — the framework never persists or generates key material itself.
bad: A narrow two-algorithm library tied to the young Kindgi SDK ecosystem (first published 2026-10, v0.1.x); browser use is only 'possible' — the implementation targets Node's crypto module; and both algorithms are commodity standard-library capabilities, so the value-add is packaging rather than capability.
didnt: Rejected — Ed25519 and HMAC-SHA256 are directly available from Node's built-in crypto, and our hash-chained ledger and attestation machinery need no external dependency for them; adopting a v0.1.x ecosystem library would add custody risk without adding capability. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dkg-notebook-memory
good: Moves explicitly cell-selected Jupyter findings into a private DKG v10 Working Memory with provenance retained (source cell, content digest, author label, status, tags) and verified readback in later sessions; the plan step is entirely offline and shows the exact outgoing triples before any push, changed findings become new revisions while older findings remain readable, unselected cells/outputs are excluded, and no notebook code is ever executed; hard limits (2 MiB notebook, 100 selected cells, 32 KiB per cell) are stated in the README.
bad: Requires a running DKG v10 node, an existing Context Graph and its bearer token — an external decentralised-graph stack we do not run; the README itself states it is 'a bounty submission candidate, not an accepted or rewarded integration', developed with AI assistance, single author, v0.1.2 published on one day (2026-09-24); finding statuses are author-supplied labels, explicitly not verification claims, and writes are serial, not transactional.
didnt: Board — board the interaction pattern for our ingest design: explicit per-item selection, an offline plan that previews the exact records before writing, and revision-instead-of-overwrite for changed findings; the DKG-node dependency and bounty-candidate maturity keep it from adoption. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @sporhq/spor
good: A shared memory substrate for teams and agents that stores decisions, rejected approaches, open questions, project norms, tasks and incidents — and their reasons — as a small typed graph (this decision supersedes that one; this task is blocked by this issue; this correction should affect future briefings); it compiles session-start briefings and per-prompt digests from the graph with links back to the source nodes, captures context at discovery, distils session ends into durable nodes, and runs fully locally with no database or server for single-user use; a briefing is itself a stored graph node that can be reviewed, corrected, versioned and rebuilt.
bad: Aimed at coding agents and teams, with a hosted product and live team-sharing server as the growth path — much of the surface (CLI, hook dispatcher, REST API) is coding-session tooling rather than personal knowledge custody; 'Spor'/'sporhq' are reserved trademarks despite the Apache-2.0 code licence; young and fast-moving (first published 2026-06, already v0.31.9).
didnt: Corroboration — a typed decision graph with supersedes edges and briefings compiled from, and linked back to, graph nodes independently confirms our supersession and compiled-briefing design; team/coding-session scope, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @dashiro/tacitus-mcp-server
good: An MCP server that turns any folder of plain Markdown notes into long-term agent memory with provenance: every fact carries its source and is returned within a token budget, contradictions are surfaced rather than silently resolved, search returns ranked snippets (never whole notes) with progressive disclosure (outline, then frontmatter, then full), and write-back is propose-a-changeset, preview the diff, commit atomically, revert by version — with read-only scopes forbidding mutation and every write audited to a JSONL log; local-first, no telemetry, no account.
bad: This npm package is the reduced 16-tool core: the flagship features (25 tools, end-to-end encrypted multi-device CRDT sync) ship only in a separate native binary via GitHub Releases, so the npm artefact is not the full system; very young (first published 2026-07, v0.1.2, single maintainer); the default embedder is a deterministic offline approximation, with neural embeddings an opt-in extra dependency.
didnt: Corroboration — provenance-carrying memory, surfaced contradictions, token-budgeted retrieval and changeset-preview/atomic-commit/revert write-back independently confirm our citation, abstention and approval-gated-write design; it is a parallel implementation, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @lionhummer/agent-memory
good: A framework-independent TypeScript memory engine that treats memory as a lifecycle: a model proposes durable facts, and code — not the model — validates source IDs, category policy, trusted authors and tenant/user/workspace/project/thread scope before anything is stored with provenance; corrections supersede prior versions with lineage exposed, recall assembles a bounded, inspectable context bundle inside a caller-supplied token budget, and human-source-required categories stop agent instructions or group chatter from hardening into personal facts; consolidation is policy-gated and compare-and-swap concurrency keeps replays idempotent.
bad: v0.1.0 and days old (first published 2026-10-11, a single release); storage is one JSON snapshot per tenant/user, so the SQLite store's reads and writes scale with total retained state and there is no automatic archival or pruning; extraction quality rests entirely on the caller's model, and the README itself concedes that source attribution does not prove a cited message entails a proposed fact.
didnt: Corroboration — code-enforced scope and attribution policy, supersede-don't-edit corrections, and bounded inspectable recall independently confirm our provenance and approval-gating design; at v0.1.0 it is far too young to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @refract-org/analyzers
good: Deterministic analyzers for public revision histories — byte-for-byte reproducible, no model involved: section extraction and diffing between revisions, citation extraction/diffing with source lineage, revert and revert-chain detection, template tracking, heuristic edit classification, borrowed-text propagation detection via n-gram similarity, citation-network concentration/diversity metrics, and semantic-enrichment signals (certainty profile, direction signal, edit magnitude, quantitative-findings extraction), all as pure library functions that run in Node, Bun or a Worker.
bad: Built for Wikipedia-style wikitext revision histories — the domain model (reverts, talk-page signals, BLP and neutrality templates) is a public wiki's, not a personal knowledge base's; AGPL-3.0 makes the code ideas-only for us; the documented workflows lean on the wider refract ecosystem (e.g. @refract-org/evidence-graph).
didnt: Board — board the deterministic, no-model analyzer ideas for our citation machinery: citation-change events with source lineage over revision pairs, and certainty-profile/direction signals as evidence features; AGPL-3.0, so ideas only, and wikitext-specific, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @svforge/graph
good: A drop-in SvelteKit component rendering an interactive, Obsidian-style force-directed knowledge graph: group-based automatic coloring from a stable hash palette, labels on hover or always, zoom/pan, reactive data updates, click/hover callbacks, and client-only dynamic import with stated deployment profiles (long-lived node, serverless, edge, separate worker — all supported).
bad: Visualization only — no storage, schema, provenance or integrity checking; hard-bound to SvelteKit/Svelte, which our Lens is not built on; a small, young package (first published 2026-09, ~210 downloads/month at catalogue time).
didnt: Rejected — a graph view is a commodity rendering layer, and this one is SvelteKit-only; our Lens renders its own views, and nothing here touches custody, citation or abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @mastra/longmemeval
licence: Apache-2.0 — the registry metadata states no licence at all; the LICENSE.md shipped inside the published package places all content outside ee/ directories under Apache License 2.0, and this package ships no ee/ content. Recorded as found from the artefact itself.
good: A complete LongMemEval harness for Mastra Memory: it runs the benchmark's 500 questions across the five long-term-memory abilities (information extraction, multi-session reasoning, knowledge updates, temporal reasoning, abstention) with automatic dataset download from HuggingFace, configurable memory modes (last-k, semantic-recall, working-memory), parallel runs with progress saving and graceful shutdown, and CLI stats/evaluate/report commands over stored results.
bad: It is a benchmark runner for Mastra's own stack, not a memory system: it wires @mastra/memory, @mastra/core, OpenAI/Google API keys and a HuggingFace token into scoring Mastra, so its numbers measure their system and say nothing portable about ours; the dependency tree is heavy (the full Mastra + AI SDK stack), and the package ships with no licence in its registry metadata at all.
took: Nothing taken from this Mastra package itself; what our programme took came from the LongMemEval benchmark directly — Tier-1 record: 'Built (marathon records): LongMemEval five-ability template with session decomposition + fact-augmented keys' (lane8-dispositions.md, Round 3 lane TB6).
didnt: Rejected — a vendor's benchmark harness for its own memory stack; our evaluation already takes LongMemEval itself as the template, and running Mastra's scorer against Mastra Memory would measure their system, not ours. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @anthropic-ai/mcpb
good: Anthropic's official MCP Bundle toolchain and specification: an .mcpb bundle is a zip holding a local MCP server plus a manifest.json describing it, enabling single-click installation in Claude for macOS and Windows; the package provides the manifest spec and schemas, a CLI (init/pack guided creation), and the host-side code Claude uses to load and verify bundles, with end-user features such as automatic updates and guided configuration of server variables.
bad: Distribution packaging for desktop MCP hosts, not knowledge machinery: it solves installing servers for end users, only works in host apps implementing the MCPB spec, and is mid-rename from DXT (format, CLI and package names all changed), so the surface is still moving; ~603k downloads/month reflect Claude Desktop's ecosystem, not wiki relevance.
didnt: Rejected — our MCP door is a local stdio server we run ourselves; bundle packaging for third-party desktop distribution sits outside the personal wiki's scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory
licence: MIT (registry license field defers to the package LICENSE file — 'SEE LICENSE IN LICENSE'; the README's License section states the MIT License)
good: The reference MCP memory server from the modelcontextprotocol project: a local knowledge graph of entities (name, type, observations), directed relations in active voice, and atomic observations, with tools to create/search/open/delete and a memory://knowledge-graph resource that emits live update notifications to subscribed clients; local file custody, no account, and both current and previous MCP protocol eras served over stdio from one process.
bad: Self-described in its own README as 'a basic implementation': observations are bare strings with no provenance, sourcing, supersession or versioning; search is substring matching over names, types and observation text; there is no abstention, citation-locking or approval machinery at all, and it now requires Node.js 24.
didnt: Corroboration — the entity/relation/observation graph is the canonical minimal shape our memory layer generalises, and its stated limits (no provenance, no supersession) mark exactly what our design adds; this is already-have ground, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-server-memory
good: A Bun-based derivative of the reference @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory offering the same local knowledge-graph memory — entities, relations and observations persisted to a knowledge_graph.json file — with the memory file path configurable via MEMORY_FILE_PATH.
bad: A personal fork 'modified for my specific needs' (its README's own words) with a single publish day (2025-04-04) and no later release; the registry README is literally unfinished, ending with the placeholder '...[rest of existing content remains unchanged...]'; ~129 downloads/month and no capability beyond the upstream reference server.
didnt: Rejected — an unmaintained single-author fork of the reference memory server with placeholder documentation; the upstream original is the one that matters, and we already cover that ground ourselves. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-knowledge-graph
good: Persistent local memory for AI models as a knowledge graph (entities, relations, observations in JSONL files) with a deliberate safety discipline: every memory file must begin with an _aim marker line and the server refuses to write to files lacking it, guarding against overwriting unrelated JSONL; project-local stores are auto-detected via an .aim directory, a master database is always available, and optional named databases split memory by context (work, personal, health).
bad: Keyword search and whole-store reads only — no provenance, sourcing, supersession or ranking; consistency is left to the model, and the README itself warns that models create near-duplicate databases and facts can land in unexpected locations; single-author project, last published 2025-12.
didnt: Board — board the file-safety-marker idea: a store that refuses writes to any file not carrying the system's own header marker is a cheap custody tripwire in the spirit of our safeguards; the server itself duplicates the reference memory shape without provenance or citation machinery, so it is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wikirefs
good: A spec-driven TypeScript utility library for [[wikirefs]]: scan() parses wikilinks/embeds/attrs with positions, buildHTML() renders canonical link/embed/attr HTML with display precedence (label > title > filename) and an explicit invalid state for unresolved refs, and mkdnToWiki() converts markdown links to wikirefs. The syntax contract is written down in a spec folder in its repo (wikibonsai/wikirefs).
bad: Still pre-1.0 (latest 0.0.14) with a broad, still-evolving API surface, and its full feature set assumes the WikiBonsai ecosystem — typed links/attrs and the caml-mkdn attrbox hand-off — rather than a plain wikilink vault; the README documents no tests or evaluation of its own.
didnt: Rejected — GPL-3.0 is ideas-only under licence discipline, and the capability duplicates our own: the Lens and our search already parse [[wikilinks]] in-house (the catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict stands). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @basicmemory/openclaw-basic-memory
good: The OpenClaw plugin for Basic Memory: agent memory stored as plain local Markdown files indexed into a semantic knowledge graph (SQLite, local), with composited memory_search across MEMORY.md text search, hybrid full-text + vector graph search, and active-task files in parallel; auto-capture writes each conversation turn into daily notes and auto-recall injects active tasks at session start. Human and agent read and write the same files; cloud sync is optional.
bad: It is a host plugin, not a standalone system: it requires the OpenClaw agent host plus the separate Basic Memory CLI (installed via uv, auto-installed on first startup), so the memory model is inherited from the parent project rather than defined here. The README states no citation locking, abstention, or approval gating for agent writes — auto-capture and auto-recall are on by default.
didnt: Corroboration — local-first plain-Markdown custody with a traversable knowledge graph and files the owner can read and edit directly independently matches our custody model; the plugin itself targets the OpenClaw host, which we do not run, and adds no locking, abstention, or approval machinery over our own memory layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @zosmaai/pi-llm-wiki
good: A self-maintaining Karpathy-pattern wiki for the Pi harness (also exposed via a stdio MCP server): immutable source capture of URLs/PDFs/markup into source bundles, automated ingest into concept/entity/synthesis pages, full-text search over a generated registry, mechanical lint (orphans, broken links, duplicate aliases, coverage gaps, stale captures), layered recall across a personal ~/.llm-wiki vault and per-project vaults, native OKF v0.2 documents with deterministic index/log generation, and guardrails that block direct edits to raw sources and generated metadata.
bad: It is bound to the Pi / oh-my-pi harness ecosystem (other hosts only via its MCP server), and the wiki is agent-maintained end-to-end: the README describes no scored abstention, citation locking, or approval gate before the agent's ingest writes land — maintenance quality rests on the harness model and its lint pass.
didnt: Corroboration — immutable source capture, edit guardrails on raw sources and generated metadata, and deterministic lint independently reproduce three of our load-bearing design choices; it is a Pi-harness product with no abstention or approval-gated writes, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: easymem
good: An agent-written local markdown wiki with deliberately no model and no database inside: the coding agent writes the pages, easymem provides storage, BM25 full-text search plus one-hop [[link]] traversal (a page that never mentions the query is still surfaced when a hit links to it), and a fixed page format. Extracted, per its README, from TencentDB-Agent-Memory's MemoryKnowledge engine — mixed Chinese/English tokenizer, multi-hop graph search, page format — behind a small CLI/MCP surface; output is plain git-committable markdown.
bad: The engine's discipline is only as strong as the skill file the agent follows — the README itself says prompt-only versions of this pattern produced differently-shaped pages daily — and retrieval is BM25-plus-one-hop only: no citation locking, no abstention, no approval gate, and no evaluation results are published in the README.
didnt: Corroboration — compile-don't-retrieve storage with BM25 + one-hop link traversal and a fixed page shape independently matches our index-first retrieval and schema discipline; it is a retrieval/storage shell without locking, abstention, or approval machinery, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @tymolu/llmwiki
good: An agent-first Karpathy-pattern vault engine with three surfaces — CLI (init/status/index/lint/search), a stdio MCP server with 7 atomic tools, and bundled librarian skill files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) — over plain CommonMark files with raw/ immutable sources and wiki/ entities, concepts and syntheses. Deterministic housekeeping reconciles index.md and detects broken links/orphans without LLM tokens; writes use atomic temp-file renames with path-containment validation, and init never overwrites existing agent files (it appends an isolated section).
bad: Early-stage (latest 0.2.0, single-author project) and functionally a subset of the pattern we already run: search is its own index lookup with no scored abstention, no citation locking, and no approval gate on agent writes; the README publishes no evaluation or scale evidence.
didnt: Rejected — a younger, smaller re-implementation of the same Karpathy pattern our stack already exceeds (citation locking, scored abstention, approval-gated writes); its atomic-write and non-destructive-init care are conventions we already hold. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @dhague/wiki-knowledge
good: The most heavily engineered package in this wave: clean-room ingestion and retrieval over a git-backed markdown vault where everything deterministic is a script, not a prompt — a single TypeScript bundle (enchiridion) does vault I/O, page placement, SQLite FTS5 indexing and commit construction with no model calls. Retrieval answers with typed-edge graph traversal and cited synthesis; derived pages trace to raw sources through an evidence chain, with bitemporal metadata (knowledge date vs written date) and volatility annotations making staleness visible. Its 20-check vault lint grades every fix auto-fix / report-only / confirm-first, and concept consolidations are assessed against one committed snapshot and refused if the cluster changed before the write.
bad: Retrieval quality leans on host-model subagents (Sonnet for ingestion judgement, Haiku for retrieval on Claude Code), so behaviour varies by host; it is a single-author project (9 stars) despite its release cadence, and there is no scored abstention — /wiki-ask always synthesises an answer from the vault.
didnt: Board — the consolidation-exclusion registry: declined merge proposals remembered in a committed YAML registry keyed by git blob OID plus a semantic fingerprint (title, summary, typed relationships, supersedes, body), so a declined consolidation is never re-proposed while content is unchanged and quietly lapses when it changes; its lint fix levels (auto-fix / report-only / confirm-first) are the same triage shape. Its bitemporal + volatility staleness surfacing also corroborates our provenance-chain design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @jackwener/llm-wiki
good: A CLI + agent-skill implementation of the Karpathy pattern: llm-wiki init scaffolds a vault with purpose/schema files, an append-only wiki-log.md, immutable date-partitioned sources/, and dual agent bootstrap files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) plus an on-demand skill playbook; operations are /ingest, /query (with write-back of valuable answers), /lint (broken links, orphans, contradictions, stale content) and /research. Search is BM25 with CJK bigram tokenization, plus graph analysis (communities, hubs, orphans, wanted pages) and SHA-256 sync tracking with optional DB9 vector search.
bad: The tool itself never calls an LLM — all judgement is delegated to whichever agent follows the skill file — and there is no citation locking, scored abstention, or approval gate: /query write-backs and /lint auto-fixes land without a human checkpoint. Vector search depends on an external DB9/PostgreSQL service, and the registry record was last modified in April 2026.
didnt: Rejected — a competent generic implementation of the pattern we already run, minus the three mechanisms that define our stack (citation locking, scored abstention, approval-gated writes); nothing in its README exceeds our in-house machinery. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @jupiterthewarlock/llm-wiki
good: A derivative of @jackwener/llm-wiki (its README says so explicitly) carrying the same vault shape — wiki/ pages, date-partitioned immutable sources/, purpose/schema/agent files, append-only wiki-log.md, dual Claude/Codex skill installs — with BM25 search, optional DB9 vector search merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion, wikilink graph analysis (communities, hubs, orphans, wanted pages), mtime + SHA-256 sync tracking, and six agent operations (/ingest, /query, /lint, /research, /enrich, /graph).
bad: A re-implementation of another wave item rather than an independent design: it inherits that design's absence of citation locking, scored abstention, and approval-gated writes, and adds only the RRF merge and /enrich on top. Single-author, and its vector path likewise depends on an external DB9/PostgreSQL service.
didnt: Rejected — a fork-lineage copy of @jackwener/llm-wiki with the same gaps against our stack (no citation locking, no abstention, no approval gates); counted as a separate package studied, not as independent corroboration of the design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-okf
good: A two-tier OKF (Open Knowledge Format) project-memory bundle: raw/ is immutable, concept pages are compiled from raw rather than from wiki text to prevent drift, and a query-first discipline requires the agent to read index.md before answering any memory question, falling back to raw only when the wiki is silent. Every factual page must carry a sources field tracing to raw/, contradictions surface as a diff the skill asks about before resolving, every page must be linked from a non-index page, and bundled Python tooling (okf_search/ingest/update/diff/status/lint/index) treats lint errors as hard stops; every ingest/update is a git commit.
bad: The discipline is enforced by a skill file the model is instructed to follow, not by machinery — nothing technically prevents an agent from skipping the index or writing without sources — and there is no scored abstention or citation locking beyond the sources-field convention.
didnt: Corroboration — mandatory index-first consultation, per-page sources tracing to immutable raw, and ask-before-resolving-contradictions independently match our index-first protocol, citation discipline, and approval posture; enforcement is prompt-level where ours is mechanical, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-stack
good: An Obsidian knowledge-base compiler distributed as five Claude Code skill commands (/kb-init, /wiki-compile, /wiki-topic, /wiki-lint, plus a status surface) over a three-layer vault (01 raw/ the LLM never edits, 02 wiki/ concept network, 03 outputs/). Notable disciplines: a concept independence test (definability, single core, multi-source) before any concept earns a page, concept evolution that appends rather than overwrites and archives superseded understandings with timestamps (conflicts kept side-by-side in a 'Different Perspectives' section), and cross-reference integrity checks (every claim linked to its raw source, bidirectional links verified each compile).
bad: It is skills and prompts only — the registry record names no repository and ships no engine, tests, or retrieval machinery of its own — and every discipline (independence test, never-overwrite, link integrity) is Claude-Code-prompt-level, dependent on the model following instructions inside Obsidian/Claude Code. No citation locking, abstention, or approval gate exists beyond the human reading outputs/.
didnt: Rejected — prompt-only packaging of the same pattern with no machinery to take; its concept-evolution rule (append, archive-with-timestamp, conflicts side-by-side) restates our supersession discipline in weaker, unenforced form. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @alekra1/llm-wiki
good: A zero-tooling markdown wiki template for agent memory: npx scaffolds a wiki/ tree (decisions, preferences, workflows, pitfalls, architecture, index.md, append-only log.md) into a project without overwriting existing files, plus entry-point files for Claude Code, Codex/OpenAI Agents, Gemini and Cursor, and a Claude Code plugin adding /wiki-update, /wiki-snapshot and /wiki-lint. Its signature convention is _snapshot.md — a ~300-token current-state page the agent reads first every session via a SessionStart hook — with a Stop hook that reminds when the session's work was never logged.
bad: A scaffold and conventions, not an engine: no search or retrieval machinery, no source capture or immutable raw layer, no citation or approval discipline — memory quality rests entirely on the agent honouring HOWTO.md conventions, and the hooks/slash commands are Claude-Code-only (other providers get file reads alone).
didnt: Rejected — a session-memory template whose snapshot-first convention is a lighter form of our standing context files; it has no knowledge machinery (retrieval, locking, abstention, gates) to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @autocut-cli/llm-wiki
good: A local, citation-aware wiki builder with the strongest governance posture in this wave: builds run only over an explicitly approved project scope (non-interactive init requires --yes plus explicit --select values), git scope verification fails closed (GIT_SCOPE_UNAVAILABLE / SOURCE_SCOPE_CHANGED / SOURCE_SCOPE_RECONFIRM_REQUIRED) rather than widening traversal, and the MCP surface is a single read-only tool (wiki_explore) — agents querying over MCP cannot mutate the wiki, which only the management CLI builds, into immutable generations with resumable batched commits. Provider credentials are accepted only via stdin or a system credential store, never in arguments or files, and semantic retrieval (off by default) requires a separate embedding profile and credential from the generation profile.
bad: Young and small (latest 0.2.0), Node 24+ only, and its guarantees guard the build scope rather than answer quality: there is no scored abstention, and enabling semantic retrieval sends a length-bounded evidence excerpt to the chosen external embedding provider, which the README discloses but cannot prevent.
didnt: Corroboration — explicitly approved source scope, fail-closed scope verification, a read-only single-tool MCP door, credentials-by-stdin/keyring, and immutable generations independently reproduce our approval-gated writes, read-door, and custody design almost point for point; it is a young single-purpose builder, so the design is corroborated, not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @codemeall/harness-wiki
good: Skill-first scaffolding for an agent-maintained markdown vault (raw/ immutable sources; wiki/ entities, concepts, sources, syntheses; index.md; append-only log.md; schema carried in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), installed as a portable skill with optional MCP/CLI accelerators for deterministic scaffold/status operations while ingest/query/lint stay agent-driven. Its distinguishing idea is a wedge: the vault registers the sibling project repos it serves (vault_link), so the wiki holds the why, repos hold the what, and a companion bridge file holds current work — with a vault_doctor health check flagging stale source pages (raw changed since ingest) and broken project links.
bad: The registry record names no repository of its own, the package is at 0.3.2 with the smallest download signal in the wave, and the vault↔repo link is a registry convention rather than enforced machinery; there is no citation locking, scored abstention, or approval gate on the agent-driven ingest/query/lint loop.
didnt: Rejected — another skill-first scaffold of the pattern we already run; the wiki↔repo↔bridge split is a filing convention our wiki + goal workspaces already embody, and there is no machinery over our stack to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-wiki
good: A Pi-harness wiki extension layering Karpathy's pattern on Ar9av's obsidian-wiki framework: /wiki-ingest (MD/HTML/JSON/PDF/URL into immutable sources/ with a .manifest.json of tracked source hashes), /wiki-query (keyword + semantic), /wiki-lint (orphans, broken links, stale), crosslink and taxonomy commands, graph export (JSON/HTML/GraphML), and bidirectional sync with an existing Obsidian vault or its own built-in vault; pages follow a fixed frontmatter schema (type, tags, sources, provenance marker, aliases).
bad: Pi-only ('Multi-agent: pi only' in its own comparison table), and several headline capabilities are self-described as Planned rather than shipped — the cross-linker, tag taxonomy audit, and QMD semantic search; PDF/DOCX/semantic support all ride on optional external installs. No citation locking, scored abstention, or approval gate is described.
didnt: Rejected — a Pi-harness skin over another framework with key features still planned; nothing in it exceeds our in-house wiki machinery, and its host lock-in is the opposite of our local door design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @sidleo3/pi-wiki
good: Pi (earendil-works) coding-agent extension that embeds the shared llm-wiki-core and registers the same 14 wiki_* tools as its sibling shells over one OKF v0.2 markdown bundle (default ~/.agents/wiki): list/search/get with automatic backlinks, create/update gated on the directory's AGENTS.md rules with human-verified marking, validate/lint (broken links, orphans, stale pages, missing index), ingest that copies sources without modifying them, deprecate-instead-of-delete, and git/Feishu sync that merges log.md by union and stops with a conflict list rather than force-pushing. A before_agent_start hook re-reads each directory's APPEND_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md every turn, so rule edits take effect immediately.
bad: A host shell, not a standalone wiki: usable only inside the Pi agent, pre-1.0 (v0.7.2, first published 2026-09-07), and the npm metadata carries no repository or homepage field, so the record points nowhere for source or issues. The README is Chinese-only, and the Feishu cloud-drive sync path depends on the external lark-cli tool and its identity state.
didnt: Rejected — a Pi-host shell over the shared core already studied at Tier 1 (@sidleo3/llm-wiki-core); the shell adds only a host binding we do not run, and nothing in it is missing from our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @sidleo3/dsh-wiki
good: DeepSeek Harness plugin embedding the same vendor-core as the other sidleo3 shells: 14 wiki_* tools over one shared OKF v0.2 bundle, two-layer prompt injection (a byte-constant tool guide that never breaks provider prefix caches, plus a per-session snapshot of bundle rules), named multi-bundle directories with session- or global-level switching, write gating read from each directory's AGENTS.md with human confirmation, git sync that never force-pushes, a Feishu backend with three-way incremental sync and an explicitly designed true-delete (both sides together, named paths only, dry-run by default, refuses when the other side has unsynced changes), optional timed autosync for the Feishu backend only, and a graphical settings surface. The README documents an extensive offline contract-test suite for the host bundle format.
bad: Bound to the DeepSeek Harness host and its release-candidate client contract (developed against DSH 0.1.7-rc.2 to 0.2.1-rc.2; a wrong engines range silently skips the whole bundle), pre-1.0 (v0.7.5), and the npm metadata carries no repository or homepage field. The Feishu sync path puts the bundle in a cloud drive via the external lark-cli — the opposite direction from our local-first custody.
didnt: Rejected — a DeepSeek-Harness host shell over the Tier-1-studied core; we run no DSH host, and its cloud-drive sync conflicts with local-first custody. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @sidleo3/codex-wiki
good: Codex plugin form of the sidleo3 suite: a bundled wiki skill, the same 14 wiki_* MCP tools (same names, parameters and outputs as the DSH/Pi forms), SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hooks that inject the current bundle's APPEND_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md rules and refresh only when content changes, and the shared registry at ~/.agents/wiki-registry.json so all five forms read and write one bundle. Zero runtime dependencies — the vendor-core and a lightweight stdio MCP transport are embedded in the package.
bad: Pre-1.0 (v0.7.2, only 3 versions since 2026-09-21) and installation is a manual local-marketplace procedure (symlink the package into ~/plugins and edit marketplace.json); the npm metadata carries no repository or homepage field. Per its own comparison table it lacks the DSH form's graphical settings and timed autosync, and non-managed hooks must be reviewed and trusted in the host before first run. Write gating lives in the shared core's AGENTS.md-rule reading with agent-mediated confirmation — there is no approval ledger.
didnt: Rejected — a Codex-host shell over the Tier-1-studied core; our Codex door is deliberately read-only, and this plugin's write path (hook-injected rules, conversational confirmation) does not meet our approval-gated write model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @sidleo3/mcp-wiki
good: Standalone MCP server (stdio) exposing the sidleo3 suite's 14 wiki_* tools to any MCP host — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex — with the same names, parameters and output text as the plugin forms, verified by a byte-for-byte parity test against the DSH plugin. Local-only by design: no ports, and no network except the explicit wiki_sync (external git or lark-cli; the core stores no tokens); logs go only to stderr so stdout stays pure JSON-RPC. Rules reach the model through four redundant channels: initialize instructions, the wiki_rules tool, rules appended to get/create/update responses, and context attached after a bundle switch.
bad: Pre-1.0 (v0.7.2); the npm metadata carries no repository or homepage field, and the README states no licence section (the licence rests on the registry field alone). Rules delivered via initialize instructions are one-shot — after a rule change the host must reconnect or call wiki_rules — and bundle switching is process-level rather than session-level. Its write tools (create/update/deprecate/sync) are gated only by the core's conversational confirmation, with no approval ledger and no abstention scoring.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent stdio MCP door over a file wiki, with cross-host tool parity enforced by byte-for-byte tests, confirms our MCP read-door design; not adopted because its write side is ungated by any approval ledger and it would duplicate our existing door over a different bundle format. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-plugin-wiki-skills
good: DeepSeek Harness plugin packaging the claude-obsidian-derived knowledge-suite skills — wiki, wiki-ingest, wiki-query, wiki-lint and save, plus think, obsidian-markdown, obsidian-bases and defuddle — mounted on the host's skill registry as a read-only bundled provider with explicit attribution (ORIGINAL_LICENSE bundled; the adaptation changes are documented). Malformed skill frontmatter fails loud at discovery instead of silently skipping a skill, and bundled-rank registration means project, runtime and user skills of the same name win over this suite.
bad: Prompt-only skills with no mechanics of their own: the upstream product scripts (transport detection, wiki-mode, vault locking, address allocation) are explicitly not bundled, so the suite does nothing without the companion dsh-plugin-wiki-tools package and a DeepSeek Harness host. It is a twice-adapted derivative (claude-obsidian's v1-era skills via a ZCode adaptation), small and young (v0.2.2, 4 versions, last modified 2026-08-27).
didnt: Rejected — DeepSeek-Harness prompt skills duplicating our own wiki skill set, derived from claude-obsidian rather than original work, and inert without a host we do not run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-plugin-wiki-tools
good: Native DeepSeek Harness tools implementing the mechanical core under the wiki skill suite: wiki_query (a quick mode returning hot.md + index.md, or full-text search with snippets and the inbound/outbound link graph), wiki_write (one page with complete bookkeeping — type-to-folder routing, frontmatter completion that preserves the created field and unknown fields, a vault-wide filename-uniqueness guard, master-index and log entries, and source-hash delta tracking that skips unchanged sources), and wiki_lint (duplicate filenames, dead wikilinks, orphan pages, frontmatter gaps, stale index entries, stale hot cache), which is report-only and writes a dated Lint Report file with suggestions instead of editing content. An independent plain-ESM implementation containing no claude-obsidian code or skill text.
bad: Works only inside DeepSeek Harness against an explicitly configured vault path (boot fails loud until vaultPath is set), and the tools read and write the host-local vault through node:fs outside any session workspace by design — cross-project referencing is the point, so there is no sandbox boundary. Writes carry no approval gate; bookkeeping correctness is the only control. Young and small (v0.14.2, last modified 2026-09-09).
didnt: Corroboration — the split between prompt-level skills and a native mechanical core, and a lint that only ever writes a dated report and never content, confirm our own scripts-plus-skills and lint-lanes design; the package itself is DSH-host-bound and ungated for writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @djolex999/vir-cli
good: CLI that builds a Karpathy-style LLM wiki retroactively from your own Claude Code and Codex session transcripts: it filters out workflow, subagent and headless noise (every skip is logged with a reason and is reversible), classifies survivors with a cheap model, and distills durable notes (patterns, gotchas, decisions, tools) with confidence scores in frontmatter, dropping anything scoring 0.6 or below before the expensive step. Notes embed into one vector space (Ollama, with a TF-IDF fallback) behind vir query and an MCP server; lessons recurring across three or more sessions become proposed rules quoted verbatim from their source notes (quotes absent from the note are discarded), and reach CLAUDE.md only through a per-rule yes in vir sync-claude, which shows a diff first. Dry-run cost estimates precede any spend, a local cost log reports actuals, and output is plain local-first markdown (1,411 tests claimed passing).
bad: Premised on reading agent session transcripts — an ingest source our programme has not approved — and on paid LLM calls for classification and distillation (mitigated, not removed, by the dry-run estimates). macOS/Linux only; Claude Code and Codex sessions only (Cursor planned); archived Codex threads are out of reach; and new Codex projects distill nothing until manually included. Its quality evidence is the author's own machine numbers (396 sessions) in the README.
didnt: Rejected — its input is session-transcript ingest, which is unapproved in our system, and its per-rule approval applies to CLAUDE.md sync, not to the vault writes themselves; the platform and provider scope fit a coding-agent desktop workflow, not our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @kybird/llm-wiki
good: LLM-friendly knowledge graph plus a file-based kanban for AI coding agents: raw daily logs (docs/raw) are the source of truth, an LLM compile step promotes cases into wiki pages (concepts, patterns, anti-patterns, answers) carrying active/deprecated/superseded status, and search always merges grep with optional local QMD semantic results. Its lint performs evidence back-matching — hash references and quoted error strings on wiki pages must exist verbatim in docs/raw — alongside broken-link, uncompiled-concept and staleness checks. The kanban half is a disciplined unattended work queue: atomic card claiming with WIP limits and claim expiry, handoff-to-human parking, mandatory reasons for abandonment (auto-logged as anti-pattern material), post-hoc verdicts on terminated cards, and a read-only live board monitor whose server rejects every non-GET method.
bad: A very large surface for a wiki tool: the intelligence lives in LLM-prompt skills, so behaviour depends on the driving agent, and the board/work-loop machinery (claims, milestones, scope seals, a fleet monitor, timelapse video) is a coding-agent work queue, not knowledge custody. Semantic search needs the optional @tobilu/qmd dependency and a roughly 300 MB model download; the package is pre-1.0 (v0.7.0, first published 2026-08-29); and parts of the README and monitor UI are Korean-only.
didnt: Corroboration — evidence back-matching in lint (every hash reference and quoted error must exist verbatim in the raw layer) and the raw-logs-as-truth to compiled-wiki flow independently confirm our citation-truth checking and raw/wiki layering; the kanban work-loop half is a different product from our knowledge OS and is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-canvas
good: Local-first visual compiler for markdown knowledge bases: it compiles Markdown, YAML frontmatter and WikiLinks into a deterministic relationship graph (stable node and edge IDs, so fixtures and git diffs are meaningful) and regenerates editable Obsidian Canvas and Excalidraw files while preserving human node positions, annotations and hand-drawn links. It checks OKF v0.2 trust signals (source, verification, freshness, lifecycle) into the graph without turning them into opaque scores, and surfaces broken or ambiguous links, missing titles and orphan pages with exact paths. It deliberately builds in no LLM, vector database, chat UI, cloud service or MCP server. Its Drafts flow registers a source with a snapshot and SHA-256, lets an agent edit only an isolated draft, and shows provenance, hash checks and blocking reasons before anything reaches the existing proposal review gate; Changes shows each proposal's status, full hashes, exact diff and affected pages and links, without the UI itself executing apply.
bad: Extremely young: v0.2.0, two versions, created and last modified on the same day (2026-08-14), with 32 downloads per month in the catalogue signal. It requires Node.js 22 or 24; the bundled example vaults are synthetic fixtures rather than real-user evidence (the README says so itself); and the main README is Chinese-first. It is deliberately only a thin visual layer — no ingest, no question answering.
