didnt: Board — the pre-apply change blueprint: a draft held against a source snapshot with SHA-256, its provenance and target-hash conflicts shown before the review gate, is a concrete pattern for our Lens and proposal surfaces; the package itself is a two-version-old visual layer we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-loop
good: Framework for self-improving markdown vaults (raw/ to wiki/ to archive/, zero database) built around mechanical grounding: check_evidence.py verifies that numbers, dates and quotes in wiki pages match the immutable raw/ sources verbatim, with strict tiers, and runs as a commit gate. Pages carry Universal Fingerprints (a git commit hash plus per-file sha256 of monitored code), so drift is detected by git diff in milliseconds with no LLM tokens; drifted pages are tagged Outdated or Disputed and archived rather than deleted. Solutions recurring two or more times in log.md are surfaced by scan:skills as auto-skillification candidates, proposal-first. One init command injects skills into seven agent runtimes; 25 tests are claimed.
bad: Created 2026-08-14 and last modified 2026-08-21 — a one-week publishing burst at v1.3.2 whose heavy marketing claims ('0-Hallucination', 'production framework') rest on the README's own demo material rather than independent evidence. Its self-organization is automatic (garbage-collection tagging, skill-promotion candidates from log repetition), which runs against our owner-gated model where nothing is promoted without a ruling; and the grounding checker verifies verbatim fact matching only — it does not score whether a claim is supported in context.
didnt: Corroboration — mechanical, zero-token evidence checking of wiki facts against immutable raw sources, plus fingerprint-based drift detection, independently confirm our citation-lockfile and change-detection core; its automatic self-organization and skill promotion are the parts our approval gates exist to prevent. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-rag
good: Governed hybrid knowledge base that keeps a human-readable Markdown wiki and a chunk retrieval index as two views of one source set, published through a single deterministic transaction: SHA256 change detection (including rename-without-content-change identity), staged builds of both layers, validation of hashes, links and source-chunk consistency, then atomic publish. Snapshots are taken before every change and rollback verifies raw-source hashes first; purging derived data is blocked until the operator deletes the source and explicitly confirms the purge. The shipped local profile (Python 3.11+, SQLite) needs no cloud vector database, and the run contract includes dry-run preview, exclusive locks, budgets, secret search, redacted approval packets, telemetry and a per-run report. LLM extraction is an explicit extension boundary, never invoked silently in the standard profile.
bad: Two versions, both published on a single day (2026-07-17) — a v1.0.2 with no track record — and the registry README is Russian-only (the English README it links is not the text the registry record carries). The shipped profile's embeddings are deterministic hashing-v1 vectors, so retrieval quality rests on hashing rather than semantic embeddings; the semantic machinery exists as extension points, not as the delivered default.
didnt: Corroboration — the closest governance analogue in this wave: one changeset transaction spanning wiki and index, snapshot-before-change with hash-verified rollback, and deletion that requires an operator's explicit confirmation independently confirm our approval-gated, provenance-first design; not adopted (single-day release history, hashing-vector retrieval). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: llm-wiki-mcp
good: MCP server implementing Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern with the canonical three layers — immutable raw sources the LLM reads but never modifies, an LLM-written wiki, and a co-evolved schema (.wiki-schema.yaml with typed page kinds and required fields) — and the three operations: ingest, query, and lint for contradictions, orphan pages and stale claims. Eight tools over stdio, with an optional Streamable HTTP transport bound to 127.0.0.1; search uses qmd when present and otherwise falls back to dependency-free substring search; the server is also usable as a TypeScript library via createServer.
bad: The LLM writes and deletes freely — wiki_delete_page is a first-class tool and the README's model is that you never write the wiki yourself — with no approval gate, confirmation step or abstention mechanism anywhere in the record. All three versions were published on one day (2026-04-06) with nothing since, and the default search is plain substring matching.
didnt: Rejected — a generic pattern server whose ungated create/update/delete tools invert our approval-gated write model, and whose schema and lint duplicate what our stack already has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-wiki-mcp
good: MCP server for Obsidian vaults (by aud1ence) built on a deliberate storage-only principle: the server stores and retrieves — with a BM25 index rebuilt after every write — while all content decisions belong to the LLM; it imposes no folder structure of its own, targets document drift across AI sessions, and ships a full English documentation set (getting started, vault structure, tools reference, workflows, configuration, troubleshooting). It works with Claude Code, Kiro CLI and Codex via npx.
bad: The storage-only principle is the opposite of our governance model — no gating, validation or provenance at the server layer, by design — and the registry README is a short Vietnamese summary naming no tool list, leaving the actual surface to the linked docs. Small and stale: v0.1.4, five versions, last modified 2026-04-29, 68 downloads per month in the catalogue signal.
didnt: Rejected — an unopinionated Obsidian storage layer that delegates every content decision to the model; our door exists precisely to gate those decisions, and generic MCP wiki servers are already well covered in this catalogue. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @thenamesalex/obsidian-mcp
good: Small MCP server bridging to Obsidian's Local REST API plugin, with read tools (API status, get note with metadata, text search with context snippets) and write tools aimed at consistent note organization: create_structured_note using a Karpathy-style template (summary, tags, related notes), upsert, append, heading/block/frontmatter patch operations, move, and delete. Read and write tools live in clearly separated modules, and the environment contract is documented (OBSIDIAN_API_KEY required; OBSIDIAN_BASE_URL defaulting to the plugin's local endpoint).
bad: Usable only inside a running Obsidian with the Local REST API plugin enabled and its API key handed to the server — a custody and dependency chain our local-first stack avoids. The registry record is thin: no repository or homepage in the metadata, a README that carries no licence statement and ends mid-section, and a delete_note tool with no confirmation or gating described. Three versions, all published within minutes on 2026-06-29, and 39 downloads per month in the catalogue signal.
didnt: Rejected — an Obsidian-plugin-dependent bridge with ungated write and delete tools and the thinnest record in this batch; nothing it offers is missing from our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @teolin/mcp-obsidian
good: Minimal stdio MCP server for a single Obsidian vault whose reason to exist is enforcement: every path is resolved inside VAULT_PATH (traversal outside the vault is rejected), and write_file/append_file are denied anywhere under raw/ at the server level, closing the hole the generic filesystem MCP server leaves open (it grants write everywhere). Five tools — read, write, append, list, and recursive regex search — local-only with no network. The README is explicit about the point: even Claude Desktop, which has no other vault access and is not governed by Claude Code's settings, cannot mutate your sources through this server.
bad: A single-version package (v1.0.0, published once on 2026-08-11) living as one directory (mcps/Obsidian) inside the author's multi-llm-mcps monorepo, so its release and issue life is tied to that repo. The tool surface is bare filesystem access — no wiki semantics, search is regex only — and beyond raw/ the vault is fully writable with no gating at all.
didnt: Corroboration — raw/ immutability enforced at the server layer rather than by prompt convention, behind a vault-scoped path boundary, independently confirms our immutable-raw custody and door design; too bare a filesystem layer to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: trilium-llm-wiki-mcp
good: 52 MCP tools over the TriliumNext ETAPI plus a companion CLI and an LLM-wiki skill (ingest/query/lint/checkpoint procedures), SessionStart/Stop hooks, and a multi-PC mode where many machines share one Trilium-hosted wiki vault.
bad: Bound to a running Trilium/TriliumNext instance: the README's own Limitations section states ETAPI exposes no revision listing/reading, no undelete, no recent-changes history and no protected-note content, so the corresponding tools are omitted as non-goals. v0.2.1, single author, ~168 downloads/month.
didnt: Rejected — Trilium-host-bound; our wiki is plain files with its own MCP door, and the ETAPI gaps omit exactly the history and protection surfaces our custody model requires. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: kobsidian-mcp
good: 66 typed, Zod-validated MCP tools for Obsidian vaults — filesystem-first (Obsidian need not be running for 55+ tools), multi-vault discovery/selection, an LLM-Wiki orchestration namespace (ingest, auto index/log upkeep, lint), plus Dataview, Canvas, Kanban, Mermaid, Marp and Templates tooling over stdio and Streamable HTTP.
bad: Obsidian-vault-centric: the REST-bridged tool namespaces require Obsidian community plugins (Local REST API et al.), and the whole surface is tied to one app's ecosystem and plugin model. Pre-1.0 (v0.3.7).
didnt: Rejected — an Obsidian-bound duplicate of our own file-based wiki and MCP read door; nothing it offers is missing from our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: xknow-mcp
good: Local stdio MCP server over the curated, cross-linked XKnow knowledge base (SEO/SaaS/LLM-wiki): ranked search, full-page reads preserving wikilinks, a graph-aware explore_concept that walks outbound links and backlinks, and a cite tool returning canonical citations. The free layer is a bundled static snapshot — no account, no API key, nothing fetched at query time.
bad: The content is the vendor's own corpus: the free layer is 57 public guides and the full 500+ note vault is a purchased product. It is a read-only window onto someone else's knowledge base, not a system for maintaining our own.
didnt: Rejected — a vendor content product; neither the corpus nor its custody is ours, and our wiki already serves our own knowledge. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: guzhi
good: Repo-local RAG infrastructure CLI for Markdown/llm-wiki repos with a strict boundary: the Markdown repo is the only source of truth and the index (.guzhi/, external DBs) is disposable and rebuildable. Structure-aware chunking, explicit link graph, incremental/full sync with journal and locks, keyword and hybrid retrieval (RRF / weighted RRF) returning evidence type, tier, facets and optional explain output, plus a read-only HTTP serve mode compatible with Dify External Knowledge API and RAGFlow; PGlite default, PostgreSQL and Milvus backends.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source: the registry record carries no license field and no repository URL, and the full README contains no licence statement — so the code is ideas-only. v0.1.0, single maintainer, Chinese-language documentation, and the vector path leans on external Milvus / OpenAI-compatible embedding services.
didnt: Corroboration — its 'repo is the sole source of truth, index is a disposable derived layer' boundary and its rule that retrieval results must honestly expose mode and hit evidence independently confirm our file-custody and evidence-surfacing design; the absent licence keeps it ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: brainmaxxing
good: Obsidian-native LLM wiki in the raw/wiki/output three-tier shape: typed semantic relationships between pages, multi-agent research orchestration (facet split, parallel research, merge with contradiction flagging), promotion of good outputs back into the wiki, tiered search and a visual dashboard, exposed to any agent via MCP.
bad: v0.2.2 from a single author with a tiny user base (~12 downloads/month on the catalogue signal); an Obsidian-bound reimplementation of the same Karpathy pattern we already run natively on plain files.
didnt: Rejected — duplication plus Obsidian binding; our wiki already implements this pattern without the app dependency. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: oh-my-llmwikimode
good: Local-first LLM-wiki workbench for OpenCode: capture lessons from sessions, search prior fixes before re-investigating, review drafts before promotion into trusted knowledge, and an operations lane that reports wiki/GitHub/Discord signals without applying changes automatically. Safety model separates inspect commands from apply commands, and Discord summaries redact secrets, webhook URLs and absolute paths.
bad: Bound to the OpenCode plugin host; it duplicates our own capture → review → promote loop and Lens-style ops reporting. Small project (~56 downloads/month).
didnt: Rejected — platform-bound duplication; its review-required promotion gate matches our approval-gated writes but adds nothing we lack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @ctxr/skill-llm-wiki
good: An Agent Skill (Claude Code, Codex CLI) that builds deterministic, token-efficient markdown LLM wikis — hierarchical indices with DAG parents — over a private git substrate: operations are snapshot-tagged, rebuilds print the diff plus per-iteration commits and prompt approve/abort/drop before validation, and any operation can be byte-exactly reset. Most retrieval resolves locally (TF-IDF + local MiniLM embeddings) with no LLM call.
bad: Hard-requires an Agent Skills-compatible harness and Node.js ≥ 18 or it refuses to run; it is a skill for building other wikis, not a knowledge system itself, and its machinery overlaps our own wiki tooling and checkpoint system.
didnt: Corroboration — its approve-before-validation workflow with snapshot/reset over a private git substrate independently confirms our approval-gated writes plus checkpoint design; nothing adopted, we already have both. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: code-brain
good: Turns a codebase into searchable knowledge for Claude Code: a tree-sitter AST index in SQLite (symbols with file:line and snippets), one wiki page per module, 18 MCP tools, activity memory of what was tried, and curated findings carrying a git-ref freshness gate that flags them stale when their cited source changes.
bad: The README's own Limitations section: keyword FTS5 search only (no semantic search), enrichment costs ~3–5K tokens per module, wiki pages can drift after refactors with no automated staleness detector, no automated test suite in the repo, memory hooks need git, and several languages (Objective-C, C, exotic) are unsupported.
didnt: Corroboration — the git-ref freshness gate on curated findings parallels our citation lockfile and change detection; codebase-scoped, so nothing to adopt for a knowledge wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @gavin-hjw/llmflow
good: One-command scaffolder that initialises a complete LLM Wiki knowledge base in an empty directory and generates slash-command skills (/llm-ingest, /llm-query, /llm-lint, /llm-reflect, /llm-merge) for Cursor, Claude, Codex and OpenCode; qmd and bun are vendored and embedding models bundled for fully offline use, with a Node-only lint health check.
bad: The registry record's README is a ~980-character stub whose own title brands the package '@thundersoft/llmflow' while the npm record is '@gavin-hjw/llmflow' — an identity inconsistency at the source itself. It is a scaffolder only, with no knowledge system of its own.
didnt: Rejected — a scaffold duplicating our existing wiki and skill structure, on a thin and internally inconsistent record. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @xdsjs/llm-wiki-invest
good: CLI plus agent-skill system that compiles sources into a continuously maintained, interlinked Markdown wiki (ingest/query/lint/research, including a reviewed-manifest dossier flow for listed companies): BM25 search with CJK bigram tokenisation, and wikilink graph analysis (label-propagation communities, hub pages, orphans, linked-but-unwritten pages). The tool itself never calls an LLM; agents operate it via skill files.
bad: Hybrid search and cloud sync depend on the vendor's DB9 hosted service — embeddings are generated server-side and the vault's embeddings are uploaded — which breaks local-first custody; the framing is investment research rather than a general knowledge OS.
didnt: Rejected — hosted-DB9 dependency and domain framing; its graph-analysis shapes are already covered by our lint lanes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @aydenden/plugin-obsidian-knowledge
good: An Obsidian-vault LLM Wiki (three layers: SCHEMA.md as single source of truth with an append-only log; raw sources; compiled entities/concepts/comparisons/queries) packaged as a plugin usable from both Claude Code and OpenCode, injecting the CC plugin structure (commands/skills/agents) into OpenCode via config hooks.
bad: The registry record names no repository and no homepage; documentation is Korean-only; and the README's own constraints section records that the Claude Code SessionStart hook does not work under OpenCode (vault-path validation becomes a manual check) and that command names differ between hosts.
didnt: Rejected — the same vault pattern we already run natively; the dual-host port adds nothing and its hook gap is a real portability limit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @pananfly/dsh-llm-wiki
good: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin implementing the OKF v0.2 LLM Wiki spec: 17 agent tools whose input schemas are strictly validated, 16 slash commands, bidirectional-link and backlink indices with atomic metadata projection, auto-rebuild guardrails and ambient recall; also runnable under the Pi / Oh-My-Pi extension spec.
bad: Exists only inside the DeepSeek Harness (or Pi) plugin hosts; a single v0.1.0 release on the record. It re-implements our wiki operations inside another agent's runtime.
didnt: Rejected — host-bound duplication of our own wiki operations and door. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: topsyde-llm-wiki-mcp
good: Bun-first, local-first MCP gateway over a checked-out llm-wiki repository: 11 tools including plan_query, get_page_neighbors, query_wiki, enrich_gap and flag_stale_answer, plus a rich llm-wiki:// resource scheme (project index, pages, tags, aliases, relationships, map). Read-only metadata and query flows run over local project files.
bad: No licence is stated at the source: the registry record carries no license field and no repository URL, and the ~1.4k-character README contains no licence statement — ideas-only. The README is a stub documenting no tests, limits or write model; single v1.0.0 release, ~17 downloads/month.
didnt: Rejected — no licence, a thin record, and a read-door shape that duplicates our own MCP read door. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @iflow-mcp/2233admin-obsidian-llm-wiki
good: MCP server plus WebSocket bridge (with filesystem fallback) letting an agent read, search, edit and compile an Obsidian vault; writes are simulated by default — the agent must explicitly opt in (dryRun: false) before anything mutates. Localhost-only socket with token auth, path-traversal guards and client/payload limits, and a zero-dependency Python companion (kb_meta.py) doing deterministic diff/hash/index bookkeeping.
bad: Full function requires its Obsidian plugin and bridge running against a live vault; v0.1.0, single release, ~19 downloads/month. Obsidian-bound throughout.
didnt: Rejected — Obsidian-bound duplication; its dry-run-by-default write model agrees with our approval gate but the stack is not ours to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-llmwiki
good: TypeScript port of llmwiki packaged as a native DeepSeek Harness plugin: injects relevant wiki knowledge into the live turn, auto-captures every turn into a daily chronicle, and layers the vault (raw / chronicle / compiled entities-concepts-comparisons-projects-queries) with keyword + wikilink-graph + temporal retrieval fused by RRF under a token budget; zero runtime dependencies beyond Node.js.
bad: Exists only as a plugin inside DeepSeek Harness (requires the dsh CLI and pnpm on PATH); v0.1.1. Its default posture auto-captures every session turn into the vault, which conflicts with our governed, deliberate ingest rule.
didnt: Rejected — host-bound, and automatic per-turn capture is the opposite of our ingest governance. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @equationalapplications/react-llm-wiki
good: React bindings (WikiProvider plus read/write/ingest/forget/maintenance hooks) over a bring-your-own SQLite adapter (e.g. sql.js WASM) giving a zero-server, in-browser RAG memory: hybrid semantic + keyword search with per-call tuning, multi-entity reads, GraphRAG traversal formatted for prompts, fact provenance distinguishing immutable document facts from librarian-inferred and user facts, maintenance jobs (librarian, heal, reembed, prune), and OKF v0.1 + v0.2 import/export.
bad: Lives entirely inside a React/Expo web app — the host must supply the SQLite adapter, the LLM provider and the embed function; there is no standalone store or file corpus. Retrieval quality depends wholly on the host's embedding setup, with keyword fallback when embeddings fail.
didnt: Rejected — browser/React-embedded app memory is a different surface from our file-based wiki; its immutable-vs-derived fact provenance split corroborates our own source-protection rule, but there is nothing here our stack lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @equationalapplications/core-llm-wiki
good: Platform-agnostic TypeScript engine for hybrid LLM memory over SQLite with zero runtime dependencies: vector + FTS5/MiniSearch keyword retrieval with per-call tuning, GraphRAG traversal as a single recursive CTE (no graph database), temporal facts with half-open validity windows, asOf reads and a supersede() that refuses immutable, foreign or already-superseded facts, OKF v0.1 + v0.2 import/export, and an opt-in grounding check that stores facts not quoting their source as drafts.
bad: Engine only — the host must bring a SQLite adapter and an LLM provider with an embed function before anything works; the default librarian strategy remains the 'legacy' one; the documented surface has draft review/promote but no approval-gated write path and no abstention behaviour.
didnt: Board — its temporal-fact model (validity windows, asOf reads, supersede refusing immutable facts) and its grounding check that demotes ungrounded facts to drafts are design patterns worth boarding against our truth-aware retrieval gap; the TypeScript engine itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @equationalapplications/schema-org-llm-wiki
good: Curated schema.org ontology manifest — 9 node types and 28 polymorphic edges in ~2 KB serialized — that seeds the knowledge graph so LLM ingest/librarian passes can only emit valid (type, source_type, target_type) triples instead of inventing edge types, while every type and property stays standard schema.org for future JSON-LD export.
bad: Data-only — no runtime code; it requires @equationalapplications/core-llm-wiki at the same release or newer, covers only warm-agent personal/professional domains (people, places, organizations, projects, events, creative works, reviews, products), and JSON-LD export is still described as future work.
didnt: Rejected — a data-only companion manifest for someone else's engine; constraining LLM edge extraction to a fixed manifest does corroborate our schema-first ingest, but our wiki's schema is our own constitution and far wider than a 9-type warm-agent taxonomy. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @atomicstrata/llmwiki-core
good: Engine-free core package exposing knowledge, profiles, retained artifacts, preparations and records services plus passive local-workflow history, with existing grants, profile checks, reviewed mutations and path confinement still applying — the README stresses that choosing core is not a grant.
bad: By its own README the package is publicly downloadable but its direct exports are internal composition contracts, not a separately supported consumer API — applications are told to import llm-wiki-compiler instead; it requires Node 24 or later, and local installation must supply matching tarballs explicitly with no runtime downloading or fallback.
didnt: Rejected — an internal composition package its own documentation says is not a supported consumer API; there is nothing to adopt and no surface our wiki could build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-memory-wiki-all-you-need
good: Extension for the pi coding agent backed by a central memory + LLM wiki server: global, user and per-project memories are injected into every request with per-prompt recall, each finished turn is sent for LLM curation (add/update/remove), a full tool set is exposed (memory_search, session_search, memory_add/replace/remove, memory_graph, wiki_search/read/write, skill_manage, memory_review with conflict-settling proposals), and the extension is fail-soft when the server is down.
bad: The npm package is only the client extension — it does nothing without the separate memory-wiki-all-you-need server running and configured; server skills sync one-way and overwrite local edits; installing it both ways (npm plus the server's install.sh) makes the extension run twice.
didnt: Rejected — bound to the pi coding agent and a separately-run server, while our agents reach the wiki through our own MCP door; its one-way skills sync overwriting local edits also conflicts with our custody model. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-weave
good: Local-first Markdown memory and knowledge graph shared by human and agent across Pi and OpenCode from one package: dictated notes keep a verbatim ## Raw tail under an agent-organised summary, notes are provenance-marked (source: human vs agent), wiki-link repair is deterministic (exact slug, then unique basename, then unique title — ambiguity reported, never guessed), every change is saved to a browsable note history, a loopback browser workspace visualises the graph, and repository/session scans build a structural index.
bad: A plugin for the Pi and OpenCode harnesses only; deep repository scans and session summaries send bounded content to the active model; v0.3.x and single-author, requiring Node 20.13 or newer.
didnt: Corroboration — its verbatim raw-tail preservation, human/agent provenance marking and link repair that reports ambiguity instead of guessing confirm our own record-keeping rules almost exactly; the Pi/OpenCode plugin itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-vault-reader
good: MCP server connecting Markdown/Zettelkasten vaults (Obsidian-compatible) to any MCP client: local vaults are indexed in place, read-only, with zero duplication; remote GitHub vaults are supported via shallow clone; MiniSearch full-text search, wikilink/backlink traversal and localised graph exploration, daily-journal retrieval, and a dedicated persistent __memory__ vault the AI can write and query across sessions.
bad: v0.1.0 with ~48 downloads/month (batch signal); user vaults stay read-only while the separate __memory__ vault is read/write with no approval gating described, and GitHub-vault support works by cloning remote repositories locally.
didnt: Rejected — a vault-reading MCP surface our own MCP read door already covers under stricter custody rules; its freely writable memory vault is the opposite of our approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @travisbergen2/second-brain-mcp
good: Local stdio MCP server over an Obsidian vault (or any Markdown folder) with an unusually explicit safety model: everything is off by default until folders are allowlisted (the allowlist is re-read live on every call), search is capped at 6 snippets / 2400 characters by a deterministic local scorer, every result discloses exactly which note paths and how many characters shipped, one audit line per call is appended to Loop/mcp-audit.md, and writes are fenced to a create-only write-back folder whose saved notes wikilink their sources.
bad: v0.1.0 with ~110 downloads/month (batch signal); v1 deliberately excludes backlink/graph queries and embedding search; its settings live in a companion Obsidian plugin, and remote-only MCP clients cannot reach a local vault by design — the README's own honesty section concedes the fences bound the blast radius rather than abolish prompt-injection risk.
didnt: Corroboration — its default-off allowlist read live on every call, per-call caps with in-result disclosure of what shipped, and an in-vault audit trail corroborate our approval-gated writes and trust-ledger design point for point; the server itself duplicates our MCP door's read surface, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @toportal/second-brain-mcp
good: MCP server that turns a Markdown folder into a structured second brain: captures are classified into readings (40-Lecturas), permanent notes (50-Notas) and concepts held as real graph nodes (60-Conceptos), matured ideas are promoted and linked with stated reasons, related notes resurface automatically while you work, graph-health tooling (pruning, concept merging) is built in, and everything stays in local plain files with no database or cloud.
bad: Documentation, tool names and the whole method are in Spanish only; it imposes its own fixed folder taxonomy and maturation workflow on the vault; v0.1.3 with ~169 downloads/month (batch signal).
didnt: Rejected — a fixed-method second brain whose taxonomy and workflow would have to displace our wiki's own schema; nothing in it fills a gap our stack has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @rulebased/second-brain
good: Claude Code plugin packaging eleven PKM skills across the CODE workflow — init, capture, organize, connect, review (spaced repetition), search, refactor, synthesize, daily, reference-check, glossary-sync — over a PARA brain structure, with a digital-garden maturity model tracked in frontmatter (seedling → budding → evergreen) and explicit growth triggers (e.g. add structure when a tag reaches 10+ files or a folder 30+) checked on every organize run.
bad: Claude Code-only surface (plugin marketplace / skills.sh); it scaffolds and prompts a methodology but provides no retrieval, citation or write-gating machinery of its own; ~26 downloads/month (batch signal).
didnt: Rejected — methodology prompts for a generic PKM method, not machinery our file-based wiki lacks; our schema, ingest and lint rules already do this work under our own constitution. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: create-obsidian-memory
good: One-command CLI that generates a structured AI memory system as an Obsidian vault: an AGENTS.md entry point agents read automatically plus a .memory/ folder (project description, progress, architecture, file-map, ADR decision records, daily session logs), from six templates — web project, research/thesis, theory assignment, career, content creator, and notes PKM — aimed at any AI coding agent.
bad: Generator only — once scaffolded there is no engine: no search, no curation or maintenance automation, and the memory stays current only if the agent or user updates the files by hand; the README is written primarily in Indonesian; the registry record names no repository.
didnt: Rejected — a static template scaffold; our wiki already has its own schema, ingest discipline and living corpus, and a one-shot generator adds nothing to it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: your-second-mind
good: npx scaffolder that creates a personalised, agent-ready PARA + Zettelkasten Obsidian vault in under a minute: numbered folders each with a Dataview _index stub, raw/ source subfolders, six note templates, per-agent instruction files (CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, AGENTS.md as selected), copy-paste agent workflow commands (weekly review, monthly lint), an index.md and a running log.md, with a non-interactive scripted mode.
bad: Scaffold only — no runtime, search or maintenance engine after generation; the generated index stubs need the user to install the Obsidian Dataview and Templater plugins themselves; v0.1.0 with ~5 downloads/month (batch signal).
didnt: Rejected — it produces an empty vault structure and stops, where our wiki is a living corpus with ingest, validation and custody rules already in place. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: polymath-world
good: One-command scaffold combining PARA folders, a Karpathy-style LLM-wiki maintainer workflow (the bundled CLAUDE.md has Claude ask one classification question per dropped source, extract takeaways, write structured entity/concept/synthesis pages, cross-reference them, and update the master index and activity log), and the Caveman output-compression skill; a beginner guide walks terminal newcomers through the whole setup.
bad: Scaffold plus prompts only — no engine, retrieval or validation; it requires Obsidian, Node 18+ and Claude Code specifically; v0.1.2 with ~15 downloads/month (batch signal).
didnt: Corroboration — its maintainer pattern (classify each source, write structured pages, cross-reference, update the index and log) is our own ingest operation in miniature and confirms the model; the Claude Code scaffold bundle itself is not adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @hydraharness/harness-obsidian-knowledge
good: Token-bounded Obsidian graph memory plugin for the Hydra harness, working through the Obsidian Local REST API's built-in MCP server (raw MCP tools never exposed to the model): recall searches once per intent and returns at most six ranked matches with ≤320-character excerpts plus up to 32 path-only graph neighbours and no embedding index; batch exact-reads fail closed on missing, invalid or oversized input; a vault-identity marker note makes a wrong open vault fail closed; and the only model-facing write path, obsidian_knowledge_save_approved, has the host ask the user to approve the exact call before saving.
bad: Release candidates only (the latest tag is 0.1.1-rc.5, with rc.10 sitting on the next tag); its own Known Limitations section states retrieval is Obsidian search plus one-hop wikilinks with no semantic index, and that Obsidian with its Local REST API plugin must be running and OBSIDIAN_API_KEY must resolve; the registry record carries no README and the repository named in the record returns HTTP 404.
didnt: Rejected — a pre-release plugin for the Hydra harness, a surface we do not run, with its source repository unreachable; its approval-gated single write path does corroborate our write-gating design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @hydra1902/harness-obsidian-knowledge
good: The same token-bounded Obsidian graph memory design as its sibling package, verified from this package's own published tarball: capped recall (six ranked matches, ≤320-character excerpts, up to 32 path-only graph neighbours, no embedding index), fail-closed batch exact-reads, a vault-identity marker that fails closed on the wrong vault, and an approval-gated save as the only model-facing write path, via the Obsidian Local REST API MCP server.
bad: Latest here is 0.1.1-rc.2 (pre-release, behind the sibling scope's rc line); the README inside its own tarball titles the package '@hydra/harness-obsidian-knowledge' — a third name matching neither this registry record nor the sibling @hydraharness scope; the registry record carries no README and the repository named in the record returns HTTP 404; it requires a running Obsidian with the Local REST API plugin and a resolved API key.
didnt: Rejected — judged on its own record and tarball: an earlier release candidate of the same Hydra-harness plugin line under the maintainer's personal scope, with the same unreachable repository; not a surface we run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @reneza/ats-adapter-obsidian
good: Storage adapter that points the Agentic Task System at an existing Obsidian vault with no migration: `ats find` fuses ranked keyword search with native vault search via RRF, a wiki layer (`ats get / url / links / open`) resolves both wikilinks and obsidian:// deep links, and an MCP server exposes the vault to Claude Desktop / Cursor — no server, OAuth, vector database or sync service required. Frontmatter is parsed only for tags/due/title/modified and everything else is left untouched.
bad: It is only an adapter: useless without the separate ATS CLI/core, and it hard-couples task identity to vault-relative file paths, so renaming a note changes its task id. The README documents no tests, evaluation, or write-safety/approval mechanism, and the adapter is a single-author project at v0.18.0.
didnt: Rejected — an adapter for the separate Agentic Task System over Obsidian vaults; our wiki is a git tree served by its own MCP doors, and its RRF-fused retrieval duplicates patterns already in our stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @vectorize-io/hindsight-obsidian
good: Obsidian plugin that incrementally syncs a vault one-way into a Hindsight memory bank (content hashes skip unchanged notes, edits upsert, deletes remove) with automatic vault/folder/date scoping tags, and adds a chat panel whose answers are grounded on the notes, cite the note each answer came from, and show a reasoning disclosure of what each step queried. A hard design rule keeps the vault canonical: Hindsight is never a second source of truth, and chat conversations are not stored by default.
bad: By default it sends vault content to an external service — Hindsight Cloud with an API key (self-hosting the Hindsight server is the alternative) — which breaks local-first custody, and turning on 'remember conversations' creates memory outside the vault. Still in beta and installed via BRAT rather than the community store, and it depends entirely on the separate Hindsight product.
didnt: Rejected — it syncs the vault into an external memory service (cloud API by default), which conflicts with our local-first custody; its one-way, vault-canonical sync and per-answer note citations corroborate our design but the architecture is not adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-brain
good: Standalone Node MCP server (18 tools) that reads vault .md files directly from disk — no Obsidian plugin, no HTTP bridge, no API key, nothing hosted, content never leaves the machine. Chunk-level semantic search (heading-aware chunking, local embeddings incl. Ollama providers) fused with FTS5 BM25 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, plus PageRank/Louvain graph analytics (influential notes, theme clusters), all indexed in SQLite with incremental re-indexing on writes.
bad: Single-author project whose write tools (create/edit/delete/move) act directly on the vault with no approval gate or preview step. First boot downloads a ~34 MB embedding model and indexes (30–60 s before tools appear), native better-sqlite3 builds cause documented ABI-mismatch failures, and three live-editor tools need the separate companion plugin with version pairing.
didnt: Rejected — a capable local-first Obsidian MCP server, but it duplicates our own MCP read door and adds ungated write/delete tools against our approval-gated write design; Obsidian-vault scope only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-mcp-server
good: Mature MCP server (14 tools, 3 resources, STDIO or Streamable HTTP) over the Obsidian Local REST API with surgical edits — replace a single heading, block or frontmatter field instead of whole files — plus text, JSONLogic and BM25 (Omnisearch) search modes. Notably it ships folder-scoped read/write permissions and a read-only switch as a built-in path policy.
bad: It only works through the Obsidian Local REST API plugin, so Obsidian must be running with an API key configured — no direct filesystem access. Write tools include whole-file overwrite, and the permission model is folder scoping rather than per-write approval; it is one maintainer's project built on the author's own mcp-ts-core framework.
didnt: Rejected — requires Obsidian running with the Local REST API plugin and duplicates our own wiki MCP door; its folder-scoped permissions and read-only switch confirm our scoping instincts but its write model is not approval-gated (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-obsidian-vault
good: MCP server giving agents direct filesystem access to a vault with no Obsidian running: 27 tools across note CRUD/search/wikilinks, multi-agent task orchestration (claim/track/complete with dependency graphs and projects), decision/discovery logging for cross-session context, human-in-the-loop review gates (review_required tasks redirect to a review queue), usage/cost tracking, and git auto-sync on write.
bad: Its own README's Known Limitations concede the safety gaps: no file locking (claims atomic only within a single server process), task scope is advisory and not enforced by the server, and webhooks are fire-and-forget. Direct filesystem writes with auto-push to git are the opposite of an approval-gated write path.
didnt: Rejected — duplicates our MCP door/gateway stack while its enforcement model is weaker (advisory scope, no locking, ungated writes with auto git push); its HITL review gates confirm the approval pattern but the implementation is not adoptable (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @huangyihe/obsidian-mcp
licence: MIT (repository LICENSE file; npm registry license field states ISC — conflict recorded in evidence)
good: MCP server for full note and folder CRUD over Obsidian with a dual API strategy (Local REST API with filesystem fallback), precision PATCH editing targeted at headings and block IDs, whole-vault auto-backlink generation with a dry-run mode, batch operations with progress tracking, and a one-click DXT package install.
bad: Prerequisites require the Obsidian desktop app plus the Local REST API plugin and an API token, and the toolset includes ungated delete for notes and folders. Single author, no GitHub releases cut, and the npm metadata licence (ISC) disagrees with the repository licence (MIT), so a consumer reading only the registry record gets the wrong licence.
didnt: Rejected — another Obsidian MCP server requiring the REST API plugin and token, duplicating our own door, with ungated deletes; its npm-vs-repository licence conflict is itself a caution against trusting registry metadata alone (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @andysama/obsidian-mcp-server
good: Small, focused MCP server exposing an Obsidian vault to AI assistants: keyword/tag/category search, full-text search, note reading, folder listing and vault structure, with YAML frontmatter parsing (category/tags/summary/folder) and simple npx or global install against any MCP client.
bad: Despite the read-oriented pitch it ships ungated create/update/delete note tools and folder creation with no approval or preview step. Chinese-language README only, single author, very small adoption (about 104 downloads/month in the catalogue signal), and no semantic search or graph features.
didnt: Rejected — a minimal single-author Obsidian MCP server duplicating our own read door, with ungated write/delete tools that contradict our approval-gated write design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-kb-cli
good: Scriptable CLI (`obkb`) for the Karpathy-style LLM-wiki workflow on Obsidian vaults, designed for the cases where no LLM is in the loop: lint walks each topic (a folder containing an index.md) and reports broken links, notes missing from the index, missing frontmatter/type, schema drift against the topic's declared CLAUDE.md schema, and stale claims judged from git history; bootstrap scaffolds per-topic CLAUDE.md/index.md/log.md from templates (papers, people, projects, books), and watch mode re-lints on every change for cron or pre-commit use.
bad: Obsidian-vault-specific and early (v0.4.0, about 21 downloads/month in the catalogue signal), single-author, and only a companion to a separate agent skill — the lint is structural (links, frontmatter, staleness) with no citation or claim verification.
didnt: Corroboration — its lint taxonomy (broken links, not-in-index, schema drift, stale claims) and per-topic CLAUDE.md/index.md/log.md scaffolding independently mirror our own validator, index and log discipline for a Karpathy-style wiki; Obsidian-specific, so nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @time4peter/foam-cli
good: Tiny focused CLI for Foam workspaces whose one documented command, verify-links, scans Markdown/MDX files, parses [[target]] and [[target|alias]] wikilinks, reports broken links with their locations, and offers script-friendly exit codes and JSON output.
bad: A single-function checker at v0.1.1 with about 15 downloads/month in the catalogue signal: the README documents no other command, no index/lint/schema checks, and no licence statement; it is published out of a monorepo whose repository is literally named foam-private, and it targets the Foam/VS Code ecosystem rather than plain vaults.
didnt: Rejected — a one-command wikilink checker for the Foam ecosystem; link integrity is already covered by our own wiki validator, and the package is pre-1.0 with minimal documentation (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @techpickles/sb
good: Second Brain CLI for Obsidian vault management designed for both humans and AI agents: multi-vault config, note create/read/move with Zettelkasten naming, an agent-routing `note context` command (extracted keywords, PARA destinations, related notes), daily-note and inbox handling — and every mutating command supports --dry-run preview, alongside `sb provenance` (current git context) and a full machine-readable command schema via `sb describe`.
bad: Obsidian/PARA-specific and tied to a config file living at ~/.claude/second-brain.md; single-author at v0.7.0, and its safety story is preview-only — a dry run shows what would happen but nothing enforces approval before a real write.
didnt: Corroboration — --dry-run preview on every mutating command plus an explicit provenance command independently confirm our preview/approval-gated-write and provenance design choices; Obsidian-specific CLI, so nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-obsidian
good: DeepSeek Harness plugin that gives a dsh agent 12 obsidian_* tools over a local vault by direct filesystem access — no MCP server, no OAuth, no Local REST API plugin. Its safety defaults are explicit: deletes only move notes into a reversible .trash/, all paths are validated to stay inside the vault root, .obsidian/ is never touched, and ripgrep is only an optional accelerator with a built-in scan fallback.
bad: It is a plugin for the DeepSeek Harness ecosystem (profile-based dsh CLI, verified by its author only against a dsh release candidate), not an MCP server, so it cannot plug into our stack. Write/overwrite tools act immediately — the guardrails are path containment and reversible trash, not approval — and the primary README is Chinese with a separate English translation file.
didnt: Rejected — a DeepSeek Harness plugin rather than an MCP component, so it does not fit our door architecture; its trash-only reversible deletes and vault-root path containment confirm our safety instincts (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @civilization/dsh-obsidian
good: DSH-native Obsidian plugin built around MOC (Map of Content) navigation instead of folders: it auto-detects and maintains MOC map notes, mounts new notes onto the right MOC to prevent orphan islands, enforces a strict YAML frontmatter schema (title/type/domain/status/created/updated/tags/related) enabling structured multi-field filtering, turns daily notes into a structured Work/Ideas incubator that spawns atomic linked notes, and perceives the active note via .obsidian/workspace.json.
bad: Bound to the DeepSeek Harness/Cordis plugin ecosystem and to Windows in places (the open-in-app tool works through the Windows system URI handler), pre-1.0 (v0.1.x) and single-organization. Its governance is convention enforced by the plugin's own tools only — nothing in the record shows citation checking or approval gating — and the README states no licence.
didnt: Rejected — its MOC-first navigation and strict frontmatter governance mirror our index-first, schema-checked design, but it is a DSH/Cordis-ecosystem, partly Windows-bound plugin that cannot serve our git-based wiki and MCP doors (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @qiqiangvae/dsh-obsidian
good: Single DSH plugin that turns an Obsidian vault into a Karpathy-pattern LLM wiki: wiki_query (BM25 retrieval returning snippets plus the link graph), wiki_write with type routing, frontmatter completion, index/log bookkeeping and source-hash dedup skipping, wiki_lint health checks (duplicates, dead links, orphan pages, missing frontmatter, stale index), wiki_scaffold with dry-run default, plus a bundled skill suite (wiki-ingest, wiki-query with citations, save, think).
bad: It exists because the upstream DSH framework keeps breaking its public Cordis API — the README says the two predecessor plugins repeatedly stopped loading — so it inherits that platform churn, and it is a young single-maintainer fork-of-forks at v0.1.2 targeting the DSH ecosystem rather than MCP clients.
didnt: Corroboration — a Karpathy-pattern wiki plugin whose wiki_write does index/log bookkeeping with source-hash dedup and whose wiki_lint checks dead links and orphans independently confirms our ingest discipline and lint design; DSH-ecosystem, so nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-client-ui-obsidian-memory
good: Small DSH plugin giving an assistant persistent memory in a local Markdown vault: five filesystem tools (read/list/search/write/append) with all paths sandboxed inside the configured vaultPath (path-traversal attempts error out), a sidebar panel showing vault status and tool descriptions, and support for the community Codex/ folder structure (AGENTS.md, TODO.md, people/, projects/, daily/).
bad: Only five plain file tools — no retrieval ranking, linking, lint or citation behaviour — and the write/append tools are ungated. It depends on a DSH sidebar slot that its own troubleshooting table says is missing in older DSH builds, is single-author, and versions before 0.3.2 silently installed without ever activating.
didnt: Rejected — five generic file tools for the DeepSeek Harness duplicate what our own doors already provide with stronger gating; DSH-ecosystem scope only (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @dingpenghui/dsh-obsidian-sync
good: DSH Cordis plugin with just two tools and a zero-prompt-injection design (default token cost is only the two tool schemas): obsidian_search over an in-process inverted index with CJK bigram tokenization and IDF-weighted ranking, incrementally rebuilt every 60 s, and obsidian_sync_session, which archives DSH sessions into the vault idempotently (date + shortId upsert, unchanged summaries skipped) under the vault's PARA rules with an auto-maintained date-segmented index note.
bad: Purpose-built for archiving DeepSeek Harness sessions, not a general knowledge layer: search covers only the vault it indexes, archived content quality depends entirely on the caller-supplied summary, and the README records a breaking hazard of its own history (dotted tool names were rejected by providers with HTTP 400). Single author; DSH/Cordis ecosystem only.
didnt: Rejected — a session-archiving plugin for the DeepSeek Harness; its idempotent, skip-if-unchanged session upserts are a sound pattern that echoes our conversation-log discipline, but it is built for the dsh session store, not our wiki (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @inovan.do/obsidian-rag-tools
good: CLI + MCP server that turns an Obsidian vault into a local RAG knowledge base: embeddings run locally via @xenova/transformers (ONNX multilingual-e5-small), hybrid retrieval fuses BM25 keyword/tag search with vector cosine similarity (RRF), and a repo importer splits external markdown into notes of at most 200 lines with YAML frontmatter and wikilinks. It separates read-only query/audit modes from an execution mode — writes require execution mode plus user confirmation — and ships a read-only pending-reviews report, per-project session memory, and vault-stored guidelines, agent profiles and skills.
bad: The README is Portuguese-only, and the npm record names no repository or homepage, so there is no public source repo to audit from the record. v2.0.0 was a breaking release (MCP tool renames, paginated response envelope) forcing client reconfiguration, and the README itself warns that semantic search can silently degrade to keyword-only results when the embedding model/provider is not working.
didnt: Corroboration — its read-only query/audit modes, writes gated behind an execution mode with user confirmation, and a read-only pending-reviews report independently confirm our approval-gated write design; the tool itself targets Obsidian vaults we do not use. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @jinlee794/obsidian-intelligence-layer
good: MCP server giving agents token-efficient, safe access to an Obsidian vault: ranked snippet search instead of full-note dumps, section-level reads, and graph traversal for related entities. Its write tools are mtime-checked — atomic_append/atomic_replace require expected_mtime and reject stale writes — and every write is recorded in an audit log (get_agent_log); a vault-health tool surfaces stale insights, missing IDs and orphaned meetings.
bad: The domain tools are shaped for CRM/customer-account vaults (customer snapshots, TPID/CRM prefetch, a Customers/People/Meetings folder schema), not general knowledge work. Writes carry no approval flow of their own — the README states approval is left to the client UI — and it is a single-author, pre-1.0 project (v0.5.3) speaking MCP over stdio only.
didnt: Corroboration — mtime-checked writes with stale-write rejection and a per-write audit log confirm our approval-gated write and audit-ledger design; its CRM-vault domain shape is not our fit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-obsidian-memory
good: Long-term memory for the pi coding agent as one-point-per-note Markdown in Obsidian vaults: typed frontmatter (rule, decision, lesson, fact, and more), a global vault plus per-project vaults, and background capture that saves, updates, archives or supersedes notes (memory_succeed links old and new both ways; notes are never deleted, only archived). dontForget notes are pinned into the system prompt, relevance-scored notes are injected per message within a character budget, and vault/shell-edit guards refuse agent writes outside the memory tools so user edits are never overwritten.
bad: It only works inside the pi coding agent, and full function depends on a paid third-party classifier API (TypeSafe 'Jev'): without TYPESAFE_API_KEY no notes are injected and every shell call is refused, while conversation content, candidate notes and shell commands are sent to TypeSafe for classification (its own Privacy section). Its Known limits admit capture quality is 'not yet measured against a real model' and that the vault guard can be bypassed by indirectly constructed paths; v0.1.1.
didnt: Board — the supersede-with-bidirectional-links note lifecycle (memory_succeed) and dontForget pinning are candidate ideas for our memory layer's supersession handling, the sharp end of our truth-aware-retrieval gap. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-zk
good: Zettelkasten MCP server for Claude Code: CRUD for fleeting/literature/permanent/MOC/project notes with proper frontmatter, automatic Luhmann numbering (1 → 1a → 1a1), typed connections (Supports/Contradicts/Extends/Related), and connection scoring from shared tags, keywords, Luhmann proximity and MOC overlap. A SQLite metadata cache with content-hash incremental indexing and mtime staleness checks keeps vault analysis (orphans, unprocessed notes with age warnings, emerging theme clusters) fast without rescanning every file.
bad: It works only with Claude Code and deliberately uses no embeddings — semantic relevance is judged by the model in context, so connection quality is only as good as the session model. It imposes its own five-folder Zettelkasten taxonomy and workflow, the record names no repository, and the record's last modification is 2026-03-19 (v0.2.12).
didnt: Rejected — fit: a Claude-Code-bound Zettelkasten workflow with its own folder taxonomy; our wiki already has its own schema, ingest and MCP door, and Luhmann numbering does not map onto our citation-locked pages. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-zk-cn
good: Chinese-first variant of the obsidian-zk design: the same Luhmann numbering, typed connections, connection scoring and SQLite incremental index, plus trilingual note generation (zh default, uk, en) with localised templates, section headings and connection types, and Chinese keyword matching over 2-character fragments of continuous text. Guided Claude Code slash-command workflows (/zk:capture, /zk:promote, /zk:finalize) mirror the original's quality pipeline from fleeting note to finalised permanent note.
bad: A derivative of obsidian-zk — its README notes it keeps compatibility with the original project's Ukrainian vault — so it inherits the same limits: Claude-Code-only, no embeddings, an imposed five-folder taxonomy. The record shows a single day of registry activity (created and last modified 2026-07-05, v0.3.0), i.e. an unproven fork rather than a maintained line.
didnt: Rejected — fit and duplication: a single-day derivative fork of obsidian-zk for Chinese-language vaults, already rejected above on fit; nothing additional it offers maps to our English-language, schema-governed wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-writer-mcp
good: The widest Obsidian MCP surface in this batch — 75 tools across notes, tasks (including an Eisenhower matrix), CRM contacts, audit (orphans, unlinked mentions, empty notes) and Syncthing sync-conflict detection/resolution. It is built for scale: direct filesystem access with SQLite WAL indexing, FTS5 full-text search (about 5–10 ms queries, about 15–20 s initial indexing of 5,000 notes), an LRU cache and watcher-driven incremental updates, plus embedding-based duplicate detection with explicit similarity thresholds and a feedback-learning loop for link suggestions.
bad: Semantic search is off by default and requires an OpenAI API key — note content leaves the machine for embeddings when enabled. It imposes a fixed French PARA/Zettelkasten folder taxonomy (RESSOURCES/GARDEN/SOURCES), and the README documents no write-approval or audit-log machinery despite the large mutating tool surface; a single-vendor project (VibeAcademy).
didnt: Rejected — fit: an Obsidian-vault tool whose semantic features depend on an external embedding service; our store is a git wiki with its own MCP read door, and its sync-conflict tooling addresses a Syncthing workflow we do not run. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @iflow-mcp/velvetmonkey-flywheel-memory
good: Local-first memory layer over Obsidian/plain Markdown: hybrid search (BM25 plus optional local semantic search) returns grounded context — frontmatter, section-aware snippets, dates and linked notes — in one call. Writes are bounded and safe: SHA-256 content-hash conflict detection, structure-preserving edits, one-call undo, and deterministic auto-wikilinking whose scoring learns from accepted/rejected suggestions; saved YAML 'policies' run search-then-write workflows atomically with a preview step, and multiple vaults can be served from one instance.
bad: Learned state (memories, link feedback, scoring) lives in a local SQLite state.db beside the vault rather than in inspectable text — it regenerates if deleted, but it is not itself readable knowledge. This npm package is a mirror of the mcp-server subpackage of the velvetmonkey monorepo (the upstream package is @velvetmonkey/flywheel-memory), its ranking and benchmark claims rest on the project's own docs, and its writes are reversible but not approval-gated.
didnt: Corroboration — hash-checked, reversible, preview-before-execute writes over plain-Markdown custody confirm our approval-gated write design; the tool itself targets Obsidian vaults and a learning link-scorer we do not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @iflow-mcp/iamtouchskyer-memex
good: Persistent agent memory as atomic Zettelkasten cards in plain Markdown with [[bidirectional links]] — no vector database and no embeddings. One shared ~/.memex/cards directory serves every client (a Claude Code plugin with SessionStart auto-recall, a VS Code extension, or the same 10 MCP tools in Cursor/Codex/Windsurf), cards can be browsed in a local timeline/graph UI, archived rather than deleted, and synced across devices through git.
bad: Recall is keyword/link-based only — there is no semantic ranking, so recall quality rests on the agent's own retrospectives after each task. Cross-device sync pushes the memory store to a GitHub repo (auto-created via the gh CLI), and the serve UI can hand memory to a hosted web app (memra.vercel.app) when sync is on — custody leaves the local machine by design; v0.1.26.
didnt: Corroboration — atomic plain-Markdown cards, readable by human and agent alike and never locked into a proprietary store, confirm our local-first custody design; its recall has no scored abstention or citation discipline to borrow. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @next-wiki/openclaw-memory-wiki
good: A disciplined one-way mirror: it scans an OpenClaw Memory Wiki vault plus memory-core files and uploads them byte-for-byte (frontmatter, links, relative paths preserved) into next-wiki's Raw space as immutable Revisions — digest-unchanged files are skipped, changed files create a new current Revision, and sources that disappear are retired from retrieval while their Raw page and revision history remain available for audit. The API key is held via an OpenClaw SecretRef with independently scoped read/write grants, failed uploads retry with bounded backoff and surface as degraded status, and the plugin never modifies the local vault.
bad: It is transport into an external hosted product: mirrored knowledge lives in an account-bound next-wiki server, the opposite direction from local custody, and it produces nothing itself — a separate producer must write the Markdown first (the README documents why in-plugin session archiving was removed in 0.5.0). Files over 512 KB are skipped, and it is young (record created 2026-09-04, v0.6.0) and bound to OpenClaw's plugin and server APIs.
didnt: Rejected — fit and custody: it mirrors vault content into a third-party hosted wiki account; our wiki stays in its own git custody. Its immutable-Revision/retire-with-audit discipline corroborates our revision handling, but the destination disqualifies it. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @openparachute/vault
good: An agent-native knowledge-graph server: 13 core MCP tools plus a full REST API over notes, tags and links, with wikilink auto-linking (aliases, anchors, embeds; unresolved links auto-resolve when the target appears) and note-path renames that rewrite wikilinks in other notes. Access is properly governed for a server — scope-narrowed hub JWTs per vault and verb (vault:<name>:read/write) — and it adds tag-schema enforcement with state machines, declarative webhook triggers with two-phase markers that prevent re-entry, chunked reads of large notes, 'changed since X' incremental queries, and bidirectional Obsidian import/export.
bad: The source of truth is a per-vault SQLite database, not plain Markdown files — Obsidian interop is import/export rather than live files, so custody is database-bound. It is one service in a multi-service Parachute ecosystem (hub OAuth, a Daily app, scribe/narrate webhook services, tunnel exposure), a large operational surface for a personal wiki, and the README itself carries vestigial legacy auth machinery; AGPL-3.0 copyleft on top.
didnt: Rejected — licence (AGPL-3.0, ideas-only under our licence discipline) and custody model: notes live in SQLite rather than inspectable Markdown under git. Its scoped-token and schema/state-machine ideas are noted but not taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sdtk-wiki-kit
good: Project-local wiki and document-graph toolkit with the strongest report-first safety model in this batch: lint, gap discovery, semantic extraction and compile are dry-run/report-only, and a compile applies only through a generated JSON sidecar with an explicit --apply --yes — create-only or same-content no-op, never overwrite, delete or archive. It keeps a metadata-only raw/provenance registry (no source payload copied), grounded Ask with primary/related source labelling and a Sources-used panel, opt-in query records that store only a redacted question and answer summary, and an optional LM Studio runtime restricted to loopback/RFC1918 origins that fails closed.
bad: Foundation/Beta maturity: the README's own not-implemented list excludes web discovery/fetch, destructive prune and query-history commands, and Ask is gated behind a 'wiki.ask' entitlement and premium runtime pack rather than being plain local functionality. It sits inside a larger SDTK monorepo ecosystem (legacy sdtk-spec atlas paths, separate design/agent kits) with heavy internal jargon, and its agent-monitoring pilot is verified only on Linux/Node 22.
didnt: Corroboration — report-first dry-runs with sidecar-approved apply, redacted query records and fail-closed local runtimes independently confirm our approval-gated, report-first design; the kit itself is a project-local toolkit tied to the SDTK ecosystem, not a fit for our wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @crewhaus/tool-wiki
good: A wiki tool vocabulary with unusually strong write governance: with requireSources enabled, wiki_write deterministically rejects any body lacking a '## Sources' heading ('no citation, no write') and extracts the listed sources into frontmatter; writes are versioned upserts (supersede, never delete) guarded by expectedVersion optimistic concurrency. Recall bodies are boundary-classified at a 'memory' TrustOrigin before reaching the model — a malicious verdict returns a redaction notice instead of the body, and lineage is tagged for egress attribution — and log_knowledge_gap records what the expert could not answer as a gap article for a study loop.
bad: It is an internal component, not a standalone product: a library inside the crewhaus/factory monorepo that needs @crewhaus/wiki-store, a tool catalog and a host composition root, with its README written as a design note (§3.2) against a sibling hosted backend ('thredz') whose parity it pins by test. All tools are scope 'internal', and the package's own description mixes a 0.3.0 memory-release note into a 0.7.0 version line — a moving internal design, not a stable surface.
didnt: Corroboration — 'no citation, no write' source-gated writes, supersede-never-delete versioned upserts, and explicit knowledge-gap logging mirror our citation locking and scored-abstention design almost exactly; as an internal monorepo library it offers nothing directly adoptable. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @dmthepm/commune
good: A personal-wiki engine on Astro whose build and CLI share one link graph and resolver: wikilinks with canonical-spelling discipline enforced by check/gate, backlinks.json written at build, and a Markdown twin served at every page URL so agents and readers get the source without scraping HTML. Dates carry provenance — frontmatter wins, then git history, then mtime — and the engine refuses to derive dates from a shallow clone rather than fabricate them; visibility defaults to private. Its authoring skills save dictated dumps verbatim, render drafts side-by-side for author review, and ship only through a gated PR — 'the author approves the content. This skill never merges.'
bad: It is a publishing engine, not an agent knowledge store: no search ranking or semantic retrieval, no MCP server, no memory layer — and it requires an Astro 7 project on Node 22.12+ with all pages and layout supplied by you. Heading links have real edges (block references and embeds unsupported), and it is a young single-author project extracted from the author's own site (record created 2026-09-03, v0.13.0).
didnt: Corroboration — date provenance with an explicit refusal to fabricate from shallow history, and a ship flow that gates, verifies and never merges without the author, confirm our provenance and approval-gate design; as a static publishing engine it has no retrieval or memory layer for us to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @oldboydev/sheldon
good: The closest design analogue to our own system in this batch: a local-first CLI that separates capture, synthesis and approval — sources are preserved, normalised to Markdown with provenance recorded, an installed agent CLI (Codex, Claude Code or Grok) drafts a knowledge proposal, and the human approves file-by-file before the wiki changes. The approved wiki is served to other projects through a local stdio MCP with an explicit per-consumer scope, a loopback-only web UI handles review and cited Q&A, and SQLite is used only for rebuildable operational state and indexes, never as the source of truth.
bad: The README is Portuguese-only, and platform coverage has hard edges: macOS lacks the image/YouTube/Instagram source connectors (signing/notarisation), and outside the four supported platform builds installation fails with no fallback. It requires Node 24 LTS and synthesises nothing itself — proposals depend on an external agent CLI being installed and authenticated; young (record created 2026-08-12, v0.2.11).
didnt: Corroboration — its propose-then-approve-file-by-file pipeline over preserved sources with recorded provenance independently validates our approval-gated ingest design end to end; we already run that architecture, so there is nothing to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: hazel-wiki
good: A small, simple Markdown wiki server for Node: markdown editing of documents, a configurable storage-provider architecture (disk, browser), an Express-based server exposed for configuration, automatic linking to existing documents based on link text, and EJS templates — with a test suite.
bad: Unmaintained: the record was created 2016-04-01 and last modified 2022-06-18, with Travis/AppVeyor-era CI badges. It is a plain document wiki — no search or ranking worth the name, no agent/MCP interface, no citation or write-governance machinery — and GPL-3.0 copyleft.
didnt: Rejected — licence (GPL-3.0, ideas-only under our licence discipline), maturity (unmaintained since 2022) and fit (a plain web wiki with no agent layer). (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: vitepress-allyouneed
good: VitePress plugin that treats an Obsidian vault as the site source directory: full wikilink forms (aliases, heading links, shortest-path resolution, Chinese filenames), note transclusion with a depth cap, embeds with an automatic asset pipeline (streamed by dev middleware, emitted hashed at build), and one systematic VaultIndex (files, aliases, tags, headings, backlinks, assets) feeding the generated Graph/Stats/Tags views; a zero-config wrapper plus a defineTheme() factory designed so third-party VitePress themes need not know the plugin exists.
bad: Very young single-author project (first published May 2026, still 0.5.x) whose own changelog leads with build-blocker fixes — wikilink parsing that could crash `vitepress build` outright — and it is a publishing layer only: no editing, memory or retrieval of its own, and hard-bound to VitePress.
didnt: Rejected — a vault-to-website publishing plugin for a stack we do not run; our Lens already renders the wiki, and its index/graph views duplicate what we have (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @quiescent/wiki
good: Astro integration that computes everything at build time over a directory of markdown notes: a remark plugin rewriting [[wikilinks]] (dead links marked and warned), a serialized MiniSearch search index, a note graph and hierarchical tag index exposed through a virtual module, plus a validateWikiLinks/reportWikiLinks dead-link CI gate; the same build runs on Cloudflare Workers (no runtime filesystem) and Node.
bad: v0.1.0 from a single maintainer and Astro-only; it is build-time only — in-browser editing and persistence require the sibling @quiescent/server and @quiescent/editor packages — and the search index and graph must be served through the host app's own auth-guarded routes, so the privacy wiring is left to the adopter.
didnt: Corroboration — build-time link validation as a CI gate, and dead links surfaced rather than silently dropped, confirm our citation-locking and validator design; Astro-bound, so nothing to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gatsby-theme-wikinotes
good: A Gatsby theme for Foam/Obsidian/plain-markdown knowledge bases in GitHub's Primer style: local full-text search, canvas graph visualisation, tag pages wired into the graph, GitBook-style SUMMARY.md sidebars, [[WikiLink]] support, nested sidebars and light/dark themes.
bad: Stuck at v0.1.0 since its only release in March 2022, and the package ships the upstream primer-wiki README verbatim — its own record does not describe this package (it even gives the other package's install command), so whatever distinguishes the fork cannot be verified from its own source; Gatsby-bound throughout.
didnt: Rejected — an unmaintained 0.1.0 fork-copy whose own README documents a different package; nothing verifiable to take (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gatsby-theme-primer-wiki
good: The original Primer-styled Gatsby wiki theme: local full-text search, canvas graph visualisation, tags-first navigation with generated tag pages connected to the graph, GitBook-style SUMMARY.md sidebars, [[WikiLink]] support, prefix paths and light/dark modes, with ready Foam, Obsidian and starter templates, and an explicit no-vendor-lock-in design principle (wikilinks the only non-markdown feature).
bad: Last published in May 2022 (v2.0.5) and unmaintained since; bound to the aging Gatsby/MDX stack, and a presentation theme only — no memory, retrieval-quality or write-safety machinery.
didnt: Rejected — unmaintained since 2022 and a rendering theme for a stack we do not use; its no-vendor-lock-in principle matches ours but is already our rule (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: gatsby-garden
good: Turns Obsidian Zettelkasten or plain markdown notes into a static digital garden: wikilink support, a graph visualisation of note linkages, backlinks at the foot of every note, tagging, and auto-generated sitemap, RSS feed and home page, over a simple frontmatter contract (slug, title, date, aliases, tags).
bad: Unmaintained since May 2022; installation is clone-the-repository rather than a composable package, the workflow is manual (notes must live in a _notes folder, copied or symlinked from the vault, and rebuilding is a separate step), and its own README says customising it means editing the Gatsby source with JavaScript knowledge.
didnt: Rejected — a stale, clone-based Gatsby publishing scaffold; our wiki already publishes through the Lens (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: nuartz
good: Quartz-inspired Obsidian publishing on Next.js 16 with shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS v4: parses wikilinks, callouts, backlinks, tags, math and graphs; D3 force-directed graph view, Pagefind full-text search with CJK support, popover previews, dead-link detection, RSS and sitemap; ships both as a headless build-time data library (buildBacklinkIndex, buildFileTree, buildSearchIndex) and as a complete starter app, deployable as a static export or server-side on Vercel.
bad: Young single-author 0.3.x project openly derivative of Quartz; its own hosting guide states the static mode loses dynamic OG images, external link previews and Next.js image optimisation, and the npm package alone ships no React components or routes — the site exists only inside the starter template.
didnt: Rejected — another vault-to-website publisher, for Next.js, a stack we do not run; the Lens covers our rendering need (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidigen
good: A CLI that serves an Obsidian vault as a live wiki: three-column interface with collapsible tree navigation, properties/table-of-contents/backlinks widgets with scroll-spy, hover link previews, Cmd/Ctrl+K live search, live reload on file change, and optional Cloudflare Tunnel plus Cloudflare Access (zero-trust email allowlist) for public access, installable as a boot service on macOS and Linux.
bad: Single-author and young (first published December 2025); it is a live server rather than static output, its public-access story leans on Cloudflare, and the README's from-source instructions still carry a placeholder clone URL (github.com/yourusername/obsidigen) — a visible sign of documentation immaturity.
didnt: Rejected — a vault web server whose tunnelled public-access model runs against our local-first, owner-only Lens custody; nothing here is missing from our stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: docusaurus-plugin-obsidian-vault
good: Docusaurus 3 plugin that syncs an Obsidian vault (local folder or GitHub repository) into docs at build time: wikilinks converted to markdown links, callouts to admonitions, assets copied, _category_.json sidebar files auto-generated, frontmatter preserved and enhanced, MDX-hostile characters escaped, plus custom banners, include/exclude filtering, multi-instance docs support and watch-mode hot reload.
bad: A single v1.0.0 release published on one day in November 2025 by one author, with no track record since; Docusaurus-only, and its GitHub-source mode still requires hand-wiring a repository checkout step in CI.
didnt: Rejected — a one-release sync plugin for Docusaurus, a stack we do not run; our wiki ingests its sources directly (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @dynamotn/datme
good: Renders an Obsidian vault as a digital garden with unusual fidelity: wikilinks, embeds and callouts plus Dataview, Tasks, Canvas, Bases, Excalidraw, Marp decks and Kanban boards rendered at build time; privacy-first — only notes marked `publish: true` leave the vault, with whole notes or single passages AES-GCM password-encrypted; static output with incremental builds (about 2.5 s for a 300-note vault), a global graph with time replay, multilingual pages, and llms.txt/llms-full.txt export.
bad: MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft puts its code in ideas-only territory for us; it demands bleeding-edge runtimes (Bun or Node 23.6+), and it is weeks old (first published October 2026) yet already at 3.1.0 — rapid churn with no settled baseline.
didnt: Board — the publish:true gating and per-passage encryption as publishing-custody ideas for any future public edition; MPL-2.0 makes the code itself ideas-only, and the private wiki does not publish from the vault (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: joplin-plugin-wikilinks
