good: Joplin plugin adding real [[wikilinks]] to the Markdown editor and preview pane: syntax highlighting, Ctrl/Cmd+click navigation (long-press on mobile), pipe-alias display text, heading anchors that scroll after opening, a four-step smart title-resolution ladder (direct note ID, exact title, case-insensitive shortest title, first-word/zettel ID), a command converting Joplin's native [text](:/noteId) links into wikilinks, and code-aware parsing that ignores wikilinks inside code.
bad: Host-bound to Joplin's plugin sandbox — useless outside that app; young (v0.4.1, February 2026) and single-author, and the registry record is sparse (no repository or homepage fields).
didnt: Rejected — a single-feature editor plugin for Joplin, which is neither our editor nor our stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @riebeckite/plugin-citations
good: Official plugin for the Riebeckite static-site framework rendering BibTeX/BibLaTeX citations in Markdown and Obsidian notes: a documented Pandoc-inspired syntax subset (bracketed citations, author-in-text, suppress-author, prefix/suffix locators like 'p. 42'), deterministic numbering with a generated References section and an optional site-wide bibliography page, careful bibliography parsing (multiline fields, nested braces, escaped characters; malformed entries reported and parsing resumes), bibliography files read at build time only and never copied into output, and six named diagnostics (unknown key, duplicate key, missing/malformed bibliography, unsupported entry type, unsupported syntax) — failures surface, never silently pass.
bad: Useful only inside the young Riebeckite framework, and it renders citations for publication without ever verifying that a citation matches its source — the half of the problem we care about; its supported syntax is deliberately a subset (@string macros render literally instead of expanding, and `#` string concatenation keeps only the first part).
didnt: Corroboration — deterministic output plus diagnostics that report malformed and unknown citations instead of failing silently confirm our citation-lockfile discipline; it is a rendering plugin for another framework, so nothing to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: wiki
good: The Node.js Federated Wiki server from Ward Cunningham's federated-wiki lineage: pages stored as flat files (default ~/.wiki, LevelDB optional), a plugin ecosystem split into its own repositories, server farms with neighbourhood seeding so federated sites discover and reuse each other's pages, and a read-only default security posture until a security module is configured.
bad: The meta-package install is fragile by its own README's account — it must be installed with --global-style, `npm update` will not update it, and the legacy database page stores do not work in farm mode; federation is a multi-writer model, the opposite of our single-custodian wiki, with no citation locking or abstention.
didnt: Rejected — federation and multi-writer editing are a design we have rejected by principle; our wiki stays single-custodian and local-first (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-memory-graph
good: Local-first MCP memory server for Claude Code and any MCP client: permanent memory in one SQLite file on the user's machine, local MiniLM embeddings (no API key, $0 per token), hybrid vector + knowledge-graph search returning confidence scores and match-type badges, bi-temporal recall, Obsidian vault sync, auto-capture/recall hooks, memory quality scoring with scheduled self-cleanup, a local web dashboard, and a committed, locally reproducible benchmark corpus — 51 tools in all.
bad: PolyForm Noncommercial licence: source-available and free only for noncommercial use, with commercial use requiring a paid licence, so its code is closed to us; the README's own Limitations discussion caps the single-process SQLite design in the low hundreds of thousands of vectors, and the first run downloads a ~30 MB embedding model from HuggingFace.
didnt: Board — bi-temporal recall and memory quality-scoring as ideas for our retrieval layer; the code itself is PolyForm-Noncommercial (ideas-only under our licence discipline), and its local memory-server role duplicates our own wiki memory design (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ori-memory
good: 'Ori Mnemos' — persistent agent memory implementing cognitive models on a markdown knowledge graph: ACT-R activation decay, spreading activation along wikilink edges, Hebbian co-occurrence and learned retrieval (Q-values, LinUCB arms), with markdown as the truth, the index derived, git as version control, and CLI, MCP-server and library surfaces all going through one recall path; its README publishes an unusually self-critical forgetting benchmark (ForgetEval: supersession, decay, amnesia, purge, drift), including an honest account of the benchmark's 35% vacuous-pass floor.
bad: Pre-1.0 (v0.8.1) and single-author; by its own benchmark account hard purge is its weak spot (64% on the discriminating purge cases), and the learned half of its state (Q-values, retrieval history) is not derivable from the markdown — it must be exported before any index rebuild or it is lost.
didnt: Corroboration — markdown-as-truth with a derived index and explicit supersession/forgetting semantics confirm our architecture and our truth-aware-retrieval direction; its forgetting benchmark is the kind of evaluation our own supersession slice needs (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: granite-mem
good: 'Granite' — a local-first markdown memory system for humans and AI agents: plain .md files with YAML frontmatter as the source of truth, a disposable SQLite FTS5 index rebuilt from the files at any time, wikilinks as the graph, typed note schemas ('types as contracts') with hooks, indexed fields and lifecycles, provenance on every note, and deterministic retrieval with no embeddings and no embedded LLM, exposed through a CLI, a web UI with a constellation graph, and an MCP server.
bad: Pre-1.0 (v0.2.0) and 'moving fast' by its own status note; the one crack in its no-cloud story is in its own FAQ — the MCP layer's Jev semantic judgment makes an outbound call requiring a self-supplied TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and Granite refuses to start without it unless run with --no-cloud; deterministic-only retrieval (no semantic search) is a deliberate ceiling.
didnt: Corroboration — markdown-as-truth, a disposable derived index, typed contracts and per-note provenance are our own design arrived at independently; the closest external confirmation of our architecture in this wave (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mnemo-agent-memory
good: A pure Node.js MCP memory engine for coding agents with no Python or native-database dependency: a persistent knowledge graph plus local ONNX embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and BM25 fused by reciprocal rank fusion, 16 MCP tools, portable single-file team memory bundles (export/import), two-way Obsidian vault mirroring, and memory hygiene — a memory_save supersedes link auto-archives deprecated notes and an audit tool repairs broken file references.
bad: Built exclusively for coding-agent project memory: the default posture is automatic context injection into agent prompts (MNEMO_AUTO_INJECT, 800-token budget), the opposite of gated, on-demand recall. Young and single-author (first published 2026-08, latest v1.3.0, quiet since late August per the record). No citation locking, evidence grading or abstention is documented anywhere in the README.
didnt: Corroboration — supersede-don't-delete memory hygiene, local-only embeddings and a Markdown notes mirror independently match our custody rules; its auto-injection design is the inverse of our approval-gated writes, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: context-mem
good: A self-described reference implementation of Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern in three layers — immutable raw sources, an LLM-maintained Markdown vault (entity, topic and session pages with backlinks, index and log), and a public schema — over an authoritative SQLite store, fully local with no API keys. Fifteen content-aware summarizers compress tool outputs adaptively (pinned entries never compress), retrieval is hybrid BM25 + vector with an optional LLM judge, and its benchmark tables are methodology-hedged (session-level recall, not end-to-end QA, stated in the README itself).
bad: Ingest is automatic and total: every tool call is captured, summarized and written without a human gate, and older observations are progressively compressed — a derived, disposable vault over SQLite, where our raw record is canonical and never compressed away. Built for coding sessions, single-author, and its headline figures (99.1% token savings, 100% LongMemEval with judge) are self-published. No citation locking or scored abstention.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent three-layer Karpathy-pattern implementation (immutable sources / maintained wiki / schema) confirms our base architecture; its auto-ingest-everything, compress-with-age custody is the opposite of our curated, approval-gated record, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: basemind
good: A Rust context layer for coding agents shipped as one MCP server: a tree-sitter code map across 300+ languages answering with paths, line numbers and signatures instead of whole files; document RAG over 90+ formats with OCR; git history/blame intelligence; per-repo shared agent memory whose mined notes enter a review queue (proposals / accept / reject) before anything is kept; and agent-to-agent comms threads. A hard credential floor keeps .env files, keys and credential stores out of the index by default.
bad: Its centre of gravity is multi-agent software development, not a personal knowledge record: memory is per-repo agent scratch with no citation locking, claim lifecycle or abstention scoring. Pre-1.0 and fast-moving (v0.30.0, 69 published versions since 2026-06), effectively single-author, and the npm package is a wrapper that downloads a pre-compiled binary from GitHub Releases on first install.
didnt: Corroboration — its approve-before-kept memory proposal queue independently matches our approval-gated writes, and its credential exclusion floor matches our custody instincts; the scope is coding-agent context, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: basemind-opencode
good: The OpenCode (and, per the README, next-release Pi) adapter for basemind: registering it as an OpenCode plugin wires up the basemind MCP server over stdio, ships the product skills into the host's skill catalog, and surfaces agent-comms inbox notifications as terminal toasts at session start and after tool calls — a tidy host-integration pattern with the packaging checks (ten skills, native extension, both adapters) run before every publish.
bad: It is only an adapter shell: it does nothing without the separate basemind binary installed on PATH and a prior basemind scan of the repo, and its Pi support is announced for 'the next release', not present. Host-bound to OpenCode/Pi, pre-1.0 (v0.30.0), and it contributes no memory, retrieval or governance behaviour of its own.
didnt: Rejected — a host-specific plugin shell for another package, dependent on the basemind binary; nothing standalone exists here to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rag-memory-epf-mcp
good: A project-local RAG memory MCP server holding knowledge graph, multilingual vector search (bge-m3) and FTS5 in a single per-project SQLite file, with 38 annotated tools. Its observation lifecycle is unusually disciplined: corrections supersede instead of overwrite, retracted facts leave search but keep their history, provisional observations need an explicit approve/decline step, and every revision keeps provenance — plus structure-anchored, codepoint-safe chunking for CJK/emoji text and measured, honestly documented retrieval trade-offs.
bad: Scoped to per-project coding-agent memory rather than a governed personal record; search returns current facts but offers no citation locking to sources and no abstention scoring. It needs Node >= 24 and a ~1.2 GB bge-m3 model download for the vector leg, its graph re-ranker is off by default after the author measured it hurting known-item retrieval, and it is a single-maintainer project.
didnt: Corroboration — its observation lifecycle (supersede-don't-overwrite, retract-keeps-history, provisional → approve) independently mirrors our claim lifecycle and approval-gated writes; the scope is project scratch memory, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rag-memory-pg-mcp
good: The PostgreSQL/Supabase sibling of the rag-memory tool family: knowledge graph, document management and semantic search (21 tools in full mode) against a Postgres backend, with one-click install deeplinks for Cursor, VS Code and LM Studio, a free local-embedding mode, and an optional OpenAI embedding mode the README prices honestly as 10–100x faster.
bad: Custody is the problem: the memory lives in a hosted Supabase project and the server connects with the Supabase service key, the credential class that bypasses row-level security — the opposite of local-first custody. Setup demands Supabase credentials before anything runs, the registry record has been quiet since 2026-02, and there is no citation locking, supersession governance or abstention.
didnt: Rejected — memory custody sits in a third-party hosted database behind a service key, against our local-first rule; nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: rag-memory-mcp
good: An MCP server extending the reference knowledge-graph memory model with documents: entities/relations/observations plus document storage, chunking and embedding, hybrid search combining vector similarity with graph traversal, and a local SQLite/sqlite-vec backend with sentence-transformer embeddings — a compact, fully local design with a clearly documented tool surface (store → chunk → embed → extract → link).
bad: Stale and derivative: the registry record has not changed since 2025-05 (latest v1.1.0), the README states it is inspired by the MCP project's own reference memory server, and the registry record itself ships no README. Retrieval carries no citation locking, provenance or abstention, and the LICENSE file its README links to is missing at the repo root.
didnt: Rejected — an unmaintained derivative of the reference memory server with no governance layer; nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-rag-memory
good: A fully offline RAG + context-management MCP server (21 tools) on built-in node:sqlite: document ingest with content-hash dedup and file-size guards, hybrid FTS5-trigram + vector retrieval fused by RRF, remember/recall with importance ratings and duplicate consolidation, and 238 stated checks. Its Performance & limits section is unusually honest — it states plainly that the default embedder is lexical hashing, not semantics, and names paraphrase recall as the known blind spot.
bad: Personal-scale by its own account: brute-force O(N) search over every chunk, an uncapped in-RAM vector cache (~800 MB at 100k chunks), and a default 'vector' leg that measures n-gram overlap rather than meaning. Recall decays by staleness instead of governed supersession with provenance; there is no citation locking or abstention. Single author, young (first published 2026-09), pre-3.0.
didnt: Rejected — sound local engineering, but personal-store scale with lexical-grade default retrieval and staleness decay where we require governed supersession; nothing taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: knowledge-rag
good: The npm distribution form of lyonzin/knowledge-rag: a 100% local RAG MCP server (13 tools, 35 file formats parsed natively, FastEmbed ONNX on CPU) whose claims apparatus is carefully hedged — a published audit report records its workload and limitations, and its agent skills encode check-first/cite-sources retrieval discipline; v4.11.0 adds a preflight that refuses to run its index under cloud-sync folders after documented index-corruption incidents.
bad: Retrieval only, exactly as the standing row found: nothing here keeps, versions, governs or supersedes a record, and 35-format ingestion breadth trades against depth on any one format. The README's own operating-model warning documents a single-writer hazard — two writer processes against one data_dir corrupt the ChromaDB HNSW segment on Windows.
didnt: Corroboration — aligned with the standing master row for lyonzin/knowledge-rag: a well-run local retrieval layer whose methodology-hedged audit claims and path:line citation discipline corroborate the wiki's retrieval standards; it keeps no record and governs nothing, so there is nothing further to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @nebutra/knowledge-rag
good: A multi-tenant hybrid-RAG library for the Nebutra-Sailor agent runtime: ingest → semantic chunk → embed → hybrid vector+keyword retrieval with optional rerank, where every persisted record carries a tenantId and tenant isolation is enforced at every store/query boundary (a tenant-A query can never return tenant-B chunks), with tenant-scoped deletes, structured errors carrying actionable suggestions, and a sub-3-second doctor health report.
bad: Self-declared 'Status: Foundation': the zero-config path is in-memory only, the production PgvectorStore is interface-only (not exercised by its tests, no migrations run), the default embedder is a deterministic local hash embedder and the default reranker is an identity pass-through. It is a multi-tenant SaaS building block inside one vendor's monorepo — the opposite shape from a single-custodian personal record — and offers no citation locking or governance.
didnt: Rejected — a foundation-stage, multi-tenant platform component whose production storage is unimplemented; wrong shape and wrong maturity for our system. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: sepia-mcp
good: A clean, self-contained MCP wrapper for the Sepia personal knowledge-graph memory server: it exposes exactly the server's 7 tools (wake, namespaces, entities, relations, memories, search, prune) over stdio or Streamable HTTP, needs no database or migrations of its own, auto-publishes in lockstep with the app via Changesets, and ships with npm provenance (OIDC) supply-chain attestation.
bad: It is only a proxy: every call is forwarded to a separate Sepia server over its REST API with a bearer token, and the default SEPIA_URL is the author's hosted instance (sepia.fly.dev) — so out of the box, memory custody sits on someone else's server. Nothing works standalone, and the underlying tool surface has no citation locking, provenance or abstention.
didnt: Rejected — a thin client for a hosted memory service; custody-by-default on a third-party server is against our local-first rule, and there is nothing here to take. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: brains-mcp
good: A personal second-brain wiki/memory server with a thoughtful session-boot pattern: one idempotent init_project call creates the project registry page, generates a platform-specific instruction file, seeds foundation pages (instruction schema, template, brain routing) and stub cross-project trackers (open loops, unanswered questions, next actions, decisions log), and returns a short pointer block for the system prompt; storage is local filesystem or Supabase Storage with Postgres full-text search, behind an OAuth 2.0 HTTP API and an MCP server.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at source (registry record, README, repository and published tarball all checked), so the code is ideas-only by default copyright. The design centres on Supabase/cloud storage and ChatGPT Actions rather than local custody, search is plain full-text with no citation locking or abstention, and the project is a single maintainer's fast-moving line (198 versions since 2026-07).
didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at source makes the code untouchable under our licence discipline, and its cloud-storage centre of gravity runs against local-first custody; the init-scaffolding idea is noted but not boarded from an unlicensed source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: agent-knowledge
good: A git-synced Markdown knowledge vault plus cross-tool session search (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Aider, Continue, Cline, OpenCode auto-discovered), with a temporal knowledge graph — edges carry valid_from/valid_to windows, as_of point-in-time queries, and an invalidate action that ends facts without deleting them — plus edge provenance (manual / auto-link / distill / reflect), freshness metadata on every search hit, confidence/decay scoring with a gated promoter that emits an auditable diary, staleness detection cross-checked against code activity, and secrets scrubbing before every git push.
bad: Its centre of gravity is coding-session recall: it auto-ingests session transcripts from seven tools (verbatim per-message indexing is on by default), auto-commits and pushes vault writes, and ranks by recency/access decay rather than governed supersession — a capture-everything posture our curated, approval-gated ingest deliberately avoids. Single author; no citation locking to sources and no abstention scoring.
didnt: Corroboration — temporal validity windows, invalidate-don't-delete, edge provenance and per-hit freshness metadata independently mirror our claim-lifecycle design; its transcript auto-ingest model is not ours, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @vib795/agent-memory
good: Durable cross-repo agent memory with exemplary supply-chain discipline: zero runtime and zero dev dependencies (enforced by a CI check that fails the build if a dependency is ever added), no install script, provenance-attested npm publishes, and a plain-Markdown store in ~/.agents/memory/ as the source of truth with a disposable SQLite FTS5 index — the same truth/index split our wiki uses. Three skills (handoff / remember / recall) ride on top, PII detectors run before capture with their three known gaps documented in the open, and 113 tests are stated.
bad: Retrieval is FTS5 keyword search only — no semantic leg, no citation locking, no abstention scoring — and the store is agent working memory (handoffs and captured facts), not a governed record with supersession or provenance per claim. Pre-1.0 (v0.8.2), single author, and it requires Node >= 22.16 for the unflagged node:sqlite FTS5 build.
didnt: Corroboration — Markdown-as-truth with a disposable index, zero-dependency discipline and documented-detector honesty independently match our architecture and custody standards; its keyword-only recall does not clear our retrieval bar, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @engramlabs/mcp
good: A local-first agentic knowledge and memory layer with a Rust core: source-grounded knowledge (every fact traces to a chunk and its source) kept distinct from experiential memory, belief synthesis with bi-temporal, recomputable stances and an explicit contradiction list, six retrieval modes fused with cross-encoder reranking, and policy, provenance and scope checked on every read and write — all data in local SQLite, no telemetry and no network on the default path. The npm package is the MCP launcher, with one-command installs per client and an adversarial read-only reviewer subagent in its agent bundle.
bad: Brand new and explicitly not production-ready: the repository's own Status section reads 'pre-1.0 — demo-driven, not production-ready', the package is an alpha (0.2.11-alpha) first published 2026-10-18, and only the memory + retrieval + knowledge subset of its contract is frozen. The registry record itself carries no README — every substantive claim rests on the repository — and the project is effectively a single maintainer's days-old codebase.
didnt: Corroboration — policy/provenance/scope on every path, source-grounded facts and contradiction tracking independently mirror our governance design more closely than anything else in this batch; at alpha age it is evidence, not a dependency, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: megamemory
good: An MCP server that lets a coding agent build and query a per-project knowledge graph of concepts, architecture and decisions, so project understanding persists across sessions: the LLM itself is the indexer (no AST parsing), storage is a local per-project SQLite database with in-process embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, no API keys), and it ships a two-way merge engine with conflict detection and AI-assisted resolution, soft-delete with history preserved, and a web graph explorer.
bad: Retrieval is brute-force cosine similarity, which the README itself scopes to graphs under ~10k nodes; the graph's quality rests entirely on what the agent chooses to write into it, and nothing at source describes citation locking, provenance to source documents, scored abstention or approval gates on writes.
didnt: Rejected — a coding-agent project-memory graph in an opaque SQLite store; our knowledge layer is owner-readable files with citation locking and approval-gated writes, and its merge machinery solves a multi-writer problem our single-custodian design does not have. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @muvon/octobrain
good: A Rust persistent-memory tool (CLI plus MCP server) with semantic and hybrid BM25+vector search, Zettelkasten-style auto-linking, Ebbinghaus temporal decay, sleep consolidation, knowledge indexing of URLs and files, git-backed knowledge boxes, and — rare in this field — published BEIR retrieval benchmarks (SciFact hybrid nDCG@10 0.742, NFCorpus 0.363) with a reproducible offline harness.
bad: Memory lives in the tool's own application data directories as an internal store, not in owner-readable documents; the README itself admits the cross-encoder reranker is currently a no-op with fastembed models, and config loading is strict enough that deleting a field by hand makes startup fail. Nothing at source describes citation provenance, abstention or approval gates.
didnt: Rejected — fit/duplication: a capable assistant-memory store, but an opaque internal database rather than owner-held files, and it carries none of the trust machinery (citation locking, scored abstention, approval-gated writes) that defines our system; its benchmark discipline is credited in good. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @iwe-org/mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (registry license field; agrees with the standing iwe-org/iwe row's repository-settled licence)
good: The npm face of the IWE core: a zero-config npx stdio binary running the IWE MCP server (iwec) directly over the markdown files in its working directory, customised only by an optional .iwe/config.toml, with prebuilt binaries for macOS (arm64/x64), Linux (x64/arm64) and Windows — the studied core's agent-memory door, installable in one line.
bad: The package README is minimal — no tool list, no licence section — and the server inherits the limit recorded in the standing study of the core: connected agents read and write the shared notes directly, bounded mainly by undo; no citation locking, provenance, abstention or approval gate is described.
didnt: Corroboration — aligned with the standing Tier 2 row for iwe-org/iwe: one of the closest living relatives of our design (shared human/agent Markdown memory in owner-held files behind an MCP door) confirms the architecture from the market side; the difference remains the trust machinery it does not describe and we built. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: mcp-agents-memory
licence: MIT (registry license field only; the README states no licence)
good: A shared, time-ordered memory pool for many agents at once (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Grok, Antigravity): every turn stored raw and chronologically in PostgreSQL+pgvector, with a hot path for instant writes and an asynchronous 'cold path' librarian that tags, embeds, clusters and promotes durable user facts, plus soft-delete archival, per-model separation and a session-startup brief.
bad: It is premised on automatically capturing full conversation transcripts into a shared central database — the opposite of local-first, owner-held custody — and its curation depends on an LLM backend (local Qwen3-14B via llama.cpp or a cloud fallback) and OpenAI embeddings; the record's README states no licence, so the licence rests on the registry field alone.
didnt: Rejected — premised on automatic session-transcript capture into a shared central store, which is unapproved in our system, and on centralised Postgres custody rather than owner-held files with approval-gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @absolutejs/agent-memory
licence: MIT (registry license field only; the README states no licence)
good: A provider-neutral memory library with unusually explicit trust design: tenant/user/agent/run scopes, mandatory provenance digests on records, taint-compatible metadata, per-operation policy, expiration, deletion and subject erasure, optimistic versions and idempotent writes, encryption through an injected codec (KMS/envelope seams), pluggable retrieval adapters, and the stated rule that retrieved records remain labelled memory data and are never promoted to trusted instructions.
bad: It is an embeddable library at v0.1.7, not a working memory system: the host must supply the codec, the retrieval adapters and the policy, and validate writes via a sibling trust package; the README documents no evaluation, storage engine or tooling of its own, and the package lives as one module inside a larger agent-modules monorepo.
didnt: Corroboration — its mandatory provenance digests, taint labels and never-promote-retrieved-memory-to-trusted-instructions rule corroborate our trust-boundary design for agent memory; nothing taken, as it is an early-stage library rather than a store we could build on. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @kiraautonoma/agent-memory-mcp
good: An MCP-native memory server whose memories carry provenance chains (source, extraction method, confidence), decay-weighted retrieval on a 30-day half-life reinforced by access, and a feedback flywheel that ranks recall by confidence × source trust × decay × usefulness — all in a local SQLite database with no API key required.
bad: Recall as documented is keyword/category search ranked by those scores — no semantic retrieval is described — and the confidence and source-trust inputs are asserted by the storing agent rather than verified against anything; v0.1.3 with very small adoption, and no citation locking or approval gate on writes.
didnt: Corroboration — provenance on every memory and decay-and-feedback-scored recall confirm the direction of our scored, provenance-carrying memory design; keyword-only recall and self-asserted confidence fall short of our citation-locked standard, so nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @danielsimonjr/memoryjs
good: A very broad TypeScript knowledge-graph library: entities, relations and observations with bitemporal versioning and contradiction-driven supersession, temporal relations with validity windows, BM25/TF-IDF/fuzzy/semantic/hybrid/temporal search, graph algorithms, RBAC and PII redaction, an agent memory system with decay, salience and consolidation, and JSONL (human-readable), SQLite or PostgreSQL storage backends.
bad: The breadth is the risk: an enormous single-author API surface that a host application must assemble into a system, with no owner-facing surface of its own; the default JSONL backend is single-process only by its own README, and its observations carry no citation lock to source documents of the kind our wiki requires.
didnt: Board — the bitemporal versioning and contradiction-driven supersession model as a design reference for our own supersession machinery (a Phase-2 question for the owner); the library itself is a component, not a fit for our file-based store. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @fgv/ts-agent-memory
licence: MIT (registry license field; the repository's root LICENSE is also MIT; the record carries no README)
good: From the record's own description: a FileTree-backed storage and retrieval substrate for agent memory and knowledge — memory kept as a plain file tree rather than a database, which is the custody shape our design also chose.
bad: The registry record carries no README at all, and the package's recorded source directory (libraries/ts-agent-memory in ErikFortune/fgv) no longer exists anywhere in the repository's current tree, so the published package's source cannot be inspected at its recorded home; the version line is a prerelease (5.1.0-36).
didnt: Rejected — maturity/verifiability: an undocumented substrate whose own source has vanished from its recorded repository location; the file-tree custody idea it names is one we already implement in fuller form. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @memongo/memory-engine
licence: Apache-2.0 (registry license field only; the README states no licence)
good: The low-level engine of the Memongo stack: MongoDB-native search, graph, episodes, structured memory, procedures, sync, reasoning chains, novelty detection and memory consolidation with lease behaviour, plus access tracking, recall traces and erasure support, and provider reranking with carefully specified window, overflow and fallback semantics.
bad: It is server infrastructure, not a memory system an owner can inspect: it requires MongoDB and the surrounding Memongo stack, exposes the lowest-level primitives rather than any agent- or owner-facing surface, and depends on an external reranking provider; its README states no licence, so the licence rests on the registry field alone.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a MongoDB-native server engine is the opposite direction from our local-first, owner-held plain files, and nothing in it fills a gap our stack has. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @hydradb/mcp
licence: Apache-2.0 (registry license field only; no repository named in the record and the README states no licence)
good: A complete MCP surface over the hosted Hydra DB memory service: unified memory-and-knowledge query with knowledge-graph context, ingest of notes, documents or conversations, subgraph traversal, inspect/status tools and per-request feedback, plus a separate Cypher property-graph surface; it runs as a local stdio binary or as a hosted HTTP server with OAuth sign-in and single- or multi-tenant modes.
bad: The memory itself lives in the vendor's hosted database behind an account API key, so custody leaves the owner's machine entirely; deletes are documented as irreversible; and the package record names no repository or homepage, so the code's home is unstated at source.
didnt: Rejected — custody: a hosted vendor database is incompatible with our local-first, owner-held custody rule, and no citation locking, abstention or approval machinery is described. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @cycgraph/memory
good: A temporal knowledge-graph memory library with design discipline rare in this field: facts carry validity ranges and are invalidated rather than deleted (so 'what was true on 2026-01-15?' is answerable), provenance on every record, a conflict detector with explicit resolution policies (supersede-on-newer, negation-invalidates-positive, manual-review), a paraphrase-aware write-admission gate that refuses re-entry of previously invalidated facts, and eval-gated retention whose decision rule uses a Welch-style test with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control and ships its own operating-characteristics validator.
bad: It is an embeddable TypeScript library at v0.8.2 (pre-1.0), not a system: stores are in-memory or a Postgres adapter from a sibling package, extraction quality depends on pluggable extractors that fall back to regex, and there is no owner-facing surface, no citation lock to source documents and no human approval gate on writes.
didnt: Corroboration — its invalidation-not-deletion temporal model, conflict-resolution policies, write-admission gate and eval-gated retention independently corroborate our supersession, gating and eval-gated promotion design; nothing taken, as our store is owner-held files rather than a library's in-memory or Postgres state. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @devinmlowe/engram
licence: MIT (registry license field, confirmed by the repository LICENSE file; no licence section in the registry-carried README)
good: A local-first, offline-capable cognitive memory system for Claude Code: conversation history is consolidated by a 'dream state' pipeline (ingest, extract, consolidate, reflect, prune) into semantic knowledge and an entity graph, with hybrid vector + FTS5 + graph search disciplined by caller-specified token budgets and progressive disclosure, FSRS decay, contradiction detection, and CLI, MCP-server and web-visualization faces.
bad: It is premised on ingesting raw conversation history — its sync reads the agent's own session archives — and its autonomous daemon extracts, merges and prunes memory without a human approval gate; the registry-carried README is truncated at 64 KB with no licence section in the carried text (the licence was settled at the repository).
didnt: Rejected — premised on session-transcript ingest, which is unapproved in our system, and its consolidation runs autonomously without the approval-gated writes our custody model requires. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memory-mcp-1file
good: The npm face of the studied single-file memory server: an npx/bunx launcher that downloads and runs the one-file binary — semantic memory with embeddings, tree-sitter code indexing, an entity/relationship knowledge graph and temporal queries — across Linux (musl), macOS (x86_64 and ARM64) and Windows, with trusted-project configuration that pins the version and keeps the database under the project's own data directory.
bad: It distributes a project the standing study found archived and superseded by its own first line; the launcher fetches a release binary at run time, so running it means trusting release assets, and the governance limits recorded for the core (a system-prompt protocol an agent may or may not follow; decay and confidence as unwritten roadmap entries) apply unchanged.
didnt: Rejected — aligned with the standing Tier 2 row for pomazanbohdan/memory-mcp-1file: a capable all-in-one store whose author has moved on; the npm launcher adds distribution convenience, not a reason to reopen the judgement. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: shelbymcp
good: A zero-dependency MCP memory server in a single SQLite file: a knowledge graph with typed edges (refines, cites, refuted_by, tags), pre-computed one-line summaries so search returns pointers instead of blowing up the context window, and a 'Forage' scheduled skill that consolidates, deduplicates, connects and backfills embeddings using the owner's existing AI subscription — no Docker, no Python, no cloud accounts.
bad: Memory quality rests on a prompt-driven memory protocol and on scheduled agent runs rather than on verified machinery: nothing at source describes citation locking to source documents, scored abstention or an approval gate on writes, and at v0.2.6 the graph's discipline is only as good as the agent following the protocol.
didnt: Corroboration — single-file local custody, typed refuted_by edges and scheduled self-maintenance corroborate our local-first, sweep-maintained design; the trust-machinery difference (no citation locking, scored abstention or approval gates) is why nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @salishforge/memforge
good: A neuroscience-inspired memory service with tiered hot, warm and cold memory, hybrid full-text plus vector search with rank fusion, and ten-phase 'sleep cycles' that score, triage, resolve conflicts, revise low-confidence memories and detect knowledge gaps; it measures its own quality (revision stability, retrieval correlation, contradiction rates) and publishes LongMemEval results (93.2% R@5 in hybrid mode, 35.0% in keyword mode).
bad: Beta software (v3.0.0-beta.4) requiring PostgreSQL 16+ and optionally Redis; its own Known Limitations section states a single-process design, no built-in scheduler, no streaming consolidation for large backlogs, and that the revision and reflection features require an LLM provider's API keys — and its sleep cycles rewrite stored memories autonomously, with no human approval gate.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a Postgres server stack whose core move, an LLM autonomously rewriting stored memories during sleep cycles, runs against our approval-gated writes and owner-readable files; its self-measurement discipline is noted, but nothing is taken. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @steno-ai/engine
licence: MIT (registry license field only — the registry README states no licence)
good: Core memory engine for the Steno agent-memory system: a heuristic-to-LLM extraction pipeline with deduplication, contradiction detection and entity extraction into a facts + knowledge-graph store, and 6-signal retrieval (vector, keyword, graph, temporal, salience decay, trigger matching) with fusion ranking and reranking; storage, LLM and embedding sit behind adapter interfaces (SQLite/Supabase, OpenAI/OpenAI-compatible).
bad: v0.2.2 and early: it is a library core, not a usable system — every deployment must supply its own storage, LLM and embedding adapters, and the official adapters are OpenAI-centric. It models tenant-scoped conversation facts, not human-curated documents, and the README documents no evaluation, citation grounding or write-approval mechanism.
didnt: Rejected — a tenant conversation-fact engine at a different layer from our citation-locked markdown wiki; its contradiction detection and multi-signal fusion converge with our retrieval design but the engine itself is not a fit (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @fancyrobot/agent-vault
good: Durable project memory as plain Markdown + wikilinks in a per-project .agent-vault/ — typed notes (phases, steps, bugs, decisions, sessions) with canonical templates and YAML frontmatter, 12 MCP tools including vault_validate (frontmatter/structure/links/orphans/doctor) and vault_prepare_context with token budgeting and explainable score reasons, schema migrations run as dry-run plan then apply with validation after each step, and read-only vault:// resources that reject path traversal and secret-like paths.
bad: Scope is software-project execution memory (phase/step workflows, bug-triage branches), not general knowledge; the surface is harness-specific, installing into Claude Code/OpenCode/pi/Codex configs, and during execution the agent updates the session note continuously and automatically — there is no approval gate on writes.
didnt: Corroboration — a Markdown vault with typed notes, a wikilink graph, an integrity validator and dry-run migrations independently mirrors our own vault discipline; its project-execution scope is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: grounder
good: Obsidian-vault memory for Cursor and Claude Code kept as plain markdown files the user owns — no database or background process. Three fixed document shapes (living plans updated in place, dated one-off notes, per-session handoff logs), setup/link commands that preview writes and ask for confirmation, and deliberate by design: nothing is read or written until a command is run, no auto-capture; the vault syncs across machines with plain git.
bad: Deliberately minimal: no embeddings, graph traversal or citation machinery; skills exist only for Cursor and Claude Code (Copilot/Codex are roadmap items), and handoffs depend on the user remembering to run the command — an auto-draft handoff on session end is only 'under consideration' in its roadmap.
didnt: Corroboration — files-you-own markdown memory with deliberate, preview-and-confirm writes, living plans plus dated logs, is the same custody posture our wiki is built on; nothing in it is missing from our stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @amemhq/core
good: TypeScript implementation of A-MEM (NeurIPS 2025): LLM note construction classifies notes as episodic memory or durable knowledge, generates bidirectional Zettelkasten links, and evolves linked notes under an EVOLVE/CONFLICT/EXPAND/NEW taxonomy with a full evolution_history audit trail; retrieval fuses local Transformers.js dense vectors with BM25 via RRF plus a relevance-gated 2-hop graph expansion, conflicting or outdated notes are temporally soft-deleted rather than overwritten, and notes carry owner/readers/writers isolation fields.
bad: Requires a running Qdrant server and an LLM API (Anthropic by default) for every write, link judgment and evolution — heavy external machinery; memory evolution rewrites notes autonomously on LLM judgment, the opposite of approval-gated writes; the README itself notes Japanese and Korean get no lexical (BM25) tokens.
didnt: Board — the EVOLVE/CONFLICT/EXPAND/NEW memory-evolution taxonomy with an evolution_history audit trail, as an idea for our claim-lifecycle work; the engine itself is not adopted (Qdrant + per-write LLM calls, and autonomous note rewriting conflicts with our approval gates) (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @touchskyer/memex
good: Zettelkasten memory for coding agents as atomic markdown cards with [[bidirectional links]] in one shared ~/.memex/cards directory used identically by Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf and Pi via MCP (12 tools) or plugins — no vector database or embeddings; link/backlink graph stats, an organize command surfacing orphans, hubs and conflicts, git-based sync, and secret guardrails that reject high-confidence raw secrets and redact credentials embedded in URLs.
bad: Cards are written automatically by the agent on task completion (auto-recall/auto-save hooks) with no approval gate, citation locking or provenance requirement; the A-MEM-inspired agentic workflow is experimental and default-off, and the README's own privacy section concedes it cannot hide unsafe tool-call arguments already shown in the transcript.
didnt: Corroboration — plain-markdown atomic cards with wikilinks under git custody is our own base design arrived at independently; its automatic write model differs from our approval-gated writes and nothing is taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: amalfa
good: Local-first knowledge graph over markdown: the files are the source of truth and the SQLite index is a disposable cache. Indexes markdown into a searchable graph exposed via 8 MCP tools (semantic search, node reading, link exploration, find_gaps for similar-but-unlinked documents) with full CLI parity, built around a structured-reflection workflow of briefs to debriefs to playbooks so past session learnings compound.
bad: Extraction (LangExtract) needs cloud LLM API keys (Gemini/OpenRouter/Mistral) or an Ollama setup plus a Python sidecar environment; the registry README leads with API-key configuration, and its performance claims ('95% search precision', '4.6x faster than grep') are stated without a cited benchmark.
didnt: Corroboration — markdown-as-source-of-truth with a disposable index cache is exactly our architecture, and find_gaps echoes our orphan/link lint; the hosted-LLM extraction layer is not a fit and nothing is taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: engramgraph
good: Deterministic code + knowledge graph memory engine needing no LLM: Tree-Sitter parsing (16 languages) builds a structural code graph in an embedded Kuzu/ryugraph store while SAGE-style self-evolving graph memory handles specs and decisions; the MCP server is deliberately read-only (write/index tools excluded — indexing is a terminal job) and the package deliberately refuses to auto-register itself into assistant configs at install time; its platform-support documentation is unusually honest, including admitting a previously cited CI release gate never actually ran.
bad: Heavy native dependencies with real platform breakage documented in its own README: the graph-DB binary is broken upstream on Linux ARM64 and on glibc < 2.38 (Ubuntu 22.04 / Debian 12), and most non-Linux-x64 platforms need a C/C++ toolchain at install time.
didnt: Corroboration — a read-only MCP door by default and a refusal to self-grant tool access at install corroborate our gateway's default-deny, approval-first posture; the engine itself is a code-graph layer we do not adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cortex-graph
good: Dual-layer knowledge graph for coding agents: an AST structural layer (symbols, imports, cross-file dependencies) joined to an episodic intent layer (verified decisions, gotchas, invariants), compacted into under-2,500-token context slices; memory updates go to an append-only event ledger in .cortex/ledger/ designed to merge in git without conflicts, new insights start tentative and are promoted to verified only when test suites pass (3-tier verification protocol), and it ships an MCP stdio server.
bad: v0.1.1 — very early; scope is codebase/coding-agent memory, not general knowledge; the README's own quickstart invokes `npx cortex-memory` although the package is named cortex-graph.
didnt: Corroboration — tentative-to-verified promotion of agent insights plus an append-only, git-mergeable ledger mirrors our trust-ledger and verification discipline; the codebase-memory product itself is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: ogm-slim
good: Fully local persistent memory + AST codebase graph for coding agents on a single SQLite file (WAL + FTS5, no API keys): Tree-Sitter call graph, hybrid recall ranking (BM25 60% + agent confidence 25% + recency decay 15%), memories anchored to code symbols with auto-supersede versioning, a bi-temporal schema separating immutable evidence episodes from distilled memories that cite them, Louvain community detection and PageRank, and 12 MCP tools including memory_feedback (confirm/reject/correct/supersede/stale) and memory_forget with audit trails.
bad: Codebase/coding-agent scoped rather than a general knowledge system; a young single-author-scale project (v1.1.0) whose README reports only 23 unit tests, and its performance figures are self-reported.
didnt: Corroboration — bi-temporal episodes-versus-memories with citation edges, a supersede/feedback lifecycle and local-first single-file custody all converge with our design; the coding-agent product is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: opentology
good: Ontology-powered project memory: codebase modules, symbols, decisions, issues and sessions stored as RDF named graphs queryable in SPARQL, with a context_impact blast-radius check the assistant runs before editing (its documented cycle confirms with the user first) and a published grep-vs-graph experiment on its own codebase showing transitive dependents that grep misses.
bad: Coding-project scope, v0.4.1; by design it goes beyond tools — it installs SessionStart hooks, writes behavioural instructions into the project's CLAUDE.md and auto-records session summaries, i.e. automatic session capture plus instruction injection into the agent's standing context.
didnt: Rejected — codebase-scoped, and its behaviour-shaping model (hooks that auto-capture sessions and injected CLAUDE.md instructions) conflicts with our deliberate, approval-gated ingest; the pre-edit impact-check pattern is noted but the package is not a fit (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: opencode-graphiti
good: Two-layer OpenCode memory: short-term structured session events (decisions, tasks, file edits, errors) held in Redis/FalkorDB and continuously rebuilt into a priority-tiered snapshot re-injected before every LLM call and compaction, while long-term recall lives in a Graphiti temporal graph updated only in the background — Graphiti is never on the synchronous path and the plugin degrades gracefully to local memory when it is down; topic-drift detection (Jaccard similarity) schedules cache refresh.
bad: Its core premise is continuous automatic capture of session events — including child/subagent sessions promoted into the root session's state — into memory; it requires Redis/FalkorDB plus a Docker-run Graphiti MCP server, and is bound to OpenCode.
didnt: Rejected — premised on automatic session-event capture and ingest, which is unapproved in our system, and host-bound to OpenCode over an external Redis/Graphiti stack (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: graphzep
good: TypeScript implementation of the Zep paper's temporal knowledge graph: episodic, semantic and procedural memory over a bi-temporal model, automated fact extraction with confidence scoring, semantic/keyword/hybrid search with MMR reranking, drivers for Neo4j and FalkorDB plus an RDF triple store with SPARQL 1.1 and RDFS/OWL reasoning, and LLM clients for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and Groq; the README claims 91+ passing tests.
bad: v0.1.0 — a first release; a from-scratch reimplementation of the Zep/Graphiti architecture rather than the original, requiring an external graph database and a cloud LLM API key for extraction and embeddings (every README example uses OpenAI), and its integration tests require a database.
didnt: Rejected — immature (0.1.0) reimplementation bound to an external graph DB + cloud LLM stack; its bi-temporal model converges with our design direction, but bi-temporal fields are an owner-gated decision in our system, not adopted from here (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @happycastle/opencode-graphiti
good: OpenCode plugin giving coding agents persistent memory via a Graphiti temporal knowledge graph: automatic context injection at session start (user profile + project knowledge), user/project scoping via group_id, hybrid semantic + keyword search through the Graphiti MCP server, a loopback-only read-only local dashboard, and a read-only 'dream' reflection mode that reviews temporal facts before any save and never mutates memory.

didnt: Rejected — host-bound OpenCode plugin shell over an external Graphiti/graph-DB stack, judged on its own record (a distinct package from vicary's opencode-graphiti); the read-only dream-reflection pattern is noted but nothing is taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: n8n-nodes-graphiti
good: n8n community node giving AI Agent workflows dual memory — recent conversation episodes plus long-term facts in a Graphiti temporal graph — with grouped semantic search that returns facts grouped by source (file vs conversation) with confidence scores, per-user session memory, and graceful fallback to in-memory chat history when the episodes endpoint fails.
bad: The node does nothing on its own: it requires the author's separate 'Graphiti Awesome Memory' FastAPI backend (with Neo4j and LLM credentials) to be deployed first; it is bound to n8n, and its README's worked example is built on medical records and carries cryptocurrency donation addresses.
didnt: Rejected — an n8n-host-bound node dependent on a separate bespoke backend stack; its source-grouped fact output echoes our citation grouping but nothing is taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @multilab/graph-memory
licence: MIT (registry record states no license field; settled from the LICENSE file in the repository named by the record)
good: Graph-as-navigation memory plugin for DeepSeek Harness/OpenClaw: TASK/SKILL/EVENT nodes, summaries and communities only navigate — the original user question and final answer remain the evidence and travel with every recall; extraction reads only the question and final answer (explicitly no reasoning/tool transcript ingestion), invalid extraction is quarantined rather than repaired into accepted data, a corrupt database is quarantined without deletion, decay deprecates then purges stale nodes with escape hatches and a revive path, and the README publishes a measured 20-turn benchmark (-80.69% first-request context) with method and limits stated; 491/498 automated tests passing.

didnt: Corroboration — 'the graph only navigates; the original Q/A remains the evidence', quarantine-don't-repair failure handling and refusal to ingest reasoning/tool transcripts all align with our citation and ingest discipline; the host-bound plugin is not adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-graphmemory
licence: MIT (registry record states no license field; the README License section and licence badge both state MIT)
good: Cross-session knowledge-graph memory for DeepSeek Harness and OpenClaw: conversations are extracted in the background into TASK/SKILL/EVENT nodes with five typed edges (including CONFLICTS_WITH), stored in a local SQLite database; recall fuses optional vector search with FTS5, community expansion and PageRank, and content recalled into the prompt is explicitly marked as untrusted reference material that cannot override the current user instruction. A dashboard shows extraction progress, recent errors and the graph itself.
bad: A plugin for DeepSeek Harness, pinned to the DSH 0.1.5 line (the 0.1.x line is bugfix-only), so it does nothing outside that host; extraction depends on a separately configured LLM route, and it is a young (v0.2.0, first published 2026-09) single-maintainer fork-line of adoresever/graph-memory.

name: dsh-kylin-memory
good: Dual-host (DeepSeek Harness + QiLin/Kylin) graph memory that manages the history surface sent to the model: recent turns stay verbatim and older prefixes are batch-archived only past a token threshold, so provider prefix caches survive; a new value for the same (subject, predicate) marks the old fact invalid and recall drops it automatically, while recall always carries the exact original question and final answer — the graph is a navigation layer, not the fact source. The README reports 194/194 automated tests, CI, and real dual-host install verification.

didnt: Corroboration — fact invalidation instead of deletion, and source-exact recall (graph as navigation, originals as truth), are our lifecycle and citation positions in another stack; host-bound to DSH/QiLin, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: graph-memory
licence: MIT (registry record states no license field; the README header and License section both state MIT)
good: OpenClaw context engine that builds a typed property graph (TASK/SKILL/EVENT nodes, five edge types including CONFLICTS_WITH) from conversations in local SQLite; dual-path recall (FTS5/vector seeds, community expansion, graph walk and Personalized PageRank, plus a community-summary path) with vector dedup, and the top recalled nodes pull their original conversation snippets back into context so a node stays tied to the dialogue that produced it. The README documents a measured 95K-to-24K token compression over a 7-round task and 80 tests.
bad: Works only as OpenClaw's registered contextEngine slot — without that config it silently never ingests; extraction and community summaries need LLM/embedding API keys; the npm registry record is metadata-poor (no repository or author field); single author.

name: nox-mem
good: Self-hosted hybrid memory engine (SQLite FTS5 + sqlite-vec + knowledge graph) with a CLI, an HTTP API and a 21-tool MCP server; files deleted from disk become tombstones whose chunks stay searchable and are listed for human review, every destructive operation (reindex, consolidate, compact, crystallize, kg-prune) takes an atomic snapshot first, an ingest guard refuses writes into a database over 10,000 chunks without explicit confirmation, and answers come with citations plus honestly documented --as-of temporal filtering.

didnt: Corroboration — its tombstone review queue, snapshot-before-destruction and large-database write guard are our approval-gated deletion and custody posture independently arrived at; a separate store we do not need, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: cogni-code
licence: MIT (registry license field only; the README states no licence)
good: Harness-agnostic agent memory spanning Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode and pi: a git-versioned knowledge graph (so memory changes can be inspected or reverted) tended by a scribe-auditor-librarian-dreamer pipeline whose auditor prioritises stale and contradictory nodes; memories an agent writes itself are marked written_via and loaded framed as unreviewed information rather than instructions, and session context is injected as compact mental models instead of raw history.
bad: Heavy machinery for memory (a background Docker daemon or API worker, per-harness hook plumbing, a separate dashboard app) that burns LLM calls continuously and writes into four harnesses' hook/config surfaces; the licence rests on the registry field alone; a young, fast-moving single-author project (registry record created 2026-07, latest 4.2.2).
didnt: Corroboration — git-versioned memory, contradiction/staleness auditing and unreviewed-agent-write marking all confirm our custody and filings design; adopting the engine would replace our wiki rather than extend it, so nothing taken (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: stratagate-dsh
good: DeepSeek Harness memory that keeps six detail layers (L0 title to L5 raw record) for every conversation block: older blocks present progressively simpler views while the full original is always retained and re-expandable on demand; extracted events keep their source and distinguish when something was said from when it happened, new events can supersede current-state graph entries while history and sources stay, and an explicit evidence gate makes the agent check whether retrieved evidence actually suffices before answering — searching further or declaring uncertainty when it does not. Retrieval hits never reinforce a memory; only evidence actually adopted into an answer does. It publishes a LoCoMo evaluation (80.46% judged accuracy vs Mem0 base 63.22% on the conv-26 sample, 152 questions).
bad: A plugin for DeepSeek Harness only (the DSH 0.2.0 version family); the published evaluation covers a single LoCoMo conversation and is self-run; the decay design deliberately lets unadopted memories sink in recall priority; and the layered machinery (six views per block plus graph, topic catalogue and profile layers) is complex.
didnt: Corroboration — the evidence gate (answer only on sufficient retrieved evidence, else search more or say so) and use-only reinforcement are our abstention and citation discipline in another system; DSH-bound, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-living-memory
licence: MIT for the code (registry field and README License section agree); the README expressly reserves the NuanNuan name and persona, which are NOT granted under the licence
good: Self-tending local SQLite memory for DeepSeek Harness: a nightly patrol deduplicates and merges entries, applies temporal decay, builds a knowledge graph with Personalized PageRank, and — when a new memory contradicts an old one — flags both for review instead of silently overwriting history; recall fuses seven signals via RRF and degrades gracefully when a channel is missing; daily snapshots and an audit trail are kept; and guard rules block credential-shaped content before it can be written to the store, with a prepublish contamination gate that fails closed.
bad: DeepSeek Harness only; the configuration surface is enormous (30+ LEGION_* disable switches); decay deliberately sinks unused memories; and it is a young single-maintainer project published under an AI persona whose name and persona the licence pointedly does not cover.
didnt: Corroboration — contradiction flagging for review (never silent overwrite) and a secrets-shaped write gate mirror our approval and custody rules; DSH-bound, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-unified-agent-memory
good: One Obsidian vault as the shared source of truth for a whole agent fleet (dsh, Codex, Claude, Hermes), with a zero-dependency Python core and a local SQLite FTS5 index; agents may write only into an inbox staging area, a Promoter reviews submissions and promotes them into the canonical vault, conflicting facts are intercepted into an adjudication queue (the agent rules first with a written rationale kept in the log, a human only when it cannot decide), credentials are auto-redacted before storage, recalled content is wrapped as data-not-instructions, superseded facts are moved into a superseded section and excluded from recall, and forgetting is reversible decay rather than deletion.
bad: The lifecycle depends on a scheduled agent actually running the daily promotion/adjudication pass; the DSH plugin half is pinned to specific DSH release-candidate lines and the host silently skips the whole bundle when the peer range mismatches; its agent-driven deployment writes memory rules into other agents' AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files — by design, but invasive; single community maintainer, first published 2026-08 (latest 0.8.7).
didnt: Corroboration — inbox-only writes with reviewed promotion, a conflict adjudication queue with logged rationales, credential redaction and supersession-instead-of-deletion are our filings/gateway/owner-decision architecture independently built; nothing adopted, because our wiki already runs this pattern (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-simple-wiki-memory
good: A deliberately minimal LLM-wiki memory for DeepSeek Harness: only the index in AGENTS.md is auto-injected into each session and one Markdown file per topic is read on demand — no RAG, no vector store, no runtime LLM calls; writes land in a pending zone immediately so nothing is lost mid-session, promotion to reference happens only when the user says archive/confirm, unattended sessions may write pending but never promote, reorganisation is proposed and executed only after user confirmation, and the vault is a git repo with automatic commits (uninstall preserves all data).
bad: DeepSeek Harness only, and it depends entirely on the host's dsh-agent-instructions injection — the README itself notes that anchored/minimal-context modes silently disable memory loading; retrieval is index-plus-directory-scan with no ranking; promotion is manual by design, so pending items wait on the user.
didnt: Corroboration — index-only injection plus pending-until-confirmed promotion is our own memory discipline in miniature (our wiki is the full system this is a simplification of); nothing to adopt (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-persist
good: Layered plain-text memory for DeepSeek Harness — USER.md/MEMORY.md profile files, per-conversation notebooks that other conversations cannot see, project memory shared by working directory, and a Zettelkasten-style vault with bge-m3 semantic search that falls back to keyword search; injection is selective and defaults to zero (nothing enters context unless the user ticks it), memory is editable in a visual tab, and the memory API is loopback-only (403 otherwise) with plainly stated privacy warnings about what the semantic path sends to the embedding provider.
bad: DeepSeek Harness only, with fiddly Node version requirements (node:sqlite flag ranges); semantic search sends every message and memory text to a third-party embedder (SiliconFlow) when enabled; static injection truncates at 100 lines; and vault.md is fully rewritten by tool operations, so hand edits can be clobbered unless re-imported immediately (all stated in its README).
didnt: Corroboration — default-off selective injection and hard per-conversation isolation confirm our context and custody discipline; a DSH plugin duplicating layers our wiki already has, nothing adopted (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @modelnorth/dsh-plugin-memory
good: Compact DeepSeek Harness plugin giving agents long-term fact and preference storage with semantic and keyword recall, exposed natively as memory_remember/memory_recall tools, plus a dsh-memory CLI to list, search, add and forget memories from the terminal.
bad: v1.0.0 with a single day of registry history (created and last modified 2026-08-26); the short README documents no storage format, tests, limits or write-safety behaviour, and the registry record names no repository (installation points at a GitHub path under a different account name than the package scope).

name: @libai168/dsh-tool-memory

bad: v0.1.0 published and last touched on a single day (2026-10-05); search is keyword-only, with timestamps, vector semantic search and multi-store isolation all listed as future directions; it requires specific DSH peer packages (@deepseek-ai/cordis, @deepseek-ai/dsh-tools).

name: zettelkasten-memory-server

good: A sibling fork of the Zettelkasten fragment design (one Markdown fragment per memory, [[links]], recursive expansion, link-weight ranking, information-divergence health scoring, read-only core fragments) that adds automatic placeholder files for not-yet-existing linked fragments, subdirectory fragment names, weight caching with automatic invalidation, and separate low-value versus isolated-fragment suggestion tools.
