name: @inchankang/zettel-memory
good: Local-first MCP memory server (14 tools): notes are Markdown files with YAML front matter organised by PARA categories, with UID-based Zettelkasten links, backlinks and broken-link detection, SQLite FTS5 search, orphan and stale note finders and an organisation-health report; deletion requires an explicit confirm flag, writes are atomic, and nothing leaves the machine.
bad: A single alpha release — v0.0.1, published 2025-11-14, self-described as alpha with APIs subject to change, and about 31 downloads a month; delete_note is permanent (the README states it cannot be undone); vector/semantic search exists only on the v1.0.0 roadmap.
didnt: Rejected — alpha maturity (one v0.0.1 release) and permanent deletion; its orphan/stale lint echoes machinery our wiki already runs (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-memory-strata
good: Four-layer stratified memory for long-horizon agent projects — L1 MEMORY.md key points auto-loaded every session, L2 project core (stable facts and ADRs), L3 dev status, L4 daily journal — with explicit promotion rules: auto-distillation moves entries L4→L3→L2→L1 as they prove stable, memory strength decays via [last_used] tags (over 14 days flagged, over 30 days auto-archived), and Zettelkasten [[...]] bidirectional links connect L2 and L3. Ships init/maintain/check commands, a daily maintenance pass (journal coverage, freshness, anchor and link integrity, daily summary) and an Obsidian vault layout.
bad: A single published version (0.1.0) from a single maintainer, with no repository or homepage named in the registry record. The README documents no tests or evaluation, and the design is a markdown-file convention for the pi coding agent rather than a general memory store — no search index and no citation or evidence machinery.
didnt: Corroboration — its L1–L4 stratification, episodic-to-semantic distillation and last_used decay independently mirror our own MEMORY.md / daily-log / distillation design and its lean-memory discipline. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-persistent-intelligence
good: Governed long-term memory for the pi coding agent whose canonical store is JSONL with Markdown as a rendered projection: L1 identity records are never auto-applied (explicit ratification required), L2 playbooks are patch-governed and confidence/evidence gated, L3 session memory lives in daily files, and content-addressed evidence records plus tombstones stop deleted records being silently re-promoted. Durable changes flow candidate → evidence → verification → inbox review → patch; recall, quality, relationship and recall-effectiveness diagnostics are review-only, preference capture is candidate-first, and export/import is redacted and preview-first.
bad: Built only for the pi coding agent host — it explicitly runs no MCP server, so other agents need the separate pi-governance-rs runtime; single maintainer and still pre-1.0 (0.17.4). The governance machinery (dashboards, audits, patch simulation) is heavy for a single-user memory, and most of its quality reporting is review-only rather than enforced.
didnt: Corroboration — patch-governed durable writes, never-auto-applied identity records, tombstones against re-promotion and redacted preview-first export independently confirm our approval-gated write and trust-ledger design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: pi-ext-tdai-memory
good: Client extension giving the pi coding agent MemoryCore (TencentDB Agent Memory) long-term memory: automatic L0 conversation capture after each turn, parallel recall of L1 atomic memories, L2 scenes and the L3 persona injected into the system prompt, a fixed-agent binding so all sessions share one isolated memory, plus a team skills library and wiki knowledge-base tools. Runs in direct-connect or public Gateway mode with zero runtime dependencies.
bad: It is only a client: all memory data is stored on a MemoryCore server whose core capabilities (the /v3 API, LLM skill extraction, knowledge-base processing) are a hosted Tencent service — the open-source side ships the client plugins/SDK and a local gateway only. Conversations are auto-captured to that server every turn, the extension is useless without credentials, a team/user identity and a running server, and the README is Chinese-only.
didnt: Rejected — memory custody sits on a third-party server under a hosted-service model, the opposite of our local-first custody; its premise is automatic capture of full conversations to that server, and it is bound to the pi agent. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @tencentdb-agent-memory/memory-tencentdb
good: Four-layer local memory plugin (OpenClaw/Hermes) from the TencentDB Agent Memory team: L0 raw conversations → L1 atomic facts → L2 scenarios → L3 persona, with heterogeneous storage (databases for the evidence layers, human-readable Markdown for the persona/scene layers) and a guaranteed drill-down path from any abstraction back to the raw L0 text. Its symbolic short-term memory offloads verbose tool logs to files and keeps a compact Mermaid canvas with node_id references in context; standalone mode runs a local gateway on SQLite + sqlite-vec + BM25 with no cloud dependency, and the README publishes benchmark tables (PersonaMem 48%→76%; WideSearch token use −61.38%).
bad: A plugin for the OpenClaw/Hermes hosts rather than a standalone system, and it needs an LLM in the loop for extraction, scene aggregation and persona generation. The headline numbers are the vendor's own measurements, and recall works by auto-capturing conversations — a capture-first posture our approval-gated writes deliberately do not take.
didnt: Corroboration — its layered L0→L3 pyramid with lossless drill-down from persona back to the raw conversation independently validates our raw-record-plus-compiled-layer design and our rule that a summary must never orphan its evidence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @arnilo/prism-memory
good: Memory and context family for the Prism agent framework: schema-shaped working memory plus semantic recall, RAG, LLM and observational compaction subpaths, and a /wiki subpath with a prism-wiki bin and bundled skills. Its consent lifecycle is unusually complete — records carry consent {source, scope, visible}, recall drops revoked or invisible entries at assembly time, correct() re-embeds corrections, forget() performs real deletes, retention runs in bounded batches, and export emits only explicitly consented visible records, redacted and size-capped; tenant/resource/thread identity is mandatory on every operation and cross-tenant recall is denied.
bad: A library inside one author's framework (single maintainer; the package sits in the prism monorepo and is not yet included in profile bundles pending a size/use review). The production path needs PostgreSQL/pgvector, it is pre-1.0 (0.12.1), and the README documents no recall-quality evaluation.
didnt: Board — per-record consent (source/scope/visible carried on the record itself and enforced at recall assembly time) as a refinement idea for our memory and claim records. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @remnic/coding-graph
good: Codebase-graph engine for the Remnic memory stack: web-tree-sitter WASM grammars (no native bindings) extract symbols and import edges for 15 tier-1 languages into a neutral FileIR consumed by a SQLite knowledge-graph store. Per-file parse failures return tagged {ok: false} results instead of aborting an index run, and the optional semantic layer (symbol embeddings, SIMILAR_TO near-clone edges via local MinHash/LSH, natural-language semantic_query) is off by default — the package states that in its default configuration it sends nothing anywhere.
bad: It is only an optional companion engine — it does nothing without @remnic/core — and its scope is code symbols, not knowledge or wiki memory. Version churn is extreme (351 published versions; latest 9.69.56 with a 10.0.5 alpha already out) under a single maintainer, signalling an unstable surface.
didnt: Rejected — scope and fit: a codebase symbol-graph engine for another agent-memory stack; our system is a knowledge wiki with citation machinery, not a code index. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: monomind
good: MCP server and CLI that extends five coding hosts (Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Codex) with a tree-sitter codebase knowledge graph in SQLite (imports, callers, blast radius), a JSON persistent-memory store with episodic recall, multi-agent 'org' coordination with policy-gated role agents, and a large pickable library of agents and skills — imported skills carry their licence, source and commit, and a catalog flow stages, approves and activates skills under policy. All of its own state stays on the user's machine.
bad: A sprawling coding-teams suite (83 pickable agents, 560 org skills, 40 slash commands) whose centre of gravity is software orchestration, not knowledge management; its memory is a JSON pattern store with no citation or evidence layer. Single maintainer despite 326 published versions, and the surface changes constantly.
didnt: Rejected — fit and scope: a multi-agent coding-orchestration suite duplicating pieces of our own agent stack, not a knowledge system we can draw a component from. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @monoes/monomindcli
good: The CLI engine package of the Monomind project (packages/@monomind/cli in the same monorepo): it carries the MCP server, the tree-sitter + SQLite codebase knowledge graph, persistent memory, multi-agent task coordination and session hooks that the user-facing monomind package exposes.
bad: A second distribution name for the same project — same repository, same README text and the same 2.24.9 version line as the monomind package studied in this batch — so it adds no independent evidence; as an engine package it carries no installable value on its own, and it inherits the project's single-maintainer churn (321 published versions).
didnt: Rejected — the same project as the monomind row in this batch under a second distribution name, with the same fit and scope reasons; judged on its own registry record, which matches the monomind record in repository, README and version. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: brito-cli
good: Coding-agent CLI (plus a native desktop app) built on an embedded code knowledge graph (LadybugDB; tree-sitter with incremental reparse by file hash) answering 'what breaks if I change this?' via graph_search / graph_callers / graph_impact, with durable memory notes tied to files and symbols. Its self-learning skills have a governed lifecycle: a skill is born 'in test', is promoted after 3 clean uses, is archived after failures or 21 unused days, risky or destructive-command skills always wait for human /skills approve, a safety lint rejects skills containing secrets, credentials-in-URL, curl | sh or prompt-injection phrases, and approved skills are versioned.
bad: Licensed PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0 — source-available for non-commercial use only, so its code is ideas-only for us. Single author, early (0.6.1, nine published versions), README in Portuguese, and by its own statement Windows is untested; it is a coding agent, not a knowledge system.
didnt: Board — the probationary skill lifecycle (skills born in test, promoted on measured clean uses, archived on failures, safety lint plus mandatory human approval for destructive commands) for our own skill governance; the package itself is not adopted — PolyForm-Noncommercial licence (ideas-only) and coding-agent fit. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @sonic182/graphmem
good: Shared local memory for coding agents: one SQLite store with local semantic search and linked entities that Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, pi and other MCP clients can all share, installed as a native binary that is downloaded and checksum-verified explicitly (SHA256SUMS). Scope discipline is built in — writes are limited to the current Git repository plus the global scope, reads always include global, and an MCP list_scopes tool exposes each scope's write permissions; optional code tools (find_symbol, code_outline, code_imports, code_diff between Git revisions) work with no embedding model at all.
bad: Single author and early (0.13.0, nine published versions). Its memory is project decision notes for coding work — no citation, evidence or approval machinery; the code tools index definitions only, not call sites or references, and Linux release binaries require glibc 2.39.
didnt: Rejected — duplication and fit: another coding-agent memory store; our wiki and its scoped MCP read door already cover shared memory with citations and gated writes. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @agent-memo/mcp-client
licence: Proprietary (registry license field: 'SEE LICENSE IN https://agent-memo.ai/terms'; README License section states 'Proprietary')
good: Thin MCP client exposing 14 tools over the Agent-Memo.AI service: memory store/recall with type, importance (1–4), topic and tags, a near-duplicate check before storing, and a knowledge graph whose facts carry temporal validity (valid_from/valid_to windows, kg_invalidate preserves ended facts for history, kg_timeline). Memories auto-scope to the detected project, with personal/project/team scopes, and optional hooks auto-save every 15 messages and again before context compaction.
bad: The memory itself lives in the vendor's cloud (api.agent-memo.ai) behind a JWT token — custody of every stored memory leaves the machine, with no local or offline mode. The client is proprietary, single-maintainer, and the service's own terms govern the data.
didnt: Rejected — cloud custody contradicts our local-first rule and the client is proprietary-licensed; its temporal-validity graph is ideas-only at most and duplicates ground our bi-temporal work already covers. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @alfe.ai/openclaw-memory-cloud
good: OpenClaw cloud-memory plugin with an unusually careful safety model: live capture state is isolated per sessionKey with serialized flushes so the memory service's high-water mark cannot observe a later batch first, a strictly monotonic owner-only epoch fences daemon restarts, and auto-capture disables itself if that state cannot be secured while recall and explicit tools remain available. memory_forget is two-step — preview up to five current matches, then confirm those exact IDs in the same order — memory_learn accepts only bounded inline text or a regular, non-symlink file under the configured workspace, and recalled context is escaped and capped at 16 KiB.
bad: No licence is granted: the registry license field reads UNLICENSED and the README states no licence — a private plugin for Alfe's own platform. The memory itself is cloud-side (Turbopuffer vectors plus a DynamoDB knowledge graph behind the Alfe Agent API), it is OpenClaw-only, and versioning is still 0.0.x despite 57 publishes.
didnt: Rejected — no licence granted at source (UNLICENSED) and cloud custody on the vendor's platform; its forget-confirmation pattern is noted but the package is unusable for us. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: memory-lancedb-pro
good: Enhanced LanceDB long-term memory plugin for OpenClaw with a serious retrieval pipeline: vector + BM25 hybrid fusion (RRF), cross-encoder reranking (Jina or a custom endpoint), recency boost, time decay, length normalization, MMR diversity, noise filtering, and adaptive retrieval that skips greetings and commands. Adds multi-scope isolation (global / agent / project / user / custom), session memory, reflection-recall for inherited rules, task-aware embeddings with any OpenAI-compatible provider (including local Ollama), and a full management CLI (list, search, stats, delete, export, import, reembed, migrate).
bad: Bound to OpenClaw's plugin API and lifecycle hooks — it is not a standalone server. Single maintainer, and the README's feature-comparison table asserts retrieval quality without any published evaluation; the store is embedding recall only, with no citation or evidence layer over what it recalls.
didnt: Board — the hybrid retrieval recipe (vector + BM25 RRF fusion, cross-encoder rerank, recency/time-decay weighting, MMR diversity, hard minimum score) as a candidate ranking upgrade for our Ask door, behind our existing abstention gate. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @cablate/memory-lancedb-mcp
good: Standalone MCP server giving any MCP-compatible agent local LanceDB long-term memory, with the hybrid recipe documented as an explicit scoring pipeline (RRF fusion → cross-encoder rerank → Weibull lifecycle decay → length normalization → hard minimum score 0.35 → MMR demotion above 0.85 cosine). Stored memories auto-link bidirectionally to related ones, contradictions are flagged at store time instead of silently overwriting, topics are auto-assigned, junk is filtered, memories promote Peripheral → Working → Core with use, updates keep a traceable version history, merges mark originals as superseded, and recall returns self-maintenance hints (duplicates, dormant entries, contradictions) alongside a memory_lint tool and an HTML graph visualizer.
bad: An embedding API key is required and the default providers are cloud endpoints (OpenAI/Jina), so memory text leaves the machine for embedding unless the user configures a local endpoint. Single author; memories are free-text notes whose refs are internal short IDs rather than citations to sources, and recall quality is asserted rather than evaluated in the README.
didnt: Corroboration — lifecycle tiers with promotion by use, supersession on merge, contradiction flagging at write time and lint-driven self-maintenance independently confirm our claim-lifecycle and corrections design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @akashahq/vidya
good: Hybrid memory plugin for OpenClaw (AkashaHQ): LanceDB vector search + BM25 keyword search fused via RRF, Voyage AI cross-encoder reranking, multi-provider task-aware embeddings (Voyage/OpenAI/Jina), multi-scope isolation with per-agent access control, LLM-judged auto-capture with a heuristic fallback, auto-recall before each turn, noise filtering, MMR diversity, recency/importance/decay post-processing, daily JSONL backups with 7-day rotation, and a CLI plus six agent tools; the repository carries CI and coverage badges.
bad: The third OpenClaw plugin in this batch built on the same LanceDB pattern, and the youngest (three published versions). It hard-depends on paid cloud embedding APIs — reranking is Voyage-only — so memory text leaves the machine by design, and its auto-capture writes memories on an LLM's judgment with no human approval step.
didnt: Rejected — duplication (the same LanceDB hybrid pattern as two other rows in this batch, in a younger package) and cloud-embedding dependence. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: semcode-mcp
good: Semantic code search as an MCP server: Tree-sitter AST chunking across 16 languages, voyage-code-3 embeddings (int8-quantised) in sqlite-vec with FTS5 full text, vector + BM25 recall fused by RRF, Voyage rerank-2.5 re-ranking and call-graph expansion, over a watchdog-watched index with multi-workspace LRU management and incremental hash-based sync.
bad: The npm package itself is only a thin npx shell that launches the Python server via uvx — the substance lives in the Python project. The whole retrieval chain hard-requires a paid Voyage API key (embeddings and rerank), with no local-embedding path documented; a young single-author project (v0.1.2, ~34 downloads/month).
didnt: Rejected — fit: semantic code search is a different problem from our knowledge wiki (our repos are read-only and the wiki's retrieval runs over compiled pages, not code), and the hard Voyage-key dependency plus shell-over-Python packaging gives us nothing our stack lacks. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @agfpd/mergemind-mcp
good: Shared memory for a team of Claude Code / Codex agents: an Obsidian-compatible markdown vault with canonical folders (knowledge, decisions, ideas, projects) plus per-agent working memory, hybrid search (BM25 + vector + rerank) exposed to any connected peer as MCP tools (vault_search / vault_read / vault_map / vault_graph), and a curator 'Index' agent that files drafts and maintains frontmatter, links and tags.
bad: The write side runs as always-on daemons that are macOS-only (launchd plists) and the curator is an autonomous live agent session — the opposite of our approval-gated single-writer model. Distribution is through the author's private plugin marketplace, it leans on sibling plugins (persistent-peer, Inter-Agent-Protocol) and a Telegram bot for the curator, and the documentation is Russian-only.
didnt: Rejected — fit and custody: a multi-agent shared vault written by daemons and an autonomous curator contradicts our approval-gated, single-writer design, and the macOS/launchd lock-in and private-marketplace distribution do not transfer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @mks-agenticslab/embeddings
licence: MIT (registry license field; README states no licence)
good: A shared embeddings + hybrid-retrieval surface for one author's agent ecosystem: Gemini embeddings with an LRU + disk cache, hybrid recall that runs FTS and vector halves in parallel and fuses them with weighted RRF (with graceful-degradation diagnostics), multi-query expansion, a fail-open LLM reranker, heading-aware markdown chunking, and a built-in golden-set evaluator reporting recall@k / MRR@k / precision@k.
bad: Hard-wired to one stack: Gemini embeddings only, a fixed 768-dimension contract, and Postgres/pgvector storage the consumer must supply (both retrieval halves and the schema are the consumer's problem). v0.1.0, Spanish-only documentation, and built for the author's own sibling projects.
didnt: Corroboration — RRF hybrid recall with degradation diagnostics, a fail-open rerank pass, and golden-set recall metrics shipped inside the retrieval library confirm the shape of our own retrieval and evaluation design; the code itself is Gemini/pgvector-bound. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @pi-mentis/pi-mentis-retrieval
good: A retrieval-fusion library whose type surface (read from the published tarball) shows weighted reciprocal rank fusion, MMR diversity selection, and a distinctive structural deduplication: fact identity is taken from write-path metadata (predicate, cardinality, fact key, set-member key) and always outranks embedding similarity, so distinct members of a fact set are never collapsed as duplicates, with per-candidate diversity traces kept.
bad: Undocumented to the point of opacity: no README in any published version (the registry shows an error placeholder, and the tarball's file list names a README.md it does not contain), no repository or homepage anywhere, no licence stated anywhere, and it depends on five sibling @pi-mentis workspace packages — there is no way in from the outside.
didnt: Board — structural deduplication (recorded fact identity outranking embedding similarity, set members never collapsed) as an idea for our retrieval/dedup layer; with no licence stated at source the code is ideas-only in any case. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @lynage/core
licence: MIT (repository LICENSE file; the npm record itself states no licence)
good: The core engine of Lynage, a long-term story-memory system for narrative agents: source text is stored verbatim and immutably in SQLite (append-only, no update or delete), AI summaries of story segments form a self-growing index tree (G0 segments to G1/G2 directories) that acts as navigation rather than storage, and layered search (FTS, then embedding, then LLM rerank) retrieves the original passages through source pointers — with a published recall benchmark (92% recall@prompt for summaries + raw source vs 83% for summaries alone).
bad: A narrow narrative-fiction domain (novels, galgames, interactive stories) far from a personal knowledge wiki; very young (v0.0.2, two published versions, single author), and the npm record itself is a stub — no licence, no repository field — so the package page alone grounds almost nothing.
didnt: Corroboration — verbatim immutable source storage where summaries are navigation indexes, never the storage, and pointers reopen the original text for verification is the same raw/compiled discipline our wiki is built on, arrived at independently. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @jeremiaheth/neolata-mem
good: A graph-native memory engine for agents with Zettelkasten-style automatic bidirectional linking, biological decay (configurable half-life, link- and access-reinforcement, category stickiness), LLM-assisted conflict resolution that archives the superseded version with its evolution history, and a quarantine lane: memories stored with claim metadata and a provenance trust score are quarantined instead of auto-superseding when trust is low or structure conflicts — aimed at poisoning resistance. Zero-config local JSON storage with keyword search and no API key needed.
bad: Elastic-2.0 is a source-available licence (it forbids offering the software as a hosted service), so the code is ideas-only for us. Decay deletes dead memories outright, where our wiki keeps history; conflict resolution needs an external LLM/embeddings provider; a young single-author project (v0.8.6).
didnt: Board — trust-gated supersession and the quarantine lane for low-trust or structurally conflicting memories as ideas for our claim lifecycle and contradiction handling; Elastic-2.0 makes the code itself ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @wiscale/velesdb-memory-node
licence: VelesDB Core License 1.0 (source-available, based on ELv2)
good: In-process Node.js agent memory with no server, daemon or API key: remember/recall over a durable on-disk store, typed links between facts, and why() — a walk over those links that returns the evidence trail behind an answer, including facts sharing no words with the question — plus the deterministic context compiler that shrinks a prompt under a hard token budget with one auditable decision per fragment (measured 82.5% smaller over its committed 12-turn corpus, byte-identical across runs), and zero AI calls on the write path.
bad: By design and by licence it is a memory wedge only — no raw VelesQL, no deep graph traversal, no collection administration (a test pins the restricted API allowlist). No musl prebuild, so Alpine-based images need a local build. The VelesDB Core licence is source-available and forbids re-hosting the engine as a multi-tenant service.
didnt: Board — as with the standing VelesDB row, why() evidence-path recall and the deterministic, auditable context compiler are the ideas worth boarding for truth-aware retrieval and context assembly; this Node binding adds no separate take, and the source-available licence keeps all of it ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: server-noonien
good: The npm distribution of the standing row's project: a drop-in replacement for the official MCP memory server (the same nine tools, inputs and outputs) plus the extension operations the official nine lack (update_*, merge_entities, read_conflicts) and an import path from the official server's JSONL; each node writes only its own append-only JSONL shard and shards merge as a CRDT LWW-Element-Set ordered by (HLC, node, sequence), travelling through a shared folder/S3 bucket or directly peer-to-peer via the nooniend daemon.
bad: As recorded for the standing row: MPL-2.0 keeps the code ideas-only under our licence discipline, and multi-writer CRDT convergence is a design this wiki deliberately refuses in favour of a single writer with an approval ledger — eventual consistency means a node acts on another node's writes only after an exchange. A young single-author project (TypeScript, Node >= 22).
didnt: Corroboration — aligned with the standing row: the single-writer-shard, operation-log and anti-entropy pattern validates our append-only discipline from the opposite direction, but CRDT multi-writer convergence stays outside our single-writer design and MPL-2.0 bars code reuse. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @kenz1117/dsh-engram
good: A cross-session long-term memory plugin for the DeepSeek Harness built on memory-palace information architecture: memories are pinned to room#slot coordinates in typed rooms (fact, preference, decision, episode, skill), an append-only tour route fixes recall order, write-time 'doorplate' scoring grades uniqueness, hybrid FTS5 + local-vector retrieval fuses by RRF, and an evidence gate (engram_assess) code-enforces that a sufficiency claim needs at least one valid in-batch evidence ref before answering; every memory carries source session/turn provenance with a full operation log, and ingest redacts credentials and personal identifiers before storage.
bad: Its growth loop is session-transcript ingest: an auto-ingest mode extracts candidate facts from session logs each round, and a backfill mode refines the host's persisted historical sessions into the palace. It is also bound to the DeepSeek Harness host, so none of it runs in our stack.
didnt: Rejected — premised on session-transcript ingest (auto-ingest from session logs plus historical-session backfill), which is unapproved in our system, and bound to the DeepSeek Harness host; its code-enforced evidence gate is a design we already practise as scored abstention. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: superskill
good: A one-entry orchestrator for coding agents: deterministic skill routing that turns a task into curated packs plus a budgeted rule plan with an audit trail, evidence gates (spec, then tickets, then evidence, then a gate check — deterministic and non-zero on failure), a project-jailed markdown vault whose FTS5 knowledge graph tags every code-graph edge EXTRACTED or INFERRED, and fail-closed safety (secret scanner, prompt-injection scan, MCP write rate limits) — all local-first.
bad: It is a coding-agent skill orchestrator, not a knowledge system; the platform contract is brittle (Node 22.16+ on the 22.x line or 24+, and official Node 22.13-22.15 builds cannot run it for lack of FTS5), and its README concedes model behaviour 'remains unproven until separate evaluations complete' — fixtures and green tests establish only the deterministic cases.
didnt: Board — deterministic evidence gates (no gate pass without cited evidence) and EXTRACTED-vs-INFERRED edge tagging as ideas for our claim/evidence layer. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @3030-labs/wotw
good: A local-first knowledge daemon that turns dropped files into an interlinked Obsidian-compatible wiki: generated pages land in a candidates/ staging area and are promoted into wiki/ only by an explicit human approve (approval appends a provenance record attributing the decision to the user), every write is signed into a SHA-256 provenance chain recording content, model, cost and source (verifiable with wotw audit and an offline Compliance Pack), and reads are served to any MCP-capable agent over ten tools with bearer-token auth — pure BM25 retrieval, no embeddings.
bad: AGPL-3.0-or-later makes the code ideas-only under our licence discipline. It is pre-1.0, with breaking changes possible at minor-version bumps, and its input diet treats meeting transcripts as a first-class source type.
didnt: Corroboration — candidate staging with human approval before a page lands, plus a hash-chained provenance ledger attributing every write, is our approval-gated-writes and trust-ledger design arrived at independently; AGPL keeps the code itself ideas-only. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @abraca/wiki
good: A streaming Wikipedia/MediaWiki to Abracadabra importer: every discovered title becomes a shell doc immediately and bodies stream in one fetch at a time, so the graph skeleton is visible before the first body lands; it follows internal links and categories to configurable depth, splits articles into section + infobox docs, rate-limits politely per Wikimedia etiquette, and offers a --dry-run that fetches only the entry article and writes nothing.
bad: A peripheral importer for one platform: it needs the Abracadabra server (ABRA_URL), an Ed25519 key file, invite-code registration and the @abraca/dabra peer package — outside that ecosystem it does nothing. It imports one source type (MediaWiki) and makes no attempt at synthesis or contradiction handling.
didnt: Rejected — fit: a single-source importer bound to the Abracadabra CRDT platform; our ingest reads sources directly into the wiki and has no use for a MediaWiki-only bridge into someone else's doc graph. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @dicsussion/core
good: The protocol engine beneath the Dicsussion SDK: Iroh QUIC and WebSocket transports, X25519 / AES-256-GCM / Ed25519 cryptography, Automerge CRDT sync with a sparse Merkle tree, and zero-knowledge anti-spam (Groth16 / RLN, RFC 001-003), with a bridged-transport seam for hosts that own their own sockets — and an unusually candid README (it states plainly that a WebSocket relay operator can reconstruct the membership graph).
bad: It is a messaging protocol engine, not a knowledge system: browser builds stub out the transport and ZK entries, proof generation is Node-only, and the whole design is multi-writer CRDT sync — the direction our single-writer wiki refuses by design. A young single-author project (v0.8.1, RFC-stage).

name: @cyanheads/cern-inspire-mcp-server
good: A polished MCP wrapper over CERN's INSPIRE-HEP: literature, author, and experiment search, full paper records, citation summaries (h-index, citation buckets, per-year counts), BibTeX/LaTeX citation export, and HEPData record linkage, over stdio, local HTTP, or a public hosted endpoint.
bad: Domain-locked to high-energy physics and wholly dependent on the remote INSPIRE API — no local custody and nothing generalizable to a personal wiki's sources; v0.1.3, single author.
didnt: Rejected — scope: excellent scholarly machinery locked to high-energy-physics literature and a remote API; nothing adoptable for a general personal wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: dsh-research-writing
good: A one-install bundle of two DeepSeek Harness plugins: dsh-lit-search (Crossref + OpenAlex literature search with GB/T 7714 / APA / BibTeX citation formatting) and dsh-latex-guard (latexmk compile checks, BibTeX lint/fill, and a citation audit).
bad: The bundle itself is only a dependency shell — both plugins are separate packages (dsh-lit-search was studied on its own record in this wave), the bundle adds no mechanism of its own, and it targets the DeepSeek Harness plugin profile, not our stack; v0.1.0.
didnt: Rejected — a bundle shell with no mechanism of its own; its components are judged on their own records (dsh-lit-search studied in this wave), and the DeepSeek Harness plugin profile is not our stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @auxiora/research
licence: Apache-2.0 (from the LICENSE file shipped in the published tarball; the registry record states no license field)
good: A deep-research engine library: a DeepResearchOrchestrator plans a question into subtopics, runs multi-source web search (a Brave Search client ships in the package), scores source credibility by domain reputation, tracks citations (formattable inline, footnote or bibliography style), assembles a knowledge graph of entities and relations, evaluates knowledge gaps and refines queries, and generates cited reports.
bad: Ships compiled dist code only: the registry record carries no README, no repository and no homepage, and the tarball adds no documentation or examples — the API surface is visible only in its TypeScript type definitions. It is one organ of a lockstep-versioned sibling stack (@auxiora/logger, @auxiora/audit, @auxiora/ssrf-guard), its built-in search is Brave-only, and it is single-maintainer with minimal adoption (catalogue signal: 76 downloads/month).
didnt: Rejected — an undocumented, compiled-only research library bound to Brave Search and the author's sibling package stack; our research lanes already do citation-tracked, multi-source research under our own verification discipline, so there is nothing missing here to adopt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: aiseo-audit
good: A deterministic, fully local, zero-API-key audit of a web page's AI-search readiness in the Lighthouse mould: 50+ content factors rolled into four pipeline stages (technical eligibility, retrieval alignment, citation fitness, provenance), every factor evidence-tiered (supported / conditional / heuristic / diagnostic / experimental) and traced to reviewed generative-engine-optimization literature, with CLI, GitHub Action, MCP server and typed API faces and baseline/diff tracking over time.
bad: Its subject is public web pages competing for generative-engine citations — a different problem from a private wiki's internal quality. The scores are expert-set heuristics, explicitly not citation probabilities; it reads fetched HTML only (no JavaScript rendering, no visual or multimodal assessment), and the v2.0 rescoring broke comparability with 1.x baselines.
didnt: Board — evidence-tier labelling for scored factors: every metric tagged with its evidence strength and traced to its source, as a discipline for our own evaluation and lint reporting, where heuristic numbers are easy to over-trust. The tool itself audits public pages, which our private, local-first wiki does not need. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @camadb/memory
licence: MIT (registry license field and the tarball's package.json agree; no LICENSE file is shipped and the README states no licence)
good: A small, runtime-neutral contracts package for AI memory: TypeScript interfaces for MemoryRecord, RetrievalResult and MemoryStore in which embedding provenance (provider, model, dimensions, creation time, revision) is a first-class field on every record — a clean separation, with implementations depending on @camadb/core and core never depending on memory or an embedding provider.
bad: Contracts only — no implementation, no store, nothing to run. The registry record carries no README, no repository, no author and no homepage, the tarball's README is three lines, and the version line is date-stamped 0.0.0-alpha pre-releases (32 versions) aimed at the CamaDB stack only.
didnt: Board — embedding provenance recorded per record (provider, model, dimensions, revision), so stale or mixed embedding spaces are detectable, as an integrity discipline for any vector index our retrieval layer keeps. The package itself is an unimplemented alpha contract for another database's stack. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @zereight/mcp-gitlab
good: A mature MCP server for GitLab with 276 tools (projects, merge requests, issues, pipelines, wiki, releases) in runtime-activatable toolsets over stdio, SSE and Streamable HTTP; PAT and OAuth auth, lean toolset defaults, JMESPath result filtering with response masking, self-hosted GitLab support, and distribution as an npm package, an MCP bundle and a gh-style CLI.
bad: Scope is GitLab only — it does nothing for a Markdown personal wiki. The default permission mode is full, delete and teardown tools included, unless the operator deliberately sets readonly or modify mode, and the 276-tool surface is heavy for clients that load all tool definitions at once.
didnt: Rejected — GitLab-specific connector; our forges are GitHub and Azure DevOps and our wiki MCP doors already cover the knowledge side. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @supermemory/memory-graph
good: A polished React graph-visualization component (Canvas 2D force layout): document nodes and memory hexagon nodes with similarity and version-chain edges, workspace/space filtering, pagination-aware layout warming that settles appended pages without disturbing manual pan/zoom, a static-layout safeguard above 6,000 nodes, console and consumer variants, and full TypeScript definitions.
bad: A front-end component only — no storage, retrieval or memory logic of its own — and its data model (DocumentWithMemories) is the Supermemory hosted platform's shape, so it is useful only with that service's data; React 18+ and browser-only. The Supermemory platform itself stands rejected in Tier 1 on custody (hosted, auto-learning from conversations).
didnt: Rejected — a visualization component bound to the Supermemory hosted platform's data model; our Lens already renders our own wiki graph from our own pages, and there is no missing capability here for a local-first markdown wiki. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @storybook/mcp
licence: MIT (registry license field; the package README opened in the repository states no licence section)
good: The official Storybook MCP library: it serves component and documentation knowledge from generated Storybook manifests (components.json, optional docs.json) through three read tools (docs-list, docs-show, docs-show-story), either as a fetch-style HTTP handler you mount on your own server or as composable tool registrations on your own tmcp server, with multi-source composition across several Storybooks.
bad: A library, not a server — the tarball ships one module and no executable, so you must host it yourself (or use the dev-server addon instead). It requires pre-generated Storybook manifests and Node 22.12+, its composition helpers work only with the tmcp server and explicitly cannot be composed into the official MCP TypeScript SDK, and its scope is UI component documentation only.
didnt: Rejected — it serves Storybook component documentation to coding agents; our stack has no Storybook corpus, and our own MCP read door already serves the wiki with the citation and abstention discipline this package does not attempt. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @productbrain/mcp
good: An MCP server that gives an agent a product team's memory — 'the Chain': orientation and search over product knowledge, capture of decisions and tensions with write-back, entry and relation management, collections, labels, workflows and session tracking, with workspace, user and scope all derived server-side from a single API key, plus an endpoint override for self-hosted deployments.
bad: Pre-GA beta (0.0.1-beta builds; the README itself instructs users to pin the beta tag). The server is a thin client for the hosted Product Brain Cloud on Convex — it requires their API key and the knowledge lives server-side by default. No licence is stated at source (checked as detailed in evidence); the catalogue's 'MIT' is not borne out at source.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted-cloud product-memory service (third-party API key, Convex cloud custody) contradicts local-first custody, and no licence is stated at source, so its code is ideas-only at best. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: security-detections-mcp
good: A unified MCP front-end over roughly 8,200 security detection rules in six formats (Sigma, Splunk ESCU, Elastic, KQL, Sublime, CrowdStrike CQL): full-text and faceted search, MITRE ATT&CK mapping (technique, tactic and actor coverage), coverage and gap analysis with Navigator-layer export, 81 tools in the local install plus 11 expert prompts, running fully locally over your own cloned rule corpora.
bad: A security-operations domain tool with nothing to do with a personal knowledge wiki; its value depends on cloning and indexing six large external rule repositories, and the zero-setup hosted variant is a read-only subset (~25 tools) capped at 200 calls/day on the free tier. Single-author project (Michael Haag).
didnt: Rejected — detection engineering for SOC teams is outside our system's scope entirely; our wiki's corpus is our own pages, not third-party detection rules. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @entrogic-net/knowledge
good: The memory/knowledge module of the BanglaClaw agent runtime, designed with unusual care: explicit remember/recall/forget tools with server-side owner scoping (the model cannot touch another owner's memories), refusal to store passwords, OTPs and PINs, near-duplicate merging, and memories injected as data-not-instructions; plus a knowledge base with multi-format loaders, Bangla-aware sentence chunking, SHA-256 skip on re-ingest, and search returning passages with source#chunk citations under a minimum-score cutoff.
bad: One module of a multi-user bot-gateway runtime rather than a standalone store: persistence needs a running Qdrant (the in-memory store loses everything on restart), its own docs state that every bot user can read all knowledge-base documents (per-user ACLs only planned), and hybrid search and re-ranking are likewise still planned. Built for Bangla-first chat channels, not a single-owner local wiki.
didnt: Corroboration — its explicit, owner-scoped memory writes with secret-refusal, retrieved content presented as data-not-instructions, and citation-bearing search with a minimum-score cutoff independently confirm our approval-gated writes and scored-abstention design. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @lovedolove/dsh-codebase-memory-mcp
good: A well-built bridge plugin for DeepSeek Harness: six knowledge-graph code tools (project list, symbol search, exact snippet, architecture summary, call-path tracing, regex code search) registered natively, an auto-started upstream daemon with a graph-visualization Web UI, graceful degradation when host services are missing, a bundled agent skill plus injected system-prompt policy for when to prefer graph queries over grep, and a real unit/integration test suite with CI.
bad: It is only a bridge — all indexing and querying live in the separate upstream codebase-memory-mcp binary, which must be installed beforehand or no tools register at all — and it is hard-bound to the DeepSeek Harness/Cordis plugin surface and its version window. It indexes software codebases, not document knowledge; single author, v0.1.x.
didnt: Rejected — a host-specific bridge for code knowledge graphs inside DeepSeek Harness; our wiki already traverses its own markdown graph through its own doors, and code-repository indexing is outside its scope. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @loongsuite/otel-util-genai
good: Alibaba's Node.js implementation of the OpenTelemetry GenAI utility: standardized telemetry handlers for LLM calls (message content, token usage, streaming time-to-first-token), agent, embedding, tool-execution, retrieval, rerank and memory operations, following the OTel GenAI semantic conventions, with event-log-to-trace conversion — the Node counterpart of the Python package of the same design.
bad: Observability plumbing, not a knowledge system: it instruments other pipelines and stores nothing. v0.1.1 is early, the GenAI semantic conventions it targets are themselves still evolving, and it has value only inside a Node stack already wired for OpenTelemetry.
didnt: Rejected — our audit trail is the wiki's own hash-chained ledger and conversation log, not OpenTelemetry spans, and there is no Node telemetry pipeline here for it to instrument. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: obsidian-to-arcadedb
good: A focused one-job CLI: it walks an Obsidian vault and upserts its notes into ArcadeDB as :Note nodes carrying content, with :Tag nodes, :LINKS_TO edges from wikilinks and :TAGGED edges, multi-vault keying by (tag, vault), and unresolved wikilinks preserved on the source note as an unresolvedLinks property instead of being silently dropped.
bad: One-shot full re-import only — its own Limitations section states no watch mode and no incremental diff; markdown parsing is regex-based and wikilink resolution is basename-only, so two notes sharing a name both get linked. It needs a running ArcadeDB (Docker) plus the suite's sibling foundation package, and the README in the registry record still describes v0.1.0 as 'not yet published to npm' while the registry's latest is 0.2.0 — the documentation lags the release.
didnt: Rejected — it mirrors a vault into a separate graph database; our wiki keeps the markdown files themselves as the store and traverses them in place, so a database mirror is duplication, and our lint already surfaces broken and unresolved links at the source. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @feelingmindful/knowledge-graph
licence: MIT (README License section; the registry record states no license field)
good: A local-first vault knowledge graph with real depth: an Obsidian vault parsed into SQLite with sqlite-vec embeddings and FTS5, hybrid search fused by Reciprocal Rank Fusion and re-ranked by PageRank, graph analytics (Louvain communities, betweenness bridge nodes, PageRank centrality), path/neighborhood/subgraph traversal via CLI and MCP, incremental indexing by file mtime, embeddings computed locally (bge-base via transformers.js), 76 tests, and a bundled prove-claim skill that decomposes a claim, searches, traces connections and reports with citations.
bad: The licence lives only in the README — the registry metadata states none, which trips automated licence checks (and the catalogue recorded it as unstated). The install story is muddled: the README's clone instructions point at obra/knowledge-graph while the record's repository is feeling-mindful/feeling-mindful-plugins. First run downloads a 109MB embedding model, PageRank may fail to converge on large disconnected graphs (degree-centrality fallback), and the graph is untyped — files are nodes, with no claim- or citation-level structure.
didnt: Corroboration — a local-first vault graph with path and neighbor traversal, hybrid search and a prove-claim citation workflow independently confirms our wiki-traverse door's design; our door is already built, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @abhishekmcp/notes
good: A complete local markdown-notes MCP server in pure JavaScript: ranked full-text search plus local semantic search (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 in WebAssembly — no API keys, nothing leaves the machine), wiki-link graph tools (backlinks, neighbors, shortest path, related notes, graph overview with orphan and broken-link counts), token-efficient reads (outline, section, character window), sandboxed filesystem access (traversal and escaping symlinks rejected, atomic writes), and a read-only mode in which the mutating tools are not even registered.
bad: Single-author and young (v0.4.1); its search and embedding indexes are JSON sidecar files written inside the vault, the first semantic search must download a ~23MB model and embed the whole vault, and there is no citation-locking or abstention discipline — search returns ranked snippets with no provenance guarantee.
didnt: Corroboration — its read-only mode (mutating tools not registered at all), path-containment sandboxing and local-only embeddings independently confirm our read-door design; its ungated write tools are the part our approval-gated writes deliberately do differently, so nothing is adopted. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: @eqman00003/knowlp-rag
good: Dual knowledge-graph retrieval for markdown notes: a prerequisite/dependency graph (P-Agent) and a similarity graph (S-Agent) fanned out together with vector and full-text engines, returning reading paths — ranked hits with their prerequisite chain and a suggested reading order — instead of flat results; it works without a GPU in n-gram mode, supports Chinese vaults, and carries a serious test suite including a packaging-closure test that exists because a previous release shipped with 16 modules missing from the tarball.
bad: Heavy machinery for a personal vault: a Python engine behind the npm/DeepSeek-Harness bundle, a ~30-second Python bootstrap on first search, and an index lifecycle that needs its own stats/status tooling. Its signature mechanism is usage-based edge decay — consumed edges strengthen, unused edges forget by half-life tiers ('use it or lose it') — which is the opposite of a durable record; single-author.
didnt: Board — reading-path retrieval: return the prerequisite chain and a suggested reading order alongside ranked hits, as an idea for our traverse/Ask layer. Its usage-decay edge forgetting is NOT boarded — our wiki's base purpose is a durable record that loses nothing. (completion pass, 2026-10-21)

name: my-wiki
good: A shared, git-synced, LLM-maintained wiki as a zero-dependency Python CLI (command `mywiki`): sources are frozen as immutable content-hash snapshots, ingest hands the calling agent a work order, pages carry [^src-id] claim citations, query returns cited answers, and lint checks broken, stale and uncited claims; git push/pull syncs one knowledge base across machines and agents (Claude Code, Codex and others), with several independent wikis per machine kept in a local registry.
bad: Very early (version 0.1.1) and the GitHub repository the record names (luohaha/MyWiki) now returns 404, so the code's home is unreachable even though the PyPI distribution survives. The CLI cannot call a model itself — all reasoning is delegated to whichever agent runs its playbook, so output quality depends entirely on the host agent.
didnt: Corroboration — its immutable hash-addressed sources, work-order ingest, per-claim citations and lint confirm our raw/compiled/schema design almost point for point; it holds nothing our stack lacks. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ex-brain
good: CLI personal knowledge base built on seekdb: page management with semantic 'Compiled Truth' updates, hybrid full-text plus vector search, automatic timeline/event extraction and entity auto-linking, an interactive 3D knowledge-graph web UI with Ask Ex-Brain Q&A that answers with [[slug|title]] citations, and an MCP server (ebrain serve) letting agents read, write, search and compile; imports Markdown, HTML (via Readability), PDF and Word.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source — no license field in the registry record, no licence in the README, no repository named — so nothing in it is reusable. Semantic features need an external LLM/embedding API configured by the user (the documented defaults point at Alibaba DashScope), and it is a single-maintainer package still at 0.5.x.
didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at source makes it ideas-only, and its compiled-truth, timeline and entity-linking design duplicates what our wiki already does. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: AutoWiki / Factory
licence: no licence stated at source (closed commercial product)
good: Factory's AutoWiki generates a living wiki for each repository via a multi-phase, multi-agent pipeline (survey, plan the structure, generate pages in dependency order, publish), then keeps it current incrementally: later runs diff against the commit hash stored in the wiki's metadata and regenerate only affected pages. Wikis ship to four surfaces automatically — Factory's cloud viewer, the GitHub wiki tab, Droid sessions via a read_wiki tool, and a droid-wiki/ folder committed into the repo — and a CI workflow (/install-wiki) can refresh on every push.
bad: It is a feature of Factory's paid hosted platform, not an openable codebase: generation runs through their Droid product and CI with access to your repositories, the browsable wiki lives in Factory's cloud, and the announcement page is the only primary source — no code, no self-hosting, no licence terms stated. Codebases only; it documents code, not general knowledge.
didnt: Rejected — a closed, hosted, codebase-only documentation feature of a paid platform; its incremental regeneration from commit diffs matches what our own staleness/lint work already does. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Stash
good: Open-source infrastructure for agents that learn from experience: captures agent session traces via hooks or API, curates them into persistent knowledge and reusable skills, and exposes them through a Python SDK, REST API, MCP and CLI; self-hostable, actively maintained (340 stars, pushed 2026-10-21). A reward-model layer derives preference pairs from reviewer comments and user reactions on traces, with each judgment attributed to its source quote.
bad: Its centre of gravity is production-trace capture and reward-model/prompt optimization for agent teams — it is premised on ingesting session transcripts, and the broader product (accounts, reward-model rollout, GEPA skill optimization) is an agent-ops platform, not a personal knowledge base. The catalogue-era description (a shared memory vault over MCP/VFS) no longer matches what the repo leads with.
didnt: Rejected — premised on session-transcript ingest, which is unapproved in our system, and its trace/reward-model focus is agent-operations tooling rather than a personal knowledge wiki. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: trip2g
good: A single Go binary on SQLite that publishes an Obsidian vault as a website and serves the same notes to agents over MCP (search, note_html, similar, federated_* tools): every edit is snapshotted into note_versions and mirrored to git, so history is a readable diff and the vault stays cloneable. It adds federation between peer hubs, per-domain routing, subscription ACLs and API keys, webhooks and cron, and Telegram publishing; actively maintained (pushed 2026-10-21).
bad: It is a publishing and hosting mesh, not a knowledge compiler — no ingest, lint or abstention discipline — and its federation, multi-user accounts and paid-content gating widen the custody surface far beyond a private single-owner wiki. The feature map is very broad for a young project (created March 2026), with some primitives only on a feature branch or still planned by its own table.
didnt: Rejected — a multi-user publishing/federation host inverts our private, local-first custody; its versioned-notes-over-git sync is sound but is already how our wiki keeps history. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: WikiBrain
good: A faithful hosted implementation of Karpathy's pattern: the same raw/ wiki/ schema/ three layers with index.md and log.md conventions, Ingest/Query/Lint operations, a six-tool MCP server (Streamable HTTP, optimistic locking, bearer tokens or OAuth 2.1), rich source import (URLs with DOI/arXiv/PubMed handling, PDF, Word, images), academic tooling (BibTeX/CSL-JSON, Zotero sync, citation rendering), version history with rollback, and full Obsidian-compatible export.
bad: It is a hosted multi-tenant service — user accounts, OAuth, revocable public share links, and a maintainer-run billed version with backups and mobile apps — the opposite of private local-first custody; the code is AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Brand new (created September 2026, 12 stars) and built on a Node/PostgreSQL service stack rather than plain files under the owner's control.
didnt: Rejected — the hosted multi-tenant model inverts our local-first custody and AGPL-3.0 is copyleft; the catalogue's own NOT FOR US verdict stands at source. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: TrueHOOHA
good: A Karpathy-pattern wiki whose three workflows are packaged as agent skills (.agents/skills: ingest, query, lint) with hard preconditions and guardrails — raw sources immutable, log append-only, index.md rebuilt on every change, an exact required step order — written specifically to enforce workflow rigidity and mitigate agent behavioural drift. The wiki tree conforms to the project's own written Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.1 spec (SPEC.md), with AGENTS.md as the single source of truth for the schema.
bad: It is prose and process only: no code, helper scripts, tests or search tooling of its own (the README says there are no helper scripts to run), so enforcement rests entirely on the agent's compliance with skill text. Small and young (22 stars, created May 2026), and the repository was renamed from LLM-Wiki-Skilled to LLM-Wiki, breaking the catalogue-era link.
didnt: Corroboration — its skill-level guardrails (preconditions before edits, append-only log, index rebuilt on every change, schema as single source of truth) confirm our own schema-discipline approach; as a scaffold it holds nothing our stack lacks. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: llm-wiki-karpathy
good: A representation-first, multimodal Markdown wiki runtime for Obsidian vaults, shipped as a standalone CLI, a stdio MCP server and an OpenClaw host entry: raw text, PDFs, images and tabular data are prepared into stored representations under .llm-kb/representations/ with compile-readiness tracking (ready / partial / needs_representation), source-id repair that migrates stale ids instead of discarding them, deterministic gap mapping and promotion, and a deterministic lint that flags contradiction candidates, stale representations, unsupported claims and isolated pages.
bad: All published versions date from a single day (2026-04-13) with nothing since, and the registry record names no repository, so the code's home and maintenance state cannot be inspected from the record. It is a young 0.4.x runtime whose synthesis is still agent-owned — the runtime owns structure only.
didnt: Corroboration — its representation-first multimodal ingest, source-id repair and contradiction-candidate lint confirm our raw/compiled discipline; the runtime itself duplicates our stack. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: LLM-WIKI-MCP
good: A local-first Markdown knowledge system (by Martin Timms / Vishva AI) that ingests Markdown, text, PDF, DOCX and source files into a wiki_vault/, indexes it in SQLite, and offers search, retrieval, context-pack generation, Mermaid graph export, linting and repair, plus provenance-aware re-ingestion. It runs as a CLI, a Python library or an MCP stdio server, and its ask workflow answers from retrieved wiki pages through a local Ollama model, with configurable context budgets and a /debug-context view of the exact prompt pack.
bad: A single burst of activity — created 2026-05-20 and last pushed 2026-05-21, nothing since — with 21 stars. Its ask pipeline deliberately falls back to a best-effort answer when the local model returns nothing rather than abstaining, and its repair --apply rewrites pages with no approval gate; both invert our scored-abstention and approval-gated-write rules.
didnt: Rejected — ungated repair/writes and an answer-anyway fallback invert our approval-gated writes and scored abstention, and the pattern duplicates our stack. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: PieKBS
good: A local-first knowledge search engine for agents in a single dependency-free Go binary: a watcher distills raw documents into structured Markdown source-notes (key claims with inlined aliases, entity annotations, authority and doc-type metadata, and related_to / supports / contradicts links), synthesized concept, comparison and decision pages are generated on demand, and agents search and deep-read through MCP tools (kb_search, kb_page, kb_add) over pure SQLite FTS5/BM25 — no embeddings required. Search results carry the linked documents, so agents expand along citation/support links and synthesize their own answers; bundles conform to OKF v0.1.
bad: Very young and little adopted (created June 2026, 6 stars, last pushed July 2026). Distillation quality rests on an external LLM the user must supply, and retrieval is keyword FTS only — there is no semantic recall when vocabulary differs.
didnt: Board — its _draft quarantine (synthesized pages with fewer than 2 sources stay unindexed until corroborated) and its typed-link graph expansion along supports/contradicts relations are ideas worth carrying to our retrieval and synthesis gates. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: llm-wiki-starter
good: A one-command bootstrap for the Karpathy pattern: a bash installer (or an equivalent agent skill) that scaffolds the three-layer raw/ wiki/ templates/ structure, pre-configures AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md guidelines, auto-configures 17 Obsidian plugins plus theme and shortcuts, and can auto-install the surrounding tools (Claude Code, Obsidian, Node.js, Git). Compatible out of the box with Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI and OpenCode; 95 stars.
bad: It is an installer, not a knowledge system — after setup it hands you the same pattern to run yourself. Its headline route is a curl-piped bash script that installs and reconfigures global tools system-wide, a heavy and opinionated footprint; the scaffold's value ends where our already-running system begins.
didnt: Rejected — a bootstrap for a stack we already run; nothing in the scaffold is missing from our system, and its global-tool auto-install is not a route we would use. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Compass
licence: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual-licensed; root LICENSE file, LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE — the repo's licence card reads NOASSERTION because of the dual layout)
good: A local-first Rust knowledge-graph engine for codebases and project artifacts: it scans repository ASTs, Git history and dependencies with no external vector database, compiles architecture maps, and exports interlinked Markdown wikis, Obsidian vaults, GraphML, Neo4j/FalkorDB and self-contained HTML workbenches. Its MCP server and CLI answer bounded graph queries (query, explain, path, affected) with evidence tiers and cursor pagination, and historical graphs are pinned to exact commits with immutable extraction fingerprints, so past states can be queried, exported and diffed. Actively developed (174 stars, pushed 2026-10-20).
bad: Codebase-only: it graphs code and project artifacts, not personal knowledge, so its centre of gravity is a different product category from a personal knowledge OS. Very young (created July 2026) with a large, fast-moving surface spanning CLI, VS Code workbench, exports and MCP transports.
didnt: Rejected — a codebase graph engine, however strong, is out of scope for our personal knowledge wiki; our repos are worked by agents directly, not maintained as a graph product. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Enzyme
good: An Obsidian plugin whose chat agent works from a pre-computed conceptual map of the vault — built from existing tags, links, folders and note recency — so it pulls the right context before a follow-up is asked, then answers quoting vault notes with clickable links and highlighting the graph nodes it used. It works with local models (llama-server/Ollama/vLLM) as well as hosted chat APIs, keeps an on-device VaultSearch index that makes no AI calls, and claims up to 90% token savings versus having a coding agent explore the vault directly.
bad: AGPL-3.0 copyleft, so its code is ideas-only for us. It is a chat layer bound inside Obsidian rather than a standalone knowledge system, and its indexing leans on external AI providers plus a sign-in 'indexing credits' system despite the local-first framing; the repo was last pushed in May 2026.
didnt: Board — pre-computed concept maps from links, tags and recency as a context-assembly layer is an idea worth carrying to our evidence packing (its code is AGPL-3.0, ideas-only). (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: llm-code-wiki
good: A Claude Code plugin (three skills: wiki, deep-research, setup-wiki) that maintains an interlinked Markdown wiki over living code repositories: the agent reads code without copying it, writes cross-referenced pages (repositories, decisions, concepts, comparisons), and flags pages stale when the underlying code changes, tracked by file hashing done with the shell's built-in tools — no dependencies. A setup wizard scaffolds the wiki in minutes, an audit pass flags out-of-date pages, orphans and gaps, and an optional Python validator enforces the schema in pre-commit/CI.
bad: No licence is stated anywhere at the source — no LICENSE file in the repository, no licence in the README — so nothing in it is reusable. It is a prose-skill pack bound to Claude Code, young (created June 2026, 11 stars), and code-only in scope.
didnt: Rejected — no licence stated at source makes it ideas-only, and as a Claude Code skill pack over code repos it duplicates the pattern we already run. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Podcast Wiki
good: A Claude Code plugin that turns the Spotify episodes you have actually heard into a Karpathy-style wiki: published transcripts are preferred, with local mlx-whisper transcription as fallback, and synthesis extends one page per topic across episodes instead of creating near-duplicates, linking every claim to its episode and speaker and keeping disagreements between guests side by side. It ships a live demo wiki, a /lint-wiki health check (broken links, orphans, drift), a /dream pass that merges duplicate concept pages, and a headless scheduled ingest in which untrusted transcripts may only write inside wiki/ and run no git.
bad: Hard platform lock-in: macOS on Apple Silicon only (for mlx-whisper), plus a Spotify account, Claude Code, uv and ffmpeg. It is a personal single-listener tool — the raw transcripts stay local by design, so the published wiki's claims cannot be re-checked against source audio from the repository alone — and it is very young (v0.1.2, 7 stars).
didnt: Board — the Disagreements convention: when sources conflict, keep both claims side by side, each attributed to its speaker and episode, instead of letting the compiler silently merge them — a named section our contradiction handling could adopt. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ICT Knowledge Library
good: A complete, self-audited worked example of the Karpathy pattern in a single domain: 226 concept files across 33 directories, each following a strict template (7 required top-matter fields, 10 required sections, and a machine-readable JSON block whose id matches the filename), 43 stable Source IDs kept in SOURCES.md, per-concept confidence grades (high / medium / community-attributed / disputed / demo-stage), an INDEX.md catalogue beside the append-only log.md, and a reported audit with all files section-complete, every JSON block parsing, zero broken cross-links and zero orphan citations.
bad: The content is one curator's definitional library of a contested trading doctrine, so nothing transfers to our system beyond pattern corroboration, and its confidence grades are assigned by the library itself. Its README's License section reads '(none yet — TBD)' and there is no LICENSE file, so the content is unlicensed for reuse.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent, audit-passed deployment of the same three-layer shape we run (raw sources with stable IDs, a compiled wiki, an AGENTS.md schema, an append-only log) confirms the architecture; its unlicensed status would bar reuse in any case. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: OKF for Crossplane
good: A versioned Open Knowledge Format v0.2 catalog for the Crossplane v2 ecosystem: small Markdown concept documents carrying OKF metadata, provenance in sources, keyed claim footnotes and relationships, served two ways — a hosted public MCP server, and a self-host container that ingests catalog/ into a DuckDB catalog and serves read-only okf-mcp tools over Streamable HTTP. Its CRD tools resolve provider versions and return definitions as token-efficient YAML from pinned Git tags, and CI validation pins the ingest tool (okf-ingest 0.11.0).
bad: The public MCP endpoint is the author's temporary early-access service: the README warns its availability is not guaranteed and it may change or be removed without notice, and it has no application-level authentication, leaving access control to the operator's reverse proxy. Scope is a single vendor ecosystem, and the catalog rides on upstream OKF tooling.
didnt: Board — serving a Markdown knowledge bundle through a DuckDB catalog behind read-only MCP tools, as a possible query layer for our own read door; our stack has the read-only MCP door but no bundle-to-DuckDB ingest today. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: "Does the Wiki Grow Smarter?"
good: A disciplined pilot negative result against the LLM-Wiki pattern itself: a corpus of ten operating manuals, a stream of forty batched training cases and a held-out set of fifty cases stratified by six exception subtypes, with four systems ranging from a strong RAG baseline to a Wiki with compiled rule-checking views, iterated three times with substantially different ingest policies. Across all iterations and subtypes no Wiki variant exceeded the RAG baseline on diagnosis accuracy or forbidden-action recall, and the paper names three degenerate maintainer behaviours — fragmentation, atomization, and over-merging — with code, prompts, corpus and run outputs promised as a reproducibility archive.
bad: The author's own limitations section bounds the result tightly: a non-frontier model (glm-4-flash), one trajectory per configuration at temperature 0, a small synthetic Chinese corpus (ten SOPs), a lenient fuzzy-match scorer, and a single exception-dense domain; the preprint is banner-marked NOT PEER-REVIEWED. The discussion itself notes the small corpus leaves little knowledge gap for a wiki to fill, so the null may not transfer to large corpora or cross-document synthesis, which were not tested.
didnt: Corroboration — its degeneration modes, and a compiler that drops exception conditions during compression, corroborate our citation locking, caveat carriage and contradiction flags over a trusting maintainer loop; the null result is evidence for that discipline, not against the pattern at our scale. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)
institution: Institute of Data Science and Intelligent Technology, NingboTech University, Ningbo, Zhejiang, China

name: annotation-tools (collignon)
good: A minimal, honest bridge from annotation tools into Obsidian: it uses karlicoss/hypexport to pull all of your Hypothesis annotations to JSON, then converts them into Obsidian Markdown notes, with an incremental last-pull date kept in a .env file so re-runs fetch only new annotations; a parallel script does the same for Pinboard bookmarks and notes.
bad: A 2021 personal script collection, untouched since August 2021: credentials sit in a plaintext secrets.py, setup is manual and multi-step, and the README's own to-do list leaves tag hierarchies, links between pages and images unimplemented. No licence file exists and none is stated in the README.
didnt: Rejected — stale personal export scripts for another vault stack; our ingest reads sources directly with citation locking, and the absence of a licence makes the code ideas-only regardless. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: PKMigrator
good: A small collection of four working one-way converters between personal-knowledge apps: RemNote JSON to Obsidian Markdown, RemNote to Org Mode / Org Roam, Roam Research JSON to Obsidian, and Roam Markdown to Org Roam — a practical escape hatch out of hosted PKM tools into plain-text vaults.
bad: The README is a bare link list with no install or usage documentation and no tests; two of the four tools are forks of other people's converters with additions, and the collection is a single-author 2021-era effort.
didnt: Rejected — one-way export converters for RemNote and Roam corpora we do not hold; our wiki ingests Markdown directly, so there is nothing for it to migrate. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Goodsidian
good: A Bash script that pulls your Goodreads currently-reading and read shelf RSS feeds and creates or updates Obsidian book notes keyed by Goodreads book ID — frontmatter, cover image and an author wikilink — and when a book is finished it swaps the shelf tag and adds year/month-read lines, giving a reading shelf a maintained notes vault without a plugin.
bad: macOS-first tooling (osascript and BSD sed, with Linux support relegated to a separate branch), brittle grep/sed scraping of RSS with the shelf owner's name hard-coded for manual replacement, and the author's own warning about possible data loss; a single-author personal script.
didnt: Rejected — a personal Goodreads-to-Obsidian sync with no fit for our citation-locked wiki, and with no licence at source the code is ideas-only regardless. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: mdzk
good: An mdBook-based Zettelkasten backend: it turns a folder of Markdown notes into a directed graph with backlinks and wikilinks, can render through static site generators, can host a language server for the note graph, and is distributed through crates.io and Homebrew — plain-text notes with graph structure and no database.
bad: The README itself warns the tool is 'CURRENTLY UNDER HEAVY DEVELOPMENT' and 'somewhat unusable at the moment', with documentation still a work in progress; there has been no release since 0.5.2 (February 2022), so the project reads as stalled mid-build.
didnt: Rejected — stalled since 2022 and self-described as somewhat unusable; MPL-2.0 copyleft would make it ideas-only in any case. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: writeup-converter
good: Dependency-light Python and Bash scripts (standard library only) that copy an Obsidian writeup folder together with its attachments to a new location — the private-to-public vault export Obsidian itself lacks — with filename prefix rewriting, plus a website formatter mode that concatenates the files, converts wikilinks to Jekyll anchors and builds a contents table.
bad: The README lists many manual post-conversion cleanup steps and open TODOs, so the automation is partial; the repository has been stale since September 2021 and is a single-author utility.
didnt: Rejected — a personal export utility for a publishing flow our wiki already handles through its own pipeline, and with no licence at source the code is ideas-only regardless. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: postgres-mcp-hardened
good: A defence-in-depth read-only PostgreSQL MCP server in Rust: SQL is AST-validated with sqlparser and run inside a read-only transaction with rollback plus a write-function denylist, an EXPLAIN cost guard rejects expensive queries, columns can be redacted, and every call lands in a tamper-evident hash-chained audit log, with OAuth 2.1, a fuzz harness and CI; it refuses to start as a network listener if its database role turns out to be able to write.
bad: A very young single-author project (3 stars, pushed days before this pass), and its own README documents an unresolved redaction equality-oracle issue — the security model is visibly still being battle-tested in public rather than settled.
didnt: Corroboration — AST-validated read-only access, a query cost guard and a hash-chained audit log mirror our gateway's deny-by-default and ledger design; there is no Postgres MCP need in our stack to adopt it for. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: NeoLi00/memX
good: Self-learning, self-maintaining memory layer for coding agents: it turns completed work into structured, searchable memory (facts, events, state, entities and graph edges) kept linked to the original turn, maintains itself by letting corrections supersede older facts and stopping stale task state from competing with current state, and injects only compact evidence lines at recall. It connects natively to Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw through lifecycle hooks and to any MCP client, and its README reports 94.2% R@3 on LongMemEval-S in its own benchmark table.
bad: Very young and already quiet: created 2026-05-08, last push 2026-05-26 (403 stars). Memory compilation, recall planning and maintenance all call an external LLM through a provider adapter (OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Google, or local Ollama), so the default path sends work content to a cloud model, and capture is automatic via native hooks rather than deliberate. Its benchmark figures are the project's own, with no independent evaluation.
didnt: Rejected — capture is ambient (native hooks record completed turns automatically), which our deliberate-capture, approval-gated write rules forbid, and its self-maintenance depends on a cloud LLM call; its supersession of stale facts confirms a mechanism we already have. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)
