name: Goldentrii/AgentRecall-X
good: Local-first memory built around a governed corrections ledger: every correction becomes a structured record (severity, evidence, applies_when, retraction) stored as plain markdown under ~/.agent-recall/, is loaded at session start before the agent acts, and is measured — each time the same situation recurs the outcome is logged as heeded or recurred, so a rule that failed to change behaviour is rewritten rather than merely re-saved. Ships as MCP server, SDK and CLI with five default tools, and rule edits stay owner-gated.
bad: Young (created 2026-03-24, 371 stars) and effectively single-author. Its optional Claude Code hooks capture corrections silently and inject ambient memories on every prompt — automatic capture by another name — and its effect numbers, including the 'Automaticity Law', are self-measured on the author's own store. The README also embeds an instruction block addressed to visiting agents, telling them to install it and what to say to their human.
didnt: Corroboration — a corrections ledger loaded before acting, heeded/recurred outcome measurement and owner-gated rule edits confirm our corrections-ledger and outcome-verified-claims design; its silent ambient-capture hooks are the part we deliberately do not copy. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Graphicle-AI/graphicle
good: One local Rust program that builds a tree-sitter code graph of a repository and layers project memory (docs, reviewed decisions, past sessions) over it, answering through MCP and its CLI with cited excerpts that name the exact file and lines, inside a token budget the user sets. Memories an agent proposes wait for the owner's approval in its app, reviewed memories are anchored to the code symbols they describe so a memory goes stale when that code changes, and it runs with no account, no API key and no telemetry.
bad: Brand new: the repository was created 2026-10-14, days before this study, and its headline speed and memory benchmarks are the project's own runs of a pre-release 0.1.1 engine against Graphify. The Windows build is an unsigned preview, and session capture keeps each finished turn automatically — the memories distilled from them are approval-gated, but the turn capture underneath is not.
didnt: Corroboration — cited file-and-line excerpts, approval-gated memory writes, and staleness anchored to the thing a memory describes confirm our citation-locking and approval-gate design. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: kleosr/cursorkleosr
good: Agent memory made a property of the repository rather than a tool invoked: an always-apply Cursor rule (.cursor/rules/workflow-memory.mdc, alwaysApply: true) makes the agent read workflow_state.md and project_config.md before acting and write state back after meaningful work, with AGENTS.md as the single agent handbook, so no session starts from zero. Zero dependencies and no build step — all state lives in plain root markdown that can be read, diffed and grepped from anywhere.
bad: The enforcement mechanism is hard-bound to Cursor's rule system, so the always-on property does not transfer to other hosts. It is a documentation-only project — the README itself states there are no tests, no compilation and no CI — and the always-loaded rule spends context in every session whether or not the stored state is relevant to the task.
didnt: Corroboration — an always-loaded markdown state file the agent must read before it thinks confirms our wiki-as-agent-memory design; the pattern is already our base, and its enforcement trick is Cursor-only. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ZSeven-W/dsh-noema
good: Long-term memory plugin that keeps memories as inspectable Markdown files under a local root (~/.agent-memory/): recall, full-text search, catalog browsing and multi-hop graph recall tools, a noema_explain tool that says why a memory was or was not recalled, a settings page where the owner can search, browse, add, review and delete stored memories, and an importer that reads the memory files of ten other agent tools with a content-keyed deduplication ledger.
bad: It is a plugin for a single host — DeepSeek Harness, tested only against DSH 0.2.0-rc.2, a release candidate — and depends on the separate Noema engine (a bundled Rust submodule/binary). Its importer ingests other tools' memory files wholesale, the opposite of a deliberate per-source ingest.
didnt: Rejected — a host-bound plugin for DeepSeek Harness with its own engine; our stack keeps memory in the wiki itself, and wholesale cross-tool memory import conflicts with our deliberate-ingest rule. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Avinash-jetwani/jevmem
good: Keeps a project's decisions, rules, bugs, to-dos and failed approaches as one-line entries in a JEVMEM.md file inside the repository: when a decision changes, the old line is crossed out as [superseded] but kept for history, and a pre-action guard checks each command or edit against the saved rules and asks the user first when one might break (66 of 68 rule breaks caught in the author's held-out test). The file travels with git, so a whole team shares the same memory.
bad: Every keep/drop decision is made by TypeSafe AI's hosted Jev model — the README states a TypeSafe API key is required and that jevmem's requests are billed to it, so chat content leaves the machine for an external judgement on each save. All effect numbers are the author's own single-run test sets (the README says so itself), and prompt-time retrieval time and cost grow with the file.
didnt: Corroboration — an in-repo decisions ledger with superseded lines retained, and a pre-action guard that asks the owner before a saved rule is broken, confirm our ledger and approval-gate design; the hosted-model dependency is the part we avoid. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: MemFree
good: Hybrid AI search engine that answers from a personal knowledge base — bookmarks, local files (text, PDF, Docx, PPTX, Markdown) and multi-image input — and from the live web through several search engines, presenting results as text, mind maps, images or video, with cross-device sync of search history; the same codebase doubles as an AI page generator producing React/Tailwind pages. Substantial adoption for its class at 1,515 GitHub stars.
bad: A hosted, multi-vendor product rather than a local-first system: deployment requires OpenAI and other model API keys plus Upstash Redis and auth secrets, answers are produced by cloud models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), and the knowledge base lives inside the service. Repository activity has also slowed, with the last push on 2026-07-06.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted search product whose storage and inference sit with external cloud services fails our local-first custody rule, and AI page generation is outside our system's scope. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: OkiDoki
good: Zero-configuration static generator for API and technical documentation: it turns Markdown files into a searchable, responsive documentation site with sub-second builds, generates API reference pages directly from OpenAPI/Swagger specs, and scaffolds a project with okidoki init (docs folder, okidoki.yaml site config, sidebars.yaml navigation). Published on npm as okidoki, with full-text search built into the generated site.
bad: Tiny and young: 18 GitHub stars, created 2025-08-26, single-author in practice, and the README is written as search-engine marketing (long comparison sections against Docusaurus, VitePress, GitBook and others) rather than engineering documentation; it documents no tests, evaluation or provenance features.
didnt: Rejected — a presentational docs generator: it publishes pages but keeps no knowledge, citations or memory of its own, so there is nothing for our wiki engine to take. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: pelican-obsidian
good: Small Pelican plugin by Jonathan Sundqvist that lets an Obsidian vault feed a Pelican blog without the syntax looking out of place: [[note name]] and [[note | custom text]] wikilinks, ![[file]] embeds, and #tag names rendered without the leading hash. A link to an article that does not exist renders as plain text, so notes that should stay inside Obsidian and posts that belong on the blog can be separated cleanly.
bad: Narrow and stale: 45 stars, created 2021-07-03, last push 2024-12-30. The README still says 'not yet on pypi', its Future features list (section embeds, draft handling) is unimplemented, and its commented-out badges show the README was templated from another plugin (pelican-series).
didnt: Rejected — a one-way rendering bridge for the Pelican blog engine; our wiki renders its own pages and already resolves wikilinks natively, so the bridge solves a problem we do not have. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ucsandman/markdown-agent-memory
good: A markdown-only hierarchical memory system for long-running agents: a routing-index MEMORY.md over people/projects/decisions/context files, where every fact carries a provenance tag ([stated]/[observed]/[inferred]/[suggested]), superseded facts are struck through in place with dates rather than deleted, and inferred lessons must pass a 3-signal recurrence gate before becoming standing rules. Zero dependencies; the README reports seven months in production across three frontier models from two vendors, including a head-to-head where a 382-dependency memory runtime returned a superseded fact while the folder returned the current one with its source.
bad: The repository was archived on 2026-09-19 — the policy, templates and install prompt moved to ucsandman/Agnostic-AI and this repo 'receives no further commits'. It is discipline without tooling: no search, index or retrieval machinery beyond the agent reading files, so the read path scales only as far as the folder stays small and well-kept.
didnt: Corroboration — provenance tags on every fact, supersession as an in-place edit with history preserved, and a recurrence gate before inferred lessons harden into rules independently mirror our citation, supersession and claim-promotion discipline. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: radimsem/remindb
good: An agentic memory database in a single portable SQLite file: it parses Markdown/HTML/JSON/YAML/TOON notes into a hashed node tree exposed through an MCP tool suite, with FTS5 ranked search trimmed to a passed token budget, hot/cold node 'temperature' that decays over time and nudges in-place summarization of cold nodes, git-style snapshots with per-node diffs so a returning agent resyncs with a small delta instead of re-reading everything, and weighted [[wikilink]] edges traversable up to 5 hops as a knowledge graph. The README claims 82–99% session-token savings.
bad: Memory lives in one binary .db file, giving up the plain-text auditability (grep, git blame, human reading) of markdown stores; the headline token-saving figure is the project's own claim, and the temperature/summarization machinery depends on the agent cooperating through the bundled skills. Single-author project shipped as a Go binary plus MCP server.
didnt: Board — hot/cold temperature ranking with decay-driven summarization, and delta resync via per-node diffs instead of whole-file re-reads, as candidate mechanisms for our retrieval ranking and session boot. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ArgentAIOS/argentos-core
good: A self-hosted personal AI operating system: SQLite + pgvector hybrid memory with auto-capture and entity tracking, a heartbeat accountability loop with a contract/promise system and scoring, an always-on contemplation loop over local models, multi-channel messaging (Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage), a visual multi-agent workflow builder with scheduling and approvals, a three-tier hierarchical intent policy engine for safe agent behaviour, AES-256-GCM encrypted secrets with OS-keychain integration, and 64 connector harnesses.
bad: Enormous scope and stack for the memory job: a macOS-first installer that pulls in Homebrew, PostgreSQL and Redis, and the README frames Core as 'the free, open-source foundation' fronting a marketplace and paid boundaries. Its continuity model is a whole agent platform, not a knowledge store a part could be lifted from cleanly.
didnt: Corroboration — the three-tier intent policy engine, workflow approvals and heartbeat promise/scoring system independently confirm our approval-gated writes and accountability design at platform scale. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: SrsBlack/ict-knowledge-library
good: A canonical LLM-maintained wiki of Inner Circle Trader concepts 2016–2026: 226 self-contained concept files across 33 directories, each with a definition, formal criteria, formula, visual, examples, common mistakes, related-concept cross-links, source citations to 43 stable Source IDs, and a machine-readable JSON block whose id matches the filename — all under a strict template (7 required top-matter fields, 10 required sections) with stated validation targets of 10/10 required sections per file, zero broken cross-links, zero orphan citations, and INDEX/TIMELINE files fully aligned with disk.
bad: Deliberately definitional only — the README's scope section excludes trading algorithms, backtests, live data and performance results — and it canonises one trading doctrine, with community-attributed and disputed concepts carried under its own confidence field. Its License section reads '(none yet — TBD)' and no LICENSE file exists, so reuse terms are unsettled.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent Karpathy-pattern wiki in an unrelated domain, held together by a schema file (AGENTS.md), stable source IDs and mechanical completeness checks, confirms our schema-plus-lint architecture. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: nutdnuy/invest-like-apo-resources
good: A Thai-language companion resource pack for a QuantCorner investment-research talk series (Claude Thailand Community): an end-to-end workflow from market data (Webull API) through research memory (an LLM Wiki setup) and reusable analysis frameworks (Book-to-Skill, portfolio analytics via Riskfolio-Lib) to dashboard output, with a Source Note template for evidence capture and a Decision Log template recording the proposal, evidence, reasoning, reviewer and next-review conditions.
bad: It is a curated link-and-template collection for one lecture series, not a maintained system: most of the value lives in the external projects it points to, the documentation is Thai-only, and the pack carries a Webull account-opening referral link for QuantCorner. No licence is stated anywhere in the repository.
didnt: Corroboration — its Source Note and Decision Log templates (evidence, reasoning, reviewer, review conditions) independently match our decision-record practice; there is no software here to take. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: cafe3310/agent-skill-memories-off
good: A local-first personal knowledge base managed like a code repository: markdown entity files under a schema defined in meta.md (entity types and relation predicates, enforced H1/H2 structure), a memocli tool (init, create-entity, search-entities, append-update, explore, doctor) and Git-driven auditing in which every script-made change lands as a commit carrying a mandatory reason; read-only external document repos such as Obsidian vaults can be attached for search and reading without converting their notes into entities.
bad: Documentation is entirely in Chinese, and the architecture has already pivoted once — the original MCP server was replaced by an Agent Skill plus Python scripts, with the old MCP version kept only on the v2 branch. A single author's personal tool with an idiosyncratic entity/relation notation.
didnt: Corroboration — git-audited knowledge changes with a mandatory recorded reason, plus a schema-first markdown entity store, mirror our ledger and schema discipline. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: VT777/pageindex-chat-studio
good: PageChat builds a document's structure before answering questions about it: layered TOC construction routed by document shape (the text layer directly for clean PDFs, OCR/VLM only for scanned or image pages, selective OCR for hybrid files, escalation to a heavier path when TOC quality gates fail), then an agent reads evidence progressively from folders, TOCs, pages, tables and images, with citations placed close to conclusions and previews back to the original page. It supports PDF, Markdown, spreadsheets, slide decks and Word documents, multi-provider custom models, optional web search, and one-command Docker Compose deployment.
bad: A heavy deployed application — Docker Compose with frontend/backend images and user-configured QA, parsing and OCR/VLM model providers — rather than a file-based store; it is a workspace over uploaded documents, not a persistent cross-source wiki, and answer quality rides on the configured models.
didnt: Corroboration — its stated philosophy (never answer from an LLM rewrite of the document; treat TOC and source anchors as the first infrastructure layer and return to original evidence for each question) matches our citation-first stance. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: niuma996/nium-wiki
good: An AI-coding-tool skill that compiles a codebase into a cross-linked wiki: import-graph module discovery, two-phase fact extraction, auto-generated Mermaid architecture/data-flow/dependency diagrams, and idempotent incremental updates — SHA256 hashing plus dependency-graph propagation regenerate only the pages affected by code changes while preserving hand-edited and domain pages. Fully offline with zero external dependencies, works across 10+ programming languages, and ships a local preview server with full-text search, Mermaid rendering and an interactive source↔doc relationship graph.
bad: It documents codebases only, not general knowledge, and output quality rides on the host coding agent's model, since the skill is a workflow the agent executes rather than a deterministic generator; its own README flags large projects (over 500 graph nodes) for special handling in the relationship view.
didnt: Board — SHA256 change detection plus dependency-graph propagation to regenerate only the compiled pages affected by a source change is a concrete incremental-maintenance mechanism for our wiki compile step. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: growilabs/growi-mcp-server
good: The official MCP server for the GROWI wiki (@growi/mcp-server on npm): page search and retrieval plus page, tag, comment and share-link management, simultaneous connections to multiple GROWI instances (v7.3.x or higher recommended), and bundled agent skills for guided setup and for smart saving with path suggestions presented to the user before writing.
bad: It is only a connector: useless without a running GROWI instance and API tokens, and it hands the agent read/write access to an organisation's hosted wiki with no approval gating of its own described in the README. Nothing about it is local-first or file-based.
didnt: Rejected — a write-capable bridge to an external hosted wiki platform; its custody and write model are the opposite of our local-first, approval-gated door. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Ciao1019/Petrichor
good: A self-hosted knowledge platform (Go + React + PostgreSQL) that compiles Markdown writing into a semantic wiki — entities, concepts and relations aggregated across articles with source citations and freshness fingerprints — while keeping retrieval and reading strictly separate (Search/Outline to locate, then Read originals as Evidence, with Trace) in an agentic RAG fusing BM25, vector and wiki signals. It can hand knowledge to other agents: REST and MCP access plus exports to OKF, Obsidian and installable Agent Skill packages, with full call auditing.
bad: A full server platform to operate: Docker Compose with PostgreSQL 16+ (with pg_trgm and pgvector extensions), Redis, S3-compatible object storage and Caddy, plus per-purpose model-provider configuration — the opposite of a local files-first store and far beyond a personal wiki's operational budget.
didnt: Board — the semantic-wiki middle layer (cross-article entity/concept pages carrying source citations and freshness fingerprints) and the locate-then-read evidence separation are ideas worth boarding for our Ask path. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: hiroto107/my-SECONDBRAIN
good: A lived personal implementation of the Karpathy LLM Wiki pattern inside an Obsidian vault (in Japanese): an 'LLM Wiki' folder holding raw sources (inbox, clipping, from-vault, assets), agent-compiled wiki pages (sources, entities, concepts, syntheses, plus index, log and overview), page templates, an AGENTS.md schema fixing the division of labour (the human selects sources, sets topics and reviews; the LLM summarises, links, applies diffs and maintains the log), and a .claude/skills/llm-wiki-ingest skill — with dozens of dated source summaries and syntheses showing sustained real use.
bad: It is the author's own vault published as-is — personal notes, reading memos and multi-megabyte images included — and the root README consists of only the project title; with no licence anywhere, nothing in it is documented or licensed for reuse by others.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent, sustained personal deployment of the same raw/wiki/schema pattern, including the human-selects-and-reviews / agent-maintains split, confirms our architecture in the wild. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: awacke1/KnowledgeGraphEditor
good: A single-file Streamlit app (app.py) for building knowledge-graph displays with Mermaid: glossary entities — bundled roleplaying and transhuman glossaries ship in the code — are rendered as link-rich nodes whose per-entity links fan out to arXiv, Wikipedia, Google, Bing, YouTube and X searches plus AI-search/refine prompt variants, so a graph doubles as a research launcher.
bad: Demo-grade and unmaintained: the Space is sleeping and was last modified 2025-01-03, much of the supposed AI pipeline in app.py is placeholder stubs (the LLM inference function returns mock text; the image, video, speech-synthesis and arXiv-search functions only print debug lines), debug helpers were left in, and four backup copies of the app file (backup1–backup4) litter the repository.
didnt: Rejected — a sleeping demo with stub AI functions; its Mermaid graph editing adds nothing our stack lacks. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: IIC/RagQuAS
good: Spanish RAG/QA evaluation dataset ('RAGMiscContextual', DOI 10.57967/hf/2044): 201 test questions across many everyday domains (health, insurance, gastronomy, first aid, scams, customer service...), each shipped with five retrieved contexts, their source links and full texts, a topic and a gold answer, distributed as parquet - a ready-made retrieval-plus-answering evaluation set.
bad: Test split only and tiny (201 examples, ~1 MB download); gated (auto-approval) on Hugging Face; Spanish-only; minimal adoption (56 downloads, last modified 2025-01-03) and a brief card whose summary trails off with 'see the full description on the dataset page'.
didnt: Rejected - a small Spanish-language RAG evaluation set under non-commercial share-alike terms; our answer evaluation is covered by our own golden set and abstention battery, and nothing here fills a gap in them. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: NextSecurity/infected_memory_dumps
good: DFIR training/research corpus of memory dumps from real cybersecurity incidents - the file listing shows WannaCry on Windows XP SP3, PSExec activity on Server 2012, Windows 2003/XP/10 images and CTF cases (Securinets Quals 2019) in .raw/.mem/.vmem/.img formats; the card says the dumps were gathered with forensic tools and anonymised.
bad: Gated behind manual approval; 'loads of GBs' of unstructured binary images whose informal card gives no per-file provenance, counts or schema; 7 downloads, untouched since 2024-04-01. 'Memory' here is RAM images - a keyword collision with knowledge memory, as the Stage B record already suspected.
didnt: Rejected - a DFIR RAM-image corpus that only shares the word 'memory' with our domain; no fit for a personal knowledge OS. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: otellm/3gpp_knowledgeGraph
licence: other - custom 'Trial Licence KU GSMA Members Knowledge Graph' (card license_name; text in the repo LICENSE file)
good: A knowledge-graph rendering of the 3GPP Release 13 specification corpus in a single GraphML file - 12,800 nodes and 9,970 edges of extracted entities, compiled by Khalifa University for telecommunications, semantic-network and graph-based AI research: a worked example of turning a whole standards corpus into a queryable graph.
bad: One frozen 2016-era release (Rel-13) with sparse connectivity (about 0.8 edges per node); gated behind manual approval; the licence is a custom GSMA-members trial licence, not an open one; 19 downloads.
didnt: Board - compiling an entire specification corpus into an entity graph with a stated node/edge census is a pattern worth boarding for our own corpus-graph views; the dataset itself is telecom content under a custom trial licence, so ideas only. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)
institution: Khalifa University

name: llm-book/bert-base-japanese-v3-crf-ner-wikipedia-dataset
good: Japanese named-entity-recognition model from the book 'Introduction to Large Language Models' (chapter 6): cl-tohoku/bert-base-japanese-v3 with a CRF output layer, fine-tuned on llm-book/ner-wikipedia-dataset; the card gives a runnable transformers-pipeline example with sample output, and declares seqeval precision/recall/F1 as its metrics.
bad: The card names metrics but reports no scores; Japanese-only and Wikipedia-domain; untouched since 2023-07-25 with 160 downloads and 3 likes - a book companion artifact, not a maintained model.
didnt: Rejected - a Japanese Wikipedia NER model; no gap in our English-first knowledge stack that a BERT token-classifier fills. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ai.libers/libers-suite
good: Libers Suite is an AI-search optimisation service for online shops: it asks six AI systems (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Grok, DeepSeek) whether they mention a shop, rewrites the shop's product data into 'Knowledge Packs', writes them back into Shopify/WooCommerce/Shopware/Magento and other shop systems, then re-measures. This MCP server exposes the authenticated account's website analyses and Knowledge Packs to agents, using OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration.
bad: An e-commerce marketing SaaS, not a knowledge tool - the 'knowledge' is product-feed optimisation. The registry record is a single line with no repository, documentation or tool list, and access is bound to a vendor account, so custody of the analyses sits with the vendor.
didnt: Rejected - AI-search shop-optimisation SaaS; no fit for a personal knowledge OS, and its custody is vendor-hosted. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ai.llamanotes/llamanotes
good: Hosted MCP study buddy ('Lucky') over the user's own LlamaNotes courses: chat about course material, progress tracking and AI course generation, served as a streamable-HTTP remote at mcp.llamanotes.ai.
bad: The registry record is the whole inspectable surface - no repository, tool list or licence - and the website the record names (llamanotes.ai) was found in Stage B to serve a different product ('SkillSend'), so the vendor's public identity trail is inconsistent; a hosted, account-bound service.
didnt: Rejected - hosted study-buddy SaaS with an inconsistent public trail and no inspectable code; our knowledge and homeschool work is local-first. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ai.meminal/meminal
good: Hosted conversational-memory MCP remote (meminal.ai/mcp) offering persistent memory for deep conversational context across platforms, with standard Bearer authentication (OAuth or personal access token) declared in the record.
bad: A one-line registry record is all that can be inspected: the repository field is empty, and there is no tool list, documentation or licence anywhere in the record; memory custody is the vendor's cloud by design - the opposite of local-first - and there is a single 1.0.0 release.
didnt: Rejected - hosted memory SaaS whose custody model contradicts our local-first design, with nothing inspectable beyond a registry line. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ai.mitosislabs/mitosis
good: Mitosis Labs runs a live agent-memory platform ('Cortex', billed as 'the source of truth for your agents') with business integrations (Snowflake, Notion, GitHub); its public MCP remote needs no auth and serves pricing, documentation search, platform status and agent skills.
bad: The MCP surface is a sales/support door, not the memory product itself; the catalogue's decentralised/Filecoin framing appears nowhere on the current site, which presents a conventional hosted platform with unquantified claims ('cutting your AI spend by up to 90%'); the registry-named repository (OperatingSystem-1/website) returns 404.
didnt: Rejected - hosted agent-memory platform; vendor custody, and the only inspectable MCP surface is marketing/support rather than the product. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: ai.smithery/plainyogurt21-clintrials-mcp
good: Structured access to ClinicalTrials.gov data - searching, retrieving and analysing clinical-trial records - as a hosted MCP remote on Smithery; version 1.16.0 indicates sustained iteration.
bad: Hosted behind a Smithery API key; the registry record's repository field is empty so no code can be inspected, and the registry itself truncates the server's description mid-sentence; it is one of several ClinicalTrials.gov MCP servers, with nothing in the record distinguishing it.
didnt: Rejected - a hosted, uninspectable single-purpose data connector, and clinical-trials data is outside our system's scope. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Compose MCP
good: Typed feature-management MCP tools (roadmap, changelog, artifact linking, journal, completion) over canonical project files (ROADMAP.md, CHANGELOG.md, docs/features/<code>/, docs/journal/), part of the Compose structured AI dev pipeline, which gates design decisions before any code, requires every step to clear postconditions, and runs review on a different model than the one that wrote the work; a slim stdio launcher pulls the full runtime transitively.
bad: BUSL-1.1 source-available licence (not open source); the tools only work inside a compose-initialised project and mutate Compose's own artifact layout, so using them means adopting that pipeline; seven releases in three weeks (September 2026) mark a young, fast-moving surface.
didnt: Board - the typed-artifact discipline (roadmap/changelog/journal as canonical files an agent must maintain, design gated before code, cross-model review) is a governance pattern worth the ideas board; the BUSL-1.1 licence bars adopting its code. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Ambix
good: Strategic product memory for product teams: strategy, initiatives, opportunities, findings and the history behind them held in one structured store - initiatives linked to the strategy they serve, findings to the decisions they should shape - so every AI session starts with the team's full context; a hosted remote MCP server with OAuth 2.1 browser sign-in (no API keys to paste), EU hosting, and a plain web overview for teammates who don't use an AI client.
bad: A closed hosted service: the README states plainly that the repository 'is a listing page for the hosted Ambix MCP server. It contains no source code'; access is membership-gated and checked server-side, and team data sits on the vendor's EU servers; very young (repository created 2026-06-17, one star, a single day of pushes).
didnt: Rejected - closed product-team SaaS; vendor custody contradicts our local-first custody, and there is no code to evaluate. Its typed strategy-initiative-finding linking mirrors what our wiki's links already do. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Cosmonote
good: AI note-taker for iPhone and Mac: records for hours, transcribes with speaker identification, converts recordings into structured notes with PDF export, and offers an offline mode (vendor site, archived 2026-01-08).
bad: The catalogue's MCP-server repository (cosmonote/pocketbase) no longer exists and the cosmonote GitHub organisation lists no public repositories at all, so the MCP surface the catalogue described could not be inspected; the product is a closed, single-developer consumer app (site copyright Jordan Bonnet) with notes held in the vendor's app.
didnt: Rejected - closed consumer transcription app whose MCP add-on has vanished from public view; our notes live as local files under our own custody. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: hiveWiki
good: A shared project wiki built for AI agents: agents read and write pages and track next actions and activity logs over a hosted MCP remote (mcp.hivewiki.ai), per its official registry record.
bad: The one-line registry record is the entire inspectable substance: the product site and even its archived snapshot are JavaScript shells with no readable content, and the record publishes no repository, tool list or licence.
didnt: Rejected - hosted agent wiki with nothing inspectable beyond a registry line; our local-first wiki already provides agent read/write with approval gates and an activity log. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: InfoLang Memory
licence: Apache-2.0 (the official SDKs — GitHub licence detection on infolang-sdk-python and across the org's SDK/integration repos; the memory service itself is a managed cloud API and states no separate licence in the SDK source)
good: A hosted semantic-memory API with a genuinely broad client surface: official SDKs for Python, TypeScript, Rust and Go plus integrations for ~25 agent frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, Mastra, Google ADK, the OpenAI Agents SDK and more). The API itself is small and clear — investigate/recall for semantic retrieval, remember/memorize with source and tags, forget and namespace reset, workspace isolation resolved automatically from the credential, hybrid recall with tag filters, and zip-archive bulk ingest.
bad: Managed-cloud first: the memory itself lives behind the vendor's gateway (api.infolang.ai), the opposite of local-first custody. The vendor is months old (org created 2026-05-21; the Python SDK repo 2026-07-26) and already churning its auth surface — dev keys and mTLS are deprecated and the old direct endpoint was removed. The catalogue's ALREADY HAVE verdict has no lane-8 disposition behind it and is corroborated by nothing at the source.
didnt: Rejected — a hosted memory substrate is the architecture our local-first design exists to avoid (the same ground on which hosted memory platforms were rejected in Tier 1), and the vendor is too new to hold a personal corpus; Apache-2.0 SDKs do not change the custody question. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: SmartMemory
licence: SmartMemory Lite Runtime License v1.0 (custom, proprietary — text read in full in the PyPI record): free use of the unmodified runtime including internal use and non-commercial distribution, but no modification or reverse engineering, commercial redistribution only under a separate agreement, and an express ban on using it to build a competing memory service; the hosted platform, server components and SDKs are licensed separately.
good: A serious typed-memory design: five core types (episodic, semantic, procedural, pending, zettelkasten) plus an expertise layer (decision, constraint, learned, opinion, reasoning, observation) whose types carry supersession and reinforcement; a bitemporal storage model (event time + system time) preserved at the storage layer; an observable 11-stage extraction pipeline reporting per-stage timing, tokens and cost; a local Lite mode (SQLite + usearch, no Docker) or a FalkorDB + Redis server mode; and a unified MCP server with multi-tenant workspaces and origin-provenance tiers.
bad: The licence is the blocker: the shipped core is a compiled 'Lite Runtime' under a custom proprietary licence that forbids modification and competing use and gates commercial redistribution — ideas-only under our discipline. Full extraction leans on an LLM API key, the dependency set is heavy (spaCy, HuggingFace hub), and the platform, server and SDK pieces are each licensed separately, making the real terms a patchwork.
didnt: Board — the expertise layer is a taxonomy idea worth carrying to the ideas board: first-class decision/constraint/learned/opinion memory types, with rejected alternatives recorded on decisions and supersession built in, maps directly onto our decision records. The runtime itself is Rejected: custom proprietary licence (ideas-only) and a compiled-runtime, separately-licensed platform model. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @quartz-community/remark-obsidian
licence: MIT (registry license field and the repository's GitHub-detected licence agree)
good: Quartz's remark plugin for the full Obsidian markdown dialect — wikilinks, embeds, callouts, tags, highlights, comments, arrows — with two presets where Obsidian and CommonMark disagree: legacy (reproducing what the author saw in Obsidian) and strict (CommonMark/GFM-compliant), every divergence individually switchable. Its parity gate is the notable engineering: a generated corpus is rendered inside real Obsidian and compared against the plugin's own output.
bad: Very young and small (repo created 2026-02, 4 stars, a community org), and the legacy default deliberately reproduces divergences Obsidian inherited from remark-parse@8 — faithful, but defects by design. The README is development-facing, with no user documentation beyond the preset table.
didnt: Board — the Obsidian parity-corpus method (render a generated corpus inside real Obsidian and diff against your own renderer) is a testing idea our Lens renderer work could borrow; the plugin itself is a JS-ecosystem component our Python-side renderer does not consume. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @flowershow/remark-wiki-link
good: A complete wikilink toolkit for remark: [[links]] with aliases and heading anchors, embeds for images, video, audio and PDFs with dimensions, Obsidian-style shortest-path resolution against a supplied file list, and an explicit permalink map so specific files can carry custom URLs; unresolved links are marked with a 'new' class instead of failing.
bad: Note transclusion is still on its own roadmap — ![[Embed note]] and note-heading embeds are listed as future support — and resolution is only as good as the caller-supplied file list; the plugin does no vault indexing of its own.
didnt: Rejected — a competent component, but it solves in the JS/remark ecosystem a problem our own Lens renderer already handles in-tree; nothing in it is missing from our stack. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: remark-wiki-link-plus
good: The original Life Itself wikilink plugin: [[links]] with aliases and heading anchors, PDF and image transclusion across many image formats with a graceful unsupported-format message, folder-index permalink collapsing ([[docs/index]] resolves to /docs), and a case-sensitivity fix for permalink paths.
bad: Unmaintained — the changelog ends at 1.1.1 (2022-11-14) and audio, video and note embeds are still listed as future support; in practice it is superseded by the scoped @flowershow/remark-wiki-link (v4.0.0) from the same lineage.
didnt: Rejected — stale since 2022 and superseded by its own successor package; our renderer already covers wikilinks. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @lxcid/remark-wikilink
licence: MIT (registry license field and the repository's GitHub-detected licence agree)
good: It fixes one real parsing bug properly: with stock remark-gfm, the alias pipe in [[target|alias]] splits a GFM table cell in two; this plugin recognises wikilink spans while the table row is still being scanned, so cells stay intact with no source rewriting, sentinel encoding or escaped pipes required from authors. The README is unusually thorough — design rationale, syntax decisions, mdast node shapes, HTML output, and a comparison with other wikilink plugins.
bad: Brand new and unproven (repo created 2026-07-16, v0.2.0, 1 star, single author), ESM-only and requiring Node 24+; its scope is deliberately narrow — a tokenizer-level fix, not a wikilink system.
didnt: Board — the tokenizer-ordering insight is worth boarding for our own renderer work: wikilink spans must be recognised before GFM table pipes are classified, or aliased links inside tables corrupt the table. The package itself is too young and narrow to adopt. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Agimem
licence: no licence stated at source (hosted service; no licence, source repository or terms stated on its listing)
good: A deliberately simple hosted memory capsule: key/value set/get/delete with tags and TTL expiration, bulk operations (set up to 20 items, get/delete up to 50 keys per call), tag listing with AND filters, substring search, and capsule introspection (memory and tag counts, limits, last activity) across 19 tools — reachable over Streamable HTTP with an API key and zero local install.
bad: Hosted-only: the memory contents live on the vendor's service (endpoint agimem.dev/api/mcp) with no self-host option, no published source and no licence stated. The model is plain key/value — retrieval beyond substring search and tags does not exist — and the vendor is a single named individual behind a marketplace listing.
didnt: Rejected — remote key/value custody is the wrong shape for a local-first personal wiki, and substring search over a capsule sits far below our citation-locked retrieval; nothing here is missing from our stack. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Brainbox
licence: no licence stated at source (hosted service in personal preview; no licence stated on its site or its registry record, and no public source)
good: Two memory kinds handled thoughtfully: memories, and lessons that are evidence-tracked — attached evidence supports or refutes a lesson ('facts outrank hypotheses'), applying a lesson promotes its retention on an FSRS schedule, corrections increment a correction count and flag the lesson for review, and pinning outranks organic salience. Provenance rides along (a write_log audits which client wrote every item), deletion is an explicit permanent 'forget' verb, snapshots restore history rather than locking it in one chat app, and a read-only Cypher graph_query is exposed as a power tool.
bad: A solo founder's personal preview: invite-only ('registering interest doesn't promise a date or immediate access'), hosted-only custody on the vendor's deployment, an unverified Smithery listing with zero recorded uses, and no licence or self-host route anywhere at the source.
didnt: Board — evidence-gated lessons (support/refute evidence attached to a stored lesson, correction counts, retention that strengthens when a lesson is actually applied) is a lifecycle idea that maps directly onto our claim-and-outcome machinery. The service itself is Rejected: hosted custody, preview maturity, no licence. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: empirical
licence: no licence stated at source (hosted deployment; no licence, source or terms in the registry record)
good: A graph-shaped personal memory: memories as nodes with edges (neighbour traversal, relationship add/remove/replace), capture that creates or merges memories from conversation context (journal notes, preferences, plans, reflections), semantic query with category, tag, date and location filters, and two governance touches — a memory_usage_guide policy tool the agent can read, and deletion that requires confirm=true — across OAuth-selected workspaces.
bad: Hosted-only, on a Smithery run.tools deployment under one individual's account (matt-ha7x): no homepage, documentation, source or licence anywhere in the record, and the product's entire public surface is this single registry listing — durability and custody rest wholly with a solo operator and the hosting platform.
didnt: Rejected — hosted custody, no licence, single-operator footprint; its confirm-gated delete is a weaker form of the approval gating we already have. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: zero-residual
licence: no licence stated at source (hosted gateway; no licence, source or terms in the registry record)
good: A single-purpose erasure gateway with a verifiable receipt: its one tool purges volatile memory buffers with multi-pass overwrites conforming to NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1 and emits an Ed25519-signed, timestamped destruction certificate that downstream audit peers can verify; the service is engineered as a static Musl Rust binary (no garbage-collector retention), with x402 micropayment and Stripe billing rails.
bad: Exactly one tool behind a hosted endpoint, from an unverified single-vendor listing with no published source, no licence and no evaluation evidence — while the claims are absolute in wording ('prove absolute data eradication'), and a remote gateway can only scrub buffers handed to it, not the caller's own process memory.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent product built around precisely our erasure premise (a signed, timestamped certificate as the trust object for destruction) confirms that design choice in our own erasure machinery; the gateway itself is not taken (hosted, single-tool, no licence stated). (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Neither MCP
licence: MIT (GitHub licence detection and the README's own 'License: MIT' line agree — covering the client/CLI source mirror; the hosted workspace service behind the API key states no separate licence in the repo)
good: Decision memory with the record types a project actually needs — Decision, Rejected and Constraint — each cited by file path, so the context an AI receives carries its source evidence with it, and the server deliberately serves selected project context rather than a corpus dump. The local stdio connector is packaged for Cursor (plugin), Claude Desktop (MCPB bundle), Claude Code and Gemini CLI, a companion CLI pushes local docs into the memory, and the repo's privacy section is candid about collection, retention (workspace data kept while the account is active; deletion removed within 30 days) and the local process keeping no second copy of API responses.
bad: The memory itself is hosted: the MIT code in this repo is a public source mirror for the client and CLI, while the workspace decision memory lives behind the vendor's API (api.neither.online, workspace API key required) and is not self-hostable from the published source. The project is very young (repo created 2026-09-03, 0 stars), and by its own README it is not yet listed on the Cursor Marketplace or any Claude marketplace — the packaging is ready, the submission pending.
didnt: Board — the record model is worth boarding: Decision/Rejected/Constraint records, each cited by file path and served as selected context, is the same shape as our own decision records, packaged for editor agents. The service itself is Rejected: hosted workspace custody, with the open code covering only the client. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Nium-Wiki
licence: MIT (npm registry record license field; the latest version record agrees)
good: A skill for AI coding tools (e.g. Claude Code) that turns a codebase into a cross-linked wiki: dependency-graph-driven module discovery with two-stage fact extraction, Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagrams, and precompiled docs in the Karpathy compile-not-retrieve pattern. Updates are idempotent and incremental — SHA-256 change detection plus dependency-graph propagation rewrites only affected pages — and it claims fully offline operation across 10+ languages, with a local preview server offering full-text search and a source-to-doc graph view.
bad: Very early and single-maintainer: the latest npm release is 0.1.1 and the registry record names one maintainer. The README is Chinese-first, and the tool documents codebases rather than keeping a personal knowledge store — no citation locking, abstention or approval gates — with output quality resting entirely on the host AI coding tool that performs the reading; the README claims an automatic quality audit but shows no accuracy evaluation.
didnt: Rejected — a codebase-documentation generator (a compile-a-wiki-from-a-repo skill for AI coding tools); our wiki compiles from ingested sources, not code repos, and its SHA-256 incremental-update mechanic is already covered by our citation lockfile and source-hash machinery. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: LLM Research Wiki
licence: MIT (LICENSE file shipped in the published sdist; the registry record states no license field and the README states none)
good: A project-memory compiler: point it at a directory of markdown, source files and (optionally) PDFs/Office docs/images and it extracts a typed knowledge graph (41 node types), writes a queryable wiki, and emits portable artifacts — a markdown projection, a Cognee-ready bundle, an agent harness, and an MCP server wireable into Claude Code, Codex or any MCP client. Compilation is deterministic (byte-identical output), ingestion is multimodal and code-aware, a multi-project registry is built in, and it works without an API key via OAuth.
bad: A single 0.1.0 release — early software. Its own README comparison table marks the per-page ask widget 'not yet' (a proposed feature), and the tool has no live edit, no real-time collaboration and no mobile-first reading; the README also carries an unresolved TODO admitting the linked demo URL is a placeholder. It is compile-from-source only by design — anyone wanting to edit notes in a UI is told to use Logseq or Obsidian instead.
didnt: Corroboration — deterministic, byte-identical compile from sources into a typed graph, with an MCP door for agents, independently confirms this system's compile-and-cite architecture; the one artifact it emits that we do not (a Cognee bundle) is a niche adapter, not a gap. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Eva-brain
good: An open-source, local-first desktop app for building a personal knowledge base with an LLM: instead of re-retrieving from raw documents at question time, an agent maintains a durable, linked Markdown brain between the sources and the user, under a versioned on-disk contract (the Eva Brain Standard v1, identified by an eva.json marker). It ships a graph explorer, deterministic structural linting in its wiki-lib (with a 16-page fixture and unit tests), read-only MCP navigation tools (search, page reads, neighbors, shortest paths), worktree-isolated ingest, cited query, and a read-only Health Check.
bad: V1 intentionally targets macOS only — the README states Windows and Linux have neither been built nor tested against the codebase, a deliberate product decision. It is a young project (created July 2026), building the app locally requires a Rust toolchain for the Tauri shell, and the README documents unit tests for wiki-lib but no evaluation of answer quality or abstention.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent convergence on this system's exact shape (local-first linked-Markdown brain, deterministic structural lint, read-only MCP navigation, cited query, health check) confirms the design; nothing it ships is missing from our stack. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: localmd
good: A browser-only, local-first markdown wiki web app: a static page with no backend reads and writes a folder the user already has, through the File System Access API — file tree, editor, preview, [[wikilinks]], backlinks, a force-directed graph and full-text search, with nothing uploaded anywhere. Its agent reads the folder's PDFs/EPUBs and the user's open browser tabs and writes linked markdown beside them; block-level document indexes make every citation a chip that clicks back to the exact paragraph, and every change waits for the user's yes in a diff review panel. Version history is a real in-browser git repository (isomorphic-git) with optional GitHub sync, and the whole application is free — no account, no paid tier.
bad: Browser-only means dependence on the File System Access API (Chromium-class browsers) and a bring-your-own-key model — the agent's quality is whatever the user's provider key buys. It is a young, small project (created July 2026, 16 stars), and by the README's own account the extensible-tool layer beyond the built-ins is 'a spec, not a release'.
didnt: Corroboration — changes that wait for the user's yes in a diff panel, paragraph-exact citation chips and strict local custody independently confirm this system's approval-gated writes and citation design. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Memento
good: Hosted MCP memory for coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, Copilot): it saves architectural decisions, gotchas and patterns as the user works and surfaces them automatically in later sessions, across sessions, IDEs and machines. Every memory is a plain-English node in a linked graph that the user can browse, read and edit in a web dashboard — no black box — with personal and team-org scopes, /remember and /recall commands, an end-of-session /sleep consolidation, 30+ pre-built coding commands, and recall blending semantic similarity, keyword matching and knowledge-graph traversal over a hierarchical context architecture. The free tier includes 200 memory files, 50 MB and the cloud dashboard.
bad: Custody is the vendor's cloud by design ('your memory lives in the cloud'), the opposite of local-first. Capture is automatic ('you don't have to ask'), and memories carry weight that decays and re-ranks what surfaces, so the record is continuously re-scored rather than held verbatim under the owner's approval; the free tier caps at 200 memory files / 50 MB, the hierarchical architecture is 'patent pending' proprietary, and the page's scale claims (200 to 200,000 memories, 500K-line codebases) are the vendor's own with no published evaluation.
didnt: Rejected — hosted cloud custody plus automatic, decay-weighted capture is the managed-memory profile this system refuses; the human-readable, editable node dashboard is credited in good. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: WikiMind (project 1)
good: A personal LLM-powered knowledge OS: feed it articles, papers, PDFs, YouTube videos, podcasts or RSS feeds and it compiles them into a structured wiki whose articles carry key claims, confidence scores and source citations, with auto-extracted concepts, bidirectional backlinks and typed relationships. It answers questions with source citations, synthesises across articles (comparative, chronological, thematic and gap analysis), lints for contradictions, orphans and stale content automatically, and exposes an MCP server (13 tools, 3 resources, 4 prompts) plus exports to Markdown, JSON, PDF and Obsidian.
bad: A heavy server stack for a personal tool — FastAPI + React + PostgreSQL + Redis, run via Docker and configured with a hosted LLM provider key — so custody is database-shaped and multi-user/hosted in orientation (OAuth accounts, public share links with expiry, a cloud live demo), not plain local files under the owner's hand. The release line is 0.1.0, and the README states its capabilities without a published abstention or answer-quality evaluation.
didnt: Corroboration — confidence-scored claims with automatic contradiction and staleness detection independently confirm this system's claim-lifecycle direction; its hosted, multi-user server stack is not a fit for our local custody and is not adopted. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: Zissa Wiki
good: A personal research knowledge base in plain markdown, maintained by the AI agent of the user's choice (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, or a plain chat app through a prompt/apply round-trip), implementing Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern: drop a source into raw/ and say 'ingest', and the agent writes a source note and updates every concept, author, debate and project page the source touches. Its scripts/wiki.py checks every direct quote word-for-word against the file it came from, validates links and structure, and can gate commits through git hooks; raw sources are immutable and there is no database, embeddings or plugin layer.
bad: A personal, single-user tool whose quality rests entirely on the maintaining agent — the README itself tells users to supervise the first 5–10 ingests closely, and the chat-app route is a manual copy-paste round-trip whose prompt bundle must be budget-capped as the wiki grows. Its checks are link- and quote-level: the README shows no abstention behaviour, no approval gate on agent writes and no claim-truth evaluation. A young project (created April 2026, 61 stars).
didnt: Corroboration — word-for-word quote verification against source files and a portable AGENTS.md schema independently confirm this system's citation discipline; nothing it ships is missing from our stack. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: CacheZero
good: An AI-powered second brain implementing Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern: bookmark anything from the web — tweets, LinkedIn posts, YouTube videos, articles and any web page — via a bundled Chrome extension (WXT, Manifest V3) or the cachezero CLI into a local Hono server (port 3777) that stores bookmarked content as plain markdown files under raw/ in ~/.cachezero/vault/, an Obsidian-compatible vault the user browses with graph view, wikilinks and tag browsing. The user's local Claude Code compiles raw/ into interconnected wiki/ articles with [[wikilinks]], YAML frontmatter and source citations following SCHEMA.md, updating INDEX.md and log.md; LanceDB vector search over Gemini text-embedding-004 indexes the vault for semantic search, cachezero ask synthesises cited answers saved to outputs/, wiki-health reviews the wiki for contradictions, gaps and orphan pages, an MCP server exposes search_knowledge, list_bookmarks and add_bookmark to Claude Code, and cachezero publish builds a Quartz v4 static site (search, graph view, wikilinks, tag pages) deployable to Vercel. Setup is one command, npx cachezero init.
bad: Compilation, Q&A and health checks depend on a locally installed Claude Code CLI and vector search requires a Google Gemini API key (free tier) set at init, so the core loop is not self-contained. The Chrome extension is not store-installed — it must be sideloaded manually via Developer Mode and 'Load unpacked'. It is a young, small project (created April 2026, 18 stars, 23 commits, 1 release in the repo metadata as opened), and the README states its capabilities without a published evaluation of compilation or answer quality or abstention behaviour; by its own design the vault is the LLM's domain — the user browses it, the LLM writes it.
didnt: Corroboration — an independent implementation of the same compile-from-raw pattern (immutable raw markdown, SCHEMA-driven compilation into wikilinked, source-cited wiki pages, an index and append-only log, health checks for contradictions, gaps and orphans, and an MCP door) confirms this system's architecture; its hosted-publishing and Gemini-embedding choices are not adopted. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @sgawarat/remark-obsidian-wikilink
licence: MIT (registry license field, the package.json in its repo directory, and the MIT LICENSE.md file in that directory all agree)
good: A remark plugin for the unified pipeline that adds Obsidian-style wikilink syntax — [[path#heading|text]] — built on micromark and mdast-util-from-markdown, written in TypeScript (ESM) and shipped with a vitest test suite in its source directory.
bad: The README is a bare title (37 characters) in both the registry record and the repository — no usage documentation anywhere; the package lives as one library inside the author's personal blog-theme monorepo rather than in its own repository, and it is pre-1.0 (v0.1.4) and single-author.
didnt: Rejected — an undocumented pre-1.0 wikilink parser from a personal monorepo; our Lens renderer already resolves wikilinks and is not a remark pipeline. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: gatsby-remark-enhanced-wikilink
licence: MIT (registry license field only — the README carries no licence section)
good: A Gatsby remark plugin supporting enhanced wikilink syntax (Obsidian internal links) for Gatsby 4: links to markdown files with heading and alias, links to other files such as PDFs, and image embeds, with heading slugs via github-slugger and a configurable wikilinkToUrl function.
bad: Gatsby-specific and stale — the latest release v1.0.1 dates from December 2021 and targets Gatsby 4; embedding whole notes is listed as unsupported in its own README's feature checklist.
didnt: Rejected — Gatsby-only and unmaintained since 2021; nothing in our stack renders through Gatsby. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: micromark-extension-wikilink-syntax

good: A syntax-only micromark extension that tokenises Obsidian-style wikilinks and embeds, distinctive in allowing the alias/alt text itself to contain markdown; actively maintained (v2.1.1, April 2026), ESM-only, from the unified ecosystem.
bad: Syntax-only by design — it ships no HTML compiler and produces nothing usable without its mdast companion package and manual tree rewriting; a narrow parsing component rather than a renderer.

bad: Only half of a pair — useless without the micromark extension, and its output nodes still need manual replacement with ordinary constructs via unist-util-visit; it has no rendering behaviour of its own.

didnt: Rejected — alias republication of markdown-it-wikilinks-plus (studied separately in this batch); markdown-it is not our renderer. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: obsidian-wikilinks
licence: MIT (registry license field and README licence badge agree)
good: A coding-agent plugin (v0.5.0, October 2026, actively developed) — not a markdown renderer: it hooks Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode so that [[wikilinks]] typed in a prompt are fuzzy-matched against the user's Obsidian vault and the resolved notes are injected as context, with the hook requiring explicit trust approval in the host agent.

didnt: Board — resolving [[wikilinks]] in agent prompts against the vault is a genuinely relevant pattern for agents working over our wiki; boarded as an idea only, since this implementation auto-injects on fuzzy matches without the approval gates our context discipline requires. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @prabhavag/rehype-citation
licence: MIT (registry license field only - the README states no licence)
good: A rehype plugin to nicely format citations in markdown documents and insert a bibliography in HTML format, integrating citeproc-js and citation-js in the remark-rehype ecosystem: it supports normal ([@foo]) and in-text (@foo) citations, author-date, numerical and note styles, BibTeX, CSL-JSON or CFF bibliography files, built-in CSL styles (apa, vancouver, harvard1, chicago, mla) and locales, and options including suppressBibliography, noCite and linkCitations, per the record's description and full README.
bad: A scoped republication duplicating the unscoped rehype-citation package - same repository, author and README, with a different maintainer (prabhavag) publishing only v2.2.1 and v2.2.2 on 2024-11-13 - so which package is canonical is muddied; it is ESM-only, meant as a server-side plugin, and note-style citations are only compatible with GitHub Formatted Markdown (the README advises running remark-gfm before it).
didnt: Rejected - a duplicate scoped republication of rehype-citation rather than a distinct project, and our rendering stack is not a rehype pipeline. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @citation-js/plugin-bibtex
licence: MIT (registry license field and README License badge agree)
good: First-party Citation.js plugin adding input and output support for BibTeX, BibLaTeX and Bib.TXT, in both text form and as a JSON representation, with format dictionary support on output; deeply configurable through its @bibtex config - strict parsing, sentence-case handling, Bib(La)TeX to CSL-JSON type mappings, required-field lists, field types, and Unicode, diacritic, ligature and formatting-command handling - and actively maintained (latest v0.9.0 in the record).
bad: A narrow component, not a standalone tool: it only works registered into @citation-js/core (listed as a peer dependency in the record), and its configuration surface is very large and low-level, exposing dozens of mutable constants; the README itself notes its argument commands do not support optional arguments yet.
didnt: Rejected - a sound first-party BibTeX/BibLaTeX format plugin, but a Citation.js core component in the JS ecosystem, not adopted as a standalone dependency for our wiki. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @citation-js/plugin-wikidata
licence: MIT (registry license field; README carries the package's npm licence badge)
good: Citation.js plugin that turns Wikidata references into citable CSL records: it accepts single IDs, whitespace/comma ID lists, API URLs, entity URLs, ID arrays and raw API responses, and exposes per-property/per-type input parsing, with a configurable label-language fallback order. Part of the long-running citation-js project (59 versions since 2018; latest 0.9.0, 2026-09).
bad: A format plugin only: it adds an input source to @citation-js/core and renders nothing itself, resolving IDs needs live access to the Wikidata API, and the README documents formats and configuration only, with no offline or caching story.
didnt: Rejected — duplication/fit: our citation machinery rests on the citation-js core already studied at Tier 1 and on claim-level source locking, not on resolving Wikidata entities into bibliographies. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @behackl/citation-js-extras
licence: MIT (registry license field and README License section agree)
good: Extends citation-js into an HTML publication-list renderer with real care for scholarly detail: custom BibTeX fields that citation-js normally drops stay available for grouping/filtering, titles are linked, DOI/arXiv/MathSciNet/zbMATH badges print once instead of duplicating URLs as text, and $...$ mathematics in titles survives formatting for KaTeX/MathJax renderers.
bad: Young and narrow: first published 2026-02 (v0.4.0, five versions, single author), aimed at academic publication lists on personal pages, and citation-js is a peer dependency the user must supply.
didnt: Rejected — scope: rendered HTML bibliography lists for academic homepages; our citation layer is provenance and locking, not reference-list rendering. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: postext-citeproc

good: Full CSL citation formatting for the Postext typesetting system: Pandoc-style citation codes in a document are rendered in 21 bundled styles (APA, Chicago, MLA, IEEE, Vancouver, ISO 690, GB/T 7714, OSCOLA and more) with 14 locales, the engine can be lazy-loaded only when a document cites, and arbitrary CSL styles can be passed whole.
bad: Brand new and churning — first published 2026-10-01 and already at v1.53.0 after 113 versions in three weeks — and wholly tied to the niche Postext document system; what it bundles is not all MIT: citeproc-js is CPAL-1.0 (dual-licensed CPAL 1.0 / AGPL 1.0) and the bundled CSL styles/locales are CC BY-SA 3.0.
didnt: Rejected — fit/maturity: a citation renderer bound to the Postext typesetting stack, three weeks old at study time; our documents do not run on Postext. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @benchmark-urbanism/remark-bibtex
licence: MIT (registry license field and README License section, 'MIT © Gareth Simons', agree)
good: Remark plugin that resolves (@citationKey) markers from a .bib file through citation-js and rewrites them as numbered footnote references with a generated footnotes bibliography, chaining with remark-gfm for the footnote machinery.
bad: Unmaintained: latest release 0.6.0 was published 2022-04-04 with nothing since; it offers a single mandatory option (the .bib file path), footnote-only output, and a hard dependency on remark-gfm.
didnt: Rejected — maturity/duplication: an unmaintained, footnote-only remark plugin; our Markdown pipeline has no footnote-citation requirement it would fill. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: bibtex-json-toolbox

good: A small JavaScript toolbox (TinyBibReader / TinyBibFormatter) that parses BibTeX, resolves pandoc-style citation codes in text, and formats citations and bibliographies (APA and Harvard-style output) as plain text, Markdown or HTML, with worked examples throughout its README.
bad: No licence stated anywhere (see licence field), so reuse rights are undefined; the record names no repository, author or support channel, and the README demonstrates APA output while its claims of several styles rest on that single example.
didnt: Rejected — licence: no licence stated at source, so ideas-only at most, and the parse/format function duplicates citation-js, already on record. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: pure-references
licence: MIT (registry license field only — the README states no licence)
good: A tiny BibTeX-to-citation-list converter ('BibToCitation') offering two output shapes, authors-first and title-first formatters, callable on a .bib file path.
bad: The README's own install and import instructions name a different package ('bibToCitation'), so the documented usage cannot be followed as written; dormant since v1.0.2 (2022-05-13), three versions total, a single-function utility.
didnt: Rejected — fit/maturity: a two-function converter whose own README misnames the package; nothing here our citation stack lacks. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @enyalai/sdk
licence: Apache-2.0 (registry license field only — the README states no licence)
good: SDK (Greenland AI Limited) layering local agent memory — SQLite-backed synchronous remember/recall — with permanent encrypted archival whose integrity is client-verifiable: content commitments (SHA-256 over a random nonce and the content), Shamir-share client-side disclosure, post-quantum hybrid decryption tiers, and agent-to-agent messaging with delivery acknowledgement. Retries with idempotency keys are built into state-changing calls.
bad: The archival, sync and messaging layers are a metered hosted service: an ENYAL API key is required, archiving 'costs joules', and the README states rate limits and daily disclosure caps; the permanent record therefore sits in the vendor's custody, not the user's. The README also limits the local store: SQLite WAL mode, never on a network filesystem.
didnt: Rejected — custody: however strong its proof machinery, a hosted, metered memory/archive service conflicts with our local-first custody rule for the wiki's records. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

name: @typegraph-ai/sdk

good: TypeScript SDK for a tenant-scoped 'business context graph': one client over documents, events, threads, entities, facts and memory, with hybrid search, extraction/ontology tooling and memory consolidation (the shipped build includes decay and forgetting engines), and a carefully specified tenancy/bucket/actor context model.
bad: No licence stated anywhere (see licence field). It is a client for a hosted stack — installation pulls companion packages including a pgvector adapter, an AI gateway and Neon serverless Postgres — and the README directs readers to a repository-root README while the record names no repository at all; pre-1.0 (0.7.0) with 41 versions since 2026-04.
didnt: Rejected — licence and scope: unlicenced, and built for multi-tenant B2B product-intelligence graphs on hosted infrastructure, the opposite of a single-user local-first wiki. (completion pass stage C, 2026-10-22)

good: A VuePress + vuepress-theme-hope template that turns Markdown notes into a shareable knowledge-base/blog site, with GitHub Actions one-click deployment to GitHub Pages or Vercel and detailed setup documentation; actively maintained (529 stars, pushed 2026-10-14) with the author's own site (newzone.top) as a worked example.
